en: Salutations to the illustrious Goddess Durgā.
The Greatness of the Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata.
She who is Sarga in the act of creation, Pālinī in the task of protecting the world, and Raudrī in its dissolution; she for whom this entire universe is a play, known as Aparā;
and thereafter, the Blessed Lady in the forms of Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī consisting of phonemes.
May she, who is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, graciously grace our speech. || 1 ||
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Jaya."
The sages said:
O Sūta, may you live long! You who cause us to hear here so many captivating and meritorious stories, O high-minded disciple of Vyāsa.
We have heard with devotion this wonderful account of Viṣṇu’s deeds, which removes all sins, is meritorious, and is endowed with the stories of his incarnations. ||4||
The divine life-story of Śiva, as well as that of sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads, along with their greatness and ancient histories, has been heard from your lotus-like mouth. (5)
Now we wish to hear that which is supremely purifying even among the purifying,
which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men with ease in every respect.
"O illustrious one, tell us that reality by which men attain perfection;
for even in this Kali age, we know of no other than you who can cut through our doubts.
Sūta said:
"Excellent, O illustrious ones, you have asked out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
I shall explain to you in its entirety that which is the essence of all the scriptures.
So long as the sacred fords, the Purāṇas, and the religious vows continue to roar [in vain],"
As long as the Devībhāgavata is not heard correctly by men. ||9||
The forest of sin remains dense with thorns and a source of suffering for men only so long as the axe named Devībhāgavata has not been obtained.
The great darkness of calamities that brings affliction to men persists only so long as the sun-like Lord of the Goddesses, the Bhāgavata, has not yet risen.
The sages said: "Speak to us, O best among speakers!
Of what nature is that Purāṇa, and what is the rule for hearing it?"
O Sūta, O highly fortunate Sūta, over how many days is this to be heard, and what is the mode of worship? By which men was it heard previously, and what various desires do they attain? (13)
=== PAGE 2 === The Greatness of the Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata, Chapter 1.
Sūta said:
A portion of Viṣṇu was born as a sage from Parāśara upon Satyavatī;
having divided the Vedas into four, he taught them to his disciples in former times. (14)
How can those who are outcasts (vrātyas), mere kinsmen of the twice-born, those ineligible for the Vedas, women, and men of dull intellect, come to possess knowledge of dharma? (15)
Having reflected upon this with his mind, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa meditated upon the Purāṇa-saṃhitā out of a desire to establish the dharma for them.
Having composed the eighteen Purāṇas, that venerable sage taught them to me alone, as well as the narrative known as the Bhārata.
There, he himself recited the Devībhāgavata Purāṇa, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, to King Janamejaya.
Formerly, his father King Parīkṣit was bitten by the serpent Takṣaka; having been purified from that, he heard the Bhāgavata.
After nine days, having worshipped the Goddess, the Mother of the Three Worlds, according to the prescribed rites from the lotus-like mouth of the illustrious Vyāsa; || 20 ||
When the nine-day sacrifice was completed, King Parīkṣit,
assuming a divine form, attained the same world as the Goddess at that very moment.
Having beheld his father’s divine departure, King Janamejaya honored the sage Vyāsa and attained supreme joy.
Among the eighteen Purāṇas, the supreme and most excellent is that named Devībhāgavata, which bestows virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. 23.
For those who always listen with devotion to the Bhāgavata narrative of the Goddess, spiritual perfection is not far off; therefore, it should always be recited by men. 24.
Whether for half a day, or half of that, or for a single muhūrta, or even for a mere moment—
those men who listen with devotion shall never encounter an evil rebirth.
Whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices, all sacred fords, and all acts of charity,
a man obtains that same fruit by listening to a Purāṇa even once.
In the Kali age, many duties have been performed, yet for men there exists no other dharma than the listening to the Purāṇas. || 27 ||
For the benefit of men who were devoid of righteous conduct and possessed of little learning and short lifespans, Vyāsa prepared in ancient times the nectar-like essence known as the Purāṇas. (28)
Just as a man drinking nectar alone would become free from old age and death, so too the nectar of the Goddess’s story shall make the entire family free from old age and death. (29)
There is no restriction here regarding months, nor even any restriction regarding days;
the Devībhāgavata should always be served, always served by men. (30)
In the month of Āśvina, or in the month of Madhu (Caitra), or likewise in the month of Śuci (Jyeṣṭha), it yields especially great fruit during the four Navarātras. ||31||
Therefore, this nine-day sacrifice is declared to be the bestower of merit for men, as it yields a fruit greater than that of all other meritorious deeds.
Those who are ill-intentioned, devoted to sin, deluded, betrayers of friends, revilers of the Vedas,
intent on violence, and attached to the path of atheism— they purify themselves in the Kali age by means of the Navāha sacrifice.

Those men who are greedy for the wealth of others, who bear the burden of the [coming] kalpa, and who lack devotion to cows, deities, and brahmins—how can they become pure without knowledge of the ninefold path? (34)

Whatever fruit is obtained by men through fierce austerities, the observance of vows and sacred fords, various restraints, sacrifices, oblations, and recitations—that is attained by the sacrifice performed on the ninth day. || 35 ||
In the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya*, Chapter 2:
Neither Gaṅgā, nor Gayā, nor Kāśī, nor Naimiṣa, nor Mathurā, nor Puṣkara [is equal to it].
O Brahmins, for this sacrifice to the Goddess instantly purifies our Badarī forest, just as it does for others. || 36 ||
Therefore, the Bhāgavata Purāṇa of the Goddess is considered the highest of all, the supreme means for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. (37)
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo,
one should worship [the Lord] seated upon the great lion-throne on the Mahāṣṭamī day.
One who, out of devotion, gives a manuscript of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata to a worthy brāhmaṇa as an object of the Goddess’s pleasure, shall attain the state of the Goddess. (39)
Whoever daily recites even a single verse or half-verse of the Devībhāgavata with devotion shall become a recipient of the Goddess’s affection.
Merely by hearing it, one destroys terrible calamities arising from portents, the outbreak of great pestilence, and all other omens of ill fortune. (41)
Whatever fear is caused by child-seizing spirits, or by ghosts and goblins, departs far away through the hearing of this *Devībhāgavata*. (42)
But that man who recites the Bhāgavata of the Goddess with devotion, or listens to it,
attains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Upon hearing this, Vasudeva rejoiced greatly when he recovered his beloved son Kṛṣṇa, who had been delayed while searching for Prasenajit.
Whoever hears this narrative of the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam with devotion,
or whoever reads it with devotion, attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One without a son obtains a son, and the poor man becomes wealthy;
the sick person shall be liberated from disease upon hearing this nectar of the Bhāgavata. (46)
Whether she be barren, or one whose children are like crows (a woman who bears only one child), or a woman whose offspring die,
by hearing the Devībhāgavata, she shall obtain a long-lived son.
That house in which the book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is constantly worshipped indeed becomes a sacred pilgrimage site, destroying the sins of those who dwell there. 48.
He who, endowed with devotion, reads or even listens to this on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the ninth lunar day, attains supreme perfection. (49)
A twice-born man who recites it becomes a leader among those learned in the Vedas; one born of the arms (a Kṣatriya) shall become a lord of the earth;
a Vaiśya who recites it attains abundance of wealth; and even a Śūdra, by listening to it, shall become most excellent in his own station.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Mānasakhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, within the Māhātmya of the Devībhāgavata. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
The sages said:
"O highly fortunate one, how did Vasudeva obtain a son?"
Where was Prasena sought by Kṛṣṇa as he wandered about, and how? ||1||
O wise Sūta, tell this story: by what rite and for what reason was the Devībhāgavata heard by Vasudeva?
Sūta said:
Satrājit, a scion of the Bhoja dynasty, lived happily in Dvāravatī;
devoted to the worship of the Sun, he was his supreme devotee and friend. (3)
Then, after some time, the Sun became pleased;
out of devotion and affection for him, he revealed his own world.
In the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamāhātmya*, Chapter 2:
To him who was thus convinced, the Blessed One granted the Syamantaka jewel.
Wearing that jewel around his neck, he indeed returned to Dvārakā.
Seeing him, the citizens were bewildered by his splendor, thinking him to be the sun;
they approached Kṛṣṇa as he sat in the Sudharmā hall and spoke to him.
"O Lord of the World, here comes Savitṛ, desiring to see you.
Having heard those words, Kṛṣṇa laughed and spoke in the assembly:
"O children, this is not Savitṛ; he is Satrājit, blazing with his jewel."
And he comes with the radiant Syamantaka jewel given by Bhāsvat.
Having summoned the brahmins and performed the rite of invoking auspiciousness (*svastivācana*),
Satrājit, after honoring them, caused the jewel to enter his own home.
Moreover, where that jewel—which constantly yields eight *bhāras* of gold—resides, there is no plague, no famine, and no fear of calamity anywhere. (10)
Then once, Satrājit’s brother, named Prasena, having tied the jewel around his neck and mounted a Saindhava horse, [set out]. (11)
Having gone to the forest for the sake of hunting, the king saw him;
having killed Prasena along with his horse, the lion seized that jewel.
Then Jāmbavān, the king of the bears, seeing that the monkey was wearing the jewel,
did not kill him after he had taken it from the cave, but instead the valiant one seized the jewel.
The lord gave that jewel to his son for the purpose of play;
then, having obtained the radiant gem, even the boy played with it.
When Prasena had not yet returned, Satrājit was filled with anxiety.
I do not know by whom he was struck down while seeking the jewel.
Then a rumor emerged from the mouths of the people in the city:
"Surely Prasena has been killed by Kṛṣṇa, who was desirous of the jewel."
Kṛṣṇa also heard that ill-repute clinging to himself;
to wipe it away, he followed in his footsteps accompanied by the citizens.
Having gone into the forest, he saw a quiver killed by a lion;
following the path stained with blood, he went in pursuit of the king of beasts.
Then, seeing the slain lion at the entrance of the cave, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa spoke these words out of compassion to the inhabitants of the city: (19)
"Stay right here until my return;
I shall enter this cave to obtain the necklace of jewels. (20)
Having said, "So be it," those inhabitants of Dvārakā remained right there;
Kṛṣṇa went to the inner cave where the home of Jāmbavān was located.
Upon seeing the son of the bear-king wearing the jewel, Kṛṣṇa then desired to seize the jewel; at that moment, the nurse cried out in fear.
Hearing the cry of the nurse, the King of Artha immediately arrived and then fought with his master incessantly, day and night.
Thus, for twenty-seven nights, a great battle took place between the two;
meanwhile, the citizens remained at the gate awaiting the arrival of Kṛṣṇa.
Then, out of fear, they returned to their own homes for twelve days;
there, they related the entire account from the beginning.
Cursing Satrājit, they were all deeply overwhelmed with grief;
and when the illustrious Vāsudeva heard that account of his son,
he fainted along with his retinue out of supreme sorrow.
He reflected in many ways: "How might my welfare be secured?
(27) Then the blessed celestial sage arrived from the world of Brahmā;
Vasudeva rose, bowed to him, and honored him. (28)
Having inquired after the welfare of the high-minded Vāsudeva, Nārada questioned that best of the Yadus: "Tell me, what are you reflecting upon? (29)
=== PAGE 5 === In the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya*, Chapter 2,
Vasudeva said:
"My son Kṛṣṇa, who was very dear to me, went to the forest with the citizens to search for Prasena; he then beheld him slain. (30)
Seeing Hari dead at the entrance of the cave after killing Prasenajit,
he stationed the citizens at the gate and entered the cave himself.
"Many days have passed, yet my son has not returned even now; therefore, I grieve. Tell me that, O Sage, by which I may obtain a son. (32)
Nārada said:
O best of the Yadus, worship the goddess Ambikā for the sake of obtaining a son;
by her very propitiation, you shall indeed immediately attain well-being in this world. (33)
Vasudeva said:
"O Blessed One, who indeed is that goddess, and what is the power of that Great Sovereign?
O divine sage, please tell me out of compassion how her propitiation is performed."
Nārada said:
O illustrious Vasudeva, listen to my account in brief;
who is capable of describing in detail the incomparable majesty of the Goddess?
She who is the Blessed Lady, eternal, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss—the Goddess higher than the highest, by whom this entire world is pervaded. (36)
Through propitiating her, Brahmā creates this world of the moving and the non-moving;
and by praising her, he was liberated from the fear arising from Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
By whose grace the Lord Viṣṇu sustains this universe,
and by the glance from the corner of whose eye Rudra withdraws it.
That which is the cause of bondage for those who are bound is itself the bestower of liberation;
she is the supreme Goddess Vidyā, she alone is the Sovereign of all sovereigns. (39)
Having worshipped the Mother of the Universe according to the ritual of Navarātra,
listen for nine days to the Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇa.
By the mere hearing of which you shall immediately obtain a son;
for men who recite or hear it, enjoyment and liberation are not far off. 41.
Thus addressed by Nārada, Vasudeva bowed to him and spoke with supreme affection to Nārada, the best of sages.
Vasudeva said:
"O Blessed One, by your word my own past life has been remembered;
listen as I shall relate that which arose from the majesty of the Goddess."
Long ago, having learned from the voice in the sky that his own death would come from Devakī’s eighth pregnancy, the wicked Kaṃsa imprisoned me along with my wife out of fear.
I dwelt in prison together with my wife Devakī;
moreover, the evil-doing Kaṃsa killed every son as soon as he was born.
When his six sons had been slain by him,
the blameless Queen Devakī was then deeply overwhelmed with grief and tormented day and night.
Then, having summoned the sage Garga, bowed to him, and honored him, I informed him of Devakī’s sorrow and spoke out of a desire for a son. (47)
O Blessed One, ocean of compassion, you are the preceptor of the Yādavas;
O Sage, tell me the means for obtaining a long-lived son.
In the *Śrīmad-devī-bhāgavata-māhātmya*, Chapter 2:
Then Garga, whose soul was serene and who was a treasure-house of compassion, spoke to me.
O illustrious Vasudeva, listen to that supreme means of accomplishment.
Worship that auspicious Goddess Durgā, who removes the distress of her devotees; for you shall immediately attain the highest good. 50.
By worshipping her, all may attain all their desires;
for men who worship Durgā, nothing in this world is difficult to obtain. (51)
Thus addressed, filled with joy, I bowed to that bull among sages with supreme devotion along with my wife, and with palms joined in reverence, I spoke.
Vasudeva said:
"O Blessed One, O ocean of compassion, if you have affection for me, then in the past you should have propitiated Caṇḍikā for my sake. (53)
"I have been confined in Kaṃsa's house; I am unable to do anything. Therefore, O high-minded one, you alone must rescue me from this ocean of misery. (54)
Thus addressed by me, that bull among sages spoke with pleasure:
"O Vasudeva, out of affection for you, I shall do what is beneficial for you."
Then the sage Garga, having been entreated by me with affection,
departed for the Vindhya mountain along with brahmins, desiring to propitiate Durgā.
Having gone there, the sage, devoted to the recitation of prayers, worshipped the Mother of the World, who grants the desires of her devotees.
When the observance was completed, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"O sage, I am pleased; the accomplishment of your purpose shall come to pass."
For the purpose of removing the burden of the earth, Hari has been sent forth by me;
he shall descend through his own portion into Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva.
Out of fear of Kaṃsa, Ānakadundubhi will immediately take that child and deliver him to the house of Nanda in Gokula.
Having taken the daughter of Yaśodā to his own home, he will give her to King Kaṃsa; then Kaṃsa, in order to kill her, will throw her down upon the earth.
Emerging from his hand, immediately assuming a divine form, she—
being a portion of myself— will dwell on the Vindhya mountains and bring about the welfare of the world.
Having heard those words and having bowed to the Mother of the World,
the sage Garga, with a tranquil soul, went to the city of Mathurā.
Having heard the boon granted by the Great Goddess, which brought happiness to Garga Ācārya,
he, together with his wife, was delighted and attained supreme joy.
From that time onwards, O celestial sage, I have known the supreme and most excellent majesty of the Goddess;
indeed, even now it has been heard by me from your lotus-like mouth.
Therefore, O Lord, please cause me to hear the Bhāgavata itself from the Goddess;
it is solely by my good fortune, O divine sage, O ocean of mercy, that you have arrived here. (66)
Having heard the words of Vasudeva, Nārada, with a delighted mind,
began the narration on an auspicious day under a favorable constellation.
To dispel obstacles to the discourse, the twice-born recited the nine-syllable mantra;
likewise, they chanted the hymn to the Goddess as proclaimed in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Beginning from the first book, Vasudeva listened with devotion to the nectar of the Bhāgavata as it issued from the mouth of the venerable Nārada.
On the ninth day, the high-minded Vasudeva, being pleased, honored the storyteller and the book upon the completion of the narrative. Then,
there within the cave, during the combat between Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavān—
With his limbs relaxed by the impact of Kṛṣṇa’s fist, Jāmbavān fell. ||71||
Then, having regained his mindfulness, he bowed down to the Blessed One and spoke with supreme devotion, seeking forgiveness for his transgression.
You are known as the best of the Raghus, for through your wrath the lord of rivers was agitated and Rāvaṇa, along with his followers, was slain at Laṅkā. (73)
In the Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamāhātmya, Chapter 3:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you are indeed that very person; O Lord, forgive my wickedness."
Tell me what must be done by me; I am your servant in every way. (74)
Having heard the words of Jāmbavān, the Lord of the World said: "O Lord of Bears, we have come here to this cave for the sake of the jewel. (75)
Then the King of the Bears, having honored him, affectionately gave his own daughter Jāmbavatī to Kṛṣṇa, as well as the Syamantaka jewel.
Taking Satā’s wife and placing the jewel upon her neck,
and having consecrated the king of bears with mantras, he set out toward Dvārakā.
On the day the story was concluded, the noble-minded Vasudeva fed the Brahmins and gratified them with sacrificial fees.
While the twice-born were offering their benedictions at that moment, Hari arrived with his wife, wearing a jewel.
Seeing Kṛṣṇa together with his wife, those led by Vasudeva, their eyes filled with tears of joy, attained supreme delight. (80)
Then the celestial sage Nārada, delighted by Kṛṣṇa’s arrival,
took leave of Vasudeva, and Kṛṣṇa departed for the assembly hall of Brahmā.

He who, with a pure heart and stainless devotion, reads or hears this account of Hari’s deeds which destroys ill-repute, shall always be filled with happiness and attain all his desires in this world; and at the end of his body, he shall find the path to liberation. (82)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Devībhāgavata," in the Mānasa-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
Now begins the third chapter.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, now listen to another ancient narrative (itihāsa).
Wherein the majesty of this Devībhāgavata is sung. || 1 ||
Once, the sage born from a jar, the husband of Lopāmudrā,
went to Kumāra, worshipped him, and inquired about various matters.
To him, the Blessed Lord Skanda related at great length various discourses enriched by the majesty of gifts, sacred fords, vows, and other such practices.
The greatness of Vārāṇasī as well as that of Maṇikarṇikā, and also the various holy sites (tīrthas) of the Gaṅgā, have been described in great detail. ||4||
Then, having heard this, that sage Agastya, born from a jar, was delighted; for the benefit of the worlds, he questioned the youth of great splendor once again.
Agastya said:
O Blessed One, O Enemy of Tāraka, O Lord, please tell me the procedure for hearing the majesty of the Devībhāgavata.
The Purāṇa named Devībhāgavata is the most excellent; therein the eternal Mother of the three worlds is directly extolled. (7)
Skanda said:
"Who is capable of describing in detail the majesty of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata?
Listen, O Brahmā; I shall now recount it to you in brief."
She who is eternal, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, the Mother of the Universe,
who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has herself taken direct refuge there.
Therefore, O Sage, that goddess whose form consists of speech is present in the Devībhāgavata;
for one who reads or hears it, nothing whatsoever in this world is difficult to attain. (10)
In the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya*, Chapter 3:
There was a son of Vivasvat known as Śrāddhadeva.
Being childless, that king, with the permission of Vasiṣṭha, performed a sacrifice.
Then Śraddhā, the beloved wife of Manu, requested Hotṛ:
"O Brahman, let her become my daughter; let a means be devised accordingly. (12)
Mentally intending [to offer] oblation, the Hotṛ priest offered the maiden herself as the sacrificial offering;
then, due to that transgression, she became the maiden named Ilā. (13)
Then the king, seeing his daughter, spoke dejectedly to the preceptor:
"O Lord, how has this discrepancy in your resolve arisen here?"
Having heard that, the sage reflected; perceiving the transgression of the Hotṛ priest, he sought refuge in the Lord out of a desire for Ilā to attain manhood.
And through the power of the Sage’s asceticism, as well as by the grace of the Supreme Lord,
while all the worlds were looking on, the earth attained the state of a man.
Then Sudyumna, the son of Manu, having been consecrated with the purificatory rites by his preceptor, became a treasury of sciences, just as the ocean is the repository of rivers. || 17 ||
Then, in the course of time, Sudyumna, having attained youth,
went to the forest for the sake of hunting, having mounted a horse from the Sindhu region.
Wandering from forest to forest with his followers, he roamed extensively;
by fate, that prince arrived at a forest at the foot of the Golden Mountain (Hemādri).
At one time, the blessed Lord Śaṅkara, the God of gods, was dwelling there in joy together with his wife Aparṇā.
Then the sages, longing for a vision of Śiva, arrived there;
upon seeing them, Girijā became bashful. ||21||
Seeing those two, Giriśa and Girijā, engaged in dalliance, the sages of rigid vows then desisted and departed for their abode in Vaikuṇṭha.
Seeking what was pleasing to his beloved, Śiva cursed the forest, saying:
"From this day forward, whatever man enters here shall become a woman. (23)
From that time on, men indeed avoided that region;
yet Sudyumna, having entered there, became a most excellent woman.
Seeing his horse followed by those who had become women, he was filled with wonder;
then that beautiful woman wandered from forest to forest.
Once, she went to the vicinity of Budha’s hermitage;
seeing her, whose every limb was beautiful and whose breasts were full and elevated—
The venerable Budha, his limbs pierced by the arrows of the bodiless god of love, desired her who had full lips, teeth like jasmine, a beautiful face, and eyes like lotuses. (27)
She too, the fair-browed one, desired that prince, the delighter of Soma;
then she dwelt in his hermitage, sporting with Budha.
After some time, she gave birth to a son, Purūravas.
Born from Mitra and Varuṇa, he begot offspring upon her. ||29||
Then, after some years had passed, she once remembered her former history at Budha’s hermitage and, filled with sorrow, departed.
Then, having gone to the hermitage of the preceptor Vasiṣṭha and bowed down to him,
she reported what had occurred and sought refuge with him, desiring manhood.
Vasiṣṭha, having learned the news, went to Mount Kailāsa;
having worshipped Śambhu, he praised him, filled with supreme devotion. ||32||
Vasiṣṭha said:
Salutations again and again to Śiva, to Śaṃkara, to the one with matted hair;
salutations to you whose body has half its limbs as the Daughter of the Mountain, and to the moon-crested one.
Salutations to you, Mṛḍa, the bestower of happiness, who dwells on Kailāsa; salutations to the blue-throated one, the granter of worldly enjoyment and liberation to his devotees. ||34||
Salutations to Śiva, whose form is auspicious, who removes the fear of those who have sought refuge, who has the bull as his vehicle, who is the worthy protector, and the Supreme Self. 35.
Salutations to the one who takes the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa during creation, preservation, and dissolution; salutations to the God of gods, the giver of boons, the enemy of Tripura.
In the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya*, Chapter 3:
Salutations again and again to the one whose form is sacrifice, who bestows the fruits upon those who perform sacrifices.
Salutations to you, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and fire. ||37||
Thus praised, that Blessed Lord, the Master of the World, appeared,
mounted upon his bull and accompanied by Ambikā, with a splendor equal to ten million suns.
Resembling a mountain of silver, three-eyed and moon-crested,
he, with a highly gratified soul, spoke to the best of sages who stood before him in prostration.
The Blessed Lord said: "Choose a boon, O brahmin-sage, whatever dwells in your mind.
Thus addressed, the sage bowed to him and, desiring manhood, made his request.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, said to the best of sages:
"For one month he shall be a man, and for one month he shall be a woman."
Having thus obtained the boon from Śambhu,
the great seer prostrated before the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, the Mother of the World, who was intent on bestowing the boon;
and having worshipped her, whose gentle smile possessed the luster of ten million crescent moons.
He constantly praised her with devotion, desiring manhood for Ilā. 43.
Victory, O Goddess, Great Goddess, you who bestow grace upon your devotees!
Victory, O you who are worshipped by all the gods; victory, O abode of infinite virtues! 44.
Salutations, salutations to you, O Goddess of gods, who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge!
Victory to you, O Durgā, destroyer of suffering, slayer of the wicked Daityas! 45.
Obeisance to you, O Great Illusion, accessible through devotion, Mother of the Universe! Your lotus feet are a boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
Even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, attain sovereignty over the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe by serving your lotus feet. (47)
Be gracious, O Goddess of gods, bestower of the four aims of life!
Who is capable of praising you, O Goddess? I am merely prostrate before you. 48.
Thus praised by the sage Vasiṣṭha with devotion, the supreme Goddess Durgā, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, became pleased at that very moment.
Then the Great Goddess, who removes the suffering of those who bow before her, said to the sage:
"Go to the palace of Sudyumna and perform my worship with devotion. (50)
O best of the twice-born, out of affection, cause Sudhūmna to hear the Purāṇa named Devībhāgavata, which is dear to me, in nine days.
"Merely by hearing this constantly, his manhood shall be restored.
Having spoken thus, Śiva and Īśvarī vanished from sight. (52)
Vasiṣṭha, having bowed in that direction and returned to his own hermitage,
summoned Sudyumna and instructed him to perform the propitiation of the Goddess.
Having worshipped the Mother of the World according to the Navarātra ritual during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, he caused the king to hear [the scripture].
Having heard the nectar of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata with devotion, Sudyumna bowed down and worshipped his guru, and thereby attained manhood permanently.
Having been consecrated upon the royal throne by the great seer Vasiṣṭha,
he ruled the earth with righteousness, delighting his subjects.
He performed various sacrifices with abundant and excellent sacrificial fees;
having entrusted the kingdom to his sons, he attained the same world as the Goddess.

Thus has it been told in its entirety, along with its history, O Brahmins. If a man recites this with true devotion or hears it, he shall attain all his desires in this world through the grace of the Goddess, and at the end, he goes to the supreme nectar—the realm of the Goddess. (58)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Mānasakhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa, within the Māhātmya of the Devībhāgavata.
In the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya*, Chapter 4.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard this divine and wonderful narrative, the pot-born Agastya,
desiring to hear more, spoke thus again to Viśākha with humility.
Agastya said:
O Lord, General of the Divine Armies, this wonderful narrative has been heard; tell me further another account of the majesty of the Bhāgavata. (2)
Skanda said: O sage born of Mitra and Varuṇa, listen to this narrative,
in which the greatness of even a single portion of the Bhāgavata is proclaimed.
The expansion of the Dharma is described with reference to the Gāyatrī;
that wherein the greatness of the Gāyatrī is found is intended as the Bhāgavata. (4)
Because this [text] belongs to the Blessed Lady (Bhagavatī), they know it as Bhāgavata;
for she, the Supreme Bhagavatī, is indeed worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. (5)
There was a highly intelligent sage renowned as Ṛtavāk;
in due time, a son was born to him under the final degree of the constellation Puṣya at the end of Gaṇḍānta.
He performed for him the birth-rites and other ceremonies according to the prescribed rules;
he also performed the purificatory rites such as the tonsure and the initiation.
From the very moment that son of that great-souled one was born,
the sage thereafter became overwhelmed by grief and affliction.
Likewise, his mother also had her mind overwhelmed by anger and greed;
constantly possessed by intense passion and other afflictions, she was deeply tormented by grief and suffering. (9)
The sage Ṛtavāk, being deeply distressed, fell into reflection:
"What is the cause of this that has occurred? My son has become utterly wicked-minded."
He forcibly abducted the wife of a certain son of a sage;
that man of deluded intellect paid no heed to the instruction of his father nor to that of his mother.
Then, with a dejected heart, Ṛtavāk spoke these words:
"Childlessness is better for men than ever having a wicked son. (12)
An evil son even casts his deceased ancestors into hell;
as long as he lives, he is nothing but a source of suffering for his parents. (13)
Fie on the birth of a wicked son who brings sorrow to his parents;
he is of no benefit to his friends, nor does he cause harm to his enemies.
Blessed are those men in this world in whose house dwells a good son, who is inclined toward helping others and brings happiness to his father and mother. (15)
By a bad son the family is ruined; by a bad son one's reputation is destroyed;
through a bad son there is suffering both in this world and the next, as well as the torments of hell.
A lineage is ruined by a bad son; birth is ruined by a bad wife;
a day is ruined by bad food; and where is there happiness with a bad friend? (17)
Skanda said: Tormented incessantly by his son’s wicked conduct, the sage went to Garga at that time and questioned him.
Thus spoke the truthful voice of the wicked one:
"O Blessed One, I wish to ask you; tell me that, O Lord!"
And [he described] the reason for the teacher's misconduct regarding his son, according to the science of astrology.
The Vedas have been studied by me according to rule; having completed the vow of a religious student, marriage was performed according to the prescribed rites. (20)
Through service to the guru, [one masters] the Vedas.
Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata Mahātmya, Chapter 4.
Together with my wife, the duties of the householder were constantly performed,
and the ritual of the five great sacrifices was carried out by me according to the prescribed rules.
O Brahmin, fearing hell and not out of a desire for sensual pleasure, I performed the rite of conception according to the rules for the sake of obtaining a son. (22)
"O Sage, this son of mine, born through the fault of my mother or my own, has become a bringer of sorrow to his parents—a man of evil character who causes grief to his kinsmen. (23)
Having heard these words of the sage at that time, Garga Ācārya,
the knower of astrology, reflected upon the entire cause and spoke these words.
Garga said:
O sage, this is no fault of yours, nor of your mother, nor of your lineage.
Rather, the Gaṇḍānta ending with Revatī is the cause of the child's lack of character.
O Sage, because your son was born at such an inauspicious time, that alone is the cause of your suffering; there is not even the slightest other cause.
O Brahmin, for the sake of pacifying that suffering, diligently propitiate the auspicious Durgā, the mother of the worlds and the destroyer of misfortune. (27)
Having heard Garga’s words, Ṛtavāk, overcome with anger, cursed Revatī: "May Revatī fall from the sky! (28)
When he had thus pronounced the curse upon Pūṣan,
the sun’s orb fell from the sky while all the world looked on from Mount Kumuda.
Due to that fall, the mountain became known as Raivataka and Kumudācala;
from that time forward, it also became exceedingly beautiful.
Having pronounced a curse upon Revatī according to the procedure prescribed by Garga,
the sage propitiated the goddess Ambikā and became a possessor of happiness and good fortune.
Skanda said:
From the splendor of the constellation Revatī, a maiden was born who was peerless in beauty in the world, like a second Śrī. (32)
Then, having seen that maiden born from the splendor of Revatī,
the sage Pramuca joyfully gave her the name Revatī.
Then he led her to his own hermitage and nourished her according to dharma,
like a daughter, on Mount Kumuda, the Brahmarṣi named Pramuca.
Then, seeing that she had reached maturity and was endowed with beauty, the sage reflected: "Who might be a suitable husband for her? (35)
Searching for her husband in many ways, she did not find the worthy one;
thereupon, entering the fire-sanctuary, the sage praised the Purifier (Agni).
Then the Fire-god, being pleased, also prophesied for him a bridegroom who would be most righteous,
powerful, heroic, sweet-spoken, and unconquered.
"O Sage, a lord of the earth named Durdama shall become her husband.
Having heard these words of Agni, the sage then became filled with joy. (38)
By chance, under the pretext of hunting, the wise king named Durdama arrived at that moment at the hermitage of the sage.
The son of Vikramaśīla was powerful and exceedingly heroic;
born from the womb of Kālindī, he was descended from the lineage of Priyavrata. ||40||
Having entered the hermitage of the sage and not seeing that great seer, the king addressed his beloved and asked Revatī: "O dear one! (41)
"O beloved, the venerable great sage Rājīva has departed from this hermitage;
O auspicious one, tell me truly, I wish to see his feet. (42)
Chapter 4 of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahātmya.
The maiden said:
"O Great King, having heard those words, the great sage arrived at the fire-sanctuary;
the king, too, having heard that speech, quickly emerged from the hermitage. (43)

Likewise, the sage saw King Durdama standing at the door of the fire-sanctuary, endowed with the marks of royalty and bowing with humility. The king prostrated before him, and the sage said to his disciple:
"Gautama, let the guest-offering (arghya) be brought; this lord of the earth is worthy of the arghya."
"Since my son-in-law has arrived after such a long time," he said, and specifically offered him the guest-offering (arghya); he too accepted it while reflecting.
Then, having greeted the king— who was seated upon his sage-like throne and holding a water-pot— with blessings for all his desires, he also inquired after his welfare.
"O King, is all well with your health, your army, your treasury, and your friends?
Is it well with your servants, ministers, city, kingdom, and yourself as well, O lord of men? (48)
Your wife is well, since she remains right here;
therefore, I do not ask after her welfare, but speak instead of the welfare of you and your other wives.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace there is freedom from ailment for me in every respect.
But this is my curiosity, O Brahmin: who is this woman who exists as my wife? (50)
The sage said:
"O lord of the earth, you have a wife named Revatī, who is peerless in beauty on this earth; how is it that you do not recognize her as your own spouse?"
The king said:
"O Lord, O Blessed One, I know those wives of mine who are in my home, such as Subhadrā and the others; however, I do not know Revatī. (52)
The sage said:
O King of great intelligence, that beloved whom you have just now called "dear" has been forgotten by you in an instant— she who was your most praiseworthy beloved.
The king said:
"O sage, what you have spoken was not false; I invited you exactly as you were addressed. My intention was not wicked; you ought not to be angry. (54)
The sage said:
"O King, what you have spoken is true; your intention has not been corrupted. These words were uttered by you in this manner because you were impelled by Agni. (55)
Today I asked the Fire-god, "Who will become her husband?
He replied, "King Durdama will certainly be her husband. (56)
Therefore, O lord of the earth, accept this maiden given by me;
she was previously addressed as "Priyā" (the Beloved), so do not hesitate, O sir! (57)
Having heard this, he remained silent, reflecting upon the words spoken by the sage;
then the sage prepared to perform the marriage rite for him.
Then, seeing him prepared for the marriage, the maiden said to the sage:
"O father, you ought to perform my marriage when the constellation Revatī is in the ascendant. (59)
The sage said:
"O child, there are indeed many constellations suitable for marriage;
why then the wedding at Revatī? The asterism of Pūṣan (Revatī) is not situated in the sky."
In the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya*, Chapter 4,
the maiden said:
"Except for the asterism Revatī, there is indeed no time suitable for my marriage;
therefore, I entreat you: perform this wedding under the constellation Pauṣṇa."
The sage said: "In former times, the constellation Revatī was cast down by the truthful-speeched sage;
if you have no affection for it, how can your marriage take place?"
The maiden said:
"What austerity has this one performed? He is merely truthful in speech alone. Have you not performed such austerity through speech, body, and mind?"
"You are capable of creating the world; I know the power of your asceticism.
O Father, having established the Revatī constellation in the sky, perform my marriage."
The sage said:
"So be it; may you be blessed. Just as you tell me, today, for your sake, I shall establish the constellation Puṣya upon the path of the Moon."
Skanda said:
Having spoken thus, O Pot-born one, the sage immediately restored the constellation Puṣya to its former state through the power of his asceticism,
according to the path of the Moon.
Under the constellation named Revatī,
the sage gave Revatī to the high-souled King Durdama according to the marriage rites.
Having performed the marriage of his daughter, the sage said to the king:
"O hero, tell me what you desire; I shall fulfill it. (68)
The king said:
"O sage, I am born in the lineage of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu;
by your grace, I desire a son who shall be the sovereign of a Manvantara. (69)
The Sage said:
"If you have this desire, perform the worship of the Goddess;
a son shall indeed be born to you, a Manu who will be the lord of a Manvantara."
Having heard that fifth Purāṇa known as the Devībhāgavata five times, you shall obtain the desired son.
The fifth Manu will be named Raivata, the son of Revatī;
he will be a knower of the Vedas, an expert in the principles of the scriptures, righteous, and unconquered.
Thus addressed by the sage, the wise king, having bowed to the sage with joy,
departed for his own city together with his wife.
That high-minded one ruled the kingdom inherited from his father and grandfather;
that righteous soul protected his subjects like his own biological sons.
Once, a high-souled sage named Lomaśa arrived;
having prostrated before him and honored him, the king spoke with palms joined in reverence.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, O Sage, by your grace I desire to hear the Purāṇa named Devībhāgavata, out of a longing for a son. (76)
Having heard the words of the Lord of Creatures, Lomaśa spoke with joy:
"O King, you are blessed; devotion has arisen in you toward the Mother of the Three Worlds, she who is the supreme Mother of the Universe, worshipped by gods, asuras, and men. (77)
If devotion toward her has arisen, the accomplishment of one's purpose will occur. || 78 ||
Therefore, O King, I shall cause you to hear the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, by the mere hearing of which nothing whatsoever remains difficult to attain. (79)
Having spoken thus, O Brahmin, he began the narration on an auspicious day;
he listened to it five times according to the prescribed rite together with his wife.
Chapter 5 of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahātmya.
On the day of completion, the righteous king, filled with supreme joy, honored both the Purāṇa and the sage.
Having offered oblations with the nine-syllable mantra and having fed the young maidens,
he gratified the Brahmins along with their wives with sacrificial fees.
Then, after some time, by the grace of the Blessed One,
that queen conceived a fetus that would bring about the welfare of the world.
Then, when the auspicious time had arrived and the planets were situated in favorable positions, Revatī gave birth to a son amidst every kind of auspiciousness. (84)
Having heard of his son's birth, the king, filled with joy, bathed and performed the birth-rites and other ceremonies with gold.
Having bestowed gifts according to the prescribed rites and gratified the brahmins,
the king had the boy undergo the initiation ceremony and taught him the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches.
Born as a treasury of all sciences, most righteous, and the best among those skilled in weapons,
he was the heroic one named Raivata, both a proponent and a practitioner of dharma.
Then Brahmā appointed Raivata to the station of Manu;
that illustrious lord of the Manvantara ruled the earth according to righteousness.
Thus, this power of the Goddess has been narrated in brief;
who is capable of describing the greatness of the Purāṇa in detail? (89)
Sūta said:
Having heard the greatness and the ritual procedure of the Bhāgavata, and having worshipped Kumāra, the pot-born sage returned once more to his own hermitage.
Thus, O Brahmins, this majesty of the Bhāgavata has been declared by me in your presence.
He who hears it with devotion or recites it here, having enjoyed all worldly pleasures, attains liberation in the end.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Śrī Devībhāgavata-māhātmya within the Mānasa-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
The sages said:
O Sūta, O Sūta, O highly fortunate one, we have heard the supreme majesty.
Now we wish to hear the procedure for listening to the Purāṇas.
Sūta said: O all you sages, listen to the procedure for hearing the Purāṇas,
by which men who hear it shall attain the fulfillment of all their desires.
First, having summoned an astrologer, the wise man should determine an auspicious moment;
beginning from the month of Śuci, a period of six months brings good fortune.

The hearing of the Purāṇas is auspicious when performed under the asterisms of Hasta, Aśvinī, Mūla, Puṣya, Jyeṣṭhā, Mantrā (Maitrā), Mṛgaśiras, and Śravaṇā; on favorable lunar days and on auspicious weekdays. ||4||
Through the sequence of four, four, eight, five, six, four, and three [syllables],
there is the attainment of dharma, the acquisition of wealth, success in one's purpose, and supreme happiness.
Suffering, then fear of kings, and the attainment of knowledge are the results in successive order;
one should purify the wheel by listening to the Purāṇas spoken by Śiva.
Alternatively, for the pleasure of the Goddess, one should listen during the four Navarātras,
or even in another month, provided the lunar day, weekday, and asterism have been purified.
The wise should diligently prepare such provisions for this new marriage rite as are required for other marriages and similar occasions. || 8 ||
One should employ many assistants who are free from deceit and greed, men who are clever, generous, and devoted to the Goddess. (9)
In the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya*, Chapter 5:
"This news should be diligently dispatched by messengers to every country and to every person."
"You must certainly come here; there will be a conversation with the Goddess."
Whether they belong to the Saura, Gāṇapatya, Śaiva, Śākta, or Vaiṣṇava sects,
she is to be served by all of them, since the gods are always accompanied by their Śaktis.
Those who are intensely devoted to love and eager for the nectar-like essence of the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata should especially come for the sake of this discourse.
The castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, as well as women and those in the stages of life (āśramas)—whether they possess desire or are free from desire—must drink this nectar of the narrative. 13.
There shall never be an occasion for them even to hear the word "no";
they must arrive at the proper time for the sacrifice, for the auspicious moment is fleeting.
The summoning of men must be carried out with propriety; likewise, for those who have arrived, a suitable place of residence must be provided. 15.
A place for discourse should be prepared on the ground, preceded by sweeping; then, in a spacious area, it should be made beautiful by smearing with cow dung. (16)
A beautiful pavilion should be constructed, adorned with pillars of plantain trees, with a canopy above, and resplendent with flags and banners. (17)
And a divine seat for the speaker, provided with a comfortable covering, should be prepared with effort, facing either the east or the north. (18)
He should provide appropriate seats for the listeners—both for men and for women—for the purpose of hearing the discourse. (19)

One who is eloquent, self-controlled, learned in the scriptures, devoted to the worship of the Goddess, compassionate, free from desire, skillful, steadfast, and an excellent speaker is considered [fit]. (20)

Devoted to Brahman, a worshiper of the deities, and intent upon the essence of the sacred narratives; magnanimous, free from greed, humble, and indeed abstaining from violence and other such acts—such is the listener. || 21 ||
One who is devoted to heresy, greedy, a womanizer, a hypocrite, cruel, wrathful, or abusive is not praised at a sacrifice to the Goddess. (22)
To sever doubts, one who is wise, possessed of such qualities, capable of awakening the listener, and composed should be appointed as an assistant to the speaker. (23)

For a moment before the day [of initiation], the acts such as the preparation of the milk-offering (kṣīrakarma) should be performed by the people, including the speaker and the listeners; thereafter follows the formulation of the observances (niyama).
At the time of sunrise, having performed purification, one should bathe;
then one should regularly perform the twilight rites and the libation (tarpaṇa) in brief.
To establish fitness for hearing the discourse, one should cause cows and horses to be given;
first, one should worship Gaṇapati, the remover of all obstacles.
Having also established the water-pots (kalaśas), one should worship there the deities belonging to the directions:
Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, the Yoginīs, and likewise the Mātṛkās.
Having also worshipped Tulasī, the planets, Viṣṇu, and Śaṅkara,
one should worship the Mother of the Universe with the nine-syllable mantra.

Having worshipped the book of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata with all ritual offerings—as the very embodiment of the speech of the Goddess Śrī, composed in beautiful script—according to the prescribed rules. 29.
For the sake of pacifying obstacles to the discourse, he should choose Brahmins;
the nine-syllable mantra is to be muttered, and the Saptashati hymn is to be recited. (30)
Having performed circumambulations and prostrations, one should at the end offer praise:
"O Kātyāyanī, O Mahāmāyā, O Bhavānī, O Sovereign of the World! (31)
O Compassionate One, lift me up who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
O Mother of the Universe, worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, be gracious! 32.
"O Goddess, grant the boon desired by my mind; salutations be unto you!
Having thus prayed, one should listen to the narrative with a restrained mind. (33)
Then, having honored the speaker with the intellect of Vyāsa and Buddha, the self-possessed one,
having adorned him with garlands, ornaments, garments, and so forth, should entreat him.
O knower of all scriptures and histories, O you who are Vyāsa in form, salutations be unto you!
Dispel the mass of inner darkness with the rising moon of this narrative.
In the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya*, Chapter 5: Furthermore,
from that point until the end of the ninth day, the religious observances (*niyamas*) must then be performed.
Having seated the Brahmins and others and honored them with food, he himself should sit down.
It should be listened to with attention for the sake of attaining the fruits of the four aims of life. Having cast aside all concern for home, children, wife, kin, and wealth,
the wise person should rest for a mere moment and recite it at midday when a small portion of the sun remains.
Beginning from sunrise, a light meal is prescribed;
one who desires the sacred narrative should eat only once, preferably sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
For the sake of conquering excrement and urine, one should either subsist on fruits, consume only milk, or eat only ghee;
a wise person should act in such a way that no obstacle arises to the recitation of the story. 40.
O twice-born ones, I shall declare the rule for those who are devoted to hearing this narrative,
regarding those who perceive a distinction between Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
Those who are devoid of devotion to the Goddess, heretics, violent, wicked, haters of Brahmins, and atheists—they are not fit to hear this narrative. (42)
In listening to discourses. ||43||
Those who are greedy for seizing the property of Brahmins, the wives and wealth of others, or the property of the gods, have no right [to this].

A celibate student (brahmacārī), one who sleeps on the ground, a speaker of truth, and one who has conquered his senses—such a self-controlled person should eat from a leaf-plate at the conclusion of the recitation. 44.
One observing a vow should avoid eggplant, kalinda, oil, legumes, honey, burnt food, stale food, and anything tainted by its inherent nature. (45)
One should avoid meat, lentil soup, and food looked upon by a woman in her courses,
as well as garlic, radish, asafoetida, onion, and leek.
One who observes the vow of the Kathā should not eat the vegetables kūṣmāṇḍa and nalikā;
he should also avoid lust, anger, intoxication, greed, hypocrisy, and pride. (47)
He who speaks with a woman in her courses, or with one who has violated the Veda, while observing a vow of silence; ||48||

One should not even hear the censure of Brahmins, those who have fallen from their status, Vratyas, dog-cookers, Yavanas, and outcastes; nor that of the Vedas, cows, gurus, and Brahmins; nor likewise of women, kings, great souls, or the gods and their devotees. (49)
One who observes the vow of sacred narrative (kathāvratī) should practice discipline, straightforwardness, purity, compassion, moderation in speech, and a noble state of mind. (50)
Whether she be barren, or one whose children are all female, or unfortunate, or one whose children have died;
or whether he be poor and childless—one who is devoted to me should listen to this narrative. (51)
This story should be heard by those who are barren, or those who bear only female offspring, or the unfortunate, or those whose children have died, or by women whose wombs are barren. 52.
He who desires dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa without exertion must listen with diligence to the Bhāgavata of the Blessed One.
For these days are indeed equal to the day of the new moon for one skilled in policy;
whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, or chanted during them becomes of infinite fruit. (54)
Having thus observed the vow for nine days, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana);
those desiring its fruit should act exactly as prescribed for the Mahāṣṭamī vow. || 55 ||
For those who are free from desire, by the mere hearing [of it], they become purified and indeed attain liberation;
since the Supreme Goddess bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men. (56)
One should always perform worship of both the book and the speaker;
one should receive the grace bestowed by the speaker with devotion. (57)
He who constantly worships young maidens, feeds them, and makes requests to them, as well as to married women and Brahmins, will achieve success without a doubt. || 58 ||
Or, at the conclusion [of the ritual], one should recite the *Nāmasāhasra* or the *Viṣṇusahasranāma* for the pacification of all defects.
One should therefore glorify Viṣṇu, by whose true name being uttered, whatever is deficient in acts such as asceticism and sacrifice attains completeness. 60.
Upon the completion of the seven-hundred-verse mantra of the Goddess,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with either the root-mantra of the Devīmāhātmya or the nine-syllable mantra.
=== PAGE 17 === 2 In the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya*, Chapter 5.
Alternatively, the oblation may be performed with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter while reciting the Gāyatrī;
for this Bhāgavata is said to be composed of the Gāyatrī.
One should properly satisfy the reciter with garments, ornaments, abundant food, and other gifts;
when the reciter is pleased, all the deities are pleased with him. (63)
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and satisfy them with sacrificial fees;
for they are the very forms of the gods upon this earth, and when they are pleased, one's desired fruit is attained.
One should feed married women and virgins with devotion to the Goddess;
having given them sacrificial fees as well, one should pray for one's own spiritual success. || 65 ||
One should give other gifts as well—gold, milch cows, horses, elephants, and land; for him, the fruit thereof shall be inexhaustible.
This Devībhāgavata, written in beautiful characters, should be placed upon a golden throne and wrapped in a silk cloth. (67)
On the eighth, the ninth, or the fourteenth lunar day, he should give gifts; having enjoyed worldly pleasures here, he shall attain liberation, which is difficult to obtain. 68.
Whether he be poor, weak, a child, a youth, or even an old man,
a physician who knows the ancient scriptures is always worthy of honor and respect.
There are many teachers in the world born of their virtues;
yet among them all, the one born of the Purāṇas is the supreme teacher.
But a Brāhmaṇa who is a reciter of the Purāṇas, while seated upon the seat of Vyāsa,
should not offer salutations to anyone until his discourse is concluded.
Even for those who listen with devotion to this divine ancient narrative, there is no fruit of merit, as they remain partakers of suffering and poverty. (72)
Those who listen to the story of the Goddess without first honoring the Purāṇa with betel, flowers, and other offerings will indeed become impoverished. 73.
Those men who, abandoning the narrative being recited, go elsewhere,
will find their wives and wealth perishing midway through their enjoyments.
And those hypocrites who, seated upon high thrones, listen to the narrative—
Having eaten there, they become crows and undergo the torments of hell.
"Those who sit in the āḍha posture and those who remain in the vīrāsana posture, and who listen to this divine narrative, shall become branches of Arjuna. (76)
Those who speak inappropriately while the Kaṣāya is being recited become donkeys in this world,
and after that, they become lizards.
Those wicked ones who revile the ancient knowledge or the discourse that removes sin shall undoubtedly become dogs for a hundred births. (78)
Those who sit upon the same seat as a speaker while he is telling a story go to the abode of hell and incur a sin equal to that of violating the preceptor’s bed. ||79||
Those who listen without bowing down become poisonous trees;
even those who listen while lying down become pythons.
Those men who never listen to the ancient stories,
having experienced a terrible hell, become village pigs.
Those who do not approve of the discourse and those deceitful ones who create obstacles, having experienced hell for ten million years, become village pigs. 82.
Those who give a seat, a vessel, a substance, fruit, garments, or a woolen blanket to one who knows the Purāṇas go to the abode of Hari. (83)
Those men who provide a new, auspicious silk cloth or fine thread for an ancient manuscript are partakers of happiness. (84)
Whatever fruit one may obtain from listening to all the Purāṇas,
one shall obtain a hundred times that merit from the Devībhāgavata.
Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya, Chapter 5.
Just as the Gaṅgā is preeminent among rivers, Śaṅkara among the gods, the Rāmāyaṇa among poetic works, and the sun among luminous bodies; || 86 ||
As the moon is among things that give delight, as fame is among riches,
as the earth is among those who possess forbearance, and as the ocean is in depth;
as the Sāvitrī is among mantras, so is the remembrance of Hari for the destruction of sin.
Likewise, among the eighteen Purāṇas, there is the Devībhāgavata.
If one hears it nine times by any means whatsoever, it is impossible to describe the fruit thereof; he indeed becomes liberated while living. 89.

When fear of royal enemies has arisen, or likewise when there is fear of a great pestilence, during famine or the ruin of the kingdom—one should listen to this for the sake of pacifying those calamities. (10)
O twice-born ones, one should listen to the Devībhāgavata for the destruction of ghosts and spirits, for the attainment of a kingdom from enemies, and for the gain of a son.
Whoever reads or even hears the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam—whether a half-verse or a quarter-verse—attains the supreme goal. (92)
That which was revealed by the Blessed Goddess herself in the form of verses and their meanings has been expanded through the lineage of disciples and grand-disciples. 93.
There is no dharma higher than the Gāyatrī; there is no austerity higher than the Gāyatrī;
there is no deity equal to the Gāyatrī; there is no Manu higher than the Gāyatrī. (94)
Because it protects the singer (gātāram), it is called Gāyatrī;
that goddess, along with her secret doctrine, is established here in this Bhāgavata. (95)
Therefore, even the great Purāṇas are not worth a sixteenth part of this Bhāgavata, which brings delight to the Goddess. 96.
The Śrīmad Bhāgavata Purāṇa is the stainless wealth of the brāhmaṇas;
herein is declared the pure dharma by Nārāyaṇa, the son of Dharma,
as well as the secret of the Gāyatrī and a description of Maṇidvīpa.
And the Blessed Gītā was sung by the Goddess herself to the Lord of the Snowy Mountains. 17.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, there is nothing else in this world equal to this Purāṇa; for this reason, the Devībhāgavata should always be served with devotion.

Salutations ever to that Mother of the Universe, whose entire power neither the Creator, nor Hari, nor Giriśa, nor even Ananta knows; what then of the gods who are but her partial manifestations, or other deities? 99.

Salutations forever to that Mother of the Universe, by obtaining the dust of whose lotus feet Brahmā creates the universe, Viṣṇu sustains it day after day, and Rudra destroys it; otherwise, they would not be capable of such deeds. 100.

Having meditated upon the Mother, who shines with a smiling countenance within the heart of Supreme Śiva—residing in a house made of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi) on the Island of Jewels (maṇidvīpa), which is adorned with groves of celestial trees at the edge of the ocean of nectar and is most wonderfully beautiful—a man indeed enjoys worldly enjoyment and attains liberation. || 101 ||
Worshipped by Brahmā, Īśa, Acyuta, Śakra, and other great sages, may she, the presiding deity of Maṇidvīpa, exist for the welfare of the world. 102.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Listening," in the *Devībhāgavata-māhātmya* within the *Mānasa-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Skanda Purāṇa*.
This concludes the *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata-Māhātmya* belonging to the *Skānda-Purāṇa*.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
The Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata, First Skandha.
— First Chapter.
Om! We meditate upon that primordial Goddess, whose nature is universal consciousness.
May that wisdom inspire us. || 1 ||
Śaunaka said: O Sūta, O Sūta, you are highly fortunate and blessed, O bull among men,
since these auspicious collections of Purāṇas have been studied by you.
O sinless one, the eighteen divine Purāṇas were formerly narrated by the sage Kṛṣṇa, and they have been studied by you, O sinless one.
O giver of honor, you have learned from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, all these [Purāṇas] endowed with five characteristics and accompanied by their secret doctrines.
By the power of our merit, you have arrived at this supreme field—divine, equal to the universe, meritorious, and free from the defects of the Kali age. ||5||
"O Sūta, this assembly of sages indeed desires to hear that which bestows merit; please speak to us with a concentrated mind regarding the Purāṇa-saṃhitā."
May you be long-lived everywhere and free from the three types of suffering;
O illustrious one, relate today the Purāṇa that is equal to the Veda.
O Sūta, those men who possess the faculty of hearing but are unskilled in discerning the true taste [of scripture] do not listen to the Purāṇas; indeed, they have been deceived by fate.
Just as the gratification of the sense of taste is experienced through the six flavors,
so too is the gratification of the sense of hearing held to be produced by the words of the wise.
Indeed, snakes, being devoid of ears, may well be deluded by the qualities of the sky;
but how is it that those who possess ears and hear with them are not likewise as if earless?
O gentle one, all these twice-born ones within the Naimiṣa forest, afflicted by the fear of the Kali age, remain with concentrated minds, desiring to hear [this].
It is taught that the passing of time may be accomplished by any means whatsoever;
for the foolish in this world, through vices, and for the wise, through reflections on the scriptures. (12)
The scriptures are also diverse and filled with disputations and debates;
the Purāṇas are of three kinds, and the Śāstras are manifold.
They were filled with cavil and fallacies, causing pride and resentment; they were endowed with various sophistical arguments, logical, and extensive. (1–13)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, First Book, Chapter 2.
Among those, Vedānta is considered sāttvika, Mīmāṃsā is regarded as rājasa, and the Nyāya-śāstra, which is constrained by the logic of causal arguments, is tāmasa. (14)
In that very same way, O gentle one, you have narrated the Purāṇas, which consist of three qualities and possess five characteristics, through various stories. (15)
In that regard, the meritorious Bhāgavata, which is equal to the Vedas and endowed with all characteristics, was previously described by you. (16)
At that time, this most wonderful [account] was proclaimed merely in outline;
it bestows liberation upon those seeking liberation, and likewise grants desires and righteousness.
"Relate that supreme Purāṇa in detail with reverence;
all these twice-born ones desire to hear the divine and auspicious Bhāgavata. (18)
But you, O knower of dharma, surely know the ancient compendium spoken by Kṛṣṇa due to your devotion to your guru, as well as the qualities of goodness and the rest;
and other [teachings] have been heard by us, O omniscient one, as they issued from your own mouth.
Today we do not reach satiety at all, just as the immortals do when drinking nectar.
O Sūta, for those who drink the nectar of worldly poetry, there is never liberation at any time;
but by drinking the Bhāgavata, a person is immediately released from all distress.
O Sūta, although thousands of sacrifices have been performed for the sake of drinking the nectar of immortality,
we do not attain peace in any way whatsoever.
For the fruit of sacrifices is heaven, and from heaven there is a fall;
thus occurs incessant wandering in this wheel of worldly existence. (23)
O Omniscient One, for men wandering here in this wheel of time composed of the three qualities, there is never liberation without knowledge. (24)
Therefore, recite the *Bhāgavata*, which is endowed with all aesthetic flavors, meritorious, purifying, bestowing liberation, secret, and always dear to those seeking release. (25)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Question of Śaunaka," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
The venerable Sūta said: "I am blessed, I am most fortunate, I have been purified by these great souls."
That which was asked is a very great merit, an ancient account renowned in the Vedas. ||1||
Therefore, I shall fully declare that which is in accordance with the meaning of all the Śrutis—the secret of all the Śāstras and Āgamas, unsurpassed. (2)
Having bowed to that beautiful lotus-foot which bestows liberation upon yogis,
which is served even by Brahmā and others intent on praise, and which is always meditated upon by the lords of sages—
I shall today describe in detail, with many flavors, that most glorious Purāṇa.
O twice-born ones, with devotion [he visited] the abode of all aesthetic flavors, renowned by the name Bhagavatī. ||3||
That which is designated as "Vidyā" on the path of the Vedas— the primordial, supreme Power (Śakti),
all-knowing, skilled in severing the bonds of worldly existence, and residing within the heart of all—
is difficult to be known by those of evil soul, yet has been brought by sages to the state of being the object of meditation.
In this world, that Blessed Lady becomes manifest; she shall always be the bestower of spiritual accomplishments. ||4||
Having created this entire universe, whose nature consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, she protects the world by means of her own power composed of the three qualities (guṇas);
having withdrawn it at the time of the cosmic dissolution, she likewise rejoices alone—I meditate upon her with my mind, the mother of the entire universe. (5)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 2:
It is well known that Brahmā creates this entire universe; indeed, this has been declared by those conversant with the Purāṇas who are knowers of the Vedas.
It is indeed said by them that his birth was from the lotus of Viṣṇu's navel; for he does not create independently. ||6||
But Viṣṇu sleeps upon the couch of Śeṣa; at that time, his birth indeed occurs within the bud of the lotus from his navel.
Since the thousand-headed one has surely become the support here, how indeed can that Blessed One, the enemy of Mura, be awakened? (7)
The water of the single vast ocean exists only in the form of flavor; indeed, there is no persistence of flavor without a vessel.
I have gone for refuge to her who, in the realm of all beings, is truly the power itself—the mother of all beings. (2)
Having seen Viṣṇu seated upon the lotus with his eyes closed in yogic sleep, the unborn Brahmā praised that Goddess; I go for refuge to her. (9)

Having meditated upon that Māyā, both with attributes (saguṇā) as the giver of liberation and likewise without attributes (nirguṇā), I shall proclaim the entire Purāṇa; let the sages here listen. (10)
The Purāṇa known as the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is the most excellent and meritorious;
it contains eighteen thousand refined verses. (11)
In this [work], twelve auspicious sections (skandhas) were composed by Kṛṣṇa;
it is remembered as containing three hundred chapters in full, augmented by eighteen.
Therein, there are twenty in the first, twelve indeed in the second, thirty in the third, and twenty-five in the fourth. || 13 ||
Thus, thirty-five chapters are proclaimed in the fifth [book], thirty-one in the sixth, and forty in the seventh. (14)
In the eighth [chapter], the enumeration of the principles (tattvas) is fifty; likewise in the ninth;
and in the tenth, it was indeed proclaimed by the Sage to be thirteen.
And likewise, O best of sages, twenty-four chapters are declared in the eleventh book, while there are exactly fourteen chapters in the twelfth. (16)
Thus has the enumeration been fully declared by the Great-Souled One in this Purāṇa;
its total number is proclaimed to be eighteen thousand.
Cosmic creation, secondary creation, genealogy, the periods of the Manus, and the history of the dynasties—thus the Purāṇa has five characteristics. (18)
She who is always devoid of qualities, eternal, all-pervading, unchanging, and auspicious;
she who is attainable through yoga, the support of all, and who abides as the fourth state (turīyā). ||19||
Her powers are indeed the Sāttvika, the Rājasa, and the Tāmasa;
these women are Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Mahākālī.
The creation characterized by the acceptance of these three powers by the gods for the purpose of emanation has been fully described by those learned in the scriptures. (21)

Then the origin of Hari, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Rudra is recorded; indeed, that is remembered as the secondary creation (pratisarga) for the purpose of preservation, origination, and destruction. || 22 ||
The genealogy of kings born from the lineages of Soma and Sūrya is proclaimed;
at the end of those lineages, the dynasties of Hiraṇyakaśipu and others are fully described.
And there is a detailed description of the Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva,
as well as the calculation of their time-periods and their respective Manvantaras.
O best of sages, the recounting of their lineages is known as the *vaṃśānucarita*, and these [Purāṇas] possess five characteristics. (25)
And likewise, the Bhārata, consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses, was composed by the Sage;
it is proclaimed as the fifth Veda, known as Itihāsa. ||26||
Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, tell us in detail what those Purāṇas are;
O omniscient one, how many in number are they? For we here are desirous of hearing them.
"We, the inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest, are terrified by the Kali age;
we have been commanded here by Brahmā after he gave us a mind-made discus. (28)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 3.
He told us that all those who follow behind him go to that place where the rim of his wheel is shattered; that region is considered purifying.
At that time, Kali will never be able to enter there;
let him remain in that very place until the Satya Yuga returns once more.
Having heard those words of his and taken up that narrative, he set out quickly, shaking [his head] with a desire to see all lands. (31)
"Having moved the wheel here both after death and in this world, the rim was shattered while he was looking on;
therefore, this most purifying sacred field is called Naimiṣa. (32)
"There is no entry for the Kali age here; therefore, this place was established by me, as well as by the high-souled sages and hosts of Siddhas who were afraid of the Kali age. (33)
It is said that sacrifices were performed even when devoid of animals, using only sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) and the like;
one should simply pass the time until the arrival of the Satya Yuga.
"O Sūta, you have arrived here entirely by the power of destiny;
therefore, tell us today the Purāṇa that is purifying and esteemed by Brahmā. (35)
"O Sūta, we are all desirous of hearing; you are the wise speaker, and we are indeed free from other occupations and likewise one-pointed in mind. (36)
O Sūta, may you be long-lived and free from the threefold afflictions;
how indeed shall you narrate today the auspicious and meritorious Bhāgavata Purāṇa?
In this [work], there is a description of dharma, artha, and kāma according to the prescribed rules;
having obtained knowledge through it, liberation is indeed said to be attained by the Sage. 38.
O Sūta, we are not satiated by hearing this delightful narrative, which was spoken by the sage Dvaipāyana and which is purifying.
It is a sacred vessel containing the entirety of all virtues, a wondrous drama of the Mother of the Entire World.
Reveal that ancient name of the Blessed One, which is joined with her own name, the destroyer of the entire multitude of impurities and the root of desire. 40.
Thus ends the second chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. ||2||
Now begins the third chapter.
Sūta said:
"O lords of sages, listen as I duly proclaim the Purāṇas."
Just as they were heard in their true essence from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī. || 1 ||
The Mahābhārata, the two Bhāgavatas, the three Vratas, and the four Vacanas, as well as the various ancient Purāṇas with their respective characteristics. ||2||
The first is proclaimed as the Matsya Purāṇa consisting of fourteen thousand verses;
likewise, there is the most wonderful Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa consisting of one thousand verses.
Fourteen thousand and five hundred [verses] are reckoned as the future extent by the sages who perceive the truth.
The Bhāgavata Purāṇa indeed consists of eighteen thousand verses,
while the Purāṇa known as the Brahmapurāṇa likewise contains ten thousand.
The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa consists of exactly twelve thousand verses and one hundred more;
likewise, the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa consists of eighteen thousand verses.
O Śaunaka, there are ten thousand known as Vāmana, six hundred belonging to Vāyu,
and twenty-four thousand.
The Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, most wonderful, consists of twenty-three thousand verses; the Vārāha Purāṇa, most wonderful, consists of twenty-four thousand verses.
The Purāṇa known as Agni consists of sixteen thousand verses;
the Nārada is considered supreme, containing twenty-five thousand verses.
The extensive work known as the Pādma is considered to consist of fifty-five thousand verses;
and that called the Liṅga is very extensive, comprising eleven thousand verses.
The Gāruḍa Purāṇa, spoken by Hari, consists of nineteen thousand verses; and the Kūrma Purāṇa, spoken by Kūrma, consists of seventeen thousand verses.
O sinless ones, I have related in detail the most wonderful Purāṇa known as the Skanda, consisting of eighty-one thousand verses and its traditional enumeration.
In the same manner, O best of sages, listen to the Upapurāṇas as well. Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa.
First Sanatkumāra, and after that Nārasiṃha.
The Nāradīya, the Śiva, the unsurpassed Daurvāsasa, the Kāpila, the Mānava, and likewise the Smṛti of Uśanas; 14.
The Vāruṇa, the one called Kālika, the auspicious Sāmba composed by Nandin, the Saura spoken by Parāśara, and the very extensive Āditya. 15.
The Māheśvara, Bhāgavata, and Vāsiṣṭha in detail—these are the Upapurāṇas declared by the high-souled ones. (16)
Having composed the eighteen Purāṇas, the son of Satyavatī created the incomparable narrative known as the Bhārata, which was augmented by them.
In all Manvantaras, during every Dvāpara Yuga,
he who seeks righteousness manifests the Purāṇas according to the prescribed rule.
In every Dvāpara age, Viṣṇu always assumes the form of Vyāsa;
out of a desire for the welfare [of beings], he divides the single Veda into many parts,
having perceived that the Brahmins in the Kali age will have short lifespans and small intellects.
In every age, he composes this meritorious Purāṇa-saṃhitā.
For women, Śūdras, and the dependents of the twice-born,
the hearing of the Vedas is not prescribed;
it was for their benefit alone that the Purāṇas were composed in ancient times.
O best of sages, in this auspicious seventh Manvantara named Vaivasvata,
when the twenty-eighth Dvāpara age has arrived.
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī and my preceptor who is most knowledgeable in dharma, will become the son of Droṇa (Drauṇi) when twenty-nine years have passed. 23.
Likewise, twenty-seven past Vyāsas have appeared,
and by them the Purāṇa-saṃhitās were narrated in age after age.
The sages said:
"Speak, O highly fortunate Sūta! Who were the Vyāsas born in previous ages, those who were the expounders of the Purāṇas in every Dvāpara age?
Sūta said:
In the first Dvāpara age, the Vedas were divided by Svayambhū himself;
but in the second Dvāpara age, Prajāpati performed the task of Vyāsa.
In the third [age] Uśanas was the Vyāsa, while in the fourth it was Bṛhaspati;
in the fifth Savitṛ was the Vyāsa, and likewise Mṛtyu in the sixth.
Maghavā is remembered for the seventh [Manvantara], Vasiṣṭha for the eighth;
Sārasvata for the ninth, and likewise Tridhāman for the tenth.
Then, in the eleventh, Trivṛṣa, and after that Bharadvāja.
In the thirteenth [kalpa] was Antarikṣa, and in the fourteenth was Dharma. ||29||
Tramyāruṇi was in the fifteenth, while Dhanañjaya was in the sixteenth;
Medhātithi was in the seventeenth, and likewise Vratī in the eighteenth;
Atri was in the nineteenth, and after that came Gautama.
Then, in the twenty-first [chapter], the one whose self is Hari (Haryātmā) is proclaimed as the most excellent. || 31 ||
Beno and Vājaśravas, Soma the son of Amuṣya, Tṛṇabindu, Vyāsa, and after him Bhārgava;
