then Śakti, Jātūkarṇya, and Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.
The number twenty-eight, which was heard by me and recounted by me, has been told.

I have heard this Purāṇa, the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, which was proclaimed by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana; it is meritorious, the destroyer of the flood of all miseries, the granter of desires and liberation, and enriched with the meaning of the Vedas. (34)
It is the garden of the essence of the flavor of all scriptures, always dear to those seeking liberation. ||35||
Vyāsa, having composed this most auspicious Purāṇa, taught it to his high-souled son Śuka, who was endowed with detachment and born from the fire-drill (araṇi).
I have heard it there and grasped it exactly as it was spoken from the mouth of Vyāsa, O lords of sages,
in the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 4.
All this ancient secret, complete and gathered together, [was obtained] through the grace of the Guru, the ocean of compassion. //37//
Questioned by the charioteer, Dvaipāyana there recounted the entirety of that ancient mystery;
indeed, I heard that which possesses great power from him, who was born not from a womb and possessed wondrous intelligence. (38)

The most excellent Śuka, desiring to dry up the waters of the ocean of worldly existence that are so difficult to traverse, brought forth the tasting of the fruit of the divine tree of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*;
with his ears as vessels, he listened with love to this wonderful work, which is the abode of the essence of various narratives.
Having heard that, who on earth of such a kind would not be liberated from the fear of the Kali age? (39)
Even a wicked person, devoid of Vedic dharma and lacking in proper conduct and intention, who listens to this supreme and glorious Purāṇa even under a pretext,
shall enjoy an abundance of pleasures here in this world and, at the end of the body, attain the beautiful, immovable state reached by yogis, marked with the name of the Blessed Goddess.

That knowledge which is devoid of qualities, unattainable even by Hari, Hara, and others, most beloved by the virtuous, and accessible through meditative absorption—it produces its presence within the hollow of the heart of one who constantly listens to the Satī Purāṇa. (41)

Having obtained a human birth endowed with all its limbs—a vessel for crossing the waters of the ocean of existence at will—yet failing to hear the Teacher, alas, that fool is deceived here by fate regarding the Purāṇa which bestows happiness. (42)

Having obtained a pair of sharp ears in human form, why does that dull-witted person on earth—who remains free from passion yet constantly listens to the slanders of others—not listen to this ancient, pure treasure of nectar that bestows all goals? (43)
Thus ends the third chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 3 ||
The Fourth Chapter.
The Sages said:
O gentle one, in whose wife was the son Śuka born by Vyāsa?
Or how, and of what kind was he, by whom this well-compounded [text] was recited? || 1 ||
"You have stated that Śuka was not born from a womb and likewise not produced by a female bird;
there is great doubt regarding this, so please explain it today, O high-minded one. (2)
It was previously heard that there was a practitioner of heat-yoga named Śuka, a man of great asceticism;
how did he formerly study the Purāṇa of such vast extent?
Sūta said: Formerly, on the bank of the Sarasvatī, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
was filled with wonder upon seeing a kalaviṅka bird in his hermitage.
The infant, as soon as it was born, was released into its nest;
it was charming, with a copper-colored beak and auspicious limbs in their entirety, yet devoid of any downy sprouts.
But those two, being utterly devoted to sexual pleasure, were intent on the fatigue of lovemaking;
they repeatedly cast food into the beak of their young one.
Filled with joy, he rubbed his own limbs against the limbs of the child,
and out of love, he kissed the auspicious face of the young parrot.
Then, having witnessed that wonderful display of love between the two young sparrows,
Vyāsa, overcome with longing, reflected deeply in his mind.
What is surprising about the love that is observed even among animals toward their offspring? It is not at all strange that humans, desiring the fruits of service, [should feel such affection]. (9)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, First Book, Chapter 4: "And why are this sparrow and his wife the means for his happiness through marriage?"
Having fashioned it, they both became happy upon seeing the auspicious face of the bride.
Or else, when old age has arrived, a most virtuous son will perform service for the sake of the merit of the two birds.
Or, having acquired wealth, he will gratify his parents;
or else, he will perform the funeral rites according to the prescribed rules.
Or rather, what need is there for the boy to go to Gayā to perform the śrāddha rites, or to perform the ritual release of a dark bull according to the rules? (13)
In this cycle of existence (saṃsāra), it is declared that the highest happiness among all pleasures is the embracing of a son’s body and, especially, fondling him.
For one who has no son, there is no destination, neither heaven nor anything else;
there is no means for achieving the world beyond other than a son. (15)
And it has been declared by the sages such as Manu and others in the Dharmaśāstras:
"One who has a son attains heaven, but one who is sonless never does so in any way. (16)
This is seen here before one's very eyes; it is not established by means of inference.

Even at the time of death, a man who is afflicted and deprived of sons, lying upon the ground as his bed, grieves in his mind:
"In my house there was abundant wealth and various vessels. || 18 ||

Since his mind wanders in distress at the time of death, one who has a deluded mind will certainly fall into an evil rebirth in every respect. (20)
Having thus reflected in many ways, the son of Satyavat sighed repeatedly with hot breath and became despondent.
Having reflected deeply with his mind and having made a firm resolve within his heart,

He reflected in his mind: "Which god shall we worship—one who is skilled in granting boons and likewise bestows desired objects?

And likewise Gaṇeśa, Kārtikeya, Pāvaka, and Vāruṇa. ||24||
As he was reflecting thus, Nārada, the best of sages,

Then, having heard that inquiry after his welfare, the best of sages asked [him in return].
"O Dvaipāyana, why are you so overcome with anxiety? Tell me.
Vyāsa said:
"For one who has no son, there is no higher goal, nor is there peace in the mind."
For that purpose, I am distressed and reflect upon it again and again:

Thus, overcome by anxiety, I have now come to you for refuge. (28–29)
"O Great Sage, you are omniscient; O treasure-house of compassion, tell me quickly:

Sūta said:
Thus questioned by Vyāsa, the high-minded sage Nārada, a knower of the Vedas,
spoke with supreme affection regarding Kṛṣṇa.
Nārada said:
O highly fortunate son of Parāśara, regarding that very matter which you ask me here, Madhusūdana was previously questioned by my father on that same subject.
Seeing Hari established in meditation, my father was filled with wonder;
he questioned the Lord of Gods, Śrīnātha, the Master of the Universe, who was radiant with the Kaustubha gem and bore the divine conch, discus, and mace. (33)
He wears yellow garments, has four arms, and his chest is marked with the Śrīvatsa.

He saw Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, the God of gods, the Teacher of the universe, the cause of all worlds, performing great austerities. (35)

O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Master of the past, the future, and the present; O Janārdana, why do you perform penance, and what are you meditating upon?
This is a source of great wonder to me: you are the Lord of all the worlds;
yet you are absorbed in meditation, O Lord of Gods—what could be more marvelous than this? (37)
"Born from the lotus of your navel, I am indeed the creator of all;
tell me, O Lord of Māyā, if there is anyone here who is superior to you. (38)
I know you, O Lord of the World, to be the primordial source and the cause of all;

O Great King, by your will I create this world;
and Hara, too, always acts according to your word when it is time for destruction.
The sun revolves in the sky, the wind blows auspiciously and inauspiciously, the fire burns, and the rain-cloud pours down, O Lord, by Your command. (41)

Having shown compassion, please speak today; I am your devotee, O you of noble vows.
For it is a traditional teaching that there is generally nothing that great souls should conceal. (43)

The power of passion (rājasī) resides in you for the creation of the world;

Separated from her, you are not capable of performing that task;

Who, having abandoned the enjoyment of prosperity along with Lakṣmī, would go among low births such as those of fish?

The Vedic scriptures and so forth are *sāttvika*; literature is *rājasa*;
and accounts of war and the exposure of others' faults are *tāmasa*. (11)
The wise and learned have declared the sattvic [nature] to be threefold:
namely, the highest, the middling, and likewise the lowest. (12)

Having deliberated, it has been determined and known by the wise that the highest [type of gift] bestows the fruit of liberation, the middling bestows heaven, and the lowest bestows worldly enjoyment.
Literature is of three kinds; it is considered best when directed toward one's own wife, middling when directed toward a courtesan, and lowest when directed toward the wife of another. (14)
The threefold nature of the *tāmasa* [type of battle] should be known by the wise who have seen the scriptures:
fighting against an assassin (*ātatāyin*) is declared to be the highest among them. (15)
Furthermore, the middling [type] arises from enmity toward the Pāṇḍavas by their enemies;
the lowest, however, occurs without cause during disputes and quarrels.
Therefore, O high-minded one, listening to this Purāṇa is the primary means;
it increases the intellect, is meritorious, and consequently destroys all sin. (17)
Therefore, O one of great intelligence, relate that auspicious ancient narrative which was previously heard from Dvaipāyana and which accomplishes every purpose.
Sūta said:
You are blessed and highly fortunate, and I too am blessed upon this earth, since you possess the inclination to hear and I indeed the desire to narrate. (19)
And formerly, when the three worlds had dissolved and become a single ocean,
Janārdana, the God of gods, was sleeping upon the couch of Śeṣa.
The two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, were born from the earwax of Viṣṇu;
those two Daityas of great strength grew up in the waters of the ocean.
Playing there, they remained moving here and there;
once, those two of massive body became absorbed in play within the great ocean.
The two brothers, remaining together as one in their hearts, reached the funeral pyre;
for nowhere does an effect arise without a cause—this is the universal law.
An object to be supported cannot exist in any way whatsoever without a support;
yet this relationship of support and supported does not appear within the range of the mind. //24//
"Where does this water, so vast and of such a pleasant nature, abide?
By whom was it created, and how did it come to be? We two are submerged, yet we remain standing in the water. How were we both born, or by whom were we both produced? (25)
"Where are our parents?"—such consciousness we do not have; indeed, such is the state of us two. (26)
Sūta said:
Desiring thus, the two of them did not reach a decision;
then Kaiṭabha spoke there to Madhu, who was standing by him in the water.
Kaiṭabha said:
"O Madhu, O brother, a great and unshakable power resides here within this water to sustain us; for that, I believe, is my reason [for staying]."
By her this water is pervaded, and it remains supported by her;
she alone is the supreme goddess, the cause, and not we two.
When those two Asuras, thus awakened and possessed by the funeral pyre,
heard a most enchanting seed-word (vāgbīja) in the sky, [they were struck with wonder].
Then, having received it, they practiced it with firm perseverance;
at that time, an auspicious flash of lightning was seen by them rising into the sky.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Book, Chapter 7.
They deliberated there: "This mantra is undoubtedly present here;
likewise, this meditation with attributes (saguṇa) has indeed been seen in the sky. (32)
Abstaining from food, having conquered their selves, with minds fixed on Him and composed,
they remained intent upon recitation and meditation after having thus reflected.
In this manner, they performed great penance for a thousand years;
consequently, that supreme Śakti became pleased with them.
Distressed upon seeing them resolved to perform austerities, an incorporeal voice spoke for the sake of showing them favor: 35.
"O Daityas, choose a boon that you desire, one that is highly esteemed;
I shall grant it, for I am indeed well-pleased by your ascetic penance. (36)
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, the Dānavas then spoke to her:
"O Goddess, O lady of noble vows, grant us this boon: death at our own will. (37)
The voice said:
"By my grace, O Daityas, death shall be according to your desire;
you two brothers shall be invincible by gods and Daityas alike—of this there is no doubt. (38)
Sūta said:
Having thus received boons from the Goddess, the Dānava, arrogant with pride,
sported in the ocean together with his hosts of aquatic creatures.
After some time, O brahmins, by chance the two Dānavas beheld the Lord Prajāpati Brahmā seated upon his lotus throne.
Seeing them, those two of great strength were filled with joy and, desiring battle, then said to him there: "O observer of noble vows, grant us a fight! (41)
If not, then leave this lotus and go wherever you wish without delay;
for if you are weak, where else could there be a suitable and auspicious seat? 42.
"This place is to be enjoyed by heroes; you are a coward, so leave at once!
Hearing these words of theirs, Prajāpati ascended the funeral pyre. 43.
And having seen those two powerful heroes, the ascetic stood there, overcome with anxiety, reflecting in his mind, "What shall I do? (44).
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 6 ||
Then the seventh chapter begins.
Sūta said:
Having seen them so powerful, Brahmā then reflected upon means [to subdue them].
And he, an expert in all strategic treatises, employed conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and other such means of war against them all.
I do not truly know the strength of these two as it actually is;
indeed, when strength is unknown, war is certainly not recommended.
If I were to offer praise today for these two wicked ones intoxicated with pride, my own weakness would surely be revealed by me. (3)
Even he alone will slay [them] once their weakness has been revealed;
therefore, neither is giving a gift appropriate today, nor how could a sowing of dissension be effected by me? (4)
Today I awaken Viṣṇu, Janārdana, who has been sleeping on the couch;
he is the four-armed great hero, and he shall be the destroyer of my suffering.
Having thus reflected in his mind, the lotus-born Brahmā, situated within the stalk of the lotus,
went for refuge in Viṣṇu, the destroyer of suffering, with his mind.
He praised Hari, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, who was motionless in his yogic sleep, with auspicious words of awakening for the purpose of rousing him.
Brahmā said:
O Hari, Lord of the wretched, Viṣṇu, Vāmana, arise, O Mādhava! O Hṛṣīkeśa, remover of the distress of devotees, abode of all, Lord of the universe! (8)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 7: O Vāsudeva, Lord of the Universe, whose inner self is immeasurable!
O wielder of the discus and mace, whose one-pointed mind is solely intent on destroying wicked enemies! || 9 ||
O Omniscient One, Lord of all worlds, endowed with all powers! Arise, arise, O Lord of gods, destroyer of suffering; protect me!
O Sustainer of the universe, large-eyed one, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious!
O Source of the Universe, formless one, you who bring about the creation, maintenance, and end [of all things].
"O Great King, these two Daityas, arrogant with pride, desire to kill me.
O Support of All, how is it that you do not know that I have fallen into calamity? (12)
If you disregard me, who am afflicted by extreme suffering and have come to you for refuge, then your status as the Protector, O Mahāviṣṇu, would become devoid of foundation. (13)
When the Lord Hari, overcome by yogic sleep, did not wake even though praised in this manner, Brahmā then reflected as follows: || 14 ||
"Surely Viṣṇu, whose measure is power, has fallen under the sway of sleep; that righteous soul has not awakened. What shall I do now, being so distressed?
"Both have arrived, desiring to kill me, O Dānava, arrogant with pride.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? I have no refuge anywhere.
Having reflected thus in his mind and reached a decision, he said:
With his heart fixed in one-pointed concentration, he offered praise to that Yoganidrā.
Having reflected thus even with my mind, I see that my power is capable of protection—by which power indeed Viṣṇu was rendered unconscious and devoid of movement. (18)
Just as the sun does not perceive the qualities such as the Vedic meters here,
so too Hari, with his eyes closed in sleep, does not perceive them.
Since you do not abandon sleep even though praised in many ways, I think that sleep is not under his control; rather, he has been brought under the sway of sleep.
It is said that whoever has fallen under another's power is indeed that person's servant;
therefore, this Yoganidrā is the mistress of Hari, the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Even the daughter of the ocean has come under her control, by whom her own husband was brought under subjection;
surely this entire world has been brought under subjection by the Blessed Lady.
I am Viṣṇu, as well as Śambhu, Sāvitrī, Ramā, and Umā;
we are all under her control—of this there is no doubt whatsoever. (23)
Even Hari lies helplessly, just like any other ordinary person;
when he is thus overcome, what can be said of other great-souled ones? 24.
Today Janārdana shall indeed enter the yoga-sleep by which the eternal Vāsudeva, when released, will engage in battle.
Having thus resolved in his mind, Brahmā, then situated upon the lotus stalk,
praised that Yoganidrā who was resting upon the limbs of Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said:

O Goddess, you are indeed the cause of this universe; this has been fully understood by me through the words of all the Vedas, O Mother, since even Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person who ordains the discernment of all worlds, has today been brought under the power of sleep.
"Who knows, O Mother, the playful sport of your delusive charm? I am a fool, and this Hari lies here helpless.
Thus addressed by her, [the Lord], the abode of the minds of all beings, the most learned among millions of gods, though devoid of qualities— ||28||
The Sāṃkhyas speak of the Puruṣa and that Prakṛti which is devoid of the nature of consciousness and is the creator of the world;
O Abode of the World, are you such? Why then have you today been made by you to be devoid of consciousness? 29.
O Bhavānī, you perform a dance of manifold kinds through your attributes, yet no one understands the application of your methods of action;
the hosts of sages meditate upon you three times daily at fixed intervals, having assigned to you the name "Sandhyā" (the Twilight) on account of your qualities.
O Goddess, you are always the intellect that brings awakening to the worlds, and you are Śrī, who eternally bestows happiness upon the gods.
*Śrīmad-devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, First Skandha, Chapter 7.
O Mother, fame, intelligence, death, splendor, faith, and delight indeed reside in all people through you. (31)
Indeed, having fallen into this miserable state, I have found no authority greater than these hundreds of conjectures;
yet you, who are truly the mother of all the worlds, were seen here by Hari as he granted him the gift of sleep.
O Goddess, you are difficult to be conceived even by those who know the Vedas; indeed, even the Veda does not know you in your entirety.
For this Śruti, having attained its origin from you, perceives all this work of yours as if it were directly before its eyes.

The wise one alone on earth knows your entire conduct; neither I, nor Hari, nor Bhava, nor the other gods, nor even the sages or my own sons are capable of knowing it. Thus, your greatness is indeed difficult to describe in all the worlds. (34)

O Goddess, even when the oblation has been offered in sacrifices by those learned in the Vedas, if they do not utter "svāhā" unto you, the gods do not constantly receive their share of the sacrifice; for you alone are the provider of sustenance even among the wise deities. (35)
O Blessed One, we were indeed first protected by you from the fear arising from the enemies of the gods;
likewise now, O Goddess, granter of boons, I am terrified and have come for refuge upon beholding the terrible Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
"Viṣṇu does not know this suffering of mine now; I know that you have brought my slender body under your own control.
Either release the Primal God, or slay the lord of the Dānavas—do as you please in this matter, O lady of great majesty. (37)
O Goddess, those dull-witted ones who do not know your supreme power even meditate upon Hari and Hara;
O Mother, today I have clearly perceived the proof, for Viṣṇu now lies utterly helpless.
O Goddess, even the river born of the Indus is not able to awaken Hari today by her power, for he is now subject to your will;
I believe that even Ramā was forcibly put to sleep by you, and having been rendered helpless, she did not wake.
Blessed indeed are those on earth who, having abandoned the worship of other deities, are intent on devotion at your feet and remain absorbed in you;
for they perform every kind of worship with great zeal, O Goddess, knowing you truly to be the Mother of all beings and the very Cow of Plenty.

Where have His luster, fame, auspicious conduct, virtues, and other qualities of Viṣṇu gone today, having abandoned Him? Surely this Hari has been made a captive here by your very power, O Goddess, who are possessed of supreme pride! 41.
You alone are the power of all worlds, possessing every majesty; indeed, everything created by you is merely a manifestation of being.
You sport within the net of delusion fashioned by yourself, just as an actor performs in a drama created by his own hand. ||42||

At the beginning of the age, Viṣṇu was manifested by you, and indeed the stainless power was granted for the sake of protection; everything has been saved and all have been brought under your control today. O Mother, you surely do exactly as pleases you. (43)
O Blessed One, if you have created me here only to destroy me, then cast aside your silence and show compassion!
Why indeed have these two been manifested in the form of Death? Or is it that you wish to mock me, O Bhavānī? (44)
I have understood your wondrous conduct; having created this entire universe, you sport therein as one who is independent.
— Śrīmad-devī-bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 8 —
O Bhavānī, you indeed cause me, who am already entirely dejected, to be struck down in that very same way; what is there to wonder at in this? ||45||
O Mother, O Ambika of the world, grant my death this very day; I have no fear here of the pain born of dying.
For you yourself first ordained him as my slayer, and thus the greatest infamy remains—that he was struck down by a demon and has died.
Arise, O Goddess; assume here a wondrous form! Either destroy me or these two as you wish, O playful child;
otherwise, awaken Hari, for he will surely slay these two—this entire undertaking was indeed meant to be accomplished by you. (47)
Sūta said:
Thus praised then by Brahmā,
the goddess Tāmasī emerged from the body of Hari and stood at his side.
Having abandoned all her limbs, that Yoganidrā then emerged for the destruction of those two [the gods] of Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable splendor.
When Janārdana was born with his body quivering, [she appeared].
Then Dhātṛ, seeing Hari, attained the highest joy.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Awakening of Viṣṇu," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The sages said:
"O highly fortunate one, there is a great and most wonderful doubt regarding this narrative."
And it has been definitively established by the wise at all times through the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas. || 1 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—these three gods are eternal;
O high-minded one, there is nothing superior to them in this cosmic egg.
Brahmā indeed creates the worlds, Viṣṇu protects the entire universe, and Rudra withdraws it at the time of dissolution; these three are the cause here.
There is one single form consisting of three gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— who,
joined with the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas, act as the agents of creation.
Among them, Hari is the most excellent, the Mādhava, the Supreme Person.
The primordial god, the lord of the world, is capable in all undertakings.
Is there anyone capable of honoring Viṣṇu, who possesses incomparable splendor?
How has that Lord been made to sleep, rendered helpless by his own yogic power (yogamāyā)?
Where has his consciousness gone, and from where does his movement come while he is still alive?
O illustrious one, this is a great doubt; tell me as it truly is.
What was that power previously described, by which the Lord Viṣṇu was conquered?
From where was she born, how is she capable, and what is her power? Tell me, O observer of noble vows.
But he who is the Lord of all, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world,
the Supreme Self, supreme bliss, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
who is the maker of all, the sustainer of all, the creator, stainless, omnipresent, and pure— || 9 ||
How could he, who is beyond the highest, be led by sleep and rendered dependent on another? || 10 ||
O scorcher of foes, this doubt that has arisen in us is indeed a matter of great wonder;
O Sūta, disciple of Vyāsa, O high-minded one, sever it with the sword of knowledge.
Sūta said:
Who in the three worlds, including the mobile and immobile beings, can pierce this doubt? Even the eternal sons of Brahmā, the sages, are surely bewildered by it.
"Nārada and Kapila are the best of sages regarding this question; O highly fortunate ones, what can I say concerning this difficult investigation? (13)
Among the gods, Viṣṇu is declared to be all-pervading and the protector of all, from whom this entire universe, including the moving and the unmoving, has arisen as the Virāṭ. (14)
In the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 8. 38.
Having bowed down to the supreme deity Nārāyaṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Vāsudeva, and Janārdana, they all worshipped him together.
Likewise, some [saw] Mahādeva Śaṅkara, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, three eyes, five faces, the trident in his hand, and the bull as his banner. || 16 ||
Likewise, in all the Vedas, the one named Tryambaka is praised—
the one with matted hair, the five-faced, who bears half of Gaurī’s body as his own.
The god who delights in dwelling on Kailāsa, who is endowed with all powers,
who is accompanied by hosts of spirits, and who is the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Likewise, O highly fortunate ones, those who know the Vedas praise the Sun with various hymns and eulogies every day at dawn, at dusk, and at midday. (19)
Just as in all the Vedas the worship of the Sun is supreme,
so too is the name of that Great Soul renowned as the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Agni is praised everywhere in the Vedas by those most learned in the Vedas.
Indra, the lord of the three worlds, and likewise Varuṇa as another. ||21||
Just as the Gaṅgā flows through many currents, even so Viṣṇu is proclaimed among all the gods by the great seers. 22.
For only three means of valid cognition have been taught by the truly wise:
perception, inference, and verbal testimony as the third. (23)
"Others, however, say there are exactly four [means of valid cognition], while still others, those of great intelligence, say there are five, including presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). (24)
The wise ones who know the ancient lore declare that this supreme Brahman is difficult to comprehend through these means of knowledge. In this matter,
one should employ both reasoning and scriptural tradition with the intellect.
And having investigated again and again with reasoning that is definitive in nature. ||26||
For those possessed of intelligence who always follow the path of the virtuous, the nature of consciousness is directly perceived through both reasoning and constant illustration. (27)
Even the learned speak thus, as it is celebrated in the Purāṇas:
"The power of creation resides in Druhiṇa (Brahmā), and the power of preservation in Hari (Viṣṇu). (28)
O Hara, the power of withdrawal resides in you; the power of illumination resides in the Sun;
and the power of supporting the earth resides in Śeṣa as well as in the Tortoise.
She is that primordial power who has evolved and is established in everything;
she is like the power of combustion in fire and the impelling nature in the wind.
Even Śiva becomes a corpse when he is devoid of Kuṇḍalinī.
"However, anyone who is devoid of power is considered incapable by the wise.
Thus it is everywhere among all beings, both stationary and moving—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—within this cosmic egg, O one of great asceticism. (31-32)
But that which is devoid of power would be contemptible, even if it were a mere entity among the moving and the unmoving;
for one who is powerless is incapable of conquering enemies, as well as of walking or eating. (33)
Thus, that all-pervading power is discerned as Brahman;
it should always be properly meditated upon through various means and thoroughly investigated by the wise. 34.
In Viṣṇu there is the sāttvika power; though devoid of it, he performs no action. In Druhiṇa (Brahmā) there is the rājasa power; indeed, devoid of it, he would not be a creator.
And in Śiva there is the *tāmasī* power; by that he is the agent of dissolution.
Thus everything should be inferred by the mind, having reflected upon it again and again. (36)
Śakti creates the universe; she indeed protects it in its entirety;
by her will, she destroys this world of the moving and the unmoving. (37)
Neither Viṣṇu, nor Hara, nor Śakra, nor Brahmā, nor Pāvaka,
nor Sūrya, nor Varuṇa is capable in any way whatsoever to accomplish their respective tasks.
For those gods perform their respective duties when joined with that [power];
she alone is perceived directly in the effects of those causes. (39)
She is declared by the wise to be twofold: with attributes (saguṇā) and without attributes (nirguṇā).
She who possesses attributes is to be served by those possessed of passion; she who is without attributes, however, by those free from passion.
She is the untroubled mistress of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
when worshipped according to the prescribed rites, she grants all desired objects. 41.
Foolish people, always shrouded by illusion, do not know her;
yet some men, even though they know, delude others as well.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 9:
"The learned, for the sake of their own bellies, indeed [propagate] various heretical doctrines."
Driven by the Kali age, those of dull intellect set them in motion. || 43 ||
O highly fortunate one, in this Kali age, various types of practices have arisen; in other ages, there were never any such dharmas that were outside the Veda.
This Viṣṇu performs fierce penance for many years;
Brahmā, Hara, and the three gods meditate upon some indeterminate, eternal Reality. 45.
Always desiring their respective desires, those three— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— indeed perpetually perform various sacrifices.
They indeed constantly meditate with their minds upon Śakti, the supreme goddess known as Brahman and identical with the Supreme Self, regarding her as eternal and everlasting. 47.
Therefore, power should always be cultivated by the wise who have reached firm resolve;
O best of sages, the definitive conclusion of all the scriptures must be understood. 48.
This was heard by me from Kṛṣṇa; he learned it from Nārada;
and he [Nārada] learned it from his father, who in turn received it from Brahmā through the words of Viṣṇu.
The wise, having reached a firm resolve, should not listen to nor consider the words of others; rather, the learned should always cultivate their own power alone. 50.
Even the exertion of one who is powerless should be observed directly;
therefore, indeed, it is power alone that must be recognized in all beings. (51)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Sūta said:
When sleep had departed from the body of that Teacher of the World—from his eyes, mouth, nose, arms, heart, and chest—[the following occurred].
Having emerged, that supreme power of darkness stood in the sky;
O Lord of the World, he arose again and again, yawning.
Then he beheld Prajāpati standing there, terrified with fear;
and the one of great splendor spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Lotus-born Lord, why have you come here, abandoning your ascetic penance?
Why are you so distressed by anxiety, with your mind overwhelmed by fear?"
Brahmā said:
"O Lord, the two Daityas Madhu and Kaiṭabha, born from the wax of your ears, have approached me with terrible forms and great strength, intent on killing me. (5)
"O Lord of the World, I have come to your presence out of fear of those two;
O Vāsudeva, protect me today, for I am terrified and deprived of my senses. (6)
Viṣṇu said:
"Stay today, for you have become fearless; indeed, I shall slay those two.
Having reached the end of their life-span, they have come before me to do battle. (7)
Sūta said: While the Lord of the Gods was speaking thus, those two exceedingly powerful Dānavas,
both arrogant with pride, searched about and arrived at that place.
Remaining there in the water without support, free from all distress, those two,
intoxicated with pride, spoke to Brahmā in the presence of the seven sages.
"What is the point of his having arrived here after fleeing?
Fight! We shall both kill him right before his very eyes. (10)
"Later we shall slay him while he is standing upon the coils of the serpent;
you, however, engage in battle today, or say, 'I am your slave.'"
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the first book, chapter nine. Sūta said:
Having heard those words, Viṣṇu Janārdana said to them both: "O foremost of Dānavas, engage in battle with me as you desire."
"I shall indeed take away the pride of you two who are intoxicated;
come, O illustrious and mighty ones, if you have faith. (13)
Sūta said: Having heard those words, both of them, their eyes agitated with anger, became intent on battle while remaining supportless and stationed within the water.
Madhu, enraged, set out quickly to engage in combat with Hari there, while Kaiṭabha remained standing as he was.
A hand-to-hand struggle took place between the two of them, like that of two intoxicated wrestlers;
when Madhu grew weary, Kaiṭabha then engaged in combat.
Furthermore, Madhu and Kaiṭabha fought again and again with their arms in hand-to-hand combat against the powerful Viṣṇu, both of them blinded by passion.
At that time, Brahmā, who was the spectator, and the Goddess, who had gone into the atmosphere, did not feel exhaustion;
however, Viṣṇu fell into a state of weariness.
When five thousand years had passed while they were fighting,
Hari reflected that the cause there was the death of those two.
"Indeed, I have fought for five thousand years;
the two terrible Dānavas were not weary, yet I am exhausted—this is truly wonderful! (20)
"Where has my strength and heroism gone, and why are these two free from disease?
What is the cause here? One must reflect upon this by means of the mind. (21)
Seeing Hari thus absorbed in anxious thought, both of them,
intoxicated with pride and possessing voices as deep as thunderclouds, spoke.
O Viṣṇu, if you do not have the strength, or if you are weary from battle, speak;
I am indeed your servant, having placed my joined palms upon my head.
If not, then engage in battle today, O high-minded one, for you are capable;
having slain you, we shall slay even the four-faced Puruṣa.
Sūta said:
Having heard their speech in that great ocean, the high-minded Viṣṇu spoke these gentle words, preceded by conciliation.
Hari said:
"Heroes do not strike one who is exhausted, terrified, deprived of weapons, fallen, or a child; this is the eternal dharma. (26)
For five thousand years, I have indeed waged war here;
I am alone, while you two brothers are both powerful and equal to me.
"You both have rested repeatedly in the midst of the fray;
having thus rested, I shall fight—of this there is no doubt.
For you two remain here for now, powerful and intoxicated with pride."
Having rested, I shall engage in battle according to the path of righteousness.
Sūta said:
Having heard his words, those two best of Dānavas,
having made their resolve for battle, stood there at a distance, full of confidence.
Seeing them from a great distance, the four-armed Vāsudeva reflected in his mind upon the cause of their death.
Knowledge arose from their meditation; since both had received boons from the Goddess, they did not wither even though they died according to their desire. Thus, these two did not decay.
"I have fought in vain; this exertion of mine has gone to waste.
Having reached such a firm conclusion, how can I continue to fight? (33)
And if the battle is not fought in that manner, how will these two—the givers of misery, always arrogant due to the boons granted to them—avoid destruction? (94)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Book, Chapter 9: A boon was granted by the Blessed Goddess, and that [boon] was indeed difficult to accomplish.
Even if one is suffering, one certainly does not desire death at will. || 35 ||
"Even one seized by disease or even one who is wretched does not wish to die;
how then will these two, intoxicated with pride, desire to die? (36)
Indeed, today I take refuge in that Vidyā, the Power who grants all desires;
for without her, who is perfectly propitious, desires are not accomplished.
While reflecting thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu beheld Śivā, who was established in the sky, the enchanting Yoganidrā.
With palms joined in reverence, that knower of yoga, whose self is immeasurable,
praised the Goddess of the World there, the bestower of boons, for the sake of the destruction of those two.

Viṣṇu said: "Obeisance, O Goddess Mahāmāyā, you who cause the creation and dissolution [of the world], who are without beginning or end, O Caṇḍī, O Śivā, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation! (40)
I do not know your form, whether it possesses attributes or is devoid of them; O Goddess, how could I know your deeds, which are beyond all numbering? (41)
Today I have experienced your exceedingly difficult-to-perform power, whereby I, though absorbed in sleep, have become unconscious. (42)
Although I was awakened again and again by Brahmā with great effort, I did not wake up at all, for my six senses had been completely contracted. (43)
O Mother, through your power I have attained freedom from disease;
released by you, I am awakened, and I have fought many battles. (44)
"I am weary, yet those two are not weary; you have granted them boons.
A Dānava, arrogant with pride, has come here to slay Brahmā. (45)
O giver of honor, when I was challenged at will by them to a duel,
I fought a most terrible battle with those two in the great ocean.
Your death was a boon granted to me; therefore, it is known as a great marvel. Having understood this, I have today come to you for refuge—you who bestow refuge. (47)
"O Mother, grant me your assistance; I am exhausted by the work of war.
Those two, arrogant due to the boon granted by you, are causing distress to the gods. (48)
"The two wicked ones are intent on killing me; what shall I do, and where shall I go?"—having been addressed thus, the Goddess then spoke with a smile. (49)
To Vāsudeva, the eternal Lord of the World, who was bowing down [to him], he said:
"O God of gods, O Hari, O Viṣṇu, engage in battle yourself once again! (50)
"Having deceived these two, they must be slain while they are utterly deluded;
I shall surely bewilder them with my Dānavī glance, which is so crooked. (51)

"Go quickly, O Nārāyaṇa, [and slay] those two who are deluded by my māyā. Having heard her words, which were imbued with the essence of affection, Viṣṇu reached the field of battle and stood there upon the great ocean.
Then those two heroes of great strength arrived, desiring battle.
Seeing Viṣṇu standing there, the two became filled with joy:
"Stay! Stay, O great-bodied one! Engage in battle, O four-armed one! (54)
Having realized today that victory and defeat are surely dependent on destiny,
the strong man attains victory through destiny, and even the weak man conquers through destiny.
A high-souled person should by no means give way to joy or sorrow;
for in the past, many Daityas were indeed conquered by the enemy of the Dānavas.
"And now, fighting alongside these two, he has been defeated.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, those two mighty-armed ones stood ready for battle.
Seeing this, Viṣṇu, whose deeds are marvelous, quickly struck them with his fist;
those two, intoxicated by their great strength, also struck Hari with their fists.
Thus a most terrible battle broke out between them;
then Nārāyaṇa beheld those two of great prowess engaged in combat.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 9.
Sūta said:
Hari cast a piteous glance directly at the Goddess;
seeing Viṣṇu in such a state, filled with the essence of compassion, [she spoke]. (60)
Then that demoness, whose eyes were exceedingly copper-red as she gazed at them,
struck them with her side-long glances as if with another set of the arrows of Kama.
Beholding the face of the Goddess, which was accompanied by gentle smiles and filled with expressions of love, those two wicked ones became utterly infatuated.
Thinking it to be a marvel, and tormented by the arrows of desire,
they remained there gazing at that goddess of radiant luster.
Hari also perceived what the Goddess intended to do there;
having recognized that they were both deluded, the Blessed One, the supreme knower of all duties, [acted].
Smiling, he spoke to them gently in a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"O heroes, choose whatever boon is desired by you both."
"Highly pleased, I shall indeed grant you both a battle;
for many Dānavas have been seen by me in combat in the past. (66)
No one like you two has ever been seen or even heard of;
therefore, I am truly pleased with your matchless strength and prowess.
"O you two of great strength, I shall grant you whatever desire you wish for like brothers.
Hearing those words of Viṣṇu, the two, filled with pride and afflicted by love, [acted].
Sūta said:
Beholding Mahāmāyā, who brings joy to the world,
the two lotus-eyed ones spoke to Viṣṇu, who was overcome by desire.
"O Hari, by this [act], what hope do you two have? What do you wish to give here?
O Lord of Gods, grant us that which is incomparable; we are the givers, not the supplicants. (70)
O Hṛṣīkeśa, ask for the boon desired by your heart;
we are satisfied with your battle and with you, O Vāsudeva, who are truly wonderful.
Having heard those words of theirs, Janārdana replied: "May both of you be pleased with me today; both of them are to be slain by me."
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, the two Dānavas were greatly astonished;
thinking that they had been deceived, they stood there filled with grief.
Having reflected upon this with their minds, those two daughters of Danu spoke to Viṣṇu,
seeing that everything was composed of water and devoid of earth or dry land.
O Hare, O Janārdana, this boon which was granted by you previously—O Lord of Gods, you are true to your word; grant that desired boon. (75)
"O Madhusūdana, slay us in this vast, waterless region;
we two are to be killed by you, O Mādhava—be true to your word. (76)
Remembering that, Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari, smiling, then said to them both:
"O illustrious ones, today I shall slay you on a vast, waterless plain."
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods, having made his thighs exceedingly broad,
displayed them there upon the water, even though they were devoid of water.
"There is no woman more generous than I who would release water upon her head here;
today I shall indeed become one whose word is true for both of you. (79)
Having heard those truthful words and having reflected upon them with their minds,
the two of them increased their bodies to a thousand yojanas.
The Blessed One then doubled their hips, leaving them astonished as they placed their heads upon those most wonderful hips.
Then, when the wheel had been severed by the powerful Viṣṇu,
their two heads were violently dragged over the hips.
Then the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, were born with their life-force departed;
at that time, the entire ocean was indeed pervaded by the fat of those two.
From that,
the name "Medinī" arose for the Earth on all sides throughout the first book of the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, chapter 10.
"For that reason, O lords of sages, clay is not to be eaten.
Thus I have told you everything with certainty, as I was asked;
the Great Knowledge, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), should always be served by the wise.
The Supreme Śakti is to be propitiated by all gods and demons alike;
there is nothing higher or more exalted than her in the three worlds. (86)
Truth, truth, and again truth is the definitive conclusion regarding the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras:
the Supreme Shakti is to be worshipped, whether she be devoid of attributes (nirguṇā) or possessed of attributes (saguṇā). ||87||
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 9 ||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
The sages said:
O Sūta, previously you spoke that which was declared by Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor.
Having composed the entire auspicious Purāṇa, he taught it to Śuka.
But how was Śuka produced by Vyāsa after he had performed penance?
Tell me all of this in detail, exactly as you heard it from Kṛṣṇa.
Sūta said:
I shall narrate the birth of Śuka from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī.
Born from me, Śuka was a sage who was visibly the foremost among yogis.
On the most delightful peak of Mount Meru, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
performed extremely severe penance, having resolved to obtain a son.
Desiring a son, that treasury of asceticism meditated upon the supreme Mahāmāyā while reciting the one-syllable mantra of speech, which he had heard from Nārada. ||5||
"May this son of mine be equal in prowess to Agni, the Earth, Vāyu, and the intermediate space," he thought.
Abstaining from food, that lord remained standing for a hundred years,
propitiating Mahādeva as well as Sadāśiva.
Having reflected again and again that power is worshipful everywhere, one who is powerless is censured in the world, while the powerful is fully honored. (8)
On that mountain peak, wonderful with its groves of vaikarṇikāra trees,
all the deities and sages preeminent in austerity sport.
Where the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and likewise the two Aśvins reside, as well as the sages and others who are the most eminent knowers of Brahman—
there, upon the peak of the Golden Mountain, resounded with the music of songs.
The righteous Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, performed austerities.
Then, by his splendor, the entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, was pervaded;
the matted locks of the wise son of Parāśara became the color of fire.
Then, perceiving his splendor, the Lord of Śacī became afraid;
seeing Turāsāh thus terrified by fear and overcome with exhaustion.
The Blessed Lord Rudra spoke thus to Maghavan as he stood there:
"O Indra, why are you afraid today? What is your sorrow, O Lord of the Gods?
Śaṅkara said:
One should never harbor resentment toward ascetics;
for the sages practice penance knowing me to be endowed with power. 15.
"But these ascetics do not wish him any harm at all.
Having spoken these words, Śakra said to that bull-bannered god: || 16 ||
"Why does Vyāsa perform penance? What is the purpose in his mind?
Śiva said:
"The son of Parāśara performs this difficult penance because he desires a son."
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Chapter 11, Part 44.
"O Vāsava, having spoken thus regarding death, the compassionate Rudra said, 'I give you today this auspicious son who has been born after a full hundred years.'"
Sūta said:
Having approached the presence of the sage, the Teacher of the World spoke to him:
"Arise, O son of Vāsavi! An auspicious son shall be born to you."
O sinless one, this son of yours shall always be composed of all splendor, wise, a maker of fame, and beloved by all people here. (20)
"His qualities will be complete, and his valor will be rooted in truth. Having heard those gentle words, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana then [spoke].
Sūta said:
Having paid homage to the trident-bearer, he went to his own hermitage;
having reached that very hermitage, he was quickly overcome by the exhaustion of many years of ascetic toil.
Desiring to produce fire by friction, he took the secret fire-drills together with the lower wood;
as he was performing the churning, a heavy burden of anxiety then arose in his mind.
He appeared suddenly at the birth of the high-souled one,
arising from the churning and the conjunction of the churning-stick and the fire-drill.
Just as it is with fire, how could there be the arising of happiness for me?
The "fire-sticks" (araṇi) for a son have been explained, yet they do not exist for me today. (25)
How can I make my beloved—who is young, endowed with beauty, born of a noble family, and devoted to her husband—equal to one bound by chains at the feet? (26)
She was skilled in procreating sons and always established in devotion to her husband;
though she was a devoted wife, capable, and beautiful, she was nonetheless full of desire. (27)
She is eternally of the nature of bondage, yet she provides the pleasure of her own will;
even Śiva, on the mountain, is constantly bound by the noose of his beloved.
"How shall I manage this household life here, which is so difficult to maintain?"—
while he was reflecting thus, the celestial nymph Ghṛtācī appeared in her divine form.
Having come within the range of his vision, she stood nearby in the sky;
and he beheld that excellent Apsaras standing close by, with her tremulous side-glances. (30)
His body completely overwhelmed by the five arrows, he quickly became firm in his vow;
and then he reflected: "What shall I do now in this crisis? (31)
If, when the irresistible power of Dharma has arrived before me, I were to accept her who has come here for the sake of deception, [it would be a transgression]. (32)
"Having performed most terrible austerities here for a full hundred years, the great-souled ascetics will laugh at me as I am distraught. (33)
Having seen the apsaras, how did that great ascetic become helpless?
Let there be even censure for desire, provided it results in incomparable happiness. (34)
It is declared by the wise to be the source of happiness for those born into the householder stage of life, bestowing sons and desires, granting heaven, and likewise bestowing liberation. ||35||
Surely that will not happen through this celestial maiden;
for I have previously heard this story from Nārada.
Just as King Purūravas was defeated by the power of Urvaśī. || 36 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The sages said:
Who was this King Purūravas, and who was Urvaśī, the daughter of the gods?
How did that high-souled king come to encounter such hardship?
"O Lomaharṣaṇaja, tell us now the entire narrative;
we are all desirous of hearing the nectar falling from the lotus of your mouth. (2)
O Sūta, your speech, which is full of aesthetic flavor, is sweeter even than nectar;
we are all not satiated by it, just as the immortals are never satiated by the ambrosia.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the first book, chapter 11. Sūta said:
O sages, I shall relate this divine and enchanting story exactly as it was heard by my intellect from the most excellent Vyāsa.
The beloved wife of the Guru was renowned by the name Tārā;
she was endowed with beauty and youth, possessed of lovely limbs, and intoxicated with passion.
Once, that beautiful wife of the sacrificer was seen by the Moon in the abode of Garta, she who was exceedingly endowed with beauty and youth.
Then the moon became afflicted by desire for her who has a moon-like face;
she too, beholding the moon, became tormented by passion.
They both became filled with love and afflicted by the pangs of passion;
like the moon and the stars, they were intoxicated with desire and tormented by the arrows of Kāma.
Thus, impelled by mutual longing,
several days passed for the two as they took their delight there.
Afflicted by grief, Bṛhaspati sent a disciple to his home to bring Tārā back, but she did not return, having been captivated [by another]. 10.
When the moon turned back toward his pupil, Bṛhaspati then became enraged and went there in person. 11.
Having gone to the house of Soma there, the noble-minded Vācaspati,
filled with wrath yet smiling, spoke to the Moon who was intoxicated with pride:
"O Dilipa, what further deed, censurable by dharma, have you committed?"
"For what reason has this beautiful woman, my wife, been protected?"
"O Lord, I am your preceptor; you are my sacrificer in every respect. O fool, how could you have enjoyed the wife of your preceptor? Or was she protected? (14)

The killer of a Brahmin, the stealer of gold, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are indeed the perpetrators of the great sins (mahāpātakin), and the fifth is he who associates with them. || 15 ||
"You are burdened with great sins, of evil conduct, and utterly contemptible;
you are not worthy of the abode of the gods if this woman has been enjoyed by you. (16)
Release this woman with dark-cornered eyes; I shall lead her to my own home.
Otherwise, I shall denounce you, O evil-souled one, as a thief who has abducted the wife of his preceptor.
To him who was speaking thus— the preceptor filled with anger and distressed by the sorrow of separation from his beloved— the Lord of Rohiṇī replied.
Indu said:
"Brahmins who are free from anger are difficult to propitiate when they are full of wrath;
those who know the treatises on Dharma are worthy of worship, but others should be avoided. (19)
That woman of excellent complexion will surely come to your house;
while the young girl remains right here, what loss do you suffer in this matter, O sinless one? (20)
For she has remained here by her own will, desiring happiness;
after staying for a few days, she will depart according to her own desire.
Furthermore, you yourself previously cited the opinion of the Dharmaśāstra:
"A woman is not defiled by her conduct, nor is a Brahmin by his Vedic ritual acts. (22)
Thus addressed by Śaśin, the Guru there became exceedingly distressed;
overcome with anxiety and afflicted by love, he went quickly to his own home. (23)
Having stayed there for a few days, the Guru, distressed with anxiety,
quickly returned home as before to that lord of medicinal herbs.
Held back by the gatekeeper at the entrance, the Moon did not enter, filled with wrath; Bṛhaspati became exceedingly angry.
"This unrighteous man, having entered into discipleship with me, has forcibly seized my preceptor's wife as if she were his mother; he must now be disciplined by me. (26)
Standing outside at the gateway, he spoke these words in anger:
"O dull-witted one, O evil-doer, O lowest of gods, why do you lie there in the palace?"
"Give me my beloved quickly; otherwise, I shall cast a curse upon you.
If you do not give me my dear one, I will surely reduce you to ashes. (28)
In the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 11.
Sūta said:
Having heard such cruel words as these from Bṛhaspati, the lord of the twice-born quickly went out from his residence. 29.
Smiling, Soma said to him: "Why do you speak so much?
This dark-eyed woman, endowed with all auspicious marks, is not worthy of you."
"O twice-born one, take another woman who is of similar appearance but of ugly form;
such a woman of excellent complexion is not suitable for the house of a mendicant. (31)
It is said that a woman’s passion is for a lover who resembles her;
you, O dull-witted one, do not understand the definitive conclusions of the science of love (kāmaśāstra).
"Go as you please, O evil-minded one; I will not give away this woman of desire.
Do whatever you can, but this woman of excellent complexion must not be given."
"O Preceptor, since you are afflicted by passion, your curse cannot afflict me; I will not give up my beloved wife—do as you wish. (34)
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by Śaśin, the worshipful one, filled with rage, ascended the funeral pyre;
then, possessed by anger, he went swiftly to the abode of the Lord of Śacī.
Seeing his preceptor standing there afflicted by grief, Śatakratu honored him with water for the feet, the guest-offering, and water for sipping, and then sat down respectfully.
The most noble one questioned the Guru, who remained in that state:
"O illustrious one, what is your concern? O great sage, you are afflicted by grief."
"By whom have you been insulted—you who are my preceptor and in my kingdom?
This entire army, along with the lords of the worlds, is under your command. (38)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Śambhu and whatever other supreme gods there may be, will provide assistance; what cause for concern is there? Tell me now.
The Guru said:
"My beautiful-eyed wife Tārā has been carried off by the Moon;
that evil-minded one does not give her back, even though he has been entreated again and again. (40)
"What shall I do, O Lord of the Suras? You alone are my refuge.
Grant me your assistance, O Lord of Devas; I am suffering, O Śatakratu. (41)
Indra said:
"Do not grieve, O knower of dharma; I am your servant, O observer of noble vows.
I shall surely bring back your wife, O high-minded one."
"If, after I have dispatched a messenger, he does not give [it] up due to his arrogance,
then I shall wage war, surrounded by the armies of the gods.
Having thus consoled his preceptor, Śakra [sent] a messenger who was skilled in speech.
He dispatched the wonderful Vātaśiṃsin to Soma. ||44||
Having gone swiftly to the world of the Moon, that highly discerning one spoke these words with his voice to the Lord of Rohiṇī.
"O illustrious one, I have been sent by Śakra with the desire to speak to you.
O high-minded one, I shall tell you that which was spoken by my lord. (46)
O highly fortunate one, you are a knower of dharma and you understand policy, O observer of noble vows;
since Atri is your father, O righteous-souled one, you ought not to do what is blameworthy.
A wife must indeed be protected by all beings according to their ability and with vigilance;
for her sake, quarrels will certainly arise—of this there is no doubt. (48)
Just as you would for yourself, so should he exert effort in protecting his wife;
O treasure-house of nectar, regard all beings as your own self. (49)
There are twenty-eight auspicious women, daughters of Dakṣa, who desire you;
O treasury of nectar, how can you wish to enjoy the wife of your guru?
"These beautiful women, Menakā and the others, dwell forever in heaven;
eat them at your pleasure according to your desire, and abandon even the wife of your preceptor."
If the lords act with contemptuous egoism,
and the ignorant follow them, then there will be a destruction of dharma.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, release the beautiful wife of your preceptor. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam*, Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 11.
"May there not arise today a quarrel among the gods caused by you. (53)
Sūta said: Having heard the words of Śakra, the Moon (Soma), somewhat agitated by anger,
then spoke this reply with sarcasm to the messenger of Śakra.
Indu said:
"O mighty-armed one, you are a knower of dharma; you are yourself the sovereign of the gods, and your priest is likewise such a person; thus, the intellect of both of you is equal. (55)
Many people are skilled in giving instruction to others, but one who performs the action himself when the time for action has arrived is difficult to find in every respect. (56)
And men accept the treatise composed by Bṛhaspati;
O Lord of Gods, what contradiction is there here for those who desire to enjoy a woman?
Everything belongs to the strong; to the weak, nothing belongs at all.
The notions of "one's own" and "another's" are merely the delusion of those with dull minds. 58.
Tārā is devoted to me, yet not as she is devoted to her guru;
how can she, being thus devoted, be abandoned according to dharma and justice? (59)
But how could the commencement of building the house take place while she was still impassioned?
Since she has now become dispassionate, she desired the wife of her younger brother. (60)
"I will not give up the beautiful woman; go, O messenger, and speak for yourself.
Even though you are the Lord, O thousand-eyed one, do whatever you wish."
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus by the Moon, the messenger went into the presence of Śakra and reported everything that had been said by the cool-rayed one to Indra.
Having heard that, Turāṣāṭ also became filled with anger;
the powerful lord then made preparations for his army in order to assist his preceptor.
But Śukra, having heard of the conflict, departed from there out of hatred for Bṛhaspati.
"Do not give it," he said these words to Śaśin.
"O high-minded one, O worthy sir, if a battle should take place between you and Indra, I shall provide you assistance through the power of mantras. (65)
But Śaṅkara, having heard of that violation of the preceptor’s wife and considering Bhṛgu to be the enemy of his teacher, then rendered him assistance.
Then a battle between the gods and the Dānavas quickly took place;
indeed, it lasted for many years, like that of the Asura Tāraka.
Having witnessed the battle fought between the gods and the asuras, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) mounted his swan and went swiftly to that place; the Grandfather,
mounted upon his swan, went quickly to that region for the sake of pacifying the distress.
Then Rākāpati said, "Bring your wife to the preceptor;
otherwise, having summoned Viṣṇu, I shall bring about his destruction. (69)
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, restrained Bhṛgu:
"O high-minded one, has an unrighteous intent arisen in you due to the fault of association? (70)
Then Bhṛgu forbade that lord of medicinal herbs:
"Leave your wife today; I have been sent to you by your father, my guru. (71)
Sūta said:
Having heard those wonderful words of Bhṛgu,
the Moon (the king of the twice-born) gave back his beloved and auspicious wife, who was pregnant with the preceptor’s child.
Having obtained his beloved, the preceptor went to his own home joyful and delighted;
thereafter, the gods and the demons likewise departed for their respective abodes. 73.
Brahmā reached his own abode, and Śaṅkara likewise reached Kailāsa;
and Bṛhaspati, having obtained his charming wife, was thoroughly satisfied.
Then, after some time, Tārā gave birth to an auspicious son on a favorable day and under an auspicious constellation; he was equal to the Lord of the Stars (the Moon) in his virtues.
Seeing that his son was born, the preceptor,
with a joyful inner soul, performed all the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman) according to the prescribed rules.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 12.
O best of sages, having heard of the birth of his son,
the high-minded Candra dispatched a messenger to his preceptor.
And this son of yours was not born from the power of your mind;
how then did you perform the rites such as the birth-ceremony and others? (78)
Having heard those words of the messenger, Bṛhaspati said:
"My son is my equal; there is no doubt in this matter. (79)
Once again, a dispute arose; the gods and demons assembled, and having come for the sake of battle, their gathering took place. (80)
Then Brahmā himself, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) desiring peace, arrived there and restrained those who were stationed at the entrance and intoxicated by the madness of war.
The righteous-souled one asked Tārā, "O auspicious one, whose son is this?
O lady of excellent hips, tell the truth so that my distress may be pacified. (82)
Though bashful and with her face cast down, that woman of excellent complexion, her outer corners of the eyes dark, spoke to him; yet, saying "Of the moon," she slowly departed within.
Soma took that son with a joyful inner soul;
he gave him the name Budha and returned once more to his own home.
Brahmā went to his own abode, as did all the gods along with Indra;
everyone, including all the people who had been spectators, departed in every direction just as they had come.
This arising of the Buddha has been told as it was heard by me previously from Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, in the field of the Guru, like [the account] of Soma. 86.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Birth of Budha," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Purāṇa. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Sūta said:
Thereafter Purūravas was born of Ilā; this I shall relate to you.
The son of Budha was exceedingly righteous in soul, a performer of sacrifices, and devoted to the giving of gifts.
A king named Sudyumna, truthful in speech and having conquered his senses,
mounted a horse from the Sindhu region and went hunting in the forest.
Chārūkuṇḍala was presented by several ministers,
who had fastened the Ājagava bow and a wondrous collection of arrows.
Wandering through that forest region accompanied by his troops, he slaughtered ruru deer,
hares, boars, rhinoceroses, and likewise gavayas.
Slaying wild buffaloes, Sāmbhara deer, and forest fowl— pure animals fit for sacrifice— the king entered Kumāravana.
At the base of Meru, there was a divine place adorned with rows of Mandāra trees,
strewn with Aśoka creepers,
and perfumed by Bakula flowers.
It was covered with sārastālas, tamālas, campakas, and likewise panasa trees,
as well as āmra, nāpa, and madhūka trees, and was surrounded by pavilions of mādhavī creepers.
It was adorned with pomegranates and coconuts, beautified by groves of plantains,
and surrounded by creepers bearing flowers of jasmine, mālatī, and kunda.
Crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, resounding with the humming of *kīcaka* bamboos, and made delightful by the songs of bees— the entire forest brought every happiness.
Seeing this, King Sudyumna, surrounded by his attendants, was filled with joy upon beholding the trees in full bloom, adorned with the warbling of cuckoos. 10.
Having entered there, the royal sage attained womanhood in an instant;
the horse also became a mare, and that king was overcome with grief.
Thinking "What is this? and being tormented by anxiety as he reflected again and again, Sudyumna, filled with shame, experienced even greater suffering.
"What shall I do? How can I go home while endowed with this female form?
How shall I rule the kingdom? By whom indeed have I been deceived? (13)
The sages said:
"O Sūta, O Lomaharṣaṇa, this wonder has been told by you—that King Sudyumna, who was like a god, attained womanhood. (14)
Tell me, what was the cause of that in that enchanting forest? Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 12.49.
O observer of noble vows, tell me in detail what was done by that king.
Sūta said:
Once, the sages headed by Sanaka, illuminating the quarters with light free from darkness, approached in order to see Giriśa.
And at that time, Śaṅkara was there together with his beloved;
the Great Goddess, the passionate Śivā, was naked and intent on play.
Seated on her husband's lap, the beautiful goddess Ambika was sporting with him;
seeing them, she became utterly ashamed, being herself unclothed.
Rising from her husband's lap and taking the garment, she put it on;
overcome with shame, the highly proud woman stood there trembling. (19)
Even the sages, seeing the intimacy of those two as they were sporting together,
turned back and quickly departed for the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Seeing the passionate woman deprived of her husband, the Lord Hara said:
"Why are you overcome with shame? I shall provide you with happiness."
O fair-faced one, from this day forward, whatever man should out of delusion enter this forest, he shall indeed become a woman.
Those people who anywhere know that the forest has been cursed by him thus avoid their desire for this forest, which is full of faults. (23)
But Sudyumna, entering that [forest] out of ignorance along with his ministers, likewise attained womanhood together with them; of this there is no doubt. (24)
Overcome by anxiety, that royal sage did not go into the cave out of shame;
he wandered here and there outside that forest region.
The message was received by that great-souled one regarding his state as a woman;
while wandering there, the youthful Budha, son of Soma, arrived.
Seeing that lovely and enchanting woman surrounded by her female attendants, and endowed with all the arts of coquetry and amorous expression, the venerable Budha desired her.
She too, in private, desired him— Budha, the son of Soma— as her husband.
There, a union was formed between those two through mutual love. ||28||
He begot upon her a son, Purūravas.
The young woman, having given birth to her son and remaining in the forest, was overcome with grief and remembered Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages and the preceptor of her own lineage. (30)
Then, seeing that condition of Sudyumna, he was filled with compassion and propitiated Mahādeva Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
The Blessed One, being pleased with him, granted his desired boon;
Vasiṣṭha then requested manhood for the beloved king.
Śaṅkara, making his own word true, said:
"The king shall indeed be a man for one month, and a woman for one month. (33)
Having thus obtained the boon, the king returned once more to his own home;
that righteous-souled one ruled the kingdom through the grace of Vasiṣṭha as well. (34)
While remaining in the female state he dwelt in palaces, and in the male state he ruled the kingdom;
yet the subjects were distressed by him and did not welcome the lord of the earth.
When his son Purūravas had reached youth at that time,
the king, having bestowed the kingdom and established him in his position, departed for the forest.
Having gone to that delightful forest, which was filled with various kinds of trees,
he received from Nārada the unsurpassed nine-syllable mantra.
With his mind overflowing with love, he chanted the mantra intensely;
then the virtuous goddess Tāriṇī, the auspicious one, became well-pleased. 38.
Mounted upon a lion, she stood before him, possessing a divine and enchanting form;
she was intoxicated by the drinking of wine, her eyes rolling from the effects of intoxication.
Having seen her of divine form, his eyes overflowing with love,
he bowed his head in devotion and praised the Mother of the Universe with joy.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 12,
Ilā said:
O Blessed One, your divine and celebrated true form, which accords with the welfare of all the worlds, has been seen by me.
I bow to your lotus feet, O Mother, which are served by the hosts of gods and which bestow both desires and liberation. (41)
O Mother, who on earth could know your desire for a human body, wherein even all the sages and gods are deluded?
O Goddess, that you display this entire sovereignty as well as compassion toward the wretched—indeed, it is all a source of wonder to me. (42)

Śambhu, Hari, the Lotus-born, Indra, the Sun, Kubera, Agni, Varuṇa, and Vāyu—even the Vasus do not truly know your power; how then could a man, devoid of qualities himself, comprehend your virtues? (43)
O Mother, Viṣṇu of immeasurable luster knows you directly as the Sāttvikī, born from the ocean, the bestower of all goals;
who indeed knows you as the Rājasī, O Hara, or as the Tāmasī Umā? But, O Ambikā, no one truly knows you as the Nirguṇā.
Where am I, of dull intellect, compared to you of incomparable power? Where is this extreme skill of yours and your great favor toward me?
I know that your conduct is endowed with compassion, for you show mercy even to those servants who are devoted to you with sincere intent. (45)
O lotus-born goddess, even though you dwell there, this Hari Madhusūdana does not experience joy;
for it is said that the Primal Being, the Purifier, having placed his feet upon that spot with fire, makes them auspicious with his own hand.
Ah, Hari, the Ancient Person, like a man overcome by passion, joyfully desires the kick of a woman's foot as much as an *aśoka* tree does;
yet you, O angry one, do that very thing when you see your husband—worshipped by all the gods and tormented by love—prostrating at your feet. (47)
O Goddess, you always dwell upon his chest, which is like a couch for your virtuous conduct—vast and exceedingly peaceful;
and since it is beautifully adorned and as dark as a dense mass of lightning, why would even this Lord of the Universe not have you as his vehicle? 48.
O Mother, if you abandon Madhusūdana out of anger, he will surely become powerless even if he is worshipped;
for people abandon a man who is right before their eyes if he is peaceful, devoid of fortune, and utterly lacking in virtues.
The hosts of gods, beginning with Brahmā, are not truly men if they do not take refuge day and night at the lotus-feet of a young woman;
I consider them to have been made so by you alone. How can I describe your power there, O You of infinite valor? (50)

"I am neither neuter nor male"—such is my conceptualization of you, O Goddess; whether you possess attributes or are indeed attribute-less, I bow to you constantly with a devoted heart, for I desire unwavering devotion toward you, my Mother. (51)
Sūta said:
Having praised her thus, the protector of the earth then sought refuge;
thereupon the Goddess, being thoroughly pleased, granted him union with her own self.
Then, by the grace of that Goddess, Sudyumna attained the supreme and eternal state, which is difficult even for sages to obtain. (53)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Praise of Sudyumna," in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Purāṇa.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Book, Chapter 13:
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Sūta said:
When Sudyumna had departed for heaven, Purūravas ruled the kingdom;
he was virtuous, handsome, and devoted to pleasing his subjects. || 1 ||
In the beautiful city of Pratiṣṭhāna, he who knew all dharmas and was devoted to protecting his subjects ruled a kingdom honored by all. ||2||
His mantra was well-guarded, as was his supernatural knowledge; he possessed constant energy-power as well as supreme lordly power. (3)
All means, such as conciliation and bribery, were under the control of that king;
indeed, he ruled his kingdom while establishing the various social orders and stages of life in their respective duties.
That king performed various sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
and then that lord of men gave pure gifts.
Having heard of his physical beauty, noble qualities, magnanimity, virtue, wealth, and prowess,
Urvaśī became subject to his influence and desired that lord of men.
Tormented by the curse of Brahmā, she descended to the world of mortals;
considering that king to be virtuous, the proud lady chose him as her husband.
Having made such an agreement, that excellent woman remained there;
O giver of honor, protect these two princes who are here as guards. (8)
"Ghee is my constant food; I eat nothing else, O King.
And I do not look upon you, O Great King, when you are naked, except during sexual union."
"O King, if this bond of speech should be broken, then I shall depart, leaving you behind; I tell you this as the truth. (10)
And that which was spoken by the passionate woman was accepted by the king;
he remained bound by her speech, desiring to grant both a curse and a favor.
Then that king, infatuated by passion for Urvaśī, abandoned his religious duties and other obligations and sported with her, absorbed in pleasure for many groups of years.
But the lord of the earth, having become single-minded and absorbed in her thought, being utterly deluded and deprived of her, was unable to endure even a moment without her. (13)
Thus, at the end of the years, the Lord of the Gods, Pākaśāsana, residing in heaven,
seeing that Urvaśī had not arrived, spoke to the Gandharvas.
"O Gandharvas, all of you together must indeed bring Urvaśī here at the appointed time, having slain the female donkey from the house of that king. (15)
"My place does not shine without Urvaśī;
by whatever means possible, bring back that beloved woman. (16)
Thus addressed, those Gandharvas, led by Viśvāvasu, then went forth;
and when a great, dense darkness had set in,
the gods, having cast off their concealments, beheld him sporting there.
Then those two, being carried away through the sky, cried out.
Hearing that cry, which was like the wailing of her two sons, Urvaśī became angry and said to the king: "This condition was established by me. (19)
"I have been lost through my lack of faith in you; I was captured by thieves who intended to kill me.
O King, these two are equal to sons to you; why do you remain indifferent toward a woman? (20)
I am ruined by this wretched protector, a eunuch who fancies himself a hero;
today my two rams, who were always dearer to me than life itself, have perished.
Seeing her lamenting thus, the king, utterly bewildered, the lord of the earth, went quickly after her while still naked. ||22||
There, in the king's palace, which was illuminated by lightning,
the king was seen by her as he was naked, while she was desirous of departing.
Having abandoned them at Uraṇa, all the Gandharvas departed on the road, O King;
the monarch, exhausted and naked, took hold of those two and went toward his own home.
Then, seeing that Urvaśī had departed, he lamented, overcome with extreme grief;
and seeing her husband naked, that woman of excellent complexion vanished.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 14:
Wailing, that king himself wandered from place to place.
With his mind fixed on that, he was distraught, grieving, helpless, and deluded by passion.
Wandering indeed over the earth of the virtuous, that best of kings beheld her at Kurukṣetra;
having seen her, with a joyful countenance, he spoke these well-spoken words.
"O cruel wife, stay! Stay! You ought not to abandon me—me, who am devoted to you, your beloved, under your control, and innocent. (28)
"O Goddess, this body of yours, having been carried far away by you, falls here;
O fair-limbed one, since it has been abandoned by you, wolves and crows devour it. (29)
