To the king who was thus lamenting— distressed, miserable, exhausted, afflicted by desire, and utterly helpless— Urvaśī spoke.
Urvaśī said:
"O tiger among kings, you are a fool; where has your wisdom gone?
O monarch, there can never be friendship with women, just as there is none with wolves. (31)
Indeed, kings should place no trust in women or thieves;
go home, enjoy happiness, and do not set your mind on despair.
Thus enlightened, the king did not understand, being utterly deluded;
bound by his attachment to his wanton wife, he fell into supreme misery. (33)
Sūta said:
Thus has the great life-story of Urvaśī been fully related;
it was expanded in the Veda, and has now been told by me in brief.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 13 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having seen her with dark-cornered eyes, Vyāsa became intent upon the funeral pyre.
What shall I do? This celestial maiden, an Apsaras, is not suitable for me. || 1 ||
Seeing Vyāsa thus reflecting, the Apsaras became terrified, thinking, "He might cast a curse upon me. (2)
Then, having assumed the form of a female parrot, she emerged, overwhelmed by fear;
Kṛṣṇa, however, was filled with wonder as he gazed upon that bird.
Upon merely seeing Vyāsa, Kāma became united with his body;
his mind became utterly amazed, and he was filled with wonder throughout all his limbs.
But even though that sage Vyāsa restrained his mind with great fortitude, he was unable to control his mind which had already run away.
Although his mind was repeatedly captivated by Ghṛtācī,
the mind of Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor was not at all disturbed, owing to his spiritual cultivation.
As that sage was performing the churning with the desire to produce fire,
his semen suddenly fell upon the lower fire-drill (araṇi).
Without noticing that fall, he continued to churn the fire-drill itself.
From that, Śuka was born, possessing a form that was captivating to the mind. ||8||
That child born in that forest grew up causing wonder,
shining with splendor like a fire kindled at a sacrifice when fed with oblations.
But Vyāsa, beholding his son, was struck with the utmost wonder;
reflecting, "What is this?", he realized it was indeed due to the granting of a boon by Śiva.
Though born from the interior of the fire-drill (araṇī), Śuka was composed of radiant energy;
blazing exceedingly with his own splendor like a second fire,
Vyāsa then gazed upon his joyful son.
Endowed with divine splendor, he was like another Gārhapatya fire.
Then, having arrived at the edge of the Gaṅgā on that mountain, he bathed [the child];
O ascetic, a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon the infant.
In the glorious Mahāpurāṇa, in the first book, chapter 14: Vyāsa performed the birth rites and other ceremonies for that great-souled one.
The celestial drums resounded and hosts of Apsaras danced.
The lords of the Gandharvas, Viśvāvasu, Nārada, Tumburu, and Śuka, being delighted, sang there at his birth. || 15 ||
All the gods and likewise the Vidyādharas, filled with joy,
offered praise upon seeing the divine son of Vyāsa, who had been born from the womb of the fire-drill (araṇi).
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of Śukra, a staff, a beautiful black antelope skin, and a divine water-pot fell from the atmosphere onto the earth. ||17||
Immediately upon being born, that boy, exceedingly radiant, became conscious;
Vyāsa, who was well-versed in the methods of learning, performed his initiation ceremony.
As soon as he was born, the Vedas, along with their secret portions and their compendiums,
approached that Great-Souled One, just as they had approached his father.
Since the form of Śukī was seen at the time of Ghṛtācī’s birth,
that best of sages gave his son the name Śuka.
Then, having appointed Bṛhaspati as his preceptor, the son of Vyāsa [proceeded].
He performed the vows of celibacy according to the prescribed rules. ||21||
Having studied all the Vedas along with their secret doctrines (Upanishads) and compendiums,
and having mastered all the treatises on Dharma, Śuka remained in the teacher’s household.
Having given the teacher’s fee to his preceptor, the sage, having completed his studies,
then returned to the presence of his father, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
Seeing that Śuka had arrived, Vyāsa rose up with affection and agitation; he embraced him repeatedly and placed his hand upon his head. 25.
Vyāsa inquired after his welfare and remained there, pure in his studies;
having comforted him, he established Śuka in that auspicious hermitage.
Then Vyāsa, desiring to perform the rite of marriage for Śuka,
quickly asked a certain lovely daughter of a sage for his hand.
Vyāsa said to his son Śuka: "The Veda has been studied by you in its entirety;
likewise all the Dharmaśāstras. O high-minded one, now take a wife. (27)
Having entered the householder’s state and obtained beautiful wives, O son, worship the gods and the ancestors, and release me from my debts.
"There is no destination for one without a son, neither in heaven nor anywhere else.
Therefore, O illustrious son, enter the householder's stage of life this very day."
"O son Śuka, having established me in the householder's life, make me happy;
O high-minded son, fulfill my great hope."
"O highly wise Śuka, having performed most formidable austerities, you have been born without a womb; you possess a divine form—protect me, your father. (31)
Sūta said:
When [the king] had spoken thus, Śuka,
who was detached, approached his own father— who was intensely attached— and spoke to him.
Śukra said:
"What do you say, O knower of dharma, O Vedavyāsa of great intelligence? Instruct me, your disciple, according to the truth; I shall fully carry out your command."
Vyāsa said:
"O son, for your sake I have performed penance for a hundred years;
and you have been obtained through great hardship and through the propitiation of Śiva."
"Having petitioned the king, I shall give you wealth;
O highly wise one, enjoy happiness after attaining excellent youth. (35)
Śuka said:
"O father, tell me what happiness exists in the world of men that is free from affliction;
for the wise do not call that happiness which is pierced by suffering."
O illustrious one, having become a woman, I shall follow after her;
for what happiness is there for one who is dependent on another, especially one who has been conquered?
In the Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 14:
One who is bound by iron, wood, and the like might perhaps be released at some time;
but one who is fettered by sons and wife shall never be liberated. (38)
The body of women arises from feces and urine, and likewise they are composed of that;
O best of Brahmins, what wise man would desire to find pleasure therein? (39)
O brahmin-sage, I am not born from a womb; what kind of inclination could there be for me toward a womb?
Even in the future, I do not desire birth within a womb at all.
Why should I desire the pleasure of the vulgar, having abandoned the wonderful bliss of the Self?
For one who delights in the Self does not become excessively greedy again. (41)
First, the Vedas were studied by me and expanded by me;
they were studied as consisting of violence and as promoters of the path of ritual action. (42)
Even Bṛhaspati, the preceptor, has fallen into the ocean of domestic life;
with his heart seized by ignorance, how is he capable of delivering others? (43)
Just as a physician afflicted by disease treats the illnesses of others, so too is this householder a guru for me who seeks liberation; it is a mere mockery.
Having paid homage to my guru, I have come into your presence;
protect me, who am terrified by the serpent of saṃsāra, through the awakening to reality. (45)
In this most terrible saṃsāra, wandering is like that of the stars in the sky;
there is no resting anywhere, just as for the sun day and night.
O father, what happiness is there in saṃsāra when one considers its nature as ending in death?
The notion of happiness among fools is like the pleasure of insects among libertines. (47)
Among those who have studied the Vedas and Shastras yet remain attached to worldly existence, there is no one more foolish than them; they are equal in nature to asses and swine. (48)
Having attained a human birth, which is difficult to obtain, and having studied the Vedas and the scriptures, if one is still bound within saṃsāra, what man could possibly be liberated? (49)
There is nothing more wonderful or marvelous anywhere in this world than this:
that a man attached to children, wife, and home is proclaimed a wise scholar. (50)
The man who is not oppressed by the three qualities of illusion within saṃsāra—
he is truly wise, he is intelligent, and he has indeed reached the further shore of the scriptures.
What is the use of this futile study, which only results in firm bondage? One should quickly study that alone which would liberate one from the fetters of worldly existence. (52)
Because it seizes a person, it is proclaimed as "house" (gṛha); where is there happiness in a prison? Therefore, O father, I am afraid. (53)
Those who are ignorant, dull-witted, and deprived by fate,
even after attaining human birth, enter into bondage once again.
Vyāsa said: A house is not a prison, nor is it the cause of bondage;
even one who is a householder is liberated if he is mentally detached.

A householder who has acquired wealth through righteous means, who performs the rites prescribed in the Vedas according to rule and sequence, who is truthful in speech and pure, shall be liberated even while living as a householder by performing the Śrāddha. 56.
The celibate student, the ascetic, the forest-dweller established in his vow, and the householder always wait upon one another when midday has passed. || 57 ||
Those established in dharma who dwell in the householder stage of life assist others through faith, the giving of food, and likewise through pleasant speech.
No dharma superior to the householder’s stage of life has been seen or heard of,
yet it was fully embraced by learned teachers such as Vasiṣṭha and others.
O illustrious one, what is unattainable for one who performs the rites prescribed in the Vedas?
Whether it be heaven, liberation, a noble birth, or whatever else he desires, that shall come to pass. (60)
"Those who know the Dharma understand that one should go from stage to stage;
therefore, having established the sacred fires, perform your duties without sloth. (61)
O son, knower of dharma, having duly gratified the gods, the ancestors, and human beings, and having procreated a son and established yourself in the householder stage of life,
you shall leave your home, go to the forest, and perform the highest vow.
Having entered the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), he should thereafter take up renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
O illustrious one, listen well: for one who is not self-controlled, these five intoxicating senses, together with the mind, lead to an endless end. (64)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the first book, chapter fifteen,
O high-minded one!
"One should practice austerity in old age"—this is the word proclaimed in the scriptures. (65)
Therefore, one should take a wife for the sake of conquering that [mind];
the highly fortunate Viśvāmitra, having performed most difficult austerities for three thousand years, remained without food with his senses subdued. (66)
Deluded by Menakā, the one of great splendor remained in the forest;
from his seed, the auspicious daughter Śakuntalā was born.
Having seen Kālī, the daughter of the fisherman, my father Parāśara,
struck by the arrows of desire, took hold of that maiden while remaining upon his raft.
Brahmā too, seeing his own daughter and being tormented by the five-arrowed god of love, was running after her; but he was stopped by Rudra, who had rendered him unconscious. || 69 ||
Therefore, O auspicious one, you too should do what is beneficial by following my word:
choose a maiden born of noble lineage and take refuge in the path of the Vedas. (70)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 14 ||
Then, in the fifteenth chapter,
Śrī Śuka said:
"O father, I shall not build a house, for it is a source of suffering in every respect."
It is like a snare, a constant bond for all embodied beings. || 1 ||
O dear one, where indeed can happiness be seen for those distressed by the lack of wealth?
For greedy people who are destitute are surely tormented by their own kinsmen. (2)
Even Indra is not as happy as one who is free from desire like a mendicant; for while the splendor of the three worlds exists here in this saṃsāra, who else could be so? (3)
Seeing the ascetic being gratified, Maghavan became distressed;
the Lord of Heaven created many kinds of obstacles for him.
Even Brahmā was happy, as was Viṣṇu, having obtained the enchanting Lakṣmī.
He constantly experiences exhaustion from battles with the asuras. He does not exert great efforts, yet he performs difficult austerities;
even the glorious Lord of Ramā—who possesses abundant happiness—belongs to whom? (To no one.)
Even Śaṅkara is always sorrowful, as I know;
he constantly performs austerities and is ever engaged in battle with the Daityas. Even a wealthy man, if he is greedy, never sleeps in peace.
But how, O dear one, does a man who is destitute of wealth attain happiness? (8)
O illustrious one, even though you know that a son is born of your own prowess,
you would nevertheless appoint him to this most terrible cycle of existence, which is always fraught with suffering.
O Father, there is the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, and likewise the suffering in death;
furthermore, there is the suffering in dwelling within the womb, which consists of feces and urine.
Therefore, excessive suffering arises from craving and greed;
O giver of honor, begging is a supreme misery even greater than death.
Brahmins subsist on the wealth they receive as gifts; they do not live by the power of their intellect.
Hope for others is the supreme suffering, and death occurs day after day.
Having studied all the Vedas and the Shastras in their entirety,
the wise should go before the wealthy and offer praise with their whole being.
What concern does one who shares a single womb have for leaves, roots, fruits, and the like?
For he is fulfilled by whatever means available and through contentment. (14)

When there is a large family consisting of wives, sons, and likewise grandsons, there is great suffering for the sake of their maintenance; what happiness, then, could there be for one's parents? (15)

"O Father, teach me the Yoga-śāstra, the science of knowledge that produces happiness; I never take delight in the entire ritualistic section (karmakāṇḍa). Tell me the means for the destruction of karma—both that which has begun to bear fruit (prārabdha) and that which has been accumulated (saṃcita)."
Just as the present [karma] perishes, so too does the threefold karma born from its root.
A woman always drinks blood like a leech;
yet the fool, deluded by her gestures and movements, does not perceive this.
Śrīmad Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, First Canto, Chapter 15:
"Vigor is [attained] through enjoyments, wealth through [possessions], and the mind is filled with crooked speech."
A beloved woman carries away one's entire wealth; what other thief is like her? 19.
The fool, deceived by the Creator, takes a wife for the sake of destroying the pleasure of sleep; it leads only to suffering, not to happiness.
Sūta said:
Having heard such words from Śuka, Vyāsa fell into great anxiety, wondering without doubt, "What shall I do? (21)
Tears born of sorrow flowed from his eyes;
trembling came upon his body, and likewise his mind fell into exhaustion.
Seeing his father grieving, dejected, and overwhelmed by sorrow,
he spoke to his father Vyāsa with eyes wide open in amazement.
Oh, how formidable is the power of Māyā, which deludes even the wise one—the author of the Vedānta, the omniscient one who is equal to the Vedas! 24.
I do not know what that illusion is, nor how it is so exceedingly difficult to overcome, since it deludes even the learned Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī. (25)
Even he who was the speaker of the Purāṇas, the author of the Mahābhārata,
and the divider of the Vedas, has fallen into delusion.
I go for refuge to that Goddess who indeed deludes the entire world, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others; what then can be said of others? (27)
Is there anyone in the three worlds who is not deluded by Māyā, since even the former gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others—were brought to delusion by her? (28)

Listen to what must be performed by a Brahmin who has taken refuge in the path of liberation:
having been initiated, he should first dwell with a guru for the purpose of studying the Vedas.
Having studied the Vedas and Vedāntas and having given the teacher’s fee,
the sage, having returned home, should dwell in the state of a householder together with his wife.
He does not engage in other occupations, but is contented, free from desire, and cleansed of all taint;
he performs the Agnihotra and other rites, is truthful in speech, and pure. 17.
Having entrusted his son with the paternal duties, he should dwell in the forest-dweller’s stage of life (vānaprastha);
having conquered the six enemies through austerity and having settled his wife upon his son. (18)
Having duly internalized all the sacred fires within himself, the knower of dharma,
being weary [of worldly life] and having attained pure detachment, should dwell in the forest hermitage.
Only one who is dispassionate has the qualification for renunciation, and never otherwise;
this Vedic statement is true, and my conviction is that it is not otherwise. (20)
Indeed, forty-eight purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are taught in the Vedas;
among them, forty are prescribed for the householder by the great-souled ones. 21.
And for one desiring liberation, the eight qualities such as tranquility and self-control have been prescribed; "one should go from stage to stage"—this is the instruction of the learned. (22)
Śrī Śuka said:
When detachment has arisen in the heart and knowledge and realized wisdom have come into being,
one must necessarily dwell in the hermitages in the forests.
Janaka said:
"The senses are powerful, O giver of honor; when not restrained, they repeatedly produce various distortions in one who is unripe. (24)
Having become an ascetic, how could one fulfill the desire for food, the desire for pleasure, and the desire for sleep of one's own son when such transformations have arisen? (25)
The web of latent impressions (vāsanā) is indeed difficult to digest and does not come to rest;
therefore, for the sake of its pacification, one should gradually renounce it.
One who sleeps facing upward surely falls; one lying face down does not fall downward.
But one who has fallen away after renouncing the world finds no path again. ||27||
Just as an ant climbs from the root to the branch, slowly and steadily reaching the fruit by walking with ease, so too does one progress.
The bird comes swiftly, casting aside all fear of obstacles;
the ant, having wandered about, moves on happily once it has rested.
But the mind is a powerful desire, unconquerable by those who have not disciplined themselves;
therefore, it must be conquered gradually, following the sequence of the stages of life (āśramas).
Even while established in the stage of life of a householder, one who is peaceful, wise, and self-possessed should neither rejoice nor grieve; he should remain equanimous toward gain and loss.
Performing the prescribed duties, abandon that which is accompanied by anxiety.
One who is satisfied with the attainment of the Self is liberated; of this there is no doubt. ||32||
Behold, although established in kingship, I am liberated while living;
I wander according to my will, and nothing whatsoever arises for me.
"O sinless one, just as I shall be—enjoying various pleasures and performing numerous duties—you too shall likewise become liberated. (34)
It is indeed said: from what is one inevitably and necessarily bound?
The five elements are visible, as are their qualities (guṇas). || 35 ||
The Self is accessible through inference; it is never perceptible by the senses.
O Brahmin, how can that which is changeless and stainless be bound? (36)
But the mind, O twice-born one, is the cause of great joys and sorrows;
when this [mind] becomes pure, everything indeed becomes pure. (37)
Though one wanders through all sacred fords, bathing again and again, as long as the mind is not stainless, all of it is in vain. (38)
O scorcher of foes, it is neither the body, nor the individual soul, nor the senses;
rather, the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings. (39)
The Self is eternally pure and liberated; it is never bound at any time.
Bondage and liberation reside in the mind; when that [mind] is stilled, they come to rest. 40.
Enemy, friend, and neutral—all these distinctions reside within the mind.
How could duality exist in the state of oneness, since it arises only from the perception of duality? (41)
The individual soul is always Brahman; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
It is only the notion of duality that persists while one remains in the cycle of worldly existence.
O illustrious one, this is ignorance, and knowledge is that which brings it to an end;
O discerning one, both knowledge and ignorance must always be understood by you. (43)
For how can the happiness of shade be known without the heat of the sun?
Likewise, how indeed can one know true knowledge (vidyā) without ignorance (avidyā)? 44.
The qualities (guṇas) abide in the qualities, and likewise do the elements;
the senses abide in the objects of the senses—what fault is there for the Self (ātman) in that? (45)

O sinless one, the boundaries [of conduct] have been established in all the Vedas for the sake of protecting everything; otherwise, there would be the destruction of Dharma, as among the followers of the Sugata.
When Dharma perishes, the conduct of the social classes (varṇas) is destroyed and transgressed;
therefore, for those who proceed by the path prescribed by the Vedas, there is auspiciousness. 47.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, a doubt remains within me that does not depart at any time, as I listen to what has been told by you, O lord of men. (48)
For in the Vedic dharma there is violence, and that is indeed full of unrighteousness;
O King, how can the dharma spoken of in the Vedas be considered a giver of liberation? (49)
But by direct perception, O lord of men, there is the practice of drinking soma, the slaughter of animals, and the consumption of their meat. (50)

Likewise, the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice was proclaimed, as was the direct consumption of liquor;
gambling was proclaimed, as well as various religious observances. || 51 ||
It is heard that in former times there was a supreme king named Śābidi,
who was a performer of sacrifices, eternally devoted to dharma, generous, and true to his promise;
he was a protector of the bridges of dharma and a punisher of those who walk on wrong paths.
By him many sacrifices were performed, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
A mountain of hides, equal in size to the Vindhya range, arose once more;
and from the flooding of the waters of the clouds, the auspicious river Carmaṇvatī was born.
That king also has gone to heaven, and his fame remains unshakable on earth;
yet, despite such dharma and the Vedas, my intellect does not incline toward them.
A human being always attains happiness through enjoyment in the company of women; in their absence, there is extreme suffering. How, then, can one be liberated while living? (56)
Janaka said:
"In sacrifices, violence is directly perceived, yet it is proclaimed to be non-violence;
for it is determined that violence exists only through the application of limiting conditions (upādhi), and not otherwise."
Just as smoke arises from fire through contact with fuel, so too, through the absence of that contact, the state of being smokeless shines forth within it.
O best of sages, know that non-violence is likewise declared in the Vedas;
yet even that is considered violence for those possessed by passion, while it is not so regarded for those free from desire.
And that action which is free from passion and likewise devoid of egoism, the wise and learned knowers of the Veda declare to be "unperformed. (60)
But for householders, O best of the twice-born, that very violence which occurs in sacrifice is [not a sin] when it is performed without attachment and likewise free from egoism.
O illustrious one, this alone is the path for those seeking liberation who have conquered their own selves. (62)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 18 ||
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Śrī Śuka said:
O Great King, this doubt exists within my heart.
Abiding in the midst of illusion, how could he be free from desire? ||1||
Even after attaining knowledge of the scriptures and investigating what is eternal and what is non-eternal, if the mind does not abandon delusion, how can that man be liberated? (2)
Indeed, it is not possible to destroy the internal darkness through the mere knowledge derived from the scriptures,
just as darkness is not dispelled by a lamp-wick that has been prepared but not lit.
Non-malice toward all beings must always be practiced by the wise;
O tiger among kings, how then might this be achieved by a householder? (4)
Your desire for wealth is not stilled, nor is your desire for the pleasures of sovereignty;
and with your stake being victory in battle, how can you be one liberated while living?
You perceive thieves as thieves, yet you perceive the ascetic as a saint.
The distinction between self and other exists for you as well; O King, how then can you be "bodiless"?
O King, you perceive the pungent, sharp, astringent, and sour tastes as both auspicious and inauspicious;
yet the mind delights in the auspicious ones, and not so in the inauspicious. (7)
O King, waking, dreaming, and deep sleep indeed occur to you according to their respective times; but how is it, O monarch, with the fourth state? (8)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Book, Chapter 19:
Foot soldiers, cavalry, charioteers, and elephants— all are indeed under my control.
"You consider yourself the master of us all, yet you do not truly acknowledge it."
O King, you always ate sweets with joy and likewise with a troubled mind;
and in the matter of the garland as well, O best of kings, how was it that you were impartial toward all? (10)
But one who is liberated, O King, regards a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal;
possessing the realization of the single Self everywhere, he acts for the welfare of all living beings.
Today my mind finds no delight anywhere in home, wife, or other such things;
it is my resolve that I shall wander alone, utterly free from desire. (12)
Free from attachment, free from the sense of "mine," peaceful, subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits,
I shall wander like a deer— beyond the pairs of opposites and without possessions.
“O King, what use have I for a house, wealth, or even a beautiful wife, when my mind is detached from passion and I have transcended the qualities? (14)
You display various forms, agitated by manifold passions;
this hypocrisy of yours indeed shines forth as you declare, "I am liberated. || 15 ||
Sometimes there is anxiety regarding the parasol, sometimes anxiety regarding wealth, and sometimes anxiety regarding the army; when, O King, will you be free from all concern? (16)
Even those Vaikhānasa sages, who are moderate in diet and firm in their vows,
are deluded within this worldly existence, even though they know its unreality.
O King, [this applies] to those born in your lineage known as the Videhas.
Know that it is indeed crooked; never otherwise. ||18||
A Vidyādhara who is a fool, a sun that is blind from birth, and one named Lakṣmīdhara who is poor—for them, their names are meaningless. (19)
Those kings born in your lineage whom I have heard of in the past were renowned by the name Videhas; they were so known neither by their actions nor by their deeds. (20)
O King, in former times there was a king named Nimi in your lineage;
that royal sage [invited] the sage Vasiṣṭha, his own preceptor, for the sake of a sacrifice.
Then the sage invited him and said to that king:
"I have indeed just now been invited by Devendra for the sake of a sacrifice."
"Having completed his sacrifice, I shall indeed perform yours as well;
meanwhile, O Indra among kings, prepare the necessary materials gradually."
Having spoken thus, that sage then departed for the sacrificial ground of Mahendra;
Nimi, having appointed another preceptor, performed an excellent sacrifice.
Hearing that, Vasiṣṭha became exceedingly angry and cursed the king again: "O violator of your preceptor, let your body fall this very day! (25)
The king also cursed him, saying, "May this [fruit] not fall upon you either.
And I have heard that those two fell due to their mutual curses.
"O best of ascetics, O lord of kings, how was your preceptor himself cursed by Videha?
This appears to my mind like a mere diversion.
Janaka said:
"What you have spoken is true; this which you hold is not at all false.
Nevertheless, listen, O best of Brahmins: my guru has been highly honored by me. (28)
Abandoning the company of your father, you wish to go to the forest;
there, you will undoubtedly have a close association with the deer. (29)
The great elements are everywhere; where will you find non-attachment? Your mind is always anxious for the sake of food; how can you be certain? (30)
Just as you have concern for the staff and the deerskin even while in the forest, so too do I have concern for the kingdom, whether I am contemplating it or not. (31)

"Afflicted by doubt, you have indeed come from a distant land."
I have no conceptual construction or doubt; I am entirely free from conceptualization. //32//
"I sleep happily, O Brahmin, and I always eat with happiness;
because of the realization that 'I am not bound,' I am forever happy, O Sage. (33)
But you are always miserable, bound by the suspicion that "I am bound.
Abandoning this suspicion, become happy and composed. (34)
"This body is my bondage; 'it is not mine'—this is liberation.
Likewise, wealth, home, and kingdom—'they are not mine'—this is the firm conviction. (35)

Having heard those words of his, Śuka became joyful in mind;
taking leave of him, he went quickly to the excellent hermitage of Vyāsa.
Seeing his son approaching, Vyāsa also attained great joy;
having embraced him and smelled the crown of his head, he inquired after his welfare once more. (37)
He remained there in that delightful hermitage by his father’s side, composed in mind,
perfected in the study of the Vedas, and an expert in all the scriptures.
Having seen the condition of the high-souled Janaka while he was established in kingship,
he attained supreme detachment and remained in his father’s hermitage.
The fortunate daughter of the Pitṛs, a beautiful woman named Pīvarī,
Śuka indeed made his wife, even though he was established on the path of Yoga.
He begot upon her exactly four sons:
Kṛṣṇa, Gauraprabha, Bhūri, and Devaśruta.
Having produced a daughter named Kīrti, the powerful son of Vyāsa gave her to the high-souled Aṇuha, the son of Vibhrāja.
The son of Aṇuha was the illustrious and powerful Brahmadatta;
that protector of the earth was born from Brahmā and originated from the daughter of Śuka. ||43||
After some time, having there attained supreme knowledge and the unsurpassed path of yoga through the instruction of Nārada, [he remained]. (44)
Then, having entrusted the kingdom to his son, he went to Badarikāśrama;
through the instruction on the seed-syllable of Māyā, his knowledge became unimpeded. 45.
Through the grace of Nārada, Śuka immediately attained that which bestows liberation; having abandoned all attachment to his father on the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, he realized this. (46)
Having resorted to extensive meditation and remaining averse to all attachments,
he flew up from the mountain peak and attained supreme perfection.
Moving through the sky with great splendor, he shone like the sun when the peak of the mountain was split in two by Śuka’s flight. || 48 ||
Many portents occurred; Śuka ascended into the sky like the wind in the atmosphere being praised by the celestial sages. (49)
Shining exceedingly with splendor like a second sun, Vyāsa, however, overcome by the pangs of separation, cried out repeatedly, "O son! (50)
He went to the mountain peak where Śuka was staying,
perceiving Vyāsa to be wailing piteously and overcome with exhaustion.
Then the witness present in all beings gave a response;
even today, on the peak of that mountain, an echo clearly arises.
Beholding Vyāsa weeping and overwhelmed by separation, crying out "O son! O son! while accompanied by Śāka, [the sage spoke]. (53)
Having arrived, she awakened the son of Parāśara.

REVET. Having approached, she enlightened the son of Parāśara.
O Vyāsa, do not grieve; your son is the foremost among those who know yoga.
He has attained the supreme goal, which is difficult to reach for those who have not disciplined themselves;
therefore, you who understand grief should not grieve for him.
"O sinless one, great fame has arisen for you because of that son.
Vyāsa said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master of the World, my grief does not depart; what shall I do? (56)
"My eyes are still unsated today, longing for the sight of my son.
Mahādeva said:
"You shall see the most beautiful shadow of your son standing by your side. (57)
"O tiger among sages, O scorcher of foes, abandon your grief upon seeing her.
Sūta said:
Then Vyāsa beheld the radiant shadow of his son.
Having granted him that boon, Hara vanished on the spot;
when Mahādeva had disappeared, Vyāsa returned to his own hermitage.
Furthermore, he was even more deeply distressed by his separation from Śuka.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 19 ||
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
The sages said:
"O best of gods, Śuka has indeed attained supreme perfection."
What did Vyāsa do after that? Tell me that in detail. ||1||
Sūta said:
Those who were the disciples of Vyāsa, devoted to the study of the Vedas, all first departed for the earth at his command. (2)
Asita Devala, Vaiśampāyana, Jaimini, and Sumantu—all those whose wealth is their asceticism—have likewise departed. || 3 ||
Having seen these [disciples] and his son who had departed to another world,
Vyāsa, overcome with grief, set his mind upon departing.
Vyāsa remembered in his mind that auspicious daughter of a Niṣāda,
his mother, who was filled with grief after being abandoned on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Having remembered Satyavatī, Vyāsa left that best of mountains.
The sage of great splendor returned to his own birthplace.
Having reached the island, he then asked, "Where has that fair-faced maiden gone?
The Niṣādas informed him, "The girl has been given to the king."
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the first book, chapter twenty:
King Dāśaratha, having honored Vyāsa with great affection, [spoke].
Having honored him with a welcome, he spoke with palms joined in reverence.
The King of the Dāsas said:
"O Sage, today my birth has become fruitful and our lineage has been purified,
since the sight of you— who are difficult even for the gods to behold— has occurred."
"O best of the twice-born, tell me that for which you have come;
O Lord, even my wife, wealth, and sons are at your disposal."
On the delightful bank of the Sarasvatī, he established a circle of hermitages;
endowed with the austerity of *nyāsa*, he remained there, fully concentrated.
The son of Śantanu of immeasurable luster was born as the son of Satyavatī;
considering those two to be brothers, Vyāsa dwelt in the forest in happiness. 12.
The first-born son of the king was Citrāṅgada, who was handsome, eloquent, a scorcher of his enemies, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
A second son was born, named Vicitravīrya;
he too was endowed with all virtues and increased the happiness of Śantanu.
Gāṅgeya was his first son, a great hero superior in strength;
likewise, two other sons of great power were born to Satyavatī.
Seeing those sons endowed with all auspicious marks, the high-minded Śantanu considered himself invincible even to the gods and other beings. (16)
Then, after some time had passed, the righteous Śantanu, by the turn of fate, abandoned his body like a worn-out garment, though he was still possessed of a soul.
When the king had passed away according to the law of time, Bhīṣma performed all the funeral rites and various kinds of gifts in accordance with the prescribed rules.
Then the heroic one installed Citrāṅgada on the throne;
he himself did not exercise sovereignty, for that reason he became one who observed a vow.
But Citrāṅgada, the son of Satyavatī, though powerful, heroic, pure, and a giver of pain to others, became intoxicated by his own pride. ||20||
Once, that mighty-armed one, surrounded by a vast army,
roamed through the forest regions, observing the deer and ruru antelopes fit for slaughter.
But the Gandharva Citrāṅgada, seeing the king traveling along the road,
descended from his excellent celestial chariot that was stationed near the earth.
There, O ascetics, a great battle took place between those two of equal prowess at the great site of Kurukṣetra for three years.
Slain in battle by a Gandharva, Bhīṣma quickly reached the world of Indra; hearing this, he then promptly performed his funeral rites.
But Gāṅgeya, having performed the funeral rites and being surrounded by his ministers,
installed the one named Vicitravīrya as the lord of the kingdom.
Later, having been exhorted by her ministers and by high-souled elders,
and seeing her own son established in the kingdom, she was still struck by grief for her [other] sons.
The beautiful Satyavatī became exceedingly gratified;
and Vyāsa too, having heard that his brother had become king, was filled with joy. (27)
Having attained the prime of youth, the auspicious son of Satyavatī,
Bhīṣma, also gave thought to the marriage of his younger brother.
The King of Kāśī had three daughters, endowed with every auspicious mark;
they were placed by that king in a svayaṃvara for the purpose of marriage.
Kings and princes by the thousands were summoned;
being duly honored, they assembled for the sake of the Svayaṃvara according to their desire.
There, the immensely powerful and heroic Bhīṣma,
having crushed the entire assembly of kings with a single chariot, forcibly carried them away.
Having conquered all those kings and taken them with him, that radiant great chariot-warrior reached the city called Gajāhvaya by the strength of his arms.
Reflecting upon them as if they were his mother, his sister, and his daughter,
he indeed brought together three beautiful-eyed maidens.
Having quickly informed Satyavatī and summoned the twice-born,
he promptly questioned the astrologers learned in the Vedas regarding an auspicious day.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, First Skandha, Chapter 20:
Having then prepared the wedding requisites for his own brother, he [proceeded].
When he married those [daughters] to the most righteous Vicitravīrya.
Then the eldest daughter, the beautiful-eyed one with dark-cornered eyes, feeling bashful, spoke thus to the son of Jahnavi.
"O son of Gaṅgā, best of the Kurus, knower of dharma, lamp of your lineage!
In the svayaṃvara, King Śālva has been chosen by me in my heart. (37)
"I have indeed been chosen by that king, whose heart is filled with love.
O scorcher of enemies, act now for the sake of this lineage in a manner that is appropriate. (38)
Therefore, O best among the upholders of dharma, I have been previously chosen by him;
you are powerful, O son of Gaṅgā, so do as you wish. (39)
Sūta said: Having been addressed thus by that maiden there, the descendant of Kuru questioned the elderly brāhmaṇas, his mother, and likewise his ministers.
Having ascertained the opinion of all, Gāṅgeya, the foremost knower of dharma, said to the maiden, "Go, O fair-faced one, according to your pleasure. (41)
Then, dismissed by him, she went to Śālva’s abode;
that woman of beautiful hips spoke to the king her heart's desire.
"I have been released by Bhīṣma according to dharma because my mind was set on you;
I have come here, O Great King, so accept my hand today. (43)
"O best of kings, I shall become your lawful wife for all time;
you were previously chosen by me, and I by you—of this there is no doubt. (44)
Śālva said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, you were seized by Bhīṣma while I was looking on;
since you have been placed upon his chariot by him, I shall not take your hand."
"What wise man would accept a girl who is the leavings of another?
Therefore, I shall not accept her, for she has been abandoned by Bhīṣma like a mother. (46)
Weeping and lamenting, having been abandoned by that high-souled one, she approached Bhīṣma once more and, weeping, spoke these words: || 47 ||
"O hero, Śālva will not accept me once I have been released by you; therefore, take me!
O illustrious one, you are a knower of dharma, for otherwise I shall die. (48)
Bhīṣma said:
"O woman of excellent complexion, how indeed can I take you when your heart is set on another?
O lady of lovely hips, go quickly and without anxiety to your father. (49)
Thus addressed by Bhīṣma, she indeed departed for the forest;
she performed austerities at a solitary and most purifying sacred site (tīrtha).
Furthermore, that king had two wives who were exceedingly beautiful.
Ambālikā and Ambikā were the two auspicious daughters of the King of Kāśī.
That mighty King Vicitravīrya took delight with those two women in various diversions, both in the palace and likewise in the grove.
Having enjoyed delightful pleasures for nine years, O Indra among kings,
he again met with death, seized by consumption.
When her son had died, Satyavatī was then overcome with extreme grief;
she caused the funeral rites for her son to be performed by the ministers.
Then, in private, she spoke these words to Bhīṣma, being exceedingly distressed:
"O illustrious one, son of your father Śaṃtanu, rule the kingdom! (55)
"Take your brother's wife and preserve the lineage, so that the lineage does not come to destruction, just as happened with the lineage of Yayāti. (56)
Bhīṣma said:
"O mother, I have heard the vow that was made by me for the sake of my father:
'I shall not rule the kingdom, nor shall I take a wife. (57)
In the glorious *Devībhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, in the first book, chapter twenty. Sūta said:
Then she became anxious with the thought, "How shall the lineage continue?
for no happiness arises for me from an idle son once a kingdom has been produced.
The son of Gaṅgā said this to her: "Do not grieve, O beautiful lady;
provide a field-born son for Vicitravīrya."
Summon a man of noble birth from the twice-born class and unite him with your daughter-in-law;
for there is no fault in this, even according to the Veda, in the matter of preserving the lineage. 60.
"O lady of pure smiles, having produced a grandson, give him the kingdom;
for I shall indeed uphold his command. (61)
Having heard those words of his, he went in his mind to Vyāsa Dvaipāyana, the sinless sage who was his own son born of a maiden.
Then, as soon as he was remembered, that ascetic Vyāsa arrived;
having established himself in his true form before his mother, the radiant sage stood there.
Honored by Bhīṣma and duly respected by Satyavatī, the one of great splendor remained there like a second smokeless fire. (64)
The mother said to that sage, "Now produce a handsome son for me in the field of Vicitravīrya, born from your own seed. (65)
Having heard the words of his mother, Vyāsa reflected upon her speech; saying "So be it," he remained there and awaited the time of her season.
When Ambika, having bathed after her menstrual period,
attained union with the sage, she gave birth to a blind son of great strength.
Seeing her son born blind, Satyavatī was also distressed;
she spoke to her second daughter-in-law, saying, "Produce a son immediately."
Then, when her season had arrived, she united with Vyāsa;
thus, on that night, the woman Ambalikā conceived a child.
Although a son was born to him, Pāṇḍu was not considered fit for the kingdom;
therefore, at the end of the year, he urged his wife once again for the sake of obtaining sons.
And having summoned Vyāsa, the best of sages, and made her request to him,
she sent him at night to her excellent bedchamber.
The bride had not yet arrived there when a maidservant was sent by her;
and from that maidservant, Vidura was born to her through a portion of Dharma. (72)
Thus were those three sons, Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others, born of Vyāsa as great heroes for the sake of protecting the lineage. We have related to you the entire account of the origin of that dynasty.
O sinless ones, the lineage has been protected by myāsa, who knows the dharma of his brother.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the first book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of ten thousand verses. || 20 ||

The sages said: "This speech concerning the cause of the conception is truly marvelous;
a doubt has arisen here within all of us ascetics. (1)

O observer of noble vows, tell me the truth regarding how both sons were born from her;
O illustrious one, relate this most purifying story in detail.
Furthermore, all the sages of rigid vows were desirous of hearing again concerning Bedavyāsa and likewise Satyavatī. ||5||
Sūta said:
Having bowed down to the Supreme Power, the bestower of the four aims of life,
the Primordial Power, I shall relate this auspicious ancient narrative.
Success becomes eternal merely by reciting it;
for even by means of a pretext, the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava is especially effective. (7)
For the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals by everyone, the Goddess, who bestows desired objects, should be remembered in every way. (8)
There was a glorious lord of the Cedi country named Rājamarīcara, who was righteous, true to his promise, and a worshiper of the twice-born. (9)
Pleased by his ascetic penance, Indra, desiring to do what was pleasing to him, gave him that beautiful and auspicious crystal celestial chariot.
Mounted upon that, the lord of the earth travels everywhere by means of the divine vehicle;
because he stands above the ground, that Vasu is known as Uparicara.
That king was constant in righteousness and was renowned throughout all the worlds;
his wife was a beautiful woman of excellent form named Girikā.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Second Skandha, Chapter 1:
"The sons of immeasurable prowess and great heroism were five in number."
Kings were established in various regions by that sovereign.
Vasostu’s wife, Girikā, presented her desires at the proper time; having bathed and become pure for the *puṃsavana* rite, she approached him during her fertile period. (14)
On that day, the Pitṛs said to him, "Slay the deer.
Having heard that, he reflected upon his wife who was in her season.
Having resolved that the father’s word must be carried out, regarding it as a guru’s command, the king went hunting while remembering Girikā in his mind. (16)
While staying in the forest, that royal sage remembered the beautiful woman in his mind—she who was endowed with exceeding beauty, like another goddess Śrī herself. (17)
As he remembered that amorous woman, his semen was discharged;
the king, however, immediately cast that which had been emitted onto a banyan leaf.
"How could this semen, having been spilled in vain, not be fruitful?"—
having realized it was the time of her season, the king then formed a plan.
"My vigor is in every way unfailing; of this there is no doubt.
I shall send this to my beloved"—thus he resolved. (20)
At the time of the discharge of semen, having observed his queen,
he consecrated that seed with mantras and placed it within a fold of banyan leaves.
Addressing the hawk standing at his side, the king said to the twice-born man:
"O illustrious one, take this and go quickly to my home."
O gentle one, taking this for the sake of my pleasure, carry it home;
give it quickly to Girikā, for today is indeed her season.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, that best of kings gave the leaf to the hawk;
having taken it, he who was most skilled in flight quickly soared into the sky.
Then another hawk saw that bird coming, having seized a hawk in flight in the hollow of its beak.
Perceiving it to be meat, he quickly rushed toward the bird;
then, in the sky, both of them raised their beaks and engaged in combat.
While they were fighting, it fell into the waters of the Yamunā;
then, when the vessel had fallen, the bird emerged at will.
At that time, a certain Apsaras named Ādrikā approached a Brāhmaṇa who had arrived there, intent upon his twilight devotions.
Engaging in water-sports, she moved about naked in the water;
that woman of excellent complexion seized the foot of the twice-born man. (29)
Then, intent on breath control (prāṇāyāma), he saw her moving at will and said:
"Since you have caused an obstacle to my meditation, become a fish! (30)
Cursed by that foremost of brahmins, she became a wanderer upon the Yamunā;
for Adrikā was indeed a most excellent apsarā who had assumed the form of a beautiful śapharī fish.
Then, as that semen fell from the talon of the hawk, the daughter of Vasava,
in the form of a fish, approached swiftly and seized it with her mouth.
Then, after some time, when the tenth month had arrived, that fisherman, having caught her, bound that beautiful female fish.
That fisherman quickly tore open her belly;
from that belly emerged a pair [of children] in human form. (34)
Seeing this wonder—the handsome young boy and the fair-faced maiden—he then attained the utmost amazement. (35)
He reported to the king that two sons had been born from the fish;
the king, filled with wonder, took hold of that auspicious son.
That king named Matsya was righteous and true to his promise;
he was the son of Vasu, possessed of great splendor, and equal to his father in prowess.
Kālikā was given by Vasu to a fisherman as a swift bride-price.
She is renowned by the name Kālī, and likewise as Matsyodarī.
By virtue of her qualities, she truly became known by the name Matsyagandhā;
that auspicious daughter of Vāsava grew up in the house of a servant.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Second Skandha, Chapter 2:
The sages said:
"The excellent Apsarā Adrikā was cursed by the sage and became a fish."
She was torn apart by the fisherman, and having died, she was further devoured.
Tell me further, O Sūta, what became of that Apsaras? How did the end of her curse come about, and how did she attain heaven? (41)
Sūta said:
When she had been cursed by the sage and was filled with astonishment,
she then offered praise to the brahmin, weeping like one in distress.
Then the compassionate Brahmin spoke to that weeping woman:
"Do not grieve, O blessed lady; I shall tell you the end of your curse."
"O auspicious one, by the power of my curse of anger you have entered the womb of a fish;
after giving birth to two humans, you shall obtain release from the curse."
Having been addressed thus by him, she attained a fish-body in the waters of a river;
after giving birth to two boys, she died and was released from the curse.
Having cast off her fish-form and attained a divine form, that woman of excellent complexion departed for the celestial realm, released from her curse.
Thus born, the excellent daughter Matsyagandhā, of beautiful countenance,
grew up being nurtured in the house of a fisherman.
Then Matsyagandhā was born as a young girl of exceeding splendor;
performing her duties, she was like Vāsavi, yet not easily won.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Lord of Matsyagandhī," in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata.
Now begins the second chapter.
Sūta said:
Once, while traveling on a pilgrimage, the sage Pārāśara—
The one of great splendor arrived at the lofty bank of the Kālindī. ||1||
Then the righteous-souled one said to the Niṣāda, who was then eating his meal:
"Take me across to the further shore by means of Kāliya’s boat."
Having heard the words of the sage and while taking his meal on the bank,
the fisherman spoke to that young daughter, Matsyagandhā, who was so enchanting.
"O young girl, O lady of pure smiles, take this righteous-souled ascetic to the further shore by means of your boat; he is desirous of departing. (4)
Having been addressed thus by her father, that beautiful Matsyagandhā, daughter of Vasu, then began to row the boat for the sage who was seated within it.
While traveling in the waters of the Yamunā,
the sage became afflicted by desire due to the power of destiny upon seeing that beautiful-eyed woman.
Desiring to take her hand, that sage, seeing that she was in the bloom of youth,
touched her right hand with his own right hand.
To him, Pāñcālī, her eyes darkened with anger, spoke these words preceded by a smile:
"Is this worthy of your lineage? Is it consistent with your learning or your asceticism? (8)
"You are indeed the heir of Vasiṣṭha, endowed with noble lineage and character;
O knower of dharma, what do you intend to do, being so tormented by love? (9)
O best of Brahmins, human birth on this earth is difficult to obtain;
even therein, I consider the status of a Brahmin to be especially difficult to attain. (10)
"O best of the twice-born, you are indeed renowned for your lineage, your conduct, and your learning, and you are a knower of dharma;
how then have you come to such ignoble behavior upon seeing me, O lord of brahmins, smelling of fish? (11)

"O twice-born one of unerring intellect, having perceived what auspicious quality in my body have you come near to take my hand? Being overcome by passion, how is it that you do not recognize your own dharma? (12)
The Second Chapter of the Second Book in the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
"Oh, this dull-witted brahmin, having seized me while I am submerged in the water, will surely sink today!
My mind is agitated and pierced by the five arrows [of love]; indeed, no one here is able to act against it. (13)
Having reflected thus, that young woman said to the great sage:
"Be steadfast, O illustrious one; I shall indeed lead you to the further shore. (14)
Sūta said:
Having heard those words full of benefit, Pārāśara released his hand, remained there for a moment, and then crossed back over to the other side of the lion.
Then the sage, overcome by lust, seized Matsyagandhā;
trembling, the maiden spoke to him as he stood before her.
"I am foul-smelling, O best of sages; why do you not shrink from me?
For the union of two who are equal in form brings happiness. (17)
When this was said, that beautiful maiden, in a mere moment,
was transformed into Yojanagandhā— possessing a lovely form and a beautiful face.
Having made that beloved and enchanting woman fragrant with musk, the sage, tormented by the god of love, took her by the right hand.
To him who desired to take her, the auspicious Satyavatī spoke by name:
"O Sage, this world and even your father look on from a neutral standpoint. (20)
"This most cruel practice of animal sacrifice does not produce joy for me;
wait, O best of sages, until the night arrives. (21)
Sexual intercourse is prescribed for a human being at night, but not by day;
indeed, men perceive great fault in union during the daytime. (22)
"O one of great intelligence, restrain your desire; public censure is difficult to withstand.
Having heard those words of hers, which were spoken with propriety, he of noble intellect [replied]: ||23||
By the power of his merit, he indeed quickly created a mist;
and when the mist had arisen, the bank was enveloped in profound darkness.
The amorous woman spoke these words, preceded by gentleness, to that sage:
"O tiger among the twice-born, I am a maiden; having enjoyed me according to your desire, you shall depart. (25)
"O Brahmā, you whose vigor is unfailing, may you become my refuge!
What shall I say to my father today, if I am to become pregnant? (26)
"Having eaten me, you will depart; tell me, what shall I do?
Pārāśara said:
"O beloved, by doing this which is dear to me today, you shall remain a maiden. (27)
"And choose a boon, O timid one, whatever you desire, O beautiful lady.
Satyavatī said:
"O giver of honor, [grant it] so that my parents in this world shall not know [of my marriage]. (28)
"O best of the twice-born, act in such a way that my vow as a maiden shall not be broken;
and may a son of wonderful prowess be born to me, equal to you. (29)
"May this fragrance be mine forever, and may my youth remain ever new.
Pārāśara said:
"Listen, O beautiful one; your son shall be born from a portion of Viṣṇu and shall be pure."
And you shall become renowned throughout the three worlds, O woman of excellent complexion;
for some reason, I have become afflicted by desire for you. (31)
"O fair-faced one, never before has there been any delusion in me;
even upon seeing the beauty of the Apsarases, I have always maintained my fortitude. (32)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Second Book, Chapter 2:
"By the turn of fate, having beheld you, I have fallen under the sway of desire."
Know that there is some cause for this, for destiny is indeed difficult to overcome.
Having seen you, who are so exceedingly foul-smelling, how could I fall into delusion?
O fair-faced one, your son shall be the author of the Purāṇas.
"He is the author of the *Vedavidbhāga* and is renowned throughout the three worlds.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, that best of sages enjoyed her as she had come under his control. (35)
Having bathed in the waters of the Kālindī, the sage departed with speed; and that virtuous Satyavatī, having been purified, immediately became pregnant.
On an island in the Yamunā, she gave birth to a son who was like another Kāma;
as soon as he was born, the radiant youth spoke to his mother. (37)
Having fixed his mind solely on asceticism, the exceedingly powerful one entered [the hermitage], saying:
"Go, mother, as you desire; I shall go from here henceforth."
Therefore, O illustrious one, when I am remembered, I shall indeed manifest myself there;
whenever there may be some supreme task for you, O mother. (39)
"I must be remembered by you then; O beautiful lady, I shall return quickly.
May it be well with you; I shall depart, leaving the funeral pyre behind—live happily. (40)
Having spoken thus, Vyāsa departed, and she too went to her father's side;
because the boy was placed by her on an island (dvīpa), he became known as Vaipāyana. (41)
As soon as he was born, he quickly attained growth through his connection with a portion of Viṣṇu;
having performed ablutions at every sacred ford, he practiced supreme austerity.
Thus Dvaipāyana was born to Satyavatī from Parāśara;
and perceiving that the Kali age had arrived, he divided the branches of the Veda.
Due to his expansion of the Vedas, the sage became known by the name Vyāsa;
he composed the Purāṇa-saṃhitās and the excellent Mahābhārata.
Having divided them into sections, he taught the Vedas to his disciples:
Sumantu, Jaimini, Paila, and Vaiśampāyana.
Asita, Devala, and even Śukra his own son—O best of sages, all this has been told as the cause. (46)
Sūta said: The auspicious birth of the son of Satyavatī likewise occurred;
O best of sages, no doubt should be entertained regarding this origin. 47.
"According to the sage, virtues alone are to be taken from the conduct of the great;
and for this reason, Satyavatī’s birth occurred within the belly of a fish. (48)
There was a union with Pārāśara, and likewise with Śantanu;
otherwise, how could the mind of the sage have become agitated by desire? (49)
How could that sage, who knew the Dharma, have performed an act favored by the ignoble?
This origin has been told as having a specific cause, even though it was contrary to proper conduct.
Having heard this auspicious narrative, the learned man who listens to it becomes entirely liberated from sin. (51)
He does not fall into an evil rebirth; he is happy at all times. || 52 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 2 ||
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the second book, chapter three.
Now begins the third chapter.
The sages said:
O Sūta, O sinless one, you have already related in detail the birth of Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor as well as that of Satyavatī.
Nevertheless, O knower of dharma, one doubt remains firmly established in our minds; it does not cease even though you have explained it, O sinless one. (2)
How did she who was declared to be the auspicious mother of Vyāsa, named Satyavatī, come to obtain Śantanu, the king and foremost knower of dharma? (3)
How did that most righteous king, the Paurava monarch, himself choose as his wife the daughter of a Niṣāda— a woman of low birth and unrefined character?
Who indeed was the first wife of Śantanu? Tell me that now;
and furthermore, how did the wise Bhīṣma become a portion of Vāsava? (5)
O Sūta, you previously stated that the heroic King Citrāṅgada,
the son of Satyavatī, was slain by Bhīṣma of immeasurable splendor.
When the heroic Citrāṅgada was slain, his younger brother,
the son of Satyavatī named Vicitravīrya, became the king.
While the eldest Bhīṣma— righteous and handsome— stood previously,
how did he exercise sovereignty, and by what means was he installed by that wise man?
When Vicitravīrya had died, Satyavatī was deeply distressed;
how did she cause her two daughters-in-law to give birth to the son Golaka? (9)
How did that woman of excellent complexion not give the kingdom to Bhīṣma?
And why was a marriage not contracted by that hero? (10)
But why was this unrighteous act committed by Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor—that he procreated two sons upon the wife of his elder brother? (11)
How did that righteous-souled sage, the author of the Purāṇas,
practice the service of another's wife, and especially that of his own brother?
How did that sage perform this loathsome deed? O Sūta, how can the conduct of the learned be the cause for inferring the meaning of the Vedas? (13)
O wise one, you are a disciple of Vyāsa; you ought to sever our doubt.
We are all desirous of hearing [the truth], having made an opportunity at this field of dharma.
Sūta said:
Born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku, he was known as Mahābhiṣa;
he was truthful, virtuous in character, a universal emperor, and the best of kings.
With a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices,
the high-minded one gratified the Lord of the Gods and attained heaven.
Once, King Mahābhiṣa went to the abode of Brahmā; all the gods assembled there for the purpose of serving the Lord of Creatures. (17)
The great river Gaṅgā was situated there to serve the Lord;
her garment was lifted up by the swift wind.
All the gods, including Adhokṣaja, remained within the three worlds and did not stay there;
however, King Mahābhiṣa beheld it without any hesitation.
That river also recognized the king as being filled with love;
seeing the two of them united in affection, shameless and infatuated by passion, [she was moved].
Brahmā became enraged and, filled with wrath, quickly cursed him:
"O King, having obtained birth among mortals, you shall again become a deer. (21)
"Endowed with great virtue,
you shall obtain the Gaṅgā in every way," Brahmā said thus, O King, beholding her full of love.
Dejected, the two of them quickly departed from the presence of Brahmā;
he, for his part, then reflected upon those devoted to dharma in the world of mortals.
He thought of his father Pratīpa, born of the Puru lineage;
at that very moment, the eight Vasus, accompanied by their wives, [arrived].
Having arrived at the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha while wandering at will,
they found someone named Dattaka among the Vasus, beginning with Pṛthu.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Second Skandha, Chapter 3:
Then his wife, named Dyu, saw a cow named Nandinī.
Having seen her, she asked her husband, "Whose excellent cow is this?"
The friend said to Gaurī: "Listen, O beautiful one!
Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever drinks her milk," (27)
"Surely he shall have a lifespan of ten thousand years and remain eternally youthful.
Hearing that, Sundarī said: "I have a friend in the world of mortals. (28)
O highly fortunate one, for the sake of the daughter of the royal sage Uśīnara— a daughter most exceedingly beautiful— he [gave] a milch cow along with her calf.
"Bring Nandinī, the auspicious cow who grants all desires, to my excellent hermitage, so that my friend may always drink her milk. (30)
"Among humans, let there be one who is free from old age and disease.
Having heard those words of hers, Dyaus carried away Nandinī.
Having insulted the self-controlled sage, the sinless [Viśvāmitra], accompanied by Pṛthu and others, departed;
meanwhile, when Nandinī had been carried away, Vasiṣṭha of great asceticism remained.
Having quickly gathered fruits, the sage returned to the path leading to his hermitage; however, when he did not see his cow and her calf in his own hermitage, [he was struck with wonder]. (33)
The radiant sage searched even in the depths of the forests;
when the cow was not found, the sage became exceedingly enraged.
Vāruṇi, having perceived through meditation that she had been carried off by the Vasus, [thought]:
"Since they have indeed disregarded me, my cow has been taken away by the Vasus. (35)
"Therefore, all of you shall be born among humans; of this there is no doubt.
Thus did the righteous-souled son of Vasiṣṭha himself curse those Vasus.
Hearing this, they all departed dejected and sorrowful;
realizing "we have been cursed," they approached that sage. (37)
Seeking to propitiate that sage, the Vasus went to him for refuge;
the righteous-souled sage spoke to those dejected Vasus standing before him.
"After one year, you shall all obtain release from the curse;
[by that time] this cow Nandinī, who is so affectionate toward her calf, will have been recovered by him. (39)
Therefore, those two shall dwell for a long time in a human body;
having seen Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, as she was traveling along the path, they were cursed.
All of them, bowing down, spoke to that river who was cursed and distressed with anxiety:
"O Goddess, how shall we gods continue to be consumers of nectar? (41)
Moreover, this [sacrificial fire] is situated within the bellies of humans;
therefore, O best of rivers, become a human woman and give birth to us. (42)
O sinless one, you were the wife of that royal sage named Śantanu;
therefore, O river of the gods, cast us out from your garment's hem.
"In this way, there shall be liberation from the curse; of this there is no doubt.
Having said, "So be it," they all returned once more to their own worlds.
The goddess Gaṅgā also emerged, being meditated upon again and again;
at that time, King Mahābhiṣa was born as the son of Pratīpa.
The royal sage named Śantanu was righteous-souled and true to his promise;
Pratīpa, however, offered praise to the Sun of immeasurable splendor. (46)
And then, that woman of excellent complexion and beautiful countenance emerged from those waters and took hold of her right thigh, which was like the trunk of a śāla tree. 47.
And he said to the woman sitting on his lap: "O fair-faced one, having asked me, why are you seated on my left side, O auspicious one? (48)
That woman of beautiful limbs said to him, "O best of kings,
O foremost of the Kurus, for whose sake I stand upon your lap, accept me, who desire you."
Then the king spoke to her, who was endowed with beauty and youth:
"O woman of excellent complexion, I would never approach another's wife out of lust. (50)
O beautiful woman, embracing my right thigh, remain there;
O lady of pure smiles, know this to be the place for children and daughters-in-law.
"O auspicious lady, become my daughter-in-law once your highly desired son is born;
through your merit, a son shall also be born to me—of this there is no doubt. (52)
Having said "So be it," that woman of divine appearance indeed departed;
and the king, having reached his home, continued to think of that woman again and again.
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the second book, chapter four:
Then, after some time had passed, when a son was born, she became a milk-giver.
Desiring to go to the forest, the king related the account to his son.

Having related this account, he spoke again to his own son: "O lord of men, if that beautiful-smiling girl of noble form goes to you in the forest, longing for you, you should enjoy the company of that charming woman;
by my command, she must not be questioned by you as to who she is."
"And by making her your lawful wife, you shall indeed become happy.
Sūta said:
Having thus instructed his son, the king, with a joyful mind, [departed].
Having bestowed his entire royal splendor [upon his son], the king indeed entered the forest;
and there, having performed austerities and propitiated the Supreme Mother (Parāmbikā), he [attained his goal].

Having cast off his body through his own splendor, that king went to heaven; having obtained universal sovereignty, the highly effulgent Śantanu, the lord of the earth who meted out punishment according to dharma, protected his subjects.
Thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Sūta said:
After Pratīpa had ascended to heaven, Śantanu, whose prowess was truth, [reigned].
The king became devoted to hunting, slaying tigers and deer. || 1 ||
Once, while wandering in a formidable forest on the banks of the Gaṅgā, the king beheld a beautiful woman with eyes like those of a young deer, adorned with lovely ornaments.
Upon seeing her, the lord of men was captivated; she was the very one described by his parents as having a most excellent countenance.
Endowed with beauty and youth, she was like another Lakṣmī manifest before his eyes.
O sinless one, drinking from her lotus-face, the king found no satiety; his hair stood on end there as if his heart were completely possessed by her.
Perceiving him to be Mahābhiṣa, she too became filled with love;
casting a gentle smile, she stood before the king.
Beholding her with dark-cornered eyes, the king, his mind greatly delighted,
spoke sweet words, consoling her with a gentle voice.
"Are you a goddess, or are you a human woman, O fair-thighed one?
Are you a Gandharva woman, or a Yakṣī, or perhaps a Nāga maiden or an Apsaras? (7)
"Where are you going? Who are you, O lady of excellent hips? Become my wife, O beautiful one!
With a smile full of love, become my lawful wife this very day. (8)
Sūta said:
The king certainly did not recognize her as the daughter of Gaṅgā;
however, Jāhnavī knew him to be a king born from a great physician.
