The woman said:
"I know you, O best of kings, the auspicious son of Pratīpa. For what other worthy husband would an Apsarā desire, considering her own noble nature?"
"O best of kings, by the binding of my speech, I shall indeed make you my husband.
Listen to my condition, O King; I choose you, O most excellent of monarchs. (12)
O King, whatever task I may perform, whether auspicious or inauspicious, you must not forbid me, nor should you speak anything unpleasant to me.
And since you, O best of kings, will not do my bidding, then, O noble one, I shall depart for my own desired land after leaving you. (14)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Second Skandha, Chapter 4.
Then Jāhnavī, remembering her birth among the Vasus within her heart with that former prayer, and having reflected upon her love for Mahābhiṣa, [departed]. 15.
Having said "So be it," that goddess then made the king her husband;
thus chosen by the king, Gaṅgā then assumed a human form.
The fortunate woman of excellent complexion reached the king’s palace;
having approached her, the king sported with her in the auspicious grove.
That beautiful woman, who understood his inner feelings, also delighted him.
Then the king, while sporting, did not perceive the many years that had passed.
He was like Śatakratu with Śacī, that fawn-eyed woman;
she was endowed with every virtue, and he too was skilled in the ways of love. (19)
They remained in that divine palace like Ramā and Nārāyaṇa. As time passed in this manner, she then conceived a child for the king; and that beautiful-eyed Gaṅgā gave birth to a son named Vasu.
As soon as his son was born, he likewise threw water upon the second one.
Then, when his son was killed in the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or even the seventh [battle], the king became consumed with anxiety.
"What shall I do now? How may my lineage remain stable on earth?
Surely these seven sons have been slain by this woman, who is the very embodiment of sin. (23)
I shall restrain her, for if she abandons this, my eighth pregnancy—long desired by my mind—will surely be lost entirely. (24)
If I do not restrain her today, she will surely be cast into the water in every way;
whether this will come to pass or not—this is my great and wondrous doubt. (25)
Even if she were capable, she might protect me or she might not;
since this matter is thus uncertain, what should I do now? (26)
"Indeed, I must exert the greatest effort for the sake of protecting my lineage;
therefore, when in due time this son was born as the eighth Vasu," (27)
Seeing that the cow Nandinī had been carried off by the sage who was conquered by a woman, the king fell at his son's feet and said to him: (28)
"I am your slave, O slender-limbed one; I entreat you, O lady of radiant smiles:
I shall nourish this one son; grant me my very life. (29)
"O lady with thighs like the trunk of an elephant, my seven auspicious sons have been destroyed by you;
protect the eighth, O fair-hipped one, for I fall at your feet. (30)
"O most beautiful one, I shall today grant you whatever else you desire, even that which is difficult to obtain; my lineage must now be protected by you. (31)
"Those who know the Vedas understand that there is no path to heaven [for me];
therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, I now entreat you for an eighth son. (32)
Although he had said, "For one who has no son," when she took him and was eager to depart,
the king then became enraged and spoke to her in great distress.
"O most wicked one, what shall I do now? Why do you not fear the hells?
Who are you, this daughter of evildoers, always devoted to sin? (34)
"Go or stay as you wish; let my son remain here.
What shall I do with you, O sinful woman, who are the end of my lineage?
While the king was speaking thus, she took her infant son.
As she was departing, filled with anger, she spoke these words to him.
Desiring a son, I protected this very child when I had gone to the forest;
now my time has come, for I must depart, as my word has been made otherwise.
"O Gaṅgā, know me to have come for the sake of the gods' mission.
In ancient times, the Vasus were cursed by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha:
'Enter a human womb,' and they remain there, distressed with anxiety."
Having seen this, O sinless one, they requested of you, our mother: "Become [our mother]. (39)
O best of kings, know that after granting them a boon, I was born as your wife for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods; this is my origin. (40)
"Your seven sons have been released from the sage's curse;
for how long a time shall this one son of yours remain? (41)
"O Śantanu, accept this son Gaṅgādatta yourself;
knowing him to be the god Vasu, enjoy the happiness arising from having a son. (42)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Second Skandha, Chapter 4.
"O highly fortunate one, this son of Gaṅgā will be superior in strength;
today I shall lead him there where you have indeed been chosen by me. (43)
"O Lord of the Earth, having protected him until he has reached youth, I shall give him away;
for a son who is deprived of his mother cannot live, nor can he be happy. (44)
Having spoken thus, Gaṅgā vanished after taking that child;
and the king, overcome with extreme grief, remained in his own palace.
Constantly reflecting upon the extraordinary sorrow born of separation from his wife as well as that of his son,
the lord of the earth continued to rule his kingdom.
As time passed in this manner, the king then went out on a hunt, slaying herds of deer, as well as buffaloes and boars, with his arrows. (47)
Then King Śantanu, having reached the bank of the Gaṅgā, was filled with wonder upon seeing that the river had only a small amount of water. 48.
There he saw the prince discharging many arrows and playing upon the bank of the river, having drawn his great bow.
Seeing him, the king was struck with wonder and knew not what to do.
The king did not regain his memory: "Is this my son, or is he not? || 50 ||
Even after seeing his superhuman feat, his light-handedness with arrows,
his incomparable knowledge, and his form resembling that of the God of Love, [he was not moved].
Filled with wonder, the king asked, "Whose son are you, O sinless one?
But that hero, discharging his arrows, said nothing at all. (52)
Then, having vanished, that king became anxious with worry:
"Who is this young son of mine? What shall I do? To whom shall I go? (53)
The king, remaining there with a concentrated mind, praised Gaṅgā;
then she, possessing her former beautiful form, granted him her vision.
Seeing her, whose every limb was beautiful, the king himself spoke:
"O Gaṅgā, who is this boy who has gone there? Show him to me now. (55)
Gaṅgā said:
"O Indra among kings, this son of yours has been protected as the eighth Vasu;
I now place this Gāṅgeya of great asceticism into your hands."
O observer of noble vows, he who has been taught all the Vedas and the eternal science of archery shall become the bringer of fame to this lineage.
This son of yours is established in the divine hermitage of Vasiṣṭha;
he is a knower of the application of all sciences, skilled in all matters, and pure.
What that son of Jamadagni knew, this son of yours knows as well;
accept him, O Indra among kings, go, and be happy, O lord of men. (59)
Having spoken thus and having given the son to the king, Gaṅgā indeed vanished;
the king, however, became filled with joy and exceedingly endowed with happiness.
Having embraced his son and smelled the crown of his head,
the king placed his son upon the chariot and set out for his own city.
Having gone to Hastināpura, the king held a magnificent festival;
he summoned an astrologer and asked him for an auspicious day.
Having gathered all his subjects and all his auspicious ministers from every quarter,
the king then installed the son of Gaṅgā as the heir apparent.
Having made his son, who was endowed with all virtues, the crown prince,
that righteous-souled king lived in happiness and no longer remembered the Ganges.
Sūta said:
Thus has all this been told to you— the cause of your curse,
as well as the birth of Gāṅgeya and the origin of Jāhnavī.
The man who hears of the meritorious descent of the Gaṅgā and likewise the origin of the Vasus is liberated from sin; of this there is no doubt.
O best of sages, this meritorious and purifying narrative has been told,
just as I heard it from Vyāsa in the past— a Purāṇa equal to the Vedas.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Second Skandha, Chapter 5:
The meritorious Śrīmad Bhāgavata, which is endowed with various narratives and stories.
It emerged from the mouth of Dvaipāyana and is endowed with five characteristics.
O best of sages, this meritorious history, which destroys all sins and likewise bestows auspiciousness and happiness, has been recited for those who listen. (69)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
The sages said: O Sūta, the origin of the Vasus has been narrated by you on account of the cause of their curse.
Thus, O Lomaharṣaṇa, the birth of Gāṅgeya has been narrated.
O knower of dharma, how was the virtuous Satyavatī, the mother of Vyāsa by name, obtained as his auspicious Gandharvī wife by Śantanu? (2)
Tell me that in detail: how was the daughter of the fisherman chosen by the king, the most excellent in righteousness? O you of noble vows, dispel my doubt. (3)
Sūta said:
There was a royal sage named Śantanu who was constantly devoted to hunting;
he went to the forest, indeed slaying deer, wild buffaloes, and antelopes.
For exactly four years, the king, taking delight with his son,
experienced happiness just as Hara does with Kumāra.
Once, while discharging arrows and slaying bears with his sword,
he reached the forest and the Kālindī, the best of rivers.
Seeking its source, he then wandered through that forest.
The lord of the earth perceived an unsurpassed, indescribable fragrance;
it was not the scent of the mandāra, nor of musk, nor was this captivating aroma that of the campaka, the mālatī, or the ketakī. (8)
"From where does this come? It is indeed the wind that deludes my vital breath."
Thinking thus, Śantanu, deluded by his longing for the fragrance and following the wind, wandered through the forest region.
He beheld a beautiful woman standing on the riverbank;
she was lovely, adorned with ornaments, well-composed, yet dressed in soiled garments.
At that, the lord of the earth, struck with wonder at her dark-cornered eyes,
became certain that this was the fragrance of her body.
Having seen that wonderful form, exceedingly beautiful, as well as the fragrance esteemed by all the world,
and such auspicious fresh youth, the king indeed became struck with amazement upon seeing it. (13)

Who is she, and from where has she come now? Is she a celestial nymph or a human woman? I wonder how this fragrant and lovely lady could be the daughter of a Gandharva or perhaps the daughter of a Naga. (14)
Having reflected thus in his mind, when that king could not reach a decision himself, he,
overcome by desire while remembering Gaṅgā, then questioned his beloved who was standing on the bank.
Who are you, my dear? Whose daughter are you? Why do you stand here alone in this desolate place, O lady of beautiful thighs? Tell me, O lovely-eyed one, are you married or are you unmarried? (16)
"O lotus-eyed one, having beheld you—my beloved and so enchanting—I have become filled with desire.
Tell me, my dear, where you are going and what it is you wish to do; tell me everything in detail. (17)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Second Book, Chapter 5:
Having been addressed thus by the king, the lotus-eyed woman with beautiful teeth spoke to him with a smile.
O King, know me to be the daughter of Dāśa, a maiden who abides by her father’s command. (18)
"O Lord of Kings, I am merely ferrying this boat across these waters for the sake of the Dharma alone;
my father has gone home today as he pleases. I speak the truth before you, O Master of Wealth. (19)
Having spoken thus, the young woman fell silent; the king, overcome by passion, addressed that hero of the Kurus: "Become my husband; let not your youth indeed pass in vain. (20)
I have no other wife; O deer-eyed one, become my lawful wife.
I am your slave, forever subject to your will; O beloved, the god of love torments me.
"My beloved wife has departed, leaving me behind; I have chosen no other, O lovely one, and I am desolate.
Having beheld you, whose every limb is most enchanting, my mind has indeed become helpless. (22)
Having heard the king's exceedingly charming words, which were like the taste of falsehood,
that maidservant Sugandhā, endowed with virtuous disposition, summoned great fortitude and spoke to the monarch.

"O King, I believe that which you have said of me to be exactly so; however, as for these words of yours, know that I am not independent. My father is the giver of me; therefore, you should quickly entreat him. (24)
I am not a wanton woman, nor even one for jesting; as the daughter of a fisherman, I always abide under the authority of my father.
If my renowned father grants his consent, then take my hand; I am subject to you.
O King, what distresses you so much in mind as it does me, who am still in the bloom of youth?
For even in that regard, one must preserve composure and remain devoted to the succession of family traditions. (26)
Sūta said:
Having heard this from her, the king, deluded by passion,
went to the house of the fisherman's lord in order to ask for her hand.
Seeing the king approaching, the fisherman was filled with great amazement;
having prostrated before the king, he spoke with palms joined in reverence. (28)
The fisherman said:
"I am your servant, O protector of the earth; my purpose has been fulfilled by your arrival. Grant me your command, O Great King: for what purpose have you come here? (29)
The king said:
"O sinless one, I shall make this daughter of yours my lawful wife;
she is being bestowed upon me by you—I tell you this truly. (30)
The fisherman said: "O King, if you seek my jewel of a daughter, she must be given;
however, I shall never give away that which ought not to be given. (31)
Therefore, O Great King, your son shall be the lord of the earth after you; he alone must be consecrated in every way, and no other son of yours, according to my view. (32)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the second book, chapter five. Sūta said:
But when the king heard the words of the fisherman, he became anxious with thought;
keeping the son of Gaṅgā in his mind, the monarch then said nothing.
Having arrived at his home, the lord of the earth sat down dejected; having entered his house, he neither ate nor drank, nor did he sleep.
Then, seeing his father dejected, Devavrata went and asked the protector of the earth the cause of his dissatisfaction. (35)
"Who is this invincible enemy of yours? I shall bring him under your control.
What is your anxiety, O tiger among kings? Speak the truth, O best of monarchs. (36)
O King, what is the use of that son who is born yet does not recognize suffering nor seek to destroy it?
He has come here to collect a debt incurred in a previous birth; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (37)
Having renounced the kingdom at his father's command, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus and son of Daśaratha, indeed went to Mount Citrakūṭa together with Lakṣmaṇa and Jānakī. 38.
O King, he was the son of King Hariścandra, famous by the name Rohita;
having been purchased by his father at the marketplace, he was indeed delivered as a slave into the house of a brahmin. (39)
Likewise, the most excellent son of Ajīgarta, renowned by the name Śunaḥśepa,
was purchased by his father and then bound to the sacrificial post, but was later liberated by Gāvisuta.
It is well known that the head of his mother was formerly severed by the son of Jamadagni at the command of his father;
even though he committed an improper act, he acted because the permission of a guru is most weighty. || 41 ||
"O King, this body of yours is no longer capable; surely you must tell me, what shall I do?
While I am still present, there is nothing that should cause you grief, for I shall accomplish even this impossible task. (42)
"Tell me, O King, what is your anxiety? Taking up my bow, I shall ward it off this very day. If you grant me the fulfillment of my purpose, let your desire become unfailing. (43)
What is the use of that son who, though capable, does not fulfill the desired purpose of his father?
Indeed, what is the use of a son born who does not lift up the deceased spirit of his father? (44)
Sūta said:
At these words of his son, "Simba," King Śantanu, feeling ashamed in his mind, quickly spoke to that son. (45)
The king said:
"O son, you are my father’s great son; you are my only child—heroic, exceedingly powerful, proud, and one who never turns his back in battles. (46)
"O father, for me who has but one child, this life is indeed in vain. If you die, I shall die somewhere; being without support, what shall I do?
This is my great anxiety, and therefore I am distressed today. (47)
"O son, there is no other thought in me that I shall speak before you."
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the second book, chapter 6, Sūta said: O Pāṇḍava...
Having heard that, the son of Gaṅgā then questioned the elder ministers:
"The king, overwhelmed today by shame, does not speak to me;
you must inquire today about the news regarding the village wealth and reach a definitive conclusion."
"Tell me everything truthfully; I shall do it without any hesitation.
Having heard that, they went to the king and, having ascertained the reason, reported it.
But Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā, who understood the matter, reflected upon it.
Accompanied by them, the son of Jahnavī then went quickly to the house of the fisherman;
bowing low with affection, he spoke these words.
Gangeya said: "Sūta..."
"Give this slender-waisted daughter to me today; I entreat you.
Let her be my mother, O scorcher of foes, for I am her slave."
The fisherman said: "O illustrious prince, accept her as your wife;
for as long as you exist, no son of hers shall become king. (54)
Gāṅgeya said:
"This daughter of the fisherman is not my mother; I shall certainly not rule the kingdom.
Her son will by all means rule the kingdom, there is no doubt. (55)
The fisherman said:
"I know this to be the truth: your son shall be powerful, and it is certain that he will seize the kingdom by force. (56)
Gāṅgeya said:
"I shall certainly not take a wife in any way whatsoever;
this is my truthful word, dear father, for I have taken the vow of Bhīṣma."
Sūta said:
Having heard this vow thus made,
the fisherman gave Satyavatī, who was beautiful in every limb, to that king.
By this method, Satyavatī was chosen by him as his beloved;
however, O best of kings, he did not know of Vyāsa’s previous birth.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Sūta said:
Thus, it is said, Satyavatī was chosen by Śantanu.
And likewise, two sons were born, yet they died as well under the power of time.
From Vyāsa’s seed, Dhṛtarāṣṭra was born, and he was indeed blind;
for when the sage was seen, the lustful woman closed her eyes.
Since the princess, upon seeing Vyāsa, turned white in color,
the son born from Vyāsa’s wrath was undoubtedly named Pāṇḍu.
Vyāsa was gratified by that maidservant, who was skilled in the arts of love;
meanwhile, Vidura was born as a portion of Dharma, truthful and pure.
Although Pāṇḍu was the younger, he was installed in the kingdom by the ministers;
however, because Dhṛtarāṣṭra was blind, he was not appointed to the office of authority.
With Bhīṣma’s consent, the mighty Pāṇḍu obtained the kingdom;
then the wise Vidura was appointed to the task of counsel.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra had two wives: Gāndhārī, the daughter of Subala, is remembered as the first, and the second was a Vaiśya woman, firmly established in the duties of domestic life.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Second Skandha, Chapter 6: It is stated by the exponents of the Vedas that Pāṇḍu also had two wives.
Śaurasenī, as well as Kuntī and Mādrī, who was born in the land of Madra. ||8||
Gāndhārī gave birth to one hundred most beautiful sons;
the Vaiśya woman also gave birth to one beloved and dear son, Yuyutsu.
But Kuntī, while still a maiden living in her father’s house, first gave birth to the charming Karṇa from Sūrya; later, she became the wife of Pāṇḍu.
The sages said:
"O Sūta, O best of sages, what is this strange thing you speak?
She was previously given birth to as a daughter by Pāṇḍu and was married by him."
Tell me in detail how Karṇa was born from Sūrya through a maiden;
and how, moreover, that maiden was born and subsequently married by Pāṇḍu.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, when Kuntī, the daughter of Śūrasena, was still in her childhood,
that auspicious maiden was requested in marriage by King Kuntibhoja.
That girl of lovely smiles was adopted as a daughter by Kuntibhoja and appointed for the service of the radiant [sage].
The sage Durvāsas arrived and stayed during the Cāturmāsya;
Kuntī served him, and the sage attained great satisfaction.
I shall give her an auspicious mantra by which, when invoked, a god will come in person and fulfill her desire just as she wishes.
When the Sage had departed, Kuntī remained in her house for the sake of making a decision; she reflected in her mind, "Which god shall I invoke? (17)
Then the sun rose, and the maker of day was seen in that manner;
having likewise performed the recitation of mantras, the one of fierce rays was then invoked.
Having assumed a most beautiful human form from the mandala,
he then descended from the sky into that temple nearby.
Seeing the god approaching, Kuntī was greatly amazed;
trembling due to the fault of the dust, that beautiful woman suddenly became impure.
Standing with her palms joined in reverence, the lovely-eyed lady spoke to the Sun:
Highly pleased by the sight of you today, go now to your own realm.
Sūrya said:
"O Kuntī, how have I been summoned by you through the power of a mantra?
Why do you not accept me, even though I have come before you after being invoked?"
"O lady with dark-cornered eyes, I am afflicted by desire; favor me with your affection!
Lead me away to sport, for I have been brought under your control by this mantra. (23)
Kuntī said:
"O knower of dharma, O witness of all, I am but a maiden; I bow before you.
Even to you, I am not one to be spoken of ill, for I am a girl of noble family, O observer of excellent vows. (24)
Sūrya said: "If I go today while my great chariot is still unprepared, I shall incur the reproach of all the gods; I will go there, of this there is no doubt. (25)
I shall praise that twice-born man today to whom this mantra was entrusted; and I shall also praise you greatly, O Kuntī, lest you fail to honor me.
Thus, your maidenly virtue will remain steadfast, and indeed people will not know [of our union]. Furthermore, O fair-faced one, a son equal to me shall be born to you.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods, the Sun, granted her most desired boon and departed after she had eaten, leaving Kuntī deeply ashamed and with her mind fixed upon him.
The fair-hipped woman remained in a well-guarded chamber, concealing her pregnancy;
only her nurse knew of it and her beloved, but neither her mother nor anyone else. (29)
A son was born in the house, exceedingly charming,
endowed with a most beautiful armor and two earrings.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the second book, chapter six: like a second sun, or like another Kumāra.
Then, placing her hand [on her shoulder], the nurse spoke to her who was deeply abashed: "I am inviting you;
O lady with thighs like the trunk of an elephant, why do you feel anxiety? Today I am standing here.
As Kuntī was placing her son into the basket, she spoke these words: "O all-pervading one..."
"What shall I do? Afflicted by grief for my son, I shall abandon you, my beloved as life itself.

Ill-fated as I am, I shall forsake you, who are endowed with every auspicious mark. May the divine Ambikā—the sovereign of all, who possesses both attributes and is beyond attributes—protect you from the wind-wolf; may Mādrī protect you.
May Kātyāyanī, the mother of the universe and granter of desires, never grant me breast milk.

When shall I behold her lovely lotus-face, having been entreated by her? For I am dearer to her life than breath itself—[yet] remembering you, she will abandon you in the lonely forest like a wicked, wanton woman who abandons the son of the Sun (Sugrīva). Thus it is for you.

In a previous birth as well, the Mother of the three worlds was not propitiated by me, nor was the bliss-bestowing lotus-foot of the Goddess Śivā meditated upon for even a moment. O son, because of that, I am perpetually unfortunate; for she has abandoned me once more in the forest, just as she did before.
"I shall suffer for the sin committed by my own hand," she thought, remembering the deed she had done. 35.
Sūta said: Having said "He is dead" regarding that son held within the basket, Kuntī—so it is told—[placed him there].

Terrified of being seen by people, Kuntī then placed her in the hands of a nurse; having bathed, she performed the rites for him, and she herself lived there in the house of her father’s kinsmen. Carried by the flowing river, the basket was indeed seized by a fisherman.
The son of Sūta indeed had a wife, and by her he was requested for a son;
thus Karṇa was born, a powerful hero, who was raised in the house of his foster-father. Kuntī was married as a maiden by Pāṇḍu at her svayaṃvara.
And his other wife was Mādrī, the auspicious daughter of the King of Madra. ||39||
While sporting in the forest on a hunt, the mighty Pāṇḍu killed a sage who was enjoying himself in the woods, mistaking him for a deer.
Then Pāṇḍu was cursed by that enraged sage:
"If you engage in sexual union with a woman, then your death shall be certain.
Having been thus cursed by the sage, Pāṇḍu was overcome with grief.

Having renounced his kingdom, he lived in the forest, deeply afflicted by grief. O best of sages, his two wives, Kuntī and Mādrī, departed together with him, devoted to the dharma of virtuous women in order to serve him.
Staying on the banks of the Gaṅgā and in the hermitages of sages, Pāṇḍu performed difficult austerities while listening to the treatises on dharma.
While the discourse was proceeding, the king at one point heard well-articulated words concerning the Dharma spoken by the sages.
O scorcher of foes, there is no way for one without a son to go to heaven;
therefore, by whatever means possible, one should bring about the birth of a son. (46)

The son born of a portion [of the body], the son of an appointed daughter, the son born of the wife, the golaka, as well as the kuṇḍa, the son received with the bride, the maiden-born, the purchased, and likewise the one obtained in the forest; || 47 ||
By whom was he given?
And those who take wealth [from the father] are considered sons who are incapable;
it is certain that sons are progressively inferior [to one another]. (48)
Having heard this, Kuntī then spoke to the lotus-eyed one:
"Go to the ascetic sage endowed with penance and quickly procreate a son. (49)
"By my command, there shall be no fault in you; formerly, I heard that the high-souled king begot a son from Vasiṣṭha named Sauvāsa. (50)
To him Kuntī spoke these words: "O Lord, I possess a mantra that grants all desires; it was given to me long ago by Durvāsas and bestows success in every way."
O King, with this mantra I shall invite whichever deity I choose. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa*, Second Skandha, Chapter 7.
Being thus invited, he shall certainly come to my side in every way. || 12 ||
Having united with the best of gods, she gave birth to a son, Yudhiṣṭhira, as her first.

“O great king, what shall I do? O Lord, destroy my sorrow. (55)

Thus, O best of the twice-born, those five Pāṇḍavas, born from the field [of Kuntī] and being sons of gods, were born year by year in that forest.
Once, having seen Mādrī in a secluded hermitage, Pāṇḍu, overcome by intense passion and driven to a state of ruin, seized her as she approached.
Although she forbade him vehemently in many ways, saying "No! No! No! Do not!", he embraced his beloved; then, by fate, he fell to the surface of the earth.
Just as a creeper clinging to a tree falls when the tree is cut down,

Having heard those words of his elder brother of immeasurable splendor,

"Because of your evil counsel, we have now encountered suffering in the forest, and the highly fortunate Draupadī has been brought here by that evil-minded one. (23)

If you, the eldest, had not been a gambler, how could there have been this destruction?
Having slain the Magadhan, I became the cook for Virāṭa.

His hands, adorned with the Gāṇḍīva bow, have been made beautiful with bracelets; having assumed this human form, what sorrow could there be beyond this? 27. O lord of men, all the Kīcakas were slain by me without even asking you;

O Indra among kings, you have displayed folly; for Duryodhana and the others, though they were enemies, have been released from the Gandharvas, while [your own] captives have been bound in chains at will.
"O protector of the earth, though urged by you in every way, I do not wish to give wealth today for the sake of Duryodhana's benefit. (32)
Having spoken thus and Bhīma having departed, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the son of Ambikā, surrounded by his three [sons], gave gifts to the Brahmins.

Having performed all the funeral rites for the deceased, the king, accompanied by Gāndhārī, [proceeded].
He quickly entered the forest together with Kuntī and Vidura.
Having been fully understood by Sañjaya, that high-minded one departed;
even as he was being restrained by his son, the daughter of Śūrasena went forth.
Bhīmasena, lamenting along with the other Kauravas,
turned back from the banks of the Gaṅgā and all departed for Hastināpura.
Having gone to the auspicious hermitage of Śatayūpa on the bank of the Jāhnavī,
they constructed huts there with grass and performed austerities with concentrated minds.
When six years had passed for those ascetics who had departed, Yudhiṣṭhira, out of longing, spoke these words to his sons: ||39||

"If it pleases you all, I shall go to the high-souled Vidura and the highly intelligent Sañjaya; this is my thought.
Then all those brothers, as well as Subhadrā and Draupadī, [agreed].
And the illustrious Vairāṭī, as well as the people of Nāgarika. || 42 ||

Free from passion, the steward wanders about, desireless and without possessions;

On the second day, while proceeding toward the Gaṅgā, King Yudhiṣṭhira beheld Vidura in the forest, emaciated and clothed in darkness through his observance of a vow.

Then Kṣatā gave up her life, and Yudhiṣṭhira grieved excessively;

As the king was listening, an incorporeal voice then spoke:

Having heard this, all those brothers bathed in the pure waters of the Gaṅgā and went to Dhṛtarāṣṭra to inform him of everything in detail.
All the Pāṇḍavas remained there in that hermitage together with the citizens;
there, the son of Satyavatī and Nārada also arrived.
Other sages and great-souled beings had also arrived at Dharmnandana;
then Kuntī spoke to Vyāsa, who was seated there with his auspicious appearance.
"O Kṛṣṇa, my son Karṇa was seen by me as soon as he was born;
my mind is tormented exceedingly. Show him to me, O one rich in asceticism!
Thus spoke Gāndhārī.
"You are capable, O illustrious one; fulfill my desire, O Lord.

Subhadrā said to him:

"O Omniscient One, O Treasure of Austerity, I desire to see [them]; show them to me today!
Having heard these words, the son of Satyavatī [replied]: 57.
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), that best of sages meditated upon the eternal Goddess when the time for twilight had arrived at the Gaṅgā.
Having bathed in the waters of the sacred river and summoned his kinsmen headed by Yudhiṣṭhira, he offered praise to the Mother of the Universe.
She who delights in both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, who possesses attributes as well as being beyond them,
the Goddess of gods, whose nature is Brahman, and who dwells upon the Island of Jewels (Maṇidvīpa).

O Goddess, you are then neither poison, nor Yama, nor even fire; I bow to her.
You are neither water, nor wind, nor earth, nor space; you are not their qualities, nor the senses, nor am I.
You are not the mind, nor the intellect, nor the sun, nor the moon—O Goddess, at that time you were she whom I revere.

Having concentrated this world of living beings within her mind and having withdrawn the sheath of the subtle body (liṅga-kośa) into meditative absorption, she remains for the duration of a kalpa, independent and self-sustained; there is no one who can know her, even though one has attained discriminative wisdom.
This world prays to me for the sight of the dead once again;
O Mother, I am not capable [of this], so show the deceased people to me quickly.

Thus praised then, the Goddess Māyā Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī summoned all the kings from heaven and revealed herself to them. 65.
Having seen Kuntī, Gāndhārī, Subhadrā, and the daughter of Virāṭa,
all the Pāṇḍavas rejoiced upon beholding their own kinsmen returned.
Then they were released again by Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor,
who, having called to mind the Goddess Mahāmāyā, made them rise up like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*).
Then all the Pāṇḍavas and the sages departed with Paṣṭrā;

Sūta said:
Then, on the third day, that king Dhṛtarāṣṭra...

Then, when the thirty-second year had passed, following the destruction of the Kauravas,

Then, having observed the body of Hari and prepared a pile of wood,

Having cremated the body of Rāma along with Revatī in the fire,

Then that city of Vāsudeva was flooded by the ocean;
Arjuna, having indeed taken all the worlds with him, departed at that time.

"Furthermore, O high-minded one, when you and Hari shall become [one],

The king set his mind on going toward the Golden Mountain (Himālaya),

Having gone to the Himalayas, those six sons of Pṛthā gave up their lives;
Parīkṣit, the royal sage, was likewise exceedingly righteous toward all his subjects.
And that lord of kings protected [the earth] for sixty years without weariness;
he became devoted to hunting and went to a great forest.
At midday, the king himself, searching for the wounded deer,
was thirsty, exhausted, and hungry, O son of Uttara.
Afflicted by his own conduct, the king beheld the sage nearby;
seeing the sage established in meditation, the king, distressed, questioned him about water. ||21||
Then the king, remaining silent, said nothing;
instead, overcome with anger, he took up the dead snake with the tip of his bow.
But with his mind possessed by Kali, he placed a serpent around his neck;
even when the serpent had been fastened there, that best of sages said nothing.
Even though he had returned to his own home, the king did not waver from his state of meditative absorption.
His son, possessed of great splendor and performing mighty austerities, was born from a cow.
Then, while playing near the edge of the forest, Mahāśākta heard his friends say to his son, "Now [the father] is upon your father's neck."
"O Lord of Sages, a dead snake has been found by someone!
Having heard those words of theirs, he then became exceedingly enraged. (26)
Taking water quickly in his hand, the enraged king cursed him:
"By him who today threw a dead serpent around my father's neck! (27)
Within seven nights, Takṣaka shall bite that sinful man;
then the disciple of the sage approached the king who was staying at home.
Having heard the curse indeed bestowed by the twice-born sage,
the son of Abhimanyu announced the curse that had been delivered by the son of the muni.
Realizing that it was unavoidable, he spoke to the elder ministers:
"Without a doubt, I have been cursed by one in the form of a brahmin out of hatred for me. (30)
"O ministers, what must be done by me? Let a means be devised here;
for those who proclaim the Vedas say that death is indeed unavoidable. (31)
Nevertheless, the effort prescribed by the scriptures must be performed in every way by the wise;
for some learned men who advocate for skillful means (upāya) have declared this. (32)
Tasks are accomplished through wise means and not by any other;
indeed, the powers of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs are difficult to comprehend.
Why should it not be so? What is the use of those well-prepared jewels?
In the past, the dead wife of a sage, bitten by a snake, was restored to life by them. (34)
Having given half of his lifespan to that excellent Apsaras, the sage said: "The wise should never place their trust in what is destined to be. (35)
O ministers, behold this direct example:
indeed, is any man seen anywhere, either in heaven or on earth?
If one should remain idle after having deliberated with the gods, he becomes a detached ascetic (yati) and goes out for alms in every respect. (37)
Whether invited at will to the house of householders, or otherwise, whether arrived by chance, or even if it has been thrust into one's mouth by someone; ||38||
And without effort, how could it enter his stomach? Effort must be exerted in endeavor; for even if success does not come, [the attempt itself is not in vain].

The wise man should fix his mind on the Lord as He stands in this manner.
The ministers said: "Which sage was it who, having given half of his own life, restored his beloved to life? (40)
"How did she die, O Great King? Tell us that in detail.
The King said:
"The wife of Bhṛgu was a beautiful woman of excellent form named Pulomā. (41)
In that lineage was born the highly renowned sage named Cyavana;
and to Cyavana and Śaryāti was born a beautiful daughter named Sukanyā.
From her was born a glorious son, renowned by the name Pramati;
and the beloved wife of Pramati was the famous Pratāpinī. 43.
A son named Ruru was born, who was likewise a supreme ascetic;
and at that time, there was a certain man known as Sthūlakeśa.
He became endowed with ascetic power, righteous in soul, and esteemed for his truthfulness.
In the meantime, the venerable Menakā, an excellent Apsaras, arrived.
The most beautiful woman in the three worlds sported on the riverbank;
having conceived a child from Viśvāvasu, that lady of excellent complexion emerged [from the water]. (46)
Having gone to the hermitage of Sthūlakeśa, that excellent Apsaras released the maiden, the most beautiful in the three worlds, upon the riverbank. 47.
Seeing the helpless girl at that time, the best of sages,
Sthūlakeśa, took her in, nurtured her, and gave her the name Pramadvarā.
In due time, she attained youth, endowed with all auspicious marks;
and Ruru, upon seeing that young woman, was indeed pierced by the arrows of love.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Parīkṣit said:
Afflicted by desire, that sage Ruru went to his own hermitage while he was asleep.
The father asked that dejected one: "O Ruru, why are you despondent? (1)
Afflicted by intense desire, he said to him: "In the hermitage of Sthūlakeśa, there is a maiden named Pramadvarā; let her become my wife. (2)
Having gone there, Pramati quickly approached the great sage Sthūlakeśa;
having bewildered him and made his face pleasant, he requested that beautiful-faced woman.
Sthūlakeśa gave his word, "I shall give her on an auspicious day," and the two of them prepared the wedding requisites in the forest.
The high-souled Pramati and Sthūlakeśa, having prepared for the sake of marriage, remained nearby in the forest of asceticism. ||5||
At that moment, a beautiful-eyed maiden, sporting in the courtyard of the house, touched with her foot a serpent that was fast asleep.
Then, having been bitten by the serpent, that beautiful woman died;
a great clamor arose upon seeing Pramadvarā dead.
All the sages assembled there cried out, overcome with grief;
seeing her fallen upon the ground, her father was exceedingly distressed.
Ruru wept for her who was lifeless yet blazing with great luster;
hearing that cry, he arrived in order to see her.
There he saw a beautiful woman fallen down as if still alive,
and he beheld Sthūlakeśa weeping, along with the other best of sages.

Ruru, having gone outside his place, wept, overwhelmed by the pain of separation.
"Aha! This most wonderful serpent has been sent by fate. || 11 ||
"This is indeed the cause of my suffering, intended to destroy my happiness;
what shall I do, where shall I go? My beloved, dearer than life itself, is dead."

Separated from this beloved woman, I truly do not wish to live. That lady of noble form has never been embraced by me, nor has she been kissed upon the face. Alas, the taking of her hand in marriage was entirely obtained by me through my own misfortune.
Furthermore, the oblation of parched grain was not performed by her together with him in the fire.
"Shame on this human state! Let my life-breaths depart this very day;
for death does not come at will to one who is thus afflicted by suffering. (15)
How then can that divine happiness desired on earth be attained?
I am falling into a terrible lake; I am falling into fire! (16)
"Even by placing poison around my neck as a noose, I shall give up my life.
Having lamented thus, Ruru then reflected further in his mind. (17)
Standing on that riverbank, he pondered a means [of escape]:
"What fruit would there be for me in death? Self-destruction is difficult to overcome. (18)
May my father be sorrowful and my mother exceedingly distressed;
yet may the gods be pleased by seeing me having renounced my life, as they wish. (19)
Everyone here would surely be overjoyed at my passing; there is no doubt of this. But what benefit could there be for my beloved in the next world? (20)
Even if she were my beloved in the next world, she would not belong to me, a self-killer, even if I were to die by my own hand or be tormented by separation from her.
"For this reason, there would be no fault in my death, but certainly not in my remaining alive.
Having reflected thus, Ruru bathed there, sipped water for purification, and stood pure.
Having taken water in his hand, the sage spoke these words:
"Whatever merit has been earned by me through the worship of the gods and other such acts," ||23||
If the gurus have been honored with devotion, oblations offered, merit earned through austerity, all the Vedas studied, and the Gāyatrī consecrated; ||24||
"May the Sun, propitiated by him, restore my beloved to life;
if my dear wife does not live, then I shall give up my own life. (25)
Having spoken thus and propitiated the deities, he cast that water upon the ground.
While he was thus lamenting and his wife was likewise distressed, the king said: (26)
Then the divine messenger approached Ruru and spoke these words.
The divine messenger said: "O Brahmin, do not commit such a rash act; how can one whose beloved is dead live? (27)
"The life of this fair-hipped daughter of a Gandharva and an Apsaras has come to an end; O you who are free from physical defects, desire another woman, for she is dead and remains unmarried. (28)
"Why do you weep, O one of very poor intellect? What pleasure do you have with her?
Ruru said:
"O messenger of the gods, I shall certainly not choose any other woman. (29)
Whether I should live by means of life itself, or whether I must now die—

Having thus understood Hari’s intention, the messenger of the gods was filled with joy.

"O best of brahmins, listen to the means ordained by the gods in the past. (31)
"By giving half of my life, restore Pramadvarā to life immediately.
Ruru said, "I shall give half of my life to the maiden; there is no doubt in this. (32)
"Today let my beloved rise up, her life-breaths restored.
Then Viśvāvasu arrived there in his celestial chariot,
having learned that his daughter Pramadvarā had suddenly died from the world of heaven.
Then the king of the Gandharvas and the most excellent messenger of the gods approached Dharmarāja and addressed him with these words:
"O Dharmarāja, this is the wife of Ṛuru and likewise the daughter of Viśvāvasu."
"O son of the Sun, this daughter Pramadvarā has just now been bitten by a serpent;

Dharma said: "O messenger of the gods, if you desire the maiden who is the daughter of Viśvāvasu," ||37||
"Having risen for the sake of life, O Ruru, go and restore her.

In this way, by means of the application of skillful methods, she was then restored to life even though she had died; indeed, such a method must be employed in every respect as sanctioned by the scriptures. ||40||
"By means of gems, mantras, and vows, one's life may be protected according to the prescribed rites.
Having said this to his ministers, the king appointed excellent guards. (41)
Then, having caused a magnificent seven-storied palace to be built,
the son of Uttara ascended it at that very moment along with his ministers.
Heroes who possessed jewels and mantras were stationed there for protection;
thereafter, the king dispatched the sage Gauramukha.
For the sake of propitiating his servant, he said "Forgive me" again and again;
and for the sake of protection, he dispatched Brahmins who were masters of perfected mantras here and there.
The minister’s son remained there and stationed elephants;
no one at all could ascend that well-guarded palace.
Even the wind did not move there; it was warded off at the entrance.
And the king, remaining stationed there, provided food, edibles, and other provisions.
Having performed his duties, such as bathing and the twilight prayers, right there,
the king carried out all matters of state while remaining in that very place.
Having consulted with his ministers and even counting the days,
there was a certain Brāhmaṇa named Kaśyapa, the best among counselors.
And thus the king heard of the curse received from the high-souled one.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter ten. 97.
And thus the king heard of the curse received from the high-souled one.
Seeking wealth, that best of the twice-born, Kaśyapa, reflected thus.
"I shall go to where the king, cursed by the twice-born, resides. Having thus resolved, the brahmin departed from his own home onto the road.
Kaśyapa, the best of sages, was a learned knower of mantras who was seeking wealth. || 51 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 9 ||
Then begins the tenth chapter.
Sūta said:
On that very day, Takṣaka by name [approached] that best of kings.
Knowing he had been cursed, O Puruṣottama, Takṣaka quickly emerged from his house.
Disguised as an old Brāhmaṇa, he came out onto the road and saw Kaśyapa walking toward the king.
That serpent questioned the brahmin, the reciter of mantras:
"Where are you going in such haste, and what task do you wish to accomplish?"
Kaśyapa said:
"Takṣaka will burn that best of kings, Parīkṣit;
therefore, I am going there in haste to make the king free from fever."
"O best of Brahmins, I indeed possess a mantra that destroys poison;
I shall certainly restore him to life, for he must now live. (5)
Takṣaka said:
"O Brahmin, I am that serpent; I shall speak to that lord of the earth.
Turn back, for you are not capable of curing one who has been bitten by me."
Kaśyapa said:
"O serpent, I shall undoubtedly restore to life the king who has been bitten by you and cursed by the twice-born."
Indeed, by the power of mantras, one may [attain] desire at will. ||7||
Takṣaka said:
"O sinless Brahmin, if you wish to live after I have bitten that best of kings, then display the power of your mantras and your strength before me."
"And today I shall indeed burn this banyan tree with my venomous fangs.
Kaśyapa said:
"O best of serpents, I shall restore to life that which has been bitten or even burnt by you."
Sūta said:
Having fallen upon the tree, the serpent reduced it to ashes;
he then spoke again to Kaśyapa, "O best of the twice-born, restore this to life."

When the tree had been reduced to ashes by the fiery poison of the serpent, Kaśyapa gathered all the ashes together and spoke these words: 5. "Having gathered all the ashes of the tree that was consumed by the fiery poison of the serpent, Kaśyapa spoke these words."
"Behold today the power of my mantra, O best of serpents! O you of great venom, I shall restore this banyan tree to life even as you watch.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the third book, chapter ten: Having spoken thus, Kaśyapa, the most excellent among those who know mantras, took up water.
He sprinkled that heap of ashes with water consecrated by mantras.
From that water-born seed grew a beautiful banyan tree as before;
seeing that mountain alive, Takṣaka was filled with amazement.
The Naga said to Kaśyapa: "For what purpose is this exertion of yours?"
"I shall fulfill that desire; speak, O Brahmin, what you wish.
Kaśyapa said:
"Desiring wealth, I perceived the king as cursed and departed, O serpent."
And from my home, I shall assist that best of kings with my knowledge.
Takṣaka said:
"O best of Brahmins, accept from the king as much wealth as you desire; I shall give it to you. Go to your own home, for by this I shall have my wish fulfilled."
Sūta said:
Kaśyapa, the knower of the supreme truth, reflected in his mind upon those words again and again: "What shall I do? (18)
If, having heard that and taken the wealth, I were to go back to my own home again, my fame in the world would perish on account of my resorting to greed. (19)
If that best of kings lives, my fame shall be unshakable;
there will be manifold acquisition of wealth, and merit from his very life. (20)
Fame should certainly be protected; fie upon wealth that is devoid of fame!
In former times, Raghu gave away his entire possession to a brahmin for the sake of renown. (21)
How could I neglect King Hariścandra, who is being consumed by the fire of grief, for the sake of my own fame, as was done extensively by Karṇa? 22.
O Queen, as long as I live today, there shall be happiness for all people;
in a kingless state, the destruction of the subjects will surely come—of this there is no doubt. (23)
If the king dies, there will be sin for me due to the destruction of the subjects, and there will be infamy in the worlds because of my greed for wealth. (24)
Having reflected thus in his mind and performed meditation, that most wise Kaśyapa realized that the king’s life had come to an end.
Having realized through meditation that the king's death was imminent, the righteous Kaśyapa went to his home, taking wealth from Takṣaka.
Having turned Kaśyapa back, the serpent, desiring to kill the king on the seventh day,
went quickly to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
At the edge of the city, he heard that Parīkṣit was staying in a palace,
being diligently protected at will by means of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs.
Then the Naga, overcome with anxiety and agitated by the fear of the Brahmin’s curse, reflected through his yogic power: "How may I enter the house? (29)
How can I deceive this king, a doer of evil, a fool struck down by the curse of a brahmin, a rogue who causes suffering to brahmins? (30)
"Born as one of the Pāṇḍavas' lineage, no one could possibly be such as this, by whom a dead snake was placed around the neck of an ascetic. (31)
Having committed a censurable deed and knowing the course of death,
the king appointed guards in his palace and ascended to the upper story.
"The king will escape death; today he moves about free from anxiety.
How shall I consume him, though impelled by the words of the Brahmins?
For that dull-witted man does not know that death is indeed irrevocable. (33)
Therefore, having stationed guards, he has ascended his palace and rejoices today.
(34) If death has indeed been ordained by the God of immeasurable splendor, how could it be averted even by tens of millions of efforts? (35)

And the king, the heir of the Pāṇḍava, though knowing that [his predecessor] had passed away, remained unperturbed in his station, fixing his mind upon living. Thus ends the tenth chapter in the third book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.
A king ought by all means to perform meritorious acts such as giving;
for through righteousness, disease is destroyed and one's lifespan becomes eternal. (37)
Having performed the ritual for a timely death and carried out such acts as bathing and giving gifts, one's death leads to the heavenly realm; otherwise, it results in hell. (38)

The sin committed by him in oppressing the twice-born, as well as that of this king individually, and likewise the terrible curse of the Brahmins, shall indeed result in his death upon his throne. (39)
There was no brahmin by his side who could awaken him;
for death ordained by the Creator is altogether and in every way unavoidable. (40)
Having reflected thus, that serpent, having placed his own nāgas nearby and disguised them in the dress of ascetics, dispatched those excellent serpents.
Then Takṣaka, having taken fruits, roots, and other items for the king,
himself entered into the middle of a fruit in the form of an insect.
Then those nāgas, having quickly taken the fruits, departed;
reaching the royal palace, they stood near the mansion.

Seeing the ascetics, the guards asked them what they intended to do. They said: "O King, we have come today from the penance grove to see the heroic son of Abhimanyu, that sun of his lineage who is so beautiful to behold;
likewise, we have come with mantras to nourish him. (44-45)
"Announce to the king that the sages have arrived for an audience;
having performed our ablutions and given him sweet fruits, we shall depart."
In the lineage of the Bharatas, doorkeepers have never been seen anywhere;
nor indeed has it ever been heard that ascetics fail to grant an audience to a king. (47)
"Let us go to that place where King Parīkṣit is;
having honored him with blessings and received his permission, we shall depart for the forest. (48)
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of those ascetics, the guards replied to the twice-born ones, regarding their request as a command from the king.
"O brahmins, it is our thought that you should not have an audience with the king today;
tomorrow, you must all come here to the king's palace along with all the ascetics."
O best of sages, the palace has no stairs for the Brahmins;
it was undoubtedly constructed by the king out of fear of the Brahmins' curse. (51)
Then those brahmins said to them: "O well-guarded ones, let the fruits, roots, and waters, as well as the blessings of the brahmins, be presented to the king. (52)
Having gone there, those people told the king that the ascetics had arrived.
The king said: "Indeed, you must bring whatever fruits, roots, and other provisions there are."
"O ascetics, ask them about their business; you may come again in the morning. Offer my salutations to them, for there shall be no audience with me today. (54)
Having gone there and gathered whatever fruits, roots, and other provisions were available,
they presented them to the King with great respect.
When those elephants, disguised in the attire of Brahmins, had departed, the king took the fruits and spoke thus to his ministers: || 56 ||
"Let my friends eat all these fruits today; as for me, I shall eat this one great fruit brought by the brahmin. (57)
Having spoken thus and given him that fruit, the king, the son of Uttara and a friend of Indra, took the ripe fruit in his hand and split it open himself.
When the fruit was split open by the king, a tiny worm emerged;
it had black eyes and copper-colored skin, and it was seen there by the monarch himself.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in classical Indic scripts typically mark the end of a section or verse. [End of Section]
Seeing him, the king then spoke to his astonished ministers:
"The sun is setting; today I have no fear of poison."
"I accept that curse; let this worm bite me.
Having spoken thus, that lord of kings placed it upon his neck.
When the lord of day had set, Kīṭaka was then seized by the throat;
he became Takṣaka, terrible and appearing as Death itself.
The king was enveloped by it and the lord of the earth was bitten;
the ministers were struck with amazement and wept, being deeply distressed.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 11:
Beholding her of terrible form, they fled, overcome by fear.
All the guards cried out, and a great hue and cry arose.
Encircled by the coils of the serpent, his many men having perished, the king said nothing; the son of Uttara did not stir.
A terrible flame of fire, born of poison from the Takṣaka forest,
arose and blazed forth, quickly causing the king to lose his life.
Having swiftly taken the life of the king, Takṣaka departed into the sky;
the people here beheld him as he was making the world appear as if it were being consumed by fire.
He fell down, lifeless, like a tree consumed by fire;
and all the people cried out upon seeing the lord of men dead.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Death of Parīkṣit," in the second book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Purāṇa.
Then begins the eleventh chapter.
Sūta said:
Having observed that the king’s young son was indeed lifeless, [he spoke].
And all the ministers performed the funeral rites for the next world for the lord of the earth;
they placed him upon a pyre that was prepared with fragrant aloe-wood.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā, they performed the funeral rites for him who had died an untimely death, his body burnt and reduced mostly to ashes,
according to the Vedic mantra injunctions through his family priest.
They gave gifts to the Brahmins— cows, gold as was appropriate,
various kinds of food, and diverse garments.
At that very moment, the ministers placed the infant son, who increased the joy of the people, upon that auspicious lion-throne.
The people of the city and the countryside named that infant king Janamejaya, who was endowed with the marks of royalty.
The nurse instructed him in all the royal insignia;
growing day by day, he became possessed of great intelligence.
When the eleventh year had arrived, the family priest imparted to him the knowledge appropriate for him, and he received that appropriate knowledge.
Kṛpa imparted the complete and well-refined science of archery (dhanurveda) to him,
just as Droṇa did for Arjuna, and as Bhārgava did for Karṇa.
He was difficult to overcome;
he had reached the further shore of both the science of archery and the Vedas, and was a knower of the supreme truth.
Having attained knowledge, he became powerful,
skilled in the meaning of the treatises on dharma, truthful, and a master of his senses;
being righteous in soul, he ruled the kingdom just as the son of Dharma did in ancient times.
Then, it is said, the king of Kāśī named Suvarṇavarman gave his auspicious daughter Vapuṣṭamā to the son of Parīkṣit.
Having obtained her, whose limbs were dark as the star Rāhu, Janamejaya rejoiced, just as a king of old did upon obtaining the beloved daughter of the King of Kāśī. 13.
Vicitravīrya rejoiced with Subhadrā just as Arjuna did;
the protector of the earth sported in the forests and the groves.
Just as Śatakratu is attended by Śacī, whose eyes are like lotus petals, so too did his subjects become thoroughly contented and cherished with happiness. (15)
By her, the ministers, skilled in action, performed all their duties in every respect.
At that very time, however, there was a sage named Uttaṅka.
Harassed by Takṣaka, he went to Hastināpura, reflecting, "Who could provide retribution for this enmity? (17)
Thinking him to be the son of Parīkṣit, he approached that king:
"O best of kings, you do not distinguish between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done at this time. (18)
Today you do what ought not to be done, and indeed you do not do what ought to be done;
why then do you now entreat me, having cast aside my resentment?
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the second book, chapter 11:
[He was] ignorant of enmity, unacquainted with the *tantras*, and possessed of the behavior of a child.
Janamejaya said:
"What enmity was not known to me? What retaliation was not performed by me? (20)
"Tell me that, O illustrious one, so that I may do what follows.
Uttaṅka said:
"O King, your father has been slain by the evil-minded Takṣaka."
"Summon your ministers and ask them about the destruction of my father.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words, the king questioned his most excellent ministers.
They said, "He was indeed bitten by a serpent and died due to the curse of a twice-born.
Ugrasena said:
"In this case, the curse by the sage was surely the cause of the king's death. (23)
"But what was Takṣaka's fault? Tell me, O best of sages.
Uttaṅka said:
"Having been given wealth by Takṣaka, Kaśyapa was dissuaded [from going]."
"O King, is that Takṣaka not your enemy, the slayer of your father?
O King, in the past, the wife of Ruru was bitten by a snake and died. (25)
But his beloved, though not yet married by the sage, was restored to life;
moreover, Śruṇa made there a most dreadful vow.
"Whichever serpent I see, that one I shall surely slay with my weapon.
Having thus made this vow, Ruru then stood with weapon in hand.
O King, he wandered the earth here and there, slaying serpents;
once, in a forest, he encountered a terrible Dundubha snake afflicted by old age.
Seeing him, he raised his staff and approached to kill him;
as he struck, the brahmin was bitten, and then the ḍuṇḍubha spoke to him.
"I have done you no wrong, O Brahmin; why indeed do you strike me?
Ruru replied, "My beloved, dearer to me than life itself, has been bitten by a snake and has died."
"O serpent, this vow was made by me while I was in distress.
The Dundubha said:
"I will not bite you; rather, those other snakes who bite shall do so. (31)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the second book, chapter eleven.
"You ought not to harm me by means of your bodily union.
Uttanka said:
Having heard those enchanting human words spoken by the serpent, [he was moved]. 32.
Ruru asked, "Who are you, and why have you come to this state of being a water-snake?
The serpent replied, "O Brahmin, I was formerly a brahmin; my friend, O sage, was named Khagama."
That brahmin, the best among the upholders of dharma, truthful and self-controlled—he was deceived by me out of delusion, having fashioned a grass snake. (34)
While staying in the *agnihotra* chamber, he was overcome with extreme fear;
trembling violently and terrified, that vile man cursed me:
"O dull-witted one! O dull-witted one! Become a serpent, you by whom I have been insulted! (35)
Having been greatly propitiated by me, that best of the twice-born, having attained some degree of peace from his anger, spoke to me:
"Ruru shall be released from this curse; he will become a serpent. (36-37)
"He spoke these words to me: 'Surely you are the son of Pramati.
I am that serpent Ruru; now hear my supreme words. (38)
Non-violence is the supreme dharma for Brahmins; there is no doubt about this.
A wise Brāhmaṇa must practice compassion toward all beings. (39)
"O best of Brahmins, it is held that violence other than in sacrifice is not considered sacrificial.
Uttaṅka said:
"That Brāhmaṇa Ruru was then released from his birth as a serpent. (40)
Having brought about the end of his curse and abandoned all violence, he married the young woman; she who had died was restored to life once more.
Remembering the enmity, you have carried out the slaughter of all the serpents;
yet now, having cast aside that enmity, you conduct yourself toward the snakes with equanimity.

Free from anger toward those who killed his father, O best of the Bharatas, my father was released into the intermediate space, though he had been deprived of ritual bathing and the giving of gifts. (43)
O Indra among kings, having slain the serpents, he does not know how to repay his father's debt; even while living, he is indeed as good as dead.
Your father’s misfortune shall continue as long as you do not kill them.
"O best of kings, having performed the Ambāmakhya sacrifice, perform the [great] sacrifice. ||45||
"O great king, remembering the enmity toward his father, he [performed] a snake-sacrifice.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of his, King Janamejaya then—
Deeply distressed, he shed tears from both his eyes and said:
"Fie upon me, the evil-minded one who has vainly indulged in pride! (47)
"Since my father, afflicted by serpents, has met a terrible end, I shall today begin a sacrifice and thereby perform the funeral rites for my father. (48)
Having undoubtedly slain the serpents while the fire blazed, the king summoned all his ministers and spoke these words. (49)
"O best of ministers, prepare the materials for the sacrifice just as I have instructed. — Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 12.103.
Having had the auspicious ground measured out on the bank of the Gaṅgā by the best of the twice-born, || 50 ||
"O ministers, being composed, let a hundred-pillared and enchanting pavilion be constructed; indeed, a sacrificial altar must be prepared for me today. (51)
Indeed, the snake-sacrifice (sarpasattra) should be performed in its full detail with Takṣaka as the sacrificial victim; there, the great sage Uttaṅka shall be the Hotṛ priest.
"Let the Brahmins—who are all-knowing and have mastered the Vedas—be summoned quickly.
Sūta said:
Then the wise ministers acted according to the king's words.
While all the preparations for the sacrifice were being made and the sacrificial altar was being extended, Takṣaka went there as the oblation was being offered.
Afflicted by fear toward Indra, he said, "Protect me!
Having comforted him who was terrified by fear and having settled him in his own place, [Indra departed]. || 55 ||
He granted him complete freedom from fear, saying, "O serpent, be fearless.
Knowing that he had sought refuge with Indra, the sage likewise granted him immunity from fear.
Uttaṅka, being anxious, made an invitation including Indra;
at that time, he was remembered by Takṣaka, who was born of the Yāyāvara lineage.
The righteous-souled sage named Āstīka, the son of Jaratkāru,
having arrived there, praised King Janamejaya while still a youth.
Having seen that boy, who was profoundly wise, the king honored him;
and having honored him, the king gratified him with his heart's desires.
But that illustrious one chose, "May this sacrifice cease";
for the king was bound by truth and had been entreated by him in that manner once again. (60)
He brought the fire sacrifice for the serpents to an end at the word of the sage;
then Vaiśampāyana recited the Bhārata in detail.
Even after hearing this, the king did not attain peace;
the monarch questioned Vyāsa, "How may my peace be restored? (62)
My mind is burning intensely; tell me, what shall I do? My father, the son of Pārtha’s son, has died like one who is truly unfortunate.
O illustrious Vyāsa, for Kṣatriyas, death in battle is preferable;
whether it be death on the battlefield or at home according to the prescribed rites.
"The death of my father occurred while he was in the intermediate space, dying helplessly;
O son of Satyavatī, tell me the means for pacification in this matter. (65)
So that my father, who has fallen into an evil state, may quickly go to heaven.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the second book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Sūta said:
Having heard those words of his, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, [spoke].
There, in that assembly, he spoke these words to the king.
Vyāsa said:
"Listen, O King, I shall proclaim this ancient, secret, and wonderful Purāṇa."
The auspicious work called the Bhāgavata, which contains various narratives,
was previously taught by me to my own son Śukra;
O King, I shall indeed recite it to you, for it is my supreme secret.
It is said that by hearing this, which is extracted from all the scriptures, one obtains the cause of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; it is auspicious, bestows happiness, and is eternal. (4)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twelve,
Janamejaya said:
"Whose son is this Āstīka? For what purpose has he come to cause an obstacle?
O Lord, what is his motive here in the protection of the serpents?"
O highly fortunate one, relate this narrative in detail;
likewise, O observer of noble vows, recount the entire Purāṇa at length.
Vyāsa said:
The peaceful sage Jaratkāru did not enter the householder's stage of life;
however, he beheld his own ancestors hanging in a pit within the forest.
Then they said to him, "O son, take a wife, for that would bring us supreme satisfaction;
indeed, we shall go to heaven, freed from suffering, once you, our son, are endowed with righteous conduct. (8)

He then said to them: "When I obtain a wife who is of equal status, unasked for, and exceedingly submissive, then I shall undertake the building of a house; this I speak as the truth, for such was the command of my ancestors."
Having spoken thus to them, the twice-born Jaratkaru departed for the sacred fords;
at that very moment, the serpents were cursed by their mother, saying, "Let him fall into the fire!"
The two wives of the sage Kaśyapa, Kadrū and Vinatā, having seen the horse on the chariot of the Sun, spoke to one another. (11)
Having seen him, she then spoke these words to Kavaṇatā: "O blessed lady, what is the color of this horse? Tell me the truth without delay. (12)
Vinatā said:
"This king of horses is indeed white; or what do you think, O auspicious one? You too tell me its color, and then let us make our wager. (13)
Kadrū said:
"O lady of pure smiles, I consider this horse to be black in color; come with me, O beautiful woman, to become my slave. (14)
Sūta said:
And Kadrū spoke to all her sons, the serpents who were standing there:
"Make them as dark as children, as many as there are hairs on the horse's body."
Some among them were armless; he then cursed them, saying:
"At the sacrifice of Janamejaya, you shall indeed go into the fire. (16)
Other serpents, with bodies of variegated colors, coiled around the tail of the four-horsed chariot out of a desire to do what was pleasing to their mother.
The two sisters, having gone together, beheld the horse;
seeing that brindled horse, Vinatā was exceedingly distressed. (18)
Then her son Garuḍa, possessed of great strength, arrived;
seeing his mother distressed, that devourer of serpents questioned her.
O Mother, why are you so deeply distressed? To me, you appear as if weeping, even though I, your son, am alive, as are the others, including the charioteer of the Sun.
"You are suffering; therefore, shame on your life, O fair-eyed one!
What is the use of a son being born if his mother is so deeply distressed? (21)
"Tell me the reason, O mother; I shall make you free from your fever.
Vinatā said:
"O son, I am the slave of my co-wife; what can I say to you in vain, for I am wounded? (22)
"O son, she speaks thus to me today; therefore, I am distressed.
[Śrīmad-devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam, Third Skandha, Chapter 12]
Garuḍa said:
"I shall indeed carry her to wherever she is eager to go. (23)
"Do not grieve, O auspicious lady; I shall make certain for you.
Vyāsa said: Having been addressed thus, Vinatā then went to the side of Kadrū.
To dispel her state of servitude, even the exceedingly powerful Garuḍa carried her along with her son and went to the further shore of the ocean.
Having gone there, Garuḍa said to her: "Speak, O Mother; salutations to you!
How may my mother be released from this state of servitude without a doubt?
Kadrū replied:
"O son, having forcibly brought the nectar from the world of the gods, restore it to me immediately; deliver my sons and release my helpless mother."
Vyāsa said:
Thus addressed, the mighty one departed swiftly for the realm of Indra;
having waged war, that best of birds quickly seized the jar of nectar.
Vainateya brought the nectar and presented it to his mother;
by that act, Vinatā was undoubtedly liberated from her state of servitude.
When the serpents had gone to bathe, Indra seized the nectar.
Vinatā was liberated from her state of servitude by the power of her husband.
There, the *kuśa* grasses were spread out, which were licked by those named *pannaga*;
by the mere touch of the tips of the *kuśa*, those double-tongued ones became fully endowed with tongues. (30–31)
And those Nāgas, headed by Vāsuki, who had been cursed by Mātṛkā, went in their grief to Brahmā for refuge and spoke of their fear born of the curse. (32)
To them the Blessed One Brahmā said: "O Jaratkāru, the great sage, hand over to him Vāsuki’s sister who bears the same name as his own. (33)
The son who is born of her shall be the protector of the lineage;
his name shall be Āstīka, of this there is no doubt. (34)
Having heard those auspicious words of Brahmā, Vāsuki went to the forest and,
with humility, gave his daughter to him.
Knowing her to be such, the sage Jaratkāru said to him:
"If she should do anything displeasing to me, then I shall abandon her. (36)
Having performed such a vow of silence, the sage accepted her himself;
and Vāsuki, having granted his desire, went to his own abode.
Having constructed a bright leaf-hut in the great forest, Jaratkāru,
the scorcher of foes, lived happily with her, taking his pleasure.
Once, after having eaten, that best of sages fell asleep;
his sister, a woman of excellent complexion, was seated upon the breast of Vāsuki.
