Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Viṣṇu, Janārdana, spoke again.
"Let us go to her side, bowing down again and again. || 1 ||
This very Varā Mahāmāyā shall indeed grant us boons, for having attained her presence by praising her, we shall move fearlessly at her feet.
If the attendants stationed at the gate do not prevent us,
we shall stand there with concentrated minds and recite a hymn of praise to the Goddess.
Brahmā said:
When these words were spoken by Hari, they became exceedingly joyful and well-composed;
both were delighted and ready to go near Kāma. || 4 ||
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahārāṇa, the Third Skandha, Chapter 4:
Having said "Om," all three descended swiftly from the celestial chariot.
Having crossed over, she emerged at the gate, her mind filled with great apprehension.
Then the divine Goddess, seeing them all standing at the door,
smiled and quickly transformed those three into bearers of female forms.
"We are young women, beautiful and adorned with lovely ornaments;
filled with great wonder, we went once more into her presence.
Seeing us there in female form standing at her feet, she—"
And Aṅganā gazed at him with a look filled with love. Having bowed to that Great Goddess, we stood before her, looking at one another, in female forms adorned with beautiful ornaments. ||8-9||
Gazing at the footstool adorned with various jewels,
which shone like ten million suns, we three remained there.
There, thousands of female companions were dressed in red garments;
likewise, there were auspicious women wearing blue garments and yellow garments.
All the goddesses, auspicious in form and adorned with variegated garments and ornaments, shone resplendently at her side, intent indeed upon her service. 12.
Other women sang and danced, attending upon them; filled with joy, they played lutes, flutes, and various musical instruments.
The entire cosmic egg, including all things mobile and immobile, is therein;
so too am I, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Vāyu, Agni, Yama, and Ravi.
Varuṇa, Śītāṃśu, Tvaṣṭṛ, Kubera, and Pākaśāsana;
likewise the mountains, oceans, rivers, Gandharvas, and Apsarases. ||16||
Viśvāvasu, Citraketu, Śveta, Citrāṅgada, as well as Nārada, Tumburu, and likewise Hāhā and Hūhū. || 17 ||
The Aśvins, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, and the Siddhas, as well as the Pitṛs;
all the Nāgas beginning with Śeṣa, along with the Kinnaras, Uragas, and Rākṣasas—18.
Vaikuṇṭha, the world of Brahmā, and Kailāsa, the best of mountains—all that was seen by him situated within the space between his fingernails. 19.
There, my birth-lotus exists, and I, the four-faced one, am situated there;
likewise are Śeṣaśāyī, the Lord of the World, as well as Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
The Blessed Lord said:
"In that place, I saw [the mark] situated upon the nail of His lotus-foot;
seeing it, I was struck with wonder and, filled with doubt, wondered, 'What is this? (21)
Viṣṇu was filled with wonder, and Śaṅkara likewise remained so;
they then regarded that goddess as the mother of the universe.
Then, as he beheld various kinds of divine sports upon that auspicious island consisting of nectar, a full hundred years passed by.
Then, the goddesses, adorned with various ornaments and appearing joyful, perceived those who were stationed there as if they were their friends.
We too, because of its extreme loveliness, became utterly infatuated; our minds were completely lost amidst those enchanting sights. (25)
At one time, the Lord Viṣṇu, established in a state of intense devotion, praised that Great Goddess, the goddess Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī.

The Blessed Lord said: Salutations to the Goddess, to Prakṛti, and constant salutations to the Ordainer; salutations again and again to the Auspicious One, the Giver of Desires, and to Vṛddhi and Siddhi.
Salutations to her whose form is truth, consciousness, and bliss; salutations again and again to you, the creator of the fivefold cosmic functions and the mistress of the universe. 28.
Salutations again and again to the one whose form is the support of all, who is immutably established;
salutations again and again to Hullekhā, who bears the meaning of the half-measure. ||29||
"O Mother, I have realized that all this is established within you; both its origin and its dissolution proceed from you.
Śrīmad-Devī-Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 4. Page 115.
And your power, whose influence is far-reaching, is now truly known to consist of all the worlds in its capacity to bring this about. || 30 ||

Having expanded everything in its entirety, you display all modifications of existence and non-existence without exception to the Puruṣa at the proper time; and by means of the sixteen and seven principles, you indeed shine like a magician’s illusion for our delight.
Without you, not even a single thing existing as an object appears; pervading, indeed pervading everything in its entirety, you abide.
O Mother, even a person is declared by wise people to be powerless in worldly activity without your power.
You constantly gladden the entire universe with your own powers and reveal everything through your splendor;
indeed, O Goddess, you shall surely devour it all by force at the time of the cosmic dissolution—who, O Goddess, truly knows your course of being?
O Mother, we have been saved by you from Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and indeed the worlds have been shown to you in their vast extent;
they have been led to the abode of happiness and to the highest pinnacle, for the sight of you, O Bhavānī, possesses great power. (34)
O Mother, neither I nor Brahmā knows [your deeds]; for who else indeed can know your inconceivable conduct?
O you of great power, how many worlds are there within this collection of creations fashioned by you? (35)
In this world, O Goddess, we have seen only Hari, Śiva, and the lotus-born Brahmā of renowned power;
are there none others in other worlds? What do we know, O Goddess, of your vast and supreme majesty? (36)
Having prostrated before your lotus feet, O Mother, I beg this much: may this form of yours always dwell within my heart;
may your name alone remain forever within the cavity of my mouth; and may there be constant vision of your two lotus feet at all times. (37)
"I am this servant who is always to be cherished by you; indeed, I contemplate you in my mind as my mistress.
O Goddess, may this bond between us be perpetual, like that between a mother and her son for the sake of their mutual welfare. (38)
You know the entire, complete expanse of the world; you have reached the ultimate stage of perfected omniscience.
O Mother of the Universe, what need is there for a common man to inform You? O Bhavānī, simply act as is fitting, for Your intention is already known.
"Brahmā creates, Viṣṇu protects, and the Lord of Umā is the agent of destruction—this is the common renown among people.
Is this indeed the truth? O Goddess, O Unborn One, we are capable of acting even in this way through Your will, for we are endowed with Your power. (40)
O Dhātrī, daughter of the mountain, the world does not shine; it is indeed Your power of support (Ādhāra-śakti) that sustains everything.
O Giver of Boons, even the sun shines because of Your light; You, being free from all passion (virajā), shine as this entire universe.

By your power, I am indeed Brahmā, the supreme Lord, and all of us are born from you; yet we are not eternal. What other gods, headed by Indra, could be eternal? You alone are the eternal Mother, the ancient Prakṛti. (42)
If you, O Ancient Puruṣa, show compassion, I know today that I am always in your presence;
yet I am lowly, while You are the All-pervading, Beginningless, Effortless Lord, whose intellect is the soul of the universe—You who are eternally beyond the nature of darkness (tamas).
Indeed, you alone are the knowledge of wise men, and you alone are truly the power of those who possess power at all times.
Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 5.
In the world of men, you alone are fame, beauty, fortune, stainless contentment, and form; you are liberation itself and renunciation. 44.
You are Gāyatrī, the first digit of the Veda; you alone are the divine Svāhā and Svadhā, the half-mora endowed with qualities.
The Veda itself is ordained as your sacred utterance (nigama), for the constant life-sustenance of the gods and the ancestors. 45.
Indeed, you create this entire phenomenal world solely for the sake of their liberation, since they have indeed attained the state of individual souls;
for they are like the vast waves of the beginningless, endless, and faultless full ocean. (46)

When the individual soul has fully understood that "this entire activity is yours alone and you withdraw it all"—as is well known—you, whose power is renowned, cease [your activity] once the internal drama, composed by the Actor (the Self), has been rendered futile. 47.
O Ambikā, great bestower of prosperity, you alone are my refuge from this ocean of existence consisting of delusion; I ever come to you.
O Savior, protect me indeed during this time that is full of manifold suffering, false, and constructed by passion and other afflictions at its end. 48.
Homage to you, O Goddess Mahāvidyā! I bow at your feet.
O auspicious one, bestower of all goals, grant me the constant illumination of knowledge. 49.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. ||4||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Brahmā said:
When Janārdana, Viṣṇu, the god of gods, had thus spoken and ceased, [Brahmā spoke].
Śaṅkara, known as Śarva, spoke while standing bowed before him.
Śiva said:

O Goddess, if Hari is your source of manifestation, and if the lotus-born Brahmā likewise is your origin, then am I not also endowed with your excellent qualities? For you, O Śivā, are skilled in the creation of all the worlds.
You are the earth, the water, the wind, as well as the ether and the quality of fire;
O Mother, you are those elements again, as well as the organs of perception, the intellect, the mind, and even the ego.

Those who do not know this, yet speak otherwise—that the entire world was created by Hari, Hara, or Brahmā—they are themselves merely the instruments of your creation; it is they alone who always fashion the universe, including all things mobile and immobile.

O Mother, if the world were produced by earth, air, ether, fire, water, and so forth, along with their objects and qualities, then how is it that it clearly manifests today from you alone, O Nectar of Kalās? 5.
You are all this, both the moving and the unmoving, fashioned in the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
O Mother, you cease from or delight in the playful curiosity of various guises according to Your own pleasure.
O Mother, whenever I, Hari, and the lotus-born Brahmā desired to create the entire world,
we indeed accomplished that only after attaining the possession of the dust from your lotus feet.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 5:
O Ambikā, if your mind were not always moist with compassion, how could I have been ordained as one characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas)?
And Kamalaja (Brahmā) is born from the quality of rajas; is Hari (Viṣṇu), who is well-established, indeed the quality of sattva? ||8||

O Ambikā, if your mind were not partial, why was this world created in such diverse ways—filled with ministers, kings, and servants, and crowded with both those possessing great wealth and those who are destitute? (9)
Indeed, your three qualities alone are always capable of manifestation, preservation, and withdrawal;
for Hari, Hara, and Guha have been fashioned by you in succession as the cause of the three worlds. 10.
"O Hari, likewise by me, the lotus-born one, while traveling through the worlds in celestial chariots, these have been fashioned;
tell me, by whom were these new worlds created? (11)
O Mother of the Universe, you create and protect the world by your own power; how much do you wish to destroy?
You always delight your husband, the Puruṣa; O Śivā, we truly do not know your course.
O Mother, grant us, though we are but worldly beings, perpetual service at the lotus feet of the Lord’s devotees as well.
Having attained manhood, where indeed could we find happiness if we were clearly deprived of Your lotus feet? 13.
O Mother Śivā, having obtained a human body and even the sovereignty over the three worlds, I have no desire at all to dwell anywhere in the worlds apart from your lotus feet. (14)
O lady with beautiful teeth, even having attained the state of youthfulness in your presence, I do not find the slightest pleasure;
for where does manhood lead to happiness when your feet are not within the range of one's vision? (15)
May this stainless fame of mine always prevail throughout the three worlds:
that, having attained the state of a young woman, I have served Your lotus feet, which destroy the cycle of worldly existence. (16)
Who on earth, having abandoned service at your feet, would desire a kingdom free of thorns?
For even a moment surely becomes like an eon if your lotus-like foot is not near.

O Mother, those stainless sages who are devoted to austerity, having abandoned the worship of your lotus feet, have indeed been deceived by fate; for they have suffered humiliation despite their great power. 18.

O Unborn One, liberation from the ocean of worldly existence does not occur through austerity, nor through self-restraint, nor through meditative concentration, nor even through sacrifices performed according to rule, as it does through the service of the pollen of Your lotus feet. (19)
O Goddess, show mercy if you have compassion for me; tell me the pure and wonderful mantra.
By reciting it with equanimity, I shall indeed become happy, possessing that most excellent and perfectly clear nine-syllabled mantra.
Although it was attained by me in my first birth, that nine-syllable mantra does not manifest now;
tell me the mantra today, O Mother, and ferry me across, ferry me across the ocean of worldly existence, O Savior! (22)
Thus addressed by Śiva of wondrous splendor, that goddess then spoke at that time. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa*, Third Skandha, Chapter 5.
The nine-syllable mantra of Ambikā was clearly uttered. ||22||
Having taken it, Mahādeva attained supreme bliss; having bowed at the feet of the Goddess, Śiva remained right there.
Then Śaṅkara remained there, reciting the nine-syllable mantra which bestows both desires and liberation, joined with the seed-syllable and uttered auspiciously.
Seeing Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, situated in that manner,
I stood at his feet and spoke to that Mahāmāyā.
The Vedas were not capable of perceiving you in this way here, for they did not declare you to be the complete and flawless sustainer of all wealth;
rather, they designated you as the Goddess who is the very essence of the *svadhā* offering in all sacrificial oblations.
At that time, O Mother, you truly became omniscient throughout the three worlds. ||26||
"I am the creator; I fashion this entire, most wonderful cosmic egg.
Who else in this triple world of moving and unmoving beings is as capable as I?
I am truly blessed here, there is no doubt, for I am Brahmā, transcending all worlds."
"I am in this vast ocean of existence due to the onset of pride. ||27||
Today, by the grace of you, I have become skilled in speaking the truth, thinking with the pride of having received the pollen from your lotus feet, "I am blessed. Therefore,
I entreat you, O Sovereign Lady, who are expert at destroying the fear of worldly existence and bestowing liberation.
Having cast off the great iron fetter created by delusion, make yourself endowed with devotion to you. ||28||
Therefore, having been born from this immeasurable lotus manifested by you, how could I not be liberated?
"I am indeed your servant, your obedient slave"—O Śivā, protect me, for I am blinded by worldly existence and submerged in delusion. (29)
Those men who do not know speak of me as the Lord; yet those priests here who sacrifice, desiring heaven, certainly do not understand your pure and ancient character or my power at will.
Created by you for the purpose of creation, I divided the first manifestation into four parts in order to fashion the world;
I alone know this—what other could have known it, O Master of Supreme Illusion? Forgive my offense, which was born of egoism.

Those fools who, having entered the eightfold path of yoga, exert themselves in meditative absorption (samādhi), do not know that which bestows liberation, even though it has been uttered by me under the pretext of being a mother. ||32||

Having abandoned those who are deluded regarding the supreme investigation, the enumeration of the principles, and the state [of liberation], are they not utterly bewildered in the ocean of existence? O Bhavānī, you alone are indeed the bestower of liberation from saṃsāra. (33)
Do those primordial beings abandon that supreme knowledge of reality which they themselves experienced?
Even for a mere half-nimēṣa, her holy conduct is pure; she is Śivā, Ambikā, Śakti, and Īśā. (34)
Are you not capable of instantly creating the entire universe with a mere glance, divided in its fourfold form? *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, Third Skandha, Chapter 6. 119.
Having fashioned me in such a manner at the beginning of creation merely for the sake of diversion, you now surely do this [to me]. (35)
Was Hari the protector not protected by you from Madhu or Kaiṭabha in the midst of the ocean?
Was Hara not withdrawn by you at the proper time? How is it that he was born from the middle of my eyebrows? (36)

Your birth has never been seen or heard of anywhere; whence could it have arisen? No one here knows its origin. Indeed, you are the primordial Śakti, the one and only Bhavānī; therefore, you are awakened by all as the independent one. (37)
Joined with you, O Mother, I am capable of destroying Hara; and joined with you, Hari is capable of protecting me.
Hara is indeed able to slay Hari when united with you here; yet today, all are powerless when separated from you.
Just as I am Hari and Śaṅkara, were others not born in that same way? Do they not exist now, or will they not come to be?
Why do those of limited intellect not become deluded regarding this most wondrous play of Yours, which serves as a ground for dispute? (39)
The Lord is indeed today a non-doer, manifest beyond the qualities (guṇas), devoid of desire, free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhi), and eternally unconditioned (akala).
Nevertheless, those who know the sacred ordinances say that Your Lordship perceives the pleasure bestowed upon You. 40.
When this distinction between the seen and the unseen has been thoroughly investigated, there is no other third person superior to you among all objects of knowledge. (41)
"The words of the Veda must never be considered false;
this contradiction has caused great anxiety within my heart. (42)
That Brahman which the Vedas declare to be indeed one without a second—is that you, or is it he? Dispel this doubt. (43)
Without doubt, my mind does not function without hesitation;
this small intellect is submerged in this investigation of duality and unity. (44)
You ought to dispel my doubt with your own mouth;
for through the enjoyment of my merit, this meeting with your feet has been attained by me. (45)
"Are you a male or are you a female? Tell me in detail;
having known you as the Supreme Power, I shall be liberated from the ocean of worldly existence. (46)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Brahmā said:
Thus was the Goddess questioned by me, who was bowed down with humility.
That venerable lady, having arrived, spoke these gentle words.
The Goddess said:

"There is always and eternally only oneness between me and this [universe], no duality at all. He who is that, I am she; I who am this, he is that. Any perceived difference exists only through the delusion of the mind. (2)
He who knows the subtle difference between these two is indeed wise;
liberated from saṃsāra, he is released—of this there is no doubt. || 3 ||
Brahman alone is indeed non-dual, eternal, and ancient;
yet it assumes the state of duality when time is designated as the "impending creation."
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter six.
Just as a lamp appears in two ways due to the presence of limiting conditions—like a shadow within a mirror or a reflection—so it is with us two. (5)
Indeed, at the time of differentiation, the Supreme Reality manifests as the enjoyer;
this distinction between the visible and the invisible exists in every way when duality is present.
I am neither woman nor man, nor am I neuter at the dissolution of creation;
when creation exists, this distinction arises, being again imagined by the intellect.
I am intellect, I am fortune, as well as fortitude, fame, and memory;
I am faith, intelligence, compassion, modesty, hunger, thirst, and likewise forgiveness;
I am luster, peace, longing, sleep, lethargy, old age, and youth.
Knowledge and ignorance, longing and desire, power and indeed powerlessness;

fat, marrow, and skin—these are my forms. My vision is both true and untrue speech; I am the supreme, the intermediate, and the intuitive (paśyantī) levels of speech, as well as the various dramatic modes (nāṭya). I am all these diverse things.
"O Lotus-born One, know this to be my firm conviction: 'What is there in saṃsāra that I do not see? Indeed, what exists apart from me? Everything is indeed myself. (11)
"Tell me, what is it that is devoid of these definitive forms of mine?
Therefore, O Creator, I have indeed become pervasive throughout this creation. (12)
"Surely among all the gods, I indeed exist under various names; in the form of Śakti, I manifest my prowess.
I am Gaurī, Brāhmī, Raudrī, Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Śivā."
I am Vāruṇī, Kauberī, Nārasiṃhī, and Vāsavī;
when all tasks arise, I enter into them and accomplish every deed, having indeed made him the instrumental cause.
As there is coldness in water, heat in fire, and light in the sun,
and as there is frost in the lord of the night (the moon), so do I manifest according to my will.
"O Creator, once abandoned by me, surely not even a living being in this world would be capable of moving; I declare this to you as a certainty. (17)
It is said that Śaṅkara was rendered powerless to slay the Daityas because he was abandoned by Mayā;
for the world calls a man devoid of power exceedingly weak. (18)
Indeed, people do not speak of one who is devoid of Rudra or devoid of Viṣṇu;
rather, they all call him the lowest of men who is devoid of Śakti. 19.
One who has fallen, stumbled, been afraid, become tranquil, or fallen under the power of an enemy is called "incapable" in the world; no one is said to be anything other than Rudra.
Know that power (śakti) is the cause by which you desire to create;
and when you are joined with power, you shall then become the creator of everything.
Likewise Hari, likewise Śambhu, likewise Indra, and then Vibhāvasu;
Śaśin, Sūrya, Yama, Tvaṣṭṛ, Varuṇa, and Pavana as well.
A house is stable and capable of being supported only when it possesses sufficient strength;
otherwise, it would be unable to support even a single atom. (23)
Likewise Śeṣa, likewise Kūrma, and all the other elephants of the quarters—
when joined with me, they are capable and have accomplished their respective tasks.
I drink up all the water, I withdraw the fire, and today I paralyze the wind; I act exactly as I desire.
O Lotus-born One, one should never at any time entertain doubts regarding the existence of any of the principles (tattvas), even those that are non-existent. ||26||
Perhaps it would be a prior absence (prāgabhāva) or even a posterior absence (pradhvaṃsābhāva), just as there is an absence of a jar in clay lumps or in potsherds. (27)
If one were to investigate where this earth has gone since it no longer exists today, it should be understood that only its atoms remain. (28)
Eternal, momentary, empty, permanent, impermanent, with an agent, and preceded by the ego—thus it is intended to be explained through these seven divisions. (29)
"O Aja, take hold of the principle of Mahat; from that, the ego (ahaṅkāra) arises.
From that, fashion all the elements as they were before. (30)
May you depart to your own abodes; having established yourselves there, may you dwell in peace.
May you, impelled by destiny, perform each your respective duties. 31.
"O Creator, accept this beautiful and sweet-smiling Śakti, the excellent Mahāsarasvatī by name, who is endowed with the quality of Rajas. (32)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter 6: [She who is] divine, wearing white garments, and adorned with celestial ornaments.
Seated upon an excellent throne, she was her companion for the sake of play. ||33||
"This excellent woman shall be your constant companion;
do not disregard my sovereignty by considering this beloved wife as merely an object of worship."
Go now with her indeed to Satyaloka quickly;
produce all four kinds of seeds right away.

The linga-kośas, together with those souls and their respective karmas, exist and remain established throughout time; restore them as they were before, including the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, just as it was previously. The whole universe is joined with its own inherent qualities through the causes known as Time, Karma, and Nature.
Viṣṇu should be honored by you and worshipped at all times;
because his nature is primarily characterized by the quality of goodness (sattva), he is always superior in every respect. (38)
Whenever you have a task that is difficult to accomplish,
Hari will indeed take an incarnation upon the earth at that time.
Then, having taken on a human body either in the animal realm or elsewhere,
Janārdana will indeed bring about the destruction of the Dānavas.
This Bhava shall also be your companion, possessed of great strength;
having created all the gods, sport as you please. 41.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, all of you being well-composed, shall perform various sacrifices according to the prescribed rules along with sacrificial fees. 42.
"O gods, by the mere utterance of my name in all sacrifices and rituals, you shall indeed always remain satisfied and content. (43)
And Śiva, who possesses the quality of tamas, is indeed to be honored in every way;
he should be worshipped with great effort in all sacrificial rites.
Furthermore, whenever fear of the Daityas shall arise for the gods, my Śaktis will then manifest in beautiful forms and take them away. 45.
Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, Gaurī, Nārasiṃhī, and Sadāśivā—
perform these and other tasks for me, O Lotus-born One.
O Lotus-born One, always reciting this nine-syllable mantra accompanied by the visualization of the seed-syllables, perform all your duties. 47.
"O one of great intelligence, you must know that this is indeed the supreme among mantras;
it should always be held in your heart for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
Having spoken thus to me, the Mother of the World, with a pure smile, spoke to Hari.
O Viṣṇu, go and accept this captivating Mahālakṣmī. 49 ||
She shall always remain in the place of your chest; of this there is no doubt.
For your pleasure, I have given you this auspicious Śakti, the bestower of all goals.
"You must never treat her with contempt; she is always to be honored.
Indeed, this union known as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa has been ordained by me. (51)
All sacrifices for the sake of livelihood have been performed by me for the gods;
one should always conduct oneself with the three [objects of life] without opposition and with proper attachment.
And you shall be Brahmā, and Śiva shall be yours; these gods shall arise from my own qualities.
They will all be worthy of honor and worship by everyone; of this there is no doubt.
Those men of deluded minds who shall create division will go to hell because of that division; of this there is no doubt.
such a man shall become. ||55||

Hari is Śiva himself, and he who is Śiva is Hari himself. One who maintains a distinction between these two goes to hell; likewise, Druhiṇa (Brahmā) should be known as such—there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
There is another distinction based on qualities; listen, O Viṣṇu, I shall tell you.
Let the quality of sattva be primary for you, O self-reflecting one;
even if it were secondary, the other two qualities—rajas and tamas—are well known. (57)
Always remaining joined with the quality of passion (rajas), sport together with Lakṣmī amidst various transformations and manifold diversities.
The seed-syllable of speech (Vāgbīja), Kāmarāja, and Māyā as the third—this mantra, O Beloved of Ramā, which bestows the supreme goal, has been given by me to you. (59)
Having taken it up, recite that [mantra] constantly and dwell at your ease;
O Viṣṇu, you shall have no fear of death, nor any fear arising from Time.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter seven.
"As long as this abode of mine remains firmly established, I shall withdraw everything—the entire universe, both moving and unmoving. (61)
At that time, you shall surely be absorbed within me as well.
This mantra, which bestows both desires and liberation, must always be remembered.
It should be performed in conjunction with the Udgītha by one desiring auspiciousness;
and having caused Vaikuṇṭha to be built, O Puruṣottama, one should dwell there.
"Dwell as you desire, contemplating me, the eternal.
Having spoken thus to Vāsudeva, that supreme Prakṛti consisting of the three guṇas [departed]. Brahmā said: [Thus ends the verse].
The Guṇa-less Goddess spoke these immortal words to the god Śaṅkara:
"O Hara, accept Gaurī; you are Mahākālī, the captivating one. (65)
Having caused Kailāsa to be built, dwell there at your pleasure;
let the quality of tamas be your primary attribute, while the qualities of sattva and rajas remain secondary.
For the sake of destroying the demons dwelling there, they performed penance to suppress the qualities of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas),
as well as for the purpose of remembering the Supreme Self.
O sinless ones, you must always adopt the peaceful quality of all beings;
in every way, you three possess the [three] qualities and are the agents of creation, maintenance, and destruction. (68)
There is no object whatsoever in this saṃsāra that is devoid of these [qualities];
indeed, whatever is perceived as a mere object in saṃsāra consists of the three guṇas.
In this world, that which is visible is never devoid of qualities, neither in the past nor will it ever be so;
yet this Supreme Self is devoid of qualities and is never an object of vision.
At the appointed time, O supreme Śaṅkara, I am both with attributes and without attributes;
O Śambhu, I am always the cause and never the effect.
Indeed, she is with attributes (saguṇā) because of her causality, yet she is without attributes (nirguṇā) in the presence of the Puruṣa;
likewise, the Great Principle (mahattattva), the Ego (ahaṃkāra), and the qualities such as sound and the rest are her attributes.
O Śivā, because I am perpetually manifest as the ego (ahaṃkāra) through the form of cause and effect day and night, I am therefore the cause.
And my ego (ahaṃkāra) must perform its function; it is established as possessing the three qualities (triguṇa).
From the ego arises the principle of the Great One (mahattattva); that is proclaimed to be the intellect (buddhi). (74)
The principle of Mahat is indeed the effect, while the ego (ahaṃkāra) is the cause;
for the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi) always arise from the ego.
The five elements are the cause for the arising of all things;
likewise, there are exactly five organs of action and five organs of cognition.
There are exactly five great elements (mahābhūtas) and the mind as the sixteenth; this group of sixteen consists of both effects and causes, and is characterized by the qualities (guṇas). (77)
The Supreme Self, the Primordial Person, is neither effect nor cause;
thus, O Śambhu, is the origin of all at the first of creation.
I have briefly described to you their origin there;
O best of beings, go now by celestial chariot for my sake.
"Even when you are in a state of distress, I shall grant you my vision through remembrance;
O gods, I, the eternal Supreme Self, am always to be remembered. (80)
"By the mere remembrance of both, the accomplishment of the task is certain.
Brahmā said:
Having spoken thus, he dismissed us after bestowing well-consecrated powers upon us. 81.
Then, Mahālakṣmī was sent from that place to Viṣṇu, Mahākālī to Śiva, and Mahāsarasvatī to me.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 7: Having reached another place, they became men like us.
They were contemplating that true nature and its most wonderful power.
Having reached that celestial chariot, the three of them indeed ascended it;
neither was that island there, nor that goddess, nor likewise the ocean of nectar.
Furthermore, we indeed saw that celestial chariot there, and not otherwise.
Having reached that vast celestial chariot, we arrived in the presence of the Lotus-born One at the great ocean,
where the two invincible ones named Madhu and Kaiṭabha were slain by Murāri.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 6 ||
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Brahmā said:
Such is the power of that Goddess as she was seen by me and by Viṣṇu.
O highly fortunate one, even by Śiva, those various goddesses were addressed individually.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his father, Nārada, the best of sages, being exceedingly pleased, questioned the Prajāpati with these words. (2)
Nārada said:
"Tell that to me, O Grandfather."

The Primordial Person is indestructible, devoid of qualities, infallible, and immutable; He is both seen and experienced, whereas the Power (Śakti) consisting of the three qualities has been observed. O Father, what is that Power which is devoid of qualities like?
O Lotus-born One, tell me the true nature of both Her and the Puruṣa.
And for the sake of which I performed great austerities on Śvetadvīpa—those high-souled Siddhas and ascetics free from anger have been seen by me. (5)
"O Lord of Creatures, that Supreme Self has not yet come within the range of my vision; for this reason, I have performed intense austerity again and again. (6)
"O dear one, you have seen the Śakti endowed with qualities, which is beautiful to the mind;
but tell me, what are those two who are devoid of qualities like? (7)
Vyāsa said: Thus questioned by Nārada, his father Prajāpati,
the Grandfather, spoke these truthful words with a smile.
Brahmā said:
O sage, the form of the attributeless (nirguṇa) cannot come within the range of vision;
since that which is visible is perishable, how can the formless be seen? (9)
The power (Śakti) is devoid of qualities and difficult to attain, and likewise the Person (Puruṣa) is devoid of qualities;
yet they are both to be understood through knowledge by the sages and likewise to be meditated upon. || 10 ||
Know that Prakṛti and Puruṣa are without beginning or end and are eternally present;
they are to be approached with trust, never with distrust. (11)
Know that consciousness which exists in all beings is of the nature of the Supreme;
it is the eternal, all-pervading light within various manifestations, O Nārada. (12)
O illustrious one, know that both He and She are all-pervading and omnipresent;
there is nothing whatsoever in this world of transmigration that is devoid of them. (13)
Always intermingled within the body, these two are eternal, immutable,
identical in nature, consisting of pure consciousness, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and of stainless luster.
That which is Śakti is this Supreme Self, and that which is the Supreme Self is considered to be Śakti;
no one, O Nārada, knows even the slightest difference between these two.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter seven.
O Nārada, even after studying all the scriptures and the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches,
one does not know the subtle difference between those two without renunciation.
The entire universe, both moving and unmoving, is created by the ego.
O son, how could that [sin] be eliminated even in a hundred kalpas? || 1 ||
O son, how can one who possesses qualities perceive that which is devoid of qualities with the eye?
O one of great intelligence, contemplate with the mind that which possesses qualities.
O best of sages, when the tongue and the eye are covered by bile, [the true nature is not perceived].
The bile perceives pungency as its flavor, yet it does not perceive form in that same way.
How can the mind, which is veiled by the qualities (guṇas), know that which is devoid of qualities?
Furthermore, since that [mind] arises from egoism (ahaṃkāra), how could it be free from it?
As long as there is no cessation of the qualities (guṇas), how can there be the vision of that [Reality]?
One perceives it in the mind when one is devoid of egoism (ahaṃkāra).
Nārada said:
O Lord of the gods, [tell me] in detail the nature of these three qualities; for Ahaṃkāra, which possesses a triple form, is indeed their very essence— namely,
the Sāttvika, the Rājasa, and the other, the Tāmasa.
O Supreme Person, describe the essential natures according to their distinctions;
O Lord, tell me that knowledge by knowing which I may be fully liberated,
as well as the characteristics of the qualities (guṇas) in their detailed divisions.
Brahmā said:
O sinless one, I shall tell you of the three powers belonging to these three:
the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and another, the power of objects (artha-śakti). 25.
The power of knowledge belongs to the *sāttvika*, the power of action to the *rājasa*, and the power of material substance to the *tāmasa*; thus have the three been described to you.
I shall now declare their respective effects; listen, O Nārada, according to the truth.
From the tamasic power of the primal substance (prakṛti), there arises sound and touch;
form, taste, and smell are called the subtle elements (tanmātras).
Space has sound as its sole quality, and wind likewise has touch as its quality.

Fire has the single quality of beautiful form, water consists of the quality of taste, and earth is to be known as having the quality of smell; these, O Nārada, are subtle. When these ten are combined, they indeed possess the power of substantiality (dravya).
That creation, which follows from that [tamas], is born of the tamasic ego and conforms to it. || 30 ||
And hear from me those things produced from the creative power of the rājasa [quality]:
the ear, the skin, the mouth, the eye, and the nose as the fifth. (31)
These are the organs of cognition, and likewise the organs of action— namely,
speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals, which are indeed five.
Prāṇa, apāna, dhyāna, samāna, and udāna—these fifteen combined together are called the rājasa creation. ||33||
These means of accomplishment (sādhana) are indeed composed of the power of action (kriyā-śakti);
their material cause (upādāna), it is said, is the persistence of consciousness (citi-anuvṛtti). ||34||
Endowed with the power of knowledge and born from the quality of sattva,
they are the quarters, Vāyu, Sūrya, Varuṇa, and also the two Aśvins.
The five presiding deities of the five sense organs are Candra, Brahmā, Rudra, and Kṣetrajña as the fourth. (36)
Thus, for that which is called the internal organ—namely the intellect (buddhi) and the rest—it has been declared that there are exactly four presiding deities. (37)
Together with the mind, these are indeed fifteen;
this is the creation of the sattvic type, proclaimed as the "sāttvika" creation.
The Supreme Self has two forms, distinguished as gross and subtle;
they declare that form which consists of knowledge and is formless to be the primary cause. (39)
For the practitioner, however, the gross form is taught for the sake of meditation and so forth;
this subtle body alone is proclaimed to belong to the Puruṣa. (40)
Indeed, my very body is designated as the Sūtra;
I shall now describe the gross body of Brahmā, the Supreme Self. (41)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 8:
Listen with diligence, O Nārada, for by hearing this one is completely liberated.
Those which were indeed previously described as the subtle elements (tanmātras) are the subtle forms of the primary elements (bhūtasūkṣmas).
Having quintuplicated those very [subtle elements], there arises the manifestation of the five gross elements;
listen now as I truly explain this process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa). 43.
First, having taken up the subtle element of taste even within the mind,
one should likewise imagine it in such a way that it becomes water.
Having divided the portions of the remaining beings individually,
one should then mix those portions into the water that has been made into the essence of flavor.
Then, when the differentiation of the elements and consciousness have been revealed, the doubt "I am that" arises from the entry of consciousness [into the body]. (46)
Because he is perceived through that very distinction by way of such conceit, the Lord is called Ādinārāyaṇa and Bhagavān. ||47||
Then, when the differentiation of the elements had become solidified and attained clarity, they grew by means of their qualities in this manner, through the successive increase of each quality. (48)
Space has only one quality, which is sound alone and no other;
wind is proclaimed to have two qualities, namely sound and touch. 49.
Sound, touch, and form—these three are the qualities of fire;
sound, touch, form, and taste are indeed the four qualities of water.
Touch, sound, taste, form, and smell are the qualities of the earth;
it is said that the creation of the cosmic egg occurs through the union of these combined elements.
All living beings, having come together, are born from a portion of the cosmic egg;
indeed, eighty-four hundred thousand species of living beings have been declared.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Brahmā said:
"O dear one, this creation has now been described to you, concerning which I was questioned by you just now."
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the true nature and configuration of the qualities (guṇas). || 1 ||
Sattva should be known as having the nature of joy, for joy arises from happiness;
likewise, it consists of straightforwardness, truthfulness, purity, faith, forbearance, and fortitude. ||2||
Compassion, as well as modesty, tranquility, and contentment—
through these, a constant and unshakable conviction in *sattva* arises. Furthermore, *sattva* is white in color and always brings delight in the Dharma.
It constantly generates true faith and wards off false faith. ||4||
Faith is said by the seers who perceive reality to be of three kinds: sattvic, rājasic, and likewise another, tāmasī. ||5||
Red-colored dust is said to be wonderful yet unpleasant;
because it involves association with suffering, displeasure certainly arises from it. (6)
Furthermore, hatred, malice, envy, and arrogance,
as well as longing and sleep— these are your rajasic forms of faith.
Pride, intoxication, and likewise arrogance are indeed born from *rajas*;
a wise person should recognize the nature of *rajas* by these characteristics. (8)
Darkness is said to be black in color; it causes delusion and produces despondency, as well as laziness, ignorance, sleep, dejection, and fear.
Dispute, as well as miserliness, crookedness, anger, partiality, extreme atheism, and the pointing out of others' faults; ||10||
The wise should recognize that [state] as characterized by darkness (tamas) in every respect;
it is joined with faith of a dark nature and produces suffering for others. 11.
A person desiring welfare should always cause *sattva* to shine forth, restrain *rajas*, and suppress *tamas* at will. (12)
Because they mutually overcome one another, they conflict with each other;
likewise, all things depend upon one another, for nothing remains without a support.
Sattva alone is never found anywhere, nor is rajas or tamas; they are always all combined, and for that reason they are remembered as being mutually dependent. 14.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter eight.
I shall now describe their expansion through mutual union;
listen, O Nārada, for by knowing this one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
No doubt should be entertained here regarding the words I have spoken after having known this.
That which is known and experienced becomes fully understood when the fruit is attained.
O Mahāmati, through hearing and seeing, and indeed immediately through the experience of mental impressions (saṃskāra), that which is fully understood is not born again.
[The sacred place] heard is holy and purifying, and faith has arisen, yet it is characterized by passion (rājasī).
Having emerged at that sacred ford, he saw exactly what he had heard.
Having bathed there and performed his duties, he gave royal gifts. Enveloped by the quality of passion (rajas), he remained there for some time.
Not liberated from passion and hatred, shrouded by desire and anger,
he returned once more to his home and remained just as he was before. O Lord of Sages, he had indeed heard about the holy ford, but he did not experience it.

"Since the fruit has not been attained, know it to be as if unheard, O Nārada (21). Know, O best of sages, that freedom from sin is the power of the holy ford; just as in this world the fruit of agriculture is the eating of prepared food (22), so too are those other transformations of the sinful body, such as desire, anger, and the rest."
Greed, delusion, as well as thirst, hatred, passion, and pride; envy, jealousy, impatience, and lack of peace—O Nārada, these are evils;
as long as they have not departed from the body, a man is possessed by sin. ||23-24||
If, once the sacred site has been prepared, these [impurities] do not depart from the body,
then it is merely fruitless labor, just like that of a farmer.
The field has been pressed by labor, the ground has been ploughed with great difficulty;
the seed sown is of high quality, and thus the livelihood is said to be beneficial. (26)
Day and night, he was exhausted from guarding [the fruit], longing for its result;
yet, having fallen asleep at the proper time during the winter in the forest, he was severely attacked by tigers and other predators. (27)
Just as everything was devoured by locusts and rendered hopeless once more, so too, O son, is the toil of visiting holy places; it brings only hardship and yields no fruit.
O Nārada, his sattva became intensely dominant and increased through the study of the scriptures; as its fruit, he attained detachment toward objects characterized by tamas.
It indeed forcibly overcomes both rajas and tamas;
rajas has become intensified and active through its association with greed.
In that same way, it indeed overcomes both [rajas and] sattva;
likewise, having become intensified through its association with delusion (moha), darkness (tamas) increases. ||31||
Both that sattva and rajas, having come together, also overcome [tamas];
today I shall explain in detail how they indeed overcome it.
When sattva has indeed increased and the intellect is established in dharma,
one does not perceive external objects arising from rajas and tamas.
He accepts wealth produced through righteous means and not otherwise;
he desires wealth, dharma, and sacrifice that are accomplished without effort. || 34 ||
Then he indeed indulges his desire only for those enjoyments that are characterized by sattva;
not for the sake of liberation in those characterized by rajas, and how much less so in those characterized by tamas? (35)
Having thus first conquered passion (rajas), there follows the conquest of darkness (tamas);
then, O son, the pure quality of goodness (sattva) alone becomes stainless. (36)
When passion (rajas) has indeed increased, having abandoned the eternal duties (sanātana-dharma),
one performs actions contrary to dharma after attaining a state of exhaustion characteristic of passion.
Through the Rajas quality, there is the increase of wealth as well as Rajasic enjoyment;
by means of that, Sattva emerges, and Tamas is likewise restrained. (38)
When darkness had increased and become intense,
there was no faith in the Veda, nor likewise in the Dharmaśāstra.
Having acquired a tamasic faith, he brings about the loss of wealth;
he practices malice toward everyone and does not attain peace. ||40||
Having conquered both passion and the quality of rajas, yet being wrathful, evil-minded, and deceitful, he conducts himself according to his own whims amidst all extended objects of experience.
Rajas does not exist alone, nor does tamas;
the qualities (guṇas) always function by depending on one another, possessing the nature of a pair.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 9:
Without rajas, sattva cannot exist; nor can rajas ever exist without sattva.
And these do not exist at all without darkness, O bull among men. (43)
But that which is devoid of both [rajas and tamas] is never alone;
indeed, all the qualities (guṇas), characterized by duality, exist within various effects.
All are mutually dependent and do not exist when separated from one another;
for they are each other's progenitors, since they possess the nature of procreation.
Sometimes sattva produces rajas and tamas; and sometimes rajas produces both sattva and tamas. (46)
Sometimes, however, darkness produces both goodness and passion;
likewise, they produce one another, just as clay produces a jar.
Established in the Buddha, those qualities mutually awaken one another, just as Devadatta, Viṣṇumitra, Yajñadatta, and others [do]. (48)
Just as a woman and a man form a couple with one another, so too do the qualities (guṇas) enter into a state of union with one another. 49.
Sattva is the pair of rajas; rajas is the pair of sattva.
Both these, sattva and rajas, are known as the pair of tamas. ||50||
Nārada said:
"Having heard this unsurpassed account of qualities and forms as told by my father, I myself then questioned the Grandfather."
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Nārada said:
"O dear one, you have indeed described the characteristics of the qualities (guṇas)."
I am not satiated, even as I drink the sweet nectar flowing from your mouth. (1)
Describe the qualities of the virtues as they truly are,
so that I may attain supreme peace within my mind.
Vyāsa said:
Thus questioned by his son, the high-souled Nārada,
the creator of the world, who has arisen from the quality of passion (rajas), spoke.
Brahmā said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall describe the qualities;
I do not know them perfectly, yet I shall tell you according to my own understanding. 4.
Sattva alone is never perceived anywhere;
rather, due to their mutual intermingling, it appears as if they are mixed together.
Just as a certain excellent woman, adorned with all ornaments and endowed with graceful gestures and expressions, brings delight to her husband through her passion; || 6 ||
She likewise brings joy to her mother and father as well as to her circle of kinsmen;
yet she indeed produces only sorrow and delusion among co-wives.
Thus, by that very same essence which had been brought to the state of womanhood—
Otherwise, the activity of both rajas and tamas would be produced. ||8||
Indeed, through the passion (rajas) created by woman and likewise through darkness (tamas), and from their mutual union, affection appears in a different way. 9.
O Nārada, because they abide within their own inherent natures, no contrary species are ever perceived anywhere through yoga,
just as a beautiful woman is adorned by her youth.
She was endowed with modesty and sweetness, as well as possessed of discipline. || 11 ||

She was knowledgeable in the rules of the science of love (kāmaśāstra) and esteemed even in the science of duty (dharmaśāstra); she became a source of delight to her husband and a cause of grief for her co-wives. 12.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter nine.

Abiding in the nature of delusion and suffering, it is called "abiding in existence" (sattvasthā) by people; likewise, when that existence undergoes transformation, it indeed appears as another state of being.
For virtuous people who are harassed by thieves, that very army brings happiness;
yet for the bandits, it is painful and bewildering—such are its qualities.
They naturally avoid erroneous perception, just as one avoids a foul day that has arisen, shrouded by dense, great clouds. (15)
Accompanied by lightning and thunder, enveloped in darkness, and raining down as it drenches the earth—that indeed is described as having the form of darkness (tamas). ||16||
That very same day which is indeed extremely distressing for farmers becomes a source of happiness when they are provided with seeds and implements. || 17 ||
And for those unfortunate householders whose houses are not well-concealed, who have taken up grass and wood, it brings particular suffering. (18)
Even for women whose husbands are away, it brings about delusion;
indeed, all their natural qualities appear as their opposites.
Furthermore, O son, listen as I describe their characteristics:
sattva is always light, illuminating, stainless, and pure. (20)
When the limbs are indeed light, as are the sense organs such as the eyes,
and when the mind is likewise pure, it perceives those objects of the senses.
Then, sattva is to be understood as being intensely manifest in the body;
furthermore, rajas is characterized by agitation, arrogance, lethargy, and restlessness.
When that [passion] becomes intense within the body of anyone whatsoever, Kali seeks to take possession of them, even as they go to another village. (23)
When that [passion] becomes excessive in one whose mind is restless and who is thus intent on dispute,
then desire, which is a heavy veil, becomes darkness (tamas).
At that time, the limbs quickly become heavy and are overcome by obstruction.
The senses and the mind are empty; he does not desire sleep at all.
"O Nārada, the characteristics of the qualities (guṇas) should be understood here in this way.
Nārada said:
"O Grandfather, the three qualities have been described as having distinct characteristics. (26)
How do they perform their eternal task together in a single place, for it is said that even enemies, though distinct, unite with one another? ||27||
"Tell me, how do they perform their functions while remaining in one place?
Brahmā said:
"Listen, my son, I shall explain; these qualities have the nature of lamps. (28)
And just as a lamp performs its function of revealing objects, wherein the wick, the oil, and the flame are mutually contradictory [yet act together]. (29)
For in that way, oil is indeed incompatible when joined with fire;
oil is opposed to the wick, and fire likewise is opposed to each other.
Remaining in one place, they provide a manifestation of all categories of objects.
Nārada said:
Thus, O son of Satyavatī, have the qualities born of Prakṛti been described. 31.
"Indeed, the cause of the universe has been told to you by me exactly as I heard it before.
Vyāsa said:
"Thus was everything explained to me in full detail by Nārada. (32)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 10:
The complete definition of the qualities (guṇas) and their respective functions, categorized individually.
The Supreme Power is to be praised, by whom all this is pervaded. ||33||
Indeed, she is always both with attributes (saguṇā) and without attributes (nirguṇā) according to the distinction of her effects;
the Puruṣa, however, is the non-agent, complete, desireless, supreme, and immutable. || 34 ||
This Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) creates the universe, which consists of both the existent and the non-existent; she is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Sūrya, Candra, and the Lord of Śacī.
The Aśvins, the Vasus, Tvaṣṭṛ, Kubera, the Lord of the Waters (Varuṇa), Vahni, Vāyu, as well as Pūṣan, Senānī, and Vināyaka; || 36 ||
All are endowed with power and capable of performing their own respective tasks;
otherwise, they would indeed be powerless and unable even to move.
And she alone, O King, is the cause and the supreme sovereign of the world;
worship her, O ruler of the earth, and perform a sacrifice, O lord of men. (38)
One should perform worship with supreme devotion according to the prescribed rite for her alone:
[as] Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, and likewise Mahāsarasvatī. (39)
She is the sovereign of all beings, the cause of all causes;
she bestows all desired objects, is peaceful, easy to serve, and endowed with compassion. (40)
She bestows the fruits of desired objects merely by the utterance of her name;
she was formerly propitiated by the gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. (41)
And by various ascetics desiring liberation who had conquered their selves, even that name which was indistinct was uttered, though only incidentally. (42)
It grants all desired objects, even those that are entirely difficult to obtain, when one utters "Ai Ai!
out of fear upon seeing a tiger or other such beasts in the forest. (43)
It has been said that it indeed bestows even the most desired object, though one may be destitute;
O best of kings, the example of Satyavrata himself is seen in this regard.
Moreover, this example of that [truth] among assemblies of Brahmins is directly perceived by us wise ones, as well as by sages of purified souls. (45)
O King, listen as I relate everything in full detail that was heard by me:
there was a twice-born man named Satyavrata who was illiterate and a great fool;
having heard the syllable "Ko," he himself then uttered it from his mouth.
By chance, he was born as this most excellent of the wise, though devoid of the bindu. || 47 ||
Then, upon the utterance of the syllable *ai*, the Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign, being moist with compassion, became pleased and made him a king of poets. ||4||
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 9 ||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
Who was that Brāhmaṇa named Satyavrata, O best of the twice-born?
In which country was he born, and what was he like? Tell me this.
How was that sound heard by him, and how was it uttered again?
And what kind of supernatural power (siddhi) arose for that brahmin at that very moment?
"How was that Bhavānī, who is all-knowing and established in all things, satisfied? Tell us today this delightful story in detail.
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by the king, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
spoke these most noble, flavorful, and pure words.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall relate this auspicious ancient narrative (paurāṇikī kathā),
which was previously heard by me in the assemblies of sages, O best of the Kurus.
Once, O best of the Kurus, while performing a pure pilgrimage to sacred fords,
I arrived at the purifying Naimiṣa forest, which is frequented by sages.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter ten. 130.
Having prostrated before all the sages, he remained there in that excellent hermitage where the sons of Brahmā resided,
who were liberated while living and observers of great vows.
While that very conversation was underway in the assembly of brahmins, Jamadagni, remaining seated there, questioned the sages in this manner: (8)
Jamadagni said:
"O illustrious ascetics, there is a doubt in my mind;

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Indra, Varuṇa, Anala, Kubera, Pavana, Tvaṣṭṛ, the General, and the Lord of the Gaṇas; || 10 ||
The Sun, the Aśvins, Bhaga, Pūṣan, the Lord of the Night (the Moon), and likewise the other planets—
who among them is most worthy of worship, who bestows the fruit of desired objects,

"Let the sages, who are all-knowing and firm in their vows, speak quickly.
When this question had been asked there, Lomaśa spoke these words:
"O Jamadagni, listen to this which has now been asked by you."
She is the most worthy of being served by all who desire auspiciousness;
she is the supreme primordial nature, omnipresent, and eternally auspicious. 14.
She alone is the mother of the gods and of the high-souled ones beginning with Brahmā;
she is indeed the primordial material cause and the root of the tree of worldly existence.
When remembered and invoked, the Goddess truly grants whatever is desired.
Always possessing a compassionate heart, she was propitiated for the granting of boons. || 16 ||
I shall proclaim this auspicious history; let the sages listen to how it was obtained by me, a twice-born, merely through the utterance of syllables. 17.
In the land of Kosala, there was a certain twice-born man renowned as Devadatta;
being childless, he performed a sacrifice for the sake of a son according to the prescribed rites.
Having established himself on the bank of the Tamasā and constructed an excellent pavilion,
he summoned the twice-born who were knowers of the Vedas and experts in the performance of sacrificial rites.
Having prepared the sacrificial altar according to the rules and established the fires,
that best of the twice-born performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice there in accordance with the prescribed rites.
He appointed the best of sages, Suhotra, as the Brahmā priest;
Yājñavalkya as the Adhvaryu; and Bṛhaspati as the Hotṛ.
Having duly appointed Paila as the Prastotṛ and Gobhila as the Udgātṛ, along with other sages as the members of the assembly, he bestowed wealth upon them according to the prescribed rites.
The Udgātṛ priest, the most excellent singer of the Sāman, sang the Rathantara hymn endowed with the seven musical notes and accompanied by modulated tones.
Then, as he repeatedly exhaled, his voice broke;
Devadatta became enraged and spoke secretly to Gobhila. (24)
"O chief of sages, you are a fool; today you have caused a break in my voice while I was engaged in a ritual for desire, performing a sacrifice for the sake of a son. (25)
Then Gobhila, being greatly provoked, said to Devadatta:

In the bodies of all living beings, however, inhalation and exhalation are very difficult to perceive;
O high-minded one, I have no fault whatsoever in this matter regarding the breaking of my voice. (27)
Having heard those words of the high-souled Gobhila,
Devadatta, fearing the curse, spoke to him in great distress.
"O Lord of Sages, why are you angry with me in vain, for I am innocent? For sages are indeed free from anger and are always bestowers of happiness.
O Lord of Sages, since my offense was so slight, why have I been cursed by you?"
"I am childless; though already deeply tormented, I have been made to suffer even more. (30)
Those who know the Vedas consider childlessness better than having a foolish son;

Like a beast and like a Śūdra, he is unfit for all ritual duties.
O best of the twice-born, what shall I do with this foolish son?
There is no doubt that a Brāhmaṇa who is foolish is just like a Śūdra.
He is unworthy of worship, unworthy of gifts, and censurable in all undertakings.
(33) In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the Third Skandha, Chapter 10. [Page 131]
Even while residing in the country, a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the Vedas should be regarded by the king as a mere laborer, equal to a Śūdra.

A king should regard such a person as equal to a Śūdra and should not employ him in any duties;
rather, even if he be a twice-born, he should be treated like a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of the Vedas.
The Śrāddha should indeed be performed with a vessel made of kuśa grass in the absence of a worthy Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Śrāddha should never be performed by a foolish Brāhmaṇa.
One should not give food in excess of what is required for sustenance to an unwise person;
the giver falls into hell, and the recipient all the more so. (38)
Indeed, that kingdom belongs to such a king in whose land ignorant people are honored—even with gifts, respect, and the like—if they are foolish brahmins. (39)
Whether in sitting, in worship, or in giving, there is no difference whatsoever;
however, the wise man must indeed discern the difference between a fool and a scholar. (40)
A wise man should by no means dwell in that country where fools are honored with gifts, respect, and patronage like the dung of a cow. 41.
The riches of the wicked serve only to benefit other evil people;
though the mango tree is laden with fruit, by whom else is it enjoyed save by crows? (42)
Having eaten food, one who knows the Vedas indeed performs the study of the Vedas;

"O best among the knowers of the Vedas, what indeed was said by you [regarding] Gobhila?
In this world, the state of being the son of a fool is more contemptible than death. (44)
"O illustrious one, show compassion and favor toward Vāpa;

Having spoken thus, Devadatta fell at his feet,

Then Gobhila, seeing him there with a dejected mind, [reproached him], for great men are indeed quick to anger, while the most wicked are angry for an entire kalpa. || 47 ||
Water is cold by its very nature; it becomes hot through contact with fire or sunlight, but in their absence, it quickly becomes cool again. (48)
The compassionate Gobhila said to the deeply distressed Devadatta:
"Though your son has become a fool, he will indeed become a learned man. (49)
Having thus received the boon, that bull among brahmins was then delighted;
having looked upon the brahmins, he dismissed them according to the prescribed rites.
After some time, his wife Rūpamatī,
who was virtuous and like Rohiṇī herself, conceived a child in due season.
The twice-born performed the rites beginning with the conception ceremony (garbhādhāna) according to the rules,
as well as the rite for ensuring the birth of a male child (puṃsavana) and the decoration of the fetus.
The parting of the hair ceremony was performed according to Vedic injunctions;
and considering the sacrifice to have been fruitful, he joyfully gave various gifts.
On an auspicious day, when the moon was in conjunction with Rohiṇī, Rohiṇī gave birth to a son;
on that day, at a most excellent and favorable moment, he performed the birth-rite (jātakarman).
Having performed the ceremony for beholding his son, he also performed the naming rite;
the knower of ancient lore gave the name "Utathya" to his son.
And in his eighth year, on an auspicious day under favorable conditions,
his father duly performed the rite of initiation for him according to the prescribed rules.
The Guru taught the Vedas to him who was established in his vow;
yet Utathya did not speak at all, remaining then like one who is bewildered.
Though repeatedly admonished by his father, the rogue did not maintain his composure;
like one utterly deluded, he remained as he was, and his father then grieved for him.
Acting thus, he became habituated through constant practice for twelve years;
yet he did not know how to perform the rite of the Sandhyā-vandana according to the prescribed rules.
He became a fool among all people; the news spread very widely among all the Brahmins, as well as among the others.
=== PAGE 132 === O Sage, the world laughed at that brāhmaṇa wherever he went. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 11.
Then his father and mother censured him, severely rebuking that fool.
Then, though censured at will by the people, his parents, and his kinsmen,
the Brahmin attained a state of detachment and went to the forest.
"A blind man is better than a son who is a fool," having been told this by his parents, he indeed entered the forest.
Having constructed an unsurpassed hut at a beautiful spot on the bank of the Gaṅgā and having resolved upon a forest-dwelling way of life, he remained there with a concentrated mind. 64.
Having made a supreme vow, I do not speak an untruth;
for he remained in that delightful hermitage, devoted to the vow of celibacy.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Lomaśa said:
He knows nothing whatsoever of Vedic study, nor likewise of recitation (japa).
Neither meditation nor the propitiation of deities is of any avail in that regard. ||1||
That brahmin did not know the *āsana*, nor again the *prāṇāyāma*; he knew neither *pratyāhāra* nor the cause that is *bhūtaśuddhi*. (2)
He did not know the mantra-kīlaka, nor the japa, nor the Gāyatrī;
nor did he know the rules for purification, the procedure for bathing, or likewise the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
That sage knew neither the Prāṇāgnihotra, nor the offering of food, nor the guest; he knew neither the twilight prayers, nor the sacrificial fuel, nor likewise the oblation.
Having risen in the morning, he performed whatever dental cleansing was necessary and bathed in the Ganges like a Śūdra, devoid of mantras.
Just as one who has taken wild fruits at will even at midday does not know the distinction between what is edible and what is inedible, so too is the rogue.
Standing there, he spoke the truth and never again uttered a falsehood;
therefore, the people gave that brahmin the name Satyatapas.
One should not do what is harmful to anyone, nor likewise what is unrighteous anywhere;
reflecting thus, one sleeps happily right there, free from fear.
"When will my death come? I live in misery in the forest;
fie on the life of a fool! Death is surely better by force. (9)
"I have been made a fool by fate; there is no other cause for this in my case. Having obtained an excellent birth, it has now become useless for me. (10)
Just as a barren woman may be beautiful, or as a tree may be fruitless,
or as a cow may yield no milk, even so have I been rendered fruitless.
"What indeed am I blaming? Surely such was my past karma; I did not give a book, having had one made, to a high-souled Brahmin. (12)
"Indeed, in a previous birth, pure knowledge was not bestowed upon me by you;
therefore, through that karma, I am a rogue and the lowest of the twice-born.
Neither have I performed penance at a sacred ford, nor have I served the holy sages."
The twice-born were not honored by him with material gifts; therefore, I have been born with a wicked mind. || 14 ||
The sons of sages, who have mastered the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, are present here;
yet, by some stroke of fate, I have become utterly deluded. (15)
I do not know how to perform austerities; what effective means can I employ?
This resolve of mine is surely in vain, for my fortune is indeed not auspicious. 16.
I consider fate alone to be supreme; fie upon useless human effort! Whatever task is performed with labor comes about entirely through fate. (17)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and indeed the gods headed by Śakra—all are subject to Time; for Time is truly difficult to overcome.
Thus endowed with such qualities, the twice-born man, performing his duties day and night,
remained there in that hermitage on the sacred bank of the Jahnavī. (19)
Having become dispassionate, that twice-born man remained in that hermitage;
peaceful, he spent his time in the solitary forest.

While he remained thus in the forest of pure waters for fifteen years at his will, he did not perform propitiation nor recitation, nor did he know any mantra; he simply spent his time there in the forest.
The world knows his vow alone to be extensive; indeed, even though he is a sage, he speaks the truth. His fame has spread among all people, for this Satyavrata constantly speaks no falsehood at will.
Once, while he was enjoying a hunt, a Niṣāda hunter named Niśaṭha arrived, carrying a bow and arrows.
Sporting in that vast forest, he possessed a body like Yama, had a cruel appearance, and was exceedingly skilled in the act of killing.
Pierced by an arrow drawn back too far by that Kirāta wielding the bow, the boar—
Fleeing and overwhelmed by fear, he ran and came into the presence of the sage. ||24||
When he, trembling and his body drenched in blood, reached the precincts of the hermitage,
the sage, seeing him so wretched, was then overcome by an exceedingly compassionate disposition.
Seeing the boar running ahead with its body drenched in blood and suddenly pierced, the sage,
trembling intensely out of an overwhelming surge of compassion, then uttered the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī.

Though he had heard of it before as something previously unknown, and though it had indeed come forth from the mouth of the gods, that deluded sage did not recognize the seed; thus that high-souled muni sank into grief.
A boar entered that circle of hermitages and, having gone into a thicket, remained hidden therein.
Having not yet attained the path, his mind was firmly despondent as he trembled from being afflicted by arrows. || 28 ||
Then, in an instant, he arrived at the edge of that place, wielding a bow drawn back to its limit, his body appearing most terrifying;
indeed, though being sought, he was the King of the Niṣādas who was Time itself.

Seeing the sage named Satyavrata, who was seated there upon a mat of kuśa grass and was without equal, the hunter bowed before him and stood at his feet, asking: "O lord of the twice-born, where has the boar gone? (30)
I know your celebrated vow of excellent conduct; therefore, pierced by my arrow today, I ask you:
I have indeed come here desiring to support my entire family, which is afflicted by hunger. (31)
"O best of Brahmins, this is the livelihood ordained for me by the Creator; there is no other, I speak the truth.
One must certainly support one's family here by some means or another, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (32)
"Tell the truth today, for you are one whose vow is truth. Your dependents are suffering from hunger.
Where have you gone, O Brahmin? I ask you: tell me quickly where the boar pierced by the arrow has gone! (33)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter eleven.
Thus questioned, that high-souled sage, though deeply immersed in reflection, readily replied:
"May my vow of truth not be broken today; for what indeed is the use of speaking of one who has not been seen? (34)

The boar has entered here with its body pierced by arrows; how can I speak today whether it be false or true? Afflicted by hunger, he seems to be questioning me, yet upon seeing him, [the hunter] will surely kill the pig.
Indeed, that which involves violence is not truth, even if it be true; whereas untruth accompanied by compassion is truly truth.
That alone is truth by which benefit comes to men in this world, and not otherwise. (36)

"How might there be benefit for both who are in opposition? What answer would not be a false word?"—pondering thus in this dilemma of dharma, O Vāḍava, he did not find the words to speak as was appropriate. (37)

Seeing the boar struck by the arrow yet filled with compassion, Śivā, who was moved by those words uttered at that moment, became pleased and granted him her own seed—the difficult-to-attain Vidyā. (38)
Through the utterance of the seed-syllable, the entire Vidyā of the Goddess manifested;
and just as it was before, the poet Vālmīki likewise came into being. (39)
The twice-born Satyakāma, righteous-souled and devoted to compassion, spoke this single verse to the hunter who stood before him with his bow:

"O hunter, seeking your own interest, you ask again and again."
Having been addressed thus by him at that time, the slaughterer of animals departed;

But there was a brahmin born as a poet, like another Prācetas, a twice-born man renowned in all the worlds by the name Satyavrata. (43)
Then he chanted the seed-mantra of Sarasvatī according to the prescribed rites:
"O twice-born one, you are a most renowned scholar upon the surface of the earth. (44)
On every festival day, the Brahmins always sing his glory,
and indeed the sages chant his very extensive narrative.
Having heard that, he went to his hermitage and reached his dwelling;
by him who had previously abandoned him, he was now led home and treated with the highest honor.
Therefore, O King, she should always be honored with devotion by the army;
for she is the primordial power, the supreme goddess, and indeed the cause of the worlds.
O great king, perform her sacrifice according to the Vedic injunctions;

When remembered, fully worshipped with devotion, meditated upon, practiced, and praised, she grants all desired objects; therefore, she is celebrated as Kāryadā (the Giver of Success).
O King, this power must be exercised in every way by the wise, having seen those afflicted by disease, the miserable, the hungry, the destitute, and the deceitful. (50)
He likewise [saw] people who were fools, constantly oppressed by enemies,

Those who are distressed by unfulfilled desires for food and enjoyments, whose senses are never subdued, who are dominated by craving, who lack capability, and who are constantly oppressed by their masters. ||52||
Likewise, they saw those endowed with wealth, increasing in sons and grandsons,
with nourished bodies, possessed of enjoyments, and expounders of the Vedas.
Then [he saw] heroes endowed with royal fortune who had brought people under their control,
as well as those separated from their kinsmen, all of whom were marked by every auspicious characteristic.
A wise person should investigate through both positive and negative concomitance;
for if the auspicious Goddess, the bestower of the fruits of all goals, is not worshipped with these [offerings], she remains unpropitiated. 55.
And thus Ambikā was always propitiated by these men in the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 12.
Therefore, all these people in this world of transmigration are undoubtedly happy. (56)
Vyāsa said:
Thus, O King, I heard there in that assembly of sages the excellent majesty of the Goddess at will from the mouth of Lomaśa.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 11 ||
