The King said:
"Tell me correctly the ritual procedure for that Goddess in its entirety."
"O Mistress, having heard this, I shall indeed act according to my ability, remaining unwearied. || 1 ||
The ritual procedure for worship, the mantras, and the materials for the fire-oblation without doubt; the number of Brahmins, as well as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). ||2||
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe the sacrifice to the Goddess according to the prescribed rules;
it should always be known as threefold, performed through rites seen in the sacred ordinances.
It is of three kinds: sattvic, rājasic, and likewise another, tāmasa.
That which is sattvic is declared for sages, while that which is rājasic is remembered for kings.
I shall describe to you in detail that which is tamasic among the rākṣasas, that which is devoid of qualities among the wise, and that which consists of knowledge among the liberated. 5.

They know that sacrifice to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika) wherein the place, the time, the materials, the mantras, the officiating priests, and the faith are all characterized by goodness. 6.
O King, if there be purity of substance, purity of action, and purity of mantra, then the fruit becomes complete; not otherwise. (7)
If a meritorious deed is performed using wealth acquired through unjust means, it yields neither fame in this world nor its fruit in the next world. (8)
Therefore, one should always perform virtuous deeds only with wealth acquired through righteous means; for such action leads indeed to fame, to the next world, and to happiness.
O Indra among kings, it is evident to you that the Pāṇḍava has performed the Rājasūya,
the best of sacrifices, which was completed with excellent sacrificial fees.
There, Hari Kṛṣṇa himself, the high-minded lord of the Yādavas,
was present, as were Brāhmaṇas who had perfected their learning, such as Bhāradvāja and others.
Having completed the sacrifice perfectly within a single month by the Pāṇḍavas,
they encountered even greater hardship and the terrible forest exile.
The oppression of the princess of Pañcāla, as well as the defeat at dice, the forest exile so full of great hardship—where has the fruit born of sacrifice gone? (13)
And servitude was performed for Virāṭa by all those high-souled ones;

What indeed is to be considered here as the cause of this deficiency in dharma,
while Keśava, the lord of gods, and Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, are present?
If it were taught that "it must come to pass," then the arrival of that [result] would be fruitless;

All means of accomplishment are fruitless and every method is useless;
yet that which is destined to happen will surely come to pass, even when it is expressed in words.

Even the sacred tradition would become mere empty praise, and all ritual actions would be purposeless;
likewise, austerity for the sake of heaven and the duty of the social classes would be in vain.
Every effort would be in vain if what is destined has already been fixed in the heart;
both must be considered: destiny and the means. (21)
If, when a rite has been performed, success should turn out to be the opposite of what was expected, then the wise—the crowns of the learned—should infer some deficiency in the procedure. 22.

That ritual action has been described in many ways by learned practitioners of ritual, again due to the differences among performers, the differences among mantras, and likewise the differences among substances. (23)
Just as in the past Viśvarūpa was chosen as his preceptor by Maghavan,
