Having repeatedly said, "Svāhā to the gods and to the Dānavas," the protection of those on his mother’s side, the Asuras, was ensured. Then,
seeing the Daityas exceedingly prosperous, Maghavan became enraged.
Hari swiftly severed his heads with the thunderbolt. ||26||
There is no doubt that the ritual was defective due to a difference in the performers;
otherwise, the rite would have been performed by the King of Pañcāla even with his wrath. (27)
For the destruction of Bhāradvāja and for the birth of a son,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna was born from the midst of the sacrificial altar, and Draupadī likewise.
Formerly, when Daśaratha also performed a sacrifice for the sake of sons,
four sons were born to him who had been childless.
Therefore, O best of kings, an action performed with proper reasoning will always grant success; if performed without reasoning, it will always have the opposite effect. 30.
O King, just as the Pāṇḍavas obtained a contrary result at their sacrifice due to some deficiency, so too did they suffer defeat at dice;
yet Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, remains a speaker of truth.
And the virtuous Draupadī, as well as his other auspicious younger brothers.
Whether a deficiency has arisen in the sacrifice due to the use of inferior materials, or a defect has occurred because it was performed by those possessed of pride. (33)
O Great King, that sacrifice which is characterized by sattva is indeed remembered as difficult to attain;
for this great sacrifice is ordained specifically for the Vaikhānasa sages. (34)
Those ascetics who always partake of sattvic food—righteously acquired, consisting of forest produce, and well-prepared with wild herbs. (35)

O King, sacrifices that are constantly devoted to sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa), performed without a sacrificial post (viyūpa), preceded by mantras, and characterized by an abundance of faith, are remembered as the supreme sāttvika sacrifices. 36.
The sacrifices of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are characterized by passion (rājasa), involve abundant materials, feature well-constructed sacrificial posts, and are performed with great pride. 37.

Those sacrifices of the Dānavas which are characterized by darkness (tāmasa), accompanied by anger, increasing intoxication, full of malice, refined for cruelty, and violent, have been described by the great-souled ones. 38.
For the sages who desire liberation, who are dispassionate and great-souled, sacrifice performed mentally is considered to be endowed with all means of accomplishment. (39)
In all other sacrifices, there may be something deficient—
whether in the ritual materials, in faith, in the performance, or likewise by the officiating Brahmins.

Through all the means consisting of place, time, distinct substances, and so forth, when [the ritual] is complete, one indeed does not become anything else; rather, the mind becomes [one with the goal]. || 41 ||
First, however, the mind must be purified, freed from all qualities;
when the mind is pure, the body is indeed pure—of this there is no doubt. (42)
When the mind has become pure, having abandoned the objects of the senses,
then he shall possess the authority for that sacrifice.
Having constructed a pavilion extending over many yojanas,
he [honored it] with extensive and elegant hymns made from sacrificial wood.
There, one should mentally visualize the Vedas clearly;
likewise, one should indeed mentally establish the fires according to the prescribed rite. (45)
Having likewise performed the selection of the Brahmins, [he appointed] the Brahmā, the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, and the Prastotṛ according to the prescribed rules. (46)
The Udgātṛ, the Pratihartṛ, and the other members of the assembly, as well as the best of the twice-born, are to be honored with effort according to the rules, even with the mind alone. 47.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 12:
Prāṇa, apāna, as well as vyāna, samāna, and udāna.
These five purifiers are to be placed upon the altar according to the prescribed rule.
Then the Gārhapatya fire is the prāṇa, the Āhavanīya fire is the apāna, the Dakṣiṇāgni fire is the vyāna, and the Āvasathyaka fire is the samāna. || 49 ||
For these purifiers are remembered as perfectly pure and supremely powerful;
and the substance should be contemplated by the mind as being devoid of qualities, supreme, and pure.
At that time, the mind itself was the Hotṛ priest and likewise the sacrificer;
it was also the supreme deity of the sacrifice—the attributeless and eternal Brahman. (51)
The power that bestows fruit is devoid of qualities; she is eternally auspicious and grants detachment.
She is the knowledge of Brahman, the support of all, pervading and abiding everywhere. (52)
With that as his objective, the twice-born one should offer that substance into the fires of the vital breaths;
thereafter, O Lord, having rendered the mind supportless, he should likewise offer the vital breaths.
One should offer oblations into the eternal Brahman through the path of the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī;
one should perceive the Self abiding within one's own experience, and all beings within the Self.
Through the yoga of concentration alone, one should meditate with an undisturbed mind upon the Self abiding in all beings, and all beings within the Self. (55)
When the elemental self (bhūtātmā) has reached its full development, then it beholds that auspicious one;
having seen her, who is the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss, it becomes a knower of Brahman.
Then, O protector of the earth, everything beginning with illusion (māyā) is burnt away;
however, only the karma that has already begun (prārabdha-karma) remains as long as the body persists. || 57 ||
Then he becomes liberated while living, and upon death, he shall attain liberation;
O dear one, he who worships the Mother of the Universe has accomplished all that was to be done. 58.
Therefore, with every effort, the illustrious Bhuvaneśvarī should be meditated upon;
she should also be heard and reflected upon in accordance with the words of the Guru. || 59 ||
O King, a sacrifice performed in this manner bestows liberation; there is no doubt about this.
Other sacrifices, however, being characterized by desire, lead toward decay.
"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma according to the rules"—this, the wise declare, is the instruction of the Vedas. (61)
When their merit is exhausted, they enter the world of mortals according to their mental disposition;
therefore, the mental sacrifice is superior, for it is indeed inexhaustible.
This sacrifice is not fit to be performed by a king who desires victory;
previously you performed the Sarpa-yajña, which was characterized by darkness (tāmasa), and now you have done so again.
O King, the enmity of the evil-minded Takṣaka has been avenged,
for it was on his account that millions of other serpents were slain by you in the fire.
"O best of kings, perform today the sacrifice to the Goddess, performed extensively according to the threefold rule, which was formerly performed by Viṣṇu at the beginning of creation. (65)
"Act accordingly, O Indra among kings; I shall explain the ritual procedure to you.
There are Brahmins present, O Indra among kings, who are experts in the ritual and most learned in the Vedas. (66)
Those who know the ritual application of the seed-syllables of the goddesses and are skilled in the path of mantras shall become the officiating priests; you yourself, indeed, shall be the patron.
Having performed the sacrifice according to the rules and having bestowed the merit earned from the rite,
O Great King, deliver your father who has fallen into an evil state.
O sinless one, the sin born of insulting a Brahmin—which is difficult to overcome and leads to hell—as well as the fault arising from a curse, has been incurred by your father. (69)
Likewise, an untimely death was met by the king through the bite of a serpent;
yet his death occurred in the interval [of the sky], and not upon the earth on the bed of kusha grass. (70) By the king;
in the interval likewise.
"O best of the Kurus, your father's death occurred there in that palace, devoid of battle or the merit of bathing and giving gifts in the Ganges. (71)
O best of kings, all these things are miserable and lead to hell;
yet, among them, there is one cause that has not arisen for him, which is exceedingly difficult to find.

Wherever the vital breath (prāṇa) may be situated, once it has recognized that the time [of death] has arrived, it is indeed helpless in the face of extreme peril, even in the absence of spiritual practices (sādhana). //73//
When one indeed attains detachment with a pure mind, thinking:
"The body consists of the five elements; what sorrow-giving thing is there in this? (74)
Today let it fall as it pleases; I am liberated, devoid of qualities, and immutable.
Since all principles are by nature subject to destruction, what cause for lamentation is there in that? (75)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter 13.
I am indeed Brahman, not a transmigrating being; I am eternally liberated and eternal.
My connection with the body is brought about by karma. (76)
All those [beings], both auspicious and otherwise, are liberated through their connection with a human body, by means of the attainment of pleasure and pain. || 77 ||
"Thus liberated from this terrible and most fearsome peril of saṃsāra"— reflecting in this manner, he remains free from both bathing and ritual offerings.
If he meets his death [at that moment], he is liberated from the suffering of birth;
this is declared to be the supreme state, difficult to attain even for yogins. (79)
O tiger among kings, having heard the curse uttered by the twice-born,
your father conceived a sense of "mine-ness" regarding his body and attained world-weariness.
"My body is free from disease and my kingdom is rid of all thorns;
how may I live as I desire? Let them indeed bring the knowledge of mantras. (81)
Then the king employed medicine, gems, mantras, as well as the supreme yantra, and likewise ascended to the pure abode.
Neither bathing was performed, nor charity given, nor was the Goddess remembered;
nor did he sleep upon the ground, considering the Lord to be supreme. (83)
In the vast and terrible ocean of delusion, he died like one struck by a serpent in his own palace;
having committed sin through the influence of the Kali age, it arose from his contempt for an ascetic.
By these very practices, hell will inevitably come to pass;
therefore, O best of kings, deliver that father from his sin. (85)
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, Janamejaya became afflicted with great sorrow, his throat choked with tears. 86.
"Fie upon this life of mine today, for my father remains in hell!
Therefore, I shall do that by which the son of Uttara may go to heaven this very day. (87)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 12 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
The King said:
O Grandfather, how was the sacrifice performed by Hari in the past?
By the powerful Viṣṇu, who exists in the form of the cause of the universe. ||1||
O high-minded one, who were the assistants there?
O scorcher of foes, tell me who were the officiating priests (ṛtvij), those who knew the true essence of the Vedas.
"Having heard of the sacrifice performed by Viṣṇu for Ambikā, I shall, with a concentrated mind, perform a sacrifice according to the rites prescribed by the sacred law. (3)
Vyāsa said:
O King, O highly fortunate one, listen to the most wonderful account in detail,
of how the sacrifice was performed by the Blessed One according to the prescribed rites.
When they had been dismissed by the Goddess after she had given them those three powers,
the men became lords of the city and ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Having reached the terrible great ocean, those three foremost of gods performed their ablutions and, having brought forth the earth for the sake of dwelling, they remained there.
Then the immovable power of support (ādhāra-śakti) was released by the Goddess herself;
supported by that, the earth, endowed with fatness (medas), became established. //7//
Because of its connection with the fat (medas) of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, it is known as Medinī;
because it supports (dhāraṇa), it is called Dhārā; and because of its vastness (vistāra), it is Pṛthvī. ||8||
And the earth, because of its great magnitude, was supported upon the head of Śeṣa;
and all the mountains were made extensive for the purpose of providing support.
Just as an iron nail [is driven] into wood, so were those mountains made for you;
O Great King, they are called "Mahīdhara" (Earth-bearer) by the wise.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, third book, chapter 139:
Mount Meru, consisting of gold and extending for many yojanas, [is situated there].
Adorned with peaks made of jewels, it was most wonderful to behold. || 11 ||
Marīci, Nārada, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Dakṣa, and Vasiṣṭha— these are the celebrated sons of Brahmā.
Kaśyapa was born from Marīci, and thirteen daughters were born to Dakṣa;
from them, indeed, gods and Daityas were produced in great numbers.
From that, the creation of the earth (Kāśyapī) proceeded in great detail, divided in many ways by the various species of humans, cattle, serpents, and so forth.
From the half-body of Brahmā, Manu Svāyambhuva was born, and from his left side, the woman Śatarūpā was likewise produced. || 15 ||
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were his two sons;
he also had three daughters of excellent form who were exceedingly beautiful. (16)
Having thus brought forth creation, the Lord born from the lotus fashioned the enchanting world of Brahmā upon the peak of Mount Meru.
Vaikuṇṭha is the supreme abode of Lord Viṣṇu, the delighter of Ramā;
it is a most beautiful place of play situated above all the worlds.
Śiva also created the supreme abode known as Kailāsa;
having reached it, he sported with his hosts of spirits according to his pleasure.
Heaven, known as Triviṣṭapa, is fashioned upon the summit of Mount Meru;
that abode of the Lord of the Gods is resplendent with various jewels. (20)
From the churning of the ocean, the Pārijāta, the best of trees, was obtained;
likewise the four-tusked elephant, and the wish-fulfilling cow that grants all desires.
Uśravas, Aśva, Raṃbhā, Ādya-prasa, and all else that was born as an ornament of heaven were indeed taken up by Indra. ||22||
And Dhanvantari and Candra emerged from the ocean;
these two gods, surrounded by many hosts, shone resplendent while stationed in heaven.
Thus, O best of kings, the threefold creation has arisen, fashioned in various ways through the distinctions of gods, animals, humans, and so forth. 24.
Indeed, living beings joined with their karma are born through four types of birth: from eggs, from sweat, from sprouts, and from wombs. (25)
Thus, having accomplished the creation, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara all engaged in their respective pastimes in their own abodes as they desired.
When the creation had thus proceeded, the Lord,
the Sovereign Acyuta, sported there in his own world together with Mahālakṣmī.
Once upon a time in the past, Viṣṇu was residing in Vaikuṇṭha;
he remembered the island situated in the ocean of nectar, which was adorned with jewels.
There, Mahāmāyā was seen and the auspicious mantra was attained; by remembering that supreme Śakti, he was transformed into the state of a woman.
The Lord of Ramā set his mind upon performing a sacrifice;
having ascended from that world, he summoned Maheśvara.
Brahmā, Varuṇa, Śakra, Kubera, Pāvaka, Yama, the divine Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Vāmadeva, and Bṛhaspati. ||31||
He prepared the sacrificial requisites on a very extensive scale;
they were endowed with great magnificence, characterized by purity (sattva), and captivating to the mind.
There, he had a spacious pavilion constructed by artisans,
and he chose twenty-seven officiating priests of excellent vows.
He caused a sacrificial altar to be constructed and very extensive altars as well;
the Brahmins recited mantras endowed with the seed-syllables of the Goddess.
They offered their oblation according to the prescribed rites in that sacrificial fire duly prepared;
and when the extensive homa had been performed, an incorporeal voice spoke.
Then, addressing Viṣṇu with a sweet voice and melodious syllables, she said:
"O Viṣṇu, O Hari, may you always be the most excellent among the gods. (36)
"Honored and worthy of worship, and even capable among the gods, Brahmā and all the others, including Vāsava, shall worship you. (37)
O Lord, through devotion, humans everywhere on earth shall become powerful;
and you indeed shall be the bestower of boons upon all among men. (38)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter fourteen.

The granter of desires to all the gods, the supreme Parameśvara, you are the chief among all sacrifices, the sacrificer worthy of worship by all. People shall worship you, and you shall become the bestower of boons.
And the gods, being greatly oppressed by the Dānavas, shall take refuge in you;
O Supreme Person, you shall become the shelter for all.
This shall be so in all the Purāṇas, in the Vedas, and in the extensive scriptures.
You are indeed most worthy of worship; your fame shall surely spread.
For whenever there is a decline of Dharma on the surface of the earth, [you appear]. (42)
"Descending swiftly with a portion of yourself, you must quickly perform the protection of Dharma. Your incarnations will be well-known on earth according to your respective parts;
indeed, O Mādhava, in all your incarnations across various wombs, you shall be honored by the great-souled ones on this earth. (43–44)
O Madhusūdana, you shall become renowned throughout all the worlds;
in all your incarnations, Śakti shall be your constant companion.
She shall manifest as a portion of myself, accomplishing all tasks in many ways through various forms such as Vārāhī and Nārasiṃhī.
Bearing diverse weapons, possessing auspicious forms, and adorned with every ornament, she shall appear in manifold ways.
O Viṣṇu, O Mādhava, joined with them, you always perform the works of the gods.
"You shall accomplish all that through the granting of boons by me;
you must never, even with the slightest trace of pride, hold them in contempt. (48)
They are certainly to be worshipped with effort and honored in every way;
indeed, those Śaktis in the land of Bhārata grant all desires. (49)
They shall be honored among men in images;
and their fame, as well as yours, O Lord of Gods, shall prevail throughout all lands. (50)
O highly fortunate one, those [rivers] renowned throughout the seven continents on the earth’s surface will indeed seek you out among the people on the earth’s surface.
O Hari, those possessed by desire will constantly worship you for the sake of their wishes, offering various articles of worship while imbued with diverse emotions. (52)
They shall worship you with mantras declared in the Vedas as well as with the recitation of your names; O Madhusūdana, your greatness shall be manifest in the mortal world and in heaven.
"O Lord of the gods, through worship by human beings, it shall attain increase.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus granted these boons, Vāṇī, who was born from the ether, became silent.
The Blessed One, the Lord Hari, having duly completed the sacrifice, became joyful in spirit, as if from hearing [the account]. || 55 ||
Then, having bid farewell to those gods, the sons of Brahmā, and the sages,
the one whose banner is Garuḍa departed for Vaikuṇṭha along with his attendants.
Then all the gods returned to their respective abodes,
while the sages, filled with wonder, conversed with one another.
Then, being greatly delighted, they went at their pleasure to their own purifying hermitages.
Having heard that most lucid voice born of the sky, which was delightful to the ears of all, a spirit of devotion toward Prakṛti arose in everyone.

All the hosts of twice-born ones and sages, filled with devotion, performed her worship according to the rites prescribed in the Agamas, O lords of sages, for she is the granter of all desires and fruits.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 13 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"O twice-born one, I have heard from you in detail how the sacrifice was prepared by Hari."
Likewise, tell me in detail the greatness of Ambā.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 14:
Having heard the life-story of the Goddess, I shall indeed perform an unsurpassed sacrifice.
And by your grace, O best of Brahmins, I shall become pure.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the supreme life-story of the Goddess;
I shall relate the history and the Purāṇa in great detail.
O Kausalya, the best of kings born of the Solar dynasty was the son of Puṣpa, known as the highly resplendent Dhruvasandhi. || 4 ||
Virtuous in soul, true to his promise, and devoted to the welfare of the social orders and stages of life,
he, pure in his vows, ruled the kingdom in the prosperous city of Ayodhyā.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other twice-born ones likewise lived according to dharma in that kingdom, each established in his own respective occupation.
In his kingdom, there were nowhere any thieves, slanderers, or rogues; indeed, no deceitful, ungrateful, or foolish men dwelt there. (7)
O best of the Kurus, while the king was living in this manner,
he had two wives who were endowed with beauty and capable of providing all sensual enjoyments.
Manoramā was his lawful wife, happy and exceedingly wise;
Līlāvatī was his second wife, and she too was endowed with beauty and virtue.
She dwelt with her two co-wives in the houses and in the groves,
upon pleasure-mountains, in long ponds, and in various palatial mansions.
At an auspicious time, Manoramā gave birth to an excellent son named Sudarśana, who was endowed with the marks of royalty. ||11||
Līlāvatī, his beautiful wife, also gave birth within one month to a handsome son on an auspicious lunar fortnight and on a favorable day.
There, the king performed the birth rites and other ceremonies for the two of them;
delighted by the birth of his sons, he bestowed gifts upon the Brahmins.
O King, the monarch bestowed equal affection upon his two daughters;
the king never made any distinction between them in his friendship.
The best of kings, that scorcher of foes, being filled with joy, performed the tonsure ceremony for the two of them according to the prescribed rite and in accordance with his means. (15)
Having had their tonsure ceremony performed, the two lovely sons, who delighted the hearts of the people as they played, captivated the mind of the king at will. (16)
Of the two, Sudarśana was the elder; the auspicious son of Līlāvatī was named Śatrujit, who was indeed full of endearing speech. (17)
He was a producer of joy for his father, possessed of pleasant speech and handsome appearance;
he was indeed beloved by the subjects as well as by the circle of ministers. || 18 ||
Thus the king felt affection for him because of his possession of virtuous qualities; however, due to his own misfortune, he did not feel such affection for Sudarśana.
As time passed in this manner, that best of kings, Dhruvasandhi,
who was always devoted to hunting, went into the middle of the forest.
Slaying ruru deer, kamba deer, boars, gavayas, hares, buffaloes,
sharabhas, and rhinoceroses, the king sported in the forest.
While the king was sporting there in that terrible and most fearsome forest,
an exceedingly wrathful lion emerged from a thicket.
First pierced by the king with a stone-tipped arrow, the lion fell under the sway of anger;
seeing the monarch before him, he roared with a sound like a thundercloud.
Raising his tail and spreading his great mane, he,
filled with extreme rage, leapt up into the air from the sky to slay the king.
Then the king, seeing him with speed, grasped a sword in his hand and, taking a shield in his left, stood like another lion. (25)
All his servants, filled with rage and possessed by fury, also discharged various arrows at will upon that lion. ||26||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter fourteen.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose and the combat became terrible;
then a fierce lion sprang upon the king.
Seeing it falling, the king struck it with his sword;
it too, having arrived there, tore him apart with its cruel claw-tips.
Struck by his claws, the king fell down and indeed died;
then those soldiers cried out and struck him with arrows.
The lion died right there, and the king likewise died; the soldiers, the chief ministers, and others arrived at that spot and reported [the news]. (30)
Having heard that the king had passed away to the other world, those excellent ministers went to the edge of the forest and performed the funeral rites.
There itself, Vasiṣṭha caused all the funeral rites to be performed according to the prescribed rules, which bring about happiness in the next world. (32)
The subjects, the ministers, and the great sage Vasiṣṭha held a consultation among themselves regarding how to make Sudarśana the king.
"The son of a lawful wife, peaceful, and a man of auspicious marks—he is indeed worthy of the royal throne," so said the best of ministers. (34)
Vasiṣṭha also spoke in the same manner: "This son of the king is worthy;
though he is but a child, he is a righteous king and deserves the royal throne here. (35)
When the counsel had been formulated by the elders of the ministers, a king named Yudhājin,
the lord of Tujjayinī, having heard of it, arrived there with speed.
Then, having heard that his son-in-law was dead, Līlāvatī’s father quickly came there, desiring to do what was pleasing to his daughter's son.
Likewise, Vīrasena arrived out of a desire for Sudarśana’s welfare,
as did the king who was the father of Manoramā, the lord of Kaliṅga.
Both kings, accompanied by their armies and overcome with trepidation,
held a consultation with those three chief ministers for the sake of the kingdom.
Then Yudhājit asked: "Of these two sons, which one shall obtain the kingdom? Surely the elder receives it, and never the younger. (40)
Vīrasena, the son of his lawful wife, spoke there as well:
"O King, according to what I have heard from those learned in the scriptures, he is indeed worthy of the kingdom."
Yudhājit spoke this again: "This one is the eldest, and likewise endowed with virtues;
he possesses the marks of a king, whereas Sudarśana does not."
A great dispute has arisen here between these two greedy kings;
who would be capable of dispelling this doubt in such an extreme crisis? (43)
Yudhājit said to his ministers: "You are indeed intent upon your own self-interest;
having made Sudarśana the king, you surely wish to enjoy the wealth. (44)
I have understood this deliberation of yours through your gestures;
therefore, Śatrujit, being possessed of strength, is approved by you for the royal throne.
While I am alive, who indeed would make my younger brother king,
abandoning the elder one who is endowed with virtues and accompanied by an army?
Surely I shall wage war; by the edge of my sword, that earth shall be split in two—what need is there for further words from you in this matter? (47)
Having heard that, Vīrasena spoke to Yudhājit:
"O wise one, there are two boys of equal intelligence; what difference is there here? (48)
While the two kings remained thus disputing,
the subjects and the sages became anxious in their minds.
And the vassal kings, intent on causing distress, gathered together with their armies;
eager for conflict with one another, they remained vigilant. || 50 ||
For the Niṣādas, who were residents of Śṛṅgaverapura,
arrived there to seize the royal property, having heard that the lord of the earth had died.
Hearing that the two young sons were engaged in mutual combat,
thieves arrived there from various regions and even from other lands.
A great crush occurred there when the battle was joined;
Yudhājit and Vīrasena both became desirous of combat. (53)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 14 ||
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book (Tṛtīyaskandha), chapter 15.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
When the battle had begun there between the two kings who had taken up their weapons for combat,
a tumultuous clash ensued as they were both equally under the sway of anger and greed.
That king, the conqueror of Pṛthulabāhu in battle, stood firm in the conflict with bow in hand;
joined by his own forces, vehicles, and attendants, the monarch was resolved upon the fray.

O Vīrasena, here in this battle, that king, equal in splendor to the Lord of the Gods, has stood firm, accompanied by his army and following the duty of a warrior for the sake of his daughter’s son. (3)
Seeing Yudhājit standing firm in battle, that king, filled with wrath and possessed of true prowess, released a rain of arrows upon him,
like a cloud charged with lightning pouring down torrents of water upon a mountain.
Vīrasena covered him with stone-sharpened arrows that were swift-moving and straight-flying;
and he, in turn, cut down with his own arrows those stone-tipped shafts discharged by the other, which fell with extreme velocity.
An exceedingly fierce battle took place between the elephants, chariots, and horses, watched by throngs of gods, men, and sages;
the sky was instantly covered by flocks of birds, such as vultures and others who feed on desire, eager to devour the flesh.
There, a wondrous and terrible river of blood flowed forth from the very herds of elephants, heroes, and horses;
it was terrifying to the eyes of men and reached its full extent among the wicked, like the path of the sun's offspring [Rāhu] at the time of an eclipse.
Human heads, covered with hair, lie scattered upon the broken sandbanks and shine just like gourd-pots placed there by those wishing to sport in the ocean,
as if they were offerings made by the sons of the Sun.
The hero is dead, gone to the earth, fallen indeed from his chariot; I think a vulture circles above for the sake of his flesh.
Yet even this soul, beholding its own lovely body, alas, desires to enter it again, despite being utterly helpless.
"O best of men, even when slain in battle, you are mounted upon a magnificent celestial chariot and speak to your beloved celestial nymph seated on your lap.
Behold, O lady with thighs like the trunk of an elephant, my beloved body, struck by arrows, has fallen upon the earth covered in dust. (10)
One enemy was slain, while another fled into the sky and reached a celestial chariot (vimāna) where he was united with a divine woman.
Meanwhile, that weak woman, having offered her body into the fire for her beloved, became strong and regained her husband.
In battle or in death, two brave warriors meet in heaven; slain by each other’s weapons, they depart together.
There, struck down for the sake of a celestial nymph, those two, overcome by passion and agitated by strife, strike one another repeatedly.
A certain youth, having obtained a celestial maiden who was indeed exceedingly beautiful, virtuous, and full of devotion.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter fifteen:
At that time, proclaiming his own expanded virtues, he, being absorbed in yoga, emulated her who bestows love.
The dust of the earth spread far and wide, reaching even into the sky; it made the night and completely veiled the sun.
That very dust suddenly appeared submerged in an ocean of blood, and the sun too became shorn of its brilliance. || 14 ||

It is said that someone who had gone to the sky, having encountered a celestial maiden of beautiful countenance who was full of devotion, did not accept her, fearing the destruction of his vows; for he thought, "This woman will come to me with flattering words in vain. (15)
When that battle had commenced there, Yudhājit, the lord of the earth,
struck Vīrasena with sharp and terrible arrows.
Slain, that lord of the earth fell to the ground with his head severed;
his entire army was shattered and fled in the four directions.
Having heard that her father had been slain at the front of the battle, Manoramā became terrified with fear as she recalled the enmity toward her father. (18)
"The evil-minded Yudhājit will surely slay my son in battle out of greed for the kingdom; that wicked soul," she thought, becoming consumed by anxiety. (19)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? My father has been slain in battle;
my husband too has died this very day; and here is my young son. (20)
Greed is exceedingly wicked; by it, who has not been brought under its sway? Possessed by it, what sin would even the best of kings not commit? (21)
A person possessed by greed kills his father, mother, brothers, teachers, kinsmen, and relatives; there is no doubt about this.
Afflicted by craving, he indeed commits the eating of forbidden food and likewise approaches those who should not be approached; furthermore, he abandons the Dharma. (23)
I have no companion here in this city who possesses great strength, upon whose support I may rely while protecting my auspicious son. (24)
Now that my son has been killed, what shall I do again, O King?
There is no protector for me in this world by whom I might truly be established in security. (25)
That co-wife Līlāvatī will always be full of enmity toward my son; she will never be compassionate toward him. (26)
If Yudhājit arrives, there will be no escape for me;
knowing my son to be a child, he will take him to prison. (27)
For it is heard that in ancient times, while still in his mother’s womb, the child was cut into seven pieces by Indra; subsequently, those seven were each cut into seven more.
Having entered his mother's womb and placed a small thunderbolt in his hand,
those who were forty-nine Maruts became fifty in heaven.
I heard before me that poison was administered by the king’s wife, his co-wife, for the purpose of destroying the fetus. (30)
Indeed, the boy was born separated from his body by another;
therefore, he became renowned on the circle of the earth by the name Sagara. 31.
While her husband was still alive, Rāma, the eldest son of King Daśaratha, was exiled by Kaikeyī, the king’s wife; meanwhile, King Daśaratha himself has died.
But my ministers were indeed helpless; those who desired to make my son Sudarśana the king went away from Yudhājit. (33)
"I have no brother so heroic who might release me from this bondage;
indeed, through the power of fate, I have encountered this great hardship. (34)
"Effort must be made by all means, for success arises from destiny;
therefore, I shall today, with great haste, devise a means for the protection of my son. (35)
Having thus reflected, that young woman considered Vidalla,
who was exceedingly proud yet skillful in all affairs, as the best among the chief ministers.
Having summoned him to a private place, she, deeply distressed, weeping and with a dejected mind, spoke while holding the boy by the hand. (37)
"My father has been slain in battle, and this son of mine is but a child;
Yudhājit and Vātrājā are here—tell me, what should be done? (38)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter 15. 145.
Vidalla said to her: "You must certainly not remain here; we shall go as we please to the forest, or indeed back again to Vārāṇasī. (39)
There dwells my illustrious maternal uncle, who is exceedingly powerful;
known as Subāhu, he shall be your protector.
With a mind eager for the sight of Yudhājit, you must go outside the city, mount a chariot, and depart; of this there is no doubt. (41)
Having been addressed thus by him, that queen went toward Līlāvatī and said, "O fair-eyed one, I am going today to see my father. (42)
Having spoken thus, she then mounted the chariot accompanied by Sairandhrī and Vidalla,
and departed from the city.
For she was distressed and most piteous, overwhelmed with grief for her father,
upon seeing King Yudhājit, her father, deprived of life.
Being prepared for the ceremony, she arrived at the bank of the Bhagirathi river after two days, filled with haste, trembling, and overwhelmed by fear. 45.
There, plundered by the Niṣādas, all their wealth was seized;
having taken even the chariot, those deceitful bandits departed.
Weeping, taking her son with her, the beautiful and charming woman went out to the bank of the Ganges, supported by the hand of the Sairandhrī.
And having quickly climbed up out of fear, she, overwhelmed by terror, crossed the holy Bhāgīrathī and went to Mount Trikūṭa. ||48||
Having reached the hermitage of Bhāradvāja, she was agitated by fear;
yet, upon seeing the ascetics there, she then became free from fear.
She was then questioned by the sage: "Who are you, and whose wife are you?"
"O lady of pure smiles, tell me truly: how did you reach this place with such difficulty? (50)
"Are you a goddess or a human woman? How is it that you, with your young son, are here in the forest?
O fair-thighed one, O lotus-eyed one, you appear like one fallen from her kingdom. (51)
Thus questioned by the sage, that woman of excellent complexion did not speak;
weeping and tormented by grief, she instead commanded Vidalla. (52)
Vidalla said this to him: "This is the lawful wife of that Dhruvasandhi, the best of kings, and her name is Manoramā. (53)
The king of the Solar dynasty, who possessed great strength, was slain by a lion;
this son of that monarch is named Caitrasudarśana. (54)
Her father, an exceedingly righteous soul, died in battle for the sake of his daughter's son;
terrified by fear, she has arrived in this lonely forest.
"Having come to you alone for refuge, O best of sages, protect this princess who has but a young son; be her protector, O highly fortunate one. (56)

The merit gained from protecting one who is distressed is declared to be greater than that of a sacrifice; it is remembered as yielding especially great fruit when protecting one who is terrified and miserable.
The sage said:
"Dwell here without fear, O auspicious one; protect your son, O lady of excellent vows.
You must not entertain any fear arising from enemies, O large-eyed one. (58)
"Protect your beloved son; he shall become your king.
Neither suffering nor grief shall ever arise for you here. (59)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by the sage, the queen became composed;
she dwelt then in the hermitage provided by the sage, free from sorrow.
Accompanied by Sairandhrī and joined by Vidalla, that charming woman lived there, protecting Sudarśana. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter sixteen.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Then the mighty Yudhājit, having returned from the battle to Ayodhyā, [proceeded].
And he questioned Manoramā with the intent to slay Sudarśana.
He sent forth his servants, asking repeatedly, "Where has he gone?
Then, on an auspicious day, he seated his grandson upon the throne.
And by the ministers and Vasiṣṭha, he was consecrated with auspicious Atharvan mantras using jars completely filled with water.
O best of the Kurus, a great festival indeed took place in the city with the sounds of kettledrums and conchs, as well as the blares of trumpets.
With the recitation of the Vedas by the Brahmins and likewise with the hymns of the bards,
Ayodhyā was filled with joy and auspicious shouts of victory.
Crowded with joyful and well-fed people and resounding with the sounds of hymns and musical instruments,
that city shone like something new under that newly installed protector of the earth.
Certain virtuous people who were staying at home prepared vegetables;
having searched for Sudarśana, they asked, "Where has that son of the king gone today? (7)
Where has that most virtuous Manoramā gone, accompanied by her son?
Her father was slain in battle by an enemy out of greed for the kingdom. (8)
Reflecting thus, those virtuous ones of even-mindedness remained there in distress,
subject to the control of Śatrughna.
Yudhājit, having installed his daughter's son according to the prescribed rites and having entrusted the kingdom to his ministers, set out toward his own city.
Having heard that Sudarśana was staying there in the hermitage of the sages,
he went quickly to Mount Citrakūṭa, desiring to kill him.
Placing before him the heroic Niṣāda chief named Bala,
he quickly went to the lord of Śṛṅgaverapura, known by the name Durdarśa.
Hearing that he was approaching accompanied by an army, Manoramā, whose young son was with her, became exceedingly distressed and overcome with fear. (13)
Afflicted with intense grief and with eyes full of tears, she said to the sage:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Yudhājit has arrived."
"My father was slain by him, and he made my grandson the king; now, desiring to kill my son, he approaches here accompanied by a great force. (15)
O Lord, I have heard before that the Pāṇḍavas were once staying in the forest, together with the princess of Pañcāla, in a holy hermitage of sages. (16)
Those five Pārtha brothers have gone out on a hunt;
Draupadī remains there in that auspicious hermitage of the sages.
Dhaumya, Atri, Gālava, Paila, Jābāli, Gotama, Bhṛgu, Cyavana of the Atri lineage, Kaṇva, Jatu, and Kratu. || 18 ||
Vītihotra, Sumantu, Yajñadatta, Vatsala, Rāgāsana, Kahoḍa, Yavakrī, Yajaka, and Kratu. ||19||
These and other auspicious sages, such as Bhāradvāja and others,
all devoted to the recitation of the Vedas, were established there, dwelling in the hermitage.
O sage, Yājñasenī was also present there together with her female attendants.
And she wandered through the hermitage, which was filled with sages, with all her limbs uncovered and without fear.
Meanwhile, the five heroic sons of Pṛthā, the scorchers of their enemies, set out for the forest, pursuing deer while bearing bows and arrows. (22)
Meanwhile, the illustrious Lord of Sindhu, accompanied by his army, was on the road;
having heard the sound of the Vedas, he then approached my presence.
Hearing the sound of the Vedas from the sages of purified souls,
the king, desiring a vision of them, quickly descended from his chariot.
When he went forth from there accompanied by two servants, he observed the sages established in their efforts, chanting the Vedas. (25)

Then Jayadratha, standing before him with his palms joined in reverence, spoke. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, Third Skandha, Chapter 16. 147. [Jayadratha], with his hands folded in *añjali*, stood before him.
The king entered the hermitage frequented by sages.
Then, desiring to see the king seated there, the women and the wives of the sages approached and asked the king, "Who is this? (27)
Among them, Yājñasenī, the lady of noble form, arrived;
she was seen by Jayadratha, appearing like another Goddess Śrī in her beauty.
Beholding her, with her dark-cornered eyes like another celestial maiden, the king asked Dhaumya: "Who is this dark-complexioned woman of beautiful face? (29)
Whose wife is she, whose daughter, and by what name is this woman of excellent complexion?
Endowed with beauty and grace, she is like Śacī descended to the earth. (30)
Standing in the midst of a grove of bamboo like a sprig of clove,
that beautiful woman truly shines forth like Rambhā surrounded by a host of Rākṣasīs.
"Speak the truth, O illustrious one! Whose beloved wife is this frail woman?
She shines like a queen; she is not the wife of a sage, O twice-born one. (32)
Dhaumya said: O Indra among the lords of Sindhu, Draupadī, the beloved wife of the Pāṇḍavas, who possesses auspicious marks and is a princess of Pañcāla, dwells here in this excellent hermitage.
Jayadratha said:
"Where have the five Pāṇḍavas gone now, those renowned heroes? Do those mighty warriors dwell here in the forest, free from sorrow? (34)
Dhaumya said:
"The five Pāṇḍavas, mounted upon their chariots, have gone out for the purpose of hunting;
at midday, those kings will return taking deer with them."
Having heard those words of his, that king rose up;
having gone into the presence of Draupadī and bowed down, he spoke this.
"Is all well with you, O lady of beautiful hips? Where have your husbands gone?
It has been eleven years today that they have supposedly remained in the forest. (37)
Draupadī, however, then said to him, "May it be well with you, O prince!
Rest in the vicinity of the hermitage; the Pāṇḍavas will arrive in a moment.
While she was speaking thus, that king became possessed by greed.
The hero carried off Draupadī, disregarding the best of sages.
The wise should never place their trust in anyone under any circumstances;
by doing so, one incurs suffering, as is evidenced by the example of Bali.
The illustrious son of Vairocana was most righteous and true to his promise;
he was a performer of sacrifices, a donor, a refuge for others, and highly esteemed by the virtuous. || 41 ||
The grandson of Prahlāda was never devoted to unrighteousness;
he indeed performed ninety-nine sacrifices accompanied by proper sacrificial fees.
Viṣṇu, whose form is pure goodness (sattva), is always to be served even by the yogis.
Although the Blessed One is changeless, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, [he acts]. ||43||
And from Kaśyapa was born Viṣṇu as the deceptive Vāmana;
by means of trickery, he seized the kingdom and the earth together with its oceans.
At that time, King Bali, the son of Virocana, became truthful in speech;
however, I have heard that Viṣṇu employed a stratagem for the sake of Indra. (45)
Why does no one else act in this way, as has been done by the one whose form is pure being (Sattva),
who assumed the form of a dwarf desiring to bring about the downfall of the sacrifice?
One should never place trust in anyone at any time;
for if greed exists within one's own mind, what fear can there be regarding the commission of sin? (47)
"Stricken by greed, living beings indeed commit sins;
O Sage, no one at any time has any fear of the next world. (48)
On account of taking what belongs to others through thought, deed, or speech, men whose minds are utterly destroyed by greed fall [into hell]. (49)
Having constantly propitiated the gods, men desire wealth;
yet the gods, even if they placed it in their hands, are not able to give it forth directly.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 17.
The wealth of another is brought [to them], and they bestow whatever is desired,
whether by means of trade, gifts, theft, or even by force.
Having taken up much grain, clothing, and other goods for the purpose of selling them, the Vaiśya worships the gods, thinking, "May there be great prosperity for me. (52)
O scorcher of enemies, do you have no desire for the wealth of others here?
For when the time for seizing it has arrived, he even longs for a great sacrifice.
"For in this way, O Brahmin, all living beings constantly exist intent upon seizing the property of others; how, then, can there be any trust? (54)
Vain is the pilgrimage, vain is the gift, and vain indeed is the study;
for those shrouded by greed and delusion, that which has been performed becomes as if unperformed.
Therefore, O highly fortunate one, O best of the twice-born, send him back toward his home;
I shall dwell with my son like Jānaki.
Having been addressed thus, that powerful sage Bharadvāja went to King Yudhājit and spoke these words to the king.
"Go, O best of kings, to your own city as you desire; this Manorama, who has a young son and is deeply distressed, does not come. (58)
Yudhājit said:
"O Sage, abandon your obstinacy; release this beautiful and charming woman.
I shall not go away having left her; today I will take her back by force. (59)
The sage said:
"If you have the power, take him away today by force from my hermitage,
just as Viśvāmitra formerly took the cow of the sage Vasiṣṭha."
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 16 ||
Then the seventeenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of that sage, the lord of the earth there—
Having summoned his aged minister, he questioned him with unwearied diligence.
"O wise one of noble vows, tell me what must be done by me today?
I shall forcibly take that sweet-spoken woman along with her son, as I desire.
Even a minor enemy should not be overlooked by one who desires prosperity in every way."
Like a fully developed royal consumption, it prepares one for death. ||3||
"There is neither army nor warrior here who might prevent me;
having seized him, I shall surely slay that enemy of my daughter's son. (4)
"The kingdom would become devoid of enemies; therefore, I shall today exert my strength. Once Sudarśana is slain, he will surely be without fear. (5)
Pradhāna said: "O King, there is nothing that should not be done; I have heard the words of Manu. O noble one, the example of Viśvāmitra was told by him."
Formerly, the illustrious and highly renowned Viśvāmitra, son of Gādhi,
while wandering about, that best of kings arrived at the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
And having paid his respects to him, the powerful King Viśvāmitra—
The best of kings sat down upon the seat provided by the sage.
Invited by the high-souled one for a meal, the highly illustrious King Gādhiputra remained there with his army. || 9 ||
Having partaken of all the excellent foods and delicacies throughout the day,
the king, together with his army, enjoyed a meal there that was exactly as he had desired. 10.
Having recognized that power of Nandinī,
the king, that best of sages Vasiṣṭha, begged Nandinī from him.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter 17.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O Sage, I shall give you a thousand cows that yield pots of milk;
O scorcher of foes, I entreat you, grant me the cow Nandini. (12)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O King, this sacrificial cow I will not give up under any circumstances;
let these thousand cows of yours remain there."
Viśvāmitra said:
"O virtuous one, I shall give you ten thousand or even a hundred thousand—whatever your heart desires. Give Nandinī to me; otherwise, I shall take her by force. (14)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O King, take Nandinī by force today as you please;
however, O King, I will not give her to you from my own will. (15)
Having heard that, the king commanded his mighty servants:
"Take the cow Nandinī away, you who are firmly established in the pride of your strength. (16)
The servants, having forcibly seized her and bound her, she—trembling and with eyes full of tears—spoke to the sage:
"O sage, why do you abandon me? They are dragging me away while I am firmly restrained."
The sage replied to her: "I will not abandon it, O lady of difficult speech. (18)
"O auspicious one, this king leads me away by force, for he has been honored by me today;
what can I do? Indeed, I do not wish to abandon you even in my mind."
Thus addressed by the sage, the cow became filled with anger;
she immediately let out a lowing sound, a cruel and most dreadful noise. (20)
Then, from her body, there emerged Daityas even more terrible, clad in armor and bearing weapons, crying out, "Stay! Stay! (21)
The entire army was slain by them, and Nandinī was set free;
King Viśvāmitra, deeply distressed, departed alone.
Alas, that sinner, his soul exceedingly dejected, censuring the great power of the kṣatriyas and considering the power of a brāhmaṇa difficult to master, remained established in austerity.
Having performed severe austerities for many years in the great forest,
Gādheya attained the status of a rishi, having once again abandoned the kshatriya way of life.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, do not engage in this extraordinary enmity;
indeed, a battle with ascetics will surely bring about the destruction of your lineage.
O best of sages, depart today after having consoled that treasure of asceticism;
O lord of kings, let Sudarśana also remain here as he pleases.
"This boy is poor; what harm can he do to you, O King? Why do you harbor such enmity toward this helpless, weak child? (27)
Compassion should be practiced toward all; this world is subject to destiny.
O best of kings, what is the use of envy? Whatever is destined to be, that shall come to pass.
O King, by the turn of fate, there is no doubt that even a thunderbolt acts like a blade of grass;
and at some time, through the turn of fate, even a blade of grass acts like a thunderbolt. (29)
A hare kills a tiger, and even a mosquito kills an elephant; O wise one, abandon this rashness and do what I say for your own benefit.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, Yudhājit, the best of kings,
bowed his head to that sage and departed for his own city, O King.
Manoramā also became healthy while staying there in the hermitage;
she protected her son Sudarśana according to the rites of immortality.
Day by day, that boy grew in stature;
playing with the children of the sages, he was fearless and auspicious in every way.
At one time, Vidalla arrived there;
the son of the sage addressed him from nearby, saying, "Klīṃba. (34)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter 17. 150.
Sudarśana, having heard that, clearly held the single syllable accompanied by the *anusvāra*; he recited it again and again,
having then grasped with his mind that seed-syllable known as Kāmarāja.
The boy chanted with great intensity, holding it respectfully in his heart;
O Great King, because of their future union, he naturally grasped this wonderful mantra known as Kāmarāja. Thus indeed was it taken up by the boy. (36–37)
Then, in his fifth year, he received that unsurpassed mantra,
which was devoid of seers and meters and stripped of meditative visualization and ritual placement.
Constantly reciting it with his mind, even while playing or sleeping,
he did not forget that mantra, knowing for himself that it was the very essence.
When his eleventh year had arrived, that prince, the son of the king,
was initiated by the sage and likewise instructed in the Vedas.

Likewise, through the power of mantras and other means, he practiced the science of archery along with its auxiliary branches, the treatises on ethics, and all branches of knowledge according to the prescribed rules. (41)
Once, he too beheld the Goddess manifest before his very eyes,
wearing red garments, red in complexion, and adorned with ornaments of red for all her limbs;
she was the wondrous power of Viṣṇu (Vaiṣṇavī Śakti), seated upon her vehicle, Garuḍa.
Upon seeing him, the prince’s face became bright with joy.
Then, staying in that forest, he who knew the true essence of all branches of knowledge lived on the riverbank, attending upon his mother.
A bow was obtained, along with arrows sharpened on stone;
and a quiver and armor were given to him by Ambika in the forest.
At that time, there was the divine daughter of the King of Kāśī, named Śaśikalā, who was beloved and endowed with all auspicious marks.
He heard from the mouths of bards that the prince Sudarśana was dwelling in the forest,
endowed with all auspicious marks like another Kāma;
having heard of the heroic prince Susaṃgata, he [approached him].
She resolved in her mind to choose that boon with her intellect. Then, in the middle of the night, the Mother of the World appeared to her in a dream and,
having consoled her as she stood there composed, spoke these words.
"Choose a boon, O lady of beautiful hips; Sudarśana is my devotee.
By my word, O beautiful woman, let him be the granter of all your desires.
Thus did Śaśikalā see that enchanting form in her dream.
Remembering her mother's words, the highly passionate woman rejoiced greatly.
Standing there, composed and attentive, the young girl was questioned again and again by her mother; yet, overcome with extreme bashfulness, she did not speak the reason for her joy.
Having laughed and attained great joy, she recalled the dream again and again;
then she told that other friend the account of her dream in full detail.
Once, for the sake of recreation, she entered a beautiful grove.
Accompanied by her friends, the large-eyed young woman,
standing beneath a campaka tree while gathering flowers,
saw a Brahmin approaching on the path in great haste. (14–15)
Having bowed to that brahmin, Śyāmā spoke these sweet words:
"O illustrious one, from what land have you come? (56)
The twice-born said:
"O child, my arrival from the hermitage of Bhāradvāja has surely occurred due to the exigency of some business; tell me, what do you ask? Speak to me. (57)
Śaśikalā said:
"O illustrious one, what indeed is there in that hermitage worthy of description? Is there anything especially transcendent of the world and most worthy of being beheld? (58)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, the illustrious King Sudarśana, the son of Dhruvasandhi, dwells there;
that Supreme Person exists with a name truly meaningful."
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 18:
"To me, his eye appears utterly fruitless."
O lady of beautiful thighs, by whom has that handsome youth not been seen? (60)
I believe that all virtues were placed together in one place by the Creator, who desired to create, as if out of curiosity to see the very mine of all virtues.
Therefore, this worthy prince ought to become his husband;
this union was ordained just like that of the jewel and gold.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 17 ||
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, Śyāmā became filled with love.
Having spoken thus, the composed Brahmin departed from that place.
But she, due to her former passion, was deeply immersed in love and exceedingly restless once that best of brahmins had entered the fire of the arrows of Kama.
Then she spoke of her passion to her friend, who followed her wishes, saying:
"A transformation has arisen in my body following that which I heard. (3)
The wicked god of love torments this prince of noble birth, who is ignorant of the knowledge of sensual pleasures; what shall I do, and where shall I go? (4)
Or was he seen by me in dreams as another five-arrowed god of love? My tender heart, distressed by separation, is tormented exceedingly.
"O beautiful lady, this sandalwood paste clinging to my body appears like poison;
this garland is like a serpent, and even the rays of the moon are like fire."
In the forest there is no peace for me from the palace, nor does it exist in the long pond; neither by day nor by night do I find happiness through the means of pleasure. (7)
Neither bed, nor betel, nor song, nor instrumental music delights my mind today; my eyes remain unsated.
Today I shall go to that forest where that rogue dwells;
for I am afraid of family shame and likewise dependent upon my father. (9)
"My father does not hold a svayaṃvara today; what shall I do?
I shall indeed give my heart to Prince Sudarśana.
There are hundreds of other rulers of the earth who possess abundant prosperity."
They are no longer delightful to me; even he, though deprived of his kingdom, is now esteemed by me as such.
Vyāsa said:
Sudarśana was alone, penniless, and devoid of strength;
dwelling in the forest and subsisting on fruits, she remained firmly established in his heart. (12)
Success has now arrived for him through the recitation of the Bāmbīja mantra;
intent upon meditation, he too recited that supreme mantra with extreme devotion. (13)
In his dream, he beheld the Goddess, the unbroken Viṣṇu-māyā, the Mother of the Universe, the unmanifest, the auspicious one who bestows all prosperity. 14.
The Niṣāda, the governor of Śṛṅgaverapura, approached him and gave him an excellent chariot equipped with all necessary implements. 15.
Knowing that the prince was victorious, he then presented him with a gift: a chariot yoked with four horses and adorned with excellent banners.
He too, out of affection, accepted him as a well-established friend and properly honored Śambara with wild roots and fruits.
When that lord of the Nipas had departed after being offered hospitality,
those sages and ascetics, filled with joy, spoke to one another concerning him.
O Prince, you shall certainly obtain the kingdom in every way; through your majesty, you will do so without agitation in a very short time—of this there is no doubt. (19)
The goddess Ambikā, the bestower of boons who deludes the universe, is pleased with you;
your assistance is perfectly secured, so do not worry, O observer of noble vows. (20)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter eighteen.
Then those sages of rigid vows said to Manoramā:
"O lady of pure smiles, today your son shall become the lord of the earth. (21)
She, whose limbs were slender, said to them: "May your words bear good fruit;
O Brahmins, this man is your servant—what is so wonderful about that, given his proper service? (22)
I have no army, no ministers, no treasury, and no ally whatsoever; by what means, then, does my son deserve to obtain the kingdom here? (23)
"By your blessings, this son of mine will surely become a lord of the earth;
of this there is no doubt, for you are the most skilled in mantras. (24)
Vyāsa said:
Mounted upon his chariot, that wise Sudarśana appeared wherever he went,
shining with such splendor that he seemed surrounded by an entire akṣauhiṇī army.
O King, there is no other power than that of the seed-mantra;
this is indeed so for one who recites it with devotion in every way. (26)
Having obtained from a true guru the wonderful seed-mantra known as Kāmarāja, he who recites it while pure and tranquil shall attain all desires. (27)
O best of kings, there is nothing on earth or even in heaven that is difficult to obtain, nor anything unattainable for one who is devoted to Śivā. 28.
They are dull-witted and extremely unfortunate, pursued by diseases, in whose minds there is no faith in the worship of the gods and other such practices. (29)
O best of the Kurus, she who was proclaimed at the beginning of the age as the mother of all the gods is therefore renowned by the name Ādimātā (the Primordial Mother).
Intellect, fame, fortitude, prosperity, power, faith, understanding, and memory—indeed, she shines forth perceptibly before all living beings. (31)
Indeed, those men who are deluded by illusion do not know; those who rely on fallacious reasoning do not worship the auspicious Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe. 32.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Śambhu, the Vāsus, Varuṇa, Yama, Vāyu, Agni, Kubera, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, the Aśvins, and Bhaga. || 33 ||
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts—all meditate upon that Goddess, the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction. ||34||
Whosoever, being wise, indeed serves that supreme power, she—the auspicious Goddess who grants all goals—is known by him through the Sudarśana. 35.
She is indeed Brahman itself, that most difficult-to-attain knowledge whose nature is both ignorance and wisdom;
she is the supreme power accessible through yoga and beloved by those seeking liberation.
Who is capable of knowing the true nature of the Supreme Self without her, she who, having created the threefold creation, reveals it to the Soul of All? (37)
But Sudarśana, reflecting upon that goddess in his mind, remained in the forest, having indeed attained a happiness greater than the acquisition of a kingdom. ||38||
And Candrakalā too, being excessively tormented by the arrows of Kama,
constantly maintained a distressed body through various means of consolation.
In the meantime, her father Subāhu, having learned that his daughter desired an excellent husband,
diligently prepared a svayaṃvara (self-choice marriage) for her.
The self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara) has been proclaimed by the learned to be of three kinds;
it is indeed suitable for the marriage of kings, and certainly not said to be for others. 41.
One was the "Self-choice by Desire" (icchāsvayaṃvara) and the second was called the "Stake" (paṇa);
indeed, it was like when the bow of Tryambaka was broken by Rāma.
The third [type of bridegroom] is proclaimed as one whose bride-price is valor;
it was for such a one that the best of kings held a *svayaṃvara* based on his own choice. (43)
The mantras were performed by artisans and provided with auspicious coverings;
thereafter, assembly halls of various forms were well-constructed.
When these extensive preparations for the wedding had been thus made, the sorrowful and beautiful-eyed maiden spoke to her friend Śaśikalā: (45)
"Speak these words of mine to my mother in private:
'The auspicious son of Dhruvasandhi has been chosen by me as my husband in my heart. (46)
"I shall choose no other boon except for that Sudarśana;
that prince alone, established in the divine power, shall be my husband. (47)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter 19.
Vyāsa said:
Having been told this, that friend went quickly and spoke these words privately to her mother in a sweet and melodious voice: "The princess of Vidarbha [has spoken thus]. (48)
"O auspicious one, listen to what your virtuous daughter, being distressed, has said to you through my mouth; perform that which is for her benefit with haste now. (49)
"In the holy hermitage of Bhāradvāja, there is the son of Dhruvasandhi;
he alone is my husband in my heart, for I choose no other king. (50)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the king, when her husband had returned home,
she then reported her daughter's speech exactly as it was.
Amazed and laughing repeatedly at these words, King Subāhu spoke this truthful speech to his wife, the princess of Vidarbha:
52. "The words [of the sage] are true. Thus spoke Subāhu to his wife, the daughter of Vidarbha.
Having heard that, O fair-browed one, you know that this boy was exiled from the kingdom and now dwells alone with his mother in the desolate forest.
For his sake, King Vīrasena was slain by Yudhājit;
O lovely-eyed one, how could such a penniless man be a suitable husband?
"Speak these words, my daughter, even if they are unpleasant:
'Kings will surely come to the svayaṃvara of this steadfast maiden. (55)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 18 ||
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having placed her young daughter upon her lap, she was thus addressed by her husband:
Having comforted her who possessed a pure smile, he spoke these gentle words.
"O fair-toothed one, why do you speak such unpleasant words to me in vain?
By these words, O lady of virtuous vows, your father suffers great distress. (2)
Sudarśana was extremely unfortunate, deprived of his kingdom, without refuge,
destitute of strength and treasury, and abandoned by his kinsmen.
Having reached the forest with your mother, you have become emaciated, subsisting on fruits and roots;
this bridegroom is indeed unfit for you, being a forest-dweller and unfortunate.
"O daughter, there are other princes who are wise, handsome, highly esteemed, and adorned with royal ornaments. (5)
His beloved brother indeed rules the kingdom among the Kosalas;
endowed with beauty and possessed of all auspicious marks, he governs it.
Furthermore, O fair-browed one, hear another reason as it was heard by me:
King Yudhājit is constantly desirous of his death. (7)
Having made a solemn pact and slain King Vīrasena, he consulted with his ministers and established his daughter's son upon the throne.
Desiring to kill Sudarśana who had arrived at the hermitage of Bhāradvāja,
he was later restrained by the sage and returned to his own home.
Śaśikalā said:
"O Mother, by the word of Śaryāti alone, the prince is indeed my desired husband, even though he dwells in the forest; and Sukanyā is devoted to her husband. (10)
And how, having attained Cyavana, she became devoted to the service of her husband;
for the service of the husband grants women both heaven and liberation. || 11 ||
"Surely that which is performed without guile brings happiness to a woman;
for the Blessed One has granted me an unsurpassed boon in a dream. (12)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter nineteen.
Without him, how could I resort to another prince?
For Sudarśana has been painted upon the wall of my heart by the Goddess herself. (13)
"Abandoning that beloved and dear husband, I shall do nothing else.
Vyāsa said:
Then the princess of Vidarbha was thus addressed by her with many illustrations.
She related everything to her husband—the words spoken intensely by her daughter, which she had received before the day of the wedding and which were consistent with what she had heard. (15)
There, Śaśikalā quickly dispatched the twice-born Sudarśana, saying:
"O lord,
go to Bhāradvāja’s hermitage with haste and speak my words, so that my father may not know."
"My father has indeed prepared this svayaṃvara for my sake.
For many kings accompanied by their armies will surely arrive.
You have been chosen by me in my heart with all affection. (17-18)
"O god-like one, commanded by the Blessed Lady in a dream, I would rather eat poison or cast myself into a blazing fire;
even if urged by my parents, I choose no other than you. (19)
"O excellent one, you have been restrained by me in thought, deed, and speech."
"By the grace of the Blessed Lady, welfare shall be ours both;
you too must come right here, making destiny your supreme strength. (21)
The entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, exists dependent upon her;
whatever has been commanded by the Blessed Lady shall not prove false. (22)

O Brahmin, that son of a king under whose control all the deities, beginning with Śaṅkara, abide— He must be spoken to by you in private. O sinless one, you must perform that task for me exactly as it is required.
Having spoken thus and given the sacrificial fee, she employed the sage for her purpose.
Having gone there and quickly reported everything, the twice-born Sudarśana returned; and having understood that, he then made the firm resolve to depart.
Urged by that sage, he performed [the rite] with the utmost reverence.
Vyāsa said:
To her son who was intent on departing, Manoramā spoke.
Trembling, afflicted by extreme sorrow, filled with terror, and with eyes full of tears, she said:
"O son, where are you going today to the assembly of kings? (27)
Alone and having incurred enmity, what is the king Yudhājit contemplating as he approaches you at the svayaṃvara, desiring you for his own sake? (28)
"You have no other companion; therefore, my son, do not go. I am an only child, exceedingly wretched, your sole support, and without any other refuge. (29)
O highly fortunate one, you ought not to leave me hopeless today;
for that king by whom your father was slain has also arrived there.
"Yudhājit will kill you there while you are alone and gone.
Sudarśana said: "What is destined to happen will surely happen; there is no need for deliberation in this matter. (31)
"And by the command of the Mother of the World, I am going today to the svayaṃvara;
do not grieve, O auspicious one, for you are a Kṣatriya woman, O fair-faced one."
I do not fear, for I am constantly sustained by the grace of the Blessed Goddess.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 19. 155.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Sudarśana mounted his chariot, desiring to depart.
Having seen her son, Manoramā congratulated him with blessings:
"May Ambikā protect you from the front; may Pārvatī protect you from behind. (34)
May Śivā protect you at your sides at all times;
may Vārāhī protect you on difficult paths; may Durgā protect you whenever there are obstacles; and may the Supreme Goddess Kālikā protect you in terrible conflict. (35)
In that pavilion, during the svayaṃvara, may Bhavānī—both as Mātaṅgī and as the gentle one—standing in the midst of the kings, protect you, she who grants liberation from worldly existence. 36.
May Girijā protect you in mountain fastnesses, Cāmuṇḍā in courtyards, and the eternal Kāmagā in the forests. (37)
O scorcher of the Raghus, may the power of Viṣṇu protect you in dispute;
O gentle one, may Bhairavī protect your feet when you encounter your enemies. (38)
May the Mistress of the World, the Great Illusion, the Sustainer of the Universe, whose form is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss, protect you at all times and in all places. (39)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to him, his mother, trembling and overwhelmed with fear, said,
"I will certainly come along with you in every way."
"Indeed, I cannot endure to remain here even for half a moment without you;
take me with you, my child, wherever your mind is set upon going. (41)
Having spoken thus, the mother then departed accompanied by her nurse;
all the brahmins, having been granted blessings, went forth filled with joy.
Then Rāghava arrived at Vārāṇasī in a single chariot;
he was recognized there by Subāhu and honored with offerings and other marks of respect.
For the sake of settling him, he gave a house as well as food, drink, and so forth; and having authorized a servant, he provided for his personal attendance. (44)
Then indeed, the kings who were lords of various lands assembled;
Yudhājit also arrived, accompanied by his grandson.
The lord of Karūṣa, as well as the king who is the ruler of Madra, the heroic Sindhu king, and the warrior who is the lord of Māhiṣmatī. || 46 ||
The Pāñcāla, the mountaineer, the highly powerful Kāmarūpa, the Karṇāṭa, the one from the Cola country, and the very mighty Vaidarbha. (47)
At that time, sixty-three akṣauhiṇīs were assembled in total;
the city was surrounded by those armies stationed everywhere.
These and many other kings, accompanied by excellent elephants, assembled there with the desire to witness the svayaṃvara.
Then, having gathered together, those princes said to one another:
"The prince Sudarśana has indeed arrived, free from all agitation. (50)
"O Kakutstha, why has that high-minded one now come here alone with his mother in a chariot for the sake of marriage? What indeed is happening now? (51)
Having abandoned these sons of the king along with their armies and weapons, will that princess now choose this mighty-armed man? (52)
Then King Yuvājit said to those lords of the earth:
"I shall slay him for the sake of the maiden; there is no doubt in this. (53)
Then the ruler of Kerala, the best among those skilled in policy, said to him:
"O King, war must not be waged here at this svayaṃvara of one's own choice."

There is no abduction of the bride here, nor is there a bride-price or a svayaṃvara; here, the selection of a husband is according to the girl's own wish—what kind of dispute could there be in this? (55)
O best of kings, previously that [son] was exiled from the kingdom by you, his mother’s father; yet now, O powerful one, the kingdom has been handed over to your grandson. (56)
"This is the illustrious descendant of Kakutstha, the son of the lord of Kosala;
how will you slay this prince who is innocent? (57)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty.
O best of kings, you will surely reap the fruit of this misconduct. O long-lived one, there is a ruler of this world who is the Lord of the universe:
Dharma triumphs, not Adharma; Truth triumphs, not Untruth.
Pay homage, O Indra among kings, and indeed abandon your sinful intent.
Your daughter’s son has arrived; he too is endowed with beauty, possessed of royal power, and illustrious—how could you not choose him? (60)
Other princes are indeed more powerful,
yet at the maiden's self-choice ceremony (svayaṃvara), she will now accept him.
“Since he has been chosen, what dispute can there be? Let the kings speak;
one who possesses true knowledge should not harbor mutual hostility in this matter. (62)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 19 ||
Now begins the twentieth chapter.

Vyāsa said: When the king, the ruler of Kerala, had spoken thus at that time, [the sages asked: "O best of Brahmins, what did the great sage Nārada say? They said: "O best of Brahmins, tell us everything exactly as it occurred. Vyāsa said: "When the king, the lord of Kerala, had spoken in this manner, the great sage Nārada, having heard those words, spoke these words to the king. Nārada said: "O King, listen with an attentive mind to what I shall tell you regarding the supreme secret of all secrets, which is difficult for even the gods to attain. Vyāsa said: "Having been thus addressed by the sage, the king, with palms joined in reverence, spoke again to the great sage Nārada. The king said: "O holy one, O knower of dharma, tell me truly and in detail about the greatness of Śrī Rāma, which is the cause of the destruction of all sins. Nārada said: "O King, listen with an attentive mind; I shall tell you the truth. There is a great mountain named Himavat, which is the source of all jewels and the abode of the gods. On its peak is a hermitage belonging to the self-born Brahmā, where the Lord of the World dwells together with the goddess Pārvatī. There, the Great Lord, the Supreme Soul, the eternal, the imperishable, the unchanging, the one without beginning or end, the unborn, the omnipresent, the one without attributes, the one without form, the one without qualities, the one without parts, the one without support, the one without decay, the one without fear, the one who is beyond the reach of thought, the one who is not an object of beyond the reach of cause, the one who is not an object of cause, the one who is beyond the reach of effect, the one who is not an object of effect, the one who is beyond the reach of birth, the one who is not an object of birth, the one who is beyond the reach of death, the one who is not an object of death, the one who is beyond the reach of old age, the one who is not an object of old age, the one who is beyond the reach of disease, the one who is not an object of disease, the one who is beyond the reach of pleasure, the one who is not an object of pleasure, the one who is beyond the reach of pain, the one who is not an object of pain, the one who is beyond the reach of happiness, the one who is not an object of happiness, the one who is beyond the reach of sorrow, the one who is not an one who is beyond the reach of existence, the one who is not an object of existence, the one who is beyond the reach of non-existence, the one who is not an object of non-existence, the one who is beyond the reach of both, the one who is not an object of both, the one who is beyond the reach of the manifest, the one who is not an object of the manifest, the one who is beyond the reach of the unmanifest, the one who is not an object of the unmanifest, the one who is beyond the reach of the known, the one who is not an object of the known, the one who is beyond the reach of the unknown, the one who is not
The highly fortunate King Yudhājit also replied. || 1 ||
O protector of the earth, this is the principle you have stated here in the assembly of kings— you who are truthful in speech and have conquered your senses.
"O upholder of the lineage, while worthy suitors are present, this jewel of a maiden is being offered to an unworthy man; O King, does this course of action please you? (3)
How indeed could a jackal deserve to enjoy a portion of a lion?
Likewise, how can this Sudarśana deserve such a jewel of a maiden? || 4 ||
For the strength of Brahmins is the Veda, while the strength of kings is that born of the bow.
O Great King, what improper thing shall I say here now? (5)
Just as the bride-price for kings is proclaimed to be strength,
