let only the strong take it, and never the weak.
Therefore, having made a formal agreement, let a policy be established here;
otherwise, there will surely be conflict among the kings. (7)
When such a dispute had arisen among the kings there,
the excellent king Suvāhu was summoned into the midst of the assembly.
Having summoned all the kings, those seers of truth said to him:
"O King, you must apply yourself with focused attention to the proper conduct regarding this marriage."
"O King, tell me with a composed mind what you intend to do;
to whom does the gift of your daughter please your heart, O Monarch? (10)
Subāhu said:
"Sudarśana was indeed chosen by my daughter's mind as her desire;
though I restrained her most earnestly, she did not heed my words."
"What can I do? My daughter’s mind does not remain under my control;
likewise, Sudarśana has arrived alone and undisturbed. (12)
Vyāsa said:
Having summoned Sudarśana, all the kings, being vigilant, spoke to him as he arrived alone and composed. (13)
"O illustrious prince of noble vows, by whom were you summoned that you have come here alone to this assembly of kings? (14)
Neither an army, nor ministers, nor a treasury, nor a great force do you possess; for what purpose have you come? Tell me the truth, O high-minded one. (15)
The kings assembled here are desirous of battle; they have come with their armies for the sake of the maiden. What do you intend to do in this situation? (16)
Your brother Subala, the hero, has arrived with the desire to seize [the city], and the mighty-armed Yudhājit has also come to provide assistance. (17)
"Go or stay, O Indra among kings; that which was spoken has been stated exactly as it is.
Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 20. 157.
Go or stay, O Indra among kings; that which was spoken has been stated exactly as it is.
"And since you are devoid of an army, do as you wish, O observer of noble vows.
Sudarśana said:
"I have no strength, no allies, no treasury, and no refuge in a fortress."
I have no friends, no affection, and no kings to protect me. ||19||
Having heard of this svayaṃvara, I have come here desiring to see it;
I have been impelled by the Goddess in a dream, of this there is no doubt. (20)
"Nothing else is intended by me today; the Goddess of the Universe has spoken to me, and whatever she has ordained shall come to pass today, without a doubt. (21)
O lords of the world, there is no enemy whatsoever here in this cycle of existence for me today, as I behold everywhere Bhavānī, the Mother of the World.
O princes, whoever shall act as an enemy toward me, the Great Vidyā shall be his punisher; I do not recognize such enmity.
O best of kings, that which is destined to be will surely come to pass and not otherwise; what cause for anxiety should there be here? I am entirely subject to fate. 24.
O best of kings, among gods, humans, and all living beings at all times, devotion toward him is produced for everyone; it is not otherwise.
O King, whatever that ruler desires to do in the evening, the lords of men carry it out; or if he wishes to make a man penniless, what concern is that of mine at all? (26)
Without that supreme power, even the gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are not able to move; what concern, then, is there for me, O kings?
Whether I am capable or incapable, whatever I may be, by his command I have arrived this very day at the svayaṃvara. (28)
Whatever she desires, let her do; what is the use of my worrying?
No doubt should be entertained in this matter; I speak this truth to you. (29)
O kings, I have not even the slightest shame here regarding victory or defeat;
however, the Blessed Lady does possess shame, and I am therefore subject to her in every way.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard that speech of his, those best of kings, the lords of men who understood the certainty of things, looked at one another and spoke. (31)
"O virtuous one, you have spoken the truth; it can never be false.
Nevertheless, the lord of Ujjayinī desires to kill you. (32)
Out of regard for you, no compassion was shown; we speak to you, O high-minded one!
O sinless one, having reflected with your mind, you should do what is right.
Sudarśana said:
"O best of kings, you compassionate friends have spoken the truth. What more can I say after having already spoken these words? (34)
Death cannot be avoided by anyone, for anyone, or at any time;
this entire world, both stationary and moving, is subject to destiny. (35)
This living being (jīva) is not independent; it is always subject to its own karma.
That karma has been declared by the wise who perceive reality to be threefold. 36.
Accumulated karma, present karma, and thirdly, commenced karma—
by means of time, action, and inherent nature, this entire world is pervaded by these.
A divine being is not able to slay a human without the arrival of the appointed time;
it is eternal Time that kills, with the [divine being] acting merely as the instrument. 38.
Just as my father, the subduer of enemies, was slain by a lion,
so too has my maternal grandfather Yudhājit been killed in battle.
Even one who exerts millions of efforts may be slain by the turn of fate;
conversely, a man might live for thousands of years without any protection at all. (40)
"O most righteous ones, I am never afraid of Yudhājita. Considering destiny alone to be supreme, O kings, I remain ever composed.
I constantly and perpetually practice the remembrance of the Blessed Goddess;
she, the Mother of the Universe, will bring about my welfare. (54:16–17)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty.

For one must experience what was previously acquired, whether it be auspicious or likewise inauspicious; when one understands that this is the experiencing of one's own past deeds, what cause for grief could there be for the wise? 43.

Having encountered suffering through the connection with the fruits of one's own karma, the insentient [body]—it is said—that being of small intellect, harbors enmity toward the instrumental cause. 44.
I do not perceive enmity, sorrow, or fear in that way;
having arrived here at this assembly of kings, I am entirely free from apprehension.
Desiring to witness the unsurpassed svayaṃvara alone,
I have arrived here by the command of Caṇḍikā, for that which was destined to happen has now come to pass.
Restrained, I know no authority other than that of the Blessed Lady;
whatever she has done will result in happiness or suffering, and it cannot be otherwise.
"May Yudhājit obtain happiness; I have no enmity toward you, O best of kings.
He who shall harbor enmity toward me will likewise receive his due reward. (48)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by him, those kings remained there well-satisfied;
he too, having reached his own hermitage, became established in a state of well-being.
On the following day, at an auspicious hour, the kings were indeed summoned by King Subāhu to his own beautiful pavilion.
And the kings, adorned with auspicious ornaments, sat upon couches prepared and furnished with divine coverings. || 51 ||
Wearing celestial attire like gods in their aerial chariots,
they stood there resplendent, desiring to witness the svayaṃvara.
Thus, all were intent on the funeral pyre, wondering, "When will she come?
When will she choose that fortunate and best of kings, whose merit is renowned? (53)
When Sudarśana happens by chance to adorn himself with a garland here, there will indeed be a dispute among kings; of this there is no doubt. (54)
While they were reflecting in this manner, seated upon their thrones,
a very great sound of musical instruments arose in the royal pavilion.
Then the Lord of Kāśī spoke to his daughter, who had bathed and was well-adorned,
wearing a garland of madhūka flowers and clothed in silken garments.
To her, who was adorned with wedding ornaments, who resembled the daughter of the ocean, who was dressed in fine garments, and who was lost in thought, he spoke these words preceded by a smile: (57)
"Arise, my son! Taking this auspicious garland in your hand, go now into the midst of the pavilion and behold the assembly of kings. (58)
O slender-waisted one, choose that best of kings who dwells in your heart—one who is virtuous, endowed with beauty, and of noble birth. (59)
"O slender-limbed one, behold all the lords of various lands reclining upon the prepared couches; choose according to your pleasure. (60)
Vyāsa said:
To her father who was speaking thus,
the young girl, who spoke with moderation, addressed these words that were both charming and consistent with dharma.
Śaśikalā said: "O father, I shall certainly not go within the sight of kings who lust after me;
other women indeed go to such lords of men. (62)
"O dear one, I have indeed heard this statement in the Dharmaśāstra:
'A woman should look upon only one man as her husband, and no other.'"
"The virtue of her chastity has departed, she who goes to another's house;
seeing her, they all imagine, 'May this happen to me. (64)
When she comes to the pavilion at the svayaṃvara holding the garland,
she then becomes like an ordinary woman, like another unchaste wife.
Just as a courtesan, having entered a gambling house, observes the men standing there and reflects within her own mind upon their merits and defects;
so too does the courtesan, being of manifold dispositions, look upon a lover in vain.
Likewise, having gone to the pavilion, I shall perform what was done by the courtesan.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter of the third book in the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. [Page 159]
"I shall not now perform the religious duty (dharma) practiced by the elders;
rather, firm in my vow, I shall observe the vow of fidelity to my husband according to my desire. (68)
Having first approached them all equally and having made many resolutions, she chooses but one; even so, how indeed shall I choose today?
"O father, O best of kings, Sudarśana was previously chosen by me with my whole being; I do not wish to act otherwise than that. (70)
O King, if you desire my welfare, bestow the gift of your daughter upon Sudarśana on an auspicious day according to the rites of marriage. (71)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 20 ||
Then the twenty-first chapter.
Vyāsa said: Subāhu, having heard what she had then spoken so appropriately, [reflected].
He was suddenly overcome with anxiety as to what should be done hereafter. ||1||
The mighty rulers of the earth, accompanied by their armies and retinues, having assembled and seated themselves upon thrones, were eager for battle. (2)
If I tell them all that she has not come now,
nevertheless those evil-minded ones, filled with anger, might kill me.
Neither do I possess such strength of an army, nor such a wondrous strength of fortresses, by which I might venture here to challenge all these kings.
Sudarśana was alone, indeed without companion, without wealth, and a mere child;
"What should be done? I am utterly submerged in an ocean of suffering. (5)
Thus lost in thought, the king went into the presence of the monarchs;
having prostrated before them, the king, bowing low with humility, then spoke to them.
"O kings, what should be done? My daughter does not enter the pavilion at will, even though she has been urged many times by her mother and by me as well. (7)
"I prostrate with my head at your feet; I am now the servant of you kings. Having accepted this honor and the rest, please return to your homes today."
"I give many jewels, garments, elephants, and chariots; having accepted these today and shown me favor, let them go to their own homes."
"If my young daughter, not being under my control, should die from distress, then I would suffer great sorrow; therefore, I am consumed by anxiety. (10)
O sirs, you who are compassionate, highly fortunate, and possessed of great luster—
what need have I for that dull-witted and ill-behaved daughter?
"I am indeed to be favored by you; I am your servant in every way. My daughter must always be regarded by you as your own daughter. (12)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of Subāhu, some of the kings did not approve;
Yudhājit, his eyes copper-red with anger, spoke to him filled with wrath. (13)
"O King, you are a fool! Why have you performed such a wicked deed?
Out of delusion, why was this svayaṃvara arranged when there was already danger? (14)
All the kings have assembled here, summoned by you to the svayaṃvara;
how is it that these monarchs are now fit to return to their own homes? (15)
Having disregarded all other kings, why do you wish to give your daughter to Sudarśana? What could be more ignoble than this? (16)
"O King, after due deliberation, a person desiring what is auspicious should indeed act; however, that which was undertaken by you was done without such knowledge."
Having abandoned these kings along with their armies and vehicles,
why do you now desire to make Sudarśana your enemy?
O most sinful one, I shall slay you first, and afterwards Sudarśana.
"My resolve is this: today I shall give my daughter to your son-in-law. (19)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty-one.
"While I am present, who else is there who wishes to abduct the maiden?
Sudarśana, how insignificant is this poor, weak child today! (20)
"Previously, at the hermitage of Bhāradvāja, I was released by me for the sake of the sage;
today, however, I will by no means release the life of this child."
Therefore, having deliberated upon this matter of righteousness together with your daughter and wife,
O fair-browed one, give your beloved daughter to my grandson.
"Having given this beautiful daughter, become her kinsman; one who desires constant welfare must always establish a high-status alliance. (23)
Having given your auspicious daughter, who is dearer to you than life itself, to Sudarśana—who is alone and without a kingdom—what happiness do you hope to obtain? (24)
"Having considered family, wealth, strength, beauty, kingdom, fortress, and friends, a daughter should be given [in marriage]; otherwise, one does not attain happiness."
Having mastered the Dharma and the eternal principles of statecraft, O King, perform your duties as is appropriate; do not set your mind on any other course.
"You are my very dear friend; for your benefit, I tell you this:
O King, bring your daughter, adorned with the rākṣī, to the pavilion. (26)
Even when she chooses someone other than Sudarśana, my body shall not suffer; let your desired marriage take place. (27)
All other kings are of noble birth, possessed of armies, and equal [to him];
O best of kings, what kind of opposition could possibly prevail against him if he were to choose [this course]? (28)
"Otherwise, I shall today forcibly seize this auspicious maiden.
O best of kings, do not enter into a conflict that is so difficult to resolve. (29)
Vyāsa said:
Commanded by Yudhājit, Subāhu, filled with grief and sighing deeply, went to his home and spoke to his wife while overwhelmed by sorrow. (30)
"O daughter, you who are well-versed in the true dharma, speak to me regarding this conflict that has arisen;
what can be done by me? I am at your mercy, O fair-eyed one. (31)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard her husband's words, she went to her daughter and said:
"O child, your father, the king, remains even now afflicted by extreme grief."
"O fair-hipped one, a conflict among the kings has indeed arisen today for your sake;
choose another king, O lady of beautiful limbs, with the exception of Sudarśana. (33)
"O child, if you forcibly choose Sudarśana,
he— being endowed with great strength— will surely slay both Yudhājit and me."
And that powerful King Sudarśana, intoxicated by his own strength, shall later become your second husband when the quarrel occurs. (35)
Therefore, O fawn-eyed one, if you desire happiness for me or for yourself, abandon Sudarśana and choose another excellent king.
Having been thus enlightened by her mother, she was subsequently enlightened by the king as well.
Having heard the words of both, the fearless maiden spoke.
The maiden said:
"O best of kings, you have spoken the truth, and you know my vow. (37)
"O protector of the earth, I choose no one else anywhere except for Sudarśana;
O Indra among kings, if you are indeed afraid of other monarchs, you are truly a coward. (38)
"Give me to Sudarśana and dismiss me outside the city;
having placed me upon his chariot, he will depart from your city. (39)
That which is destined to happen must indeed come to pass later, and it cannot be otherwise;
O best of kings, you should not entertain any anxiety regarding what is destined.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty-one. [Page 161] 165.
"What is destined to happen will certainly happen; there is no doubt about this in any way.
The king said:
"O daughter, the wise should never act with recklessness."
"Those who know the Vedas understand that one should not oppose many;
how then shall I abandon my daughter after having given her to the king's son? (42)
What improper act would kings endowed with excellent qualities not perform?
If it pleases you, my child, I shall establish a wager. (43)
Just as Janaka previously acted at Sītā’s svayaṃvara,
so too did he hold the bow of Śiva, having made it the stake.
Likewise, O slender-limbed one, I shall today perform that which is difficult to achieve, so that when it has been done, the dispute among the kings may indeed be settled. (45)
"He who shall fulfill your desire—whether it be Sudarśana or any other who is more powerful—he shall become your husband. (46)
Having fulfilled his wager, he will certainly choose you in every way;
if this is done, the dispute among the kings will be pacified. (47)
"After that, I shall arrange your marriage with ease.
The maiden said, "I do not sink into doubt at all, for this is a deed of fools. (48)
Sudarśana was previously held in my mind, and not otherwise;
for the mind alone, O Lord of the Earth, is the cause of merits and sins. (49)
"O father, having mentally chosen him, how could I choose another?
O great king, once a wager has been made, I am indeed under the control of all of you.
Whether there be one protector, two, or many, let it be so. (50)
O father, what should be done then when a dispute has arisen? (51)
"Since I do not perform any action when a task is beset by doubt, do not worry, O Indra among kings; give me to Sudarśana."
Having performed the marriage according to the prescribed rites, Caṇḍikā will bestow welfare;
by the mere chanting of her name, the flood of miseries shall go to its dissolution.
Remembering that supreme power, perform your duty without indolence;
go now and speak to the kings with your palms joined in reverence.
"Tomorrow all the kings must come here to the svayaṃvara.
Having said this, you should quickly dismiss the entire circle of monarchs. (55)
"O King, perform my marriage ceremony at night according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas;
having given him suitable wedding gifts, dismiss him. (56)
"It is said that Dhruvasandhi’s son will indeed take me away;
perhaps those kings, becoming enraged, will prepare for battle. (57)
Then that goddess will come into being and she will provide us with assistance;
he too will engage in battle with those sons of the king.
If by fate he should die in battle, I too shall surely perish;
therefore, grant me leave and stay at home with your army, and may blessings be upon you.
"I alone shall go with him, desiring to sport with him.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of hers, that king made his resolve. (60)
Having thus resolved in his mind and gained confidence, he proceeded to act accordingly.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 21 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 22.
Then the twenty-second chapter. Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of his son, the king of blameless soul went to the other kings and spoke to them.
"Let the kings depart for their camps as they please; tomorrow, indeed, we shall arrange the wedding. (1)
"Eatables and drinks have been provided by me; let everyone accept them with full confidence in me.
Tomorrow, indeed, the ceremony to take place here in this pavilion must be performed by all of you gathering together. || 2 ||
"The daughter has not come to the pavilion today; what shall I do, O kings?
Having comforted my daughter tomorrow morning, I shall lead her away. Therefore, let the kings depart from their camps. (3)
The wise do not engage in conflict with their own dependents; for compassion must always be shown toward one's offspring.
Having made this arrangement, I shall bring back my daughter; let the kings depart as they please.
"Or, having reflected upon my heart's desire, I shall perform the marriage ceremony tomorrow morning;
or else, having assembled here with all the gathered kings, a *svayaṃvara* (self-choice) should be held with the consent of everyone."
Having heard this and realizing his words were infallible, those kings departed for their own abodes;
having established a guard around the city, they performed the rites prescribed for midday.
Subāhu, accompanied by noble people, performed the rites at the time of the wedding;
having summoned his daughter to a well-guarded chamber in his home, he did so in the presence of the foremost among those who know the Vedas and the family priests.
Having performed the bathing and other rites for the bridegroom, and likewise having adorned him with wedding ornaments,
the lord of the earth brought him to the house where the altar had been prepared and offered him due honor.
O lord of men, having duly offered him a seat, water for rinsing the mouth, a pair of garments, a cow, and two earrings,
that king of undiminished strength desired to give away his daughter.
He too, his mind intoxicated by pride, accepted everything; then the anxiety regarding Manoramā subsided.
He then regarded the maiden Sukeśī as equal to a daughter of the Nidhis and considered himself to be unsurpassed.

Then all those ministers, filled with joy and free from fear, led him— who had been well-honored with gifts of ornaments and garments and who was most excellent— to the interior of the festive pavilion.
The women, their ornaments duly completed, having placed the princess upon a fine vehicle,
led her to the pavilion indeed furnished with four pillars, which was the repository of excellent treasures.
Having established the sacred fire and offered oblations according to the prescribed rites during that interval, the family priest [performed the ceremony].
*The Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 22.* Page 163.
The bride and groom, having performed the auspicious rites and being filled with love, called out to one another intensely.
Having performed the ritual scattering of parched grain according to the rules and having circumambulated the sacrificial fire,
they both carried out there every appropriate rite pertaining to their family and lineage as was fitting.
That lord of men gave to Sudarśana two well-adorned chariots, yoked with horses of the Āśvayuja breed and equipped with showers of arrows— a highly honored dowry for the wedding.
Then that lord of kings, filled with affection, gave to the prince one hundred and twenty-five elephants, rutting and adorned with gold, their bodies resembling the peaks of mountains. (16)
At the time of the wedding, the king, filled with joy, repeatedly presented to the bridegroom a hundred female slaves adorned with gold and a hundred very beautiful female elephants. (17)
Furthermore, he gave a thousand servants, all equipped with weapons and fully adorned, as well as gems, garments appropriate for each, and various divine and woolen cloths. (18)
Furthermore, he gave him long, beautiful, and variegated dwelling-houses;
and he bestowed two thousand most lovely, excellent horses born in the land of Sindhu. (19)
He indeed assigned three hundred very beautiful camels carrying loads, and he gave him two hundred excellent wagons filled with grains and liquids. (20)
Having bowed before the beautiful princess, he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence:
"O most excellent princess, I am your servant; therefore, tell me whatever is in your heart. (21)
She too spoke those pleasing words: "May it be well with you, O King; may there be prosperity for your lineage!
I am honored by you, since you have bestowed your own daughter, Ratnavarā, upon my son. (22)
O King, I am neither the daughter of a bard nor the princess of Magadha; why then do I praise you here as my own most eminent kinsman?
For today my son has been made equal to Mount Sumeru by this most excellent sovereign, my relative.
Oh, how exceedingly wonderful and supremely purifying is the conduct of you, O King! What more can I say?
For today you have bestowed upon my son, who has been deprived of his kingdom, your most venerable and excellent daughter.
To him who lived in the forest, who was indeed penniless, who was bereft of his father, who was without an army,
who had abandoned all these kings, who subsisted on fruits, and who was devoid of wealth— (25)
Furthermore, a king gives his daughter to one who possesses equal wealth, a lineage, and strength; no one would give a virtuous and beautiful daughter to my son, who is destitute of means. (26)
But all [the kings], having entered into an alliance with one another against their enemies, who were surrounded by excellent troops, [prepared for battle].
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty-two:
"Now that my daughter Sudarśanā has been entrusted to you, how can I describe this fortitude of yours?"
Having heard these words, the king was delighted and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke again:
"Accept my well-known kingdom; from this day forth, I shall be your general. (28)
If not, then having accepted half of that, enjoy the fruits of sovereignty here together with your sons;
abandon your residence in Vārāṇasī, for from now on I have no dwelling either in the forest or in the city.
"There are indeed kings who possess great beauty; having gone there, I shall first employ conciliation.
After that, I will use two other means, and if those fail, I shall wage war. (30)
Victory and defeat depend on destiny; nevertheless, victory belongs to righteousness even when unrighteousness has been committed.
How indeed will it be for those kings who are unrighteous? Their ill-considered plans will surely fail.
Having heard his meaningful speech, Manoramā, who had attained honor from him, spoke these beneficial words to him; she was delighted and serene in every way. (32)
"O King, may it be well with you; rule your kingdom, casting aside all fear along with your sons.
Surely my son too, having obtained the kingdom in the city of Sāketa, will carry on his rule here. (33)
"Dismiss us so that we may go to our own home; Bhavānī will provide for your welfare.
O King, no anxiety exists for me as I meditate upon the Supreme Mother. (34)
The lamps had been extinguished by the various words and phrases of the *rasāla* trees, as well as by the nectar-like words of their mutual conversation;
in the morning, the kings, having learned that the marriage had taken place, went outside the city filled with rage and spoke thus: (35)
"Let us kill that prince, the bearer of the king's disgrace, and likewise that boy who is indeed unfit for marriage;
let us seize Śaśikalā and the fortune of the king. Having incurred shame, how shall we return to our own [country]? (36)
"Let them hear the sounds of trumpets being played; indeed, the sounds of the mṛdaṅgas overwhelm the blasts of conchs.
And we perceive various sounds of song and the resonance of the Vedas; we believe that the king has performed the wedding ceremony here. (37)
Having deceived us, he has indeed performed the grasping of the hand according to the ritual of marriage by means of the marriage rite;
what must be done now? O kings, consider this among yourselves and deliberate upon a course of action. (38)

While the kings were speaking thus, the Lord of Kāśī, possessing incomparable majesty, performed the marriage rites for the maiden and quickly departed with his friends of renowned power to invite the monarchs. And then the kings, seeing the Lord of Kāśī approaching...
Out of anger, they did not say anything at all, but remained standing, observing silence. 40.
Having gone there and prostrated, he spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"All the kings must come to my house for the sake of a meal. (41)
"This king has been chosen by my daughter; what can I do, whether it be beneficial or harmful?
You must act auspiciously for him, for the great are indeed compassionate. (42)

Having heard those words of his, the kings were overwhelmed with anger. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa*, Third Skandha, Chapter 23. [Page 165] === PAGE 165 === Having heard those words of his, the kings were overwhelmed with anger.
They replied, "We have already eaten; O King, please go to your own home. (43)
Perform all your duties as you wish; a good deed has been done.
Let all the kings today indeed depart for their respective homes. 44.
Having heard that, Subāhu also went home apprehensive, wondering, "What will the best of kings do when they are agitated and filled with anger? (45)
When he had departed, those rulers of the earth again made a pact:
"Having blocked the path and slain Sudarśana, we shall seize the maiden. (46)
Some said: "What have we to do with that king?
Having seen all this curiosity, we shall go back just as we came. (47)
Having spoken thus, all those kings took their leave and departed;
Subāhu, having returned to his own home, performed his subsequent duties.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 22 ||
Then the twenty-third chapter. Vyāsa said:
Having then duly prepared foods worthy of honor for him, according to the prescribed rites, he...
And for six days, the king fed [him] with devotion. ||1||
Having thus performed all the marriage rites, the king,
after bestowing the wedding gifts, then consulted with his ministers.
Having heard what was told by his attendants regarding the obstruction of the path,
King Subāhu, of immeasurable splendor, became despondent.
Then Sudarśana, firm in his vows, said to his father-in-law:
"Dismiss us quickly; we shall depart without any apprehension."
"O King, having gone to the holy hermitage of Bhāradvāja, you must by all means deliberate there with a concentrated mind regarding our dwelling. (5)
O sinless one, you should not feel even the slightest fear of the serpents;
Bhavānī, the mother of the world, will surely provide me with assistance.
Vyāsa said:
Having understood this intention of his son-in-law, that best of kings dismissed him after giving him wealth; he, too, departed in haste.
Possessed of great strength, that best of kings proceeded forward;
Sudarśana, surrounded there, moved along the path fearlessly.
The hero, seated upon his chariot with his wife, was likewise surrounded by his own forces.
As he went along, the joy of the Raghus beheld the armies of the kings.
Subāhu, too, having seen them, became overcome with anxiety;
he joyfully sought refuge in Śivā within his heart according to the prescribed rites.
He recited the unsurpassed Kāmarāja mantra, which consists of a single syllable;
free from fear and devoid of sorrow, he remained together with his newly wedded wife.
Then all the rulers of the earth, having raised a great clamor,
rose up accompanied by their armies, desiring to kill the maiden.
Upon seeing them, the King of Kāśī indeed became intent on killing them;
however, he was then strongly restrained by Rāghava, who desired victory.
There too, conchs, kettledrums, and small drums resounded as Subāhu and the kings, desiring to slay one another, clashed.
Śatrughna, well-prepared and stationed there with the intent to slay [his enemies],
and Yudhājit, equipped for the sake of assisting him, stood ready.
And some spectators stood there with his armies;
Yudhājit, having gone forward, approached Sudarśana.
Accompanied by Pātrujitta, the younger brother set out to kill his elder brother;
overcome with rage, they mangled one another with floods of arrows.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter thirteen.
A very great tumult then broke out there among those excellent archers;
at that time, the Lord of Kāśī, surrounded by a vast army, arrived swiftly.
She went quickly for the sake of assistance to her blameless son-in-law.
While this terrible, hair-raising battle was thus proceeding,
the Goddess suddenly appeared, seated upon a lion.
Bearing various weapons, beautiful, adorned with excellent ornaments,
dressed in divine garments, and well-endowed with garlands of mandāra flowers—
seeing her, those kings then attained the utmost amazement. ||20-21||
"Who is this woman mounted upon a lion, and from where has she come? Thus the inquiry arose;
but Sudarśana, beholding her, said to Subāhu:
"Behold, O King, the Great Goddess of divine appearance who has arrived. (22)
"Surely she has appeared out of compassion to favor me.
O Great King, having become fearless even from fear itself, Sudarśana and Subāhu beheld that lady of the beautiful countenance. (23–24)
Delighted by the sight of her, they both offered their salutations;
at that moment, the lion roared and the elephants, terrified, trembled.
Terrible winds blew and the quarters of the sky became most dreadful;
then Sudarśana spoke to his own commander-in-chief.
Proceed quickly along the path where the kings are stationed;
what can these kings do, even if they are enraged and evil-minded? (27)
For she is our divine lady who has come for the sake of refuge;
we must proceed along this path crowded with kings, free from fear. (28)
"I have remembered the Great Goddess, who has arrived for the sake of protection.
Having heard those words, the commander-in-chief proceeded by that path. (29)
But Yudhājit, greatly enraged, said to those lords of the earth:
"Why do you stand here terrified by fear? Slay him along with the maiden! (30)
And disregarding all of us, who are superior in strength, that child, though himself weak, has taken the maiden and proceeds with speed and fearlessness. (31)
"Being afraid upon seeing a woman seated on a lion, you must not neglect her; O highly fortunate ones, she must be slain here with focused minds. (32)
"We shall seize the forest and the maiden with her beautiful ornaments;
this jackal does not deserve to take what has been claimed by the lion. (33)
Having spoken thus, Yudhājit, accompanied by his army and joined by Śatrughna,
arrived there desiring to fight, overwhelmed with rage.
Drawing his bow back to his ear, he quickly released arrows that were polished by smiths, sharpened on stone, and fitted with matching feathers.
Then the evil-minded one, desiring to kill Sudarśana from above, [attacked];
but Sudarśana, in an instant, cut those arrows down as they fell with his own shafts.
When the battle had thus commenced, Caṇḍikā became exceedingly enraged;
then Goddess Durgā discharged arrows toward Yudhājit.
Then the auspicious Mother of the World, assuming various forms and bearing various weapons, arrived there and created a tumultuous uproar. (38)
There, Śatruñjaya was slain, and King Yudhājit also fell;
as both of them tumbled from their chariots, a cry of victory arose at that moment. 39.
Seeing her and the death of their maternal uncle as well as their nephew in battle, all the ornaments attained the utmost astonishment.
Subāhu, too, seeing their death in battle,
was supremely delighted and praised Durgā, the destroyer of difficult calamities.
Subāhu said: Salutations to the Goddess, the mother of the universe; constant salutations to Śivā.
Salutations again and again to you, the Blessed Durgā, the granter of desires.
Salutations to Śivā, to you who are peace; salutations to the Knowledge that grants liberation.
O Mother of the world, O Sustainer of the universe, salutations to you, O Śivā, who pervades the entire cosmos.
O Goddess, though reflecting deeply upon your course, I do not know it; for you, who are indeed devoid of qualities, are said to be possessed of all qualities.
Śrīmad-devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam, Third Skandha, Chapter 24.160.
How can I praise her, the mother of the universe, whose power is manifest, who is intent on destroying the suffering of her devotees, and who is the supreme Śakti? (44)
You are the goddess of speech, omnipresent indeed; you are the intellect, knowledge, and understanding, as well as the refuge of every living being.
Why do I praise you? For you are the controller of all minds; indeed, how can one's own true nature ever be praised? 45.

Even Brahmā, Hara, and Hari—the best of the gods—have indeed reached no end while incessantly praising Your qualities. O Ambā, where am I, possessed of a mind full of distinctions; alas, how can I, being so unrenowned, be capable of recounting Your deeds? 46.
Oh, how can association with the virtuous not produce its desired effect, even when it occurs incidentally, since it surely brings about purity of mind?
Indeed, through this meeting arranged for my son-in-law, I have obtained this wonderful vision of you. (47)

O Mother, even Brahmā, Hara, Hari, the gods led by Indra, and the sages who have realized the truth of reality, always long for that vision of yours which today I have obtained— though it is so difficult to attain— even without self-restraint, tranquility, or meditative absorption.
Where am I, of such dull intellect, compared to Your swift glance; and where is this, O Bhavānī, Your peerless medicine for worldly existence?
For You, O Goddess, are indeed eternally endowed with compassion, devoted to showing mercy to Your devotees, and worshipped by the assembly of the immortals.
O Goddess, how can I describe this conduct of yours, that Sudarśana has been protected here in such peril?
Today, by you, the powerful enemies have been swiftly slain; O compassionate one toward your devotees, your conduct is supremely pure. (50)
"O Goddess, this is no wonder," you reflected; "having considered the matter, you indeed protect everything in its entirety, both the stationary and the moving.
Having struck down the enemy out of compassion, you have now protected this son of Dhruvasandhi. (51)
O Bhavānī, you have fashioned this life-story to make your own fame, which is devoted to serving your devotees, exceedingly radiant;
otherwise, how could Kuśalavā, who is of irreproachable character, have become so skillful in battle after having well-accepted your daughter?
O Mother, you are capable of destroying the fears of birth, death, and so forth; what wonder is there in this regarding the desire of your devotee?
You are sung of as boundless by your devotees, O Mother; you are devoid of both sin and merit, yet you possess attributes and are also without attributes.
O Goddess, Sovereign of the World, by the sight of you I have become a man of great merit, one who has achieved his life’s purpose; I am blessed in my birth, O Mother!
Indeed, I knew neither your seed nor your worship, yet today your greatness and manifest power have been realized by me.
Vyāsa said: Thus praised, the goddess Śivā, with a gracious countenance, then spoke to the king: "O observer of noble vows, choose a boon."
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 23 ||
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of Bhavānī, that best of kings—
There, Subāhu, filled with devotion, spoke these words: || 1 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty-four.
Subāhu said:
"On one side is the kingdom of the world of the gods and the circle of the earth; on the other side is the sight of you indeed—and these two are never equal."
"There is nothing in the three worlds equal to this sight for me. O Goddess, what boon shall I ask for? I have achieved my purpose on the face of the earth. (3)
O Mother, I desire to ask for this cherished boon:
may my devotion to you always remain unfailing, O Protectress of the Universe. (4)
"O Mother, you must remain here in this city at all times;
established here as Śakti, you shall indeed be known by the name Durgādevī. (5)
And you must always provide protection for this city,
so that it may remain free from disease, just as Sudarśana was protected from the hosts of enemies.
Likewise, O Ambikā, you must provide protection here for Vārāṇasī until the city becomes well-established and firmly situated upon the earth. (7)
O Goddess, treasure-house of compassion, you must remain here in this fortress for that long;
this boon should be granted to me by you—what else could I possibly ask for? (8)
Grant me all various desires and slay my enemies;
and always bring about the destruction of all that is inauspicious for the world.
Vyāsa said: Thus entreated by him who was overcome by distress, the goddess Durgā, the destroyer of difficulties,
stood before that king and, having praised him, spoke to him there.
Durgā said:
"O King, my permanent residence shall be in Muktipurī for the protection of all the worlds as long as the earth endures. (11)
Then Sudarśana, having arrived there filled with joy,
bowed down with supreme devotion and praised the Mother of the Universe.
Oh, how great is your compassion! What can I say? For you have indeed saved one who was devoid of devotion.
Everyone is compassionate toward their devotees; however, the protection of those who have abandoned devotion is your specific vow.
O Goddess, it has been heard by me that you create the entire phenomenal world; you protect what you have created;
and at the time of dissolution, you consume it. Therefore, my protection by you is not at all surprising.
"What shall I do for you? Tell me, O Goddess, what task must be done, or where should I go? Grant me your permission at once.
I am bewildered as to my duty; by your command, O Mother, I shall go, stay, or move about."
Vyāsa said:
To him who was speaking thus, the goddess, filled with compassion, replied:
"Go to Ayodhyā, O highly fortunate one, and rule the kingdom befitting your lineage."
"I am always to be remembered by you and to be worshipped with effort;
O best of kings, I shall eternally bestow welfare and sovereignty upon you. (17)
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and especially on the ninth day,
my worship should be performed according to the ritual for offering oblations (bali).
"O sinless one, my image should be installed by you in the city;
it must be worshipped with effort and devotion three times a day. (19)
In the autumn season, a great worship of me must always be performed according to the ritual of Navarātra, endowed with a spirit of devotion—endowed with a spirit of devotion. (20)
A great festival should be celebrated in the months of Caitra, Āśvina, Āṣāḍha, and Māgha;
O Great King, worship should be performed especially during Navarātra.
O tiger among kings, those endowed with devotion to me should always perform [this rite] on the fourteenth day and likewise on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, as prescribed by the wise. (22)
In the glorious Mahāpurāṇa Śrīmad Bhāgavatam, in the third book (Tṛtīyaskandha), chapter 24. Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, vanished;
she was then bowed to and praised at great length by Sudarśana.
Seeing her vanished, all those kings approached him and bowed down, just as the gods bow to Śakra.
Subāhu also, having bowed to him, stood there filled with joy;
then all the kings spoke to the lord of Ayodhyā.
Our own lord and teacher is your servant, and we are always yours;
O best of kings, rule the kingdom in Ayodhyā and protect us.
O Great King, by your grace, I have beheld the auspicious Viśveśvarī, Bhavānī, the primordial Śakti who bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. (27)
You are one who has fulfilled his purpose and possesses great merit upon the earth, since for your sake the eternal Goddess has manifested. (28)
O best of kings, we all did not know the power of Caṇḍikā, for we were always deluded by her darkness-filled illusion. 29.
They are always delighted in thinking of their wives and sons,
submerged in a terrible great ocean agitated by the fish of lust and anger.
O illustrious one, we wish to question you; you are omniscient, O high-minded one!
Tell us: what is this power, from where has it arisen, and what is its influence? 31.
O descendant of Kakutstha, you are a boat for us in this saṃsāra, and the virtuous are exceedingly compassionate;
therefore, tell us the supreme majesty of the Goddess.
O best of men, we wish to hear everything regarding that goddess—her true nature and her origin, as well as how her power has departed; please tell us.
Vyāsa said:
Thus questioned by them at that time, the king who was the son of Dhruvasandhi,
having searched for the Goddess with his mind, spoke to them filled with joy.
Sudarśana said:
O protector of the earth, what can I say of her supreme conduct?
Even Brahmā and the other hosts of gods, together with Śiva, do not know it.
O protector of the earth, she is the primordial Mahālakṣmī of all, the most excellent and supreme power; she is of the nature of sattva and is intent upon the protection of the world.
She who takes the form of *rajas* during creation, the form of *sattva* during preservation, and the form of *tamas* during dissolution—she is always considered to consist of the three *guṇas*. (37)
The supreme power is devoid of qualities (nirguṇā) and bestows the fruits of all desires;
for she, O best of kings, is indeed the cause of all beings, beginning with Brahmā. (38)
O kings, she who is devoid of attributes is impossible for yogis to know in every respect;
however, she who possesses attributes is easily served and should always be meditated upon by the wise. 39.
The kings said:
"Though you reached the forest while still a child, you were surely overcome by fear;
how was the Goddess, the supreme and most excellent Śakti, recognized by you? (40)
O King, how was she served and how was she honored, that she, being well-pleased, rendered assistance with great haste? 41.
Sudarśana said:
"O kings, out of childishness I obtained its seed-mantra through close association; I remember reciting daily that which is known as the Kāmabīja. (42)
That supreme Ambikā Śivā, being described by the sages, has been known by me;
I remember her day and night with the highest devotion.
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of his, the kings, intent on devotion and regarding her as the supreme power, departed toward their own homes.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty-five.
Subāhu went to Kāśī after taking leave of Sudarśana;
and the righteous Sudarśana also departed from the land of Kosala.
But the ministers, having heard that Śatrujit had been killed in battle and that Sudarśana had indeed been victorious, were filled with affection.
Hearing that the king was approaching, the inhabitants of Sāketa [prepared to welcome him].
Taking up various offerings, the people went forth into his presence. || 47 ||
Likewise, all the subjects, with various gifts in their hands, joyfully departed after having presented the son of Dhruvasandhi.
Then, accompanied by his wife, that handsome Sudarśana reached Ayodhyā;
after honoring all the people, the king went to his palace.
He was being praised by bards, saluted by ministers,
and showered with parched grain and flowers by young maidens.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 24 ||
Then the twenty-fifth chapter. Vyāsa said:
Having gone to Ayodhyā, that best of kings, surrounded by his friends, entered the palace of the king.
Śatrujit, having prostrated before his grief-stricken mother, spoke to her. ||1||
"O mother, your son has certainly not been slain by me in battle, nor has your father Yudhājit; I swear this by your feet. (2)
He was slain in battle by Durgā; indeed, there is no fault of mine in this matter.
Against events that are destined to occur, no remedy exists.
O proud lady, you should not feel grief here for your deceased son;
living beings, subject to the power of their own karma, experience pleasures and pains.
O Mother, I am your slave; just as Manorama is mine, so too are you, O knower of dharma—there is not even the slightest difference between us. (5)
One must inevitably experience the results of whatever action has been performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
therefore, you should never grieve over pleasure or pain.
In times of suffering, one should look upon those who suffer more than oneself; in times of happiness, one should look upon those who are happier than oneself.
One should not surrender oneself to grief and joy as if they were two enemies.
All this is dependent on destiny and never dependent on oneself;
therefore, a wise man should not wither his soul through grief. (8)
Just as a wooden puppet moves through the manipulation of actors and others, so the embodied soul, subject to its own karma, functions everywhere. (9)
"O mother, having gone to the forest, my mind was not filled with sorrow;
reflecting upon my own past deeds, I know that they must be experienced. (10)
My maternal grandfather has died right here, and my mother, overcome with grief and stricken by fear, took me and departed for the dense forest. (11)
Plundered by thieves on the road, she was likewise stripped of her clothes;
all her provisions were taken away, leaving her with her young son and without any refuge.
My mother took me and arrived at the hermitage of Bhāradvāja;
this Vidalla has also arrived, as has Dhātreyikā. (13)
Filled with compassion, the sages and their wives nourished those three who were staying there on all sides with fruits and wild grains (nīvāra).
At that time I felt no suffering, nor do I feel happiness now upon the arrival of wealth;
there has never been any enmity or envy in my mind at any time. (15)
In the heat of austerity, eating wild rice (nīvāra) is superior to the enjoyments of kings;
one who aspires for that [higher state] goes to hell, but one who merely eats wild rice never does so.
A wise man should practice righteousness, having truly conquered the group of senses, so that he does not go to hell. (17)
O Mother, human birth in this auspicious land of Bhārata is difficult to obtain; indeed, the comforts of food and so forth may be found in all [other] wombs. (18)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 25:
Having cast off that human body, one must perform the means for attaining dharma.
It bestows heaven and liberation upon men, and is difficult to attain in other wombs.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by him at that time, Lolāvatī, overcome with extreme shame, cast aside her grief for her son and spoke to him with tearful eyes. (20)
"O son, I am guilty; I was made so by my father Yudhājit, who indeed killed your maternal grandfather and seized his kingdom. (21)
I was not able to restrain my son then;
whatever deed was done by him alone, there is no fault of mine, O son. (22)
In their deaths, you were not the cause by your own doing, nor were they;
I do not grieve for that son, but I always grieve for what he did. (23)
"O son, you are auspicious; Manoramā is my sister.
I have not the slightest anger or sorrow toward you, my son. (24)
Rule the kingdom, O highly fortunate one; protect the subjects, O observer of noble vows.
By the grace of the Blessed Goddess, this realm has been obtained free from all thorns.
Having heard those words of his mother and having bowed to her, the prince went to the beautiful palace where Manoramā formerly resided.
Having gone there, Yavanasattva summoned all his ministers and astrologers, and then inquired about an auspicious hour and day.
Likewise, he had a beautiful golden throne fashioned.
I shall always worship the Goddess seated upon the lion-throne. ||28||
Having seated the Goddess, who bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, upon her throne,
I shall thereafter govern the kingdom just as it was ruled by Rāma and the others.
The Goddess should always be worshipped by all people of the city;
she is the venerable Śiva-Śakti, the bestower of the fulfillment of all desires and aims. (30)
Thus addressed, those ministers carried out the king's command;
they had a most beautiful palace constructed by artisans.
Then, having had an image fashioned on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, the king summoned the twice-born who were learned in the Vedas and established it. (32)
Having performed the oblation according to the rules and having worshipped the deity,
the wise king installed her in the temple of the Goddess.
O King, a festival took place there with the sounds of musical instruments,
the Vedic chants of the Brahmins, and various songs.
Vyāsa said:
Having installed the goddess Śivā according to the prescribed rites by those who recite the Vedas, the king performed various kinds of worship with great ritual precision. (35)
Having performed the rites of worship and regained his ancestral kingdom, the king became renowned,
and the goddess Ambikā indeed became famous among the Kosalas.
Having obtained the kingdom, the king, a victor through the true Dharma, brought all the neighboring kings—who were exceedingly righteous—under his control. (37)
Just as Rāma was in his own kingdom, and as Raghu was in that of Dilīpa,
so too did the happiness of the subjects and the established order of conduct flourish.
Likewise, the dharma of the castes and stages of life became four-footed;
on the surface of the earth, the minds of no one took delight in unrighteousness. (39)
In every village, all the lords of men constructed palaces;
at that time, the worship of the Goddess was joyfully established throughout the Kosala lands.
Subāhu also, having had a beautiful image of Durgā fashioned in Kāśī, installed it in a temple with devotion. || 41 ||
There, all the people there, devoted to loving devotion,
performed her worship according to the prescribed rites, just as they would for Viśveśvara.
Then she became renowned as the goddess Durgā upon the surface of the earth;
O great king, her devotion increased in every land. 43.
At that time, Bhavānī became the object of worship for everyone in every way, throughout the whole world of Bhārata and among all social classes. 44.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty-six.
O King, all became devoted to Śakti and Bhakti, full of self-respect, and intent upon the recitation of mantras, meditation, and hymns as prescribed in the Āgamas. (45)
During all the Navarātras, all the people, devoted to the Goddess, performed worship, oblations, and sacrifice according to the prescribed rules.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 25 ||
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"O best of the twice-born, when the Navarātra has arrived, what should be performed?"
Please explain the ritual procedure according to the rules, especially for the autumn season.
O Great-minded One, what indeed is the fruit and what rite is to be performed there?
O best of the twice-born, please explain this in detail out of compassion. (2)
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the auspicious Navarātra vow;
it should be performed according to the prescribed rules, especially during the autumn season.
In the springtime, it should likewise be performed with love;
for indeed, among all people, there are two seasons known as the fangs of Yama—
the autumn and the spring— which are truly difficult for living beings here to overcome.
Therefore, one who desires auspiciousness in all matters should perform this rite with diligent effort. || 5 ||
Only two seasons are exceedingly terrible and cause disease for men;
both spring and autumn alone bring about the destruction of all.
Therefore, O lord of men, the wise should perform the worship of Caṇḍikā there with devotion during the auspicious month of Āśvina.
Having reached the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should prepare auspicious materials;
on that day, one should eat only one meal consisting of sacrificial food (haviṣya) and meatless fare.
The pavilion should be constructed on level ground in an auspicious location,
measuring sixteen cubits in size and provided with pillars and banners.
Then, one should have the area smeared with white clay and cow dung;
in its center, a bright, level, and stable altar (vedikā) should be constructed. 10.
The site for the pedestal should be four cubits on each side and one cubit in height;
one should then arrange variously decorated arches and a canopy.
Then, at night, he addressed the twice-born who were experts in the true nature of the Goddess—
those devoted to right conduct, self-controlled, and masters of the Vedas and their auxiliary branches.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, one should perform the morning bath according to the prescribed rules,
whether in a river, a stream, a lake, a pond, a well, or even at home.
Having performed the daily morning rites, one should then proceed with the formal invitation of the Brahmins.
All rites, beginning with the offering of water for honor (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya), should be performed preceded by honey (madhu). || 14 ||
Garments, ornaments, and other such items should be given according to one's own capacity;
one should never practice stinginess regarding wealth when resources are available.
When satisfied by the Brahmins, the task shall be entirely fulfilled.
For the recitation of the Goddess, nine, five, or three Brahmins are prescribed. (16)
Then, one should select a peaceful Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of reciting the Pārāyaṇa;
the rite of Svastivācana should be performed according to the injunctions of the Vedic mantras. ||17||
Having placed a lion-throne upon the altar, furnished with silken cloth,
the goddess Ambikā should be installed there, endowed with four hands and her weapons.
Adorned with jewel ornaments and radiant with pearl necklaces, wearing divine garments, gentle, and endowed with all auspicious marks. || 19 ||
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, seated upon a lion, auspicious, and possessing eighteen arms, the eternal Goddess should be installed. (20)
In the absence of an image, one should likewise place a yantra conjoined with the nine-syllable mantra;
there, for the purpose of worshipping the pedestal (pīṭha), one should set down a water-pot (kalaśa) at its side.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty-six:
[The vessel] joined with the five sprouts, consecrated with Vedic mantras, filled with water from excellent holy sites, and endowed with gold and gems. (22)
Having arranged the necessary materials for the worship of Pārśva on all sides,
one should indeed cause the sounds of songs and musical instruments to be made for the sake of auspiciousness.
O King, worship on the first day, when the lunar day is joined with the Hasta constellation and is a Nandā tithi, is excellent; performed according to the rules, it grants the desires of men. (24)
Having first established the observance (niyama), one should thereafter perform the worship,
either by fasting, eating only at night, or by taking a single meal.
"O Mother, I shall observe the unsurpassed vow of Navarātra;
O Goddess, Mother of the Universe, grant me your full assistance. (26)
One should observe the restrictive vow (niyama) for the sake of the religious observance (vrata) according to one's capacity;
thereafter, worship should be performed according to the rules, preceded by the recitation of mantras. ||27||
With sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and with fragrant flowers—mandāra, karaja, aśoka, campaka, and karavīra. ||28||
One should worship the Sustainer of the worlds with *mālatī* flowers, *brahmakā* flowers, and auspicious *bilva* leaves, according to the prescribed ritual, using incense and lamps. (29)
There, indeed, an offering (arghya) should be presented with various kinds of fruits,
such as coconuts, citron fruits, pomegranates, and plantains.
O lord of men, one should perform the gift of food with devotion, using oranges, jackfruits, and likewise auspicious fruits that are fully ripe. (31)
Those who consume meat must perform the slaughter of animals;
among these, the offering of buffaloes, goats, and boars as a sacrificial oblation (bali) is considered superior.
O sinless one, animals slain in the presence of the Goddess go to the imperishable heaven; for there is no violence born of the animal in that case, as they are killed for her sake.
In the definitive conclusion of all scriptures, non-violence is declared to be the true nature of sacrifice;
for animals offered for the sake of the deities, there is certainly the attainment of heaven. (34)
For the purpose of the fire sacrifice (homa), a triangular pit (kuṇḍa) must be constructed;
or else, an auspicious triangular sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared according to the prescribed measurements. ||35||
Worship should be performed constantly at the three times of day with various pleasing substances,
and a great festival should be celebrated with songs, instrumental music, and dances.
One should always sleep on the ground and worship young maidens with divine garments and ornaments, as well as with foods consisting of nectar. (37)
One should worship each one daily, increasing by one [deity] at a time,
or likewise doubling or tripling them, or even nine for each.
Indeed, worship should be performed according to one's means;
O King, one should never practice stinginess regarding wealth in a sacrifice when one has the capacity. (39)

O King, a girl who has reached only one year of age should not be employed in the ritual of worship; however, even a young child may be the supreme knower of enjoyments such as perfumes and the like. (40)
She who is two years old here is called Kumārikā;
Trimūrti is three years old, and Kalyāṇī is four years of age. (41)
Rohiṇī is known as five years old, and Kālikā as six years old;
Caṇḍikā would be seven years old, and Śāmbhavī eight years old.
Durgā should be nine years old, and Subhadrā ten years old;
beyond that age, she should not be made [as an image], for it is censured in all ritual matters.
Worship should be performed with these names according to the prescribed ritual;
I shall now describe the fruits of always worshipping these nine.
A maiden, when worshipped, brings about the destruction of suffering and poverty;
she indeed effects the ruin of enemies, the increase of wealth and longevity, and the growth of strength. (45)
From the worship of the Trimūrti, there shall arise longevity, the fruits of the three aims of life, the acquisition of wealth and grain, and the increase of sons, grandsons, and progeny. (46)
One seeking knowledge, one seeking victory, a king seeking sovereignty, and one seeking happiness should always worship Kalyāṇī, the granter of all desires. 47.
One should worship Kālikā with devotion for the purpose of destroying enemies;
and one who desires sovereignty and wealth should fully worship Caṇḍikā.
One should worship the Śāmbhavī [goddess] daily for the sake of enchanting kings, for the destruction of suffering and poverty, and for victory in battle. (49)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book (Tṛtīya Skandha), chapter twenty-seven.
For the sake of destroying cruel enemies, as well as for accomplishing fierce rites,
and for the happiness of the next world, one should worship Durgā with devotion.
For the sake of accomplishing one's desired object, one should always worship Subhadrā;
for the destruction of disease, a person should worship Rohiṇī according to the prescribed rite. (51)
And with the mantra "Śrīrastu," one intent on devotion should perform worship;
either with the mantra containing the word "Śrī," or else with seed-syllable mantras (bījamantra). ||52||
I worship that Kumārī who, even in play, creates the principles (tattvas) of Kumāra as well as those gods beginning with Ka.
I worship the Trimūrti, that power which, through the qualities of sattva and the others, possesses manifold forms and pervades the three periods of time. 54.
She who eternally brings about auspiciousness for her devotees and is worshipped incessantly—I worship that auspicious one, the granter of all desires, with devotion. (55)
I worship that goddess Rohiṇī who causes the seeds accumulated in previous births to sprout for all living beings. (56)
Time impels everything within the entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving;
at the time of the end of the kalpa, I worship her as Kālikā.
I worship that Caṇḍikā, the remover of fierce sins. || 58 ||
I worship that goddess Śāmbhavī, who is thus celebrated and who bestows happiness. ||59||
I worship that Durgā, who arises without cause, who always protects her devotee from distress, who destroys all misfortune, and who is difficult to be known even by all the gods. (60)
When worshipped, she always brings auspiciousness to her devotees;
I worship the goddess Subhadrā, the destroyer of inauspiciousness. (61)
By these mantras, young maidens should always be worshipped by the wise with garments, ornaments, garlands, and various kinds of fragrant unguents.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 26 ||
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Vyāsa said: One should avoid a maiden who is deficient in limbs, afflicted with leprosy, or marked by ulcers.
Her body was devoid of the fragrance [of fine perfumes], yet she was born of a noble lineage.
One should reject a maiden who is blind from birth, squint-eyed, one-eyed, ugly, excessively hairy, diseased, or marked with red flowers and the like. (2)

One who is emaciated, one whose pregnancy has recently ended, a *golaka* (a child born to an unmarried woman), and one born of a *kanyakā* (an unmarried woman)— these should always be avoided in all rites such as worship and the like.
One should properly honor a maiden who is healthy, beautiful in limb, lovely, free from blemishes, and born of the same lineage. ||4||
A Brahmin woman is considered suitable for all undertakings; one born of the royal lineage for the sake of victory; one born of the Vaiśya lineage or even of the Śūdra lineage for the sake of profit.
Those born of Brahmā are to be honored by Brāhmaṇas; those born of the lineage of Brahmā by Rājanyas;
those born of the three classes by Vaiśyas; and all four who are produced from the feet [of Viṣṇu].
One should always worship the bamboo images produced by artisans according to the appropriate rite for Navarātra, performed with devotion. (7)
If one is unable to perform the worship regularly during the Navarātra,
especially on the eighth day, the worship must always be performed [at that time].
The destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
the most terrible Yoginī, manifested together with ten million [other] Yoginīs.

In ancient times, Bhadrakālī [was worshipped] on the eighth day; therefore, worship should always be performed especially on the eighth day with various kinds of offerings, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 27:
Through milk-rice offerings, meat offerings, burnt oblations, and the feeding of Brāhmaṇas.
And one should satisfy the Mother of the World with offerings of fruits and flowers.
O King, for those who are unable to observe the fast, three days of fasting have been prescribed during the Navarātra vow, which grant the same fruit as previously described.
Likewise, on the seventh, eighth, and ninth [lunar days], by performing the three-night rite with a spirit of devotion, the entire fruit is obtained through worship.
O Kumāra, that vow is declared to be complete through worship, fire-offerings (homa), as well as by feeding people and brahmins. || 14 ||
Whatever other vows and various kinds of gifts there may be, none on this earth are even equal to this Navarātra vow. (15)
It constantly bestows wealth and grain, increases happiness and progeny,
grants long life and health, and likewise bestows heaven and liberation.
Whether a man seeks knowledge, wealth, or a son,
he should then perform this auspicious vow according to the prescribed rules, for it bestows good fortune.
Indeed, one who seeks knowledge attains all branches of learning through the accomplishment of this vow.
A king who has fallen from his throne always regains his kingdom.
Those by whom no supreme vow was truly performed in a previous birth become diseased, impoverished, and destitute of sons.
If there be a woman who is barren, a widow, or destitute of wealth, one should infer in that case: "She has not performed this vow.
The Navarātra vow has been proclaimed; it has not been performed by her on this earth.
How does he, having attained such power, rejoice likewise in heaven?
He by whom Bhavānī is worshipped with tender bilva leaves mixed with red sandalwood shall become a king upon the earth. (22)
That man by whom the eternal Śivā— the remover of the pain of suffering, the bestower of perfection, and the most excellent in the world— is not propitiated,
shall surely become afflicted by misery, beset by enemies, and truly destitute upon this earth.
(23) She whom Viṣṇu, Indra, Hara, the Lotus-born Brahmā, as well as Agni, Kubera, Varuṇa, and the Sun-god [worship]...
Do men not worship that Caṇḍikā, who is meditated upon by those delighted by the fulfillment of all their goals? 24.
By the power of Manu, the gods and likewise the ancestors are satisfied by the names Svāhā and Svadhā;
the lords of sages joyfully take up that pair of names in all sacrifices through the sacred scriptures. (25)
By whose will the Lord of Creatures creates this universe, and Hari assumes various incarnations;
indeed, Śambhu surely reduces the world to ashes—how then can a human being not worship her who bestows such bliss? (26)

In all the worlds, there is indeed not a single god, man, bird, or serpent who is bereft of her; even among the gandharvas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and nāgas, there is certainly none who possesses the power to move at will. (27)
Who would not serve that auspicious Caṇḍī, who grants all desires and goals? Who would not observe her vow, desiring the fourfold aims of life? (28)
One who is joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) should observe the vow of Navarātra;
he is liberated from all sins—no deliberation is required in this matter. ||29||
O best of kings, in ancient times there was a certain merchant in Kosala who was miserable, devoid of wealth, deeply distressed, and burdened with a family.
He had many offspring who were tormented by hunger;
however, his young children obtained some food in the evening.
Then, though hungry himself, that performer of duties ate the food of another;
there, he maintained his family with complete composure.
Always delighting in the Dharma, peaceful, of virtuous conduct, and truthful in speech;
free from anger, steadfast, devoid of pride, and without malice. ||33||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty-seven.
Having daily worshipped the deities, as well as the ancestors and guests, the merchant then took his meal once his dependents had eaten. (34)
As time passed in this manner, one named Suśīla, who was [renowned] for his virtues, being afflicted by poverty and overcome by extreme hunger, questioned a peaceful brahmin. (35)
Suśīla said:
O Brāhmaṇa, O high-minded one, having shown compassion, tell me today with certainty how the destruction of poverty may come about. (36)
"O giver of honor, O best of the twice-born, I have no desire for wealth, nor do I wish to be wealthy; I ask you only for the sake of maintaining my family. (37)
"My young son, my daughter, and I am crying out intensely for food;
there is not even that much food in the house, so I give him but a single handful. (38)
"Since this foolish boy was sent away from home by me weeping, my heart burns excessively because of it; what can I do without wealth? (39)
"I have a daughter for whom there is a marriage; yet I have no wealth—what shall I do?
For one who is over ten years old, even the time for giving her away is passing away. (40)
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, I grieve; you are omniscient, O ocean of compassion.
Tell me of some austerity, charity, or vow, as well as a mantra for recitation. (41)
"O twice-born one, may I receive only as much food as is necessary for me to provide sustenance for my family; indeed, I do not pray for more. (42)
"By your grace, may my family become happy and prosperous in this world; therefore, O illustrious one, act accordingly after having ascertained the matter through your knowledge. (43)
Vyāsa said: Thus questioned by him, O best of kings, that Brahmin of rigid vows, being exceedingly pleased, spoke to that Vaiśya.
The worship of the Blessed Lady, as well as the fire-oblation and the feeding [of the deities], likewise. || 45 ||
"Perform today, according to your ability, the complete study of the Vedas, as well as the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, and so forth; thus your purpose will be accomplished. (46)
O Vaiśya, there is no other vow on this earth superior to this one;
it is known as Navarātra, and it is both purifying and a bestower of happiness. (47)
The Navarātra vow always bestows knowledge and liberation, increases the continuity of happiness, and fulfills desires while destroying enemies. 48.
Deprived of his kingdom and separated from Sītā, Rāma,
indeed afflicted by grief, performed this very vow in Kiṣkindhā.
Although Rāma was scorched by the fire of separation from Sītā,
the Goddess was indeed worshipped according to the prescribed rites through the Navarātra vow.
Then, having built a bridge across the great ocean and having slain the immensely powerful Kumbhakarna, the lord of Mandodari, he reached Vaidehi.
Having slain his son Meghanāda and installed Vibhīṣaṇa as king,
he subsequently returned to Ayodhyā and obtained a kingdom free from all thorns.
O best of men, by the power of this Navarātra vow, Rāma of immeasurable splendor attained happiness upon the surface of the earth. (53)
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of the Brahmin, O King, that Vaiśya took him as his preceptor and received the excellent mantra known as Māyābīja.
With supreme devotion, she recited [the mantra] tirelessly throughout the nine nights,
and she worshipped with various kinds of offerings with great reverence.
Devoted to the seed-syllable of Māyā for nine years,
at the end of the ninth year, on the Mahāṣṭamī day, Maheśvarī [appeared].
At midnight, he granted a direct vision;
by bestowing various boons, he made him successful in his purpose.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. ||27||
In the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 28.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
How was that vow, which bestows happiness upon the Goddess, performed by Rāma?
How did he, having been deprived of his kingdom, [behave], and how was Sītā taken away again?
Vyāsa said:
In ancient times, there was a glorious king named Daśaratha, the ruler of Ayodhyā and upholder of the solar dynasty, who was a worshiper of the gods and the brāhmaṇas.
To him were born four sons, renowned throughout the worlds.
By name they were Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata. || 3 ||
All were dear to the king and equal in their virtues and appearance;
Rāma was known as the son of Kausalyā, and Bharata as the son of Kaikeyī.
Two charming twin sons were born to Sumitrā;
indeed, they were born as youths already bearing bows and arrows.
The king’s ministers were well-guided, refined in conduct, and increasers of his happiness;
then Kauśika, having arrived, made a request to the joy of the Raghus.
For the sake of protecting the sacrifice, he gave his sixteen-year-old son Rāma,
together with Lakṣmaṇa, to that Kauśika.
Having approached the sage on the path, those two of beautiful appearance departed;
on the way, the Rākṣasī Tāṭakā, who was terrible to behold, was slain.
With a single arrow, Rāma brought an end to the one who always caused suffering to the sages;
there, the sacrifice was protected and the treacherous Subāhu was slain.
Then Mārīca, who was essentially a spirit, was cast away by the force of the arrow;
thus he performed this great deed for the protection of the sacrifice.
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Viśvāmitra all went to Mithilā;
there, that woman Ahalyā was freed from her sin by being released from the curse.
They both went with the sage to the city of Videha;
there he broke the bow of Śiva, which had been staked by Janaka.
Then the king married Sītā, the daughter of Janaka born from his final portion;
likewise, he gave his other daughter, Umilā, to Lakṣmaṇa.
Both brothers, Bharata and Śatrughna— who were virtuous and possessed auspicious marks— likewise obtained the two daughters of Kuśadhvaja as their wives.
In this manner, O King, the marriage rites of those four brothers were performed in Mithilā according to the prescribed rules and ordinances. (15)
Then, seeing his son fit for the kingdom, King Daśaratha set his mind upon bestowing the burden of sovereignty upon his own descendant, Rāghava.
Seeing that the preparations had been made, Kaikeyī requested the two boons previously promised from her husband, who was under her influence. (17)
He gave the kingdom to his high-souled son Bharata,
and likewise granted fourteen years of forest exile to Rāma.
At her word, Rāma, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
went to the Daṇḍaka forest inhabited by rākṣasas.
King Daśaratha, afflicted by the separation from his sons, gave up his life; he of immeasurable soul did so while recollecting his former curse.
Seeing his father dead indeed because of his mother's deed, Bharata did not accept the prosperous kingdom out of a desire to do what was pleasing to his brother.
While Rāma was dwelling in Pañcavaṭī in the forest, [he encountered] the younger sister of Rāvaṇa.
He indeed made Śūrpaṇakhā deformed and afflicted by excessive passion.
But when the night-stalkers, Khara and the others, saw her with her nose severed,
they waged an incomparable battle against Rāma of immeasurable splendor.
Seeking the welfare of the sages, Rāma, whose prowess is truth, slew Khara and the other Daityas endowed with exceeding strength. (24)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter twenty-eight.
Having gone to Laṅkā, Śūrpaṇakhā, defiled by the slaughter of Khara and Dūṣaṇa at the hands of Rāghava, reported it to Rāvaṇa.
Hearing of that destruction, that wicked man, overcome by anger,
mounted his chariot and then went to the hermitage of Mārīca.
Rāvaṇa dispatched the illusory Asambhava to capture a golden deer in order to entice Sītā.
Then, having become a golden deer with most variegated limbs, that master of illusion appeared before Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, coming within the range of Sītā's vision.
Seeing him, Jānakī, impelled by fate, spoke to Rāghava:
"O beloved, bring the hide," just like a woman who has her husband under her control.
Then Rāma, without further deliberation, stationed Lakṣmaṇa there and,
taking up his bow with an arrow, followed the tracks of the deer.
Sāraṅga, too, being an expert in millions of illusions, upon seeing Hari,
became visible and invisible at will, and then departed into the depths of the forest.
Realizing that the deer was within his grasp, Rāma, drawing his bow with fury once more,
