struck the artificial animal with an exceedingly sharp arrow.
Struck by him with extreme force, that wicked, illusory, and perishable being cried out in great agony: "Alas, Lakṣmaṇa! I am slain!
At that moment, that tumultuous sound was heard by Jānakī.
Thinking it was Rāghava’s, she, distressed, spoke to her husband's brother.
"Go quickly, Lakṣmaṇa! This joy of the Raghus has been slain. He is calling for you, O son of Sumitrā; provide him assistance at once.
Thereupon Lakṣmaṇa said to Sītā, "O Mother, even more than the slaying of Rāma..."
I shall not go today, leaving you here in this hermitage without a companion.
"O daughter of Janaka, Raghava’s command is for me to remain here;
fearing to transgress it, I do not leave your side.
Indeed, having seen Raghava far away in the forest, [I remained] by a certain illusory means."
Having abandoned you, O lady of pure smiles, I cannot take even a single step.
"Take heart; I do not think you are capable of killing Rāma today, even though you have been cast down.
I shall not depart, having disregarded the words spoken by Rāma."
Vyāsa said: Then,
urged by fate, the weeping Sudatī spoke these cruel words to the auspicious Lakṣmaṇa, who was free from cruelty.
"O son of Sumitrā, I know him; he is full of affection for me, and it was at Bharata's instigation that he has come here for my sake. (41)
O lowest of deceivers, I am not such a wanton woman;
even though Rāma is dead, I do not wish to make you my husband out of lust. (42)
If Rāma does not come, I shall give up my life;
without him I cannot live, for I am utterly distressed and miserable. 43.
"Go, or stay, O son of Sumitrā; I do not know what you desire.
Where has your affection for your elder brother, who is devoted to dharma, gone today? (44)
Having heard those words of hers, Lakṣmaṇa, with a dejected mind and a voice choked with tears,
then spoke to that daughter of Janaka.
"O noble one, why indeed do you speak such exceedingly cruel words to me, a mere mortal?
What is it that you say? For by my intellect, I know that what you speak will surely come to pass as a great misfortune for you."
Having spoken thus, O lord of the earth, the hero departed, abandoning her while weeping bitterly; afflicted with grief, he went on, looking back at his elder brother.
Then, after Lakṣmaṇa had departed, Rāvaṇa, assuming a deceptive form and donning the garb of a mendicant, entered that hermitage.
Thinking him to be an ascetic, Jānakī respectfully offered half of her forest-gathered alms-food to the evil-minded Rāvaṇa.
That evil-minded one, bowing with a voice intoxicated with pride, asked her:
"Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, in this lonely forest? (50)
"O fair-limbed one, who is your father? Or who is your brother? And who is your husband, since you remain here all alone, O woman of excellent complexion? (51)
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the third book, chapter 29:
"O beloved, why are you in this desolate forest? You are worthy of a palace."
In the hermitage, she possessed a splendor equal to that of a celestial maiden, like the wife of a sage. ||52||
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words and recognizing by divine fortune that the ascetic was the husband of Mandodarī, the daughter of Videha then replied.
The illustrious King Daśaratha had four sons;
the eldest among them is my husband, renowned by the name Rāma. (54)
Now, having been exiled by the king on account of a boon granted to Kaikeyī,
Rāma shall dwell here for fourteen years together with Lakṣmaṇa.
I am the daughter of Janaka, renowned by the name Sītā;
having broken Śiva’s bow at will, I was wedded to Rāma.
"By the strength of Rāma’s arms, we dwell here in the forest without fear;
yet, having sighted a golden deer, my husband has gone out to kill it. (57)
Lakṣmaṇa, too, having heard the cry again, has now gone after his brother;
therefore, I dwell here indeed without fear, by virtue of the strength of their arms. (58)
"O dweller in the forest, I have related all this account to you;
having arrived here, they will indeed honor you according to the prescribed rites.
You are the very embodiment of Viṣṇu in the form of an ascetic; therefore, you have been worshipped by me."
An hermitage has been established in this terrible forest by a family of Rākṣasas. || 60 ||
Therefore, I question you: speak the truth before me.
Who are you that have come to this forest in the form of a triple-staffed ascetic? (61)
Rāvaṇa said: "O lotus-eyed one, I am the illustrious Rāvaṇa, lord of Laṅkā and husband of Mandodarī;
for your sake, O lady of beautiful form, I have assumed this appearance. (62)
"O lady of beautiful hips, I have indeed come here at the instigation of my sister, having heard that her two brothers, Khara and Dūṣaṇa, have been slain in Janasthāna. (63)
Accept the king; do not abandon that human husband who has been stripped of his kingdom, deprived of his fortune, rendered powerless, and is now a forest-dweller.
"Clearly, O Mandodarī, become my chief queen;
I am your slave, O fair-limbed one—be my mistress, O beautiful lady."
"Victorious over the world-protectors, I fall at your feet;
take my hand today, O Jānakī, and make me your protector."
"O timid one, your father was previously entreated by me for your sake.
Your father spoke thus to me: 'O base man, you have been made my son-in-law.'"
Out of fear of Rudra’s bow, I did not attend the svayaṃvara;
meanwhile, my mind remained fixed there, submerged and distressed by separation.
"O lady with dark-cornered eyes, hearing that you are staying here in the forest, I have come, deluded by my former passion; make my labor fruitful. (69)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 28 ||
Then the twenty-ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those wicked words, Jānakī was overwhelmed with fear.
Trembling, she steadied her mind and spoke these words.
"O descendant of Pulastya, why do you speak such improper words, deluded as you are by passion?
I am certainly not a wanton woman, but rather one born of Janaka’s lineage.
Go back to Laṅkā, O ten-faced one; Rāma will surely slay you."
For my sake, death will occur there; of this there is no doubt. ||3||
Having spoken thus, she went to the leaf-hut near the fire;
saying "Go! Go! to Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 29.
Then, assuming his own form, he approached the hut;
he forcibly seized that young girl as she wept, overwhelmed by fear.
Crying out "Rāma, Rāma! and "Lakṣmaṇa!
again and again, the wicked man seized her, placed her upon a chariot, and departed in haste.
As he was proceeding, he was blocked on the path by Jaṭāyu, the son of Aruṇa;
a most fierce battle then took place between the two of them in that forest region.
Having slain him and seized her, that lord of the Rākṣasas departed for Laṅkā; O dear one, she was crying out like a female osprey before that evil-minded one.
She was placed in the Aśoka grove together with the rākṣasīs;
indeed, she did not waver from her own conduct despite [attempts to sway her] by means of conciliation, gifts, and other such methods.
Rāma, too, having killed that deer, went away taking it with him, feeling satisfied.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa approaching, he asked: "What have you done, O younger brother? (10)
"Having abandoned your beloved wife all alone, for what purpose have you come here?
Hearing Rāma's voice, the descendant of Raghu spoke these words.
But the son of Sumitrā, tormented by the word-arrows of Sītā, spoke these words:
"O Lord, I have arrived here due to the turn of time; of this there is no doubt. (12)
Then, having gone to the leaf-hut and seeing [it empty], the two of them became deeply distressed;
both exerted themselves to make an effort to search for Jānaki. ||13||
Searching for him, they arrived at the place where that bird had fallen—
Jaṭāyu, who lay fallen upon the surface of the earth with only his life remaining.
Rāvaṇa said: "Today that daughter of Janaka was carried off by me;
that evil-souled one was restrained by me, and I, in turn, was struck down in battle. (15)
Having spoken thus, he departed his life; he was indeed consecrated with funeral rites by Rāghava.
After performing the post-mortem ceremonies, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa then departed from that place.
Having slain Kabandha, that Lord liberated him from his curse;
at his request, Rāghava then formed a friendship with Hariṇa.
And having slain the heroic Vālin, Rāma gave the excellent kingdom of Kiṣkindhā to Sugrīva, who had formed an alliance with him for the sake of their common purpose.
Right there, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, he remained for the months of the rainy season,
reflecting in his heart upon his beloved Janakī, who had been carried away by the Ten-faced one.
Rāma, however, afflicted by the pain of separation from Sītā, said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O Saumitri, the daughter of Kaikeyī has attained her full desire. (20)
Jānakī has surely not been found; I shall certainly not live without her, nor shall I return to Ayodhyā without the daughter of Janaka.
The kingdom is lost, my dwelling is in the forest, my father is dead, and my beloved has been abducted;
that evil-minded one is tormenting me, so what can fate do further? || 22 ||
"Indeed, the destiny of living beings is difficult to comprehend, O younger brother of Bharata. What will our fate be, dear one? It will be full of great suffering. (23)
Having indeed obtained birth in the lineage of Manu as both princes,
they became subjects of extreme suffering in the forest due to their past deeds.
Having renounced all enjoyments, you too have gone forth with me;
yet, O Saumitri, by the turn of fate, you must endure this insurmountable suffering.
Never before in my family has there been a man who shared such suffering as I;
one so destitute, powerless, and afflicted has never existed, nor will there ever be.
"What shall I do today, O Saumitri? I am submerged in an ocean of sorrow, and for me, who am truly without assistance, there is no means of crossing over.
I have neither wealth nor strength, O hero; you alone are my companion."
O younger brother, toward what should I direct my anger today—toward this enjoyment which was produced by my own actions?
The kingdom that was in my hands has gone, like a seat of sand shifting in an instant;
yet now residence in the forest has been attained—who knows what is ordained by destiny? (29)
And due to her youthful nature, Vaidehī departed with us;
yet she has been led by wicked fate to a state of even greater suffering, she who is so darkly beautiful.
How could the dark-complexioned Vaidehī, who is devoted to her husband, virtuous, and deeply affectionate toward me, suffer while in the house of the Lord of Laṅkā? And,
O Lakṣmaṇa, she would certainly not come under his control.
How could the daughter of Janaka be like a wanton woman, O lady of beautiful limbs? (32)
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, Third Skandha, Chapter 30:
"O younger brother of Bharata, Maithilī would rather give up her life than remain under another's control."
"It is certain that she shall not fall under the power of Rāvaṇa. ||33||
O hero, if Jānakī is dead, I shall undoubtedly give up my life;
if that lady with dark-cornered eyes is dead, O Lakṣmaṇa, what is the use of my body?
To him who was thus lamenting, the lotus-eyed one,
the righteous Lakṣmaṇa spoke, consoling him with truthful words.
"Be steadfast, O mighty-armed one, casting aside all cowardice here;
I shall bring back Vaidehī after slaying that lowest of Rākṣasas. (36)
Those who remain equal in both adversity and prosperity due to their fortitude are the wise;
however, those of small intellect sink into distress even when in a state of affluence. 37.
Both union and separation are dependent upon destiny;
what then is the nature of grief regarding the body or the self? (38)
Just as there was the loss of the kingdom and dwelling in the forest, and just as the abduction of Vaidehī occurred, so too shall our reunion come at the proper time. (39)
The cessation of the experience of pleasure and pain must occur somewhere;
it cannot be otherwise, O Knower of Janaki. Therefore, abandon your grief now. 40.
"There are many monkeys who will go in the four directions;
they will surely bring back news of Janaka’s daughter."
Having ascertained his location on the path and having gone there and exerted my prowess,
I shall slay that evildoer and bring back Maithilī.
Or else, having summoned Bharata along with his army and his younger brothers, we shall slay the enemy; why do you grieve in vain, O elder brother?
In former times, all the quarters were conquered by Raghu alone with the strength of his arms;
O Raghava, how can you, born of that lineage, allow yourself to be overcome by grief? 44.
I alone am capable of bringing all the gods and asuras;
how much more so, when accompanied by allies, can I bring Rāvaṇa, that disgrace to his lineage? ||45||
Or, O delight of the Raghus, having summoned Janaka to our aid,
I shall slay the evil-doing Rāvaṇa, that thorn in the side of the gods.
In the arising of pleasure and pain, he is submerged in an ocean of sorrow and shall never be happy. 47.
O descendant of Raghu, after his period of happiness had passed, Indra formerly met with calamity; indeed,
Nahuṣa was established by all the gods in the place of Maghavan.
And Maghavan, out of fear, abandoned his own station and remained for many groups of years in the midst of a lotus, living in concealment. 49.
When time had passed and he returned once more to his own place,
Nahuṣa fell to the earth in the form of a serpent due to the curse.
Desiring Indrāṇī and having insulted the Brāhmaṇas,
that lord of the earth was born with the body of a serpent due to the wrath of Agastya.
Therefore, O Raghava, one should not give way to grief when misfortune occurs;
rather, having resolved the mind upon exertion, a wise person must indeed remain steadfast.
O illustrious one, you are omniscient; O Lord of the world, you are capable.
Why do you grieve so excessively within yourself like an ordinary man? (53)
Vyāsa said:
Thus enlightened by the words of Lakṣmaṇa, the joy of the Raghus abandoned his excessive grief and became free from his feverish distress.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the third book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. ||29||
Now the thirtieth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Thus, having made that agreement, as soon as the two of them became silent, [the conversation continued].
Then the venerable sage Nārada arrived from the sky. || 1 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Third Skandha, Chapter 30.
Then, sounding his great lute adorned with the scales and notes, Gāyava approached him, singing the Rathantara Sāman.
Seeing him, Rāma rose and then gave him an auspicious bull; he of immeasurable luster also offered him a seat, water for honor (arghya), and water for his feet (pādya). || 3 ||
Having performed the supreme worship, Hari stood with palms joined in reverence; then, having received permission from the sage, he sat down near him. ||4||
Then, as Rāma sat with his younger brother, his mind filled with sorrow,
Nārada, the best of sages, affectionately inquired after their welfare.
O Raghava, how is it that you are afflicted by grief like an ordinary man?
I know that Sita has been carried off by the evil-minded Ravana;
having gone to the abode of the gods, I heard news of the daughter of Janaka.
She was abducted by the descendant of Pulastya out of delusion, while he himself remained unaware of his own impending death.
O descendant of Kakutstha, O lord of men, your birth was indeed for the sake of the destruction of Paulastya, and the abduction of Maithilī occurred for this very purpose. (8)
In a previous birth, Vaidehī was the ascetic daughter of a sage;
while performing penance in the forest, she of the pure smile was seen by Rāvaṇa. (9)
O Raghava, when she was entreated by Ravana, saying, "Become my wife," he was rebuffed by her;
nevertheless, he seized her hair with force.
O Rāma, at that moment the ascetic woman, being greatly enraged and desiring to cast off her body defiled by his touch, severely cursed Rāvaṇa.

"O evil-souled one, for the sake of your destruction, I shall become an excellent woman born not from a womb upon the surface of the earth; having abandoned [this] body, I shall even cast it off. (12)
This woman, born from a portion of Ramā, was seized by that Rākṣasa like a venomous serpent or a garland out of haste, for the very purpose of destroying his own lineage. (13)
And your birth, O Kakutstha, was for the sake of his destruction,
brought about by the immortals through a portion of Hari, who, though unborn, was born in the lineage of Aja.
"Take heart, O mighty-armed one! There she remains, helpless—Sītā, the virtuous lady devoted to righteousness, meditating upon you day and night. (15)
Having placed the milk of the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu into a vessel, Maghavan himself sent it for him to drink; and he drank it as if it were nectar. || 16 ||
From drinking the milk of Surabhi, she became free from the suffering of hunger and thirst;
with eyes like lotus petals, she was seen by me as she remained there.
O Raghava, I shall now tell you the means for his destruction;
with faith, perform this vow at the present time, in the month of Āśvina.
O Rāma, fasting during the nine nights and the thorough worship of the Blessed Lady,
performed according to the rules of recitation and fire-offerings, brings about all spiritual accomplishments.
Having offered a sacrificial oblation to the Goddess with pure animals,
and having performed the fire-offering ten times, you will become empowered.
It was practiced in the past by Viṣṇu, Mahādeva, and Brahmā;
likewise, it was performed by Maghavan while he resided in the midst of heaven.
O Rāma, this auspicious Navarātra vow should be observed by those who are happy; indeed, it must especially be performed by a man who has fallen into distress.
O descendant of Kakutstha, this was undoubtedly performed by Viśvāmitra, as well as by Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa. (23)
This great vow was undertaken by my preceptor after his wife had been abducted;
therefore, O Indra among kings, you too must act for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa.
In ancient times, an unsurpassed vow was undertaken by Indra for the destruction of Vṛtra,
and likewise by Śiva for the destruction of Tripura.
O high-minded descendant of Kakutstha, this was performed by Hari on Mount Meru for the destruction of Madhu; perform this vow according to the rules without sloth.
Śrī Rāma said:
Who is that goddess, what is her power, from where was she born, and what is her form?
O ocean of compassion, you are omniscient; tell me duly what the vow is. (27)
Nārada said:
Listen, O Rāma, to the Goddess who is eternally constant, the primordial and everlasting power; when worshipped, she is the bestower of all desires and the destroyer of suffering. (28)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the third book, chapter 30:
O descendant of Raghu, you are the cause of all living beings, beginning with Brahmā.
Without her power, no one would be capable of even moving.
That power of protection belonging to Viṣṇu is the creative power (kartṛśakti) of my father;
that power of destruction belonging to Rudra is another supreme power, Śivā. 30.
Whatever object there may be, whether existent or non-existent, anywhere within the three worlds—the power that belongs to all of that, from what could its arising occur? (3.1)
When there was neither Brahmā nor Viṣṇu, neither Rudra nor the Sun, neither all the gods beginning with Indra, nor the earth, nor the mountains; || 32 ||
Then that primordial nature (prakṛti), complete and devoid of qualities (nirguṇā), being united with the supreme Puruṣa, sports indeed at the beginning of the age, O Auspicious One.
Having subsequently become possessed of attributes (saguṇā), she creates the three worlds,
first bringing forth Brahmā and the other gods and bestowing all their powers in every respect.
Knowing her, a living being is released from the bondage of birth and the cycle of existence;
she is to be known as the supreme knowledge, the source of the Vedas and the cause of all that is known. (35)
It is said that her names are indeed innumerable, fashioned by Brahmā and the other gods according to her qualities and activities; what more can I say? (36)
O descendant of Raghu, when joined with the vowels beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', as well as with the consonants, there arise innumerable names.
Rāma said:
"O brahmin-sage, tell me the procedure for this vow in brief;
endowed with faith, I shall perform the worship of the Goddess Śrī this very day. (38)
Nārada said:
"O Rāma, having prepared a seat in a level place and having installed the Mother of the Universe, observe nine fasts according to the prescribed rule. (39)
"O Lord of the Earth, I shall be the preceptor in this rite;
I am exerting my efforts for the purpose of performing the ritual of the gods. (40)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words and considering them to be true, the powerful Rāma had an auspicious pedestal constructed and installed the goddess Ambikā Śivā.
When that month of Āśvina had arrived, Hari, observant of his vow, performed her worship according to the prescribed rites on that excellent mountain.
Devoted to fasting, Rāma performed the supreme vow;
there he duly performed the fire-oblation, the offering of bali, and the worship.
Out of love, the two brothers observed the vow approved by Nārada;
for on the eighth day at midnight, that goddess, the Blessed One, indeed [manifests].
Mounted upon a lion and duly worshipped, she granted him her vision;
standing upon a mountain peak, she addressed Rāghava and his younger brother with these words.
Pleased by this [prayer] uttered with a spirit of devotion as deep as a thundercloud, the Goddess said:
"O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! I am gratified by your vow. (46)
"Choose whatever boon you desire that dwells in your mind;
for you, O sinless one, are born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa in the twentieth Manvantara."
In former times, having assumed the form of a fish and having slain the terrible Rākṣasa, you were indeed sought after by the gods for their destruction. ||48||
Desiring the welfare of the gods, you indeed protected the Vedas from Rāvaṇa;
having assumed the form of a tortoise, you supported Mount Mandara. 49.

I have no desire for sensual pleasure or happiness, which destroys both well-being and dharma. || 55 ||
"How could a wise man take delight even in the commonality with beasts?
The Apsarases replied:
"Among the five [objects of the senses], beginning with sound, the pleasure of touch is the best. (56)
Indeed, there is no other happiness whatsoever that has the essence of bliss as its root;
therefore, O Great King, by all means do as we say. (57)
Attaining abundant happiness, dwell on Mount Gandhamādana;
for if you desire heaven, there is nothing superior to Gandhamādana.
"Enjoy yourself here in this auspicious place, having obtained all the celestial nymphs. (58)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 6 ||
Then the seventh chapter begins.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the powerful son of Dharma [Yudhiṣṭhira]—
He made this reflection in his mind: "What should be done by me now? || 1 ||
Today, through this association, I shall become an object of ridicule among the hosts of sages;
that this suffering has been obtained due to egoism is beyond doubt. (2)
Since the Great Soul has declared that the root of the tree of saṃsāra is speech, I remained silent upon seeing him arrive and composed myself in meditative absorption. ||3||
Because I indulged in a multitude of courtesans, I became a vessel for suffering; likewise, by the destruction of dharma, I have indeed caused my mothers to be born as women.
Those excellent women, afflicted by desire, have set out to obstruct me;
today I am like a spider caught in its own web.
"I am bound here by very firm [bonds]; what is to be done after this?
If I abandon the funeral pyre and leave these women behind, [what will become of them]? (6)
Having been cursed, they shall all depart fallen, their desires shattered;
I, being liberated, shall wander in solitude performing supreme austerity.
Therefore, having aroused my wrath, I shall abandon this host of beautiful women.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus reflected in his mind, the sage Nārāyaṇa then—
He reflected upon the means for generating happiness in the mind:
"This second great enemy, anger, is the cause of torment. (9)
Even more powerful than desire in this world, and more terrible even than greed,
one overcome by anger commits violence that destroys life. (10)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter seven:
[She who is] a source of suffering for all beings, a deep pool within the pleasure-garden of hell.
Just as fire, once kindled by friction, would burn down a tree, so too [is it]. || 11 ||
"Likewise, the fierce anger born within the body consumes the body itself.
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus upon his brother, who was dejected in mind... (12)
Nara, the younger brother of Dharmaputra, spoke these truthful words:
Nara said, "O illustrious Nārāyaṇa, O high-minded one, restrain your anger. (13)
"Resorting to a state of tranquility, destroy this supreme egoism;
for in the past, our ascetic merit was surely destroyed by the fault of egoism. (14)
A most wonderful battle indeed took place between those two beings and the asura Prahlāda for a thousand divine years.
O best of gods, we have experienced much suffering there;
therefore, O lord of sages, abandon your anger and become peaceful. (16)
"Quiescence is proclaimed by the sages to be the root of austerity.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the son of Dharma became tranquil.
Janamejaya said:
O best of sages, this is a doubt of mine:
how was battle formerly fought by the high-souled Prahlāda, who was a devotee of Viṣṇu and tranquil?
How did the two sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, engage in battle?
How did the meeting between those two ascetics, both sons of Dharma with perfectly tranquil minds, and the son of the Daitya come to pass? (19)
How was that battle waged by him with those two great-souled ones?
For Prahlāda too was exceedingly righteous, wise, and devoted to Viṣṇu.
Likewise, Nara and Nārāyaṇa were ascetics established in goodness;
yet, because of that, enmity arose between them. (21)
At that time, in austerity and in dharma, there was indeed nothing but exhaustion;
for where was recitation, and where was the practice of penance, even in the former Age of Truth?
The mind, enveloped by anger and egoism, has not been conquered by such as these;
for neither anger nor envy exists without the sprout of egoism. (23)
It is said that desire, anger, and the like arise from the ego (ahaṅkāra);
yet, having performed most rigorous penance for thousands of millions of years, [they were subdued]. (24)
Once the sprout of egoism has arisen, everything becomes entirely futile;
just as when the sun has risen, that which is of the nature of darkness does not remain. || 25 ||
Likewise, merit does not remain at the tip of the sprout of egoism;
even the illustrious Prahlāda fought with Hari. (26)
Then, indeed, all the merit performed on earth was rendered fruitless, for Nara and Nārāyaṇa had abandoned their supreme asceticism and become tranquil. ||27||
Since they have already engaged in battle, where then is peace, and what good can come of it?
For if such as these, endowed with such strength, are invincible, then my own pride is justified. (28)
And what talk can there be, O Sage, regarding those like me when egoism has been destroyed?
Is there anyone at all in the three worlds who is entirely free from egoism? (29)
That which has not been, will not be, and does not exist at all—by abandoning that, one is released from iron shackles as well as those made of wood. (30)
One who is bound by egoism is never liberated. *Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa*, Fourth Skandha, Chapter 7. 201 === PAGE 201 === One who is bound by egoism is never liberated.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, is enveloped by egoism.

Indeed, one wanders in this very cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is defiled by excrement and urine; how then can there be knowledge of Brahman in this saṃsāra enveloped by delusion? (32) [Defiled by excrement and urine:
knowledge of Brahman.]
O observer of noble vows, O sage, this doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas indeed appears highly esteemed;
yet even great men are always bound by desire, anger, and other such passions. (33)
"O best of sages, what talk can there be for those like me in this Kali age?
Vyāsa said:
"O Bhārata, how indeed can an effect be distinct from its cause? (34)
Just as a bracelet and an earring are essentially the same gold, so too the entire universe, including all moving and non-moving beings, arises from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). ||35||
A cloth is said to be dependent upon its threads; how could it exist when separated from them?
All that is stable and moving is fashioned by the three qualities of Māyā. (36)
When even a blade of grass is consumed by fire, what lamentation can there be?
Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are deluded by egoism.
O best of kings,
even the most supreme sages of knowledge, such as Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and others, wander in this deep and vast cycle of worldly existence.
Overpowered by these, O best of kings, embodied beings transmigrate again and again in this world; there is no bearer of a body in the three worlds who is not subject to this.
Freed from these qualities of illusion, peaceful, and established in the bliss of the Self,
he is likewise free from desire, anger, greed, and delusion born of egoism.
O best of kings, it does not leave any embodied being, even after they have studied the Vedas and Shastras and investigated the Puranas. 41.
Having performed pilgrimages, giving, meditation, and the worship of the gods, one who is attached to sense objects performs all such actions like a thief. (42)
O descendant of Kuru, even in the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages, one who is possessed by lust, delusion, and pride does not reflect beforehand.
Even dharma has been pierced here; what need is there to speak of it today in the Kali age?
There is constant rivalry and malice, along with greed and indignation at all times. (44)
Such is the nature of this saṃsāra; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
In this world, virtuous people who are free from envy are rare. (45)

"Those who have conquered anger, who have overcome resentment, and who are established in the meaning of the illustrative examples—the King said: 'They are blessed, they have performed meritorious deeds, and they are devoid of intoxication and delusion. (46)
Those who have conquered their senses and follow righteous conduct have, in effect, conquered the three worlds;
yet, remembering the sin of my high-souled father, I am filled with grief.

therefore, O best of sages, what can happen to him in my presence? (48)
I do not know what will happen due to this confusion of my intellect;
the fool sees the honey, but does not see the precipice at all. (49)
He performs censurable deeds and does not fear the hells;
tell me in detail how that battle occurred in the past.
And just as [the battle] was fierce between Prahlāda and Nara-Nārāyaṇa, tell me how it was that Prahlāda went from Pātāla. (51)
At the great and holy pilgrimage site of Sārasvata, in the sacred hermitage of Badarikāśrama,
Nara and Nārāyaṇa dwell as peaceful ascetics, the best of sages.
O giver of honor, for what reason did they engage in such a battle?
Enmity arises between people either for the sake of wealth or for the sake of wives. (53)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter eight.
Why did these two, who are free from all worldly desires, engage in this great battle?
And how was it that even the righteous-souled Prahlāda, having recognized the two as eternal gods, [did so]? (54)
O Brahmā, I wish to hear in detail the reason for this: how did those two sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, engage in battle? 55.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Sūta said:
Thus was the Brahmin questioned at that time by King Pārīkṣita.
Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, spoke all of this in detail.
The righteous Janamejaya also attained a state of supreme detachment,
considering the mind of the son of Vairāṭī to be characterized by evil conduct.
He constantly set his mind upon the means for the deliverance of that very person who,
through the sin of insulting a brahmin, had indeed gone to the realm of Yama.
O lords of sages, because he protects his own father from the hell named Punnāma and others, his name "putra" (son) is truly meaningful for him.
Having heard that the king had been bitten by a serpent and likewise died upon his horse, [the sage] Auttareya,
due to a brahmin’s curse, was deprived of bathing and giving gifts.
Having heard of his father’s fate, the illustrious King Pārīkṣita fell into a state of world-weariness; he was deeply distressed and overwhelmed by fear.
Then, the blameless one questioned the sage Vyāsa, who had arrived at his home,
regarding this most extensive narrative of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
Vyāsa said: O King, when that fierce Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain,
his son named Prahlāda was then consecrated in the kingdom.
While that lord of the Daityas, a worshiper of gods and Brahmins,
was ruling, kings on earth performed sacrifices with great faith.
The Brāhmaṇas perform austerities and religious duties and undertake pilgrimages;
the Vaiśyas remain established in their respective vocations, and the Śūdras are devoted to service. 10.
Then, having been established in Pātāla by Nṛsiṃha, that king of the Daityas ruled right there, devoted to the protection of his subjects. ||11||
Once, the son of Bhṛgu, known as Cyavana, a man of great austerity,
went to the holy ford of Vyāhṛtīśvara on the Narmadā to bathe.
Having seen the great river Revā, he then descended into it;
as he was crossing over, a serpent-maiden seized him, terrifying with her venom.
Seized and terrified, that best of sages remembered Viṣṇu, Janārdana, the God of gods, within his mind in the netherworld (pātāla).
When the lotus-eyed Lord was remembered, the great serpent became free from poison;
Cyavana felt no suffering even while being led down to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Abandoned by the double-tongued one, despondent and filled with great apprehension, the sage might curse me in his anger, thinking, "This ascetic is a great man. (16)
Honored by the daughters of the Nāgas, that best of sages wandered about;
then he entered the great city of the Nāgas and the Dānavas.
Once, that king of the Daityas, Prahlāda, who was devoted to dharma, beheld the son of Bhṛgu as he was wandering in that excellent city.
Having seen him, the lord of the Daityas then worshipped the sage and asked:
"Tell me, what is the reason for your coming to Pātāla?"
"O best of the twice-born, tell me truly:
have you been sent by Indra, who is filled with hatred for the Daityas and desires to see my kingdom? (20)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter eight.
Cyavana said:
"O King, what have I to do with Maghavan, since I, while performing the duty of a messenger, have been sent back and have arrived here in your city? (21)
"Know me to be that son of Bhṛgu, Svanaetra, who is devoted to righteousness. O Lord of Daityas, do not entertain any doubt regarding me, for I have indeed been sent by Vāsava. (22)
O best of kings, having arrived at the Narmadā at a holy bathing place for the purpose of bathing,
I descended into the river itself and was seized by a great serpent.
He became a snake devoid of venom, as if from the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu;
by the power of that very remembrance, I too was liberated from that serpent.
"O Indra among kings, by coming here I have obtained the sight of you. O Lord of Daityas, you are a devotee of Viṣṇu; therefore, regard me as one devoted to Him. (25)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those gentle words of Hiraṇyakaśipu’s son,
he asked with great affection about various sacred fords (tīrthas).
Prahlāda said:
O best of sages, which sacred places on earth are meritorious?
Likewise, tell us in detail those in the netherworld (pātāla) and in the sky. 27.
Cyavana said:
O King, for those whose mind, speech, and body are pure, there is a sacred ford at every step;
but for those with defiled minds, even the Gaṅgā is but a mere puddle in Kīkaṭa.
If the mind first becomes pure and freed from evil, then indeed all sacred fords become purifying. (29)
For along the entire course of the Gaṅgā’s bank dwell cities, as well as cow-pens, mines, villages, and all other types of settlements. (30)
O best of Daityas, there are also the dwellings of the Niṣādas, as well as others such as the Kaivartas, Hūṇas, Vaṅgas, Khasas, and Mlecchas.
O Lord of Daityas, people always drink the water of the Gaṅgā, which is ever equal to Brahman; they bathe there at their own will during the three periods of the day.
In that regard, O noble one, not even a single person becomes pure of soul;
what then is the fruit of a sacred ford for those whose selves are afflicted by sense objects?
O King, reflect that the mind alone is the cause here and nothing else;
one who desires purity must constantly practice the purification of the mind. (34)
One who dwells at a sacred ford (tīrtha) becomes a great sinner by his own word;
the sin committed right there leads to his downfall. ||35||
Just as a ripe mango from the Indra-vāruṇa tree does not become sweet, so too the disposition of one who has bathed ten million times at a sacred ford does not wither.
One who desires what is auspicious must first purify the mind;
when the mind is pure, the purity of the ritual substance follows, and not otherwise. (37)
In that very way, purity of conduct must exist; through that, the sacred site (tīrtha) becomes effective.
Otherwise, however, everything performed becomes useless at that very moment. 38.

"One should always avoid the company of those of low caste when going to a sacred ford (tīrtha). Compassion for all living beings must be practiced through both action and thought. If you ask me, O Indra among kings, I shall describe the unsurpassed sacred ford."
First is the meritorious Naimiṣa, then Cakratīrtha and Puṣkara;
there is no counting the other sacred sites on the surface of the earth.
O best of kings, there are many purifying places as well.

Having heard those words, the king prepared to go to Naimiṣa.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter nine.
With a mind overflowing with joy, he did not urge the Daityas forward.
Prahlāda said:
"O illustrious ones, arise; today we shall go to Naimiṣa."
"We shall see the lotus-eyed, yellow-robed, and infallible one.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by that devotee of Viṣṇu, all those Dānavas then [departed].
Together with him, those mighty Daityas and Dānavas emerged from Pātāla with supreme joy, having come together.
Having reached the Naimiṣa forest, they joyfully performed their ablutions;
there, Prahlāda, accompanied by the Daityas, wandered through the sacred bathing places.
O best of kings, he beheld the highly meritorious Sarasvatī of pure waters at that sacred ford belonging to the high-souled Prahlāda. (46)
Having bathed in the waters of the Sarasvatī, the mind of the lord of the Daityas became serene; there, in that auspicious place, he duly performed his ablutions, offerings, and other rites.
With a serene soul, he also performed [his rites] at that most purifying sacred ford. ||47||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said: While performing the rites for the holy ford there, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu—
Then he saw before him a very large banyan tree with a vast shade. || 1 ||
Then he saw other arrows of various kinds—fierce, whetted on stone, brilliantly radiant, and furnished with vulture feathers. ||2||
He mentally meditated upon Him whose arrows are these very ones here,
in this holy hermitage of the sages, a most purifying sacred ford.
While he was reflecting thus, the two sons of Dharma were then seen by him as sages wearing black antelope skins and bearing lofty masses of matted hair.
Before them were two bright bows, anointed with ghee and endowed with auspicious marks—
the Śārṅga and the Ājagava— as well as two inexhaustible quivers.
Then the lord of the Daityas beheld there the two sons of Dharma, the highly fortunate sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, established in meditation.
With eyes red with anger, the guardian of the asuras spoke to them both:
"Why have you begun this hypocrisy that destroys dharma? (7)
Indeed, neither has it been heard nor ever seen in this cycle of existence that there was such a performance of severe austerity as well as the wielding of a bow. (8)
This is a contradiction; how is it appropriate in this present age, which is dear to Kali, for a Brahmin to practice asceticism while carrying a weapon? (9)
Where is the wearing of matted hair on your body, and where are these quivers—a mere mockery?
For you two, who possess divine natures, the practice of dharma is truly appropriate.
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of his, O Bhārata, Nara spoke:
"O Lord of Daityas, what is your anxiety here? Why this fruitless asceticism on our part?"
Whatever one who possesses capability might do, that indeed would be accomplished;
for we two are renowned in the world as being incompetent in these two tasks. (12)

In battle and in austerity you possess such power; what, then, will you do? Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Fourth Skandha, Chapter 9. 205. In battle and in austerity you possess such power; what, then, will you do?
"Go along the path as you please; why do you boast here?
You are deluded and do not know that the splendor of Brahman is difficult to attain.
Those who desire happiness should not engage in contentious debate with living beings. (13-14)
Prahlāda said:
"You two are ascetics of dull intellect, deluded by false pride while I, the lord of the Daityas and upholder of the bridge of dharma, am present. (15)
"This is not fitting; furthermore, the practice of dharma does not belong in this sacred ford.
What power do you have in battle? Show it now, O ascetic! (16)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the man replied to him:
"If such is your mind, then fight with me today! (17)
"Today, O lowest of Asuras, I shall shatter your head; thereafter, you shall never again have any desire for battle.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the lord of the Daityas then became enraged. (18)
The powerful Prahlāda then made this vow:
"By whatever means possible, I shall conquer both of them. (19)
The two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa were self-controlled and endowed with ascetic power.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken these words, the Daitya took up his bow.
Having swiftly drawn his bow, he made the sound of the bowstring;
Nara also, taking up his bow, [prepared] sharp arrows whetted on stone.
O King, out of anger, he released [them] many times upon Prahlāda.

The king of the Daityas, having swiftly approached, cut those arrows down with his own shafts tipped with gold; seeing that the arrows he had discharged were severed, Nara, filled with wrath, quickly released other weapons.

The lord of the Daityas, having cut those [arrows] as well with arrows of fierce velocity, struck that lord of sages in the chest; Nara also, enraged, struck the lord of the Daityas on the upper arm with five swift arrows.
The gods, together with Indra, remained in their celestial chariots in the sky there to witness the battle between those two;
they repeatedly praised the prowess of Nara as he stood firm in combat, and likewise that of the lord of the Daityas.
The lord of the Daityas, having taken up his bow, rained down arrows like a cloud pouring forth water;
taking up the immeasurable Śārṅga bow, he released sharp, gold-feathered shafts.
A tumultuous battle took place between those two, the king and the god-demon, both desiring victory;
standing in the path of the sky, they, with joyful hearts, rained down divine flowers.
The lord of the Daityas became enraged at Hari and released arrows of extreme velocity;
the son of Dharma then swiftly cut them down with very sharp, flame-tipped shafts discharged from his bow.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book (Caturtha-skandha), chapter nine.
Then Prahlāda showered Nārāyaṇa—
the hero, the son of Dharma, the eternal one who stands firm— with exceedingly sharp arrows.
Nārāyaṇa also [struck him] with arrows whetted on stone, released with great speed.
He struck the lord of the Daityas who stood before him;
at that moment, a great gathering of those desiring to witness the sight took place in the sky.
When the sky was covered by the rain of arrows from both sides as the gods and the dānavas raised shouts of victory, (31)
Even by day, a great darkness arose like that of night;
the gods and the Daityas, being greatly amazed, spoke to one another.
A battle never seen before is now taking place today, most terrible;
[therein are] the celestial sages, as well as the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Pannagas.
The Vidyādharas and the Cāraṇas were filled with the utmost wonder;
the two sages, Nārada and Parvata, stood there for the sake of witnessing the scene.
Nārada said to Parvata: "Such a thing has never occurred before, nor did such a battle take place with the demon Tāraka or with the demon Vṛtra. (35)
Such was the battle waged by Hari against Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
for Prahlāda was a powerful hero who was [confronted] by Nārāyaṇa.
He engaged in a battle equal to that of the Siddha of wondrous deeds.
Vyāsa said: Day after day and night after night, he did this again and again. (37)
Then those two, the Daitya and the ascetic, engaged in a supreme battle;
Nārāyaṇa, however, cut asunder Prahlāda’s bow.
With a single swift arrow, he did not take up another bow;
but Nārāyaṇa, having swiftly released another shaft, [pierced him].
At that very moment, the light-handed one cut the bow in the middle;
as soon as it was cut, the demon took up another bow. (40)
But Nārāyaṇa, provoked to anger, swiftly cut [the bow] with his arrows;
when the bow was severed, the lord of the Daityas took up a mace.
Extremely enraged, he quickly struck the son of Dharma between the arms;
as he was approaching, that powerful sage [struck him] with nine arrows.
He shattered that terrible iron club with ten arrows and struck him; then,
seizing a firm mace made entirely of iron,
the lord of the Daityas swiftly struck the god Nārāyaṇa on the knee in a rage.
And with his mace, he stood firm like a mountain, his mind steady.
The exceedingly powerful son of Dharma swiftly released his arrows;
then the Blessed One shattered the firm mace of the lord of the Daityas.
The spectators stationed in the sky were struck with supreme amazement;
meanwhile, Prahlāda, the slayer of enemy heroes, took up his spear.
Enraged, he forcefully hurled it by strength at the chest of Nārāyaṇa;
seeing it coming toward him, [Nārāyaṇa] effortlessly [cut it] with a single arrow. (47)
Having quickly cut him into seven pieces, he struck him with those seven; that supreme battle between the two lasted for a thousand divine years.
O King, that which had occurred there in the hermitage was a source of wonder for everyone;
then, the four-armed one clad in yellow garments arrived with speed.
There, the four-armed Gadādhara, beloved of Ramā, bearing the discus, mace, and lotus, spoke at the hermitage of Prahlāda.
Seeing him arrived there, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu bowed with supreme devotion and, with palms joined in reverence, replied.
Prahlāda said:
"O God of gods, Lord of the universe, you who are affectionate toward your devotees, O Mādhava! (51)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fourth Skandha, Chapter 10:
"How is it that I did not defeat these two ascetics in battle?"
"O Lord, I have waged war for a full hundred years."
"Why have they not been conquered by the gods? This is my great wonder.
Viṣṇu said:
"These two are perfected beings (siddhas) and portions of myself; what cause for wonder is there in this, O noble one?"
Those two ascetics, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, have not conquered their own selves; you have been conquered.
Go now, O King, to Vitala and practice unwavering devotion to me. 54.
"O high-minded one, do not cause harm to the two ascetics at the navel.
