Thus commanded, the king of the Daityas set out together with the asuras.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa once again became engaged in ascetic penance. ||55||
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 9 ||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Janamejaya said: "O son of Parāśara, there is a great doubt here regarding this narrative."
Nara and Nārāyaṇa were indeed peaceful Vaiṣṇavas rich in asceticism.

Those two high-souled sons of Dharma were ascetics established in truth; they resided in hermitages at sacred fords, were endowed with courage, always subsisted on forest fare, and remained steadfast in their vows. || 2 ||
How did they become possessed by passion and born into mutual conflict?
Why did they wage war, abandoning their unsurpassed asceticism? (3)
O sages, how is it that they abandoned the bliss of peace and engaged in battle for a full hundred divine years together with Prahlāda? (4)
How did those two sages wage war with Prahlāda?
O illustrious one, tell us the reason for this conflict.
The beloved woman is gold, and she is indeed the cause of their physical conflict;
how did the desire for battle arise between those two who were so detached from it?

O scorcher of foes, for what reason did those two perform such asceticism—was it for the sake of delusion, for the sake of enjoying pleasures, or for the sake of heaven? They performed that most intense penance which bestows all fruits. (7)
"What wonderful fruit was obtained by the two sages of tranquil minds?
Their bodies were emaciated by asceticism and repeatedly subjected to battle. (8)
For a full hundred divine years, they were oppressed by toil;
neither for the sake of sovereignty nor wealth, nor for wives or homes.
For what purpose was this battle waged by him with those two high-souled ones? Why would a man who is free from worldly desire engage in such a conflict? (10)
Knowing that the body is in every way a source of suffering and that dharma is eternal,
the wise person always performs actions here that grant happiness.
O knower of dharma, these do not cause suffering; this is the eternal state.
The son of Dharma is a portion of Hari, omniscient and adorned with all virtues.
"How did you two engage in that battle, which is so painful and destructive to dharma?
Having abandoned it, you have now brought back this great fruit, the pleasure-grove. (13)
O Kṛṣṇa, even a fool does not desire a terrible conflict;
I have heard that King Yayāti fell from heaven.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter ten. 208.
Felled to the surface of the earth by the sin arising from egoism,
he was a performer of sacrifices, a giver of gifts, and a righteous lord of the earth.
I was struck down by Vajrapāṇi with a mere utterance of words;
without egoism, there is certainly no battle—this is certain. (16)
"What is the fruit of this battle that destroys the merit of a sage?
Vyāsa said: "O King, the root of saṃsāra is indeed proclaimed to be threefold. (17)
Since he was deemed by all-knowing sages to be fit for the determination of the Dharma, how indeed could he have been so harshly addressed by the Sage among those who bear bodies? (18)
It is certain that an effect cannot exist without a cause;
austerity, charity, and likewise sacrifices—all these originate from the quality of goodness (sattva). (19)
O illustrious one, from the *rājasa* or the *tāmasa* [nature] arises such strife;
O Lord of Kings, not even the slightest action ever occurs without egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). (20)
Whether it be auspicious or even inauspicious, the certainty that arises—whether it binds or liberates—is none other than egoism (ahaṃkāra) on this earth. (21)
How could that by which this universe was created be devoid of it?
For Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu—all these are possessed of egoism (ahaṅkāra). || 22 ||
What then can be said of other sages, O lord of the earth?
This entire universe of moving and non-moving beings wanders about, enveloped by egoism.
Rebirth and repeated death—all follow the power of karma for gods, animals, and humans in this cycle of existence, O Lord of the Earth. (24)
The constant wandering [of the breath] through all the limbs, like the spokes of a chariot wheel, is thus remembered.
Furthermore, what man can know the total number of the incarnations of Viṣṇu? 25.
But in this saṃsāra, among the highest and lowest wombs,
Nārāyaṇa Hari himself has assumed the form of a fish.
In age after age, Vāsudeva Janārdana, the Lord of the World, appears as Kāmaṭha, Saukara, Nārasiṃha, and Vāmana. (27)
O great king, in the seventh Vaivasvata Manvantara, the Lord Hari, constrained by the divine ordinance, effects innumerable incarnations.
Listen now to the truth regarding the incarnations he indeed assumed during the Manvantaras:
O great king, due to the curse of Bhṛgu, Viṣṇu, the lord and best of gods, [took these forms].
"Into how many incarnations did the Lord of All enter?
The King said:
O highly fortunate one, this doubt arises within my heart. (30)
O Grandfather, how was the Blessed Viṣṇu cursed by Bhṛgu? And what unpleasant act was committed against that sage by Hari, O Sage? (31)
"Because of whose anger Viṣṇu, who is worshipped by the gods, was cursed by Bhṛgu?
Vyāsa said:
"Listen, O King, I shall explain the cause of Bhṛgu’s curse. (32)
Formerly, when King Hiraṇyakaśipu, the descendant of Kaśyapa, was ruling,
a mutual conflict was waged between him and the gods.
When that conflict had been joined, the entire world became utterly distressed.
When that king had perished, King Prahlāda was born.
Prahlāda, the harasser of his enemies, oppressed the gods;
then a terrible battle took place between Śakra and Prahlāda.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter 1. [Page 209]
O King, for a full hundred years, a fierce battle that caused wonder to the world was waged with the gods, and Prahlāda was defeated.
Having attained supreme detachment and realized the eternal Dharma,
King Bali installed Virācana’s son upon the throne.
Having obtained the kingdom, the illustrious Bali waged war against the gods; he went to Mount Gandhamādana to perform intense austerities.
Then a most terrible battle took place between them.
Thereupon, O King, the Daityas were defeated by Indra of immeasurable splendor,
with Viṣṇu as his ally, and were deprived of their kingdom.
Then the defeated Daityas went for refuge to Kāvya.
"O Brahmin, why do you, being so powerful, not provide us with assistance? For we are unable to remain here; indeed, we shall enter the netherworld. (41)
"If you, the best of those who know the mantras, are not my companion [in this task]," Vyāsa said;
thus addressed, the compassionate sage Kāvya spoke to the Daityas. (42)
"Do not fear, O gods; I shall sustain you with my own splendor. Indeed, I shall always provide you assistance through mantras as well as medicinal herbs. (43)
"I shall do it; let them be full of energy and free from anxiety.
Vyāsa said: Then those Daityas became fearless, having taken refuge with Kāvya.
Indeed, the entire account was heard by the gods from the mouths of their spies;
having consulted there with one another and with Śakra, those gods [acted].
Greatly agitated, they performed a mantra through the power of the Kāvya-mantra, saying:
"Let us go quickly to fight, before they indeed cause us to fall."
"Having forcibly slain them, we shall cause the survivors to reach Pātāla.
Then the gods, enraged and with weapons in hand, went toward the Daityas.
Addressed by Hari, those Dānavas went forth accompanied by Viṣṇu;
but as they were being slain, those Daityas became terrified and oppressed by fear.
They sought refuge with Kāvya and cried out, "Protect us! Protect us!
Seeing those mighty Daityas afflicted by the gods, the powerful Śukra spoke these words: "Do not fear," by the power of his mantras and medicinal herbs.
Having seen the poem, all the gods abandoned them and indeed departed. 50.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Vyāsa said:
When the gods had departed, Kāvya replied to them.
O best of Dānavas, listen to that which was previously spoken by Brahmā.
Janārdana Viṣṇu, intent on the destruction of the Daityas, will slay them;
having assumed the form of a boar, he will kill them just as Hiraṇyākṣa was slain.
Just as Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by him in the form of Nṛsiṃha, so too will he, having exerted his full effort, slay all; it shall not be otherwise.
The power of the mantra appears clearly to me, just as it did to Hari;
you are capable of conquering the gods sent by me. (4)
Therefore, wait for some time, O best of Dānavas;
today I shall indeed depart for the sake of counsel with Mahādeva.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the fourth book, chapter eleven:
"Having received the mantras from Mahādeva, I shall now depart."
"O best of Dānavas, I shall give them to you according to their true nature."
The Daityas said:
"O best of sages, having been defeated, how shall we be able to remain on earth?
We are powerless, yet we must wait for that time. (7)
All the powerful ones have been slain, and only a few Dānavas remain;
they are no longer fit for battle today, nor can they bring such happiness.
Śukra said:
"Until I have brought back the knowledge of mantras from Śaṅkara,
you must remain engaged in austerity and endowed with self-restraint."

The wise have declared that conciliation, bribery, and the other [stratagems] are appropriate for the occasion, once they have understood the place, the time, the strength, the hero, the power, and the force. (10)
At times, service should be rendered to enemies with a desire for one's own welfare;
however, when the time comes for the increase of one's own power, they should be destroyed by the wise. (11)
Therefore, having today employed discipline preceded by conciliation and indeed using guile,
remain in your own dwellings while longing for my return.
"O Dānavas, having obtained mantras from Mahādeva, I shall return;
then, relying on the power of those mantras, we shall fight the gods once again. (13)
Having spoken thus to them, Bhṛgu, the best of sages, having made his resolve, departed for Mahādeva, the great king, for the sake of counsel, O great monarch. (14)
The Dānavas sent Prahlāda into the presence of the gods—
he who was truthful, immutable, and a source of confidence for the deities.
Then Prahlāda, the king, together with the asuras, bowed down with humility and spoke these words full of modesty to the gods. (16)
Having laid down our weapons and likewise cast off our armor,
we shall all perform penance like the gods, clothed in bark garments.
Having heard those words of Prahlāda, which were spoken as the truth,
the gods then desisted, freed from their feverish anxiety and filled with joy.
When the Daityas had laid down their weapons, the gods then desisted;
having returned to their own homes with confidence, they remained there well-settled, intent on their pleasures.
The Daityas, resorting to hypocrisy, and the ascetics, endowed with their penance,
took up residence in the hermitage of Kaśyapa, desiring the arrival of Kāvya.
Then Kāvya, having gone to Kailāsa and bowed down to Mahādeva, was asked by the Lord, "What is your business? and the master replied. (21)
"O God, I desire those mantras which do not exist with Bṛhaspati, for the defeat of the gods and for the victory of the asuras. (22)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the omniscient Śaṅkara, who is auspicious, reflected in his mind: "What should be done after this?"
Now, with a mind intent on hostility toward the gods, this son of Kavi has arrived here for the sake of counsel and for the victory of those Daityas; he is their guru.
Thinking, "The gods must be protected by me," Maheśvara Śaṅkara spoke to him regarding that most fierce and difficult vow.
If you drink the smoke of chaff for a full thousand years with your head hanging downwards—may prosperity be yours—then you shall obtain the mantras. (26)
Thus addressed, he bowed to the Lord and spoke these words:
"O God, O Lord of the Suras, commanded by you, I shall perform the vow. (27)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to Śaṅkara, Kāvya undertook an excellent vow;
devoted to inhaling smoke, he became tranquil, having reached a firm resolve regarding the meaning of the mantra.
Then the gods, having understood that Kāvya was devoted to his vows while the Daityas were devoted to deceit, became intent on holding counsel.
O King, having deliberated thus with their minds, they all prepared for battle. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, Fourth Skandha, Chapter 11.211.
Armed with weapons, they went to where those foremost of Dānavas were. Then, seeing them arrived— equipped with weapons and clad in armor—
the Daityas became agitated with fear on all sides before the gods.
Suddenly, those who were armored and terrified by fear rose up and spoke these truthful words to the gods who were arrogant in their strength: ||32||
When the Blessed One had laid down his weapons and was established in the vow of an ascetic, the gods previously approached us with the intent to kill, having granted us their protection. (33)
O gods, where has your truth gone, and where is the dharma taught in the Vedas?
Those who have laid down their weapons must not be slain, nor those who are terrified and have come for refuge.
The gods said:
"Kāvya has been sent by you for the purpose of counsel and through deceit;
indeed, your power lies in austerity and knowledge, and because of that, we shall certainly fight."
"Be prepared for battle, eager and with weapons in hand;
he must be slain at the enemy's moment of vulnerability—this is the eternal law. (36)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words and deliberated among themselves, all the Daityas, overwhelmed by fear, set out to flee. ||37||
Terrified, the Dānavas went for refuge to the mother of Kāvya;
seeing them deeply distressed, she then granted them fearlessness.
Kāvyamātā said:
"Do not fear, do not fear! Cast away your fear, O Dānavas! For those who abide in my presence, there ought to be no more fear. (39)
Having heard those words, the Daityas remained there free from distress;
for the Asuras stood in that excellent hermitage unarmed and unperturbed.
Seeing those Dānavas followed by the gods, their own followers attacked them by force, without considering the relative strength of the two sides. ||41||
All the gods arrived there, intent on slaying the Daityas;
yet, though restrained by Kāvya alone, they slaughtered those staying in the hermitage.
Seeing them being slain by the gods, Kāvya’s mother trembled violently and said to all those who were still asleep, "I shall indeed deprive you of your power through my ascetic penance. (43)
Having spoken thus, Nidrā was dispatched; she arrived and fell upon them.
Along with Indra, the gods succumbed to the power of sleep and remained as if mute. (44)
Seeing Indra overcome by sleep and dejected, Viṣṇu said:
"Enter me; may it be well with you; I shall lead you away, O best of gods. (45)
Having been addressed thus, Purandara then entered Viṣṇu;
protected by Hari, he became fearless and free from sleep.
Seeing Śakra there, protected by Hari and free from distress, Kāvya’s mother then became enraged and spoke these words: ||47||
"O Maghavan, by the power of my asceticism, I shall indeed devour you along with Viṣṇu;
behold such is the power of my asceticism while all the gods look on. (48)
Vyāsa said:
Thus addressed by her, the two high-souled ones, Viṣṇu and Indra, were overcome by her yogic power and became paralyzed. (49)
Then, seeing those two thus overwhelmed, the gods were struck with wonder;
yet, with dejected minds, they broke out into cries of "kilakila."
Seeing the gods crying out, the Lord of Śacī said to Viṣṇu:
"O Madhusūdana, I am being especially overwhelmed by you."
O Viṣṇu, O Lord, slay her by force before she consumes us;
O Mādhava, do not hesitate regarding this wicked woman who is arrogant because of her asceticism. 52.
Thus addressed by Śakra and the renowned [Viṣṇu],
Mādhava then cast aside his compassion and swiftly called to mind his discus.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter twelve: As soon as it was remembered, the discus, acting under the control of Viṣṇu, arrived.
And, incited by Śakra, he held it in his hand in anger for the purpose of slaying him.
Having seized the umbrella in her hand, he swiftly cut off her head;
seeing her slain, Śakra then became joyful.
The gods were exceedingly delighted; crying out "Victory! Victory to Hari!", they all praised him with joy, their afflictions having vanished.
At that very moment, Indra and Viṣṇu were born with pain in their hearts,
fearing the slaying of a woman and the insurmountable curse of Bhṛgu.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 11 ||
Then, the twelfth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having witnessed that terrible slaughter, the venerable Bhṛgu became enraged.
Trembling and afflicted by extreme sorrow, he spoke to Madhusūdana.
Bhṛgu said:
O Viṣṇu of great intelligence, though you know it to be a sin, you have committed what should not have been done;
this killing of one born of the brahmin caste was impossible for you even to contemplate. (2)

You are declared to possess the quality of goodness (sattva), while Brahmā is remembered as being of the nature of passion (rajas); likewise, Śambhu is of the nature of darkness (tamas). How then is this [your status] considered the opposite? ||3||
How have you become possessed by tamas? Why was such a most censurable deed committed?
O Viṣṇu, why did you kill a woman who was innocent and not to be slain? (4)
I curse you, O man of evil conduct; what else can I do?
O sinful one, I have been rendered helpless by you for the sake of Śakra.
I do not curse Śakra in that manner; rather, I curse you, O Madhusūdana!
You are always intent on deceit, born from the womb of a worm, and evil-minded.
Those sages who indeed call you *sāttvika* are fools;
for you, O Janārdana, are manifest before my eyes as one of *tāmasa* conduct and wicked behavior.
May there be incarnations in the world of mortals arising from my curse;
O Janārdana, because of your sin, may you mostly experience the suffering born of the womb. (8)
Vyāsa said: Then, when Dharma had thus been destroyed again and again by that curse,
he was born here among human beings for the sake of the welfare of the world.
The king said:
"The wife of Bhṛgu was killed there by that wheel of immeasurable splendor;
how then did the state of householdership arise again for that high-souled one? (10)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus cursed him, Hari, out of anger, quickly took that head;
then Bhṛgu, who knew what was to be done, swiftly joined it back to the body and spoke.
"O Goddess, if the entirety of dharma is known or even practiced by me, then I shall restore my own [wife] slain by Viṣṇu to life. (12)
If I speak the truth, by that truth may I live; let all the deities witness my great splendor and power. (13)
"Sprinkling her with cool water, I shall restore her to life by the power of my asceticism, provided that truth, purity, and modesty constitute the strength of my penance. (14)
Vyāsa said:
Sprinkled with water, the goddess was then instantly restored to life;
the wife of Bhṛgu, possessing a pure smile, rose up filled with supreme joy.
Then all living beings, seeing her as if she had just awakened from sleep, [were filled with wonder].
*Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa*, Fourth Skandha, Chapter 12. 213.
Then all living beings, seeing her as if she had just awakened from sleep, [were filled with wonder].
"Excellent! Excellent! they cried, praising him and her from every direction. 16.
Thus restored to life by that Bhṛgu, the woman of excellent complexion caused the gods, including Indra, to experience supreme wonder upon seeing it in the three worlds.
Then Indra said to the gods: "Now that Śataparvan has been restored to life by the sage, what will Kāvya do, he who is an expert in mantras after performing such severe penance?"
Vyāsa said:
O King, sleep has departed from the body of the lord of the gods,
and distress has arisen as he recalls the account of Kāvya and the exceedingly terrible purpose of the mantra.
Then Śakra, having reflected with his mind upon his daughter Jayantī,
spoke these words with a smile to the maiden Avaṅgī.
"Go, my daughter; you have been given by me to the ascetic Kāvya. Propitiate him, O slender-limbed one, and bring him under your control for my sake. (21)
"O Sage, having quickly gone there to that excellent hermitage, dispel my fear by propitiating him with those various services that are pleasing to his mind."
Having heard her father’s words, the beautiful Manorama went there;
the large-eyed woman saw her father amidst the smoke in the hermitage.
Then, beholding his body and remembering his father's words,
he took a plantain leaf and fanned that sage.
Having quickly brought pure, cool, and well-perfumed water, she prepared it for drinking with supreme devotion;
and when the sun was at its zenith, she provided shade with a cloth parasol.
The slender-limbed Satī, herself established in dharma, composed it. ||26||
Having brought divine fruits that were ripe and sweet, he placed them before the sage, prepared for him to eat.
Then, for the fulfillment of his daily rites, he held at the tip [of his hand] green kuśa grass, a span in length and resembling parrots in color, along with flowers.
He prepared a bed strewn with sprouts for the sake of sleep; and while that sage was there, she stood respectfully and slowly fanned him.
At that time, fearing a curse from the sage, Jayantī did not display any gestures of amorous allure (*hāva*) or other such expressions that might produce a transformation in him. (30)
The slender-limbed woman, being eloquent, offered praise to that high-souled one with well-spoken, favorable, and pleasing words. || 31 ||
When he had awakened, she took water and held it for him to sip;
constantly acting in a manner pleasing to his mind, she then moved about.
Indra, too, being clever, dispatched his servants there,
desiring indeed to learn news of that self-controlled sage.
In this manner, for many years she remained devoted to service—
unchanging, having conquered her anger, and dedicated to the life of celibacy.
When a full thousand years had passed, Maheśvara, the captivating one, being thoroughly pleased, invited Kāvya to choose a boon.
Īśvara said:
O Brahmin, son of Bhṛgu, whatever little exists that you perceive—all that must not be spoken of to anyone. 36.
O best of the twice-born, you will undoubtedly become the subduer of all, the controller of all beings, and the lord of creatures.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus granted the boons, Śambhu vanished right there;
then Kāvya, beholding Jayantī, spoke these words.
"Who are you, whose daughter are you, O fair-hipped one? Tell me, what do you intend to do? For what purpose have you arrived here? Speak your business; I am your suitor. (39)
"What do you desire? Shall I perform today even that which is difficult to accomplish, O fair-eyed one? I am pleased by what you have done today; choose a boon, O lady of virtuous vows. (40)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter thirteen.
Then Jayantī, with a joyful countenance, spoke to the sage:
"O Blessed One, you ought to know what I intend to do through my ascetic penance. (41)
Vyāsa said:
"I already know it; nevertheless, tell me what you desire in your heart.
I shall fulfill it in every way, O blessed one, for I am pleased with your service."
Jayantī said:
"O Brahmin, I am the daughter of Śatru; I have been entrusted to you by my father. O Sage, I am Jayantī by name, the younger sister of Jayanta. (43)
"O Lord, my desire for you is fulfilled; now grant me my wish.
O illustrious one, I shall enjoy with you in accordance with dharma and with love. (44)
Śukra said: "O fair-hipped, O beautiful woman, remain here with me for ten years,
invisible to all beings, and sport as you please."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, he went home and took the hand of Jayantī in marriage;
the descendant of Bhṛgu lived with that goddess for ten years.
The Lord, concealed by his illusory power (māyā), became invisible to all beings;
and the Daityas, hearing that he had arrived accompanied by his mantra and having accomplished his purpose, [were filled with fear].
Joyful and desiring to see him, they arrived at his house;
however, they did not find him wandering about in union with Jayantī.
Then they all became dejected and their efforts were shattered;
overcome with anxiety and deeply distressed, they looked back again and again. ||49||
But not seeing him, those foremost of Daityas, overcome with anxiety and stricken by fear, returned to their own homes just as they had come. || 50 ||
Perceiving him thus enjoying himself, Śakra spoke to his preceptor, the illustrious Bṛhaspati: "What should be done after this?"
"Go today, O Brahmin, and entice the Dānavas with your illusory power;
having reflected with your intellect, O giver of honor, accomplish our task. (52)
Having heard those words of Kāvya, which were delightful and well-composed,
and having understood their intent, the Guru assumed that very form and went toward the Daityas.
Having gone there with great devotion, he summoned the Dānavas;
all those Asuras arrived and beheld Kāvya before them.
Having prostrated, they all stood there, utterly bewildered, regarding Kāvya as a supreme being;
they did not recognize the guru’s illusion manifested in the form of Kāvya. 55.
To them, the Guru, in the form of Śukra, spoke through his concealed power of illusion:
"Welcome! I have indeed arrived for the benefit of you, my patrons. (56)
"I shall awaken you to the knowledge obtained through non-deception;
Śambhu, being gratified by my ascetic penance, has done so for the sake of your welfare. (57)
Having heard that, those best of Dānavas became joyful in mind;
considering their preceptor’s task accomplished, they, being utterly deluded, rejoiced.
Filled with joy, free from fear and devoid of distress, they prostrated themselves;
having cast off all dread of the gods, they all remained in a state of perfect well-being. 59.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 12 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
The King said:
What was done by the Guru, who subsequently appeared in the form of Bhṛgu?
Indeed, by means of his guile alone, through the office of priest held by that wise one, [he acted against] the Daityas. || 1 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter thirteen: The preceptor of the gods, who was constantly devoted to all branches of knowledge.
How is it that this sage, being the son of Aṅgiras, is a practitioner of deceit?
In all the treatises on Dharma, the sages have declared truth and righteousness to be the cause by which even the Supreme Self is attained. || 3 ||
If even Vācaspati speaks falsely toward the Dānavas, who then will be a speaker of truth in this world while living as a householder? (4)
There is no food greater than nourishment, even within the vastness of the universe;
O Sage, why then do sages engage in falsehood for its sake? (5)
In the absence of the learned (śiṣṭas), has the authority of verbal testimony not been abolished?
Or, when one is engaged in deceitful actions, how can there be non-reproach toward a teacher?
The gods are said by the sages to have arisen from sattva, human beings from rajas, and animals from tamas at the time of their origin. 7.
If even the preceptor of the immortals were himself a speaker of falsehood, then who could be a speaker of truth, especially one who is passionate and ignorant? (8)
Where does that Dharma abide? This is my own doubt. What is the destiny of all living beings in this triple world which is illusory in nature? (9)
Hari, Brahmā, the beloved of Śacī, and other foremost of the gods—all are skilled in the art of deception; what then need be said of human beings?
All the gods and the sages whose wealth is austerity are consumed by desire and anger, their minds struck down by greed; they are all skilled in deception. (11)
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Viśvāmitra, and likewise the preceptor—these were devoted to sin; what, then, O giver of honor, is the destiny of dharma in this world?
Indra, Agni, the Moon, and Brahmā are all lusting after the wives of others;
O Sage, tell me, where in these worlds does true nobility reside? (13)
O sinless one, whose word should be accepted as instruction?
For all those gods and sages are likewise overcome by greed.
Vyāsa said:
Is it Viṣṇu, or Śiva, or Brahmā, or Indra, or Bṛhaspati? One who possesses a body is indeed subject to transformation and is always joined with the modifications [of nature].
"Viṣṇu possesses passion; Śiva possesses passion; even Brahmā is endowed with passion.
O lord of men, what improper act indeed would one who has passion not commit?"
Though possessed of passion, he appears like Videha due to his cleverness. || 16 ||
Even he, when a crisis has arrived, is indeed constrained by his own qualities;
for how can an effect exist apart from its cause? (17)
Indeed, for all beings beginning with Brahmā, the qualities (guṇas) alone are the cause;
their bodies arise from the twenty-five principles, and not otherwise. (18)
O King, there is no doubt that you are subject to death in due time; what hesitation can you have in this matter?
For all the learned become perfectly clear-sighted when it comes to advising others. (19)
For when one's own duty has presented itself, there is indeed a confusion characterized by lack of discrimination:
desire, anger, greed, malice, egoism, and envy. (20)
O Great King, this worldly existence is always remembered as being of such a nature that an embodied being is never able to abandon those [attachments] again. (21)
Indeed, the world consisting of good and evil does not arise otherwise;
for at times the Lord Viṣṇu performs severe ascetic penance.
Sometimes the Lord of the Gods performs various sacrifices;
at other times, the Supreme Lord is delighted by the stage of Ramā.
It is said that the youthful Lord Vaikuṇṭha once took delight [in sport],
and at one time there was a most terrible battle with the Dānavas.
Afflicted intensely by his arrows, that ocean of compassion sometimes achieves victory, and sometimes, by the power of fate, he too suffers defeat. (25)
Overcome by pleasure and pain, he certainly becomes so; there is no doubt.
At other times, when these two have subsided, he is enveloped in yogic sleep.
At the proper time, the Universal Soul, awakened by his own nature, manifests as Śarva,
Brahmā, Hari, and likewise Indra and all the other gods.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter thirteen: Indeed, the sages wander about, having fashioned their own lifespans.
When the end of the night had arrived, the world, with its moving and unmoving beings, [awoke].
O King, there is no doubt that no one ever dies prematurely;
O Ruler of the Earth, even those born from the lotus (Brahmā) and others meet their end only at the conclusion of their own lifespan.
Furthermore, the gods such as Viṣṇu, Hara, and Śakra arise [from it];
therefore, an embodied being undergoes states such as desire and the like. (30)
O King, you should never feel astonishment at this;
for this cycle of worldly existence, O Monarch, is fraught with uncertainty due to desire, anger, and other such passions.
Rare is the person who is liberated from that [bondage] and knows the ultimate truth;
he who fears this worldly existence does not even take a wife.
Liberated from all attachments, he wanders about without fear;
therefore, the wife of Bṛhaspati was taken back by the Moon.
The wife was offered by the elder brother to his younger brother;
thus, in this wheel of saṃsāra, one is enveloped by passion, greed, and other such afflictions.
And having entered the state of a householder, how may a man become liberated?
Therefore, with every effort, one should abandon the notion that worldly existence possesses any essence. (35)
One should propitiate the Great Sovereign Goddess, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is concealed by the qualities of Her Māyā;
O King, it all wanders like one intoxicated, like one drunk with wine. (36)

By propitiating her alone and crushing all [other] qualities, the wise man shall attain liberation; there is no other path beyond this. As long as the Great Goddess, being propitiated, does not bestow her grace, [liberation is not attained]. ||37-38||
Until then, how could there be happiness? For who else is endowed with compassion?
Therefore, one should worship this ocean of mercy without guile. (39)
But he who, having attained this human birth so difficult to obtain, does not serve the Great Goddess—by whose very worship one attains liberation while living—is truly lost. (40)
Then we know him as one fallen from the top of a ladder;
we know him as one enveloped by egoism—the universe enveloped by egoism and endowed with the three qualities. 41.
Otherwise, how could one be liberated even when bound by untruth?
Therefore, having abandoned everything, she who is the Sovereign of the World should be served by all. (42)
The king said:
"What was done there by the preceptor who had assumed the form of Kāvya?
When did Śukra arrive? Tell me that, O Grandfather. (43)
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall tell you what was then done by the high-souled Guru,
who assumed the form of Śukra and acted in secret.
Instructed by their preceptor, the Daityas, considering Kāvya to be their own teacher,
placed supreme trust in him and then became absorbed in him.
Thinking him to be Bhṛgu, they, being utterly deluded, sought refuge with him for the sake of knowledge;
having been deceived by their preceptor out of greed, who indeed does not become deluded? (46)
Then, when the full period of ten years had elapsed,
Kāvya, having played with Jayantī, began to reflect upon his patrons.
"Indeed, they stand waiting, watching my path with longing;
I shall go and see those sacrificers who are overcome with great fear. (48)
"Let there be no fear of the gods for those devotees of mine; O Āvā, having reflected and applied your intellect, speak thus to Jayantī. || 49 ||
"O fair-eyed one, my sons go only unto the gods;
today your agreement has been fulfilled, for this ten-year period has come to an end. (50)
Therefore, O lady of slender waist, I shall go to see my patrons;
I will return to your presence immediately thereafter. 51.
"So be it," said Jayantī, the most proficient in dharma, and she added:
"Go as you wish, O knower of dharma; I shall not cause your dharma to be violated. (52)
Having heard those words, Kāvya departed from there in haste;
he then beheld Vācaspati standing by the side of the Dānavas.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the fourth book, chapter 14:
[He saw him] assuming a deceptive form, gentle in appearance, and deceiving them through guile.
He himself established the Jaina dharma, which was likewise intent upon the censure of sacrifice.
O enemies of the gods, I speak the truth for your own benefit:
non-violence is the supreme dharma, yet those who are aggressors must indeed be slain.
Indeed, the slaughter of animals was prescribed in the Veda by twice-born men devoted to worldly enjoyments;
intent on the taste of their tongues, they considered the great buffalo of desire to be the supreme goal. 56.
Hearing his guru speaking such words, which were consistent with the Vedas and the Shastras, that son of Bhrigu was filled with wonder.
He reflected in his mind: "My preceptor is indeed my enemy;
there is no doubt that these patrons of mine have been deceived by this rogue. (58)
Fie on greed, the seed of evil and the powerful gateway to hell, by which even a teacher, impelled by that sin, speaks untruth! (59)
Even he whose word is authoritative is a bearer of heresy;
for [Brahmā] is the preceptor of all the gods and the promulgator of the treatises on dharma.
What does one whose mind is defiled by greed not obtain? Even another person, even a teacher, becomes such a pseudo-scholar of heresy through greed. (61)
"Adopting all the behaviors of an actor, this best of the twice-born deceives even my extremely deluded Daitya patrons. (62)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 13 ||
Then, in the fourteenth chapter, Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus in his mind, he spoke to them as if smiling.
"Have the Daityas not been deceived by my own form; what indeed is the need for a preceptor? ||1||
"I am Kāvya and this is my preceptor, the accomplisher of the gods' work;
you have been deceived by him in my sacrifice—of this there is no doubt. (2)
"O noble ones, do not believe his words; this man who has my form is a hypocrite. Follow me, abandon this Bṛhaspati as your officiating priest."
Having heard his words and seeing those two again as identical,
they were struck with supreme wonder and concluded, "This is Kāvya. Seeing them utterly bewildered, the Guru spoke these words:
"This guru is surely deceiving me; he is Bṛhaspati in the form of my father. ||5||
"He has arrived to deceive you for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods;
O best of Daityas, do not place your trust in his words."
"I have obtained the knowledge of Śambhu; I shall teach it to you.
I will surely bring victory over the gods; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard these words of the Guru, who had assumed the form of Kāvya, they—
They attained the highest confidence, certain that he was Kāvya. ||8||
Although the Dānavas were awakened there in many ways by Kāvya,
they did not understand the illusion of their preceptor, being deluded by the turning of time.
Having thus made their resolution, they then said to the descendant of Bhṛgu:
"This righteous-souled one is our preceptor, and his intellect is devoted to our welfare. (10)
"For ten years this descendant of Bhṛgu has constantly ruled over us. Go away; you appear to be a deceiver and are certainly not our guru. (11)
Having spoken thus, O descendant of Bhṛgu, and having rebuked the fool again and again,
they affectionately took hold of that teacher after bowing down and saluting him.
But Kāvya, seeing them absorbed in that [meditation], became enraged and then cursed them, perceiving that the Daityas had been awakened by him and utterly deceived by their preceptor. || 13 ||
"Because you did not accept my words even though I awakened you, therefore, having lost your senses, you shall surely meet with defeat. (14)
"You shall certainly reap the fruit of your contemptuous disregard in a very short time;
then all his deceit will be fully recognized. (15)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter fourteen.
Having spoken thus, that descendant of Bhṛgu departed swiftly, filled with anger;
Bṛhaspati, having attained joy, remained there with a composed mind. ||16||
Then, having learned that those Daityas had been cursed by Bhārgava,
the Guru quickly departed, abandoning his own form and assuming another.
Having gone there, he then said to Śakra: "The task has certainly been accomplished by me;
those Daityas have been cursed by Śukra and have indeed been abandoned by me."
"O best of gods, you have surely been rendered supportless;
O illustrious ones, strive for battle, for you have been consumed by my curse. (19)
Having heard these words of the preceptor, Maghavan attained great joy;
and all the gods rejoiced, having honored Bṛhaspati in return.
Having deliberated among themselves once more, they resolved to engage in battle;
all the gods then set out together, facing toward the Dānavas.
Perceiving that the Suras were prepared and exerting great effort,
and seeing that their preceptor had vanished, they became filled with anxiety.
Then, deluded by his illusory power, they said to one another:
"That high-souled one was to be propitiated, yet he has departed with his mind lost;
having deceived us, that wicked teacher, a scholar of deceit, has gone away. (23)
He generally seduces the wives of his brothers; he is impure within, though pure without. 24.
What shall we do, and where shall we go? How may we make this incensed poem become favorable and joyful in spirit for the sake of our assistance? (25)
Having thus reflected, they all gathered together, trembling with fear;
placing Prahlāda at their head, they went once more to the descendant of Bhṛgu.
Then they bowed at the feet of that sage who was observing a vow of silence;
thereupon Bhārgava, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke to them.
Though awakened by me, you were deluded by the great illusion;
at that time, you did not accept my worthy, pure, and beneficial words. 28.
"At that time, I was disregarded by you who had fallen under his sway;
surely, being intoxicated with pride, you have now reaped the fruit born of my humiliation. (29)
Go there, you who have fallen from the right path, to where that one of deceitful form resides;
he is a deceiver seeking to serve the cause of the gods, for I am not such a deceiver. (30)
Vyāsa said:
To Śukra, who was speaking thus with a voice faltering with words,
Prahlāda then spoke after seizing his feet.
Prahlāda said:

O descendant of Bhṛgu, you ought not to abandon us, who have come today seeking sacrificial offerings and are thus distressed; for we are your sons, O omniscient one, and devoted to your welfare. (32)
But while you were away on a mission, we have been deceived by that evil-minded actor with his sweet-sounding words of feigned devotion to you. (33)
One who is peaceful does not become angry in this way due to a fault committed through ignorance; you are omniscient and know that our minds are exceedingly inclined toward you. (34)
"Knowing our disposition through our asceticism, O high-minded one, abandon your anger;
for all sages declare that the virtuous are indeed quick to forgive. (35)
Water is cold by its very nature; it becomes hot through contact with fire and sunlight, and upon separation from them, it returns to its state of coldness. (36)
Anger, indeed in the form of a caṇḍāla, must be abandoned in every way by the wise;
therefore, O observer of noble vows, renouncing wrath, grant me your favor. (37)
If you do not abandon your anger, you will abandon us who are deeply distressed;
O illustrious one, abandoned by you, we shall go to the netherworld (rasātala). 38.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of Prahlāda and having looked upon them with the eye of knowledge, Bhārgava became well-disposed and spoke to them as if smiling.
"O Dānavas, you must neither fear nor go to the netherworld (rasātala). [Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Fourth Skandha, Chapter 15]
"I shall indeed protect you, my patrons, with unfailing mantras. (40)
"O knowers of dharma, listen now to my certain and beneficial words regarding the truth, which you have heard from Brahmā in the past. (41)
Events, whether auspicious or inauspicious, that are destined to occur inevitably come to pass;
no one on the face of the earth is capable of altering destiny.
Today, undoubtedly, due to the turn of time, you have become weak;
having been defeated by the gods even once, you shall descend to the netherworld.
"The time for succession has arrived," Brahmā declared;
"the entire prosperous and flourishing kingdom has been enjoyed by you. (44)
Having ascended to the very heads of the gods for ten full yugas, you have enjoyed the powerful three worlds through the power of destiny. (45)
That sovereignty over the Manu-period will come to pass once more;
your grandson Bali, the conqueror of the three worlds, shall obtain the kingdom. 46.
When the land was taken by the Lord Viṣṇu in the form of a dwarf, at that very time your grandson was addressed by the divine Jiṣṇu: ||47||
"By whom the kingdom was seized from Bali for the sake of accomplishing the gods' desire—you shall become Indra first, when the Sāvarṇika Manu is established. (48)
The Bhāgavata said: Thus addressed by Hari, O Prahlāda, your grandson now wanders incognito like one afraid, invisible to all beings.
This Bali, having assumed the form of a donkey, was alone with Vāsava;
staying in an empty house, he was filled with fear of Śatakratu at his will. (50)
Then Vāsava saw Bali in many forms and asked: "O bull among the Daityas, for what purpose have you assumed the form of a donkey?"
"You are the enjoyer of all the worlds and the ruler of the Daityas;
O best of Rākṣasas, you feel no shame in the form of a donkey.
Having heard those words of his, Bali, the king of the Daityas, then [replied]. 52.
He spoke these words to Śakra: "O Śatakratu, what cause for grief is there here?
Just as Viṣṇu of great splendor assumed the forms of a fish and a tortoise."
Thus, by the force of time, I have assumed the form of a donkey,
just as you remain dissolved within the lotus, possessed by the sin of killing a Brahmin.
For thus am I now afflicted, standing here assuming the form of a donkey.
O Pākaśāsana, what sorrow or what joy can there be for one who is subject to destiny? (55)
"Time indeed acts in whatever way it desires.
Bhārgava said:
Having thus established that supreme agreement between Bali and the Lord of the Gods, [he spoke].
They regained consciousness at will and went to their respective places;
thus have I fully explained to you the supreme power of destiny.
The entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, is dependent on destiny.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 14 ||
Then the twenty-fifth chapter. Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the high-souled Bhārgava, [the sages asked:]
But Prahlāda, O prince, became exceedingly joyful.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter fifteen.
Having realized that destiny was all-powerful, Prahlāda said to them:
"Even if a battle were fought, victory would never be achieved. (2)
Then those victorious Dānavas, arrogant with pride, said:
"War must indeed be waged; do we not know the power of destiny? (3)
For those who make no effort, O Lord of Asuras, destiny is indeed paramount.
By whom has it been seen? Where has it been seen? Of what nature is it, and by whom was it created? (4)
Therefore, we shall now wage war, relying upon our strength;
O best of gods, you stand before us, for you are omniscient, O high-minded one.
O King, having been addressed thus by them, Prahlāda, the commander of the army against the powerful enemy, then challenged the gods to battle.
Seeing those asuras assembled for battle there,
all the gods, having gathered their full equipment, fought against them.
Then a terrible battle took place between Śakra and Prahlāda;
it lasted for a full hundred years and filled the sages with wonder.
O King, while that great battle was raging, the Daityas led by Prahlāda, protected by Śakra, then achieved victory.
At that very moment, at the word of his preceptor, Indra mentally recalled the goddess Śivā— the supreme bestower of liberation who destroys all suffering.
Indra said:
Victory, O Goddess Mahāmāyā, wielder of the trident, O Mother Ambikā!
You who hold the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and sword in your hands, and who bestow fearlessness! 11.
Salutations to you, O Sovereign of the World, O Leader who reveals the Power (Śakti)!
O Mother, whose essence consists of the ten principles, you who are the very nature of the Great Bindu! 12.
O you who are in the form of Mahākuṇḍalinī, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
O you who are the knowledge of Prāṇāgnihotra, salutations to you who are the essence of the lamp’s flame! 13.
O Mother, who resides within the five sheaths, who is subtle, whose nature is Brahman, who is a digit of bliss, and who is praised by all the Upanishads! 14.
O Mother, be gracious; be well-disposed toward us, O Janani, and protect us who are weak in spirit and defeated by the Daityas.
O Goddess, you are our refuge and the ultimate authority in this abode; endowed with all power, you are capable of pacifying our suffering. (15)
Those who meditate become exceedingly happy; others likewise, freed from sorrow and fear, are possessed of suffering;
yet the virtuous, seeking liberation, free from pride and released from attachment, cross over the waters of the ocean of saṃsāra. (16)
O Goddess, Mother of the Universe, you whose power is renowned, who have arisen with terrifying majesty for the sake of protection;
indeed, you take the form of Time (Kāla) to withdraw this entire world—who, then, of dull intellect could truly know your conduct, O Mother? (17)

Brahmā, Hara, the one with the green-horsed chariot (Viṣṇu), Hari, Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Agni, and Samīraṇa—as well as the sages of great majesty and even the Vedas and Āgamas—are not capable of knowing her incomparable power. (18)
Blessed indeed are those great souls devoted to you, who are freed from the miseries of saṃsāra and immersed in an ocean of bliss;
whereas those devoid of the sentiment of devotion never cross the ocean of suffering, which is filled with waves that neither diminish nor end. 19.
I reflect that you were surely worshipped with various offerings in a previous body by those fortunate ones who, seated upon palanquins and fanned with white chowries, sported in delight. (20)

Those who, mounted upon excellent elephants, move about playfully in the company of their retinues, attended by subordinate kings who have approached them—I believe that you were indeed honored by them. (21)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter 15. Vyāsa said:
Thus praised by Maghavan, the Goddess, the Sovereign of All,
then suddenly manifested, mounted upon a lion and possessing four arms.
The goddess, possessing beautiful eyes, bore the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
she was clad in red garments and adorned with divine garlands and ornaments.
He spoke to those gods with a gracious countenance and a gentle voice:
"O gods, cast away your fear; I shall indeed now provide for your welfare."
Having spoken thus, that exceedingly beautiful goddess, mounted upon a lion,
then went swiftly to where the intoxicated Daityas were.
Seeing the Goddess standing before them, all of them, headed by Prahlāda, spoke to one another in fear: "What should be done here now? (26)
Indeed, the goddess Caṇḍikā, the slayer of Mahiṣa and the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, arrived here at this very place before Lord Nārāyaṇa.
"Ambikā will slay us all; there is no doubt about this—she by whom, with a sidelong glance, Madhu and Kaiṭabha were previously slain. (28)
Seeing them thus distressed with anxiety, Prahlāda said to them:
"O lords, O best of Dānavas, you must fight; you must not flee. (29)
Intent on flight here,
the Mother of the World, it is said, will strike them down in her wrath with her weapons.
Then Namuci said to them:
"O fortunate ones, act in such a way that no suffering arises;
let us go this very day to Pātāla, having praised her with her permission."
Prahlāda said: I praise the Goddess Mahāmāyā, the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction;
the power who is the mother of all, and the bestower of fearlessness upon her devotees. (32)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, Prahlāda, the devotee of Viṣṇu and knower of the supreme truth,
then praised the Mother of the worlds with his palms joined in reverence.
Salutation to her whose form is *hrīṃ*, who is the substratum of all, in whom the entire world of moving and non-moving beings appears like a garland of snakes. (34)
From you proceeds this entire universe, both the stationary and the moving;
others are merely instrumental causes, created by you as its agents. (35)
Salutations to the Goddess Mahāmāyā, who is remembered as the mother of all.
What difference is there for you between the gods, the Daityas, and those created by yourself? (36)
What difference can there be for a mother between sons who are wicked and those who are virtuous? Likewise, you must not now make any distinction between us gods. (37)
O Mother, those sons of yours, the Dānavas, are indeed as they are;
for you are proclaimed in the Purāṇas as the mother of the entire universe. 38.
They too were surely intent on their own self-interest, and we likewise; there is no difference between the Daityas and the Suras—this distinction arises from delusion. (39)
O Goddess of the gods, we are attached day and night to the enjoyment of wealth, wives, and other pleasures;
it is exactly the same for the gods—what difference is there between asuras and gods? (40)
"We too are indeed the descendants of Kaśyapa and born from him;
O Mother, how has this occurrence of hostility now arisen between us? (41)
O Mother, source of all things, you have not acted in such a way;
indeed, you must maintain equanimity toward both the gods and us.
Since all gods and asuras have arisen from the intermixture of the qualities (guṇas), how could those embodied beings be immortal while still being endowed with the qualities? (43)
Desire, anger, and greed reside within all bodies; since they are always present, what person could possibly be free from conflict? (44)
"Surely this mutual conflict was devised by you out of curiosity; we consider it certain that you desire to witness a battle through their division. (45)
Otherwise, O sinless one, what kind of discord exists among brothers?
If you, Cāmuṇḍā, indeed wish to witness this quarrel. (46)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter fifteen.
O knower of dharma, I know the dharma and I know Śatakratu;
nevertheless, O Goddess, there is always a quarrel between us for the sake of enjoyment.
O Mother, there is no teacher whatsoever in this world other than you;
for what wise person who possesses desire is capable of acting according to [the words of] another? (48)
At one time, this ocean was churned by the gods and asuras;
indeed, Viṣṇu brought about a division under the pretext of the nectar and the jewels.
By you, that Śauri, the teacher of the world, was appointed to the office of protector;
by him, out of greed, Lakṣmī—the beauty of the immortals—was personally seized.
Likewise, Airāvata was taken by Indra, and Pārijāta as well as the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhuk;
Uccaiḥśravas was taken by the gods—all this indeed being by the will of Viṣṇu.
"Having committed such an injustice, how have the gods become virtuous? Surely the gods are unjust; behold the true nature of dharma!
Surely the gods were established by Viṣṇu, who is full of self-conceit. || 52 ||
Surely the Daityas have been defeated; behold the characteristic of Dharma!
Where is Dharma? What is Dharma like? Where is duty, and where is goodness?
And before whom shall I declare my established doctrine of Mīmāṃsā?
[There are] logicians who know the arguments of reasoning, those who know the ritual procedures, and proponents of the Vedas. (54)
Those whose nature is inert dispute that the universe has a creator;
yet, indeed, if there were a creator in this vast cycle of existence— (55)
What kind of mutual contradiction exists there regarding a single action? Why is there a single-minded agreement with the Veda, and likewise again among the various Śāstras? (56)
Furthermore, even the speech of those who know the Vedas is not of one voice, because the entire world, both stationary and moving, is intent upon its own self-interest. (57)
There has been no one in this world free from desire, nor will there ever be;
even Śaśinātha, having learned of it, forcibly took the wife of his preceptor.
Likewise, although Indra knew Gautama’s certainty regarding the Dharma, his elder brother forcibly enjoyed his younger brother’s wife while she was pregnant. (59)
The child was cursed while still in the womb and likewise rendered blind;
furthermore, the head of Rāhu was forcibly severed by Viṣṇu with his discus.
O Mother, at that time, though he was without fault, that grandson of yours—who was full of courage, devoted to dharma, heroic, and dedicated to truth—was at the mercy of desire. (61)
A performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, peaceful, omniscient, and a worshiper of all—
[he was deceived] after Hari, who knows how to outwit, assumed the form of a dwarf.
It is said that in former times Bali was deceived and his entire kingdom was taken away;
nevertheless, the wise declare that the gods remain established in dharma.
Having gone there, they speak flattering words and words of righteousness;
knowing this, O Mother of the World, do as you wish.
"All the Dānavas have come for refuge; either slay them or protect them.
The Goddess Śrī said:
"All of you go to Pātāla, and there dwell as you desire. (65)
"O Dānavas, all of you act without fear and free from resentment;
time must be awaited by you, for it is the cause of both good and evil."
For those who are intent on complete detachment, there is happiness everywhere and at all times;
yet even in the sovereignty over the three worlds, there is no happiness for those whose minds are possessed by greed.
Even when accomplished, there is no complete happiness for those who still possess desire, even through fruits;
therefore, having abandoned this earth, let him go today to the netherworld.
Placing my command before them, may you all be freed from all taints.
Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Fourth Skandha, Chapter 16. 223.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the goddess, he said, "So be it," and went to the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Having bowed down, all the Dānavas departed, protected by Śakti;
then the Goddess vanished, and the gods returned to their own abode.
Then all those gods and dānavas remained there, having abandoned their enmity;
whoever hears or recites this entire narrative [shall attain merit].
Completely liberated from all suffering, he proceeds to the supreme state. ||71||
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 15 ||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
O best of sages, [tell me] of Hari, the performer of wondrous deeds, regarding the curse of Bhṛgu.
O Lord, how were the incarnations born, and in which Manvantara did they occur?
O Knower of Dharma, O Brahmin, tell me in detail the narrative of Hari’s descent, which destroys sins and brings all happiness when heard.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe the incarnations of Hari according to which Manvantara they occurred and in which Yuga, O lord of men.
O King, I shall now describe to you in brief all those forms in which Nārāyaṇa indeed performed his various deeds. (4)
During the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, Dharma himself appeared;
he became known on the surface of the earth as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the sons of Dharma.
Then, in this second age known as Vaivasvata,
Hari again took birth as Dattātreya, becoming the son of Atri.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra— these three most excellent gods—
became sons to Atri, having been chosen by his wife.
And Anasūyā, the wife of Atri, was the most excellent among virtuous women;
by her, the gods were entreated and became her three sons.
Brahmā became Soma-rūpa, Dattātreya was Hari himself,
and Durvāsas, in the form of Rudra, attained the state of being your sons.
