now tell me of those other portions of the gods who were born therein. (28)
"O sinless one, it was indeed at the request of the gods for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden that [I was born].
Vyāsa said: "Those who were the renowned portions of the gods and the asuras upon the earth... (29)
I shall declare them to you; listen to them in brief:
Vasudeva was a portion of Kaśyapa, and Devakī likewise was Aditi.
Among those who exist in the present, Baladeva is a portion of Ananta;
he who is known as the illustrious Dharmasuta (the son of Dharma) is celebrated as Nārāyaṇa.
Vāsudeva was an incarnation of that [portion] while the sage was still present;
and Arjuna was indeed an incarnation of his younger brother, Nara.
Yudhiṣṭhira was a portion of Dharma, and Bhīma likewise a portion of Vāyu;
the two sons of Mādrī, possessed of great strength, were declared to be portions of the Aśvins. (33)
Karṇa is said to be a portion of the Sun, and Vidura is remembered as a portion of Dharma;
Droṇa was a portion of Bṛhaspati, and his son was born from a portion of Śiva.
Samudra is declared to be Śantanu, and Gaṅgā is considered his wife by the wise; Devaka, moreover, is proclaimed in the Āgama to be the lord of the Gandharvas.
Vasubhīṣma and Virāṭa are remembered as the Marudgaṇa;
the son of Ariṣṭa is celebrated as Haṃsa and Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The host of Maruts is said to be Kṛpa, and likewise Kṛtavarman;
Duryodhana is a portion of Kali, and know Śakuni to be Dvāpara.
The son of Soma, known as Suvarcas, is declared to be Somapraṇa;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna is a portion of Pāvaka, and Śikhaṇḍin is likewise a Rākṣasa.
Pradyumna is proclaimed to be a portion of Sanatkumāra;
Drupada is a portion of Varuṇa, and Draupadī is born from a portion of Ramā.
The five sons of Draupadī are remembered as being born from portions of the Viśvedevas.
Kuntī is Siddhi, Mādrī is Vṛtti, and Gāndhārī, the daughter of the king of Gāndhāra, is Mati.
Likewise, all the wives of Kṛṣṇa are remembered as celestial courtesans;
and all the kings, as well as the Asuras, were incited by Śakra. || 41 ||
Śiśupāla is declared to be a portion of Hiraṇyakaśipu;
likewise, Jarāsaṃdha is Vipracitti, and Śalya is Prahlāda. (42)
Likewise, Kālanemi, Kaṃsa, Keśin, Hayaśiras,
Ariṣṭa, and Bali’s son Kakudmin were slain at Gokula.
Anuhāda became Dhṛṣṭaketu, Bhagadatta became Bāṣkala, Lamba became Pralamba, and that Khara became Dhenuka. (44)
The Daityas Vārāha and Kiśora, who were exceedingly fierce,
became wrestlers known as Cāṇūra and Muṣṭika.
Likewise, Diti’s sons were Ariṣṭa, Gaja, and the one named Kuvalaya; Baki was known as the daughter of Bali, and her younger brother is remembered as Baka. (46)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fourth Skandha, Chapter 23.
Yama, Rudra, as well as Kāma and Krodha as the fourth—the son of Droṇa, possessed of great strength, was born from portions of them. || 47 ||
In the partial incarnations, all those former Daityas and Rākṣasas were born as portions of the gods for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth.
O King, this descent of portions of the gods and the asuras has been described to you; it is proclaimed in the Purāṇas, O Ruler. (49)
When the gods, headed by Brahmā, went to Hari for the sake of a boon,
Hari then indeed granted them two hairs, one white and one black.
Then Kṛṣṇa was dark-complexioned, and Saṃkarṣaṇa was white;
for the purpose of relieving the burden of the earth, those two were born from the portions of the gods.
Whoever hears this account of the partial incarnations with a spirit of devotion,
being liberated from all sins, rejoices surrounded by his own kinsmen.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 22 ||
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Vyāsa said: When six sons had been slain by the son of Ugrasena, Devakī—
When the seventh embryo had fallen, it was due to the words of Nārada.
And for the sake of protecting his eighth pregnancy,
the king, reflecting upon his own death, made an unremitting effort.
At the appointed time, Hari entered the womb of Devakī;
having arrived with Vasudeva in due order, he did so by means of a portion [of himself]. (3)
Thus, this goddess Yogamāyā entered Yaśodā at her will for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. 4.
Rāma, the son of Rohiṇī, was born in Gokula,
for that lovely woman remained there, agitated by fear of Kaṃsa.
Then Kaṃsa placed Devakī, who is praised by the gods,
in prison and appointed guards for her protection.
But Vasudeva, constrained by the love of his beloved and reflecting upon the birth of a son, entered [the cave] together with his wife.
Viṣṇu, having entered the womb of Devakī for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods,
grew up in due order after being praised by hosts of immortals.
Then, when the tenth month had arrived— the auspicious month of Śrāvaṇa—
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, conjoined with the lunar mansion Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī).
But Kaṃsa, overwhelmed by fear, said to all the Dānavas:
"Devakī must be protected by you within the inner chamber of her womb."
"The eighth child in Devakī's womb will become my enemy;
that boy, who is the very form of death, must be protected with great effort. (11)
"Having killed this child, O Daityas, I shall sleep happily in my palace,
now that the eighth son— the misery devoid of fulfillment— has been destroyed."
May they all bear swords and spears, and carry bows;
may they be free from sleep and lethargy, with their eyes fixed everywhere.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus commanded the hosts of Asuras, Kaṃsa, overwhelmed by extreme fear, quickly went to his own palace; that Dānava found no peace.
At midnight, Devakī spoke there to Vasudeva:
"What shall I do, O Great King? The time of my delivery has arrived.
Many terrifying guards are stationed here."
Formerly, an agreement was made by me together with Nandapalyā. || 16 ||
"O proud lady, you must send your son to my palace;
there I shall indeed protect him with all my heart. (17)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter twenty-three. [Page 241]
"I shall give you an offspring as proof against Kaṃsa.
O Lord, what must be done now that this crisis has arrived? (18)
"O Śauri, how would you be able to effect a reversal of this lineage?
Stay far away today, O beloved; my shame is exceedingly difficult to overcome. (19)
"O Lord, having turned my face away, what else could I do?
Having spoken thus to that illustrious one, who was honored by the gods, Devakī—
There, at midnight, she gave birth to a most wonderful boy;
seeing that auspicious child, Devakī was filled with amazement.
The highly fortunate woman, her body blossoming with joy, said to her husband:
"Behold the face of your son, O beloved; for it is indeed difficult for you, my lord, to obtain. (22)
"Today this brother’s son, appearing in the form of Death, will slay him.
Vasudeva, saying "So be it," took his son by the hand.
And he beheld the face of his son of wondrous deeds;
upon seeing his son's face, Śauri was indeed overcome with joy.
"What shall I do? How can there be no suffering for me on account of him?"—while he was thus distressed with anxiety, an incorporeal voice spoke.
Addressing Vasudeva with clear syllables in the sky:
"O Vasudeva, take him and lead him to Gokula quickly;
all the guards have been rendered unconscious by me through sleep."
The eight doors and the chains were thrown open. ||27||
"Having released him from the house of Nanda, you must bring back the Yogamāyā.
Upon hearing this, Vasudeva went to that prison cell.
O King, seeing that the gate was open,
he quickly took him and departed at once, unobserved by the gatekeepers.
Having reached the bank of the Kālindī and seeing the flood with certainty,
that best of rivers instantly became waist-deep at that very moment.
By the power of his yogic illusion, Ānakadundubhi crossed [the river];
having gone to Gokula at nightfall on a deserted path, O Śauri.
Standing at the gate of Nanda, beholding the manifestation known as the bound soul (paśu),
Yaśodā, born from his own womb, was then and there produced.
The goddess, born from a portion of Yogamāyā, possessing the three qualities and divine form,
took that divine girl who had been born into her lotus-like hands.
Having arrived there, the queen, assuming the form of a maidservant (sairandhrī), [received him];
Vasudeva, having placed his son into the lotus-like hand of the maidservant, [departed].
Taking that girl with a joyful heart, he went quickly;
then, having gone to the prison, he placed the daughter upon Devakī’s bed.
Having cast it aside, he stood by the side, overcome with anxiety and afflicted by fear;
at that very moment, the girls who had regained their consciousness wept piteously.
Having heard that news at night, the king's servants rose up;
they went to the monarch in great haste and extreme agitation and spoke to him. (37)
"A son has been born to Devakī; come quickly, O high-minded one! Having heard those words of theirs, the lord of the Bhojas departed at once.
Seeing the door closed, Kaṃsa then called out to Vasudeva.
Kaṃsa said:
"O high-minded Vasudeva, bring the son of Devakī here; my eighth pregnancy is death itself, and I shall slay that enemy, Hari."
Vyāsa said: Having heard Kaṃsa’s words, Śauri, his eyes trembling with fear,
took that daughter by the hand and quickly gave her [to him], as if weeping.
Then, having seen the girl, the king was struck with the utmost wonder.
The speech of the gods and the words of Nārada have proven futile;
how could Vasudeva, even while standing in the midst of a crisis, utter a falsehood? (42)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter twenty-four.
"All my guards are undoubtedly attentive;
how then could a maiden have entered here at will, and where indeed has that son gone?"
"One must not entertain doubt in this matter; the course of time is treacherous.
Having reflected thus, the wicked man seized that young woman by her feet.
That merciless defiler of his lineage dashed her against a stone;
released from his hand, the young girl ascended into the expanse of the sky.
Then, assuming a divine form, she spoke to him in a gentle voice:
"O wicked one, what is gained by killing me? A powerful enemy has been born for you. (46)
"He will destroy you, the lowest of men, for he is difficult to propitiate in every way.
Having said this, that auspicious maiden, who could travel anywhere at will, departed into the sky.
Kaṃsa, however, filled with astonishment, then went to his own home; having summoned all the Dānavas, he spoke these words: ||48||
"Overcome with rage and afflicted by fear, let all the Dānavas, including Baka, Dhenuka, Vatsa, and the others, go for the sake of accomplishing my purpose. (49)
"Wherever infants are born, they must be killed;
let this Pūtanā, the slayer of children, go today to Nanda’s cowherd settlement. (50)
By my command, Dhenuka, Vatsaka, Keśin, Pralamba, and Vaka were there, slaughtering infants as soon as they were born. 51.
"Let all remain right there out of a desire to perform my work"—
having thus commanded the Asuras, the wicked Kaṃsa went to his own home.
Overcome with anxiety and deeply dejected in spirit, he reflected upon that matter once more.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 23 ||
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
In the morning, a great festival for the birth of a son took place in the house of Nanda.
Now, it is said that this was also heard by Kaṃsa from the mouths of his spies.
He knows that Vasudeva’s wife resides there;
indeed, all the cattle and the group of servants are in Nanda’s cowherd settlement.
O descendant of Bharata, filled with apprehension because of that,
Nārada also previously explained all the reasons concerning Gokula.
Those in Gokula, such as Nanda and others, and their wives who were born from portions of the gods, as well as Devakī, Vasudeva, and the rest— all of them were indeed his enemies.
Thus enlightened by the words of Nārada, O King, that lowest of his clan, Kaṃsa— the perpetrator of supreme evil— became filled with rage. There, Pūtanā was slain by Kṛṣṇa of immeasurable splendor.
Baka, Vatsāsura, and the exceedingly powerful Dhenuka as well. || 6 ||
Having heard that Pralamba had been slain by him and that Govardhana had likewise been held up,
Kaṃsa considered his own death to be certain.
When Keśin had been thus slain, Kaṃsa, realizing this, became exceedingly dejected;
under the pretext of a bow-sacrifice, he quickly set about bringing those two [Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma] there.
Then the cruel one of sinful mind,
possessing immeasurable prowess, dispatched Akrūra in order to bring Rāma and Kṛṣṇa for their slaughter.
Having mounted the chariot from Gokula, Gopāla, the son of Nandinī,
arrived in Mathurā and indeed remained there at the command of Kaṃsa.
Then, having arrived there, they both broke the bow;
then, having slain the washerman at will, as well as the elephant, Cāṇūra, and Muṣṭika.
Then Hari slew both Śala and Tośala;
the Lord of Gods effortlessly seized Kaṃsa by the hair and killed him.
Then, having liberated his parents, the destroyer of enemies made them free from sorrow;
he bestowed that kingdom upon Ugrasena.

There, the high-minded Vasudeva caused the two of them to undergo the formal investiture of the sacred thread (vratibandha) according to the prescribed rites, preceded by the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter 243:
Then, having been initiated, the two of them went to the abode of Sāṃdīpani.
Having thoroughly mastered all branches of knowledge, they returned again to Mathurā. || 15 ||
Twelve years after their birth, the two heroic sons of Ānakadundubhi, who were accomplished in learning and possessed of great strength, resided in Mathurā. (16)
But Jarāsandha of Magadha, distressed by the slaughter of his son-in-law,
assembled a multitude of troops and arrived at the city of Mathurā.
Having encountered him in battle, he was defeated seventeen times by Kṛṣṇa, who had made up his mind [to fight] while residing in Madhupurī.
And later, impelled by him, that one named Kālayavana—the brave lord of all the Mlecchas and a source of terror to the Yādavas—[attacked]. || 19 ||
Having heard that the Yavana was approaching, Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Madhu, summoned all the best of the Yadus as well as Rāma and spoke to them.
"Great fear has arisen here for us from the mighty Jarāsaṃdha;
what should be done, O illustrious one, for the Yavana is indeed approaching? (21)
One should protect one's life even by abandoning home, strength, and wealth;
indeed, that country where one dwells in happiness is one's true ancestral land.
Although it certainly causes constant agitation, what should be done that is appropriate for one's lineage?
One who desires happiness must remain in the presence of mountains and oceans. (23)
The wise should dwell where there is no fear of enemies;
Hari himself rests upon the ocean, reclining on the bed of Śeṣa.
And likewise, the destroyer of Tripura remained on Kailāsa out of fear;
therefore, we, tormented by our enemies, must not remain right here. 25.
"We shall all go together to Dvāravatī;
today Garuḍa has described to us that beautiful city of Dvāravatī. (26)
"In the vicinity of Mount Raivata, on the shore of the ocean, she is enchanting.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those truthful words, all the foremost of the Yādavas [acted accordingly].
Together with their families and their vehicles, they resolved to depart;
likewise, there were wagons, camels, mares, horses, and buffaloes.
Having filled [the carts] with wealth, they all set out from the city,
placing Rāma and Kṛṣṇa at their head, accompanied by all their attendants.
Placing all their subjects at the forefront, Cilla and all those best of the Yadus reached the city of Dvāravatī after some days, it is said.
Mādhava indeed caused the restoration of the ruins to be carried out by artisans;
having established the Yādavas there, he [honored] these two, Bala and Keśava.
Having arrived swiftly at Mathurā, they took up residence in that deserted city;
then, the powerful lord of the Yavanas reached that very place.
Knowing that he had arrived, Kṛṣṇa went out from the city; Janārdana was on foot at the head of his procession as he approached the forest.
Wearing yellow garments, the glorious Madhusūdana smiled;
seeing that lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa proceeding before him, [he was filled with joy]. (34)
The wicked Yavana, being on foot, followed from behind while the royal sage Mukunda, who possessed great strength, was fast asleep. (35)
The Lord Hari, accompanied by Kālayavana, proceeded there; and having looked upon Mucukunda, Viṣṇu vanished right then and there.
Right there, a Yavana arrived and saw him as if he were asleep;
thinking him to be Vāsudeva, he struck the king with his foot.
Awakened, the immensely powerful one, his eyes red with rage, consumed him;
having burnt him, Mucukunda then beheld the lotus-eyed Lord.
Having bowed down to Vāsudeva, the lord of the virtuous gods, he set out for the forest;
accompanied by Baladeva, Kṛṣṇa went to Dvārakā. || 39 ||
Having made Ugrasena the king, he sported according to his pleasure; and at the svayaṃvara of Śiśupāla, he carried off Rukmiṇī as he desired.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter twenty-four.
By means of the Rākṣasa form of marriage, Hari performed the rite of taking a wife;
thereafter [he took] Jāmbavatī, Satyā, and the beautiful Mitravindā.
Having brought together Kālindī, Lakṣmaṇā, Bhadrā, and the auspicious Nāgnajitī,
each individually, Janārdana married them.
O protector of the earth, Rukmiṇī gave birth to eight most beautiful sons, including Pradyumna, who was lovely to behold. (43)
Madhusūdana performed for him the birth-rites and other ceremonies;
he had been carried away from the lying-in chamber by the powerful Śambara.
The boy was led back to his own city and handed over to Māyāvatī;
Vāsudeva, seeing that his son had been taken away, was overcome with grief.
With a mind full of devotion, he sought refuge in the Goddess, by whom Vṛtāsura and the other Daityas were slain as if in mere sport. (46)
Then he directed his supreme mindfulness toward Yogamāyā with most noble words and auspicious, imperishable hymns of praise.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Mother, you were propitiated by me through intense penance in a previous birth, and you were worshipped with flowers and other offerings.
O Janani, has your state of devotion toward me been forgotten by the son of Dharma in the midst of the Badarī forest?
"Has my infant been carried away from the lying-in chamber by someone of wicked intent, or perhaps out of curiosity?
Surely, O Mother, it is only proper for you to feel shame today before me, who have stripped you of your honor; for such shame is indeed fitting for one who has a devoted person. (49)
The city of Durgā is exceedingly well-guarded and highly secure; even there, my residence is reportedly situated in the very center.
Within the inner apartments, the lying-in chamber is indeed secluded; yet, despite all this, the child has been taken away solely through my own fault. (50)
I have not gone to the enemy's city, nor have the Yādavas, nor indeed the city of Rākṣāvatī with its heroic men;
O Mother, this is surely your own illusion of manifest power, for by some deceiver has my child been carried away.
O Mother, who can know your well-guarded conduct? I am but a dull-witted person of little learning, a mere embodied soul.
Where has he gone, that thief whom my soldiers did not see? O Ambika, this is merely a curtain you have fashioned.
It is no wonder that you, by means of your illusory power, brought this child from your mother’s womb to me before my very eyes at the halfway point;
for Rohiṇī, remaining far away and devoted solely to her husband even without being with him, gave birth to the world-renowned Haladhara.
You create the worlds, you protect them, and likewise you bring about their destruction again and again through your qualities without ceasing;
O Mother, who can know your conduct, which brings an end to all sins? For almost everything entirely ordained here has been accomplished by you alone.

Having first produced the joy born of a son's birth, and then indeed bestowed the heavy burden of suffering arising from separation, you truly sport with those very same charming pastimes; otherwise, how could my delight in attaining a son be in vain? (55)
His mother weeps bitterly like a female osprey; she who is always by my side spreads sorrow for me.
Alas, O Lalitā, you do not perceive this, you of immeasurable power! O Mother, you alone are the refuge for those afflicted by worldly existence. 56.
O Goddess, the wise declare that the birth of a son is the limit of happiness and his loss is the limit of suffering within one's home.
Therefore, O Mother, what shall I do? O Mother, now that my first son has perished, my heart seems to burst asunder this very day.
I perform sacrifices for your gratification, as well as vows and divine worship; you are the destroyer of all suffering. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa*, Fourth Skandha, Chapter 25. 245.
If my son survives here until morning, you must indeed show him quickly, for forgiveness is the destroyer of all sorrow. (58)
Vyāsa said: Thus praised then by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds, the Goddess,
appearing visibly before him, spoke to that teacher of the world.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, do not grieve; this curse of yours is ancient.
By its power, your son was forcibly carried away by Śambara."
Therefore, in his sixteenth year, having slain that Śambara by force, your son shall go [to heaven] through my grace; of this there is no doubt. (61)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess Caṇḍikā, of fierce prowess, vanished;
and the Blessed One, too, having abandoned grief for his son, became happy.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 24 ||
Chapter Twenty-Five.
The King said:
O best of sages, a doubt arises in me from your words.
And having observed the arising of suffering within the Blessed One, who possesses a Vaiṣṇava portion. || 1 ||
How was that powerful Vāsudeva, born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa,
carried away as a child even from Hari by Mūrtikā?
Then, having entered a well-guarded lying-in chamber within the beautiful city of Sugupta, how was that infant seized by that Daitya? (3)
"It was not known by Vāsudeva; this is a marvel to me, a great wonder arising in my heart, O son of Satyavatī."
O Brahmin, tell me the reason for that which was unknown to Keśava: why did he, while staying there, carry off the infant from the maternity chamber?
Vyāsa said:
O King, the Māyā of Śambhu is powerful and deludes the intellects of men; it is renowned in the world—who indeed does not fall into delusion?
Having attained human birth, all qualities indeed become human;
they are born of the body at will, but not so for gods or asuras.
Hunger, thirst, sleep, fear, lassitude, delusion, grief, doubt, joy, pride, old age, death,
ignorance, exhaustion, lack of pleasure, envy, malice, intoxication, and fatigue—
these states born of the body arise, O lord of men.
Just as Rāma did not perceive the golden deer standing before him, so too he was unaware of Jānaki’s abduction and the death of Jaṭāyu.
On the day of his consecration, Rāma did not know of his exile to the forest; likewise, Rāma did not learn of his father’s death from his own grief.
Investigating like one ignorant, though searching forest after forest,
he did not find Jānakī, who had been forcibly abducted by Rāvaṇa.
Having made the monkeys his allies, having slain the son of Śakra by force,
and having built a bridge across the ocean, he crossed over that lord of rivers.
He dispatched those elephant-like monkeys in all directions;
he engaged in a terrible battle and met with suffering on the field of combat.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fourth book, chapter twenty-five.
The mighty Rāma, the joy of the Raghus, was bound by the serpent-noose,
and subsequently experienced liberation from Garuḍa.
Enraged, the joy of the Raghus slew the exceedingly powerful Kumbhakarṇa in battle, as well as Meghanāda and Nikumbha.
Janārdana did not know that Jānakī was beyond reproach;
nevertheless, he caused her to undergo the divine ordeal by fire.
Furthermore, due to public censure, the son of Daśaratha abandoned his beloved Sītā, whom he considered blameless, thinking her to be defiled. (18)
Neither his own two sons nor Kuśīlava were known by that Rāma;
however, the sage declared that those two were his exceedingly powerful sons.
And Rāghava, not having learned through his supernatural knowledge that [his brother] had indeed gone to Pātāla, was filled with anger and prepared to slay his brother. || 20 ||
The slayer of Khara did not even perceive the arrival of Time;
having assumed a human body, he performed human actions. ||21||
In the same way, one should not entertain any doubt regarding human affairs;
for previously, the joy of the Yadus arrived at Gokula out of fear of Kaṃsa.
Out of fear of Jarāsaṃdha, Hari subsequently went to Dvāravatī;
furthermore, Kṛṣṇa committed an unrighteous act in the abduction of Rukmiṇī.
And knowing the eternal dharma,
Kṛṣṇa grieved for the child Śiśupāla, who had been forcibly abducted by Śaṃvara.
Then, recognizing him as his son, he rejoiced, filled with waves of joy;
indeed, by the command of Satyabhāmā, he fought [with him] as if he had descended from heaven.
For the sake of a tree, Indra displayed his state of being conquered by women; he who, having defeated Śatakratu, carried off the Kalpavṛkṣa.
To protect the pride of the proud Satyā, the Lord Hari bound himself to a tree; then Satyā gave her husband to Nārada.
Then, having given birth to Kāla and Kṛṣṇa,
Mochanāminī subsequently bore sons of many virtues, headed by Pradyumna.
The distressed Jāmbavatī sent Kṛṣṇa toward the Yavanas;
having resolved to perform austerities, Kṛṣṇa went to that mountain.
Where the sage Upamanyu, a devotee of Śiva and a scorcher of foes, resided;
there Hari, having taken Upamanyu as his guru, received the Pāśupata initiation.
Desiring a son, he took them up and became one with shaven head and a staff;
there he performed severe penance for one month, subsisting on fruits alone.
Hari, intent on meditation upon Śiva, chanted the Śiva-mantra;
in the second month, Hari remained standing on one foot, subsisting only on water.
In the third [period], he subsisted on air alone, standing on the tips of his toes;
and in the sixth, the Blessed Lord Śiva became pleased with him due to his state of devotion.
And there Soma, the bearer of the lunar digits, beheld the sight;
he arrived mounted upon his bull, surrounded by the gods beginning with Indra. (34)
Accompanied by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and attended by Yakṣas and Gandharvas,
Gaṅkara spoke to Vāsudeva, awakening him.
"I am well-pleased, O high-minded Kṛṣṇa, by your fierce austerity. I grant you your desired boons; speak, O delight of the Yādavas! (36)
"When I am seen, who fulfills all desires, no trace of desire shall remain.

Having been addressed thus by the Lord of the Gods, that messenger departed in haste;
he went to the intoxicated Mahiṣa, and after bowing down, he replied.
The messenger said:
"O King, the lord of the gods does not disregard you at his pleasure;
surrounded by the divine army, he considers his own strength to be complete. (23)
"Since that fool has spoken thus, how can I say anything else?
A servant must speak what is both pleasing and true in the presence of his master. (24)
"O Great King, the auspicious maxim that 'one who desires what is beneficial should speak what is pleasant and true in the presence of a lord' remains ever vigilant. (25)
If you speak only what is pleasant, your purpose will not be accomplished;
nor should anything harsh ever be spoken by one who desires what is auspicious. (26)
O Lord, just as words resembling poison issue forth from the mouths of enemies, how is it that words likewise issue forth from the mouths of your servants? (27)
O Lord of the Earth, such words as those spoken by him here—my tongue is never able to utter even one like them. (28)
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of his, which were full of reason, Mahiṣāsura, who feeds on grass, became intensely overcome with anger.
With eyes bloodshot with rage, he summoned the Daityas while placing his tail upon his back and passing urine.
"O Daityas! This lord of the gods is in every way desirous of battle. Make preparations for force; this lowest of gods must certainly be conquered. (31)
Who could be a hero in my presence? Even if there were ten million such as you, I do not fear them alone; I shall slay Kāma today by all means.
He is surely a hero among the peaceful and one who excels in strength among ascetics;
for he is a deceitful libertine who seizes the wives of others, a creator of mere physical force.
Intoxicated by the power of the Apsarases, that wicked man caused obstacles to his asceticism;
he was a sinner who struck at vulnerabilities and was constantly a betrayer of trust.
By him, having first made various oaths through deceit and fear, the evil-minded Namuci was slain after he had established a pact.
Viṣṇu, however, is a teacher of deceit, a fraud, one who makes false oaths;
he assumes various forms at will, bestows strength, and is a scholar of hypocrisy. (36)

"O sons of Danu, I shall certainly not fall under the power of him by whom Hiraṇyākṣa was struck down after he had assumed the form of a boar, nor of that Nṛsiṃha by whom Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain. (37)
I do not place trust in the gods at any time or in any place whatsoever.
"What can Viṣṇu do to me, or even the more powerful Indra?
Nor even Rudra is capable of countering me on the field of battle. (39)
"I shall seize the triple heaven after conquering Indra, Varuṇa, and Yama, as well as Kubera and Agni, and having defeated both the Moon and the Sun. (40)
"Today we shall all become partakers of the sacrificial portions and drinkers of Soma;
and having conquered the host of gods, I shall sport with the Dānavas. (41)
"O Dānavas, by virtue of this boon, I have no fear of the gods;
nor is there death for me from men; and what can a woman do to me? (42)
And let swift messengers, having summoned the most excellent Dānavas from the mountains of Pātāla, appoint them as commanders of my army. 43.
"Alone, I am capable of conquering all the lords of the gods;
having summoned you for the sake of glory, I shall lead you to the assembly of the immortals. (44)
"I shall indeed strike the gods with my two horns and my two hooves;
by the power of the boon granted to me, I have no fear of the gods. (45)
"I am invincible by the hosts of gods, asuras, and likewise by humans;
therefore, prepare yourselves today for the conquest of the world of the gods."
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter four.
"Having conquered the abode of the gods, I shall sport in the Nandana grove, wearing garlands of Mandāra flowers and accompanied by celestial women. (47)
Sprinkled with the milk of the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhenu and gladdened by the drinking of nectar, they were accompanied by the songs, dances, and graceful movements of gods and gandharvas. ||48||
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Ghṛtācī, Tilottamā, Pramadvarā, Mahāsenā, Miśrakeśī, and Madotkaṭā. (49)
Vipracitti and the others, who are experts in dance and song,
will delight you all with various kinds of intoxicating drinks.
"Let everyone be ready today; let the journey to heaven be pleasing, having performed the most excellent auspicious rites for the sake of battle with the gods. (51)
And for the sake of protecting everyone, having summoned the best of sages, Bhārgava, and having honored and established him as the supreme preceptor in the sacrifice, [he installed him]. (52)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus instructed the lords of the Daityas, O King, the sinful Mahiṣa then departed quickly for his own abode, filled with joy.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Mobilization of the Daitya Army," in the fourth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Vyāsa said: After the messenger had departed, the lord of the gods (Indra) then summoned the deities.
He spoke these words to Yama, Vāyu, Dhanādhyakṣa, Varuṇa, and Agni. ||1||
The lord of the Daityas named Mahiṣa, the son of Raṃbha, was possessed of great strength;
intoxicated by the pride and arrogance of having received boons, he was expert in a hundred forms of illusion.
"O gods, a messenger sent by that greedy man who desires heaven has arrived today; he spoke these words to me. (3)
"O Śakra, abandon the abode of the gods; go wherever you wish, O Vāsava, or else perform service to the high-souled Daitya Mahiṣa. || 4 ||
That compassionate lord of the Dānavas will provide you with a means;
he never becomes angry with those who have become his servants.
Otherwise, O Lord of Gods, prepare the army yourself for battle;
once I have departed, that lord of the Daityas will quickly approach.
Having spoken thus, that messenger of the evil-minded Dānava departed.
"O best of gods, consider what must be done next. (7)
O gods, even a weak enemy must not be neglected by one who is powerful,
especially one who is constantly industrious, strong, and arrogant of his might.
One must indeed exert effort according to one's intellect and according to one's strength;
for victory or defeat is surely dependent upon destiny.
There is no alliance here; an alliance with the wicked is useless. In every matter, the virtuous should deliberate again and again.
Furthermore, one must not embark upon a journey now in such haste.
The spectators and those to be entertained should be swift-moving and easy to enter. || 11 ||

Perceptive of gestures, free from attachment, devoid of desire, and truthful in speech, they reported the enemy's mobilization, their departure, and the actual strength of their forces exactly as they were. (12)
Having ascertained the identities of the heroes, let them proceed with haste, once they have understood the strength and weakness of that lord of the Daityas and his army. 13.
"Therefore, I shall quickly prepare for departure or the consolidation of the fort.
Indeed, a task must always be performed by a wise person after due deliberation;
an action undertaken impulsively will result in suffering in every respect. (14)
Therefore, the wise should always act with deliberation so as to bring about happiness;
in this matter, it is not right to employ a policy of division among the Dānavas under any circumstances.
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the fifth book, chapter four:
"Therefore, let spies indeed go forth with one-pointed minds for this task."
Having understood their strengths and weaknesses, and having subsequently deliberated upon the proper policy, || 16 ||
Those who know the rules should carry out the duties properly toward those intent on their tasks;
otherwise, a duty performed contrary to the rule yields a contrary result. || 17 ||
"In every respect, that would surely be like an unknown medicine.
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus, all of them [sought] one who understood how to carry out the mission.
The king, the lord of the gods, dispatched a messenger to ascertain the facts;
the messenger, having gone swiftly and approached the sovereign of the gods, [reported]. (19)
Then he reported the entire strength and weakness of his army;
having learned of that force and the exertion [of the enemy], Turāṣāṭ was greatly amazed.
Having quickly summoned his domestic priest, the lord of the thirty gods urged the gods forward and, being the best among those who know mantras, performed the ritual recitation.
He spoke to the best of the Aṅgirasas as he sat upon an excellent seat.
Indra said:
"O O Teacher of the Gods, O learned one, tell us what must be done."
"You are omniscient; when this task has arisen, you are our refuge today.
There is a Dānava named Mahiṣa, possessed of great heroism and filled with pride. (23)
"Desirous of battle, he approaches, surrounded by many dānavas;
now, you who are skilled in mantras must take countermeasures there. (24)
"Among them, you, O Śukra, are my remover of obstacles, being well-restrained.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, Bṛhaspati spoke to Turāsāha (Indra).
Having mentally resolved upon his desire, being intent on accomplishing his task, the Guru said: "Be composed, O Lord of the Gods; take courage, O noble one. (26)
When calamity has arisen, one must certainly not abandon fortitude immediately;
for victory and defeat, O Lord of the Gods, are always dependent upon destiny.
Therefore, O Śatakratu, one who possesses intelligence should always remain firm by relying upon fortitude; for even while knowing it, that which is destined to happen will surely come to pass.
One must exert effort in every way according to one's own human capacity;
for even the sages are always devoted solely to effort for the sake of liberation. (29)
Knowing that [the fruits of action] are dependent on destiny, those devoted to yoga and meditation should therefore always exert effort as prescribed for the destruction of suffering. (30)
Whether there be happiness or not, what lamentation can there be regarding destiny?
Without human effort, one might never attain success. (31)
Just as one might feel at ease with a blind man or a lame man, so too one may feel complacent if success does not arise even when human effort has been exerted. (32)
In that regard, there is no blame for him when the embodied being is subject to fate;
for the accomplishment of the task depends neither on the army, nor on counsel, nor on deliberation.
"Neither in the chariot nor in the weapon, O Lord of Asuras, is there surely any [certainty];
for it is under the sway of destiny that the strong encounters suffering while the weak enjoys happiness. (34)
The intelligent man sleeps while hungry, whereas the witless man may possess enjoyments;
the coward achieves victory, while the hero suffers defeat. (35)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book (Pañcama-skandha), chapter five.
Since this worldly existence is dependent on destiny, what lamentation can there truly be?
O Lord of the Gods, one should certainly apply oneself to effort; yet that which is destined to be must come to pass. (36)
In that regard, one should not discriminate between what gives pain and what gives pleasure;
rather, in suffering one should see those who suffer more, and in happiness one should see those who are happier. (37)
One should not surrender oneself to joy and sorrow as if they were two enemies; rather, the wise should understand that steadfastness alone must be maintained when joy and sorrow arise. (38)
The kind of suffering that arises from a lack of fortitude does not exist when there is fortitude; indeed, the capacity for endurance during times of both pleasure and pain is difficult to find. (39)
Where, through the certainty of awakened intellect, neither joy nor sorrow arises, one realizes:
"What is suffering? Whose is the suffering? I am eternally devoid of qualities and immutable."
I am beyond the twenty-four [tattvas]; what suffering or pleasure can there be for me?
Hunger and thirst belong to the vital breath (prāṇa), while grief and fainting belong to the mind (manas). (41)
Śiva is free from the six afflictions of the body, which are old age and death;
grief and delusion are attributes of the body—what concern is there for me in this? (42)
I am not the body, nor am I its possessor;
I am distinct from the seven, the one, the sixteen, and so forth, and I am eternally blissful.
"I am neither nature nor its transformation; what sorrow can there be for me forever?
Thinking thus, O Lord of the Gods, remain free from the sense of "mine" in your mind. (44)
O Śatakratu, this is the first means for the destruction of your suffering:
possessiveness is the supreme suffering, while freedom from possessiveness is the supreme happiness. (45)
O Lord of Śacī, there is no state of happiness greater than contentment;
or rather, if one lacks the knowledge that truly destroys the sense of "mine. (46)
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, detachment must be practiced regarding that which is destined to be;
for it is said that the destruction of prārabdha-karmas is not observed through mere enjoyment.
O best of beings, whatever is destined to happen will surely come to pass; there is no anxiety regarding pleasure or pain, whether through all the gods, through allies, or through your own intellect.
O noble one, happiness leads to the exhaustion of merit, while suffering leads to the exhaustion of evil;
therefore, the wise should in every way rejoice at the exhaustion of happiness. (49)
Alternatively, O Great King, exert yourself today according to the rules by means of mantras; when effort has been made, that which is destined to happen will come to pass.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this, the thousand-eyed one spoke again to Bṛhaspati.
I shall indeed undertake preparations for battle for the destruction of the enemy of horses.
Without exertion, there is neither kingdom, nor happiness, nor indeed fame;
the timid do not praise one who lacks effort, nor do those who possess it.

Knowledge is the ornament of ascetics, while contentment is indeed the ornament of the twice-born; for those desiring prosperity, industriousness and the destruction of enemies are their ornaments. (3)
O best of sages, just as the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, Namuci, and Bala were slain by effort,
so shall I slay this Mahiṣa.
O Lord, you are my strength; you are my supreme weapon, the thunderbolt.
You are truly the great Hari, as well as the imperishable Lord of Umā.
"O virtuous one, recite for me the mantras that destroy demons; O giver of honor, today I shall make an effort to station my army and confront Mahiṣa."
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by the King of the Vedas, Vācaspati then spoke these words with a smile to the Lord of the Gods, who was intent on battle.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 5. Bṛhaspati said:
I neither urge you forward nor do I restrain you;
for when victory is uncertain, there is no point in fighting, let alone in defeat.
O Lord of Śacī, there is no fault whatsoever in this matter of what must come to pass;
whether it be happiness or suffering, it shall occur as it has been ordained.
O Vāsava, you indeed know that future suffering as well as happiness which was experienced by me long ago when my wife was abducted. (10)
"O crusher of enemies, my wife has been carried off by the Moon, who acted as my friend; while staying in my own hermitage, I have encountered this sorrow that robs one of all happiness. (11)
O Lord of the Gods, I am known throughout all the worlds as being wise;
where did that wisdom of mine go when my wife was carried off by force?
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, wise men should always employ skillful means; for the accomplishment of one's purpose is always certainly dependent upon destiny.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those truthful words of his preceptor, the Lord of Śacī went for refuge to Brahmā, and after bowing down, he spoke these words. (14)
O Grandfather, Lord of the Gods, the demon named Mahiṣa, desiring to seize my heaven, is making a great effort with his forces. (15)
And all the other Dānavas, possessing great heroism and skilled in battle, having assembled with that army, stood there desiring to fight. || 16 ||
Therefore, being terrified, I have come here into your presence;
you are omniscient and possessed of great wisdom, so you ought to grant me your assistance. (17)
Brahmā said:
"Let us all go today to Kailāsa with haste,
placing Śaṅkara and Viṣṇu, the best among the strong, at our head."
Then, having assembled and deliberated upon a plan, and having determined the proper place and time, war must be waged by all the hosts of gods together.
A man who acts with rashness, failing to discern strength and weakness and abandoning discrimination, meets with downfall. (20)
Vyāsa said: Having heard that, the thousand-eyed one departed from Kailāsa,
placing Brahmā before him and accompanied by the guardians of the worlds.
Having approached Maheśvara, Śaṅkara, he praised him with Vedic mantras;
having secured his favor, he departed toward the city of Viṣṇu.
Having praised that Lord of the Gods of gods, he spoke of his own business:
the fierce fear arising from Mahiṣa, who was arrogant due to the granting of boons.
Having heard that, Viṣṇu spoke to the gods out of fear:
"We shall wage war and slay this invincible one. (24)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus made this resolution, the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Īśvara—
mounted their respective vehicles and departed.
Brahmā was mounted upon a swan, Viṣṇu had Garuḍa as his vehicle,
Śaṅkara was mounted upon a bull, and Vṛtrahā (Indra) was seated upon an elephant.
Skanda with his peacock vehicle and Yama with his buffalo vehicle—once the gods had assembled their armies, they set forth. (27)
Just then, the arrogant army of the Daityas, led by Mahiṣa, arrived;
thereupon, a tumultuous battle took place between the armies of the gods and the Dānavas.
With arrows, swords, as well as spears, maces, and axes;
with clubs, sharp-edged spears, tridents, discs, javelins, and lances. ||29||
With mallets, javelins, and plows,
as well as other various weapons, those most cruel beings struck one another.
The Fifth Chapter in the Fifth Skandha of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
His general, Cikṣura, who was mounted upon an elephant and possessed great strength,
struck Maghavan with five of those arrows.
Turāṣāḍ, being skillful, also swiftly cut those arrows with his own arrows and struck him in the heart with a crescent-headed shaft.
Struck by the arrow, the commander-in-chief fell into a swoon atop his elephant;
then, with a blow from his thunderbolt, he struck Varuṇa on the hand.
Struck by that thunderbolt, the elephant was broken and fled toward the army.
Seeing this, the king of the Daityas became enraged and then spoke to the one named Viḍāla.
Go, O hero of mighty arms, and slay Indra who is arrogant with pride;
having struck down Varuṇa and the other supreme gods, return to my presence. (35)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the exceedingly powerful one named Viḍāla mounted a rutting elephant of Varuṇa and went to the lord of the gods.
Seeing him approaching, Vāsava, filled with rage, struck him with sharp arrows possessing a luster like that of venomous serpents. ||37||
Having swiftly cut down those arrows with his own shafts released from the bow,
he quickly struck Vāsava with fifty feathered arrows.
Then Indra also, filled with wrath, cut those arrows and struck him with sharp shafts possessing a luster like that of venomous serpents.
Having quickly cut down those arrows with his own shafts released from his bow,
he struck the elephant on its trunk with a mace.
Slain by his own hand, the Naga repeatedly uttered cries of distress;
turning back, he swiftly struck the army of Daityas, which was overcome with fear. 41.
But the Dānava, seeing that the elephant had turned back and departed from the battle,
whirled [the elephant] around in his beautiful chariot and quickly went toward the gods in the fray.

Turāṣāḍ, too, beholding him returned once more standing upon his chariot, struck him with sharp arrows possessing a luster like that of venomous serpents. He, the mighty one, also became enraged and unleashed a fierce shower of arrows;
a tumultuous battle then ensued between those two who were desirous of victory.
But Indra, seeing him so powerful, his senses agitated by anger,
placed Jayanta at his front and fought in conjunction with him.
Jayanta, however, struck that asura, who was arrogant with pride, in the middle of his chest with five sharp arrows drawn with great force.
Struck by the arrows, he fell down even from his chariot;
having drawn the chariot away, the charioteer departed from the field of battle.
When that Daitya named Viḍāla had thus departed, rendered unconscious, there arose a great sound of "Victory! and the resonance of kettledrums.
All the gods, greatly rejoiced, praised that Lord of Śacī;
the lords of the Gandharvas sang, and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
Hearing the shout of victory raised by the gods, Mahiṣa became enraged;
he dispatched right there Tāmra, the destroyer of great pride.
Tāmra, having encountered many [enemies] on the field of battle,
quickly unleashed a shower of arrows, like a cloud pouring rain upon the ocean.
Then Varuṇa, raising his noose, went forth in haste;
and Yama, mounted upon his buffalo and taking up his staff, set out.
There, a fierce battle took place between the gods and the dānavas with arrows,
swords, maces, spears, and axes.
Struck by the staff raised in Yama’s hand,
the mighty-armed Tāmra did not waver from the field of battle at that time.
Drawing his bow with great force and discharging sharp iron arrows,
Tāmra swiftly struck Indra and the other gods on that field of battle.
Those gods also [attacked] with divine arrows, whetted and sharpened on stone.
They struck down the enraged Dānavas and cried out, "Stay! Stay! ||56||
Struck by those gods, the Daitya fell into a swoon upon the field of battle;
a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the Daitya army, overcome with fear.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Defeat of the Daitya Army," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Purāṇa.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Then, while the Daitya was unconscious, Mahiṣa was filled with rage.
Having raised his heavy mace, he indeed approached the gods.
"Today I shall surely slay all these gods with my mace;
for they are all merely crows, always devoid of strength as they please. (2)
Having spoken thus, that mighty-armed one, overcome by intoxication, approached him who was mounted upon an elephant and swiftly struck him on the base of the arm with his mace.
He too, with his terrible thunderbolt, swiftly cut that mace asunder;
then, desiring to strike, he quickly advanced toward Mahiṣa.
The enemy of horses (Garuḍa), also out of anger, took up a brilliantly shining sword and approached this one of great prowess as if intending to strike him.
And between those two there occurred a battle that brought fear to the world of mortals,
performed with various weapons and causing wonder to the sages.
Then the Daitya quickly employed the Śāmbarī illusion, which causes delusion,
destroys all the worlds, and bewilders even the sages.
There, crores of buffaloes, possessing that same form and that same prowess,
all armed with weapons, were seen slaughtering the army of the gods.
Seeing that illusion created by the Daitya there, Maghavat was struck with wonder;
indeed, he became exceedingly agitated with fear at that deluding magic.
Varuṇa was also greatly terrified, as were the lord of the clouds,
Yama, Hutāśana (Fire), Sūrya, and Śītaraśmi (the Moon), all afflicted by fear.
All the gods became intent on flight, bewildered;
they exerted themselves and called to mind Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. || 11 ||
And as soon as they were remembered, the supreme gods, the lords of their respective vehicles, arrived at the sacrifice,
mounted upon swans, Garuḍas, and bulls, bearing excellent weapons and desiring to protect him.
Seeing that Mohinī, Śauri then discharged his blazing Sudarśana; by its very splendor, that illusion was brought to dissolution.
Beholding them there— the creators, sustainers, and destroyers of the world— the buffalo,
desiring to fight, seized an iron club and rushed toward them.
The great hero named Mahiṣa, as well as Senānī, Cikṣura, Ugrāsya, and Ugravīrya, all ran forth, desiring battle. ||15||
Asiloman, the three-eyed one, Bāṣkala, and Andhaka—
these and many others set forth, desiring to fight.
Equipped with armor, holding their bows, and mounted upon chariots, those men, arrogant with pride,
surrounded all the gods like wolves surrounding a fine calf.
Then the Dānavas, arrogant with pride, and the gods as well, desiring to slay one another, unleashed showers of arrows and discuses. || 18 ||
Having approached Hari, Saṃghaka released five arrows whetted on stone,
drawn back to his ear, possessed of great force, and smeared with poison.
Vāsudeva, the destroyer of enemies, then cut down with swift arrows those shafts before they had even reached him; he then released five more.
A battle took place between those two, Hari and the Daitya,
with arrows, swords, discuses, clubs, maces, spears, and axes.
A tumultuous battle between Maheśa and Añcaka, causing the hair to stand on end,
took place between them for a duration of fifty days.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter six.
Likewise between Indraba and Skala, and between Mahishasura and Rudra;
similarly between Yama and Trinetraka, and between Mahahanu and Dhaneśa. ||23||
The battle between Asiloman and Varuna was exceedingly terrible;
the Daitya struck Garuda, whose vehicle is Hari, with a mace.
With his limbs exhausted by the blow of the mace, he stood there sighing;
Śauri quickly comforted him with his right hand.
The Lord of Gods steadied the mighty Vainateya;
drawing his Śārṅga bow, he released many arrows.
Janārdana, desiring to slay Andhaka out of anger,
[discharged his arrows], but the Dānava also cut those shafts with his own sharp arrows.
In his wrath, Hari struck him with fifty arrows whetted on stone;
Vāsudeva, however, quickly evaded those excellent shafts.
He released the thousand-spoked Sudarśana discus with great force;
the Sudarśana, once released, was warded off from afar by his own discus.
And it whirled about, O Great King, as if to utterly confound the gods;
for the discus of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow was seen to have become fruitless.
All the gods fell into grief, while the Dānavas likewise rejoiced;
and Vāsudeva, seeing the gods overwhelmed with sorrow, acted with speed.
Grasping his mace Kaumodakī, Hari rushed toward the Dānava;
with great force, he struck that master of illusion on the head.
Struck by the mace, he fell to the ground in a deep swoon;
seeing him fallen in that manner, the enemy of the horse (Kārttikeya) became exceedingly enraged.
He approached the Lord of Ramā, terrifying him with his exceedingly loud roars;
Vāsudeva, for his part, saw him approaching, filled with wrath.
He made a fierce twanging sound from his bowstring, gladdening the gods;
the Blessed One swiftly unleashed a shower of arrows upon Mahiṣa.
He too, with a flood of arrows, cut down those shafts discharged by the son of Gaṇeśa;
O King, a battle ensued between the two that struck fear into one another.
Keśava struck him upon the head with his mace;
struck on the crown of his head by that mace, he fell to the earth in a deep swoon.
A great and most terrible cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among his army.
Having cast off his pain, that Daitya rose up again after a moment.
Taking a club to his head, he struck Madhusūdana;
hit by that club, Janārdana fell into a swoon.
Garuḍa swiftly bore that unconscious one away from the battle;
when the Lord of the World had turned back, the gods, led by Indra, [returned]. ||40||
Afflicted by great suffering, they fell into fear and cried out upon the field of battle;
seeing the gods wailing, Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident, then [acted].
Approaching the buffalo with speed, he, filled with rage, struck him; the buffalo, in turn, clearly hurled a spear at the chest of Śaṅkara.
And that evil-minded one roared, having deceived him with the trident;
yet even then, Śaṅkara felt no pain, though struck upon his chest. 43.
With eyes red with anger, he struck him with his trident upon seeing Śaṅkara closely engaged in combat with the evil-minded Mahiṣa.
At that moment, Hari regained consciousness and rose from his swoon caused by the blow;
meanwhile, Mahiṣa beheld both Hari and Śaṅkara approaching him.
Desirous of battle and possessed of great heroism, that excellent one, bearing a discus and a trident,
became filled with wrath upon seeing those two approaching him.
Then that mighty-armed one, assuming the form of a buffalo with a raised tail, went forward to face him for the sake of battle. 47.
He let out a terrifying roar, frightening even the immortals;
shaking his head, his massive body was as formidable as a fierce rain-cloud. (48)
With his two horns, he violently hurled away the mountain peaks that were exceedingly formidable.
O best of gods, having seen those two of great prowess, the Dānava—
They both rained down a terrible shower of arrows upon the Dānava;
seeing Hari and Hara thus pouring forth that rain of shafts, Hari [beheld them].
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter seven: He covered the formidable mountain peak with his tail and hurled it.
Beholding the mountain rushing toward him, the Blessed Lord, the protector of the Sātvatas, [acted].
With his discus, he swiftly struck him with arrows that were split into a hundred pieces;
struck by Hari’s discus in battle, that king of the Daityas fell into a swoon.
And in an instant he indeed rose up, assuming a human form—the most terrible Dānava, resembling a mountain, with a mace in his hand. (53)
He roared loudly at Meghanāda, terrifying even the immortals;
hearing that, the Blessed Viṣṇu blew his radiant conch, Pāñcajanya.
He swiftly filled [the air] with a harsh-sounding roar;
by that sound of the conch, the Dānavas were terrified with fear.
The gods and the sages whose wealth is asceticism became joyful. || 55 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. ||6||
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Then, seeing the Asuras dejected in mind, Mahiṣa—
Having abandoned that buffalo form, he became the king of beasts, terrifying the army of the gods with the sight of his claws.
Letting out a most terrible roar and lashing his great tail,
the lion fell upon Garuḍa, drenching him in blood with the blows of his claws;
and with a blow from his claws, he struck Viṣṇu on the arm.
Vāsudeva, too, seeing him, raised his discus with speed;
Hari, filled with wrath and desiring to slay him, quickly attained his desire.
Just as he struck that enemy with his discus with great speed,
even so did the exceedingly powerful Śṛṅgin strike Hari with his two horns.
Struck on the chest by the two horns, Vāsudeva became overwhelmed and fled with speed to his own abode.
Having seen Hari depart at his will, Śaṅkara was filled with fear;
considering him to be supreme and unslayable, he went to Mount Kailāsa.
Brahmā also fled quickly to his own abode out of fear;
and the mighty Indra, seizing his thunderbolt, stood firm like a horse.
Varuṇa stood firm, leaning upon his noose and maintaining his composure;
Yama too, taking up his staff, remained vigilant and intent on the battle.
Then the lord of the yakṣas became intent on battle according to his desire;
Pāvaka, taking up his spear, set his mind upon fighting there. (10)
The lord of the stars, Sūrya, and [Śiva], both standing together,
beheld that best of Dānavas and resolved to engage him in battle.
In the meantime, the enraged army of the Daityas advanced,
discharging nets of arrows resembling cruel serpents.
Having assumed the form of a buffalo, the king then stood there;
a tumultuous roar arose from the warriors of the gods and the dānavas. (13)
In that most terrible battle between the armies of the gods and the Dānavas, the striking of the bowstring and the clapping of hands became like the roar of clouds.
With his two horns, the immensely powerful Dānava, arrogant with pride, hurled mountains and struck down the hosts of gods.
Filled with rage, that most wonderful Mahiṣa struck the gods with kicks from his hooves as well as by whirling his tail. || 16 ||
Then the gods, along with the gandharvas, were seized by fear as they stood ready for battle;
but upon seeing Mahiṣa, Maghavan became intent on flight.
When Śakra, the lord of Śacī, had completely abandoned the combat and departed, [the gods fled].
Yama, the lord of wealth, and Pāśī—all of them went forth, overcome with fear.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter seven.
Then Mahiṣa, having achieved victory, went to his own home;
meanwhile, Indra, as he was departing, took the elephant Airāvata that had been abandoned [by Mahiṣa].
Likewise, surrounded by his own army, he quickly set his mind on going to heaven, taking with him Uccaiḥśravas, the sun, and the milch-cow Kāmadhenu.
Having gone swiftly to the abode of the gods, that Mahiṣāsura seized the sovereignty of the deities, which had been abandoned by the gods who were overcome by fear.
Then the Dānava sat down upon the beautiful throne of Indra;
he established the Dānavas in the positions of the gods.
Thus, having waged that most terrible battle for a full hundred years,
the Dānava, intoxicated with pride, reached his limit at this point.
Nirjarā had departed from Nāka, and because of that, everyone was greatly tormented;
thus they wandered for many years within the mountain caves.
Then, O King, all of them, being exhausted, went for refuge to Brahmā—the Lord of Creatures, the Master of the World, who is of the nature of passion (rajas) and possesses four faces. (25)
The lotus posture, which is frequented by the sages born of his own lineage—
such as Marīci and others who are peaceful and have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences— is the womb of the Vedas.
Terrified by fear, the Kinnaras, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Uragas, and Pannagas praised the God of gods, the Teacher of the World.
The gods said:

O Lotus-born One, destroyer of all suffering, why do you show no compassion toward us gods, who have been utterly defeated by the lord of the asuras in battle, driven from our positions, and forced to dwell in mountain caves? (28)
What hundred offenses have you committed that a father, free from greed, would abandon his sons and leave them in extreme distress?
Yet you, today, neglect the gods who are devoted to your lotus feet and the wretched Daityas who were once tormented by them.
By him the sovereignty of the immortal realm was enjoyed to the utmost; he also bestows upon Brahmins sacrificial oblations worthy of such offerings.
That evil-minded one enjoys the flower of the most excellent celestial tree, and he also enjoys that cow who is the very treasure-trove of the ocean.
What wonderful deed of yours shall we proclaim? O Lord of Gods, you know the activities of the enemies of the gods;
through your wisdom, you are the knower of all matters without exception. Therefore, O Lord, we bow at your feet. (31)

Wherever the gods have gone, that wicked-minded one of diverse conduct surely inflicts suffering upon them; having witnessed his deeds, O Lord of Gods, you are our protector—O All-pervading One, grant us well-being! 32.

Afflicted by the great fire of the forest, we do not stir; whom else but the Lord of Creatures, possessed of infinite splendor, the beloved of the gods, the primordial Creator, and the auspicious one, shall we go for refuge as our peacemaker? (33)
Having thus offered praise, all the gods bowed down to that Prajāpati;
with their palms joined in reverence, they all stood with deeply dejected faces. (34)
Seeing them thus afflicted, the Grandfather of the World then spoke in gentle words, as if generating comfort for them.
Brahmā said:
"O gods, what desire of mine shall I fulfill? This Dānava is arrogant because of the boons he has received;
he is to be slain by a woman, not by a man. What, then, should be done in this matter?"
"O gods, let us all go today to Kailāsa, the best of mountains, placing Śaṅkara—who is skilled in all matters—at our head. (37)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 7: "Then let us go to Vaikuṇṭha, where the Lord Janārdana resides."
Having assembled, let us deliberate especially upon the task of the gods.
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, for the sake of accomplishing his task, mounted a swan and,
placing the gods behind him, departed toward Kailāsa.
Meanwhile, Śiva also, having quickly perceived through meditation that the Lotus-born was approaching along with the gods, went outside his own abode.
Having seen each other, they both offered a profound salutation; and being deeply bowed down by all the gods, they both became fully satisfied. || 41 ||
Having provided separate seats for the gods, the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain sat down upon his own seat once they had all taken theirs.
Having inquired after Brahmā’s welfare, the omnipresent Lord whose banner bears the bull asked him the reason for the gods' arrival at Kailāsa.
Śiva said:
O Brahman, for what purpose have you and the gods, including Indra, come here?
O highly fortunate one, tell me truly the reason for this.
Brahmā said:
O Lord of the Gods, the inhabitants of heaven have been oppressed by Mahiṣa;
including Indra himself, they wander through mountain fastnesses, terrified with fear.
The buffalo of the sacrifice has been born, as have other enemies of the gods;
the guardians of the worlds are oppressed and have today come to you for refuge. (46)
"O Śambhu, I have brought them to your abode because of the gravity of the task;
O Lord of the Gods, now perform whatever is appropriate for the sake of the gods. (47)
"O Creator of Beings, the burden of all the gods rests upon you.
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words, Śaṅkara laughed and spoke this. 48.
With gentle speech, he addressed the Lotus-born One.
Śiva said:
"O Lord, this task was already accomplished by you alone through the granting of boons in the past. (49)
And what should be done next regarding this one who brings misfortune to the gods, who is so powerful and heroic, and who strikes fear into all the deities? (50)
What excellent woman is capable of slaying him who is so arrogant with pride?
Neither my wife nor yours is fit to go into battle against him. (51)
O highly fortunate lady, how indeed could they have fought by means of their gait alone?
For the highly fortunate Indrāṇī is certainly not skilled in combat.
What other power is there capable of slaying that sinner, who is arrogant with pride?
It is my opinion that this very day I shall go to the god Janārdana.
We shall urge him very swiftly for the sake of the gods' mission;
he is Viṣṇu, the foremost among the highly intelligent, in accomplishing all purposes.
Having praised and assembled together, they must deliberate upon the task to be performed regarding Vāsudeva; through his intellect and strategic means, he will provide the necessary resources.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Rudra, Brahmā and the other foremost of the gods,
saying "So be it," quickly approached him together with Śiva.
Seeing auspicious omens that were sealed with success and brought about the fulfillment of their purpose, they all departed toward the city of Viṣṇu on their own vehicles.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter eight.
Auspicious, calm, and fragrant winds blew, proclaiming good fortune;
and everywhere along the path, birds uttered auspicious cries.
The sky became stainless and the quarters likewise pure;
as the gods proceeded there, everything appeared as if auspicious.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Then, having swiftly reached Vaikuṇṭha, the beloved abode of Viṣṇu...
They beheld it, rich in every beauty and adorned with celestial dwellings. ||1||
It was auspicious and bliss-bestowing, endowed with lakes, ponds, and rivers, and resplendent with the warbling of swans, cranes, and ruddy geese. ||2||
With *caṃpaka*, *aśoka*, *kahlāra*, *mandāra*, and *vakula* trees; with *mallikā*, *tilaka*, *aprāta*, and *kurabaka* flowers and others. ||3||
It was endowed with divine groves, delightful with the warbling cries of cuckoos, beautified by dancing peacocks with their fanned tails, and charming with the humming of bees.
He was accompanied by his attendants, such as Sunandananda and others, who were devoted to him with fervent devotion,
and by bhaktas whose mental activity was focused on no other than Bhava.
It was joined by auspicious palaces, inlaid with jewels and adorned with gold,
which were brilliantly decorated and rose high enough to touch the clouds.
It was constantly delighted by singing deva-gandharvas, dancing throngs of apsarases,
and enchanting kinnaras with their sweet voices.
And likewise, the abode of Hari was adorned by peaceful sages who were devoted to the recitation of the Vedas and who praised Him with Vedic hymns.
Having reached the abode of Viṣṇu, they beheld the two gatekeepers of auspicious form,
Jaya and Vijaya, standing there holding golden staffs, and spoke to them.
Let even one person go between the two and announce their arrival to Brahmā,
Rudra, and the others standing at the gate, who are longing for a vision of Viṣṇu.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, Vijaya went into the presence of Viṣṇu and,
after bowing down to all the assembled gods, spoke with haste.
Vijaya said:
O God of gods, O Great King, O Beloved of Ramā, O Slayer of the enemies of the gods! O Lord, all the deities have arrived and are indeed standing at the gate.
Brahmā, Rudra, as well as Indra, Varuṇa, Pāvaka, and Yama—
the immortals, desiring a vision of you, praise you with Vedic utterances.
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of Vijaya, Viṣṇu, the Lord of Ramā,
departed quickly from his home with even greater festivity toward the gods.
Having gone there and seen the gods standing at the gate, exhausted and parched with thirst,
Hari gladdened those distressed ones with a gaze full of affection.
All those gods bowed down to Janārdana, the God of gods,
and they praised the slayer of the enemies of the gods with words established in the Vedas.
The gods said:
"O God of gods, Lord of the universe, cause of creation, preservation, and destruction; O Great King, ocean of compassion!"
Protect us who have come to you for refuge! ||17||
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter eight. Viṣṇu said:
"May all you gods enter; may you speak of your welfare.
For what purpose have you come together and gathered here upon these seats? (18)
"Why have you become so overcome with anxiety, dejected, and dejected in spirit?
Together with Brahmā and Rudra, tell me quickly what must be done. (19)
The gods said:
"O great king, we have been oppressed by Mahiṣa, a man of evil deeds, who is incurable, exceedingly wicked, sinful, and protected by a boon. (20)
He enjoys the sacrificial portions offered by the Brahmins,
while the gods wander through mountain fastnesses, overcome with fear.
O Madhusūdana, because of the boon granted by the Lord, he is difficult to conquer;
therefore, recognizing the gravity of that task, we have come to you for refuge.
"You are capable of uprooting him, O expert in the illusions of the Daityas!
O Kṛṣṇa, crusher of the Dānavas, devise a means for his destruction. (23)
Indeed, a boon was granted to him by the Creator: "You shall certainly be invulnerable to men.
What woman, then, could this young girl be who would slay such a rogue in battle? (24)
"Who among Umā, Māyā, Śacī, or Vidyā is capable of slaying this most wicked Mahiṣa, even by virtue of the power of his boon? (25)
Having reflected with your intellect upon everything that is the cause of this death,
O mountain, you who are kind to your devotees, perform the service for the gods.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, Viṣṇu spoke to them as if smiling:
"A battle was fought by us in the past, yet he did not die."
If that woman of excellent limbs were born today from the combined splendor and perfection of form of all the gods, she would surely slay him by force in battle.
"A woman fashioned from a portion of our power would indeed be capable of slaying this enemy of horses, who is arrogant and skilled in a hundred illusions. (29)
And let those seekers of splendor pray for us in such a way that, through the portions of their splendor produced by them, there may arise a mass of splendor. (30)
We all, led by Rudra, give her all our divine weapons,
including the trident and whatever others there may be.
A woman bearing all weapons and endowed with all splendor shall slay that evil-minded sinner who has violated my command. (32)
Vyāsa said:
When the Lord of Gods had spoken thus, a mass of effulgence, exceedingly unbearable, manifested of its own accord from the mouth of Brahmā. 33.
Red in color, of auspicious form, with the luster of a ruby gem;
slightly cool and likewise warm, adorned with a network of rays. (34)
It was seen by Hari and by the high-souled Hara;
O great king, those two of wide stride were filled with wonder.
Emerging from the body of Śaṅkara, there issued forth a great wonder:
intense, white as silver, difficult to behold, formidable, and vast.
It was terrifying to the Daityas and a source of wonder to the gods; it was of a formidable form, resembling a mountain, like another manifestation of the quality of darkness (tamas).
Then, from the body of Viṣṇu, there appeared another being of great splendor, dark blue in color and endowed with the quality of sattva, like a mass of radiant energy.
Then, from the body of Indra, there emerged a multiform and invincible manifestation of energy, perfectly formed and consisting of all qualities.
From the bodies of Kubera,
Yama, and Agni, as well as from that of Varuṇa, a great splendor issued forth on all sides.
And from the bodies of the other gods as well, that great splendor emerged, exceedingly radiant, becoming a mass of intense light. || 41 ||
The Eighth Chapter in the Fifth Book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Seeing him, all the gods, led by Viṣṇu, were struck with wonder;
he was a mass of splendor, most divine, like another Himalaya mountain.
While the gods were watching there, a most excellent woman, beautiful and causing wonder, was born from the mass of radiant energy. 43.
She is Mahālakṣmī, composed of the three guṇas, born from the bodies of all the gods;
she has eighteen beautiful arms, possesses three colors, and is the enchantress of the universe.
With a white face, black eyes, and sprout-like lips deeply reddened, she had copper-colored palms; beloved and adorned with divine ornaments.
The goddess, possessing eighteen arms and adorned with a thousand arms, was born from a mass of splendor for the destruction of the asuras. 46.
Janamejaya said:
O Kṛṣṇa, O God, O highly fortunate one, O omniscient best of sages,
tell me in detail the origin of that body.
Is the splendor of all of them unified as one, or does it exist separately? And are her limbs likewise composed of all that splendor? (48)
Those limbs which are produced through the division of distinct parts—such as the distinctions of mouth, nose, and eyes—are nevertheless of a single nature throughout. (49)
O Vyāsa, tell me that in detail regarding the origin of the limbs of his body;
for what limb of that deity was born from his splendor, so wondrous?
I desire to hear from the lotus of your mouth everything regarding how and by whom the weapons, ornaments, and other items were bestowed. 51.
O Brahman, I am not satiated while drinking the nectar-like essence of the life-story of Mahālakṣmī as it flows forth from the lotus of your mouth.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the king, the son of Satyavatī spoke sweet words, as if delighting the adorned monarch. (53)
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O illustrious King, I shall tell you in detail, according to my understanding, O best of the Kurus, how her body came into being. 54.
Neither Brahmā, nor Hari directly, nor Rudra,
nor even Vāsava is ever capable of describing that form according to its true nature.
How can I know the form, the nature, or the origin of the Goddess?
I say that she has arisen as a mere verbal designation (vācārambhaṇamātra). || 56 ||
She exists eternally at all times for the sake of accomplishing the purposes of the gods;
though she is of one form, she appears in manifold forms according to the gravity of the task.
Just as an actor on the stage assumes various forms, even though his own nature is of a single form, for the sake of pleasing the world. (58)
In the same way, for the sake of the work of the gods, she— though formless and devoid of qualities by her own play—
assumes many forms, both with and without attributes.
Indeed, they proclaim names according to their functions and activities;
there are also very many secondary names endowed with the meanings of verbal roots and specific qualities.
O lord of men, I shall describe her beautiful form, from which splendor arose, according to the Buddha’s teaching. (61)
And by that splendor of Śaṅkara, his lotus-face became exceedingly great, white in color and of auspicious form. 62.
By that splendor, her hair became glossy,
with curved tips, exceedingly long, cloud-colored, and captivating.
Her three eyes were born from the fiery splendor;
they were adorned with the three colors—black, red, and white.
With her two eyebrows, which were glossy, black in color, and radiant with the splendor of twilight,
the goddess’s eyes became possessed of great luster, like the two bows of Kāma.
And from the wind and the fire, the two ears were produced;
they were neither too long nor too short, like two swings for the god of love.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 9:
Her nose, resembling a sesame flower, is exceedingly beautiful.
Indeed, through the splendor of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), her complexion became truly lustrous.
O King, his teeth became even, smooth, and radiant with the splendor of Prajāpati, resembling the tips of kunda flowers and as high as mountain peaks.
Her lower lip became intensely red through the brilliance of Aruṇa,
while her upper lip likewise became beautiful through the splendor of Kārttikeya.
The eighteen arms took on the form of Viṣṇu’s splendor,
while the fingers became red in color through the splendor of the Vasus.
From gentle splendor, her pair of excellent breasts was born;
likewise, from the splendor of Indra, her waist was formed, endowed with three folds.
Then his shanks and thighs were produced from the splendor of Varuṇa;
but that broad hip was born from the splendor of the Earth.
In this way, O King, that woman of auspicious form, beautiful appearance, and most melodious voice was born, having arisen from a mass of splendor.
Seeing her, who was beautiful in all her limbs, with lovely teeth and charming eyes,
all the gods who had been oppressed by Mahiṣa attained great joy.
Viṣṇu said to all the gods: "O gods, let all auspicious ornaments and weapons be bestowed upon her right now. (75)
"Quickly producing weapons endowed with splendor from their own arms, let them all today indeed present various weapons to the Goddess. (76)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Goddess's Own Form," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu, all the gods were then greatly delighted.
And they quickly gave them ornaments, garments, and their own weapons.
And Kṣīroda gave her a divine necklace that was red, subtle, ageless, stainless, well-adorned, and pleasing.
He gave him a divine crest-jewel with a luster equal to ten million suns, as well as two bright earrings and bracelets for his arms. || 3 ||
