With his senses and mind serene, Viśvakarman gave her divine armlets and bracelets, resplendent with various jewels;
as well as anklets of beautiful sound and lovely appearance, pure and adorned with gems.
Tvaṣṭṛ gave her two beautiful feet, which resembled the sun.
Likewise, the great ocean gave her a beautiful neck-ornament and radiant jeweled rings of every kind.
Varuṇa likewise presented a garland of unfading lotuses, rich in fragrance and followed by bees, as well as the Vaijayantī garland.
Then Himavat, being well-pleased, [gave] various kinds of jewels.
And he gave him a beautiful, golden-hued lion as a vehicle.
Adorned with divine ornaments, that excellent and auspicious woman shone resplendent;
mounted upon a lion, she of beautiful form was endowed with all auspicious marks.
Viṣṇu, having produced it from his discus, gave her that wheel-weapon,
which possessed a thousand spokes, was brilliantly radiant, and was the destroyer of the heads of the enemies of the gods.
Having produced from his own trident that most excellent spear, Śaṅkara gave it to the Goddess; it was the destroyer of the enemies of the gods and the dispeller of fear.
And Varuṇa, with a gracious soul, produced from his own conch a most auspicious, resonant, and brilliantly shining conch and gave it to him. ||12||
Then Hutāśana, with a gracious soul, bestowed upon her the Śakti weapon, the Śataghnī, and the Sumanojavā, which were destroyers of the Daityas.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 9.
And Māruta gave her a quiver filled with arrows and a bow of wondrous appearance, which was difficult to draw and produced a harsh sound.
Producing a most formidable thunderbolt from his own feathers, Indra gave it to him;
and he quickly took from Airāvata a beautiful bell that produced an excellent sound. (15)
Yama gave him the staff born from the rod of Time (Kāladaṇḍa) at his will,
by which he brought about the end of all beings when their time had come.
Brahmā, filled with joy, gave her a divine water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) filled with the waters of the Gaṅgā, and Varuṇa likewise gave her his noose (pāśa).
Kāla then gave her a sword and a shield, O lord of men;
and Viśvakarman likewise gave her a sharp axe.
Dhanada, moreover, gave her a drinking vessel made of gold, filled with wine.
Varuṇa gave her a divine, celestial, and captivating lotus.
Tvaṣṭṛ, with a gracious mind, gave her the mace Kaumodakī, which resounded with the noise of a hundred bells and was the destroyer of the enemies of the gods.
Tvaṣṭṛ gave the Mother of the World missiles of many forms as well as impenetrable armor; and the Sun-god gave her his own rays.
Seeing her equipped with weapons and adorned with ornaments, those gods were filled with wonder;
they praised that auspicious goddess, the enchantress of the three worlds.
The gods said: Salutations to Śivā, the auspicious one; salutations again and again to Peace and Nourishment.
Salutations to the Blessed Goddess, to Rudrāṇī; salutations eternally.
Salutations again and again to Kālarātri, to Ambā, and to Indrāṇī;
salutations again and again to Siddhi, to Buddhi, to Vṛddhi, and to Vaiṣṇavī. ||24||
I bow to that supreme Goddess who, though situated within the earth, is not known by the earth, and who, while remaining within, governs the earth. 25.
We praise Śivā, the impeller, who, though herself unborn, abides within Māyā and is known through Māyā, yet is not [limited] by it;
she, dwelling within, impels that which impels. 26.
"O Mother, do what is auspicious; protect us who are tormented by enemies!
O Enemy of Haya (Hayāri), destroy the evil that has deluded us with its own brilliance! (27)
He was a wicked, deceitful, and terrible being, arrogant due to a boon, who deserved to be slain by a woman;
he was a bringer of suffering to all the gods, a rogue who assumed various forms. (28)
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, you alone are the refuge of all the gods;
O Goddess, protect us today from the oppressed by the Dānava; salutations be unto you! (29)
Vyāsa said: Thus praised then by the gods, the Great Goddess, the bestower of all happiness,
spoke these auspicious words preceded by a smile to them.
The Goddess said:
"O gods, cast away your fear of the dull-witted Mahiṣa;
today itself, in battle, I shall slay him who is arrogant due to his boon and utterly deluded. (31)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to the gods, the goddess laughed most melodiously;
"How strange is this world in saṃsāra, filled with wandering and delusion! (32)
Indeed, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, along with Indra, the horse-riders, and other gods,
were trembling and terrified by Mahiṣa.
O best of gods, the power of destiny is great, terrible, and difficult to conquer;
Time is the creator of sorrows and the sovereign lord of joys. 34.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 9: 271.
Even when you are capable of creation, preservation, and destruction, [if you do not act...]
Tormented by afflictions and oppressed by the buffalo, they become bewildered. ||35||
Having thus smiled, the goddess let out a loud, most terrible, and bone-chilling laugh that struck fear into the Dānavas. (36)
Upon hearing that wondrous sound, the earth trembled there;
all the mountains shook, and the powerful ocean was agitated.
Mount Meru trembled at the sound, and all the directions were filled with it;
hearing that great noise, the Dānavas were then seized with fear.
"Victory! Protect us! the gods said to her, filled with supreme joy;
but Mahiṣa, hearing that sound, became enraged, intoxicated by his own pride.
Unperturbed by the sound, he asked those Daityas, "What is this?
and commanded, "Let messengers go quickly to ascertain the source of this noise."
"By whom has this most fierce sound, which causes pain to the ears, been produced? Is it a god or even a dānava who is the maker of this noise? (41)
"Having seized that evil-minded one, let them bring him here into my presence;
I shall slay this man of wicked conduct who roars with the arrogance of pride. (42)
With my life-span exhausted and my intellect dulled, I am being led to the abode of Yama;
the gods, utterly defeated and overcome by fear, no longer roar at will. (43)
"The Asuras are not under my control; whose foolish deed is this?
Let them come to me quickly, having learned the cause of this sound. (44)
"I shall go and slay that wicked man of futile exertion.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by him, those messengers [approached] the Goddess, who was beautiful in every limb. 45.
Divine, with eighteen arms, adorned with all ornaments, endowed with all auspicious marks, bearing excellent weapons, and beautiful. ||46||
Seeing her holding a cup in her hand and repeatedly drinking the honey-wine, they became terrified with fear and departed in great alarm and apprehension. ||47||
They quickly went into the presence of Mahiṣa and told him the reason for their coming.
The messengers said:
"O Lord of the Daityas, a certain bold woman is seen there. (48)
Adorned with ornaments on every limb and graced by all kinds of jewels, she was neither human nor asura; she possessed a divine form and was captivating to the mind. 49.
Mounted upon a lion, bearing weapons, and possessing eighteen excellent arms,
that woman utters a roar and appears intoxicated with pride.
We know that she, though devoted to drinking liquor, was certainly not married;
the gods stationed in the intermediate space praise her with great joy. (51)
"Victory! Protect us! "Slay the enemy!"—thus [I cried], O Lord.
I do not know who that woman of beautiful hips is, nor whose wife she may be. (52)
"For what purpose have you come here, and what does the beautiful lady intend to do? We are not at all able to look upon her, being overwhelmed by her splendor. (53)
"Abounding in the sentiments of love, heroism, and humor, and endowed with the sentiments of wrath and wonder—having seen such a woman, you have returned without even speaking to her. (54)
"O King, what further must we do according to your command?
Mahiṣa said:
"Go, O hero, my best minister, accompanied by troops, as commanded by me. (55)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter ten.
Win over that fair-faced woman by means of conciliation and the other expedients;
if that woman does not come here even through these three methods beginning with conciliation, [then act accordingly].
"Without killing that woman of beautiful hips, bring her to my presence;
I shall joyfully make that lady with eyebrows like a swan's the chief queen. (57)
When that fawn-eyed woman approaches filled with love, act according to my desire so that there may be no interruption of our passion. (58)
"By hearing of the excellence of her form, I have been benefited today.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these elegant words of Mahiṣa, the best of ministers [replied]. (59)
Accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots, he proceeded swiftly according to his desire;
having gone a great distance and halted, he spoke to that high-minded woman.
Bowing with humility, the minister, speaking gently with sweet words, said:
"O lady of sweet speech, who are you? What is the purpose of your visit here? (61)
"O illustrious lady, my lord asks you through my mouth:
'He is indeed the conqueror of all the gods, yet he is supposedly incapable of being slain by men.'"
O fair-eyed one, that powerful lord of the Daityas, who could always assume any form at will, was made arrogant by the granting of a boon from Brahmā. (63)
"Having heard that you have arrived, beautifully attired and captivating,
the king named Mahiṣa, a ruler of the earth, desires to question me."
"Assuming a human form, he will come into your presence;
O lady of beautiful limbs, we consider it as you wish. (65)
"Come then, O fawn-eyed one, to the presence of that wise man;
otherwise, I shall bring that king, who is so devoted to you, here."
O Queen of the Gods, I shall act in such a way that your heart’s desire is fulfilled;
for he is exceedingly captivated by your voice and the hearing of your beauty.
O lady with thighs like an elephant's trunk, tell me quickly how I should act accordingly.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Devīmāhātmya of the glorious Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 9 ||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, that most excellent of women laughed.
He spoke to him, O great king, with a voice as deep as a thundercloud.
The Goddess said: "O best of ministers, know me indeed as the mother of the gods;
I am renowned as Mahālakṣmī, the destroyer of all the Daityas. (2)
I was requested by all the gods for the sake of slaying Mahiṣa— by Indra,
who was oppressed by his enemies, and by those who had been excluded from their shares of the sacrifice.
Therefore, O best of ministers, I have come here today alone, without an army, having made an effort to slay him.
O sinless one, because you have welcomed me with respect, preceded by conciliation, and addressed me with sweet words, I am pleased with you. (5)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter ten. 203.
"I shall surely release you by piercing you with the arrow of Time, which is like the fire of universal destruction;
indeed, who would not find pleasure in the deception of sweetness? (6)
"Go and speak these words of mine to that wicked buffalo:
'If you have any desire for life, go now to the netherworld.'"
Otherwise, I shall slay you, O wicked one who has committed an offense, upon the field of battle;
with your body mangled by my arrows, you will go to the abode of Yama.
"Knowing this compassion of mine, depart quickly!
O fool, once you are slain, the gods will swiftly attain heaven. (9)
Therefore, O dull-witted one, go alone, abandoning this earth with its oceans,
and dive into the netherworld before my arrows fall upon you.
O Asura, if there is a desire for battle in your mind, then come quickly;
I shall send all you heroes of great strength to the abode of Yama.
"O great fool, in age after age, countless beings like you have indeed been slain;
likewise, I shall surely slay you on the field of battle.
Make your weapons effective, otherwise your labor in wielding them is in vain."
Therefore, being tormented by desire, fight with me in battle.
Do not act thus, O evil-minded one, for I possess a boon from Brahmā;
you fools, though I am not to be slain, have oppressed the best of the gods.
"Your word must be carried out; therefore, having assumed this incomparable female form, I have come to you to slay the truth-killer who has committed an offense. (15)
"Go as you please, O fool, even to the netherworld (pātāla) inhabited by serpents, having abandoned the abode of the Brahmins today, since you still have a desire for life. (16)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by the goddess, that best of ministers, endowed with strength,
listened to her words filled with reason and replied.
"O Queen, you speak words like a common woman; you are intoxicated with pride.
Where is he? Where are you? How can this battle even be conceived? This is truly impossible! (18)
Moreover, she is alone, young, having just begun her youth, and tender;
he is a buffalo of massive body—truly, this encounter is difficult to conceive. (49)
His army was of many kinds, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots; it was joined by throngs of foot soldiers and shone with various banners.
What effort is required for a king of elephants to crush a mālatī flower? Or what effort, O fair-thighed one, is required for you to slay Mahiṣa in battle? (21)
If I were to speak even a very slight harsh word to you, it would indeed be contrary to the erotic sentiment; for I fear the disruption of the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
"The king, the enemy of the gods, is devoted to you;
therefore, I must speak words of conciliation accompanied by an offer of gifts. (23)
If not, I shall this very day strike you with an arrow—you who are skilled in false pride and arrogant regarding your beauty and youth—were I a speaker of falsehood. (24)
"My lord has been captivated upon hearing of your form, which transcends the world;
therefore, for the sake of his pleasure, you must grant the beloved desire that I shall speak to you. (29)
The kingdom is yours, all the people are your servants, and Mahiṣa is indeed your slave;
cast aside this anger that brings death, O large-eyed one, and assume a favorable disposition.
O beautiful lady, with a heart full of devotion I fall at your feet;
O lady of pure smiles, quickly become the chief queen of the great king. (27)
Through the possession of the earth, you shall obtain the entire, unblemished sovereignty of the three worlds and all the happiness born of worldly existence. (28)
The Goddess said:
Listen, O minister, I shall declare the supreme essence of words, having reflected upon wisdom according to the path seen in the scriptures. (25)
I have indeed come to know through my intellect that you are the chief among buffaloes; from your speech just now, it is clear that your nature is that of a beast.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 10.
How can he whose minister is such as you be considered wise?
Indeed, this union of two such like natures was surely brought about by Fate. (31)
"As for what was said—that you are of female nature—consider that, O fool!
I am not a man; I became a woman while wearing female attire. (32)
Since death occurred previously for the woman just as it did for you, her lord,
I consider him to be exceedingly foolish and not the most skilled in the sentiment of heroism.
The death of the beloved woman, which brings joy to the impotent and sorrow to the brave,
was requested by that lord Mahiṣa, who possessed his own intelligence.
Therefore, having assumed the form of a woman, I have come to accomplish my purpose;
how could I fear your words, which contradict the treatises on dharma? (35)
When fate is adverse, O Lord, even a blade of grass becomes like a thunderbolt;
but if fate is favorable, then even a thunderbolt is like cotton-wool.
What is the use of armies, weapons, or elaborate fortifications?
For one whose death is imminent, what fruit is there in having an army? (37)
When this connection with a body occurs for the individual soul through the conjunction of time,
then all that— happiness, suffering, and likewise death— is already inscribed.
In whatever manner death is ordained for anyone by destiny, it shall occur for him in that very way and not otherwise; such is the certainty. (39)
Just as the destruction and arising of Brahmā and the other gods are ordained by time, so too it is for you; why then should there be any deliberation regarding others? (40)
Those who are subject to death, yet become arrogant because of the granting of boons, do not consider that they will die; they are fools of dull intellect. (41)
Therefore, go quickly and speak these words to the king:
"Whatever the monarch commands must indeed be carried out by you. (42)
"Let Maghavan attain heaven; let the gods be eaters of the oblation.
You all go to Pātāla, if you wish to live! (43)
O dull-witted one, if your mind is otherwise inclined toward that evil-souled Mahīpa,
then exert yourself together with me to bring about his death.
"You think that the gods, led by Viṣṇu, were broken in battle;
however, destiny was the cause there—the boon granted by Prajāpati. (45)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the goddess, the Dānava reflected:
"What should be done? Should I fight out of fear, or should I go toward the king? (46)
"I have been commanded here for the sake of marriage by the king who is indeed overcome by desire;
how then could I go into the presence of the monarch having made it unpleasant? (47)
This is the correct understanding: that I shall go without delay;
I shall inform the king exactly as I came, so as I go. (48)
Furthermore, that king, the best among the wise, will deliberate with his skillful ministers and then act as the authority regarding what must be done. 49.
"I must not engage in battle with her impulsively;
for whether there be victory or defeat, it would be unpleasant for the king. (50)
"If Sundarī should kill me, or if I should kill her again, by whatever means possible, that king will surely be provoked to anger. (51)
Therefore, having gone there myself, I shall inform that king so that he may do as the Queen has commanded today, according to his own inclination.
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus, the wise Asātyaka went into the presence of the king;
having prostrated before him, he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence. (50)
The minister said:
"O King, the goddess of beautiful form is seated upon a lion;
she has eighteen arms, is lovely, and is supreme, bearing excellent weapons. (54)
I said to her, "O great king, O beautiful woman, enjoy Mahiṣa;
become the queen of the king, the beloved of the lord of the three worlds. (55)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 11:
"You alone shall be his principal queen; of this there is no doubt."
He will become your obedient servant and will remain under your control. || 56 ||
"O fair-faced one, having enjoyed the sovereignty of the three worlds for a long time, and having obtained Mahiṣa as your husband, become the most fortunate among women. (57)

Having heard these words of mine, that large-eyed woman, deluded by the onset of passion and pride, spoke these words to me with a smile: Thus, having heard my speech, she, infatuated by the possession of pride, addressed me with this word preceded by a smile. (58)
"Born from the womb of a buffalo, the lowest among animals, I shall offer this as a sacrifice to the Goddess out of a desire for the welfare of the gods. (59)
"What deluded woman in this world would indeed choose a buffalo as her husband? O dull-witted one, why would someone like me resort to the state of a beast in this world? (60)
The female buffalo makes the male buffalo her lord, possessing horns and joined with him even as she cries out; indeed, I am not such a deceitful woman as she.
"I shall wage war in battle and slay you, the enemy of the gods;
or go to the netherworld, O wicked one, if you have any desire for life. (62)
"O King, having been addressed with such harsh words out of intoxication, I have returned here after reflecting upon them again and again. (63)
Having perceived the destruction of my purpose, I did not engage in battle;
for without your command, how could I undertake such a futile effort? (64)
O King, that beautiful woman remains utterly intoxicated by her own power;
I do not know what destiny awaits, nor what will come to pass.
In this matter, you alone are our authority; the counsel is exceedingly difficult to fathom.
Whether battle or flight is better, I know not for certain. (66)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, Mahiṣa, overwhelmed by intoxication, [spoke].
Having summoned the elder ministers, the king spoke these words.
"You are skilled in this task and discerning in means; speak with confidence regarding what must be done through conciliation and the other methods, without delay. (2)
"Has this illusion, fashioned by the gods like that of Śambara, arrived?
Tell me, what among the means such as conciliation (sāma) should be employed by me here? || 3 ||
The ministers said: "O best of kings, one should always speak the truth and that which is pleasant;
indeed, wise men, having deliberated, should certainly act only for what is beneficial."
O King, truth should be both beneficial and exceedingly pleasing;
for just as armor in this world is unpleasant to men, it is nonetheless the destroyer of disease.
O Lord of the Earth, one who hears and reflects upon the truth is rare;
indeed, while speakers are many, one who speaks [the truth] is difficult to find.
O King, how can we speak in this matter? For in this profound inquiry, who in the three worlds knows what is auspicious or even what is inauspicious? (7)
The king said:
"Let each speak separately according to his own inclination; having heard what the disposition of each is like, I shall reflect upon it."
Having ascertained the opinion of many and having deliberated upon it again and again,
one who is skilled in discerning what ought to be done should indeed perform that which is most beneficial.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the exceedingly powerful Virūpākṣa quickly spoke these words, pleasing the lord of the earth.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 11.
Virūpākṣa said:
"O King, this wretched woman speaks on my behalf;
you should understand that these words are merely intended to terrify you. (11)
Who would be afraid of the words of women— whether harshly spoken, uttered in the madness of battle, untruthful, or reckless— knowing them to be the natural behavior of females?
O King, having conquered the three worlds today out of fear for his beloved,
even in this state of wretchedness, a hero will surely incur infamy throughout the world.
Therefore, O Great King, I shall go alone to do battle against Caṇḍikā; I will slay her, so be fearless now.
Surrounded by my army, I shall go there and surely destroy that wicked-minded Caṇḍikā of fierce prowess with various weapons and missiles. (15)
"Having bound her with snares made of serpents, I shall lead her to your presence;
she shall always remain under your control. Behold, O King, my power! (16)
Vyāsa said: Having heard the words of Virūpākṣa, Durdhara spoke these words:
"O King, the speech spoken by the wise Virūpākṣa is true. (17)
My words, too, should be heard with faith by you, who are wise;
for that fair-toothed woman appears to be afflicted by passion, even by inference. (18)
Granted, such a heroine may indeed be proud of her beauty;
yet, having struck terror into you, O best of boars, she desires to bring you under her control. (19)
This is indeed the *hāva* (coquettish gesture) of proud women; he who knows it is the best among those who understand aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
This is the *vakrokti* (indirect speech) of a loving woman, which is entirely devoted to her beloved. (20)
Or perhaps some man, an expert in the science of love, might say:
"I shall indeed slay you in the forefront of battle," just as Bāṇa is said to have done. (21)
This statement, which contains a reason within itself, should be understood by those most skilled in logic:
it is well known that for proud women, side-long glances are indeed their arrows. (22)
O King, having already offered this handful of flowers and these indirect words, what power do other arrows have to strike you? (23)
Such a power does not exist even among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others, as was said by you with your eyes and words: "O fool, I shall kill the king. (24)
"Indeed, that which was understood perversely by you, the one who knows no flavor [of dharma], I shall cause you, my husband, to fall upon a bed made of battle. (25)
That speech she uttered, "I shall deprive him of his life," should indeed be understood as a playful utterance of perverse intent. (26)
"Vīya" is said to mean "vital breaths," and without that [breath], it is not otherwise.
O King, by means of this sentence with its suggested meaning (vyaṅgya), the excellent woman chooses him. 27.
"Everything should be understood through investigation by one who is expert in the texts on rasa; having realized this, O Great King, that which is endowed with rasa must be performed. (28)
O King, in her case there are only two means—conciliation and bribery—and no other;
for even when she is angry or arrogant, a proud woman can be brought under control. (29)
With such sweet words as these, I shall bring her into your presence. What need is there for much talk, O King? She must be made subject to your will.
"Having gone [there], I shall now always serve you like a maidservant.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words in this manner, Tāmra, who was discerning of the truth, [acted accordingly]. ||31||
He spoke these words, O King: "Listen to what I have said—reasoned, consistent with dharma, delightful, and endowed with novelty. (32)
"O giver of honor, this young woman is not afflicted by passion, nor is she lacking in devotion; she is discerning, and no words of reproach were ever spoken by her. (33)
It is a marvel here, O mighty-armed one, that this single woman, solitary, without support, and of wondrous form, approaches so captivatingly. (34)
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 11: "A woman with eighteen arms has never been heard of, nor has she ever been seen."
"O King, no one in the three worlds possesses such auspicious prowess;
even all those powerful weapons have been taken up [by others].
I consider all this to be contrary to the natural order, brought about by Time. (35-36)
"Indeed, I have seen evil omens in dreams during the night; by this I know for certain that a great slaughter has arrived. (37)
If a woman wearing black garments is seen weeping in the courtyard of one's house even in a dream at the time of dawn, its adverse consequence must be contemplated.
Deformed birds shrieked "roru" in every house throughout the night;
O King, various portents manifested in every single home.
Therefore, I know for certain that there must be some underlying cause why this young woman, having made her resolve, seeks you for battle.
She is neither a human, nor a Gandharva, nor likewise an Asura.
O Lord, this which has been created must be understood as the delusive power (māyā) that causes bewilderment, O All-pervading One.
"You must not yield to cowardice; this is my firm resolve. War must be waged by all means; whatever is destined to happen will happen. (42)
Who knows what the work of destiny shall be, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious?
Therefore, O wise one, you should remain firm, relying upon fortitude with your intellect. (43)
O Lord of Men, the life and death of human beings are dependent upon destiny;
no one at all in the three worlds is capable of making them otherwise. (44)
Mahiṣa said:
"Go, O illustrious Tāmra, resolved for battle;
having conquered her by righteous means, bring back that proud woman of beautiful form. (45)
If that woman of yours does not come under control in battle, she must be slain; otherwise, she should by all means be honored with great effort. (46)
"You are a hero, O Omniscient One, and an expert in the science of love;
by whatever means possible, that woman of excellent complexion must be won over. (47)
Hastening there, O hero of mighty arms, surrounded by a great army, you must ascertain the situation after deliberating upon it again and again. (48)
For what purpose has she come? That reason must indeed be known:
Is it out of desire, or from love, or is this an illusion? And whose is she? || 49 ||
Having first made a firm determination regarding that which one intends to do, one should know what is to be accomplished;
thereafter, battle should be waged as is appropriate and according to one's strength. (50)
You must not display cowardice, nor should you be merciless;
indeed, you should act exactly according to her state of mind. (51)
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of his, Tāmra, falling under the power of time,
departed accompanied by his army after bowing down to King Mahiṣa.
As he was traveling on the road, that evil-minded man, seeing dreadful omens that revealed the path of Yama, was struck with both wonder and fear.
Having gone there and beheld that goddess seated upon a lion, being praised by all the gods and adorned with all her weapons; ||54||
Standing there, bowed down with humility and resorting to a conciliatory disposition, he spoke these words to her in a sweet voice with a humble manner. (55)
O Goddess, Śṛṅgin, the lord of the Daityas, infatuated by your beauty and virtues,
and Mahiṣa as well, desire to take your hand in marriage.
"O large-eyed one, conceive a desire for that husband who is invincible even to the gods;
having obtained him, O lady of delicate limbs, sport in the wonderful Nandana grove. (57)
Having obtained a body beautiful in all its limbs, which is the abode of all happiness,
it is the established principle that pleasure should be embraced with one's whole being and suffering should be abandoned.
O lady with thighs like an elephant’s trunk, for what purpose have you taken up these weapons?
Your hands, as delicate as lotuses, are fit only for flowers and balls. (59)
While the bow of her eyebrows exists, what need is there for a [physical] bow?
Since her side-long glances are her arrows, what is the use of useless shafts? (60)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twelve.
A wise person should not engage in war, which brings suffering in saṃsāra;
yet those attached to greed wage war against one another. (61)
One should not even fight with flowers, much less with sharpened arrows;
for whom would the piercing of one's own limbs bring joy? (62)
Therefore, O slender-limbed one, you too ought to show favor;
accept my husband as your lord, he who is worshipped by gods and dānavas.
He will fulfill all your desires and your heart's wish here;
you shall become the king’s chief queen in every respect—of this there is no doubt. (64)
"O Goddess, follow my word and you shall attain supreme happiness;
there is no doubt that you will meet with suffering in battle, yet victory is certain. (65)
O lady of excellent complexion, you know the principles of statecraft exactly as they are;
enjoy the full happiness of sovereignty for tens of thousands upon tens of thousands of years.
"A beloved son shall be born to you, and he too shall become a king;
having sported in his youth, you will attain happiness in old age. (67)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 1 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of Tāmra, the Mother of the Universe—
Laughing, she spoke to him with a voice as deep as a thundercloud. ||1||
The Goddess said:
"Go, Tāmra, and speak to that husband of yours, who is slow-witted and desirous of death—the buffalo-demon who is afflicted by excessive lust, deluded, and devoid of wisdom. (2)
Just as your mother is a mature buffalo that eats grass, I am not like her; I am Śṛṅgavatī, with a long tail, a large belly, and horns. ||3||
I do not desire the Lord of Gods, nor Viṣṇu, nor Śaṅkara;
nor the Giver of Wealth, nor Varuṇa, nor Brahmā, nor Pāvaka.
"Setting aside these hosts of gods, for what reason indeed would I choose an animal in vain? What reproach might befall me? (5)
I am not a woman choosing her own husband; my husband is the Lord, the doer of all, the witness of all, indeed the non-doer, free from desire, and steadfast.
Devoid of qualities, free from the sense of "mine," infinite, without support, and without refuge;
all-pervading, omnipresent, the witness, the full one, whose intention is full—He is Śiva. ||7||
He who dwells in all abodes, who is patient, peaceful, all-seeing, and the creator of all beings—having abandoned that [Lord], how could I venture to serve this dull-witted buffalo? (8)
"Once I have awakened, I shall, at my pleasure, make those who fight my vehicle;
or indeed, I shall make human beings my water-carriers. (9)
"O wicked one, if you have a desire to live, go quickly to the netherworld along with all the dānavas; otherwise, I shall slay you in battle."
Granted that in this world, a union between two equals may bring happiness;
otherwise, if it is brought about through ignorance, it will result only in suffering. (11)
"You are a fool that you say, 'O beautiful woman, accept me as your husband.
Where am I, and where is a horned buffalo? What kind of relationship could there possibly be between the two of us?"
"Go, or fight as you wish; I shall slay you along with your kinsmen.
Otherwise, abandon your share of the sacrifice and the world of the gods, and be happy. (13)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess then let out a most wonderful roar;
she made a sound like that at the end of an eon, which struck terror into the Daityas.
The earth trembled and the mountains shook at that sound;
and from the roar of the thundering, the fetuses of the Daityas' wives were cast out.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twelve:
Having heard that sound, Tāmra, his mind then terrified with fear, [acted].
Then, having fled from there, he went into the presence of Mahiṣa.
O King, those Daityas who were in his city also reached the funeral pyre,
their ears deafened and intent on flight.
Then, with his mane bristling, the lion also roared fiercely out of anger;
by that roar, the Daityas clearly fell into a state of fear.
Seeing them assembled together, even the enemy of horses (Kārttikeya) was bewildered;
he deliberated with his ministers as to what should be done hereafter:
"Should the siege of the fortress continue, or should we go out once more for battle?"
O best of Dānavas, it would be better for you to flee. ||20||
Intelligent, invincible, and all proficient in the scriptures—
a counsel must indeed be kept strictly secret for the successful accomplishment of the task.
The kingdom is traditionally held to be rooted in counsel; therefore, it must be thoroughly protected by wise ministers who always observe virtuous conduct. (22)
If there is a disclosure of the mantra, there will be the destruction of both the kingdom and the king;
therefore, one who desires prosperity must keep it secret for fear of such disclosure. 23.
Therefore, in this matter, the ministers should speak words that are reasoned and beneficial, having deliberated upon a decision according to policy in accordance with the time and place. (24)
This woman who has arrived here, powerful and fashioned by the gods, is alone and without support; let her reason be investigated. 25.
This fool seeks war; what could be more astonishing than this?
Who in the three worlds knows whether what is beneficial here is actually its opposite? (26)
Victory does not belong to the many, nor is there defeat for the one;
victory and defeat in battle should always be known as dependent upon destiny. (27)
Those who propound the doctrine of means (upāyavādins) ask: "O Lord, by whom has God been seen? That which the wise call 'the unseen' (adṛṣṭa) [is what we mean]. (28)
Even if that [divinity] exists, what proof is there for it other than the reliance on the hopes of the faint-hearted?
For nowhere is a god observed to be of any avail to capable men. (29)

For exertion and destiny—these two are considered the factors for the brave and the cowardly respectively; having deliberated upon everything today with the intellect, one should perform what must be done with diligence. (30)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the king, which were pregnant with reason,
the great sage named Viḍāla spoke thus to the great king with palms joined in reverence.
O King, this large-eyed woman must be investigated with great care: for what purpose has she arrived here, from where does she come, and whose wife is she? (32)
Having fully understood that death [was imminent] for the woman, the gods sent her forth with all their might; she, lotus-petal-eyed, was produced by means of their own splendor.
They too, all desiring to witness the battle, remained there in the sky concealed;
at the proper time, they will become her allies, eager for combat.
Placing a beautiful woman before them, those led by Viṣṇu will indeed slay us all; she, moreover, shall kill you in battle.
"O lord of men, I have understood this which they intend to do;
however, I possess no knowledge whatsoever regarding what is destined to happen. (36)
"O Lord, I am not able to say whether you must fight today or not; O Great King, you alone are the authority in this matter ordained by fate. (37)
"For your sake, we must die incessantly due to the gravity of our duty;
yet you must sport together with us—this is the dharma of those who live in service. (38)
O King, there is great deliberation here as to how a single woman seeks battle with us, who are accompanied by armies and proud of our strength. (39)
Durmukha said:
"O King, I truly know that victory will be ours in battle today;
one must not flee, for it causes the loss of fame among men. (40)
That which was not done even in battle by Indra and the other gods—what man indeed, having encountered a woman alone, would flee in disgrace? (41)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twelve.
Therefore, war must be waged, for there is either death or victory in battle. Whatever is destined to happen will surely come to pass; what anxiety can there be for one who sees clearly? (42)
"In this matter, there is the attainment of fame in death and likewise happiness in life;
having considered both in your mind, you must indeed engage in battle today. (43)
In flight there is loss of honor, and in battle, the exhaustion of life;
therefore, one should not indulge in vain grief over either living or dying. (44)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of Durmukha, Bāṣkala—skilled in speech—bowed down with joined palms upon the ground and addressed the king with these words. (45)
Bāikala said:
"O King, you should not feel anxious regarding this task which is disagreeable to Kāla;
I alone shall slay Caṇḍī, she of the flickering eyes. (46)

O best of kings, enthusiasm is to be cultivated as the stable emotion (sthāyibhāva) of the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa), while fear is the stable emotion of the terrifying sentiment (bhayānakarasa). 47.
Therefore, O King, casting aside fear, I shall engage in a wondrous battle;
O lord of men, I shall lead Caṇḍikā to the abode of Yama.
I do not fear Yama and the others, nor even Kubera, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Vāsava, Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, the Moon, or the Sun. 49.
If even a woman alone is thus [powerless], how much more so one who is arrogant with pride?
I shall slay her with arrows sharpened on stone.
Behold my strength of arms today; sport as you please.
You must not go away from here, even in this battle of mine.
Vyāsa said:
While Vākala, arrogant with pride, was speaking thus to the king of kings,
Durdhara bowed there to the monarch and spoke these words.
Dudhara said:
"O Mahiṣa, I shall conquer the goddess created by the gods—charming, with eighteen arms, who has arrived here for a specific purpose. (53)
"O King, this was indeed created by the gods to terrify you;
recognizing this as a mere illusion (vibhīṣikā), abandon the delusion within your mind. (54)
O King, listen to this policy of statecraft and likewise to the practice of diplomacy:
some are of the nature of sattva, some are rājasa, and others are tāmasa.
O Lord of the Dānavas, there are three kinds of ministers in the world:
the *sāttvika* ones accomplish the tasks of their master through their own powers. (56)
They perform their own duties without contradicting the master's work;
they are single-minded, devoted to dharma, and proficient in the treatises of counsel (maṃtraśāstra). || 57 ||
Those characterized by passion (rājasa) have divided minds and are always intent on their own affairs; they perform the master's work only occasionally and by chance.
Those characterized by tamas are devoted to greed and always intent on their own interests;
having destroyed the body of the master, they accomplish only their own ends. 59.
Their agreements fall apart, while others are utterly deceived;
staying at home, they point out their own vulnerabilities to those on the enemy's side. (60)
Constantly causing a division of duties and always sheathed like a sword in its scabbard, they always strike fear into their master when a conflict arises. (61)
O King, you must never place trust in them;
for by placing trust, there will surely be a loss of one's purpose and a constant betrayal of one's counsel.
What will the wicked not do when they have gained confidence, being intent on greed, dark-natured, devoted to sin, devoid of intellect, and likewise deceitful? (63)
Therefore, O best of kings, you should not worry in any way; I shall go to the front of the battle and accomplish my task.
"Having seized that woman of wicked conduct, I shall return with all haste;
behold today my strength and fortitude as I perform my master's task to the best of my ability. (65)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 12 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter thirteen. Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to those two mighty-armed Daityas, Bāṣkala and Durmukha—
who were skilled in all weapons and missiles and whose limbs were smeared with the rut of elephants— they departed.
Having gone to the battlefield, those two Dānavas, intoxicated with pride, then spoke these words to the Goddess in voices as deep as thunderclouds.
"O lady of beautiful hips, choose as your husband that high-souled Mahiṣa, by whom the gods and goddesses were conquered, the sovereign lord of all the Daityas."
Having assumed a human form endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with divine ornaments, he will indeed come to you in secret.
O lady of pure smiles, you shall obtain every desire for the sovereignty of the three worlds;
O beloved, direct your heart's supreme devotion toward Mahiṣa.
Having made the great hero your husband, you shall indeed obtain the wonderful happiness of saṃsāra, O sweet-voiced cuckoo, which is truly desired by women.
The Goddess said:
"O fool, what do you know? This woman is deluded by passion;
being of dull intellect and utterly weak, she would serve the wicked Mahiṣa."
Noble women honor him who is equal to them in lineage, conduct, and virtue, even if he excels them in beauty, cleverness, intellect, character, fortune, and other such qualities.
What woman, afflicted by desire, would resort to one in the form of a beast—
the buffalo, surely the lowest of beasts— were she not a devourer of gods?
"Go quickly to that king Mahiṣa, who is intoxicated by his own wicked pride;
speak those words to that Daitya, who possesses horns like maces. (10)
"Either go to the netherworld (pātāla) or come and engage in battle with me;
for once the combat has begun, it is certain that the thousand-eyed Indra will be free from fear. (11)
"Having killed you, I shall depart; there is no other way for me to go.
Knowing this, O evil-minded one, do as you wish. (12)
"Without first conquering me, you shall never have a place on this earth, nor in the four quarters, nor in heaven, nor in mountain caves. (13)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by her, the Daitya, his eyes agitated with anger, became a hero bearing a bow and arrows; both were desirous of battle.
Having let out a very great roar, that goddess stood there fearless;
and both of them, O bull of the Kurus, rained down a fierce shower of arrows.
The Dānava also released a torrent of arrows toward the Blessed One,
uttering an exceedingly sweet roar for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Of those two, Bāṣkala quickly came face-to-face on the field of battle,
while Durmukha remained there as a spectator, standing opposite the Goddess.
Then a terrible battle took place between those two, whose thighs had been severed,
which was terrifying to those of feeble minds due to the blows of arrows, swords, and iron clubs.
Then the Mother of the World, enraged upon seeing him intoxicated with the pride of battle,
struck him with five arrows whetted on stone and drawn back to her ear.
The Dānava also cut the goddess’s arrows with his own sharp shafts,
and struck the goddess, who was seated upon her lion, with seven more.
She too, having cut down those arrows with ten sharp and well-whetted shafts, struck him and laughed again and again. (29)
With a crescent-shaped arrow, he severed the bow;
Bāṣkala, seizing a mace, also advanced to slay the Goddess.
"Do not approach the Dānava who wields a mace and is incited by me!
Thus [commanded], Caṇḍikā struck him down to the ground with blows from her own mace.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter thirteen.
Bāṣkala fell to the ground, but after a moment he rose again;
and he too, of fierce prowess, hurled his mace at Caṇḍikā.
Seeing him approaching, the goddess, enraged, struck Bāṣkala in the chest with her trident; he fell down and died.
When Bāṣkala had fallen, the army of that evil-minded one was broken;
and the gods, stationed in the sky, cried out "Victory! with joy. || 26 ||
When that Daitya had been slain, Durmukha, endowed with great strength,
arrived at the battlefield before the Goddess, his eyes bloodshot with rage.
"Stay! Stay, O weakling! he cried again and again, while that illustrious one, clad in armor and holding his bow and arrows, remained stationed upon his chariot.
Seeing him approaching, the goddess sounded her conch and made a twanging sound from her bowstring,
thereby provoking that Dānava.
He too quickly discharged sharp arrows resembling venomous serpents;
Mahāmāyā cut them down with her own arrows and let out a roar.
O King, a tumultuous battle took place between the two of them with the blows of arrows,
spears, and maces, as well as with clubs and javelins.
Then, on the field of battle, a river carrying floods of blood was produced;
the heads that fell upon its banks then shone brilliantly.
Just as the Yamakiṃkara leaders, for the sake of crossing over,
brought taṃvī fruits, while those intent on new training brought guḍa.
Then the battlefield became exceedingly terrible and impassable,
with bodies fallen upon the ground being devoured by wolves and other beasts.
Carrion-eaters, dogs, crows, *kaṅkas*, iron-beaked birds, vultures, and hawks were devouring the bodies of the evil-minded.
(35) A foul stench arose from the corpses, and there was a tumultuous clamor of the flesh-eating birds. (36)
Then that evil-minded one, deluded by the time of suffering, became enraged;
raising his right hand auspiciously, he spoke to the gods with arrogance.
"Go away, Caṇḍī! I shall kill you, you utterly foolish woman!
Or else, O fair-thighed one, resort to the Daitya Mahiṣa, who is arrogant with pride. (38)
The Goddess said:
"O you who are destined for death, you may prattle as you please today, deluded as you are;
this very day I shall slay you, just as this Bāṣkalī was slain. (39)
"Go or stay, you fool—if death pleases you!
Having slain you, I shall surely kill this foolish son of the queen. (40)
Having heard those words of hers, Durmukha prepared for death;
he released a terrible shower of arrows toward Caṇḍikā.
She too, having swiftly cut down that shower of arrows with her own sharp shafts,
angrily struck the Dānava as Indra strikes Vṛtra with his thunderbolt.
A mutual battle then broke out between the two, exceedingly fierce, terrifying to the faint-hearted, and increasing the strength of the brave. (43)
The Goddess swiftly cut the bow held in his hand;
likewise, with five arrows, she shattered his excellent chariot.
When his chariot was broken, the mighty-armed Durmukha then took up an invincible mace and, on foot, advanced toward Caṇḍikā.
With great force, he dealt a blow with his mace upon the crest of the lion;
yet Hari, possessed of immense strength, did not waver from his place even though struck.
Seeing him standing before her with a mace in hand,
Ambikā severed his head, including its crown, with a sharp-edged sword.
When his head was severed, Durmukha fell dead upon the ground;
then the delighted gods raised a great shout of victory. 48.
When Durmukha had been slain, the immortals then praised that goddess;
standing in the sky, they showered flowers and raised shouts of victory.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 14:
The sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Kinnaras.
Seeing that Dānava slain at the forefront of the battle, they rejoiced.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 13 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Having heard that Durmukha had been slain, Mahiṣa was overwhelmed with rage.
He spoke to all the Dānavas, asking repeatedly, "What has happened? (1)
The two heroic Dānavas, Durmukha and Bāṣkala, were slain in battle by that slender woman;
let them behold this supreme marvel, the deed of the gods.
For Time is indeed the powerful agent of the constant experience of pleasure and pain for men who are dependent on others, according to their connection with merit and demerit.
"O best of Dānavas, the two have been slain; what should be done after this?
Let everyone assembled here say what is appropriate in this crisis of action."
When the exceedingly powerful Mahiṣa had spoken thus, O Indra among kings,
the great car-warrior named Cikṣura addressed the commander of the army.
"O King, I shall slay him; what anxiety is there regarding the injury of a woman?
Having said this, he was released by his own forces and departed, surrounded by chariots.
Making Tāmra, who possessed great strength, his second hand,
he filled the sky and the quarters with the great roar of his army.
Seeing him approaching, the divine and auspicious Goddess Śivā made a most wonderful sound by striking the rim of her conch shell and clashing her cymbals.
Then, at that sound, all those enemies of the gods, trembling with fear, fled while crying out, "What is this? ||1||
But seeing them intent on flight, the one named Trikṣurā, being exceedingly enraged, said: "What fear has come upon you? (10)
"This very day I shall slay with my arrows the young woman who is arrogant with pride;
O Daityas, remain here at the front of the battle, casting aside all fear. (11)
Having spoken thus, the best of the Dānavas, endowed with strength and holding a bow in his hand,
approached the Goddess in battle and spoke these words, free from distress.
"Why do you roar, O large-eyed one, terrifying other men?
I am not afraid, O lady of beautiful limbs, having heard your conduct today. (13)
O lovely-eyed one, my mind remains indifferent even after recognizing the fault in killing a woman, as well as the resulting infamy. (14)
O beautiful one, for women, battle is waged with side-long glances and graceful gestures;
it is never anywhere conducted with weapons for those like you. (15)
One should not even fight with flowers, much less with sharpened arrows; for even a petal of the *mālatī* flower causes pain to the bodies of those like you. (16)
Fie upon this birth in the human world for those who subsist by the dharma of the warrior! This cherished body, so long pampered, must now be cut asunder by sharp arrows. (17)
This dear body, nourished by oil massages, flower-fragrances, and the eating of sweet foods, must be destroyed by the arrows of others.
Having cut his body with sword-blades, a man is born as a granter of wealth;
fie on that wealth which gives pain at first—what could it possibly give happiness later? (19)
"O lady of beautiful thighs, since you desire battle like one ignorant even of yourself, what quality do you perceive in combat that makes you abandon the pleasure born of union? (20)
The falling of swords, the blows of maces, and being pierced by arrows;
at the end of life, there is the cremation rite and being dragged by the mouths of jackals. (21)
Poets and rogues have excessively praised that very thing;
the attainment of heaven for those who die in battle is merely an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). || 22 ||
Therefore go, O lady of beautiful hips, wherever your heart delights;
or else serve the lord of kings, the enemy of horses (Garuḍa), the crusher of the gods.
The Fourteenth Chapter in the Fifth Book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
To that Daitya who was speaking thus, the Mother of the World replied:
"O fool, why do you speak falsely, like a wise scholar? (24)
You do not know the science of ethics (nītiśāstra), nor likewise the science of inquiry (anvīkṣikī);
you have not served the elders, and you possess no inclination toward dharma.
Since you are devoted to the service of fools, you yourself are indeed a fool;
you do not know the duty of kings—what are you saying before me? (26)
Having slain Mahiṣa in battle and created a mire of blood,
and having erected a firm pillar of glory, I shall go as I please.
"I shall slay that evil-doing Dānava, who gives pain to the gods and is arrogant with pride; fight and remain firm! (28)
O fool, if you have a desire for life just as the buffalo does,
then let all those Dānavas go to the netherworld.
If the desire for death has arisen in your minds, then fight with haste;
I shall slay every one of you—this is my firm resolve now.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of his, the Dānava, arrogant in his strength,
released a shower of arrows like another rain from a cloud.
Then she cut his arrows with her own sharp shafts and likewise struck him with terrible arrows resembling venomous serpents.
A battle took place there between them that was filled with wonder;
then the Mother of the World struck him from his chariot with a mace.
Struck violently by the mace, that evil-minded one fell unconscious;
for about two moments he remained motionless like a mountain on the floor of his chariot.
Seeing him thus unconscious, Tāmra, the crusher of enemy forces, came to the battlefield out of impetuosity to fight against Caṇḍikā. (35)
Seeing him approaching, Caṇḍikā said with a laugh:
"Come, come, O best of Dānavas! I shall lead you to the world of Yama."
"What is the use of your arrival, you weaklings whose lives are spent?
What can a foolish buffalo do with his efforts for life within his own house? (37)
"What is the use of killing you? Even my own effort would be in vain as long as that wicked, evil-minded enemy of the gods, the sinful Mahiṣa, remains unslain. (38)
Therefore, let him go home and send Mahisha here;
let that dull-witted one see me standing exactly as I am.
Having heard those words, Tāmra,
with his bow drawn back to his ear, discharged a shower of arrows in anger toward Caṇḍikā.
The Blessed Lady Tāmrākṣī also, having drawn her bow, swiftly released arrows, desiring to slay the enemy of the gods. ||41||
The powerful one named Cikshura, having recovered from his swoon, rose up again;
seizing his bow along with an arrow, he stood before him in an instant.
Both the one named Cikṣura and Tāmraśva, who were exceedingly fierce and possessed of great strength, those two great heroes fought with the Goddess on the field of battle. (43)
Enraged, Mahāmāyā rained down a continuous stream of arrows,
making all the Dānavas have their armor pierced by her shafts.
Struck by arrows, the Asuras became bewildered with rage;
filled with fury, they hurled nets of shafts toward the Goddess. (45)
All those rākṣasas there, wounded by arrows, shone like flowering kiṃśuka trees in a forest during the springtime. ||46||
A tumultuous battle took place with Tāmra in that encounter;
the gods who stood as spectators were struck with the utmost amazement. || 47 ||
Taking up a fierce, firm iron mace made of copper, he struck the lion on the head; and he laughed and roared.
Seeing him roaring then, the goddess, filled with rage,
swiftly severed his head with a sharp-edged sword.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 15:
When his head was severed, the powerful Tāmra, though headless, remained armed with a mace.
He wandered for just a moment and then fell upon the field of battle.
Seeing the copper vessel fallen, the exceedingly powerful one named Cikshura seized his sword and rushed swiftly toward Caṇḍikā.
The Blessed Lady also, seeing that Dānava approaching with sword in hand,
swiftly struck him with five arrows in the battle.
By one [arrow] his sword was felled; by the second, his hand;
and by another, his head was severed from his neck with arrows.
Thus those two Rākṣasas, Karanidhata and Raṇadumada, were slain;
their army was quickly broken and fled in all directions with terrified minds. (54)
And all the gods, seeing those two slain in battle, were delighted;
standing in the sky, they joyfully showered flowers and raised shouts of victory.
The ṛṣis, gods, gandharvas, vetālas, siddhas, and cāraṇas cried out again and again, "Victory to the Goddess! O Ambikā! (56)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 14 ||
Then, the fifteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Having heard that those two had been slain by her, Mahiṣa was filled with amazement.
He dispatched the mighty Daityas for the purpose of slaying him.
[He saw] those led by Asiloma and Viḍāla, who were fierce in battle,
accompanied by a great army, equipped with weapons, and provided with all their attendants.
There they beheld the divine goddess seated upon a lion,
possessing eighteen arms and holding a sword and a shield.
Asiloma, having gone before her, spoke to the goddess who was intent on slaying the Daityas, smiling as it were, humble with modesty and tranquil. (4)
Asilomā said:
O Goddess, speak the truth; for what purpose have you come here, O beautiful one? And why do you slay these innocent Dānavas? (5)
Tell me the reason today, and I shall make peace with you;
[I shall give] gold, gems, jewels, and excellent vessels.
"O lady of noble limbs, take whatever you desire and depart without delay.
For what reason do you wish for battle, which only increases suffering and torment? (7)
The Great-Souled One says: "War takes away all happiness;
it strikes that exceedingly tender body with blows as fierce as those of flowers. (8)
"Why do you endure the falling of weapons? he wondered in amazement; for the fruit of wisdom is peace and the constant enjoyment of happiness. (9)
So why do you wish to engage in battle, which is a cause of suffering?
In this cycle of existence, the established rule is that pleasure is to be embraced and suffering is to be abandoned. (10)
That happiness is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being eternal and non-eternal:
the knowledge of the Self is eternal happiness, while that born of enjoyment is remembered as non-eternal. (11)

O fair-faced one, if you accept the doctrine of the Buddhists, then that [doctrine], which is characterized by destruction, must be abandoned by those who contemplate the meaning of the Vedic scriptures. (12)
Nevertheless, having attained youth, enjoy unsurpassed pleasures;
O slender-waisted one, if you have any doubt regarding the next world.
O beautiful lady, remain constantly devoted to the enjoyment of heaven upon this earth;
knowing that youth in the body is impermanent, one should perform virtuous deeds.
The wise should always avoid causing pain to others.
The pursuit of dharma, artha, and kāma should be practiced without mutual conflict. ||15||
Therefore, O auspicious one, you too should always apply your mind to dharma;
why do you slay the Daityas without cause, O Ambikā?
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter fifteen.
"Compassion is his duty, truth is proclaimed to be his body, and his life-breaths reside therein;
therefore, compassion as well as truth must always be protected by the wise.
O lady of beautiful hips, tell me the reason for your slaughter of the Dānavas."
The Goddess said:
"O mighty-armed one, you have asked why I have come here."
Therefore, O Daitya, I shall fully explain the purpose for my slaying; I always wander through all the worlds at all times. || 19 ||
She, appearing as a witness, observes the right and wrong conduct of living beings;
I have never had a desire for enjoyment, nor greed, nor enmity. (20)
I wander here in this saṃsāra for the sake of dharma, protecting the virtuous;
I always steadfastly observe this vow of mine.
The protection of the virtuous must be performed, and even those who are wicked must be slain;
the preservation of the Vedas must be accomplished through numerous incarnations.
In age after age,
I indeed assume those incarnations;
meanwhile, the wicked Mahiṣa was intent on slaying the gods.
"O Rākṣasa, having learned this, I have now arrived for the purpose of slaying him;
I shall kill that evil-doer, the enemy of the gods, who possesses great strength. (24)
"Go or stay as you wish; this truth has been spoken.
Or rather, speak to that evil-minded king, the son of the queen. (25)
"Why do you send others here? Fight yourself!
If you, O King, desire to make peace with me," (26)
Let everyone go to Pātāla at their ease, having abandoned enmity;
whatever property of the gods was seized after defeating the deities in battle [shall be returned]. (27)
"Having given that [wealth], let them go to Pātāla, where Prahlāda resides.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the goddess, Asiloman stood before her. (28)
Asiloma asked the great hero named Biḍāla with affection:
"O Biḍāla, have you heard that which was spoken by Bhavānī? (29)
"This being the case, what should be done—war or peace?
Viḍālākhya said: "The king is full of pride and has no desire for peace; moreover, he knows that death in battle is certain."
Having seen those who were slain, it impels us as well; for who indeed is capable of overstepping destiny? (30)

"Let the duty of servants here always be difficult to fulfill for those devoid of honor—servants who are intent on obeying orders and remain under control like puppets, due to the breaking of the thread [of their own will].
(1) Having gone before him, how could this harsh thing be spoken by you and by me as well? (31)"
"Let all of you go from here to the netherworld (pātāla) after giving the gods jewels and wealth;
for one should speak what is pleasant even if it be untrue, but that which is beneficial, though unpleasant, should be spoken."
"Truth, what is pleasing, and desire are our goals here; therefore, silence is established for those who are wise. (2)
"A king should not be awakened by trivial words, but rather by heroes"—such is the teaching of the treatises on statecraft.
Surely one should not go there, nor speak for his welfare with earnestness, nor even inquire after him; for once he has gone, the king will become filled with anger. 33.
Having reflected thus, one should engage in battle when life is in peril, considering the master’s duty to be supreme and death as insignificant as a blade of grass. (34)
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus, those two heroes stood intent on battle,
equipped with bows and arrows, armored, and stationed upon their chariots.
First, the one named Biḍāla released seven arrows;
Asiloman, a master of supreme weapons, stood at a distance as a spectator.
Ambikā likewise cut down those arrows as they reached her with her own shafts,
and she struck the one named Biḍāla with three stone-sharpened arrows.
Having suffered the agony of the arrow, the Daitya fell upon the field of battle;
then, rendered unconscious, the Dānava quickly died by the turn of fate. 38.
Seeing the one named Biḍāla slain in battle by a multitude of spears and arrows,
Asiloman stood with bow in hand, intent on combat.
Raising his left hand, he spoke these measured words to her:
"O Goddess, I know of the death of the evil-minded Dānavas."
Nevertheless, I, being subject to another's will, must indeed wage war;
for the dull-witted Mahiṣa does not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful.
In his presence, I must not speak even beneficial words that are unpleasant;
I must die according to the dharma of a hero, whether it be for good or for ill.
I consider destiny alone to be supreme; fie upon useless human effort!
For the Dānavas fall swiftly to the earth there, struck by his arrows. (43)
Having spoken thus, that best of Dānavas unleashed a shower of arrows;
the Goddess, however, cut them down with her own shafts before they could reach her presence.
Then Asiloman, her face filled with rage and watched by hosts of immortals, swiftly pierced him with arrows that travel as fast as thought.
Pierced by arrows, the Dānava indeed shone at will,
with streams of blood flowing from his body like a blossoming *kiṃśuka* tree.
Amiloma, seizing a heavy iron mace with speed,
rushed toward Caṇḍikā in rage and struck her on the head like a lion.
The lion, disregarding the blow of the mace struck by that powerful one, tore him apart in the middle of his chest with the strikes of its claws.
Leaping up with speed, the most terrible Daitya, mace in hand,
mounted upon the lion’s head and struck Ambikā with his mace.
But having evaded that blow, O lord of the people,
he severed his head at the neck with a sharp-edged sword.
When his head was severed, the lord of the Daityas fell swiftly to the earth; a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose within the army of that evil-minded one.
"Victory to the Goddess!"—thus did the gods praise that Mother of the World. The celestial drums resounded, O King, and the Kinnaras sang.
Seeing the Dānava slain and both [his companions] fallen upon the field of battle, and seeing all the soldiers there forcibly killed by Kesarin, [he was struck with grief]. || 53 ||
Some were devoured, and thus that entire host was rendered completely extinct;
some were broken, while others, being sluggish, fled toward Mahiṣa in distress.
O best of kings, Asiloman and Viḍāla were slain; they cried out and wept with cries of "Save us! Save us! (55).
"O King, those other soldiers who were devoured by the lion," saying this, they then committed a slaughter against the king. (56)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the First Skandha, Chapter 16.
Having heard those words of theirs, Mahiṣa then became dejected;
he was overwhelmed with anxiety, distressed, and filled with sorrow. || 57 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 15 ||
Then the sixteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the lord of men was filled with anger.
He quickly spoke to Dāruka: "Bring me my wonderful chariot."
It was yoked to a thousand donkeys, adorned with banners and flags,
equipped with weapons, white, with excellent wheels and beautiful poles.
The charioteer, having brought the chariot, spoke to him with haste:
"O King, this chariot has been brought; it stands adorned at the gate. (3)
Equipped with all weapons and furnished with excellent coverings,
the mighty lord of the Dānavas, having learned that the chariot had been brought, [prepared for battle].
Having assumed a human body, he was intent on going to battle;
and having reflected thus in his mind, the goddess, beholding me with a foul countenance, [spoke]. (5)
"She will surely be dejected at the sight of that horned buffalo;
for to women, beauty and cleverness are both dear. (6)
Therefore, I shall not go toward her by assuming a clever disguise, so that upon seeing me, that young woman will be filled with love. (7)
"May happiness belong to me alone at that time, and not to anyone else"—
having thus reflected in his mind, the immensely powerful lord of the Dānavas [spoke].
Having abandoned that buffalo form, he became an auspicious man,
bearing all weapons, glorious, and adorned with beautiful ornaments.
Wearing divine garments, handsome like another god of love with his flower-arrows,
he sat upon a chariot, adorned with armlets and garlands, bearing the bow of speech.
Surrounded by his army, the god, intoxicated with pride, went forth,
assuming a charming form that captivated the hearts of the proud.
Then, beholding that lord of the Daityas arrived and surrounded by many heroes, the Goddess sounded her conch shell.
Having heard that sound of the conch which caused wonder among the people,
he approached the presence of the goddess and spoke to her as if smiling.
O Goddess, a person existing in this wheel of saṃsāra—whether a man or likewise a woman—indeed desires happiness in every way. (14)
The happiness born of union for men does not exist here in the absence of union;
union is divided into many kinds, which I shall declare—listen indeed. (15)
There are numerous varieties arising from joy, arising from the cause, and arising from their own nature;
among these, I shall first describe those born of joy according to my understanding. (16)
The union of a son with his mother and father is considered the highest;
likewise, the union of a brother with a brother is regarded as middling for a specific reason. || 17 ||
He is remembered as the highest because he is the giver of the highest happiness alone;
and he is the middle one because he is the giver of only limited happiness. (18)
But the association of boatmen with those whose minds are shrouded by various [impurities] and who revolve in worldly attachment is considered natural by the wise. (19)
Because it bestows only very slight happiness, this [lower union] is considered inferior by the wise;
however, the supreme union (saṃyoga) bestows both happiness and suffering within saṃsāra. (20)
The union that is always proclaimed between a woman and a man who are equally beautiful and of equal age is considered the most excellent of all. || 21 ||
He is of such a nature because he is the bestower of the most supreme bliss; likewise, he possesses skill, beauty, dress, and so forth, as well as noble lineage, good conduct, and virtues.
For it is said that mutual excellence is achieved through mutual [elevation];
if you would enter into union with me, a hero. (23)
Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 16. 289.
You shall attain the highest bliss itself; of this there is no doubt.
O beloved, I assume various forms according to my own will.
All the gods, beginning with Indra, have been conquered by me in battle;
whatever divine jewels are now in this palace of mine— || 25 ||
Enjoy all of those as you wish, or give them away as you please;
become the chief queen today, O beautiful one, for I am your slave.
"I shall abandon my body at your word, O Lord; of this there is no doubt.
I shall indeed act in such a way that you may obtain happiness. (27)
"Command me, O large-eyed one, and I shall do exactly so;
for my heart has been infatuated by your beauty, O sweet-spoken lady. (28)
I am yours, O lady of beautiful hips; I have indeed come to you for refuge.
Protect me, O timid one, for I am tormented by the arrows of love. (29)
The supreme among all dharmas is the protection of those who have come for refuge.
I am yours, O dark-eyed one; I am your servant, O slender-waisted lady. (30)
My word is true unto death; I shall not act otherwise. O lady of true limbs, I bow at your feet, having cast aside my various weapons.
Have mercy, O large-eyed one; I am tormented by the arrows of love. O lovely-limbed one, from birth until now, I have never practiced wretchedness.
"Having approached the lords beginning with Brahmā, I shall place that [burden] upon you;
for in battle, the gods beginning with Brahmā know my conduct. (33)
"I too am there as a servant; look upon my face, O beautiful lady.
Vyāsa said:
To that Daitya who was speaking thus, the goddess Bhāgavatī replied: 34.
Laughing with a smile, the woman of excellent complexion spoke these words.
The Goddess said:
"I do not desire a man other than the Supreme Puruṣa. (35)
And if I so desire, O Daitya, I create the entire universe;
that Soul of the Universe beholds me, for I am his auspicious Prakṛti.
"By the power of its very proximity, consciousness is eternally present in me;
though I am insentient, through union with it, I become endowed with consciousness. (37)
Just as iron acquires consciousness through the proximity of a magnet, so too does the desire for worldly pleasures never arise in me at any time. (38)
"You are a fool, O dull-witted one, that you desire union with a woman;
a woman is proclaimed to be a chain for the bondage of a man. (39)
One bound by iron may be released, but one bound by women is never released.
O dull-witted one, do you desire the service of a latrine? (40)
Bestow peace for the sake of happiness; through tranquility you shall attain bliss.
Knowing that union with women brings great suffering, why do you become deluded? (41)
Abandon your enmity toward the gods and roam the earth as you please;
or go to Pātāla at your will, if there is any desire for life remaining in you. 42.
Or else, wage war; I am powerful at this moment.
O Dānava, I have been sent by all the gods for your destruction.

I speak the truth: I am pleased by the kindness of speech shown by you today; therefore, go alive and at your ease. Friendship with the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together; for that reason, I release your life.
O hero, if you have the desire for death, then fight as you please. 45.
O mighty-armed one, I shall slay you; of this there is no doubt.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter seventeen,
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of hers, the Dānava was infatuated by lust.
Then, with gentle speech, he spoke these sweet words:
"O lady of excellent limbs, O fair-faced one, I am afraid to strike you."
Having completely conquered Hari, Hara, and the other guardians of the world, he took a woman who was tender, beautiful in all her limbs, and enchanting to men. 48.
"O lotus-eyed one, is a battle with you appropriate for me?
O beautiful woman, if it pleases you, let us marry; accept me."
Otherwise, go to that place as you wish from which you have come;
I shall not strike you, since you have shown me friendship.
Beneficial and auspicious words have been spoken; therefore, go as you please.
What beauty would there be for me in the end after killing you, O lovely-eyed one?
"O fair-faced one, having taken you home today, I shall surely depart; for the killing of a woman, the killing of a child, and the killing of a Brahmin are difficult to overcome. (52)
"Even so, there would be no fruit for me; how then could there be the happiness of enjoyment?
Therefore, O lady of beautiful hair, I speak to you, bowing down with humility. (53)
A man finds no happiness apart from the lotus-face of his beloved;
likewise, women find no such happiness without a man. (54)
In union there arises happiness; in separation, the birth of suffering.
You are lovely, endowed with beauty, and adorned with every ornament. (55)
"O, is there no cleverness in you that you do not attend upon me?
By whom was this abandonment of enjoyments taught to you? (56)
O lady of sweet speech, you have been deceived here by some enemy; release this obsession with your beloved and perform what is truly beneficial.
"O Mountain, if you grant me your daughter, happiness shall indeed be mine as well as yours;
for Viṣṇu shines with Lakṣmī, and the Great-Souled One with Sāvitrī."
Rudra shines together with Pārvatī, and likewise does Indra with Śacī;
what woman, deprived of her husband, can ever obtain perpetual happiness?
O lady with dark-cornered eyes, why do you not choose a husband?
O beloved, where has that Kāma gone today, he who [pierced] you with his most tender arrows?
"The dull-witted Madana does not strike Kāma with his five arrows;
I believe that even Kāma is compassionate toward you, O beautiful one, just as I am. (61)
Thinking her to be a mere child, he does not discharge his arrows;
or perhaps he harbors some ancient enmity toward me from the God of Love. (62)
And for that reason, O lady with beautiful eyes, he does not release his arrows at you;
or rather, that god whose banner is a fish has been restrained by my malevolent deities.
Because of those things which destroy happiness, he does not strike you;
yet, O fawn-eyed one, having abandoned me, you will later feel remorse.
Like Mandodarī, O slender-limbed one, having first abandoned a virtuous and well-disposed king,
she later made a deceitful man her husband.
And when the people, afflicted by desire, have their inner selves agitated by delusion, (65)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the account of the Goddess's deeds, in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 16 ||
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the goddess questioned the Dānava.
Who was that woman Mandodarī, and who was that manifest king by her?
"Who was that deceitful king? Tell me that story later;
tell it in detail, how she again experienced suffering. (2)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter 17:
Mahiṣa said:
There is a country named Siṃhala, renowned upon the surface of the earth;
it is filled with forest trees and abounds in wealth and grain. (3)
There, a king named Candrasena reigned, devoted to righteousness,
wielding the rod of justice with equity, peaceful, and intent upon protecting his subjects.
He was truthful, gentle, brave, and patient; an ocean of statesmanship, a knower of the scriptures, an expert in all dharmas, and highly proficient in the science of archery.
His wife was of beautiful limbs, lovely, fortunate, and auspicious;
she was of virtuous conduct, exceedingly pleasant, and devoted solely to her husband.
In her first pregnancy, that beloved wife, named Guṇavatī and endowed with all auspicious marks, gave birth to a daughter who was exceedingly beautiful.
The father was exceedingly delighted to have obtained such a beautiful daughter;
filled with joy, he gave her the name Mandodarī.
Like the digit of the moon, she grew exceedingly day by day;
when she had become ten years old, the maiden was most enchanting.
And day after day, the king obtained anxiety regarding his excellent chariot;
so too did the brave ruler of the Madra country, the monarch named Sudhanvan.
His son was Atimedhāvin, renowned as Kaṃbugrīva;
he was described by the Brahmins to the king as a suitable and auspicious husband for her.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and having reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge,
he was then seen by the king, who had a beloved queen named Guṇavatī.
