"I shall give my own daughter, of excellent complexion, to Kaṃbugrīva.
Having heard her husband's words, she respectfully questioned her daughter. (13)
"Your father desires to perform your marriage with Kaṃbugrīva.
Having heard that, Mandodarī then spoke these words to her mother: ||| 14 ||
"I will not take a husband, nor do I have any desire for marriage; having undertaken the vow of lifelong maidenhood, I shall spend my time in every way. (15)
"I shall indeed always practice intense austerity with complete independence;
for dependence, O Mother, is the supreme misery in the ocean of saṃsāra. (16)
"Scholars who are experts in the scriptures say that liberation comes from independence;
therefore, I shall become liberated, and I have no need for a husband. (17)
While the marriage ceremony was taking place in the presence of the sacred fire, these words were properly spoken: "I am forever dependent upon you. (18)
Servitude to the group of mothers-in-law and brothers-in-law, and obedience to the father-in-law and the husband—this is considered more painful than pain itself. (19)
If at some time her husband should resort to another loving woman,
then there would arise a far greater suffering born of a co-wife.
Consequently, jealousy arises toward her husband and further affliction occurs;
O Mother, where is there happiness in saṃsāra, especially for women? (21)
"O Mother, I previously heard from the mouth of Tānacara that among those dependent on their own nature within this dream-like cycle of existence,
there was a king who was the youngest brother of Dhruva, supreme and a knower of all dharmas. (22)
His wife was devoted to dharma, virtuous, and dedicated to the service of her husband.
Without any fault, he abandoned his beloved wife in the forest;
such are the miseries that exist even while the husband is still alive.
If he dies due to the conjunction of time, the woman shall become a vessel of suffering;
widowhood is the supreme misery, causing grief and torment. (25)
Even when living as another's wife, there would be even greater suffering at home;
for one consumed by the fire of passion, what happiness can there be from union with a husband? (26)
"Therefore, it is my opinion that one should never take a husband.
Thus addressed, the princess then spoke to her mother regarding a husband. (27)
Observing the vow of lifelong maidenhood, she did not desire a husband;
constantly devoted to her vows and recitations, she was always turned away from worldly existence.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter ten.
Discerning the many faults involved, he did not wish to carry out the execution;
having heard what his wife had said, the king remained exactly as he was.
Knowing that her daughter had been won over by his power, he did not arrange a marriage;
she remained in the house itself, protected by her father and mother.
The sprouts of youth have arisen in women, which kindle desire;
nevertheless, she was urged again and again by her female companions. (31)
Speaking words of wisdom and meaning, she desired to become his wife;
once, she went to wander in a garden region filled with many trees.
Attended by a group of maidservants, the fair-faced and slender-waisted woman went there with love; she enjoyed herself and beheld the flowering creepers.
While the beautiful woman was gathering flowers, surrounded by her companions,
the lord of Kośala happened upon her on that path by the power of fate.
The great hero Vīrasena, who was exceedingly famous, arrived;
he was mounted alone upon his chariot, accompanied by only a few attendants. (35)
And his army followed behind him, approaching very slowly;
then the king was seen from afar by her companions.
Thus it was said to Mandodarī: "A man comes along the path, mounted upon a chariot, long-armed and handsome like another Madana. (37)
"I think some king has arrived here by the power of fortune.
While she was speaking thus, the lord of Kośala arrived there.
Upon seeing her with dark-cornered eyes, the king was struck with wonder;
quickly descending from his chariot, he questioned the female attendant. (39)
"Who is this young woman with large eyes? Whose daughter is she? Tell me quickly.
Thus questioned, the Sairandhrī, with a pure smile, spoke to him.
First speak to me, O hero; I ask you, O fair-eyed one:
who are you, why have you come here, and what is your purpose? Tell me now.
Thus questioned by the Sairandhrī, the lord of the earth said to her:
"There is a country named Kośala on this earth, most wonderful. (42)
And I, O beloved, am his protector, named Vīrasena;
my fourfold army follows behind me at will.
"Know me to be the lord of Kosala, who has arrived here by mistake on the road.
Sairandhrī said: "O King, I am indeed Mandodarī by name, the daughter of Candrasena. (44)
"This lotus-eyed woman has arrived at the garden desiring to sport.
Hearing those words, the king replied to his attendant: 45.
"O Sairandhrī, you are clever; awaken the princess. O fair-eyed one, I am a king born of the lineage of Kakutstha. (46)
"O lovely woman, become my wife through the Gāndharva rite of marriage;
O fair-hipped one, I have no wife, for I am in the prime of youth. (47)
"I truly desire a beautiful woman of noble birth;
or rather, your father ought to give her to me according to the prescribed rites. (48)
"And I shall become a devoted husband; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard these words, Mahiṣa, the sairandhrī then spoke to her. (49)
O Mandodarī, expert as you are in the science of love, speak sweet words to the householder;
a king born of the Solar dynasty has arrived. (50)
O beautiful one, a king has been born who is handsome, powerful, and lovely; moreover, he is equal to you in age and is entirely devoted to you. (51)
O large-eyed one, your father also suffers in every way,
having learned at the time of your marriage that you were possessed by world-weariness.
"Thus spoke that king to us, sighing again and again. Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 18. 293.
"Let these maidservants, devoted to their duties, awaken this daughter."
We are not able to speak to you again, for you are devoted to the way of obstinacy;
Manu has declared that for women, the supreme duty is service to their husband.
"Indeed, by serving her husband, a woman attains heaven;
therefore, O large-eyed one, perform the marriage ceremony according to the prescribed rites. (55)
Mandodarī said:
"I will not take him as my husband; I shall perform wonderful penance.
O girl, restrain the king; why does he look at me so shamelessly? (56)
Sairandhrī said:
"O Goddess, this desire is difficult to conquer; this time is difficult to overcome.
Therefore, O beautiful one, you ought to act upon my wholesome advice. (57)
"Otherwise, a calamity will surely befall us; this is certain.
Having heard these words of hers, the maiden then spoke to her friend: 58.
"Whatever may happen, let it happen through the power of destiny; there is no doubt about this. O attendant, I will not perform the marriage ceremony under any circumstances. (59)
Mahiṣa said:
Having understood her persistence, he spoke again to the king:
"Go, O King, as you please; she does not desire a virtuous husband."
Having heard those words, the king departed with his army;
his mind turned toward Kośalā, becoming free from desire for the lustful woman.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 37 ||
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Mahiṣa said:
Her sister was a maiden, auspicious by name, Indumatī.
Then the youngest sister, being beautiful, became fit for marriage.
Her marriage was performed and the svayaṃvara took place;
kings from many lands assembled there in that pavilion. ||2||
By her, a certain king was chosen— one who was powerful, endowed with marshy lands, possessed of noble lineage and good character, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
Then, having seen the king as a libertine, she became afflicted by desire;
by the turn of fate, she lusted after that rogue who was adorned with cleverness. ||4||
The slender-limbed maiden said to her father, "O father, arrange my marriage;
having seen the lord of Madra here today, a desire has arisen within me."
Having heard those words spoken by his daughter in private, Candrasena,
with a gracious mind, became intent upon accomplishing that task.
Having summoned that king to his home,
he gave him his daughter Mandodarī according to the marriage rite, as well as abundant wedding gifts.
Cārudeṣṇa, having obtained that beautiful woman, became joyful;
the king also, delighted, went to his own home accompanied by the woman.
That tiger among kings sported with his beloved for many days;
it is said that once, while sporting in secret with a female servant, he was alone with her.
Sairandhrī told her what she had seen regarding her husband;
filled with anger, she rebuked him with a smile.
Once, while the king was sporting with and fondling Sāmānyā in private, he saw Rūpavatī; at that very moment, she fell into distress.
"This rogue was not recognized before when he was seen at the svayaṃvara."
"What have I done out of delusion that I have been seized by the king? (12)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 18.
"What shall I do now with this torment, O shameless, pitiless, and deceitful one? What joy can there be in such a husband? Fie upon my life today! (13)
From this day forward, I have indeed renounced all pleasure in this worldly existence;
I have now attained contentment regarding everything arising from union with a husband.
An action that ought not to have been done has been performed; it has become a source of suffering for me.
If I were to commit suicide by abandoning my body, it would be an exceedingly grave sin.
"I shall go quickly to my father's house, yet even there no happiness will be found;
I shall undoubtedly become an object of ridicule for my friends. (16)
Therefore, having abandoned the pleasures of desire once again, I must dwell right here with one possessed of dispassion, in accordance with the requirements of time. (17)
Mahiṣa said:
Having reflected thus, that woman, devoted to misery and grief, abandoned her husband’s home and the pleasures born of worldly existence, and remained there. (18)
Therefore, O auspicious lady, disregarding me, the lord of the earth, you will, afflicted by passion, take refuge with another—a base and wretched man. (19)
Follow my truthful word, which is most beneficial for women;
by doing so, you will avoid supreme grief—of this there is no doubt. (20)
The Goddess said:
"O dull-witted one, go to Pātāla, or engage in battle now!
Having slain you and all the asuras, I shall proceed according to my pleasure. (21)
Whenever, O Dānava, suffering befalls the virtuous,
then for their protection I assume a body.
Know for certain, O Daitya, that for the sake of protecting the gods, I—who am formless—have assumed form, and I—who am unborn—have taken birth. (23)
I speak the truth; know this: I have indeed been requested by the gods, O enemy of horses, that for the sake of slaying you, having killed you, I shall remain steadfast. (24)
Therefore, either fight or go to Pātāla, the abode of the asuras;
in every way I shall slay you—I tell you this truth.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by the goddess, that Dānava took up his bow and stood there on the battlegrounds, desiring combat.
She swiftly released arrows, whetted on stone and drawn back to her ear;
the Goddess cut them down with iron-tipped shafts discharged in fury.
A terrifying battle took place between those two, as the gods and the dānavas, each desiring victory over the other, engaged one another. ||28||
Durdhara, arriving in their midst, discharged toward the goddess extremely fierce arrows smeared with poison, thereby provoking her wrath.
Then the Blessed Lady, enraged, struck him with sharp arrows;
Durdhara fell lifeless upon the earth like a mountain peak.
Seeing him thus slain, the Three-eyed Lord, the supreme knower of weapons, [acted].
Having arrived, he struck the Supreme Goddess with seven arrows.
But the Goddess cut down those future arrows with her own shafts;
then the Mother of the World struck the Three-eyed One with her trident.
Seeing the Three-eyed Lord slain, Andhaka quickly arrived;
with an iron mace, he swiftly struck the lion on the head.
But the lion, having slain that exceedingly powerful one with a blow of his claws, consumed Andhaka's flesh with speed and fury. (34)
Seeing those arrows destroyed by Tāraṇa, the Dānava was filled with wonder;
he swiftly discharged extremely sharp arrows that had been whetted on stone.
The Goddess split those arrows into two with her own stone-tipped shafts before they could reach him;
then Ambikā struck the Daitya on the chest with her mace.
Struck by the mace, that tormentor of the immortals fell into a swoon;
yet that evil-souled one, enduring the agony, quickly returned.
Filled with rage, he struck the bewildered lion with his mace. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa*, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 18. [Page 295]
The lion also tore that great asura with the strokes of his claws.
Abandoning his human form, he too became a lion;
with his claws, he tore apart the lion of the Goddess, who was fierce with pride.
And seeing that lion, the queen, filled with rage,
overwhelmed him with sharp iron-tipped arrows as if with venomous serpents.
Abandoning his form as Hari and becoming an elephant with flowing rut,
he took a mountain peak in his trunk and hurled it toward Caṇḍikā.
"Come, O Goddess!"—with these words, the Mother of the World shattered the mountain peak into pieces as small as sesame seeds with her stone-sharpened arrows, and she laughed aloud. (42)
Then, leaping up, the lion stationed himself upon his head and tore with his claws the buffalo who was in the form of an elephant.
Abandoning his elephant form, Hari likewise became a fierce eight-legged beast;
enraged and desiring to kill, he was exceedingly powerful.
Seeing that śarabha, the goddess, filled with wrath, quickly struck him on the head with her sword; he, too, then struck her.
A battle between the two of them took place, inspiring great terror;
then, assuming the form of a buffalo, he struck him with his two horns.
By whirling his tail and striking with blows from his horns, the great asura— terrible in form and fearsome— swiftly struck the slender-limbed woman.
Seizing the mountain peaks with his tail and whirling them by force,
that evil-minded one sent them forth, laughing with supreme joy.
Intoxicated by his strength, he said to her: "Stay, O Goddess, on the field of battle!
Today I shall slay you, who are adorned with beauty and youth. (49)
"You are a fool, intoxicated by pride today, that you engage in combat with me;
utterly deluded, you are a false, powerful she-ass. (50)
Having slain you, I shall destroy the gods who are experts in deceit—those rogues who, placing a woman at their forefront, desire to conquer me. (51)
The Goddess said:
"Do not boast, O dull-witted one! Stay, stay on the field of battle!
Having slain you, I shall make the best of the gods free from all affliction. (52)
"Having drunk the sweet Madhavī wine today, O lowest of men, I shall strike down in battle that sinner who causes suffering to the gods and fear to the sages. (53)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, she took a golden goblet filled with liquor and,
desiring to slay the great asura, drank from it again and again out of anger.
Having drunk the sweet grape-wine, the Goddess, taking up her trident with haste,
rushed toward the Dānava, gladdening the hosts of gods.
The gods praised her with love and rained down flowers;
they cried out, "Victory! Live long!", amidst the sounds of kettledrums.
The ṛṣis, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, Cāraṇas, and Kinnaras, having beheld the battle, stood joyfully in the sky. (57)
That master of deceit, having repeatedly assumed various bodies composed of illusion, committed sins in battle against the Goddess.
And Caṇḍikā, her eyes red with rage, forcefully struck that wicked one in the heart with her sharp trident.
Struck by him, he fell down and remained unconscious for a moment;
rising again, Cāmuṇḍā struck him forcefully with her two feet.
Having struck him with blows of his feet, he laughed again and again with those kicks;
he uttered a terrible sound that caused fear among the gods.
Then the Goddess, taking the supreme thousand-spoked wheel with its beautiful nave in her hand,
spoke to the demon Mahiṣāsura who stood before her.
Behold, O you who are blinded by intoxication, the wheel that shall now sever your neck;
stand still for just a moment and go now to the realm of Yama. (63)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter nineteen.
Having spoken thus, the Mother of the World released her terrible discus;
then, in that battle, the head of the Dānava was severed by the weapon.
Warm blood flowed from his throat-trachea like vomit,
as red as ochre and resembling a powerful, surging mountain torrent.
The headless trunk of that Daitya, while spinning, indeed fell upon the earth;
and a cry of "Victory! arose from the gods, increasing their joy.
Then the exceedingly powerful Siṃha devoured the Dānavas, who were intent on flight there in battle, as if he were tormented by hunger.
O King, when the cruel Mahiṣa was slain, the Dānavas were oppressed by fear;
those who remained alive fled to Pātāla.
When he had been struck down, the gods, the sages, the men, and all other virtuous beings on earth attained supreme joy. (69)
Caṇḍikā too, having abandoned the battle, then settled in an auspicious place;
the gods quickly arrived there, desiring to praise her who bestows happiness. (70)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Slaying of the Asura Mahiṣa," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 18 ||
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Then all the gods, led by Indra, were greatly rejoiced.
Seeing the buffalo slain, they praised the Mother of the Universe. ||1||
The gods said:
Brahmā creates, Viṣṇu protects this world, and Maheśa indeed withdraws it by your power alone at the time of its end;
even those lords cannot exist without you. Therefore, you alone are the cause of the world's sustenance and destruction.
You are celebrated as Smṛti and Gati; you are Karuṇā, Dayā, Śraddhā, Dhṛti, Vasudhā, Kapilā, and Jayā;
you are Puṣṭi, Kalā, Vijayā, Girijā, Jayā, Tuṣṭi, Prabhā, Buddhi, Umā, and Ramā. (3)
Knowledge, forbearance, splendor, and even intelligence—thou alone art known as all these in this world of the three realms.
O thou who art the dwelling place of all the worlds, who else indeed would be capable of acting swiftly without these powers of thine?
(4) Surely thou art *dhāraṇā* (retention); for if thou wert not, how could the Tortoise and the Serpent be capable of supporting even this earth?
O Mother, if you were not the earth, how could all this world, burdened with such great weight, remain suspended in the sky? ||5||

Or those deluded men who praise the immortals—the four-faced Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—along with the Moon, Fire, Wind, and the foremost of the Gaṇas, O Mother; for apart from You, they have no power to accomplish their task.

O Mother, those of small intellect who, having appointed the gods as their presiding deities, offer abundant oblations in the sacrifice spread out before them with the cry of "Svāhā"—if you were not there, how could they have truly attained [their goal]?
For do they not, in fact, worship you alone? It is for this reason that they are deluded. (7)
O Mother, you are the bestower of enjoyments here for all things moving and unmoving; indeed, through your own portions, you grant them eternal life.
Just as you nourish your own gods here, so too do you protect others; for this reason [you are called Bhogavatī]. (8)
O Mother, you who have yourself playfully fashioned in the forest trees that are barren, devoid of leaves, and bitter;
Skillful men do not destroy them by any means; therefore, you too protect the Daityas exceedingly well.

But as for you, who slay your enemies at the head of battle with arrows after perceiving that they are intent on the amorous play of celestial nymphs—even while in another body, you take up the essence of compassion; this is your conduct for the sake of fulfilling the desires [of others].
It is wonderful that these demons of renowned power do not perish despite being deprived of their lives by your mere glance;
for the sake of whom you, O Mother, assume this bodily form, such is your relish for play, and neither of the two [the demons' strength nor your own] is the cause here.
Alas! When the most wicked age of Kali has arrived, men do not worship you; indeed, they have been deceived.
By clever deceivers of old, people were made devoted to the service of Hari and Śaṅkara, while those fashioned by you were neglected.
Having learned that the gods have come under your control and that those who worship you on earth with devotion are destined for the state of asuras,
men— though holding a truly stainless lamp in their hands— fall into a waterless, most terrible well.
O Mother, you alone are knowledge that bestows happiness, and you are ignorance that bestows misery; you alone are the remover of the births of men.
You have indeed been sought by those of dull intellect for the sake of liberation, yet you were not worshipped by the ignorant who are intent on worldly enjoyment, O Mother.
Brahmā, Hara, Hari, and likewise the other gods, constantly worship Your lotus feet, which are the refuge for all;
yet those of small intellect who do not worship them with their minds fall perpetually into the ocean of worldly existence, deluded.
O Caṇḍī, by the grace of the dust arising from the lotuses of your feet, Brahmā creates the entire universe at the beginning of existence;
Śauri protects it, and Hara indeed destroys it; yet that unfortunate man here does not serve you.
O Goddess, you are the deity of speech; even the foremost among the immortals, the gods and asuras, are not capable of describing your power.
For if you do not dwell within their mouths, those humans who are devoid of it cannot exist at all. (17)
Hari was indeed cursed by the enraged Bhṛgu to become a fish, a tortoise, and a boar;
thereafter, he became the Man-lion (Nṛsiṃha) who acted with deceit upon the earth—O Mother, could there not be fear of death for those who serve them? (18)
O Mother, this famous *liṅga* of Śambhu fell to the earth by that curse when Bhṛgu had gone to the forest;
how can there be happiness, both here and in the hereafter, for those men on earth who worship that wearer of the skull? (19)

Those men who worship the elephant-faced Lord of the Gaṇas, having taken refuge in the false [Ganeśa] away from Maheśvara, do not know you, O Goddess—the Mother of the Universe, the bestower of the fruits of all goals, who is easily served for happiness. (20)
It is wonderful that even your enemy’s people, having been slain in battle by you with sharp arrows out of a heart moistened with compassion, have been sent to the heavenly realm;
for otherwise, they would have fallen into a state of extreme suffering in hell, which is filled with the consequences of their own past deeds.
Even Brahmā, Hara, and Hari—those very gods—do not know your power due to their state of pride;
what other mortals are capable of knowing it? They are utterly deluded by your qualities, O You of immeasurable majesty.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter 19. 298.
Even those sages suffer, their minds being utterly deluded, for they do not worship Your lotus feet, which are difficult to conceive;
though intent on serving the sun and fire, they have not realized the essence of the Vedas—the ultimate reality—even through hundreds of scriptural revelations.
I believe that your virtues, whose power is renowned throughout the world, indeed cause those who are averse to the spirit of devotion to turn toward Viṣṇu, Śiva, the Sun, and Gaṇeśa. (24)

O Mother, you do not become angry with those foremost of men who, being averse to your feet, create various worlds and diverse scriptures through their own intellects and their own proclaimed traditions, [teaching] the yoga of devotion and the worship of Hari and Hara; rather, you show them compassion and utterly subdue those who are experts in the mantras of delusion.
In the fourth age, the exceedingly powerful fourth quality (tamas) prevails; by it, the false scriptures are churned up.
Yet in the Kali age, skillful poets indeed protect you, and they even offer praise to the hosts of asuras fashioned by you.
Sages of exceedingly pure being meditate upon the supreme knowledge, perfected through yoga, which bestows the fruit of liberation on this earth;
yet even they do not avoid the suffering within a mother’s womb. Blessed indeed are those men who have merged into You.
There exists a consciousness within the Supreme Self by which even He becomes manifest and known throughout the worlds as the performer of the acts of existence;
for who else, devoid of these three, is capable—by their own power—of bringing this world into being, maintaining it, and causing it to move? (28)
O Mother of the Universe, how could the principles of existence, devoid of consciousness, be capable of creating the world, since they are insentient?
Furthermore, O Goddess, how could the sense organs, though endowed with qualities and functions, bestow their fruits when separated from You? (29)
O Mother, would not the gods accept their own portion, duly offered according to the rules, even when it has been presented by sages in sacrifices?
If you, Svāhā, were not the instrumental cause therein, then surely you alone protect the entire universe.
All this has been ordained by you from the beginning of existence; you indeed protect the lords of the directions, headed by Hari and Hara.
At the time of dissolution, even the gods do not know your primordial deeds, O Bhava; how then could men of meager fortune ever know them? (31)
O Mother, having slain the fierce asura who had assumed the form of a buffalo, this host of gods was indeed protected by you;
what praise can those of dull intellect offer you, O Janani, for even the Vedas did not reach your true nature? (32)
The task has been accomplished in this world, for that evil-minded enemy, an inconceivable thorn in the side of the universe, has been slain;
indeed, fame has been established throughout the worlds, yet compassion must still be exercised—protect us as well, O Mother of renowned power! (33)
Vyāsa said: Thus praised by the gods, the Goddess spoke to them in a gentle voice:
"O best of gods, speak of any other task that is difficult to accomplish."
Whenever there may be a task for the gods that is exceedingly difficult to accomplish, I should then be remembered; I shall swiftly destroy their calamity. 35.
The gods said:
"O Goddess, everything has been accomplished by you; indeed, our task is now complete, since this enemy of ours, Mahiṣāsura, has been slain. (36)
O Mother, act in such a way that we may always remember Your lotus feet, and that our devotion to You, O Mother of the World, may remain unwavering. (37)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 20: 299.
A mother alone always forgives thousands of offenses.
Knowing this, why do people not worship the source of the universe? ||38||
In this body there are two birds; their friendship is constant.
There is no third friend who could indeed endure such an offense.
Therefore, what indeed will that evil-souled and unfortunate jīva do after abandoning you, his friend, throughout the births of gods and humans? (40)
Having obtained this body so difficult to attain, the lowest of men would not remember you;
we say this repeatedly as a truth, in thought, deed, and word. (41)
Whether in happiness or in sorrow, you are our wonderful refuge;
protect us always, O Goddess, with all your excellent weapons. (42)
"Otherwise, there is no refuge other than the dust of your lotus feet.
Thus praised by the gods, the Goddess vanished right there.
Seeing her emerge, the gods were filled with supreme wonder.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 19 ||
Then the twentieth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
O Sage, having then beheld the wonderful power of the Goddess, which brings supreme peace to the world—
O best of the twice-born, there is no satiety for me in hearing the nectar of your discourse born from your lotus-like mouth. || 1 ||
When Bhavānī had vanished, what did those gods, led by Indra, do?
[They recounted] the supreme and most purifying life-story of the Goddess, which is indeed difficult to attain for men of meager merit.
Who, possessing keen channels for the ears yet separated from fortune by meager merit, does not attain satisfaction through this nectar of narrative?
For by drinking it, one attains immortality; fie on those men who do not drink it with reverence! || 3 ||

How could those who are grateful ever abandon the playful deeds of the Mother of the World, which provide protection for gods and great sages, serve as a raft for men to cross the ocean of worldly existence,
and are cherished by those already liberated, those seeking liberation, those wandering in saṃsāra, and even those afflicted by disease? 4!
Those who know the Vedas declare that this, which grants all goals, should always be drunk by their ears.
Likewise, O Sage, for kings who are always devoted to virtue, wealth, and pleasure, it is especially so;
since even those liberated ones indeed drink from that [stream], how could it not be drunk by those who are devoid of them? 6.
It can indeed be inferred that those who in a previous birth worshipped Bhavānī with excellent kunda flowers, campaka flowers, bilva fruits,
and darbha grass, become kings endowed with enjoyments upon this earth.
Those who, having obtained this human body in the land of Bhārata, are devoid of devotion and have not worshipped You—
destitute of wealth and grain, afflicted by disease, and bereft of progeny— they [suffer].
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the fifth book, chapter twenty:
"Indeed, they wander perpetually as slaves, obedient to commands, carrying nothing but burdens."
Devoted only to their own interests day and night, they never even obtain enough to fill their bellies.
And as for others on earth who suffer misery—those who are mute, deaf, lame, or afflicted with leprosy—the poets should infer therein that Bhavānī was not constantly propitiated by them. (10)

Those who possess royal enjoyments and are full of prosperity, who are served by many people, or those who are seen endowed with great wealth—it must be inferred that they have been honored by Ambā. (11)
Therefore, O son of Satyavatī, having shown compassion, please narrate the supreme life-story of the goddess; for you are now truly merciful.
Having slain that wicked buffalo and being praised and honored by the gods, where has that Mahālakṣmī gone, she who is born from the essence of all splendor? || 13 ||
"O illustrious one, it has been told to you that she, the Mistress of the World, quickly vanished;
whether she is established in heaven or in the world of mortals."
Has she gone to dissolution, or has she taken refuge right there in Vaikuṇṭha? Or is she on the Golden Mountain? Tell me now according to the truth. (15)
Vyāsa said: Previously, I described to you the enchanting Maṇidvīpa,
the eternal playground of the Goddess, which is remembered as her supreme favorite.
Therein, Brahmā, Hari, and Sthāṇu assumed the state of women;
having regained their manhood once more, they performed their respective duties.
In the midst of the ocean of nectar there is an exceedingly beautiful island;
there Ambikā always sports in various forms.
Praised and worshipped by the gods, that auspicious Śivā went right there, where the eternal power of Māyā constantly sports. (19)
Seeing that goddess, the sovereign of all, thus departed,
the gods established a mighty protector of the earth born of the solar dynasty.
He installed the heroic king named Śatrughna, the lord of Ayodhyā,
who was endowed with all auspicious marks, upon the splendid throne of Mahiṣa.
Having then bestowed the kingdom upon him, all the gods, headed by Indra,
departed for their own abodes on their respective mounts.
O lord of the earth, while those hosts of gods were present upon the earth,
there then arose a kingdom of righteousness, and the subjects likewise became happy.
The rain-cloud poured forth at the proper season, the earth was covered with the excellence of grain,
and the trees, rich in fruits and flowers, were always a source of happiness.
The cows were abundant in milk, yielding pots full of it and granting the desires of men;
the rivers flowed along excellent paths, clear, cool, and filled with birds. 25.
The Brāhmaṇas were conversant with the true essence of the Vedas and likewise devoted to the performance of sacrificial rites;
the Kṣatriyas were endowed with righteousness and intent upon giving gifts and Vedic study. ||26||
All the kings were constantly devoted to the science of weaponry, intent on protecting their subjects, wielders of just punishment, and endowed with tranquility. (27)
There was indeed no conflict among any living beings;
there were mines yielding treasures and wealth, and herds of cattle accompanied by flocks of cows.
O best of kings, on the surface of the earth, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras all became devoted to the Goddess. (29)
Everywhere there were sacrificial posts and enchanting pavilions;
the earth was filled with sacrifices performed by Kṣatriyas for the sake of Brāhmaṇas. 30.
The women were devoted to their husbands, possessed of good character, and endowed with truthfulness;
the sons were intent on filial devotion to their fathers and dedicated to righteousness.
Neither heresy nor unrighteousness existed anywhere upon the surface of the earth.
There were only the doctrines of the Vedas and the doctrines of the Shastras; no other doctrines existed in that way. 32.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 21:
There was no quarrel among anyone, nor any wretchedness, nor any inauspicious thought.
May all people be happy everywhere, and likewise may they die at the proper time. ||33||
There shall never be separation from friends nor any calamity; there shall be no drought, no famine, and no plague that brings suffering to men. (34)
There was no disease, nor envy, nor mutual hostility;
everywhere men and women were endowed with happiness and possessed of joy. (35)
All the people sported like hosts of gods in heaven;
there were no thieves, nor heretics, nor deceivers, nor hypocrites. (36)
O King, lord of the earth, at that time there were no backbiters, no libertines, and no arrogant men;
nor were there any sinful people who hated the Vedas. (37)
All were constantly devoted to the Dharma and dedicated to the service of the twice-born;
thus, from the threefold creation of Dharma, the Brāhmaṇas became threefold. (38)
Some were of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), some of passion (rājasa), and others likewise of darkness (tāmasa);
yet all were knowers of the Vedas, skillful, and characterized by the quality of goodness (sāttvika) and virtuous conduct.
Devoid of accepting gifts and devoted to compassion and self-restraint,
they performed sacrifices with food characterized by *sattva*, being intent upon righteousness.
Never by means of sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa), nor by animal sacrifices, [is merit gained];
rather, giving, study, and thirdly, performing sacrifice [are the means]. (41)
O King, those Brahmins who take delight in the three types of ritual action are indeed Sāttvika;
those who are Rājasa are knowers of the Vedas and serve as domestic priests for Kṣatriyas.
All were devoted to the six duties and ate meat according to the prescribed rites; they performed sacrifices, officiated at sacrifices, gave gifts, and likewise accepted them. (43)

Furthermore, the study of the Vedas and likewise their teaching— these six [occupations] belong to those who are characterized by darkness (tamas), joined with anger, and devoted to passion and hatred.
The servants of kings were always devoted to some form of study;
now that Mahiṣa has been slain, they are all happy and intent upon the Vedas.
The Kṣatriyas were devoted to their vows and dedicated to the duty of giving; they were intent on protection, while the Vaiśyas followed the occupation of trade. (46)
Others followed the livelihoods of agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and usury;
thus the world rejoiced when Mahiṣa was struck down.
Indeed, there was no distress among the subjects, and wealth flowed in;
the cows yielded much milk and were auspicious, and the rivers likewise abounded with water. (48)
The trees were laden with abundant fruit, and the people were free from disease; there were no mental anxieties nor deceivers anywhere who could cause suffering to the subjects. (49)

Those living beings who are devoted to the dharma ordained by the Vedas and whose minds are fixed on serving the lotus feet of Caṇḍikā do not meet their end prematurely; they remain forever endowed with all prosperity and free from disease. (50)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 20 ||
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the supreme life-story of the Goddess.
It bestows happiness upon all living beings and destroys all sins. ||1||
Just as Śumbha and Niśumbha, those two exceedingly powerful brothers, were great heroes who were indeed incapable of being slain by men.
Surrounded by many followers, the hero was always a source of suffering for the gods;
he was of evil conduct, arrogant with pride, and accompanied by many dānavas.
In that exceedingly terrible battle, they were both slain by Ambikā,
along with all their attendants, for the sake of the welfare of the gods.
Caṇḍamuṇḍī, the mighty-armed Raktabīja who was exceedingly terrible,
and the one named Dhūmralocana— all of them were slain upon the field of battle.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-one.
Having slain them, she removed the supreme fear of the gods;
she was praised and worshipped on the auspicious mountain Mācala, the Mountain of the Gods.
The king said:
"The two asuras have been described; how did those two become the best among the strong?
By whom were they established here, and why did they come to be slain by women? (7)
By what asceticism and by what granting of boons were these two of great strength born?
And how were they slain? Tell me everything in detail.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, to this divine narrative which destroys all sins, which is joined with the life-story of the Goddess, and which is auspicious, bestowing the fruits of all desires. (9)
Formerly, two Asuras named Śumbha and Niśumbha, brothers of auspicious appearance, arrived from the netherworld upon the surface of the earth.
Having reached the prime of youth, they both performed supreme austerity at Puṣkara, the purifier of the worlds, having renounced food and water.
For as many as ten thousand years, devoted solely to the science of yoga,
they performed supreme austerity, remaining seated together in one place.
Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, was pleased with the two of them;
and the Blessed One arrived there, having mounted the lord of swans.
And the Creator of the World, seeing both of them absorbed in meditation, said:
"Arise, O highly fortunate ones; I am indeed pleased with your austerity."
Vyāsa said: "I shall grant whatever desired boon or wish you speak here;
I have come as the granter of desires, having witnessed the power of your asceticism. (15)
Having heard these words of his, the two of them became awakened and composed;
they performed a circumambulation and then offered their salutations. (16)
Having prostrated themselves like a staff, those two of weakly built forms, distressed, spoke sweet words with voices faltering with emotion. (17)
O God of gods, ocean of mercy, bestower of fearlessness upon the non-devotees! O Brahman, if you are pleased, O Lord, grant us immortality. (18)
There is no fear whatsoever on the surface of the earth greater than death;
terrified by that fear, we have come to you for refuge. (19)
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O Creator of the universe, O Treasure of Forgiveness!
O Soul of the Universe, dispel at once the fear born of death.
Brahmā said:
What is this that you desire? It is entirely contrary [to reason].
It is something that cannot be given by anyone to anyone at all in the three worlds.
For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died.
Indeed, the boundaries were established in the world of old by the Creator of the Universe.
"All living beings must die by all means; there is no doubt in this.
Ask for another desire, and I shall grant whatever you wish. (23)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words and having reflected well upon them, Dāna and Trai then bowed down and spoke to Brahmā, who stood before them.
O Ocean of Compassion, grant us our desired boon: invincibility against men, gods and others, humans, beasts, and birds. (25)
"Which woman is so powerful that she will bring about our destruction?
O lords, there is no woman in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, who possesses such power as you desire. (26)
O Lotus-born One, these two brothers shall be invulnerable to men;
nor shall they have fear from women, for by their very nature, women are weak.
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the fifth book, chapter 21. Vyāsa said:
Having heard their words, Brahmā, with a gracious mind, granted them the desired boon and then departed for his own abode.
Then, having gone to that palace, the two Dānavas returned to their own home; having appointed Bhṛgu as their domestic priest, they then performed worship.
On an auspicious day and under a favorable constellation, the sage fashioned a divine and beautiful throne made of gold and bestowed it for the sake of his sovereignty. (30)
He gave the auspicious royal throne to Śubha, who was the eldest;
at that very moment, the best of the Dānavas quickly arrived to serve him.
The two great heroes, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, brothers arrogant in their strength,
arrived accompanied by an army and provided with chariots, horses, and elephants.
One named Dhūmralocana, possessing a form and fierce prowess like his [Shumbha's],
having heard that King Shumbha had arrived, then came accompanied by an army;
likewise the heroic Raktabīja, who was superior in strength due to the granting of a boon.
Accompanied by two akṣauhiṇīs, he arrived at that very place and joined him. ||34||
O King, there is one cause for this for him who always fights in battle:
the flow of blood from his body when he is struck by weapons. (35)
And when such cruel men, numerous and with weapons in their hands, are born and arise in great numbers upon the earth, [then this occurs]. (36)
Men born from blood arise with those very forms, those same appearances, and those same prowess; moreover, they engage in battle. (37)
Therefore, that great Asura Raktabīja, possessing immense prowess, was exceedingly difficult to defeat in battle and was incapable of being slain by any living beings.
And many other heroes, endowed with the fourfold army, considering Śumbha to be their king, became his servants. ||39||
At that time, an innumerable army arose for Śumbha and Niśumbha;
by their great power, the entire kingdom of the earth was seized. (40)
Then, having formed that military array, Niśumbha, the slayer of enemy heroes,
went swiftly to heaven in order to conquer the Lord of Śacī.
He waged a great battle on all sides with the world-protectors;
the slayer of Vṛtra struck him in the chest with the fall of his thunderbolt.
Struck by the vajra, that younger brother of the Dānavas fell to the ground;
then the army of that great-souled Niśumbha was shattered.
Hearing that his brother had fainted, Śumbha, the crusher of enemy forces,
arrived there and struck all the gods with arrows.
A great battle was fought with that Śumbha of unwearied deeds;
indeed, all the gods, including Indra, and all the guardians were utterly defeated. 45.
Then, by virtue of his great strength, he seized the station of Indra,
which was endowed with the wish-fulfilling tree and accompanied by the cow of plenty.
The three worlds and the sacrificial portions were seized by that great-souled one;
having reached the Nandana grove, the great asura became joyful.
By drinking the nectar, the great asura attained happiness;
and having conquered Kubera, he indeed ruled over his kingdom.
Likewise, he established his authority over the sun and the moon;
and having utterly defeated Yama, he seized that very office as well.
Likewise, Niśumbha, endowed with his own strength, exercised the sovereignty of Varuṇa and performed the functions of Agni; he also carried out the duties of Vāyu.
Then the gods, shaken off, deprived of their kingdom and robbed of their splendor,
all abandoned the Nandana grove and departed for mountain caves.
Deprived of their authority, they all wandered through the lonely forest—
without support, without refuge, devoid of splendor, and without weapons.
All the immortal gods, along with the ministers, were in the caves of the mountains,
in empty gardens, and in the deep recesses of the rivers.
Deprived of their positions and deprived of their senses, O Great King, those guardians of the world found no happiness anywhere; indeed, happiness depends upon destiny. 54.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-two.
O lord of men, those who are powerful, highly fortunate, possessed of great knowledge, and endowed with wealth,
likewise encounter suffering and wretchedness in due time.
This is a marvel, O Great King, the very working of Time itself:
that which makes a man a king, and then subsequently a beggar. (56)
The giver and the beggar, the powerful and the weak, the wise and the disabled, the lustful and the hero, and even the extreme coward—[all these he treats with impartiality]. (57)
Having performed a hundred sacrifices and attained the supreme throne of Indra, he again encountered supreme suffering; such is the course of time.
Time makes a man most righteous and endowed with knowledge;
yet it makes that very same person exceedingly wicked and utterly devoid of even a trace of knowledge.

One should not feel astonishment in any way regarding the workings of Time; even for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others, such miserable conduct occurs. Viṣṇu undergoes birth in wombs such as that of a boar, and Hara became a skull-bearer (Kapālī) solely through the power of mighty Time.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Fifth Book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, within the Glorification of the Blessed Goddess.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Vyāsa said:
All the gods were defeated, and Śumbha ruled over the kingdom.
In this manner, O best of kings, a thousand years passed away.
Then the gods, having been deprived of their kingdom, fell into an insurmountable anxiety;
afflicted by grief, they respectfully questioned their preceptor as follows. || 2 ||
"O Guru, tell me what must be done; you are the omniscient Great Sage. O Illustrious One, there exists a means for the cessation of suffering as well. (3)
Surely the Vedic mantras by the thousands are intent upon ritual practice;
indeed, it is said that the Sūtras have been observed to grant one's desired objects. (4)
Various sacrifices have been proclaimed which bestow the fruits of all desires;
perform them indeed, O sage, for you are well-acquainted with their performance.
Perform today, according to the prescribed rites, that method for the destruction of our enemies as taught in the sacred scriptures, so that there may be an end to our suffering.
O son of Aṅgiras, you ought to act this very day in such a way that,
according to your wisdom, there may be the destruction of the Dānavas through a malevolent rite (abhicāra).
Bṛhaspati said: "O Lord of the Gods, all mantras declared in the Vedas have their fruits dependent upon fate;
they are not independent, nor do they invariably bestow results. (8)
You are the deities of the mantras, yet you have become the sole vessel for suffering;
we have come into being through the power of time—what means of remedy can I employ? (9)
In sacrificial rites, Indra, Agni, Varuṇa, and others are worshipped;
having fallen into calamity, what will you, who are objects of such worship, do for us? (10)
"There is no remedy for events that are destined to happen;
nevertheless, one must employ a means—this is the instruction of the learned. (11)
For some wise men proclaim that destiny is powerful;
those who advocate for human effort declare that destiny is useless.
Fate and human effort—these two alone are considered the means for men;
one should never remain relying solely upon fate. (13)
The means must be determined in every way by reflecting again with one's own intellect;
therefore, I speak to you all after having reflected upon it repeatedly. (14)
In former times, the Blessed Lady, being pleased, slew the demon Mahiṣa;
then, praised by you, the Goddess granted a boon.
"Whenever you encounter calamities arising from the gods, O lords of the gods, I shall surely destroy those misfortunes whenever I am remembered. (16)
The twenty-second chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. [Page 305]
"Then, when you so desire, I should always be remembered by the gods;
being remembered, I shall destroy your greatest calamities. (17)
Therefore, having gone to the Himācala mountain, which is most beautiful,
perform the propitiation of Caṇḍikā with love.

"Those who know the ritual procedures for the seed-syllable of Māyā and are devoted to its preparatory practice (puraścaraṇa)—through the power of yoga, I know that she will become well-disposed toward me. (19)
"The end of your suffering is seen today; there is no doubt about this.
I have heard that the Goddess always resides on that mountain peak. (20)
When praised and fully worshipped, she will immediately grant your desired objects;
having made this firm resolve, go indeed to the Himalayas.
"The goddess shall perform all your tasks according to your desire.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, those gods departed for the mountain.
O great king, all those queens, intent on meditation, remained in the Himalayas,
constantly chanting the seed-syllable of Māyā with their hearts.
They paid homage to Mahāmāyā, the bestower of fearlessness upon her devotees,
and, filled with supreme devotion, they praised her with hymns and mantras.
Salutations to the Goddess, Sovereign of the Universe, the Mistress of Life, whose form is eternal bliss, who bestows joy upon the gods;
salutations to her who brings an end to the Dānavas, who grants manifold goals to human beings, and whose true nature is accessible through devotion. (25)
There is no limit to your names, nor is your form such as this; you exist in the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others.
You alone are the embodiment of power within all beings, always present at the times of the creation and dissolution of the world.
You are mindfulness, you are fortitude, and you alone are intelligence; you are old age, nourishment, contentment, firmness, splendor, and peace.
You are true knowledge, true prosperity, the goal, fame, and wisdom; you alone are the ancient seed of the universe. (27)
We bow today for the sake of peace to those very forms by which you perform the work of the gods here;
you abide within all beings as forgiveness, yogic sleep, compassion, and speech, through these auspicious forms. (28)
You have already accomplished the task for the gods at the outset, for that great enemy, blinded by pride, has been slain.
O Goddess, your compassion toward all the deities is well-known in the Purāṇas and sung in the Vedas.
What wonder is there in this, that a mother should joyfully protect and properly nourish her own son?
Since you are the mother of the ancient ones, perform this entire task with a single-minded heart as my helper. ||30||
O Goddess worthy of worship, we do not know the extent or the true nature of your virtues;
yet, considering us merely as objects of your compassion, O you who are capable of protecting, always shield us from all fears.

Without the discharge of arrows, without the striking of fists, and without spears, swords, or clubs, you alone are capable of slaying enemies; yet even so, O Lord of a hundred [eyes], your playful sport here is for the benefit of the world.
Fools do not know this eternal truth: that an effect cannot possibly exist without a cause;
we consider inference to be the means of valid knowledge, and you alone are the creator of this universe. (33)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-two.
Aja is the creator, Mukunda is the protector, and Hara is renowned in the Purāṇas as the destroyer;
yet these three were born from you at the beginning of the Yugas. You alone are the source of everything, and therefore you are the Mother.
O Goddess, you were propitiated by the three in ancient times, and you bestowed upon them the entire, formidable power (śakti).
United with you, they fulfill their desire for the very creation, protection, and destruction of the world.

Are those ascetics not of dull intellect and utterly deluded who do not take refuge in you, the mother of the universe—the supreme knowledge that bestows the fruits of all desires, grants liberation, and whose resolve is highly praised by the hosts of the wise? (36)
Those who are Vaiṣṇavas, Pāśupatas, and Sauras surely appear to be mere hypocrites;
they meditate neither upon you nor upon Lakṣmī, nor upon modesty, splendor, stability, fame, or even nourishment.
O Mother, you are served here by Hari, Hara, and others, as well as by the best of gods and asuras;
those men of small intellect on earth who do not worship you are surely deceived by fate. (38)
Hari himself colors the lotus feet of the ocean-born goddess with lac-dye; even the three-eyed Śiva is intent upon serving the pollen of the lotus feet of the mountain-born goddess. (39)

What is the use of stories about other men? Who does not worship the pair of your lotus feet? Even sages who have abandoned passion and home, whose intellects are perfected, worship your compassion and forgiveness.
O Goddess, those people who are not devoted to the worship of your feet have indeed fallen into the pit of saṃsāra;
afflicted by leprosy, abdominal tumors, and diseases of the head, they are burdened by poverty and wretchedness, being utterly deprived of floods of happiness. (41)

O Mother, we know that those who are skilled in carrying loads of wood or in the work of gathering fodder, yet are destitute of wealth and wives, must have never performed service to your feet in a previous birth due to their small-mindedness. (42)
Vyāsa said:
Thus praised by all the gods, Ambikā, filled with compassion, suddenly manifested herself, endowed with beauty and youth. (43)
The goddess was clad in divine garments, adorned with divine ornaments,
endowed with divine garlands, and anointed with divine sandalwood paste.
Possessing a beauty that deludes the world and endowed with all auspicious marks, she of peerless form came into the sight of the gods. 45.
Desirous of bathing in the Jāhnavī, that goddess, who possesses a divine form and is the enchantress of the enchantment of the universe, emerged from the mountain cave.
Smiling with affection, she who spoke as sweetly as a cuckoo addressed the gods, who were intent on her praise, with a voice as deep as a thundercloud. (47)
The Goddess said: "O best of gods, who is being praised so intensely by you?
For what purpose? Tell me your business; why are you overcome with anxiety, and from where has it arisen? (48)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of hers, the best of the gods, infatuated by the perfection of her beauty and their hearts stirred with love, spoke to her. (49)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 23.
The gods said:
O Sovereign of the Universe, we praise you; prostrate, we are at your feet, O ocean of compassion.
Protect us from all sufferings—we who are agitated and have been shorn by the Daityas. 50.
O Great Goddess, in the past, after you had slain Mahiṣa, the thorn in the side of the gods, you granted us this boon: "I am to be remembered always in times of distress. (51)
"By remembering you, I shall undoubtedly destroy the affliction born of the Daityas;
therefore, O Goddess, you have surely been remembered by us. (52)
"Today two asuras, Śumbha and Niśumbha, who are terrible to behold, have arisen as creators of obstacles for that man who is indeed to be slain today.
Also [arisen are] the powerful Raktabīja and the two asuras Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa."
By these and other very powerful ones, the kingdom of the gods was seized.
O lady of slender waist and great power, we have no other refuge; you alone are our recourse.
Therefore, perform the task for the sake of the distressed gods. 55.
The gods, ever devoted to the service of your feet, have been brought to calamity by the exceedingly powerful Dānavas.
O Goddess, make them free from suffering; O Mother, you alone be the refuge for those who are distressed. (56)

O Goddess, the protection of the entire world must now be undertaken by you, knowing that this universe was created by you at the beginning of the age; O Mother, O Mātaḥ, the Dānavas, filled with pride and intoxicated by their own strength, are inflicting suffering upon the world.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 22 ||
Then the twenty-third chapter.
Vyāsa said: Thus was the Goddess then praised by the deities, who were tormented by their enemies.
From his own body, he caused a supreme form to manifest.
Then Ambikā indeed emerged from the body of Pārvatī;
she is thereafter celebrated in all the worlds as Kauśikī. (2)
But when she had emerged, Pārvatī, due to the exchange of bodies, became black in form; she was then celebrated as Kālikā.
Dark as ink, most terrible, and increasing the fear of the Daityas, she was called Kālarātri; she bestows the fruits of all desires.
The supreme form of Ambikā shone forth, enchanting to the mind.
Adorned with every ornament and endowed with the quality of loveliness.
Then Ambikā, smiling, spoke thus to the gods:
"Dwell here without fear; I shall slay the enemy here."
Your task must certainly be accomplished; I shall roam through the battlefield and slay Niśumbha and the others for the sake of your happiness.
Having spoken thus, that goddess Kālikā, mounted upon a lion and intoxicated with passion,
took [the enemy] by the side and went to the city of the foe.
Having gone there, Ambikā stood in the grove accompanied by Kālikā;
then she sang there a sweet melody that deludes even the Deluder of the World.
Hearing that sweet song, the birds and deer fell into a state of enchantment,
while the gods stationed in the sky attained the highest joy.
At that moment, two fierce Dānavas named Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, servants of Śumbha, were sporting there by chance.
Upon their arrival, they then beheld Ambikā, who possessed a divine form, standing before them as Kālikā accompanied by song. 12.
O best of kings, having seen her of divine form, the two Dānavas were filled with wonder and quickly went to the side of Śumbha.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-three.
Having gone to his house and approached the lord of the Daityas as he sat there,
they bowed their heads to the king and spoke these sweet words.
O King, a beautiful woman, enchanting with desire, endowed with all auspicious marks, has arrived from the Himalayas, mounted upon a lion. (15)
"Such a woman as this does not exist in the world of the gods, nor likewise in the city of the Gandharvas; such a most excellent of women has never been seen or heard of anywhere on earth. (16)
And she performs such singing, O King, that it delights the people;
even the deer stand by her side, enchanted by her sweet voice. (17)
"Let it be known whose daughter she is and for what purpose she has come here;
O tiger among royal sages, let her be taken, for she is a woman worthy of you."
"Having understood this, take the beautiful-eyed woman as your wife in your home;
for it is certain that there is no woman of such a kind in this world. (19)
"O King, you have taken all the jewels of the gods;
why, O best of kings, do you not accept this woman of beautiful limbs?
[For she possesses] Indra’s glorious elephant Airāvata and likewise the Pārijāta tree."
"O King, it is said that you forcibly seized a seven-headed horse. (21)
O King, by your power you have seized that divine celestial chariot, made of precious gems and adorned with a swan-banner; it is truly wonderful.
O King, the lotus-treasure of Kubera has been seized by you;
that bright umbrella of the Lord of Waters has also been taken by you by force. (23)
Moreover, O best of kings, the noose of Varuṇa, who was conquered by force, has also been seized by your brother Niśumbha at his will. (24)
The ocean gave you a garland of unfading lotuses, O Great King, as well as various jewels out of fear of you. (25)
O King, having conquered and seized even the power of Death and the most terrible staff of Yama at will, what else remains to be described? 26.
"O King, the wish-fulfilling cow born from the ocean has been seized today;
likewise, Menakā and the other celestial nymphs remain under your control.
Thus, all these jewels have been taken by you, even by force."
Why is this excellent woman, a jewel of the wilderness, not taken [by you]? ||28||
O Lord of the Earth, all those radiant treasures of yours in the household shall likewise come into being through her, becoming as precious as jewels themselves.
O Lord of Daityas, no woman so dear exists in the three worlds;
therefore, bring her quickly and make that captivating lady your wife. (30)
Vyāsa said: Having heard those sweet words, spoken with sweet syllables, he,
with a serene countenance, spoke to Sugrīva who was standing nearby.
"Go, Sugrīva, and perform the duty of an envoy; O wise one, you must speak there in such a way that the slender-waisted lady comes to us. (32)
A wise man should employ two means toward beloved women;
those skilled in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) say they are conciliation and bribery. (33)
Even when a deviation is employed, a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) arises;
however, in the case of suppression, there is a disruption of rasa (rasabhaṅga). Therefore, these two are censured by the wise.
O messenger, what woman, when afflicted by desire, does not come under one's control through words characterized by conciliation and generosity, as well as gentle speech accompanied by jesting? (35)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words spoken by Śumbha, which were very pleasing and eloquent, Sugrīva went swiftly to that place where the Mother of the World resides.
He beheld the lovely, fair-faced lady seated upon the lion;
having bowed down, he addressed these sweet words to the Mother of the World: ||| 37 ||
The messenger said:
"O lady of beautiful thighs, Śumbha—the enemy of the gods, handsome in every limb, the sovereign of the three worlds, the heroic and all-conquering king—shines with splendor. (38)

I have been sent as a messenger to you by that high-souled one, according to his desire. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa*, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 23. 309. "I am a leader who has been dispatched to your presence at the will of that Great-Souled One."
With a mind intensely distressed by its attachment to hearing of your form. ||39||
O slender-limbed one, listen to his words preceded by love, just as the lord of the Daityas spoke to you after prostrating himself. 40.
"All the gods have been conquered by me; I am the sovereign of the three worlds.
O beloved, standing here forever, I receive the sacrificial portions. (41)
"Surely the sky has been robbed of its essence by me and rendered devoid of jewels;
for whatever jewels belonged to the gods, those I have carried away. (42)
"O beautiful lady, I am the enjoyer of all jewels in the three worlds;
all the gods, the Daityas, and human beings are subject to my will. (43)

Having reached Karna through your virtues and entered the interior of his heart, he has been made entirely subject to you; I am your servant—what shall I do? (44) Command me, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks; I shall do that, following your will.
I am your slave, O beautiful-limbed one; protect me from the arrows of Kama! (45)
"O lotus-eyed one, resort to me, who am overwhelmed by passion and dependent on you;
having become the mistress of the three worlds, enjoy unsurpassed pleasures. (46)
"O beloved, I shall be your servant until death;
O lady of noble hips, I am forever invulnerable to both asuras and humans. (47)
O fair-faced one, you shall always be endowed with good fortune;
O beautiful lady, sport wherever your heart finds delight. 48.
Having reflected upon his words in her heart, she, slow with intoxication, spoke these sweet words out of love: "Tell me whatever must be said. (49)
"O lady with tremulous eyes, I shall tell that to Śumbha immediately.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the messenger, she smiled very charmingly.
The Goddess, who accomplishes the purpose of the gods, spoke these sweet words to him.
The Śrī Devī said:
"I know Niśumbha and the exceedingly powerful King Śumbha. (51)
The conqueror of all gods, the slayer of enemies, the repository of all virtues, and the enjoyer of all prosperity. || 52 ||
He was a donor, exceedingly brave, handsome, and possessed a form like that of the god of love;
endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, he was incapable of being slain by gods or humans. ||53||
Having learned this, I have come here desiring to see the great Asura;
for even gold and jewels arrive to increase their own splendor. (54)
I have indeed come from afar to see my own husband;
I have seen all the gods and the humans on earth. || 55 ||
The Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and others who were exceedingly handsome—all of them, terrified by the fear of the auspicious [deity], trembled and lost their senses. || 56 ||
"Having heard of your auspicious qualities here, I have come today with the desire to see you.
Go, O illustrious messenger, and speak to the mighty Śumbha."
In a secluded place, with gentle words, he spoke these words at my request:
"Knowing you to be the best among the strong and the most beautiful among the handsome. (58)
A donor, virtuous, heroic, and proficient in all branches of knowledge;
a conqueror of all the gods, skillful, fierce, and of noble lineage. (59)
"O lord of men, I am truly desirous of you as my husband—you who enjoy all jewels, who are self-dependent, and exalted by your own power; I am worthy of you. (60)
O high-minded one, O best of Rākṣasas, they have come here to this city of their own will; however, I have a certain purpose regarding my marriage.
"O King, in my childhood, while playing with my companions in a secluded place by chance, I previously observed some minor vow. (62)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-four.
Out of pride in the strength of his own body, he said in secret before his friends:
"A hero with a strength equal to mine will clearly defeat me in battle. (63)
"Having ascertained his strength and weakness, I shall choose that desire.
Upon hearing these words, her friends laughed, their minds filled with astonishment. (64)
What cruel and truly wonderful vow has she performed so swiftly?
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too, having recognized such power as mine, [should act accordingly].
Having defeated me today by your own strength, fulfill your own desire—
either you or your younger brother, O sibling, having come together upon the field of battle.
"O handsome one, having defeated me here in battle, perform the marriage."
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. ||23||
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the goddess, that messenger spoke in amazement.
"What do you say, O lady of beautiful eyes? For [this] is due to the audacity inherent in the nature of women. (1)
"O Goddess, O beautiful lady, how can you wish to defeat in battle him by whom Indra and the other gods, as well as the Daityas and others, were conquered?
There is no one such as he in the three worlds who could achieve victory in battle."
Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one, standing before him now in battle?
O beautiful one, one should never speak a word without due reflection;
having ascertained the strength of both oneself and the other, one should speak what is appropriate for the occasion. (4)
"Śumbha, the lord of the three worlds, has been infatuated by your beauty;
that king entreats you, so fulfill his desire, my dear. (5)
Abandoning your foolish nature and honoring my words, devote yourself to either Śumbha or Niśumbha; I tell you this for your own benefit.
The erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), the most excellent of the nine sentiments, should be cultivated with supreme joy by all sentient beings who possess intelligence in every respect. (7)
O child, if you do not come, the enraged lord of the earth will now send other obedient messengers and carry you away by force.
"O lady of beautiful thighs, those Dānavas, arrogant in their strength, will surely drag you by the hair and carry you with force into the presence of Śumbha. (9)
"O slender-limbed one, preserve your own modesty; abandon all rashness. Go to his side with honor, for you are indeed worthy of respect. (10)
Where is battle with sharpened arrows, and where is the pleasure born from sexual union?
Discerning the essential from the non-essential, carry out my words effectively. 11.
"Worship either Śumbha or Niśumbha; you shall obtain supreme fortune.
The Goddess said:
"O messenger, O highly fortunate one, it is true that you are indeed skilled in speaking. (12)
"I know for certain that Niśumbha and Śumbha are powerful; how could my vow, made since childhood, be rendered otherwise? (13)
Therefore, tell me whether Niśumbha or Śumbha is the more powerful;
for without a battle, no one shall become my husband by mere excellence of form.
"O King, having conquered me by force at will, take my hand now;
know me to be a woman who has come here with a desire for battle. (15)
Give me battle, for you are capable; practice the duty of a hero!
If you fear my trident, go to the netherworld without delay.
"O messenger, go quickly and respectfully tell your master: 'If you still have a desire for life, then abandon the three cities and the earth. (17)

Having reflected upon what is appropriate, that one of great strength will act accordingly. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 24. [Page 311] 311. Having reflected upon what is appropriate, that one of great strength will act accordingly.
In this cycle of existence, it is indeed the duty of a messenger to speak only the truth. (18)
"O knower of dharma, act accordingly toward both the enemy and your husband; do not delay.
Vyāsa said: Then, having heard those words endowed with sound policy... (19)
Then, filled with wonder, the messenger departed, speaking with reason and confidence; having gone to the lord of the Daityas, he reflected upon it again and again. (20)
Bowing at his feet with humility, he replied to that king with words consisting of statecraft, gentle in manner and pleasing in speech.
The messenger said:
"One must speak what is both true and pleasing; for that reason, I am indeed consumed by anxiety.
O Indra among kings, words that are both true and pleasing are indeed difficult to find. (22)
The king may indeed become angry in every way with those who speak unpleasant words;
but how could he [be angry] with one who has appeared before him in person, or whose strength and weakness belong to whom? 23.
I shall say nothing of her conduct, which is beyond the scope of knowledge;
I saw her desiring battle, arrogant, and speaking harsh words.
O Mahāmati, listen correctly to what was said by her:
"In my youth, this vow was previously made by me in jest. (25)
"In the presence of my friends, he has declared that I shall certainly marry him who truly defeats me in battle and shatters my pride. (26)
"I shall choose that very man as my husband, for he is indeed equal in strength;
O best of kings, I must not make my vow false. (27)
"Therefore, fight, O knower of dharma; having conquered me, bring me under your control.
Having heard these words uttered as "So be it," I approached him. (28)
"O Great King, do as you wish for your own pleasure;
she has set her mind on battle, equipped with weapons, and moves with the gait of a lion. (29)
"O King, she remains steadfast; let that which is appropriate be done.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Sugrīva, the lord of men—
He questioned his heroic brother, who was standing nearby and possessed of great strength.
Śumbha said:
"O brother, tell me truly, O high-minded one, what should be done here? (31)
"There is a certain woman who desires to fight; she now challenges me.
I shall go to the battle, or you, endowed with strength, may go. (32)
"Whatever pleases you, Niśumbha, that indeed must be done by me.
Niśumbha said:
"O hero, neither I nor you shall go to the front of the battle."
"O Great King, dispatch Dhūmralocana with haste;
having gone there and conquered her in battle, let him bring back that woman of lovely eyes."
"Śumbha will arrive here; let the wedding preparations be made."
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-four,
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of his younger brother, Śumbha—
In anger, he dispatched Dhūmralocana, who was standing by his side.
Śumbha said:
"Dhūmralocana, go at once, surrounded by a great army! (36)
"Let whoever—be it a god, a dānava, or a man of great strength—seize and bring back this innocent girl, who is deluded by the pride of his own prowess. (37)
Having become his ally, he must be slain by you with speed;
then, having killed Kālī who stands at his side, take her back again. (38)
"Come here quickly after having accomplished this unsurpassed task;
you must protect that virtuous woman while she is discharging her soft arrows. (39)
O hero, with great effort, those soft-bodied ones with slender waists must be slain along with their companions who bear weapons in battle. (40)
"In every way she must not be killed; she must be protected with great effort.
Vyāsa said:
Thus commanded by the king, Dhūmralocana then departed with speed.
Having offered salutations, surrounded by his auspicious army, he went quickly to the battlefield,
likewise accompanied by sixty thousand wicked men.
Then he beheld the goddess situated in a lovely grove;
seeing her, whose eyes were like those of a young deer, he was filled with humility.
He spoke these gentle words, adorned with logical reasoning:
"Listen, O illustrious goddess; Śambhu is afflicted by the pain of separation from you. (44)
The one skilled in policy, fearing a breach in the aesthetic flavor (rasa), has himself sent a messenger to your side with words of conciliation. (45)
O lady of beautiful countenance, the leader arrived and spoke words that were contrary [to the truth];
by those words, my husband, the king, became despondent at heart regarding the funeral pyre.
Śumbha, deluded by passion, became one who knew only the path of sensual pleasure;
he did not understand the words of that messenger, which were pregnant with reason. 47.
"O proud lady, he who defeated me in battle and spoke those harsh words did not understand that battle is indeed of two kinds. (48)
The [sorrow] arising from love and that arising from exertion are intended according to the distinction of the recipient;
O fair-thighed one, yours is remembered as born of love, while that of the enemy is born of exertion. (49)
"O beloved, the first [son] is known to bestow happiness, while the one born from the enemy [of the moon] bestows sorrow;
O lady of excellent limbs, I truly know your heart's desire. (50)
"The disposition for battle is revolving within your heart.
Having understood from this that it was born of him, the lord of men sent me to your presence, O King. (51)
Today the auspicious one dispatched her, surrounded by a great army;
O highly fortunate one, listen to my gentle words. 52.
Worship the auspicious Lord of the three worlds, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods;
having become his beloved chief queen, enjoy unsurpassed pleasures. (53)
"The mighty-armed Śumbha, who understands the power of desire and its objects, will defeat you; employ various amorous gestures (hāvas), and he too will manifest corresponding emotions (bhāvas). (54)
In that time, this Kali will indeed be a witness to our sport;
thus, through the union of our agreement, my husband shall be a knower of the supreme truth.
Having conquered you, he will leave you exhausted upon his comfortable bed—
your body stained with blood from the wounds of his nails, and your lower lip torn by his teeth.
The king will restore you, who are broken and drenched in sweat;
there shall arise within your mind a desire born from the battle for Rati.
O beloved, by the mere sight of you, Śumbha remains completely subdued in every respect. *Śrīmad-devī-bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 25. [Page 313]
"Follow my word; it is wholesome, beneficial, and pleasing."
Victory to the leader of the hosts, the inauspicious one! O highly esteemed one, you who are exceedingly proud, those who are fond of combat with missiles are surely of little fortune. 59.
O beloved, you who are ever fond of amorous play, it does not befit you to leave King Aśoka withered; rather, cause him to blossom by striking him with your foot.
Sprinkle the bakula tree with rum and likewise treat the kurabaka in the same way.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Goddess," in the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 24 ||
Then, the twenty-fifth chapter: Vyāsa said—
Having spoken these words, Dhūmralocana ceased his speech.
Then Kālī, smiling, replied with these charming words. || 1 ||
"You are a buffoon, you scoundrel; you speak like an actor.
You harbor vain desires in your mind while speaking so sweetly. (2)
"Strong and endowed with power, you have been sent by that evil-minded one;
engage in battle now, O dull-witted one, and abandon your futile talk. (3)
Having slain Śumbha, Niśumbha, or even others more powerful than you,
the enraged Goddess returned to her own abode, victorious through the impact of her arrows.
Where is that dull-witted Śubha, and where is she who deludes the entire world?
Indeed, this marriage arrangement between these two in this worldly existence is utterly improper.
Does a lioness, afflicted by excessive lust, ever make a jackal her mate? Or does a female elephant, or even a cow, make a donkey or a gayal her husband? (6)
Go, Śumbha, and speak these true words to Niśumbha:
"Engage in battle; otherwise, depart for the netherworld immediately by force."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of Kālikā, that Daitya Dhūmralocana, his eyes bloodshot with rage, spoke to her, O highly fortunate one. (8)
"Having slain you, who are difficult to behold, in battle like a lion intoxicated with pride, I shall indeed take her and go before the king every day. (1)
