O you who delight in quarreling, I am now afraid here at this moment for fear of the destruction of my aesthetic flavor; otherwise, O lover of strife, I shall slay you today with my sharpened arrows.
Kālikā said:
"O dull-witted one, why do you boast? This is not the way of archers.
Discharge your arrows according to your own strength; you shall go to the assembly of Yama. (11)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words, the Daitya took up his firm bow and showered Kālikā with arrows whetted on stone.
The gods, stationed there upon their excellent celestial chariots, with Indra at their head, praised her and cried out, "Victory! to the goddess. 13.
A most terrible battle ensued between the two of them,
fierce with arrows, swords, maces, spears, clubs, and other weapons.
Having first slain the donkeys with the discharge of her arrows, Kālikā shattered that arrayed chariot and laughed again and again. (15)
Having mounted another chariot and blazing as if with fury,
O Bhārata, he unleashed a fierce shower of arrows upon Kālika.
She too swiftly cut down his unerring arrows, while Kālikā released other shafts of fierce velocity upon the Dānava.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-five.
By those arrows, his thousands of rear-guards were struck down;
and having slain the charioteer and the mules, he shattered the chariot with great force.
She immediately cut that bow with arrows resembling serpents;
she brought joy to the gods and likewise blew her conch shell.
Deprived of his chariot, the enraged Dhūmralocana seized a firm iron club made entirely of metal and approached the seat of the chariot.
Threatening her with his voice, Karāla, who resembled Time itself, said:
"O you of ugly form and tawny eyes, I shall slay you this very day! (21)
Having spoken thus, when he suddenly approached and hurled his iron club,
Ambikā instantly reduced him to ashes with a mere roar of "huṃ."
Seeing the Daitya reduced to ashes, the soldiers, overwhelmed by fear, immediately fled, crying out "Alas, O Father! along the way.
Seeing that Dānava Dhūmralocana slain, the gods,
standing in the sky, joyfully released a rain of flowers.
Then, O King, the battlefield became terrible,
strewn with slain dānavas, horses, donkeys, and likewise elephants.
Vultures, crows, ravens, hawks, jackals, and likewise hyenas danced and wheeled around the deceased who had fallen upon the battlefields. (26)
Ambikā, having abandoned that battlefield and gone to a distant place,
uttered a fierce and terrifying blast on her conch shell.
Hearing that sound of fear while staying in his palace,
Śumbha then saw the Dānavas returning, broken and drenched in blood.
And those with their feet and hands severed, even those placed upon couches,
with their backs, hips, and necks broken, crying out many times— (29)
Seeing them, Śumbha and Niśumbha asked: "Where has Dhūmralocana gone?
Why have they returned defeated? And why has that fair-faced woman not been brought back? (30)
"O dull-witted ones, tell me where the army has gone;
who is it whose conch-blast, increasing our fear, is heard today? (31)
The Gaṇas said:
"All the forces have been struck down and Dhūmralocana has been slain;
Kālikā has performed superhuman deeds upon the field of battle. (32)
The sound of the conch shell, pervading the sky, shone forth;
it brought joy to the hosts of gods and caused grief among the Dānavas. || 33 ||
O Lord, when all [the enemies] had been struck down by that lion, the chariots were shattered and the horses destroyed by the falling of his arrows. (34)
Seeing the entire army shattered and Dhūmralocana struck down, the gods stationed in the sky joyfully showered a rain of flowers.
"We have reached the firm conclusion that victory will certainly not be ours;
O Indra among kings, deliberate upon this with your ministers who are most skilled in counsel. (36)
This is a marvel, O Great King, that the Mother of the World, who is alone and devoid of an army, stands ready for battle with you;
a young girl, fearless and solitary, mounted upon a lion and intoxicated with passion.
O Great King, this wondrous and marvelous thing appears immediately.
O Great King, having deliberated upon peace, war, staying put, or marching forth today, perform your duty as you see fit.
"O scorcher of enemies, although there is no force in his presence,
it is said that in times of calamity all the gods will indeed become his rear-attackers."
At that time, Hari and Śaṅkara were known to be standing near him;
today the world-protectors remain nearby, stationed in the sky. (41)
O scorcher of enemies, the hosts of Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and likewise humans,
as well as their allies, should be considered [as present] at that time.
By our own intelligence, it is known in every way to be thus:
there is no hope for Ambikā's assistance, nor any hope for the success of that task. (43)
"One alone is capable of destroying the entire world, including all things moving and stationary;
what then need be said of all the Dānavas? This is certain. (44)
"O highly fortunate one, having understood this from the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 26, do as you please.
Followers should speak words that are beneficial, truthful, and measured. (45)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of theirs, Śumbha, the crusher of enemy forces,
summoned his younger brother and questioned him while standing in private.
"O brother, Dhūmralocana has been slain this very day by Kālikā;
his entire army has been destroyed, and the assembled hosts have been broken."
Ambikā, intoxicated with pride, indeed utters a sound like a conch;
the course of Time is in every way difficult to comprehend even for the wise.
Grass indeed acts like a thunderbolt, and a thunderbolt itself acts like grass;
the strong may become weak—the course of destiny is such. (49)
I ask you, O illustrious one, what must be done hereafter? Ambikā is surely unapproachable; for what reason has she come here? (50)
"O hero, it is appropriate for you to either flee or fight; tell me quickly!
In this crisis, I consider you to be light-headed despite being my elder. (51)
Niśumbha said:
"O sinless one, neither flight nor taking refuge in a fortress is appropriate;
for battle alone is in every way the highest good against her."
Accompanied by my army and relying upon the foremost warriors, I shall go to battle;
having slain that weak woman, I will return here with speed.
If it shall come to pass that I die, you must deliberate upon what is to be done again and again.
Or perhaps, due to powerful destiny, it shall turn out otherwise.
Having heard these words of his, Śumbha spoke to his younger brother:
"You stay here; let Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa go forth accompanied by their forces."
In this matter, it is not appropriate to release the elephant in order to capture a hare;
Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa are both exceedingly powerful and are entirely capable of killing her.
Having spoken thus to his brother and addressed those two of great strength, King Śumbha spoke these words to Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, who were standing before him.
"Go, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, surrounded by your own armies, to quickly slay that shameless woman who is arrogant with pride. (58)
Then, having seized and slain the tawny-eyed Kālikā in battle, O highly fortunate ones, you may return after having accomplished this great task. (59)
If that proud Ambikā does not come even when seized,
then she must be slain with extremely sharp arrows upon the field of battle.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 25 ||
Then the twenty-sixth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Thus commanded, the two heroes Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, who were possessed of great strength, [set forth].
Accompanied by a vast army, they both proceeded with great speed into the battle.
Seeing the goddess, who acts for the welfare of the gods, standing there,
those two of great prowess then spoke words of conciliation.
O foolish girl, do you not know Śumbha, the oppressor of the hosts of gods, and Niśumbha, who possesses great heroism and is arrogant from his victories over Indra? ||3||
O lady of beautiful hips, you are alone, accompanied only by Kālī and a lion;
O poorly bound one, you wish to conquer Śumbha, who is endowed with all powers. (4)
There is no one at all to slay you, whether woman or man;
even those gods who impel you toward your own destruction are but yourself.
O slender-limbed one, reflect and perform your duty by weighing the strength of yourself and your opponent;
because you possess eighteen arms, you harbor pride that is utterly false.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-six.
Of what use are many arms that cause pain, or weapons that bring only exhaustion, before Śumbha, the conqueror of the gods who is resplendent in battle? (7)
O elephant-tamer who severed the trunk of Airāvata and caused the destruction of the tuskers,
O victor over the hosts of gods, accomplish the purpose cherished in your heart.
O beloved, you vainly indulge in pride; do my pleasing word, which is beneficial for you, O large-eyed one, and which bestows happiness and destroys suffering. (9)
Actions that cause suffering should be abandoned from afar by the wise; those that bestow happiness should be cultivated by those proficient in the true principles of the scriptures.
O cuckoo with four fangs, behold the great army of Śumbha, which brings about the supreme triumph of the gods through its crushing of their enemies. 11.
Indeed, to abandon direct perception and rely on inference alone is surely in vain;
for a wise person does not engage in an action that is accompanied by doubt. (12)
"Śumbha, the enemy of the gods, the supreme foe who is invincible in battle—for that reason the gods, oppressed by the lord of the Daityas, are impelling you here. (13)
Therefore, O lady of pure smiles, you have been deceived by their affectionate words;
this instruction of the gods, which accomplishes their own purpose, will lead only to your sorrow. (14)
Having set aside a friend for worldly affairs, one should rely upon a friend for the Dharma;
the gods are intent on their own interests, but I have spoken the truth to you. (15)
Worship Śumbha, the lord of the gods, the conqueror and sovereign of the world—clever, handsome, heroic, and an expert in the science of love. (16)
"By the command of Śumbha, you shall obtain sovereignty over all the worlds;
having made this firm resolve, worship your husband, the auspicious one. (17)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Caṇḍa, the Mother of the World roared with a sound as deep as a thundercloud and spoke again.
"Go away, you fool! Why do you speak such deceptive words?
Having abandoned Hari, Hara, and the others, why would I worship Śumbha as my husband? (19)
"I must not have any husband, nor must I act with a husband;
behold, I alone am the mistress of all beings. (20)
Many Śumbhas have been seen by me, and Niśumbhas by the thousands;
hundreds of Daityas and Dānavas have already been slain by me. (21)
Before me, hosts of gods have perished age after age;
likewise, the multitudes of Daityas shall surely meet their destruction once again today.
O Daitya, Time itself has arrived here as the destroyer;
you are exerting yourself in vain for the protection of your progeny. (23)
O high-minded one, engage in battle for the sake of protecting the dharma of heroes;
death is inevitable and difficult to avoid, but fame must be preserved by great souls. (24)
"What business have you with Niśumbha and the evil-minded Śumbha?
Having attained the supreme duty of a hero, go to heaven, the abode of the gods! (25)
Śumbha, Niśumbha, and all your other kinsmen here shall now follow behind you as your attendants. (26)
"Today I shall gradually bring about the destruction of all the Daityas.
Cast aside your despondency, O dull-witted one; engage in battle, O lord of men! (27)
I shall now slay you, your brother,
as well as Śumbha, Niśumbha, and the blood-seeded Raktabīja who is intoxicated with pride.
Having slain all the other Dānavas on the field of battle, I shall go to my proper place; stay or depart quickly.
"Take up your weapon quickly, O wicked one, and fight with me now! Why do you prattle false words that are entirely pleasing only to cowards? (30)
Vyāsa said:
Thus incited by her, the two Daityas, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa,
filled with rage and proud of their strength, swiftly made a terrible sound with their bowstrings.
She too made the sound of a conch shell, filling the ten directions;
and the powerful lion, becoming enraged, let out a roar at that moment.
At that sound, Śakra and the other immortals rejoiced then. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 26. 317.
The sages, yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, sādhyas, and kinnaras. 33.
A fierce battle then took place there between Caṇḍikā and Caṇḍa, terrifying to the cowardly, fought with arrows, swords, maces, and other weapons.
The Goddess cut down the fierce, released arrows with her own sharp shafts;
then Caṇḍikā again discharged fierce iron bolts like serpents.
Then, in that battle, the sky was covered with arrows,
like locusts appearing at the end of the clouds, bringing terror to the farmers.
Even though he was shaven-headed, Muṇḍa fell impetuously into the battle along with his soldiers;
enraged and extremely fierce, he indeed released a rain of arrows.
Seeing that great mass of arrows, Ambikā became intensely enraged;
through her anger, her face became like a dark cloud.
Then Kālī, whose eyes were like plantain flowers and whose brows were knit in a frown,
quickly emerged from the surface of her forehead.
Clad in tiger skins, she was cruel, with an elephant hide as her upper garment;
she bore a garland of severed heads, was terrifying, and had a belly like that of a dried-up well.
Holding a sword and a noose, she was exceedingly terrifying and a giver of fear;
bearing a skull-topped staff, she was fierce like another Kālarātri.
With her expansive face, repeatedly flicking her tongue,
and possessing broad hips, she swiftly struck down the asura soldiers.
Having seized those great heroes with her hands, she, filled with rage,
forcefully cast the Daityas into her mouth and slowly crushed them with her teeth.
Seizing by the hand elephants equipped with bells, she placed them in her mouth;
having devoured them along with their riders, she let out a loud, boisterous laugh.
In the same way, having seized horses and camels along with their charioteers,
he bit them in the mouth with his teeth most terribly.
Seeing the army being slaughtered, the two great asuras Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa covered the Goddess with a continuous stream of arrows.
And Caṇḍa, with great force, hurled at the Goddess a discus that possessed the brilliance of the fierce-rayed sun and was the weapon of the wielder of the discus; and he roared again and again.
Seeing him roaring and that Sudarśana discus, which possessed the luster of the sun, Kālī severed that radiant weapon with a single arrow.
The fierce Caṇḍī struck him with sharp arrows whetted on stone;
severely afflicted by the goddess’s shafts, he fell to the earth in a swoon. 49.
Seeing his brother fallen, Muṇḍa was then overcome with grief;
out of anger, he unleashed a shower of arrows upon Kālikā.
With the weapons of reeds discharged by his power, he instantly reduced Caṇḍikā’s most terrible shower of arrows, released from her severed head, to pieces as small as sesame seeds.
He struck him again with a crescent-shaped arrow;
that one of great prowess fell upon the earth, deprived of his intoxication.
Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the host of Dānavas;
all the immortals, free from distress, rejoiced as they stood in the sky.
Recovering from his swoon, Caṇḍa seized a massive club and swiftly struck Kālikā on her right arm.
Having evaded that blow from the mace, Kālikā swiftly bound that great asura with a noose of arrows released by means of a mantra.
Then Muṇḍa, rising up and seeing his younger brother forcibly bound,
arrived fully armed, holding a spear firmly in his hand.
Then Kālī, seeing the Dānava approaching, quickly and with great force bound her second brother. ||57||
Having seized those two of great prowess like the moon and the sun, Caṇḍa and Muṇḍī,
laughing loudly, approached Ambikā.
Having arrived, he then said to her: "O beloved, take these two animals;
these two Dānavas, invincible in battle, have been brought for the sake of the sacrifice of war."
Then, seeing those two brought before her like two wolves, Caṇḍikā,
the Mother Ambikā, spoke these words full of sweetness to Kālikā.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-seven.
Do not kill, do not release; O four-armed one, you who delight in battle!
The accomplishment of the gods' purpose must be swiftly achieved by you.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, Kālikā spoke to her again:
"When the sacrifice of battle is highly renowned and the sword is established as the sacrificial post (yūpa)..."
"I shall perform the ritual slaughter so that no violence occurs," having said this, the goddess then [struck] the heads of those two with her sword.
Kālī swiftly cut [him] apart and joyfully drank his blood;
seeing the two Daityas thus slain, Ambikā spoke with delight.
The task of the gods has been accomplished by you; therefore, I grant you today an auspicious boon:
since Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa have been slain by you, your name shall be Kālikā.
She shall become widely renowned on the surface of the earth as Cāmuṇḍā. ||65||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having seen those two Dānavas slain, the remaining soldiers fled.
Then, having fled from there, they all went toward the king. || 1 ||
Some with their limbs shattered by arrows, others with their hands severed, and still others with bodies streaming with blood, advanced while wailing. || 2 ||
Having gone there, they all joyfully raised a great cry to the lord of the Daityas:
"Protect us! Protect us, O Great King! Today Kālikā is devouring us! (3)
By her, the two great heroes Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the tormentors of the gods, were slain;
all the soldiers were devoured, and we have been broken, overcome with fear.

O Lord, the battlefield was made terrifying by Kālikā through the fallen elephants, heroic horses, and blood-stained foot-soldiers. A small stream was created flowing with floods of blood, with flesh for its mud,
hair for its moss, and adorned with the broken wheels of chariots.
Abounding with fish whose fins and tails were severed, and filled with heads and seeds,
it brought fear to the timid while increasing the joy of the gods.
"Protect your family, O Great King; go quickly to Pātāla.
The enraged Goddess will bring about your destruction immediately; of this there is no doubt. (8)
O Lord of the Danujas, the lion also devours the Dānavas as they come;
likewise, the goddess Kālikā strikes them down in many ways with her arrows.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too, with a provoked mind, are forming a false intention for death along with your brother Śumbha.
"What will this cruel woman do, this destroyer of her family, for whose sake, O Great King, you desire to kill your kinsmen? (11)
O Great King, victory and defeat in this world are dependent on destiny;
a wise man should not bring about great suffering for the sake of a small gain. (12)
Behold the wondrous work of Fate, O Lord, upon which the world depends:
all these Rākṣasas have been slain by this single woman. 13.
"You are indeed the conqueror of the world-protectors, accompanied as you now are by your army;
yet a single young woman seeks you in battle—how very surprising! (14)
Formerly, you performed austerities at Puṣkara, the abode of the gods.
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived there to grant you a boon.
O great king of noble vows, you were addressed by the Creator: "Choose a boon."
At that time, you indeed requested immortality from Brahmā.
May there be no death for me from gods, daityas, or humans; nor from snakes, kinnaras, or yakṣas, even from those denoted by masculine gender. (17)
Therefore, O Lord, this woman has arrived through a female form with the intent to kill you.
"Do not wage war, O Indra among kings; reflect upon this now with your intellect. (18)
For this goddess is indeed considered the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the supreme primordial nature (Prakṛti);
O Indra among kings, at the time of the end of the aeon, she is the bringer of universal destruction.
The auspicious Goddess, the sovereign of the worlds and of the gods, is composed of the three qualities yet characterized by tamas, and is endowed with all powers. (20)
Invincible, imperishable, eternal, omniscient, and ever-arisen;
she is Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā), and the abode of all the gods. || 21 ||
She is without attributes and yet possesses attributes; she is perfected, the bestower of all perfections, and imperishable.
She is bliss itself, the giver of bliss, Gaurī, who grants fearlessness to the gods.
Knowing this, O Great King, abandon this state of enmity;
seek refuge, O Lord of Kings, and the Goddess will protect you. (23)
"Be her obedient servant; restore your own lineage to life, and let those Daityas who remain after the slaughter become long-lived. (24)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, Śumbha, the crusher of the hosts of gods,
spoke these truthful words, O best of heroes, which were endowed with merit.
Śumbha said:
"O fools, you who have been broken on the field of battle, preserve your pride!
Go quickly to the netherworld; the hope for life is very strong. (26)
The entire world is subject to destiny; what anxiety, then, do I have regarding victory? Just as Brahmā and the other gods are likewise subject to destiny, so too are we.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and this Rudra, as well as Yama, Agni, Varuṇa,
Sūrya, Candra, and Śakra— all these are indeed subject to the power of fate.
What is the use of this sluggish mind of mine? Whatever is to be, will be.
Let there be such exertion as is appropriate; such is the nature of destiny. (29)
Having reflected in this way in every respect, the wise never grieve;
here in this world, the men of knowledge do not abandon their own duty out of fear of death.
Happiness, suffering, as well as the lifespan, life, and death of human beings, occur when the proper time has arrived; in every respect, they are ordained by the gods. (31)
Brahmā falls at his own appointed time, as does Viṣṇu and the Lord of Pārvatī; at the end of their lifespan, all the gods, including Indra, meet their destruction.
Likewise, I too am now entirely subject to the power of Time;
I shall go either to destruction or to victory by means of fulfilling my own duty.
"Even though challenged by this weak woman for battle, how could I live for a hundred autumns as one intent on flight? (34)
Today I shall engage in battle; let whatever happens here happen. Whether it be victory or even death, I accept it however it may be.
"Destiny is false," so say the wise who advocate for human effort;
their words are consistent with reason, for they know how to speak. (36)
Without effort, desires are certainly not fulfilled;
it is only the cowardly who prattle, "What is to be will be. (37)
The foolish, not the wise, proclaim that the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is powerful; what proof is there for its existence? How can that which is unseen be seen? (38)
That something unseen might ever be seen anywhere is a mere terror instilled by fools;
this is merely the mind’s fixation upon suffering without any basis. (39)
Seated near the wheel and remaining there, she who brings about nourishment [says]:
"Without exertion, flour can never be ground in any way whatsoever. (40)
When effort is exerted, a task invariably reaches completion in every way;
however, if there is a deficiency in that effort, the task may not even come to fruition.
Having understood the place and the time, as well as one's own strength and the enemy's force, the task will surely be accomplished; such is the word of Bṛhaspati.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus resolved, the lord of the Daityas dispatched the great asura Raktabīja to battle, surrounded by a vast army.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 27.
Śumbha said:
"O mighty-armed Raktabīja, go to the field of battle!
O illustrious one, wage war according to the strength that has been bestowed upon you. (44)
Raktabīja said: "O Great King, you need not worry even the slightest bit;
I shall slay her and bring her under your control."
Behold my skill in battle! Where is this young girl, beloved of the gods?
Having conquered her by force in combat, I shall make her your slave. (46)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, O best of the Kurus, the great asura Raktabīja mounted his chariot and departed, surrounded by his own army.
Surrounded [by his retinue], he mounted his chariot and went forth to see the Goddess stationed upon the mountain. ||48||
And seeing him approaching with multitudes of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, the Goddess blew her conch shell,
which struck fear into all the Daityas and increased the joy of the gods. (49)
Hearing the fierce sound of the conch, the exceedingly swift Raktabīja approached Cāmuṇḍā and spoke these gentle words.
Raktabīja said: "O child, why do you terrify me, thinking me to be a coward, my dear?
O slender-limbed one, do you not know Dhūmralocana by the sound of his conch?"
"I am Raktabīja by name; I have come here into your presence. O speaker of unseasonable words, if you desire battle, be ready; I have no fear."
"Behold today my power, O beloved! Those cowards whom you have seen—I am not among their number; engage in battle as you wish. (53)

You have previously served the elderly, you have heard the treatises on ethics (nītiśāstra), you have studied the knowledge of worldly affairs, or perhaps you have participated in the assemblies of the learned. (54)
O beautiful one, if you possess knowledge of literature and the science of the Tantras, then listen to my words, which are wholesome, true, and supported by valid cognition. (55)
Among the nine rasas, indeed, only two attain preeminence in the assemblies of learned men: the erotic rasa and the rasa of tranquility.
Of these two, the erotic sentiment alone is established first in the state of kingship;
indeed, Viṣṇu dwells with Lakṣmī, and the four-faced Brahmā with Sāvitrī.
Indra lies with Śacī, and Śaṅkara with the Daughter of the Mountain;
the tree with its creeper, the deer with the doe, and the pigeon with the female pigeon.
Thus, all living beings are intensely addicted to union; so too are those other men who are timid and have not attained the power of enjoyment. (59)
Those who [act thus] are indeed self-mortifiers; they are fools deceived by fate.
Not knowing the true essence of worldly existence, they are deceived by those intent on deception.
For they are devoted to the essence of tranquility and are skilled in sweet conversation; where is there knowledge, and where is dispassion, while the god of love reigns supreme? (61)
When greed, fierce anger, and destructive delusion exist,
you too, O auspicious lady, must make your husband charming.
"Whether it be Śumbha, the conqueror of the gods, or the exceedingly powerful Niśumbha," Vyāsa said;
having spoken thus, that Raktabīja ceased speaking as he stood before him.
Having heard this, Cāmuṇḍā, Kālikā, and Ambikā likewise laughed.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 27 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-eight. [Page 321] 323.
Then the twenty-eighth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O lord of the people, having laughed, the goddess then spoke to him.
With a voice as deep as a thundercloud, he spoke these words, which were endowed with logical reasoning. || 1 ||
"O dull-witted one, I have already spoken; why do you boast before this messenger with words that are appropriate yet fraught with malice? (2)
If there should be anyone in the three worlds who is my equal in beauty, strength, and wealth, him I choose as my husband. (3)
"Speak, Śumbha and Niśumbha! A vow was made by me long ago;
therefore, fight me, and having conquered me, perform the marriage according to the prescribed rites."
Indeed, you have come here by his command for the sake of accomplishing his purpose;
either wage war or go to the netherworld with your husband.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the goddess, that Daitya, filled with indignation,
swiftly loosed terrible arrows upon the lion.
Seeing those arrows resembling serpents in the sky, Ambikā,
with great lightness of hand, cut them down in an instant with her own sharp shafts.
Ambikā struck the great asura Raktabīja with arrows released from her bow, drawn back to her ear and sharpened on stone. ||8||
Struck by the goddess’s arrow, the wicked one fell into a swoon upon his chariot;
and when Raktabīja had fallen, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose. ||9||
All the soldiers cried out and said, "We are slain!
Then, hearing that most dreadful tumultuous roar, Śumbha [was filled with rage].
He indeed commanded all the Daitya forces to exert themselves.
Śumbha said:
"Let all the Dānavas, including the Kāmbojas, set forth, surrounded by their own armies. (11)
"Others too are exceedingly powerful heroes, especially the Kālakeyas.
Vyāsa said:
Thus was the entire fourfold army commanded by Śumbha.
The Goddess went forth onto the field of battle against him who was possessed by pride;
and seeing that Dānava Bala approaching, Caṇḍikā [confronted] him.
The Mother of the Universe quickly and repeatedly made a terrifying and fear-inducing sound with her bell,
and she likewise produced the twang of her bowstring and the blast of her conch.
By that sound, Kālī became wide-mouthed;
and having heard that terrible roar, the lion, the vehicle of the Goddess, [also reacted].
That powerful one also roared, producing a most extraordinary fear;
hearing that sound, the Dānavas were overcome with rage.
In that very long and terrible battle, which caused the hair to stand on end, all those of great strength hurled their weapons at the goddess.
And the powers of Brahmā and the other gods, as well as those of the Vedas, went to Caṇḍikā; whatever was the form, ornament, and vehicle of each respective deity [was likewise bestowed]. (18)
At that time, the goddesses set out for the field of battle in such forms: Brahmāṇī, mounted upon a swan and bearing a rosary and a water-pot, went to the field of battle. (19)
The power of Brahmā has arrived, celebrated as Brahmāṇī;
likewise Vaiṣṇavī, mounted upon Garuḍa and bearing the conch, discus, and mace. (20)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-eight.
Padmahastā arrived, adorned with yellow garments;
Śāṅkarī, however, was mounted upon a bull and bore an excellent trident.
The goddess Śivā bears a crescent moon and has a serpent for her bracelet;
Kaumārī is mounted upon a peacock, holds a spear in her hand, and possesses a beautiful countenance. 22.
Desirous of battle, Indrāṇī arrived, possessing the form of Kārttikeya,
with a beautiful face and mounted upon a magnificent white elephant.
With a vajra in her hand and exceedingly fierce, she advanced toward the battle;
Vārāhī is considered to have the form of a sow and to sit upon a mature corpse. (24)
Nārasiṃhī, assuming a form resembling that of Nṛsiṃha, and Yāmyā, mounted upon a buffalo, holding a staff in her hand and inspiring fear. (25)
Then, in the battle, Śucismitā arrived with the form of Yama;
likewise came the spear Vāruṇī and Kauberī, who was intoxicated with pride.
Such beings of such forms, surrounded by their respective armies, departed;
and seeing them arrive, the Goddess attained great joy.
The gods rejoiced in their own state, while the Daityas fell into fear;
there, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, was surrounded by them.
Having arrived at the battlefield, he spoke thus to Caṇḍikā:
"Let the asuras be slain quickly for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods."
Having slain both Niśumbha and Śumbha, as well as whatever other Dānavas remained,
and having destroyed the entire Daitya army, she made the world free from fear.
Let the Śaktis return each to their respective abodes;
let the gods who partake of the sacrifice be present, and let the Brāhmaṇas be devoted to the performance of the sacrifice. ||31||
May all living beings, both stationary and moving, be content;
likewise, may calamities and epidemics be pacified once again. (32)
"May the clouds rain abundantly in due season, and may agriculture likewise yield great fruit.
Vyāsa said:
While Śaṅkara, the Lord of Gods and benefactor of the world, was speaking thus, (33)
From the body of Caṇḍikā, however, there emerged a wondrous power— terrifying,
exceedingly fierce, and resounding with the howls of hundreds of jackals.
Then, with a smiling face, she of terrible form said to the five-faced one:
"O God of gods, go quickly toward the lord of the Daityas."
O Śaṅkara, enemy of Kāma, act accordingly and speak to Śumbha, who is agitated by passion, and to Niśumbha, who is arrogant with pride, according to my word. (36)
"Leaving Triviṣṭapa, you must go quickly indeed to Pātāla;
let the gods return to heaven, and let Turāṣāṭ occupy his auspicious throne. (37)
May the deities obtain their station in heaven and their shares of the sacrifice, if your desire for life should be even greater. (38)
"Friends, go quickly to Pātāla where the Dānavas dwell;
or else, summoning your strength, if you desire battle, then come for death. (39)
"Then let my auspicious attendants come and feast upon your flesh.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of hers, the wielder of the trident (Śiva) acted with haste.
Having gone to the king of the Daityas, Śumbha, as he sat in his assembly, Śiva said: "O King, I have been sent by Ambā; I am Hara, the destroyer of Tripura. (41)
Having come here into your presence to accomplish every benefit for you,
leave both heaven and earth and depart quickly.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter 29: Pātāla, where Prahlāda and Bali, the best among the strong, reside.
"Or, if you have the desire for death, then go quickly!
I shall surely slay all of you swiftly in battle.
Thus spoke the Great Queen for the sake of your welfare.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus caused those excellent Daityas to hear these words, which were like nectar,
the benevolent wielder of the trident returned.
Impelled by her toward the nature of Śambhu against the Dānavas,
she became renowned throughout the entire three worlds as Śivadūtī.
Having heard those words of the goddess, which were difficult even for Śaṅkara to perform, they too quickly went forth to battle, armored and with weapons in hand. || 47 ||
Having swiftly approached the battlefield against Caṇḍikā,
the Dānavas struck her with sharp arrows, whetted on stone and drawn back to their ears.
Tearing them apart with her mace and spear, she moved about there, devouring the dānavas by striking them down at their vital points.
There on the field of battle, he rendered the mighty Dānavas lifeless by hurling water from his water-pot, and he reduced them to the state of Brahmāṇīs.
Māheśvarī, mounted upon her bull, struck down the Dānavas in battle with her trident of extreme velocity and cast them to the ground.
By the falling of her discus and the blows of her mace, Vaiṣṇavī swiftly deprived the Dānavas of their lives and stripped them of their heads.
With a blow from his Indra-like thunderbolt, he cast them to the ground;
the foremost of the Daityas were crushed by the strike of Airāvata’s trunk.
With blows from the snout of a boar and by striking with her tusks,
she, filled with wrath, slew hundreds of Daityas and Dānavas.
Tearing apart the foremost of the Daityas with her fierce claws, the Nārasiṃhī roamed the battlefield devouring them and roared again and again. (55)
Śivadūtī cast them down upon the ground with a loud burst of laughter;
then Cāmuṇḍā and Kālikā, filled with haste, devoured them. 56.
Stationed upon his crest, Kaumārī, drawn by the ears with arrows sharpened on stone, indeed struck down the enemies in battle for the sake of the gods. || 57 ||
At the forefront of the battle, he struck down the Daityas— who were bound by the Vāruṇa and Upāṃśu nooses—
upon his back, rendering them unconscious and deprived of their senses.
Thus, the army of Dānavas, though possessing great vigor and prowess, was crushed by the host of Mothers and became intent on flight. || 59 ||
A great roar arose there from that ocean of forces;
then the gods showered flowers upon the Goddess and her hosts.
Hearing that terrible roar and the cry of victory,
and seeing the Daityas fleeing, Raktabīja quickly became enraged.
Then, beholding the gods roaring in that manner, the mighty and radiant Daitya Raktabīja advanced toward the battle.
Armed and seated upon his chariot, making a wondrous sound with his bowstring,
he then approached the goddess, his eyes raised and blood-red with rage.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 28 ||
Now the twenty-ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said: This boon was granted to that Dānava by Śiva.
O King, listen to that which is most wonderful; I shall relate it to you. || 1 ||
Whenever drops of blood fall from his body onto the earth,
Daityas arise, identical in form and identical in prowess to him.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-nine.
"May the innumerable Dānavas born of blood possess great heroism"—thus was an exceedingly wonderful boon granted by Rudra. (3)
Proud because of that boon and filled with wrath,
he swiftly advanced in battle to slay the Goddess together with Kālī.
Seeing the Vaiṣṇavī power seated upon Garuḍa,
the lord of the Daityas struck that lotus-eyed goddess with his spear.
She parried it with her mace; that Śakti, joined with her own power, struck the great asura Raktabīja with her discus.
From his body, struck by the wheel of the chariot, much blood flowed forth,
like red mineral streams from the peaks of a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Wherever and whenever drops of blood fell upon the ground, thousands of men arose there, possessing forms identical to those [who had fallen]. || 8 ||
Aindrī struck the terrible demon Tamasura with her thunderbolt;
overcome with rage, she also struck Raktabīja, and blood flowed forth.
Then, from that blood, many Raktabījas were born;
they possessed his vigor, bore his form, were equipped with weapons, and were intoxicated by the frenzy of battle.
Enraged, Brahmāṇī struck him violently with the Brahma-staff,
and Māheśvarī tore the Dānava apart with her trident.
The Nārasiṃhī pierced that great asura with blows from her claws;
enraged, she struck that lowest of Rākṣasas with a blow from her snout.
And Kaumārī likewise struck him in the chest with her spear;
he too, enraged, pierced them all with showers of sharp arrows.
With blows from his mace and spear, he struck each of the Mothers individually.
Enraged by that, the Śaktis pierced him with blows from their arrows.
Caṇḍikā cut his weapons apart with her own sharp arrows;
and the goddess, being exceedingly enraged, struck him with other shafts.
From his body there flowed forth blood in many streams,
and from that, thousands of heroes resembling him appeared.
The world was pervaded by Raktabījas, born from floods of blood, who,
with their loud shouts and weapons, were engaged in a truly marvelous battle.
Seeing those Raktabījas striking them repeatedly, the gods became terrified; they were deeply dejected and overcome with grief. || 18 ||
How will the thousands of Daityas—those Dānavas of massive bodies and great prowess, born from blood—meet their destruction today? (19)
"Only Caṇḍikā is here, as well as Kālī and the Mothers;
all the Dānavas must be conquered by these—this is indeed a difficult task. (20)
Either Niśumbha or Śumbha, endowed with great strength, will suddenly come to the battle; from that, a great calamity will arise.
Vyāsa said: When the gods, thus agitated by fear, had reached the highest state of despondency,
then [Brahmā] spoke to Ambikā, the lotus-eyed Kālī.
O Cāmuṇḍā, quickly make your mouth wide open;
O swift one, drink with haste the blood produced from the stroke of my weapon! 23.
"Roam today through the battlefield at will, devouring the Dānavas;
I shall slay them with sharp arrows, as well as with maces, swords, and clubs."
"Act accordingly, O large-eyed one, so that not even a single drop of her blood shall fall upon the ground right now. (25)
Being devoured at that time, no other Daityas shall arise;
thus their destruction will surely come to pass, and not otherwise.
"I shall slay the Daitya; you, meanwhile, drink quickly, drinking all the blood as you strive for the destruction of the enemy. (27)
Having thus brought about the destruction of the Daityas and having granted the entire stable kingdom of the celestial realm to Indra, we shall go wherever we please.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter twenty-nine. Vyāsa said:
Thus addressed by Abhikā, the goddess Cāmuṇḍā, of fierce prowess,
drank all the blood produced from the body of Raktabīja.
Ambikā quickly struck him with a sword and a mace;
then Cāmuṇḍā, the slender-waisted one, devoured the fragments of his body.
When he too, enraged, struck Cāmuṇḍā with blows,
she nevertheless quickly drank his blood and devoured him.
Those other cruel blood-born ones, the mighty Raktabījas—they too have all been struck down, devoured, and drained of their blood. 32.
All the artificial ones were devoured; as for that one who was a natural asura, he too was struck down and slain, having been utterly mangled with a sword.
When the fierce Raktabīja was slain, the other dānavas in the battle fled from there, trembling with fear. ||34||
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", they spoke to Śumbha while utterly overwhelmed; their bodies stained with blood, they spoke in great distress, their weapons fallen away and their senses lost. (35)
That Raktabīja was struck down by the Queen Mother (Ambikā),
and Cāmuṇḍā drank all the blood from his body.
And whatever other heroic dānavas there were, all were slain by the lion with its exceedingly swift mount, while others were devoured by Kālī.
O King, we have come to tell you of your deeds in battle, as well as the most wonderful conduct of the Goddess in the conflict. (38)
"O Great King, I am invincible in every respect by the Daityas and Dānavas, as well as by the Gandharvas, Asuras, Yakṣas, Pannagas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas. (39)
O great king, other goddesses led by Indrāṇī arrived there in great numbers,
fighting with their mounts and weapons.
By them, with their excellent weapons, the entire army of the Dānavas was destroyed;
even Raktabīja, O lord of kings, was swiftly struck down.
Even a single goddess is difficult to withstand, how much more so when accompanied by them?
Even a lion of immeasurable luster slays the rākṣasas in battle.
Therefore, having deliberated with your ministers, let that which is appropriate be carried out;
hostility with her is not fitting, for peace alone brings happiness. (43)
It is entirely wonderful that she has slain these Rākṣasas;
even Raktavīja has been killed, and his blood too has become like a child's.
Other Daityas were struck down in battle by Ambikā, O King,
and all their flesh was indeed devoured by Cāmuṇḍā on the field of war.
O Great King, it would be better to enter the netherworld or even to serve her; however, you must not engage in battle with Ambikā.
This woman is indeed no ordinary mortal; she is a fulfiller of the purpose of the gods' mission.
She has arisen as this powerful goddess, Māyā, who destroys [all obstacles]. 47.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these truthful words of theirs, Śumbha, deluded by fate and desiring to die, replied thus with his lips quivering. (48)
Śumbha said:
"Go to Pātāla for refuge, or else, overcome by fear;
today itself, with my weapons raised, I shall slay her and them."
Having conquered all the gods and established a most prosperous kingdom, how can I, agitated by fear of women, enter the netherworld? (50)
Having slain all the attendants headed by Raktabīja in battle, why should I depart for the sake of saving my life, abandoning such vast fame? (51)
Death, ordained by Time, is indeed unavoidable for living beings;
who would abandon that fame so difficult to attain out of fear of it, which is acquired through birth? (52)
"Niśumbha, I shall go mounted upon my chariot to the field of battle;
having slain her, I will return, or else I will not return at all. (53)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter thirty.
But you, O hero, accompanied by your army, become my rear-guard;
by your own prowess, lead that woman to the abode of Yama with your sharp arrows. (54)
Niśumbha said: "I shall go today and slay that wicked Kālikā;
I will return quickly after having seized that Mother Ambikā."
Do not worry, O Indra among kings, on account of this wretched woman;
where is this young girl, and where is the strength of my arms that brings the entire universe under its control? (56)
"O brother, casting aside this great distress, enjoy excellent pleasures;
I shall bring back that proud woman, filled with honor, according to your desire. (57)
O King, while I am present, it is not fitting for you to go into battle;
having gone myself, I shall surely bring back the glory of victory for your sake.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to his eldest brother, the younger one, proud of his strength,
mounted a vast chariot, equipped for battle and surrounded by his own forces.
Having performed auspicious rites for battle, he proceeded swiftly and with great speed,
accompanied by bards and panegyrists, equipped with weapons and his full regalia.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now the thirtieth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Having made a firm resolve for either death or victory, Niśumbha—
Exerting himself, powerful, and heroic, he approached the goddess in battle. ||1||
Śumbha also arrived there, surrounded by his own army;
the king, an expert in the delights of battle, became a spectator of the fight. ||2||
Then the gods stationed in the sky, shrouded by masses of clouds,
as well as the hosts of Yakṣas led by Indra, remained there desiring to witness the battle.
Then Niśumbha, having entered the battle and taken up his Śārṅgaka bow,
unleashed a rain of arrows, terrifying the Mother of the Universe.
Seeing Niśumbha discharging volleys of arrows in battle, Caṇḍikā took up her excellent bow and laughed repeatedly with a loud voice. ||5||
The goddess Kālikā said: "Behold the foolishness of these two!
O Kāli, they have now come here into my presence for the sake of death."
Having witnessed the terrible slaughter of the Daityas as well as the destruction of Raktabīja, these two,
deluded by my Māyā, still maintain their hope for victory.
For this hope is indeed powerful; it never leaves a man, even when his strength is broken, his power taken away, he is ruined, deprived of his wings, and rendered senseless. (8)
Bound by the snares of desire, these two have come together for battle;
O Kālī, Śumbha and Niśumbha must be slain by me in combat. (9)
"These two are on the verge of death, having been overtaken by divine delusion;
while all the gods look on, I shall slay them this very day. (10)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to Kālikā, Caṇḍī swiftly covered Niśumbha, who stood before her, with a multitude of arrows drawn back to her ear.
The Dānava also cut her arrows with his own sharp shafts;
a most terrifying battle took place between the two of them.
Shaking his mane, the powerful lion plunged into the ocean of the army like an elephant into a lake,
[striking] the Dānavas standing before him with his claws and the blows of his tusks.
And he devoured those whose limbs were shattered, like elephants intoxicated with rut.
Thus,
while the army was being churned by Kesarin at that time, in the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 30.320.
Then Niśumbha, having drawn his excellent bow, rushed forward.
Many other Daitya lords, enraged, with their tongues pressed against their teeth and eyes bloodshot, approached the Goddess in order to kill her. || 16 ||
Thereupon Śumbha, surrounded by his army, arrived with speed;
falling upon Kālikā in rage, he sought to seize the Mother of the World.
Having arrived there, he beheld Ajāmbikā standing before him—
both fierce with the sentiment of wrath and lovely with the sentiment of love.
Beholding her, whose eyes were wide and cast sidelong glances, the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, lovely with blood-red eyes, yet likewise with eyes reddened by anger; (19)
Abandoning his desire for marriage and likewise casting hope for victory far away,
he stood with his bow strung, having made a firm resolve to die.
To that Dānava, the Goddess spoke these words preceded by a smile,
while those Daityas were listening on the summit of the battlefield.
"Go away, you wretches! Either go to the netherworld or into the ocean, casting off your weapons right here and fixing your hope firmly on life!"
Alternatively, let all those whose lives were taken by me through envy or malice on the field of battle,
having attained the bliss of heaven, sport there free from all distress.
Cowardice and heroism do not exist at all in any way;
I truly grant the gift of fearlessness, so let everyone go as they please.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard her words, Niśumbha, his heart agitated by passion,
took up a sharp sword and a shield marked with eight moons.
Running with speed, he struck the lion— who was fierce with his paw—
on the head with his exceedingly powerful sword, while whirling the Mother of the World.
Then the goddess, having evaded the falling sword with her own mace,
struck him on the base of the arm with an axe at that time.
Struck by the sword at the base of his arm, that Mahāmada then endured the pain and struck Caṇḍikā once more.
She too let out a terrible sound from her bell, which struck fear into men;
desiring to slay Niśumbha, she drank the liquor again and again.
Thus occurred a battle between the gods and the dānavas, both seeking victory over one another, which was exceedingly terrifying.
Carnivorous birds, cruel dogs, jackals, vultures, herons, and crows, being exceedingly delighted, danced. (31)
The battlefield shone, strewn with the fallen bodies of the foremost gods, joined by streams of blood and crowded with the carcasses of elephants and horses.
Seeing the Dānavas fallen, Niśumbha, filled with extreme rage,
quickly advanced toward Caṇḍikā, seizing his terrible mace.
Intoxicated with pride, he struck the lion on the head with his mace;
having struck it, he smiled and struck the goddess once more.
Then the Goddess, seeing Niśumbha standing before her striking her while he was exceedingly enraged, spoke these words.
The Goddess said:
"Wait, O dull-witted one, until I drive this sword into your neck; then you shall go to the abode of Yama. (36)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the goddess Caṇḍikā, composed in mind, swiftly severed the head of Niśumbha with her sword.
With his head severed by the Goddess,
that most terrifying headless trunk (kabandha) wandered about with a mace in hand, striking terror into the hosts of deities.
The goddess severed his feet and hands with her sharp arrows;
then that sinner, resembling a mountain, fell down lifeless into the water. 39.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter thirty.
When that Daitya Niśumbha of terrible prowess had fallen, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from his army, which was trembling with fear.
Abandoning all their weapons, the soldiers, drenched in blood,
went toward the royal palace while all of them raised a tumultuous cry.
Having observed them closely as they arrived, Śumbha, the slayer of enemies, asked: "Where is that Niśumbha? How have you been defeated and fled?"
Having heard those words of the king, they, bowing deeply, said:
"O King, your brother lies slain at the forefront of the battle. (43)
The heroes who were struck down by her, as well as their followers and subordinates—we have all come here to report the entire account of what has transpired to you. (44)
Niśumbha has now been slain there by that Caṇḍikā;
O King, this is no longer the time for battle upon the field of the wounded. (45)
Reflect thus: "Surely some supreme woman has arrived here for the sake of the gods' mission, in order to slay the race of Daityas. (46)
This is not merely an ordinary woman; she is the unsurpassed power of the Goddess, whose conduct is inconceivable and who is difficult to be known even by the gods. 47.
Assuming various forms, she is exceedingly skilled in the root of illusion;
the auspicious goddess wears diverse ornaments and bears all weapons. 48.
Profound and of secret conduct, she is like another Kālarātri;
she reaches the further shore of the shoreless, she is full, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
The gods stationed in the intermediate space praise her, free from fear from any quarter.
And [he saw] the most wonderful Śrī Devī, performing the work of the gods.
Fleeing is the highest duty; by all means, one must protect the body.
For it is said that when this body is preserved, our own happiness will be attained in due time.
O King, victory in battle shall be yours; of this there is no doubt.
Time makes one strong at one moment and weak at another. (52)
Furthermore, having made him powerful, Time indeed places him at the disposal of victory;
for at some point, Time makes the giver a beggar. (53)
Within a short time,
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, or even the Lord of Pārvatī will surely make the giver of wealth a beggar, brought under the power of Time.
Indra and all the other immortals—time itself is their sovereign lord.
Therefore, wait for time; it is now adverse to you.
O King, he stood face-to-face with both the gods and the demons as the cause of their destruction; indeed, there is but one destiny for all, and none can escape Time.
One must understand his activity even as he assumes various forms:
at times there is the manifestation of men, and likewise at times their dissolution. (57)
Time is one cause of arising, and another is the cause of destruction;
O Great King, all these, including Indra himself, are directly perceived by you, O Goddess. (58)
Those Asuras who were previously made to pay tribute by Kāla when he was face-to-face with them, have now become powerful through that very same Kāla when he has turned his back on them. || 59 ||
Kāla utterly destroys and brings about both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
in this matter, neither Kālī nor the eternal gods are the cause. (60)
O King, having reflected upon it, do as seems best to you;
this is the time, and there is no other reason for this, nor for the Dānavas again. (61)
Śakra, having gone before you, was defeated in battle and rendered weaponless;
likewise were Viṣṇu, Rudra, Varuṇa, Dhanada, and Yama.
Likewise, O Indra among kings, having observed that the world is subject to the power of time, go quickly to Pātāla; living there, you shall attain well-being.
But when you have died, O Great King, your enemies, filled with joy,
will wander everywhere singing auspicious songs.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. ||30||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter thirty-one.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, Śumbha, the lord of the Daityas,
then spoke quickly to his soldiers with eyes agitated by anger.
Śumbha said:
"O wretches! Why do you speak such foul words? Having killed my ministers and brothers, how can I, devoid of shame, continue to live and roam about?"
Time is the most powerful agent of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds;
what concern is it to me, when that irresistible Lord is formless?
Let that which is to be happen; let him do what he does.
I have no anxiety whatsoever regarding either death or life.
Even Time itself, though it may be conceived otherwise, is nowhere able to act differently.
And the rain-cloud never rains during the month of Śrāvaṇa. ||5||
Sometimes, during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa, Māgha, or Phālguna, it rains suddenly out of season; therefore, this [rain] is not considered primary.
Time is merely an instrument, for destiny is indeed more powerful;
everything is ordained by destiny and does not happen otherwise—this is the truth.
I consider fate alone to be supreme; fie upon useless human effort!
For even Niśumbha, who was the conqueror of all the gods, has been slain by her. (8)
When even that great archer Raktabīja has met his destruction, then why should I abandon my fame and cling to the hope for life? (9)
When the time arrives, measured by two parārdhas, Brahmā himself,
the creator of the world and the sovereign lord, meets his end with speed.
Indeed, during a single day of Brahmā, which consists of a thousand cycles of the four yugas,
five and nine Indras respectively fall from their celestial abodes, and then [others] arise again.
In the same way, when the three qualities (guṇas) are present, Viṣṇu prepares for death;
likewise, when two qualities are present, Śaṅkara attains peace.
Some, deluded by the thought of death, remain motionless as if ordained by fate;
yet even the earth, the mountains, and the sun and moon shall perish. (13)
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Since this body is impermanent, it is fame that must be preserved as something enduring. 14.
"Let my chariot be prepared quickly; I shall go to the field of battle.
Let victory or even death come this very day through destiny. (15)
Having spoken thus to his soldiers, Śubha quickly mounted his chariot and set out for where Ambikā was situated on the Himālaya mountain.
His fourfold army—
consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry— set forth there, well-equipped with many weapons.
Having gone there, Śumbha beheld the Mother of the Universe seated upon Mount Acala— she who fascinates the three worlds, the beloved one, riding upon a lion.
Richly adorned with all ornaments and endowed with all auspicious marks,
she was being praised by the gods dwelling in the sky, as well as by gandharvas, yakṣas, and kinnaras.
She was being worshipped with flowers, specifically those born from the Mandāra trees,
as she produced the sound of a conch shell and the enchanting resonance of bells.
Upon seeing her, Śubha, deluded by passion, fell into a state of infatuation;
struck by the five-arrowed god of love, he reflected thus in his mind: ||21||
"Oh, how perfect is this form! Oh, how wonderful is this youthfulness! And how marvelous is this tenderness and fortitude, which are usually mutually contradictory! (22)
Delicate, with exceedingly slender limbs, and having manifested youth all at once—how strange it is that this young girl is devoid of any signs of amorous passion! (23)
Equal in beauty to Kāmakāntā and endowed with all auspicious marks, who is this Ambikā? Indeed, she destroys even those of great strength.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter thirty-one.
What means should be employed here by which she might come under my control?
For neither mantras nor other methods are effective in the presence of that swan-eyed one for my accomplishment. || 25 ||
"For she consists entirely of mantras, she is enchanting and proud with passion;
how might this beautiful woman of excellent complexion come under my control? (26)
"It is not proper for me to go to the netherworld from this battlefield; this one of great strength must be won over through conciliation, bribery, or sowing dissension. (27)
"What should be done, and where should one go, when such a crisis has arisen?
Death here is not the best course, for it would destroy the reputation earned through my wife. (28)
The sages have declared that death in battle is a source of auspiciousness, provided it occurs between two warriors of equal strength who are indeed fighting one another. (29)
This woman, created by fate, the best among hundreds of women, has arrived here;
she is exceedingly powerful and will surely bring about the destruction of our lineage. (30)
Why should I now employ conciliatory words in vain? For she has come here for the purpose of killing me; will she be appeased by conciliation? (31)
She cannot be moved by gifts, being adorned with various weapons; and sowing dissension is likewise fruitless, for she is entirely under the control of all the gods. (32)
Therefore, death is better than fleeing from battle;
let there be either victory or death today according to the prescribed rule.
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected thus, Śumbha took recourse in the quality of goodness (sattva);
becoming firmly resolved for battle, he spoke to her who stood before him.
"Drink and fight today, O beloved; this exertion of yours is in vain.
You are indeed a fool among women, for this is never the proper conduct. (35)
The eyes of women are their arrows; their eyebrows alone are the bow;
their gestures and expressions are the weapons; and the wise man is the target. (36)
In this [battle], armor and body-unguents are the adornments, and the chariot is the mind's desire;
the low murmur of speech is the sound of the kettledrum, and never anything else. (37)
For women, wielding other weapons is undoubtedly a mockery;
O beloved, modesty alone is their ornament, and never indeed audacity.
A noble woman engaged in combat appears as if harsh;
how, indeed, can her breasts, which ought to be well-concealed, endure the drawing of a bow? (39)
Where is slow movement, and where is running while wielding a mace?
Here, Kālikā bestows wisdom, while Cāmuṇḍā is the supreme mistress.
Seated in the midst of the mantra of Caṇḍikā, Śivā is of harsh voice in her fondling;
her vehicle is the king of beasts, who strikes fear into all living beings.
"O woman of excellent complexion, you have abandoned the sound of the lute to produce the sound of a bell; everything regarding beauty and youth is contradictory [to this]. (42)
"If you have a desire for battle, O beautiful woman, then become ugly:
have protruding lips, deformed nails, be cruel, and have eyes the color of a crow."
With long legs, protruding teeth, and the appearance of cat-like eyes—
assuming such a form, remain steady in battle.
Speak harsh words, and then I shall engage in combat.
Having seen such a woman with beautiful teeth, my hand does not feel at ease. || 45 ||
"O fawn-eyed one, resembling the beloved of Kāma, I shall slay you in battle!
Vyāsa said:
Seeing him speaking thus, afflicted by lust, the Mother of the World [spoke]. (46)
Preceded by a smile, she spoke these words, O best of the Bharatas.
The goddess said:
"O dull-witted one, deluded by the arrows of passion, why do you despair? (47)
"O fool, I am standing here as a mere spectator; engage in battle with Kālikā!"
Or they shall do so with Cāmuṇḍā on the battle-field suitable for you.
"Strike me as you please; I do not venture to fight with you.
Having spoken thus, the Goddess addressed Kālikā with sweet words. (49)
"Kill him, O Kālikā, you who are cruel, in this cruel battle dear to the Kurus!
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, Kālikā, impelled by Time and possessing the form of Time, [acted].
Seizing her mace, she stood in the battle with swift exertion;
between the two of them, a most terrifying combat ensued.
While all the gods and the high-souled sages were looking on,
Śumbha then raised his mace and struck Kālikā in battle.
Kālikā struck the king of the Daityas violently with her mace;
Caṇḍī shattered his chariot, which was radiant with gold.
Having killed the donkeys, she of the dreadful roar quickly struck Dāruka;
then, filled with rage, he took up a heavy mace and proceeded on foot.
Then, laughing, he struck between Kālikā’s arms;
having evaded the blow of the mace, he quickly seized his sword.
He severed his left arm, which was adorned with sandalwood paste and still grasping a weapon;
with his arm cut off and deprived of his chariot, he leaped forward with a mace in hand.
Then, having arrived shortly thereafter, Kālī struck Kālikā; with her sword, she then severed her right arm.
Laughing, she indeed severed him along with his mace and his arm-guard;
enraged, he rushed forward with speed to deliver a kick to her feet.
Kālī, acting with great haste, severed his feet with her sword;
even though his hands and feet were cut off, he cried out, "Stay! Stay! (59)
He ran swiftly toward Kālikā, as if terrifying her;
seeing him approaching, lotus-like [Viṣṇu], Kālikā—
He violently severed the head from the neck, which flowed profusely with a torrent of blood;
when that head was cut off, it fell to the ground like a mountain.
His vital breaths departed swiftly from his body;
seeing the Daitya fallen and lifeless, the gods, including Indra, [rejoiced].
Then they praised that goddess Cāmuṇḍā as well as Kālikā;
auspicious winds blew there, and the quarters of the sky became exceedingly clear.
The fires used for the oblation became auspicious, with their flames turning to the right;
and those Daityas who remained after the slaughter, having bowed down to the Mother of the World, [departed].
Having cast aside their weapons, O King, they all departed for Pātāla.
Thus has this entire supreme account of the Goddess’s deeds been told to you—
the slaying of Śumbha and his followers, as well as the protection of the gods.
Human beings on earth recite this entire narrative.
Those who always listen with devotion indeed become successful in their aims;
one without a son obtains sons, and one without wealth obtains great riches.
The sick person is freed from disease and shall obtain all desires;
he who recites this auspicious life-story shall have no fear of enemies.
The man who constantly hears and recites this becomes possessed of liberation. ||68||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Slaying of Śumbha," in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"O Sage, the greatness of Caṇḍikā has been fully described by you."
And by whom was she previously propitiated through the practice of the three modes of conduct? || 1 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter thirty-two.
To whom did she become gracious and grant her boon? By whom was this great fruit obtained? O ocean of mercy, tell me how one propitiates the Goddess who fulfills all desires. || 2 ||
O Brahman, O highly fortunate one, tell me in detail the procedure for worship, as well as the procedure for ritual service,
and furthermore, the procedure for the fire sacrifice.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the king, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Satyavatī, was pleased and replied to the monarch regarding the worship of Mahāmāyā.
Vyāsa said: Formerly, in the Svārociṣa Manvantara, there was a king named Suratha,
who was supremely noble and devoted to the protection of his subjects.
He was a speaker of truth, devoted to his duties, and a worshiper of the Brahmins;
he was constantly intent on devotion to his guru and remained faithful to his own wife.
Generous, ethical, and non-opposing, he was the sole master of the science of archery;
while he was thus protecting the kingdom, the Mlecchas dwelling in the mountains [attacked].
Having forcibly become enemies, they formed a fourfold army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; intoxicated with pride, they were filled with arrogance.
The destroyers of Kolā arrived, intent on seizing the earth;
Suratha, taking his army with him, came forward to face them.
A terrible battle took place between him and those most fierce [foes];
the army of the Mlecchas was small, while that army of the king was marvelous.
Nevertheless, though he was emboldened by them in battle, the king was defeated by fate;
broken, he reached his own city, which was well-protected and adorned with fortifications.
The wise king, skilled in statecraft,
became anxious upon seeing his principal ministers had taken refuge with the enemy faction.
Having seized a vast position fortified with moats and difficult to assail, one should await the [proper] time; or is battle considered better? (13)
"Those ministers who have fallen under the power of the enemy are indeed unfit for counsel.
Thus the king reflected in his mind, "What shall I do? (14)
Perhaps those of evil conduct, relying on others, will seize me and hand me over to their enemies; what then will happen? (15)
One should never place trust in those of evil intent;
what indeed can those men do who are under the sway of greed?
[They would betray] even a brother, a father, a friend, a well-wisher, or a kinsman.
A man possessed by greed always hates his venerable teacher and the twice-born.
Therefore, I must by no means place my trust now in this most wicked circle of ministers who have taken refuge with the side of the enemy. (18)
Having reflected thus in his mind, the king, deeply distressed,
mounted his horse alone and departed from that city.
Then, having departed without a companion and taken refuge in the dense forest, the wise one reflected: "Where should I go next? (20)
Having learned that the supreme hermitage of the sage Sumedhas was located at a distance of only three yojanas, the king went to the ascetic.
It was filled with many trees, situated upon a riverbank, crowded with beasts of prey that were free from enmity, and adorned with the warbling of cuckoos. ||22||
It was rich with the sounds of students' recitations, surrounded by hundreds of herds of deer,
abundant with well-cooked wild rice, and filled with trees bearing beautiful flowers and fruits.
Always bringing delight to living beings with the sweet fragrance of sacrificial smoke, it was more enchanting than even heaven, being pervaded by the sound of the Vedas. 24.
Having seen that hermitage, the king became filled with joy;
casting off his fear, he set his mind on taking rest in the brahmin’s hermitage. 25.
Having tethered his horse to a tree, he proceeded with humility,
seeing that sage seated there, taking refuge in the shade of a *sāla* tree.
He was seated upon a deer-skin, peaceful, exceedingly emaciated by asceticism, upright,
teaching his disciples, and perceiving the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras. || 27 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 32:
[He who is] free from anger, greed, and the like, beyond the pairs of opposites, and devoid of envy.
One who delights in self-knowledge, speaks the truth, and is endowed with tranquility. || 28 ||
Beholding him, the king then fell prostrate like a staff upon the ground before him,
his eyes filled with tears and his heart overflowing with love.
"Arise, arise; may it be well with you," the sage then said to him. Then, urged by his teacher, the disciple gave him a grass mat (bṛsī).
Having risen and seated himself before her by her command, King Sumedhas offered the guest-offering of water for the feet and other honors according to the prescribed ritual.
He asked him there: "From where have you come? Who are you, and why are you intent on the funeral pyre?
Tell me freely the cause that has led to this."
"Tell me the purpose of your arrival; speak the matter that is in your mind. I shall fulfill your desired wish, even if it be impossible for you. (33)
The king said:
"I am a king named Suratha, defeated by my enemies;
having abandoned my kingdom, home, and wife, I have come to you for refuge. (34)
"O Brahman, whatever you command, I shall carry out with devotion;
there is no protector for me other than you on the surface of the earth. (35)
"I have terrible fear from my enemies; today I have come into your presence.
Save me, O tiger among sages, you who are compassionate toward those who seek refuge! (36)
The sage said:
"Dwell here without fear, O Indra among kings; indeed, no enemies shall come against you here, for by the power of your asceticism, they will surely be overcome. (37)
O best of kings, one should not practice violence here while living by the forest;
one's livelihood should be sustained by the auspicious wild grains, fruits, and roots. (38)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, that king, free from fear, then dwelt in that very hermitage, pure and subsisting on fruits and roots. (39)
Once, while taking refuge in the shade of a tree there, that king,
afflicted by anxiety and with his heart longing for home, began to reflect.
My kingdom has been seized by enemies who are Mlecchas always devoted to sin;
the worlds would be oppressed by those ill-behaved and shameless men. (41)
All the elephants and horses will become weak and deprived of food;
they will be tormented by the enemy—of this there is no doubt. (42)
All those servants of mine who were formerly protected by me have now become subject to my enemies and have surely become miserable.
Indeed, my wealth has been squandered by wicked and evil-minded enemies, who have consigned it to gambling, liquor, and the service of slaves. (44)
Those of evil intellect will exhaust the treasury through calamities;
even those Mlecchas who are my ministers are not skilled in the giving of worthy gifts. 45.
While the king remained at the foot of the tree, absorbed in such reflections,
a certain merchant, who was likewise extremely distressed, arrived there.
Seen by the king in front of him, he was seated there at his side;
the king asked him, "Who are you, and from where have you come to this forest? (47)
"Who are you, and why are you so dejected, green, and afflicted by grief?
Speak the truth, O illustrious one; friendship is said to be formed by walking seven steps together. (48)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the king, that best of men sat down, became composed, and, considering it a meeting with the virtuous, spoke to him.
The Vaiśya said:
"I am indeed a Vaiśya by birth, well-known by the name Samādhi;
I am wealthy, skilled in dharma, truthful in speech, and free from malice. (50)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter thirty-three.

I am now reduced to the state of one who has given away his son by wicked men greedy for wealth; making a pretext of being "miserly," they abandoned me after casting off their most difficult-to-relinquish deceit.
Abandoned even by my own kin, I have indeed quickly reached this forest.
"Who are you? You appear fortunate; tell me now, O beloved.
The king said: "I am a king named Suratha, and I have been oppressed by bandits. (52)
"I have arrived here, deprived of my kingdom and deceived by my ministers;
by good fortune, O best of men, you have met me here as a friend. (53)
We shall dwell happily here in this forest of auspicious trees;
abandon your grief, O one of great intelligence, and be at ease, O best of men. (54)
"And stay here with me at your pleasure and in comfort.
The Vaiśya said:
"My family, deprived of me and without support, is suffering greatly."
And he will become tormented by anxiety, afflicted by disease and grief. 55.
"O King, my mind is distressed by the thought that there is no happiness in the body of my wife, nor is there happiness in the body of my son; thus, my heart does not find peace. (56)
"When shall I see my son, my wife, my home, and my own kin? O King, my mind is not at ease; it is deeply distressed by anxiety for my household. (57)
The king said:
"O high-minded one, having seen those sons and others who were of wicked conduct and utterly foolish, by whom you were cast out—will there be any happiness for you today? (58)
A benefactor is the best enemy; where are friends who cause suffering?
Therefore, making your mind firm, sport with me.
The Vaiśya said:
"O King, my mind is not steady today; it is deeply distressed by anxiety for this family, which is so difficult for the wicked-hearted to abandon. (60)
The king said: "The sorrow born of sovereignty torments my mind as well;
let us today question the peaceful sage, who is the medicine that destroys grief. (61)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus resolved their minds, both the king and the Vaiśya,
filled with humility, went to the sage to ask the cause of his sorrow.
Having approached and prostrated before that unsurpassed sage who was seated, the king, himself seated properly, calm and having attained tranquility, spoke to him. (63)
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the fifth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 32 ||
Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
The King said:
"O Sage, this Vaiśya has now become my friend in the forest."
"Cast out by his sons and wife, he has come here to meet with me.
Due to separation from his family, he is exceedingly sorrowful and dejected;
likewise, even now, he finds no peace in my presence."
"O Great-minded One, I am afflicted with grief by the suffering of having lost my kingdom. ||1||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Fifth Skandha, Chapter 33:
"And this causeless anxiety does not depart from my heart."
Would my horses become weak, or would my elephants fall under the power of the enemy? (2)
Likewise, the circle of servants will become miserable without me;
moreover, the enemies, being exceedingly powerful, will exhaust the treasury in an instant.
As I was reflecting in this way, sleep came easily upon my body;
for I now know that this entire world is indeed false, just like a dream.
O Lord, even though I know this, my mind is deluded and finds no steadiness;
who am I, who are these horses and elephants, and who are these brothers of mine? They are not mine, nor am I theirs.
Neither sons nor friends cause me such pain as this suffering;
I know it is but an illusion, yet it still weighs upon my mind. (6)
Delusion does not depart at all; what is the cause of this wonder?
O Lord, you are omniscient and the destroyer of all doubts. (7)
"O ocean of compassion, tell me the cause of this delusion of mine.
Vyāsa said:
Thus questioned then by the king, Sumedhas, the best of sages, [replied]. (8)
He spoke to him that supreme knowledge which destroys sorrow and delusion.
The sage said:
"Listen, O King, I shall explain the cause of bondage and liberation. (9)
She is renowned here as Mahāmāyā among all living beings;
[so too are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśāna, Indra, Varuṇa, and Vāyu.
All the gods and humans, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas; various trees and creepers, as well as beasts, wild animals, and birds. || 11 ||
And they are all subject to Māyā, being the vessel for both bondage and liberation;
by her this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, has been created.
He surely exists in such a state, bound by the snare of delusion;
what are you, a single human being, a kṣatriya turbid with passion? (13)
For she deludes even the minds of the wise in various ways;
indeed, Brahmā, Śiva, Vāsudeva, and others remain subject to her influence despite their possession of knowledge.
They too, deluded by passion, wander in this world;
O King, in former times, during the Satya Yuga, Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa himself—
Having reached Śvetadvīpa, he performed extensive penance for ten thousand years in order to attain devotion to the knowledge of Brahman.
Then, desiring imperishable bliss, Brahmā himself went to a solitary and most wonderful place beyond that. (17)
O Indra among kings, that Vāsudeva Hari, the Lord who removes delusion, once remained engaged in ascetic penance; at another time, he moved to a different location.
