Rising from that place, O king of kings, he departed with a desire to see another;
the four-faced one likewise emerged from the dry land.
Having met on the way, the four-faced and the four-armed ones asked one another, "Who are you? Who are you? indeed.
Brahmā said to that god, "I am indeed the creator of the universe.
Viṣṇu said to him, "O fool, I, the infallible one, am the creator of the universe. (21)
How much powerless you are, being dependent upon the quality of passion (rajas)!
Know me to be Vāsudeva, the eternal, who is established in goodness (sattva). 22.
"Having fought a most terrible battle, you were protected by me this very day;
you came to me for refuge, oppressed by two Dānavas. (23)
I have indeed slain the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
why do you boast, O dull-witted one? Abandon this delusion at once!
In this vast expanse of saṃsāra, there is no one superior even to me.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the fifth book, chapter thirty-three,
the sage said: Thus did Brahmā and Viṣṇu speak to one another.
With quivering lips and trembling, their eyes turned red;
while they were thus disputing, [the sword] suddenly appeared before them.
In the midst [of it], there was a vast, long, and wonderful linga, white as nectar;
then, suddenly, an incorporeal voice spoke there from the sky.
Having addressed those two illustrious ones who were disputing with one another, [he said]:
"O Brahmā, O Viṣṇu, do not engage in mutual dispute. (28)
"Whoever among you two can go from the bottom to the top of this supreme pinnacle of the Liṅga, which is fixed above and below—he shall indeed always be the superior one between you. (29)
"Let one go to the netherworld and the other to the sky now;
my word must be carried out, abandoning this useless dispute. (30)
"In this dispute between the two of you here, an arbiter must always be appointed.
Having heard those divine words, the sage said, "We have both prepared ourselves and made our effort. (31)
They went to measure the linga of wondrous appearance standing at the forefront;
Viṣṇu descended to the netherworld (pātāla), and Brahmā ascended to the very sky.
In order to increase his own greatness, Viṣṇu went some distance to measure the Great Liṅga, yet he became exhausted because it extended in every direction.
He did not reach the end of the liṅga, but turned back and went to dry land;
then Brahmā arrived at the spot where a fallen ketakī petal lay.
Having received it from the head of Śiva and returned filled with joy,
Brahmā quickly came and gave the *ketakī* petal to Viṣṇu.
Having shown it to be false, he, deluded by pride, said:
"This ketaki petal was taken from the top of the linga. (36)
"It was brought for the sake of recognition and for the pacification of your mind.
Having heard those words of Brahmā and having seen the petal of Keśaka, Hari replied to him:

Hearing those words, the women bowed before him and said:
"Do not fear, O Lord of Gods; we shall strive to entice him."
O one of great luster, you must act in such a way that no fear arises from him, by means of enticing that sage with dance, song, and diversions. (48)
"O Lord, having deluded the sage with side-long glances and various gestures of the limbs, we shall bring him, who is greedy and constrained, under our control. (49)
Vyāsa said:
Having thus addressed Hari, the women went beyond Triśiras,
displaying various gestures appropriate even to the treatises on love.
Singing with various rhythmic patterns and dancing before the Sage, those beautiful women attempted to seduce him by manifesting diverse emotions. (51)
That mass of asceticism did not perceive the mockery of women;
having brought his senses under control, he remained as if mute, blind, and deaf. (52)
For some days those women remained in that excellent hermitage,
performing songs, dances, and other diversions that produce great enchantment.
When the sage Triśiras did not stir from his meditation at will,
the goddesses turned back and again approached Śakra.
All of them, with palms joined in reverence,
then spoke to the king of the gods,
being exhausted, miserable, terrified by fear, and with their faces exceedingly pale. (55)
O God of gods, O Great King, the utmost effort has been made;
yet that invincible one cannot be shaken from his fortitude, O Lord.
"O Indra, subduer of Paka, another means must be devised by all means;
our strength is of no avail against this ascetic who has conquered his senses. (57)
In the Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 2:
"By good fortune we have not been cursed by this high-souled one."
For by the sage, who was like fire, he was indeed illuminated through his ascetic heat.
Having dismissed the apsarases, Śakra, dull-witted and evil-minded as he was, reflected upon an improper means for his destruction.
Having cast aside worldly shame and likewise the intense fear of sin,
O Lord of the Earth, he formed a wicked intent for his slaughter.
Thus ends the first chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Then that lord of the gods, having succumbed to greed, approached and sat upon his elephant-throne.
Then, with a wicked mind toward Triśiras, he beheld the sage of immeasurable prowess. || 1 ||
Beholding him seated firmly upon his seat, with speech conquered and brought under the power of perfect concentration,
resembling the sun or fire in his splendor, the Lord of the Gods encountered supreme distress.
How can I slay this sage, who is indeed renowned for his sinless mind?
How can I disregard this enemy, whose power of asceticism is so fully kindled, while he is intent on seizing my throne? (3)

Having reflected thus, the Lord of the hosts of gods himself released the thunderbolt, his supreme weapon, at the sage established in austerity—an arrow resembling the moon and the sun, possessing three points. (4)
Struck by that blow, the ascetic indeed fell upon the surface of the earth and died;
it was like a mountain peak struck by a thunderbolt, falling to the ground as a wondrous sight.

Having slain him, the Lord of the Gods attained joy, as did the wielder of the thunderbolt; but the sages remained there, uttering cries of intense distress, "Alas! Alas! exclaiming, "What has been done by the sinful Indra?"
The lord of Śacī, a treasure-house of asceticism, has been slain by this evil-minded, wicked soul despite his innocence;
let this sinner now swiftly reap the fruit arising from that murder.
Having struck him down with force, the king of the gods quickly departed for his own abode;
though slain, that great-souled one, a treasury of splendors, shone as if he were still alive.
Seeing him fallen upon the ground as if still alive, the slayer of Vṛtra fell into anxiety, his limbs overwhelmed with distress, wondering: "Could he possibly live again?"

Having reflected deeply in his mind and beholding the carpenter standing before him, Maghavan spoke words appropriate to his own purpose: vimṛśya manasā'tīva takṣāṇaṃ purataḥ sthitam | maghavā vīkṣya taṃ prāha svakāryasadṛśaṃ vacaḥ ||10||
"O carpenter, cut off his heads; do as I say!
Let this one of great splendor not live—he shines as if he were alive himself. (11)
Having heard his words, Takṣaka spoke in reproach:
[Śrīmad-devī-bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 2] 347. [Page 347]
The carpenter said:
"With its massive trunk, it shines so brightly that the axe will not be able to cut through it."
Therefore, I shall not perform this despicable deed;
for you have committed an act censured by the virtuous. ||13||
I truly fear sin, as well as the killing of one who is already dead;
this man is as good as dead, so what is the use of cutting off his head? (14)
"O Pākaśāsana, what fear has arisen in you here? Tell me.
Indra said:
"This body appears with its clear form as if it were still alive. (15)
"Therefore, I am afraid lest this sage, my enemy, should live.
Takṣa said:
'O learned one, are you not ashamed here at such a cruel deed? (16)
"Having killed this son of a seer, do you have no fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin?
Indra said:
"I shall indeed perform an expiation later for the destruction of my evil. (17)
"But an enemy, O high-minded one, must be dealt with by all means, even through deception.
Takṣaka said:
"O Maghavan, struck down by greed, you commit a sin here. (18)
"Without him, how can I commit sin? Tell me, O Lord.
Indra said: "I shall indeed always grant you a share in the sacrifices. (19)
"Men will offer the head as your portion in the sacrifice;
for this fee, cut off his heads and do what is pleasing to me. 20.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Mahendra, the carpenter was filled with joy;
he indeed cut off his heads with a very firm axe.
When the three heads were severed and fell upon the ground,
thousands of birds suddenly flew out from them.
Then, kalaviṅkas, tittiris, and likewise kapiñjalas, each separately, rushed forth swiftly from his mouth. 23.
From that mouth by which he studied the Vedas and likewise drank the Soma,
it is said that all the Kapiñjala birds emerged.
Because he gazed at all directions as if drinking them in at his will,
from that [act] the partridges (tittira), possessed of fierce luster, emerged there.
That mouth of Triśiras which drank liquor, O King, from it indeed emerged sparrows; thus did those birds come forth.
O King, having seen those egg-born beings thus emerged, Śakra rejoiced in his mind and returned once more to the third heaven.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter 2:
When Śakra had departed, Takṣaka also went swiftly to his own home.
Having obtained a supreme share of the sacrifice, O lord of the earth, he attained great joy.
Then Indra, having returned to his own home and slain the mighty enemy,
considered himself to have accomplished his purpose, disregarding the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Upon hearing that his supremely righteous son had been slain, Tvaṣṭṛ—
He became exceedingly angry in his mind and spoke these words: ||30||
"Since you have slain my innocent son, a sage, I shall therefore procreate another son for the sake of his destruction. (31)
"Let the gods behold my heroism as well as the power of my asceticism;
let that evil-souled one know the full extent of the great fruit of his own actions. (32)
Having spoken thus, Tvaṣṭṛ, overwhelmed with anger, then offered oblations into the fire with mantras proclaimed in the Atharva Veda for the purpose of producing a son.
When the oblation had been performed for eight nights from the kindled fire,
a person resembling fire suddenly emerged with speed.
Seeing that son before him, endowed with splendor and strength, appearing as if he were a blazing fire manifested from the speed of Vahni, Tvaṣṭṛ—
Tvaṣṭṛ, beholding his son standing before him, spoke these words:
"O enemy of Indra, grow strong through the power of my asceticism."
When these words had been spoken, Tvaṣṭṛ, blazing with anger,
grew in size until he touched the heavens, possessing a splendor equal to Vaiśvānara.
Born with the form of a mountain, resembling Time and Death, and possessing sovereign power, he said to his father, who was extremely distressed, "What shall I do?
"O Lord, O you of noble vows, give me a name and tell me what must be done."
Why are you so full of anxiety? Tell me the cause of your grief. (39)
"I shall destroy your grief today"—this is the vow I have undertaken.
Why, then, having been born, does my father remain so sorrowful? (40)
I shall drink up the ocean instantly, I shall pulverize the mountains,
and today I shall ward off the rising sun of fierce radiance.
I shall instantly slay Indra along with the gods, or Yama, or any other deity;
I shall cast them all into the ocean and uproot the very earth.
Having heard these eloquent words of his son, Tvaṣṭṛ,
exceedingly delighted, replied to that son who was like a mountain.
"O son, because you are now able to rescue [the world] from evil (vṛjina), therefore your name shall be known as Vṛtra. 44.
O highly fortunate one, your brother was an ascetic named Triśiras;
he indeed possessed three heads that were full of prowess.
A knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and an expert in all branches of learning,
he remained engaged in ascetic penance, which generally inspires wonder throughout the three worlds.
But today he has been struck by Śakra with the blow of his thunderbolt;
their heads were suddenly severed without any fault on their part.
Therefore, O tiger among men, slay Śakra for his transgression.
The sin of ten thousand killings of Brahmins belongs to you, who are shameless, evil-minded, and deceitful. ||48||
Having spoken thus, Tvaṣṭṛ, overwhelmed with grief for his son,
then fashioned various divine weapons.
And for the sake of slaying the thousand-eyed one, he gave him powerful weapons,
namely swords, spears, maces, javelins, lances, and so forth.
Likewise, the Śārṅga bow and arrow, the iron club (parigha), the sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa), and the divine discus with a thousand spokes, possessing a splendor equal to the Sudarśana. || 51 ||
An inexhaustible and divine quiver, and most beautiful armor;
a chariot resembling a cloud, firm, capable of bearing great weight, and swift.
O King, having prepared all the implements of war and given them to his son,
Tvaṣṭṛ, filled with rage, dispatched him.
Thus ends the second chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 2 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the sixth book, chapter three.
Now begins the third chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having had rites for his welfare performed by Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, the mighty Vṛtra mounted his chariot and set forth to slay Śakra.
At that very time, the cruel Rākṣasas, who had previously been defeated by the gods, assembled for the sake of service, knowing Vṛtra to be possessed of great strength. ||2||
But the messengers of Indra, seeing that he had arrived for battle, came with speed and reported the news of his actions to him. ||3||
Vyāsa said: "O Lord, your enemy named Vṛtra is quickly approaching here;
he is indeed powerful and has been fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, mounted upon a chariot."
Indeed, by you who were filled with wrath and tormented by the slaughter of your son, he was joined with Rākṣasas— namely Duḥsaha— for the purpose of destruction through malevolent magic (abhicāra).
Exert yourself, O illustrious one;
a terrible and most dreadful sound, resembling Mount Meru and Mount Mandara, is approaching right now.
In the meantime, the hosts of gods, being greatly terrified there,
approached and spoke to the Lord of the Gods as he listened to the messenger's words.
The Gaṇas said:
"O Maghavan, many ill omens are appearing in the abode of the gods, as well as the cries of birds foreboding great danger."
Crows, vultures, hawks, and fierce kāka birds, along with other dreadful winged creatures,
shriek with loud, discordant cries above the palace.
The birds uttered loud cries of "cī-cī-kū-cī," and streams of water fell down from the eyes of the mounts.
O illustrious one, a very great and terrible sound of weeping Rākṣasīs is heard upon your palace at night. (11)
O giver of honor, banners fall swiftly even without wind;
great portents arise in the heavens, on the earth, and in the intermediate space.
Women wearing black garments wander from house to house with distorted faces, crying out, "Go away! Go quickly from this house!
And at night, within their own homes, they appear in the dreams of sleeping lovers.
The Rākṣasīs, extremely distressed and terrifying him, tore out his hair.
O Lord of Gods, such portents as earthquakes and meteors occurred, and jackals howled in the courtyards of the mansions during the night. (15)
And webs of lizards appear in every house; there are ill omens everywhere, such as the twitching of limbs and so forth. (16)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the Lord of the Gods ascended the funeral pyre;
then, having summoned Bṛhaspati, he questioned him regarding what was in his mind.
Indra said:
"O Brahmin, why indeed do such terrible omens appear?
Fierce winds blow and fireflies fall from the sky. (18)
"O illustrious one, you are omniscient and capable of destroying obstacles;
you are wise, a knower of the true principles of the scriptures, and likewise a preceptor of the deities. (19)
O knower of the rites for pacification, perform that which brings about the destruction of my enemies;
let the ritual be performed in such a way that no further suffering may befall me. (20)
Bṛhaspati said:
"O thousand-eyed one, what shall I do? A wicked deed has been committed by you today;
having slain an innocent sage, what fruit have you acquired?"
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter three.
The fruit of merit and sin is exceedingly fierce and ripens swiftly;
therefore, one who desires prosperity should indeed perform an action only after careful deliberation. (22)
One should never perform an action that causes suffering to others; a living being devoted to the torment of others finds no happiness. (23)
O Śakra, out of delusion and greed, the murder of a Brahmin was committed by you just now;
the fruit of that sin has suddenly arrived.
This one known as Vṛtra was born invincible to all the gods;
surrounded by many Dānavas, he comes here to slay you.
And having taken up all his divine weapons, equal to the thunderbolt and given by Tvaṣṭṛ, O Vāsava, he has arrived. 26.
The invincible and powerful one, mounted upon his chariot, will arrive bringing about the destruction of the Lord of the Gods; he shall be his death.
A great clamor then arose as Vākpati spoke thus;
the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and sages whose wealth is their austerity [all gathered]. (28)
Abandoning their abodes, all the immortals fled;
seeing that great refuge, Śakra took it as his ultimate resort.
Then he commanded his servants for the mobilization of the army:
"Bring the Vasus, the Rudras, the Aśvins, and the Sun. (30)
Having ascended their celestial chariots, Pūṣan, Bhaga, Vāyu, Kubera, Varuṇa, and Yama— the best of the gods— stood equipped with their weapons.
"Come quickly! The enemy is approaching now!
Having thus commanded, the Lord of the Gods mounted his excellent elephant.
Having placed Bṛhaspati at their head, they departed from their own abode;
likewise, all the gods mounted their respective vehicles. 33.
Having resolved to fight, they set forth with weapons in hand;
then Vṛtra, joined by the Dānavas, reached the Mānasottara mountain.
Indra also came to the delightful mountain Mānasottara, the abode of deities adorned with trees, and,
accompanied by the gods and preceded by Vācaspati, he waged war upon that mountain. (35)
Then, a fierce battle took place there between Vṛtra and Vāsava.
With maces, swords, clubs, nooses, arrows, spears, and axes,
he fought in human form for a hundred autumns.
He became a source of terror to men and to the sages of purified souls;
indeed, Varuṇa was first broken, and then the host of Vāyus.
Then Vibhāvasu, Śakra, and all of them departed from the battle; seeing the gods, led by Indra, intent on flight, they left the field.
Vṛtra also went with joy to his father, who was staying in the hermitage;
having prostrated before Tvaṣṭṛ, he said, "The task for my father has been accomplished by me. (40)
All the gods, including Indra, were completely defeated while standing in the midst of battle;
they fled and went to their own abodes, just as deer and elephants flee from a lion. 41.
"O Lord, Indra came on foot, and this best of elephants was brought by me;
this is Airāvata, the most excellent of tuskers—please accept him. (42)
"They were not killed by me; therefore, killing those who are afraid is improper.
Command me again, dear father: what desired task of yours shall I perform? (43)
All the gods fled, terrified by fear and overcome with exhaustion;
even Indra, abandoning Airāvata, fled in terror. || 44 ||
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his son, Tvaṣṭṛ spoke, filled with joy:
"Today I have become a father of a son; my life has borne fruit. (45)
"O son, I have been purified by you; the fever of my mind has departed.
My mind has become steady upon seeing that wonderful prowess."
Listen, my son; I shall speak what is for your benefit today—pay close attention.
O fortunate one, perform penance with mindfulness and a steady posture.
One must never place trust in anyone, O subduer of Pāka.
Your enemy is a practitioner of deceit, skilled in various forms of dissension. || 48 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the sixth book, chapter 4:
Prosperity is attained through austerity; through austerity, supreme sovereignty is attained.
Through austerity, there shall be an increase in strength as well as victory in battle.
Having propitiated the god Druhiṇa and obtained an unsurpassed boon,
slay Śakra, who is of evil conduct and enveloped by the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Becoming steady and attentive,
worship Śaṅkara, the giver;
for when he is satisfied, that four-faced one will grant you the desired boon.
Having gratified Brahmā, the source of the universe, who possesses immeasurable splendor,
and having attained indestructibility, slay Śakra, who has committed an offense.
"O son, enmity born from the slaughter of my son dwells within my mind;
I find no peace, nor do I sleep in comfort. (53)
"Since my innocent son, an ascetic, has been slain by you, O sinful one, I find no peace; O Vṛtra, deliver me from this sorrow. (54)
Vyāsa said: Having heard those words of his father, Vṛtra was then filled with anger;
taking leave of his father’s command, he departed joyfully for the sake of ascetic penance.
Having reached Gandhamādana, he bathed in the auspicious and holy Devadhunī river; then, having prepared a seat of kuśa grass, he remained there with his posture steady.
Having renounced both food and the drinking of water, devoted to the practice of yoga,
he sat upon a firm seat, meditating on the Creator of the Universe within his mind.
Knowing him to be performing penance, Maghavan, the subduer of Pāka, became anxious with worry and dispatched Gandharvas to create obstacles.
And [he saw] yakṣas, pannagas, serpents, and kinnaras of immeasurable prowess;
vidyādharas, apsarases, and numerous messengers of the gods.
Deceptive means were employed by those illusionists to obstruct his austerities;
yet the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, that supreme ascetic, did not waver from his meditation.
Thus ends the third chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Those gods, who had come forth to cause obstacles to his asceticism, turned back and departed.
Despairing of the successful accomplishment of their task, they beheld him of firm resolve. ||1||
When a full hundred years had passed, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, arrived there with speed, mounted upon his swan and possessing four faces. ||2||
Having arrived, he said this to him: "O son of Tvaṣṭṛ, may you be happy! Abandoning your meditation, choose a boon; I shall grant you whatever you desire. (3)
"I am pleased with you today because of your austerity, seeing you so exceedingly emaciated.
Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—that which is desired by your heart. (4)
Vyāsa said:
Then Vṛtra, having heard before him those exceedingly clear words from the sole Creator of the world— words whose flavor was like nectar—
suddenly cast off his state of meditative absorption and rose up, his eyes filled with a multitude of tears born of joy.
Having bowed his head at the feet of the Creator out of affection, he stood before him with palms joined in reverence;
bowing low with humility, he addressed that bestower of boons—who had been approached through penance—with words faltering with love.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 4.
O Lord, today I have attained the station of all the gods, for the vision of you, which is so difficult to obtain, has swiftly come to pass.
O Protector, there is a desire in my devoted mind that is hard to fulfill; I shall declare it, O Lotus-seated One, for you know the inner state of beings.
"May death not come to me from iron weapons, nor from dry or wet bamboo, nor from other arms;
may my prowess increase exceedingly in battle, so that I shall be unconquerable even by the gods together with their hosts. (8)
Vyāsa said: Thus entreated, Brahmā spoke to him as if smiling:
"Arise, go; may it be well with you; your desire shall always be fruitful."
Your death shall not come by means of anything dry, nor by anything wet, nor by stone, nor by wood; I tell you this as the truth. (10)
Having thus granted the boon, Brahmā departed for the supreme realm;
Vṛtra, having obtained that boon, went to his own home filled with joy.
The high-minded one related that granting of the boon before his father;
and Tvaṣṭṛ, being delighted, then beheld his son who had obtained the boon.
May it be well with you, O illustrious one! Slay Śakra, my enemy;
having slain him, go forth against the slayer of Triśiras, who is joined with evil. (13)
"O Lord of the Thirty-three, having attained victory in battle, become my sovereign;
I shall bear the immense grief arising from the loss of my son. (14)

By carrying out the instructions of a living father, by providing abundant food on the anniversary of his death, and by offering funeral cakes at Gayā—a son attains the status of a true son through these three acts. (15)
Therefore, my son, you ought to destroy this excessive grief of mine;
for Triśiras never departs from my mind.
Virtuous, truthful, an ascetic, and the foremost knower of the Vedas—he was slain by that evil-minded one without any fault. (17)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the exceedingly invincible Vṛtra mounted his chariot and swiftly departed from his father’s house.
Having caused the sound of battle-drums and the blast of conchs to be made,
he, intoxicated with pride, set out on his expedition.
Accompanied by his ministers, he set forth, speaking thus to his attendants:
"Having slain Śakra, I shall seize the kingdom of the gods, free from all thorns."
Having spoken thus, he quickly went forth, surrounded by his own army,
terrifying Amarāvatī with the great roar of his troops.
O descendant of Bharata, perceiving that he was approaching, Turāṣāṭ, terrified by fear, also quickly mobilized his army;
that subduer of enemies swiftly summoned all the world-protectors.
Impelling them all toward battle, he of great splendor shone brilliantly.
Then, having formed the Guṅghra array, the subduer of Pāka took his stand;
thereupon Vṛtra, the crusher of enemy forces, arrived there with speed.
A tumultuous battle then took place between the god and the Dānava,
Vṛtra and Vāsava, as they both desired victory over one another in that conflict.
Thus, while the battle was blazing fiercely between them and inspiring great terror,
the deities perceived their inner resolve and attained supreme joy.
[They fought] with javelins, slings, swords, axes, and spears.
The gods and the Daityas struck one another with their respective excellent weapons.
While this fierce and hair-raising battle was thus proceeding,
Vṛtra, filled with rage, suddenly seized Śakra.
Having opened his mouth and cast Śatakratu inside, Vṛtra stood there, O great king, filled with joy as he recalled their former enmity. (29)
Then, when Śakra was seized by Vṛtra, the gods were bewildered;
overcome with supreme distress, they cried out "Alas, Śakra! again and again.
=== PAGE 353 === 23 In the glorious Mahāpurāṇa Devībhāgavata, in the fifth book, chapter 4. 353
Seeing Śakra with his mouth wide open, all the inhabitants of heaven, their minds distressed, bowed to Bṛhaspati and said:
"O best of the twice-born, what should be done? You are our supreme preceptor. (31)
Śakra, though seized by Vṛtra, was protected by the other deities.
"What can we all do without Śakra, for our prowess has been diminished?
O Lord, perform an act of sorcery quickly for the sake of liberating Śakra. (33)
Bṛhaspati said:
"O gods, what must be done? Vāsava has been cast into the mouth;
though struck down by Vṛtra, he remains alive within the belly of his enemy."
Vyāsa said: All the gods, overcome with anxiety upon seeing Indra thus treated, reflected and swiftly made an effort for his liberation.
They created a great being, a yawning demoness who destroys enemies;
then, as he yawned, his mouth became wide open. 36.
Then, as Vṛtra was yawning, the slayer of Bala emerged from his mouth, having withdrawn even his own limbs. 37.
From that time forth, yawning has remained among living beings in the worlds;
and all the gods rejoiced upon seeing Śakra emerge.
Then a battle commenced between them that struck terror into the worlds;
it lasted for ten thousand years, being fierce and hair-raising.
On one side all the gods stood ready for battle;
on the other side, the powerful son of Tvaṣṭṛ advanced in the conflict.
When Vṛtra, protected by his boon, grew powerful in battle,
Śakra was then defeated and overcome by his splendor.
Then Maghavan suffered in the battle, having met with defeat;
and the gods fell into despair upon seeing Śakra vanquished. ||42||
All the gods, led by Indra, abandoned the battle and departed,
for Vṛtra had arrived with great speed and seized the *devasavana* vessel.
That Dānava forcibly enjoys all the celestial gardens;
even Airāvata, that best of elephants, has been seized by the Daitya. (44)
And all the celestial chariots were seized, O lord of the people;
furthermore, Uccaiḥśravas, the best of horses, then came under his control.
The wish-fulfilling cow, the Pārijāta tree, and likewise the host of Apsarases were taken as mere jewels by that son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
All the gods, fallen from their positions and dwelling in mountain fastnesses,
suffered misery, having been deprived of their sacrificial shares and their celestial abode.
Having attained the status of a god, Vṛtra became exceedingly arrogant;
and Tvaṣṭṛ, having obtained extreme happiness, rejoiced together with his son.
O Bhārata, when this occurred, the gods, bewildered by fear, consulted together with the sages as to what should be done, reflecting deeply. 49.
The gods, accompanied by Śakra, went to Mount Kailāsa;
bowing deeply to Mahādeva with palms joined in reverence, they spoke. ||50||
O God of gods, Mahādeva, O Maheśvara, ocean of compassion!
Protect us, who are terrified by fear and utterly defeated by Vṛtra.
"O Lord, that powerful one has seized the abode of the gods;
O Śambhu, tell us truly today, O Śiva: what should be done after this?"
"What shall we do, and where shall we go, O Maheśvara? Having been deprived of our station, O Īśvara, we find no means for the destruction of our suffering. (13)
"O Lord of Beings, bestow your assistance; we are distressed, O treasure-house of compassion!
O All-pervading One, slay Vṛtra, who is intoxicated with pride by the power of the boon he received. (54)
Śiva said:
"Placing Brahmā at our head, we all went to the abode of Hari;
having approached Viṣṇu, we deliberated upon the plan for his slaughter."
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, the sixth book, chapter five.
Vāsudeva Janārdana is capable, skilled in detecting deception, powerful, and possessed of supreme intelligence; he is the refuge of all and an ocean of compassion.
"Without that Lord of the Gods of gods, no success in one's purpose will come to pass;
therefore, you must go to him for the sake of accomplishing all your tasks. (57)
Vyāsa said:

For that which is the cause of experience—of pleasure and pain—for the embodied being, [is the result] of karmas accumulated over many births. (19)

In the course of time, through the ripening of one's karma, an impulse arises within someone; by the power of that *prārabdha* (commenced karma), he performs meritorious acts in whatever manner they may be.
O King, a human being commits evil, as do the gods and others;
likewise, O King, both Nārāyaṇa and A-ra, the two born of Dharma, do so as well.
Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna were born as portions of Nārāyaṇa according to his will;
this is indeed the ancient foundation proclaimed by the sages.
He who possesses great wealth should be known as a portion of the gods;
for no one who is not a Ṛṣi composes poetry, nor does anyone who is not Rudra worship Rudra. (23)
O King, neither one who is not a portion of the gods, nor one who is not Viṣṇu, can become a lord of the earth;
[one becomes so] from Indra, Agni, Yama, Viṣṇu, or Kubera. (24)
"Taking sovereignty, power, wrath, and prowess, it is surely fashioned as the body; this is certain.
Whoever in this world is powerful, fortunate, or possessed of enjoyments,"
Whether he possesses knowledge or is devoid of it, he is proclaimed to be a portion of the gods.
In the same way, O lord of the earth, the Pāṇḍavas have described this to me:
that Vāsudeva is a portion of the gods, possessing a splendor equal to Nārāyaṇa. (27)
The body of living beings is surely a vessel for pleasure and pain;
the embodied soul shall accordingly experience either pleasure or pain without interval. (28)
There is no embodied being who possesses any autonomy; for everyone is always subject to destiny.
Helpless indeed, one undergoes birth, death, suffering, and happiness. (29)
Those Pāṇḍavas, who were born in the forest, have returned once more to their own home;
subsequently, by the strength of their own arms, they performed the Rājasūya, the most excellent of sacrifices.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 11:
They returned once more to forest life, which is supremely fraught with manifold sufferings.
Indeed, Arjuna performed a penance that is difficult even for those who have not conquered their senses.
The gods, being satisfied, granted once more an auspicious boon: "Where has the merit produced by the human body gone? Where has that born of dwelling in the forest gone? (32)
The severe austerity performed by Arjuna in the body of a human being at the Badarikāśrama indeed became the source of its fruit within his very body.
In relation to the bodies of living beings, the course of karma is profound;
it is difficult to understand in every respect even for the gods, so what need be said of human beings? (34)
Vāsudeva was also born in the extremely cramped prison;
he was then led by Vasudeva to the cowherd settlement of Nanda Gopa.
O descendant of Bharata, he remained there for exactly eleven years;
then, returning again to Mathurā, he forcibly slew the son of Ugrasena.
He released his two parents from their bonds, which had caused them great suffering,
and installed King Ugrasena in the city of Mathurā.
Out of fear of the Mleccha king, he went again to Dvāravatī;
Kṛṣṇa performed all this great manly effort under the power of destiny.
Having performed many deeds in Dvāravatī, Janārdana abandoned his body at Prabhāsa along with his family and ascended to heaven;
so too did his sons, grandsons, friends, brothers, and sisters-in-law.
At Prabhāsa, all the Yādavas met their destruction due to the curse of the Brahmins.
Thus, O King, has this profound course of karma been described to you;
even Vāsudeva met his end by the arrow of a hunter.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"The birth of the two Kṛṣṇas has been narrated for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden."
O best of the twice-born, this doubt remains within my heart.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, the Earth, extremely distressed and oppressed by a heavy burden, went for refuge to Brahmā in the form of a cow. ||2||
Requested by the Creator, Viṣṇu, the Lord and husband of Kamalā, [appeared] for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth and for the protection of the virtuous. ||3||
O Lord Janārdana, together with the gods, quickly take birth in the house of Vasudeva within the land of Bhārata, O All-pervading One.
Thus entreated by the Creator, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī,
together with Rāma, indeed became [incarnate] for the sake of removing the burden of the earth.
How much of the burden has been removed after he has slain numerous wicked ones?
Having recognized all those kings here as being of evil conduct and sinful intent.
Bhīṣma is slain, Droṇa is slain, as are Virāṭa and Drupada;
Bāhlīka, Somadatta, and Karṇa Vaikartana likewise.
Why were those wicked ones who remained on the surface of the earth not destroyed—those by whom all wealth was plundered and the wives of Hari were carried away? (8)
There were Ābhīras, Śakas, Mlecchas, and Niṣādas by the millions;
what was that "removal of the burden" accomplished by the wise Kṛṣṇa? (9)
O highly fortunate one, this doubt does not depart from my mind;
for I behold all people in this Kali age to be resolved upon evil. (10)
Vyāsa said:
O King, in whichever yuga the subjects become such according to time, it certainly cannot be otherwise; here, the nature of the yuga is the cause.
Those living beings who were devoted to the essence of dharma existed indeed in the Satya Yuga;
those who were devoted to the essence of dharma and artha existed indeed in the Tretā Yuga. ||12||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter eleven: The Paths.

In the Dvāpara age, people were devoted to the pursuit of dharma, artha, and kāma; indeed, in this Kali age, all become intent upon artha and kāma. O Indra among kings, the nature of each yuga does not undergo a reversal.
Time is the agent of dharma, and indeed, it is likewise the agent of adharma.
The King said: "Those living beings in the Satya Yuga were devoted to righteousness;
O highly fortunate one, where do those partakers of merit reside today? (15)
O Grandfather, tell me where those excellent sages who act like Dānavas exist during the Tretā or the Dvāpara ages. (16)
Where will those most sinful revilers of the gods go in the first age—those shameless ones who exist here in the Kali age, characterized by wicked conduct? (17)
"O Mahāmati, explain all of this in detail;
explain it fully, for I am desirous of hearing this entire determination of the Dharma.
Vyāsa said:
O King, those human beings are indeed born here in the Kṛta Yuga;
having performed meritorious deeds, they truly go to the worlds of the gods.
O best of kings, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are devoted to their own duties indeed go to worlds won by their actions. 20.
Truthfulness, compassion, as well as generosity, and likewise fidelity to one's own wife; non-malice toward all beings and equanimity toward all creatures. (21)
Having established this common dharma once again in the Satya Yuga, other castes, such as washermen and others, go to heaven in accordance with dharma.
Likewise, O King, in the Tretā age, in the Dvāpara age, and in this Kali age,
sinful men go to hell;
they remain there until the completion of the cycle of the ages.
And again, they become human beings on the earth in the world of men. ||24||
O King, when the beginning of the Satya Yuga and the end of the Kali Yuga occur,
it is said that meritorious men are born from heaven.
When the beginning of the Kali Yuga and the end of the Dvāpara Yuga coincide,
all sinful men emerge from hell onto the earth.
Thus, the conduct of the age was never otherwise; therefore, Kali is a doer of evil, yet the people in that age are of such a nature.
Sometimes, by the power of destiny, a reversal may occur among living beings;
those who are virtuous in the Kali age may be born in the Dvāpara age.
Likewise, some in the Tretā age and some in the Satya age;
those who were wicked in the Satya age remain so even in the Kali age. (29)
Having attained various pleasures through the power of performed actions,
they again perform similar actions according to the nature of the age.
Janamejaya said: O highly fortunate one, tell me all the duties of the ages (yugas) in their entirety;
in which age such-and-such a duty exists, that I wish to know exactly as it is.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O tiger among kings, for I shall tell you an illustration:
even the minds of the virtuous are indeed affected by the influence of the age.
O Indra among kings, just as your father—a high-souled knower of dharma—was treated with contempt by Kali through the impairment of his intellect, so indeed was it done, O King. (33)
Otherwise, why would a Kṣatriya king, born of such a noble lineage,
have placed a dead snake around the neck of an ascetic?
O King, all this must be understood as the power of destiny by one who possesses true knowledge.
For indeed, religious duty must be performed with diligent effort, especially so.
"O King, in the Satya Yuga, the Brāhmaṇas were masters of the Vedas, devoted to the worship of Parāśakti, and longing for a vision of the Goddess. (36)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 11:
Those who are devoted to the three-syllabled *praṇava* and who perform meditation on the Gāyatrī;
They were intent on the recitation of the Gāyatrī, chanting the single seed-syllable of Māyā.
In every village, all were eager to build temples for Parāmbā; they were devoted to their own duties and endowed with truthfulness, purity, and compassion. (38)
There, the Kṣatriyas were devoted to their assigned duties, proficient in the knowledge of reality, and intent upon the support of the subjects. (39)
O King, in that meritorious Satya Yuga, the Vaiśyas were devoted to agriculture, trade, and the tending of cattle, while the Śūdras were intent upon service.
In the supreme age (Kṛtayuga), all social classes were devoted to the worship of Parāmbā;
likewise, in the Tretāyuga, the establishment of Dharma was slightly diminished. ||41||
And in the Dvāpara age, the condition of the Satya Yuga is especially diminished.
O King, those who were Rākṣasas in former times are known as Brāhmaṇas in the Kali age. (42)
Those devoted to heretical paths are generally deceivers of people;
they are all speakers of untruth and are devoid of the Vedic dharma. || 43 ||
Some were hypocritical, clever in worldly affairs, proud, and devoid of Vedic knowledge; others were devoted to serving Śūdras and were promoters of various heterodox doctrines. || 44 ||
O King, as the Kali age advances, there arise those who revile the Vedas, who are cruel, fallen from the Dharma, and excessively boastful. (45)
There would be a total destruction of Dharma, which is rooted in truth;
likewise, the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras would become devoid of Dharma. (46)
In the Kali age, the wicked speak untruths, as do those of other castes;
Brahmins delight in the duties of Śūdras and are devoted to accepting gifts.
O King, in the Kali age, women will indeed have grown excessive; acting according to their own desires, they will be possessed by lust, greed, and delusion.
O King, they are wicked, speakers of falsehoods, always delighting in afflictions, constant deceivers of their own husbands, and experts in preaching the dharma. (49)
In this way, women become exceedingly wicked in the Kali age;
however, O King, through purity of food, purity of mind arises. (50)
O best of kings, when the mind is pure, there is the manifestation of Dharma;
through the fault of confusion in conduct, confusion of Dharma arises. (51)
When the confusion of dharma arises, there will surely be a confusion of castes;
so it shall be, O King, in the Kali age which is devoid of all righteousness. (52)
This report concerning the nature of gold is not found anywhere;
even great men who know the Dharma commit unrighteous acts, O King. (53)
This is the very nature of Kali; it cannot be avoided by anyone.
"O Indra among kings, there can be no atonement through ordinary means.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, expert in all the scriptures! (55)
In this Kali age, which abounds in unrighteousness, what will be the destiny of men?
If there exists a means for that, tell it to me.
Vyāsa said:
O great king, there is only one means for that, and no other;
to eliminate all defects, one should meditate upon the lotus feet of the Goddess. (57)
Indeed, there are no sins so great as the power that exists in the name of the Goddess for burning away evil; therefore, O King, whence can there be fear? 58.
If even that which is uttered playfully, though involuntarily, bestows such [blessings], neither Hara nor any others are capable of knowing what it grants. (59)
The remembrance of the name of the Illustrious Goddess is indeed the atonement for sins;
therefore, O King, a man dwelling in a sacred field out of fear of the Kali age [is purified]. 60.
One should constantly practice the recollection of the Name of the Supreme Mother;
even after cutting through, piercing, and slaying all beings and this entire world.
In the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 12:
He who bows to the Goddess with devotion is not smeared by sins.
O King, the secret of all scriptures has been declared by me.
Having reflected upon this in its entirety, take refuge in the lotus feet of the Goddess;
all people mutter the Gāyatrī known as Ajapā.
They do not know my greatness or the vast power of my illusion;
all the Brāhmaṇas chant the Gāyatrī within their hearts.

They do not know the greatness [of the Lord], nor the vast power of Māyā. O King, all that you asked regarding the establishment of the duties of the Yugas has been fully explained; what more do you wish to hear? 65.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
The King said:
"O best of sages, tell me of the meritorious holy places (tīrthas) upon the earth."
The sacred fields and likewise the rivers are accessible to both men and gods. || 1 ||

And what kind of fruit is obtained from bathing and giving gifts at various sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as the procedure for pilgrimage to these fords and the specific observances (niyamas). ||2||
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall describe various sacred fords (tīrthas),
and those among the sacred fords where the journeys of the goddesses are highly praised.
Among rivers, the Jāhnavī is the best, as are the Yamunā and the Sarasvatī;
likewise the Narmadā, Gaṇḍakī, Sindhu, Gomatī, and Tamasā. ||4||
The Kāverī, the Candrabhāgā, the meritorious Vetravatī, the auspicious Carmaṇvatī, the Sarayū, the Tāpī, and likewise the Sābhramatī; || 5 ||
These have been described, O King, as well as hundreds of others;
among them, those flowing to the ocean are meritorious, while those not reaching the sea possess little merit.
Those rivers that flow into the ocean and carry all their waters at all times are considered sacred;
however, for two months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, they are all in their menstrual period.
Likewise, by means of rain, there arise rivers carrying village waters;
as well as Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, and the most purifying Dharmāraṇya. ||8||
Prabhāsa, Prayāga, and Naimiṣāraṇya,
as well as the renowned Arbudāraṇya and the purifying mountains.
Śrīśaila, Sumeru, and Mount Gandhamādana; as well as the meritorious lakes, and the world-renowned Mānasa. ||10||
Likewise, there is the most excellent Bindusaras, the purifying lake named Acchoda,
as well as the meritorious hermitages of sages of purified soul.
The sacred hermitage of Badarikāśrama is ever-renowned and famous, where the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa performed their austerities. (12)
The hermitage called Vāmana-āśrama and likewise Śatayūpa-āśrama are renowned by those names because of the penance performed there by each of them.
"O Lord of the Earth, there are indeed countless such meritorious places upon the surface of the earth, celebrated by the sages as purifying. (14)
O King, in all these places there dwell shrines of the Goddess that remove sin through the mere sight of them, and they reside there according to fixed rule.
O King, I shall first describe those sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as certain gifts, vows, and sacrifices, in connection with this topic.
O Lord of the Earth, ascetic practices and meritorious deeds are dependent;
they depend upon the purity of material substances, the purity of ritual action, and the purity of the mind. (17)
For sacred fords, austerities, and vows are indeed purifying;
yet the purification of material substance occurs only at certain times, and the purification of ritual action only at others. (18)
In the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 12:
"O King, purity of mind is difficult for all to attain at all times."
But the mind, O King, is fickle and rests upon many objects. (19)
O King, how can that which is based on various states of being become pure?
For desire, anger, greed, egoism, and pride likewise [obstruct it]. (20)
For these indeed cause all obstacles to asceticism, sacred fords, and vows:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses. || 21 ||
O King, the observance of one's own duty bestows the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites;
[otherwise], through the abandonment of obligatory rites and the fault of association on the road, [one falls]. ||22||
Visiting sacred fords in vain leaves only sin remaining;
for sacred fords wash away all impurities born of the body in every way. (23)
O King, they are indeed not capable of washing away the mind;
if they were capable, then everyone dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā would be so.
How could sages who were filled with malice ever have the Lord as their object of meditation?
For it is said that those such as Viśvāmitra and others were humble, being equal to Vasiṣṭha.
All are always devoted to passion and hatred and are agitated by desire and anger;
the sacred ford consisting of purity of mind is far more purifying than the Gaṅgā and other holy waters. (26)
If, by the turn of fate, one should wash away internal impurity—
especially through association with the virtuous, O King— for one who is established in knowledge.
Neither the Vedas nor the scriptures, neither vows nor austerities, neither sacrifices nor gifts are the cause of the purification of the mind. //28//
Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā and an expert in Vedic knowledge,
though he was free from passion and hatred, once resided on the banks of the Gaṅgā at his will.
[There occurred] the great battle between Viśvāmitra and Vasiṣṭha known as Āḍībaka.
Born from hatred, it was useless and caused wonder among the gods. ||30||
Viśvāmitra was born there as Baka, characterized by supreme tamas;
he was indeed cursed by Vasiṣṭha on account of Hariścandra.
Having cursed Vasiṣṭha as well, Kauśika was born from an āḍī fruit due to the power of that body; by that curse, both sages of pure luster became āḍībaka birds.
The two ascetics reached their dwelling on the shore, devoted to dharma;
they engaged in a fierce battle with blows from their claws and beaks.
For as long as ten thousand years, those two sages,
filled with wrath and intoxicated by pride, fought each other like two lions.
The king said:
"How did those two tigers among sages, those ascetics devoted to dharma, come to harbor mutual enmity? By what cause did this arise? (35)
For what reason did those two of great intelligence bestow curses upon one another—curses that cause mutual affliction and bring suffering to human beings? (36)
Vyāsa said: In ancient times, Hariścandra, the son of Triśaṅku, was the best of kings; he belonged to the solar dynasty and was the elder brother of Rāmacandra.
Childless, that royal sage, desiring a son, offered a human sacrifice— difficult to perform— to Varuṇa at a great ritual.
Varuṇa was pleased with him when that sacrifice had been duly performed;
the king’s wife, who was most beautiful, conceived a child.
Seeing his wife pregnant with longing, the king was filled with joy;
he performed, according to the prescribed rites, the ceremonies for the consecration of the embryo.
The woman gave birth to a son endowed with all auspicious marks;
O lord of the people, the king attained great joy there upon the birth of his son.
He performed the supreme rites of purification, beginning with the *jātakarman*,
and gave gold and milch cows especially to the Brāhmaṇas.
O great king, when the birth festival had fully concluded in the house,
the Lord of the Sea arrived there, likewise wearing the guise of a brahmin.
Then, having been honored by the king and provided with a seat according to the prescribed rite, Varuṇa, when asked about his business, spoke these words to the monarch: "I am Varuṇa. (44)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 12.
O Indra among kings, perform a sacrifice after making your son the most purifying sacrificial animal; be true to your word, for a solemn resolve has been made by you.
Having heard those words, the king, overwhelmed and distressed by extreme pain,
steadied his grief and spoke to Varuṇa with his hands joined in reverence.
"O Lord, I shall perform that sacrifice in every way according to the prescribed rites;
I shall make my promise to you come true. (47)
O best of gods, after a full month has passed, the lawful wife shall be purified;
once the wife is purified, the sacrifice accompanied by the animal victim must be performed.
Vyāsa said:
When these words had been spoken by the king, Varuṇa went to his own home;
the king became satisfied, yet he was somewhat anxious as well. (49)
When the month was complete, he returned once more to the king's palace for the sake of testing him; having assumed the form of a brahmin, well-attired and speaking eloquently. ||50||
Then the king, filled with humility, addressed these words full of reason to that best of gods, who had been duly honored and was seated comfortably.
"O Lord, how can I bind that unconditioned son to the sacrificial post?
Having consecrated him and made him a Kṣatriya, I shall perform the supreme sacrifice. (52)
O Lord, if you take pity upon me, your wretched servant,
know that one who is unrefined and a child has no entitlement anywhere.
Varuṇa said:
O Indra among kings, you deceive me after having first made a solemn agreement; for I know that your affection for your son is difficult to abandon, especially since you have no other offspring.
"O protector of the earth, I shall go home at your gentle word;
after waiting for some time, I will return to your house. (55)
O dear one, you must then act in accordance with truthful speech. ||56||
The King said:

"O Lord of aquatic creatures, after performing the concluding rites of my return from student life in every respect, I shall sacrifice my son as an animal in a sacrifice according to the prescribed rules. (57)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the king, Varuṇa, with a pleased mind, said "So be it" and departed quickly; the king, however, became composed.
His son, known by the name Rohita, grew up to be intelligent and became an expert in all branches of knowledge. (59)
By him, the entire cause of the sacrifice was understood in full detail;
then, perceiving his own impending death, he too became terrified with fear.
Having fled, that hero went into a mountain cave;
afflicted by fear, he remained there in a place inaccessible to kings.
Then, when the time had arrived, Varuṇa, desiring to perform a sacrifice, went to the king's palace and said to that ruler of the earth: "O lord of people, perform a sacrifice."
With a withered face and agitated senses, the king said to him:
"O best of gods, what shall I do? My son has gone somewhere."
Having heard those words of the king, that Yāsamati became enraged;
in her fury, she severely cursed the king for being a speaker of untruth.
"O King, may the disease known as *jalodara* (ascites) afflict your body, since you have deceived me by acting as a hypocritical scholar. (65)
Having thus uttered the curse, the one bound by the noose then departed for his own abode;
the king remained in his palace, overcome with anxiety and afflicted by disease.
When the king was severely afflicted by a disease born of a curse,
then the son also heard that his father was tormented by illness.
The traveler said: "O prince, your father is indeed deeply distressed by the affliction of dropsy born of a curse. (68)
O evil-minded one, born in vain, your life is now destroyed today. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 13. 377.
Since you have abandoned your father, who was in distress, and reached this mountain cave. (69)
"O lowest of sons, what fruit of birth have you obtained with this body? Having made the giver of this body miserable, you remain here."
"It is the settled conviction that a virtuous son must sacrifice his life for the sake of his father;
for your sake, the king is grieving and wailing like one afflicted by disease. (71)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those truthful words from the traveler, which were consistent with dharma, he then set his mind upon going to see his father who was afflicted by grief. (72)
Then, O descendant of Bharata, Vāsava, assuming the form of a brahmin, approached him and spoke these beneficial words in private, as if out of compassion.
"You are a fool, O prince; you vainly set your mind on departing.
Today you do not realize that your father is filled with anguish. (74)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 12 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Indra said:
"The king previously performed a rash act, namely, the sacrifice that was described."
Having made his beloved son a sacrificial animal, he promised him to Varuṇa.
O one of great intelligence, once you have departed, your pitiless father, tormented by distress, will bind you again to a sacrificial post, treat you as a beast, and slaughter you.
Thus forbidden by Śakra of immeasurable splendor, his son remained right there,
utterly deluded by the illusion of Māyeśī.
But when, having heard again and again that his father was afflicted by disease, he set his mind on departing, Indra then forbade him. (4)
Hariścandra, afflicted by extreme sorrow, questioned his preceptor Vasiṣṭha, who was seated nearby in private— the omniscient one ever intent on his welfare.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, what shall I do now? I am cowardly and overwhelmed by distress. Protect me, whose mind is sorrowful and who is afflicted by the fear of a great disease."
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O King, there is a praised remedy for the destruction of disease;
thirteen kinds of sons have been described in the Compendium of Dharma (Dharmasaṃgraha).
Therefore, having adopted a purchased son, perform the most excellent sacrifice;
give the wealth as prescribed and bring back that best of the twice-born.
"O King, when the sacrifice has been performed in this manner, there will be a destruction of the disease, and Varuṇa too will become gracious in spirit and at ease. (9)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the king spoke to his minister:
"O man of great intelligence, search with the utmost effort throughout the realms."
Sometimes a father, driven by greed, gives away his own son; even as he pleads, "Bring him back after giving me wealth," the son is already gone.
The young brahmin must by all means be brought here for the sake of the sacrifice;
you must not entertain a pitiable thought on my account.
"You must request a son from some Brahmin;
for the sake of the sacrifice, you must indeed provide him with wealth and offer him as the sacrificial animal. (13)
Thus urged by him for the sake of his duty, the minister searched throughout the city, from village to village and house to house.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter thirteen.
While he was searching in this manner within his domain, there was a certain sick man who was destitute and had three sons; he was known by the name Ajīgarta.
Then that best of ministers, having given him the requested wealth, brought his middle son, Śunaḥśepa. || 16 ||
Having brought Śunaḥśepa, the son of a brahmin who was fit for sacrifice, the minister, intent on his duty, presented him to the king. (17)
The king, exceedingly delighted, summoned from all sides the best of Veda-knowing Brahmins and had them prepare the necessary materials for the sacrifice.
But while that sacrifice was underway, the great sage Viśvāmitra,
seeing Śunaḥśepa bound, then forbade the king.
"O King, do not act rashly; release this young brahmin boy.
I entreat you, O long-lived one; today there shall be happiness for you. (20)
This Śunaḥśepa is crying out; his piteous state distresses me as well. Be compassionate, O Indra among kings; O King, do my bidding.
In former times, those Kṣatriyas who were devoted to compassion, desiring heaven and pure in their vows, gave up their own bodies for the protection of others' bodies. (22)
For the sake of protecting your own body, you are forcibly killing this son of a brahmin;
O Indra among kings, do not commit such an act, but be compassionate toward the child.
O King, you yourself know that affection for one's body is equal toward all;
therefore, release this child if my word is authoritative to you. (24)
Vyāsa said:
Disregarding those words, the king, being deeply afflicted by grief, did not release the sage; the ascetic became exceedingly enraged with him. (25)
Then the compassionate Kauśika, the foremost knower of the Vedas, gave instruction to Śunaḥśepa, who was bound by the noose of the mantra.
Śunaḥśepa also, repeatedly reciting that mantra with an elongated tone as he was being dragged toward the sacrificial post,
cried out while intensely remembering Varuṇa.
Knowing that the son of the sage was indeed praising him, the Lord of the Sea,
an ocean of compassion, came there and released Śunaḥśepa.
Having freed the king from disease, Varuṇa went to his own home;
Viśvāmitra, for his part, made that son released from death.
The king did not heed the words of the high-souled Kauśika;
that son of Gādhi, harboring resentment in his mind, directed his anger toward the king.
At one time, the king, mounted on a horse, went to the forest;
desiring to hunt a boar, he was at the bank of the Kauśikī at midday. (31)
Deceived by Viśvāmitra in the guise of an old Brahmin,
he was asked for his entire possession and gave up his wonderful kingdom.
Since that Hariścandra, performing the sacrifice, was being greatly oppressed,
Vasiṣṭha spoke to Kauśika, who had arrived in the forest by chance.
O lowest of Kṣatriyas, O evil-minded one, you who wear the dress of a Brāhmaṇa in vain! O hypocrite, why do you carry such pride for no reason, following the conduct of a crane? (34)
"O fool, why have you brought this best of kings—who was performing a sacrifice for me as well—into such extraordinary suffering without any fault on his part? (35)
"Since you are intent on harming the Kaśyapas, therefore you shall indeed become a crane.
Having been cursed thus by Vasiṣṭha, Kauśika spoke to him again: || 36 ||
"You too, O long-lived one, shall become a crane, and I shall likewise become a crane"—
having thus mutually uttered this curse, the two were tormented by anger.
Vyāsa said:
Two birds were born from an egg in the lake; one was a crane and the other a heron.
Having built a nest in a single tree, that one took the form of a crane.
Viśvāmitra remained there at the divine Mānasa lake,
while Vasiṣṭha made an excellent nest upon another tree.
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, Sixth Book, Chapter 14:
Assuming the form of Āḍi, they stood facing one another, intent on mutual hatred.
Day after day, filled with wrath, the two of them engaged in combat.
Causing suffering to all the worlds, both cried out intensely,
striking one another with blows from their beaks and wings and with the scratching of their claws.
Drenched in blood, they struck each other like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom;
thus did the two sages, assuming the forms of birds, [fight] for many years.
"O Great King, while they were staying there, they were restrained by the noose of a curse.
The king said:
"How were the two best of sages, Vasiṣṭha and Kauśika, released from the curse? (43)
"Tell me that, O brahmin-sage, for my curiosity is great.
Vyāsa said:
"Seeing both of them engaged in combat, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds," [44]
There the Creator of the World arrived, surrounded by all his unblinking attendants who were intent on compassion; having consoled them both and restrained them from battle, he spoke.
He released the curse that had been cast between them;
then all the gods and the Lotus-born One returned to their respective abodes.
The powerful Viśvāmitra, mounted upon a swan, went swiftly to Satyaloka;
Vasiṣṭha also departed quickly and returned to his own hermitage.
Then, having formed a mutual affection due to the instruction of Prajāpati,
the son of Mitra and Varuṇa likewise engaged in this causeless war.
O King, who indeed in this world—whether a human, a god, or even a demon—could endure such mutual suffering together with Kauśika? (49)
Having achieved victory over the ego, one shall always partake in happiness;
therefore, O King, purity of mind is difficult to attain even for the great. (50)
That [wisdom] must be accomplished with effort; everything else devoid of it—whether pilgrimage, charity, austerity, truth, or any other means of dharma—is useless. (51)
In this regard, faith is said to be threefold among embodied beings in their religious duties and actions within all bodies: the *sāttvika*, the *rājasa*, and likewise the *tāmasa*. (1)

The *sāttvikī* [pūjā] is difficult to find in this world, for it always bestows the fruit as described; the *rājasī*, when performed according to the prescribed rules, is said to bestow half of that fruit.
But that which is characterized by darkness (tāmasī), O King, yields no fruit and brings no fame;
it belongs, O best of monarchs, to those people who are overcome by desire and anger.
Having rendered that mind free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through hearing [the scriptures] and other means,
one should dwell constantly at sacred fords and other holy places, intent upon the worship of the Goddess,
uttering her names with speech and praising her qualities.
Afflicted by the fear of the defects of the Kali age, he meditated upon her lotus feet.
For one who acts in this manner, there is never any fear of the Kali age;
even a sinful person is liberated from saṃsāra without effort.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 13 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"How did that sage come to be called 'Maitrāvaruṇi'?"
Of the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā. || 1 ||
O best among speakers, tell me: did he obtain his name from his actions or from his qualities? Explain to me the cause for that name's origin.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the Sixth Skandha, Chapter 14,
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O best of kings: Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, having cast off his body due to the curse of Nimi, was born again with great splendor.
Because it belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa, O King, its name is renowned everywhere in this world as "Maitrāvaruṇi."
The king said:
"Why was that righteous-souled sage, the son of Brahmā, cursed by the king?
This is a marvel—that such an exceedingly terrible curse should have fallen upon the sage from the king."
"O Sage, why did the king curse this sinless sage?
O knower of dharma, tell me the reason for that curse from its very root."
Vyāsa said:
"O King, I have already explained to you the determined cause:
this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is indeed pervaded by the three qualities of Māyā."
Let the king practice dharma and let the ascetics perform their penance;
yet, pierced by the faults of all, it shall not shine brightly here.
And kings as well as sages, overcome by anger and pride, and joined with greed and egoism, perform difficult austerities. (9)
O King, there are Kṣatriyas who are endowed with the qualities of royal power,
and likewise, O King, there are some Brāhmaṇas who are possessed of great strength of character (sattva).
That Nimi was cursed by the Ṛṣi, and the sage was cursed by him in turn;
both of them, by the power of fate, experienced a state more painful than pain itself.
Purification of the body, purification of action, and the radiant purification of the mind—
these, O King, are difficult for living beings to attain in this world composed of the three qualities.
This power of the Supreme Śakti cannot be transgressed by anyone at any time;
she who desires to bestow grace upon someone liberates that person in an instant. (13)
Even great ones such as Hari, Brahmā, and Hara are not liberated,
whereas even commoners such as Satyavrata and others are liberated.
No one in the three worlds knows her heart;
nevertheless, it is certain that she remains subject to the devotion of her devotees. 15.
Therefore, devotion to that [Lord] should be cultivated for the sake of uprooting defects;
yet, if that devotion is joined with passion, hypocrisy, and the like, it becomes destructive. || 16 ||
Born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku was a lord of men named Nimi,
who was handsome, endowed with virtues, a knower of dharma, and a delighter of the world.
A speaker of truth, devoted to charity, a performer of sacrifices, wise and pure;
the twelfth son was intelligent and intent upon the protection of his subjects. (18)
He established a city named Jaya near the hermitage of Gautama for the welfare of the Brāhmaṇas.
A rajasic thought arose within that Buddhist:
"I shall perform a sacrifice with many rituals over a long period of time, accompanied by sacrificial fees. (20)
O King, having seen his father Ikṣvāku, he caused the preparations for the sacrificial rite to be made exactly as prescribed by the great-souled ones.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Vāmadeva, Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Ṛcīka, Pulaha, and Kratu. ||22||
He invited sages who were omniscient, masters of the Vedas,
experts in the science of sacrifice, ascetics, and the most eminent among those who know the Vedas.
Having gathered the necessary materials and honored his own preceptor, the king,
who was knowledgeable in dharma and endowed with humility, spoke to Vasiṣṭha.
"O tiger among sages, I wish to perform a sacrifice; O treasure-house of compassion, please officiate for me.
You are my guru and an all-knowing one; perform this task for me now. (25)
All the sacrificial implements have been brought and well-prepared;
my mind is resolved to perform the initiation for five thousand years.
In this sacrifice, having propitiated the Goddess Śrī Jagadambikā,
I perform the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites for the sake of her pleasure.
Having heard those words of Nimi, Vasiṣṭha spoke to the king. Śrīmaddevībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 14. 23. Having heard those words of Nimi, Vasiṣṭha spoke to the king.
"O best of kings, I was previously chosen by Indra according to the truth. (28)
Desirous of performing a sacrifice to Parāśakti,
the Lord Indra was initiated for a period of five hundred years.
Therefore, O King, wait for an interval until this sacrifice to Indra is completed, having performed the task of the Lord of Heaven.
"I shall come, O King; therefore, please wait for me.
The king said:
"Other sages have been invited by me for the sake of the sacrifice. (31)
"All the requisites have been gathered; how then shall I protect [the kingdom], O Guru?
O Brahmin, you are the best knower of the Vedas and the preceptor of the Ikṣvākus. (32)
"Why have you now abandoned my task and prepared to depart so quickly?
O best of the twice-born, it is not proper for you to leave my sacrifice."
With his mind agitated by greed for wealth, the Guru set out for the sacrifice of Indra even though he was forbidden by the king. (34)
The king, too, becoming despondent, paid honor to Gautama;
he performed sacrifices on the slopes of the Himalayas near the ocean.
O King, abundant sacrificial fees were given to the Brahmins during the performance of the sacrifice;
there, Nimi underwent the initiation ceremony for five thousand [years].
The officiating priests, having been honored at their pleasure with wealth and cattle,
were filled with joy when the Śakra-sacrifice, lasting five hundred years, was completed.
Vasiṣṭha arrived, desiring to see the king’s sacrificial session;
having arrived, he stood there for the purpose of seeing the monarch.
Then the king, having fallen into a deep sleep, was completely overcome by slumber;
he was not awakened by his servants, nor did the king come to the sage. (39)
Then, due to that insult and because Nimi was no longer visible there, the anger of Vasiṣṭha arose; that best of sages became enraged. (40)
And, overcome by anger, he uttered a curse upon that king:
"Since you have abandoned me, your guru, to take another as your own preceptor... (41)
"O dull-witted king, you have been initiated against my will for the sake of my destruction;
therefore, even though you were forbidden by me, you shall remain in this very body. 42.
"Let this body of yours fall; become bodiless, O lord of the earth!
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the king, his attendants were struck with astonishment.
They immediately awakened the sage, who was said to be provoked;
having approached him while he was still angry, the king was cleansed of all sin.
He spoke words that were gentle, pregnant with reason, and logical:
"O knower of dharma, it is not my fault; you have gone forth agitated by thirst. (45)
O best of the twice-born, having abandoned me as I am performing a sacrifice— even though I entreated you most earnestly— you feel no shame for having committed such a loathsome deed.
O best of Brahmins, recognize the certainty of dharma in contentment;
you are truly the son of Brahmā himself, the foremost among those who know the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
"You do not understand the subtle course of the law of the Brahmins, which is difficult to traverse;
having recognized my own fault in you, you are prepared to curse me falsely. (48)
Anger must be abandoned by the virtuous, for it is worse than a caṇḍāla;
overcome by useless wrath, you have cast this curse upon me. (49)
"And may this body of yours also fall today, filled with anger.
Thus was the sage cursed by the king, and the king likewise by the sage.
Having incurred curses from one another, they both became distressed;
Vasiṣṭha, however, being exceedingly afflicted with grief, went to Brahmā for refuge.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter fifteen:
He likewise reported the great curse inflicted by the king.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"I have been cursed by the king, saying: 'Let this body of yours fall today! (52)
"What shall I do, father? This suffering born of falling into a body has been reached;
tell me now what will cause the production of another body. (53)
O Father, may my connection with this body be restored as it was before; whatever knowledge existed in this body, let that same knowledge remain there.
"You are capable, O Great King; you ought to show favor.
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, Brahmā spoke to that son.
"Entering the splendor of Mitra and Varuṇa, become firm;
therefore, you shall be born not from a womb at the proper time—of this there is no doubt. (56)
Having regained a body once more, you will be endowed with righteousness;
as the self of all beings and a knower of the Vedas, you will be desired by all and honored everywhere.
Thus addressed by his father, he then departed for the abode of Varuṇa,
having affectionately circumambulated and bowed down to his grandfather.
Then Vasiṣṭha, having abandoned that unsurpassed body, entered the bodies of Mitra and Varuṇa by means of a portion of his vital spirit (jīva). 59.
Once, O King, the beautiful Urvashi, surrounded by a group of her female companions, came to the abode of Varuna by chance.
O King, having seen that divine apsaras endowed with beauty and youth, the two goddesses then became overcome with desire and spoke to her.
"Helpless and agitated, we two choose you, O lady of faultless limbs, who are as beautiful as a celestial maiden with every limb lovely. (62)
"O lady of excellent complexion, dwell in this place as you desire. Having been addressed thus by those two, the goddess remained there, constrained against her will.
Having made her disposition firm in the house of Mitra and Varuṇa, that goddess of beautiful appearance remained there, having adopted their state of being.
O King, the semen of those two fell into a jar that was not covered by the gods;
from that were born two sages who were exceedingly beautiful.

Among them, Agasti was the first, and Vasiṣṭha was the other; those two best of sages were ascetics born from the seed of Mitra and Varuṇa. The first, a great ascetic, reached the forest while still a child;
however, Ikṣvāku chose that boy Vasiṣṭha as his domestic priest.
For the welfare of this lineage, the king protected him;
having recognized him specifically as a sage, he became filled with affection for him. (68)
All this has been told to you,
as well as the cause regarding Vasiṣṭha and how he attained another body through a curse within the lineage of Mitra and Varuṇa.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 14 ||
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"The acquisition of a body by Vasiṣṭha has indeed been narrated by you."
Tell me how Nimi again obtained a body. || 1 ||
Vyāsa said:
O lord of men, Vasiṣṭha regained his body once more;
however, Nimi did not regain his body in the same way after the curse.
When he was cursed by Vasiṣṭha,
all those brahmins who had been chosen as officiating priests (ṛtvij) for the sacrifice by the king deliberated together.
What indeed should be done by us now? Alas, the lord of the earth has been consumed by a curse!
Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 15. 383.
What indeed should be done by us? Alas, the lord of the earth has been consumed by a curse!
But while this sacrifice was still incomplete, he was righteous and engaged in the initiatory rite.
"What should be done? This task has indeed turned out contrary [to our wishes].
Because it was an inevitable occurrence, we were powerless to prevent it. (5)
Then, by means of various kinds of mantras, they maintained his body— belonging to that great-souled one—
and kept it protected, with just a slight trace of breath remaining.
Being worshipped repeatedly with various perfumes and garlands,
he was installed as changeless and well-honored through the power of mantras.
When the sacrifice was completed there, O King, all the gods assembled and, being praised by the officiating priests, became well-pleased.
Addressed by the sages with hymns of praise, they spoke to their weary selves:
"O protector of the earth, we are pleased; choose a boon, O you of noble vows. (9)
O royal sage, by means of this sacrifice, an excellent birth is ordained—whether it be a divine body or a human body, whichever is desired in your mind. (10)
"Let your proud priest remain at his pleasure in the world of mortals.
Having been addressed thus, the soul of Nimi, being well-pleased, spoke to them.
I have no desire for this body, which is ever-perishing;
O best of gods, my dwelling is in the vision of all living beings. (12)
"I move about as the wind within the eyes of all beings.
When he had spoken thus, the gods there addressed Nimi’s own self.
O Great King, pray to the Goddess Śivā, the sovereign of all;
being satisfied by this sacrifice, she will grant you your heart's desire.
Thus addressed by the gods, he offered prayers to the deity with various kinds of divine hymns, out of devotion and with a voice faltering with emotion.
Then that goddess, being pleased, granted a direct vision,
