appearing in a form radiant with beauty and resembling ten million suns.
Seeing this, everyone was delighted and felt in their hearts that they had accomplished their purpose;
and when the goddess was thus propitiated, O King, the monarch chose a boon.
Grant that stainless knowledge by which liberation may be attained, so that my dwelling may be in the eyes of all living beings. (18)
Then the Goddess of gods, the Mother of the World, being pleased, spoke:
"May your knowledge become stainless, [only] remaining for the sake of what is left of your prārabdha karma. (19)
He shall also become the dwelling place for all beings within their eyes;
it is by your very act that the eyes of embodied creatures close in a blink. (20)
Because of your dwelling here, human beings and animals shall become blinking, and even the gods shall again become unblinking. (21)
Having thus granted him that boon, the goddess Śrīvarā then took leave of all the sages and vanished right there.
When the goddess had vanished, the sages remaining there searched everything according to the prescribed rites and recovered the body of Nimi.
Then, having established the fire-drills there, those great-souled ones performed the mantra-recitation and oblations for the sake of a son for Nimi, just as prescribed by the mantras. ||24||
Then, as the fire-drill was being rubbed in the forest, a son appeared, endowed with all auspicious marks, like another Nimi in person. (25)
Because he was born from the churning of the *araṇī* wood, he is remembered as Mithi;
because he was born from Janaka, he became known as Janaka. (26)
Since Nimi was born as Videha, therefore the kings who arose in his lineage are celebrated as the Videhas. ||27||
Thus King Janaka, the son of Nimi, became renowned;
by him was built a captivating city on the bank of the Gaṅgā. (28)
Mithilā was well-renowned, endowed with gate-towers and watchtowers,
filled with wealth and grain, and adorned with marketplaces and halls.
All those kings who were in this lineage were likewise Janakas;
they were all renowned as wise men and celebrated as Videhas. (30)
This supreme narrative has been told to you, O King;
I have related in detail how he attained bodilessness as a result of a curse.
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhaskandha*), chapter fifteen. 384.
The king said:
"O Blessed One, you have explained the cause of Nimi’s curse;
having heard it, my mind has fallen into doubt and is exceedingly restless. (32)
Vasiṣṭha, the best of brahmins and the royal priest, was the son of the Lotus-born; how was that sage cursed by the king? (33)
Having recognized the Guru as a Brahmin, Nimi did not show forbearance;
after performing the auspicious sacrificial rite, how is it that he has fallen into anger? (34)
Having understood the true nature of dharma, how could one born of the Ikṣvāku lineage fall under the sway of anger and curse his guru, a brāhmaṇa? (35)
Vyāsa said:
O King, forgiveness is exceedingly difficult for living beings who have not conquered their own selves;
one who possesses forgiveness, especially one who is highly capable, is rare in this world. (36)
Let him be a sage who has renounced all attachments, an ascetic who has conquered sleep and hunger, and one firmly established in the practice of yoga. (37)
Lust, anger, greed, and egoism as the fourth—these enemies residing within the body are difficult to discern; therefore, they must be overcome in every way. (38)
Never before in saṃsāra has there been such a man, nor does one exist now, nor will there ever be anyone who could conquer these enemies. (39)
Neither in heaven, nor on the earth, nor in the world of Brahmā, nor at the abode of Hari, nor on Kailāsa, is there anyone such as this who could conquer these enemies. (40)
Even the sages, the sons of Brahmā, and other such supreme ascetics are pierced by the three qualities; how much more so, then, the humans on earth?
Kapila was a knower of Sāṃkhya, devoted to the practice of Yoga, and pure;
yet, by the turn of fate, it was he who utterly consumed the sons of Sagara.
Therefore, O King, since the three worlds have arisen from this ego-consciousness (ahaṃkāra), how could they be separated from it, given the relationship of cause and effect? (43)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śrava (Viṣṇu), and Śaṅkara, being permeated by the three qualities, manifest within bodies; their respective dispositions are distinct from one another.
And what need is there to speak of human beings, O lover of truth, when you are established in your state?
O King, a confusion of qualities is present everywhere.
Sometimes there is an increase of sattva, sometimes indeed of rajas, sometimes an increase of tamas, and at other times there is equilibrium. 46.
This Supreme Self is devoid of qualities, untainted, supreme, and imperishable;
it is unperceivable by all living beings, immeasurable, and eternal.
In the same way, the supreme power, devoid of qualities and established in Brahman—the foundation of all beings—is difficult to be known by those of small intellect. (48)
Likewise, the Supreme Self and His Power are indeed always one;
by knowing that their form is non-different, one is liberated from all defects. (49)
"Liberation arises from the knowledge of that alone"—this is the drumbeat of the Vedānta.
He who knows this is liberated from this saṃsāra composed of the three guṇas. (50)

Knowledge is said to be of two kinds; the first is known as verbal knowledge, which arises from the understanding of the meaning of the Vedas and scriptures through the application of the intellect. ||51||
In that regard, many conceptual constructions arise, fashioned by the intellect;
some are fabricated by fallacious reasoning, while others are fabricated by correct reasoning.
"From discursive thought arises delusion; from delusion comes the impairment of the intellect;
and from the impairment of the intellect, the destruction of knowledge for living beings is proclaimed. ||1||
But the second knowledge, called "experience," is difficult to attain, O King.
That [result] is attained by the knower only when there is attachment to it;
O Bhārata, the accomplishment of an action does not arise from the mere knowledge of the word. (53)
Therefore, a superhuman knowledge of direct experience is not possible;
for verbal cognition alone is not capable of cutting through the darkness residing within.
Just as darkness is not destroyed by the mere report of a lamp having been lit, so too is that action which leads to bondage; whereas that is true knowledge which leads to liberation. 55.
Other action leads to exhaustion; other knowledge is skill in the arts;
virtue consists in benefiting others, freedom from anger, forbearance, and fortitude. (56)
The Sixteenth Chapter in the Sixth Book of the Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa. Page 385.
And contentment is the brilliantly radiant fruit of the ripening of knowledge;
it is nourished by knowledge, by austerity, or even by the practice of yoga. (57)
Without the arrows of desire and the like, there is never any destruction [of the mind].
But the mind, O King, is fickle by nature and exceedingly difficult to grasp;
under its sway, every living being in the three worlds is of three kinds.
1 || "States such as desire, anger, and the like are proclaimed to be born of the mind. || 58 ||
They truly do not exist at all when the mind has been completely conquered;
therefore, O King, forgiveness was not practiced by Nimi toward the sage.
Just as in the past, when Śukra,
the son of Bhṛgu, had committed an offense, King Yayāti, the best of monarchs, was cursed by him.
The king did not curse the sage out of anger; rather, he had taken upon himself old age.
One person may be gentle, while another becomes cruel, O King. (61)
O King, since there is a difference in their inherent natures, whose fault can be imputed here?
In ancient times, the Haihayas, out of greed for wealth, [deposed] the Bhārgavas who were their family priests.
Overwhelmed by anger, they cut down all the Brahmins from their very roots,
casting behind them the sin arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 15 ||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"In whose lineage were those Haihaya Kṣatriyas born?"
Disregarding the sin of killing a Brahmin, those who struck down the descendants of Bhṛgu; || 1 ||
O Grandfather, tell me the cause of their hostility; how can these most excellent beings harbor anger without any apparent provocation? (2)
Why did that enmity arise between them and the family priests? For this hostility of the Kṣatriyas could not have arisen from a trivial cause. (3)
Otherwise, how could they have slain the blameless Brāhmaṇas who are worthy of worship? And why were those powerful Kṣatriyas not afraid of sin? (4)
O bull among Kṣatriyas, why would he kill the Bāḍavas for such a slight offense?
O best of sages, I have a doubt; you ought to tell me the reason. (5)
Sūta said:
Thus questioned by him at that time, the king, the son of Satyavatī,
being greatly pleased, spoke while recollecting the story in his mind.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O son of Parīkṣit, to this ancient account of the Kṣatriyas, which is truly marvelous and was fully understood by me in the past. (7)
By the name Kārtavīrya, there was a lord of the earth named Arjuna,
who possessed a thousand arms, was powerful, and was devoted to righteousness.
He was a disciple of Dattātreya, like an incarnation of Hari;
he was a perfected Siddha who bestowed all objects of desire, a devotee of Śakti, and indeed the one to be worshipped by the Bhrigus.
A performer of sacrifices, supremely righteous, and ever devoted to giving,
he offered wealth to the Bhṛgus after having performed numerous sacrifices.
O King, through their acts of giving, those twice-born ones became wealthy Bhṛgus;
enriched with an abundance of precious horses, they became renowned throughout the earth.
O tiger among kings, when Kārtavīryārjuna was born again,
the Haihayas became impoverished over the course of great time, O King.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter sixteen:
Once, a grave matter arose concerning the Haihayas.
O King, those Haihayas went to Bhūgu as supplicants.
Having established the discipline, the Kṣatriyas requested much wealth;
yet, afflicted by excessive greed, they did not give it, saying repeatedly, "There is none, there is none. || 14 ||
Some Bhṛgus buried their excellent wealth in the ground,
while others gave it to the twice-born, having perceived the danger from the Kṣatriyas.
Having moved their wealth to another place, the Brāhmaṇas, overwhelmed by fear,
all abandoned their hermitages and departed, driven by thirst for sustenance.
Seeing the supplicants in distress, they, deluded by greed, gave nothing;
having fled, they all went and took refuge in mountain fastnesses. || 17 ||
Then, O dear one, those Haihayas, the bulls among Kṣatriyas, being distressed by the gravity of their situation, went to the hermitages of the Bhṛgus for the sake of wealth. (18)
Then, seeing that the Bhṛgus had departed and their houses were empty and abandoned,
the Haihayas dug deeply into the earth there for the sake of wealth.
All the kṣatriyas, emaciated by their toil, beheld the wealth that had been obtained by digging in the dwelling of a Bhṛgu. || 20 ||
Whatever abundant wealth then arose from the surface of the earth in various places,
it went even to the houses of the Brahmins at your side.
Having pierced through the wealth, the Haihayas beheld it out of a desire for riches;
all the brahmins cried out in fear and sought refuge.
While the Brahmins were searching extensively, much [wealth] emerged from their dwellings;
out of anger, they struck down those Vāḍavas who had sought refuge with arrows. 23.
They went through mountain fastnesses where the Bhṛgus resided; they wandered over this earth, following them even from the womb.
Slaying all the Bhrigus as they arrived with sharpened arrows— killing them from the children to the elderly— and disregarding the sin of this further atrocity.
While the Bhārgavas were being uprooted in this manner from here and there,
the Haihayas violently seized and killed the fetuses of women.
Those women wept as much as they desired, distressed like female ospreys, whose fetuses had been torn out by Kṣatriyas of evil resolve. (27)
Other sages dwelling at sacred fords also spoke to those arrogant ones:
"O Kṣatriyas, abandon this fear-inspiring anger toward the Brāhmaṇas. (28)
"This reprehensible deed you have undertaken is improper—that these bulls among Kṣatriyas should slay the fetuses of the wives of Bhṛgu.
One reaps the fruit of exceedingly fierce merit and sin even in this very world. (29)
Therefore, one who desires prosperity for oneself should avoid despicable actions.
Then they addressed those compassionate sages who were enraged:
"All of you are virtuous men, yet you are like women toward those of sinful deeds. (31)
All this wealth of their high-souled ancestors has been seized by these men, who, skilled in deception, have robbed them on the road like highwaymen. (32)
These were deceivers, hypocrites, and those who acted like herons; yet when a great task arose, they were entreated with humility.
O Brahmins, though requested even by increasing the price fourfold, they did not grant what was asked for.
The proponents of nihilism remained stubborn when they beheld the priests in distress. ||34||
For what reason was the wealth obtained from Kārtavīrya not protected? Why were no sacrifices performed by them, nor were gifts given in abundance to supplicants? (35)
Brahmins should never, under any circumstances, hoard wealth anywhere;
rather, they should perform sacrifices according to the rules, give gifts, and enjoy themselves as they please.
O twice-born ones, fear of thieves regarding wealth is proclaimed, as well as fear of kings;
there is most terrible fear of powerful men, and likewise great fear of rogues. (37)
By whatever means possible, one should give away wealth that acts as a protector;
or else, having died, he departs leaving his wealth behind and attains a happy rebirth.
Thus we, full of humility, requested an increase by a quarter;
nevertheless, our priests, clouded by greed, did not grant it. (39)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 17:
Such is the destiny of wealth— donation, enjoyment, and destruction.
For the virtuous, there is both giving and enjoyment; for the sinful, however, there is indeed destruction.
Neither a giver nor one who enjoys [the fruit], but a miser intent on guarding his wealth—
that deceitful man, a partaker of suffering, must be punished in every way by the king.
Therefore, we are all prepared to slay these gurus, who are deceivers and the lowest of Brahmins; the high-souled ones should not be angry.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken these reasoned words and thus comforted those sages,
they then departed, searching for the wife of Bhṛgu in many places.
Afflicted by fear, the wives of Bhṛgu, weeping, trembling, and extremely emaciated, took refuge on the Himavat mountain. ||44||
Thus those brahmins, oppressed by the Haihayas who were greedy for wealth,
were slaughtered at will by those furious evildoers.
Greed alone, residing within the bodies of men, is their great enemy;
it is declared to be the source of all suffering, the giver of misery, and the destroyer of life. (46)
For he is indeed the root of all evil, always possessed by craving;
he creates opposition toward the three castes and is likewise the cause of all suffering.
Out of greed, they indeed abandon dharma as well as family tradition;
they even kill their mother, brother, father, and kinsman.
Driven by greed and deluded by sin, what improper or wicked act would one not commit toward a teacher, a friend, a wife, a son, or even a sister? (49)
From anger, from desire, and from egoism, greed alone is the great enemy;
it causes one to abandon even their very life through greed—how much more so that which is not yet covered?
O Great King, your ancestors, who were knowers of dharma and established on the path of the righteous—
the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas alike— met their destruction through greed.
Where Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, Karṇa, and Bāhlika are, as well as Bhīmasena, the son of Dharma, and likewise Arjuna and Keśava. (52)
Nevertheless, they waged a most fierce battle against one another;
driven by greed, they caused a great slaughter of their own kin here on earth.
Droṇa has been slain, Bhīṣma has been slain, and likewise the sons of the Pāṇḍavas;
brothers, fathers, and sons—all have indeed been killed in battle.
Therefore, what indeed might a man overcome by greed not do?
By those of sinful intent, all the Bhṛgus were slaughtered by the Haihayas. (55)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 16 ||
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
How did all those women [cross] over the ocean of suffering of the Bhrigus?
The lineage of those Brahmins became liberated and stable once again. || 1 ||
Tell me, what deed was accomplished by the Haihayas after they killed even those brāhmaṇas?
Speak of that which was done by the kṣatriyas, who were possessed by greed and followed sinful conduct.
O Brahmin, I am not yet satiated; I thirst for your nectar-like discourse, which purifies men, bestows auspiciousness, and yields fruit in the world beyond.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall relate a story that destroys sin, by which those women were liberated from that suffering so difficult to overcome. 4.
O King, when the wives of the Bhṛgus went to the Himavat mountain, terrified with fear and their hopes shattered, having been severely oppressed by the Haihayas. ||5||
Having installed an earthen image of Gaurī there on the bank of the river,
they remained intent on fasting until death on that very night.
In the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 17:
Then, having gone to them in a dream, the Goddess spoke to those most excellent women.
Among you, there shall be a man born from the thigh of a certain woman.
"Pervaded by a portion of my power, he shall accomplish your task.
Having thus instructed Parāmbā, she subsequently vanished from sight.
Then all those excellent women woke up and attained great joy;
among them, one clever woman was exceedingly agitated by fear.
When that Brāhmaṇa woman was seen by the Kṣatriyas intent on flight, she bore the embryo in one thigh for the sake of the lineage's prosperity. (10)
Overwhelmed and struck by his splendor, they then fled in great haste, crying out, "Seize her! Kill her! This pregnant woman is escaping quickly! (11)
Speaking thus, they arrived with swords in hand before the woman;
seeing them approach, she, afflicted by fear, wept.
For the sake of protecting the fetus, she cried out, overcome by extreme fear;
hearing her mother weeping, distressed, and as if deprived of life, [he acted].
Supportless and weeping, she was tormented by the kṣatriyas like a pregnant doe seized by a lion. || 14 ||
Then Vālaka, becoming enraged, quickly emerged from her thigh—she who was trembling with tears in her eyes—just as another sun might burst forth. || 15 ||
The auspicious boy, by his splendor, eclipsed the visions of the Kṣatriyas;
at the mere sight of the boy, they all quickly regained their sight.
Like those born blind, the Kṣatriyas wandered through the mountain fastnesses;
everyone wondered in their minds, "What is this now? (17)
That we were all born deprived of sight because of seeing a child is due to the power of this Brāhmaṇī; great indeed is the strength of her vow of chastity.
"Or in a moment their resolutions will be in vain; what can they do, being miserable?"—having reflected thus in their minds, those who were blind and without refuge [remained there]. (19)
The Hehayas, their minds overwhelmed by fear, sought refuge with the Brahmin woman;
trembling with terror, they bowed down to her with their palms joined in reverence.
Agitated by fear, those bulls among kṣatriyas spoke to her for the sake of seeing her: "Be gracious, O blessed mother; we are indeed your servants. (21)
O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, these Kṣatriyas of sinful intent who have committed offenses have all become sighted through the mere sight of you, O slender-limbed one. (22)
O beautiful lady, we do not even see your face, like those born blind;
wonderful is the power of your asceticism—what can we do, being evildoers? (23)
We have come to you for refuge; O giver of honor, grant us our eyesight!
You ought to show mercy, for this blindness is more terrible than death. (24)
Furthermore, by granting us our sight, make the kṣatriyas your servants;
then, having desisted from our evil deeds, let us go together.
Henceforth, such an act must never be committed again;
for we are indeed the servants of all the Bhārgavas. (26)
Whatever sin has been committed through ignorance, that must now be brought to an end by you;
henceforth, there shall be no enmity anywhere with the Kṣatriyas of the Bhṛgu lineage.
"O fair-hipped lady, you must be properly restrained by oaths; remain with your sons, for we are all bowed down before you. (28)
"Be gracious, O auspicious lady; we shall never look [upon you again].
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the Brāhmaṇī was filled with wonder. (29)
To those who were prostrate, distressed, and deprived of sight, he spoke, consoling them:
"O Kṣatriyas, I have indeed not taken away your vision. (30)
"It is not out of anger that I speak; hear now the true reason:
this Bhārgava, born from your thigh, has surely become angry with you today. (31)
Therefore, your eyes have been paralyzed by that wrathful one;
having learned of this, the Kṣatriyas have themselves slain even those still in the womb. 32.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter ten:
[He seized] those innocent ascetics devoted to dharma out of a desire for their wealth.
O sons, even when you were slaying the Bhṛgus while they were still in the womb.
Then this embryo was carried by me in my thigh for a hundred years;
and by him, the entire Veda with its six limbs was grasped directly.
Even while remaining in the womb, that child, surely inflamed with anger for the sake of increasing the lineage of Bhṛgu,
desires to kill him, as if he were his father.
"By the grace of the Blessed One, this boy has been born to me;
by his divine splendor, my eyes have been robbed of their sight. (36)
Therefore, I have heard this today: "Entreat him with humility;
for he, being pleased by your prostration, will restore your sight. (37)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of hers, the Haihayas praised him;
filled with humility, they bowed down to that best of sages, the thigh-born one.
Then, being well-pleased, he spoke to those wise ones:
"O kings, go to your own homes; my word has been fulfilled. (39)
Those events ordained by the gods are inevitable;
a wise man should not feel grief on this account. (40)
As before, may all the sages attain their desires as they please;
free from anger, may they depart for their own abodes at their ease. 41.
Thus instructed by him, the Haihayas, having regained their sight,
took leave of Aurva and departed for their homes as they pleased.
O protector of the earth, the Brāhmaṇī took that divine son and went to her own hermitage; there, she tirelessly nurtured that radiant child.
Thus, O King, has been told to you the destruction of the Bhṛgus, and indeed the sin that was committed by the Kṣatriyas out of greed toward the Brahmins. 44.
Janamejaya said:
"I have heard of the great and terrible deed of the Kṣatriyas;
in this matter, greed alone was the cause, for it brought suffering to both sides."
I wish to ask something regarding a doubt concerning Vāsavi:
how did those sons of kings, the Haihayas, become famous on earth by that name? (46)
Let it be that the Yādavas [descended] from Yadu and likewise the Bhāratas from Bharata;
however, there was a certain king of the Haihayas established in their lineage. (47)
Therefore, O treasury of compassion, I wish to hear the cause:
how did those Haihayas become Kṣatriyas, and by what deed? (48)
Vyāsa said:
O King, listen in detail to the ancient and highly meritorious account of the origin of the Haihayas, which destroys all sins.
O King, at one time there was a very handsome son of the Sun,
renowned as Revata, who was beautiful and possessed immeasurable luster.
Mounting the beautiful jewel among horses, Uccaiḥśravas,
the son of the Sun-god went to Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Viṣṇu.
When he arrived mounted on a horse, desiring a vision of the Blessed One,
the son of the Sun was seen by Lakṣmī while still standing upon his horse.
Having beheld the divine horse and her brother born from the ocean,
Ramā was struck with wonder by his beauty and stood there with her eyes transfixed.
The Lord Viṣṇu, seeing him approaching mounted on a beautiful horse, affectionately questioned Ramā.
"O lovely-limbed one, who is this approaching like another mounted on a horse?
O beautiful one, his body is the very splendor of the God of Love, enchanting the three worlds. (55)
Then Lakṣmī, her mind fixed upon him, gazed at him; though questioned again and again, she did not utter a single word by the power of fate.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter eighteen.
Vyāsa said:
Having observed her whose mind was attached to the horse, who was utterly infatuated with passion,
gazing with supreme love, with tremulous eyes and fickle nature— (57)
The Lord, filled with anger, said to her: "What do you see, O fair-eyed one?
Deluded upon seeing Hari, you do not speak even when questioned."
Since you delight everywhere, you shall therefore become Ramā; and because of your fickleness, you shall be called Cañcalā—of this there is no doubt whatsoever. (59)
Just as an ordinary woman is surely fickle, so too you, O auspicious lady, have never been steady at all. (60)
O fair-thighed one, if you, standing near me, become deluded upon seeing the horse,
then become a mare in this most cruel world of mortals.
Thus cursed by Hari due to the turn of fate, the goddess Ramā wept,
trembling, terrified by fear, and deeply distressed.
Having bowed her head to the god, her own husband, the charmingly smiling lady, filled with apprehension and endowed with humility, spoke to that Lord of Ramā.
O God of gods, O Lord of the universe, O Keśava, O Govinda, source of compassion, why do you bestow a curse upon me for such a slight offense? 64.
O Lord, such anger as this has never before been seen by me;
where has your innate affection for me gone, that which is not subject to destruction? (65)
The thunderbolt-strike should be directed at an enemy, not at a friend;
since I am worthy of being chosen by you, how have I been made worthy of a curse? (66)
O Govinda, I shall give up my life today even as you look on;
how can I live, deprived of you and tormented by the fire of separation?
"O Lord of Gods, show favor toward me; from this most terrible curse, O All-pervading One, grant that I may attain your bliss-bestowing presence at what time shall I be released? (68)
Hari said:
"O beloved, when you shall have a son on earth equal to me,
then, O slender-limbed one, having obtained me, you will become happy."
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. ||17||
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"Thus was the daughter of the ocean cursed by the Blessed One due to her improper conduct."
How was she born as a mare, and what was done by Revanta? (1)
In what land was the goddess born, who, assuming the form of a mare, remained all alone like a young woman whose husband has gone abroad? (2)
"O venerable one, for how long was Ramā separated from her husband while dwelling in the lonely forest, and what did she do thereafter?"
When did the daughter of the ocean attain union with Vāsudeva? And how was a son obtained by her while she was separated from Nārāyaṇa?
O Noble Lord, relate this account in detail;
O best of Brahmins, I am desirous of hearing this unsurpassed narrative. (5)
Sūta said:
O brahmins, having been thus questioned by the son of Parīkṣit, Vyāsa then related this story in great detail.
Vyāsa said: Listen, O King, I shall relate this auspicious ancient narrative,
which is purifying, bestowing happiness upon the ear, and composed of clear syllables.
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the sixth book, chapter three: But Revanta, seeing the passionate Ramā cursed by the Lord, [was overcome with grief].
Out of fear, he departed from afar after bowing down to the Lord of the worlds.
Seeing the anger of the Lord of the World, he quickly went into the presence of his father and reported to Bhāskara the story concerning the curse.
Commanded by the Lord of the Universe,
the lotus-eyed one arrived in the world of mortals.
Afflicted with grief, that goddess Ramā, having offered a most solemn salutation,
quickly departed from that very spot,
assuming the form of a mare. || 11 ||
In the past, Sūryapatnī performed penance at that place where the Kālindī meets the Tamasā, to the north of Suparṇākṣa—
suparṇākṣa being the name of the mountain— at a site that grants all desires and is adorned with a most beautiful forest, [where she worshipped] Candraśekhara.

Remaining there, she meditated with a single-minded focus upon Mahādeva Śaṅkara, who bears half of Gaurī’s body, whose form has the luster of camphor-white, who grants all desires, and who possesses a trident, a blue throat, and three eyes. 14.
Having five faces and ten arms, with a serpent as his sacred thread. || 15 ||
The Lord, who wears a tiger skin and has an elephant hide as his upper garment, and who is adorned with a garland of skulls—
the son of the Ocean, having assumed a charming female form,
performed difficult penance at that sacred site in the presence of the Lord of Ramā. || 16 ||
Meditating upon the Supreme God and having fully resorted to dispassion,
a thousand divine years passed there, O lord of the earth.
Then Mahādeva, the three-eyed Lord who rides upon the bull, being pleased,
appeared in person together with Pārvatī, the sovereign Maheśāna.
There, Śambhu, accompanied by his attendants, spoke to that beloved of Hari,
who was performing penance and had assumed the form of Aśvinī, O highly fortunate one.
O auspicious one, O Mother of the World, tell me why you are performing penance;
for your husband is the bestower of all goals and the creator of all worlds. (20)
O Goddess, why do you praise the Lord of the Universe, Vāsudeva, the Master of the World who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, today after having abandoned Hari? 21.
The word spoken in the Vedas must be followed: for women, the husband is their deity; they must never, under any circumstances, nor at any time or place, direct their affection toward another.
Service to the husband is the eternal dharma of women;
whatever his nature may be, he must be served in every way by those desiring their own welfare. (23)
"Nārāyaṇa alone is indeed always to be served and worshipped by all;
O daughter of the Ocean, having abandoned that Lord of the gods of gods, why do you meditate upon me? (24)
Lakṣmī said:
O Īśāna, you who are easily pleased, I have been cursed here by my husband, O Śiva;
O Lord of Gods, O ocean of mercy, deliver me from this curse. (25)
Thus it was said by Hari to Śambhu: "O Śambhu, when I was entreated by you, Viṣṇu, filled with compassion, [granted] the cause for both curse and favor as desired. (26)
When you have a son, then there shall be liberation from the curse,
and your residence shall be in Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Kamalā.
Having been addressed thus, I have come to this penance grove to perform austerities;
I have propitiated you, O God, the bestower of all goals. (28)
O God of gods, how can I obtain a son without a wife?
For he dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, having abandoned his blameless and beautiful consort. (29)
"O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, if you are pleased with me, grant me a boon;
for there is certainly never any duality in your disposition. (30)
O Hara, beloved of Umā, I have understood this before my husband:
he who is you is indeed he, and he who is he is you; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having realized our oneness, O Śiva, I have called you to mind; otherwise, blame would fall upon me for having taken refuge in you.
Śiva said:
"O Goddess, O beautiful one, daughter of the ocean, how was the identity between me and that Hari known by you? Tell me the truth. (33)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter eighteen.
Neither the gods nor the sages, nor even the wise who know the truth of the Vedas, truly understand oneness; they are, it is said, afflicted by fallacious reasoning.
Many of my devotees likewise revile Vāsudeva, and many devotees of Viṣṇu are intent upon reviling me. (35)
O Goddess, time becomes especially distinct through its divisions;
O auspicious one, how was it born from you, such that it is difficult to be understood even by those who have disciplined their souls? (36)
"In every respect, however, the state of oneness between Hari and me is difficult to attain.
Vyāsa said:
Thus was that beloved of Hari questioned by the gratified Śambhu.
Having learned the account of him, Ramā, with a very gracious countenance, began to speak to Śiva there. (38)
Lakṣmī said:
O Lord of the gods, once I saw Viṣṇu in solitude, intent on meditation, performing penance while seated in the lotus posture. (39)
Then, O Lord, filled with wonder, I questioned that husband of mine,
knowing him to be awakened and well-pleased, with humility:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, when I emerged from the ocean..."
O Lord, [he was] honored by all the gods and Daityas, beginning with Brahmā.
At that time, I observed them all with the desire for a husband,
and having reached the firm conclusion that you are the best among all the gods, you were chosen by me.
"O Lord of All, whom do you meditate upon? This is a great doubt of mine.
You are dear to me, O Slayer of Kaiṭabha; tell me what is in your mind. (43)
Viṣṇu said:
"At the conclusion of the ritual, I shall describe that supreme god whom I meditate upon in my heart— the Great Lord who is easily pleased, the beloved of the Daughter of the Mountain."
Sometimes the God of gods, who possesses immeasurable prowess, meditates upon me;
and I, in turn, exert myself in meditation upon the Lord of gods, Śaṅkara, the destroyer of Tripura.
I am the dear life-breath of Śiva, and Śaṅkara is likewise mine;
there is no difference between us two, whose minds are mutually attached. 46.
Those who hate Maheśvara surely go to hell;
O large-eyed one, I declare this truth to you: they are my devotees. 47.
Thus was it spoken by Viṣṇu, the powerful God of gods,
when he was questioned by me in private, O beloved of my son.
Therefore, knowing you to be the beloved of Viṣṇu, I have meditated upon you;
O Maheśāna, act in such a way that there may be a reunion with my beloved.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of Śrī, Maheśvara,
who is skilled in speech, comforted her with affectionate words and replied according to the truth.
"Be at ease, O lady of broad hips; I am pleased with your asceticism.
You shall be reunited with your husband, of this there is no doubt. (51)
"O Kāma, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the World, urged by me, will come in the form of a horse to fulfill your desire. (52)
In that manner, I shall impel that god Madhusūdana so that he,
intoxicated with pride, will come to you in the form of a horse.
"O fair-browed one, you shall have a son on earth equal to Nārāyaṇa;
he shall become a protector of the world, honored by all people. (14)
O highly fortunate one, having obtained that boon, you shall go with that husband to Vaikuṇṭha, O Goddess, and you will become his beloved. 55.
"This son of yours shall become famous by the name Ekavīra;
from him, indeed, a lineage shall spread across the earth. (56)
Blinded by intoxication and with a maddened mind, you have therefore obtained such a fruit. ||57||
Therefore, O daughter of the ocean, for the sake of pacifying that fault, seek refuge with the Supreme Deity residing in the heart by means of the state of being the self of all.
"Otherwise, O best of horses, how could your mind go [to its destination]?
Vyāsa said:
Having thus granted the boon to the goddess, the Blessed Lord, the Creator of the World, [departed]. (59)
Śiva himself, together with Umā, vanished from sight;
and that beautiful goddess, seated upon a lotus, remained right there.
Meditating upon the supremely beautiful lotus-feet of the Goddess— the circles of whose toenails were touched by the crest-jewels of gods and asuras—
she praised them again and again with a voice faltering with love,
while awaiting her husband, Hari, who had assumed the form of a horse. (62)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 18 ||
Then the nineteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having granted him that boon, Śambhu departed swiftly for Kailāsa.
Delightful, frequented by hosts of gods and adorned with celestial nymphs; it was graced and embellished by hosts of gods and celestial nymphs.
Having gone there, he dispatched the group Citrarūpa, who was skilled in action,
to Vaikuṇṭha for the sake of accomplishing Lakṣmī’s purpose.
Śiva said:
"O Citrarūpa, go to Hari and speak these words on my behalf, so that he may free his distressed wife from her grief. (3)
Thus addressed, Citrarūpa departed in great haste for the supreme abode of Vaikuṇṭha, which is surrounded by hosts of Vaiṣṇavas.
It was adorned with hundreds of ponds and filled with swans, ducks, peacocks, parrots, and cuckoos. ||5||
It was joined with lofty palaces, adorned with banners,
filled with the arts of dance and song, and graced by mandāra trees.
It was adorned with Bakula, Aśoka, Tilaka, and Campaka trees,
and filled with the warbling of birds that brought delight to the ears.
Having beheld the palace of Viṣṇu,
the two gatekeepers named Jaya and Vijaya, who were stationed there as protectors of the sacred precinct, bowed down and spoke.
Citrarūpa said:
"O, announce quickly to Hari, the Supreme Soul:
'A messenger has arrived here sent by Hara, the wielder of the trident.'"

O fair-faced one, embrace Vyāsa and give birth to a wonderful son, the founder of the Kuru lineage and one worthy of the kingdom. (15)
Then the bride, filled with shame, said not a word;
at her mother's command, I went to the bedchamber that night.
A maidservant of Vicitravīrya, endowed with beauty and youth, adorned with various ornaments and garments, was sent here by Ambikā. (17)
Her body reddened with sandalwood paste, adorned with flower garlands, endowed with graceful gestures, possessing beautiful hair, and walking with the gait of a swan, she arrived. (18)
Having seated me upon the couch, she remained there filled with love;
O sage, I then became delighted by her playful charm.
O Nārada, during our intense amorous play with her at night, I,
being well-pleased, granted a boon to her once again.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter twenty-five.
O fortunate lady, you shall have a son endowed with all auspicious marks;
he will be handsome, a knower of all dharmas, truthful, and devoted to tranquility. (21)
At that time, Vidura was born, and thus there were three sons together;
O virtuous one, my illusion (māyā) had increased due to its birth in another field.
The separation from Śuka, which was the cause of his grief,
was forgotten as he beheld his three sons— who were indeed heroic and esteemed for their prowess— according to his heart's desire.
O Brahmin, illusion is powerful and indeed difficult to abandon for those who have not disciplined themselves;
though formless and without support, it deludes even the wise. 24.
Bound by affection for my mother and likewise constrained by my sons,
O best of sages, my mind found no peace in the forest.
The mind became like one mounted on a swing; at times it was in Hastināpura, and again on the banks of the Sarasvatī, having no fixed abode anywhere. (26)
At one time, as he reflected, knowledge indeed appeared in his mind:
"Who are these sons? Where is this delusion? They are not worthy of the funeral rites for my deceased father."
"How indeed could sons born of infidelity bring me happiness?
For powerful illusion spreads delusion within the mind. (28)
"O Sage, knowing that I have fallen into this blind well of delusion in vain," I once performed this rite in secret, being well-composed in meditation. (29)
Then the powerful Pāṇḍu, approved by Bhīṣma, obtained the kingdom;
at that time, my mind became serene on account of his son. (30)
He had two beautiful wives, Kuntī and Mādrī;
Kuntī was the daughter of Śūrasena, and the other was the daughter of the King of Madra.
Having received that curse from the twice-born, he, though endowed with a pair of beautiful women,
became filled with world-weariness due to his pale complexion and, abandoning his kingdom, went to the forest.
Then, hearing that my son was staying in the forest, grief entered me;
I went to that place where he was dwelling together with his two wives.
Having comforted Pāṇḍu in the forest, I returned once more to Hastināpura;
after addressing Dhṛtarāṣṭra, I went to the banks of the Brahmajā river.
Having lawfully begotten five sons born of the field (kṣetraja) in the forest hermitage—namely the five Pāṇḍavas from Vāyu, Śakra, and the two Aśvins—he [departed]. || 35 ||
Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīmasena, and likewise Arjuna—
these sons of Kuntī are renowned as being born from Dharma, Vāyu, and the Lord of the Gods (Indra).
Once, in private, the lord of the earth embraced Mādrī, who was the daughter of the King of Madra and the mother of Nakula and Sahadeva.
Having died by the curse of the sages, he was consecrated in the mouth of the fire;
there Mādrī, being a virtuous wife, entered along with her husband.
Kuntī remained with her sons in the blazing fire;
at that time, the sages [beheld] the daughter of Śūrasena accompanied by her children.
They brought that sorrowful woman, bereft of her husband, to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura);
she was then entrusted to the high-souled Bhīṣma Vidura.
Having heard that my sons were protected by Bhīṣma, I was indeed afflicted by both joy and sorrow, reflecting upon them as being [both] my own and those of others.
Likewise, out of affection, Vidura and the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra [spoke],
as did his sons, Duryodhana and the others, who were cruel-minded.
Having come together in one place, they engaged in a wonderful conflict;
then Dronācārya arrived there and was honored by Bhīṣma. 43.
When Karna was an infant abandoned by Kuntī, he was settled in that city for the purpose of teaching her sons.
Protected by his charioteer Adhiratha, he reached the river;
thus Karṇa became dear to Duryodhana and likewise the most heroic of men.
Mutual hostility arose among Bhīma, Duryodhana, and the others;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, however, reflected upon the suffering caused by those sons and himself.
He established a residence for the high-souled Pāṇḍavas in the city of Vāraṇāvata solely for the purpose of pacifying the conflict.
Right there, out of malice, Duryodhana had divine lac-houses constructed by sending his friend Purocana.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter 26:
Having heard that the Pāṇḍavas, together with Pṛthā, had been burnt in the house of lac, [Dhṛtarāṣṭra...]
O best of sages, because of my lack of a grandson, I am submerged in an ocean of calamity.
Afflicted by intense grief, beholding them day and night in the desolate forest, I saw the Pāṇḍavas, emaciated by suffering, in Ekacakrā. (50)
Then, having beheld the sons of Pṛthā, I became joyful in mind;
and I quickly dispatched them toward the city of Drupada.
Afflicted by grief, emaciated, and wearing the garments of Brahmins and deer-skins, they went there and then took their places in the assembly hall.
Having displayed his prowess and conquered the daughter of Drupada, the victorious one performed the marriage with that proud lady five times, according to the word of his mother.
Having witnessed their marriage, O sage, I was then exceedingly joyful;
thereafter, we arrived at the city named after the Nāgas, accompanied by Pāñcālī.
O best of the twice-born, Khandavaprastha was prepared as the residence for the Pandavas by Vasudeva’s son and Dhritarashtra.
There, the sacrificial fire was gratified by Viṣṇu along with Jiṣṇu;
when the Rājasūya sacrifice was performed, I then became joyful.
Then, having seen their prosperity as well as the assembly hall constructed by Maya,
Duryodhana became deeply distressed and subsequently engaged in gambling.
Śakuni was unskilled at the gambling board and Yudhiṣṭhira had no knowledge of dice;
thus the kingdom, all wealth, and everything were lost, and Yājñasenī was subjected to suffering.
Those Pāṇḍavas have been exiled to the forest for twelve years together with the princess of Pañcāla; because of that, great sorrow has been produced within me. (59)
"O Nārada, thus am I deeply immersed in this worldly existence, which consists of both pleasure and pain, wandering through delusion even while knowing the eternal Dharma. (60)
"Who am I? Whose daughter am I? Who are these [people]? Who is my mother? And what is happiness?
For because of delusion, my heart wanders thus day and night. (61)
What shall I do? Where shall I go? Contentment is not attained.
My mind is mounted upon a swing; it is restless here and does not become steady.
"You are omniscient, O best of sages; dispel my doubt.
Act in such a way that I may become happy and free from distress.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of mine, Nārada, the knower of the supreme truth, [spoke].
And having smiled, she spoke to me as I asked about the cause of my delusion. ||1||
Nārada said:
O son of Parāśara, knower of the Purāṇas, what do you ask for the sake of certainty?
In this saṃsāra, there is no embodied being whatsoever who is free from delusion.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Sanaka, and Kapila—all are enveloped by Māyā and wander upon the path of worldly existence. ||3||
People know me as one possessed of knowledge, yet I am deluded like all the world;
listen to my former history, which I shall relate with complete certainty. (4)
O son of Vāsavi, because of my own delusion regarding a wife, I previously experienced a far greater suffering than this. (5)
Once, Parvata and I descended from the world of the gods to the surface of the earth,
in order to behold the excellent land of Bhārata.
Wandering together upon the earth, they beheld the circle of sacred fords,
purifying places, and the auspicious hermitages of sages.
Having first conversed with one another from the world of the gods,
they deliberated and, having reached a firm decision, indeed set out while observing this agreement.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, the sixth book, chapter twenty-six.
However, the mental disposition that arises in anyone—whether auspicious or inauspicious—must be expressed; it should never be concealed. (9)
Whether there be a desire for food, a desire for wealth, or even a desire for pleasure—whatever exists in one's mind should be spoken of to another. (10)
Having thus made this agreement, we two have come from the heavenly realm to the world of mortals;
with one mind, having become sages, we wander according to our will. (11)
Thus wandering in this world, when the end of summer had arrived,
they reached again the delightful city of King Sañjaya.
Honored with devotion by the king and highly esteemed by him,
they remained there in the house of that high-souled one for the duration of the Cāturmāsya.
The four months of the rainy season are always difficult to traverse on the road;
therefore, it is the settled conclusion that a wise person should remain in one place. (14)
A twice-born man may always travel abroad for eight months due to the exigencies of his duties;
however, one who desires happiness should not go on a journey during the rainy season. (15)
Having thus reflected in his mind, he then remained in the house of Sañjaya,
honored by the high-souled king who had offered him hospitality.
The daughter of that lord of the earth was renowned as Damayantī;
she, possessed of beautiful teeth and great beauty, was strictly commanded to perform service.
The princess, who possessed discerning knowledge and large eyes, exerted herself and performed service to both of them at all times. || 18 ||
At the proper time, she gives water for bathing, delicious and abundant food, mouth-fresheners, and whatever else is desired. (19)
The maiden also provided for both of them all the desired objects of their hearts, such as fans,
seats, beds, and so forth, even those they had not requested.
While being thus served, we two indeed remained in the king’s house, intent on the study of the Vedas and devoted to Vedic observances. (21)
Holding the lute in my hand and having perfected the most excellent notes, I sang the Sāman chant, sweet-sounding and a tonic for the ears. (22)
But having heard that enchanting song of the Sāmaveda, O wise one, the princess became filled with passion for me and endowed with affection.
Day by day, her passion for me has increased to the highest degree;
likewise, my mind has become filled with longing for her who is full of affection. (24)
Filled with affection, that maiden never made even the slightest distinction between me and him regarding food and other services; she served us both without any difference in her devotion.
She provided hot water for my bath and cool water for Parvata;
likewise, she prepared curd for me and buttermilk for Parvata as well. (26)
She prepared a bright bed and coverlet for my sake with such supreme affection as she had never shown even toward Parvata. (27)
The beautiful woman gazed at me with love, and not at the mountain;
then, seeing her look in such a way, Parvata understood the cause of her affection.
Filled with wonder, he reflected in his mind, "What is this?
and asked me in private: "O Nārada, tell me clearly and in every way. (29)
The princess, filled with joy, feels great love for you; full of affection, she bestows all kinds of food and delicacies upon you from every side. (30)
Such a difference regarding me does not produce doubt here;
rather, the daughter of Sañjaya considers you in every way to be her husband.
I also recognize such a state of yours through your physical characteristics; the cause of your affection is known by the changes in your eyes and face. (32)
"Speak the truth; you must not utter a false word, O Sage. Remember now the agreement you made while in heaven; do not deviate from it. (33)
Nārada said:
When I was thus questioned by Parvata regarding this matter with such persistence, I was overcome with shame; yet, having become composed, I spoke again.
"O Parvata, this large-eyed woman is intent on making me her husband; likewise, my own heart's desire is especially fixed upon her. (35)
Having heard those truthful words, Parvata was filled with anger. *The Sixth Book, Chapter 26 of the Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa* [Page 413]
The sage spoke these words to me, saying "Fie! Fie! again and again. ||36||
"Since I have been deceived by you after first making oaths, O betrayer of my friend, become one with the face of a monkey by virtue of my curse. (37)
Thus cursed by that enraged high-souled one, I suddenly became cruel, with the face of a monkey. (38)
I, too, did not show forgiveness toward that son of my sister;
out of extreme anger, he indeed cursed me, saying, "Surely there shall be no place for you in heaven."
"O Parvata, since you have cursed me for such a trivial offense, therefore, O dull-witted one, your own stay shall indeed be in the world of death. (40)
But Parvata departed from that city deeply dejected;
at that very moment, however, I was transformed into the face of a monkey.
Seeing me, a cruel monkey, the princess became embarrassed;
she grew exceedingly despondent, longing only for the sound of the lute.
Vyāsa said:
O Brahman, what happened after that? How was the curse revoked? You were born again with a human face; tell me this according to the facts. (43)
"Where did Parvata go again, and where did your meeting with him take place? O son, when and how did it all happen? Tell me everything in detail. (44)
Nārada said:
O highly fortunate one, what can I say of the great deeds of Māyā?
I am deeply distressed there on that mountain now that she has departed in anger.
Furthermore, the princess became exceedingly devoted to my service;
when Parvata had departed as he pleased, I remained right there in that very residence.
Overcome by sorrow, wretched, and with a face like that of a monkey,
I was especially tormented by anxiety, brooding over what might happen to me.
Then Sañjaya, seeing his daughter whose youth was slightly manifest,
questioned his minister regarding the marriage of the princess.
"The time for my daughter's marriage has now arrived;
tell me of a worthy prince who is a suitable groom. (49)

"I shall now indeed perform the marriage of my daughter according to the prescribed rites with one who is endowed with the qualities of physical nobility and beauty, who is heroic, and born of a noble family. (50)
But Pradhāna said, "O King, there are indeed many princes on earth who are worthy of your daughter and endowed with all virtues. (51)
O Indra among kings, having summoned that prince in whom you have interest,
give him your daughter along with abundant wealth consisting of elephants, horses, and chariots.
Nārada said: Having learned of her father’s intention, Damayantī, skilled in speech, then spoke to the king while he was seated in private through the mouth of her nurse.
The nurse said:
"O great king, your daughter Damayantī has spoken thus to me:
'O nurse, speak to my father on my behalf words that are full of joy. (54)
Then, infatuated by passion, I chose the wise Nārada, who was accompanied by Mahatī;
no one else was dear to me. 55.
"O father, fulfill my desire for marriage with the sage;
O knower of dharma, I shall choose no other husband than Nārada. (56)
I am indeed great, O ocean of sound, devoid of men, consisting of essence, free from salt, filled with bliss, and shunned by the timi and timiṅgila fish. || 57 ||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 26 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 27.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Nārada said:
Then, having heard those words of his daughter from the mouth of the nurse, the king...
He spoke to his wife Kaikeyī, the beautiful-eyed one who was standing nearby.
The King said:
"O beloved, you have heard those words that were spoken by the nurse."
This sage Nārada, though possessing the face of a monkey, has indeed been chosen according to his desire.
"What is this thoughtless and misguided act conceived by my daughter?
How could I give my daughter to that one with the face of a monkey? (3)
"Where is the ugly monk, and where is my daughter Damayantī?
This matter is inverted; it can never be understood. (4)

O Sukeśānta, restrain that daughter of yours by force in private; use skillful means to turn this innocent girl away from her devotion to the sage, in accordance with the teachings of the elders learned in the scriptures. (5)
Having heard these words of her husband, the mother then said to her:
"How could that sage, who has the face of a monkey and whose wealth is his asceticism, ever desire your beauty?"
"How have you, who are clever, fallen into delusion once again, O mendicant?
You possess a body as delicate as a creeper, while he has a body as coarse as ashes. (7)
O sinless one, how is it appropriate for you to have news from the mouth of a monkey? O lady of pure smiles, what pleasure can there be in a despicable man?
"Let the prince be your husband; do not persist in this futile obstinacy.
Your father will fall into sorrow upon hearing these words from the mouth of the nurse. (1)
Seeing the tender *mālatī* creeper entwined with a *babbūla* tree, whose wise mind would not fall into sorrow? (10)
On this earth, who—even a fool—would give tender betel leaves for consumption to a servant? (11)
Seeing you with your hand clasped [in marriage] near Nārada while the wedding ceremony was underway, whose heart would not burn with grief? (12)
Therefore, conversation with this foul-mouthed one does not produce any pleasure;
how then are you to pass the time with him until death?
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of her mother, the slender-limbed Damayantī,
deeply distressed and having made her resolve regarding him, spoke to her mother.
What is the use of a face or beauty for a fool, and what is the use of wealth for one? What is the use of a kingdom for one who is unrefined and ignorant of the path of aesthetic flavor? 15.
Even the does in the forest are blessed, for they have been so captivated by his roar that they offer up their very lives; fie upon the foolish men on this earth!
O Mother, Nārada alone knows this Vedic knowledge consisting of the seven musical notes;
indeed, no other man besides Śiva knows it. 17.
Dwelling with a fool is death at every moment;
a man who is handsome and wealthy, yet devoid of virtue, should always be abandoned.
O fool, when a king is possessed of vain pride, it is better for a virtuous beggar to grant happiness through his words alone. (19)

One who knows the notes, understands the scales, and possesses the distinctions of the knowledge of the *mūrcchanās*—such a person is indeed difficult to find, even if he is weak, provided he also knows the eight aesthetic sentiments (*rasas*). (20)
Just as the Gaṅgā and the Sarasvatī lead to Kailāsa, so too does one who is proficient in the knowledge of the celestial realms lead to Kailāsa. ||21||
He who knows the resonating sound, though being human, is a god;
he who does not know its sevenfold division, even if a god, is a beast. (22)
He who does not experience joy upon hearing the path of melodies and scales should be known in every way as a beast; for deer are not beasts. 23.
Better is a venomous serpent that, upon hearing a captivating sound, experiences joy even though it lacks ears; fie upon those humans who possess ears!

Even as a child, having heard a song of beautiful melody, his mind was filled with joy. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 27. [Page 415] Even as a child, having heard a song of beautiful melody, his mind was filled with joy.
But those elders do not understand; fie upon them!
Does my father not know the many virtues of Nārada?
There is no second chanter of the Sāman hymns equal to him in the three worlds. 26.
Therefore, he was surely chosen by me before our meeting;
subsequently, under the power of a curse, he became this mine of virtues with the face of a monkey.
To whom would the Kinnaras not be dear? For what purpose does one possessing horse-like faces exist? What is the use of an excellent face when one is fully endowed with the science of song? 28.
"O mother, tell my father: 'This best of sages has been chosen;
therefore, having joyfully released me from him, give me to him.'"
Nārada said:
Having heard these words of her daughter,
O sage, the queen informed the king of Sundarī’s insistence upon Nārada.
"O Indra among kings, perform the marriage with Damayantī on an auspicious day;
for that omniscient sage has already been chosen by her in her mind.
Nārada said:
Thus urged by the queen, Saṃjaya, the lord of the earth,
then duly performed every rite pertaining to the wedding.
Having thus taken a wife, the enemy-subduing Vānarāsya remained right there,
burning day after day in his mind.
When the princess came into my presence for the sake of service, I, whose face was that of a monkey, became tormented by sorrow. (34)
But Damayantī, seeing me with my lotus-face in full bloom, once took me for a monkey and offered me vegetables. (35)
As time passed in this manner, the sage Parvata suddenly arrived here to see me while visiting various sacred pilgrimage sites.
Having been honored by me with great respect and worshipped according to the prescribed rites,
he sat upon a divine seat and, seeing me, became truly distressed.
To me, his maternal uncle, who was dejected, deeply distressed by anxiety, married, monkey-faced, and emaciated, the compassionate Parvata spoke these words: ||38||
"O best of sages, you have been cursed by me out of anger, O Nārada;
listen now as I perform the atonement for that curse. (39)
O Nārada, by my merit, may you become handsome-faced;
having seen the princess, compassion has now arisen in my heart. (40)
Nārada said:
Having made my mind inclined toward him and having heard his speech,
I immediately bestowed a favor upon him at that very moment, nullifying the curse.
"Nephew, may you too have access to the abode of the gods;
this favor for the curse has indeed been granted by Parvata. (42)
Nārada said:
"I was born with a beautiful face from his speech while he was looking on.
Then the princess, being well-pleased, quickly spoke to her mother. (43)
A son of auspicious countenance has been born to you, and a son-in-law of great luster;
by the word of the mountain, the curse of the sage has been released today. (44)
Having heard those words spoken by the queen to the king,
Sañjaya then went there with joy to see the sage.
Then, the high-souled king, being well-pleased, bestowed upon me and my sister’s son a great amount of wealth as a marriage gift.
Thus has all this ancient conduct been related to you,
as well as the greatness of Māyā's power exactly as it was experienced by me.
O illustrious one, in this saṃsāra, which is unreal and produced by the qualities of māyā, there is no embodied being who is happy—none who has been so, nor shall there ever be. (48)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter twenty-eight.
By whom have all these mighty ones been conquered: lust, anger, greed, envy, possessiveness, egoism, and pride? (49)
"O Sage, these three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are indeed the cause in every respect for the production of the bodies of living beings. (50)
O Vyāsa, at one time while I was traveling through the forest with Viṣṇu, I was turned into a woman in an instant by his playful jesting. 51.
Having become the king's consort, she was utterly deluded by the power of Māyā;
indeed, many sons were born to her in the palace of that monarch.
Vyāsa said:
O virtuous one, having heard your words, this doubt has indeed become great:
"O sage, how did you, who are so exceedingly wise, come to attain womanhood? (53)
And how was this man born? Tell me everything without omission. How were your sons born, and in whose king's house did he dwell?
Relate this great and most wonderful deed involving illusion, and how all this—both the stationary and the moving—is deluded. (55)
I do not reach satiety while listening to the nectar of your discourse, which contains the true essence of the meaning of all philosophical systems and destroys all doubts. (56)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 27 ||
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Nārada said:
Listen, O best of sages, as I relate this virtuous narrative.
The power of illusion is extremely difficult to comprehend, even for sages who are the most proficient in yoga.
The entire world, both moving and unmoving, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is deluded by Māyā through her unconceivable power of Ajā.
Once, desiring a vision of Hari of wondrous deeds, I went from Satyaloka to the enchanting Śvetadvīpa.
Playing upon a great lute adorned with beautiful tones and strings,
he sang while singing the Sāman hymns endowed with the seven musical notes.
I have beheld the God of gods, the wielder of the discus and the mace, whose chest is illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, who is dark as a rain cloud, and who possesses four arms. (5)
Clad in yellow garments, adorned with a crown and armlets,
he sports with the playful Lakṣmī, filled with joy.
Having beheld me, the goddess Kamalā— endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament— vanished from my presence.
The beloved of Vāsudeva, possessing the luster of excellent gold, was the most eminent among women, proud of her beauty and youth, and deeply cherished by him. (8)
Seeing the daughter of the ocean (Lakṣmī) having entered the inner apartments along with her attendants,
I questioned the God of gods, the wearer of the forest garland, the Lord of the universe.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Padmanābha, slayer of the enemies of the gods!
Why did she flee upon seeing me approaching from nearby? 10.
"I am neither a libertine nor a rogue; I am an ascetic, O Teacher of the World! I have conquered my senses, I have conquered my anger, and I have conquered my deceit, O Janārdana. (11)
Nārada said:
Having heard those words somewhat filled with pride, Janārdana,
smiling, spoke to me in a voice as sweet as the sound of a lute.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Nārada, such a policy must never be adopted by a woman: to remain in the presence of anyone other than her husband."
