O wise one, Māyā is exceedingly difficult to conquer even for yogis who have mastered their vital breaths,
for those learned in Sāṃkhya, for ascetics who abstain from food, and for those who have subdued their senses.
O tiger among sages, as for those words you have just spoken to me, "I am a conqueror of Māyā, O knower of song"—such a thing should never be said. (15)
Neither I, Śiva, nor Brahmā am capable of conquering that Unborn One;
even the sages beginning with Sanaka are unable—what then of you, or who else is able to conquer her? (16)
Whether he bears a divine body, a human body, or even the body of an animal, how could such a person conquer that Unborn One? (17)
How can a man, even if he is a knower of the Vedas, a knower of yoga, omniscient, and one who has conquered his senses, be able to conquer that Māyā when he is joined with the three [guṇas]? || 18 ||
Time indeed makes even that which is formless into a form; it brings about its own nature.
Under its control dwells every embodied being—whether learned, foolish, or mediocre.
Time makes even one who knows the Dharma deficient at times;
whether by its own nature or through karma, its activity is difficult to comprehend. (20)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu ceased; with a mind full of wonder, I addressed that Lord of the World, the eternal Vāsudeva.
O Lord of Ramā, what is the nature of that Māyā? Furthermore, of what kind is it? What is its power, what is its configuration, and upon what does it rest? Tell me this.
"I desire to see that illusion; show it quickly, O Upholder of the Earth! I wish to understand it thoroughly; grant me your grace, O Lord of Māyā. (23)
Viṣṇu said: She consists of the three guṇas, she is the support of all, omniscient, and honored by all;
invincible and possessing manifold forms, she stands pervading the entire universe. (24)
"If there is a desire to see [it] in your mind, O Nārada, ascend Garuḍa; accompanied by me today, let us go elsewhere now. (25)
I shall show you my illusion, which is difficult to conquer for those who have not mastered their selves;
having seen it, O son of Brahmā, do not set your mind on despair. 26.
Having spoken thus, the God of gods remembered the son of Vinatā;
and as soon as he was remembered, Garuḍa arrived in the presence of Hari.
Seeing that the Garuḍa had arrived, Janārdana mounted him;
having placed me upon his back, he prepared with due respect for the journey.
The son of Vinatā, possessing the speed of the wind, moved from Vaikuṇṭha when urged by Kṛṣṇa, who desired to go to the forest.
The great divine forests, lakes, and likewise rivers; cities, villages, mines and the like, as well as hamlets, market towns, and cow-pens.
I shall go to the hermitages of the sages, as well as to the most beautiful ponds,
vast pools, and lakes adorned with lotuses.
And having also observed herds of deer and boars,
we two went to the vicinity of Kānyakubja, O Garuḍāsana.
There he beheld a beautiful, divine lake adorned with lotuses,
teeming with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and graced by ruddy geese.
It was adorned with various colors by blooming lotuses, possessed pure and sweet water, and was made resplendent by the humming of swarms of bees. ||34||
Beholding that most wonderful lake, which rivaled the ocean and possessed especially sweet water like milk, the Blessed One spoke.
The Blessed Lord said: "Behold, O Nārada, this deep lake resounding with cranes, covered everywhere with lotuses, and filled with pure water. (36)
"Having bathed here, we shall go to Kānyakubja, the most excellent city," he said, and quickly taking me down from Garuḍa, he set me ashore. (37)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter twenty-nine.
Smiling there, the Blessed One took hold of my finger;
praising the lake further, the Lord led me to the shore. (38)
Having rested on that delightful bank, which was pleasant with its cool shade,
he said to me, "O sage, perform your bath in these pure waters;
afterwards, I shall do so in this most auspicious pond."
And their waters were as pure as the hearts of the virtuous. ||40||
"Especially with the fragrant pollen of lotuses"—
having been addressed thus by the Blessed One, I set aside my lute and deer-skin.

Having resolved to bathe, filled with love, he went to the bank; having washed his feet and hands, tied his topknot, and taken hold of *kuśa* grass, he sipped water (*ācamana*) and, being pure, bathed in that water. While Hari was looking on, I bathed in that delightful water. (43)
Having abandoned his masculine form, he attained an unsurpassed feminine state;
meanwhile, Hari took my lute as well as my auspicious black antelope skin.
Having swiftly mounted Garuḍa, he went to his own home in an instant;
then I attained womanhood, adorned with beautiful ornaments.
At that very moment, the memory of her former body arose in her mind;
she forgot that Lord of the World, and thus a great forgetfulness occurred once again.
Having assumed the form of the Enchantress (Mohinī) and emerged from the pond,
I beheld that lake of pure water, frequented by lotuses.
"What is this?"—thus I repeatedly felt wonder in my mind as I measured that one who had assumed a female form with these three [measures]. (48)
Suddenly, King Tāladhvaja appeared within the range of vision there, mounted upon his chariot and accompanied by multitudes of elephants, horses, and chariots. || 49 ||
Seeing me there, adorned with divine ornaments, the king—himself a youth, decked out in finery like the god of love incarnate—[was struck with wonder]. (50)
Filled with supreme wonder at the woman whose face was like the full moon, he asked: "Who are you, O auspicious lady? Whose daughter are you—of a mortal or of a god?"
O beloved, how can this young girl, adorned with beauty and youth, be alone—whether she belongs to a human, a Gandharva, or a serpent? (52)
"Whether you are married or a maiden, tell the truth, O fair-eyed one!
What do you see in this pond, O lady with beautiful hair and slender waist? (53)
O enchantress of the mind, tell me what you wish to do amidst the warbling of the cuckoos;
O lady with eyes like a swan’s, O slender-waisted one, enjoy the pleasures together with me.
Having surely made me, the most excellent one, her husband according to her heart's desire. ||54||
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 28 ||
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Nārada said:
Thus was I addressed at that time by that king, Tāladhvaja.
Having reflected deeply with his mind, O lord of people, he spoke to him.
"O King, I do not know for certain whose daughter I am;
where are my parents, and by whom was I placed in this lake? (2)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may my merit increase?
O Indra among kings, I am without support; I ponder what ought to be done. (3)
"O King, fate alone is supreme; here, there is no human effort on my part.
You are a knower of dharma, O protector of the earth; do as you wish. (4)
"O King, I am dependent upon you; I have no protector at all—neither father nor mother, neither a place of refuge nor any kinsman. (5)
Thus addressed by me, that king became afflicted with passion;
and beholding me, O large-eyed one, he spoke thus to his servants: || 6 ||
"Bring the chariot for Narayana, which has four horses and is captivating to the mind. Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 29. 419.
For the purpose of ascending it, let there be a covering of silk cloth.
It was provided with soft coverings, adorned with a network of pearls,
square, spacious, fashioned from gold, and auspicious.
Having heard those words of his, the servants, moving with haste,
brought a divine palanquin wrapped in cloth for my sake.
Then, desiring to do what was pleasing to him, I ascended that [chariot];
having brought me to his home, that lord of the earth was then filled with joy.
Then, according to the marriage rites, on an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, the king married me there in the presence of the sacrificial fire.
I became his beloved, dearer to him than even his own life;
thus was my name established there as Saubhāgyasundarī.
Delighting with me, the lord of the earth obtained happiness through various enjoyments and pleasures as prescribed in the treatises on love.
Having abandoned his royal duties, he was devoted to play day and night;
absorbed in the arts of love, he did not perceive the passing of time.
In delightful gardens, in ponds, and in houses; in palatial mansions, on choice mountains, and in excellent long lakes.
Intoxicated by the liquor of Varuṇī, while wandering in that beautiful forest,
he abandoned all duties and became utterly subject to his intoxication.
I am Vyāsā, and because I was so deeply attached to him, I was overcome by the savor of our play;
I did not remember my former body, nor my male state, nor my birth as a sage.
"This man is my very husband; I am his beloved wife among wives, the crowned queen who understands the arts of pleasure—my life is truly fruitful. (18)
Thus, as he was thinking, she remained under his control, bound by love day and night;
devoted to play and longing for pleasure, she stayed obedient to him.
The realization of Brahman and the eternal knowledge of Brahman were forgotten;
she remained with her mind intent upon the thorough mastery of the Dharmaśāstras. ||20||
O Sage, as I dwelt there thus, devoted to the play of desire, those twelve years passed for me like a single moment.
When I became pregnant, the king then attained great joy;
he performed the rites for the consecration of the fetus according to the prescribed rules.
The king asked me about my pregnancy longing again and again, seeking to please me;
yet, feeling great shame, I did not speak to the king, though his mind was deeply intent on my pleasure.
Then, when the tenth month was complete, a son was born to me on an auspicious day endowed with the strength of the planets, lunar mansions, ascendants, and stars.
In the palace of the king, there was a great festival for the birth of a son;
the king became supremely delighted by the birth of his son.
At the end of the period of impurity, the king beheld his son and attained great joy; "O scorcher of foes, I was the beloved wife of that lord of the earth," [she thought]. (26)
Then, at the end of two years, I indeed conceived again;
a second son was born, endowed with all auspicious marks.
Then the king gave the name Sudhanvan to that son;
furthermore, urged by the Brahmins, he gave the name Vīravarman to the eldest. (28)
In this way, twelve sons were born who were highly esteemed by the king;
at that time, I was infatuated with them through my affection for their protection and pampering. (29)
Furthermore, eight sons of beautiful form were born to me from time to time;
thus, my life as a householder became complete, having attained the means for happiness.
The king performed their marriage ceremonies at the appropriate time; likewise, through daughters-in-law, his sons and great retinue increased.
Then their sons, grandsons, and descendants, filled with the relish for play and endowed with various pleasures, greatly increased delusion. (32)
Sometimes there was happiness and sovereignty, and sometimes there was extraordinary suffering caused by disease among his sons, which brought torment to his body.
At times, a most terrible conflict arose between them, whether among the sons or the daughters-in-law; from that, great distress was born.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the sixth book, chapter twenty-nine.
O best of sages, I am deeply submerged in this terrible and miserable state, consisting of pleasure and pain, produced by mental constructs, characterized by false conduct, and utterly trivial. (35)
My prior wisdom has been forgotten, and likewise my knowledge of the scriptures has vanished; in the absence of a woman, I have become utterly dissolved in domestic chores. (36)
But egoism has arisen, which greatly increases delusion—yes, it increases delusion.
"These are my powerful sons; these daughters-in-law are born of noble families. (37)
"These sons of mine, well-armed, play within my mansions;
oh, among all women in this world, I am indeed most blessed!"
"I am Nārada, indeed deceived by the Lord through his illusory power (māyā);
never indeed has such a thing been even conceived by me in my mind. (39)
"The king's wife is of auspicious conduct, has many sons, and is devoted to her husband;
I am indeed blessed in this world"—thus was I deluded by Kṛṣṇa. (40)
Then, O giver of honor, a certain great king, the ruler of a distant land,
became an enemy toward his lord.
Having assembled his army, complete with chariots and elephants,
he arrived at the city of Kānyakubja and resolved upon battle.
The city was besieged by that king together with his army;
then my sons and grandsons emerged from the city.
A tumultuous battle was waged there by those sons of Aṭa;
all the sons were slain in combat by their enemy through the turn of fate.
The king, defeated in battle, returned once more to his own home;
I have heard that my sons were slain in that most terrible conflict. (45)
Having slain my sons and grandsons, that king, endowed with great power, departed;
then I went there to the field of battle while crying out in lamentation.
Seeing those sons and grandsons fallen, I, afflicted by grief, lamented, O long-lived one, as I was submerged in an ocean of sorrow. (47)
"Alas, my sons! Where have you gone today? Alas, I am destroyed by this wicked-souled, most powerful, and irresistible fate, which is exceedingly sinful! (48)
In the meantime, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana,
having assumed the form of an aged and most handsome brahmin, arrived there.
Well-attired and a knower of the Vedas, he approached me at his will;
on the field of battle, he spoke to me as I was crying out in extreme distress. (50)
The Brahmin said:
"Why do you despair, O slender-limbed one? This delusion has been manifested through your infatuation with the sweet warbling of the cuckoo, which consists of husband, son, and home. (51)
"Who are you? Whose daughter are you? Who are these people? Reflect upon your own supreme state. Arise, O fair-eyed one; abandon this weeping and become composed."
O beloved, perform the ritual bathing and the offering of sesame seeds for your sons who have departed to the next world, indeed for the sake of preserving the bounds of dharma.
A bath at a sacred ford must be performed in every way, but never at home;
such is the determination of the Dharmaśāstras regarding deceased kinsmen. (54)
Nārada said:
Having been thus addressed and enlightened by that aged brahmin,
I then arose, accompanied by the king and surrounded by my kinsmen.
The Lord, the creator of all beings, appeared before me in the form of a brahmin;
thereupon, I quickly set out for that supremely purifying sacred ford.
There, at that Puṃtīrtha lake, the Lord Hari, the Blessed Janārdana in the form of a brahmin, took me with compassion and said: ||57||
O lady who moves with the gait of an elephant, perform your bath in this purifying lake.
Abandon your grief; it is the time for action, and [dwelling on] the sons is useless.
Tens of millions of sons born in birth after birth have died, as have fathers, husbands, brothers, and sisters-in-law. (59)
For whom should you feel sorrow regarding this delusion born of the mind—this vain thing, resembling a dream, which brings torment to embodied beings here? (60)
Nārada said: Having heard these words of his, I entered that sacred ford known as Puruṣa, desiring to bathe there, urged by Viṣṇu.
Merely by bathing in the sacred fords, even for a moment, the man was instantly born as Hari,
standing on the bank with a lute in his hand and possessing his own divine body.
And having emerged upon the shore, O best of the twice-born, I beheld that lotus-eyed one;
then, O foremost of brahmins, recognition arose within my mind.
"I have reflected upon that matter; I am Nārada who has come here, having attained the state of a woman along with Hari, deluded by Māyā. (64)
When I was thus born as Citāpara, Hari said to me:
"Nārada, come! What are you doing staying in the water? (65)
Then, remembering that terrible female state so intensely, I was struck with wonder:
"By what cause has this male state been attained once again? (66)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 29 ||
Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Nārada said:
Upon seeing me, the Brahmin Nārada, that lord of the earth was struck with wonder.
"Where has that wife of mine gone, and from where has this best of sages come? || 1 ||
There the king lamented again and again, "O my beloved!
Where have you gone, abandoning me as I wail in separation? (2)
"O lady of broad hips, without you my life, my home, and my kingdom are in vain, O lotus-petal-eyed one; what shall I do, O girl of pure smiles? (3)
My vital breaths do not depart from me now because of separation from you;
indeed, the duty of affection has departed, for [my life] exists only to sustain my breaths without you.
I lament, O large-eyed one; give me a dear reply. Where has that affection gone which existed at our first meeting? (5)
Has she, O fair-browed one, been submerged in the water and devoured by fish and turtles?
Or has she been swiftly seized by Varuṇa through the power of my own misfortune? (6)
Blessed are you, O lady of beautiful limbs, who have been reunited with your sons;
your affection for your children is indeed genuine, O speaker of nectar-like words.
"It is not right that you have now gone to the third heaven, abandoning me—me who am wailing, miserable, and constrained by affection for my son. (8)
"O beloved, both [of you] have come to me; you are my son, O dear one as dear as life.
Nevertheless, O beloved, there is no death for one who is so deeply afflicted by sorrow."
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? Rāma is no longer on this earth.
Only the joy of the Raghus knows the sorrow born of separation from Rāma. (10)
By this cruel rite performed here on earth, the contrary has occurred:
the death of a husband and wife who were entirely equal in mind, now separated. (11)
Indeed, a benefit for women has been ordained by the sages, namely that which is stated in the treatises on dharma: cremation together with the husband.
As the king was thus lamenting, the Blessed Lord Hari then restrained him with words endowed with reason.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the sixth book, chapter thirty.
The Blessed One said: "Why do you despair, O Indra among kings? Where has your beloved wife gone?
Have you not heard the scriptures, or have you not taken refuge in the wise? (14)
Who am I? Who are you? What is our union? And what is your separation like?
In this worldly existence, which is like the flow of a river, men are like those carried away by a boat. || 15 ||
Go home, O best of kings; what is the use of your weeping in vain?
For men, union and separation are always subject to destiny.
O King, your union with her was brought about here;
you have enjoyed this large-eyed, beautiful woman of slender waist. (17)
Her parents were not seen by you when you reached the lake; what happened by way of the "crow-and-palm" coincidence has passed accordingly. (18)
Do not grieve, O lord of kings; time is exceedingly difficult to overcome. Having encountered the course of time, enjoy the pleasures in your home as you did before.
That woman of excellent complexion departed just as she had come;
go there as you were before and accomplish your task, O Lord. (20)
"O King, by weeping today, your beloved will not return;
you grieve in vain, so now become absorbed in yoga. (21)
Enjoyment comes under the power of time and likewise departs again;
therefore, one should not feel grief here on this fruitless path of worldly existence.
Union with happiness does not last in one place, nor does union with suffering remain in one place;
rather, there is a constant wandering between pleasure and pain, like the rotation of a waterwheel. (23)
O King, having made your mind steady, rule the kingdom as you please;
or else, having entrusted it to your heir, retire to the forest now.
The human body of living beings is difficult to obtain and is fragile as a moment; once it has been attained, one must by all means accomplish the realization of the Self. (25)
O King, the tongue, the generative organ, and taste exist in animal wombs;
however, knowledge exists only in the human body and not in other base wombs. 26.
Therefore, go and abandon the grief arising from your beloved;
this is but the illusion of the Blessed Lady by which the entire world is deluded.
Nārada said: Having been addressed thus by Hari, the king bowed to the Lord of Kamalā and,
having properly performed the ritual of bathing, went to his own palace.
Having bestowed the kingdom upon his grandson and attained a profound sense of world-weariness,
the king departed for the forest and attained the knowledge of reality.
When the king had departed, I beheld the Lord Adhokṣaja;
as he was laughing at me again and again for the sake of the world’s welfare, I spoke to him.
"I have been recognized by you, O Lord; the great power of my illusory art (māyā) is known.
I remember all the deeds that were performed by me while in the body of a woman. (31)
"Speak to me, O Lord of the gods! Having entered the lake, my previous consciousness vanished simply by bathing; how did this happen, O Hari? (32)
"O Teacher of the World, having obtained a woman's body, I have been deluded, just as Pulomā became infatuated upon obtaining Vāsava as her husband, O best of kings. (33)
O Lord of Gods, that very mind is the consciousness, and that ancient body is the *liṅga*; O Hari, how then can there be a destruction of memory? (34)
O Lord, this is a great wonder to me regarding the destruction of my knowledge;
O Beloved of Ramā, tell me today the supreme cause of it. (35)
Having obtained a female body, I indeed abandoned many enjoyments;
yet I constantly drank liquor and ate food in a manner contrary to the prescribed rules.
At that time, I did not clearly realize that very thing—that I am Nārada; today I know everything as it truly is, whereas at that time I did not perceive it with such clarity. (37)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter thirty-one. Viṣṇu said:
Behold, O high-minded Nārada, this play of illusion:
the manifold variations of conditions among the bodies of all living beings. (38)
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state are the conditions of embodied beings;
likewise, when another body is attained, what kind of doubt can there be? (39)
A sleeping man does not know, nor does he hear, even though he speaks;
yet once awakened, he knows everything without exception. ||40||
The mind is stirred by sleep, and the occurrences of dreams arise;
there are indeed manifold varieties of mental distinctions and numerous states of mind. (41)
"The elephant is coming to kill me; I am not able to flee.
What shall I do? There is no place for me where I might go with speed."
In a dream, he sees his grandfather come to his own home; he imagines union with him, conversation, and eating together. (43)
Indeed, one who has awakened knows the pleasure and pain seen in a dream;
having remembered it, he can even describe it in detail to all people. //44//
In a dream, no one knows for certain that "this is an illusion";
just so, the manifestation of māyā is indeed difficult to comprehend. 45.
O Nārada, I do not know that which is extremely difficult to comprehend—the succession of the qualities of Māyā; indeed, neither Śambhu nor the Lotus-born knows it. 46.
Furthermore, what other dull-witted mortal would have been capable of knowing this?
In this world, no one could have attained a full understanding of the qualities of Māyā. (47)
The entire world, both stationary and moving, is produced by the three qualities (guṇas);
without the qualities, this transmigratory existence does not exist at all.
I am characterized by the quality of sattva, yet endowed with rajas and tamas;
O Lord of the World, I am never devoid of these three qualities.
Likewise, Brahmā is proclaimed here as your father, characterized primarily by *rajas*, yet joined with *tamas* and *sattva*; indeed, he is not devoid of those two qualities.
Śiva is likewise characterized by darkness (tamas) as his primary quality, while Rajas is enveloped by Sattva;
however, I have never heard of anyone who is entirely devoid of the three qualities (guṇas). || 51 ||
Therefore, O Lord of Sages, one should not give way to delusion in this saṃsāra—which is fashioned by illusion, essence-less, shoreless, and extremely difficult to traverse. (52)
You have seen the illusion this very day, and indeed you have experienced manifold enjoyments;
O illustrious one, why do you ask about its wondrous course?
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 30 ||
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O Great King; I shall speak in clear syllables.
Indeed, I have heard from Nārada the greatness of Māyā.
Furthermore, having heard that account concerning the origin of Nārada’s body from that sage, I questioned Nārada, the sage who is the best among all knowers.
"Tell me, Nārada, what was said by Hari afterwards?
And where did Mādhava, the Lord of the World, go along with you? (3)
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus at that exceedingly beautiful lake, the Blessed One mounted Garuḍa and set his mind on going to Vaikuṇṭha.
The beloved of Ramā said to me: "O Nārada, go wherever you wish;
or come to my world—do as you please. (5)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Sixth Skandha, Chapter 31.
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, I took leave of Madhusūdana;
and at that very moment, the Blessed Lord, the sovereign of the gods, mounted upon Garuḍa.
Having instructed me as he pleased, Vaikuṇṭha departed quickly;
then, Janārdana having gone, I went to the abode of my father.
Reflecting upon all suffering and most wonderful happiness,
he went and prostrated before his father, remaining there in front of him.
Thus questioned by his father, O Sage, Brahmā looked at me who was distressed with anxiety and said:
"O illustrious son, where have you gone? Why are you so overcome with anxiety?"
O best of sages, I do not see your mind at all composed today;
have you been deceived by someone, or have you seen some great wonder?
"I see you dejected and deprived of consciousness, my son; how is this?
Nārada said:
Thus questioned by his father, he was then seated upon a grass mat (bṛsī).
I told him my own story, arising from the power of illusion:
"O father, I have been utterly deceived by the all-powerful Viṣṇu."
Having entered into the state of womanhood for many, indeed very many years, she experienced great suffering arising from grief for her son. || 13 ||
Awakened by him with the nectar of gentle words, I bathed once more in the supreme-most [waters] and was born as the man Nārada. 14.
O Brahman, what was the cause that I fell into such delusion then? My prior realization was forgotten, as I was suddenly made one with that [state]. (15)
O Brahmā, I do not understand this power of Māyā, which is so difficult to overcome;
it has clearly become the root of delusion that destroys true knowledge. (16)
"I have experienced and correctly understood all that is auspicious and inauspicious;
tell me, dear father, how you conquered it—explain that method to me. (17)
Nārada said:
"O son of Vāsavi, after I had thus addressed the Creator with affection,
my father smiled and spoke to me."
Brahmā said:
"She is difficult to conquer by all the gods, by the high-souled sages, by ascetics endowed with knowledge, and by yogis who subsist on air. (19)
Neither Viṣṇu nor the Lord of Bhūru can know her, for she is the immensely powerful Māyā who cannot be understood in any way whatsoever.
That Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), which brings about creation, maintenance, and destruction, is difficult to comprehend;
she is enveloped by instrumental causes such as time, karma, and inherent nature.
Do not grieve, O wise one; that illusion belongs to the one of great power.
You should not feel astonishment, for we have all been deluded.
Nārada said:
Thus addressed by my father, O Vyāsa, I took leave of him and, freed from pride, have come here while visiting various excellent sacred fords (tīrthas). 23.
Therefore, you too, having completely cast aside the delusion born from the destruction of the Kauravas, [should act accordingly].
O best of the Kurus, remain seated comfortably in this place until the end of time.
One must inevitably experience the results of the deeds one has performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
having made this firm resolve in your heart, move about as you please.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, O King, Nārada departed after awakening me;
I then reflected upon those words which had been spoken by the sage at that time.
Abiding on the bank of the Sarasvatī during the excellent Sārasvata Kalpa,
this Bhāgavata was composed by me for the purpose of passing the time.
O King, this Purāṇa is supreme, the destroyer of all doubts, endowed with various narratives, and resting upon the authority of the Vedas. (28)
O best of kings, you must not entertain any doubt in this matter at all;
it is just as when a certain magician holds a wooden Pāñcālī puppet in his hand.
Having fashioned the course of the lineage according to its own will, it makes Kāma dance at its pleasure;
likewise, O Mother, it makes me and the entire world, with its moving and unmoving beings, dance.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including gods, asuras, and humans,
it is endowed with the five senses and follows the lead of the mind and consciousness.
O King, all three qualities are in every way the cause of all things; it is a settled conclusion that everything exists as a combination of cause and effect. (32)
These qualities, arising from Māyā, possess distinct and diverse natures; for they are threefold, being respectively peaceful, passionate, and deluded. (33)
A person is eternally conjoined with that; how could he ever be devoid of it?
In this world, a cloth cannot exist at all when separated from its threads. (34)
Likewise, O lord of men, it is certain that one who is devoid of the three qualities is not a possessor of a body—whether that body be divine, human, or animal. (35)
One who is devoid of qualities cannot exist, just as a jar cannot exist without clay;
likewise, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—these three—are the substrata of the qualities.
At times they are endowed with affection, and again they are endowed with aversion;
likewise, they become possessed of dejection due to the conjunction of the qualities (guṇas). ||37||
Sometimes Brahmā, abiding in sattva, is then peaceful and possessed of meditative absorption;
endowed with knowledge, he becomes filled with love for all beings.
Furthermore, when devoid of *sattva* and enveloped by the quality of *rajas*, he then becomes terrible in form and filled with dissatisfaction everywhere. (39)
When the Creator is predominantly possessed by the quality of darkness (tamas),
then he becomes dejected and deluded, and not otherwise.
Mādhava, too, should always be entirely devoted to goodness (sattva), so that he may become peaceful, full of joy, and endowed with knowledge. || 41 ||
That very same [being], through the predominance of *rajas*, becomes joined with displeasure;
he is terrible toward all beings and experiences pleasure and pain according to the *guṇas*.
Rudra, too, when joined with *sattva*, becomes full of joy and peaceful.
Even that wise man, blinded by passion, was devoid of affection. 43.
Even he, possessed of the quality of tamas, becomes deluded and overcome by dejection.
If Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others are thus dependent on the qualities (guṇas),
as are those born of the Solar dynasty and likewise those born of the Lunar dynasty;
And those such as Manu and others who are proclaimed in each and every cycle of four ages; ||45||
O best of kings, what can be said of others in this saṃsāra?
This entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, is subject to illusion (māyā). 46.
Therefore, O King, you should never entertain doubt in this matter;
for an embodied being, being subject to illusion (māyā), acts in accordance with its own latent impressions (vāsanā). (47)
And that illusion (māyā) is always dependent upon and impelled by Him, even within the supreme reality which is the nature of consciousness; therefore, it [acts] perpetually among living beings. 48.
Then [he beheld] that supreme goddess, the Mistress of Illusion (Māyeśvarī), who is superior to illusion itself, the Blessed One whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss. ||49||
One should meditate upon her, worship her, bow down to her, and also recite her mantra;
by that, she becomes compassionate and surely liberates the embodied soul.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the sixth book, chapter thirty-one.
She indeed withdraws her own māyā by bestowing self-experience;
for māyā is the world, and its mistress is the Sovereign Goddess (Īśvarī). 51.
Then the goddess Bhuvaneśī, the beauty of the three worlds, was proclaimed;
O Lord of the Earth, if the mind were always fixed upon her form, [then all would be attained]. (52)
O King, what can arise from that illusion which consists of both the existent and the non-existent?
Therefore, for the purpose of dispelling illusion, there is indeed no other deity whatsoever.
But without the Goddess, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, darkness would not be capable of destroying the mass of darkness; indeed, it would have no power to do so.
However, the radiance of the sun, the moon, lightning, fire, and so forth [are surpassed by her];
therefore, one should know that Ambā, the Mistress of Māyā, is self-luminous consciousness.
One should propitiate [the Lord] with extreme devotion for the sake of turning away from the qualities of Māyā.
Thus, the slaying of the Asura Vṛtra and other events have been correctly narrated by me. (56)
O tiger among kings, what else do you wish to hear that was asked?
O you of noble vows, this first half of the Purāṇa has been narrated to you. (57)
In this [work], the greatness of the Goddess has been established in detail;
this secret of the Illustrious Mother must not be given to just anyone. (58)
It should be given to a devotee who is peaceful, who is devoted to the Goddess, to a disciple, to an eldest son, and to one endowed with devotion to the Guru. (59)
This Purāṇa is the essence of all narratives, equal to the entirety of the Vedas, and permeated by authoritative evidence.
The man who reads it with supreme devotion or hears it here with faith shall indeed become wealthy and possessed of knowledge in this world. (60)
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Goddess," in the sixth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 31 ||
With eighteen hundred and eighty-four auspicious verses composed in the *vasantatilakā* meter,
the sixth book of this *Devībhāgavata* has reached its conclusion.
This sixth book is completed.

It is purifying, pleasing to the ear, and endowed with righteousness, knowledge, and other virtues;

"Deliberate together as to how there might truly be welfare for me.

"How can this exceedingly beautiful girl be given to an unfortunate man?

Then, seeing their father overwhelmed with anxiety, the ministers [spoke]. (33)

"Indeed, you are distressed in countenance and agitated by grief on my account;

"O father, I shall indeed make him pleased by the gift of my own self.

With a serene soul, he spoke to her while his ministers listened:

Out of a desire for his own happiness, I give my daughter to one whose body is seized by old age and who is ignorant of strength; even so, a father must bestow his daughter upon one who is unknown. (39)
Never for the sake of evil;

O lotus-petal-eyed one, how am I to be imagined by you?

O sweet-voiced one, this gift does not please you;

"Be steadfast, O lady of beautiful hips; I will never give myself to a blind man.
