"O girl, I will not give you to him because he has taken away your eyes.
Hearing these words of her father, Sukanyā then said to him: (45)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 3:
These words, exceedingly full of affection, were spoken by her with a gracious countenance.
Sukanyā said:
"O father, you need not worry for me; give me to the sage now. (46)
"May there be happiness for all the worlds through my deed;
being fully contented, I shall serve my most purifying husband. (47)
And with supreme devotion, I, devoted to the dharma of a chaste wife, shall attend upon my aged husband in the lonely forest, conducting myself in perfect harmony.
"O father, I have no desire for enjoyments; my mind is at peace, O sinless one.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of hers, the ministers were filled with wonder. (49)
And the king, exceedingly delighted, went into the presence of the sage;
having arrived and bowed his head to him, he spoke to that one whose wealth is asceticism.
"O Lord, accept my daughter for the sake of service according to the prescribed rites, O All-pervading One.
Having said this, the king gave his daughter to him according to the marriage ceremony. (51)
Having accepted the maiden, the sage Bhārgava became pleased;
he did not accept the dowry being offered by the king.
He chose the maiden herself for his own service;
when that sage was thus pleased, happiness then arose for the soldiers.
At that very moment, supreme joy arose within the king as soon as he had given his daughter away and was departing for home. (14)
Then the slender-limbed daughter made up her mind and spoke to the king;
Sukanyā said:
"O father, take my clothes and my ornaments."
Give me bark garments and an excellent deerskin for my clothing;
having assumed the attire of a sage’s wife, I shall devote myself to ascetic practice. (56)
"O father, I shall act in such a way that your imperishable fame will exist upon the surface of the earth, as well as in heaven and in the netherworld. (57)
For the sake of happiness in the next world, I shall practice day and night;
having given me, a beautiful young woman, to a blind man and an old man. (58)
You must not perform a funeral pyre that would result in the destruction of your virtue, just as Arundhatī was the lawful wife of Vasiṣṭha on this earth. (59)
In that very same way shall I become; there is no need for deliberation here, just as the virtuous Anasūyā is renowned on earth as the foremost of wives.
"O daughter, just as I shall become a bringer of fame for you," having heard these words of Sukanyā, the king, who was supremely conversant with dharma, [replied]. (61)
Having given away his deerskin, he wept immediately upon seeing his daughter of lovely smiles,
who had cast off her ornaments and garments and was wearing the dress of a sage.
With his face turned pale, the king remained right there;
all the queens, seeing their daughter clad in bark garments and deerskins, [were struck with grief].
Afflicted by intense grief, they wept and became as if trembling;
having taken leave of her, the protector of the earth, surrounded by his ministers, departed.
O King, having left his daughter behind, overcome with grief, he departed for his own city.
Thus ends the third chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 3 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Book, Chapter 4.
Now begins the Fourth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
When the king had departed, that young woman, devoted solely to the service of her husband,
became likewise intent on dharma through the tending of the sacred fires.
Taking various sweet fruits and roots,
that young woman, devoted to the service of her husband, gave them to the sage.
Having quickly placed it upon hot water and wrapped it in a deer skin,
she then set it down upon an auspicious seat.
Having first arranged sesame seeds, barley, and kuśa grass, as well as a water-pot, he said to him: "O best of sages, perform your daily rites."
Having raised him up and taken him by the hand once her daily rites were completed,
the young woman seated her husband upon a cushion or a spread of grass.
Afterwards, having brought ripe fruits,
the princess fed Cyavana with well-prepared food made from wild rice.
After her husband had eaten and was satisfied, she respectfully gave him water for rinsing his mouth;
thereafter, full of devotion, she offered him betel nuts and leaves.
Having provided him with mouth-fresheners and seated him upon an auspicious throne,
she then took leave of her body and performed the rite of spiritual accomplishment (sādhana).
Having herself prepared food from fruits and returned to his presence, she spoke with affection: "O Lord, what do you command? (9)
"If you so desire, I shall massage your feet today. Thus she became constantly intent on service, eager to fall at his feet.
At the conclusion of the evening fire-oblation, that beautiful woman, having gathered fruits,
offered to the sage those that were both sweet and soft.
Then, filled with love, she ate the remaining food at his command;
having prepared a very soft bed, she joyfully laid him down upon it.
When her beloved was asleep, the slender-waisted beloved wife then performed the massaging of his feet,
inquiring about the dharma of noble women.
Having massaged his feet at night, she, devoted to him with deep affection,
perceived that the sage was asleep and lay down near his feet.
Seeing her husband established in purity, the beautiful woman constantly served him, creating a cool breeze with a palm-leaf fan.
In the winter, having gathered a store of wood and kindled a fire before him,
he likewise asked him repeatedly, "Are you well?"
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, the beloved wife, having provided water, a vessel, and earth for the sake of purification, rose up [to attend] her husband. (17)
Having established him in another place and gone far away, she remained steady;
then, perceiving that her husband had performed his purification, she went back and took hold of him again. (18)
Having brought him to the hermitage and seated him calmly upon an auspicious seat,
she washed his feet according to the prescribed rite with earth and water.
Having offered the vessel for sipping water, she brought the tooth-stick;
and having presented the tooth-wood as prescribed, the daughter of the king [performed her duties]. (20)
Having brought pure, very holy, warm water for the purpose of bathing, she, filled with affection, asked: (21)
What do you command? Indeed, the tooth-cleansing twig has been prepared by the Brahmin; take a bath with the proper mantras using this well-prepared warm water.
This time for the fire-oblation has arrived, and the morning twilight is beginning;
having performed the ritual purification according to the rules, perform the worship of the deities. (23)
Thus the blameless maiden, having obtained a husband who was an ascetic,
constantly attended upon him with affection, through austerity and religious observance.
Always performing service to the sacred fires and to guests, that lady of beautiful countenance joyfully propitiated Cyavana. (25)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter four:
Now, at a certain time, both the Aśvins, the sons of the Sun, [appeared].
While playing, they arrived at the hermitage of Cyavana. || 26 ||
Having bathed in the water, the two sons of the Sun beheld that maiden, beautiful in all her limbs, returning toward their own hermitage as she was walking along.
Seeing that celestial maiden,
the two Nāsatyas, utterly infatuated, approached her with reverence and, hastening toward her, spoke.
"Wait a moment, O lady of excellent hips, O you who walk with the gait of an elephant; we have come as the sons of gods to question you. Speak the truth, O lady of pure smiles. (29)
"Whose daughter are you? Who is your husband? How have you come alone to this garden, O lovely-eyed one, for the purpose of bathing in this pond?
O lotus-eyed one, you shine with such splendor like a second Śrī."
We desire to know; tell us the truth, O beautiful one. (31)
O beloved with tremulous eyes, your tender feet, though standing uncovered upon the ground,
cause pain in my heart as they move.
"O slender-limbed one, you are worthy of a celestial chariot; why do you travel here on foot?
Why are you traveling through this forest without being veiled? (33)
"Accompanied by a hundred female slaves, why have you not come out?
Are you a princess or an apsaras? Tell the truth, O fair-faced one! (34)
Blessed is your mother from whom you were born, and blessed is your father;
O sinless one, they are not even able to describe the good fortune of your husband.
O Sulocanā, this ground is indeed superior even to the world of the gods;
yet today your foot, as it moves, sanctifies the surface of the earth.
The deer in the forest who behold you at their pleasure possess good fortune;
so too do all the other birds, and this earth is exceedingly purified. (37)
Enough with your excessive praise; speak the truth, O fair-eyed one. Who is your father, where is your husband, and who is it that you wish to see with such reverence?
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the king’s daughter, that most beautiful maiden, overcome with shame, spoke to those two sons of gods, O prince. (39)
"Know me here to be the daughter of Śaryāti, the virtuous and beloved wife of the sage Cyavana, given by my father to you both according to his will. (40)
I have a god as my husband, who is exceedingly aged and an ascetic;
with a joyful mind, I serve him day and night. (41)
"Who are you two, and why have you come here? Your husband remains in the hermitage; having arrived there, make this hermitage pure today. (42)
Having heard those words, O lord of men, the two Dasras said to her:
"How is it, O auspicious lady, that you were given by your father to an ascetic? (43)
You shine in this forest region like the lightning of the clouds;
indeed, O beautiful woman, no one equal to you has ever been seen even among the gods.
You are worthy of divine garments; you do not shine when covered with deerskins.
Adorned with all ornaments, you possess a mass of dark, curling locks. 45.
Alas! How cruel is the working of fate, that you, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, despair here in this forest;
for you, O beloved with large eyes, have obtained as a husband this blind sage who is utterly afflicted by old age. (46)
O expert in the art of beautiful dancing, having attained fresh youth, you do not shine by wandering in vain like a female rhinoceros;
for the arrows of the God of Love, already well-aimed, will soon fall—who indeed shall be your husband? (47)

"O lady with long, dark eyes, you have been made a wife to a blind man by a creator of dull intellect, though you are endowed with fresh youth; you do not deserve such a husband—choose another instead! 48.
O lotus-eyed one, your life is as good as wasted now that you have obtained as a husband a sage who has turned his gaze away from you.
*Śrīmad-devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 5.134.
We do not consider dwelling in a cane hut or wearing garments of deerskin to be more appropriate. (49)
Therefore, O lady of faultless limbs, O fair-eyed one, choose one of these two with focused attention.
O proud woman, why do you waste your youth in vain, serving a sage, O beautiful one?
Why do you serve that one who is devoid of fortune and abandoned by both nourishment and protection?
O Sage, leaving behind him who is deprived of all happiness, worship the One who possesses faultless limbs and is common to both [parents]. (51)
O beloved, perform your celebrated pastimes in the Nandana and Caitraratha groves;
for how, O proud lady, will you spend your time deprived of honor with one who is blind and aged? (52)

You are a princess, endowed with auspicious marks, and you understand the nature of wandering through this worldly existence; why then, being destitute of fortune, do you pass your time in vain here in this desolate forest?
Therefore, O sweet-voiced one with a lovely face and wide eyes, choose one of these two for your own happiness;
O slender-waisted daughter of a king, enjoy pleasures in the temples of the gods, quickly abandoning this aged sage.

"O fair-haired one, O deer-eyed daughter of a king, what happiness do you find here in this lonely forest with an old man? What do you think of such service to a foot, and of your own fresh youth? What is it that you consider to be suffering? (55)
O fair-complexioned one with tremulous lashes, you who desire the pleasures and enjoyments of youth;
O moon-faced one, you are exceedingly delicate, and the carrying of water and fruit is not suitable for you. (56)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 4 ||
Then the fifth chapter. Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the princess began to tremble.
Maintaining her composure, she, who was wont to speak sparingly, addressed him there. ||1||
O gods, sons of the Sun, you who are omniscient and honored by the immortals, it does not behove you to speak thus to me, a virtuous woman of righteous character. || 2 ||
O best of gods, she was given by her father to a sage who follows the path of yoga;
how can I go upon that path frequented by throngs of unchaste women? (3)
This sun, the witness of the deeds of all the worlds, was born from Kaśyapa; you ought not to speak in such a manner.
How could a woman of noble family, knowing the determination of dharma, abandon her husband and resort to another man in this worthless cycle of existence? (5)
"Go as you wish, O gods, or else I shall cast a curse upon you, O sinless ones;
for I am Sukanyā, devoted solely to my husband Śaryāti."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard his words, the two Nāsatyas were greatly amazed;
suspecting fear on the part of the sage, they spoke to her again. (7)
"O Princess, O woman of excellent complexion, I am pleased with you because of your righteousness.
Choose a boon, O lady of beautiful hips; I shall grant it for your ultimate welfare."
"Know for certain, O young woman, that we two are the foremost physicians of the gods;
we shall restore your husband to youth and endow him with perfect beauty. (9)
"Therefore, O wise and clever one, choose one husband from among these three of us, who are identical in form and body. (10)
=== PAGE 438 === Having heard their words, she was then struck with wonder at her husband. *Śrīmaddevībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa*, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 5.
Having gone there, he related their words, that wonderful thing which had been spoken by them.
Sukanyā said:
"O Lord, O son of Bhṛgu, two gods, the sons of the Sun, have arrived at Cyavana’s hermitage;
I saw one of them, Nāsatya, possessed of a divine body. (12)
Beholding me, whose every limb was beautiful, both Jāti and Kāma became afflicted with passion and spoke these words: "O Mistress, he who possesses fresh youth is your husband. (13)
"We shall indeed make the sage possessed of divine form and sight;
listen now to this agreement spoken by me. (14)
And we shall create a husband for you whose form is composed of equal parts;
from among us three, choose one as your husband. (15)
"I have come here to ask you about a wonderful matter.
O virtuous one, tell me what must be done in this difficult situation."
Even the divine illusion is difficult to discern; I do not know the deception of those two.
O Omniscient One, whatever you command, that which is desired by you, I shall perform.
Cyavana said:
"Go today, O beloved, at my command, O lady of virtuous vows;
bring the two best of divine physicians to my side quickly. (18)
"Let her words be carried out quickly; no deliberation should be made in this matter.
Vyāsa said:
Thus permitted, she went there and spoke these words.
"O best of gods, Nāsatyas, let this be done quickly according to our agreement.
Having heard those words of hers, the two Aśvins arrived there.
The two princesses said to her, "Let your husband Cyavana enter the water quickly for the sake of his beauty"; thereupon, he entered the water.
The two Aśvins also subsequently entered that excellent lake;
thereupon, those three emerged from it at that very moment.
At that time, they were indeed equal in form, possessed of divine bodies, and youthful; they were alike, adorned with divine earrings, and had symmetrical limbs.
They all spoke together: "O lady of excellent complexion, O auspicious one with a stainless face, choose us as your husband—this is our desire. (24)
"O fair-faced one, choose whichever among them you feel greater affection for.
Vyāsa said:
Having seen them all identical in form and likewise equal in age, she— || 25 ||
Seeing those three, who resembled sons of gods, identical in voice and identical in appearance, she fell into a state of doubt.
Not knowing [which was her husband], she became deeply distressed and reflected:
"What shall I do? These three are equal; whom shall I choose? I do not know."
For these are indeed the sons of gods; I have fallen into a state of peril. This is a complete illusion (indrajāla) devised here by the two deities. (28)
"What must I do here now that death has arrived?
By no means should I abandon my husband to choose another. (29)
Thinking in his mind, "Some modern person has become a god"—this is my conviction—he [worshipped] the supreme Śivā, the Sovereign of the Universe. (30)
The slender-waisted lady meditated upon the divine Goddess and offered hymns of praise.
*Śrīmad-devī-bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 5. [Page 439]
Sukanyā said: "O Mother of the World, I have come to you for refuge, being deeply afflicted by sorrow. (31)
O beloved of Śaṅkara! ||32||
Protect my virtue today; I bow at your feet. O Goddess born from the lotus, salutations to you, beloved of Viṣṇu! Salutations, Lakṣmī, Mother of the Vedas, Sarasvatī!
This entire world, both stationary and moving, has been created by you.
Behold this with an undistracted mind; let it be so for the peace of the world.
You are the highly esteemed mother of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
You are the giver of intelligence to the ignorant and always the giver of liberation to the wise;
you are the primordial nature (prakṛti), the full and ignorant one, whose appearance is dear to the Puruṣa. 35.
You are the bestower of enjoyment and liberation to living beings of pure soul;
you are indeed the giver of suffering to the ignorant, yet the means for the happiness of virtuous beings.
O Mother, you are the bestower of success to yogis, and furthermore, the giver of victory and fame;
I have attained supreme wonder and have come to you for refuge.
"O Mother, show me my husband; I am submerged in this ocean of grief.
Deceived by these two gods who have created this trap, whom shall I choose? (38)
"O Omniscient One, having recognized my vow of chastity, show me my husband.
Vyāsa said: Thus was the Goddess Tripurasundarī then praised.
Then, having mentally determined those who were equal to her in age and beauty, the virtuous woman quickly bestowed upon him in her heart that knowledge which brings about the arising of bliss.
Having carefully observed them all, the young woman chose her own husband;
once Cyavana was chosen, both the god and she became satisfied.
Having observed the dharma of Satī, those two best of gods were filled with joy; pleased by the grace of the Blessed Lady, they granted her a boon.
Having addressed the sage, both were eager to depart quickly;
but Cyavana, having regained his eyesight, his wife, and his youth, [remained]. (43)
Filled with joy, the one of great splendor spoke these words to the two Nāsatyas:
"O best of gods, this service has been rendered to me by you both."
What can I say of the happiness attained in this unsurpassed cycle of existence?
Having obtained a wife with beautiful hair-ends, my suffering has increased day by day. (45)
To the blind man, who was very old and destitute of enjoyments in the forest, you two gave eyes, youth, and wonderful beauty. (46)
Having thus accomplished something, I speak now to offer you some assistance;
for how could one who has been helped by a friend not, in turn, assist that friend? (47)
"Curse that man, O Lord, for he would become a debtor on this earth;
therefore, I now wish to grant you both whatever you desire. (48)
"For the sake of liberating yourselves from debt and for the sake of the new [temple], O Lords of Gods, I shall grant you whatever you request, even that which is unattainable by gods or asuras.
Speak what is intended by your minds; I am pleased with your virtuous deed."
Having heard those words of the sage, they consulted with one another.
They spoke to that best of sages who was standing there with Sukanyā:
"O Sage, by the grace of our father, everything desired by our minds has been attained. (51)
"We have a longing to drink the Soma together with the gods. Thus addressed by the god, the two physicians were forbidden from taking up the cups. (52)
When Śakra performed a sacrifice for Brahmā on the Golden Mountain (Kanaka-giri),
you too, O knower of dharma, ascetic, should do so if you are capable.
"This task must indeed be performed by you two, for it is highly desired and conducive to our well-being.
Having understood this, O Brahman, act accordingly for us both, O drinkers of Soma. (54)
"Thirst is extremely difficult to satisfy; it will surely come upon you.
Having heard those words, Cyavana spoke softly to the two of them.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter six.
"That I am endowed with beauty and possessed of youth, and that, though having become old, I have obtained a wife—all this has been brought about by you two. (56)
"Therefore, out of affection, I shall become a drinker of Soma along with you, even while the King of the Gods looks on; I tell you this as the truth. (57)
Having heard these words regarding King Śaryāti of immeasurable splendor while his sacrifice was being performed, they both departed for heaven, filled with joy.
Having taken her, Cyavana went to the circle of the hermitage.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Janamejaya said: "How were those two physicians made drinkers of Soma by Cyavana?"
And how did the word of that great-souled one become true?
"What was the strength of Mānasa compared to the strength of the King of the Gods? Why were those two Soma-drinkers forbidden by him and rendered physicians?
O Lord, please tell me this in detail and immediately."
Today I am desirous of hearing, in every respect, the life-story of Cyavana. ||3||
Vyāsa said: Listen, O great king, to this most wonderful account of Cyavana’s sacrifice for Śaryāti on this earth, O Bhārata.
Having obtained the beautiful Sukanyā, Cyavana, resembling a celestial being, sported with a serene soul as if with another daughter of the gods. ||5||
Then once, the beloved wife of Śaryāti, being deeply distressed with anxiety,
spoke these words to her husband while trembling and weeping.
"O King, your daughter was given by you to a blind sage in the forest;
whether she is dead or alive, she must certainly be seen by you. (7)
"Go, O Lord, to the hermitage of the sage with reverence to see him; what is that Sukanyā doing now that she has obtained such a husband? (8)
"O royal sage, I am utterly consumed in my heart by grief for my daughter;
bring that large-eyed girl, emaciated by asceticism, into my presence. (9)
I see my daughter in every respect— slender-limbed, clad in bark garments,
thin-waisted, and now sharing the burden of sorrow after having obtained a blind husband.
Śaryāti said:
"O large-eyed one, O lady of beautiful hips, go today with respect to see Sukanyā, my beloved daughter, and that sage of rigid vows. (11)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to the woman who was overwhelmed with grief, Śaryāti mounted his chariot and departed quickly for the hermitage of the sage.
Having approached the vicinity of the hermitage, the lord of the earth beheld that sage,
endowed with fresh youth and resembling the son of a god.
Beholding him with the form of an immortal, the king was struck with amazement:
"What despicable deed, censured by the world, has been committed by my daughter? (14)
That aged sage has been slain by her, and another husband—though peaceful and utterly destitute—has been chosen by her who is tormented by lust. (15)
This flower-bowed god is difficult to withstand, especially in youth;
by her, a very great stain has been cast upon the human race. (16)
The life of one who has a contemptible daughter in this world is wretched;
indeed, for embodied beings, a daughter leads to suffering through all manner of evils. (17)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 6:
"An improper act was committed by me for the sake of achieving my own self-interest."
Indeed, that daughter who has been given with her whole being to an old man and a blind man— || 18 ||
"A daughter must indeed be given by her father with all his heart to a worthy man;
for such a fruit has been obtained as was surely sown by me. (19)
If I were to kill my daughter today—she who is ill-behaved and a doer of evil—the sin of killing a woman would be difficult for me to overcome, especially since she is my own daughter. (20)
The renowned lineage of Manu has been rendered stained by me;
public censure is powerful, and the chain of affection is difficult to cast off. (21)
When that king was submerged in an ocean of anxiety, wondering "What shall I do?",
his father, distressed with worry, was seen by Sukanyā by chance.
Having seen him, Sukanyā went quickly to her father's side;
having arrived, she questioned the king with a heart filled with love. (23)
"O King, why do you brood with a face distressed by anxiety, having beheld this seated sage who is youthful and lotus-eyed? (24)
"Come, come! Bow down to my husband, that tiger among men.
O best of kings, do not give way to despair now, O mortal. (25)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his daughter, Śaryāti, afflicted by anger, then spoke these words to his daughter standing before him. (26)
The king said:
"O daughter, who is this sage Cyavana? He is old, blind, and the best among ascetics;
yet who is this youth intoxicated with pride? I have a great doubt in this matter. (27)
"O sinful woman, perpetrator of evil deeds, why was the sage slain by you? O destroyer of the family, this husband of yours was chosen out of lust. (28)
Thus, overcome with anxiety, I do not see him staying in the hermitage;
what evil deed has been committed, surely the conduct of an unchaste woman? (29)
"I am now submerged in an ocean of grief caused by you, due to my wicked conduct, because I have seen this divine person but have not seen the sage Cyavana. (30)
Having heard her father’s words, she laughed and quickly spoke to him;
then, taking her father with her, she respectfully led him into the presence of her husband.
O dear one, that sage Cyavana is undoubtedly your son-in-law;
such a lovely, lotus-eyed man has been made [beautiful] by the two Aśvins.
When the two Nāsatyas arrived here at my hermitage by chance, they surely restored Cyavana to such a state out of compassion. (33)
"I am not your daughter, O father; I would not be such an evildoer as you imagine me to be, O King, deluded by the uncertainty of appearances. (34)
"O King, father, bow down before the sage Cyavana of the Bhṛgu lineage;
inquire of him, and he will explain the entire reason in detail. (35)
Having heard these words of his daughter, Śaryāti then went quickly to that place,
bowed to the sage, and questioned him with respect.
The king said:
"O Bhārgava, tell me your own story quickly as it truly is;
how were your eyes restored, and where did your old age go again? (37)
"O Brahmin, having seen this exceedingly beautiful form, a great doubt has arisen within me; tell me in detail, for by hearing it, I shall attain happiness. (38)
Cyavana said: "O best of kings, both the Nāsatyas, the physicians of the gods, have arrived here; they have rendered assistance out of compassion. (39)
I granted a boon to those two for the sake of their service:
"In the sacrifice of the king, you shall become a drinker of the Soma. (40)
"In this way, youth has been attained by me, and likewise my eyes have become clear;
be at ease, O Great King, and sit upon your auspicious throne. (41)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Book, Chapter 7.
Thus addressed by the Brahmin, the lord of the earth, together with his wife,
sat down comfortably and engaged in auspicious conversation with that high-souled one.
Then the descendant of Bhṛgu, consoling the king, said to him:
"O King, I shall perform the sacrifice for you; prepare the necessary materials."
"I have promised those two that you both shall be drinkers of Soma;
therefore, O best of kings, this must be performed by you in your most extensive sacrifice. (44)
"I shall indeed restrain the enraged Indra by means of my own splendor and strength;
O lord of kings, I shall cause you to drink the Soma at your Soma sacrifice. (45)
Thereupon, O great king, Śaryāti, the lord of the earth, being exceedingly gratified, honored those words of Cyavana.
Having honored Vyavana, the king, together with his wife and exceedingly satisfied, returned toward the city, while the sage indeed continued to perform his duties. 47.
On an auspicious day suitable for sacrifice, Śaryāti, possessing the fulfillment of all desires,
caused an excellent sacrificial ground to be prepared.
Having brought together the venerable sages headed by Vasiṣṭha,
Cyavana, the descendant of Bhṛgu, caused that lord of the earth to perform a sacrifice.

When that sacrifice had been thus expanded, all the gods together with Indra arrived there, and the two Aśvins also came for the sake of the Soma. But Indra became suspicious upon seeing those two Aśvins there.
And he asked all the gods, "Who are these two who have arrived?"
During the king’s extensive sacrifice, the immortals did not say there, "The physician is not worthy of the Soma; by whom has he been brought here? (52)
Then Cyavana took the Soma for the two divine Aśvins;
Śakra tried to stop him, saying, "Do not take the draught for these two. (53)
Thereupon Cyavana said to him: "O Lord of Śacī, tell me the truth: why are these two sons of the Sun not worthy of being called *nāsatyas*? (54)
Born of a lawful wife, he was not of mixed caste;
O Lord of the Gods, by what fault did the excellent poison not enter Soma? (55)
"O Śakra, a decision must be made here at this sacrifice by all the deities.
I shall cause Soma to be accepted; both of us have now become drinkers of Soma. (56)
"O Maghavan, that king has indeed been incited by me for the sake of a sacrifice;
for this purpose I shall act, my word is true, O Lord. (57)
O Śakra, since they have rendered assistance by granting me this new youth,
I must therefore perform a return favor for them in every way.
Indra said:
"These two Nāsatyas are physicians; they have been censured by the gods.
Neither of them is worthy of the Soma; do not take a draught for them. (59)
Cyavana said:
"O paramour of Ahalyā, restrain your anger today, for it is useless.
O slayer of Vṛtra, why indeed are those two not truthful? Is the son of a god not worthy of the Soma?"
When the dispute had thus arisen, O King, no one spoke a word to him;
then Śukra, possessing the fierce luster of fire, caused the two of them to engage in combat by the power of his asceticism.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 6 ||
Then the seventh chapter begins.
Vyāsa said:
O Indra among kings, when the planet had been given away, Vāsava became exceedingly enraged.
There he spoke to Cyavana, displaying his own power.
"O wretched Brahmin, you ought not to transgress this boundary;
I shall slay you, my enemy, like another Viśvarūpa. (2)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 7.
Cyavana said:
Do not despise these two high-souled ones,
O Maghavan; they possess the splendor of beauty and wealth, and it was they who made me appear like another celestial being.
"O Indra, O God, O scorcher of foes, know that apart from you, how could any other gods take their share? Even the two Aśvins [cannot do so]."
Indra said:
"Physicians do not deserve a share of the sacrificial offering by any means whatsoever.
If you wish to give it, O dull-witted one, I shall cut off your head this very moment."
Vyāsa said:
But disregarding those words of Vāsava, Bhārgava seized him as a captive, rebuking him severely as it were.
When the Soma vessel had been taken by the two of them out of thirst,
the god Indra, the slayer of Bala, observed this and spoke these words.
If you yourself cause Soma to be seized for the sake of these two, I shall strike you with my thunderbolt, like another Viśvarūpa. (8)
Thus addressed by Vāsava, the exceedingly arrogant Bhārgava,
filled with great resentment, accepted the Soma according to the prescribed rites, excluding the two Aśvins.
Indra also, out of anger, hurled his own weapon at him—
possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns— in the sight of all the gods.
Then, seeing the thunderbolt hurled by Śakra of immeasurable splendor, Cyavana paralyzed that vajra through his ascetic power.
With that magical rite (*kṛtyā*), the mighty-armed one, intent on slaying Indra here,
that best of sages offered the prepared oblation into the fire with a mantra.
There, by the power of Cyavana’s asceticism, a *kṛtyā* was produced—
a powerful, cruel, and massive-bodied great asura.
What is called intoxication is a most terrible and fearsome thing for living beings here;
in the body it is like a mountain, with sharp fangs and terrifying. (14)
His four long fangs were each a hundred yojanas in length,
while his other teeth were ten yojanas long.
His two arms were like mountains, long and fierce in appearance;
his tongue was terrifying and cruel, licking the very sky.
His neck, resembling a mountain peak, was hard and exceedingly fearsome.
His nails resemble the claws of a tiger, and his hair is exceedingly terrifying. 17.
His body had the luster of collyrium, and his face was terrifying;
his two eyes were like forest fires, formidable and exceedingly fearsome.
One jaw of his remained on the earth and one went to heaven;
such was the great-bodied being named Mada who was thus born.
Beholding him, all the gods were instantly struck with fear;
even Indra, trembling with terror, set his mind not upon battle.
The Daitya also stood with his mouth wide open, holding a thunderbolt;
with his terrible gaze, he seemed to pervade the sky and the three worlds as if about to devour them.
Desiring to devour him, he rushed furiously toward Śatakratu;
and all the gods, standing there, cried out, "Alas! We are slain! || 22 ||
But Indra, his arm paralyzed and desiring to release the thunderbolt from his side, was unable, O chastiser of Pāka, to strike with that weapon at him. ||23||
Seeing him resembling Time itself, Vajrahasta, the lord of the gods,
then remembered in his mind his preceptor, who was well-versed in the sacred commitments (samaya).
Upon being remembered, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati arrived quickly;
the preceptor, seeing that great occasion which resembled a calamity, [acted accordingly].
Having reflected upon the matter in his mind, he said to the Lord of Śacī:
"O Vāsava, this great mantra is difficult to accomplish with the thunderbolt."
O one of great strength, the Asura named Mada arose from the sacrificial pit, having fully acquired the ascetic power of the sage Cyavana.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter [Number].
"For this enemy is indeed unstoppable by you, by the gods, or likewise by me;
O Lord of Gods, seek refuge with the high-souled Cyavana. (28)
He will surely ward off the magical spell (kṛtyā) wrought by himself;
for those devoted to Śakti are never able to restrain the wrath of Śakti.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by his preceptor, Śakra then approached the sage;
bowing with his head and being humble, he spoke to him while filled with fear.
Forgive me, O tiger among sages; pacify the Asura who has risen up. Be gracious, O Omniscient One; I shall do as you command. (31)
"O Bhārgava, from this day forward these two Aśvins shall be worthy of the Soma;
this word of mine is true, O Brahmin, be gracious to me. (32)
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, this effort of yours is indeed in vain; yet let it be so.
I know, O knower of dharma, that you will certainly not act falsely. (33)
These two Aśvins, the drinkers of Soma, shall indeed always be created by you;
and the fame of Śaryāti shall become vast. (34)
O best of sages, whatever deed has been performed by me should in every way be understood as being for the sake of testing you and for the manifestation of your prowess. (35)
O Brahman, show me favor; restrain this arisen pride of mine, and let what is auspicious for all the gods be further established.
Thus addressed by Śakra, Cyavana, the knower of the supreme truth,
withdrew the ascetic power born of anger and produced by that conflict.
Then Bhārgava, having consoled the agitated Deva,
distributed his pride among women, drink, gambling, and hunting.
Having dispelled the pride of the Lord of the Gods and consoled him who was terrified with fear,
and having restored all the deities to their places, he brought that sacrifice to an end.
Then the Bhārgava, whose very soul was dharma, caused the consecrated Soma to be drunk by the high-souled Vāsava and the two Aśvins.
Thus, O King, those two noble Aśvins, sons of the Sun, were made drinkers of Soma by Cyavana through the power of his asceticism in every respect.
That lake also became famous, adorned with sacrificial posts;
and the hermitage of the sage became renowned throughout the entire earth. ||42||
Śaryāti also became highly gratified by that deed;
having completed the sacrifice, he returned to his city accompanied by his ministers.
The powerful son of Manu, who knew the dharma, ruled the kingdom;
Ānarta was his son, and from Ānarta, Rava was born.
Having constructed the city of Kuśasthalī within the ocean,
that subduer of enemies took up residence there and enjoyed the territories of Ānarta and other regions.
To him were born a hundred sons, with Kakudmin as the eldest and most excellent;
and a daughter named Revatī, who was beautiful and possessed of auspicious marks.
When she had become marriageable, King Revata,
the lord of kings, reflected upon princes born of noble lineage.
And having taken refuge on the mountain named Raivata, that powerful lord of men, the ruler of the earth, governed his kingdom among the Ānartas. || 48 ||
Having reflected in his mind, the king thought: "To whom should my daughter be given?
I shall go and ask Brahmā, the omniscient one worshipped by the gods. (49)
Having reflected thus, the king took his daughter Revatī and went quickly to the world of Brahmā, desiring to question the Grandfather.
There the gods and sacrifices, the Vedic meters as well as the mountains, and even the oceans and rivers, stood assuming divine forms. (51)
The sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Pannagas, and Cāraṇas—all those ancient ones—stood with palms joined in reverence, offering hymns of praise. ||52||
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter eight.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Janamejaya said: O Brahmin, this great doubt dwells within my mind:
how did the king, having reached the world of Brahmā, go there himself accompanied by Revatī? || 1 ||
Previously, I heard this entire matter from Brahmins during the course of their conversation:
"A Brahmin who knows Brahman and is tranquil shall attain the world of Brahman. (2)
How did the king himself go there, accompanied by Revatī, from the world of mortals (bhūrloka) to Satyaloka, which is so difficult to reach? This is my doubt. (3)
"The deceased attains heaven; this is the conclusion in all the scriptures.
But how can there be a journey to the world of Brahmā with a human body?
And how does one's course lead from heaven back to birth in the human world? (4)
O wise one, you ought to sever this doubt of mine at once:
how it was that the king went there desiring to question Prajāpati.
Vyāsa said: O King, upon the peak of Meru all the worlds are established—
the world of Indra, the world of Agni, and the city of Saṃyamanī.
In the same way, Satyaloka and Kailāsa are likewise there;
furthermore, Vaikuṇṭha is also there, which is called the station of Viṣṇu.
Just as Arjuna, the son of Pṛthā and wielder of the bow, went to the world of Śakra.
The son of Kuntī remained there in the abode of the gods for five years.
Indeed, with a purely human body, he stood in the presence of Vāsava;
likewise, other kings as well, headed by Kakutstha, were there.
Afterwards, even the exceedingly powerful Dānavas,
having gone to the world of the gods and conquered the abode of Indra, remained there according to their desire.
In ancient times, King Mahābhiṣa, a self-ruling sovereign, went to the world of Brahmā;
there, the king beheld Gaṅgā approaching, exceedingly beautiful.
O King, by fate her garment was carried away by the wind;
then that beautiful woman was seen by the king in such a state, almost naked.
Afflicted by desire, he smiled, and she indeed laughed slightly;
then, seen by Brahmā, they both were cursed and born upon the earth.
Even in Vaikuṇṭha, all the gods were oppressed by the Daityas and Dānavas;
they went to Hari, the Lord of the World, and praised the Consort of Kamalā.
No doubt should be entertained here in any way, O best of kings;
all worlds are accessible to human beings, O lord of men. 15.
"O lord of men, for ascetics who have certainly performed meritorious deeds, it is the very presence of their merit alone that is the cause for going there, O King. (16)
In the same way, for those sacrificers whose souls were purified by sacrifice—Janamejaya said:
"Revata took the maiden Revatī, who possessed beautiful eyes. (17)
After he had gone to the world of Brahmā, what did that king do?
What was commanded by Brahmā, and to whom was his daughter given? (18)
"O Brahman, relate all of that to me now in detail.
Vyāsa said: "Listen, O protector of the earth; there was once, it is said, a king named Revataka."
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter eight.
When he had gone to the world of Brahmā to inquire about a boon for his daughter,
he remained for a moment in the celestial music, having found an opportunity.
Listening with a joyful heart in the assembly along with his daughter, he was not satiated;
and when the musical performance there had concluded, having bowed to the Supreme Lord, [he departed].
Having shown him his daughter, he declared his intention.
The king said:
"O Lord of Gods, choose a boon; this maiden is my daughter. (22)

"To whom should it be given by me, O Brahmin? It is for this reason that I have come to question you. Many princes of noble birth have been observed by me, yet my fickle mind finds no rest in desire for any one of them. (23)
Therefore, O Lord of the gods of gods, I have come here to question you.
Therefore, O Omniscient One, command a suitable bridegroom for the prince—one who is of noble birth, powerful, and endowed with all auspicious marks. (25)
"Instruct the prince, who is a donor and of virtuous character.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the king, the Creator of the World then [spoke].
Seeing the reversal of time, Brahmā spoke these words with a smile: "O King, those boons which you have held in your heart, O Prince— " (27)
All have been swallowed by Time, together with their fathers, grandsons, and kinsmen;
today itself is the twenty-seventh [cycle], and the Dvāpara age has begun.
All those born of the lineage have died, and the city has been plundered by the Daityas;
indeed, a king born of the Lunar dynasty now rules the kingdom there.
It is said that there was a king known as Ugrasena, the ruler of Mathurā, born in the lineage of Yayāti in the region of Māthura. (30)
Kaṃsa, the son of Ugrasena, a hater of the gods and possessed of great strength, was the lord of the Daityas;
he even cast his own father into prison.
Proud with the intoxication of power, he himself ruled over the kingdoms of kings;
and the earth, oppressed by excessive burden, went to Brahmā for refuge.
Overwhelmed by the weight of the armies of wicked kṣatriyas,
the best of the gods declared that an incarnation (aṃśāvataraṇa) must take place there.
Vāsudeva, the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa,
who is that sage Nārāyaṇa, was born from Devakī, who possesses a divine form.
The eternal son of Dharma, accompanied by Nara, performed difficult austerities on the sacred bank of the Gaṅgā at the hermitage of Badarikāśrama. (35)
Having descended into the Yadu clan, he became renowned as Vāsudeva;
by him, O best of beings, that sinful Kaṃsa was slain by Kṛṣṇa.
Having slain his wicked son, the kingdom was indeed given to Ugrasena; meanwhile, the sinful and mighty Jarāsandha, the father-in-law of Kaṃsa, remained [a threat]. || 37 ||
Having arrived at Mathurā, that mighty Jarāsandha joyfully engaged in battle out of anger; however, he was defeated in combat by Kṛṣṇa.
Then he dispatched the Yavana king along with his army for battle;
and [the enemy] heard that the great hero, the lord of the Yavanas, was approaching with his forces.
Kṛṣṇa, however, having abandoned Mathurā, went to the city of Dvāravatī;
Kṛṣṇa, together with assembled artisans, [rebuilt] that city which had been destroyed.

In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 9: The powerful Vāsudeva, having first undertaken the restoration of the dilapidated city, caused it to be adorned with markets, halls, and strongholds.
And he brought King Ugrasena under his control.
The best of the Yadus established the Yādavas in Dvāravatī;
Vāsudeva, however, resides there even today together with his kinsmen.
His elder brother is the renowned Baladeva, whose weapon is the plow;
he is a portion of Śeṣa, a hero who wields a mace, and let him be your excellent choice according to your approval.
"Then, quickly bestow the lotus-eyed maiden Revatī upon Saṃkarṣaṇa, that is, Balabhadra, according to the rites of marriage."
O best of kings, having given away your daughter, go to Badarikāśrama to perform penance in that sacred grove of the gods, which purifies and grants the desires of men. (43)
Vyāsa said:
Thus commanded by Brahmā, the lotus-born one, O King,
the monarch departed swiftly for Dvārakā accompanied by his daughter.
He gave that maiden, endowed with auspicious marks, to Baladeva;
then, after performing intense penance, the king, at the turn of time, [attained his goal]. (45)
He went to the abode of the thirty gods after casting off his body on the riverbank.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, a great marvel has been recounted by you."
But Revata remained there in the world of Brahmā for the sake of his son;
indeed, one hundred and eight yugas passed while he was there.
The maiden has not grown old, nor indeed has the king;
how then could their lifespan have been so fully completed for such a long time? (48)
Vyāsa said: O sinless one, neither old age, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor death, nor fear,
nor even exhaustion ever prevails in the world of Brahmā.
The lineage of Śaryāti, having gone to Mount Meru, was destroyed by Rākṣasas;
terrified with fear, they abandoned Kuśasthalī and fled here and there. 50.
And as Manu was yawning, a son of even greater vigor was born;
he became renowned as Ikṣvāku, the founder of the Solar dynasty.
For the sake of his lineage, having received the unsurpassed initiation through the instruction of Nārada, he practiced austerity while meditating on the Goddess with undivided devotion.
O King, it is well known that Ikṣvāku had a hundred sons;
among them, Vikukṣi was the first, endowed with strength and heroism.
In Ayodhyā there dwelt a king renowned as Ikṣvāku;
he had fifty sons, the most powerful of whom was Śakuni. || 54 ||
O King, it is said that those sons of his were appointed by him as the protectors of the northern region, and likewise, they were assigned to the southern region.
Forty-eight [attendants] were stationed by the high-souled one for the sake of protection, while two others stood at his sides for the service of that king. (56)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Once, during an Aṣṭakā Śrāddha ceremony, King Vikukṣi—
The undeluded one commanded: "Bring meat quickly! ||1||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Book, Chapter Nine.
"Go to the forest with honey for the sake of the *śrāddha* offering, out of respect for your son.
Being thus addressed, he replied, "So be it," and that wielder of weapons quickly departed for the forest.
Having gone there, he killed boars, wild pigs, deer, and even hares with his arrows;
then, being exhausted, he became hungry.
He had forgotten the Aṣṭakā festival and gave the hare to him in the forest;
he then offered the remaining excellent meat to his father.
Then, seeing the meat brought for sprinkling, the preceptor, that best of sages, realized it was unfit and became enraged. (5)
"It is the established rule that what remains after eating should not be sprinkled with water at a śrāddha;
Vasiṣṭha then informed the king of the defilement of the cooked food."
Having learned from his preceptor that such was the son's deed, the king became enraged due to the violation of the sacred law and banished him from the country.
The prince was born renowned by the name Śaśāda;
however, due to his father’s anger, Śaśāda went to the forest in great agitation. (8)
Devoted to dharma, he spent his time subsisting on forest fare; when his father passed away, the kingdom was obtained by that great-souled one.
Śaśāda himself ruled the kingdom as the lord of Ayodhyā;
on the banks of the Sarayū, he performed numerous complete sacrifices.
Śaśāda had a son renowned as Kakutstha;
indeed, due to his various names, he was also known as Indravāha and Purañjaya. || 11 ||
Janamejaya said:
O sinless one, how did the change of name of the prince come about?
Tell me the entire cause and by what deed it came to pass.
Vyāsa said: When Śaśāda had gone to heaven, there was a king named Kakutstha;
that knower of dharma ruled his ancestral kingdom by means of his strength.
In the meantime, all the gods were defeated by the Daityas.
They went for refuge to Viṣṇu, the imperishable lord of the three worlds;
then the eternal Mahāviṣṇu spoke to those gods.
Viṣṇu said:
"O best of gods, let them entreat the king born of Śaśāda to act as their rear-guard;
he will surely slay the Daityas in battle."
The righteous Parāśaka, wielder of the bow, will come for the sake of assistance;
by his grace, his power shall be incomparable.
O great king, at the well-spoken words of Hari, all the gods, including Indra, went to Ayodhyā toward the son of Śaśāda.
The king honored those gods who had arrived according to dharma;
then, unwearied, he asked them the purpose of their coming.
The king said:
"I am blessed and I am purified; my life has become fruitful, since the gods have come to my home and granted me their great vision. (19)
"O lords of the gods, speak your task, even if it be difficult for humans to accomplish;
I shall perform this great deed, which is of great importance for you in every respect. (20)
The gods said:
"O Indra among kings, grant us your assistance; become the friend of the Lord of Śacī!
Conquer, conquer in battle the lords of the Daityas, who are difficult even for the thirty gods to defeat! (21)
By the grace of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), there is nothing whatsoever that is difficult for you to attain.
Impelled by Viṣṇu, we have thus come into your presence. 22.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 9. 449.29.
The king said:
"O best of gods, today I shall become the bridegroom of the deities;
provided that Indra, the lord of the gods, becomes my vehicle therein. (23)
"O Lord, I shall now wage war against the Daityas for your sake;
I shall ascend Airāvata—this I tell you in truth. (24)
Then the gods said to Vāsava: "O Lord of Śacī, casting aside shame, become the leaf of the king; a wondrous task must be performed."
Then Śakra, being greatly urged by Hari and feeling ashamed,
quickly became a bull, like another great bull of Rudra.
That king indeed ascended it for the purpose of going into battle;
because he stood upon its hump (kakuda), he became known as Kakutstha.
Because he was made the vehicle (vāha) of Indra by that name, he became known as Indravāhaka;
and because he conquered the cities of the Daityas, he became Purañjaya. || 28 ||
Having conquered the Daityas, the mighty-armed one bestowed their wealth upon them;
and having thus questioned the royal sage, a friendship indeed arose between them.
And Kakutstha was a most renowned king; those born of his lineage became the highly celebrated Kākutsthas, kings upon the earth. (30)
Kakutstha had a son of great strength born of his lawful wife;
from him was born the famous Pṛthu, a heroic son.
He is known as a direct portion (aṃśa) of Viṣṇu and the designator of the state of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti);
he should be understood as Viśvarandhi, the son of Pṛthu and lord of men. (32)
His son was the illustrious Candra, remembered as the king who perpetuated the lineage;
his son was Yuvanāśva, radiant and exceedingly powerful.
Śāvanta, the most righteous, was born of Yuvanāśva;
by him the city Śāvantī was built, which was equal to the city of Śakra.
Vṛhadaśva was the son, and Śāva was the son of that great-souled one;
Kulavāyāśva became his son and the lord of the earth. (35)
The Daitya named Dhundhu was slain by him on the surface of the earth;
consequently, he obtained the highly renowned name "Dhundhumāra. (36)
His son was Dṛḍhāśva, who protected the earth;
the illustrious son of Dṛḍhāśva is celebrated as Haryaśva.
Nikumbha is said to have been his son, and he became a lord of the earth.
Varhaṇāśva was the son of Nikuṃbha, and Kṛśāśva was indeed his son. || 38 ||
Prasenajit was the powerful son of Kṛśāśva, whose valor was truth;
his illustrious son was renowned as Yauvanāśva. (39)
The illustrious son of Yuvanāśva, King Māndhātṛ,
was the lord of the earth by whom one thousand and eight palaces were constructed.
O giver of honor, for the sake of pleasing the Blessed Lady,
he was not born from a mother’s womb, but was produced from the belly of his progenitor in great sacred fords.
Then the son emerged again, having burst through the belly of his father.
The king said:
"Has that which was described never been heard or seen by you? (42)
O highly fortunate one, the birth of him as it was described is inconceivable;
tell me today in detail the cause of Māndhātṛ’s birth.
"Just as a son born from the king's own body is beautiful in all his limbs," Vyāsa said:
"King Yauvanāśva was supremely righteous, yet he remained childless."
O King, that monarch had a hundred wives;
the king was constantly absorbed in anxiety and reflected upon it daily.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter ten.
For the sake of offspring, King Yauvanāśva, being distressed and despondent, went to the forest and stayed in a holy hermitage of sages. (46)
Distressed, he heaved sighs while the ascetics looked on;
and seeing him so sorrowful, O brahmins, they were moved with compassion. (47)
The Brahmins said to him: "O King, O ruler of the earth, why do you grieve?
What is your sorrow, O Great King? Tell us truly what is in your mind. (48)
"We shall provide every kind of remedy for your suffering.
Yauvanāśva said:
"O sages, my kingdom, wealth, and excellent horses are all at your disposal."
I have a hundred pure wives of radiant luster; moreover, there is no man at all in the three worlds who is my equal in strength. (50)
The vassal kings and likewise the ministers remain obedient to my command;
O ascetics, I see no other sorrow than that which arises from [the lack of] offspring. (51)
"For one without a son there is no destination, neither heaven nor even [the higher realms].
Therefore, O lords of brahmins, I grieve intensely for the sake of progeny. (52)

May the ascetics, who know the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras and have exerted themselves in their practice, consider my sacrifice to be appropriate for one desiring progeny and grant it to me. (53)
"O ascetics, if you have compassion, please perform my task.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of the king, their minds were filled with pity.
Undistracted, they performed his sacrifice dedicated to Indra as the deity;
there, a water-pot was placed by the Brahmins, filled to the brim with milk.
Consecrated with Vedic mantras for the sake of obtaining a son for that king,
the monarch entered the sacrificial hall at night, feeling thirsty.

Seeing the Brahmins lying asleep, he himself drank the consecrated water that had been prepared by the Brahmins for his wife’s sake, sanctified with mantras and drawn up according to the prescribed rite.
O best of kings, the king, afflicted by thirst, drank from it out of ignorance;
seeing the waterless pitcher, O brahmins, they were then filled with apprehension.
Those twice-born ones asked the king, "By whom was the water drunk?
Having realized that it had been drunk by the king, they understood the great power of destiny.
They completed the sacrifice and those sages returned to their homes;
thereafter, by the power of the mantras, the king conceived an embryo.
Then, in due time, having burst through his right side, the ministers brought forth a son for that king. (61)
By the grace of the gods, the lord of the earth did not die there;

That king, true to his promise, became a universal monarch (cakravartin).

Terrified by fear of him, the bandits fled into mountain caves.

From Purukutsa was born a son named Araṇya, who was supremely righteous. His son was Bṛhadaśva, who was devoted to filial piety.

The illustrious son of Aruṇa was known as Satyavrata;
he was a lover who moved at will, for he was dull-witted and exceedingly greedy. (7)
That evil-souled son of the king, deluded by lust, caused an obstacle to his marriage by abducting the Brahmin’s daughter. (8)
O King, the brahmins gathered there, afflicted by intense sorrow, said to King Aruṇa repeatedly, "Alas! We are destroyed! (9)
The king questioned those distressed Brahmins, the inhabitants of the city:

Having heard those words of the king spoken with humility,
the brahmins, having pronounced their blessings, then spoke very earnestly to Aruṇa.
The Brahmins said:
"O King, O best among the strong, today at your son's wedding, the daughter of a Vitra was indeed abducted and forcibly married by him."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard their truthful words, the most righteous king spoke to his son with affection: "O Vṛthā, this name has been given to you because of your wicked deed."
Go far away, O dull-witted one of wicked conduct, from my house!
You, O sinner, must not remain in my domain under any circumstances.
To his father, who was enraged, he said repeatedly, "Where shall I go?
Aruṇa then said to him, "Live together with the outcaste dog-cookers."
The act committed by the outcaste was the abduction of a brahmin’s wife;

"I do not desire a son through you, O defiler of the lineage! Go wherever you wish, O evil-minded one; you have brought about the destruction of my fame. (17)
Having heard the words of his enraged father, that high-souled one departed swiftly from that city and went toward the Śvapacas.
At that time, Satyavrata remained there among the outcasts;
though glorious, bearing a bow and arrows, clad in armor, he was an abode of compassion. (19)
When he had been expelled by his angry father, that lord of the earth was then urged on by the high-souled preceptor Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, Satyavrata became filled with anger toward Vasiṣṭha, the knower of the treatises on dharma, who remained averse to restraining him. (21)
Then, for a certain reason, his father, the lord of the earth,

O Indra among kings, because of that complete unrighteousness, the subduer of Pāka did not send rain upon that region for twelve years.
Then, O King, having settled his wife on the bank of the Kośikī within that territory, Viśvāmitra practiced intense penance.
Your wife, the daughter of Kauśika, is indeed timid;
that woman of excellent complexion is distressed for the sake of maintaining her household. (25)
Seeing her children overcome by hunger and weeping intensely as they begged for wild grains, the devoted wife fell into great distress.
Afflicted with grief upon seeing her children tormented by hunger, she reflected:

"Without my husband, by what means shall I support these children?
All my sons will die, severely tormented by hunger. (30)
"By selling one son for some amount of wealth, I shall protect my other sons; this is the course of action ordained for me. (31)
The killing of all beings is certainly not appropriate for me in this reversal;

Having made her heart hard and having reflected thus in her mind,

The wife of the sage, having tied her middle biological son around her neck and taking him with her for the sake of supporting the remaining one, departed from the house.
Having seen the distressed female ascetic filled with grief, King Satyavrata questioned her: "O beautiful one, what do you intend to do? (35)
"Having bound this weeping child to your neck, where are you taking him now?
For what purpose, O lady of beautiful limbs? Speak the truth before me. (36)
The wife of the sage said:
"I am the wife of Viśvāmitra, and this is my own biological son, O prince;

"O King, there is no food; my husband has gone somewhere to perform austerities.
Afflicted by hunger, I am indeed selling [my body] in order to support those who remain. (38)
The king said:
"O devoted wife, protect your son; I shall provide for your maintenance.
Your husband will return from the forest at that very time. (39)
Having tied some food continuously to a tree near your hermitage, I shall depart; I tell you this truly. (40)
Thus addressed by the king at that time, the beloved of Kauśika took her son Viśvāmitra and departed for the circle of the hermitage.
Due to his throat being bound, that great ascetic became known by the name Gālava;

But Satyavrata, overwhelmed by devotion and compassion,

Having killed deer, boars, and buffaloes dwelling in the forest,

Then, taking that meat, the wife of the sage gave it to her sons;
having obtained that unsurpassed food, she attained supreme satisfaction. (45)
When that king had departed to perform austerities, the sage Vasiṣṭha protected Ayodhyā, the kingdom, and likewise the inner apartments.
Satyavrata, whose soul was devoted to righteousness, remained outside the city in the forest,

For King Satyavrata, due to some cause or other,
constantly harbored an excessive resentment toward Vasiṣṭha.
The sage Vasiṣṭha did not prevent his son, who was most righteous and dear to him, from being abandoned in the forest by his father, for there was a specific reason.
"The completion of the marriage mantras occurs at the seventh step;
even though he was aware of this, that righteous soul [proceeded] with the taking of the Brahmin's wife."
On a certain day, when there were no deer in the forest,
the lord of the earth saw Vasiṣṭha’s milch-cow wandering in the middle of the woods.
Afflicted by hunger, he struck her out of anger and delusion like a bandit;
having tied her to a tree, he took that meat and ate it himself. (52)
Then, O observer of noble vows, the wife of the sage fed all her sons,
suspecting that they were deer and not cows.

Vasiṣṭha, having learned that the milch-cow had been killed, spoke to him in anger.
O evil-souled one, what sin have you committed by killing a cow, that you have become like a piśāca? (54)
Thus, let those three cruel spikes fall swiftly upon you, due to the slaughter of a cow, the abduction of a wife, and likewise the intense anger of your father. (55)
"You shall indeed become renowned on earth by the name Triśaṅku, manifesting yourself in the form of a Piśāca to all embodied beings. (56)
Vyāsa said:
Thus cursed by Vasiṣṭha, King Satyavrata then remained in that very hermitage and performed intense penance.
Having received an unsurpassed mantra from a certain son of a sage, he meditated upon the Blessed Goddess, the supreme and auspicious Prakṛti. (58)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"That son of a king, Triśaṅku, was cursed by Vasiṣṭha."
O high-minded one, tell me how he was liberated from that curse.
Vyāsa said: Thus cursed, Satyavrata attained the state of a Piśāca;
he remained in that very hermitage, devoted solely to the worship of the Goddess.
Once, having recited the nine-syllable mantra there,
the king approached the brahmins for the purpose of performing the fire sacrifice and, having prostrated, spoke to them with devotion.
O gods of the earth, listen indeed to the words of me who am prostrate before you;
may all of you here act as my officiating priests.

And a fire-offering (homa) should be performed according to the rules, consisting of one-tenth of the recitation (japa), by you who are knowers of the Vedas and full of compassion, for the sake of accomplishing the task. (5)
"O best among the knowers of Brahman, I am Satyavrata, the son of a king;
my body must be disposed of in every way for the sake of happiness. (6)
Having heard that, the brahmins there said to the king’s son:
"You have been cursed by your preceptor; you have now attained the state of a piśāca."
Therefore, you are not worthy of sacrifice because you lack the qualification for the Vedas;
you have attained this state of being a Piśāca, which is despised in all the worlds.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of theirs, the king indeed fell into grief: "Fie upon this life of mine today! What shall I do, remaining here in the forest? (9)
Abandoned by my father and severely cursed by my preceptor,
fallen from my kingdom and having attained the state of a *piśāca*, what shall I do?
Then, having made the funeral pyre even wider with wood, the prince remembered the goddess Caṇḍikā, intending to enter it.
Having remembered the goddess Mahāmāyā and having prepared the funeral pyre blazing before him,
he bathed and stood with palms joined in reverence at the front, ready to enter.
Having perceived that the lord of the earth desired to die, the Blessed Lady then came through the sky and appeared visibly before him.
Then, having granted him her vision, the Goddess, mounted upon a lion, spoke to that prince with a voice as deep as a thundercloud, O Great King.
The Goddess said:
"O virtuous one, what is your resolve? Do not, O despairing one, abandon your body.
Be firm, O illustrious one; your father is overcome by old age. (15)

"Having given the kingdom to you, he will indeed go to the forest for asceticism;
cast away your despondency, O hero, O lord of the earth, for it shall be on the day after tomorrow. (16)
Your father’s ministers will come to take you away;
and by my grace, your father, having consecrated you upon the royal throne, [will depart].
"Having conquered desire, he will go to the world of Brahmā; this is certain.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus to him, the goddess then vanished right there.
Then, having been rescued from death by the fire, the prince returned to Ayodhyā along with the high-souled Nārada. (19)
The entire account was related to the king quickly from the beginning;
having heard that news regarding his son and his such resolve for death, the king [was moved]. (20)
Feeling weary in his mind, the righteous king, overwhelmed by grief for his son, lamented in many ways and spoke to his ministers.
"You have learned of my son's exceedingly fierce conduct;
my wise son Satyavrata has been abandoned by me in the forest. (22)
Worthy of sovereignty and a knower of the supreme truth, he departed immediately by his own command;
yet, though devoid of wealth, he remained right there in that very realization, endowed with patience.
Having been cursed in that manner by Vasiṣṭha, he was turned into something like a Piśāca;
tormented today by grief, he intends to enter the fire.
Having been restrained by the illustrious Mahādevī, he stood back after having been prepared for action;
therefore, let them go quickly to that eldest son of great strength.
Having comforted him with these words, let them quickly bring him here;
having consecrated his own biological son, who is capable of protection, in the kingdom.
"I shall go to the forest; I am at peace, having resolved to practice austerities.
Having spoken thus, the king dispatched all his ministers. (27)
With their minds inclined toward joy for the sake of bringing him back,
those ministers went and consoled the prince.
Having brought the high-souled Satyavrata to Ayodhyā with due honor,
the king beheld him looking weak and clad in soiled garments.
Wearing his matted locks, cruel and overcome with anxiety, he thought:
"What harsh deed have I done that my son has been exiled?"
"He is worthy of the kingdom and exceedingly wise, knowing the certainty of dharma"—having reflected thus in his mind, the lord of the earth embraced him. (31)
Having comforted him, he had him sit upon a seat placed near himself;
once his son was seated, the king spoke to him with affection. (32)
With a voice faltering with affection, the king, who was an expert in the treatises on ethics, said:
"O son, you must set your mind upon dharma; those born from my own mouth are to be honored. (33)
Wealth acquired through righteous means should be accepted, and the subjects must always be protected;
one should never speak untruth anywhere, nor should one ever deviate from the path. (34)
That which is proclaimed by the learned should be performed; ascetics are to be honored;
cruel bandits are to be slain; and likewise, there must be mastery over the senses. (35)
O son, for the sake of accomplishing his duties, a king must always act; however, the counsel shared with his ministers must be kept secret under all circumstances. (36)
O son, a foe, however small, should not be neglected by a wise man with all his soul;
likewise, one should not trust a minister who is attached to others or who is subservient.
Spies should be stationed everywhere among both enemies and friends in every way;
one's mind should always be fixed on righteousness, and one should give gifts constantly. (38)
One should not engage in empty talk and should avoid the company of the wicked;
various sacrifices should be performed and the great seers should be honored. (39)
One should never place trust in a woman anywhere, nor in a man who is addicted to women or gambling.
One should never show excessive devotion to hunting. ||40||
He himself should certainly turn away from gambling, intoxicants, singing, and courtesans,
and he should protect his subjects from these.
One should always rise at all times during the Brāhma-muhūrta;
having likewise duly performed the bath and all other prescribed rites according to the rules. (42)
A well-initiated person should perform the supreme worship of Parāśakti with devotion;
O son, the worship of Parāśakti alone makes that birth fruitful. 43.
Having performed the great worship once and drinking the water from the Goddess’s feet, one shall never again enter a mother’s womb; this is the certain conclusion.
"O Great Goddess, all that is visible is she alone; she indeed is the seer and the witness.
Thus, filled with that state of being, one should remain with a fearless mind. (45)
Having properly performed the daily rites, one should go to the assembly of the twice-born;
having summoned them, the determination of the legal codes (dharmaśāstra) should be inquired about.
Having honored the venerable Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
one should always give gifts such as cows, land, and gold to those worthy recipients.
No ignorant Brāhmaṇa is ever to be honored;
never should anything more than mere food be given to a fool. 48.
O son, you must not, out of greed, commit an act that diminishes dharma;
henceforth, you must never again show disrespect toward brahmins. (49)
The Brāhmaṇas, the gods upon earth, must be honored with great effort;
for there is no doubt that the twice-born alone are the cause of the Kṣatriyas' prosperity. (50)
From the Brahmin, fire arose; from stone, iron.
Their all-pervading energy is extinguished within their own sources.
Therefore, those born from the mouth [the Brahmins] should be especially honored by a king who desires prosperity in every way, through both gifts and humility. 52.
The science of government should always be practiced in accordance with the treatises on dharma;
indeed, the treasury must be filled with wealth acquired through righteous means.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Thus enlightened by his father, King Triśaṅku bowed down.
"So be it," he said to his father, with a voice faltering with affection.
Having summoned Brahmins who were knowers of mantras and experts in the Vedas and Shastras,
he quickly had the requisites for the consecration prepared.
Having brought together the waters of all the sacred fords,
the lord of the people likewise summoned the subjects, the vassals, and the kings.
On an auspicious day,
having duly consecrated his son Triśaṅku upon the throne, the father bestowed upon him an excellent seat according to the prescribed rites.
Accompanied by his wife, he entered the third meritorious stage of life and practiced austerities difficult to perform in the forest on the banks of the triple-pathed river.
When his time had come, he went to heaven, honored even by the thirty gods;
seated near Indra’s throne, he shone forever like the sun.
The king said:
Previously, it was stated by your holiness through the course of this narrative that Satyavrata was indeed cursed by Vasiṣṭha for the slaughter of a milch cow.

Indeed, one who is still possessed by a curse would not be worthy of the lion-throne;

Cursed by Vasiṣṭha, he immediately attained the state of a Piśāca;

O King, as soon as the Goddess was worshipped with devotion by Satyavrata, she,
being pleased, instantly granted him a divine body.
His state as a piśāca vanished and his sin was utterly destroyed;
through the nectar of her compassion, he became free from evil and endowed with great splendor. (13)
Vasiṣṭha also became serene in soul through the grace of Śakti;
and his father too, by virtue of that favor, became filled with love for him.
When his father had passed away, that righteous king ruled the kingdom and performed various sacrifices to the eternal Goddess of the gods.
Then he had a son, the most beautiful Hariścandra,
who was endowed with the auspicious marks prescribed by the scriptures and was exceedingly handsome.
Having made his son Triśaṅku the crown prince,
the lord of the earth resolved to enjoy the pleasures of heaven with his human body.
Having gone to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha and having prostrated according to the prescribed rites, the king,
being pleased, then spoke these words with his palms joined in reverence.
The king said:
"O son of Brahmā, illustrious one, expert in all mantras! O ascetic, you ought to listen with a well-disposed mind to my petition. (19)
A desire has arisen in me today for the happiness of the heavenly world, so that I may enjoy superhuman pleasures with this very body. (20)
One shall dwell together with Apsarases and sport in the Nandana grove;

O great sage, perform for me quickly such a sacrifice by means of which I may dwell in the celestial realm of Triviṣṭapa with this very body.
"You are capable, O best of sages; perform my task now.
Having completed the sacrifice, quickly lead me to the celestial realm, which is difficult to attain. (23)
Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, burner of men, residence in heaven is very difficult to attain;
for it is taught that heaven is certain for one who has died through meritorious deeds. (24)
Therefore, O Omniscient One, I am afraid of this desire which is so difficult to attain;
for it is hard for one who is still living to dwell together with the Apsarases. (25)
"O highly fortunate one, perform sacrifices; when dead, you shall attain heaven.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the king was deeply distressed in mind.
He spoke these words once more to Vasiṣṭha, who had been angered before:
"O Brahmin, if you do not officiate at my sacrifice because of an obsession with pride..."
"Having appointed another as my domestic priest, I shall indeed perform the sacrifice now.
Hearing those words of his, Vasiṣṭha was filled with anger. ||28||
And he cursed the king, saying: "O evil-minded one, become a Cāṇḍāla!
With this very body, become a dog-eater (Śvapaca) immediately! (29)
O destroyer of heaven, most wicked one, defiled by the slaughter of Surabhi, you who have severed the wife of Brahmā and are a corrupter of the path of dharma! 30.
O sinful one, there is no way for you to attain the heavenly realm even after death.
