Vyāsa said:
O King, having been addressed thus by his preceptor, Triśaṅku, at that very moment, [departed].
There, with that body, he took on the form of an outcaste;
and at that very moment, his earrings became made of stone.
Then, while the body was of divine blue color and clad in yellow garments, the sandalwood fragrance vanished and a foul odor arose. (33)
The body of that great-souled one became the color of an elephant;
O King, this was the fruit resulting from his anger toward a devotee of Śakti.
Therefore, a devotee of Śakti should never be disregarded;
for Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, was devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī. || 35 ||
Beholding his own loathsome body, the king was overcome with grief;
distressed, he did not go home but wandered instead toward the forest.
Afflicted by grief and overwhelmed with sorrow, Triśaṅku reflected:
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? My body is utterly contemptible. (37)
I do not see anything that must be done by which my suffering might come to an end;
if I go home, my son will surely be distressed today. (38)
Even my wife, upon seeing a dog-eater, will not grant her consent; and my ministers, seeing me in such a state once again, will show me no respect. (39)
My kinsmen and circle of relatives will no longer associate with me;
for one abandoned by all, death is surely better than life. (40)
"Either by consuming poison today, or by falling into a body of water, or by placing a noose around my neck, I shall abandon this body. (41)
Either I shall offer my body as an oblation into a blazing fire according to the prescribed rites with all my strength,
or, having undertaken a fast unto death, I shall cast off these utterly defiled vital breaths.
Indeed, self-destruction will surely occur birth after birth;
furthermore, due to the fault of such killing, one may even incur the state of a dog-eater (outcaste) and a curse. (43)
Reflecting further, the king thought within his mind:
"I must by no means commit suicide at this time."
One's own performed karma must be experienced by this person here in the forest;
through the experience of its ripening, there will be a complete exhaustion of it in every way. (45)
The exhaustion of prārabdha-karmas cannot occur except through their experience;
therefore, I must here experience the fruits of the deeds I have performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (46)
While staying near the holy hermitage, he likewise performed the service of sacred fords, the remembrance of Ambikā, and the attendance upon the virtuous. ||47||
Thus, dwelling in the forest, I shall surely bring about the exhaustion of my karma;
perhaps, through the power of fortune, there may even be a meeting with a holy man.
Having thus reflected in his mind and abandoned his own city, the king went to the bank of the Gaṅgā and remained right there, grieving at will.
Then King Hariścandra, having learned the cause of his father’s curse,
was filled with grief and dispatched his ministers there.
Having gone there quickly, the ministers, filled with humility, bowed down to him who had the appearance of a dog-eater and was sighing again and again, and spoke to him. (51)
"O King, know us to be your ministers who have indeed come here sent by your son, remaining under the command of Hariścandra. (52)
The son of the crown prince said: "O lord of men, listen to what he says:
'Bring the king here, honoring my father.'"
Therefore, O King, come back to your kingdom free from distress;
all your ministers and subjects alike will serve you.
We shall propitiate the Guru so that he may indeed show us compassion; once he is pleased, that one of great splendor will bring an end to our suffering.
"Thus, O King, has it been told by your son in many ways;
therefore, let going to your own home be pleasing to you immediately. (56)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter thirteen.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, the king, who was in the form of a dog-cooker (śvapaca),
did not set his mind on returning to his own home.
Then he spoke these words to them: "Let the ministers go to the city;
having gone to the city, O illustrious ones, speak my words. (58)
"I shall not return, my son; rule the kingdom without sloth, honoring the Brahmins and the gods, and performing sacrifices many times over. (59)
"I will not enter Ayodhyā while wearing this despised garb of a dog-cooker, which is condemned by the great-souled ones; let everyone depart from here without delay. (60)
"Having installed my son, the mighty Hariścandra, upon the lion-throne, you all must carry out the affairs of state there by my command. (61)
Having been thus instructed, those ministers, overcome with intense distress, wept bitterly;
they then bowed to him and departed quickly for the forest hermitage.
Having arrived at Ayodhyā on an auspicious day,
they then performed the consecration upon the head of Hariścandra according to the prescribed rites.
Having been consecrated, the radiant and most righteous king, mindful of his father, ruled the kingdom by the command of his father along with his ministers.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 21 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
The King said:
"By the command of the monarch, Hariścandra was made king by his ministers."
But how was Triśaṅku liberated from that body of a Cāṇḍāla?
Either he died in the midst of the forest or was immersed in the waters of the Gaṅgā;
or else, the Guru, having shown compassion, liberated him from that curse. ||2||
Relate this entire account before me;
I am eager in every way to hear the life-story of that king. (3)
Vyāsa said: Having installed his son on the throne, the king, with a contented mind,
passed the time there while meditating upon Śivā.
As time passed in this manner, the sage Kauśika, having performed his austerities with a concentrated mind, then went to see his wife, sons, and others.
Having arrived and seen his kinsmen well-established, he attained joy;
the wise man questioned his wife, who stood before him in succession.
"But how was the time spent by you during the famine, O fair-eyed one?
Tell me, by what means were these children sustained in the absence of food?"
"Listen, O beautiful one: I have not come because I am engaged in asceticism. What have you done, O lovely and auspicious one, without any wealth?"
Having heard of that extraordinary famine, I prepared a funeral pyre there;
but having reflected thus, "I have not come [here], for what shall I do being destitute? I did not go.
O lady of exceedingly beautiful thighs, I too, tormented by hunger in the forest, entered a certain dwelling of a Śvapaca with the intent of a thief. (10)
Seeing the dog-cooker asleep and being severely oppressed by hunger, he recognized the kitchen and approached it for the sake of food. || 11 ||
When I opened the vessel and was about to take the cooked flesh of the dog's offspring for the purpose of eating it, I was indeed seen by him.
Questioned respectfully, "Who are you? How have you come to my house at night?
Tell me, for what purpose do you open the chest? (13)
Thus addressed by the dog-cooker, I, being severely tormented by hunger, spoke to him with a faltering voice, O lady of beautiful hair: (14)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Book, Chapter 13:
"O illustrious one, I am a Brāhmaṇa, an ascetic, afflicted by hunger."
Having fallen into the state of a thief, I see food in the vessel.
"O high-minded one, I have arrived as your guest without any intention of theft;
I am hungry, so give me permission, for I shall eat well-prepared meat. (16)
Viśvāmitra said: Having heard the words of the outcaste, he spoke to me with firm resolve:
"O foremost of the castes, do not eat me; know this to be the dwelling of an outcaste. (17)
Human birth is indeed difficult to obtain, and within that, the status of the twice-born;
and within the status of the twice-born, the state of being a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to attain—do you not realize this? 18.
One who desires the welfare of the world must never consume forbidden food;
Manu has declared that the seven lowest-born castes are untouchable by virtue of their occupation. (19)

"O Brahmin, this dog-eater must be avoided by one's actions; of this there is no doubt. O twice-born one, I am not restraining you from eating him out of greed, but directly [out of concern for your welfare]. (20)
"O best of the twice-born, let this fault of the mixture of castes fall upon me and not upon you.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O outcaste, you speak the truth; O knower of dharma, your intellect is clear. (21)
Nevertheless, O giver of honor, I shall describe the subtle path of dharma in times of distress;
for the protection of the body must be ensured by all means.
At the conclusion of a sinful act, one must again perform expiation for the sake of purification;
otherwise, from sin, a miserable rebirth will occur—both when there is no distress and even when there is distress.
Furthermore, for one who dies hungry, there is no doubt that hell awaits;
therefore, he who desires his own welfare must eliminate hunger. (24)
Therefore, O outcaste, I shall protect my body by the practice of theft;
for it has been stated by the wise that whatever sin is incurred through theft during a drought [is equal to the merit of other acts]. (25)
"That which the rain-cloud does not rain down shall belong to him.
Viśvāmitra said:
"When these words were spoken, O beloved, the rain-cloud suddenly descended. (26)
Desiring showers from the sky as thick as an elephant's trunk,
I was filled with joy upon seeing a cloud raining along with lightning.
Then, having left that house, I departed with supreme joy;
tell me, O lady of beautiful hips, how was this time spent by you? (28)
"In this wilderness, there is a supreme and cruel destroyer of the lives of living beings here.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, Priyaṃvadā spoke to her husband. (29)
Listen as I describe how this most terrible time was spent:
O best of sages, when you had departed, a famine arrived.
For the sake of food, all the little sons became exceedingly distressed;
seeing their hungry children, they wandered from forest to forest in search of wild rice (nīvāra).
Overwhelmed by anxiety, I was deluded; yet at that time, some small fruit was obtained.
In this manner, several months were passed subsisting on wild grain.
In his absence, O beloved, I thought again in my mind:
"Indeed, there is no alms to be found during this famine, nor are there wild grains (nīvāra) even in the forest. (33)
There were no fruits on the trees, nor were there roots upon the ground;
tormented by hunger, the children wept intensely, overcome with distress.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I say to those afflicted by hunger?"—having reflected thus in my mind, I made this resolution: (35)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 13.
"I shall give one son today to some wealthy man; having taken his price, with that wealth [I shall ransom] the other children. (36)
"I shall protect those afflicted by hunger; there is no other means for their protection.
Having reflected thus in his mind, he sent this son [of mine]. (37)
O illustrious one, for the sake of selling him, I, overcome with intense distress and devoid of shame, took hold of this weeping child and went out while he was crying aloud. (38)
Then the royal sage Satyavrata, seeing me on the road and extremely distressed, asked him, "O child, why are you weeping? (39)
Then, O best of sages, I spoke these words to him:
"O King, this boy is being led by me today for the purpose of sale. (40)
Having heard my words, the king, his heart softened with compassion, then said to me: "Take this young boy and go home."
"For the sake of the princes, food has been prepared for you;
I shall provide it to you daily until your meeting with the sage. (42)
Day after day, this king, filled with compassion, goes forth having placed deer and pigs upon this tree, intending to kill them. (43)
By him alone, O beloved, were the children protected from the ocean of misfortune;
then, for my sake, that king was cursed by Vasiṣṭha.
On a certain day, meat was not obtained by him in the forest; consequently, he killed Vasiṣṭha’s milch cow, and because of that, the sage became enraged. (45)
The name Triśaṅku was bestowed upon the king by that high-souled one;
and because of his execution, the king was turned into a Cāṇḍāla out of wrath.
Therefore, O Kauśika, I have become sorrowful because of his grief;
for the sake of my cause, this prince has attained the state of a dog-cooker (outcaste). (47)
By whatever means possible, O King, you must indeed provide protection for him through powerful asceticism. 48.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his wife, Kauśika, the best of sages and subduer of enemies, spoke with consoling words to that distressed woman.
Viśvāmitra said: "O lotus-eyed one, I shall release that king from his curse,
for he has rendered you a service by protecting you from the wilderness."
"By the power of my knowledge and asceticism, I shall bring about the destruction of suffering," thus consoled his beloved there, Kauśika, the knower of the ultimate truth. (51)
He reflected on how the king's sorrow might be destroyed;
having deliberated there, the sage went to where the monarch was.
Triśaṅku, wretched and appearing like a dog-cooker (outcaste), was staying in a hamlet;
seeing the sage approaching, that lord of men was struck with amazement.
Then Kauśika, seizing the king by the hand as he had fallen to the ground, quickly prostrated himself on the earth like a staff at the feet of the sage.
Raising him up, that best of the twice-born spoke these words with conciliation:
"O protector of the earth, since you have been cursed by the sage on my account..."
"I shall fulfill your desire; tell me, what may I do for you?
The king said:
"Vasiṣṭha was previously entreated by me, repeatedly entreated for the sake of a sacrifice. (56)
"O best of sages, perform a sacrifice for me; I shall perform the most excellent rite.
O lord of brahmins, act as you desire so that I may go to heaven. (57)
"O evil-minded one, having become enraged, this Vasiṣṭha has said to me: 'By this very body, you shall go to Śakra’s world, the abode of happiness. (58)
"How indeed can you dwell in heaven with a human body?
O sinless one, I was addressed thus again by the Blessed One, who was himself longing for heaven.
Having appointed another as my domestic priest, I shall perform an excellent sacrifice. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam*, Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 14. 461.
Then he cursed me: "Become a Cāṇḍāla, a low-born outcaste! (60)
Thus, all this cause arising from the curse has been told;
O Lord of Sages, you are capable of destroying my sorrow.
Having spoken thus, the king, afflicted by the pain of grief, fell silent;
Kauśika, for his part, reflected on how to avert his curse.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 13 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having reflected with his mind upon what was to be done, the son of Gādhi, a man of great asceticism, [acted].
Having arranged the preparations for the sacrifice, he then addressed the sages.
Knowing that sacrifice and having been invited by Viśvāmitra,
all those sages did not come, for they had been forbidden by Vasiṣṭha.
Having understood that command, the son of Gādhi, dejected and exceedingly sorrowful, went to the hermitage where that king was staying.
The enraged Kauśika said to him: "We have been forbidden by Vasiṣṭha."
O best of kings, all the brahmins have not yet arrived for the sake of the sacrifice.
Behold the perfection of my ascetic power, O great king, as I shall cause you to reach the abode of the gods;
I shall fulfill your desire.
Having spoken thus, that best of sages took water in his hand and then bestowed upon him the merit arising from the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
Having then bestowed this merit upon the king, he said to that lord of the earth:
"O royal sage, go without delay to Triviṣṭapa as you desire."
O Indra among kings, by virtue of my merit accumulated over a long time, go joyfully to the city of Śakra; may it be well with you in the abode of the gods.
Vyāsa said:
When the lord of brahmins had spoken thus, Triśaṅku then immediately flew up like a swift bird by the power of his asceticism.
When the king, having flown into the sky, reached the city of Śatru,
he was seen there by the hosts of gods, wearing the cruel guise of a Cāṇḍāla.
He was told by the Lord of the Gods: "Who is this who approaches so swiftly through the sky like a god, yet is difficult to behold despite having the form of a dog-cooker (outcaste)? (11)
Rising up suddenly, Śakra beheld that lowest of men;
recognizing him as Triśaṅku, he rebuked him and spoke with force: 12.
"O dog-cooker, where are you going? You are loathsome even in the world of the gods.
Go quickly back to the earth; it is not fitting for you to remain here. 13.
Thus addressed by Śakra, O crusher of enemies,
the king stumbled from heaven and then fell like a god whose merit has been exhausted.
Again the king cried out repeatedly, "O Viśvāmitra!
I am falling; protect me, who am afflicted by suffering and swiftly falling from heaven. (15)
O King, hearing that cry of his as he was falling, the sage Kauśika looked at the king falling down and said, "Stay! (tiṣṭha).
At his word, O King, he remained right there in the sky,
even though he had been moved from the abode of the gods by the power of the sage’s asceticism.
Viśvāmitra, too, having touched water, performed an extensive sacrifice in order to create a new creation—a second heavenly world. (18)
Having thus perceived his exertion, the Lord of Śacī quickly and suddenly went there toward the sage born of Gādhi.
"O virtuous one, what is being done by Brahmā? Why are you so overwhelmed with anger? Enough of this creation, O best of sages; tell me, what may I do for you? (20)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter fourteen.
Viśvāmitra said: "O Lord, out of a spirit of affection, take back to his own residence the protector of the earth who has fallen from your abode— Triśaṅku, who is exceedingly distressed."
Vyāsa said:
Having understood his resolve, Turāṣāṭ (Indra) became greatly apprehensive;
then, perceiving his formidable strength, Vāsava said, "So be it."
Having restored the king to a divine body and seated him upon an excellent celestial chariot,
Śakra took leave of Kauśika and then departed for his own city.
When Śakra had departed for heaven accompanied by Triśaṅku,
Viśvāmitra then attained peace and became firmly established in his own hermitage.
Then Hariścandra, having heard that account of Viśvāmitra’s assistance and desiring his father’s ascent to heaven, joyfully ruled the kingdom.
The lord of Ayodhyā, filled with affection, engaged in dalliance with his wife,
who was endowed with beauty, youth, and grace.
In the past, that young woman was indeed never pregnant;
at that time, the king became overwhelmed with anxiety and was exceedingly distressed. ||27||
Having gone to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha and bowed his head to the sage,
he informed his preceptor of the anxiety born of childlessness.
"You are indeed an astrologer and an expert in the science of mantras;
O knower of dharma, O giver of honor, devise a means for the continuation of my lineage. (29)
"There is no destination for one who is sonless; you know this, O best of the twice-born.
Why do you remain indifferent, knowing my suffering and being capable [to help]? (30)
"Blessed indeed are these sparrows who dote upon their young;
I, however, am unfortunate, for I think of him incessantly, day and night. (31)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, which were imbued with world-weariness, the sage,
the son of Brahmā, reflected thoroughly in his mind and spoke to him as follows.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"You speak the truth, O great king; in this world of transmigration, there exists no sorrow so extraordinary as the sorrow born of childlessness. (33)
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should diligently propitiate Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures; he will accomplish your task for you.
"There is no god superior to Varuṇa as a bestower of progeny;
worship him, O most righteous one, and the accomplishment of your purpose will come to pass. (35)
Fate and human effort—these two must be honored by men;
for how can the accomplishment of a task arise without exertion? (36)
However, O best of kings, men who perceive the truth must exert effort in accordance with what is right; when that is done, success will follow, and not otherwise. 37.
Having heard these words of his guru Amitatejas,
the king bowed down and departed, having resolved upon asceticism.
Seated in the lotus posture at an auspicious spot on the banks of the Gaṅgā, the king,
meditating upon the Holder of the Noose (Varuṇa) in his mind, performed a penance difficult to practice.
While he was thus performing penance, Pracetas came within the range of his vision.
By his grace, O Great King, his lotus-like face became serene.
The Lord of aquatic creatures spoke these words to Hariścandra:
"Choose a boon, O knower of dharma; I am pleased with your austerity."
The king said:
"O Lord of Gods, I am childless; grant me a son who bestows happiness.
This endeavor has been undertaken by me for the sake of removing the three debts. (42)

Having heard the bold words of the king who was filled with grief, [the sage spoke]. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam*, Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 15. 463. Having heard the bold words of the king who was filled with grief...
Then, preceded by a smile, the Lord of the Noose spoke to him who stood before him.
Varuṇa said:
"O King, if a virtuous son, desired in your heart, should be born, then after that task is accomplished, what further favor will you do for me? (44)
O King, if you would worship me with that very son as an unhesitating sacrificial animal, I shall grant you a boon.
The king said:
"O Lord, let there not be fruitlessness for me; I shall sacrifice to the Lord of Waters, making my own son the victim. I tell you this truly. (46)
O giver of honor, on this earth, the state of childlessness is the supreme and unbearable sorrow;
therefore, grant us an auspicious son who shall extinguish the fire of grief for men. (47)
Varuṇa said:
"O King, a son shall indeed be born according to your desire; go now to your home.
You must fulfill those words of truth which you have spoken in my presence. (48)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by Varuṇa, that Hariścandra went home and related to his wife the account arising from the granting of the boon.
He had a full hundred wives who were exceedingly beautiful;
his chief queen was Śaivyā, an auspicious and devoted wife, faithful to her husband. (50)
When the time had passed, that woman of excellent complexion conceived;
the king became joyful upon hearing of her pregnancy-longings and activities.
Then the king had the purificatory rites performed according to the prescribed rules;
and when the tenth month was complete, she gave birth on an auspicious day.
When the son, who resembled the offspring of a god, was born under the auspicious conjunction of the stars and planets, the king bathed and was surrounded by Brahmins. (53)
He performed the birth rites and other ceremonies, and gave gifts in abundance;
there was great joy for the king arising from the birth of his son.
He became exceedingly noble, endowed with wealth and grain, distinguished by his practice of giving, and filled with the sounds of song and instrumental music. || 55 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. 14.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
When the great festival for the son of that king had commenced in the palace...
Then the auspicious Pāśī, wearing the guise of a Brahmin, arrived there.
Having said "Svasti" to the king, Varuṇa spoke: "Listen, O Lord;
a son has been born to you. Sacrifice me with him quickly, O King. (2)
O King, make true your word which was spoken by you previously;
indeed, through my granting of this boon, your childlessness has today come to an end.
Having heard these words of his, the king fell into deep reflection:
"How can I kill my own son, who has been born with a face as beautiful as a lotus?"
The powerful guardian of the world arrived in the guise of a brahmin:
"One who desires well-being in every way must not, under any circumstances, show disrespect to the gods. (5)
Affection for one's son is always extremely difficult for living beings to sever in every way; what shall I do, and how may there be for me the happiness arising from my progeny? (6)
Maintaining his composure, the king bowed to him and honored him in return,
then spoke words that were gentle, appropriate, and preceded by humility.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 15.
The king said:
"O God of gods, O ocean of compassion, I grant you permission to perform a sacrifice with abundant sacrificial fees according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas."
When a son is born, the father becomes fit for ritual acts after ten days;
the mother becomes pure after a month; in this matter, the couple [are the basis]. (9)
"You are omniscient, O wise one; you know the eternal Dharma. Show mercy, O Lord of Waters; forgive me, O Supreme Lord. (10)
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus, Pracetas replied to that lord of people:
"May it be well with you; I shall depart. Perform your duties, O King."
"I shall arrive at the end of the month; you must by all means perform the sacrifice, O best of kings, after performing the auspicious rites for your son's departure."
Having spoken thus with gentle words to the king, the lord of aquatic creatures departed;
and when the wielder of the noose had gone, King Hariścandra attained great joy.
He gave away ten million cows, each with a calf and filled with gold,
to the Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, as well as mountains of sesame seeds.
Having beheld his son’s face, the king attained a most great happiness; he then performed the naming ceremony according to the prescribed rites, giving him the name Rohita.
When the month was complete, Pāśī then suddenly came to the king’s house in the guise of a brahmin, repeatedly saying, "Sacrifice! (16).
Beholding that god, the king was submerged in an ocean of grief;
having prostrated before him and offered hospitality, he spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"By good fortune, O Lord, you have come to my home; it has been purified by you, O Master."
O Lord of Waters, I shall perform for you a sacrifice according to the rules, as you desire.
"The untrained beast is not to be praised," say the exponents of the Vedas;
therefore, once its tusks have grown, I shall perform a great sacrifice for you. (19)
Vyāsa said: Having been addressed thus by him, Varuṇa replied, "So be it," and departed;
then Hariścandra, having attained joy, lived out his life in the householder stage.
Then, perceiving that his teeth had grown back, Pracetas, assuming the form of a brahmin,
came to his house saying, "Perform your duty."
The protector of the earth, seeing that the Lord of Waters had arrived in the form of a brahmin,
bowed down and honored him with seats and other marks of respect, worshipping him with devotion.
Having offered praise, with his neck bowed in humility, he spoke these words:
"I shall duly perform the sacrifice as desired, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees."
"Even this child, though his tonsure ceremony has not yet been performed, is not considered [fit for sacrifice] because he still has hair from the womb;
I have heard this from the mouths of the elders regarding the use of animals for the sake of sacrifice. (24)
"O Lord of Waters, please wait for a moment; you know the eternal law.
Indeed, the sacrifice must be performed in every way at the conclusion of the child's tonsure ceremony. (25)
Having heard those words of his, Pracetas spoke to him again:
"O King, by speaking this over and over again, you are deceiving me."
O King, do you now possess all the necessary conditions?
Bound by affection for your son, you are indeed deceiving him at this moment. (27)
"If you do not perform the sacrifice after having carried out the rite of shaving, then, filled with anger, I shall utter a terrible curse. (28)
"O Indra among kings, O giver of honor, I depart today at your command.
You, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage, must not make your word false.
Having spoken thus, Pracetas quickly departed from the king's palace.
Then the king, supremely satisfied, rejoiced in his palace.
But when the time for the tonsure ceremony had arrived and a supreme festival was underway,
the Lord of the Noose (Varuṇa) once again reached the king’s palace with speed.
When the queen, having taken her son onto her lap, was seated in the presence of the king at the time of the ritual, Varuṇa arrived right then.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 15:
Speaking these clear words, "Perform your duty," to the king—
Bearing the form of a brahmin, he was glorious, like the fire-god Agni manifest before one's eyes. ||33||
Upon beholding him, the king became exceedingly overwhelmed; with palms joined in reverence, he bowed to that supreme being out of fear.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, the king spoke with humility:
"O Lord, today I shall perform the work of the sacrifice according to the rules."
There is something more to be said even in that regard; listen with a focused mind, O Lord.
If you deem it appropriate, O Master, I shall speak it before you. (36)
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are the twice-born; those who have not been consecrated by the sacraments are Śūdras; thus the knowers of the Veda understand. (37)
"Since this son of mine today behaves like a Śūdra, it is established in the Vedas that once initiated, one becomes fit for the sacred rites. (38)
The initiation ceremony for Kṣatriyas is traditionally prescribed for the eleventh year;
for Brāhmaṇas it is in the eighth, and for Vaiśyas indeed in the twelfth. 39.
O Lord of Gods, if you take pity on me, your wretched servant,
then bring one and I shall perform a supreme sacrifice with that animal.
"You are a guardian of the world, O knower of dharma, proficient in all the scriptures;
since you consider your word to be true, go now to your abode, O Lord. (41)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, the compassionate lord of the waters,
O King, said "Om" and departed quickly with a serene countenance.
When Varuṇa had departed, the king became filled with exceeding joy;
having thus obtained the happiness of his son, the king indeed attained great delight.
Then King Hariścandra performed his royal duties;
as time passed, a son was born who was ten years old.
The king, accompanied by learned Brahmins as well as his ministers, provided for him a collection of sacrificial requisites befitting his prosperity. (45)

In the eleventh year of his son's life, during the ceremony for the binding of the sacred thread (vratibandha), the king performed the rites according to the rules; yet he remained anxious in his heart once again.
While the rite was thus proceeding and the boy had been brought forward,
Varuṇa then arrived, wearing the guise of a brahmin.
Beholding him, the king quickly bowed down and stood before him;
with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy, he replied to the supreme god: ||| 48 ||
"This son of mine is invested with the sacred thread and is fit for the status of a twice-born;
by this grace, my grief born from the reproach of being barren has vanished. (49)
"I desire to perform a sacrifice with abundant and excellent sacrificial fees;
listen at this opportune time, O knower of dharma, for I speak the truth today. (50)
"At the conclusion of the rite of returning home, I shall fulfill your desire;
therefore, having shown compassion toward me, you ought to forgive me for now. (51)
Varuṇa said: "O King, you are greatly deluding me, being intensely overwhelmed by affection for your son; O high-minded one, you repeatedly employ arguments that seem well-reasoned. (52)
"I shall go today, O Great King, impelled by your word;
I will return at the appointed time for the ceremony of my return. (53)
Having spoken thus and taken leave of him, O lord of the people, Varuṇa departed;
and the king, greatly delighted, carried out his duties accordingly.
Seeing that Varuṇa had arrived and perceiving the timing of the sacrifice, the highly discerning prince then became anxious with thought. ||55||
He inquired here and there about the cause of the king's grief;
having learned that it was the king’s intention to commit suicide, O long-lived one, he set his mind upon departing.
Having made a firm resolve and consulted with his ministers and sons,
he departed from that city and went forth into the forest.
When his son had departed, the king then became exceedingly sorrowful at will;
he dispatched his own messengers with the desire to search for him.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 16.
When time had passed in this manner, Varuṇa went to that house, saying to the king who was tormented by grief, "Perform a sacrifice. (59)
The king, having prostrated before him, said: "O God of gods, what shall I do?
I do not know where my son has gone today, overwhelmed by fear. (60)
O Lord of aquatic creatures, though he was searched for by my messengers everywhere— in mountain fastnesses and in the hermitages of sages— he was not found.
"Command me, O Great King; what shall I do now that my son has departed?
O Omniscient One, I am not at fault here; rather, this is entirely due to the fault of my own destiny. (62)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the king, Pracetas became exceedingly enraged;
deceived again and again, he cursed the king out of anger.
"O King, because I have been deceived by your words, therefore let this most dreadful disease of dropsy afflict you. (64)
Vyāsa said: Thus cursed by the enraged Pracetas,
the protector of the earth was then afflicted by a disease that brought him great suffering.
Having thus cursed the king, the wielder of the noose (Varuṇa) departed for his own abode;
the king, having contracted a great disease, became exceedingly distressed.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 15 ||
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
After Varuṇa had departed, the king was then exceedingly afflicted by disease.
Having encountered suffering after suffering, he then became exceedingly distressed. || 1 ||
O King, having heard in the forest that his father was afflicted by disease, the prince, constrained by affection, made up his mind to go.
When a year had passed, knowing that he wished to go with reverence to see his father, Śakra arrived there.
Then Vāsava, quickly assuming the form of a brahmin, skillfully restrained the prince who was intent on departing. ||4||
Indra said:
"O prince, you do not know the extremely difficult principles of statecraft;
therefore, being deluded, you vainly set your mind on going."
O highly fortunate one, your father will have the Brahmins, who have mastered the Vedas,
perform a fire sacrifice for you once the sacrificial fire has been kindled.
For the self, O dear one, is indeed beloved to all living beings;
for its sake, sons, wives, wealth, and so forth, are held dear.
Having killed you, his beloved son, for the sake of protecting his own body,
he will have a fire sacrifice performed and shall be freed from disease.
Therefore, O prince, you must not go to your father’s house;
however, once your father has died, you must by all means go there for the sake of the kingdom.
O King, having been thus forbidden there by Vāsava,

"O twice-born one, tell me what is desired by you; indeed, I shall grant your wish. (23)
"Even though it is something that cannot be given away in this world, I now desire fame;
for indeed, the life of one who has attained wealth is truly in vain. (24)
"No pure fame, which bestows happiness in the next world, has been acquired.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O Great King, grant me the kingdom along with its attendants as a boon. (25)
Rich with elephants, horses, chariots, and jewels, [it was situated] in the midst of the most sacred altar.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of the sage, the king was deluded by his illusory power. (26)
Having said "It is given," he [Rāma] accepted the kingdom without hesitation and at his own will;
then Viśvāmitra, being exceedingly harsh, said to him, "It has been taken. (27)
"O Indra among kings, O high-minded one, give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) worthy of being given;
Manu has declared that a gift devoid of a sacrificial fee is fruitless. (28)
"Therefore, for the sake of the fruit of your gift, give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as prescribed.
Thus addressed, the king, being greatly amazed, then spoke to him.
"O Brahmin, O Master, how much wealth should now be given to you by me?
O holy one, please state the exact measure for the fee of the sacrificial gift. (30)
"I shall bestow this for the sake of the merit of my gift; be at ease, O you whose wealth is asceticism.
Having heard that, Viśvāmitra spoke to that lord of the earth: || 31 ||
"Now give me two and a half bhāras of gold as my fee.
Having promised him, "I shall give it," the king was greatly astonished.
At that very moment, his soldiers arrived while looking on;
seeing the lord of the earth agitated, they praised him, filled with joy.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard their words, the king, without saying anything good or bad,
went from there into the inner apartments while reflecting upon his own past actions.
"What gift have I accepted that my entire possession has been surrendered?
I have been cheated here in the forest by this brahmin, as if by thieves. (35)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 19.
"The entire kingdom along with its appurtenances was promised by me to him, as well as two bhāras of gold and a half-bhāra as a sacrificial fee.
What shall I do? My mind is deluded; I did not recognize the deception of the sage."
I have been suddenly deceived by this ascetic Brahmin. ||37||
"I do not know the work of destiny; alas, O Fate, what will happen? Thus lost in thought, the king returned home, extremely overwhelmed.
Seeing her husband deeply distressed, the queen asked him the reason:
"O Lord, why do you appear so dejected? Tell me now, what is your anxiety?"
"Your son has returned from the forest; the Rājasūya sacrifice was performed long ago.
Why do you grieve, O Indra among kings? Tell me the cause of your sorrow. (40)
Nowhere does an enemy exist, whether powerful or weak;
even Varuṇa is well-pleased, for you have accomplished your purpose on this earth. (41)
The body is wasted away by anxiety; there is no death equal to anxiety.
O tiger among kings, let it be abandoned; be composed, O wise one. 42.
Having heard those affectionate words, the lord of men, filled with joy,
spoke somewhat regarding the cause of his anxiety, both auspicious and inauspicious.
O King, being thus possessed by anxiety, he took no food;
and though the lord of the earth lay upon a white bed, he found no sleep. (44)
As the king, distressed by his thoughts, was performing his morning rites such as the twilight prayers after rising at dawn, Viśvāmitra arrived.
The sage, who had taken away all his possessions, was reported to the king by the attendants;
having arrived, he spoke to the king as the latter bowed down to him again and again.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O King, relinquish your own kingdom and give me that which was promised by your word.
O Indra among kings, touch gold and become true to your word this very moment. (47)
Hariścandra said:
"O friend, this kingdom is now indeed given by me to you;
having abandoned it, I shall go elsewhere. Do not worry, O Kauśika."
"O Brahmin, O Lord, you have duly accepted my entire property.
O twice-born one, being unable to give a gift of gold at this time,
I shall now give you whatever gift I can until my wealth returns."
Furthermore, if by the turn of time it should be so, then I shall give the sacrificial fee.
Having spoken thus, the king said to his son and to his wife Mādhavī:
"Indeed, this kingdom has been bestowed by me upon him in great abundance upon the sacrificial altar."
Having abandoned the three bodies, all this— including elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as jewels and gold— has been surrendered to you.
"Having abandoned Ayodhyā, I shall go somewhere into the depths of the forest;
let this sage properly accept the kingdom, which is fully endowed with all prosperity. (53)
Having thus addressed his son and his wife, the virtuous Hariścandra departed from his own palace,
honoring that best of the twice-born.
Seeing the king departing, both his wife and son,
overcome with anxiety and with dejected faces, then followed behind him.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in the city upon seeing them in such a state;
all the living beings residing in the city of Sāketa wailed aloud.
"Alas, O King! What deed has been done? From where has this suffering come?
You have been deceived, O Great King, by Fate, that most clever one. (57)
Then all the social classes (varṇas) would suffer misery upon seeing that lord of the earth together with his wife and his high-souled son. 58.
The city-dwellers, including the Brahmins and others, afflicted by grief, censured that Brahmin of wicked conduct, saying, "This man is a rogue. (59)
Having emerged from that city, Viśvāmitra approached the king as he was departing and spoke these harsh words to him.
"O lord of men, go after giving me the gold of the sacrificial fee;
otherwise, say that I will not give it, for the gold has been relinquished by me. (61)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Book, Chapter 20:
"Either take the entire kingdom, or let greed and ambition turn away."
If you consider it given, O King, then give that which was promised.
To Gādheya, who was speaking thus, King Hariścandra,
with a deeply distressed soul, bowed down and spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 19 ||
Now the twentieth chapter. Hariścandra said:
"Without having given you gold, I shall certainly not take my meal."
This is my vow, O best of sages; cast off your despondency, O you of noble discipline.
I am a Kṣatriya king born of the Solar dynasty,
a sovereign who has performed the Rājasūya sacrifice and is a ruler who grants desired boons.
"O Lord, how can I avoid taking on a form at will?
O best of the twice-born, a debt must certainly be repaid to you. (3)
"Be at ease; I shall give you gold as desired by your heart.
Wait for some time until I have acquired wealth. (4)
Viśvāmitra said:
"O King, how will you obtain wealth beyond this?
Your kingdom has gone, as have your treasury, your army, and the means for achieving your goals."
"O protector of the earth, your hope for wealth is in vain; what can I do?
O King, how could I afflict you, who are destitute, with greed? (6)
Therefore, O protector of the earth, tell me now: "I will not give.
Having cast aside my hope like an unchaste woman, I shall depart from here as I please. (7)
"Go as you wish, O Indra among kings, accompanied by your wife and son.
Gold is not what you lack; tell me now what I shall give to you. (8)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of the brāhmaṇa while traveling, the king replied to the sage, "O brāhmaṇa, perform this; I shall give it."
"My body, as well as that of my wife and son, is indeed free from ailment;
having purchased that very body, O twice-born one, I shall surely give it to you free of debt. (10)
"O Lord, O best of Brahmins, look for a master in the city of Vārāṇasī;
I, along with my wife and my son, shall enter into the state of servitude."
"O Sage, O Supporter of the Earth, take this full vessel of gold weighing two and a half bhāras;
having given it at its value, be satisfied with us all. (12)
Speaking thus, he then departed with his wife and accompanied by his sons,
together with his beloved Umā, to where Śaṅkara himself resided.
And having beheld that beautiful city, which brings delight to the mind,
he said, "I have achieved my purpose, beholding this city of such great splendor."
Then, having reached the Bhāgīrathī, bathed, performed the libations for the gods and others,
and completed the worship of the deities, he cast his gaze in all directions.
Having entered the divine city of Vārāṇasī, the protector of the earth [thought]:
"This is not for human enjoyment; it is the domain of the wielder of the trident. (16)
Afflicted by grief and deeply distressed, he went on foot together with his wife;
having entered the city, the king then heaved a deep sigh.
Then he saw the best of sages, a Brahmin seeking sacrificial fees;
seeing that he had arrived, he became humble with courtesy.
And Hariścandra, having joined his palms in reverence, said to the great sage:
"O Sage, these are my very life-breaths, as well as my son and my beloved wife.
O best of the twice-born, accept whatever you require from them this very day."
And whatever other task we must perform, you should tell me that as well. || 20 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter twenty.
Viśvāmitra said:
"The month is complete—blessings upon you! Let my sacrificial fee be given, provided that your own word is remembered as being true to its purpose."
The king said: "O Brahmin, whose power is knowledge and austerity, even now the month is not yet complete; let half a day remain, and wait for that, and no longer. (22)
Viśvāmitra said:
"So be it, O great king; I shall return again.
If you do not grant [the request] today, I will cast a curse upon you. (23)
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed; and then the king reflected:
"How shall I bestow upon him the sacrificial fee that was promised? (24)
Where are my well-nourished friends? Where now is my wealth?
Since accepting gifts is so corrupt for me, how could I possibly make a request there? (25)
"The threefold conduct of kings has been declared with certainty in the treatises on Dharma;
yet, if I were to give away the sacrificial fee, I would forfeit my life."
By seizing the property of a Brahmin, I shall become a sinful worm, the lowest of the low;
or else I shall go to the state of a hungry ghost—therefore, the sale of my own self is indeed better.
Sūta said:
Then the wife replied to the king, who was agitated, dejected, and reflecting with his face cast downwards, in a voice choked with tears.
O Great King, protect your own dharma;
for a man excluded from truth is to be shunned like a ghost.
They say there is no higher dharma for a person than this.
O tiger among men, such is the observance of one's own truth.
The Agnihotra sacrifice, Vedic study, and all other rites such as giving gifts—all these become fruitless for that person whose speech is untruthful. (31)
Truth is indeed exceedingly pleasing to the wise in the treatises on Dharma;
likewise, falsehood leads to the crossing over [of the world] for some, yet to the downfall of those of unrefined self. (32)
Disregarding hundreds of horse-sacrifices and even the Rājasūya, the king, having performed [those rites], fell from heaven once due to his untruthful speech. (33)
The king said:
"This son, who increases the lineage, remains as a child.
O lady with the gait of an elephant, speak whatever words you desire to say. (34)
The wife said:
"O King, let there be no falsehood in you; for men, women bear fruit in the form of sons.
Therefore, having given me away with wealth, bestow me as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) upon the Brahmin."
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words, the lord of the earth fell into a swoon;
and having regained consciousness, he lamented, being exceedingly distressed.
"O blessed lady, this is a great sorrow that you speak thus to me:
have my smiles and conversations with you been forgotten by you, a sinner? (37)
Alas, alas! O lady of pure smiles, how is it fitting for you to speak such words?
O beautiful one, why do you utter this speech which is so difficult to bear? (38)
Having spoken thus, that best of kings, who was not steadfast in the selling of his wife,
fell upon the surface of the earth, overwhelmed by a swoon.
Seeing the lord of the earth lying on the ground, overcome by a swoon, the princess, deeply distressed, spoke these words with great compassion: (40)
Alas, Great King! From whose ill-will has this come upon you, that you, who are worthy of refuge, must fall to the ground like a beggar? (41)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Seventh Book, Chapter 21: By whom indeed has wealth been bestowed upon crores of Brahmins?
That very lord of the earth, my husband, sleeps upon the ground.
Alas, what a tragedy! O Fate, what has this king done to you, that he who was equal to Indra, the lord of the gods, has been brought to this wretched state? (43)
Having spoken thus, that woman of beautiful hips fell down unconscious,
for she was utterly overwhelmed by the great burden of grief for her husband.
Seeing this, the child, overcome by hunger and deeply distressed, spoke these words:
"Father, father! O mother, give me food to eat. (45)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Hariścandra episode of the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 20 ||
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Sūta said:
In the meantime, Viśvāmitra, the great ascetic, arrived.
Enraged, he was like Death himself in his heart's desire to beg for his own wealth.
Upon seeing him, Hariścandra fell to the ground unconscious;
sprinkling the king with water, he spoke these words to him. (2)
"Arise, arise, O Indra among kings! Give the desired sacrificial fee.
For those who bear a debt, suffering increases day by day. (3)
Then, being refreshed by that water cold as ice,
the king regained consciousness and beheld Viśvāmitra.
Again he fell into delusion, and then the sage gave way to anger;
having consoled the king, that best of the twice-born spoke these words.
Viśvāmitra said:
"Let that sacrificial fee be given to me, if you have regard for steadfastness;
by truth the sun shines, and upon truth the earth stands firm. (6)
Truth has been declared the supreme dharma; heaven is established upon truth.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once held on a scale. (7)
"Indeed, truth alone excels a thousand horse-sacrifices;
or rather, what need have I for this that has been said? (8)
"O King, if you do not give me my sacrificial fee,
I shall certainly curse you once the sun has set behind the western mountain."
Having spoken thus, the brahmin departed; and the king became afflicted by fear, miserable, destitute, and tormented by the sage’s harsh words.
Sūta said:
In the meantime, a Brāhmaṇa who had mastered the Vedas went out from his own house, accompanied by other Brāhmaṇas and kinsmen.
Then, seeing that ascetic standing there as he approached, the queen spoke these words to the king, which were consistent with righteousness and purpose.
Among the three castes as well, the father is called a Brāhmaṇa;
for there is no doubt that the paternal property must be taken by the son. || 13 ||
"Therefore, it is my opinion that he should be entreated for the sake of wealth.
The king said, "O slender-waisted one, I do not desire a gift; I am a Kṣatriya."
Indeed, begging is not found among Brahmins;
for a Brahmin is the teacher of all castes and must be honored in every way. (15)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Book, Chapter 22.
Therefore, a guru should not be entreated [for instruction] by Kṣatriyas, especially;
for sacrifice, study, and giving are prescribed for the Kṣatriya. (16)
Granting fearlessness to those who have come for refuge and protecting the subjects—this is what must be done; one should never utter such piteous words as "Give [me something]. (17)
"O Goddess, the words 'I give' alone are fixed in my heart;
whatever wealth I have acquired from anywhere, I give it to a Brāhmaṇa. (18)
The wife said:
Time makes things equal and unequal; time bestows both humiliation and honor. It is time that makes a man a giver or a beggar. (19)
Behold the workings of Time: the king was cast out from his kingdom and his happiness by a learned brahmin who, though exceedingly powerful, was filled with wrath. 20.
The king said:
"It would be better for my tongue to be cut in two with a sharp-edged sword than for me, having abandoned pride, to utter the words, 'Give, give! (21)
"O highly fortunate lady, I am a Kṣatriya; I do not beg for anything at all.
Indeed, I always give away wealth acquired through the prowess of my own arms. (22)
The wife said:
"O Great King, if indeed your mind is not inclined to beg,
I have been given to you rightfully even by the gods together with Indra."
O one of great splendor, I am to be instructed by my father and protected by my husband; therefore, having taken my price, let that which is due to my preceptor be bestowed. (24)
Having heard these words, King Hariścandra, crying out "Alas! Alas!", lamented, being exceedingly distressed.
And his wife spoke further: "Let my word be done;
because you have been consumed by the fire of a brahmin's curse, you will fall into a low state. (26)

Not for the sake of gambling, nor for the sake of wine, nor for the sake of sovereignty, nor for the sake of enjoyments—give this for the sake of your preceptor; therefore, make your vow of truth fruitful.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the Hariścandra episode of the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 21 ||
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Thus urged again and again by his wife, the king—
He said, "O blessed lady, I, utterly merciless, shall carry out your sale. || 1 ||
I shall do that which even a cruel person is unable to do,
if your speech shines forth so exceedingly harsh as this.
Having spoken thus, the king, the best of monarchs, went to the city in distress; then, having brought his wife down into the arena, he [proceeded]. || 3 ||
Then, with a throat choked with tears, he spoke these words:
"O all you citizens, listen to my words! (4)
If anyone has a task to be done by me through this life-breath of a maidservant, let him speak with haste while I still sustain my own body. (5)
Those wise men said: "Who are you that has come here to sell your wife?"
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 22:
The King said:
"Why do you question me? Who are you, O one? I am a cruel being, not human."
"Or perhaps I am a cruel Rākṣasa, and therefore I commit this sin.
Vyāsa said:
Having suddenly heard that sound, Kauśika, who was assuming the form of a Brahmin, [acted].
Assuming the form of an old man, he spoke to Hariścandra:
"Hand over a female slave to me; I am the purchaser and shall provide the wealth. (8)
"I possess incomparable wealth and my beloved wife is delicate;
she is unable to perform household chores, therefore grant her to me. (9)
"I shall take a female slave, but how much wealth will I give you?"—
when the Brahmin had spoken thus, [the reply came] from King Hariścandra.
His heart was rent with grief, yet he said nothing to him at all.
The Brahmin said:
"In your actions, age, appearance, and character, you are like a woman."
"Take this wealth which is appropriate; give me back my wife. For the price of a woman and a man has been seen in the treatises on Dharma. (12)
Endowed with the thirty-two marks, skillful, and possessed of virtuous conduct,
[he gave] thirty million gold pieces for women and likewise ten million for men.
Having heard these words of his, King Hariścandra was overcome with great sorrow and said nothing at all to him.
Then that brahmin, having placed the wealth upon a bundle of grass before the king, seized the queen by her hair and dragged her away.
The queen said:
"O noble one, release me immediately! Let me see my son;
O Brahmin, it will be difficult to behold him again. (16)
"Behold me here, my son, your mother, reduced to such a state of servitude!
Do not touch me, O prince; I am no longer to be touched by you now."
Then that boy, suddenly seeing his mother in such a miserable state, ran toward her with tears in his eyes, crying out "Mother!
while pulling at the garment in his hand, stumbling as he wore the sidelocks of a youth.
Then, out of anger, the twice-born man struck that child as he approached.
Even while saying "O Mother," he would not let go of his mother at all.
The queen said: "O Lord, show me favor; please buy this boy. (20)
"Even though I have been purchased, I shall not be effective in accomplishing this task without him.
O Lord, show favor to me, a woman of such little fortune. (21)
The Brahmin said:
"Let this wealth be taken; let my boy be given to me.
For he is a knower of the Dharmaśāstras, both in woman and man; indeed, his fee has already been paid. (22)
Worth hundreds, thousands, lakhs, and even crores according to others, she is endowed with the thirty-two marks, skillful, and possessed of the virtues of moral conduct. (23)
The value of women is said to be ten million [gold pieces], and that of a man is likewise one hundred million.
Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 22.

In that very manner, his wealth was again cast upon the cloth before him.
Taking the boy, he bound him together with his mother in one place;
filled with joy, he set out quickly for home along with her.
Having performed a circumambulation, she knelt down in prostration and, distressed and overwhelmed with tears, spoke these words: (26)
If I have given gifts, if I have offered oblations, and if I have gratified the Brahmins, by that merit may my husband Hariścandra indeed be restored to me once again. (27)
Seeing her fallen at his feet—she who was dearer to him than his own life—the king cried out, "Alas! Alas! and lamented with his senses overwhelmed.
How has she, who is endowed with truthfulness, virtue, and excellence, become separated?
Even the shade of a tree never abandons that tree at any time. (29)
Having thus spoken to his wife with these well-connected words to one another, he then said this to his son: "Where will you go, leaving me behind? (30)
"In which direction shall I go? Who will dispel my sorrow?
O twice-born one, I have no grief in the renunciation of the kingdom, nor do I have any grief in dwelling in the forest. (31)
"That which causes my separation from my son," the king spoke thus; "for in this world, wives are indeed always to be enjoyed by a virtuous husband. (32)
"O auspicious lady, you have been abandoned by me and cast into misery—you who were born in the lineage of Ikṣvāku and were worthy of all the pleasures of sovereignty. (33)
Having obtained me as such a husband, you have indeed fallen into the state of a slave;
for I am sinking in such a vast ocean of grief. (34)
"O Goddess, who will deliver me by means of the extensive ancient narratives?
Sūta said:
While that royal sage was looking on, [he was struck] with most terrible lashes of a whip.
Having slain them, the lord of brahmins proceeded to lead them away;
but seeing his wife and daughter being led away, that king— || 36 ||
Afflicted by extreme sorrow, he lamented, sighing hot breath again and again—
she whom neither wind, nor sun, nor moon, nor ordinary people had ever seen.
He has delicate fingers and toes. ||38||

"I have seen her before as my wife; now she has fallen into slavery. This boy, born of the Solar dynasty, has been brought to the point of sale! Fie on me, the evil-minded one! Alas, my beloved! Alas, my child! O dear one, this is the wicked conduct of an ignoble man like me. (39)
"Having fallen into a state dependent on fate, yet I have not died—fie upon me!
Vyāsa said: As the king was lamenting thus, the Brahmin vanished before his eyes.
In the meantime, the best of sages, possessed of great ascetic power, arrived there in haste.
Taking with him trees, houses, and other such objects, that cruel and fierce-looking lord of the Kauśikas, accompanied by his disciples, spoke thus:
Viśvāmitra said:
O King, that sacrificial fee for the Rājasūya which was previously mentioned by you— || 42 ||
"O mighty-armed one, give her up if truth is held paramount.
Hariścandra said:
"I pay homage to you, O royal sage; please accept this as your own sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)."
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 23: O sinless one, that which was previously described by me regarding the Rājasūya sacrifice—
Viśvāmitra said: "From where was this wealth obtained that is being given as a sacrificial fee? (44)
"O Indra among kings, tell me how this wealth was won by you.
The king said:
"O illustrious one, O sinless one, what is the use of telling you this? (45)
"O Brahmin of noble vows, my grief increases because of this learning.
The seer said:
"I do not accept what is improper; give me only what is proper. (46)
"O King, tell me exactly how the wealth came to you.
The king said: "That queen, my wife, was sold by me for ten million [gold pieces]. (47)
"My son Rohitākhyo has been sold for ten billion niṣkas;
O Brahmin, please accept from me eleven crores of gold. (48)
Sūta said:
Observing that the wealth obtained from the sale of his wife was so meager, Kauśika became angry and spoke to the king, who was overwhelmed by grief. 49.
The sage said: "This is not the sacrificial fee for the Rājasūya sacrifice;
produce something else quickly, by which it may become complete. (50)
O kṣatriya, if you consider this worthy bride of mine to be a fitting sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
then behold my supreme power immediately.
Of this well-performed austerity, of this stainless Brahmin, of my own fierce power, and of his pure study; (52)
The king said:
"O Blessed One, I shall give you something else; please wait for a short time.
My wife and my young son have been sold this very moment. (53)
Viśvāmitra said:
"O best of men, this very fourth part of the day that remains must be awaited by me; you need not say anything further. (54)
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 32 ||
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus spoken these merciless and cruel words to the king, [he departed].
Having taken that full wealth, the enraged Kauśika departed. ||1||
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter twenty-three:
When Viśvāmitra had departed, the king then fell into a state of grief.
Having repeatedly heaved deep sighs, he spoke aloud with his face cast downward.
"Let him who has departed by means of wealth purchased with excessive pride speak quickly—he, the Sun, who still remains for me. (3)
Then there arrived in haste one who had assumed the form of a Caṇḍāla;
he was foul-smelling, with a deformed chest, beardless, protruding teeth, and devoid of compassion.
Kṛṣṇa was pot-bellied, oily-skinned, and formidable— the lowest of men—
carrying a staff worn out by his hands and adorned with garlands of corpses.
The Cāṇḍāla said:
"I accept you into servitude; my need for a servant is very great. Quickly tell me, what is the price that is to be given to you?"
Vyāsa said:
Then, observing him to be such—a man of cruel gaze, utterly merciless, and speaking with extreme wickedness—the king asked, "Who are you? (7)
The Cāṇḍāla said:
"O best of kings, I am known here as the Cāṇḍāla named Pravīra;
I always abide by your command, removing the garments of the dead. (8)
Thus addressed, the king then spoke these words:
"Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya, let him take [it]; this is my intention. (9)
The wise have declared that for the highest there is the highest dharma, for the middling the middling, and for the lowest the lowest. (10)
The Cāṇḍāla said:
"O best of kings, you have indeed described the Dharma in this very way;
O King, what you have just spoken before me was not subject to doubt. (11)

I [beheld] the face of my lotus-eyed son who had been bitten by a great serpent. (31)
"Beholding him today, I am now overcome by terrible poison.
Having spoken thus, he took up that boy with a faltering voice.
Having embraced him, Niśśreṣṭha fell down in a swoon;
then, seeing him fallen, Śainyā revived him.
A tiger among men is recognized by his voice alone;
Hariścandra is the moon to the minds of the learned—of this there is no doubt. (34)
Such is the nose of this high-souled one of renowned fame: it is lofty, auspicious, and resembles a sesame flower; and his teeth are like flower buds. (35)
"Why has that lord of men come to the cremation ground in such a state? Having abandoned his grief for his son, she beholds her husband fallen there. (36)
Exultant, astonished, and distressed, she was deeply pained by her husband and son;
looking about, she then fell to the surface of the earth in a swoon.
Having regained her composure, she slowly spoke with a sobbing voice:
"Fie on you, O Lord! You are merciless, devoid of restraint, and loathsome! (38)
By whom this king, who was like an immortal, was reduced to the state of an outcaste, suffering the loss of his kingdom, the death of his friends, and the sale of his wife and son. (39)
"Even after having brought him here, by whom this king was made a Cāṇḍāla today?
I do not see your royal umbrella nor even your lion-throne today. (40)
Or even these yak-tail fans—what is this reversal of fate, that the kings who once preceded him have now fallen into a state of servitude? (41)
The water-clock cloth is in constant contact with the skull-cup. ||42||
They made the surface of the earth free of dust with their own upper garments; yet this very ground was adorned with great, dry, motionless cloths that had served as shrouds,
and was rendered most dreadful by hair caught within the threads of discarded funeral wreaths.
Distressed by the cries of vultures and jackals, with its small birds nourished and fat.
In that place terrifying with the clashing of ashes, charcoal, half-burnt bones, and marrow, where the night-stalkers were being dragged away; 45.

"O Indra among kings, afflicted by suffering, he wanders joyfully in the cremation ground— a place of impurity where the smoke of funeral pyres acts as a veil and darkens the horizons— feeding upon corpses.
Having spoken thus, the princess then embraced the king around his neck.
Alas! Overcome with grief, she lamented with a piteous voice:

"O illustrious one, let this be told; my mind is bewildered.

"Likewise, in the worship of Brahmins, gods, and others, and in the protection of truth—where you, who were devoted to dharma, have been deposed from your own kingdom, there is no dharma; how then can there be truth, uprightness, or compassion? (1)

Having heard these words of hers, he sighed hotly and spoke with a faltering voice.
He related to the slender-limbed woman how he had attained the state of a dog-cooker;

The timid one reported the matter exactly as it was;
having heard those words, the king fell to the surface of the earth.
Bringing his dead son and repeatedly licking him with his tongue,
he then spoke to Hariścandra and Śaivyā in a voice faltering with emotion: (53)
Become the servant of your master by having my head cut off;

In the Śrīmaddevībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 26:
"O King, truthfulness is yours; however, malice toward others is a sin."

"How can that deed be performed which is impossible to describe?
The wife said:

Then, filled with grief, he kissed the face of his deceased son.
The King said:

"O slender-limbed one, I am not my own master; behold my misfortune! If I enter the blazing fire without being permitted by the Caṇḍāla," (60)
I shall again become a slave to a Cāṇḍāla in another birth;
having reached even hell, I shall experience terrible distress.
Having reached the Mahāraurava and Raurava hells, I shall suffer torment;
for one submerged in an ocean of misery, separation from life is better.
Even this one son, who was the sole child destined to continue my lineage, has died through the powerful decree of fate. (63)
"How shall I give up my life, for I am dependent on others and fallen into misery?

In the three worlds, there is no such suffering as that found in the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana), nor likewise in the Vaitaraṇī river; how much less could there be such as that which occurs during the calamity involving one's son?
Therefore, O slender-limbed one, I shall cast myself into the blazing fire with my son’s body; you must now forgive me for this.

"O auspicious lady, that twice-born man must not be treated with contempt out of pride in being the wife of a king;

Of the righteous royal sage who was devoted to Śatākṣī with his whole being. ||1||

by his splendor, the worlds, including both gods and asuras, were scorched.
Then the blessed Lord, four-faced and mounted upon a swan,

"Today, pleased by your asceticism, I have come as the bestower of boons.

Due to the absence of sacrificial offerings and other rites, the gods became subject to old age;
at that time, the Daitya besieged the city of Amarāvatī.
Being unable to fight that asura whose body was like adamant, the gods then fled and disappeared somewhere. 19.
Established in mountain fastnesses and in caves upon jeweled peaks,
they remained meditating upon that supreme power, the Supreme Mother.
O King, due to the absence of oblations and other rites in the fire, there was also an absence of rain;
and with the absence of rain, the surface of the earth became parched and devoid of water. (21)
Wells, step-wells, tanks, and rivers have all gone dry;
O King, this drought has lasted for a hundred years.
The subjects died in many ways, as did cows, buffaloes, and others; in every house of men, there was a collection of corpses. (23)
When this misfortune had thus arisen, the Brāhmaṇas, with tranquil minds,
went to the side of the Himavat mountains, desiring to propitiate Śivā.
Day after day they praised the Goddess with offerings of meditative concentration and dhyāna;
abstaining from food and absorbed in her, they took refuge in her alone.
O Great Goddess, show compassion indeed toward these base people who are guilty of every offense; O Mother, this [harshness] is not worthy of you.
"O Goddess of gods, O you who exist as the inner controller of all, withdraw your anger!
This person acts exactly as he is impelled by you. (27)
There is no other refuge for these people; why do you look again and again?
O Maheśvarī, you are capable of doing whatever you wish.
O Maheśānī, deliver us from this great calamity that has arisen.
O Ambikā, how could our existence possibly endure without life? 29.
Be gracious, O Great Sovereign; be gracious, O Mother of the Universe!
Salutations again and again to you, the Mistress of infinite millions of cosmic eggs. (30)
Salutations to her whose form is the immutable, salutations again and again to her whose form is consciousness;
salutations to her who is known through the Vedānta, the Mistress of the World, salutations again and again. || 31 ||
We bow with our whole being to that Goddess, the cause of all, who is indicated by the words "not this, not this" in all the scriptures.
Thus entreated, the Goddess Pārvatī, the sovereign of the world and the Great Mistress,
manifested a form consisting of infinite eyes.
It resembled dark collyrium and possessed long eyes like blue lotuses.
[Her breasts were] very firm, perfectly high, rounded, full, and dense. ||34||
He offered an arrow, a fistful [of grain], a lotus, flowers, shoots, and roots; vegetables and the like, combined with fruits and endowed with various flavors. ||35||
Holding in her hand a great bow that dispels hunger, thirst, and old age,
she possessed a form that was the very essence of all beauty, adorned with exquisite charm.
Having manifested herself as one who resembles ten million suns and is an ocean of the essence of compassion,
that Mother of the World appeared, born from infinite eyes.
He released thousands of streams of water upon the worlds;
for nine nights, there was a great rain from the waters born of his eyes.
Beholding those suffering, he relinquishes his fields of arts;
by him all those worlds and even all medicinal herbs were satisfied. 39.
O King, by those waters, the currents of the rivers and streams were formed;
those gods who had previously remained hidden now emerged outside. 40.
Having gathered together with the gods, the Brahmins praised the Goddess:
"Salutations to you, who are to be known through the Vedānta; salutations to you, whose nature is Brahman. (41)
Salutations again and again to you, the creator of the entire universe through your own *māyā*;
O Goddess, who hold the wish-fulfilling tree for the sake of your devotees;
salutations to you, the eternal, satisfied, and incomparable Sovereign of the World.
For the sake of our peace, [grant] an incomparable thousand eyes.
O Goddess, since you have been held by me, therefore you shall be known as Śatākṣī. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa*, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 28. [Page 499]
O Mother, afflicted by hunger, we do not have the power to offer praise. 44.
"O Great Goddess, show mercy; O Ambikā, bring forth even the Vedas.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of theirs, [she took] the vegetables held in her own hands. 45.
Śivā gave sweet fruits and roots for the purpose of eating, as well as various kinds of food, including those fit for animals. 46.
O King, she granted him a vehicle produced from the most excellent materials, joined with those desired by his heart;
and from that day forth, she also acquired the name Śākaṃbharī.
Then, when a great clamor arose, the asura named Durgama, awakened by the words of the messenger, set out with his army and weapons to fight. (48)
Accompanied by a thousand *akṣauhiṇīs* and discharging arrows with great haste,
he besieged that army of the gods which had previously stood before the Goddess.
Likewise, he blocked the assembly of Brahmins on all sides;
then a tumultuous roar arose throughout the circle of the gods.
"Save us! Save us! all the twice-born and the immortals cried out these words.
Then, Śivā stood around the gods and their discus, which was composed of radiant energy.
She herself stood outside him for the sake of protection;
then a battle ensued between both the Goddess and the Daitya.
The sun’s orb was wondrously shrouded by a rain of arrows, brilliantly illuminated by the fire produced from the clashing of their weapons against one another. ||53||
Then, from the body of the Goddess, intense powers emerged, deafening the quarters of the horizon with the harsh twanging of their bowstrings.
Kālikā, Tāriṇī, Bālā, Tripurā, Bhairavī, Ramā, Bagalā, Mātaṅgī, and likewise Tripurasundarī. (55)
Kāmākṣī, Tulajā Devī, Jambhinī, Mohinī, as well as Chinnamastā, Guhyakālī, and Daśasāhasrabāhukā. (56)
There were thirty-two other powers, and sixty-four supreme ones;
from those, innumerable goddesses emerged, equipped with their weapons.
The battlefield resounded with the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, conchs, lutes, and other instruments,
as hundreds of akṣauhiṇīs of the Daitya army were destroyed by the Śaktis.
The commander of the army became the leader at the head of the difficult-to-traverse force;
and first, the enemy engaged in battle with the Śaktis.
A great battle took place wherein a river of blood flowed;
all those akṣauhiṇī divisions were destroyed within ten days.
Then, when the eleventh day, which was most terrible, had arrived,
he wore red garlands and garments and was anointed with red perfumes and unguents.
Having held a great festival, he mounted his chariot for battle;
and having conquered all his enemies with great fury, he was indeed powerful.
The Great Goddess stationed her own chariot at the front of his chariot;
then a great battle ensued between both the Goddess and the Daitya.
Causing terror to the heart, it extended for two *praharas*;
then the Goddess released fifteen exceedingly fierce arrows.
With four arrows he struck down the four horses; with one, the charioteer;

Then Brahmā and all the others, led by Viṣṇu and Śiva, praised the Mother of the Universe with devotion and voices faltering with emotion.

"This body of mine is excellent and must be especially protected;

"I am always to be honored by you at all times;

He who utters my name "Durga" because I am the slayer of the demon Durga, and [my name] "Śatākṣī," pierces through illusion and proceeds [to liberation]. 79.
What is the use of much speaking here? I shall state the essential truth:
I am to be constantly served by all the gods, as well as by all the Suras and Asuras.
