Having spoken thus, the Goddess, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, vanished while the gods were looking on, thereby producing great satisfaction. 81.
All this has been told to you, the supreme and great secret;
it must be guarded with effort, for it brings about all auspiciousness. ||82||
Whoever should constantly listen to this chapter with devotion shall attain all desires and be glorified in the world of the Goddess. (83)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 28 ||
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Thus ends the excellent account of the deeds of the kings belonging to the Solar dynasty.
And how much can be described by me of those born from the lunar dynasty? || 1 ||
By the grace of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), they attained greatness;
O King, know for certain that [this] is through the grace of the Supreme Power.
Whatever being possesses grandeur, beauty, or power,
know that each and every one of them has arisen from a portion of My supreme Śakti.
These and other kings, O King, became axes for the root of the tree of saṃsāra, devoted to the supreme power.
Therefore, with every effort, one should serve Bhuvaneśvarī;
like one seeking grain, one should discard everything else entirely, even as if it were mere straw.
O King, having churned the ocean of the milk of the Vedas, I have obtained this jewel;
by [attaining] the lotus feet of Parāśakti, I have achieved my life’s purpose.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 29: Seated upon the throne of the five Brahmans, there is no other deity whatsoever.
From that very source, the Great Goddess established the seat of the five Brahmans.
It is declared in the Veda that there is a reality superior to these five;
she in whom all things are woven across and lengthwise is indeed Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī.
O Indra among kings, as long as men do not understand that [reality], they shall not be liberated;
only when men shall wrap up space like a hide will liberation be attained.
Then, by not knowing Śivā, there will be no end to suffering;
therefore, the Śvetāśvataras, who follow the Vedic branches, have declared this in the Śruti.
Following the yoga of meditation, they beheld the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities, through every effort for the sake of making their birth fruitful. (11)
Whether out of shame, fear, devotion, or love-filled affection,
having abandoned all attachments and restrained the mind within the heart— one should therefore become established in That and intent upon That; such is the drumbeat of the Vedānta.

By whatever means possible—even while sleeping, standing, or walking—one should constantly glorify the Goddess; such a person shall indeed be liberated from bondage. Therefore, O King, worship the Great Sovereign (Maheśvarī) with every effort.

First, [one should contemplate] her who has the form of a *birā*, the form of a *sūtra*, and the form of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), by means of the sequence of the steps; thereafter, when the mind is purified... (15)
Worship that Supreme Śakti, whose nature is Brahman, whose form is the ultimate meaning of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, and who is devoid of the expansion of the phenomenal world. 16.
The absorption of the mind in her is known as her propitiation;
thus have I related the conduct of kings, queens, and devotees of the Supreme Power.
It is purifying for the righteous kings born of the solar and lunar lineages; it bestows fame, awakens the intellect to dharma, and grants an auspicious rebirth. (18)
"This merit-bestowing account has been told; what else do you wish to hear?
Janamejaya said:
"Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī were previously given by Parāmbā. (19)
Likewise, it is well known that Gaurī was the daughter of Himavat and Dakṣa, born from the lotus of his navel. (20)
It is recorded that she is the daughter of Hara and Hari, and of the Ocean of Milk, and is known as Mahālakṣmī;
yet how can there be the status of being a daughter for the other two who have originated from the Root Goddess? (21)
This appears inconceivable; there is doubt here, O Great Sage.
Being intent on cutting through doubt, do you sever it with the sword of knowledge. (22)
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim a most wonderful secret; for one who is devoted to the Goddess, there is indeed nothing that should not be told to you. 23.
When the Supreme Mother gave the three goddesses to the three gods,
from that time forward those gods performed the tasks of creation.
O King, at one time there arose Daityas named Hālāhala who possessed great prowess; by them the three worlds were conquered in an instant.
Proud due to the granting of a boon by Brahmā, they besieged the Silver Mountain (Kailāsa) with their own armies,
as well as Vaikuṇṭha itself.
The enemy of Kāma (Śiva) and Keṭāri engaged in battle;
for sixty thousand years, there was a most fierce war.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the armies of the gods and the Dānavas;
then, with great effort, those Dānavas were slain by the two of them.
Having returned to their respective abodes, those two conceived pride, thinking:
"O King, it was solely by the power of our own strength that they were slain. (29)
Perceiving their arrogance, Mahālakṣmī and Gaurī both uttered mocking laughter; and seeing their laughter, those two likewise [laughed].
As if greatly enraged by the primordial illusion that deludes them, the two gods gave him a difficult-to-overcome response preceded by insults. (31)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 30.
Then, at that very moment, those two deities abandoned them and vanished once more; indeed, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose there at that time.
Then, due to the humiliation of those two, Hari and Hara became lusterless, devoid of majesty, distracted, and senseless.
Brahmā became anxious with thought: "What is this that has arisen?
How is it that these two foremost among the deities are incapable of performing their duty? (34)
Why has this calamity arisen so unexpectedly?
Will there be a dissolution of this innocent world? (35)
"I do not know the cause at all; how should a remedy be applied?
Thus, extremely distressed by anxiety, he meditated with his eyes closed. (36)
"O best of kings, knowing then that this had arisen from the provocation of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), the lotus-born Brahmā became vigilant. (37)
Then, for some time, that treasure of asceticism performed whatever task was required for those two by his own power and through the influence of his hundred disciples.
Then, for the sake of their well-being, that righteous-souled one quickly summoned his sons, Manu and the others, as well as Sanaka and the rest.
The treasury of asceticism spoke these words to them as they bowed before him:
"I am occupied with a task commanded by my father; I am not able to perform penance. (40)
For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), I am burdened by the weight of the universe;
and both Śiva and Viṣṇu have been cast down due to the wrath of the Supreme Power.
Therefore, endowed with supreme devotion, you should perform most wonderful penance and then propitiate that Supreme Śakti.
"O my sons, act in such a way that those two may become endowed with power as they were in their former existence; for in this way, your own fame shall increase. (43)
Whichever family those two Śaktis are born into, that family shall purify the entire world and itself become one that has fulfilled its purpose. || 44 ||
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of the Grandfather (Brahmā), Dakṣa and all the others, their inner selves purified, departed into the midst of the forest, desiring to propitiate him. (45)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 29 ||
Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Then, in a forest region situated on the slopes of the Himalayas, they...
Devoted to the recitation of the seed-syllable of Māyā, they performed austerities with concentrated minds.
O King, as they meditated upon the supreme power for a hundred thousand years,
the Goddess became pleased and granted them a direct vision of herself.

She has four arms holding a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness; she is three-eyed, completely filled with the essence of compassion, and her form consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Having beheld her, the mother of all beings, the stainless sages offered praise:
"Salutations to you, whose form is the universe, and who possesses the beautiful form of Vaiśvānara! (4)
Salutations to her whose form is splendor, salutations to her whose body is the *sūtrātman*, in whom all subtle bodies (*liṅgadeha*) are established, woven like warp and woof. (5)
Salutations to her whose nature is supreme wisdom; salutations to her whose form is manifest;
salutations to her whose nature is direct perception; salutations to you, the embodiment of Brahman.
"Salutations to you who possess all forms, whose very embodiment is the soul of all that is perceivable.
Having thus praised the Mother of the Universe with words flowing from the staff of devotion, [he spoke]. (7)
The pure sages, headed by Dakṣa, bowed at her lotus feet;
then that goddess, speaking with the voice of a cuckoo, spoke to them with a gracious mind.
"Choose a boon, O highly fortunate ones; I am always considered a giver of boons.
Having heard her words, [the two] made their request equally from the bodies of Hara and Viṣṇu. (9)

O best of kings, they both chose the attainment of that power from her. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa*, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 30. Then Dakṣa spoke once more: "O Goddess, [grant] birth for me in my own family. (10)
"O Mother, may there be for you that by which I may become one who has fulfilled his purpose"—
thus [he spoke of] recitation, meditation, worship, and various sacred sites.
"Tell me, O Supreme Goddess, by your own mouth alone. The Goddess said: "The condition of those two has arisen from the contempt shown toward my powers."
I have never committed any offense;
now, by a mere fragment of my grace, those two have regained health in their bodies.
"Such a thing must not be done;
for you shall have power over the Ocean of Milk in your own home.
There, two [beings] shall be born, and they, impelled by me, shall obtain [their goals]."
Indeed, the seed-syllable of Māyā is my primary mantra, always dear to me; likewise, my meditation is upon the Virāṭ form, or else [I am] standing right before you. 15.
Or rather, this entire world is my abode, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss;
and I am always to be worshipped and meditated upon by you at all times. (16)
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Goddess who dwells in the jeweled lamp vanished;
then Dakṣa and all the other sages returned once more to Brahmā.
They respectfully related the entire account to Brahmā;
O King, both Hara and Hari remained intent on their respective duties.
Then, by the grace of Parāmbā, the two were freed from pride;
subsequently, after some time, the Śākta festival descended.
O great king, in the house of Dakṣa, as well as throughout the three worlds, there was a festival;
all the gods were delighted and showered down flowers. (20)
O King, kettledrums struck with drumsticks resounded in heaven,
and the minds of the pure-souled virtuous became serene.
The rivers flowed along their courses, and the sun shone with brilliant light.
When Maṅgalā has been born, everything that is born becomes auspicious everywhere. ||22||
He gave her the name Satī because of the truthfulness of her supreme consciousness;
then he gave her to Śiva as his own power (śakti).
Furthermore, O King, by the turn of fate, she was burned in a fire while in her mind.
Janamejaya said:
"O Sage, this speech you have made me hear is productive of no good. (24)
O Hutāśana! By the mere remembrance of Your name, people indeed have no fear of the fire of saṃsāra. ||25||
"How was such a great object burnt?
By what ripening of karma was it burnt by Manu?
Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, to the account of what occurred in the past regarding the cause of Satī’s cremation.
Then, on one occasion, Durvāsas went to Jāmbūnadeśvarī;
having seen the Goddess there, he muttered the seed-mantra of Māyā.
Agitated by the intoxication of nectar. ||28||
Then the Goddess of gods, being pleased, gave him that garland which was upon her own neck and was frequented by wandering bees; the sage accepted it as a mark of grace and placed it upon his head.
Thereupon, the ascetic departed swiftly by way of the sky.
He went to where Dakṣa, the father of Satī herself, was staying; for the sake of seeing his mother, he prostrated at the feet of Satī.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter thirty.
Questioned by Dakṣa, that sage [said]: "Whose is this extraordinary garland?
O Lord, how was it obtained by you, which is difficult for men on earth to obtain? (31)
Having heard those words of his, his eyes filled with tears and his heart faltering with love, he spoke of the incomparable grace of the Goddess.
The father of Satī requested that garland from the sage,
for there is nothing in the three worlds that cannot be given to a devotee of Śakti.
Thus the Buddha gave that garland to Manu;
the garland was taken by Manu and placed upon his own head in his palace.
There, a most beautiful bed was prepared for the couple;
at night, he, delighted by garlands and perfumes, was intent upon the act of love.
O King, due to that sin toward Śaṅkara,
that protector of the earth became one whose mind was filled with hatred for Śiva and likewise for the goddess Satī.
O King, by that offense, her very body— which was produced from it—
was consumed by the fire of yoga while she remained true, out of a desire to witness the dharma of Satī.
Furthermore, that great light appeared once more upon the back of the Himavat mountain.
Janamejaya said:
"When Satī’s body was being consumed by fire, what did Śiva do? (38)
She was dearer to him than life itself, and he was distressed by her separation.
Vyāsa said:
"Beyond that, what occurred cannot be told by me. (39)
O King, the destruction of the three worlds occurred through the fire of Śiva’s wrath;
Vīrabhadra emerged, accompanied by the hosts of Bhadrakālī.
When Vīrabhadra was intent on destroying the three worlds,
the gods, headed by Brahmā, then went to Śaṅkara for refuge.
Even when their entire possessions had been lost, the Lord, a treasure-house of compassion,
granted them fearlessness by means of that mantra through the mouth of the goat.
Then that great-souled Maheśvara, becoming despondent because he could not bring [the victim] back to life,
approached the sacrificial enclosure and wept, deeply afflicted by grief.
He beheld that virtuous woman being consumed by fire like a mere spark of consciousness, and placing her upon his shoulder, he cried out repeatedly, "Alas, Satī! ||44||
With his mind bewildered, Śaṅkara wandered through various lands;
at that time, the gods, headed by Brahmā, fell into the highest anxiety.
But Viṣṇu, acting with haste, raised his bow there and severed Satī’s limbs with arrows; they fell at their respective locations.

In those various locations, Hara remained there assuming diverse forms. Then he said to the gods: "For those who worship Śivā with supreme devotion in these places, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain."
The supreme Mother is eternally present there within her own limbs. 48.
For those mortals who perform the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) in these places,
their mantras become successful, especially the Māyā-bīja.
Having spoken thus, O best of kings, Śaṅkara, afflicted by separation from them, passed his time in those places through recitation, meditation, and absorption.
Janamejaya said: O sinless one, what are those places that are seats of the Siddhas?
How many are they in number, and what are their names? Tell me these. (51)
O Great Sage, O Compassionate One, tell me quickly the names of the goddesses residing there, so that I may achieve my purpose. (52)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter thirty-five. Vyāsa said:
Listen, O King, I shall now proclaim the seats of the Goddess (Devīpīṭhas), by the mere hearing of which a man becomes free from sin. (53)

I shall now describe in accordance with reality those various seats (pīṭhas) upon which I am to be worshipped by those desiring spiritual perfection (siddhi), and meditated upon by those desiring worldly prosperity (bhūti).
In Vārāṇasī she is Viśālākṣī, and she dwells in the mouth of Gaurī;
in the sacred field of the Naimiṣa forest, she is called Liṅgadhāriṇī.
Lalitā is said to be at Prayāga, Kāmukī at Gandhamādana;
Kumudā is said to be at Mānasa, as well as in the south and the north.
The Blessed Lady fulfills all desires;
she is Gomatī at Gomanta and Kāmacāriṇī on Mount Mandara. ||57||
Madotkaṭā is in Caitraratha, Jayantī in Hastināpura;
Gaurī is said to be in Kānyakubja, while Rambhā is on the Malaya mountain. (58)
On Ekāmrapīṭha she is proclaimed as Devī Kīrtimatī;
in every world they call her Viśveśvarī, and at Puṣkara she is Puruhūtā.
The goddess who bestows the true path is proclaimed to be at Kedārapīṭha;
she is Mandā on the back of the Himalayas and Bhadrakaṇikā at Gokarṇa.
Bhavānī is indeed at Sthāneśvara, while Bilvapatrikā is at Bilvaka;
Mādhavī is said to be at Śrīśaila, and likewise Bhadrā at Bhadreśvara.
Jayā is on Vārāhaśaila, Kamalā is in Kamalālaya,
Rudrāṇī is in Rudrakoṭi, and likewise Kālī is on Kālañjara.
The Great Goddess resides at Śālagrāma, Jalapriyā at the Śivaliṅga,
Kapilā at Mahāliṅga, and Kuṭeśvarī at Mākoṭa.
In Māyāpurī she is Kumārī; in Saṃtāna she is Lalitāmbikā; in Gayā she is called Maṅgalā; and in Puruṣottama she is Vimalā. In Sahasrākṣa she is Utpalākṣī, and in Hiraṇyākṣa she is Mahotpalā.
Amoghākṣī is on the Vipāśā, and Pāṭalā is in Puṇḍravardhana. || 65 ||
Nārāyaṇī is on Supārśva, Rudrasundarī is on Trikūṭa; the goddess Vipulā is on Vipula, and Kalyāṇī is on the Malaya mountain.
On the Sahya mountain she was Ekavīrā; on Hariścandra she was Candrikā;
at Rāmatīrtha she was Ramaṇā; and in the Yamunā she was Mṛgāvatī.
Koṭavī is at Koṭatīrtha, Sugandhā is in the Mādhave forest,
Trisandhyā is on the Godāvarī, and Ratipriyā is at Gaṅgādvāra.
Śivakuṇḍa is Śubhānandā, Nandinī is on the bank of the Devikā;
Rukmiṇī is in Dvāravatī, while Rādhā is in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Devakī is in Mathurā, while Parameśvarī is in Pātāla;
likewise, Sītā is at Citrakūṭa, and Vidhyādhivāsinī is on the Vindhya mountains.
Mahālakṣmī is at Karavīra, the goddess Rumā is at Vināyaka;
Ārogyā is at Vaidyanātha, and Maheśvarī is at Mahākāla. (71)
Abhayā is at the Uṣṇa tīrthas; Nitambā is on the Vindhya mountain;
Māṇḍavī by name is at Māṇḍavya; and Svāhā is at Māheśvarīpura.
Pracaṇḍā is at Chagalaṇḍa, while Caṇḍikā is at Marakaṇṭaka;
Varārohā is at Someśvara, and Puṣkarāvatī is at Prabhāsa. (73)
Devamātā is remembered on the banks of the Sarasvatī at Pārāvāra;
the highly fortunate Piṅgaleśvarī is at Mahālaya on the Payoṣṇī. (74)
Siṃhikā is at Kṛtaśauca; in the month of Kārttika, she is Atiśāṅkarī; she is Lolā at Utpalāvartaka, and Subhadrā at the confluence of the Śoṇa.
She is Mātā in Siddhavana, Lakṣmī in Bharata’s hermitage, Anaṅgā in Jālandhara, Viśvamukhī in Kiṣkindhā mountain, and Tārā on Mount Kiṣkindha. ||76||
Puṣṭi is in the Devadāru forest, Medhā in the region of Kaśmīra;
Bhīmā is the goddess on the Himālaya, and likewise Tuṣṭi is Viśveśvarī.
At Kapālamocana, the mother is Śuddhi; at Kāyāvarohaṇa, she is Dharā; likewise, at Śaṅkhoddhāra, she is named Dhṛti, and at Piṇḍāraka, she is the same.
Kalā is in Candrabhāgā, Acchodā is Śivadhāriṇī, Amṛtā by name is in the Veṇā, and likewise Urvaśī is in Badarī. (79)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter thirty-one.
Auṣadhi is in Uttarakuru; Kuśodakā is in Kuśadvīpa;
Manmathā is on Hemakūṭa; and Satyavādinī is on Kumuda. (80)
She is to be saluted at the Aśvattha tree, she is indeed the treasure in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa;
she is Gāyatrī at the mouth of the Vedas, and Pārvatī in the presence of Śiva. 81.
Likewise, she is Indrāṇī in the world of the gods, Sarasvatī in the mouths of Brahmās, and in the solar orb she is named Prabhā; she is indeed considered Vaiṣṇavī among the Mothers.
Arundhatī is the foremost among chaste women, and Tilottamā is the most beautiful;
yet in the heart of all embodied beings, there is the power named Brahmakalā.
O Janamejaya, there are these eight hundred sacred seats (pīṭhas); an equal number of their presiding lords and goddesses have also been proclaimed. (84)
The sacred seats (pīṭhas) that constitute the limbs of the goddess Satī have been described, as well as other principal ones on the surface of the earth that arose incidentally. (85)
Whoever should remember or even hear this supreme hundred-and-eight names shall be cleansed of all sins and go to the supreme world of the Goddess.

One should go to all these sacred seats (pīṭhas) according to the prescribed rules for pilgrimage, and having performed the śrāddha rites and other ceremonies, one should satiate the ancestors and others with libations.
One should perform a great worship of the Blessed Lady according to the prescribed rite, and one should repeatedly ask forgiveness from the Mother of the World, the Sustainer of the Universe. (88)
O Janamejaya, one should consider oneself to have accomplished all that was to be done;
thereafter, one should feed all the Brahmins with various kinds of foods, both solid and soft. 89.
O King, [he honored] the married women, the maidens, the young students, and others;
O Lord, even those who were Cāṇḍālas and so forth who resided in that sacred field.
All of them are remembered as having the form of goddesses; therefore, they are to be worshipped.
One should avoid all such things as accepting gifts from them in those sacred fields.
The best of beings should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) of the mantra according to his capacity;
[he should worship] the Goddess who dwells upon each respective seat with the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ). 92.
O King, by worshipping thus, a man becomes one who has performed the *puraścaraṇa* rite;
a person devoted to the Goddess should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
He who performs such a pilgrimage with a delighted mind shall dwell for a thousand kalpas in the most exalted world of Brahmā. 94.
His ancestors likewise go to Devīpura;
and he too, having attained supreme knowledge at the end, shall be liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
By reciting the name one hundred and eight times, many have attained accomplishment; wherever this is written, whether in a manuscript or otherwise, it remains present in person. (96)
Indeed, planetary afflictions, fears, and the like do not exist there at all;
rather, good fortune increases constantly, just as the ocean swells on a festival day.
For one who recites the eight-hundred-name mantra, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain;
devoted solely to the Goddess, he shall surely achieve all his purposes. 98.
The deities indeed take pleasure in him, for he is remembered as being of divine form;
he is worshipped in every way by the gods, how much more so by the best of men? || 99 ||
One should recite this supreme eight-hundred-name hymn at the time of a śrāddha ceremony;
all those ancestors, being satisfied, shall attain the highest state. (100)
O King of kings, a wise man should take refuge in these fields of liberation, which are directly composed of pure consciousness, as well as in the seats of the Siddhas. (101)
O King, everything that you asked regarding the Great Lord has been told to you, including the most secret of secrets; what more do you wish to hear? (102)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 30 ||
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"The supreme light manifested upon the crest of the lord of the mountains."
Tell me that which was previously spoken by you in detail. ||1||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 21:
Who that is wise would grow weary while drinking the nectar of the stories of Śakti?
Death may indeed come to those who drink nectar, but it shall not come to one who hears this.
Vyāsa said:
You are blessed, you have accomplished your purpose, and you have been instructed by the great-souled ones;
you are fortunate that you possess such sincere devotion toward the Goddess.
Listen, O King, to an ancient account: when Satī’s body was consumed by fire, Śiva wandered in confusion until he finally came to rest in a certain place. (4)
Free from the conceit of conceptual proliferation, with his mind attained to meditative absorption,
that self-possessed one passed his time meditating upon the very form of the Goddess.
The three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, have become bereft of fortune;
the entire universe, along with its islands and mountains, has been deprived of power.
Joy has become parched within the hearts of all; all people have become indifferent, their minds worn out by worldly accumulation. (7)
At that time, they were constantly submerged in an ocean of suffering and afflicted by diseases;
the planets and deities behaved with hostility, and kings became true embodiments of the elemental and divine powers. (85)
Now, at this very time, there was a great asura named Tāraka. ||9||
Having received a boon from Brahmā, the Daitya became the leader of the three worlds;
however, that son who is born of Śivīrā shall be your slayer.
Thus,
that great asura, whose death had been ordained by the gods of gods,
roared and bellowed because he lacked a legitimate son born of Śiva. ||11||
Harassed by him and driven from their own abodes, all the gods fell into extreme distress due to the absence of Śivīrasa’s son.
Śaṅkara has no wife; how, then, could there be the birth of a son for him?
For us, who are devoid of fortune, how will our purpose be accomplished? (13)
Thus, all of them, overcome with anxiety, went to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha;
they praised Hari in private, and he spoke a means to them.
From whom all those afflicted by the fever of desire find auspiciousness—the Goddess of the World, the wish-fulfilling tree for all desires, who dwells on the Island of Jewels—is awake. 15.
Our indifference toward her is due solely to our own lack of discernment, and not otherwise;
for this very world-mother has provided this instruction for our own training. (16)

Just as there is no cruelty on the part of a mother toward her child, whether she is fondling or striking him, so too there is no cruelty on the part of the Mother of the World when she restrains beings regarding their virtues and faults.
A son indeed commits an offense at every step;
who else in this world, save for his mother alone, can endure it? (18)
Therefore, seek refuge in that Supreme Mother without delay;
with a sincere disposition of mind, she will accomplish your purpose.
Having thus instructed all the gods, Mahāviṣṇu,
the lord of the deities, departed quickly accompanied by his wife and the gods.
He went to the great mountain Himavat, the lord of mountains;
and all the gods became engaged in the performance of preparatory rites.
O King, those who were experts in the ritual procedures for the Ambā sacrifice performed the Ambā sacrifice;
all the gods quickly observed the vows beginning with the third day.
Some were proficient in meditative concentration, some were devoted to the recitation of names;
some were intent on the hymns, and some were eager for the complete recitation of the names. ||23||

Some are devoted to the recitation of mantras, some perform penances such as the kṛcchra; some are intent on internal sacrifice, and some are dedicated to the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa). ||24||
With unwearied devotion, they performed the worship of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) by means of the Hṛllekhā mantra;
in this manner, O Janamejaya, many years passed away.
Suddenly, on the ninth day of the month of Caitra, on a Friday,
that splendor revealed by the Vedas manifested before him.
He was praised from the four directions by the personified four Vedas;
He was resplendent like ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons.
That supreme light, red in hue and possessing a brilliance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
could not be grasped as being either above, nor across, nor in the middle.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 31.
That [reality], however, is devoid of beginning and end; it is not joined with hands or other limbs, nor does it have the form of a woman, nor the form of a man, nor both.
O Lord of the Earth, the lamps became a covering for their eyes;
yet, once again summoning their fortitude, those gods looked out.
At that moment, that very same triad appeared in a captivating female form—a maiden of fresh youth with exceedingly beautiful limbs. (31)
Her rising, full breasts surpassed the beauty of lotus buds;
her girdle, anklets, and clusters of tinkling bells produced a sweet jingling sound.
Adorned with golden armlets, bracelets, and necklaces,
she shone with an invaluable jewel set in her throat.
O King, she had a slender waist, hair as dark as blue bees,
hips that were beautiful like lotus stalks, and was adorned with a line of body hair.
Her mouth was filled with betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor,
and her lotus-face was adorned with shimmering golden earrings.
Her forehead resembles the orb of the eighth-day moon, her eyebrows are long,
her eyes are like red lotuses, her nose is prominent, and her lips are sweet.
Her tips of teeth were like jasmine buds, she was adorned with pearl necklaces,
her crown was inlaid with jewels, and she was graced by a crescent moon as an ornament.
Her mass of hair, beautified by garlands of *mallikā* and *mālatī* flowers, shone brilliantly.
Her forehead is adorned with saffron dots, and her eyes are playful like young barley grains. || 38 ||
She has four arms holding a noose, a goad, a boon-granting gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness; she is three-eyed, wears red garments, and has the luster of a pomegranate flower.
She is enriched with every kind of graceful adornment, saluted by all the gods, the fulfiller of all desires, the mother of all, and the enchantress of all. ||40||
The gods beheld before them a form of unfeigned compassion, whose mantra-like face was bright with grace and whose lotus-face was adorned with a gentle smile.
Seeing her, the embodiment of compassion, the gods bowed with reverence;
their eyes filled with tears, they were unable to say anything at all. (42)
Having somehow regained their composure and with their necks bowed in devotion, their eyes filled with tears of love, they praised the Mother of the World. 43.
The gods said: "Salutations to the Goddess, to Mahādevī; constant salutations to Śivā.
Salutations to Prakṛti, to Bhadrā; being self-restrained, we bow down before her. (44)

I take refuge in that goddess Durgā, who is fire-colored, blazing with ascetic power, and honored for her fruits of action; O you who are easy to cross over, salutations to you who enable one to cross. 45.
The gods brought forth divine speech; animals of every form speak it.
May that cow-like Speech, yielding us joy, refreshment, and nourishment, flow toward us with well-praised milk. 46.
We bow to Kālarātri, praised by Brahmā, the consort of Viṣṇu, the mother of Skanda, Sarasvatī, Aditi, and the daughter of Dakṣa—the purifying and auspicious one. (47)
We know Mahālakṣmī; we meditate upon her as the power of all;
may that Goddess inspire us. 48.
Salutations to her whose form is the Virāṭ, salutations to the embodiment of the Sūtrātman;
salutations to her whose form is the Vyākṛta, salutations to the venerable embodiment of Brahman. || 49 ||
We bow to that Sovereign of the World, through whose ignorance the universe appears like a snake in a rope or a mirage in the desert, and through whose knowledge it attains dissolution. 50.
She whose nature is the singular essence of consciousness, whose form is indivisible bliss—she is the ultimate goal of the Vedas' intended meaning. ||51||
We bow to Her who is the indicated meaning of the word "That," who transcends the five sheaths, and who is the witness of the three states;
we bow to Her who is the indicated meaning of the word "Thou," whose nature is the inner Self.
In the glorious Mahāpurāṇa Devībhāgavata, in the seventh book, chapter thirty-one:
Salutations to her whose form is the Praṇava; salutations to her whose embodiment is the syllable Hrīṃ.
Salutations again and again to you, whose very nature consists of various mantras, O Compassion!
Thus praised by the gods at that time, the Goddess dwelling on Maṇidvīpa spoke with sweet words, sounding like the call of a cuckoo in rut.
The illustrious Goddess said:
"O wise ones, tell me the purpose for which you have assembled here.
I am always the bestower of boons, and I am the wish-fulfilling tree for the desires of my devotees."
While I remain present, I shall uplift you, who are full of devotion,
from this ocean of miserable saṃsāra, for you have become one with me.
"O best of the wise, know this promise of mine to be true.
Hearing these words, which were overflowing with love, they were satisfied in their minds. (57)
The fearless and ageless goddesses spoke of their own suffering.
The goddesses said: "There is nothing in these three worlds that is unknown to you. (58)
O Supreme Goddess, who are omniscient and the witness of all, we are oppressed day and night by Tāraka, the lord of the asuras. (59)
O Śivā, his death was ordained by Brahmā through the limbs of Śiva;
yet there is no wife of Śiva at all—this you know well, O Maheśvarī.
What indeed could be said before the Omniscient One by vulgar people? This has been stated in brief; consider the rest for yourself, O Ambikā. (62)
May your devotion to my lotus feet be unwavering at all times;
this is my primary prayer, while another is for the sake of a body. 62.
Having heard these words of theirs, the Supreme Goddess spoke:
"My own Śakti shall become Gaurī in the Himalayas."
She should be given to Śiva; she will accomplish your purpose.
May devotion to his lotus feet arise within you with great earnestness. 64.
"For the Himalaya worships me with his mind through supreme devotion;
therefore, taking birth in his house is considered pleasing to me. (65)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those exceedingly gracious words, Himālaya,
his throat and eyes choked with tears, spoke these words to the Great Queen.
You treat as more important him whose favor you desire;
otherwise, I am a dull-witted log, while you are of the nature of pure existence and consciousness.
O sinless one, the status of being my father is impossible to attain even in hundreds of births,
whether through meritorious acts such as horse-sacrifices or through merits born of meditative absorption equal to them.
"Today fame shall spread throughout the world, for the Mother of the Universe has become his daughter!
Oh, how blessed and fortunate is this Himālaya! (69)
Who indeed on earth could be equal to him whose daughter she has become— she in whose womb reside millions of cosmic eggs?
I do not know what supreme abode has been prepared for our ancestors, for such as they, in whose lineage there is one like me to dwell. (71)
Tell me likewise how this was given to me by you out of compassion and full of love,
and describe my own form as it is established in all the Vedāntas.
O Supreme Goddess, since you alone are I, please speak of yoga accompanied by devotion and of the knowledge approved by the Vedas. (73)
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, that Mother, her lotus-like face serene,
began to speak the secret that had been concealed from the Vedas.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 31 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 32.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
The Goddess said:
Merely by hearing [this], one attains the state of being a lord of Madra. ||1||
"Let all the immortals listen to the words I speak:
that whose consciousness is known by the single name 'Supreme Brahman'. (2)
O Lord of Mountains, that which existed previously was indeed myself; it was the very form of that [Self], a certain power established by itself, renowned as Māyā. 3.
Inconceivable, indescribable, incomparable, and free from ailment—
she is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is she of a dual nature due to contradiction; rather,
there exists something distinct from these, which is always a real entity.
Just as heat belongs to fire, as radiance to the sun, and as moonlight to the moon, so too is this my innate and constant [nature]. (5)
In that [state], the actions of living beings, the living beings themselves, and time circulate;
they become merged without distinction, like worldly activities during deep sleep.
Through the conjunction with my own power, I have attained the state of being the seed-soul (bījātman).
And its status as a fault arises from the obscuration of its own support. ||7||
Inherence is stated [as the definition]. || 8 ||

Due to its conjunction with consciousness, it is also described as the instrumental cause. Because of its transformation into the phenomenal world (prapañca), some call it *tapas*, others call it *tamas*, while still others call it the insentient (*jaḍa*).
It is called *jñāna*, *māyā*, *pradhāna*, *prakṛti*, and the unborn *śakti*.
Those who contemplate the noble reality of the Vedas have declared [this]. || 10 ||
Those proficient in the Śaiva scriptures call that state *vimarśa*; others, however, call it *avidyā*.
Thus, there may be various names for it in the Vedas and other traditions.
Its insentience (*jaḍatva*) follows from its being an object of perception, and therefore it is non-existent once knowledge is destroyed.
Consciousness is not an object of sight; that which is an object of sight is indeed insentient.
Consciousness is self-luminous and is not illumined by another.

Because of the fault of infinite regress, it is not illuminated even by itself; otherwise, there would be the contradiction of the object and the agent being identical. Therefore, it is self-illuminating like a lamp. (13)
O Parvata, know that which shines forth for others to be the illuminator;
for this very reason, my own nature as consciousness is established as eternal.
Because the visible object deviates during the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, whereas no deviation of consciousness has ever been experienced at any time. (15)

If there is an experience even of that [mind] during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, then that very witness by whom it is experienced remains here as the primordial essence of consciousness.
For this very reason, her eternality has been proclaimed by those learned in the true scriptures;
and her nature as bliss is due to her being the object of supreme love. (17)
"May I indeed become the existence"—this [desire] resides in the Self out of love;
for since everything else is illusory, my state of non-attachment is manifest. (18)
For this very reason, I maintain that indefiniteness is likewise [the nature of consciousness];
moreover, that knowledge is not a property of the self, for if it were a property, the self would be insentient. (19)
The insentience of knowledge has never been observed, nor is it possible;
likewise, it does not possess the quality of consciousness, for there is no consciousness within consciousness. (20)
Always true, full, and unattached, it is devoid of the web of duality. ||21||
Therefore, [the self] consists of the knowledge of the self and the nature of bliss, even as it undergoes the ripening of time and karma. ||22||

Furthermore, O Lord of Mountains, he [the individual soul] is described as being joined with desire, karma, and so forth, through his own māyā and the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of previous experiences. (23)
And from that state of isolation (kaivalya), when desiring to emit creation, this non-intentional emission arises, which is also called "the variegated Māyā" (māyā-śabala). (24)
For this which has been described by me is my extraordinary form; it is called the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and the unevolved (avyakta) in all the scriptures, the cause of all causes,
the primordial source of the principles and names, and whose very body is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 32:
[The Self] is the condensation of all actions and is the substratum of will, knowledge, and action.
That which is called the primordial reality (āditattva) is expressed by the mantra consisting of the syllable *hrīṃ*.
From that, space is produced, having the nature of the subtle element of sound;
from that, wind arises, consisting of the nature of touch; and then fire, consisting of the nature of form. (27)
Subsequently, water consists of the quality of taste, and from that, the earth consists of the quality of smell;
space has sound as its sole attribute, while wind is endowed with both touch and sound.
Fire is said by the wise to have the qualities of sound, touch, and form;
water is traditionally remembered as having four qualities: sound, touch, form, and taste. (29)
Earth possesses five qualities: sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. From these arose the Great Thread (Mahat-sūtra), which they call the Liṅga.
That is declared to be the essence of all; this is the subtle body of the Self. Indeed, it was already stated previously that this is the unmanifest causal body.
In that [subtle body] the form of the seed of the world resides, from which the emergence of the *liṅga* occurs;
from that [seed], the gross elements arise through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*).
Five [elements] are produced; now their specific types are described.
One should divide each of the previously mentioned elements into two parts. (33)
O Mountain, one should divide each single part of the one into four;
by joining each with its own second part and the other's second part, those [parts] become five each.
And the effect of that is the Virāṭ body; this is the gross body of the Self.
Through the sattva portions residing in the five elements, there arises the emergence of the sense organs, such as hearing and the rest. (35)
O King of kings, when the organs of knowledge are each combined,

they become the single internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is fourfold due to the difference in its functions. When its activity consists of volition and doubt, it is then designated as the mind (*manas*).
And when he understands that which is designated as "intellect" (buddhi) with perfect certainty, in a form free from doubt; ||37||
That mind is proclaimed to be of the nature of synthesis;
yet, through the activity of the self consisting of egoity, it attains the state of the ego (ahaṃkāra). ||38||
From portions of those [subtle elements], the organs of action (karmendriya) are known to arise in succession;
and from all of them combined together, the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes fivefold.
Prāṇa is in the heart, apāna is in the anus, and samāna resides in the navel; udāna is in the region of the throat, while vyāna pervades the entire body. (40)
There are exactly five organs of perception and five organs of action;
likewise, there is the group of five beginning with prāṇa, and the mind together with the intellect (dhī). || 41 ||
This subtle body is what is called my *liṅga*;
O King, the *prakṛti* described therein is traditionally held to be of two kinds.
Māyā, however, consists of the sentient being (sattva) and is mixed with the qualities of ignorance (avidyā); that which protects its own substratum is designated as māyā. (43)
That which is the reflection of that [intellect], which serves as the prototype for the Lord, is declared to be the Supreme Lord (Īśvara), who possesses knowledge residing within Himself. (44)
He is omniscient, the creator of all, and the bestower of grace upon all;
yet, O Lord of Mountains, whatever reflection appears within ignorance— ||45||
That very [state] is designated as the "living being" (jīva), which is again the locus of all suffering;
here, it is declared that for both [the individual and the universal], there are three bodies due to ignorance.
Furthermore, due to the identification with the three bodies, there arose again a triad of names:

the one who possesses the causal body is Prājña; the one who possesses the subtle body is Taijasa; and the one who possesses the gross body is known as Viśva. Thus, he is proclaimed to be threefold. (47)
In this way, the Lord (Īśa) is also fully described by means of the terms "Lord" (Īśa), "Sūtra," and "Virāṭ. ||48||
The first is known as the Supreme, whose nature is the Samaya and who exists in the form of individual manifestation;
for He is the Lord of All, acting directly out of a desire to bestow grace upon living beings. (49)
O King, impelled by my power and eternally established within me, he constantly creates the manifold universe, which is the locus of names and enjoyments.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter thirty-three. 512
Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
The Goddess said:
"The entire universe, including all things moving and stationary, is fashioned by my power of Māyā."
That illusion (māyā) also does not exist as something separate from me in the ultimate sense.
From the perspective of conventional discourse, this very [reality] is renowned as "knowledge" (vidyā) or "illusion" (māyā);
however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it does not exist at all—only reality itself exists in its absolute purity. ||2||
Having created the entire world, O Mountain, I enter into its midst, accompanied by Māyā, Karma, and the rest, with the vital breaths (prāṇas) as my forerunners.
If there were no transition to another world, how could it be? For this reason, just as [the world] comes to be, so too do the various manifestations of illusion arise.
Just as the space within jars and other such things appear distinct due to the difference in their limiting adjuncts, so too the Sun always illumines objects such as the high and the low. ||5||
In that same way, I am never tainted by defects;
others attribute the agency of intellect and so forth to me, yet it belongs only to the Witness.
Likewise, by way of division. ||7||

Those who are deluded and lack true wisdom say that the self is karma; likewise, due to the differentiation of ignorance, the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is imagined by māyā alone,
just as the distinction between the space within a jar and the great universal space is imagined.

In the same way, the distinction between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) is merely imagined; just as the multiplicity of individual selves exists only through māyā and not by its own nature.

Likewise, the plurality of Īśvaras exists through *māyā* and not by their own nature. The differentiation of the individual souls (*jīva*) is caused by ignorance (*avidyā*), which is divided by the distinctions of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the aggregate of bodies and senses; no other cause is proclaimed.
That which is the division of the latent impressions of the *guṇas* is [the cause] for each [individual]. 1130–1131.
That Māyā is the cause of the differentiation of the Supreme; it is never anything else.
O Supporter of the Earth, all this is woven across and through me.
I am the Lord, and I am the Sūtrātman; I am also the Virāḍātman.
I am Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; I am Gaurī, Brāhmī, and Vaiṣṇavī. (13)
I am the sun, I am the stars, and likewise I am the lord of the stars; I am the form of beasts and birds, and I am the outcaste and the thief.
I am the tiger; I am the one of cruel deeds; I am the one of virtuous deeds; I am the great multitude of people; and I alone am the form of woman, man, and neuter—of this there is no doubt.
Whatever is seen or even heard anywhere,
whether internal or external— all that I pervade and remain within at all times. There is not a single thing, moving or unmoving, that is abandoned by me.
If it were to exist, it would be empty, for it would be like the son of a barren woman. || 17 ||
Just as a single rope appears as various forms such as a snake or a garland, so too do I manifest in the forms of Īśa and others; there is no doubt in this. 18.
That which is imagined does not appear apart from its substratum;
therefore, this [world] possesses existence only through my existence, and not otherwise. (19)
Himālaya said:
O Goddess of gods, if you are compassionate, O Devi, I wish to behold this body which is the collective self exactly as you describe it. (20)
Vyāsa said: [He spoke] those words. (21)
Having heard these words of his, all the gods, together with Viṣṇu, rejoiced with delighted souls and offered worship. Then,
perceiving the intention of the gods, the auspicious Goddess— who fulfills the desires of her devotees and grants their every wish— revealed her own form.
They beheld the supreme Virāṭ form of the Great Goddess, whose head was the sky and whose two eyes were the moon and the sun. (23)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 33:
The directions are proclaimed as his ears, the Vedas as his speech, and Vāyu as his vital breath (prāṇa).
They say the universe is the heart; the earth is remembered as the private parts.
The vault of the sky is the navel-lake, the circle of luminaries is the region of the chest;
Maharloka is the neck, and Janaloka is remembered as the mouth. (25)
The world of heat (tapoloka) is the forehead, situated below the world of truth (satyaloka);
Indra and the other gods are the arms, and sound is the ear of the Great Lord.
The two Nasatyas and Dasras are known as the nostrils; scent is considered by the wise to be the vital breath (prāṇa);
Agni is declared to be the mouth; and day and night are the two eyelashes.
The abode of Brahmā is the expansion of the eyebrows, the waters are proclaimed to be the palate;
taste is declared to be the tongue, and the Yamas are proclaimed to be the fangs. ||28||
The teeth are his portions of affection; his smile is proclaimed to be Māyā;
the emission of side-glances is creation; and the upper lip of the Great Lord is Modesty. 29.
Her lower lip is greed (lobha), while the path of righteousness (dharmamārga) is her back;
and he who is the creator upon the surface of the earth, Prajāpati, is her generative organ (meḍhra). || 30 ||
The womb of the Great Goddess Maheśvarī is the oceans, and her bones are the mountains; her channels are declared to be the rivers, and her hair is celebrated as the trees.
Her supreme movement consists of childhood, youth, and old age;
the clouds are her hair, and the two twilights are the garments of the All-pervading Lord.
O King, the Moon is remembered as the mind of Śrī Jagadambā;
Hari is her power of cognition (vijñāna-śakti), and Rudra is remembered as her internal organ (antaḥ-karaṇa). ||33||
All the species of horses and other animals reside in the region of the hips of the Lord;
the great worlds, beginning with Atala, have come to occupy the portion below his waist. (34)
The foremost of the gods beheld such a great form, rich with thousands of garlands of flames and licking with its tongue. (35)
That which makes a "kaṭa-kaṭa" sound with its fangs, consumes with its many eyes,
wields weapons as its name, is heroic, and is the devourer of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
He has a thousand heads and eyes, as well as a thousand feet;
he resembles ten million suns and possesses a splendor equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
All the gods beheld that terrifying and most dreadful sight, which caused alarm to their hearts and eyes, and they raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! (hāhākāra).
With their hearts trembling, they fell into an insurmountable swoon;
even their memory that "she is the Mother of the Universe" vanished. (39)
Now these Vedas, situated in the four directions of the Great Lord, awakened the gods who were extremely fierce and had fainted from their swoon. ||40||
Therefore, maintaining their composure and having attained that supreme revelation, the gods stood with eyes filled with tears of love and throats choked with emotion. (41)
With voices faltering with tears, the gods began to offer praise. The gods said:
"O Mother, forgive our transgression; protect us, the wretched ones born from you. (42)
"O Goddess of the gods, restrain your anger; we are filled with fear at the sight of your form.
What praise could be offered to you here by us, mere mortals and non-gods? (43)
Even for himself, that [Brahman] and whatever constitutes his own power are indeed unknowable;
how then could they be an object for those born after him? (44)
Salutations to you, O Sovereign of the World; salutations to you, whose essence is the Praṇava.
Salutations to the one established in all Vedānta, to the embodiment of the syllable Hrīṃ. 45.
Salutation to that Soul of All, from whom fire has arisen, from whom the sun and the moon have come forth, and from whom all medicinal herbs originate. || 46 ||
Salutation to that Soul of All, from whom the gods, the Sādhyas, the birds, the animals, and human beings have come into existence. ||47||
Salutations again and again to Him from whom come inhalation and exhalation, rice and barley, austerity, faith, truth, as well as celibacy, ritual injunction, and sacred learning. 48.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter thirty-four.
Salutations to that Soul of All, from whom there are seven breaths as flames, seven indeed as fuel-sticks, seven as oblations, and likewise seven worlds.
Salutations again and again to Him from whom the oceans, mountains, and rivers flow forth, and from whom all herbs and juices arise. 50.
Salutations to that Soul of All, from whom sacrifice arose, as well as initiation, the sacrificial post, the priestly fee, the Rig-veda verses, the Yajur-veda formulas, and the Sama-veda chants.
Salutations in front and behind; salutations to you on both sides;
below and above, in the four directions—O Mother, repeated salutations to you!
O Goddess of gods, withdraw this extraordinary form;
show us instead that most beautiful of forms. (53)
Vyāsa said:
Seeing the gods thus terrified, the Mother of the Universe, that ocean of compassion, withdrew her terrible form and revealed her beautiful one. (54)
Holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, with all his limbs tender, his eyes full of compassion, and his lotus-face adorned with a gentle smile. (55)
Having seen that beautiful form, they were then freed from fear;
with peaceful minds, they bowed down, their voices faltering with joy.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 33 ||
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
The Goddess said:
"Where indeed are you, O unfortunate ones, and where is this most wonderful form?"
Nevertheless, out of affection for my devotees, I have shown myself in such a manner. ||1||
This form cannot be seen through the study of the Vedas, nor by yogic practices, nor by gifts, austerity, or sacrifice; it is possible only through my grace alone.

Listen to the subject at hand, O Indra among kings: here, the Supreme Self, through association with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), assumes the state of a living being as well as agency and other such attributes. ||3||
It performs various actions, for which dharma and adharma are the sole causes; having thereby attained various wombs, it is joined with happiness and suffering. (4)
Furthermore, due to the power of that [past] conditioning, one is always intent on various actions and attains diverse bodies, becoming joined with both happiness and suffering. || 5 ||
Indeed, like a water-wheel, for this [mind] there is never any rest;
ignorance alone is its root, from which arises desire, and from that, actions.
Therefore, a person should strive with constancy for the destruction of ignorance;
for this indeed is the fulfillment of birth: the eradication of ignorance. (7)
The attainment of the goals of human existence and even the state of liberation while living are accomplished by knowledge alone;
indeed, knowledge is the most powerful agent in destroying ignorance.
O Mountain, because there is no contradiction with meditation (*upāsti*), action and that which arises from it do not [obstruct it];
on the contrary, once ignorance and desire are destroyed, there can be no further concern with action. (9)
For they repeatedly desire actions that bring no benefit;
from that arises passion, from that arises hatred, and from that great misfortune ensues. (10)
Therefore, with every effort, a person should acquire knowledge;
yet, because it is said "even while performing actions here," action is also indispensable. (11)
For liberation comes from knowledge alone; therefore, there should be a combination of the two.
Karma, being beneficial, may serve as an auxiliary to knowledge. (12)
Thus some say here; however, that cannot be possible because it contradicts [the following]:
from knowledge comes the breaking of the heart-knot, and within the heart-knot, karma originates. (13)
Simultaneity is not possible for those two because of their contradiction,
just as simultaneity is impossible for darkness and light.
Therefore, O high-minded one, all Vedic rituals [should be performed].
Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 14. 515.
Therefore, O high-minded one, all Vedic rituals...
These should be performed with effort, for they lead precisely to the purification of the mind.
Tranquility, self-control, endurance, and dispassion arise from the quality of goodness (sattva);
ritual actions exist only up to that point, and not beyond it. (16)

At the conclusion of that very [practice], the self-possessed one, having renounced, should again take refuge with a guru who is learned in the Vedas and established in Brahman, with sincere devotion.
One should constantly listen to the Vedānta in this manner, remaining ever vigilant;
one should perpetually contemplate the meaning of such statements as "That thou art" (tattvamasi). || 18 ||
But the statement "That thou art" (tattvamasi) and others reveal the identity of the individual soul and Brahman;
once this identity is known, one becomes fearless and is indeed born in my own form. || 19 ||
First comes the comprehension of word-meanings, and from that, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; and the meaning of the sentence is proclaimed by me as the meaning of that word. (20)
And there is no doubt that the expressed meaning of the word "thou" (tvam-pada) is indeed the individual soul (jīva);
the identity of these two is declared by the wise through this [supreme] word. (21)
Since the two literal meanings are contradictory, their identity cannot possibly be established;
therefore, one must employ figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) for those two principles situated in the sacred revelation.
Pure consciousness alone is the objective referent (lakṣya) of those two; thus, the possibility of their identity exists.
Having realized their identity in that manner, one becomes non-dual through non-distinction from oneself. ||23||
Just as in the expression "this is that very Devadatta," it is held that [the term] is used figuratively (lakṣaṇā);
thus, a person, being freed from the gross body and so forth, attains Brahman. ||24||
The gross body is produced from the fivefold great elements;
it is the locus of experience, joined with old age and disease, and the site of all karmas. (25)
"This [world] appears clearly as false because it consists of illusion;
this, O Lord of Mountains, is that gross limitation (upādhi) of my self. (26)
The wise know that subtle body to be endowed with the organs of knowledge and action, joined with the five vital breaths, and possessed of mind and intellect. (27)
This subtle body of the self, arising from the unquintuplicated elements, is the second limiting adjunct (upādhi); it is the means by which pleasure and other experiences are perceived. (28)
This third [element], O Lord of Mountains, is beginningless, indefinable ignorance;
it appears as this body, the causal self of the Ātman. (29)
When the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) has occurred, the absolute Self alone remains;
yet the five sheaths (pañcakośa), situated within the three bodies, exist at all times. (30)
And by renouncing that treasury, indeed the "tail of Brahman" is obtained—that form of mine which is described by such statements as "not this, not this. (31)
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it never ceases to be.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain. (32)
If the killer thinks he has killed, or if the slain thinks he is slain, both of them do not understand; this one neither kills nor is killed. (33)
Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the secret cave of this creature;
through the grace of the Creator, the one who has transcended sorrow beholds Him and His majesty. 34.
Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself. Know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins. (35)
The senses are said to be the horses, and their objects are the paths;
the wise say that the Self, joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer. (36)
But he who is ignorant, lacks mental control, and is always impure, does not attain the [inner] space and instead enters into the cycle of worldly existence. || 37 ||
But he who possesses discernment, who is possessed of a controlled mind and is ever pure, attains that state from which he is not born again. (38)
But that man who has consciousness as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind reaches the end of the path—that supreme state which is mine. (39)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter thirty-five.
Having thus ascertained the Self by means of both scripture and one's own intelligence,
one should meditate upon Me as being of the nature of the Self, even while engaged in profound contemplation (nididhyāsana).
Prior to the practice of yoga, one should contemplate the three syllables within oneself for the purpose of meditating upon the Goddess who is expressed by the mantra known as the Praṇava. (41)
The syllable *ha* is the gross body, the syllable *ra* is the subtle body, and the syllable *ī* is that causal self; the syllable *hrīṃ* is I, the fourth state (*turya*).

Having thus understood the three seed-syllables in sequence within the collective body as well, the wise one, whose essence is pure consciousness, should contemplate them within both the individual and the collective. 43.

But before the time of meditative absorption (samādhi), having cultivated [the visualization] with such devotion, one should then meditate upon me, the Goddess, the Sovereign of the World, with eyes closed in concentration. 44.
Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal as they move within the nostrils, one whose desire for sense objects has ceased, who is free from defects, and devoid of envy; || 45 ||
Endowed with sincere devotion, in a cave or in a place free from noise,
one should dissolve the universal self, which is the letter *ha*, into the letter *ra*.
One should dissolve the fiery deity represented by the syllable *ra* into the syllable *o*;
one should dissolve the individual self (*ātman*) represented by the syllable *ī*, which consists of breath, into the syllable *ho*.

One should meditate within the interior of the crest-lock upon that which is devoid of the relationship between the expressed and the expresser, free from the state of duality, indivisible, and consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss. 48.
Thus, O King, by means of meditation, that best of men, having realized me directly,
becomes my very self, since there is oneness between the two.
Having seen me, the Self who is higher than the highest, through this application of yoga,
one becomes at that very moment the destroyer of ignorance and its effects.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 34 ||
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
Himālaya said:
O Maheśānī, speak of Yoga together with its ancillaries (sāṅga), which bestows pure consciousness (saṃvit).
By performing that through which I may become fit for the vision of reality. ||1||
The Goddess said:
"Neither in the vault of the sky, nor on earth, nor in the subterranean realm (rasātala) is there yoga;
those proficient in yoga declare that yoga is the unification of the individual soul (jīva) and the Self (ātman). (2)
O sinless one, their six obstacles have been declared as those which cause hindrances to yoga:
desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy. (3)
By means of the limbs of yoga themselves, having pierced through those [obstacles], yogins shall attain yoga:
first restraint (yama), then observance (niyama), posture (āsana), and breath control (prāṇāyāma). ||4||
Withdrawal of the senses, that which is called concentration, meditation, together with absorption—these they say are the eight limbs for yogis in the practice of yoga. (5)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, straightforwardness, forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten restraints (yamas). 6.
Austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Divine, listening to the established doctrine, devotion, recitation of mantras, and burnt offerings. (7)
O Lord of Mountains, these ten observances have been declared by me:
the lotus posture (padmāsana), the auspicious (svastika), the fortunate (bhadra), and likewise the thunderbolt posture (vajrāsana). ||8||
This is declared to be the vīrāsana; thus, in order, the fivefold set of postures [is described].
Having properly placed the auspicious soles of the feet upon the thighs— [this is the vīrāsana]. (9)
Then, the two thumbs should be drawn out from them in reverse order;
this is called the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is heart-pleasing to yogins. (10)
Having placed the soles of his auspicious feet correctly between the knees, the yogin should enter with an upright body; that is proclaimed as the Svastika posture.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 35:
Having firmly placed the pair of ankles on both sides of the sīvanī (the perineal raphe), [one should perform the following].
One should bind the two testicles below with the hands, reaching as far as the ankles.
This is called the Bhadrāsana, highly honored by yogis:
having placed the feet successively upon the thighs, with the knees facing outward and the fingers turned inward.
One should assume the unsurpassed vajrāsana posture with the hands placed on the lap,
having lowered one foot and likewise placed the other thigh upon it.
The yogi should sit with the body straight; this is called the vīrāsana posture.
He should draw in the external air through the iḍā [nāḍī] for sixteen mātrās. (15)
The yogi should restrain the filled [breath] for sixty-four measures,
and then slowly release it through the center of the suṣumnā for thirty-two measures.
The best among those who know yoga should exhale through both the Gāḍī and the Piṅgalā;
those proficient in the Yoga scriptures call this prāṇāyāma. (17)
In this manner, one should repeatedly perform the external practice for him in sequence;
by the gradual increase of the measures (mātrā), [the breath] should properly reach twelve and sixteen [counts].
The wise know that [prāṇāyāma] together with recitation, meditation, and so forth, to be "with seed" (sagarbha); they know that which is devoid of these to be "seedless" (vigarbha). || 19 ||
For a person practicing in due order, the emergence of sweat in the body is considered the lowest [stage];
that accompanied by trembling is the middle; and the abandonment of the ground is held to be the highest.
For the superior [practitioner], the attainment of qualities is desired as long as the practice continues.
Of the senses wandering without restraint among their objects.

The forceful extraction [of the breath] from those [locations] is called *pratyāhāra*. [This is performed] according to the prescribed method in the thumbs, ankles, knees, thighs, *mūlādhāra*, *liṅga*, navel, heart, neck, throat region, uvula, then the nose, the middle of the eyebrows, the crown of the head, and at the *dvādaśānta*. (117–211) (23)
The retention of the vital breath is designated as *dhāraṇā*, performed with a concentrated mind abiding within consciousness. (24)

In this context, meditation is said to be the constant contemplation of one's own chosen deity, as well as the cultivation of the identity between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). (25)
The sages have declared that samādhi is characterized by eight limbs;
now I shall describe to you the unsurpassed mantra-yoga. (26)

O Mountain, it is said that the body consists of the five elements; it is the form of the unity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, illumined by the splendors of the moon, the sun, and fire. It is held that there are thirty-five million channels (nāḍīs) within the body;
among them, ten are declared to be principal, and from those, three are established as the most essential.
Here, within the spinal column (merudaṇḍa), the primary channel takes the form of the moon, sun, and fire;
the white channel Iḍā is situated on the left, having the form of the moon. (29)
That channel, however, is of the nature of *śakti* and is directly the embodiment of nectar;
that which is on the right, called Piṅgalā, is of the form of *puṃs* and has the nature of the sun.
That Suṣumnā, consisting of all splendor, is of the nature of fire;
in its center, within the place called Vicitra, resides that which consists of will, knowledge, and action. 31.
In the center is the self-manifested liṅga (svayambhūliṅga), possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
above that is the seed-syllable of Māyā, whose essence is Hara, consisting of the bindu and nāda.
Above that, however, is Kuṇḍalinī, shaped like a crest and having a red form;
she is declared to be of the nature of the Goddess, O Lord of Mountains, and non-different from me. (33)
Outside of that, one should visualize a lotus with four petals beginning with 'va' and ending with 'la', which has the luster of gold and is as radiant as a freshly blossomed flower.
Above that is the unsurpassed Svādhiṣṭhāna, resembling fire, with petals having the luster of diamonds, and marked by the six syllables ending with *vādi*. 35.
The root is the six-cornered base; therefore they know it as the Mūlādhāra. By the word "self" (sva), they know the supreme Liṅga as the Svādhiṣṭhāna. || 36 ||

Above that, in the region of the navel, is the Maṇipūra [cakra], which possesses great luster; it has the appearance of a cloud, the appearance of lightning, and is composed of manifold splendor. ||37||
That lotus is called a "jewel-lotus" (*maṇipadma*) because it is split like a jewel;
it is endowed with ten petals and is inscribed with the letters beginning with *ḍa* and ending with *pha*.
This lotus is presided over by Viṣṇu and is the cause for the vision of Viṣṇu.
Above that is the unstruck lotus, resembling the rising sun. || 39 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 35.
It is supported by leaves consisting of one half of each letter from *ka* to *ṭha*, and in its center is a Bāṇaliṅga, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns. (40)
There, the unstruck sound (anāhata), consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahma), is perceived;
that lotus is celebrated by the sages as being called "unstruck" (anāhata). ||41||
That is indeed the abode of bliss, presided over by the Supreme Puruṣa;
above that is the petal known as Viśuddha, a sixteen-petaled lotus.

Endowed with sixteen vowels, smoke-colored and of great splendor, it is called *viśuddha* because, through the perception of the world as a *haṃsa*, it expands for the sake of the individual soul (*jīva*). 43.
The pure lotus, called the sky, is described as most wonderful;
above that is the wheel of command (ājñācakra), which is supreme and presided over by the Self.
The transmission of the command occurs therein; therefore, it is proclaimed as "the Command" (ājñā).
Dilam, conjoined with Hṛkṣa, is that most beautiful lotus. 45.
Above that is the one called Kailāsa, and above that is Rodhinī;
thus, O observer of good vows, the ādhāra-cakras have been described to you. 46.
The place of the bindu is said to be ten thousand yojanas above that;
thus has this entire unsurpassed path of yoga been described. (47)
First, by means of the practice of inhalation (pūraka), one should fix the mind upon the foundation (ādhāra).
Between the anus and the genitals lies the Śakti; by contracting it, one should awaken her. 48.

One should lead the wheel of consciousness through the very sequence of the piercing of the centers (liṅgabhedakrama), and one should contemplate that supreme Śakti as having become one with Śambhu. 49.
There, having caused her to drink that nectar which has arisen— resembling molten lac— the power known as Māyā, which bestows the perfection of yoga;
There, having satiated the deities of the six cakras with a stream of nectar,
the wise one should then bring [the nectar] back to the mūlādhāra by that same path.
Even for one practicing in this manner day after day, all the previously mentioned corrupted mantras will certainly attain success; it cannot be otherwise.
One is liberated from the bondage of existence through the sufferings of old age, death, and the like;
such are the qualities that reside in me, the Goddess, the Mother of the World. (53)
These qualities arise indeed in the supreme practitioner and not otherwise;
thus, O dear one, has this supreme retention of air been described. (54)
Now, listen attentively to me regarding that which is called *dhāraṇā*: having fixed the mind upon the Goddess who is undivided from the guardians of the quarters and the rest. (55)
One quickly becomes absorbed in that through the union of the individual soul and Brahman;
or, if the mind is still defiled and does not quickly become pure, [one should practice further]. (56)
Then, through the application of its constituent parts, the yogi should practice the yogas;
O Mountain, my hands, feet, and so forth are indeed sweet upon your peak.
The practitioner of mantra should stabilize the triple [world]; furthermore, through mastery of the locations, he whose mind is purified should fix the mind upon every form.
O Mountain, as long as the mind remains dissolved in the Goddess, who is pure consciousness,
for that long the practitioner should practice the recitation of the desired mantra along with fire offerings.
Through the practice of mantra and yoga, one becomes fit for the knowledge of that which is to be known;
for there is no mantra without yoga, nor indeed is there yoga without mantra. (60)
For the yoga of practicing these two is the cause of the perfect realization of Brahman;
just as a jar hidden in a house enveloped by darkness is seen by means of a lamp.
"Thus the Self, though veiled by illusion, has been made an object of perception by Manu;
in this way, the entire method of yoga, complete with its ancillaries, has now been declared by me."
This is to be known from the instruction of the Guru, and not otherwise, even by means of millions of scriptures.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Book, Chapter 36.
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
The Goddess said:
O King, one whose self is thus united with yoga, seated upon his seat, should meditate upon me in the form of Brahman with sincere devotion. (1)
Manifest is the hidden, moving in secret, the great state;
herein all this is deposited—whatever moves and whatever breathes.
Know this as the existent and the non-existent, the most excellent, the supreme beyond consciousness, the highest among creatures;
that which is unswallowed and subtler than the minute, in which the worlds and the inhabitants of the worlds are contained.
This is that syllable, Brahman; it is life-breath, and it is speech and mind.
This is truth, this is the immortal; know this, my dear, as that which is to be pierced. 4.

Taking up the great weapon of the Upaniṣadic bow, one should fix the sharpened arrow of meditation; drawing it with a mind absorbed in that state, O gentle one, know that very Imperishable as the mark to be pierced. (5)
The syllable Om is the bow, the self is indeed the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target.
With undistracted mind, one must pierce it; like the arrow, one shall become absorbed in that.

In whom heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and the mind, along with all vital breaths, are woven—together know Him alone as the Self; cast off other words, for He is the very bridge to immortality. (7)
Wherein the channels converge like the spokes in the hub of a chariot wheel—that very one moves within in many ways, being born in many ways. (8)
"Om"—thus meditate upon the Self; may there be well-being for you as you cross over to the further shore beyond darkness.
That Self is firmly established in the divine city of Brahman, in the ether. || 9 ||

The mind-made [self], the leader of the body of vital breaths, established in food and having placed its seat in the heart—the wise behold it through the knowledge of that [Self], which shines as the immortal form of bliss. 10.
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen. (11)
In the supreme golden sheath, there shines the resplendent Brahman, partless;
that is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self know. 12.
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire.
Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. 13.
To the south and to the north;
Brahman alone is this immortal [reality] in front, Brahman behind, and Brahman has spread out below and above.
This entire universe is Brahman, the most excellent. 14.
He who has such an experience is one who has accomplished his purpose, the best among men;
having become Brahman, with a serene self, he neither grieves nor desires. (15)
O King, fear arises from a second; in the absence of that, one does not fear.
For me, there is no separation from Him, nor for Him is there separation from me.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Purāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter thirty-seven.
"Know for certain, O Parvata, that I am indeed he and she is indeed I;
my vision is present wherever a knower of me resides. (17)
I do not dwell in a sacred ford, nor on Kailāsa, nor in Vaikuṇṭha, nor anywhere else;
rather, I reside in the very center of the lotus-heart of my devotees.
The worship of one who possesses knowledge of Me even once yields the fruit of ten million My own worships;
his lineage becomes pure, and his mother has fulfilled her purpose. (19)
