The earth is meritorious for one whose mind has its abode in consciousness;
as for the knowledge of Brahman that you have asked about, O best of mountains. (20)
All of that has been told by me; indeed, there is nothing further to be said.
This [teaching] is for an eldest son who is endowed with devotion and virtuous conduct. || 21 ||
This should be told to a disciple who is as described above, and never otherwise;
to one who possesses supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru just as for the Divine.
For these truths explained here shine forth clearly to that great-souled one;
he to whom this knowledge has been imparted is indeed the Supreme Lord himself. (23)
He who is unable to perform meritorious deeds for one [who has bestowed the Veda] becomes a debtor to that person;
he who bestows the birth of Brahman is said to be even greater than one's own parents. (24)
O Mountain, the birth derived from one's father is lost; such a birth as this has never occurred before.
For it is said in the Veda: "To him [the gods] do not come," and so forth. (25)
Therefore, according to the established conclusion of the scriptures, the Guru is the supreme bestower of Brahman;
when Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector, but when the Guru is angry, not even Śaṅkara can save one.
Therefore, O Mountain, one should please the venerable Guru with every effort;
one should always be devoted to him through body, mind, and speech.
Otherwise, one would be ungrateful, and for the ungrateful, there is no atonement.
This was told to Atharvaṇa by him, accompanied by a vow to cut off his head.
When his head was severed by the two Aśvins and his body by the wielder of the thunderbolt,
the two physicians, seeing that horse-head of his had been lost, [acted] toward the two best of gods.
Then, O Lord of Mountains, those two reattached their own heads to the Sage;
thus, the knowledge of Brahman is to be attained through great hardship.
O Supporter of the Earth, he by whom this has been obtained would be fortunate and one who has fulfilled his purpose. 30.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 36 ||
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
Himālaya said:
O Mother, tell me of your own devotion, by which knowledge indeed comes easily.
This might arise in this person of middling capacity who is free from passion.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Lord of Mountains, three paths of mine are renowned for the attainment of liberation."
O best of beings, [these are] the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, and the yoga of devotion. ||2||
This practice can be performed by all three [vehicles] in every respect, because it is easily accessible, mental in nature, and because it does not afflict the body or mind. (3)
That devotion is considered to be of three kinds according to the differences in the qualities of men:
[the first] is that which is directed toward harming others, preceded by hypocrisy. ||4||
The devotion of one who is possessed by envy and anger is *tāmasī*; it is devoid of causing pain to others and consists solely of the desire for one's own welfare. (5)
Constantly desiring [worldly] objects, seeking fame, and greedy for enjoyments,
those men worship with extreme devotion in order to attain each respective fruit.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Seventh Book, Chapter 37:
"But due to the increase of the sense of duality, the fool perceives me as other than himself."
O Lord of Mountains, his devotion is declared to be of the rājasa type.
Action dedicated to the Supreme Lord for the washing away of sins must certainly be performed by me incessantly, because it is prescribed in the Vedas. (8)
Thus, with a mind firmly resolved yet relying on the perception of duality, one performs action for the sake of joy; that devotion, O Mountain, is *sāttvika*. (9)
This attainment of the Supreme is possible through devotion because it relies upon the cognition of difference;
for the two types of devotion previously mentioned are not considered to lead to the Supreme.
Now, listen to me as I describe supreme devotion:
it consists of constantly hearing of my qualities and the perpetual chanting of my names. (11)
May my mind’s movement toward you, the mine of the jewels of virtuous qualities, remain steadfast and constant, like a steady stream of oil.
In that state, no cause whatsoever could ever exist;
nor is there any longing for the states of proximity (sāmīpya), equality (sārūpya), union (sāyujya), or co-residence (sālokya).
He never perceives anything whatsoever as superior to service unto Me;
because of the state of being the served and the server, he does not desire liberation therein.
He who, unwearied by supreme devotion, meditates upon me alone,
knows me eternally as non-different from himself, and not through any sense of separation.
But he who contemplates all living beings as being of the same nature as himself—just as he has love for his own self, so too does he have love for the Supreme Self. (16)
But he who does not make a distinction among those that exist everywhere, in all forms, and at all times, because consciousness is the same in all of them; || 17 ||
O Lord, he bows to and worships everyone, even down to the outcaste;
because he has abandoned all sense of duality, he harbors no thought of malice toward anyone whatsoever.
O Lord, there is faith in beholding my abodes, as well as in beholding my devotees, and faith in hearing about me, in mantras, tantras, and so forth. (19)
With a mind agitated by love for me, her body always bristling with horripilation, her eyes filled with the tears of love, and her voice faltering in her throat; || 20 ||
O Lord of Mountains, worship me alone with undivided devotion—me, the Sovereign, the source of the universe, the cause of all causes. (21)
My divine vows, both daily and occasional,
he who performs them constantly with devotion, free from stinginess regarding his wealth— (22)
O Blessed One, that desire to behold my festival and likewise the performance of my festival arise in him inevitably from his very nature. (23)
Indeed, singing my very names, he dances, free from egoism and the like, having conquered the identification with the body. (24)
Whatever is done by means of a chariot should be done in that same manner;
I have no concern even in that regard, such as for the protection of the body. (25)
That which is called supreme devotion (parabhakti) is remembered as that in which nothing whatsoever is conceived apart from the Goddess. (26)
O Upholder of the Earth, for one in whom such supreme devotion has truly arisen, at that very moment there occurs absorption into my own nature, which is pure consciousness alone. (27)
That which is the highest limit of devotion is proclaimed as knowledge;
and that which is the pinnacle of detachment is also knowledge, because both of these reside within knowledge. (28)
O Mountain, even for one who has performed devotion, if my knowledge does not arise due to the power of *prārabdha* karma, he goes to Maṇidvīpa.
Having gone there, O Mountain, even if one does not desire them, one experiences all enjoyments;
at the end of that, the knowledge of my true form shall arise perfectly.
By that [knowledge] one should always be liberated; liberation comes from knowledge and not otherwise.
For whomsoever there is knowledge of the inner Self right here in this world, [for him there is liberation]. ||31||
The vital breaths of that one who is dependent on my consciousness do not depart;
O Brahmin, he attains that very Brahman who knows Brahman as Brahman. || 32 ||
The throat, which is equal to refined gold, was concealed by ignorance;
indeed, through knowledge and the destruction of ignorance, that which was already attained is truly obtained. //33//
O Best of Mountains, there is nothing for me other than the known and the unknown;
as it is in a mirror, so it is in the self; as it is in water, so it is in the world of the ancestors.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 38.
Just as shadow and sunlight exist distinctly within a clear medium, even so may my knowledge arise in this world, entirely devoid of dualistic states. (35)
But he who dies while possessing detachment yet devoid of knowledge shall dwell eternally in the world of Brahmā for the duration of a kalpa, and thereafter [attain liberation]. ||36||
Furthermore, his birth shall take place again in the home of those who are pure and prosperous;
thereafter he performs spiritual practice, and from that, knowledge indeed arises. (37)
O King, knowledge is attained through many births, not by means of a single birth;
therefore, with every effort, one should apply oneself to the pursuit of knowledge.
Otherwise, there would be a great destruction, and such a birth is difficult to obtain again;
even therein, in the first category, the attainment of the Vedas is difficult to achieve. (39)

The attainment of the six qualities beginning with tranquility (śama), as well as the perfection of yoga, and likewise the meeting with a supreme guru—all of this is indeed difficult to obtain here. 40.
Likewise, through the sharpness of the faculties and the refinement of the body by means of the merits accumulated over many births, the desire for liberation arises thereafter. (41)
Even when the means of accomplishment have thus become fruitful,
the birth of that man who does not strive for the sake of knowledge is useless.
Therefore, O King, one should apply effort toward the goal of knowledge according to one's ability.
At every step, one certainly obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. ||43||
Like clarified butter hidden within milk, consciousness dwells within every single being;
it must be constantly churned with the mind serving as the churning-stick.
"Having attained knowledge, one becomes fulfilled"—thus proclaims the drum of the Vedānta.
Everything has been told in brief; what more do you wish to hear? || 45 ||
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 37 ||
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter.
Himālaya said:
"O Goddess, how many sacred places are to be seen upon the surface of the earth?"
These are the principal purifiers and most beloved of the Goddess.
Likewise, tell me, O Mother, of those vows and festivals that grant contentment, so that by them a person may become one who has accomplished his purpose. ||2||
The Goddess said:
"Everything visible is my abode; all times consist of vows.
Since I am the embodiment of all forms, there are festivals at all times. (3)
Nevertheless, out of affection for my devotee, I shall say something, little by little;
O King of Mountains, listen attentively to my words. (4)
Kolāpura is a great sacred site where Lakṣmī is eternally present;
it is the second city of the Mother, the supreme abode presided over by Reṇukā.
Tulajāpura shall be the third, and likewise Saptaśṛṅga;
there is the great site of Hiṅgulā, and similarly Jvālāmukhī.
The supreme abode of Śākambharī, the most excellent abode of Bhrāmarī,
the abode of Śrī Raktadantikā, and likewise the abode of Durgā.
The abode of the Goddess residing on Vidhyācala is the most excellent of all;
the great seat of Annapūrṇā is the unsurpassed city of Kāñcī.
The supreme abode of Bhīmādevī, as well as the Vimalā abode, the great abode of Śrī Candralā, and the abode of Kauśikī. ||9||
The supreme abode of Nīlāmbā is on the peak of the Blue Mountain;
likewise, there is the abode of Jāmbūnadeśvarī and the auspicious Śrīnagara.
The great abode of Guhyakālī is established in Nepal,
and that which is declared to be the supreme abode of Mīnākṣī is in Cidambaram.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter thirty-eight:
"The great sacred site of Vedāraṇya is presided over by Sundarī;
the great sacred site of Ekāmbara is established by Parāśakti."
Madālasā is the supreme abode of the Mistress of Yoga (Yogeśvarī), and likewise,
the abode of Nīlasarasvatī is renowned among the Chinese.
In Vaidyanātha, however, the abode of Bagalā is considered the most excellent of all.
The jewel island of the illustrious Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī has been remembered by me. ||14||
The maṇḍala of Kāmākhyā belongs to the illustrious Tripurabhairavī;
it is a jewel among sacred fields on the earth’s surface, consecrated by Mahāmāyā. 15.
She is visibly menstruating. ||16||
There is no place superior to this anywhere upon the surface of the earth. Every month, the Lord becomes present there, and all the deities residing in that place attain the nature of mountains;
indeed, even the great deities dwell within those mountains.
The entire earth there is considered by the wise to be the form of the Goddess;
there is no place higher than this, the source of Kāmākhyā. (18)
The supreme abode of the Gāyatrī is said to be the glorious Puṣkara;
Caṇḍikā is at Amareśa, and Puṣkarekṣiṇī is at Nabhāsa.
In the great place named Nāmaṣa, there is the goddess Sāliṅgacāriṇī;
in Puṣkarākṣa are Puruhūtā, Āpaḍhī, and likewise Rati.
At the great site of Caṇḍamuṇḍa is Daṇḍinī Parameśvarī;
at Bhārabhūti is Bhavabhūti; and at Nākula is Nakuleśvarī.
Candrikā is remembered as Śāṅkarī at Hariścandra on Śrīgiri;
she is Triśūlā at Japyeśvara, and Sūkṣmā at Āmrātakedavara.
Śāṃkarī is in Mahākāla; Śarvāṇī is in the one called Madhyama;
and in the great sacred field named Kedāra, that Goddess is Bhārgadāyinī.
She is known as Bhairavī in the place called Bhairava, and she is remembered as Maṅgalā in Gayā;
she is Sthāṇupriyā in Kurukṣetra, and likewise in Svāyaṃbhuva and Nākula.
Ugrā is at Kanakhala, Viśveśī at Vimaleśvara,
Mahānandā at Aṭṭahāsa, and Mahāntakā at Mahendra.
In Bhīma, Bhīmeśvarī is proclaimed; furthermore, in the place of Vastrāpatha, Bhavānī is proclaimed as Śāṅkarī; and in Ardha-koṭika, she is Rudrāṇī.
The large-eyed one is at Avimukta; the highly fortunate one is at Mahālaya;
Bhadrakarṇī is at Gokarṇa; and Bhadrā is at Bhadrakarṇaka. (27)
Utpalākṣī is in Suvarṇākṣa; Sthāṇvīśā is in the place known as Sthāṇu;
Kamalā is in Kamalālaya; and Pracaṇḍā is in Chagalaṇḍaka. (28)
At Kuraṇḍala there is Trisaṃdhyā; at Mākoṭa, Mukuṭeśvarī;
at Maṇḍaleśa, Śāṇḍakī; and again at Kālañjara, Kālī. (29)
Sound is said to reside in Śaṅkukarṇa; it becomes gross in Sthūlakeśvara.
In the lotus of the heart of the wise, the Supreme Goddess is Hṛllekhā. (30)
O best of mountains, these places have been declared as most beloved by the Goddess; having first heard of the majesty of each respective sacred field (kṣetra), [one should visit them]. 31.
Thereafter, one should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite;
or else, O best of mountains, all sacred fields are present here in Kāśī. (32)
And there indeed he should dwell constantly, devoted to the Goddess, beholding those sacred places and reciting the mantra to the Goddess without interruption. (33)
Meditating upon her lotus feet, one is liberated from bondage;
whoever recites these names of the Goddess after rising in the morning, [shall attain liberation]. (34)
O Mountain, sins are reduced to ashes at that very moment;
one should quickly recite these purifying verses before the foremost of the twice-born during the time of a Śrāddha ceremony.
All his ancestors, being liberated, attain the supreme goal.
Now, O you of excellent vows, I shall describe the religious observances (vratas) to you.
Both women and men should diligently perform this vow known as Anantatṛtīyā, the Rasakalyāṇinī vow.
The vow known as Ārdrānandakara, the vow for the third lunar day, the Friday vow, and likewise the Kṛṣṇa-caturdaśī; ||38||
Therein are the vow of Saturday (Bhaumavāra-vrata) and the vow of evening (Pradoṣa-vrata),
where the god Mahādeva, having established the Goddess upon a seat, [resides].
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Book, Chapter 39:
At the onset of night, she brings death before her, together with the gods.
Having fasted there through the night, one should worship Cīrā at the beginning of the evening.
O Mountain, the Somavāra-vrata is especially an antidote to that [sin] and brings delight to that Goddess; it is exceedingly dear to me.
There too, having fully worshipped the Goddess, one should take a meal at night;
this vow for two Navarātras is indeed pleasing to me.
O Lord, he who, free from envy, performs these and other obligatory and occasional vows for the sake of pleasing me,
attains union with me; he is my devotee, he is dear to me.
O Lord, one should also perform festivals, beginning with the festival of the swing.
Just as you would perform the festival of the bed, so too should you perform the festival of the vigil,
the chariot festival for me, and the damana festival.
My devotee should always perform this Pavitrōtsava in the month of Śrāvaṇa, which brings great joy, as well as other great festivals. 46.
One should joyfully feed my devotees, as well as married women, virgins, and vaṭukas, with the thought that they are I myself, having fixed one's inner focus upon Me. (47)
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, one should worship these [deities] with *sumanās* flowers and other offerings;
whoever performs this with devotion every year, remaining untiring. || 48 ||
He is blessed and has fulfilled his purpose; he is truly a worthy recipient of my affection. Everything that bestows joy upon me has been told to you in brief.
It must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who is not devoted.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 38 ||
Then the thirty-ninth chapter.
Himālaya said:
O Goddess of gods, O Maheśānī, O Ambikā, ocean of compassion!
Now, tell us correctly and as it truly is your own ritual procedure for worship.
The illustrious Goddess said:
"O King, O preeminent among mountains, listen with extreme faith as I shall describe the procedure for the worship of Ambikā, which is dear to her."
My worship shall be twofold: external and internal as well.
The external is also said to be twofold: Vedic and likewise Tantric. (3)
O Upholder of the Earth, the Vedic [form of worship] is also of two kinds according to the distinction of the images;
the Vedic rite should be performed by those who are initiated into the Vedas and accompanied by Vedic mantras.
However, for those who have received the initiation prescribed in the Tantras, the Tantric [method] should be resorted to;
otherwise, by not knowing this secret of worship, one acts contrarily. ||5||
Whatever great deed a man performs, he inevitably falls;
among those, I shall first describe that which is declared in the Veda. (6)
O upholder of the earth, that supreme form which you have seen directly before me is infinite—
possessing endless heads and eyes, and endless feet, it is vast.
One should constantly worship that which is endowed with all powers, the impeller, and higher than the highest; one should not meditate upon or even remember anything else.
O Mountain, thus has the nature of the first image been described.
Peaceful, with a concentrated mind, and free from hypocrisy and egoism.
Be devoted to that, perform sacrifice for that, and go for refuge to that alone;
behold that with your mind, and always chant and meditate upon it.
Resorting to my state through exclusive devotion joined with love,
worship me alone with sacrifices, austerities, and gifts, and thus fully satisfy me.
"In this way, through my grace, you shall be liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Those who are devoted to me, whose minds are attached to me, are considered the best of devotees. (12)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 39:
"I promise that I shall deliver you from this state of existence before long, either through meditation combined with ritual action, or again, through devotion and knowledge. (13)
O King, I am attained in every way, but not by mere ritual actions alone;
devotion arises from dharma, and through devotion, the Supreme is attained. (14)
That which is declared by the Śruti and Smṛti is proclaimed as Dharma;
that which is propounded by another scripture is called a semblance of Dharma (dharmābhāsa). || 15 ||
The Veda has arisen from me, who am omniscient and omnipotent;
because ignorance does not exist in me, the Śruti is not invalid.
And the Smṛtis have indeed emerged after grasping the meaning of the Śruti;
therefore, the authority of both Manu and others as well as of the Śrutis is accepted. (17)

Sometimes and in certain places, they proclaim a dharma uttered by others through a glance for the sake of wealth; however, that partial teaching is certainly not to be accepted by those who follow the Vedas.
The teachings of other authors of treatises lack authority because they arise from ignorance and are corrupted by the defect of that ignorance. (19)
Therefore, one who desires liberation should in every way rely upon the Veda for the sake of dharma;
for just as the king's command in this world is never ever transgressed.
That command of mine, which is the Śruti, is supreme over all; how could it be abandoned by men?
Indeed, the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya castes exist for the purpose of preserving my command.
Therefore, O Supporter of the Earth, you should know that this secret word of mine, revealed by Śruti, is as follows:
whenever there is a decline of dharma... (22)
At that time, when unrighteousness arose, I assumed various forms;
it was for this very reason, O King, that the distinction between gods and Daityas came into being.
For those who do not practice that Dharma, I have always prepared hells so that terror may arise from merely hearing of them. (24)
If anyone should abandon the dharma of the Vedas and take recourse to another dharma,
the king should banish those unrighteous men from his own realm.
They are not to be conversed with by Brahmins, nor are they to be admitted into the row for meals by the twice-born;
as for whatever other various scriptures exist in this world, [they are likewise rejected]. (26)
Those [teachings] which contradict the Śruti and Smṛti are entirely of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), such as the Vāma, the Kapālaka, the Kaulaka, and the Bhairava Āgama. (27)
It was brought forth by Śiva for the purpose of deluding [the gods], and not for any other reason;
[it occurred] due to the curse of Dakṣa, the curse of Bhṛgu, and the curse of Dadhīci.
For the sake of uplifting those excellent Brahmins who have been burnt and cast outside the path of the Vedas, [this work is composed] always according to the sequence of steps. 29.
The Śaivas, Vaiṣṇavas, Sauras, Śāktas,
as well as the Gāṇapatyas and the Āgamas, were indeed composed by Śaṅkara;
however, even that which is not contrary to the Vedas was spoken there in certain instances.
For those who follow the Vedas, there is never any fault whatsoever in accepting that [scripture]. ||31||
In no way may a twice-born man be entitled to a matter that contradicts the Veda;
however, one who is devoid of entitlement to the Veda may have entitlement therein. //32//
Therefore, with every effort, one following the Veda should take refuge in the Veda;
for knowledge conjoined with dharma reveals the Supreme Brahman. || 33 ||
Having renounced all desires, they have come to me alone for refuge;
they are compassionate toward all beings and free from pride and egoism.
With their minds fixed on Me, their lives surrendered to Me, and delighting in discourse concerning My abode—
whether they be renunciants, forest-dwellers, householders, or celibate students— (35)
They always worship with devotion the yoga known as the Divine;
for them, who are eternally liberated, I [dispel] the darkness born of ignorance.
"I shall destroy [all ignorance] by the light of the sun of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O Lord of Mountains, is the first [stage] of Vedic worship. (37)

The essential nature of the second [vow] has been briefly stated; now I shall describe it [regarding its application] upon an image, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or likewise within the orbs of the sun and moon. (38)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter forty.

Then, having meditated upon the Goddess who is higher than the highest— whether in water, or in a Bāṇaliṅga, or in a mantra, or on a great cloth-painting, or likewise in the lotus of the heart of Śrī— [one should worship her].
A young woman, as red as the dawn, the ultimate limit of the essence of beauty, beautiful in every limb. (40)

[I bow to] the Mother who possesses auspicious qualities, who is full of compassion, who is always distressed by the suffering of her devotees, whose face is gracious with favor, and who has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament. 41.
It should be filled with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa) according to one's available wealth. || 42 ||

One should worship her, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and whose nature is bliss, with ritual offerings as long as one does not possess the qualification for internal worship; indeed, as long as that [qualification] has not arisen, one should resort to this external worship, but once it has arisen, one should abandon it. 43.
Form is devoid of limiting adjuncts for me. ||44||

But that worship which is internal is known as the dissolution into consciousness (*saṃvit*). Since consciousness alone is supreme, the mind should be established without support within my own form, which is consciousness.
The world, however, which is beyond the nature of consciousness, is false and composed of *māyā*. (45)
Therefore, for the destruction of saṃsāra, one should meditate upon her who is the witness and whose nature is the Self, with a mind free from mental constructs (nirmanaska) and joined in yoga. 47.
Henceforth, O best of mountains, I shall describe the expansion of the external worship; listen with an attentive mind. 48.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 39 ||
Now begins the fortieth chapter.
The Goddess said:
Having risen in the morning, one should meditate upon a radiant lotus on the head.
There, one should meditate upon one's own Guru in his true form, radiant as camphor. ||1||
Having prostrated before the Goddess, who is exceedingly serene, adorned with radiant ornaments, and endowed with power, the wise man should then meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī.
I take refuge in that woman whose nature is bliss, who shines forth at the first departure and who becomes like nectar upon the return;
she whom I follow within the path of my inner being.

Having thus spread [the breath] into the middle of that crest-lock (śikhā), one should meditate upon me, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss; then, thinking "I grieve," one should complete all the ritual actions.

Then, having performed the Agnihotra sacrifice for my pleasure, O best of the twice-born, that most excellent brahmin, remaining on his own seat at the conclusion of the oblation, should perform the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) for worship. ||5||
Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa),
one should always perform the placement of the Mātṛkās of Hullekhā (hullekhāmātṛkānyāsa).
One should place the syllable *ha* at the *mūlādhāra*, the syllable *ra* at the heart, likewise the syllable *ī* between the eyebrows, and the syllable *hrīṃ* on the crown of the head.
One should perform all other ritual placements (nyāsa) prescribed by their respective mantras;
furthermore, one should conceive of a sacred seat (pīṭha) within one's own body by means of Dharma and the other [qualities].
Then, when the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) has fully manifested, the wise one should meditate upon the Great Goddess in the lotus of my heart, situated upon a seat of five corpses.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—these five great spirits (mahāpreta) stand at my feet. || 10 ||
For these [beings] consist of the five elements and likewise consist of the five states;
but I am of the nature of unmanifest consciousness, and am entirely beyond them.
Then, having visualized me as always assuming the form of the seat (viṣṭara) within the Śaktitantras,
one should worship me with mental enjoyments and also perform recitation.
Having offered the recitation (japa) to the Śrī-devī, one should then perform the ritual placement of the arghya vessel;
having arranged the vessels, one should purify the articles of worship.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Seventh Skandha, Chapter 40:
With that water and with the Astra-mantra, the bodily [impurity] was purified by Manu.
Having first performed the binding of the directions and thereafter bowed to the gurus; || 14 ||
Having received his permission, [one should then worship] with the Brāhma-pīṭhas my divine and heart-stealing form, which is meditated upon as residing within the heart. (15)
Then, one should invoke [the deity] onto the seat by means of the vidyā for the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana);
likewise, [one should perform] the offering of the seat, the invocation, the arghya, the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, as well as the water for sipping (ācamana).
Having offered with one's own devotion to the Goddess a bath, two garments, and all kinds of ornaments, as well as sandalwood paste and flowers as is appropriate, ||17||
One should perform the worship of the coverings situated within the yantra correctly;
for those who are unable to do so every time, worship on Fridays is prescribed.
The limb-deities, whose forms are light, should be remembered as the Root Goddess;
one should contemplate the three worlds pervaded by the mass of their radiance. (19)
One should worship the Root Goddess (Mūladevī) together with her retinue of returning deities,
using fragrant substances such as perfumes and likewise with well-scented flowers.
One should satisfy me with food offerings, libations, betel leaves, sacrificial fees, and so forth,
as well as with this thousand-name hymn composed by you.
O Lord, with the Kavaca Sūkta, with the hymn beginning "Aham Rudrebhiḥ," and with the mantras from the Devī-atharvaśiras and the Hṛllekhā Upaniṣad; ||22||
A man, his heart softened by love, should repeatedly praise me with this great mantra of great knowledge and seek forgiveness from the Mother of the World. (23)

With all his limbs bristling with horripilation, his voice choked by tears that obstructed his eyes, he should repeatedly please me with the sounds of dancing, singing, and other such performances. 24.
Since I am indeed to be propounded by the complete study of the Vedas as well as by all the Purāṇas, therefore one should satisfy me.
One should constantly offer even one's own entire possession, including one's body;
thereafter, one should perform the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma) and [make offerings] to Brāhmaṇas and married women.
One should feed the *vaṭukas*, the commoners, and others with the thought that they are the Goddesses;
then, having bowed, one should dissolve them back into one's own heart in reverse order.
O observer of noble vows, you should perform my worship with the *hṛllekhā* mantra;
for *hṛllekhā* is remembered as the supreme sovereign of all mantras. (28)
I am eternally reflected in the mirror of Hṛllekhā;
therefore, everything given by Hṛllekhā is offered by all the mantras. (29)
Having worshipped the Guru with ornaments and other offerings, one should attain a sense of fulfillment;
whoever thus worships the Goddess, the illustrious Bhuvanasundarī, [attains that same state]. 30.
Indeed, for him nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain anywhere at any time;
at the end of the body, he certainly goes to Maṇidvīpa by every means.
He is to be known as the very embodiment of the Goddess, and the gods always bow down to him.
Thus, O King, the worship of the Great Goddess has been described to you.
Having reflected upon this in its entirety, yet according to your specific qualification, perform my worship; by that, you shall become one who has achieved his purpose.
However, one should never speak this scripture of the Gītā to anyone who is not a disciple.
It must not be given to one who is not a devotee, nor to a rogue, nor to one of evil intent. ||34||
This revelation is the uncovering of the Mother’s breasts;
therefore, this must always be guarded with diligent effort. (35)
It should indeed be given to a devotee, to a disciple, and also to an eldest son—one who is well-behaved, well-attired, and endowed with devotion to the gods. (36)
One should recite this in the presence of Brāhmaṇas at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony;
then all those ancestors, being satisfied, proceed to the supreme state. ||37||
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lady vanished right there;
and all the gods became joyful from the sight of the Goddess.
Then that lady Haimavatī was born on the Himālaya;
she who was renowned as Gaurī was given in marriage to Śaṅkara.
Then Skanda was born, and by him Tāraka was slain.
O lord of men, previously, during the churning of the ocean, the jewels were obtained.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the seventh book, chapter forty.
There the Lord [was worshipped], and for the sake of attaining the goddess Lakṣmī, they praised her with devotion;
then, for the purpose of bestowing grace upon them, Ramā emerged from that place.
Because he was given Vaikuṇṭha by the gods, he became equal to Him.
Thus, O King, I have narrated to you this supreme majesty of the Goddess. 42.
This subject concerning the origin of Gaurī and Lakṣmī, which grants all desires, must not be told to anyone else, for it is a secret that has been revealed [only to you]. (43)
This Gītā is the very secret; it must be guarded with great effort.
O sinless one, everything that was asked by you has been explained in brief.
It is sacred, purifying, and divine; what more do you wish to hear? ||44||
Thus ends the fortieth chapter of the Devīgītā in the seventh book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 40 ||
The seventh book of this glorious Bhāgavata, consisting of two thousand two hundred and fifty verses, has been proclaimed as having issued from the mouth of Dvaipāyana. (1)
