The Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata,
Eighth Skandha; now the first chapter.
Janamejaya said:
You have narrated the life-stories of kings born of the solar and lunar lineages, which are based on noble accounts; having heard them, they have become for me a source of nectar. (1)
Now I wish to hear how that Goddess, the Mother of the Universe,
is worshipped in whatever form she is adored throughout all the Manvantaras.
In whatever place and by whatever rite,
O Goddess of Devas, she who bestows fruits should be worshipped with the body.
By whichever mantra-syllable it is worshipped, and wherever it is worshipped—
And the description of the Goddess’s universal form (virāṭsvarūpa) exactly as it is. ||3||
O brahmin-sage, tell me all about that meditation by which the mind may attain its own subtle nature, so that I may obtain the highest good.
Vyāsa said:
This is the supreme propitiation of the Goddess, by performing or even hearing which a person attains welfare in this world. (5)
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim that which the Lord, the initiator of the practice of yoga, has spoken.
Thus was Nārāyaṇa questioned by Nārada in the past.
Once, while wandering this earth, the illustrious Nārada reached the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa and remained there, his fatigue dispelled. (7)
Having bowed to that soul of sacrifice, the one born from the body of the god Brahmā questioned him regarding this very matter which you have asked, O sinless one.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the eighth book, chapter one. 530
Nārada said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, Purāṇa-Puruṣottama, support of the universe, omniscient one, you whose noble virtues are worthy of praise! (9)
Tell me, as I desire, that which is the primordial reality of the world;
from where indeed is this born, and upon what is it established? (10)
When will its end be reached? At what time does the arising of all fruits occur? By knowing what would this illusion—the ground of delusion—come to destruction? (11)
O Lord, by what worship, by what recitation, or by what meditation within the lotus of one's own heart does illumination arise, like the rising of the sun in the darkness? (12)
O Lord, speak this answer to the question in its entirety and without omission, so that the world may easily cross over this profound darkness. (13)
Vyāsa said:
Thus questioned by the celestial sage, the ancient and best of sages,
the great yogi Nārāyaṇa, greeted him and spoke these words.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O best of divine sages, here is the supreme reality of the world,
by knowing which a mortal indeed is no longer born into the delusion of the world.
"Listen, O Goddess, to the reality of the world"— thus have I indeed spoken,
as well as the sages, gods, gandharvas, and other wise men.
That Goddess creates the world, and by her it is sustained.
And by that [ignorance], everything is destroyed; thus it has been declared from the perspective of the three qualities.
I shall describe the true nature of that Goddess, who is worshipped by the Siddhas and the Ṛṣis;
she destroys all sins for those who remember her, and likewise grants desires as well as liberation.
The first Manu was Svāyaṃbhuva, the powerful son of the Lotus-born One.
The illustrious lord of Śatarūpā, the sovereign of all the Manus.
In former times, Manu served his father, the god Prajāpati, who is free from all blemish, with devotion; then the Self-born One spoke to his son.
"O son, O son, you must perform the supreme worship of the Goddess;
by her grace, my dear, the creation of progeny shall be accomplished for you.
Having been addressed thus, the all-pervading Manu Svāyambhuva, the creator of progeny and the cosmic Virāj, then gratified the Goddess, the source of the universe, through austerity.
With a concentrated mind, he indeed praised the goddess, the queen of gods—the primordial Māyā, the possessor of all powers, the cause of all causes. (23)
Manu said:
Salutations, salutations to you, O Goddess of gods, the cause of the cause of the universe;
you who hold the conch, the discus, and the mace in your hands, and who reside within the heart of Nārāyaṇa. 24.
O embodiment of the Vedas, Mother of the World, whose form is the causal abode; O Śivā, who knows the authority of the three Vedas and is praised by all the gods! 25.
O Maheśvarī! O highly fortunate one! O Mahāmāyā! O source of great prosperity! O abode of Mahādeva’s beloved! O bringer of delight to Mahādeva!
O elder sister of Gopendra’s beloved! O Great Bliss! O Great Festival! 26.
Homage to you, who removes the fear of great pestilence, and who is worshipped by gods and others. ||27||
O auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, O Śivā, who accomplishes all goals,
O refuge, O Tryambakā, O Gaurī, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations be to you!
Since this entire universe is in every way woven across and through this, it is a single consciousness—without beginning or end—a treasury of splendors. (29)
By his mere glance, Brahmā always performs all [creation], and Hari likewise protects;
by whose grace the Lord of the Universe is the destroyer.
The Lotus-born [Brahmā] was afflicted by the fear arising from Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
By whose hymn of praise [the sage] was liberated from the terrible ocean of existence as a Daitya. ||31||
You are modesty, fame, mindfulness, splendor, Lakṣmī, and Satī, the daughter of the mountain;
you are the daughter of Dakṣa, the womb of the Vedas, the bestower of perfection, and forever fearless.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter two:
"I shall praise you, I bow to you, I worship you, and I chant your name."
I meditate, I contemplate, I behold, and I shall hear; O Goddess, be gracious to me! 33.
Brahmā, the treasure-house of the Vedas; Kṛṣṇa, the abode of Lakṣmī; Purandara;
the sovereign of the three worlds; the wielder of the noose; and the supreme lord of aquatic creatures.
Kubera became the lord of treasures, Yama was born as the king of the departed; Nairṛta became the lord of the Rākṣasas, and Soma was indeed born consisting of water.
O Lord of the World, worshipped by the three worlds, you whose form is the embodiment of supreme auspiciousness!
Homage be unto you; again and yet again, O Mother of the Universe, salutations, salutations! (36)
Nārāyaṇa said: Thus praised, the supreme Goddess Durgā, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, spoke these words, O divine sage, to the son of Brahmā: || 37 ||
The Goddess said: "Choose a boon, O Indra among kings, O son of Brahmā, whatever you desire;
for I am pleased here by this hymn of praise, by your devotion, and by your worship. (38)
Manu said:
"O Goddess, O most excellent among the compassionate, if you are pleased with my devotion, then by your command may the creation of progeny proceed without obstacle. (39)
The illustrious Goddess said: "O Indra among kings, by my grace, let the creation of progeny indeed proceed without obstacle, and may there be ever-increasing prosperity. (40)
O Lord, for whoever always recites this hymn composed by you with devotion to me, there shall indeed be the attainment of knowledge, progeny, fame, and the rising of splendor. (41)
Wealth and grain abound, and the power of men remains unassailed;
there is victory everywhere, O King, as well as happiness and the destruction of enemies. (42)
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having thus granted these boons to Manu, the son of Brahmā,
the Goddess vanished from sight even as that wise one was looking on.
Then the powerful king, the son of Brahmā, having obtained the boon, said to Brahmā: "O Father, let a secluded place be granted to me."
"Command me without delay as to that place where, having established myself, I shall create abundant progeny and worship the Lord of Gods with sacrifices. (45)
Having heard these words of his son, the all-pervading Lord Prajāpatipati reflected for a very long time: "How is this matter to be accomplished?"
As I was creating, a vast period of time, infinite in number, has passed;
the earth, submerged and overwhelmed by waters, has sunk and become entirely dissolved into the primordial fluid (rasa). 47.
The Blessed One, the primordial Person, will perform this task conceived by my mind; for I have taken refuge in his command as my companion. (48)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Cosmos," in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 1 ||
Then begins the second chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O scorcher of foes, while the lotus-born one was thus reflecting, [the following occurred].
By the eminent sages such as Manu and others, and by Marīci and the rest, on all sides.
O sinless one, as Viriñci was thus meditating, a young boar the size of a single finger suddenly emerged from the tip of his nose.
Even as he was looking on, O Nārada, it grew to the size of an elephant in a mere moment; indeed, that was most wonderful.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the eighth book, chapter two.
O Nārada, having seen that boar-form, the lotus-born Brahmā, along with Marīci and the other chief sages and Sanaka and the others, began to reflect.
"What is this divine being that has taken the guise of a pig?
This most wonderful thing has arisen, having emerged from its snout. (5)
"One moment he was seen as no more than the tip of a thumb, and the next he was like the king of mountains;
is this the Blessed One, or is it my sacrifice that troubles my mind?"
While that Brahmā, the Supreme Self, was thus reflecting,
the Blessed Lord, in the form of a boar, roared like a mountain.
Making the far reaches of the quarters resound with the mere sound of his own roar, he delighted Viriñci and the assembled best of the twice-born.
Hearing that deep, rumbling sound which portended the destruction of their own suffering,
the foremost of the immortals dwelling in Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka [were moved].
O best of the twice-born, they enveloped the primordial Puruṣa with excellent hymns consisting of meters, arising from the Ṛg, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, and with sacred utterances.
Having heard their hymn of praise, the primordial Lord Hari, the Sovereign,
having favored them by a mere glance of compassion, entered the waters.
At its edge, afflicted by the blows of twenty cruel bristles, the ocean then spoke as if in distress: "Protect me, O Destroyer of those who seek refuge!
Having heard these words spoken by the ocean, Hari, the Lord, [responded].
Tearing apart the aquatic creatures, the Lord went into the depths of the water. || 13 ||
Running hither and thither and searching the earth,
the Lord of All gradually reached the ground, sniffing it again and again.
Then that Lord of the Gods of gods extracted with his tusk that earth which had gone into the water and serves as the support for all sentient beings.
Having lifted her up with the tip of his tusk, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Person of Sacrifice,
shone like a world-elephant after lifting up a lotus-pond.
Seeing him, Viriñci, that Manu, the self-ruling lord of gods,
praised with words the Lord of Gods, who had lifted up the earth with his tusk.
Brahmā said:
Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one, destroyer of the afflictions of your devotees!
You who have humbled the support of the gods and who bestow the fruits of all desires.
And this earth, O King, shines as your domain, like a lotus-pond rich with beautiful petals upturned by the trunk of a mighty elephant. (19)
And this body of yours shines by contact with the earth, resembling the body of a lordly elephant with its trunk-tip raised like a lotus stalk.
Salutations, salutations to you, O Lord of Gods, the cause of creation and destruction;
O Lord who has assumed various forms for the sake of destroying the Dānavas.
Let there be salutation to You in front, and salutation, salutation behind;
O support of all the immortals, O Great Abode, let there be salutation to You.
"By you I have been appointed to the creation of beings, empowered by your power;
under the authority of your command, I perform the work of creation and transformation. (23)
O Lord of Gods, O Hari, in ancient times, with you as their ally,
all the immortals divided the nectar according to the time and according to their strength.
By your command, Indra obtained the sovereignty of the three worlds;
worshipped by the hosts of gods, he enjoys abundant prosperity.
Having attained the state of fire through its various divisions such as the digestive fire (jāṭhara) and others, it likewise provides nourishment for gods, asuras, and humans. ||26||
Then Dharmarāja, the sovereign of the ancestors and the witness of all actions, is the bestower of the fruits of deeds; he is the supreme lord by your command. (27)
Nairṛta, the lord of the Rākṣasas, the sacrifice that destroys obstacles, and the witness of the actions of all living beings—all these are born from you. (28)
Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, the world-protector, and the sovereign of the waters, attained the status of a world-guardian by relying on the strength of your command. (29)
Vāyu, the bearer of fragrance and the cause of the vital breath of all beings, has been born by your command as a guardian of the world and a teacher of the universe. (30)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, eighth book, chapter three:
Kubera is the source of livelihood for the Kinnaras and other Yakṣas.
Included within your command, you have become honored among all the lords of the worlds. ||31||
Īśāna is the lord of all Rudras, the sovereign who brings an end to Īśvara; born as one to be venerated by the lords of the world, he is the protector of all the gods. ||32||
We pay homage to you, the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, from whose portions all the gods have indeed been born by the thousands. (33)
Nārada said:
Thus praised by the Creator of the Universe, the Blessed One, the Primordial Person, bestowed his grace merely by casting a glance in sport.
Right there, he beheld the great Asura Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa who had arrived.
As he was traversing the path, Hari struck him fearfully with his mace.
With his limbs smeared by the mud of that blood, the Lord, the Primordial Person,
having effortlessly lifted the earth from the waters with his tusk,
the Master of the Lords of the Worlds, established her [in her place] and departed for his own abode.
This supreme lifting up of the earth by the Blessed One is marvelous.
Whatever man should hear or recite this supreme account, being liberated from all sins, he shall attain the state of Viṣṇu. || 38 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said: O Nārada, having established the earth in its proper place, the Lord—
He went to the world of Vaikuṇṭha; Brahmā spoke to his own son.
O Svāyambhuva, O mighty-armed one, O best among the radiant,
remain in this place composed of earth and create subjects as is fitting for the beginning.

O Lord, worship the Supreme Person, the Lord of Sacrifice, according to the distinctions of place and time; O Master, perform the sacrifice with various articles, both high and low, as the means of the rite.
Practice the Dharma as taught by the Teacher, which is bound to the system of social classes and stages of life;
by this gradual application, the increase of progeny will come to pass.
Having begotten sons who were endowed with virtues, fame, and beauty like his own self— sons perfected in learning and humility, the best among those of virtuous conduct.
Having given his daughters in marriage to those who were virtuous and renowned, he remained composed,
having properly concentrated his mind upon the Supreme Puruṣa, the Pradhāna.
Through the yoga of the practice of devotion and by means of service to the Blessed One, you have attained the desired goal, which is ever to be venerated by yogins. (7)
Having thus consoled his son Manu, the lotus-born Prajāpati, having assigned him to the creation of progeny, returned to his own abode.
Obeying his father’s command, "Create offspring,
my son," Svāyambhuva, the lord of the earth, undertook the creation of living beings.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were the two sons of Manu, possessed of great luster;
three daughters were also born to them—listen to their names from me. (10)
Ākūti was the first daughter, the second was Devahūtikā, and the third was indeed Prasūti, renowned as the purifier of the world. || 11 ||
Ākūti gave [her daughter] Ruci to Kardama, and she gave Madhyamā to Dakṣa; she also gave Prasūti to Dakṣa, from whom these progeny in the world have descended.
From Ruci was born the lord named Yaja, the primordial Puruṣa;
and that Kapila was born from Kardama through Ākūti and Devahūtī.
The powerful Kapila, the teacher of Sāṃkhya, was renowned throughout the entire world;
from Dakṣa, through his daughter Sūti, many offspring were born.
From their own continuums were born gods, animals, humans, and others;
all those renowned in the world were produced as the Savartakas. (15)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the eighth book, chapter four.
And in the Svāyaṃbhuva Manvantara, the omnipresent Lord Yajña,
surrounded by the divine hosts of Yama, protected the mind from the Rākṣasas.
The venerable Kapila, the great yogi, while staying in his own hermitage,
[taught] the supreme knowledge that removes all ignorance to Devahūti.
The Kāpila scripture, which destroys all ignorance, is declared to be the specific yoga of meditation, consisting of certainty regarding the knowledge of the supreme self. (18)
Having given this instruction, the great yogi departed for the hermitage of Pulaha;
even today, that illustrious deity remains there as a teacher of Sāṃkhya.
I bow to that teacher of yoga, Kapila, the bestower of all boons, by the mere remembrance of whose name both Sāṃkhya and Yoga are perfected. (20)
This supreme description of the lineage of Kanyā destroys all sins for those who read it or even hear it. (21)
Thus has been told [the lineage] of Manu; hereafter I shall proclaim the auspicious succession of Manu’s sons, by the mere hearing of which one may attain the supreme state. || 22 ||
For the attainment of happiness for all beings. ||23||

The arrangement of the continents, regions, oceans, and so forth, which has been described by the sons [of Manu] for the sake of establishing worldly convention—thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the World-Sphere," in the eighth book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 2 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
To Svāyaṃbhuva Manu there was an eldest son named Priyavrata.
He was constantly devoted to the service of his father and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
And he married Barhiṣmatī, the beautiful daughter of Prajāpati Viśvakarman, who was equal to him in character and conduct. (2)
She gave birth to ten sons endowed with tenfold virtues and of purified souls, and also a daughter, Urjasvatī, who was the youngest.
On it is a golden ornament with a fringe. ||4||

Āgnīdhra, Śreḍhmajihva, and Yajñabāhu as the third; Mahāvīra as the fourth, and Dhṛtapṛṣṭha as the fifth; Savana, Medhātithi as the eighth, Vītihotra, and Kavi—these are the names of the fires as they appear. (5)
Among these ten sons, three were free from passion:
Kavi, Savana, and Mahāvīra—these three.
Having fully realized the knowledge of the Self, they were all indeed perpetual celibates; in the stage of life known as the Paramahaṃsa, they lived joyfully, free from all desire.
And upon his other wife, three sons were born,
renowned as Uttama, Tāmasa, and Raivata.
These sons of great prowess were the lords of the Manvantaras;
that king of kings, Priyavrata,
enjoyed this earth for eleven billion years, his strength and senses unimpaired.
When the sun shone upon the first division of the earth.
It is said that in the second part of that [night] there was the onset of darkness;
having thus observed this occurrence for a long time with his mind, the king—
"While I am ruling the earth, how could darkness appear?
Thus, by the power of yoga, I shall ward it off from the earth. (12)
Having thus resolved, that son of Svāyambhuva,
illuminating [the world] seven times with his chariot which had the color of the sun, set forth.
As that king was proceeding, the wheel-rims of his chariot fell upon the earth and, for the sake of the world, came to be known as "oceans" (samudra). || 14 ||
These seven regions were born on the earth as distinct continents;
the seven oceans arose from the rims of the wheels of the chariot as their moats.
Because they arose from that [primeval egg], those seven worlds are remembered as the continents (dvīpas):
Jambūdvīpa, Plakṣadvīpa, and the one known as Śālmalīdvīpa. ||16||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter five:
Kuśadvīpa, Krauñcadvīpa, Śākadvīpa, and Puṣkara.
And their measurement increases twofold for each subsequent one. ||17||
And it was prepared all around, arranged in an outward sequence:
the salt-water ocean, the sugarcane-juice ocean, the wine ocean, and the ghee-water ocean.
Kṣīroda, Dadhimaṇḍoda, and Śuddhoda—
these seven oceans are remembered as being celebrated upon the earth at that time.
The first [continent], named Jambudvīpa, which is surrounded by the salt ocean—the king appointed his son, named Āgnīdhra, as its ruler. (20)
In this second continent, Plakṣadvīpa, which is flooded with sugarcane juice,
the lord of that land was born as Prayāvrata, whose tongue was like a flame.
In this Śālmalīdvīpa, which is surrounded by the Surā ocean,
Priyavrata made Yajñabāhu its sovereign.
In the most beautiful continent of Kuśadvīpa, which is surrounded by the ocean of clarified butter (ghṛtoda),
there was a king named Hiraṇyaretas, born from the son of Priyavrata.
In the fifth continent, Kauñca-dvīpa, which is surrounded by the Ocean of Milk,
there was a mighty lord named Ghṛtapṛṣṭha who ruled with great effort.
In Śākadvīpa, which is most beautiful and filled with the waters of curd-cream (dadhimaṇḍoda), Medhātithi, the excellent son of Priyavrata, became king. (25)
In Puṣkaradvīpa, which was filled with pure waters and rivers,
there was a king named Vītihotra, who was highly esteemed by his subjects.
The powerful lord gave a daughter named Ūrjasvatī to Uśanas;
from her was born the renowned daughter of Kāvya, Devayānī. (27)
Having thus divided the seven continents among his sons, Priyavrata,
coming under the sway of discernment, took refuge in the path of yoga.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Cosmos," in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O divine sage, listen to the detailed account according to the divisions of the continents and regions.
Just as it was ordained by the gods for the entire circle of the earth. || 1 ||
I shall explain it briefly, for it is not possible to do so in detail anywhere;
first, Jambudvīpa is one hundred thousand [yojanas] in measurement.
It is vast and circular in shape, like the pericarp of a lotus;
it consists of nine regions and measures nine thousand yojanas.
On the earth, they are completely enumerated by their lengths and surrounded by mountains; they are well-distributed on all sides, being eight in number and long in form.
The two regions, situated to the south and north, should be known as being shaped like a bow;
among them, four are long and Ilāvṛta is square. (5)
Ilāvṛta is the central region; this king of mountains, made of gold, is well-established between the two [ranges] and rises for a hundred thousand yojanas.
This very form of Karṇikāra constitutes the pericarp of the earth-lotus;
it extends thirty-two thousand yojanas above [the surface]. (7)
At its base, it is sixteen thousand [yojanas] wide, and by that same measure it extends into the earth; to the north of Ilāvṛta are the Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgavān mountains.
Those mountains which have been described as forming the boundaries in the three regions— namely,
in the second region called Ramyaka and likewise in Hiraṇmaya— [are now to be enumerated].
In the third region, Kuruvarṣa, they manifest the boundaries;
extending eastward, they likewise reach as far as the salt ocean on both sides.
Each one is successively twice as wide as the preceding one, increasing by a tenth part from each earlier one toward the north. ||11||
These very same [mountains], laughing with their various sounds and rivers,
extend in length from Ilāvṛta toward the south— Niṣadha and Hemakūṭa.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter six.
And the Himālaya—these three are extensive in the east, most beautiful, and are proclaimed to be ten thousand yojanas in height. || 13 ||
These three boundary mountains describe, according to their true nature, the divisions of Harivarṣa, Kimpuruṣa, and Bhārata.
To the west of Ilāvṛta is the mountain named Mālyavat, and to its east is the glorious Gandhamādana mountain. (15)
These two boundary-marking mountains, Ānīla and Niṣadha, extend for two thousand yojanas in length and reach a width of two thousand yojanas;
they are renowned as the boundaries between the regions known as Ketumāla and Bhadrāśva.
And Mandara, as well as Merumandara and Supārśvaka. ||17||
And the mountains known as Kumuda, which are the foothills of Meru,
extend ten thousand yojanas in width and height on the four sides of Meru.
Those supporting pillars, radiant on all sides, are present;
and upon these mountains are found trees such as the ashvattha and the jambu.
The four mountains known as Kadamba and Nyagrodha are situated there;
their banners on the kings of mountains rise eleven hundred [yojanas] in height. (20)
Each of these has branches extending as far as its own extent and a circumference of one hundred [yojanas];
within them are four lakes containing waters of milk, honey, sugarcane juice, and pure water.
By touching which the gods obtain the sovereign powers of yoga, they enjoy the four divine gardens, finding delight in the company of celestial nymphs. (22)
The Nandana, Caitraratha, Vaibhrāja, and Sarvabhadra gardens,
wherein the hosts of immortals dwell together with their throngs of celestial nymphs.
Their greatness sung by hosts of secondary deities, those high-souled ones wander independently according to their desire and according to their pleasure. 24.
From the summit of the celestial mango tree situated on the lap of Mount Mandara,
fruits that shine like nectar fall from a height of eleven hundred [yojanas].
The fruits were as large as mountain peaks, delicious, and soft; and from the juice of those fruits as they were being crushed, [a stream flowed].
With the color of the Aruṇoda lake, the river Aruṇodā flows forth; it possesses beautiful waters and is worshipped by the kings of the gods and the daityas. (27)
O Great King, there exists the sin-destroying goddess named Aruṇā;
they worship that goddess, who bestows the fruits of all desires. (28)
With various offerings and oblations, they propitiate her who destroys all evils and bestows fearlessness;
by her compassionate glance, they attain well-being and health. (29)
The primordial Māyā is peerless and infinite; she is the nourishment that swallows the Lord, the destroyer of the wicked, and she is remembered on earth as the bestower of splendor.
By the power of her worship, [the land] is declared to be Jāmbūnada.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Cosmic Egg," in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Nārada, as for the river Aruṇodā which was mentioned by me, [it is as follows].
Falling from Mount Mandara, it would float across the eastern continent of Ilāvṛta.
By whose proximity even the wind carrying the bodily fragrance of the women who are attendants of Bhavānī, as well as the wives of the Yakṣas and Gandharvas, [is rendered fragrant]. || 2 ||
It perfumes the surrounding ground for a distance of ten yojanas,
due to the fruits of the Jambū tree falling from such a great height.
From the marrow of the bones of those who had reached the full measure of their bodies through old age,
a river named Jambū flowed from Mount Meru, which is like Mount Mandara.
Falling upon the ground, she went to Dakṣiṇelāvṛta;
the goddess, satisfied by tasting the jambū fruit, is known as Jambvādanī.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the eighth book, chapter six:
[He became the protector] of the people there, as well as of the gods, nagas, sages, and rakshasas.
Her feet are worthy of worship and honor; she is the one who bestows compassion upon all living beings. || 6 ||
She purifies sinners, destroys the diseases of those who remember her, removes obstacles when praised, and is worthy of honor by the gods. (7)
Kokilākṣī, Kāmakalā, Karuṇā, and Kāmapūjitā; Kaṭhoravigrahā, Dhanyā, Nākimānyā, and Gabhastinī. ||8||
These names should always be recited at will by men;
[and one should take] that earth which grows along the banks of the Jambū river.
Pierced by the rays of the Jambū tree and joined with the wind and the sun,
it became a great and manifold ornament for the women of the Vidyādharas and the gods.
And Jambūnada gold is said to be fashioned by the gods;
it is that gold for which the gods and lustful women always yearn. 11.
They fashion crowns, waist-bands, armlets, and so forth;
that is declared to be Mahākadamba, situated on the Supārśva mountain. (12)
From the hollows of that mountain, five streams are said to flow;
these, having descended from the summit of Mount Supārśva, fall upon the earth.
Those five streams of honey overflow into the western region of Ilāvṛta;
and as they are being enjoyed by the gods, they bear the fragrance of their mouths.
Then, from there, she who dwells a hundred yojanas away—the great goddess Dhāreśvarī, who accomplishes the needs of her devotees—went forth. 15.
Worshipped by the gods, possessed of great energy, having the form of Time (Kāla) and a large face, she dwells as the mistress of the forest and the planet, bestowing the fruits of karma. 16.

The Goddess, the sovereign of all the gods, is to be worshipped with these names: Karāladehā (She of the Terrifying Body), Kālāṅgī (She of the Black Limbs), and Kāmakoṭipravartinī (She who Governs the Pinnacle of Desire). 17.
Thus, from the branches of that banyan tree named Śatabala, which grows upon the Kumuda mountain,
rivers flow downward from its trunks and emerge from the summit of Kumuda.
With milk, curd, honey, ghee, molasses, food, and other offerings, as well as beds, seats, ornaments, and so forth, they shall all be fulfillers of every desire for you. (19)
To the north of Ilāvṛta, they flood it on all sides;
in that place resides the goddess Mīnākṣī, who is worshipped by gods and asuras.
Clad in blue garments, with a fierce countenance and dark tresses,
she is the bestower of fruits and the granter of boons to the celestial hosts of the gods.
She is highly esteemed and most worthy of worship, possessing the gait of an elephant in rut;
she intoxicates with passion, is fond of honor, and dwells within those who cherish honor. 22.
She who bears the onset of Māra, who is worshipped by Māra, and who is the subduer of Māra;
she who is enriched with the splendor of the excellent peacock, and whose womb is the vehicle of the crested one (Śiva). 23.
By these names and words, that goddess Mīnalocanā,
who bestows honor upon those who recite and remember her and who is united with the Lord, is to be praised.
For those people whose minds are intent on drinking the water of those rivers,
the signs of aging— such as wrinkles and graying hair— shall never occur.

Fatigue, perspiration, and other foul odors; the delusions of old age, disease, and death; cold, heat, wind, discoloration, and the accumulation of facial afflictions—these calamities do not arise, and there would be happiness for as long as one lives.
Indeed, that happiness would be continuous and unsurpassed.
Thereafter, I shall describe the arrangement of that lord of mountains, Sumeru, who is indeed named Suvarṇamaya, as well as the individual mountains [surrounding him].
Like twenty petals around a flower's pericarp,
all those mountains have become like filaments at the base of Mount Meru.
And they were prepared all around for those who heard their names:
Kuraṅga, Kuraga, Kusuṃbha, and Vikaṅkata. (30)
Trikūṭa, Śiśira, Pataṅga, Rucaka, Niṣadha, Śinīvāsa, Kapila, and Śaṅkha. (31)
Vaidūryacāru, Viś, Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, Nāga, Kālañjara, and Nārada—these are the twenty. (32)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 6 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the eighth book, chapter seven.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
To the east of Mount Meru, at a distance of eighteen yojanas, there are two [mountains].
Extending for a thousand [yojanas] and rising to a height of a thousand,
these two excellent mountains, Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa,
are situated to the west of Meru; the other is Pāriyātra.
Pāriyātra—these two are renowned for their height and extent;
Kailāsa and Karavīraka are known to be situated to the south of Meru.
The great king of mountains, Mahāmeru, extends eastward from its eastern base;
likewise, to the north of Meru, there are the mountains Triśṛṅga and Makara.
And this mountain Sumeru, the golden mountain, shines forth like the sun, surrounded by these eight surrounding mountain ranges.
Indeed, on the summit of Mount Meru is the city of the one born from the lotus (Brahmā);
it is laid out in the center with a diameter of ten thousand yojanas.
The high-souled wise ones, who know the higher and the lower, describe the city as being made of gold and perfectly square.
Beyond that city of the worlds, there are eight cities of blessings,
renowned for their golden forms, situated according to their respective directions.
Just as Rūpa has been made with one thousand five hundred eyes, so there shall be nine cities on Meru: Manovatī, Amarāvatī, and the rest. (9)
Tejovatī, Saṃyamanī, and another, Kṛṣṇāṅganā; Śraddhāvatī, Gandhavatī, and likewise Mahodayā.
And Yaśovatī belongs respectively to Brahmā, Indra, Agni, and the others;
there likewise [is she] for the omnipresent Lord Viṣṇu, whose emblem is the sacrifice.
And, O Nārada, from the center of the aperture in the upper part of the egg, which has been pierced by the nail of the big toe of his left foot, he enters heaven.
This Gaṅgā, whose waters are filled with the removal of the sins of all the worlds, enters the head of the Lord. (13)
And this very foot of the Blessed One is renowned throughout the worlds;
yet, after a long time—specifically, after a thousand yugas—it [shall disappear].
Having reached the summit of heaven, the goddess, sovereign of the divine river, arrived at that place renowned throughout the three worlds known as Viṣṇupada. ||15||
There dwells Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, the supremely purifying one, who bears upon his head the dust from the lotus-bud-like feet of the Blessed Lord. (16)
Even today that royal sage remains, having taken refuge in an immovable path;
there dwell the seven great-souled sages who know his power.
Those who desire the welfare of all the world perform circumambulations;
this is the ultimate perfection that bestows success upon those who practice austerity.
And they honor her by bowing their heads, even those bound with matted locks;
then, from the abode of Viṣṇu, the Goddess [descends] with many thousands of crores.
Descending through the path of the gods crowded with celestial chariots,
she fell, flooding the lunar orb, into the abode of Brahmā.
O Nārada, being divided fourfold in the world of Brahmā,
that goddess has spread in the four directions under four names.
And Sītā and Alakanandā followed that very lord of rivers and streams under the names Caturbhadra and so forth. || 22 ||
And from the abode of Brahmā and from the peaks of the mountains, the celestial river known by the name Kesara flows forth as the Sītā. (23)
The form of Gandhamādana, which removes sins, has fallen here;
it has arrived from the east, situated between the region of Bhadrāśva.
Having reached the salt ocean, that celestial river, worshipped by the gods,
then issued forth from the second peak of Mālyavat.
Then, becoming Vegavatī, she arrived in Ketumāla. *Śrīmad-devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇam*, Eighth Skandha, Chapter 8. 539.
The celestial river named Cakṣus has arrived from the western direction. || 26 ||
Having entered the lord of rivers, that Gaṅgā, who is worshipped by the gods,
then became known by the name of the third stream, O Nārada.
Indeed, the auspicious Alakanandā, having been given by the Lotus-born Lord (Brahmā), has come from the south,
passing beyond forests and mountain peaks.
Having reached Hemakūṭa, the best of mountains, she emerged from here;
becoming exceedingly swift, she arrived at Bhārata as the supreme [river]. 29.
That third excellent river reached the southern ocean;
for men traveling there to bathe in it, [the merit] is at every step. (30)
Indeed, the fruit of the Rājasūya, Aśvamedha, and other sacrifices is not difficult to attain;
thereafter, however, the fourth stream flows from Mount Śṛṅgavān.
Named Bhadrā, the Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds, having satisfied the Northern Kurus with her flow, reached the ocean.
Indeed, O Nārada, there are many other male and female rivers as well in every region, produced from Mount Meru and Mount Mandara.
Even there, they indeed declare Bhārata-varṣa to be the field of action (karmakṣetra),
while the other eight regions are bestowers of celestial bliss upon the earth.

O Nārada, these are the places of enjoyment for those who have gone to heaven due to the remainder of their merit; there, the men live for ten thousand years, possess bodies as firm as adamant, resemble the gods, and are attended by ten thousand Nāgas. (35)
They were exceedingly joyful, well-satisfied, enriched with wives, and endowed with happiness.
For even women whose embryos have reached maturity live for a lifespan of one year less [than a century],
and the time always remains equal to the Tretā Yuga.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In those regions, the lords of the gods always [worship] with the hymns previously mentioned.
They worship the Great Goddess through recitation, meditation, and absorption.
The forest groves there are adorned with rows of blossoms from every season, and the splendor of fruits and tender shoots is continuous throughout. (2)
In those forest regions, on the ridges of the boundary mountains, in all the mountain valleys, and in the reservoirs of pure water; ||3||
In those very places, which were interspersed with garlands of blooming lotuses and filled with the warbling of flocks of swans and cranes; ||4||
And beautiful women sport with water-games and other diverse diversions in the abodes of graceful amorous pastimes, where their eyebrows are elegantly arched.
There the Blessed One, the Primordial Person, dwells at his own will together with young women, even during the nine months.
Known as Nārāyaṇa, he remains thus for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds;
worshipping the Goddess, he is honored by all.
Through the manifestation of his own self and through worship, he, being composed, becomes present.
In Ilāvṛta, however, the Lord Bhava— the god born from the lotus-eyed one—
dwells eternally alone, accompanied by his consort.
No one else at all gains entry into that sacred field;
due to the curse of Bhavānī, any man there clearly becomes a woman.
The Lord of Gods, being surrounded by countless crores of Gaṇas who were the husbands of Bhavānī’s women, was devotedly worshipping the god Saṃkarṣaṇa.
By means of his own self through the yoga of meditation, and out of a desire for the welfare of all beings,
he [perceived] that fourth form of his own nature, which is characterized by darkness (tāmasī).
And with one-pointed mind, he approaches the unborn Blessed One.
Śrīmad-Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Eighth Skandha, Chapter 8.
The Blessed One said: "Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the Great Person, the one who embodies all qualities, the infinite, the unmanifest; salutations! || 12 ||

I worship You, the Lord, the source of worldly existence, whose lotus feet are to be meditated upon by those seeking refuge; the supreme goal of all prosperity; the creator of beings who is fully intent upon His devotees; and the one who brings about liberation from *saṃsāra*. 13.

For one whose vision is not affected even in the slightest degree when observing the activities of another’s illusory qualities and actions—just as the Lord is not overcome by the sin of those who have conquered anger—who that desires to conquer his own self would not revere him? (14)
He who appeared like an unreal being through illusion, his intellect like the honeyed wine of those with copper-red eyes;
he was not merely a slayer of serpents, for even the lords were unable to offer him worship out of shame, their senses overwhelmed by the touch of his feet.
The sages call that which is devoid of the three—the maintenance, birth, and restraint of this world—Yama, the infinite;
it is not known to exist anywhere within the abodes of his thousand heads, like a perfected object of knowledge. 16.
From whom, it is said, there arose today that great Lord, unborn and the abode of pure consciousness, whose form consists of the [three] qualities;
enveloped by His own threefold splendor, I create the Vaikārika, Tāmasa, and Aindriya [ego-senses].
We who abide under the control of that Great Soul, like birds bound by a string—
our great ego, our senses, and our darkness— all these we create through His grace alone.
This world, deluded by the heavy weight of its own creation, never perceives the illusory nature of this cycle of karma which He has fashioned.
One does not easily know the method for crossing over; salutations to You, whose nature is both dissolution and emergence. 19.
Nārāyaṇa said:
Thus that blessed Śūdra, with his mind concentrated on the host of gods, should worship the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa in Ilāvṛta.
In that very same way, this son of Dharma was named Bhadraśravas;
the men who were the lords of his family were also called Bhadrasevakas.
In the Bhadrāvatāra, that famous form of Vāsudeva was manifested;
indeed, through its transformation into the form of a horse, it was marked with the feet of Hayagrīva.
Restrained by that supreme, unsurpassed power of concentration,
they likewise grasp that very form and approach it.
The Bhadraśravas said:

"Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, the Dharma that purifies the self; salutations! "Aha! How wondrous is the activity of the Blessed One! This person, though watching, does not see the infinite wealth [of the Dharma]. For, while meditating, he does not perceive it, yet desires to live by casting away his son and father in order to pursue unrighteous conduct. (24)
The seers declare the universe to be perishable, and the wise who know the supreme self perceive it as such;
yet even they are deluded by Your power of illusion, O Unborn One. I bow to that Unborn One whose actions are most wondrous.
For you, though devoid of agency, have undertaken the task of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe; yet you remain unattached.
Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, Eighth Skandha, Chapter 9. [Page 541]
It is not surprising that this is so in your case, for you are the cause and the effect, the self of all, yet in reality distinct from them. (26)

Salutations to You, whose efforts are rendered fruitless by others, who, assuming the form of a man-horse at the end of the age when the Vedas had been obscured by darkness, recovered them for the sake of the sage who entreated You. 27.
Thus those named Bhadraśravas praise Hari, the Lord of Gods who has the horse-head, and they describe his qualities.
Whoever reads or causes others to hear this account of their deeds shall cast off the cloak of sin and go to the world of the Goddess. (29)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
And in Harivarṣa, the Lord is Nṛhari, the destroyer of sins.
He abides with his self united in yoga, bestowing grace upon his devotees. || 1 ||
Beholding that manifested form, the highly fortunate asura, endowed with devotion and knowing the reality of His qualities, offers praise.
Grahlāda said:

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Narasiṃha; obeisance to you, the Splendor! Manifest, manifest! O you with adamantine fangs, rend, rend the latent impressions of karma! Devour, devour the darkness! Oṃ svāhā!
May there be abundant fearlessness within my self. Oṃ kṣom.

May there be well-being for the universe; may the wicked be propitiated; may all beings contemplate auspiciousness toward one another with their intellects; may the mind attain auspiciousness in Adhokṣaja; and may our thought be absorbed in Him even without cause. (3)

If we should have attachment to house, wife, children, wealth, or kinsmen, rather than to those dear to the Blessed One—then he who is self-possessed and content with the mere sustenance of life succeeds before long; not so the one who is fond of sense-objects.

The unborn Lord, having emerged from the Vedas, repeatedly touches the minds of those who frequent this sacred ford—attained through the majesty of His own prowess—and removes their internal passion; who indeed would not serve the valor of Mukunda? (5)

In him who possesses unselfish devotion to the Blessed Lord, all the gods abide with all their virtues; but for one who lacks devotion to Hari, how can there be great qualities, as he runs outward after unrealities through the power of his desires? (6)
Lord Hari himself is the desired soul of all embodied beings, just as water is to fish;
if one who is great abandons Him and becomes attached to the household, then the greatness of such couples consists merely in their age.

Therefore, having abandoned the home—the wheel of worldly existence rooted in passion, attachment, dejection, anger, envy, longing, fear, and wretchedness—what fear can there be for those who worship the feet of Nṛsiṃha? (8)
Thus that lord of the Daityas also worships daily with devotion Nṛhari,
the lion for the elephant of sin, who dwells within the lotus of the heart.
And in the region of Ketumāla, the Blessed One indeed dwells, assuming the form of Smara;
he is always to be worshipped by the lords of that region.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter nine.
By means of this net of hymns, the daughter of the ocean—who is the sovereign of that [ocean] and the constant bestower of honor upon the great—is worshipped. (11)
Rāma said: Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hūṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Hṛṣīkeśa, whose self is distinguished by all special qualities;
to the Lord of intentions, thoughts, consciousnesses, and distinctions; to the one consisting of sixteen digits, who is composed of the Vedic meters, of food, of nectar, and of everything.
Salutations to you, the great splendor, the power, and the beauty; may it be with you in both worlds.
Women, having worshipped You, the Lord of the Senses, through their own vows, seek another husband in this world;
yet for them, You do not protect their offspring, their beloved, their wealth, or their lives, because they are dependent on others.
He indeed shall be a lord, free from fear from any quarter; he protects from all sides the person afflicted by fear.
He alone is such, for otherwise there would be mutual fear; nothing is considered superior to the attainment of the Self.
She who does not desire the worship of Your lotus feet is one who is greedy for all worldly desires;
yet she alone is truly desired by You, O Blessed One, who is sought after by those whose prayers have been broken and who now suffers in remorse.
O Unconquered One, for the sake of attaining me, the gods, lords, asuras, and others perform fierce austerities with their minds fixed on sense-pleasures;
yet, apart from those who have taken refuge at your feet, they do not truly know me, because their hearts are not yours. 15.
O Acyuta, you who have placed your lotus-hand—which is worshipped even by me—upon the heads of the Sātvatas;
O most excellent Lakṣmī, you bear me [on your chest] through your illusory power (māyā). Who indeed is capable of fathoming the intended purpose of the Lord? || 16 ||
Thus, while praising Kāma—who is the very embodiment of the Friend of the World—the lords of the rain-gods, headed by Prajāpati, [praised him] for the sake of Kāma’s success. (17)
And in the region named Ramyaka, Manu constantly praises the supreme form of the Blessed One as the Fish, which is worthy of worship by both gods and asuras. (18)
Manu said: Om, salutations to the most preeminent; salutations to the Being, to Prāṇa, to Ojas, to Bala, and salutations to the Great Fish.

Moving with a mighty roar, your form unseen by all the world-protectors both within and without, you are that Lord who brings this universe under his control, just as a man controls a wooden puppet woman by means of a string. 19.
That which the world-protectors, it is said, afflicted by the fever of envy—whether acting individually or together—were unable to drink, even though they strove;
that [nectar] is seen here as something stationary, like a pillar, whether it be a biped, a quadruped, or a reptile. (20)

O Lord of wide strides, O Unborn One, you who by your own power [sustained] this earth—a treasure-house of medicinal herbs and creepers—amidst the garlanded waves of the ocean at the end of the eon; together with me, salutations to You, whose self is the aggregate of the vital breaths of the universe.
Thus did Manu, the best of kings, praise the Lord of Gods,
the Fish Incarnation, who is the cause of the destruction of all doubt.
By means of the yoga of meditation, his every impurity has been washed away;
as the most excellent of great devotees, he remains serving the Lord with devotion. (23)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Cosmic Egg," in the eighth book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata Purāṇa.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter ten.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the region named Hiraṇmaya, the Blessed Lord, the Master of Yoga, dwells assuming the form of a tortoise; he is worshipped and praised by Aryaman.
Aryamā said:

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Akūpāra, who is distinguished by the qualities of all sentient beings, who is distinguished by the qualities of all sentient beings; homage to you whose station is unperceived; homage to the Body, homage to the Shaker, homage to the Abiding; homage to you!
This form of his, which is presented by his own māyā as the nature of objects, is manifested in manifold forms.
Salutations to You, whose nature is indefinable, and for whom no number exists because of Your perception beyond all categories.
The womb-born, the sweat-born, the egg-born, and the soil-born; the moving and the unmoving; the gods, sages, ancestors, and elemental beings; the senses;
heaven, space, earth, mountains, rivers, and oceans; and that which is designated as the continents, planets, and stars—all this is the One. (3)

Salutations to you, the system of Sāṃkhya, by which this world— conceived by poets with its innumerable distinctions of name, form, and shape— is dispelled through that vision of reality known as *saṃkhyā*.
While Aryaman, together with the lords of the rain-gods, was thus praising the Lord of Gods,
he sang and worshipped the Master who is the source of all beings.
Likewise, in Uttarakuru, the Blessed One, the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa),
is always worshipped by the Earth in the form of the Primordial Boar (Ādivārāha).
Having worshipped the Lord according to the prescribed rites with a heart-lotus moistened by devotion to Him,
the Earth praised Hari in His form as the Sacrificial Boar, the crusher of the Daityas.
The Earth said:
Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, whose mark is the essence of mantra, who is the sacrificial rite, who is the constituent part of the great sacrifice;
salutations to the Great Boar, who is pure through action, who possesses the three ages; salutations to you! (8)
To him whose true nature wise poets—desiring to behold it with their minds as a churning-stick churn fire from wood—churn within his qualities; to him whose self is proclaimed through ritual acts;
to him whose self is beheld through the substances of the modes of *māyā* acting as the cause, the instrument, the locus, the goal, and the agent of the sacrifice. (9)
Salutations to You, whose manifestation is free from illusion, and who are perceived by those whose intellects have surpassed the constituent factors through analytical inquiry. ||10||

Salutations to You, the witness of qualities and actions, by whose desired attributes the Prāṇa— the source upon which Māyā rests— revolves, while the Seer desires neither the creation nor the dissolution of the universe. Salutations to You,
the Primordial Boar of the world, who, having crushed the Daitya Prativāruṇa in battle, [rescued] me from the netherworld (Rasā).
Having made his foremost tusk the point of entry, he emerged from the ocean like a sporting elephant; I bow down to that all-pervading Lord.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter eleven.
In this region of Kiṃpuruṣa, Śrī Hanumān praises the Blessed One, the son of Daśaratha, the Lord of all, the divine Sītārāma, the primordial Puruṣa. || 13 ||
Hanūmān said:
"Oṃ, obeisances to the Blessed One, the one of supreme renown; obeisances to him whose character and vows possess the marks of nobility;

obeisances to the self-disciplined one who has instructed the world; obeisances to the one who refines the reputation of the virtuous; obeisances to the god who is devoted to the brāhmaṇas, the Great Person."
Salutation to the one of great fortune.
I take refuge in that which is my singular self, consisting of pure experience, by whose own splendor the arrangement of the qualities has been destroyed;
which is inward-turned, tranquil, perceived by the wise, and is indeed nameless, formless, and devoid of "I-ness."
The descent of the Lord into the mortal world for the instruction of mortals was indeed solely for the purpose of slaying the Rākṣasas;
otherwise, how could there be such sufferings caused by Sītā for the Self-sufficient Lord who delights in his own self? (15)
Indeed, that Blessed Vāsudeva, the dearest friend of those who possess a self, is not attached to the three worlds;
He would not suffer the distress caused by a woman, nor could He ever abandon Lakṣmaṇa.
Surely neither noble birth, nor great fortune, nor eloquence, nor intellect, nor physical form is the cause of being honored;
for despite these qualities, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa has, alas, made even the forest-dwellers his friends.

Whether he be a god, an asura, a human, or even a non-human, whoever with his whole being worships Rāma—the supreme knower of good deeds, Hari in human form—who led the people of Kośala from the north to heaven; (18)
Nārāyaṇa said: Thus, in the land of Kiṃpuruṣa, Hanumān, the best of monkeys, [beheld] Rāma, whose promise is true, firm in his vows, and whose eyes are like lotus petals.
He praises, sings, and worships with devotion in every way—
he who hears this wonderful narrative of Rāmacandra.
With his soul purified of all sins, he attains the same world as Rāma. || 20 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
In this land known as Bhārata-varṣa, I am the primordial Puruṣa.
I remain here, and you yourself offer praise to me incessantly. ||1||

Nārada said: "Om! Salutations to the Blessed One, whose nature is tranquility, who has ceased from the sense of self; salutations to Him whose only wealth is His lack of possessions, the bull among sages, Nara-Nārāyaṇa; salutations again and again to the supreme teacher of the Paramahaṃsas, the sovereign Lord who delights in the Self."
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the eighth book, chapter eleven. (Page 545) [Verse 515]

Salutations to that unattached, distinct witness— the agent in creation and other cosmic processes who is neither bound nor slain even while situated within the body by bodily afflictions, and who, as the seer, is not defiled by the qualities of the seen.
For this is the skill in yoga, O Lord of Yoga, which the Blessed Hiraṇyagarbha proclaimed:
that at the time of death, one who has cast off the miserable body should fix the mind with devotion upon you, who are beyond all qualities (nirguṇa). ||3||

Just as one who is greedy for sensual pleasures in this world and the next, brooding over children, wives, and wealth, might fear some calamity from an evil deed—that effort of his is merely exhaustion. (4)

Therefore, O Lord Adhokṣaja, please grant us that yoga born of Your own nature, by which we may quickly shatter this "I-ness" and "mine-ness" bestowed upon our wretched bodies through Your Māyā—a shattering so difficult to achieve. 5.

In a single moment, that Lord of the gods of gods, who pervades the universe, traverses two thousand yojanas and more— a cow’s hide [of land]— continuously and without interval.

Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, therefore, let the wondrous account of the departure and other events concerning Soma and the others be heard.

The omnipresent Lord enjoys each individual constellation for thirty muhūrtas;

[the source] of gods, sages, ancestors, humans, and so forth, as well as of reptiles and all plants.

For all [these], the inauspicious [result] is declared to be mild by the best among those who know the times.

He, who is the source of sustenance for those who live for an eon, attends upon the feet of the Blessed One, [the master] of all the hosts of luminaries—the planets, constellations, stars, and so forth. (4)

Arranged within the Kālacakra according to the division of internal and external, they are impelled by the wind while firmly supported by the Pole Star (dhruva). || 8 ||
Until the end of the kalpa, they move through the sky like hawks and other birds;

O Sage, for you whose head is downward and whose body is coiled like a serpent,
