The God of gods, always endowed with the splendor of the humming of intoxicated swarms of bees,
was dressed in blue garments and adorned with a single earring.
The imperishable Mahendra had his very thick arm placed upon the peak of Mount Halāhala, just as Airāvata had placed his golden tusk there.
The Lord of Gods, of noble play, the bull among the virtuous, has been described. ||37||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. ||20||
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Nārāyaṇa said:
The eternal Lord, the son of Brahmā, [described] his majestic power.
They wait upon him, singing in the assembly hall of Brahmadeva. || 1 ||

The cosmic ages (kalpas), beginning with Sattva, which are the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti) and serve as the causes for its origination, maintenance, and dissolution—He knows their path by His very glance. 2.

How indeed did He, who made the eternal, uncreated, and singular form manifold within Himself, assume a physical body for us out of His great compassion— that pure essence in which this world of being and non-being shines forth?
He of noble prowess assumed that faultless play-form in order to win over the hearts of His own people, even as the lion assumes his majestic sport.

If one should happen to recite what has been heard—whether out of sudden impulse, or if afflicted, or fallen, or even for deception—it instantly destroys all the sins of men without exception; what other refuge, then, would a seeker of liberation seek than the Blessed One, who remains as the ultimate remnant?

Who, even with a thousand tongues, could enumerate the heroic deeds of the Infinite One of immeasurable prowess, for whom the entire terrestrial globe—with its mountains, rivers, blood, and minute creatures—is like a tiny atom placed upon the crown of his thousand heads? (5)
Such is the power of the Blessed One, whose heroism is boundless and whose majesty consists of vast virtues;
he who, established at the root of the earth and independent of all, sustains the world for its stability as if in play.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter twenty-two:
"O best of sages, these indeed are the destinies for men in this world."
Just as they must go many times, being fashioned according to their karma. ||7||
And by those who always desire sensual pleasures according to their instructions, O Indra among kings, there are [only] this many [pleasures] among humans, beasts, and birds. (8)

The destinies resulting from karmic maturation have been declared, as well as those subject to the power of phenomena; listen now, according to the question, to those that are high, low, and dissimilar.
Nārada said:
"This diversity of the world—how was it brought about by the Blessed One?
Since all actions are equal, tell me that exactly as it is."
Nārāyaṇa said:
"The destinies of the agent are indeed diverse solely by virtue of his faith;
because they always consist of the three guṇas, their fruit here is dissimilar."
Through sattvic faith, the performer of action always experiences happiness; likewise, through rajasic faith, the performer of action experiences suffering. (12)
Suffering and delusion arise from faith characterized by tamas;
however, due to the gradations among various forms of faith, a diversity of fruits is proclaimed. (13)
O best of the twice-born, thousands of destinies have indeed come forth, produced by the transformation of karmas fashioned by beginningless ignorance.
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe its various divisions in detail;
here, within the interior of the three worlds, in the southern direction,
O Nārada, it lies beneath the earth and above the netherworld (atala).
The groups of ancestors known as the Agniṣvātta-pitṛs indeed abide there; for in that place,
the supreme blessings of one's own lineages exist,
which they quickly bring to fulfillment through their meditative concentration while offering prayers on your behalf.
The Blessed Lord, King of the Ancestors, when beings have passed away and have been brought here to his domain by his own messengers,
remains devoted to the commands spoken by the Blessed One and maintains self-restraint along with his retinue.
The one whose vision is discerning ordains [retribution] according to the action and according to the fault. (19)
The wise king always urges on all his own attendants— who know the reality of the Dharma and carry out his commands— employing them as assigned according to their respective duties.
Indeed, they describe twenty-one hells by number; some, however, state there are twenty-eight. I shall now describe them in their proper order. (21)
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Raurava as the third, and that named Mahāraurava; Kumbhīpāka is considered another. || 22 ||
Likewise, Kālasūtra, Asipatravana, and the Forest are cited; as well as Sūkaramukha, Andhakūpa, and Kṛmibhojana. ||23||
The Sandaṃśa, the Taptamūrti, and the Vajrakaṇṭaka;
then the Śālmalī, O divine sage, and likewise the one named Vaitaraṇī.
Then there is Buyoda, Prāṇaropa, and likewise Viśasana is considered;
thereafter come Lālābhakṣa and Sārameyādana. (25)
They also spoke of molten iron for drinking, as well as alkaline mud; then the feast known as the assembly of the hosts of Rākṣasas, and thereafter being impaled on spikes.
Daṇḍaśūka, Vaṭāroṣa, Paryāvartanaka, and Paramasūcīmukha—these are declared to be the twenty-eight hells. ||27||
Thus, O Lotus-born One, these supreme places of torment are known as the hells, which are reached by living beings through their own actions. (28)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 21 ||
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Nārada said:
O eternal sage, how many kinds of divisions of karma are there for me?
These grounds for undergoing torments must certainly be heard in every respect. || 1 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter twenty-two.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
He who indeed seizes the wealth, wives, and children of another is a wicked soul who falls into the domain of Yama’s attendants.
Bound by the noose of Time and seized by the most terrifying messengers of Yama,
he is cast into the hell named Tāmisra, a place of torment;
there he undergoes beating, punishment, and thereafter, threats.
The messengers of Yama, equipped with nooses, seize them, and he indeed falls into a state of utter dejection.
The son of Padmabhū, the denizen of hell, falls into a state of unconsciousness, rendered helpless, he who, having deceived his husband, enjoys his wife and other women. (5)
He is cast into the Andhatāmisra hell by the servants of Yama;
while being cast down, the creature becomes overwhelmed by agony,
where his sight is instantly lost and his intellect likewise perishes without delay.
Just as a tree whose roots are being severed here in this world, ||7||
For this reason also, it has been called by the ancients "Andhatāmisra" (Blinding Darkness),
because it consists solely of the thought "this is mine, this is I," arising from injury to living beings.
Devoted to his work, he nourishes his own family every day; yet, having abandoned this very duty, he shall fall right here due to his own inauspiciousness.
In the hell named Rorava, which brings terror to all sentient beings,
those creatures who were previously harmed by him in this world [suffer].
Having become those very ruru deer, they cause him torment in the next world;
therefore, the wise who know the Purāṇas call it Raurava.
The ancient sages have declared that the creature known as the Ruru is more cruel than a serpent;
likewise, there is the hell named Mahāraurava, where such a person resides.
Indeed, those who have taken birth in another body and undergo torment there are called *kravyāda* ruru deer; they cause him to be slain by devouring his raw flesh.
That foolish man who is fierce and cruel, who even oppresses herds of beasts and flocks of birds, is himself tormented by the messengers of Yama.
O Nārada, in the Kumbhīpāka hell and likewise in the Taptataila hell,
one remains for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on the body of a beast.
In the *Pitṛviprabrāhmaṇadhuk-kāsūsūtra*,
that hell-dweller was cast into a hell being scorched by fire and the sun.
Burning within and without the body with hunger and thirst, it sits, lies down, moves about, stands still, and runs. (17)
O divine sage, even in times of non-distress, the guards seize that sinful man who, having departed from the path of his own Veda, resorts to heresy.
And they cast him into the hell named Asipatravana; there, the wardens indeed strike with swords, and the denizen of hell likewise [is struck].
Running hither and thither, excessively agitated and with extreme speed,
he was cut by sword-leaves on both sides by their sharp edges.
With all his limbs being cut asunder, crying out "Alas, I am slain! he faints;
having reached the height of agony, he indeed falls at every step.
The king or royal official who punishes unjustly, that one of small intellect, enjoys the fruit of heresy while following his own duty.
If he inflicts corporal punishment upon a twice-born man, that most sinful man goes to hell;
he is cast into the Sūkaramukha hell by the servants of Yama.
With his limbs crushed by those powerful beings like a stalk of sugarcane,
he cried out with a piteous voice, fainting and fallen into a state of utter distress.
Being oppressed in many ways, he indeed undergoes extreme suffering;
for even one who is detached from harming others is not detached from the pain of others. (25)
He himself inflicts suffering upon those whose livelihoods are marked by the Lord; and he falls into a blind well, bound by the machine of that very malice.
There, he was surrounded by cruel creatures—beasts, wild animals, birds, reptiles, mosquitoes, gadflies, and species of bedbugs. (27)
There he is tormented by flies and biting insects in the darkness, and he wanders about within that wretched body like a small creature.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the eighth book, chapter twenty-two.
But he who performs the five sacrifices according to the rules yet is praised only by crows, and who eats whatever he obtains without distributing it [to others],
that sinful man is cast by the cruel messengers of Yama into the Kṛmibhojana hell.
In the terrible hell, one is cast down by one's own evil karma. ||30||
In a terrifying worm-pit extending for a hundred thousand yojanas,
having assumed the form of a worm, he himself will be devoured by those worms.
He who eats what has not been offered or presented indeed incurs sin therein;
likewise, he who by theft or by force takes gold or even precious gems.
O divine sage, those who seize the property of a Brahmin or of anyone else when there is no emergency, are pursued by the followers of Yama in the hereafter.
They tear her apart with iron balls as hot as fire;
she who goes to a forbidden woman or to a forbidden man [is thus punished]. (34)
There, even in that other world, the followers of Yama strike him with whips and embrace him with a sharp,
iron-made sun.
And the followers of Yama force that woman to embrace a glowing iron image—
this being the fate of the man who has sexual intercourse with all women and has accumulated a mass of sin.
In that hell, the servants of Yama plant him upon a Śālmali tree made of iron,
which is covered with thorns as hard as adamant.
Those kṣatriyas, royal officers, or those who follow heretical paths, who tear down the bridge of dharma—those men, having departed this life, go to the lower realms. (38)
O Nārada, those who have violated the bounds of propriety through their sins fall indeed into the Vaitaraṇī river, which is the moat surrounding the fortress of hell.
O Nārada, though being devoured on all sides here and there by herds of aquatic creatures, they were neither separated from their bodies nor even from their life-breaths.
And they are tormented on all sides by the ripening of their own karma, amidst excrement, urine, pus, and blood, as well as hair, bones, nails, and flesh. (41)
Those who are husbands of Śūdra women, who have lost their purity and are devoid of shame, fall into a river filled with marrow, fat, and grease. (42)
Those who have abandoned the rules of conduct and are devoted to the behavior of beasts go here to the lower realms, [feeding] upon feces, urine, phlegm, and blood. (43)
When it is filled with phlegm and impurities, those of wicked intent fall upon it;
then the hosts of Yama’s attendants devour these very things.
Those twice-born ones who are masters of dogs, donkeys, and the like, who are constantly addicted to hunting, and who kill deer at improper places, [go to hell]. (45)
The soldiers of Yama pierce with arrows those lowest of men who have come to such misconduct, once they have been targeted as their prey. (46)
Those lowest of men who, out of hypocrisy, slaughter animals in hypocritical sacrifices— them the soldiers of Yama shall then cast into the Vaiśasa hell in that world beyond.
Having cast him down, they thus torment him with lashes difficult to endure—
the twice-born man who, deluded by passion, has violated his wife of equal caste.
The fool who emits semen is cast by the servants of Yama into a pit of semen in the next world,
where they force him to drink that very semen.
Those who are robbers, those who offer fire [as a pretext for theft], those who administer poison, and those who plunder caravans—kings and royal officials who seize villages and caravans. (50)
The messengers of Yama lead them away to the Śvānakādana hell;
there, more than twenty-one thousand most formidable dogs [await them].
O Sage, those who are described in the Saptashati are violently devoured in the dreadful hell named Sārameyādana.
Henceforth, O Sage, I shall describe those hells headed by Avīci.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 22 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter twenty-three. 563
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Those men who always speak falsehood when giving testimony, [fall into hell].
O divine sage, those of sinful intellect engage in the giving and exchanging of wealth. || 1 ||
Indeed, they fall headlong from the summit of a mountain a hundred yojanas high into that most terrible hell called Avīci,
which is not open space but lies below.
And where a place is seen that is like water, joined with waves. ||3||
Because there is no interval [of rest] there, O divine sage, one whose body is cut into pieces as small as sesame seeds neither dies nor is one ever replanted again. (4)
Whether he be a twice-born Brahmin, a Kshatriya, or a Vaishya born of the Brahmanic lineage, he who drinks liquor here—whether he himself or his wife who has partaken of the Soma—is [guilty]. || 5 ||
O Sage, due to their negligence, those messengers of Yama indeed cause them to fall into hell and make them drink molten iron.
O you who are born of Brahmā, even that lowest of men, though he be base, is utterly consumed by fire when confronted with the mere possibility of his own [inferiority]. (7)
The lowest of men does not hold in high regard those superior persons who possess learning, noble birth, austerity, and the conduct prescribed for their caste and stage of life.
Led by the messengers of Yama, he is cast head-downward into the hell named Kṣārakardama,
where he undergoes terrible and endless torments.
O great sage, those men who, being deluded, sacrifice another man with a human sacrifice, or even women who devour a human beast, [suffer here]. (10)
Those slaughtered animals, having gathered in the abode of Yama, were all torn apart by him with his white-edged blade like butchers. (11)
O sage, they drink blood, dance, and sing in many ways,
just like those insatiable man-eaters here who devour flesh.
O son of Brahmā, even those who are innocent, whether in the forest or in the village,
desire to live when they have been approached by deceivers and made to feel secure.
They cause those who are like children playing at throwing up to fall down;
and after death, they indeed fall upon the point of a spike.
With their bodies impaled on stakes, threads, and other such things, they are excessively tormented by hunger and thirst;
they are struck here and there by herons with sharp beaks.
For those men of violent conduct who terrify living beings, when they are afflicted, indeed remember their own many impurities. (16)
Just as those [sinners] such as serpents also fall into hell,
specifically into that called Dandaśūka, where snakes rise up from every side.
O Brahmin, those with five faces and seven mouths, endowed with cruel intellects, devour the inhabitants of hell like creatures dwelling in holes.
Those who confine [beings] in wells, granaries, caves, and the like, are servants of the Kīnāśas with their hands raised aloft. (19)
And having seated themselves upon those very [seats], they restrain with fire and smoke those men who are devoted to evil deeds. (20)
If a twice-born householder should look upon guests who have arrived at the proper time with an eye as if wishing to burn them, he looks upon himself with sin. (21)
For that person of evil views as well, in hell, there are the servants of Yama, those with vajra-beaks, the kaṅkas, the kāka-vaṭas, and so forth. (22)
For even vultures, being exceedingly cruel, forcibly tear away that man who goes about with the conceit of wealth, excessively arrogant due to his egoism. (23)
In this matter, the lowest of men, full of apprehension, casts sidelong glances at everything, constantly calculating the future expenditure and income of his wealth.
With his heart and mouth parched, he finds no peace at all;
like a planet, that preta guards his wealth from the servants of Yama.
By his own karma, he is cast into the Sūcīmukha hell.
And like weavers with a man who has seized their wealth, the messengers of Yama [drag him away]. ||26||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the eighth book, chapter twenty-four.
Indeed, the servants wrap threads all around their limbs;
these, O wealthy one, are the various hells for those of sinful deeds. (27)
O celestial sage, there are indeed hundreds of places of torment for men, and even thousands more, both those explicitly mentioned and those not yet mentioned. (28)
O Sage, those who act thus enter these hells abounding in torment;
likewise, those devoted to dharma go to worlds arising from happiness. (29)
O great sage, one's own duty (*svadharma*) has been described there in many ways;
for it consists of the worship of the Goddess and is characterized by the propitiation of the Goddess. (30)
Merely by performing that [rite], a person shall not go to hell;
that Goddess, when worshipped, delivers men from the ocean of worldly existence. (31)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter of the Devīgītā in the eighth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 23 ||
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Nārada said:
"O dear one, what is the nature of that dharma characterized by the propitiation of the Goddess?"
How is that Goddess propitiated so that she bestows the supreme state? ||1||
What is the method of propitiation? How was she propitiated, and when?
By whom does she, as Durgā, grant protection from the difficult hells? (2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O divine sage, best among the wise, listen with one-pointed concentration to how the Goddess herself becomes pleased through the practice of dharma.
O Nārada, listen to me regarding the nature of one's own duty as it has been described;
in this beginningless cycle of existence, the Goddess herself is worshipped. (4)
O Sage, she protects [her devotees] from terrible calamities and the like;
that Goddess is worshipped by the worlds according to the proper rite—listen now to that procedure. (5)
Having reached the day of the new moon, one should worship the Goddess with clarified butter;
by giving ghee to a Brāhmaṇa, one shall always be free from disease. (6)
On the second day, one should worship the Mother of the World with sugar;
by giving sugar to a Brahmin, a man becomes long-lived. ||7||
On the third day and subsequent days, by offering milk to the Goddess during the rite of worship and giving milk to the foremost of the twice-born, one shall transcend all suffering. (8)
On the fourth day, during the worship, cakes (apūpa) should be offered to the Goddess and to the twice-born;
indeed, only cakes should be given, and one will not be overcome by obstacles.
On the fifth [lunar day], one should offer the fruit produced on a plantain tree to the Goddess;
that very same fruit should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, whereby one becomes a man of great intelligence. ||10||
On the sixth lunar day, honey is prescribed for the rite of worshipping the Goddess;
it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa so that one may possess the radiance of honey.
On the seventh [lunar day], O best of the twice-born, by offering molasses as a sacrificial gift to the Goddess and giving molasses to a brahmin,
one becomes free from sorrow.
Furthermore, on the eighth lunar day, one should offer a coconut as an oblation (naivedya) to the Goddess;
it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, and that man shall become free from suffering.
On the ninth day, having offered parched grain to the Mother and to a brahmin, one shall become exceedingly happy in this world and the next. (14)
O Sage, by offering black sesame seeds to the Goddess on the tenth day and giving them to a Brāhmaṇa, one indeed has no fear of the world of Yama.
He who offers curd to the Goddess on the eleventh day and gives it to a Brāhmaṇa shall become most beloved by the Goddess.
O best of sages, he who, having given flattened rice to the Goddess on the twelfth day, gives it to the preceptor as well, shall attain the state of being dear to the Goddess.
On the thirteenth day, one offers chickpeas to Durgā;
by giving those very same to a Brahmin, one shall possess a continuous lineage of progeny.
And on the fourteenth day, O celestial sage, he offers groats to the Goddess;
by giving those very same to a Brahmin, he shall become beloved of Śiva. (19)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter twenty-four: On the full-moon day, one offers milk-rice (pāyasa) to Aparṇā.
And he who gives [this] to the foremost of the twice-born delivers all his ancestors. ||20||
O great sage, the performance of oblations on those respective lunar days is declared for the pleasure of the Goddess;
it brings about the destruction of all misfortunes through the substances prescribed for each specific day.
On Sunday, milk-rice (pāyasa) is prescribed as the food offering (naivedya);
on Monday, milk is declared [as the offering], and for enjoyment, the kandalī fruit [is recommended]. 22.
O twice-born one, it is declared that fresh butter should be offered on Wednesday,
sugar on Thursday, and white sugar on Friday.
On Saturdays, cow's ghee is proclaimed as the appropriate food offering (naivedya).
O Sage, now hear about the food offerings for the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakṣatras). 24.
Sesame, sugar, curd, milk, inspissated milk (kilāṭaka), *dadhikūcī*, sweetmeat balls (*modaka*), *pheṇikā* cakes, and fried cakes in ghee (*ghṛtamaṇḍaka*). || 25 ||
Kaṃsāra, vaṭapattraka, and thereafter ghṛtapūra;
vaṭaka, kokarasaka, pūraṇa, honey, and sūraṇa. ||26||
Jaggery, parched grain, grapes, dates, and sugar-candy; cakes, fresh butter, mung beans, and sweetmeats. || 27 ||
O Nārada, it is declared that the offering of food (naivedya) should consist of citron;
now I shall describe the offerings for the various yogas, beginning with Viṣkambha.
When these items are prepared for the sake of the ritual objects, the Mother of the World is pleased:
jaggery, honey, ghee, milk, curd, buttermilk, and cakes. (29)
Fresh butter, crab, pumpkin, and sweetmeat;
jackfruit, plantain, rose-apple, mango fruit, and sesame.
The orange, the pomegranate, and likewise the jujube fruit;
the myrobalan fruit, milk-rice, flattened rice, and similarly chickpeas. (31)
O Brahmin, coconut, jambu fruit, kaseru, and likewise surana—these, in their respective order, are auspicious offerings for the food. (32)

O Sage, the [auspicious and inauspicious] determinations regarding the Viṣkambha and other yogas have been ascertained by the wise; now I shall describe the food offerings for the Karaṇas individually.
Kaṃsāra, maṇḍaka, pheṇī, modaka, vaṭapatraka, laḍḍuka, ghṛtapūra, sesame, curd, ghee, and honey. (34)
This has been declared with reverence as the offering for the Goddess among all ritual acts;
now I shall further describe another supreme means that brings great delight to the Goddess. (35)

O sage Nārada, listen with reverence to the entire procedure. On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, a person should worship a Madhuka tree and offer the five kinds of edible foods as an oblation.
In this manner, throughout the twelve months, on the third lunar days in sequence. ||37||
O Nārada, we shall now describe the offering of food (naivedya) according to the rules during the bright fortnight; in the month of Vaiśākha, the food offering should be accompanied by jaggery.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, honey is prescribed for the sake of pleasing the Goddess alone; and in Āṣāḍha, fresh butter and the offering of Madhūka flowers [are prescribed]. (39)
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, curd is the offering; in the month of Bhādrapada, sugar;
in Āśvina, milk-rice is prescribed; and in Kārtika, milk is said to be the best.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the best of froth is prescribed; in Pauṣa, the curd-mixture (dadhi-kūcikā);
and in the month of Māgha, one should offer cow's ghee as the food offering.
And the coconut is proclaimed as the food offering for the month of Phālguna;
thus one should worship with twelve food offerings in sequence throughout the month. 42.
Maṅgalā, Vaiṣṇavī, Māyā, the insurmountable Kālarātri, Mahāmāyā, Mātaṅgī, Kālī, and Kamalavāsinī. ||43||
One should worship the Goddess upon a Madhūka tree with these names: Śivā, Sahasracaraṇā (the thousand-footed), and Sarvamaṅgalarūpiṇī (she whose form is all-auspiciousness). 44.
Then, for the sake of fulfilling all desires and for the successful completion of the vow, one should praise the Great Goddess, the Sovereign of the Gods, who resides in the Madhūka tree.
Salutations to the lotus-eyed one;
salutations be to you, the mother of the world, the Great Goddess of Maheśvara, whose form is the embodiment of supreme auspiciousness. || 46 ||
She is the supreme destroyer of sins and the bestower of the supreme path;
she is the Supreme Goddess, the source of the birth of progeny, and whose nature is the Supreme Brahman. ||47||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eighth book, chapter twenty-four.
The giver of joy, intoxicated with bliss, accessible through honor, exalted by pride;
the wise one, meditated upon by sages, the companion of the Sun. || 48 ||
Victory to you, O wise Goddess of the World, who resemble a cloud at the time of universal dissolution;
for the sake of destroying great delusion, you are worshipped by both gods and demons. 49.

Salutations again and again to her who brings about the non-existence of the world of Yama, who is worshipful to Yama, who is the elder sister of Yama, and whose form is the subduer of Yama; salutations to her who is worthy of sacrifice.
She is of the nature of equanimity, the sovereign of all, and entirely free from attachment;
she is the destroyer of attachment, possessing a desirable form, and having compassion as her very embodiment. || 51 ||
Kaṅkālakrūrā, Kāmākṣī, Mīnākṣī, Marmabhedanī, Mādhuryarūpaśīlā, and Madhurasvarapūjitā. || 52 ||
Possessing great mantras, accessible through mantra, she who makes mantra dear;
she who is reached by the pride of men, she who makes the enemy of Manmatha (Śiva) dear. ||53||
O you who reside in the Aśvattha, Nimba, Āmra, Kapittha, and Badarī trees; O you whose nature is like milk in the Panasa, Ārka, Karīra, and other plants! 54.

Victory to you, O beloved of the Omniscient One, who are worthy of dwelling in the milk-vine, who are compassionate toward the pitiable, who abound in mercy, and whose very form is courtesy and compassion! 55.
Thus, at the conclusion of the worship, one should praise that Goddess of gods with this hymn;
by doing so, a man always obtains the entire merit of the vow.
For that man who constantly recites this hymn which brings delight to the Goddess,
there is indeed no fear of mental anguish or physical disease, nor any fear of enemies.
One who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth; one who seeks dharma shall obtain dharma. ||58||
The Brāhmaṇa shall be perfected in the Vedas, the Kṣatriya shall be victorious, the Vaiśya shall be rich in wealth and grain, and the Śūdra shall possess abundant happiness. (59)
The man who, being self-restrained, recites this hymn at the time of a śrāddha ceremony,
brings about inexhaustible satisfaction for his ancestors that lasts for an entire kalpa.
Thus has been declared the propitiation of the Goddess, honored by the gods;
the man who performs it with devotion shall become a partaker of the world of the Goddess. 61.

Those who have arisen from Kalā, having been constantly worshipped with devotion by sages with flowers, incense, and other offerings, are likewise worshipped in Bhārata. 157.
O Sage, village deities are worshipped both in villages and in cities;
thus has the entire auspicious history of Prakṛti been told to you.
According to the scriptures, what further characteristic do you wish to hear? || 158 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
Nārada said: "O Lord, I have heard the entire account of the goddesses in brief."
For the sake of awakening to enlightenment, you ought to speak at length.
O best among the knowers of the Vedas, tell me how she, the primordial source of creation, manifested at the beginning of the act of creation, and how she became fivefold?
O wise one, by what portion of her being she was born as such in this world of the three qualities (triguṇa), and by whom their life stories were expanded— that I now desire to hear,
as well as the account of their births and the rules for their worship and meditation.
Recite the hymn of praise, the armor, the sovereignty, the valor, and the auspicious description. ||4||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The self is eternal, the sky is eternal, time is eternal, and the directions are likewise eternal;
the sphere of all universes is eternal, and Goloka itself is indeed eternal.
Vaikuṇṭha is but a single portion of that [reality], following the path of the bowed-down state;
likewise, Prakṛti is eternal, and the divine play (līlā) of Brahman is everlasting.
Just as burning power in fire, beauty in the moon, and radiance in the sun are eternally joined and not separate from them, so too is primordial nature (prakṛti) in the Self (ātman). //7//
Without gold, a goldsmith is unable to fashion earrings;
indeed, without clay, a potter is not able to make a jar. ||8||
For the Self is not capable of creating creation without that [power];
she is the embodiment of all powers, by which it is always possessed of power.
The syllable *śa* signifies sovereignty, as well as power and valor;
she who bestows the essential nature of those two is proclaimed to be *Śakti*. (10)
Knowledge, prosperity, success, fame, strength, and fortune—
by means of these she is the Empowered Goddess (Bhagavatī), and she is eternally of the nature of the Bhaga.
The Blessed One is always said to be the Self (ātman) endowed with that [power];
and that God consists of His own will, being both with form and without form.
Yogis always meditate upon that which is of the nature of light and formless;
they declare it to be the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of supreme bliss. (13)
The Vaiṣṇavas do not recognize Him who is invisible, the seer of all, the omniscient, the cause of all, the giver of all, and whose form is everything.
And they say: "Whose splendor is this, apart from the Splendid One, who dwells in the midst of the circle of splendors—the Supreme Brahman, the Radiant One? (15)
He whose form consists of His own will, who is the embodiment of all forms, the cause of all causes, bearing an exceedingly beautiful and most captivating appearance. (16)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter 2:
[He who possesses] a dark-complexioned form. 17.

He was of youthful age, peaceful, and supremely beautiful; he was the one supreme light, possessing the luster of a fresh rain-cloud. His eyes released the splendor of autumnal lotuses at midday, and his row of teeth was as enchanting as a string of pure pearls.
He has a crest of peacock feathers and is adorned with garlands of jasmine;
he has a beautiful nose, smiles gently, is lovely to behold, and acts for the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees.
He is beautifully adorned with a pure yellow garment glowing like fire, has two arms, holds a flute in his hand, and is decorated with jewel ornaments. ||20||
The support of all, the Lord of all, endowed with all powers, the all-pervading one;
the bestower of all sovereignty, the independent one, the source of all auspiciousness. ||21||
The Vaiṣṇavas constantly meditate upon the eternal God of gods, who is most perfectly accomplished, the Lord of Siddhas, and the bestower of spiritual perfection. ||22||
It is the supreme remover of birth, death, old age, disease, grief, and fear;
it is that for which even the entire lifespan of Brahmā is reckoned as a mere blink of an eye.
That Self, that Supreme Brahman, is designated as Kṛṣṇa; the syllable *kṛṣi* signifies devotion to Him, and the syllable *na* denotes servitude to Him. (24)
He who bestows devotion and servitude is celebrated as Kṛṣṇa;
the word "kṛṣi" signifies everything, and the letter "na" signifies the seed. (25)
That Lord Kṛṣṇa, the creator of all, was alone at the beginning;
desiring to create and intent on emanation, the Lord was impelled by his own portion, Time (kāla). ||26||
Consisting of his own will, he became twofold by his own will:
the left portion was remembered as female form, and the right portion as male.
The eternal one, possessed of great desire, beheld her who was the support of desire.
And she was exceedingly lovely, resembling a beautiful lotus. ||28||
She was the supreme goddess, whose pair of hips surpassed the orb of the moon; she was beautiful with a waist that surpassed the lovely trunk of a plantain tree;
she was delightful with a pair of breasts shaped like auspicious bilva fruits;
she was graced by flowers, possessed of beautiful curls, slender at the waist, and captivating to the mind.
Exceedingly beautiful, peaceful, smiling, and with arched eyes;
pure as fire, wearing white garments, and adorned with jewel ornaments.
And who, with their two eyes, constantly and joyfully drink in the moon-like face of Kṛṣṇa, which puts to shame ten million moons? (32)
She bore a drop of musk, a drop of saffron, and a drop of sandalwood paste, along with vermilion, upon the center of her forehead. (33)
She bore her mass of hair in a curved braid adorned with garlands of jasmine, and she wore a necklace of the finest gems; she was a woman who desired her lover.
She was endowed with a full and radiant beauty polished by the light of ten million moons;
by her gait, she destroyed the pride of royal swans and elephants.
Having seen her, the Lord of the Rāsa dance,
delighting in the joy of the rāsa, performed the rāsa-play with her in the circle of the rāsa.
Adorned with various kinds of ornaments, like the god of love incarnate,
he enjoyed amorous pleasures for as long as a day of Brahmā.
Then, exhausted, the Father of the World discharged his seed into her womb—
she who was auspicious of aspect and eternally blissful.
O observer of noble vows, at the conclusion of their union, perspiration born of fatigue issued from every limb of that woman as she grew weary with the power of Hari. (39)
As she took great strides, there was indeed a heavy sighing;
then, all that sweat born of exertion drenched the entire cosmic egg.
And that breath-wind became the support of all;
indeed, the breath-wind is the support for all living beings throughout their various states of existence. ||41||
From the left side of Vāyu, who had become incarnate, there appeared Pramāṇavallabhā;
she became his wife, and their sons were the five vital breaths (prāṇas) of living beings. 42.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—these five vital breaths (prāṇas) indeed became his sons. ||43||
And from the water of the Dharma, the great god Varuṇa came into being;
and from his left side, his wife Varuṇānī was born. (44)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter two: Now,
that Śakti of Kṛṣṇa’s consciousness indeed conceived Kṛṣṇa within her womb.
It blazes with the splendor of Brahman for as long as a hundred intermediate kalpas (manvantaras). ||45||
She is the presiding deity of Kṛṣṇa’s life-breath, dearer to Him than His own life-breath;
she is Kṛṣṇa’s eternal companion, ever residing upon the surface of Kṛṣṇa’s chest. (46)
And when a period of one hundred intermediate kalpas (manvantaras) had passed, Sundarī gave birth to a supreme infant, golden-hued and the abode of the support of the universe. 47.
Upon seeing Ḍibha, that goddess was pierced in her heart;
and out of anger, she cast him into the waters within the cosmic egg.
Seeing her abandonment, Kṛṣṇa raised a cry of "Alas! Alas!
(hāhākāra), and the Lord of Gods immediately cursed the Goddess in a manner that was appropriate for the occasion.
"Since you have abandoned your offspring, O wrathful and cruel woman, therefore, from this day forward, you shall certainly remain childless. (50)
Whichever celestial women shall become portions of your own form,
they shall all be childless, equal to you, and eternally youthful.
In that very moment, from the tip of the Goddess's tongue,
there suddenly appeared a single maiden, white in complexion and captivating to the mind.
Clad in white garments, holding a lute and a book, she is richly adorned with jewel ornaments; she is the presiding deity of all the scriptures.
Then, out of fear, she became twofold;
from her left half emerged Kamalā, and from her right half emerged Rādhikā.
In that interval, Kṛṣṇa became twofold in form:
his right half had two arms, and his left half had four arms.
Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to her: "Become his beloved;
right here, O proud Rādhā, your welfare shall be secured. (56)
Thus, being pleased, he bestowed Lakṣmī upon Nārāyaṇa;
and the Lord of the World departed for Vaikuṇṭha together with those two.
And although you were childless, two sons were born to you at the end of the night;
they were born from the body of Nārāyaṇa as four-armed attendants (pārṣadas).
In brilliance, youth, beauty, and virtues, they were equal to Hari;
and from the body of Kamalā, ten million female attendants were born who were likewise equal to her.
Then, O sage, from the pores of the hair of the Lord of Goloka,
there arose innumerable cowherds who were equal to him in age and splendor.
By their beauty, virtues, strength, and prowess, all the attendants of the Lord became as dear to him as his own life. (61)
From the pores of Rādhā’s body, cowherd girls were born;
they were all equal to Rādhā, her maidservants, and sweet-spoken.
Richly adorned with jewel ornaments and eternally fixed in youth,
they were all perpetually childless due to the curse of a man.
In the meantime, O Brahmin, the goddess Kṛṣṇā suddenly manifested—
she who is Durgā, the eternal Māyā of Viṣṇu.
The Goddess Nārāyaṇī is the sovereign, whose very nature is all-powerful energy;
she is the presiding deity of the intellect of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
She is the seed-form of all goddesses, the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), and the supreme mistress.
She is the most perfectly full, whose nature is splendor, and who consists of the three qualities (guṇas). || 66 ||
Having the luster of the color of molten gold, with a radiance equal to ten million suns,
she has a slightly smiling and serene countenance and is endowed with a thousand arms.
Bearing a multitude of various weapons and missiles, that three-eyed goddess wore a garment as pure as fire, was seated upon a parrot, and was adorned with jewel ornaments.
And by even a minute fraction of a fraction of her portion all women came into being; and all the worlds situated within the universe are deluded by her illusory power (māyā).
She is the bestower of all sovereignty upon householders who possess desires,
and she is the Vaiṣṇavī who grants devotion to Kṛṣṇa for the Vaiṣṇavas.
She is the bestower of liberation to those seeking release and the giver of happiness to the happy;
she is the Fortune of Heaven in the heavens and the Fortune of the Home within homes.
She is the ascetic power among ascetics and the form of prosperity among kings;
she is the nature of burning heat in fire and the form of radiance in the sun.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter three.
She is the form of splendor in the moon and she is beautiful in the lotuses;
she who is the very embodiment of all powers resides in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul. (73)
By which power the Self is empowered, and by which power this world is empowered;
without which all the world remains as if dead while living. (74)
And she who is the eternal seed-form of the tree of saṃsāra, O Nārada, is also its form as stability, its form as intellect, and its form as fruit. (75)
She takes the form of hunger, thirst, and so forth, as well as sleep, drowsiness, patience, intellect,
tranquility, modesty, contentment, nourishment, delusion, splendor, and other such qualities.
Having praised the Lord of All, she remained there, intent upon Him.
The Lord of Rādhikā presented her with a jeweled lion-throne.
In the meantime, O great sage, the four-faced Brahmā emerged from the navel-lotus of Padmanābha along with his wife.
Carrying a water-pot, glorious, an ascetic and the best among the wise,
he, blazing with the splendor of Brahman, praised him with four mouths.
Then that beautiful woman was created, possessing a radiance equal to a hundred moons,
wearing garments pure as fire, holding a parrot, and adorned with ornaments of precious gems.
Having praised the Cause of All on a beautiful jeweled throne,
he rejoiced with his lord before Kṛṣṇa.
In that interval, Kṛṣṇa became twofold in form:
Mahādeva was the left half of his body, and the Lord of the Gopīs was on the right.
Resembling pure crystal, possessing the brilliance of a hundred million suns,
bearing a trident and a sharp-edged spear, Hara is clothed in a tiger skin.
Resplendent with the hue of molten gold, bearing a mass of matted locks,
his body adorned with ashes, he was the supreme one, the moon-crested Lord, smiling gently.
Naked, blue-throated, and adorned with ornaments of serpents,
he held a well-refined garland of jewels in his right hand.
Muttering with the five-faced [mantra] the eternal Brahma-light, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self and Lord, whose nature is truth. ||86||
The cause of all causes, the most auspicious of all auspicious things, the supreme remover of birth, death, the king of diseases, sorrow, and fear. (87)
Having praised that Death of death, from whom he is named "Conqueror of Death," he sat upon a beautiful jeweled throne before Hari.
Thus ends the second chapter in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Then the child remained in the water for as long as the lifespan of Brahmā.
Then, in due time, she suddenly became divided into two parts.
In their midst was a single infant, possessing the brilliance of a hundred million suns;
for a moment he cried out piteously, his mouth thirsting for the breast and tormented by hunger.
Abandoned by his father and mother, without refuge in the midst of the waters,
he who is the lord of countless universes looked upward like one who is helpless.
He, the Lord Mahāvirāṭ, is even more gross than the gross;
yet he is also like an atom, being subtler than the subtle and likewise greater than the gross.
This [Viṣṇu] is a sixteenth part of the splendor of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self;
he is Mahāviṣṇu, the support of all universes, yet still subject to primordial nature (prākṛta). ||5||
Within each and every pore of his skin, all things in their entirety exist;
even Kṛṣṇa is not capable of describing their number.
If there is never any number for the dust motes of all the worlds,
likewise, no number exists for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others.
In this manner, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others exist in every universe;
that which extends from the netherworld (pātāla) up to the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) is proclaimed as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter 3.
Above that is Vaikuṇṭha, which is indeed outside the cosmic egg;
and above that is Goloka, extending fifty crore yojanas.
Just as Kṛṣṇa is eternal and of the nature of truth, so too is he;
likewise, the earth consists of seven islands and is endowed with seven oceans.
It is endowed with forty-nine subcontinents, innumerable mountains, and forests;
above it are the seven heavenly worlds, together with the world of Brahmā.
There are seven netherworlds (pātālas) below, as well as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
above the earth are Bhūrloka and, beyond that, Bhuvarloka.
Beyond that is Svarloka, and likewise Janaloka beyond that;
beyond that is Tapoloka, and Satyaloka beyond that. ||13||
Beyond that is the world of Brahmā, resembling molten gold;
thus, everything—both external and internal—is artificial.
Upon its destruction, O Nārada, there is the destruction of all things;
the entire aggregate of the universe is impermanent, like a bubble on the water. (15)
Goloka and Vaikuṇṭha are declared to be eternal and perpetually uncreated;
it is certain that within every single pore of the skin, there exists a universe.
Kṛṣṇa does not know their number, so what can be said of anyone else?
Within each and every universe, there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others. (17)
O son, there are thirty million gods everywhere;
likewise, the lords of the directions, the guardians of the quarters, the lunar mansions, the planets, and so forth. || 18 ||
On earth there were the four castes, and below, the moving and unmoving beings including the nāgas;
then, in the course of time, that Virāṭ looked upward again and again. (19)
Within the child's belly there was indeed emptiness, and there was nothing else whatsoever;
afflicted by hunger, he fell into anxiety and wept again and again.
Having attained that knowledge, he then meditated upon Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person;
thereafter, he beheld right there the eternal light of Brahman.
Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, two-armed, clad in yellow garments, smiling, with a flute in hand, and intent on bestowing grace upon His devotees. 22.
Seeing his father, the Lord, the child laughed with joy;
then the Lord of Boons granted him a boon appropriate for the occasion.
"O child, remain until the time of dissolution, equal to me, endowed with knowledge, free from hunger, thirst, and other such afflictions, and having your abode in the countless cosmic eggs."
Free from desire and free from fear, be the bestower of boons upon all; be one who is never afflicted by old age, death, disease, grief, or pain.
Having said this, he whispered that supreme six-syllabled great mantra— the most excellent of the Vedāṅgas— into his ear three times.

Having given the supreme mantra— beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), ending in the dative case, consisting of the two syllables "Kṛṣṇa," followed by the fire-seed (*vaṃ*) and the word "iṣṭam" (desired), which removes all obstacles— the All-pervading Lord then provided him with food.
Listen to that, O son of Brahmā; understand it, for I shall tell it to you.
Whatever food offering a Vaiṣṇava person gives to every single universe,
Viṣṇu’s domain consists of one sixteenth part of that, while fifteen parts belong to him (the individual).
For the Self, which is devoid of qualities and most perfectly full,
and for Kṛṣṇa, who is established in the three Vedas, there is indeed no purpose whatsoever.
Whatever offering a person gives to that deity,
Lakṣmīnātha, the Virāṭ, likewise eats all of that.
Having bestowed that supreme mantra, the Lord spoke to him again:
"Tell me what other desired boon you wish for; I shall grant it to you."
Having heard Kṛṣṇa’s words, the all-pervading Virāṭ spoke to him;
meanwhile, the boy [Kṛṣṇa] addressed those words to Kṛṣṇa that were appropriate for the occasion.
The boy said:
"May unwavering devotion toward your lotus feet be my boon—constant for as long as my life lasts, whether for a moment or for a very long time. (34)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth skandha, chapter three.
In this world, one endowed with devotion to you is perpetually liberated while living;
whereas one devoid of devotion to you is a fool, for though living, he is indeed dead. (35)
Of what use is the muttering of mantras, austerity, sacrifice, worship, religious observance, fasting, merit, or the visiting of sacred fords? (36)
The life of a fool devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa is in vain;
for he does not even regard as his own self that very soul by which he lives. (37)
As long as the self remains in the body, it is endowed with power;
afterwards, once that self has departed, all powers become independent. (38)
He and you, O illustrious one, are the Self of all, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of your own will, the first of all, the eternal light of Brahman. ||39||
Having spoken thus, O Nārada, the boy ceased there;
Kṛṣṇa then uttered a sweet reply, beautiful to the ear.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Remain very firm for a very long time; as I am, so shall you become. Even when there is the fall of countless Brahmās, no fall shall befall you. (41)
By a portion [of yourself], you shall become the Kṣudravirāṭ within every Brahmāṇḍa;
and from the lotus of your navel, Brahmā shall arise as the creator of the universe.
On the forehead, there shall indeed be Brahmā and those eleven Rudras;
by means of a portion of Śiva, they will surely exist for the purpose of creation and dissolution.
Among them, Kālāgnirudra alone shall be the cause of the dissolution of the universe;
and Viṣṇu, as the enjoyer of objects, shall become its protector through a portion of Rudra.
By my boon, he shall always be endowed with devotion to me;
through meditation, you will certainly behold me, who am ever desirable, eternally. 45.
Having said to his mother, who was beautiful and resting upon his chest, "I am going to the other world; stay here, my child," he vanished from sight.
Having gone to his own world, he spoke to Brahmā and Śaṅkara—
that very moment— to the Creator and the Lord capable of both creating and destroying.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Go, my child, to create the creation; become the one born from the navel-lotus.
Listen, O Creator, to how the Mahāvirāṭ arises within the pore of the minute [Virāṭ]."
Go, my child Mahādeva; become born from the forehead of Brahmā.
And by a portion of yourself, O illustrious one, perform penance for a very long time.
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the worlds, the son of Vidhi, ceased;
Brahmā bowed to him and departed, as did Śiva, the bestower of auspiciousness.
Within a single pore of the Mahāvirāṭ, in the cosmic egg amidst the waters,
there now exists a minute Virāṭ, manifesting by a portion of the Virāṭ.
Śyāma, the youth, clad in yellow garments, reclining upon a bed of water;
with a slight smile and a serene countenance, Janārdana pervades the universe.
In that navel-lotus, Brahmā, born from the lotus, came into being;
having emerged, he wandered for a hundred thousand ages within the stalk of the lotus.
The lotus-born Brahmā could not reach the end of the lotus-stalk that served as his staff,
nor did your father find the limit of the lotus born from his own navel.
Having returned to his own place, he meditated upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa;
then, through meditation with his divine eye, he beheld that wretched man.
And while he was reclining upon a bed of water, submerged within the sphere of the cosmic egg, there was a cosmic egg within every single pore of his skin; that he made into the Supreme Lord. (56)
Having praised Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who was accompanied by the cowherds and cowherdesses in Goloka, he obtained a boon from him and then brought about creation.
The mind-born sons of Brahmā, Sanaka and the others, came into being;
thereafter, the eleven portions of Rudra are also remembered as belonging to Śiva.
And Viṣṇu became the protector from the left side of the base one;
the four-armed Lord resided there in Śvetadvīpa.
And in the navel-lotus of Kṣudra, Brahmā indeed created the universe: heaven, the mortal world, and the netherworld—the three worlds with all things moving and unmoving. (60)
Thus, in every single pore of the skin, there is a universe; indeed, in each and every one, there is a universe.
In every universe, there are the minor Virāṭs, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others.
Thus has been narrated, O Brahmā, this auspicious glorification of Kṛṣṇa, which bestows happiness and liberation. O Brahmā, what more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the third chapter in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Nārada said:
"Everything has been heard by me previously through your grace, and it was like nectar."
Now, describe the individual worship of the Prakṛtis as well.
Whose worship was performed by whom, and how was it propagated among mortals?
O Lord, who has worshipped which goddess, and who has praised which one? (2)
You should explain to me their hymn of praise, their meditation, their power, and their auspicious conduct; by whom and to whom was the boon granted? (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Gaṇeśajanani, Durgā, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī,
as well as Sāvitrī— these five are remembered as Prakṛti in the process of creation.
The worship of these goddesses is well-known, and their power is most wonderful;
their life-story is like nectar and is the cause of all auspiciousness.
Their portions are the *prakṛtis* and the *kalās*, and their conduct is virtuous.
O Brahmin, I shall tell you everything; listen attentively.
Kālī, Vasundharā, Gaṅgā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Maṅgalacaṇḍikā, Tulasī, Manasā, Nidrā, Svadhā, Svāhā, and Dakṣiṇā.
I shall relate their beautiful life stories, which are concise, merit-bestowing, and pleasing to the ear, as well as the beautiful account of the ripening of their past actions.
The extensive and great life-story of Durgā and Rādhā as well, I shall relate later; listen now according to a brief sequence. || 9 ||
In the beginning, the worship of Sarasvatī was established by Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
by whose grace, O best of sages, even a fool becomes a scholar. (10)
Just as the goddess had appeared from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa,
that woman, capable of assuming any form at will, being full of desire, longed for Kṛṣṇa out of passion.
And he, the omniscient one, having understood her state of mind, spoke to that mother of all beings words that were beneficial, true, and conducive to happiness in the end. (12)
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O virtuous lady, worship Nārāyaṇa, who is a portion of Me, four-armed,
youthful, beautiful, endowed with all virtues, and equal to Me."

If you wish to remain here, O beloved, you must make me— your lover, who understands the desires of women and fulfills their every wish, whose beauty is like ten million Cupids, and who is adorned with grace— their own beloved.
“Rādhā is more powerful than you; no good shall come to you.
O Vāṇī, he who is stronger than another is capable of protecting anyone other than that person.
How can one subdue others if one is not oneself a master? (15–16)
I am the Lord of all and the Teacher of all, yet I am unable to overcome Rādhā;
she is equal to me in splendor, and equal in beauty and virtue.
She is the presiding deity of my very life-breaths—who is capable of abandoning those life-breaths?
To whom, indeed, is even one's own life dearer than a son?
O blessed lady, go to Vaikuṇṭha; it shall be well with you.
Making that Lord your husband, rejoice in happiness for a very long time.
Free from greed, delusion, lust, anger, pride, and violence,
Lakṣmī is equal to you in splendor, beauty, and virtue.
Out of love for you, she shall always accompany you.
And Hari will show equal respect toward both of them. || 21 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth skandha, chapter 4.

By whom the great sage Yājñavalkya praised her in former times.
Due to the curse of his preceptor, that sage became one whose knowledge was destroyed;
