Then the thirty-third chapter.
Dharmarāja said:
"O virtuous lady, one who is devoted to the service of Hari, pure, perfected in yoga, and observant of vows—"
An ascetic and a celibate student certainly do not go to hell. || 1 ||
That powerful man who, out of pride in his strength, burns his kinsmen with harsh words,
goes to the fire-pit.
Having remained there in that fire for as long as it takes to pluck a hair from one's own body,
one attains the womb of a beast, tormented by fierce suffering, for three births.
That fool who does not feed a thirsty, weary, and hungry Brahmin who has come to his house goes to the Taptakuṇḍa hell.
Having remained there for a period equal to the number of hairs on his body, amidst that suffering,
he becomes a bird for seven lifetimes upon a scorched ground resembling fire.
On Sundays, during the solar transits (saṃkrānti), on the new moon day, and on the day of a Śrāddha ceremony,
a man who merely subjects his clothes to alkaline substances [commits a fault].
He goes to the Kṣārakuṇḍa hell and also to the Sūtramāna hell;
he shall enter the womb of a washerman for seven births in Bhārata.
That lowest of men who reviles the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), as well as the Vedas, the scriptures, and likewise the Purāṇas; || 8 ||
Likewise, people are always intent on censuring Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, as well as Gaurī, Vāṇī, and the other goddesses. || 9 ||
All of them go to that terrifying pit in hell;
there shall be no pit more painful than this.
Remaining there for many kalpas, one shall again enter the womb of a serpent;
there is no atonement for the offense of reviling a goddess.
Whether it be a means of subsistence given by oneself or given by another, he who takes away the property of a god or a Brahmin goes to Viṭkuṇḍa for sixty thousand years.
For that same number of years he remains there subsisting on excrement;
then, for sixty thousand years, he dwells again on earth like a dung-worm.
And he who constructs a tank on another's tank shall, due to the fault of the deity, go to Mūtrakuṇḍa after abandoning his own. || 14 ||
He remains there for a rain of those particles, consuming them;
then, upon the completion of another hundred years, that bull shall be born again in Bhārata.
He eats sweet food all alone and enters a pit of phlegm;
having eaten that, he remains there for a full hundred years.
Then, for a full hundred years, he shall become a preta in Bhārata;
thereafter, he repeatedly consumes only phlegm and urine, and finally becomes pure.
He who does not support his father, mother, teacher, wife, son, daughter, or the helpless, goes to the Garakuṇḍa hell.
O Candra, having eaten that [food], he remains there for a full hundred years;
thereafter he goes to Bhūtayoni, and after a hundred years, he becomes pure.
Indeed, that sinful man who looks upon a guest with a sidelong glance— neither the ancestors nor the gods will accept his water offering.
Whatever sins one may commit, such as the killing of a Brahmin and others, one experiences their consequences right here at the end, and then one goes to the Dūṣikā-kuṇḍa.
Having enjoyed that [food] there for a full hundred years, he remains;
thereafter he goes to Bhūtayoni, and after another hundred years, he becomes pure.
If, after giving wealth to a brahmin, it is given to another,
he remains in a pit of fat for a hundred years, eating that very substance.
He shall become a lizard for seven births in Bhārata;
thereafter, he shall be extremely fierce, impoverished, and short-lived.
Whether it be a lustful woman who makes a man drink semen, or a man who makes a lustful woman drink semen, he indeed goes to Śukrakuṇḍa.
Having eaten there for a full hundred years, he remains in that state; then, after becoming pure, he shall enter the womb of a worm for a hundred years.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter thirty-three.
Having struck a Brahmin preceptor and caused him to bleed,
he remains in a pit of blood for a hundred years, subsisting on that very blood.
Then, for seven births in Bhārata, he shall obtain birth as a tiger;
thereafter, that human being indeed attains purity in due course. (28)
That man who, upon seeing a devotee shedding tears while singing, laughs with a choked voice during the chanting of the virtues of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (29)
He shall dwell for a hundred years in a pit of tears, subsisting on that [food];
thereafter he becomes a Cāṇḍāla for three births, and after that, he becomes pure.
Likewise, that man who constantly practices deceit toward a friend goes for a hundred years to a pit of bodily impurities. (31)
Thereafter, she enters the womb of a female donkey for three births;
for three births she enters the womb of a female jackal, after which she certainly becomes pure.
He who, out of arrogance, laughs at or reviles one who is deaf, shall dwell for a hundred years in the pit of excrement, subsisting on that very filth. (33)
He shall become deaf and poor for seven births;
then, for seven births, he shall be physically disabled, after which he will certainly attain purification.
That man who, out of greed for his own sustenance, takes the life of another,
shall dwell in the marrow-pit for a hundred thousand years, subsisting on that very marrow.
Thereafter, he shall become a hare for seven births and a fish for seven births;
for three births he shall be a boar, and a cock for seven births. (36)
And by performing the rites beginning with the *eṇa* sacrifice, one shall certainly obtain purification from those [sins].
As for that man who, having raised his own daughter, sells her— || 37 ||
Out of greed for wealth, that great fool goes to the Pit of Flesh;
eating there, he remains for as many years as there are hairs on the body of a maiden. (38)
And the messengers of Yama strike him with blows;
placing a burden of flesh upon his head, he licks a burden of blood out of hunger. (39)
For that reason, in the land of Bhārata, a sinful man shall become a worm in a girl's [vagina] for sixty thousand years, and he shall be a hunter for seven births.
In three births he was a boar, in seven births a cock, and indeed in seven births in Bhārata he was a frog and a leech. (41)
One shall certainly obtain [the fruit] at the conjunction of vows, fasts, śrāddhas, and so forth. || 42 ||
Having been a crow for seven births, he who performs the rite of shaving thereafter becomes impure for all ritual acts;
O beautiful one, he remains in the cavity of the nails and other such places. 43.
He who strikes with a staff, or who worships the royal emblem together with its hair, O Bhāra; ||44||

He remains for a year measured by the duration of your day within a mass of hair, increasing in size by the amount of dust on a grain of mud; at the end of that period, due to the wrath of Hara, he enters a womb of a Yavana woman.
After a hundred years, he attains purification; otherwise, he will certainly become a Rākṣasa—he who does not offer a funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) for his ancestors at the foot of Viṣṇu.
And he remains in a pit of bones for a year of his own lifespan in that most terrible place;
thereafter, having attained a good womb, he becomes lame in seven births.
That great fool who serves his own pregnant wife shall become extremely impoverished, and thereafter he shall indeed be purified from the body.
And he remains for a hundred years in a heated copper cauldron—he who eats the food of a woman in her courses, or the food of one who has bathed after her menses. (49)
And he remains for a hundred years in a heated iron cauldron;
he shall then go to the womb of a washerwoman and [be born as] crows for seven births.
A man who touches the property of the gods with his hand inside a leather bag shall first become one with a great ulcer and then poor; only thereafter does he become purified.
And he who, permitted by a Śūdra, eats the food of a Śūdra, remains in a leather vessel for a duration of one hundred years.
That twice-born man remains in a pit of liquor for seven hundred years;
thereafter, he becomes a Brahmin who performs sacrifices for Śūdras for seven births.
One who eats food at a *śrāddha* ceremony offered by a Śūdra shall certainly become pure thereafter;
however, one who is corrupt in speech, harsh in his words, and constantly strikes his master with his tongue [is not so purified]. (54)
In the *Śrīmad-devībhāgavatam*, the Great Purāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter thirty-three:
He remains there, eating that [food] in the pit of sharp thorns.
He was struck fourfold with a staff by the messenger of Yama. ||55||
Then, for seven births, Uccaiḥśravas was indeed pure;
however, that merciless man who kills living beings with poison [is born as such]. || 56 ||
And having eaten that [food], he remains for a thousand years in a pit of poison;
thereafter, there shall be the destruction of his family and sores for a hundred births. (57)
For seven births he shall suffer from leprosy, and thereafter he becomes pure.
Indeed, one who drives a bull should strike both the cow and the bull with a staff.
Whether acting independently or through the agency of a servant, he remains for the duration of four yugas in the sacred field of Bhārata, within a blazing pit of oil and fire.
After a period of years equal to the number of hairs on a cow’s body, he becomes a bull;
thereafter, he who kills a living being with ease using a spear made of fire-iron [is reborn as such].
O virtuous lady, he shall dwell in Kuntakuṇḍa for ten thousand years;
thereafter, having attained a good birth, he will be afflicted by diseases within the womb.
A man who, out of greed for meat, eats meat with hypocrisy— this most base of the twice-born— shall become pure from that sin after a single birth.
O Hara, he who eats while making it perceptible to others goes to the Kṛmikuṇḍa hell; remaining there, he stays for as many years as there are hairs on his body, eating those very worms.
Then, in three births, he becomes born as a low-caste person (mleccha), and thereafter a twice-born;
[specifically] a Brāhmaṇa who performs sacrifices for Śūdras and eats at the end of a Śūdra’s funeral feast (śrāddha).

And one who burns the corpse of a Śūdra shall certainly dwell in the Pit of Putridity (pūyakuṇḍa) for as many years as there are hairs on the body, O lady of excellent vows, being punished by the rod of Yama.
Beaten by the messenger of Yama, that eater of [forbidden] food remains there;
thereafter, having returned to Bhārata, that Śūdra [remains so] for seven births.
That man who kills the snake that devours his black lotus shall become afflicted by a great disease, impoverished, deaf, and mute.
He goes to the Serpent-Pit, which lasts for a period of years equal to the number of his own body hairs;
there he is devoured by serpents and struck by the messengers of Yama.
He shall live as one who eats the excrement of snakes, and thereafter he will certainly become a snake;
then he shall become a human being again, short-lived and afflicted by leprosy. (69)
Through great affliction, his death is certain, as if he were devoured by a serpent;
for he kills even small creatures that have been granted their span of life by destiny. (70)
Day and night he was devoured by gnats, mosquitoes, and even ants within that pit; though he made no food for himself, he remained full of sound.
And like his hands and feet, he is struck by the messenger of Yama;
thereafter, he becomes a lowly creature and may even be born as a member of the Yavana race.
He who, being foolish, eats honey after having killed honey-bees, shall become a man without a body, without arms, and without a chest; yet he shall be pure [thereafter]. (73)
Thus he shall dwell for one year in a pit of poison,
bitten by venomous creatures, scorched, and struck by my messenger.
From that [act], one becomes a member of the species of flies; from that, a man becomes pure.
He inflicts punishment upon one who does not deserve it, and he inflicts punishment upon a Brahmin. (75)
He quickly goes to the pit of ten million Vajradaṃṣṭras;
there he remains day and night for as many years as there are hairs on his body. (76)
"O auspicious lady, Śabdakṛt has been devoured by them; struck by my messenger, he cries out 'Alas! Alas! at every moment. (77)
Furthermore, he is born in the womb of a pig for seven births;
then, in three births in the womb of a crow, the man thereafter becomes purified. (78)
That fool who, out of greed for wealth, imposes taxes upon his subjects, shall dwell in the excrement of a pit of scorpions for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
Then, for seven births in Bhārata, he will be born as a species of scorpion;
thereafter, he will certainly become a human being who is free from disease, though lacking limbs.
A Brahmin who bears weapons, one who serves as a messenger for others, one who neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and one who is devoid of devotion to Hari—[these are to be avoided]. || 81 ||
He dwells for as many years as there are hairs on his body within pits made of arrows and the like;
being constantly pierced by arrows and such, the man thereafter becomes purified.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter thirty-three.
He who, being negligent due to his own fault, causes his subjects to perish in a dark prison, goes to Golakuṇḍa. ||83||
Then he went to that terrifying, pitch-black mire, a pit filled with sharp-fanged insects. (84)
Pierced by insects like worms, he shall dwell there for one year with his hair intact;
thereafter he becomes a servant to his offspring, and from that point on, he gradually becomes purified.
And that man who, having risen from the lake, kills crocodiles and other creatures, goes to the Nakrakaṇṭaka hell on account of killing crocodiles. || 86 ||
Then he may become one born among crocodiles and the like;
thereafter, he becomes purified immediately by means of repeated punishment alone. (87)
He who, being lustful, gazes with desire upon the chest, hips, breasts, or face of another's wife in the meritorious field of Bhārata; ||88||
He shall dwell in Kākatuṇḍa with his eyes pecked out by crows;
thereafter, for as many years as there are hairs on his body, he shall be burned through three births.
O beloved of the gods, that fool who steals gold in Bhārata shall certainly dwell in the Manthānakaḍa hell for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
Struck by the messenger of Yama with his eyes covered,
he ate that very food right there, and consequently, in his next birth, [he became a dog].
For seven births he was poor, a glutton, and a sinner;
in Bhārata, he was a goldsmith who lived by the trade of gold.
O beautiful one, whoever in Bhārata is a thief of copper or a thief of iron goes to Bījakuṇḍa for as many years as there are hairs on his own body.
In that very place, one who eats seeds and excrement, and whose eyes are fixed on the seed, shall be struck by a messenger of Yama; thereafter, that man becomes pure.

In Bhārata, a thief of the gods' horses or one who steals the wealth of the wealthy shall certainly dwell for as many years as there are hairs on his body in the Vajra-kunda, which is difficult to cross. (95)
Even if his body is burnt by those fires, and he remains without food while making sounds, and is even struck by the messengers of Yama, the man then becomes purified. ||16||
He who steals silver, cows, or fine garments from gods or Brahmins will certainly dwell for a long time in a pit of heated stones, his own body hair serving as fuel.
And Kṛṣṇa also has three births; in his birth as Śveta, he possesses three births. His birth-mark is the sign of consciousness, while others are white-winged birds.
Thereafter, that man shall become afflicted with blood disorders and colic for seven lifetimes, and he shall have a short lifespan; only after that shall the man become purified.
That man who steals a vessel made of brass or bell-metal belonging to a deity or a Brahmin shall dwell for as many years as there are hairs on his body within a pit of sharp stones.
He who eats the food of an unchaste woman and lives by the livelihood of an unchaste woman will certainly dwell in a pit of saliva for as many years as there are hairs on his own body.
He shall be born as a horse for seven lifetimes in Bhārata;
thereafter, he shall be born with redundant limbs, then as one afflicted with a disease of the feet, and finally become pure.
Beaten by the messenger of Yama and eating that [food], he suffered there;
thereafter his eyes became afflicted with the disease of colic, and finally, he was purified in due course. (103)
That Brahmin on the land of Bhārata who serves Mlecchas and lives by ink shall dwell for as many years as there are hairs on his body in a pit of ink, experiencing great suffering. (104)
Beaten by the messenger of Yama, he who eats that [food] remains there;
thereafter, O Kṛṣṇa, for three births he becomes a black-colored beast, O virtuous lady.
In three births he shall become a black-colored goat; in three [more] births, he shall become a palm tree; thereafter, that man shall become pure.
He who steals grain and other crops, betel leaf,
a seat, or a bed from a king or a Brahmin, goes to the Cūrṇakuṇḍa hell.
There he shall dwell for a hundred years, struck by the messengers of Yama;
thereafter, he shall become a goat for three births and a cock for three births.
Then he shall become a monkey on earth, afflicted with the disease of cough;
thereafter, he will be of low lineage, poor, short-lived, and finally pure.
That person who seizes the property of Brahmins and thereby creates a circle of enmity shall dwell in the Cakrakuṇḍa for a hundred years, being beaten with clubs.
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, Ninth Skandha, Chapter 34:
Thereafter, he becomes a human being and an oil-presser for three births.
He shall be afflicted by disease, then devoid of lineage, and thereafter pure. 111.
O virtuous lady, that man who treats Brahmins who possess divine wealth as if they were mere wheels goes to the Vakrakuṇḍa hell,
where he shall remain for a hundred yugas.
Then, for seven births, he shall have crooked limbs and deficient limbs;
thereafter, he shall be poor, lacking a lineage, and deprived of a wife, until he becomes pure.
Thereafter, he would be born as a vulture for three lifetimes, and as a boar for three lifetimes;
then as a cat for three lifetimes, and as a peacock for three lifetimes.
If a Brāhmaṇa eats the forbidden flesh of a tortoise, he shall dwell for a hundred years in the shell of a tortoise, having become a tortoise himself. (115)
From that, there would be birth as a tortoise; in the second birth, a boar; in the third birth, a cat; and thereafter a peacock, after which one becomes pure. 116.
O Caitra, that sinner who steals ghee, oil, or other such items from gods or Brahmins goes to the Pit of Flames and the Pit of Ashes.
Having remained there for a hundred years, he shall be cooked in oil;
then, after seven births as a fish and a mouse, he becomes pure.
Whoever steals fragrant oil, the dhātrī fruit, or any other fragrant substance from a god or a brahmin in the meritorious land of Bhārata; || 119 ||
He shall dwell in a burnt pit for as many days as there are hairs on his body; thereafter, he shall become foul-smelling.
For seven births he is foul-smelling; for three births he is musk; for seven births he is a churning-stick; thereafter, he indeed becomes a human being. (129)
In the land of Bhārata, one who is powerful may seize the ancestral land of another through force alone, through deceit, or even by means of violence. (122)
He shall dwell upon a heated needle and remain burning day and night,
just as a living being is continuously scorched in boiling oil.
The embodied soul does not perish even when reduced to ashes while experiencing its karma;
however, the sinner remains there, tormented, for seven *manvantaras*.
Struck by a messenger of Yama, he makes no sound and remains without food;
thereafter, he becomes filled with worms for sixty thousand years.
From that, he becomes deprived of his caste and poor; then he becomes pure;
then, having attained his own birth again, he performs auspicious deeds once more.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the ninth book of the glorious Devī-mahāpurāṇa. || 33 ||
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
Yama said:
Devoid of compassion and extremely cruel, he cuts the living being with a sword.
In Bhārata, he who kills a human being out of greed for wealth dwells in the Asipatra hell for as long as fourteen Indras reign;
he who kills Brāhmaṇas among them shall dwell there for the duration of a Manvantara.
With his limbs severed, he dwells there constantly with sword-wielders;
deprived of food and struck by a messenger of Yama, he utters loud cries.
Maṃthāna was a boar for one hundred births, a cock for one hundred births, and a jackal for seven births. (4)
Struck by the messenger of Yama, he became a tiger for seven births, a wolf for three births, and a frog for seven births. ||5||
In the land of Bhārata, he shall then become a pure buffalo;
likewise for one who sets fire to villages or cities.
O virtuous lady, he might even dwell for three yugas on the edge of a razor with his limbs severed;
thereafter, he would immediately become a *preta* with a mouth of fire, wandering the earth.
For seven births he shall be a pigeon that feeds on impure things;
thereafter, for seven births he shall become a human afflicted with severe colic.
A man who whispers slander into another's ear will suffer from leprosy for seven births; thereafter, he shall become pure.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter thirty-four.
He who praises his own faults while greatly extolling himself, and who reviles gods and brahmins,
shall dwell in the Sūcīmukha hell for three eons, pierced by needles.
Thereafter, he shall become a scorpion and a snake for seven births;
then a diamond-insect for seven births, and after that, a firefly-insect.
Then he shall become a human being afflicted with a great disease, and thereafter he becomes pure;
for he who, having broken into the house of householders, commits the theft of property [attains this].
He who goes to cows, goats, sheep, or horses at the mouth of the Gokāmukha,
being struck by a messenger of Yama, shall dwell there for three yugas.
Thereafter, for seven births he shall be born as a cow afflicted by disease;
for three births he shall be born as a ram, and for three births as a goat.
Thereafter, that man shall be chronically ill and impoverished;
he shall be deprived of his wife and his kinsmen, and thereafter, being purified, he shall suffer great anguish.
A thief of common property goes to the mouth of a crocodile;
beaten there by the messenger of Yama, he shall dwell there for three *akṣaya* periods.
Thereafter, for seven births, he shall be a cattle-herder afflicted by disease;
then he shall become a human being, and thereafter he shall be pure.
He kills cows, elephants, horses, and likewise mountains;
that great sinner goes to the Gajadaṃśa hell for three yugas.
Constantly beaten by the messenger of Yama with the tip of his elephant’s tusk,
he shall become a species of elephant and a horse for three births.
A man who turns away a thirsty cow as it drinks water shall thereafter become pure, even if he belongs to the caste of a cowherd or a barbarian. || 20 ||
The hell is shaped like a cow’s mouth and filled with heated water and worms;
there he remains tormented for as long as a manvantara.
Then that man shall be deprived of cattle, afflicted by great disease, and impoverished;
for seven births he shall belong to the lowest caste, after which the man becomes purified.
Alas, he who approaches a woman who should not be approached commits the sin of cow-slaughter and the sin of killing a Brahmin;
and he who commits the murder of a woman likewise [commits these sins].
Even that great sinner who commits the murder of a monk or the destruction of an embryo in Bhārata shall dwell in Kumbhīpāka for as long as fourteen [ages].
Beaten by the messenger of Yama and being constantly ground to powder,
he falls into fire for a moment and falls upon thorns for a moment.
If for even a moment one should fall into boiling oil, for a moment into heated iron,
for a moment into molten metal, and for a moment into molten copper; [as a result of such acts],
one becomes a vulture for thousands of births and a pig for hundreds of births.
And as a crow for seven births, and as a serpent for seven births.
For sixty thousand years he is born as a worm in excrement;
thereafter, through various births, he becomes a bull, then a leper, and finally a pauper. (28)

Sāvitrī said: What constitutes the killing of a Brahmin and the killing of a cow? What is the sin of a preceptor? Who among men is unapproachable, and who is one devoid of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā)?
Who is the man who has not been initiated? Who is the one who accepts gifts at sacred fords?
What twice-born man is a village priest? And what brahmin is a temple-priest?
The cook of the Śūdras, and the intoxicated husband of a Vṛṣalī—
O best of those who know the Vedas, tell me all the characteristics of these.
The King of Dharma said: "When Śrī Kṛṣṇa and his image, others and their material nature, Śiva and the Śivaliṅga, and likewise the Sun and the sun-gem [are present]... (32)
O beautiful one, whether it be Gaṇeśa or Durgā, he who maintains a sense of difference between them in this way regarding any [deity] whatsoever shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. (33)
He who conceives a sense of duality toward his own guru, his chosen deity, his father who gave him birth, or his mother, incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who harbors a sense of distinction between Vaiṣṇava devotees and others, whether they be Brāhmaṇas or anyone else, incurs the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
He who conceives a sense of duality between the water from the feet of a Brahmin and the water from a Śālagrāma stone shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter thirty-four: Regarding the food offerings (naivedya) of Śiva and likewise the food offerings of Hari.
He who harbors a sense of duality incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O cause of all causes! O primordial source of all! O one to be served by all the gods! O inner self of all! || 38 ||
In Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all lords,
who by his *māyā* appears in manifold forms yet remains truly one and devoid of qualities—
he who creates a sense of duality therein shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. (39)
Whether toward Śakti, toward one who possesses the intellect of Śakti, or likewise toward the scripture of Śakti, that mortal who harbors hatred shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. ||40||
He who abandons the worship of the ancestors and the gods as ordained by the Vedas,
or he who performs what is forbidden, shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who bows to Hṛṣīkeśa, as well as to his devotee of that mantra—the eternal bliss of knowledge, the purifier of purifiers—[attains the highest state]. ||42||
Those who do not worship the Lord, the chief of the Kaṇavas and the one served by the gods, they incur the sin of killing a Brahmin and destroy themselves. (43)
Those who revile the Great Goddess, who is the embodiment of the causal Brahman, who is the very nature of all powers, and who is Prakṛti, the Mother of All; 44.
Those who [speak ill of her] incur the sin of killing a Brahmin, for she is the embodiment of all the gods, is eternally worshipped by all, and is the form of the cause of all things.
The Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī and Rāmanavamī, which bestow great merit, as well as Śivarātri, Ekādaśī, and likewise the day of the Sun (Sunday). ||46||
Those men who do not observe the five auspicious festivals incur the sin of killing a Brahmin and become more sinful than even Cāṇḍālas. ||47||
Those who dig the earth or perform the purification of water and other such acts on the banks of the Yamunā in the land of Bhārata incur the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
He who does not support his guru, mother, father, virtuous wife, son, or daughter—
being devoid of knowledge— he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who has no marriage, he who does not see a son,
and he who is devoid of devotion to Hari— he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He who constantly eats the food offerings (naivedya) of Hari but does not worship Viṣṇu,
and who worships the meritorious earthen liṅga— he is proclaimed to be Brahmā.
He who, seeing one striking a cow, does not restrain him,
goes between the cow and the Brahmin and incurs the sin of cow-slaughter.
That fool who, as a Brahmin, strikes cows with sticks while using a bull as a vehicle [incurs the same].
Day after day he incurs the sin of killing a cow; of this there is no doubt. || 53 ||
He who gives the remnants of his food to cows, or causes a bull-driver to eat [with him],
or eats the food of a bull-driver, will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
Any man who eats the food of one who has defeated the husband of a *vṛṣalī* incurs the sin of killing a hundred cows; of this there is no doubt. (55)
If one gives a quarter of the food to the fire and strikes it with his foot,
or enters the house with unwashed feet after bathing, he incurs the sin of killing a cow.
He who eats with greasy feet, he who sleeps with greasy feet,
and he who eats at sunrise— such a person will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
The twice-born who eats the food of those who have no heroic sons, of one who lives off his wife,
and he who neglects the three daily junctures (sandhyā), incurs the sin of killing a cow.
She who conceives a sense of separation from her own husband, whether he be a human or a god, or who strikes her beloved with harsh words, will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow. 59.
If one gives grain after having cleared a cow-path,
or gives it near a pond or a difficult pass, he will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
He who commits a transgression regarding the expiation for killing a cow—whether out of a desire for a son or through ignorance—will certainly incur the sin of cow-slaughter himself. (61)
If a cowherd does not protect his cow through diligent effort against royal or divine threats, that fool surely incurs suffering and certainly incurs the sin of killing a cow. 62.
Indeed, he who steps over a living being, an image of a deity, fire, water,
an offering, a flower, or food, will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
He who asserts that [the self] does not exist eternally is a speaker of falsehood, a deceiver, a hater of the gods, and a hater of the guru; he will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow. (64)
The Glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Ninth Skandha, Chapter 34.
If one sees an image of a deity, or a guru, or a Brahmin,
and does not bow out of negligence, he will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
That twice-born man who, out of anger, does not grant a blessing to one who bows before him,
nor imparts knowledge to one seeking it, will certainly incur the sin of killing a cow.
The killing of a cow and the killing of a Brahmin have been described as cases of extended application;
now listen as I tell you about those women who may be approached by men. (67)
"One's own wife is to be approached by all; this is the instruction of the Vedas.
And those other than her are not to be approached; thus know the experts in the Vedas. (18)
Everything general has been told; now hear the particulars, O beautiful one. Learn of those women who are indeed unapproachable; I shall describe them to you.

A Brahmin woman among Śūdras, and a Śūdra woman who desires Brahmins, are both exceedingly unfit for sexual union and are censured in the world, the Vedas, and by those devoted to their husbands. (70)
A Śūdra who has approached a Brāhmaṇa woman incurs the sin of one hundred Brahman-murders;
and the Brāhmaṇa woman, being equal to him in that act, will certainly fall into the Kumbhīpāka hell. 71.
The wife of a Brahmin among Śūdras, and the Śūdra woman who desires a Brahmin—
if a Brahmin should approach a Śūdra woman, he indeed becomes the husband of a Vṛṣalī.
He has fallen from the status of a Brahmin and is considered the lowest of Cāṇḍālas;
his funeral cake is equal to excrement, and his libation is like urine. ||73||
What is given by him does not reach the ancestors or the gods;
his merit earned over ten million births and that acquired through asceticism [are lost]. (74)
Due to lust for a Śūdra woman, the twice-born perishes without a doubt;
he becomes a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor, eats excrement, and is the husband of a Śūdra woman. (75)
A twice-born man whose body has been branded with heated seals, likewise one marked with a heated trident,
and one who eats on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī), shall go to the Kumbhīpāka hell.

The wife of a guru, the wife of a king, a co-wife, one's mother, a daughter, a daughter-in-law, a mother-in-law, a pregnant woman, a sister, and a chaste woman—[these must not be looked upon with lust]. (77)
The wife of a uterine brother, a maternal aunt, a paternal grandmother,
a maternal grandmother, her sister, a [paternal] sister, and a brother’s daughter— ||78||
The wife of a disciple, the beloved of a nephew, and the wife of a brother’s son—these are declared by Padman to be women who must not be approached. (79)
That lowest of men who, out of lust, approaches these beautiful women in Vraja, is considered a violator of his mother in the Vedas and incurs the sin of a hundred Brahman-murders.
Though unworthy of ritual action and untouchable, he is censured in both the world and the Veda;
that great sinner goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell, which is most difficult to endure.
He who performs the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) improperly, or does not perform it at all,
or avoids the three daily twilights— he is devoid of the twilight devotion and is an enemy.
He who does not accept a mantra—whether Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Śākta, Saura, or Gāṇapa—is considered uninitiated (adīkṣita). || 83 ||
Taking the current as the limit, for a distance of four cubits from the interior of the Gaṅgā, O dear one, Nārāyaṇa himself dwells as the lord.
One who dies there in the Nārāyaṇa-kṣetra goes to the abode of Hari; as do those who die in Vārāṇasī, at Badarī, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. (85)
At Puṣkara, at the sacred field of Hariharakṣetra, at Prabhāsa, at the site of Kāmarūpa, at Haridvāra, at Kedāra, and likewise at Mātṛpura— 86.
On the bank of the river Sarasvatī, in the meritorious forest of Vṛndāvana, at the Godāvarī and the Kauśikī, at Triveṇī, and on the Himālaya; ||87||
He who, out of desire, accepts gifts at these sacred fords— he, as a recipient at a non-ford, goes to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
One who serves Śūdras, performs sacrifices for Śūdras, or acts as a priest for a village is known as a Grāmayājī; likewise, one who subsists on the service of gods is proclaimed a Devala. (89)
He who lives by cooking for Śūdras is known as a *sūpakāra*;
one who neglects the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) and is heedless is considered fallen (*patita*). ||10||
"O blessed lady, I have described to you all the characteristics of the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī).
These great sinners indeed go to the Kumbhīpāka hell. (91)
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the ninth book, chapter thirty-five:
"Listen as I describe to you those who go to other sacred pools (*kuṇḍas*)."
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the ninth book of the Śrī Devībhāgavata, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa, within the narrative of Sāvitrī. || 34 ||
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
Dharmarāja said:
"O virtuous lady, service to the gods performed during the day does not result in the fulfillment of one's actions."
Pure action results in a pure seed, while hell results from evil action. || 1 ||
O devoted wife, that twice-born man who eats the food of an unchaste woman or has sexual intercourse with her goes, after death, to the most difficult-to-traverse Kālasūtra hell.
For a hundred years he will certainly remain fixed in the Kālasūtra hell;
in another birth he shall be diseased, and thereafter the twice-born becomes purified.
A woman devoted to her husband is known as *pativratā* in the first [period]; in the second, she is considered a *kulaṭā*;
in the third, she should be known as a *dharṣiṇī*; and in the fourth, she is called a *puṃścalī*.
In the fifth [birth] she is a courtesan, in the sixth a *puṅgī*, and in the seventh and eighth;
beyond that, she becomes a great courtesan (*mahāveśyā*), untouchable among all castes.
That twice-born man who approaches an unchaste woman, a widow, an adulteress,
a male-impersonating woman, a prostitute, or a high-class courtesan, certainly goes to the Matsyoda hell.
One who approaches an unchaste woman incurs [the sin] for a hundred years; one who approaches a bold woman, fourfold;
one who approaches a wanton woman, sixfold; and one who approaches a prostitute, eightfold.
One who approaches a *puṅgī* woman shall dwell there for ten times that duration, without a doubt;
and one who is a lover of a great courtesan (*mahāveśyā*) shall dwell there ten times longer than that.
Right there, beaten by the messengers of Yama, he suffers torment:
the partridge who goes to an unchaste woman, and the crow who goes to a bold woman. (9)
One who approaches an unchaste woman becomes a cuckoo; one who approaches a prostitute is remembered as a wolf;
and one who approaches a cow becomes a boar for seven births in Bhārata.
And he who, devoid of knowledge, eats during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, is born as a *śālmalī* tree frequented by great courtesans. (11)
He surely goes to a state where his food causes pain, and he suffers from the ocean of pride;
thereafter, he becomes a human being afflicted by disease in the stomach.
He who, being pure, gives his own daughter in marriage to another; 13.
O virtuous lady, he who steals that wealth shall dwell for a hundred years in a pit of dust, afflicted with a tumor, one-eyed, and toothless,
subsisting on that very dust.
Struck by my messenger, he shall dwell upon a bed of arrows;
and that Brahmin who does not worship the earthen Śivaliṅga with devotion [shall likewise suffer]. 15.
Due to that sin, he goes to the most terrible Śūlaprota hell belonging to the Wielder of the Trident;
having remained there for a hundred years, he becomes a beast of prey for seven births.
Thereafter he shall become Devala for seven births, and thereafter he becomes pure;
out of fear of that [sin], O twice-born one, even a dull-witted Brahmin trembles.
She who dwells in Prakaṃpana shall live for one year as a female monkey;
and she who, with a face full of rage, looks upon her husband out of anger [shall become] Prakopavadanā.
He speaks harsh words to him and indeed approaches with a firebrand; my *kṛkara* always places that firebrand in his mouth.
One should strike him on the head with a staff [the height of] which is equal in measure to the number of years of his hair.
Then she would become a human widow for seven births. || 20 ||
Having experienced widowhood and being afflicted by disease, that Brahmin woman who was enjoyed by a Śūdra, though pure, goes to the Andhakūpa hell.
In darkness where the water for purification is heated, eating that [water] as food day and night, she shall dwell there unsatisfied while being struck by my messenger with heated [weapons]. (2)
As she remained submerged in the water for the duration of fourteen Indras, she became a crow for thousands of births and a sow for hundreds of births. (23)
For a hundred births she is a jackal, for a hundred births a hen;
for seven births a pigeon, and for seven births a monkey. (24)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth skandha, chapter 35.
Then she shall become a Cāṇḍālī, to be enjoyed by all in Bhārata;
thereafter she shall become a washerwoman, afflicted with consumption and a wanton woman.
Then the oil-maker shall be afflicted with leprosy and subsequently purified;
the prostitute shall reside in a brothel, and the betel-seller shall be beaten with a staff.
The fair-complexioned woman shall dwell in a water-hole; the unchaste woman in the powder of a corpse;
the wanton woman in the crushing of leaves, and likewise the bold woman in the drying up [of fluids].
The one intent on destroying the clouds shall be struck by my messenger.
O virtuous lady, she shall constantly consume feces and urine for as long as a manvantara.
Then he shall become mixed with the class of Viṭ for a hundred thousand years, and after that he becomes pure;
a Brāhmaṇa may approach a Brāhmaṇī woman, or a Kṣatriya may approach a Kṣatriyā woman.

If a Vaiśya should go to a Vaiśya woman or a Śūdra woman, and a Śūdra likewise should go [to a Śūdra woman], those people fall into a state of impurity through their union with women of the same caste who are the wives of others. (30)
Having consumed a decoction of bitter herbs or boiled water for a hundred years, a Brahmin shall then become pure;
thereafter, those of the Kṣatriya and other castes likewise become pure.
"Women also become purified," so said the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
O devoted wife, if a Kṣatriya or even a Vaiśya should approach a Brāhmaṇa woman... [32]
He who approaches his mother shall dwell in the Śūrpa hell;
there, together with the Brāhmaṇī, he is devoured by worms shaped like winnowing baskets.
And he who eats heated urine, struck by my messenger,
suffers torment in that very place for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
For seven births he shall be a boar, and thereafter a goat; yet he becomes pure once he holds tulasī in his hand but fails to fulfill his vow. (35)
He who makes a false oath shall go to Jvālāmukha;
likewise, he who, having extended his right hand, does not fulfill his promise. 36.
He who, having taken water from the Ganges in his hand, does not fulfill his vow, shall go to Jvālāmukha like one who has struck a stone image of a deity. (37)
Having stayed even in a temple, he shall go to Jvālāmukha;
and having touched a Brāhmaṇa and a cow, and having offered [oblations] into the blazing fire. 38.
He who does not fulfill his promise shall go to Jvālāmukha;
so too shall he who betrays a friend, the ungrateful, and he who is a violator of trust. (39)
And he who gives false testimony shall go to Jvālāmukha;
these indeed dwell there for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Those who are scorched by glowing coals and struck by the messengers of Yama become pure after seven births by touching Tulasī, even if they were outcastes (cāṇḍālas). ||41||
O beautiful one, a Mleccha who touches the water of the Gaṅgā becomes pure after five births;
however, one who touches the stone [of Śiva] becomes a worm for seven births.
The Brahmakṛmi worm becomes touchless and pure after seven births;
likewise, one who gives with the right hand alone becomes a serpent for seven births.
Then that man becomes bereft of Brahman, and thereafter he is purified;
however, one who speaks falsely in a temple of the gods becomes a *devala* for seven births.
One who touches a Brahmin or others will certainly be born as a tiger;
thereafter, he shall be mute and deaf for three births.
Deprived of a wife, deprived of kinsmen, and then deprived of his lineage, Nakula was pure; yet he was a betrayer of friends, ungrateful, and a rogue.
A betrayer of trust becomes a tiger for seven births in Bhārata;
one who gives false testimony when it ought to be spoken becomes a frog for seven births.
He destroys seven ancestors, seven descendants, and himself.
And that twice-born man, being devoid of his daily rites, was possessed by dullness. || 48 ||
He who has no faith in the words of the Vedas laughs constantly and feebly;
he is devoid of vows and fasts, and is a reviler of the words of the virtuous. (49)
He shall also dwell for a hundred years in the Dhūmrāndha hell, subsisting on smoke;
and thereafter, he shall become an aquatic creature through a succession of one hundred births.
Then there are various species of fish, and then the pure;
[and he who] mocks the gods and brahmins during a sacrifice.
Having caused ten generations of ancestors and ten generations of descendants to fall, he goes to that smoke-blind darkness filled with the gloom of smoke. 52.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter thirty-six: One who is afflicted by smoke and eats smoky food shall dwell there for four times that duration.
Then, for seven births in Bhārata, he was born into the species of mice.
From that [arise] various species of birds along with various species of worms;
from that [arise] various kinds of trees, then animals, and then human beings. (54)
A Brahmin who lives by astrology, one who lives as a physician, a practitioner of medicine, one engaged in the trade of lac, salt, and poison, and one who sells mercury and similar substances; ||55||
He goes to Nāgaveṣṭa and indeed to Nāgarveṣṭita;
there, bound by the noose of the Nāgas, he shall dwell for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
Then he becomes various species of birds, and then a human being; thereafter, for seven births, he shall become an astrologer and a physician.
The cowherd, the artisan, and the dyer—these are pure;
and the well-known sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) have been described, O devoted wife.
Among them, those who have committed sins are the ones who experience the fruits of their own actions.
Furthermore, there are indeed other unknown and minor beings there;
they exist and wander through various wombs. What more do you wish to hear? (59)
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 35 ||
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
Sāvitrī said:
"O you who have reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences!"
Reveal that which is the essence found within the various Purāṇas and Itihāsas.

O illustrious Dharmarāja, that which is the essence of all things, desired by all, and approved by all; which takes the form of the seed for the cessation of karma, and is praised as the giver of happiness to men—[that I shall tell you]. (2)
It bestows everything upon all and brings about every auspiciousness;
indeed, by means of it, all human beings behold neither fear nor suffering.
They do not see those pits, nor do they fall into them;
tell me now what that action is by which there is no further birth and so forth.
What are the shapes of those pits, and how were they constructed? And in what form do the sinners remain there? (5)
When one's own body has been reduced to ashes, the person goes to another world;
with what body, then, does he experience the fruits of his auspicious and inauspicious deeds?
O Brahman, how is it that the body does not perish after such a long time of enduring afflictions? Or what is the nature of this body? You should explain this to me.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having heard the words of Sāvitrī, Dharmarāja, remembering Hari,
began to relate the narrative that cuts asunder the bonds of karma.
The King of Dharma said:
"And in the Pāñcarātra and other [scriptures]..."
O child, among the four Vedas, the Dharmashastras, the Samhitas, the Puranas, and the Itihasas, the service of the five deities is paramount. (10)
O lady of virtuous vows, among all other Dharmaśāstras and Vedāṅgas, this is the most desired, the very essence,
the embodiment of all auspiciousness, and the cause of supreme bliss.
It destroys birth, death, old age, disease, grief, and torment; it cuts down the tree of karma. ||12||
It is known as the cause of all perfections, the means of crossing the ocean of hell, that which produces the sprout of the tree of devotion,
and the auspicious bestower of the states of *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, *sārūpya*, and *sāyujya*. (13)
O auspicious lady, this is the staircase to liberation and the state of imperishability; these sacrificial pits are always guarded by the messengers of Yama.
Indeed, men who worship the five deities do not even see them in their dreams.
Those who are devoid of devotion to the Goddess may see my abode, or they may go to the sacred ford of Hari (Haritīrtha), or observe the day of Hari (Harivāsara). || 15 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth skandha, chapter thirty-seven.
Those who constantly bow to Hari and perform service for Hari—those wise ones do not go to my terrible city of Saṃyamanī. 16.
Even Brahmins who are pure at the three junctions of the day and endowed with virtuous conduct will not attain liberation without the service of the Goddess. (17)
My servants, though their conduct was devoted to their own duties and they were likewise intent on their own dharma, have now gone to the world of death; what a miserable fate for me! (18)
Terrified of the devotees of Śiva, like serpents before Garuḍa, I shall restrain you as you go with noose in hand, moving swiftly. (19)
And they shall go everywhere, except for those who take refuge in Hari’s servants and those who worship the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, just as serpents flee from Vainateya (Garuḍa). ||20||
And Citragupta, as if terrified, erases the names of those who worship the goddess-mantras with the nail-scraper. (21)
O virtuous lady, he repeatedly offers them the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other honors;
having transcended the world of Brahmā, he goes to that world.
Those for whom even the mere mention of heaven removes their sins are indeed highly fortunate, purifying a thousand lineages. || 23 ||
And just as dry grass reaches a blazing fire, so does delusion reach utter confusion upon seeing those [fires], as if terrified. 24.
Desire departs from the desirous man, and with it, greed and anger;
when these exist no longer, death dissolves away, as do disease, old age, sorrow, and fear.
Time, auspicious and inauspicious karma, joy, and likewise enjoyment—O virtuous lady, I have described those who do not undergo that suffering. 26.
Listen, I shall describe the constitution of the body according to the scriptures:
earth, wind, space, fire, and water—this is clearly evident. (27)
It is the seed of the bodies of embodied beings and delights in the act of creation by the Creator; it is that body which is constructed from the five elements, beginning with earth. (28)
That which is fashioned as the individual soul (jīva), the person (puruṣa) of the size of a thumb, is artificial, perishable, and here it becomes ashes. (29)
He manifests a subtle body of that same form for the sake of experience;
that body shall not turn to ashes in the blazing fire of my abode,
nor shall it be dissolved by water, even if struck for a very long time.
Neither by a weapon nor by a missile, nor likewise by a very sharp thorn. || 31 ||
In molten liquid, in heated metal, and likewise in heated stone, as well as in embracing a glowing image, and even upon falling down previously [into such things]. (32)
Neither burnt nor broken, he experiences only intense suffering;
thus has the account of the body's condition been told, along with its cause, according to the scriptures.
I shall describe to you the characteristics of all the sacrificial pits for the sake of enlightenment.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 36 ||
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
Dharmarāja said:
"The entire sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is circular, having the shape of the full orb of the moon."
When there is a low-lying area, it is cooked by many stone-breakers.
It is not perishable, nor is it a dissolution created by the will of Īśvara;
it is that abode which bestows affliction, consists of various forms, and is the source of sins. ||2||
The fire-pit is described as having the form of blazing coals, with a hundred fathom-high crests of flame, white in color,
and extending for a krośa in every direction.
It was filled with sinners making a great clamor,
and it was constantly guarded by my messengers who were striking them down.
It was filled with boiling water, infested with predatory creatures,
most terrible, and let out a harsh cry due to the forceful impact.
Then, measuring half a krośa,
there was a pit belonging to me, filled by my attendants with boiling alkaline water and further swarming with crows; it was filled with those who had been struck by me.
[Verse 6]
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter thirty-seven: It was crowded with sinners, crying out and filled with fear.
And by my messengers, who were struck and crying out the word "Save us! (7).
With throbbing, foodless bodies, their throats, lips, and palates parched,
they filled the entire *krośa* with their wailing and loathsome cries.
It is perpetually filled with an extremely foul stench, crowded day after day by sinners who have been beaten by my messengers and are tormented by their food.
It was filled with the sound of those very insects crying out "Protect us! as they were being devoured, and it was crowded with urinal pits full of boiling liquid urine.

It was constantly infested by great sinners who were like insects devouring it; it extended for a distance of two miles, was shrouded in darkness, and was perpetually filled with the sounds they made.
Then, struck by those excellent [beings] who were roaring loudly, with their throats, lips, and palates parched,
that [place] was completely filled and pacified by millions of phlegm-filled insects.
Surrounded on all sides by those who eat that [flesh] and by sinners,
the Garakuṇḍa hell extends for half a krośa and is filled with those who consume the fetus.
It was completely filled with sinners being devoured by Garakoṭas,
and with those being beaten by my messengers, who were making loud noises and trembling.
With snake-like vajra-fangs, parched throats, and most dreadful forms, their eyes were filled with mud and they cried out, swarming with insects. (15)
It is perpetually crowded with sinners, infested by worms that devour them, filled with the essence of marrow and fat, extending for four *krośas*, and most difficult to endure. (16)
By those sinners who eat that [flesh], and by my messengers who strike them,
Śukra-kuṇḍa— one krośa in extent— is filled with śukra-insects.
It was constantly crowded with wicked people fleeing from it, infested by insects, filled with foul-smelling frogs, and possessed deep pools.
It was crowded with those who ate that [food] and with sinners; it was infested by insects, filled with tears from eyes, scorched, and attended by many wicked people. (19)
And the fourth pond was filled with weeping insects that had been devoured;
it was joined by those sinful beings who had eaten the bodies of men. (20)
It was filled with my beaten messengers, with those distracted by them, and with those eaten by insects;
its ears were completely full, and it was joined by those who eat such things and by sinners.
And by those speaking of the dimensions of the pond as being four [cubits], it was filled with the marrow of men devoured by insects, and possessed a most foul odor. (22)
It was filled with great sinners, measuring four times the size of a well,
completely full of glistening flesh, and struck by messengers.
The pond was crowded with evildoers and terrifying;
it was filled with those who sold their daughters, with those who ate them, and with those devoured by insects.
With terrifying beings who, being frightened, cried out the word "Protect!", [he struck] the four [beings] beginning with Nakhin, each measuring a pond and a musical instrument respectively. ||25||
It was constantly filled with sinners being beaten by my messengers,
and it contained a cauldron of molten copper accompanied by flaming brands upon the copper.
There, the hell named Pratimālakṣa is constantly occupied by glowing-hot [iron] images;
it is filled with each sinner embracing an image while wailing.
It was a vast expanse measuring a gavyūti, struck by my messengers,
filled with streams of molten iron, and joined with blazing coals.
It was filled with sinners embracing iron images while weeping, each one constantly embracing an image that blazed with fear;
they cried out the words "Save me! Save me! as they were struck by clubs.
It was two gavyūtis in extent and was filled with those who had committed great sins (mahāpātakin).
The terrifying pit of darkness is proclaimed as the Iron Pit (lohakuṇḍa);
the Leather Pit (carmakuṇḍa) is likewise half the size of the Hot Liquor Pit (taptasurākuṇḍa). || 31 ||
It was filled with those who eat and drink there, as well as my struck messengers;
therefore, it is the Śālmalikuṇḍa, adorned with the thorns of trees.
It was a hundred thousand paces in extent and one *krośa* in length, causing great suffering;
it was encircled by bow-lengths and extremely sharp thorns.
It was filled with great sinners whose limbs were pierced one by one,
falling from the tops of trees, and struck down by my messengers.
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the ninth book, chapter thirty-seven:
[The demons appeared] crying out the words "Give us water! with their palms parched dry.
And by those who were greatly terrified and extremely agitated, their heads were shattered by blows with staffs. || 35 ||
It was as if it were being agitated by those who live by boiling hot oil, and likewise by the Takṣakas with their poison, while previously it had been crying out in distress. 36.
It was filled with sinners who feed upon that [flesh] and were being beaten by my messengers;
it was full of boiling oil and devoid of insects and other such creatures. (37)
It was filled with great sinners, surrounded by burning coals,
uttering piteous cries, moving about, and tormented by the heat.
Enveloped in darkness, crying out, causing affliction, and terrifying,
it was surrounded by iron weapons with very sharp points shaped like spikes.
And the nature of the bed of weapons (śastratalpa) is four krośas in measurement;
it is surrounded by sinners who have been pierced by spears and are themselves enveloped [in flames].
And by my messengers who were beaten, their throats, lips, and palates parched, and by terrifying crawling insects as large as spikes; (41)
O virtuous one, it was filled with those having sharp teeth and deformed features, shrouded in darkness,
and crowded with great sinners who were being beaten by my messengers.
And they describe the pit of pus as being two gavyūtis in measure;
it is filled with creatures that serve as its food and with my messengers who have struck them down.
It was covered by tens of millions of serpents as large as palm trees,
with the bodies of the sinners entwined by snakes and devoured by them.
It was crowded with my messengers who were making noise and with those they had struck; and the three pits were filled with mosquitoes and other such insects.
And the entire area, measuring half a krośa, was filled with great sinners,
their hands, feet, and other limbs severed, and covered with blood from their wounds.
While my attendants were being beaten and crying out "Alas! Alas!", the two of them completely filled the pit with thunderbolts and scorpions. 47.
Furthermore, there was a half-pond filled with sinners bitten by thunderbolts and scorpions;
and three pits for mosquitoes and other insects were completely filled with those very creatures. 48.
Pierced by those [instruments], he enters the Golakuṇḍa, which is filled with blood-red water, full of boiling liquid, and enveloped in deep darkness. ||49||
It was filled with sinful beings being devoured by insects as large as spikes,
and it was being tormented by those same sinful beings who, having been eaten by insects, were now terrified.
It was filled with those weeping and crying out as they were struck by my messengers;
it was pervaded by an extreme stench and was a constant source of suffering for sinners.
It was filled with cruel, deformed sinners who were devouring one another,
and it was completely full of tens of millions of crocodiles dwelling in the water.
It was filled with hundreds of millions of those who consume feces, urine, and phlegm,
and was joined by sinful beings being devoured by crows of hideous form.
The Mathānakuṇḍa and the Bījakuṇḍa extend for a full hundred bow-lengths;
they are filled with sinful beings who have been devoured and are constantly making loud noises.
It was always crowded with sinful beings equipped with bows and bowstrings; it was filled with a dense darkness and with those who made noise and possessed adamantine fangs. 55.
Twice the size of the pond, it was constructed of heated stones,
resembling blazing coals, and was filled with moving sinners.
There was a supreme pit made of stone, resembling the edge of a razor and filled with sharp [weapons],
as well as a pit of saliva and blood, frequented by those who have committed great sins.
And for the distance of one krośa, it was filled to the depth of a hundred bows by my struck messengers, who resembled mountains of heated collyrium.
It was filled with moving sinners being struck by my messengers,
