Possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons. ||40||

Having worshipped her according to the prescribed rites, Yajña then joyfully praised her—she who possessed the luster of molten gold, who was exceedingly lovely, beautiful, and most enchanting; whose face was like a lotus, whose limbs were tender, and whose eyes were as broad as lotuses. ||41||
Born from the body of Kamalā,
pure as fire, possessing the brilliance of a parrot, with full lips and beautiful teeth, she was a virtuous woman.
She is worthy of worship by the one seated upon the lotus, adorned with garlands of jasmine flowers,
her face bright with a gentle smile, and decorated with ornaments of precious gems.
Wearing her mass of braided hair, richly adorned and well-bathed, she captivated the minds of the sages;
she was fragrant with musk, camphor, and sandalwood paste mixed with moon-like perfumes.
Her region below the hair-parting was made radiant by even a tiny dot of vermilion;
she possessed highly praiseworthy hips and large buttocks and breasts. ||45||
Seeing her, who was tormented by the arrows of desire and so exceedingly beautiful, Yajña indeed fell into a swoon.
He took her as his wife, who possessed a form that was the very support of Kāmadeva, according to the rites prescribed by the Creator;
and having taken her to a secluded place, he remained there for a hundred divine years.
Yajña rejoiced, filled with joy, while Rāmeśa was with Ramā;
that goddess conceived a divine embryo for twelve years. (48)
Then she gave birth to a son, who was indeed the fruit of all her actions;
and when the rite was fully completed, that son became the bestower of its fruit.
Those who know the Veda understand that sacrifice, together with the sacrificial fee, the son, and the fruit, is the bestower of results for those who perform ritual actions. 50.
O Nārada, having received the sacrificial fee and his son who bestows the fruit, the sacrifice granted the fruit to all the performers of the ritual.
Then the gods and others, satisfied and with their desires fulfilled, all went to their own abodes; this was heard from the mouth of Dharmavaktra.
Having performed the rite and being the performer, one should quickly give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
at that very moment one obtains the fruit—this has been declared by the Vedas, O Sage. (53)

If the performer of the rite, upon the completion of the ritual, should not give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins at that very moment, whether out of ignorance or by the will of fate; || 54 ||
When one muhūrta has passed, it certainly becomes twofold;
when one night has passed, it becomes thirty millionfold.
In three nights, it is said to be a hundredfold; in seven days, twice that;
in a month, it is declared to be a hundred-thousandfold, and for Brahmins, it increases even further.
But when a year has passed, that [merit] becomes three crore-fold;
otherwise, all the ritual action of the patrons shall indeed become fruitless. ||57||
That man who steals the property of a Brahmin is impure and unfit for ritual action;
by that sin he becomes a sinner, impoverished and afflicted by disease.
Lakṣmī departs from that house after uttering a most terrible curse;
furthermore, the ancestors do not accept the śrāddha offerings or the libations given by him. (59)
In this way, the gods receive that worship from him, as well as the oblation of fire offered by him;
he does not give a gift that has not been given, nor does he ask for what has been received.
If the patron does not bestow the sacrificial fee upon those who have piled the altar, both of them go to hell like a jar with its rope severed.
One who steals the property of a Brahmin will certainly go to Kumbhīpāka;
there he shall dwell for a hundred thousand years, beaten by the messengers of Yama.
Consequently, he shall become a Cāṇḍāla, afflicted by disease and impoverished;
he shall cause the downfall of seven generations of men before him and seven from his own birth.
"Thus has it been told, O Brahmin; what more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said: "O Sage, who enjoys the fruit of that action which is devoid of a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)?"
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the ninth book, chapter forty-five.
"Tell me first how the ritual of worship for the sacrificial fee was performed in ancient times.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O sage, how indeed can there be any fruit from a rite that is devoid of a sacrificial fee?"
O Sage, only that action which is accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) yields its fruit; as for that action which is without a sacrificial fee, Bali alone reaps it.
O Sage, in former times Vāmana gave that [gift] to Bali;
for one who is not learned in the Vedas is like a gift of Śrāddha materials given without faith. (67)

Whatever worship, wealth, and other offerings are performed for Brahmins who are husbands of Śūdra women, and whatever sacrifice is performed by unworthy twice-born men, and whatever worship is offered to the impure; ||| 68 ||
For one who lacks devotion toward the Guru, Bali consumes his ritual action; there is no doubt of this.
Furthermore, whatever is the departure from the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), as well as the hymn and the sequence of the rite of worship—[all these are consumed]. 69.
I shall proclaim all of that as declared in the Kaṇva recension; listen.
Long ago, having obtained her, Yajña received Dakṣiṇā, who was skilled in ritual action.
He was bewildered by her form and, overcome with desire, offered praise.
Yajña said:
"In former times you were a cowherd girl in Goloka, the most excellent and best among the cowherd girls. (71)
Her dear friend, equal to Rādhā, is the beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
on the full moon day of Kārtika, during the great festival of Rādhā at the Rāsa dance.
Because she appeared together with Lakṣmī on his right side, she is called Dakṣiṇā;
and formerly you were known by the name Suśīlā, O beautiful one, renowned for your virtuous character.
O Lakṣmī, you were separated from your portion due to Rādhā’s curse;
fallen from Goloka, you have appeared here by my good fortune.
"Have mercy, O illustrious one; make me alone your husband.
O Goddess, you alone are always the bestower of the fruits of the actions of those who perform deeds. (75)
Without you, all the actions of everyone are fruitless;
likewise, without you, the ritual action of those who perform rituals does not shine.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and even the guardians of the quarters and others are not capable of bestowing the fruit of action without you.
Brahmā himself is the embodiment of action, Maheśvara is the embodiment of the fruit,
Viṣṇu is the embodiment of sacrifice, and I am you— the essence of these.
The Supreme Brahman is the bestower of fruits; Prakṛti is supreme and devoid of qualities;
and the Lord Kṛṣṇa himself is capable [of this] along with you.
O beloved, you alone are my power in birth after birth;
O fair-faced one, I am capable in every action only when accompanied by you. (80)
Having spoken thus, the presiding deity of the sacrifice stood before him;
that goddess, a portion of Kamalā, became pleased and attended upon him.
And whoever should recite this hymn of praise to Dakṣiṇā at the time of a sacrifice—
And one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices; there is no doubt in this matter. || 82 ||
In the Rājasūya, Vājapeya, Gomedha, Naramedha, Aśvamedha, Lāṅgala, and the glorious Viṣṇuyajña; ||83||
To Dhanada, Bhūmida, Pūrta, Phalada, Gajamedhaka, Lohayajña, Svarṇayajña, Ratnayajña, and Tāmraka; (84)
In the Śiva-sacrifice, the Rudra-sacrifice, the Indra-sacrifice, and the Baṃdhuka;
in the rain, the Varuṇa-worship, the Kaṇḍaka, and the Vairimardana. ||85||
She is Śuci in the sacrifice of purity, Dharmayajñā in the sacrifice of dharma, Ghaṃ in the rite that liberates from sin,
Brahmāṇī in the application of ritual action, and Bhadrakā in the auspicious sacrifice of the womb.
And whoever recites this hymn at the commencement of these [rites], that entire undertaking will certainly be accomplished without obstacles. 87.
This hymn has been told; now listen to the method of meditation and worship.
One should worship with devotion in a Śālagrāma stone or even in a bell. 88.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth skandha, chapter 46:
[She is] the bestower of fruits for all actions. (89)

I worship her who was born from the right shoulder of Lakṣmī, who is Dakṣiṇā and a portion of Kamalā; she who is the very embodiment of Viṣṇu’s power in all rites, who is honored and saluted, auspicious, the giver of purity, pure, of virtuous character, and the bestower of welfare. (90)
Having meditated thus, the wise one should worship the Granter of Boons with this very root mantra;
O Nārada, having offered water for the feet and other offerings to the Goddess according to the Vedic injunctions.
The wise one should worship Dakṣiṇā, who is honored by all, according to the prescribed rite with the mantra: "Oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Dakṣiṇā. (92)
Thus, O Brahman, has this narrative known as the Dakṣiṇā been told;
it bestows happiness, grants joy, and yields the fruit of all ritual actions. (93)
And whoever listens with a concentrated mind to this narrative of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
no action resulting in physical deficiency shall occur for them on the earth of Bhārata.
A sonless man obtains a son who is certainly endowed with virtues;
one devoid of a wife obtains a wife who is highly virtuous, beautiful, and supreme. 95.
A wife who has beautiful hips, who has borne sons, who is humble, who speaks kindly,
who is devoted to her husband, pure, and of noble birth— such is the excellent woman.
One lacking knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one lacking wealth shall obtain wealth;
one lacking land shall obtain land; and one lacking progeny shall obtain progeny. ||97||
Upon hearing this for one month, one is released from distress caused by separation from kinsmen, as well as from calamity and imprisonment; of this there is no doubt. (98)
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the dialogue between Nārada and Nārāyaṇa. || 45 ||
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter.
Nārada said:
I have heard the excellent narrative concerning many goddesses.
O Brahmin, best among those who know the Vedas, please tell me of the conduct of the others as well.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O Brahmin, you now desire to hear here the individual life stories of all those goddesses previously mentioned, as well as their deeds among the gods.
Nārada said:
Ṣaṣṭhī and Maṅgalacaṇḍī are portions of Prakṛti manifested through the mind. I desire to hear their origin and life stories in accordance with reality. (3)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: She who is the sixth part of Prakṛti is celebrated as the sixth [Goddess];
she is the presiding deity of children, the Māyā of Viṣṇu, and the bestower of children.
And she who is renowned in the Mātṛkās by the name Devasenā, that virtuous woman of excellent vows, dearer than life itself, was the wife of Skanda. (5)
Bestowing long life upon children and acting as their protector, she remains constantly by the side of the infant; through her yoga, she is a perfected Yoginī.
O Brahmin, listen to this history regarding her method of worship, which was heard from the mouth of Dharma; it is supremely bestowing happiness and granting sons. (7)
King Priyavrata was the son of Svāyaṃbhuva Manu;
though a lord among yogis, he was always devoted to ascetic practices and did not take a wife here.
However, by the command of Brahmā, he diligently took a wife.
O Sage, although he had been married for a very long time, he did not obtain a son.
Kaśyapa also caused that Putreṣṭi sacrifice to be performed;
the sage gave the sacrificial oblation to his beloved Mālinī.
And having consumed that sacrificial oblation (caru) of hers, she immediately became pregnant;
and that goddess bore the god for twelve years.
Then, O Brahmin, she gave birth to a boy with the luster of gold,
endowed with all limbs, yet dead and with wide-open eyes.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Ninth Skandha, Chapter 46.
Seeing him, all those women of the family wept;
his mother, moreover, fell into a swoon from the intense grief for her son.
O Sage, taking the boy with him, the king went to the cremation ground;
there in the wilderness, placing his son upon his chest, he wept.
Not casting off his young son, the king prepared to give up his life;
through this most agonizing grief for his son, he forgot the yoga of knowledge.
In the meantime, he beheld there a celestial chariot,
resembling pure crystal and fashioned from the finest of jewels.
Blazing with splendor, adorned with ten horses, and clothed in silken garments;
richly endowed with various wonderful patterns and graced by garlands of flowers. || 17 ||
There he beheld a goddess, lovely and captivating, possessing the luster of a white lotus and eternally fixed in youth. (18)
Her face was brightened by a gentle smile; she was adorned with jewel ornaments, full of compassion, perfected through yoga, and intent on bestowing grace upon her devotees. (19)
Seeing her before him, the king praised her with supreme devotion;
setting the child down upon the ground, he performed worship for her.
O Nārada, the king questioned that gratified woman, who possessed a luster like the summer sun, who was blazing with splendor, yet peaceful and beloved of Skanda. 21.
The king said:
"Who are you, O most beautiful one? O lovely lady, whose beloved are you, O lady of virtuous vows?
Whose daughter are you, O woman of excellent hips—you who are blessed and honored among women?"
Having heard the words of the lord of men, that Devasenā, the Caṇḍikā who is the auspiciousness of the world and the one who causes battle for the gods, spoke.
In ancient times, that army of the gods was seized by the Daityas;
because she granted victory to them, it was therefore called Devasenā.
Śrī Devasenā said: "O protector of the earth, I am the mental daughter of Brahmā, the sovereign Devasenā;
having created me from his mind, the Creator gave me to Skanda. (25)
She is renowned in the Mātṛkās as the wife of Skanda and is of excellent vows;
she is celebrated among all as Ṣaṣṭhī, the supreme sixth part of Prakṛti.
I am the giver of sons to the childless, and the giver of beloved things to those who love; I am the giver of wealth to the poor, and the giver of their own karma to those engaged in action.
Happiness, suffering, fear, grief, joy, and even auspiciousness—[all these are from me].
Both prosperity and adversity—everything comes about through karma. ||28||
By one's own karma one has many sons, yet by one's own karma one's lineage may perish;
by karma one has dead children, and by karma one lives for a long time. (29)
By his own karma he is possessed of virtues, and by his own karma he is deprived of limbs;
by his own karma he has many wives, and by his own karma he is without a wife.
By karma the possessor of dharma becomes endowed with form; by his own karma he is constantly subject to disease;
through karma there arises illness, and through karma alone there is health.
"Therefore, O King, action is supreme above all things; thus it is heard in the Śruti.
Having spoken thus, O Sage, that goddess took the boy.
By means of her great wisdom, that goddess restored him to life with her glance;
the king beheld that child, smiling and possessing the luster of gold.
Then the goddess Devasenā, having taken the boy and having bid farewell to the king who was watching her, prepared to ascend into the sky. 34.
Then the king, with his throat, lips, and palate parched, praised her once more;
by that hymn of praise from the monarch, the goddess became truly well-pleased.
O Brahmin, he spoke to that king regarding the action ordained by the Vedas.
The Goddess said: "In the three worlds you are the king, the son of Svāyambhuva Manu. (36)
Having caused my worship to be performed everywhere, perform it yourself as well.
Then I shall give you a son, a charming lotus of the family.
He was renowned by the name Suvrata, virtuous and highly learned;
he was a master of yoga, a knower of his past lives, and an embodiment of a portion of Nārāyaṇa. (38)
It was the most excellent performer of a hundred sacrifices, honored by the kṣatriyas,
and possessed the auspicious strength of a hundred thousand rutting elephants.
He is wealthy, virtuous, pure, and beloved by the learned;
he is the very embodiment of success for yogis, the wise, and ascetics. 40.
"Famous throughout the worlds and a giver of all prosperity"—having spoken thus, that goddess gave the boy to him. 41.
King Priyavrata accepted [the proposal] for the sake of worship, and the Goddess, having granted him an auspicious boon, went to heaven. 42.
He returned to his own home with his ministers, his mind filled with joy;
having arrived, he related the news concerning his son.
O Nārada, having heard this, the excellent women became highly satisfied;
she caused auspicious rites to be performed everywhere for the sake of her son. ||44||
He worshipped the Goddess and gave wealth to the Brahmins;
and every month, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, the king held a great festival.
With great effort, he caused the rite for the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī to be performed everywhere,
with due care on the sixth day in the lying-in chamber of infants.
And on the twenty-first day, as well as for auspicious rites for children and the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), [these are favorable]. ||47||
He caused that worship to be performed and indeed performed it himself;
now hear from me the meditation, the ritual procedure for worship, and the hymn of praise. 48.
The one of noble vows himself caused all that which he had heard from the mouth of the Dharma-preacher and was taught by Kauthuma to increase everywhere—
whether at Śālagrāma, or in a water-pot, or at the root of a banyan tree, O Sage.
Or the wise one, having fashioned an image on a wall, should worship it;
having installed that radiant form, which is the pure sixth part of Prakṛti. 50.
She is the mother of the world in the form of compassion,
possessing the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, and adorned with ornaments of jewels.
"I worship the supreme one who bestows good sons and grants auspiciousness. Having meditated thus, the wise man should place a flower upon his own head.
Having again meditated upon the supreme divine army, which is of a purifying nature, one should worship that virtuous lady of excellent vows with the root mantra,
offering water for the feet, the arghya, water for sipping, fragrance, flowers, and a lamp.

A person should recite the eight-syllabled great mantra according to their capacity;
then, having offered praise, they should bow down with devotion and a concentrated mind. || 55 ||

And he who recites one hundred thousand times the hymn declared in the Sāmaveda—which is excellent and bestows the fruit of a son—as well as the great eight-syllabled mantra (aṣṭākṣara), [attains his desire]. || 56 ||
"He shall surely obtain a virtuous son," so said the Lotus-born One.

salutations again and again to the Goddess, the Great Goddess, to Siddhi, and to Śānti. 58.
Salutations again and again to the auspicious Devasenā, to the Goddess of the Sixth Day; salutations again and again to the giver of boons, the giver of sons, and the giver of wealth. || 59 ||
Salutations again and again to the Goddess who is the giver of happiness and the giver of liberation, the sixth [digit];
salutations again and again to the one whose form is the sixteenth digit of creation, and to the Perfected One (Siddhā). || 60 ||

And [the fruit] of actions. 62.

Salutations again and again to Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, the presiding deity of children; salutations again and again to the auspicious Goddess Ṣaṣṭhī, the giver of welfare, the bestower of fruits, who is manifest before her own devotees. Salutations to the one worthy of worship, the beloved of Skanda, who is present for all beings in all their undertakings.

In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth skandha, chapter 47.

Having thus praised the Goddess, Priyavrata,
the king of kings, obtained a glorious son through the grace of the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī.
O Brahmin, he who listens to this *Ṣaṣṭhīstotra* for a year shall obtain a son, even if childless—one who is supreme and long-lived. (69)
He who, having worshipped with devotion for one year, listens to this,
is liberated from all sins, and even a woman long barren gives birth.
By the grace of the Goddess, she gives birth to a son who is heroic, virtuous, learned, illustrious, and endowed with a very long life.

then the gods, including Indra, approached Manas in their minds.
And Mahendra, overwhelmed and distressed by fear, praised her;
then Āstīka arrived at the sacrifice by the command of Manu.
He begged the supreme lord of the earth for the lives of Mahendra and Takṣaka;
out of compassion and at the command of the Brāhmaṇa, that best of kings granted the boon. (111)
Having completed the sacrifice, he joyfully gave sacrificial fees to the Brahmins;
and the Brahmins, sages, and gods, having gone to the presence of Manasā with their minds, [honored her]. 112.
They worshipped Mananā and praised him individually;
Śakra, having gathered the necessary offerings, was filled with devotion and ever pure. (113)
He praised him with supreme devotion,
having performed the sixteen-fold service (ṣoḍaśopacāra) and the offering dear to him at that time.
He honored Manasā and, being well-pleased, bestowed gifts by the command of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; having fully worshipped the goddess Manasā, they departed for their own abodes.
"Thus everything has been told; what more do you wish to hear?
Nārada said: "With which hymn did Mahendra praise the virtuous Manasā? (116)
"I wish to hear the sequence of the ritual for her worship according to its true nature.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"Having bathed well, being pure and having sipped water, one should put on two washed garments. (117)
With devotion, he seated the Goddess upon a jeweled lion-throne and bathed her with water from his own Gaṅgā, which was held in a precious pitcher.
Mahendra bathed Manasā with Vedic mantras,
and Vāsavi settled her in a beautiful place purified by fire.
Having applied sandalwood paste to all his limbs and with devotion,
he [worshipped] Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Agni, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Śivā.
Having first worshipped the group of six deities, he then worshipped that Satī with the mantra:
"Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ, svāhā to the Goddess through the mind. (121)
With the ten-syllable root mantra, the leader of the gods offered everything as was appropriate;
having bestowed the sixteen services that are difficult even for gods to obtain. (122)
Impelled by Viṣṇu, he joyfully worshipped with devotion and indeed played various kinds of musical instruments there.
And by the command of Devapriya, as well as by the command of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon Manasa.
He became filled with joy, praised [the Lord], and his body was marked with horripilation as his eyes welled with tears.
Purandara said:
O Goddess, I desire to praise you, the most excellent and best among virtuous women.
I am truly not capable now of praising her who is higher than the highest and supreme.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the ninth book of the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*.
The characteristic of hymns in the Veda is that they are primarily devoted to the description of natural phenomena.
It is not possible to enumerate your virtues in their entirety;
you are the very embodiment of pure being, free from anger, violence, and all such faults.
And the sage was not able to refuse it because he had made a request:
"O virtuous lady, you have been honored by me like my own mother Aditi. (128)
O Goddess of the Suras, you are compassion incarnate, like a sister, and like a mother in the form of forbearance; by you my life, sons, and wife have been protected.
I perform this worship for you, and may my love always increase;
although you, O Mother of the World, are eternally worthy of worship everywhere. (130)
Nevertheless, O Goddess of the gods, I shall increase your worship;
those who shall worship you with devotion on the day of the Āṣāḍha-saṃkrānti—131.
On the fifth lunar day known as Manasī, or at the end of the month, or on every single day,
their sons, grandsons, and so forth, as well as their wealth, truly increase.
Those people who, though illustrious, famous, learned, and endowed with virtues, do not worship you, will instead revile you out of ignorance. 133.
They shall be bereft of fortune, and they will always face fear from the Nāgas;
you yourself, however, are the sovereign of all fortune and Kamalā, whose abode is the lotus, in Vaikuṇṭha.
The lordly sage Jaratkāru, an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa,
created you through his austerity, his splendor, and his mind, O father.
For our protection alone, you were addressed by him with his mind as Manasādevī; by your power, you are a perfected yoginī through your own self.
Therefore, O Goddess Manasā, may you be worshipped and saluted by him;
for those who constantly and fervently worship the gods with devotion through the mind [attain this]. (137)
Therefore, the wise proclaim you as the goddess of the mind;
O Goddess, you are the embodiment of truth because of your constant devotion to the truth of the giver.
For whoever would constantly meditate upon you, being devoted to you, shall attain you;
and Indra, having praised you with his mind, took the boon from his sister.
Adorned with ornaments and accompanied by her retinue, that queen went to her own abode;
together with her son, she remained for a long time in her father’s house.
Honored by her brothers, worthy of respect like a spear, and to be saluted from all sides,
O Brahmin, Surabhi arrived there from Goloka and was most highly honored.
Having bathed her with milk, he worshipped her with devotion and imparted the entire secret knowledge that is so very difficult to attain. (142)
Thus honored by the god, she returned once more to the heavenly realm;
one should worship and recite this hymn to Indra, which is a seed of merit for the mind. (143)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Ninth Skandha, Chapter 49:
There is no fear of serpents for him, nor for those born in his lineage.
Poison becomes equal to nectar when one has accomplished the hymn of praise.
By reciting this hymn five hundred thousand times, a man becomes a perfected practitioner (siddha);
he shall certainly become one who sleeps upon a serpent and has a serpent as his vehicle. || 145 ||
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 48 ||
Now begins the forty-ninth chapter.
Nārada said: Who indeed was that goddess Surabhi who came from Goloka?
O Brahman, I desire to hear with great effort the account of his birth and deeds. || 1 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Surabhi, the presiding deity of cows, the first of cows, and the progenitor of cows— the foremost among cows— is born in Goloka.
Listen as we narrate the history of the Lord of the first creation;
hear how his birth occurred long ago in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Once, the Lord of the Night (Kṛṣṇa), full of curiosity,
went with his beloved to the holy Vṛndāvana, surrounded by cowherd women.
There, in that secluded place, he sported spontaneously out of curiosity;
and for him, who was composed of his own will, there arose a desire to drink milk.
He effortlessly created from his left side the goddess Surabhi, who was accompanied by her calf and yielding milk; her calf was named Manoratha.
Having seen her with her calf, Śrīdāmā milked her into a new vessel;
the milk was superior to nectar and removed birth, death, and old age.
And having himself drunk that sweet milk produced from it, the Lord of the Gopīs became a lake through the overflowing of the vessel of water.
Extending both in length and breadth for a hundred yojanas all around, this famous Ocean of Milk is also present in Goloka. (9)
And by the will of the Lord, that pool became a playground for Gopikās and Rādhā;
fashioned from precious gems, it was made complete by the Lord's desire.
Suddenly, there appeared hundreds of thousands of millions of wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus), as many as there were cowherds there, emerging from the pores of his skin. || 11 ||
Many sons, beyond counting, were born to them;
thus the creation of cows was described, and by them the world was filled.
O Sage, in ancient times the Blessed One performed worship with the Surabhi cow;
thereafter, that mode of worship became difficult to find even in the three worlds.
On the following day, by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Hara’s Surabhi became worthy of worship; this was heard from the mouth of Dharma.
O highly fortunate one, listen as I tell you the meditation, the hymn of praise, the root mantra, and whatever sequence of worship rituals has been declared in the Vedas. (15)
"Oṃ surabhyai nabhaḥ"—this six-syllabled mantra of hers is perfected by a mere hundred thousand recitations; it is a wish-fulfilling tree for devotees. (16)
Vyāna is celebrated in the Yajurveda, and her worship is performed everywhere;
she bestows prosperity, growth, liberation, and all desired objects. || 17 ||
She who is the very embodiment of Lakṣmī, the supreme companion of Rādhā, the presiding deity of cows, the primordial cow, and the mother of cows. 18.
I worship that goddess Surabhi, who is of a pure form, sanctified, and the granter of all desires to her devotees; by whom the entire universe is purified. 19.
A twice-born man should worship Surabhi in a water-pot, on the head of a cow, at a tethering post for cattle, on a śālagrāma stone, or in water or fire. 20.
On the following day, during the forenoon, he who, endowed with devotion, worships Surabhi together with lamps, shall himself become worthy of worship on earth. (21)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Ninth Skandha, Chapter 50.
Once, when the boar [incarnation] was in the three worlds by the illusory power of Viṣṇu,
Surabhi carried off the milk, and the gods and others became distressed.
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, they then praised Brahmā;
and by his command, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, praised Surabhi.
Purandara said:
Salutations to the Goddess, to the Great Goddess; salutations again and again to Surabhi.
Salutations to you, O Mother of the Universe, whose very nature is the seed of cows.
Salutations again and again to the beloved of Rādhā and to Padmāśā;
salutations to the beloved of Kṛṣṇa and salutations again and again to the mother of the cows. ||25||

Salutations again and again to her who is the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), who is eternally supreme to all, the giver of milk, the giver of wealth, and the giver of wisdom.
Salutations again and again to the auspicious one, to Subhadrā, and to the giver of cows.
Salutations again and again to Yaśodā, the giver of fame, the giver of dharma. ||27||
Merely by hearing the hymn of praise, the eternal Mother of the World was delighted and manifested right there in the world of Brahmā.
Having granted a boon to Mahendra, even one that is difficult to obtain and desired,
she departed for Goloka, and the gods and others returned to their own homes.
O Nārada, the entire universe suddenly became filled with milk;
from that milk came clarified butter, from that the sacrifice, and from that the satisfaction of the gods.
Whoever recites this hymn, which is endowed with great merit,
shall possess cattle, wealth, fame, and likewise sons;
he has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes at the end to the abode of Kṛṣṇa. ||32||
One may dwell there for a very long time and perform service to Kṛṣṇa;
one does not return to rebirth there, and from that state, one becomes a son of Brahmā.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the ninth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 49 ||
Now begins the fiftieth chapter.
Nārada said:
"I have heard the entire narrative of the primary elements exactly as it is."
Having heard which, a living being is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra. || 1 ||
Now I desire to hear the secret hidden by the Vedas—
the ritual procedure for Rādhā and Durgā as enjoined by the Śruti.
O Lord of Sages, having heard that supreme majesty of the other two described by you so extensively, whose mind would not be captivated? (3)
The entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is a portion of you both;
tell me now the method by which liberation from those two may be attained.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen, O Nārada, I shall declare the secret taught by the Vedas,
which has not been told to anyone, the essence of essences, higher than the highest.
Having heard this, it must not be told to another, for it is an extreme secret concerning the consciousness that takes the form of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) in the arising of the universe.
A pair of powers, presiding over vital breath and intellect, manifested;
they are the constant restrainers and impellers of all living beings.
The entire universe, including the Virāṭ and all things moving and unmoving, is dependent upon them.
As long as faith in these two does not arise, liberation is indeed difficult to attain. ||8||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth book, chapter fifty:
Therefore, for the sake of obtaining their grace, one should constantly serve those two.
In that regard, O Nārada, first listen with devotion to the mantra of Rādhikā.
He who is the supreme beyond the supreme, eternally served by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others;
after that [name] followed by the dative case-ending "śrīrādhe," then the wife of Agni (svāhā) follows. 10.
This six-syllabled great mantra reveals the meaning of the Dharma and other truths; beginning with the seed-syllable of Māyā, it is remembered as the wish-fulfilling gem of desires. (11)
Even with thousands of millions of mouths and hundreds of millions of tongues, it is simply not possible to describe the majesty of this mantra. (12)
Devoted to devotion, Śrī Kṛṣṇa first received the mantra from the instruction of Mūladevī in the Rāsa-maṇḍala at Goloka. (13)
Viṣṇu was instructed by him, and by him Brahmā and likewise Virāṭ;
by him Dharma, and by him I—such indeed is this lineage.
I recite that mantra; therefore, I am praised by the sages. All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, constantly meditate upon her with joy. (15)
Since there is no authority for the worship of Kṛṣṇa without the worship of Rādhā, therefore the worship of Rādhikā must be performed by all Vaiṣṇavas. (16)
Kṛṣṇā is his presiding deity, for the Lord is dependent upon her;
she is the Mistress of the Rāsa dance, and he never remains separated from her. ||17||
She fulfills all desires; therefore, she is celebrated as Rādha.
Furthermore, I myself am the seer (ṛṣi) of the mantras spoken herein. 18.
The meter here is the Gāyatrī, the deity is the goddess Rādhikā;
the seed-syllable (bīja) is Tāra, and the power-seed (śakti-bīja) is proclaimed to be Śakti herself. || 19 ||
And these [rites] should be performed elsewhere as well.
Then, one should meditate upon the Great Goddess Rādhikā, the mistress of the rasa-dance. || 20 ||
O Sage, according to the primary method and the previously mentioned manner, the six limbs [of the ritual] are recited in the Sāmaveda with a distinct melody:
[one should meditate on her] possessing the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, with a face like the autumnal moon. (21)
Resembling ten million moons, with eyes like autumn lotuses,
she was free from blemishes, possessed broad hips, and had a waist adorned with a girdle.
She was adorned with rows of teeth as brilliant as a line of jasmine flowers;
she was clothed in silken garments, pure as fire, and accompanied by parrots.
With a face brightened by a gentle smile, her breasts like the frontal globes of an elephant, eternally twelve years of age, and adorned with jewel ornaments; 24.
She is a wave from the ocean of erotic sentiment, eager to bestow grace upon her devotees,
and she is resplendent with a mass of hair adorned with garlands of jasmine and *mālatī* flowers.
She has a delicate throat, stands in the midst of the circle of the rāsa dance, grants boons and fearlessness with her hands, is peaceful, and possesses eternal, firm youth. ||26||
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, she is the leader of the circle of gopīs,
dearer than life to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Goddess revealed by the Vedas.
Having meditated thus, one should then worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite outside [the self], either in a Śālagrāma stone, in a jar, or upon an eight-petaled yantra.
Having invoked the Goddess, thereafter the seat and other offerings should be presented;
having recited the root mantra, one should arrange the seat and the rest. (29)

One should offer water for the feet (pādya) at the feet, water for the honorific offering (arghya) on the head, and water for sipping (ācamanīya) in the mouth; this should be done three times with the root mantra (mūlavidyā).
Then one should offer the madhuparka and a single milch cow;
thereafter, one should lead her to the bathing hall and contemplate her right there.
Having prepared the ritual for bathing, including the application of oil and so forth, one should then offer two garments followed by sandalwood paste and various ornaments.
Pārijāta blossoms, lotuses, and so forth. || 33 ||

Then, one should prepare various kinds of flower garlands along with *tulasī* blossoms, and perform the worship of the Lord’s retinue and the sacred thread (*pavitra*). Following this, one should perform the worship of the limbs [of the deity] in the southeast, northeast, south, northwest, the center, and the sky; thereafter, on the eight petals, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise.
One should place Mālāvatī on the foremost petal and Mādhavī in the southeast corner.
Having completed [this],
in the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the ninth skandha, chapter 50.
A wise man should worship Ratnamālā on the southern petal, Suśīlakā in the southwest, and Śaśikalā on the western petal. (36)
In the northwest one should worship Pārijātā, and in the north, Parāvatī;
in the northeast corner, Sundarī, who acts for the pleasure [of the deity], should be worshipped.
One should worship Brahmā and the others outside of that, the guardians of the quarters in the earth-fortress (bhūpura), and the weapons such as the thunderbolt; thus one should worship the Goddess.
Then, a wise person should worship the Goddess, together with her retinue, using offerings such as perfumes and other services accompanied by royal honors.
Thereafter, one should praise the Queen of the Gods with hymns and the Thousand Names.
And one should diligently perform the recitation a thousand times every day. ||40||
Whoever thus worships the goddess Rādhā, the supreme mistress of the rāsa dance,
shall become equal to Viṣṇu and go eternally to Goloka.
The supreme Rāseśvarī grants her presence to that wise person who celebrates the festival of Rādhā’s birth on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika.
For a certain reason, Rādhā, who eternally resides in Goloka, was born in the forest of Vṛndāvana as the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu. 43.

Regarding the mantras mentioned here, according to the prescribed number of syllables, the rite of *puraścaraṇa* has been declared; one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a tenth part [of that number]. (44)
One should offer oblations with sesame seeds combined with the three sweets, with a spirit of devotion.
Nārada said: O Sage, tell me the hymn properly by which the Goddess becomes pleased. (45)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Salutations to you, O Supreme Goddess, dweller in the circle of the Rāsa dance;
salutations to you, O Queen of the Rāsa, who are dearer than life to Kṛṣṇa.

Salutations to you, O Mother of the three worlds; be gracious, O ocean of compassion, whose lotus feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods. Salutations to you in the form of Sarasvatī; salutations, O Sāvitrī, O Śaṅkarī!
O Gaṅgā, O Padmāvatī, O Ṣaṣṭhī, O Maṅgalacaṇḍikā! ||48||
Salutations to you in the form of Tulasī; salutations to you whose nature is Lakṣmī. Salutations to the divine Durgā; salutations to you who possess all forms.
We worship you, who are the form of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) and an ocean of compassion;
O Mother, lift us up from this ocean of worldly existence and show us mercy. 50.
That man who recites this hymn at the three junctions of the day while remembering Rāghava will never find anything difficult to attain. (51)
And at the end of the body, one shall dwell eternally in Goloka, in the circle of the Rāsa dance.
This supreme secret must not be told to anyone. || 52 ||
Now listen, O best of Brahmins, to the ritual procedure for Goddess Durgā, by the mere remembrance of whom great calamities flee away. (53)
Indeed, there is no one anywhere who does not partake of her;
for the Śiva-power, the mother of all, is the object of worship for all and is most wonderful. 14.

She is the supreme goddess of all Buddhas, whose essential nature is that of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin); she is renowned on earth as Durgā, the destroyer of difficulties, distresses, and fears.
She is to be worshipped perpetually by both the Vaiṣṇavas and the Śaivas;
she is the form of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
I shall now declare her nine-syllable mantra, the most excellent of all mantras:
first the Vāgbhava, then Śambhu’s consort (Hrīṃ), and after that the Kāmabīja. (57)
The word *cāmuṇḍāyai* followed by the two syllables *vicce* constitute the nine-syllable mantra, which is said to be a wish-fulfilling tree for those who worship it. (58)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are proclaimed as its seers (ṛṣis);
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, and Anuṣṭubh are constantly stated to be its meters (chandas).
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Ninth Skandha, Chapter 50: Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Sarasvatī are also deities.
There may be the seed-syllable of Raktadantikā, as well as Durgā and Bhrāmarī.
The goddesses Nandā, Śākaṃbharī, and Bhīmā are remembered as the Śaktis;
their application is declared to be in the pursuit of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 61 ||
One should place the sages, meters, and deities on the crown, the face, and the heart;
for the sake of accomplishing all goals, one should place the seed-syllables of the Śaktis on the two breasts. (52)
The preceptors should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of the mantra, joined with the seed-syllables (jāti), by means of the three seeds, the four, the two, and indeed by the whole [mantra].

One should place the syllables of the mantra on the crest-lock, the two eyes, the ears, the nose, and the mouth; then one should place them on the anus, and perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the entire mantra.
She holds in her hands a sword, a discus, a mace, arrows, a bow, as well as an iron club, a trident, a *bhuśuṇḍī* weapon, a severed head, and a conch shell.
I worship Mahākālī, who has three eyes, is adorned with various ornaments,
resembles dark collyrium in appearance, and possesses ten feet and faces.
One should meditate upon Mahākālī, who embodies the seed-syllable of Kāma, whom the Lotus-seated Lord praised for the sake of destroying Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
And [he held] a rosary, an axe, maces, arrows, and thunderbolts;
likewise a lotus, a bow, a water-pot, a staff, and a spear. 68.
She holds a shield, a lotus, a bell, a vessel for wine, a trident,
a noose, and the Sudarśana discus, and she possesses a ruddy luster.
One should thus worship Mahālakṣmī, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura, who is seated upon a red lotus throne and whose very nature is the seed-syllable *Māyā*.
Holding a bell, a trident, a plow, a conch, a mace, and the Sudarśana discus, as well as a bow and arrows in her lotus-hands, she is radiant like a kunda flower. (71)
One should meditate upon Mahāsarasvatī, whose form consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who embodies the nature of the seed-syllable Vāṇ. 72.
O wise one, hear now her yantra, the destroyer of the Daityas such as Śumbha: it consists of a triangle joined with a hexagon, followed by an eight-petaled lotus and a twenty-four-petaled one. (73)
One should thus contemplate the machine (yantra) as being joined with the underground chamber;
whether in a śālagrāma stone, or in a jar, or in a yantra, or in images.
One should worship the Goddess with undivided mind;
one should worship the Goddess upon a pedestal conjoined with the powers (śaktis) such as Jayā and the rest. || 75 ||
Or, at a Bāṇaliṅga or before the Sun, one should worship the Lotus-born (Brahmā) together with Sarasvatī in the eastern corner;
there, in the southwestern corner, one should worship Hari together with Śrī.
One should worship Śambhu together with Pārvatī in the northwest corner;
to the north of the Goddess, the lion is to be worshipped, and on the left, Mahāsura.
At the end, one should worship Mahiṣa; then, one should worship in sequence within the six corners Nandajā, Raktadantā, Śākambharī, and the auspicious Śivā.
Durgā, Bhīmā, and Bhrāmarī; then, upon the eight petals, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī. (79)
Then, one should worship Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Aindrī, and likewise Cāmuṇḍā, starting from the east upon the petals of the elements.
[He created] Viṣṇu’s Māyā, consciousness, intellect, sleep, as well as hunger;
the supreme Shadow, thirst, peace, and birth along with shame.
Śānti, Bhadrā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Vṛtti, Śruti, Smṛti, Dayā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Mātṛ, and Bhrānti—thus in order. (82)
Then, at the corners of the outer square (bhūpura), a wise man should worship Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapālaka, Vaṭuka, and the Yoginīs.

Then, one should worship Indra and the other [guardians], together with their vehicles and equipped with their weapons such as the thunderbolt, according to this method; thereafter, one should worship the Goddess along with her retinue.
One should offer various services of royal homage for the pleasure of Ambā;
thereafter, one should recite the nine-syllable mantra and first contemplate the meaning of the mantra. 85.
Then one should recite the Saptashati hymn before the Goddess;
indeed, there exists no hymn equal to this in the three worlds. (86)
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the ninth book, chapter fifty.
Then, by this means, a man should satisfy the Lord of Gods every day;
that man becomes an abode of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
Thus, O Brahmin, I have related to you the ritual procedure of Śrī Durgā;
by this, one attains the fulfillment of all goals—this very thing has been told to you. 88.
All the gods, headed by Hari and Brahmā, as well as the Manus, the sages established in knowledge, the yogis, and those in the stages of life (āśramas). || 89 ||
Likewise, Lakṣmī and all the other goddesses meditate upon that Śivā;
indeed, there is fulfillment of one's birth in this world if there is remembrance of Durgā. (90)
Having meditated upon his lotus feet, even the fourteen Manus attained the status of Manu,
and the gods likewise returned to their respective positions.
All this has been declared, including the most secret of secrets:
the description of the fivefold primary natures (prakṛtis) and their constituent parts.
Having heard this, a person shall always obtain the four goals of human existence; there is no doubt in this matter. What I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth. (93)
A childless woman obtains a son, and a seeker of knowledge shall attain that knowledge;
whatever desire one may contemplate, having heard this, one shall surely achieve it.
If one recites this with a concentrated mind before the Goddess during the Navarātra, the Mother of the World will certainly be thoroughly pleased. 15.

O Lord, dispeller of the suffering of your devotees, why do you distance yourself from me? (10)
"I have uttered no slander against others, nor calumny, nor falsehood;
by the ripening of what karma do you keep me far from Kāśī? (11)
Having thus made that request for the sake of time, the pitcher-born sage went to the Lord of Obstacles as his witness, the dispeller of all impediments.
Having seen him, worshipped him, and offered prayers, the illustrious Agastya, the husband of Lopāmudrā, then departed from the city toward the southern direction.
Tormented by separation from Kāśī, that sage, a treasure-house of great fortune,
went with his wife, constantly remembering Kāśī at every moment.
Having ascended, as it were, the vehicle of austerity, the sage, in half a moment,
beheld before him that Vindhya mountain, lofty and obstructing the sky.
Upon seeing the sage standing before him, the mountain trembled quickly,
shrinking down as if wishing to touch the earth, desiring to speak.
He prostrated himself on the ground with his eight limbs outstretched out of a spirit of devotion;
seeing him with his head bowed low, he beheld the great mountain named Viṣya.
With a serene countenance, the sage Agastya then said to Vindhya:
"O child, wait for a moment until I have returned."
"O son, I am unable to climb your boulder-like cheek," having spoken thus,
the sage, eager to depart, set out toward the southern direction.
Having ascended its peaks, he descended from them in succession;
and having traveled toward the southern direction, he beheld Śrīśaila on the way.
Having reached the Malaya mountain, he became devoted to a hermitage there;
and that goddess also arrived at Vindhya there, having been worshipped by Manu.
O Śaunaka, she is renowned throughout the worlds as Vinyavāsinī.
Sūta said:
This supreme life-story is the most excellent destroyer of enemies. (22)
The narrative of the mountain Agastyavidhya destroys sins;
it grants victory to kings and increases the wisdom of the twice-born. (23)
It bestows grain and wealth upon Vaiśyas and likewise grants happiness to Śūdras;
one seeking dharma attains dharma, and one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth.
A seeker of desires shall obtain his desires merely by hearing this once with devotion;
thus did the divine Manu Svāyambhuva, having propitiated [him] with devotion. (25)
He obtained the sovereignty of the earth during his own Manvantara;
thus, O gentle one, has this account concerning the Manvantaras been narrated by me.
This is but the first account of the illustrious Goddess; what more shall I tell you? ||26||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 7 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the tenth book, chapter eight.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Śaunaka said: "The first Manvantara has been described by you as this most excellent one."
Tell me of the emergence of the other Manus of divine splendor. ||1||
Sūta said: Having thus heard the origin of the first [Manu], Svāyambhuva,
he then inquires about the successive birth of the others.
Nārada, the supreme knower, skilled in the true meaning of the Goddess’s reality,
said:
"O Eternal One, tell me fully of Manana and its excellent origin."
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O great sage, this first Manu, Svāyaṃbhuva, has been described;
by him, having bowed down to the Goddess, a kingdom free from all thorns was obtained.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda, the two sons of Manu, possessed great majesty; they were renowned on the surface of the earth as the protectors of the kingdom. (5)
And the second Manu is said by the wise to be Svārociṣa,
the illustrious son of Priyavrata, possessed of immeasurable prowess.
That Manu, named Svārociṣa, who acts for the welfare of all beings, established his residence on the bank of the Kālindī.
Becoming one who eats only withered leaves and being devoted to the practice of austerity, he worshipped an earthen image of the Goddess with devotion. ||8||
Thus, O dear one, as he was performing austerities in the forest for twelve years,
the Goddess appeared, possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns.
Then the Goddess of the Gods, being pleased by that king of hymns, O Suvrata,
granted to Svārociṣa the refuge of all the Manvantaras.
Thus, through the propitiation of Tāriṇī by King Svārociṣa Manu, she attained renown as the sovereign protectress of the world.
And that powerful lord attained sovereignty, free from all enemies;
having duly established the Dharma, he ruled the kingdom together with his sons.
Having eaten, he went to his own world, Tapoloka, because of his reliance upon his own manvantara. The third Manu, named Uttama, the son of Priyavrata,
performed penance on the bank of the Gaṅgā, intent on the constant recitation of the Vāgbhava mantra.
Having fasted for three years, he entered into the favor of the Goddess.
Having praised the Goddess with a mind imbued by devotion to this supreme hymn, he obtained a kingdom free from thorns and a long-lasting lineage. (15)

Having abandoned the pleasures arising from sovereignty, he too followed the path cultivated by the best of kings who were devoted to Dharma. (16) The fourth Manu, named Tāmasa, the son of Priyavrata, having propitiated the Goddess who is identical with the universe on the southern bank of the Narmadā, [attained his goal]. (17)
Maheśvarī is devoted to Kāmarāja and Kuṭaja during the autumn season, specifically during the Navarātra.
The Queen of the Gods worshipped the peerless lotus-born goddess;
having obtained her grace and bowed down with unsurpassed hymns of praise, [she offered oblations]. 19.
Free from fear, he enjoyed a vast kingdom without thorns,
having begotten ten heroic sons who were reservoirs of valor and held their palms joined in reverence.
Having procreated with his own wife, he departed for the highest heaven;
he is known as the fifth Manu, Raivata, the younger brother of Tāmasa. ||21||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the tenth book, chapter nine: [The refuge of the practitioner]. (22)
Resorting to the bank of the Kālindī, he muttered the seed-syllable known as "Kāma," which bestows supreme pride,
the unsurpassed prosperity of self-sovereignty,
invincible strength in the world, and the granting of all perfections. || 23 ||

By propitiating him, he obtained a long-lasting and auspicious lineage consisting of sons and grandsons; and having established his sons in the duties of dharma and enjoyed the objects of the senses, [he attained his goal].
The peerless hero went to the supreme abode of Mahendra.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, therefore, let the wonderful and supreme majesty of the Goddess be heard.
Just as the supreme kingdom was [obtained] by Manu, the son of Aṅga.
The son of King Aṅga was the excellent Manu Cākṣuṣa;
as the sixth [Manu], he went for refuge to the Brahman-sage named Supulaha.
O Brahman-sage, destroyer of the distress of those who bow before you, I have come to you for refuge;
instruct me, your servant, O Lord, so that I may attain prosperity.
"May I possess sovereignty over the earth exactly as it is, unimpaired;
may my strength of arm be unimpeded and capable, skilled in the use of hand-held weapons and missiles. Therefore, instruct me today. (4-5)
"Even though my lineage is of long standing, may I attain an unbroken and excellent lifespan, and at its conclusion, may there be the attainment of liberation"—
these words reached the path of Manu's ears.
The illustrious sage replied that the supreme means for this is the propitiation of the Goddess.
O King, listen to my words, which are greatly pleasing to the ear:
worship Śivā today, and through her grace this shall come to pass.
Cākṣuṣa said:
What kind of worship is most purifying for this Goddess?
In what form should it be performed? Out of compassion, you ought to tell me. (8)
The sage said:
O King, listen to the supreme and imperishable worship of the Goddess;
likewise, one should incessantly mutter the unmanifest seed-syllable Vāgbhava.
By reciting it three times a day, a mortal shall indeed obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O delighter of the royal line, there is no seed-mantra other than Vāgīśvarī.
Through its recitation, it brings about success and is the supreme means for increasing vigor and strength;
by the recitation of this, even the mighty Brahmā, the creator of the universe, is subdued.
O King, Viṣṇu is proclaimed as the protector of creation through the recitation of that [mantra], and Maheśvara also became the destroyer through its recitation. (12)
Arrogant with the intoxication of strength and heroism. || 13 ||
The world-protectors and others as well, who are capable of both restraint and favor, came into being by taking refuge in her;
likewise, O King, you too shall soon obtain them by propitiating the Great Goddess, the Mother of the World, and the great sage. (14)
Thus enlightened by Pulaha, the best of sages,
the son of Aṅga went to the Virajā river to perform austerities.
And that powerful protector of the earth performed intense penance, devoted to the recitation of the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava, subsisting on withered leaves.
In the first year he subsisted on tender shoots; in the second, he consumed only water;
in the third year, he fed on air alone, remaining as motionless as a pillar.
Thus, for twelve years, as the king remained abstinent from food and constantly recited the Vāgbhava mantra, his mind became endowed with auspiciousness.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the tenth book, chapter ten.
And so, as he was privately reciting the supreme mantra of the Goddess, the Mother of the World, the illustrious Supreme Sovereign herself, appeared in person. (19)
Resplendent, invincible, and the sovereign embodying all the gods, she,
being pleased, spoke to that son of her own body in sweet-sounding words.
The Goddess said:
"O protector of the earth, tell me whatever supreme boon you have desired; being well-pleased by your asceticism, I shall grant it to you. (21)
Cākṣuṣa said:
O Goddess of the lords of gods, O you who are worshipped by the gods, you know everything that is desired and sought by the mind, for you exist as the inner controller (antaryāmin). || 22 ||
Nevertheless, by my good fortune, the sight of you has occurred;
O God, I say this: grant me the kingdom, O best of kings. (23)
The illustrious Goddess said: "O best of kings, the sovereignty of this Manvantara has been granted to you;
and your sons shall be exceedingly powerful and endowed with superior virtues. (24)
"The kingdom shall be free from thorns, and liberation at the end is certain.
Having thus granted this most excellent boon to Manu, the Goddess—
Praised by him with devotion, she immediately vanished from sight;
and that king Manu, the sixth, likewise [attained his goal] through her grace and by taking refuge in her.
He became honored by men, surrounded by the pleasures of a universal monarch;
his sons were devoted to military exercises and intent upon bearing the weight of state affairs.
Devotees of the Goddess, as well as heroes possessed of great strength and prowess, are to be honored elsewhere and are the recipients of the happiness of great kingdoms. ||28||
And thus, through the propitiation of the Goddess, the lord Manu Cākṣuṣa became the best of Manus; at the end, he went to the abode of Śiva.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Devī-carita of the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: The seventh Manu has been described; now the lord Vaivasvata Manu [is to be told].
The god of the ancestral rites (Śrāddhadeva), the enjoyer of supreme bliss, is indeed worthy of honor by kings. || 1 ||
And Vaivasvata Manu, likewise through the grace of Paradevī and by means of his own austerity, was born as the sovereign of a Manvantara. ||2||
He was celebrated on earth as Manu Sāvarṇi;
having propitiated the Goddess in a previous birth, he obtained her boon. (3)
He was born as the lord of a Manvantara, honored by all the kṣatriyas;
he was of great prowess, steadfast, and solely devoted to the service of the Goddess. ||4||
Nārada said:
How was the propitiation performed by that Manu in a previous birth?
You should tell me that regarding the Goddess born from the Earth. (5)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: In the Svārociṣa Manvantara, there was a king born of the lineage of Caitra,
renowned by the name Suratha, who possessed great strength and prowess.
He was a perceiver of virtues, a wielder of the bow, honorable, eminent, a poet, and accomplished;
he was a collector of wealth and a giver within the circle of supplicants.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the tenth book, chapter eleven:
The proud and powerful crusher of enemies, skilled in all weapons.
Once, those kings who were destroyers of the Kola city rose up against him. ||8||
Then the powerful enemies, accompanied by their armies, surrounded him and besieged the city of that king whose wealth was his honor. (9)
Then that king named Suratha, the destroyer of all enemies, set out from his own city surrounded by his army.
Then, in that battle, King Suratha was defeated by his enemies;
his wealth, which had been stored in the treasury, was seized by his ministers and counselors.
When everything had been taken away without exception, the king then felt great remorse;
that monarch of supreme splendor was even expelled from the city.
Then, mounting his horse under the pretext of hunting, he went to the forest;
alone in the desolate wilderness, he wandered about with a bewildered mind.
Having come to the hermitage of a certain sage whose mind was tranquil,
[he found it] inhabited by peaceful creatures and joined by hosts of the sage’s disciples.
For some time that king dwelt in the most beautiful hermitage of the eminent sage Sumedhas, who possessed far-reaching vision.
Once, at the conclusion of the worship of the sage, that protector of the earth went there, bowed down quickly, and, filled with humility, questioned him.
O Sage, O God upon Earth, mental anguish born of worldly distress constantly oppresses me, even though I have realized the truth and am devoid of worldly wisdom. (17)
Even for one who has been utterly defeated by enemies and stripped of his kingdom in every respect, a sense of "mine-ness" (mamatva) clearly arises in their mind nonetheless. (18)
"What shall I do? Where shall I go? How may I obtain peace, O Sage?
I hope for your favor; speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas. (19)
The sage said:
Listen, O protector of the earth, to this supreme and most wonderful account of the Goddess’s majesty, which is incomparable and bestows all desires. 20.
The Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), who pervades the world and arises from Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Hara, indeed forcibly seizes away the minds of living beings. 21.
Know, O protector of the earth, that she withdraws [the world] for the sake of delusion;
she creates the entire universe and she protects it at all times. (22)
O protector of the earth, in the form of Hara during the dissolution, she indeed withdraws all things;
she is Mahāmāyā, the granter of desires, the night of time (Kālarātri) that is difficult to overcome.
Kālī is the destroyer of the universe, Kamalā is she whose abode is the lotus;
in her the entire world was born, and in her the universe is established. (24)
And because it will find repose in her, she alone is higher than the highest;
O man, the grace of that Goddess shall belong to him upon whom it falls.
He alone transcends delusion, and not otherwise, O Lord of the Earth. (25)
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 10 ||
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The King said:
"O best among those who know Time, tell me, who is that goddess spoken of by you?"
What deludes sentient beings, O twice-born one, and what would be the cause? || 1 ||
From what does she arise, O Goddess? What is her form and what is her nature?
O Bhūdeva, out of compassion, tell me everything in its entirety. (2)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the tenth book, chapter eleven.
The sage said:
O King, listen as I describe to you the true nature of the Goddess,
how she originated, and by what means she became identical with the universe.
When the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Yoga, having withdrawn the universe, spread out Śeṣa and the Blessed One lay asleep upon the ocean. ||4||
At that time, while Janārdana, the God of gods, was under the power of deep sleep,
the two Dānavas Madhu and Kaiṭabha were born from the wax of his ears.
Then the two Dānavas of terrible form, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, prepared to kill Brahmā; seeing them, the lotus-born Lord [intervened].
While the Lord of the gods was asleep, he fell into an insurmountable anxiety;
for the Blessed Lord was sleeping, and the two Dānavas were difficult to withstand.
"What shall I do? Where shall I go?
How indeed may I obtain peace?"—as that high-souled one was thus reflecting, O dear one, an intellect capable of accomplishing his task then arose within him.
Under whose control the divine Lord Hari remains even while asleep. ||9||
"I go for refuge to that goddess, Nidrā, the progenitress of all.
Brahmā said:
"O Goddess, O Goddess, Mother of the Universe, bestower of the fruits of the desires of your devotees! (10)
O Illusion of the World, O Great Illusion, O Auspicious One who reclines upon the ocean!
All beings, subject to your command, perform their respective duties.
She is the Night of Time, the Great Night, the Night of Delusion, and she who is fierce with intoxication;
she is all-pervading, she who is under her own control, she who is to be honored, and the sole treasure-trove of great bliss. 12.
Worthy of honor, most adorable, illusory power, honey-sweet, and vast;
you are proclaimed as the supreme among all things high and low.
You are modesty, nourishment, patience, fame, and splendor, the very embodiment of compassion.
She is the beloved of the world, the kinswoman of the universe, whose nature consists of the waking state and the others. ||14||
She is supreme, the sovereign mistress, and devoted to supreme bliss;
though she is one and of a single nature, she is also accompanied by a second and consists of a duality.
She is the triple Veda, the abode of the three goals of life; she is the fourth state, whose essence is the state beyond the fourth;
she is the fifth, the mistress of the five elements; and she is the sixth, the sovereign of the sixth sense.
The seventh is the mistress of the seven days of the week, the bestower of the sevenfold boons;
the eighth is the mistress of the Vasus, the sovereign composed of the nine planets.
She is the delightful essence of the nine passions, the number nine, and the sovereign of the nine;
she is the tenth, worshipped in the ten directions, and the goddess Ramā who pervades the ten quarters.
She consists of eleven aspects, is served by the eleven Rudras,
is pleased by the lunar day Ekādaśī, and is the sovereign of the eleven Gaṇas.
The goddess is the twelfth day, twelve-armed, and the birthplace of the twelve Ādityas;
she is the deity whose nature consists of thirteen and who is dear to the thirteen Gaṇas.
The thirteenth [digit] is divided into the thirteen names, with the Viśvedevas as its presiding deities;
the fourteenth is the bestower of boons from Indra, the progenitor of the fourteen Manus.
She is to be known as the fifteenth plus five (the twentieth); she is the lunar day consisting of fifteen plus five;
she is the sixteenth, possessing sixteen arms, and composed of the sixteen digits of the moon.
O Goddess of gods, you whose divine body is pervaded by the rays of the moon consisting of sixteen digits—such is your form, O Nirguṇā, when the quality of Tamas arises. (23)
The Blessed One, the God of gods, the Lord of Ramā, has been seized by you;
these two Daityas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, are powerful and difficult to overcome.
"And for the sake of slaying these two, awaken the Lord of Gods.
The sage said:
"Thus praised, the Blessed Goddess, who is of the nature of *tamas* and beloved by the Blessed One," [25]
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the tenth book, chapter twelve:
Then, having abandoned the God of gods, the demoness began to delude him.
At that very moment, the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self and Lord of the Universe, [appeared].
The Lord of Gods regained consciousness and beheld the two foremost Dānavas;
then those two terrible Dānavas saw that Madhusūdana.
Having resolved to fight, they went into the presence of Hari;
and then the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana fought with them both.
The all-pervading Lord, whose weapon is his arms,
[confronted] those two who were then intoxicated by excessive strength and deluded by the world-illusion.
"Five thousand years," they thus spoke to the Supreme Lord.
Having heard these words of theirs, the Blessed One, the Primordial Person, [responded]. (30)
"O Bestower of Boons, may you be pleased," they said again to Hari. ||31||
"It is certain that both of you shall be slain by me today in the forest. When they said, "O Lord,
slay us when the earth is submerged by water," the Blessed One,
the wielder of the mace and conch, replied, "So be it," O King.
Having severed their heads and hips with his discus,
O King, the Goddess was thus born and praised by Brahmā.
O Great King, Mahākālī is the sovereign of all the lords of yoga;
likewise, O Lord of the Earth, listen to the origin of Mahālakṣmī. 34.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Devīmāhātmya of the tenth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
The sage said:
Born from the womb of a buffalo queen, he possessed great strength and prowess.
Having defeated all the gods, Mahiṣa became the lord of the world.
Having forcibly conquered the offices of all the world-protectors, the great asura enjoyed the wondrous sovereignty over the three worlds.
Then all the gods, having been defeated and cast down from heaven,
placed Brahmā at their head and went to the highest world.
Wherein the two supreme gods, Śaṅkara and Acyuta, being established,
related the account of the wicked-souled Mahiṣa.
Having forcibly conquered the abodes of all the gods, the asura, arrogant with the intoxication of his own strength and heroism, enjoys them himself.
O Goddess who torments the asuras, this wicked Daitya named Mahiṣāsura is a thorn to the lords of the immortals; therefore, let a means for his swift destruction be considered.
Having heard these words of the gods, which were like a yoke of affliction, that Blessed One became exceedingly enraged, as did Śaṅkara and the Lotus-born Brahmā.
O lord of the earth, from the mouth of Hari, who was thus filled with wrath,
there emerged a divine splendor possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns.
Then, in due order,
the splendor of all the inhabitants of heaven issued forth from their bodies, gladdening the lord of the gods.
From the splendor that belonged to Śambhu, his head was produced;
from the southern [splendor] and that of Viṣṇu, his arms came into being.
By the grace of Soma, his two breasts were formed; by that of Mahendra, his waist;
then, O King, by that of Varuṇa, his thighs came into being;
by the splendor of Bhūmi, his hips; and by the splendor of Brahmā, his feet.
The toes [were fashioned] by Bhānu, and the fingers of the hands by Vāsava.
Likewise, O lord of the earth, his nose and teeth were produced then by the supreme splendor of Kaubera and Prajāpati.
The three auspicious eyes produced by Pāvaka became knit with a frown due to the twilight radiance, O storehouse of splendors.
O lord of men, her two ears were born from the wind and from splendor;
and by the splendor of all [the gods], the goddess who slays Mahiṣa was born.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the tenth book, chapter twelve.
Śiva gave him a trident, Viṣṇu a discus and a conch, and the wielder of the noose (Varuṇa) a noose;
Agni gave him a spear, and Vāyu a bow and arrows.
Maheṃdra gave him a thunderbolt and a bell from the elephant Airāvata.
Yama holds the staff of death, while Brahmā holds a rosary and a water-pot.
Divākara bound his garland of rays upon the pores of the skin;
likewise, Kāla [brought] a sword and a stainless shield, O lord of the earth. (18)
O King, the ocean gave him a stainless necklace, two ageless garments,
a crest-jewel, earrings, bracelets, and likewise armlets.
Filled with joy, he gave to that goddess a spotless crescent moon, as well as anklets, a neck-ornament, and other decorations.
O Lord of the Earth, Viśvakarman gave her bangles, and Himavat gave her a lion as a vehicle and various kinds of jewels. (21)
The Lord of Wealth gave her a drinking vessel filled with wine,
and the powerful Lord Śeṣa gave her a necklace of serpents.
Honored by all other gods without exception, she who pervades the universe—
the great goddess— was praised by the gods who were oppressed by Mahiṣa.
The Great Goddess, the sovereign of the gods who is worshipped by the wise, heard their various hymns of praise addressed to her, the cause of the world's manifestation.
For the sake of slaying Mahiṣa, he let out a great roar;
by that roar, O Lord of the Earth, Mahiṣa became terrified.
Surrounded by his entire army, he approached the Mother of the World;
then that great asura named Mahiṣa fought with the Goddess.
Filling the expanse of the sky with various weapons and missiles hurled in many ways—[namely] Cikṣura, Grāmaṇī, Senāpati, Durdhara, and Durmukhī—[they advanced]. (27)
Bāṣkala, Tāmraka, Fastos, and Arcispara—along with these and countless others who were like the Ender of Battles (Yama). ||28||
When the hero Mahiṣa, the best of the Dānavas,
was thus surrounded, the goddess, who deludes the worlds, then had eyes copper-red with anger.
The goddess, mounted upon Mahiṣa, struck down the warriors in battle;
then, when they had been slain, that Daitya was overwhelmed with rage.
Then the lord of the Dānavas, skilled in illusion, quickly approached the goddess; by means of his magic power, he assumed various other forms.
Then she destroyed all those various forms of his;
finally, he assumed the form of Mahiṣa, the tormentor of the immortals.
Having bound him very firmly with a noose and severed his head with her sword,
the Goddess struck down Mahiṣa, the destroyer of the hosts of gods.
Then the remaining army, crying out "Alas! Alas!", was broken and fled in the ten directions;
all the gods, filled with joy, praised the Goddess of the lords of gods.
Thus Lakṣmī, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura, was born;
O King, hear now how the manifestation of Sarasvatī occurred. 35.
Once there was a Daitya named Śumbha, fierce with the intoxication of his own power;
and his brother Niśumbha was likewise possessed of great strength and valor.
O King, all the gods, oppressed by him and deprived of their splendor,
approached the Himalayas and praised the Goddess with great devotion.
The gods said:
"Victory to you, O Lord of Gods, skilled in destroying the afflictions of your devotees!
You are the one who brings an end to the Dānavas, free from old age and death, and sinless. (38)
O Goddess of gods, who are easily accessible through devotion, possessed of great strength and prowess, whose nature is that of Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Brahmā, and others, and who possess infinite valor! 39.
O you who cause creation and maintenance, O you who bring about destruction, O bestower of luster,
O you who are well-pleased by the great *tāṇḍava* dance, O giver of joy, O Mādhavī!

"Be gracious, O Goddess of the lords of gods; be gracious, O treasure-house of compassion! Lift us up, who have sought refuge in you, O destroyer of the distress of those who seek shelter, from the shoreless ocean of fear born of Niśumbha and Śumbha.
O Lord of the Earth, while the thirty gods were thus offering praise..."
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Tenth Skandha, Chapter 12:
Pleased, Girijā said: "Tell me the reason for your hymn of praise."
In the meantime, she emerged from her treasury-form.
That Kauśikī, who is worshiped by the world, spoke this to the gods out of affection:
"O best of deities, I am pleased with your hymn of praise, which is of the highest form. (44)
When it was said, "Let a boon be chosen," the gods deliberated upon the boon;
Śumbha by name was the younger brother, and Niśumbha was his renowned elder brother.
O Goddess, the three worlds have been overwhelmed by the powerful Daitya;
let the slaying of that evil-souled lord of the Dānavas be considered.

I shall now fully declare that which must be performed day by day by a twice-born man after rising in the morning, for the benefit of the twice-born.
From sunrise until sunset, the twice-born should perform virtuous deeds,
engaged in obligatory and occasional rites, as well as other blameless optional rites.
Neither father nor mother remains as a companion for oneself;
neither son, wife, nor kinsman remains—only Dharma alone remains.
Therefore, always accumulate Dharma as a companion by means of its practices.
But by means of dharma alone, with it as his companion, he crosses over the darkness that is difficult to cross.
Conduct is the primary dharma, as declared in the Śruti and the Smṛti;
therefore, a twice-born man should always be fully engaged in this for his own sake.
Through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct one obtains progeny;
through right conduct food becomes inexhaustible; and bad conduct destroys the protector.
Proper conduct is the supreme dharma that brings about the welfare of men;
having become happy in this world, one attains happiness in the next. (11)
But for people blinded by ignorance, whose minds are deluded and wandering, Dharma is the great lamp that reveals the path to liberation. 12.
"Excellent dharma is attained through right conduct; through right conduct, one gains mastery over action;
from action, knowledge is born—such is the statement remembered by Manu."
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter one.
This conduct is the most excellent of all dharmas and the supreme austerity;
that alone is designated as knowledge, by which everything is accomplished.
O best of the twice-born, he who conducts himself here devoid of proper conduct should be excluded like a Śūdra; for he is exactly like a Śūdra.
Conduct is said to be of two kinds: scriptural and likewise worldly;

O Sage, the customs of villages, the customs of castes, the customs of regions, and those arising from families must be observed by all men; one should never transgress them.
For a man of evil conduct is indeed censured in the world;
he is constantly a partaker of suffering and is truly pervaded by disease. 18.
One should abandon wealth and pleasure if they are devoid of dharma; and one should also abandon dharma if it results in unhappiness or is despised by the world. (19)
Nārada said: O Sage, since the scriptures here are so numerous, how can there be certainty?
Tell me what the authoritative measure is for determining the path of dharma.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Dharma exists only in what is declared by these three; it is not found anywhere else. (21)
But where there should be a mutual contradiction among these three, the Śruti is the authority; in a conflict between two, the Smṛti is superior. (22)

O Sage, what is the use of speaking much or describing it again and again? (35)
The Lord is constantly worshipped and the supreme goal is attained;
therefore, at least one rudrākṣa should be worn on the head with devotion by the best of the twice-born.
A garland for the head consists of twenty-six beads, while that for the heart consists of fifty.
