The armlets were made with six hundred thousand eyes, and the wrist-bindings with twelve hundred thousand eyes.
O Six-faced One, having fashioned a rosary of rudrākṣas with one hundred and eight, or fifty, or even twenty-seven [beads]. (38)
Indeed, through either its wearing or its recitation, one attains infinite fruit;
if a rosary of one hundred and eight rudrākṣas is worn. (39)
O Six-faced One, at every moment he obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter.
The Lord said:
O Six-faced One, listen; I shall describe the characteristics of the rosary for recitation.
The face of the rudrākṣa is Brahmā; the bindu is said to be Rudra. || 1 ||
Viṣṇu shall indeed be the tail, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it consists of twenty-five akṣas, having five faces and provided with thorns. ||2||
The rosary should be made of red-colored beads mixed with white ones, strung together with knots, and shaped like a cow’s tail or a bracelet.
Having joined the mouth with the mouth, one should join the tail with the tail;
one should make Meru face upward, and above that, the serpent-noose (nāgapāśaka).
Thus, having strung together this garland which bestows the perfection of mantras, [in the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, eleventh book, chapter five].
Having washed it with scented water and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) on top.
Then, having washed it with the water of Śiva, one should install the groups of mantras;
having touched it with the Śivāstra mantra, one should veil it with the Kavaca mantra.
Having sprinkled [the object] with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta, up to one hundred and eight times.
Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the root mantra (mūlamantra) as before;
having recited the root mantra and placed it upon pure ground, one should then place Śiva, the supreme cause, together with Ambā upon it.
She is the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
Whichever mantra belongs to whichever deity, one should worship that deity with that very mantra.
The garland should be placed upon the head, or on the neck, or one should place the rosary on the ear;
likewise, with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, one whose self is restrained should perform the recitation.
Endowed with supreme devotion, one should constantly wear rudrākṣas on the neck, the head, the heart, the extremities, the ears, or both arms. (11)
What is the use of much speaking or repeated description in this matter?
Therefore, the constant wearing of rudrākṣas is praised. (12)

During bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, the Vaiśvadeva rite, worship of the gods, penance, as well as at a Śrāddha ceremony, and especially at the time of initiation; ||13||
If a Brahmin, out of delusion, performs any Vedic rite while not wearing rudrākṣa beads, he certainly falls into hell. (14)
One should wear a Rudrākṣa on the head, around the neck, on a thread, or on the hand;
it should be pure, set with gold and gems, auspicious, and not previously worn by others. 15.

One who is impure should not wear the rudrākṣa; one should always wear it with devotion alone. Even blades of grass blown by the wind that have touched a rudrākṣa will go to the world of merit from which rebirth is difficult to attain.
A human being wearing a rudrākṣa, even while committing sin, [attains the same]. (17)
For the Jābāla Śruti declares that one crosses over all evil;
indeed, by wearing Rudrākṣa beads, even animals attain the state of Rudra.
How much more so for those men who wear a rosary of rudrākṣa beads!
Indeed, at least one rudrākṣa should always be worn on the head by those devoted to Rudra. (19)
Those who utter the names of Śambhu, the Supreme Self, proclaim the destruction of all sufferings and liberation from all sins. 20.
Those who are adorned with rudrākṣas are indeed the best of bhāgavatas;
the wearing of rudrākṣas should be performed by lords seeking all that is auspicious.
In the ear-lobes, the crest-lock, the neck, the hands, and likewise the abdomen,
reside Mahādeva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and their manifestations.
Likewise, other gods as well as all the ancestral sages (gotrarṣis)—who are the primordial and foundational forms of all beings—wear rudrākṣas out of devotion. (23)
All the sages born in their lineage were indeed pure, devoted to the Vedic dharma, and wearers of rudrākṣa beads. (24)
By the grace of Mahādeva. ||25||

Faith does not arise directly toward that which grants liberation and is established by the Vedas; rather, at the end of many births, a desire for wearing the rudrākṣa arises spontaneously. Indeed, the majesty of the rudrākṣa has been proclaimed with reverence by the Jābālas. (26)
O son, it is recited by all the sages as well as by me;
the fruit of the rudrākṣa is indeed renowned throughout the three worlds. (27)
The merit from seeing the fruit becomes ten millionfold through touching it;
by wearing it, a man obtains merit a hundred millionfold. (28)
And from recitation, one always obtains [the fruit]; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. 29.
He who wears on his hand, chest, neck, ears, and likewise on his head thousands of lakhs of crores,
or hundreds of lakhs of crores of Rudrākṣas, is Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt.
Invulnerable to all beings, he shall indeed wander upon the earth like Rudra;
he is to be venerated by both gods and asuras, just like Śiva.
One who constantly wears Rudrākṣa beads is always worthy of salutation by men, even if he is impure, engaged in improper acts, or burdened with all manner of sins. 32.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter six.
One is liberated from all sins by wearing a rudrākṣa;
even if a dog dies while wearing a rudrākṣa around its neck, it is likewise freed. (33)
Even he attains liberation, how much more so a human being—if he should wear a rudrākṣa, even if devoid of recitation and meditation. (34)
Freed from all sins, he goes to the supreme goal;
for even by making an effort to wear a single rudrākṣa, one attains this. 35.
Having extracted twenty-one [beads], one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Hereafter, I shall again proclaim the ritual procedure for the rudrākṣa.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter.
The Lord said: "O Mahāsena, Kuśagranthi, Putrajīva, Ādi, and others are [the names of] the supreme [deities]."
Not even a single one of them is worth a sixteenth part of the rudrākṣa. || 1 ||
Just as Viṣṇu is among men, and as the Sun is among the Brahmins;
just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, and as Kaśyapa is among sages. (2)
Just as Uccaiḥśravas is among horses, just as the Lord of the Gods is among gods,
and just as Gaurī is among goddesses, so too may this [text] be the most excellent.
There is no hymn superior to this, nor is there any vow superior to this;
among gifts that yield inexhaustible merit, the rudrākṣa is preeminent. (4)
One should give an excellent rudrākṣa to a peaceful devotee of Śiva;
I am not able to describe the end of the fruit of his merit. ||5||
He who offers food to one who wears rudrākṣas around his neck rescues twenty-one generations of his family and goes to the world of Rudra.
That Brahmin on whose forehead there is no sacred ash, nor the wearing of Rudrākṣa beads,
nor worship in the temple of Śambhu, is the lowest of outcasts.
Even one who eats meat, drinks liquor,
or associates with those of the lowest castes shall be liberated from sins if a rudrākṣa remains upon his head.
Whatever fruit is obtained through all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and the study of the Vedas—that fruit one obtains immediately by wearing the rudrākṣa. 9.
Whatever merit is gained through the four Vedas and by reading the Purāṇas, as well as that which comes from visiting sacred fords and likewise from all branches of knowledge; || 10 ||
One immediately obtains that merit by wearing a rudrākṣa;
if one dies while wearing a rudrākṣa at the time of departure [from this life], [one attains liberation]. || 11 ||
He attains the state of Rudra, and for him there is no further rebirth;
if one dies while wearing a rudrākṣa on the neck or on the arms, [this result is attained].

Having ascended through twenty-one generations of his lineage, a man shall dwell in the world of Rudra— whether he be a Brāhmaṇa or a Cāṇḍāla, devoid of merit or possessed of merit. Whoever wears sacred ash and Rudrākṣa beads shall attain the divine state of Śiva,
whether he be pure or impure, and even if he is an eater of forbidden food.
Whether he be a barbarian, an outcaste, or even a murderer, by the mere wearing of rudrākṣas, he becomes Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt. (15)
When worn on the head, it is ten million; on the ears, one hundred million;
bound around the neck, one billion; and on the crown of the head, ten billion. (16)
If one hundred thousand Rudrākṣas are placed on the sacred thread (upavīta) and ten million on the upper arm,
then the Rudrākṣa at the wrist is the supreme means for attaining liberation.
Having become a wearer of rudrākṣas, a brahmin who always performs any Vedic rite with devotion obtains the great fruit thereof. 18.
Even one devoid of devotion who wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads around his neck, if he is constantly engaged in sinful deeds, is liberated from all bondage. 19.
He whose mind is dedicated to the rudrākṣa and who indeed wears a rudrākṣa is a devotee of Maheśvara in this world; he is to be saluted like the Liṅga itself. 20.
Whether ignorant or learned, by wearing the rudrākṣa, one [attains the highest state]. Śrīmaddevībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, Eleventh Skandha, Chapter 6. 747.
One would attain the world of Śiva, just as the donkey did in Kīkaṭa.
Skanda said:
O Lord, for what reason did the donkey wear rudrākṣas?
Or by whom were they given to him in Kīkaṭa? Tell me that, O Supreme Lord. (22)
The Blessed Lord said:
Listen, my son, to an ancient account concerning a donkey in Vidarbha;
he was made to carry a heavy load of rudrākṣa beads by a traveler on the road.
Exhausted and unable to bear that burden, he fell to the ground;
then Maheśvara, the three-eyed one who holds the trident in his hand, cast him down.
O Mahāsena, by my grace,
he who has come into my presence shall be honored in the world of Śiva for as many thousands of yugas as there are beads on the rosary of Rudrākṣas, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (25)

It should be spoken to one’s own disciples, but never to those who are not disciples (26). One should never reveal it to those who lack devotion or to fools. Whether one be devoted or lacking devotion, whether lowly or even lower than the lowest—[it should be taught to such as they].
Whoever wears rudrākṣas is liberated from all sins;
with what indeed could the merit of wearing rudrākṣas be compared? (28)
Sages who perceive the truth declare this to be a great vow:
he who, firm in his observance, wears a thousand Rudrākṣas. (29)
All the gods bow down to him; he is just like Rudra.
In the absence of a thousand arms, however, there are sixteen on each side.
One [mudrā] at the crest-lock, twelve on each of the two hands,
thirty-two in the region of the throat, and forty on the head.
He who wears one Rudrākṣa on each ear, six on his ears, and one hundred and eight on his chest, is honored like Rudra himself.
He who wears Rudrākṣas combined with pearls, coral, crystal, silver, lapis lazuli, and gold shall become Śiva himself.
Even if one wears only rudrākṣas out of laziness, sins do not touch him, just as darkness does not touch the sun. 34.
A mantra chanted with a rosary of rudrākṣas bestows infinite fruit;
even a single rudrākṣa on one's body grants great merit. (35)
His birth would be as useless as one devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), he who bathes his head while wearing a rudrākṣa on his crown. (36)
The fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā arises for him; there is no doubt in this matter.
[There are those] with one face, five faces, and eleven faces, O excellent one. (37)
Some rudrākṣas have fourteen faces and are worshipped by the world;
this rudrākṣa, whose essence is Śaṅkara, should always be worshipped with devotion. 38.
It can even make a poor man a king on earth;
in this regard, I shall relate to you the supreme ancient doctrine. (39)
In the land of Kosala, there was a certain twice-born man known as Virinātha;
he was immensely wealthy, righteous in soul, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. ||40||
The son of that performer of sacrifices who was initiated for the rite was of beautiful form,
a renowned treasury of various virtues, youthful, and as handsome as the god of love.
Then the wife of the wise preceptor Sudhiṣaṇa, adorned with strings of pearls, infatuated him with her beauty, youth, and intoxication.
Having united with her for some time, he then, out of fear, gave poison to his preceptor; afterwards, however, he was free from fear.
At whatever moment his mother or father knew of some deed [of his],
at that very instant he killed both his mother and father with poison.
When his wealth had been exhausted through various pleasures and enjoyments,
that wicked man then began to commit theft in the houses of the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, intoxicated by the madness of drinking liquor and cast out by his kinsmen,
he was expelled from the village by everyone and became a forest-dweller.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter seven:
Together with Muktāvalī, he went into the dense forest.
Standing on the path, out of greed for wealth, he slew many Brahmins. 47.
When much time had passed in this manner, that lowest of men then died;
and thousands of messengers of Yama arrived to lead him away.
Likewise, the attendants of Śiva arrived from the world of Śiva;
O son of the Mountain-Daughter, a debate took place between the two of them.
Then the messengers of Yama said: "O servants of Śambhu, tell us what merit this man has, if you wish to lead him away. (50)
Then the messengers of Śiva said: "In the spot where he died, ten cubits below the ground, there is indeed a rudrākṣa."
"By its power, O messengers, we shall lead him into the presence of Śiva.
Then, having ascended a celestial chariot, the twice-born one assumed a divine form.
The treasury of virtues, accompanied by the Dṛta, has gone to the abode of Śaṅkara.
Thus, O you of noble vows, the greatness of the rudrākṣa has been told to you.
Thus, the greatness of the rudrākṣa has been briefly described by me;
it causes the destruction of all sins and bestows the fruit of great merit. (54)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 6 ||
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Thus, O Nārada, the six-faced one was enlightened by Giriśa.
And having realized the greatness of the rudrākṣa, he became one who had accomplished his purpose. || 1 ||
Thus have I described the Rudrākṣa of such power in connection with the topic of virtuous conduct; now listen with a concentrated mind to something else.
Just as the greatness of the rudrākṣa, which bestows infinite merit, has been described,
so shall I describe to you its characteristics and the arrangement of the mantra.
From seeing it, one gains a hundred thousandfold merit; from touching it, ten millionfold;
and by wearing it, a man obtains merit a hundred million times greater than that.
A person obtains the merit of hundreds of millions and thousands of millions of recitations by wearing rudrākṣa beads. (5)
Indeed, from wearing auspicious rudrākṣas there arises a great fruit;
that which is the size of an emblic myrobalan fruit is declared to be the best. (6)
The wise declare that [the size] equal to a jujube fruit is the medium; the inferior is the size of a chickpea. This is the promise proclaimed by me. (7)
By the command of Śiva, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras were born from the tree upon the earth; indeed, those auspicious dice belong to their respective castes.
The Brāhmaṇas are to be known as white, the Kṣatriyas as red-colored;
the Vaiśyas are to be understood as yellow, and the Śūdras are proclaimed to be black.
A Brāhmaṇa should wear white garments;
a king, however, should wear red ones; a Vaiśya should wear yellow ones, while a Śūdra should wear black ones.
Those that are even, glossy, firm, and provided with auspicious thorns are excellent;
likewise, those that are bitten by insects, cut, split, or devoid of thorns are inauspicious.
One should avoid those Rudrākṣas that are covered with sores or are not smooth;
however, a Rudrākṣa that has its own opening formed naturally is considered the best in this world.
That which is made by human effort is considered mediocre;
one should wear [the beads] that are even, smooth, firm, and round, using a linen thread. (13)
• Where a line is seen that is uniform across all limbs, perfectly even yet highly extraordinary, appearing like a streak of gold when rubbed. (14)
One should know that to be the supreme rosary; it is to be worn by the worshippers of Śiva.
One should carry a single rudrākṣa on the crest-lock and three on the head. (15)
Thirty beads should be worn on the neck, sixteen on each of the two arms;
twelve beads at the wrists, and there should be fifty on the neck. (16)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter seven: One should fashion a sacred thread (upavīta) from a garland consisting of one hundred and eight beads.
One should wear [the sacred thread] around the neck in a double or triple strand; likewise,
[one should wear it] on earrings, a crown, in small circular pendants and necklaces, on armlets, bracelets, and even upon the waistband.
A person should wear Rudrākṣas at all times, whether asleep or awake;
three hundred are said to be the lowest, while five hundred are called the middle.
A thousand is declared to be the supreme; one should thus wear [the ashes] according to the divisions:
on the head with the Īśāna mantra, and on the ear with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
Furthermore, one should hold [them] in the two hands. || 21 ||
With the Aghora seed-mantra, one should place [the beads] on the forehead and likewise on the heart;
with the Vāmadeva mantra, those strung with fifty beads on the belly; and thus, by means of the five Brahmans and the ancillaries (aṅgas), is the wearing of the Rudrākṣa beads performed.
One should wear all the Rudrākṣas while reciting the well-known root mantra.
A single-faced Rudrākṣa reveals the supreme reality. (23)
That manifestation arises;
O best of sages, he becomes Ardhanārīśvara with two faces. (24)
Because he holds the supreme reality (paratattva) and because he is the bearer (dhāraṇa), Ardhanārīśvara is eternally pleased with him;
and the three-faced Fire himself instantly burns away his sin of killing a woman. 25.
The three-faced rudrākṣa is also the very embodiment of the triple fire;
by wearing it, the Consumer of Oblations (Agni) is perpetually satisfied.

The four-faced Rudrākṣa is indeed the very form of Pitāmaha (Brahmā); by wearing it, one becomes possessed of great fortune and attains supreme, great health. The Rudrākṣa is the embodiment of the five Brahmans. ||28||
A person should wear this for the sake of purification, as it is a great accumulation of knowledge. By the mere wearing of it, Maheśvara, who has five faces, is satisfied.
Furthermore, the six-faced Rudrākṣa has Kārtikeya as its presiding deity. (29)
The presiding deity of the seven limbs. || 30 ||
The wise also declare that the deity of this [bead] is the god Vināyaka. The seven-faced rudrākṣa has the seven sages as its presiding deities;
by wearing it, one becomes greatly prosperous and attains supreme, great health. (31)
The rudrākṣa with seven faces has the Sun as its presiding deity, while the one with eight faces has Rudra as its presiding deity. ||32||
A man who is pure and possesses great wealth of knowledge should wear it; for it has eight faces, it is auspicious, it pleases the eight Vasus, and it pleases Gaṅgā.
By wearing it, these [deities], who are speakers of truth, become pleased.
The nine-faced Rudrākṣa is declared to have Yama as its presiding deity; by wearing it, the fear of Yama never arises in any way whatsoever. (34)
The ten-faced rudrākṣa is remembered as the protector of the ten directions; there is no doubt that it generates joy for the ten directions when worn. (35)
It has Rudra as its eleventh deity;
they call that [deity] Indra, who always increases happiness. (36)
The eleven-faced rudrākṣa is indeed the eye, while the twelve-faced rudrākṣa has the nature of Mahāviṣṇu;
it also represents the twelve Āditya deities, for he who is devoted to that [rudrākṣa] bears these [qualities].
Kāmadeva is pleased. ||38||
The auspicious one with thirteen faces and twenty eyes is the granter of desires and the bestower of success; by the mere wearing of it, he grants long life and health. (32)
The fourteenth-faced Akṣa was born from the eye of Rudra; he is the remover of all diseases. Therefore, one should avoid liquor, meat, garlic, onion, śigru, śleṣmātaka, and village-pig in eating.
During an eclipse, at the equinoxes, at the solstices, as well as on the new moon and full moon days, and on other auspicious days;
By wearing rudrākṣas, one is immediately liberated from all sins. ||41||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. ||7||
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter eight.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O great sage, I shall now describe the method for the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having raised Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity, from the Mūlādhāra, [one should proceed]. 1.

Resorting to the path of the *suṣumṇā*, the practitioner should contemplate [the soul] reaching the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), having united the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman by means of the *haṃsa* mantra. ||2||
One should meditate upon the mandala of the earth as being from the feet up to the knees, four-cornered, adorned with vajras, enriched with the seed-syllable *laṃ*, and golden in color.

One should meditate upon the mandala of water, which begins at the knees and extends to the navel; it resembles the half-moon, is marked with two lotuses, is conjoined with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, and possesses a white luster. (4)
One should meditate upon the circle of fire, red in color, extending from the navel to the heart, triangular in shape, adorned with a svastika, and joined with the seed-syllable *raṃ*.
One should meditate upon the mandala of wind, which is smoke-colored, marked with the letter Yaṃ, and encircled by the syllable Phaṭ up to the space between the eyebrows from the heart.

One should visualize the sphere of space (ākāśamaṇḍala), which is clear, beautiful, and extends from the center of the earth up to the aperture of Brahmā (ābrahmaraṃdhra), joined with the seed-syllable "Haṃ."
Having thus reflected upon these [elements], one should dissolve each one individually:
earth into water, water into fire, fire into air, and that [air] into space.
Having dissolved space into the ego, and the ego into the principle of Mahat,
one should dissolve Mahat into Prakṛti, and Prakṛti into the Self within Māyā.
Having become composed of pure consciousness, one should meditate upon the personification of sin (pāpapuruṣa),
situated in the left side of the belly, black in color, and the size of a thumb.
It has the head of the murder of a Brahmin, the arms of the theft of gold,
the heart of the drinking of liquor, and is joined with the hips of violating the teacher’s bed.
O Kṛṣṇa, that pair of feet associated with him, which is the pinnacle of minor sins,
bears a sword and shield, faces downward, and is most difficult to endure.
Meditating on the seed-syllable of air, one should fill the air and cause it to enter [the body];
then the mantra, joined with one's own body, should burn it away with the seed-syllable of fire.
Then, having expelled the external ash produced from the "sin-man" by means of the mantra repeated during the *kumbhaka* (retention), one should exhale the air with the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The wise one should drench the ashes produced from the body with the seed-syllable of nectar (sudhā-bīja), and then,
having solidified those ashes like a golden stalk with the seed-syllable of earth (bhū-bīja).
Meditating on the seed-syllable of the sky as having the form of a pure mirror,
the wise one should fashion the limbs from the head down to the feet.
Furthermore, the mind should re-create the elements, beginning with space;
then, by means of the "I-am" mantra (so'ham), one should lead the Self into the lotus of the heart.
Having taken the life-force of the Kuṇḍalinī, which has become composed of nectar through union with the Supreme,
and having established it in the lotus of the heart, one should remember it as residing in the Mūlādhāra.
Red in color, seated upon a boat in the midst of the ocean, she stands upon a fierce lotus;
with her lotus-like hands she holds a trident, a bow, a jewel-garland, a goad, and five arrows, as well as a fresh skull; she is adorned with three eyes and possesses full, swelling breasts.

May the Goddess, the supreme power of life (prāṇaśakti), who has the color of the rising sun, be the bestower of happiness upon us. (19) Having thus meditated upon the power of life, whose nature is that of the Supreme Self, one should perform the wearing of the sacred ash for the sake of attaining mastery over all things. (20)
I shall describe in detail the majesty [of ash] and the great fruit of wearing it;
the wearing of ash is supreme, as established by the authority of the Śruti and Smṛti. (21)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 8 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter nine.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: To those twice-born ones who have duly performed this Śirovratam,
one should impart the supreme knowledge that dispels ignorance.
For those by whom the head-vow (śirovrata) has not been performed according to rule and with faith,
the practice of the Śrauta and Smārta traditions provides no benefit.
O learned one, it was solely through the practice of the head-vow (śirovrata) that Brahmā and the other deities became gods, and certainly not by any other cause.
The greatness of the Śirovrata was established by the ancients even earlier than the ancients;
for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and all the deities as well [practiced it]. (4)
O wise one, even one who is burdened with every sin is liberated from all sins by him who has performed this Śirovratam according to the prescribed rule.
This is indeed called the "Head Vow" (Śirovrata), which was declared in the Atharvaṇa Śruti upon the head;
for it is nothing other than that, and it is obtained through merit.
O tiger among sages, the names of this vow are recited differently according to the various Vedic branches; for that vow is indeed one and the same across all the branches.
In all the branches [of the Vedas], there is one single reality called Śiva, which is a mass of truth and consciousness;
likewise, there is knowledge concerning that [reality], and likewise the Śirovrata.
Even one who is devoid of the head-vow (śirovrata) and has abandoned all [other] religious duties is nonetheless entitled to all branches of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
This head-vow (śirovrata) should be performed; it burns away the wilderness of sins and is the means for attaining all vidyās. Therefore, one should practice it correctly.
One should always properly observe that vow which the subtle Atharvaṇa Śruti, illuminating its subtle meaning, has declared with affection.
With the six mantras beginning with "Agni," one should perform the smearing of all limbs with pure ash; this is called the Śarava-vrata.
One should perform this vow of the head with reverence during the periods of the twilights;
until the dawning of knowledge, his knowledge shall indeed be supreme. 13.
One should perform the Śirovrata for twelve years, or one year, or half of that, or half of that again; or alternatively, one may perform it for twelve days by means of a formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
One should not instruct that person who has performed the ritual bath after the *śirāvrata*;
his knowledge shall be destroyed, for such a teacher is indeed merciless.
The sage who is the direct teacher of the knowledge of Brahman is indeed compassionate, just as the glorious Lord of All is gentle and truly compassionate. 16.
Only for those men who have practiced dharma throughout thousands of previous births does faith indeed arise, and never otherwise. (17)
On the contrary, due to an abundance of ignorance, only aversion arises;
therefore, for one possessed of such hatred, self-realization will not occur.
[18] [This applies even to those who are directly qualified for the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman.]
O wise one, they alone are such and not others who have performed the head-vows of ablution. 19.
"The Pāśupata vow must be taught only to those twice-born who have performed it with devotion; such is the injunction of the Vedas. (20)
He who, by means of this vow, renounces both the animal and that state of being an animal, does not become a sinner even after killing them; such is the certainty of the Vedānta.
The wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) has been proclaimed with reverence by the Jābālas,
using the Tryambaka mantra, the Satarudriya, and the Śiva mantra.
One who has entered the stage of a householder should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), applying the three lines with the syllable Om uttered three times. || 23 ||
"A mendicant should always wear [it]," so says the Jābāli Śruti;
[he should do so] with the Tryambaka mantra, the Praṇava, and the Śiva mantra. ||24||

Both the householder and the forest-dweller should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka), as should the student (brahmacārī) day after day, according to the verse beginning with "medhāvī" (the wise one). 25.
One should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ash, even if it is mixed with water;
for a Brāhmaṇa born according to the sacred law, the triple mark is indeed made with ash alone.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter ten.
"One should always wear the horizontal smearing of ashes on the forehead;
through its connection with Mahādeva, there is a corresponding affinity in that dharma. A Brāhmaṇa should always properly observe the practice of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). (27)
Since the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) was worn with ashes by the primordial Brāhmaṇa,
therefore a Brāhmaṇa should always wear the triple mark.
One should not, even out of delusion, abandon the smearing of the body with ash proven by the Vedas and the application of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), nor the worship of the Liṅga of Rudra. 29.
With the Tryambaka mantra, likewise with the one accompanied by the stars (the Saptarṣi mantra),
with the five-syllabled mantra, and likewise with the Praṇava.
O great sage, one who has entered the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, the heart, and between the eyebrows.
The Tripuṇḍra should be worn with ashes— either by means of the Tṛyāyuṣa mantra beginning with "medhāvī," or else by means of the secondary (gauṇa) ashes— by the religious student (brahmacārin).
A Śūdra, devoted to service, should always perform the smearing of ashes and the wearing of the Tripuṇḍra with devotion, using the mantra "Namaḥ" alone preceded by the name of Śiva. 33.
O Sage of noble vows, for all others as well, the smearing of ashes and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) should be performed with devotion, even without a mantra. (34)
The smearing with ashes and the wearing of the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra) are superior to all other religious duties; therefore, one should practice them constantly. ||35||
Then, having respectfully taken either the ashes produced from the Agnihotra fire or those originating from the Virajā fire, and having placed them in a pure vessel; || 36 ||
Having washed his feet and hands and sipped water twice with a concentrated mind, he should take up the sacred ash while slowly reciting the Pañcabrahma mantras. (37)
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should consecrate [the water] three times with those same seven mantras, beginning with "Agnir it."
Having recited "Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ" and meditated, one should utter the mantras;
first, having thoroughly smeared the body with white ashes. (39)
Free from sin and free from passion, the mortal is born; of this there is no doubt.
Then, having meditated upon Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord of the World and the Master of Waters, [he attains liberation].
Having mixed water with ashes while reciting "Agnir ityādi" and other mantras,
and having wiped [the vessel] while meditating on Sāmba, one should scoop up [the mixture] toward the top of the head.
And they [should mark] their foreheads, chests, and shoulders with white ashes produced through meditation and made sacred, according to the mantras appropriate for their own stage of life.
One should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with devotion at the three times of day, using the middle, ring, and thumb fingers in both forward and reverse order. ||43||
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 9 ||
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: This [chapter] concerning Agni is secondary, yet it destroys ignorance and accomplishes knowledge.
Know, O Brahmin, best among the knowers of Brahman, that the secondary [teachings] are of various kinds.
O Sage, likewise [the fire] born from the Agnihotra fire, that born from the Virajā fire, that produced from the Aupāsana fire, and that originating from the Samidh fire. ||2||
[The fire] produced from a cooking fire, that arising from a forest conflagration, and for all members of the three castes, that produced from the agnihotra sacrifice. (3)
O great sage, one should wear the ash produced from the fire of the *virajā* plant;
for householders especially, it should be that produced from the *aupāsana* sacrificial fire.
The fire produced from the sacrificial fuel (samidh) must indeed be maintained by the student (brahmacārin);
for Śūdras, it is the fire arising from the cooking hearth in the house of a learned Brāhmaṇa.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter ten. 753.48.
This [remedy] arising from a forest fire should be maintained by all others as well;
the full moon day at the time of the dissolution, one's own country, and one's possessions [are the means]. //6//
A field, a grove, or a forest that is auspicious and possesses favorable characteristics is recommended.
There, on the thirteenth day of the waxing moon, having bathed well and properly prepared the sacrificial fire,
he should request permission from his own preceptor, worship him, and prostrate before him.
Having performed a special worship, he himself, wearing white garments, [should proceed]. ||8||
Wearing a pure sacred thread, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
seated upon a seat of darbha grass and holding a handful of darbha grass, he [should remain].
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), facing either east or north,
one should meditate upon the God and the Goddess by way of petitioning them.
He should be initiated by his resolve for as long as the body lasts, or for twelve years.
Thinking, "I shall perform this vow," for that purpose, one may practice for twelve months,
or half of that, or a quarter of that, or even for just one month. || 12 ||
Whether for twelve days, or even six days,
or half of that, or for a single day, until the time of making the formal vow (saṃkalpa) for the observance.
Having established the sacred fire for the purpose of performing various oblations free from blemish,
he offered clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, and cooked rice according to the prescribed ritual.

Having become purified, and further aiming for the purification of the principles (tattvas), he should offer oblations with the root mantra using those very same sacrificial fuels (samidh) and other materials. || 15 ||
Recalling, "May these principles within my body be purified," one should then [meditate upon] the elements and subtle elements,
as well as the five organs of action.
Through the division of knowledge and action, there are five each;
the seven elements beginning with the skin, the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa,
the mind, intellect, ego, the [three] qualities, primordial nature (prakṛti), and the individual soul (puruṣa).
Passion, knowledge, and indeed the limited power (kalā), as well as necessity and time. || 18 ||
Māyā, Śuddhavidyā, Maheśvara, Sadāśiva, Śakti, and Śivatattva—these they know as the principles (tattvas) in their respective order. || 19 ||
Having struck with the *viraja* mantra, that Hotṛ priest shall become free from passion (*viraja*).
Then, having taken cow dung, formed it into a ball, and consecrated it with mantras— || 20 ||
Having deposited that [image] in the fire and guarding it on that day while subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya),
one should perform everything previously described at dawn on the fourteenth day.
On that day, remaining without food, one should complete the remainder of the time;
likewise, on the morning of the festival, having performed [the rites] up to the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa).
Having withdrawn the fire of Rudra and taken the ashes,
he then became one with matted hair, one with a shaven head, and one with a single lock of hair.
Having bathed after having been so, if he should again be free from shame, he may be a naked ascetic (digambara),
or one whose garment is another's body, or one whose heroic raiment is a hide.
Clad in a single garment or wearing bark, carrying a staff and a water-pot, he should then wash his feet, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and purify his mind and body.
Having combined that [earth], which was produced from the stainless Nala, he [anointed it] in due order with the six Atharvaṇa mantras beginning with "Agnir" (Fire). 26.
Having wiped the limbs starting from the head down to the feet, one should touch them with those [ashes];
then, having likewise raised [the ashes] from that same sequence, one should apply the ash.
One should perform the touching of all limbs with either the *praṇava* or the *śiva-mantra*;
thereafter, one should apply the *puṇḍra* known as *tryāyuṣa*.
Having attained the state of Śiva, one should act in accordance with that state of Śiva;
one should likewise perform this Pāśupata vow during the three junctions of the day.
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and it brings about the cessation of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva).
Having abandoned that state of being a bound soul and having performed the Pāśupata vow, [one attains the goal]. ||30||
The Great God Sadāśiva, whose form is the Liṅga, is worthy of worship;
the ash-bath is supremely meritorious and the highest bestower of all happiness. (31)

Since it increases longevity, strength, health, glory, and nourishment, [this is done] for the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, and for the complete fulfillment of all prosperity. (32)
For those who are anointed with the unctuous ash, there is no fear of great pestilence;
this ash, which bestows peace and nourishment, shall become the granter of all desires at the three junctions of the day.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 10 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter eleven.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Nārada said: How is this threefold nature of the sacred ash proclaimed?
Tell this to me, O Lord; I have a great curiosity.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O divine sage, listen as I describe the threefold nature of the sacred ash (bhasman),
which destroys great sins and brings about supreme, great fame.
Cow dung that is connected to its source is taken with one's own hand;
when burnt while reciting a Brāhmaṇa-mantra, it is said here to bring about peace.
A man, being attentive, should indeed take up that cow-dung; having taken it while it is in the air, he should then burn it with his own limb.
That is declared to be nourishing (pauṣṭika), and now hear about that which grants desires (kāmada).
By means of grace, one should burn this; it is celebrated as the ash that grants desires.
O divine sage, having risen early in the morning, pure and devoted to the vow of sacred ash,
one should go to the cow-pens and pay homage to the herd of cows.
One should take auspicious cow dung from cows that correspond to their respective castes:
the cow of a Brāhmaṇa is white, and the cow of a Kṣatriya is red.
The [sacred thread] of a Vaiśya is said to be yellow in color, while that of a Śūdra is black;
one of purified intellect [should perform this on] the full moon, the new moon, or the eighth lunar day.
Having taken auspicious cow dung with the *prasāda* mantra,
one should then form it into a ball with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Heated by the rays of the sun in a clean and beautiful place,
he should not place it in a palace, whether with husks or even with chaff.
One should place that fire— either produced from a forest or born from the house of a Vedic scholar—
into that [vessel] with the mantra using the seed-syllable of Śiva.
Then the wise one should take ash from the fire-pit there;
having taken a new vessel, he should deposit it with a gracious mind.
Likewise, [he should take] ketaki, pāṭalī, uśīra, and sandalwood.
And various fragrant substances, such as saffron and others. || 13 ||
Having first performed the ritual bath with water, the pure-minded one should thereafter perform the ash-bath and then place [the substance] into that vessel while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra.
If one is unable to bathe in water, one should perform the ash-bath;
having washed both feet and hands, one should bow to the head with the mantra.
Then, having rubbed [the body], one should worship the face with Tatpuruṣa,
the heart with Aghora, and thereafter the navel with Vāmadeva.
Having rubbed all his limbs with the *sadyojāta* mantra,
the wise man should discard his former garment and take up a pure garment.
Having washed his feet and hands, he should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
In the absence of smearing with ashes on the navel, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is prescribed.
Before midday, one should apply [the tilaka] with water, and after that, without water;
one should also apply the Tripuṇḍra with the middle fingers, the ring finger, and the index finger.
The locations for the ritual placement (nyāsa) are said to be the crown of the head, the forehead, the ears, the throat, as well as the heart and the arms.
With five fingers, the preceptor should apply [the ash] upon the head by means of grace and the mantra;
with three fingers, he should apply it on the forehead with the *śiromantra*.
With the *sāvya* mantra he should touch the right ear, with the *vāmadeva* mantra the left, and with the *aghora* mantra the throat; then, with the middle fingers, he should touch the anus.
The preceptor should touch the heart with the heart-mantra using three fingers;
he should place [the mantra] on the right arm with the śikhā-mantra.
The wise one should place [the mantra] on the left arm with the *kavaca* [mantra] using three fingers; he should touch the navel with the middle finger while reciting the mantra "Īśāna. (24)
The three lines are traditionally known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
the first is Brahmā, then Viṣṇu, and above that is Maheśvara. (25)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter twelve.
That which is placed with a single finger-breadth [of space] has Īśvara as its deity;
Brahmā himself is in the middle of the head, while Īśvara is on the forehead. (26)
The two Aśvin deities are in the ears, and Gaṇeśa is likewise in the throat;
the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra should likewise abandon the smearing with holy ash.
For all those of the lowest castes, it should be devoid of mantra;
even for uninitiated men, it should likewise be without mantra. (28)
The eleventh chapter of the eleventh book in the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O divine sage, listen to all that fruit which arises from the smearing of ashes.
And it contains the secret ritual procedures, which bestow the fruits of all desires. || 1 ||
Having taken up this entire pure water, it falls through the sky;
yet it is neither wetted, nor hardened, nor foul-smelling, nor dried up. (2)
If one should pick up something fallen after having left it above,
one should form it into a ball and cast it into the fire of Śiva or elsewhere, consecrated with the root mantra.
Having taken it and covered it with a cloth, one should cast it into a vessel for ashes that is well-made, very firm, pure, washed, sprinkled, and auspicious. || 4 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with the mantra, the practitioner should cast ashes into the vessel—
whether it be made of metal, wood, clay, or even cloth.
Or one should prepare another beautiful and pure vessel for the ashes;
or one may place the thick ashes upon a very pure linen cloth.
One who has set out on the journey should take the ashes himself or have his attendant do so;
one should not give them to an untrustworthy person, nor should one throw them upon an impure surface.
One should not touch it with the lower limbs, nor throw it away, nor step over it; therefore, having taken the consecrated ash, one should employ it [for its intended purpose]. 8.
The procedure for wearing the sacred ashes (vibhūti), as proclaimed by me and taught in the Smṛtis, has been declared;
by the mere performance of this rite, one becomes equal to Śiva—of this there is no doubt.
The ash prepared by Śaivas should be accepted with supreme devotion from those who resemble Śiva; having requested it, one should worship it. (10)
The ash perfected by means of the Tantric path is to be accepted by Tantric worshippers;
however, if it has been offered anywhere at all, it must not be accepted by Vaidikas. (11)
Neither Śūdras, nor Kāpālikas, nor other heretics should wear that triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with devotion; one should not even mentally transgress this rule.
Since it is ordained by Śruti, one who abandons it becomes fallen;
likewise, the wearing of the Tripuṇḍra with devotion and the covering of the body [with ashes]. (13)
A twice-born man should indeed perform these with mantras; for one who abandons them becomes fallen.
Those who do not practice the smearing of ashes (udbhūlana) and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with devotion [are likewise fallen].
O bull among sages, for those by whom this path spoken of as "ashes" has not been maintained, there is no liberation from saṃsāra even through millions of births. (15)
Know, O Sage, that the birth of those men whose bodies are devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is as fruitless as that of a pig. (16)

That forehead, devoid of ashes and the sacred mark, would be like a cremation ground and should not be beheld by those who perform meritorious deeds; shame on that village, an abode of inauspiciousness! (17)
Fie upon a birth that does not worship the Lord! Fie upon knowledge that takes refuge in the inauspicious!
Those who revile the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) revile Śiva himself. (18)
And those who bear [this teaching] with devotion, they alone truly bear Him;
for just as a mountain does not shine when deprived of fire, so it is with them. //19//
Even when all other means are present, those who do not perform the worship of Śiva with faith—omitting the smearing with ashes, the *udbhūlana*, and the *tripuṇḍra*—[are deficient]. (20)
By them, everything previously performed may even become contrary;
[this includes] the warding off of the Tripuṇḍra by means of ashes and Vedic mantras.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter thirteen.

Without conduct appropriate to the Vedas, even that which is performed according to the Smṛtis becomes a cause of misfortune; by such a person, what has been done is as if undone, and even what has been heard becomes as if unheard.

Whether one has studied the Vedas or not, he who does not wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) has his Vedic study in vain, his sacrifices in vain, his gifts in vain, and his austerities in vain. || 23 ||
He who does not wear the Tripuṇḍra despite observing vows and fasts in vain,
that man who desires liberation while abandoning the wearing of ashes— 24.
Indeed, by means of drinking poison, he makes himself eternal;
under the pretext of creation, the Creator has thus prescribed the wearing of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
He created the forehead as oblique and upward, not circular;
indeed, oblique lines are seen upon the foreheads of all embodied beings. (26)
Nevertheless, foolish men do not apply the Tripuṇḍra;
for them there is no meditation, no liberation, no knowledge, and no austerity. (27)
Just as a Śūdra has no entitlement to the study of the Veda,
so too a Brahmin who performs his rites without the horizontal *tripuṇḍra* has no entitlement to the worship of Śiva. (28)
Facing east, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) as before, [he should proceed]. ||29||
Having restrained the breath and performed the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the ash-bath;
taking pure ashes produced from the Agnihotra fire. (30)
One should place it upon one's own head with the Īśāna mantra;
then, taking that ash, one should apply it to the mouth with the Puruṣa mantra.
One should apply ashes to the heart with that called Aghora, to the secret place with that called Vāma, and to both feet with that named Sadyojāta.
Then, the strengthening of all the limbs with the mantra consisting of the *praṇava* alone—
this is declared by the supreme sages to be the *āgneya* bath.
For the sake of the successful accomplishment of all rites, the wise man should first perform this;
then, having washed his hands and other limbs, he should sip water according to the prescribed rule.
One should apply a horizontal tilaka on the forehead, the heart, and the throat with ashes, using either the five Brahma-mantras or the prescribed ritual method.
This triple mark made with ghee is purifying for all ritual acts;
however, Śūdras and those of the lowest castes must never wear ashes held in their hands at any time.
One should perform ritual action smeared with ashes from the Agnihotra fire;
otherwise, all ritual actions will never bear fruit.
Truthfulness, purity, recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, visiting sacred fords, and the worship of gods and other deities—all these are in vain for one who does not wear the Tripuṇḍra. (38)
The most excellent of Brahmins who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), who bears rudrākṣa beads, and is pure, destroys diseases, calamities, epidemics, famine, and thieves. (39)
He attains the supreme Brahman from which he does not return again;
such a person is a purifier of the assembly at a śrāddha ceremony, worthy of worship by Brahmins and even by the gods.
In ancestral rites, sacrifices, recitations, burnt offerings, the Vaiśvadeva ceremony, and the worship of the gods,
a person who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) becomes purified in soul and conquers death.
I shall describe to you once again the greatness of wearing the sacred ash (bhasma).
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 12 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"The multitudes of great sins (mahāpātaka) and other sins as well—"
They perish, O tiger among sages; this is the truth, the truth, and not otherwise. || 1 ||
Listen to the fruit of merit for one by whom even a single portion of ash is worn:
it is said to bestow knowledge upon ascetics and to grant detachment to forest-dwellers. (2)
O Sage, it likewise increases the merit of householders,
and for those established in the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya), it bestows the fruit of Vedic study.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatamahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter thirteen: [This work] constantly bestows merit upon Śūdras and destroys the sins of others.
Likewise, the smearing with ashes and the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra). ||4||
For the protection of all beings, the Vedic revelation ordains both the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍraka).
The Vedic revelation prescribes for all these very as a sacrifice:
the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
The Vedic revelation ordains for them, by virtue of their being all-encompassing dharmas,
both the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
The Vedic Śruti ordains for the sake of the Liṅga-worshippers (Māheśvaras) the smearing with ashes as well as the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra). ||8||
And for the sake of the realization of all [the truths], the Vedic revelation ordains both the smearing with ashes and likewise the horizontal triple mark (tripuṇḍra). ||9||
The ash, consisting of the triple-tilaka and the smearing [of the forehead], was held by Hiraṇyagarbha, by his incarnations such as Varuṇa and others, and by the deities. (10)
Umādevī, Lakṣmī, Vāc, and other faithful women—all of them wore sacred ash in the form of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing of the body. || 11 ||
And the sages have maintained the ash in the form of the triple-mark (tripuṇḍra) and its smearing.

The ashes, worn in the form of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and as smearing the body, have been maintained by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others, as well as by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even those of mixed castes, using even Apabhraṃśa languages.
O bull among sages, only those by whom the smearing of ashes (*uddūlana*) and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) have been joyfully practiced are truly cultured and wise, and no others.
The Śiva-linga, the jewel, the rosary, and likewise the five-syllabled mantra—
It is a medicine that destroys anger for men, and it is like a woman in the rite for subjugation.
Wherever one who has smeared his body with ashes— whether he be a fool or even a scholar— enjoys [the food],
there Mahādeva, the bull-bannered god, enjoys it together with his consort.
Whatever man there may be, even if he is burdened with every sin, once worshipped, that human being is soon [purified]. ||17||
He who follows one whose entire body is covered in ashes, and praises him with faith—even if that person is burdened by all manner of sins—he is soon honored by men. (18)
By merely giving alms to one who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra),

that [person] has indeed studied, that person has heard the scriptures, and by that person everything has been performed. That Brahmin on whose head the triple mark has been made with sacred ash— [by him all is accomplished].
Even in the lands of Kīkaṭa, where Bhūtivibhūṣaṇa resides.
A human being should always dwell there, for that place is indeed equal to the sacred field of Kāśī;
whether one is ill-behaved or endowed with good character, whether one is engaged in yoga or devoid of auspicious marks. (21)

Or, one who is endowed with the teaching of prosperity (bhūti) is to be honored by me like a son; for even if he should practice the divine teaching of prosperity through a disguise, he is worthy of respect.
Even with hundreds of sacrifices, one does not attain that destination which he who holds [the scripture] attains—whether through association, playfully, or even out of fear. (23)
But he who possesses power acquired through the prescribed rites is indeed worthy of worship, just as I am;
for he is the cause of satisfaction for Śiva, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Brahmā.
It is the cause of satisfaction for Pārvatī, Mahālakṣmī, and Bhāratī;
it is very difficult to attain through charity, sacrifice, or austerities. (25)
Neither by pilgrimage nor by the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is merit obtained;
[rather, it is obtained through] charity, sacrifices, religious duties, and pilgrimages, O Nārada. (26)
Meditation does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the *tarpa* forehead mark (*tripuṇḍra*).
Just as a king always regards one who bears his own insignia as his own kinsman, so too Śiva [regards] one marked with the *tripuṇḍra*; by that [mark], Rudra is brought under control.
Whether a twice-born or of another caste, with pure ashes and faith, || 28 ||
He regards [the world] as his own;
though he has abandoned the conduct of all stages of life and all ritual actions have ceased for him, [he remains thus]. (29)
Whoever should wear the mark of the triple-tilaka even once, or should wear the triple-tilaka mark, even he is liberated;
one should not examine his knowledge, nor his lineage, nor likewise his vows. (30)
O Nārada, one whose forehead is marked with the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) is indeed worthy of worship;
there is no mantra superior to the Śiva-mantra, and nothing equal to Śiva.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter fourteen.
Indeed, there is no merit higher than the worship of Śiva, nor any sacred site (tīrtha) equal to the ash;
that which is the supreme sacred site of the fire of Rudra is proclaimed to be this ash. (32)
It is the destruction of all sufferings and the purification of all sins;
whether one is an outcaste, the lowest of men, a fool, or even a scholar.
In whatever land he who is endowed with the authority of prosperity may dwell, there Sadāśiva, accompanied by Soma and surrounded by hosts of all beings, shall ever reside.
Endowed with all sacred fords (tīrthas), it always maintains their presence. ||34||
These ashes, purified by the five Śiva-mantras and adorned with the limbs of the burner of desire (Kāma),
when fashioned as sectarian marks (puṇḍraka) upon the surface of the forehead, erase the ill-fated syllables written by destiny.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 9 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: To one whose body is smeared with ashes, he who joyfully gives wealth—
All his sins are destroyed; of this there is no doubt. || 1 ||
All the Śrutis, all the Smṛtis, and even all the Purāṇas proclaim the greatness of Bhūti; therefore, a twice-born man should wear it.
One should apply the triple-mark (tripuṇḍra) with white ashes at the three junctions of the day;
being liberated from all sins, one is glorified in the world of Śiva. ||3||
The yogi should daily perform a full-body bath from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head at the three junctions of the day; thus he shall swiftly attain yoga. ||4||
By bathing with ashes, a person becomes a savior of his lineage;
bathing with ashes possesses innumerable qualities superior to bathing with water.
Whatever merit exists in all sacred fords, whatever fruit exists in all sacred fords—one obtains all that fruit from the ash-bath; of this there is no doubt.
Whether one is burdened by great sins (mahāpātaka) or even burdened by minor offenses (upapātaka),
all that is burnt away by the ash-bath, just as fire consumes fuel.
"There is no purifying bath superior to the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
Thus was it said by Śiva in the beginning, and then Śiva himself performed the bath. (8)
From that time forward, Brahmā and the other sages, as well as those devoted to Śiva, diligently performed the ritual bath with ashes in all their rites. ||9||

Therefore, he who performs this head-bath, which is of the nature of fire (āgneya), is indeed Rudra himself in this very body; of this there is no doubt. Those who become fully satisfied upon seeing one who wears the sacred ash (bhasma)—
The gods, asuras, and lords of sages are always to be worshipped; of this there is no doubt. || 11 ||
Upon seeing that man who rises with all his limbs covered in ashes,
even the King of the Gods will prostrate himself before him like a staff.
O Sage, for those who consume what is forbidden to eat while preceded by the smearing of ashes, that very thing becomes edible for them; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he be a student, a householder, or a forest-dweller, one who constantly bathes with ashes after first bathing in water does so with devotion. (14)
Completely liberated from all sins, he goes to the supreme goal;
for ascetics, bathing with the ashes of fire is especially distinguished. 15.
An ash-bath is superior to a bath with water; the destruction of moisture is certain.
One should know that moisture is the primordial nature (prakṛti), and they know the primordial nature to be bondage. (16)
For the sake of abandoning primordial nature (prakṛti), bathing with ashes is prescribed;
O Brahmin, there is nothing equal to ashes even within the three worlds. (17)
O Sage, in ancient times, having seen the ash, the gods formerly gave it to their beloved goddess for the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, and for the sake of purification.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter fourteen:
Therefore, whoever should perform this head-bath (śiras-snāna) pertaining to Agni, [attains the fruit].
Freed from the bonds of existence, he is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 19 ||
Fever, rakṣas, piśācas, pūtanās, leprosy, abdominal tumors, all types of fistula-in-ano, and the eighty varieties of wind-diseases (vātaroga). || 20 ||
There are sixty-four diseases of bile (pitta), thirty-seven of phlegm (śleṣman), as well as the fear of tigers and thieves, and other malevolent planets as well. (21)
By means of the ash-bath, [sins] perish just as elephants do before a lion;
likewise, by pure cold water and the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) made with ash.
Whoever maintains the supreme Brahman attains it, there is no doubt;
and whoever, anyone at all, maintains the supreme triple mark with sacred ash.
He attains the world of Brahmā, freed from sin; of this there is no doubt.
By wearing the seed of Fire upon the forehead according to the prescribed rite. (23)
It certainly destroys the Yama-script written on the forehead;
by wearing it upon the neck, it destroys the sin committed above the throat.

By wearing it on the neck, sins committed through the enjoyment of sensual pleasures and the like are removed; by wearing it on the arms, sins committed by the arms are removed; and by wearing it on the chest, sins committed by the mind are removed. (25)

O Brahmin, by holding [the breath] at the navel, one removes the sin committed regarding the genitals; by holding it at the anus, one removes the sin committed regarding the anus; and by holding it at the sides, one removes such acts as embracing another's wife.
The wearing of those ashes is praised everywhere as being of three types;
it is the wearing of the ashes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśāna, as well as of the three sacred fires.
By that [rite], indeed, the maintenance of the three worlds and their qualities was accomplished;
the learned twice-born man, though covered in ashes, was freed from the occurrence of great sins. ||28||
He is instantly united with the Vajra and liberated without a doubt;
for one who is devoted to the ash, his defects are burned away by the contact of the ash and fire. (29)
One whose self is purified by the ash-bath is known as one established in the Self;
he is a Bhasmin who has all his limbs and directions smeared with ash and bears the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka).
The man who sleeps on ashes is known as one established in ashes;
[for him], ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and other such beings, as well as diseases, become exceedingly difficult to endure. (31)
By the mere proximity of one who is devoted to the sacred ash (bhasmaniṣṭha), [all sins] flee away; of this there is no doubt.
It is called *bhasita* because it illuminates (*bhāsana*), and it is called *bhasma* because it consumes impurities (*kalmaṣa*). (32)
With spirits and ghosts as their precursors. ||33||

Prosperity is the bringer of prosperity for men, and protection was the provider of protection in ancient times. Upon seeing one who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), the [obstacles] become terrified and tremble; they perish quickly, there is no doubt.
Just as sin is destroyed by the mere remembrance of Rudra, so too [does it vanish]. ||34||
Having performed thousands of evil deeds, he who bathes with ashes—
those ashes burn it all away, just as fire consumes a forest by its heat.
Even if he has committed incomparable sin, that twice-born man who, at the time of death,
becomes a bhasmasnāyin (one who bathes in ashes), is swiftly liberated from his sins.
One whose soul is purified by the ash-bath, who has conquered anger and subdued the senses, having come into my presence, does not return to worldly existence again. (37)
When the moon has entered the constellation of Bṛhaspati, one whose body is smeared with ashes, upon seeing Śaṅkara worshipped, is liberated from all sins. (38)
Whether desiring long life, or seeking prosperity, or desiring liberation, a wise man should always wear the sacred ash; he indeed is a true twice-born.
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is supremely meritorious and consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Those terrible Rākṣasas, Pretas, and other lowly creatures— || 40 ||
Upon seeing one who wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), they flee without a doubt;
having performed the rites of purification and so forth, and having bathed in pure water. (41)
One should perform the smearing with ashes from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
this is the purely Vāruṇa bath, which removes external impurities from the body.
Having abandoned all external and internal impurities through that [practice], one should drink the Aruṇa [nectar] and be intent upon that bath; of this there is no doubt. 43.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter fifteen.
O Sage, even that which has been performed is truly as if unperformed without the bath of ashes;
the bath of ashes is declared in the Vedas and is called the Agneya (fiery) bath. (44)
One shall obtain the fruit of Śiva-worship, which purifies both the interior and the exterior;
that indeed is the bath which destroys even external impurity. 45.

He explains that: even after constantly and respectfully performing ten million ritual baths with water, one must still diligently remove the external and internal impurity of living beings by means of intense [spiritual practice].
O Sage, one does not become a purified soul without the ash-bath;
only he truly knows the greatness of the ash-bath according to reality. ||47||
Or rather, Mahādeva— the crest-jewel of all the Vedas—
knows that even without performing the ash-bath, one performs a Vedic rite improperly.
He who shall diligently perform the ash-bath according to the prescribed rite does not actually obtain even a sixteenth part of the merit of that action. (49)
He alone is the one authorized for all rites, as heard in the Vedas;
the ash-bath, the purifier of purifiers, is likewise heard in the Vedas. (50)
He who, being deluded in soul, does not perform this shall become a perpetrator of great sins;
[for he fails to obtain] that merit which is acquired by twice-born men through infinite ablutions in the waters of Varuṇa.
From the ash-bath, merit many times greater than that is obtained.
The ash-bath should be performed with diligence at all three periods of the day.
The ritual bath with ashes (bhasmasnāna) is prescribed by the Śruti; its abandonment would cause one to fall [from grace].
After the discharge of urine and other excretions, one must diligently perform the ash-bath.
Otherwise, human beings will not become purified;
even a twice-born man who has performed his ablutions according to the rules will not be pure without the bath of ashes. 54.
One will not become a purified soul, nor is one qualified for ritual action, when the downward wind has been expelled, during yawning, ejaculation, or sneezing. (55)
Even when phlegm is expectorated, one should diligently perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
Only a single portion of the majesty of the glorious ash-bath has been described here.
Furthermore, O bull among sages, I shall declare again the fruit arising from the ash-bath;
it should be heard with an attentive mind.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 14 ||
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having respectfully purified the ashes with the mantras beginning with "Agniriti," etc., [one should apply them].
The triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead and other parts of the body is to be worn exclusively by the twice-born.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—all these are traditionally known as the twice-born (dvijas).
Therefore, the tripuṇḍra should be worn daily with great effort by the twice-born.

O Brahmin, he alone for whom the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) has been performed is called a twice-born (*dvija*). Therefore, the wearing of the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) and the application of sacred ash (*vibhūti*) must be performed by the twice-born.
(3) If one performs virtuous deeds while abandoning the wearing of sacred ash, those deeds become as if unperformed; of this there is no doubt. (4)
Even the instruction for the Gāyatrī mantra is not [complete] without the wearing of ashes;
therefore, having applied ashes to one's body, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī. (5)
O bull among sages, they say that the Gāyatrī is the very root of Brahmanhood;
in the absence of the wearing of ashes, it is not imparted by anyone at all.
O sage, there is no eligibility whatsoever for the reception of the Gāyatrī [without it].
As long as the ashes produced from fire have not been applied to the forehead and other parts of the body. ||7||
The absence of sacred ash on the forehead is not an indicator of Brahminhood;
in this very way, O Brāhmaṇa, I have stated the cause that bestows great merit.
He on whose forehead white ashes purified by mantras are worn—he alone is a learned Brāhmaṇa; this I say as the truth, the absolute truth. (9)
O Brahmin, he who possesses an innate joy in gathering ashes as if they were jewels—he alone is a true Brahmin; this truth, indeed, is spoken by me.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter 15: [The one] for whom there is none... [page 761]
He who feels spontaneous joy at the collection of ashes as if it were a jewel should be known as a Caṇḍāla, certainly for birth after birth. || 111 ||
He who has no natural affection for the triple-tilaka, the smearing with ashes, and other such rites, should be known as a Cāṇḍāla; this I speak as the truth, the absolute truth.
Those who, having abandoned the wearing of ashes, eat fruits and other such things, all of them undoubtedly fall into a terrible hell. || 13 ||
"He who abandons the wearing of the *vibhūti* and worships Śiva is unfortunate,
a hater of Śiva, full of hatred, and one who brings about hell."

"One who stands outside of all ritual actions and is devoid of the wearing of ashes—having abandoned the wearing of *vibhūti*, even if he performs the *hematula* rite, he does not obtain its fruit; indeed, he becomes fallen and is lost. (1–2)
Just as the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) are not performed by twice-born men who are devoid of the sacred thread (upavīta),
so too the twilight prayers should not be performed by those who are devoid of the sacred ash (vibhūti).
In some cases, when the sacred thread has been lost during the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā), a substitute may be employed;
this applies likewise to the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra, as well as to fasting and other such rites.
In the wearing of sacred ash, however, there is no substitute whatsoever anywhere;
if anyone performs the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) having abandoned the wearing of sacred ash, [he is at fault]. 17.
By that very act, the twice-born man indeed falls from his status and is no longer qualified;
just as an outcaste falls upon hearing the Vedas, so does the twice-born man.
One who performs the twilight rites without using ash undoubtedly falls [from grace];
therefore, the twice-born should always diligently procure consecrated ash (śrīta-bhasma).
In its absence, however, those who are composed should use either that prescribed by the Smṛtis or that which is worldly;
let it be of whatever kind it may be, provided the sacred ash is applied continuously.
This dhāraṇī should be diligently maintained by the twice-born during the twilight rituals and other rites;
consequently, sins never find a place within them, just as they do not remain in ashes. (21)
The wearing of ashes by Brahmins must indeed be performed with effort,
using precisely the three middle fingers of one's own right hand.
The measurement [of the forehead] should be six finger-breadths long, or even more;
upon the forehead, one should apply a radiant Tripuṇḍra according to the measure of the two eyes.
Sometimes he may perform it with ashes; he is indeed Rudra, there is no doubt about this.
The letter *A* is said to be the ring finger, and the letter *U* is the middle finger.
The letter *ma* is the index finger; therefore, the *tripuṇḍra* consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*).
The *tripuṇḍra* is applied in the natural direction using the middle, index, and ring fingers.
In this regard, I shall relate to you this ancient history:
once, Durvāsas went to the world of the ancestors.
With all his limbs smeared with ashes and adorned with ornaments of rudrākṣa beads, he said:
"O Śiva, O Śaṃkara, O Soul of All, O Glorious Mother, O Mother of the Universe! (27)
Proclaiming aloud the names of the ascetics, that crest-jewel of sages was met by Kavyavāḍ and the others with rising from their seats and respectful salutations.
They showed him great honor with offerings such as seats and other services;
then they engaged in conversation with one another through various discourses.
At that time, however, there arose a terrible cry from the sinners situated in the Kumbhīpāka hell, as they cried out, "Alas! We are destroyed! (30).
"‘We are dead,’ said some; others cried out, ‘We are burnt! ‘We are cut asunder! ‘We are shattered!’—thus they wailed.
(31) Hearing that piteous sound, the king of sages was grieved at heart and asked those lords of the ancestors: ‘Whose voice is this? (32)"
They said, "O Sage, right here lies the supreme city of Saṃyamanī, where King Yama resides, bestowing the fruits of experience upon the sinful. (33)
O sinless one, the leader of that city is present right here, accompanied by various messengers who are dark-complexioned, terrifying, and like the very form of Time (Kāla). (34)
Therein are many pits that provide the experience for sinners, surrounded by eighty-six messengers of terrible form. (35)
Therein exists the greatest and vast hell named Kumbhīpāka; now follows the description of the torments undergone by those who have entered it.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter fifteen:
It cannot be accomplished by anyone, even in hundreds of years.
Those who are traitors to Śiva, as well as those who revile the Goddess, [are destroyed]. || 37 ||
O sage, those who are enemies of Viṣṇu fall right here;
as do those who are revilers of the Vedas, of the Sun, and of Gaṇeśa.
O Sage, those who are hostile toward Brāhmaṇas fall right here;
as do those who act according to their own whims and those who are marked with heated seals.
O Sage, those who bear tridents and those who revile their mother, father, guru, elders, and the Purāṇas and Smṛtis fall right here.
O Sage, those who are corrupters of Dharma fall right here;
this is their most terrible sound, harsh to hear. (41)
"We hear constantly that dispassion arises from the study of the Vedas.
Having heard these words of theirs, the king of sages, desiring to see that [dispassion], [proceeded].
Having risen, he departed quickly and went near the pool;
at that very moment, O sage, he looked down with his face cast downwards.
For the sinners dwelling there, however, the happiness was even greater than that of heaven;
some laughed, while others sang and danced.
Intoxicated by the increase of their pleasure, they also take delight in one another amidst the sounds of mṛdaṅgas,
murajas, vīṇās, ḍhakkās, and duṃdubhis.
Sweet breezes, fragrant with the scent of spring creeper flowers and adorned with the fifth musical note, blew forth.
But the sage, being startled, and the messengers of Yama, being amazed,
quickly reported it to the learned Dharmarāja.
O Great King, O Lord, a great wonder has just occurred:
even for sinners situated in the Kumbhīpāka hell, there is a happiness greater than that of heaven. 48.
"O Lord, we do not know at all the cause for which this has occurred;
we are all terrified and have come into your presence, O God.
Having heard those words of the messenger, the King of Dharma rose up immediately.
Mounted upon a great buffalo, he went to where those sinners were.
He sent that news to Amarāvatī by means of a messenger;
having heard it, the King of the Gods also arrived together with the hosts of deities.
From the world of Brahmā came the Lotus-born one, and from Vaikuṇṭha came Viṣṭaraśravas;
and from their respective worlds, the guardians of the quarters arrived together with their hosts.
Having surrounded Kumbhīpāka on all sides, they all saw the living beings within it, who were endowed with a happiness even greater than that of heaven. 53.
They were all struck with terror and did not know the cause;
"Alas! This pit has been fashioned for the sake of enjoying the fruits of sin! (54)
In that state, since happiness has arisen by its very nature, what fear can there be of sin?
How could the boundaries of the Vedas established by the Supreme Lord be destroyed? (55)
"How has the Blessed One made his own resolve false?
This is a marvel! This is a marvel!"—thus they spoke. (56)
All those who were on the bank did not know the cause there;
in the meantime, Śauri, having consulted with the gods and others, [acted].
Some, accompanied by hosts of gods, went to the abode of Śaṅkara,
to the Lord who was with Pārvatī and as beautiful as ten million Kandarapas.
His limbs were most beautiful, a wondrous mine of loveliness;
he was eternally sixteen years of age and adorned with various ornaments. (59)
He beheld the moon-crested Lord, surrounded by various divine qualities and fondling the supreme Śivā; he bowed down to him who is the embodiment of the four Vedas.
He related the account very clearly and with wonder, saying:
"O Lord, we do not know the cause of this in any way whatsoever."
"O Lord, tell me the cause of that, since you, O Master, are omniscient.
Having heard those words of Viṣṇu, his lotus-like face became serene.
He spoke these sweet words with a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"Listen, O Viṣṇu, to the reason for that; there is no refuge to be found here. (63)
This is indeed the majesty of the ashes; for what could not become ash?
Durbāsas, who had gone to Kumbhīpāka, beheld Śiva’s attendants there.
By the power of fate, particles of ash from his forehead fell there.
By that [fire], all this world was produced; such is the greatness of the ash.
