But beyond this, that water belongs to those dwelling in the world of the ancestors.
There is no doubt that one will become happy by bathing there; from now on, it shall be known as Pitṛtīrtha after his name. (67)
O most excellent one, the installation of Mallikā and the Goddess should be performed there;
those residing in the world of the ancestors will worship them there. (68)
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist in the three worlds, this one shall be the most excellent among them;
by worshipping Pitṛīśvara, the three worlds become worshipped. || 69 ||
Nārāyaṇa said:
Having heard these words of the god and having bowed his head to the god,
Hari took his permission and went into the presence of the gods.
He related all that reason as it had been spoken by Śaṅkara;
the immortals, shaking their heads, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (71).
Hari, Brahmā, and the other gods, as well as the ancestors and the deities, praised the greatness of the sacred ash,
O scorcher of foes, for they were all satisfied by the attainment of that holy site.
On its bank, the immortals installed a *liṅga* and an image of the Goddess according to the prescribed rites, and they worshipped them daily.
There, living beings who had been established for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their sins ascended that celestial chariot and went to the region of Kailāsa. (74)
Those known by the name Bhadraganas indeed still dwell there even today;
furthermore, in a distant region, Kumbhīpāka was constructed.
On that very day, the gods caused the departure of Śaibya to cease;
thus has the entire supreme majesty of the sacred ash been recounted to you. (76)

O Sage, there exists nothing superior or more excellent than this, nor indeed any further rule for the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) according to the distinctions among those entitled to its practice. (77)
O tiger among sages, I shall explain the divine measurements for the vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* according to the divisions of the fingers, based on the study of the Vaiṣṇava scriptures. (78)
I shall now declare the mantras for the colors and the goddesses, as well as their fruits;
[these should be performed] on a mountain peak, on a riverbank, and especially in a sacred field (śivakṣetra).
One should collect these types of clay—from the banks of the Indus, from an anthill, and from the base of a *tulasī* plant—and avoid all other kinds of earth. (80)
The dark [color] is declared to bring peace; the red brings subjugation (vaśya).
They say the yellow brings prosperity (śrī), while the white is said to bestow dharma. (81)
The thumb is nourishment; the forefinger is said to be the lord of longevity; the middle finger always bestows food; and the index finger grants liberation.
One should fashion these with various finger-divisions, but one should not touch them with the sacrificial blades (makhaiḥ).
They may be made in the shape of a wick-lamp row or likewise in the shape of a bamboo leaf.
One should diligently fashion it in the shape of a lotus bud, or likewise in the form of a fish or a tortoise, and thereafter in the shape of a conch shell. (84)
A length of ten finger-breadths is said to be the highest of the high;
nine finger-breadths would be the middle, and eight finger-breadths is beyond that [the lowest]. (85)
The middle *puṇḍra* is recorded as being of three kinds, measuring seven, six, or five [aṅgulas];
the smallest *puṇḍra* shall likewise be of three kinds, measuring four, three, or two aṅgulas. ||86||
One should know Keśava to be on the forehead, and Nārāyaṇa on the abdomen;
having placed Mādhava on the heart, one should place Govinda in the hollow of the throat.
In the belly on the right side, he is designated as Viṣṇu;
and between that side and the arm, he is indeed Madhusūdana. (88)
One should place Trivikrama at the region of the ear, Vāmana on the left side of the abdomen,
Śrīdhara on the left arm, and Hṛṣīkeśa at the tip of the ear.
One should remember Padmanābha on the back and Dāmodara on the hump;
these twelve names [are assigned], with Vāsudeva at the head. 10.
At the time of worship or during the fire sacrifice, being composed in mind both morning and evening,
one should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) according to the prescribed rite while pronouncing the names [of the deities].
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter fifteen.
Even if one is impure, lacks proper conduct, or commits sin with the mind, a man marked with the *puṇḍra* on his forehead shall always remain pure. 92.
Wherever a mortal dies while wearing the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra),
even if he be a dog-cooker (outcaste), he is honored in my world, seated upon a celestial chariot.
The exclusive devotees, who are great souls, knowers of my true nature, and stainless, apply sectarian marks (puṇḍra) in the shape of Viṣṇu’s foot, leaving a gap in between. ||14||
Even those who are supremely devoted to me, being solely intent upon my feet, [should offer] pure [substances], such as those shaped like skewers (śūlākāra) mixed with turmeric powder. ||15||
Other Vaiṣṇavas, out of devotion, should apply marks (*puṇḍra*) that are even without gaps, having shapes resembling a lamp, a lotus, or a bamboo leaf.
Even those who are exclusively Vaiṣṇava may make them with gaps;
for them, no fault is found in making them with gaps. (1198–1199)
For those who are single-minded devotees and even for those who possess supreme devotion, a great transgression would occur if they fail to apply the flawless sectarian mark (puṇḍra). || 18 ||

Furthermore, those who are Vaiṣṇavas should apply an auspicious vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) shaped like a staff, with a hole in the middle, while reciting the names beginning with Keśava and ending with "namaḥ. (99)
That man who applies pure *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* marks with proper intervals between them, he builds for me a vast temple therein. 100.
In the center of the broad and most beautiful vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the imperishable Viṣṇu rejoices, seated together with Lakṣmī. 101.
That lowest of the twice-born who makes an *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* without a gap indeed drives away both Viṣṇu and Śrī who reside therein. (102)
But he who, being of deluded intellect, makes an upward sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) that is not continuous, goes in succession to those twenty-one hells.
One should apply straight vertical marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) with distinct sides and proper intervals, resembling a staff, a lotus, a lamp, or a fish. 104.

O great sage, the topknot and the sacred thread must be worn by a twice-born man, and likewise the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) must be maintained; for without these, all ritual acts become fruitless.
Therefore, in all ritual activities, the wise Brahmin’s duty is [to apply] the vertical *puṇḍra*, the trident, the circular, and the square [marks]. 106.

One who is devoted to the Vedas and has taken refuge in the path of the Vedas should not wear a linga in the shape of a half-moon or other such forms, even if he was born with that [particular] caste status. || 107 ||
One should never wear a mark on the forehead that is incomplete or blurred,
even for the sake of achieving renown, beauty, and other perfections, as prescribed in the Viṣṇu-āgamas and other scriptures.

A person following the Vedic path should never wear another *puṇḍra* while one is already established; having abandoned the horizontal *tripuṇḍra*, how could he ever, even through delusion, wear the *śrīta* mark?
(109) By wearing the horizontal *tripuṇḍra* with ashes on the forehead without any other *puṇḍra*, out of ignorance, one becomes a denizen of hell. (110)
If one who is devoted to the path of the Vedas is marked even by delusion, he surely falls;
of this there is no doubt, as it is with any other sectarian mark (puṇḍra).
One who has taken refuge in the path of the Vedas should not perform branding during a formal rite;
for those solely devoted to the Śrauta dharma, the mark must indeed be that of the Śrauta tradition alone.
For those devoted to non-Vedic practices, a non-Vedic emblem is prescribed;
however, for those deities established by the Vedas, the emblem is indeed Vedic. (113)
For those who are devoted to the non-Vedic tantras, their path is indeed non-Vedic;
however, Mahādeva, established by the Vedas, is the direct liberator from saṃsāra. 114.
And for the benefit of his devotees, he bears the auspicious Liṅga;
for Viṣṇu, who is established by the Vedas, there is only the auspicious Liṅga, and nothing else. 115.
Indeed, for his various manifestations as well, that very same scriptural mark—namely, the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) and the smearing of ashes (uddhūlana)—is to be understood as the sign. 116.
For those who are inferior in the Vedic path, vertical marks such as the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* and so forth are not prescribed, nor is the horizontal *tripuṇḍra*;
rather, they should follow only the path declared by the Vedas.
Indeed, a horizontal sectarian mark (tripuṇḍra) made with ash must be worn on the forehead by one who has taken refuge in the god Nārāyaṇa, the supreme state.
One should always apply a trident mark on the forehead with fragrant water.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 15 ||

Now, therefore, let the meritorious and supreme practice of the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) be heard;

O sinless one, I shall describe to you the procedure for the morning twilight devotion:
the morning twilight [should be performed] while the stars are still visible, and at midday when the sun is at its zenith.
They worship the three junctions of the day, including the evening twilight when the sun is still present.
O best of divine sages, listen as I describe their divisions.
The morning twilight is considered to be threefold: the best is accompanied by stars, the middling has its stars obscured, and the lowest is illumined by the sun. 4.

The twilight accompanied by the sun is considered the best; that occurring when the sun has set is middling; and that accompanied by stars is the lowest. Thus, the evening twilight is regarded as being of three kinds.
The Brahmin is a tree; here, the roots are the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), the Vedas are the branches, and righteous deeds are the leaves.
Therefore, the root must be protected with effort; for when the root is severed, there is neither tree nor branch.

He by whom the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) are not known, and he by whom the twilight devotions are not performed, shall become a corpse even while living, and after death he is born indeed as a dog. (7)
Therefore, the supreme twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) must always be performed;
in its absence, one would certainly not be qualified for other rites and the like.
One should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) for as long as three ghaṭikās after sunrise or sunset; beyond that, it constitutes an expiation (prāyaścitta). ||9||
If a lapse of time has occurred, one should cause the fourth *arghya* offering to be presented;
or else, having first recited the mantra of the Goddess eight hundred times, one should perform that [offering].

At whatever time a particular rite is to be performed, one should first perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) dedicated to the presiding deity of that time, and thereafter carry out the rite appropriate for that specific occasion.
In the home, she is said to be common; in the cow-pen, she is indeed middling;

The three junctions of the day (saṃdhyā) should be performed; then it leads to infinity.
O King, there exists no other deity for the Brahmins than this one;
neither is there eternal worship of Viṣṇu nor likewise of Śiva. (14)
Just as it is ordained by the Vedas for the Great Goddess Gāyatrī,
so too is the worship of Gāyatrī the very essence of all the Vedas.

they worship Ādiśakti, Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Vedas.

Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka) are proclaimed as prāṇāyāma in all the scriptures by yogis of restrained mind. (31)

O Great Sage, I shall first describe the ritual placement of syllables (akṣaranyāsa);

Having first uttered the Praṇava, the deposition of the letters (varṇanyāsa) is proclaimed. Having first uttered the syllable "tat," one should deposit it on both big toes. 85.

One should meditate upon Maheśvarī, who has four feet, eight bellies, and seven heads;

one should meditate upon the Goddess Maheśvarī as residing within the solar orb. 97.

The *saṃpuṭa*, the *vitata*, and likewise the *vistṛta*;

And with services such as offering a seat and so forth, one should always bathe that Supreme Goddess, who is endowed with devotion and love, with the essence of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other substances.

Having given two garments of linen and a thousand fruit-bearing trees to the Goddess, he goes to the world of Vāyu;

In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient and eternal account concerning the royal sage Bṛhadratha—a narrative that is pleasing and bestows devotion. 49.
In a certain region of the Himalayas, there was a bird who was a cakravāka;

In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter twenty-one.

In the performance of rituals prescribed by the Śruti, Smṛti, and other sources, breath control (prāṇāyāma) is "with seed" (sagarbha); that which consists of meditation alone is "without seed" (agarbha), and it is proclaimed to be without mantras. 34.
Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth, otherwise the rite is not said to be effective;
having meditated upon the deity along with its *lakṣa*, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*). (35)
At the evening twilight, the wise man should perform meditation upon the goddess Sarasvatī, who is aged, dark-limbed, and clad in black garments.
She holds a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus in her hands, has Garuḍa as her vehicle,
is adorned with various glittering jewel ornaments, and wears tinkling anklets and a girdle.
She wears a crown of priceless jewels and is adorned with strings of pearls;
her cheeks are made beautiful by the luster of rubies set in her earrings.
The Goddess, wearing yellow garments, whose nature is pure consciousness, bliss,
and existence, was accompanied by the Sāmaveda and joined with the path of goodness (sattva).
Established in the heavenly world and traversing the path of the sun, I invoke the Goddess who is coming from the solar orb. (40)
Having meditated upon that goddess in this manner, one should perform the twilight ritual resolve (saṃdhyā-saṃkalpa) with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and likewise with "agnir vai".
One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana); the remainder is declared to be as previously stated.
Having recited the Gāyatrī mantra for the pleasure of Śrī Nārāyaṇa... [42]
The practitioner, with a pure mind, should offer the *arghya* to the Sun,
placing both feet evenly together and holding a handful of water in his hand.
Having meditated upon the deity situated within the mandala, one should then offer the arghya water in due order;
for that foolish soul devoid of knowledge who offers the arghya directly into the water [is at fault]. (44)
Having transgressed the Smṛtis and the Mantras, the twice-born man must perform expiation;
thereafter, he should also worship the Sun with the Āditya-mantras. (45)
Then, sitting upon a grass mat (bṛsī), one should perform the recitation (japa) of the Gāyatrī mantra either a thousand times or half of that, preceded by meditation on the Goddess Śrī.
Just as in the morning, one should likewise perform the ritual attendance and other rites;
at the evening twilight and the water libation, one should recite [the mantras] in their proper sequence. ||47||
In this [verse], the sage is proclaimed to be Vasiṣṭha, the deity is Sarasvatī in the form of Viṣṇu, and the meter is indeed Sarasvatī. (48)
This is the application for the libation (tarpaṇa) during the evening twilight:
having uttered "Svaḥ," as well as the Puruṣa [sūkta] and the Sāmaveda. (49)
Having thus addressed Maṇḍala, as well as Hiraṇyagarbha, likewise Paramātman, and then Sarasvatī; ||50||
In this context, one should likewise approach the Mother of the Vedas, who is the embodiment of refinement,
as well as the aged Sandhyā, who is the very form of Viṣṇu, and Upasī.
And likewise [he saw] Nimṛji, who brings about all accomplishments,
as well as the Lord of all mantras, and the Puruṣa of the worlds Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
Thus should the libation be performed, as sanctioned by the Vedas for the twilight rite;
and so has been described the procedure for the evening twilight, which destroys all sins. (53)
O bull among sages, the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) is the foremost among virtuous practices; it destroys all suffering, eliminates disease, and likewise bestows liberation.
By performing the twilight rites, the Goddess grants the desires of her devotees.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 20 ||
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Now, therefore, O Brāhmaṇa, listen to the sin-destroying [mantra] of Gāyatrī.
The merit of the *puraścaraṇa* rite bestows desired fruits according to one's wish. ||1||
On a mountain peak, on a riverbank, at the foot of a bilva tree, by a reservoir of water, in a cow-pen, in a temple, under an aśvattha tree, in a garden, or in a grove of tulasī; ||2||

A practitioner of mantra who performs the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) in a field of merit, in the presence of a guru, and in a place of one-pointed concentration, certainly attains success; of this there is no doubt. (3)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter twenty-one:
One may begin the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) for any mantra whatsoever.
One should recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, conjoined with the three Vyāhṛtis.
Without first chanting the Gāyatrī, all recitation of the Tantric and Vedic mantras of Nṛsiṃha and Varāha shall be fruitless. (5)
All twice-born ones are said to be Śākta, neither Śaiva nor Vaiṣṇava;
they worship Ādiśakti, Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Vedas.

Having purified the mantra with effort, one who is intent on the *puraścaraṇa* rite should first perform the supreme purification of oneself, which is the preliminary limb (*pūrvāṅga*) to the purification of the mantra. (7)
To purify the reality of the self, the wise one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, or else one hundred thousand times, by way of the path proclaimed in the Śruti. (8)
Without purification of the self, rituals such as recitation and fire-offerings performed by the agent are to be known as fruitless; this is the reason enjoined by the Śruti. 9.
One should scorch the body with austerity and satisfy the ancestors and the gods;
through austerity one attains heaven, and through austerity one finds the Great.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortunes by the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya by his wealth; but a Śūdra and the best of the twice-born by recitation and burnt offerings.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, one should perform penance with great effort;
for ascetics declare that the emaciation of the body is the highest form of penance.
One should purify [the transgression] by means of the path of penance through such rites as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa.
Now, O Nārada, listen as I describe the method for purifying food. (13)

The fourfold modes of subsistence on alms—namely, *ayācita* (unasked), *uñcha* (gleaning), and *śukla* (pure)—as well as the purity of food prescribed by both the Tantrikas and the Vaidikas, have been declared. (14)
Having brought pure alms-food and divided it into four portions, one portion is for the twice-born, while the second is a mouthful for the cow. 15.
The third portion is for guests; thereafter, one should provide morsels of food to one's two wives according to the order of their respective stages of life (āśrama). 16.
Having first drunk cow's urine according to one's capacity and in the proper sequence,
thereafter shall be the number of morsels for the forest-dweller and the householder.
The size of a morsel is prescribed as being equal to a hen’s egg;
eight morsels are for a householder, and half of that for a forest-dweller. (18)
The celibate student (brahmacārī), according to his desire and following the prescribed rule, should sprinkle cow urine nine times, six times, or three times. ||19||
Having made the hand free from gaps and mentally reciting the mantra "tat savitur vareṇyam," the procedure for sprinkling is thus declared.
Whether it be a thief, a Cāṇḍāla, a Vaiśya, or likewise a Kṣatriya—whosoever, even one of the lowest status, should give food, that is declared to be the rule. (21)
Those who eat the food of a Śūdra, have contact with a Śūdra, or dine together with a Śūdra,
go to a terrible hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
One should likewise perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite for as many hundred thousand times as there are syllables in the *gāyatrī* meter of the mantra. (23)
Likewise, the system of Viśvāmitra consists of thirty-two lakhs;
for just as a body devoid of life is incapable of performing any action, [so too is a ritual without this]. || 24 ||

A mantra is likewise proclaimed to be ineffective when devoid of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa). Furthermore, the months of Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Bhādrapada, Pauṣa, and the intercalary month (malamāsa) [are also unfavorable]. || 25 ||
On a Tuesday and a Saturday, during the Vyatipāta and Vaidhṛti yogas, and on the eighth, ninth, sixth, fourth, and thirteenth lunar days; || 26 ||
On the fourteenth day, the new moon, at dusk, and likewise during the night; on the days of Yama, Agni, Rudra, Sarva, Indra, Vasu, Śravaṇa, and Janma-bha. (27)
One should avoid Aries, Cancer, Libra, Aquarius, and Capricorn;
all of these are to be avoided during the rite of *puraścaraṇa*. (28)
One should perform the *puraścaraṇa* practice especially during the bright fortnight when the moon and stars are favorable; thus, the perfection of the mantra is produced. (29)

One should perform the recitation of auspicious benedictions (svastivācana) and the nāndī-śrāddha according to the prescribed rules, diligently satisfying the Brahmins with food, clothing, and other offerings. 30.
Thereafter, preceded by formal permission, a twice-born man, facing westward in a place dedicated to Śiva, should perform the recitation (japa) in one of the other [prescribed] ways. 31.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter twenty-one.
Kāśīpurī, Kedāra, Mahākāla, Nāsika, and Tryambaka—these five are the great sacred fields (mahākṣetra) on earth. || 32 ||
Indeed, the lamp is everywhere remembered as the tortoise-seat (kūrmāsana), from the day of commencement until the day of completion. 33.
One should perform the recitation day after day neither deficient nor excessive;
the lords of sages perform the *puraścaryā* with uninterrupted continuity. (34)
Beginning at dawn and continuing according to the rules until midday, one should perform the withdrawal of the mind, purification, meditation, and reflection on the meaning of the mantra. (35)
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) should be performed for as many hundred thousand times as there are syllables in the mantra according to its Gāyatrī meter.
One should perform oblations with that [substance] combined with its ten-fold auxiliary (daśāṅga), along with ghee and milk,
as well as with sesame seeds, leaves, flowers, and barley, all mixed with honey.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth [of the recitations]; then the mantra becomes perfected.
Furthermore, the Gāyatrī should be cultivated, for it bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa. 38.
In the triad of daily, occasional, and optional rites, one should have the Gāyatrī as the supreme refuge;
indeed, there is nothing higher than the Gāyatrī in this world and in the next.

At midday, eating sparingly and observing silence, the wise man, intent on bathing and worship three times a day, performed the ritual of reciting the *Nanyamāna* mantra three hundred thousand times while in the water.

One who performs recitation as part of a ritual, or subsequently, or even by one's own will, should continue the recitation and other such practices for as long as the task has not been accomplished. 41.
The procedure for general rites performed out of desire and so forth is stated as follows:
having bathed at sunrise, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times every day. (42)
One certainly obtains long life, health, sovereignty, and wealth;
within six months, three months, or at the end of a year, one shall attain perfection.
By performing one hundred thousand homas of lotuses ending with clarified butter in the fire, one attains complete liberation; it is certain that success is achieved, there is no doubt. || 44 ||
Without the attainment of mantra-siddhi, the rituals of the practitioner—such as japa, homa, and so forth, whether for the sake of worldly desires or liberation—all of that shall be fruitless. 45.
When extracted with twenty-five hundred thousand portions of either curd or milk, the living being is perfected within his own body, according to the doctrine of the great seers. (46)

Whatever fruit a man attains through the perfection of the eightfold yoga, that same fruit of perfection he attains here; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (47) Whether capable or incapable, one should practice a regulated diet.
For one who is always devoted to the guru, success shall be attained within six months. 48.
For one day I shall subsist on the five products of the cow; for one day I shall subsist on air;
for one day I shall eat the food of Brahmins and perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī. (49)
Having bathed in sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā, one should mutter [the mantra] a hundred times while submerged within the water;
then, by drinking the water a hundred times, one is liberated from all sins.
Whether he be a king or a brahmin, if one performs penance in one's own home, one certainly attains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa and other kṛcchra vows.
Whether a householder, a student, or even a forest-dweller,
by being intent upon their respective duties, they obtain the fruit preceded by sacrifices and other rites.
Rites such as those prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti are performed by those desiring liberation;
he maintains the sacred fires, follows right conduct, and is well-instructed by the learned. (53)
Thereafter, one should diligently provide [offerings] with fruits, roots, water, and so forth;
one should eat pure alms-food and consume eight morsels oneself. (54)
Having thus performed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), one shall attain success in mantra;
O divine sage, by the performance of which poverty shall go to its destruction.
And even by merely hearing that, one shall attain great perfection of merits. ||55||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 21 ||
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter twenty-two.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: This has also come to my memory.

The sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to Brahman, the sacrifice to all beings, the sacrifice to the ancestors, and the sacrifice to humans—these are the five sacrifices for a person. Now, O Brahmin, listen to the procedure for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice in connection with the preliminary practice (puraścaryā). ||2||
For the pacification of evil. || 3 ||
A householder has five slaughterhouses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water jar; or [one may perform these acts] even upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should not perform the Vaiśvadeva rite in a small pan, nor in an iron vessel, nor on the ground, nor in a broken pot; rather, one should perform it in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). ||5||

One should not blow upon the fire with the hand, nor with a winnowing basket, nor with pure skins and the like; one should blow upon it with the mouth alone. If done with a vessel, disease arises; with a winnowing basket, there is loss of wealth;
by using the hand, one meets death; but by using the mouth, there is success in one's undertakings.
One should perform [the offering] with fruits, curd, ghee, roots, vegetables, water, and so forth;
in their absence, with whatever is available, such as wood, roots, grass, and the like.
One should offer oblations smeared with clarified butter, avoiding oil and alkaline substances;
or smeared with curd, or smeared with milk-rice (pāyasa); or, in the absence of these, even with water alone.
By offering dry food one becomes afflicted with leprosy; by stale food, one falls under the power of enemies;
by harsh food, one enters into poverty; and by offering alkaline substances into the fire, one goes to a lower state.
Having removed the embers mixed with ashes to the north of the fire,
one should indeed perform the Vaiśvadeva offering, but not with anything mixed with salt or similar substances.
That dull-witted twice-born who eats without having first performed the Vaiśvadeva rite goes,
headlong, to the Kālasūtra hell.
Whether it be a vegetable, or a leaf, or a root, or a fruit—
whatever food one intends to eat, with that one should also offer oblations into the fire.
If a mendicant arrives for alms while the Vaiśvadeva offering has not yet been performed,
one should set aside a portion for the Vaiśvadeva and, having given him alms, dismiss him.
A mendicant is capable of removing the fault committed by the Vaiśvadeva offering,
but the Vaiśvadeva offering cannot remove the fault committed by the mendicant.
Both the ascetic and the celibate student are the rightful owners of cooked food;
having eaten without first giving food to these two, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And after the Vaiśvadeva offerings, one should present a morsel of food to a cow;
I shall explain its ritual procedure, so listen, O you who are honored by gods and sages. (16)
Surabhi is indeed the mother of Viṣṇu, eternally established in the station of Viṣṇu;
O Surabhi, please accept this mouthful of grass offered by me. (17)
Having offered worship with the words "Salutation to the cows," one should present [the fodder] to the cow;
by the offering of a morsel to the cow, Surabhi, the mother of cows, becomes well-pleased.
Then, one should remain in the courtyard of the house for the duration of time required for milking a cow.
From whose house a guest returns with his hopes frustrated, [that man incurs great sin]. || 19 ||
Having assigned his misdeeds to him and taking his merit, he departs;
[this applies to] the mother, father, teacher, brother, offspring, servant, and dependents. (20)
A guest who has arrived and the sacred fire—these are declared to be those whom one must support.
Knowing this, he who out of delusion does not undertake the householder's life, [is at fault].
For him, by the nature of things, there is neither this world nor the next;
for he obtains that fruit which a wealthy twice-born man attains through the Soma sacrifice.
By means of the five great sacrifices performed correctly, even a poor man may attain [that goal].
Now, O bull among sages, I shall describe the Prāṇāgnihotra.
Knowing which, a living being is liberated from birth, death, old age, and the like;
through full understanding, men are released from sins and transgressions. (24)

By that rite through which one is liberated, a Brahmin may be released from the three debts; he uplifts his lineages and [rescues] twenty-one generations from hell. This is the rite known as Manthāna. 26.
One attains the fruit of all sacrifices and goes to all the worlds; [this is the result for] one whose heart-lotus is the abode of the Immortal.
In the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh skandha, chapter twenty-three:
One should churn fire with the rope of life (prāṇa) and the eye shall be the Adhvaryu priest;
one should offer the oblation of udāna with the index finger, middle finger, and thumb.
One should offer the oblation for apāna with the middle, ring, and thumb fingers;
immediately thereafter, that for vyāna with the little, ring, and thumb fingers. (28)
One should offer an oblation to Udāna with the little finger, the index finger, and the thumb;
taking the food with all the fingers, one should offer an oblation to Samāna. (29)
One should recite the name-mantras preceded by the Praṇava and ending with Svāhā;
the Āhavanīya fire is in the mouth, while the Gārhapatya fire is in the heart.
The navel is the Dakṣiṇā fire, while below are the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires;
Speech is the Hotṛ, Breath is the Udgātṛ, and Sight is the Adhvaryu. (31)
The mind becomes Brahmā, and the ear indeed occupies the position of the Āgnīdhra priest;
here, the ego is the sacrificial animal, and the Praṇava is declared to be the milk. (32)
And the intellect is declared to be his wife, for the householder is dependent upon her;
the chest is the altar, the body hairs are the *darbha* grass, and the two hands are the sacrificial ladles (*sruva*). (33)
The seers (ṛṣis) of the Prāṇamantra are Rukmavarṇa and Kṣudhāgnika;
the deity here is Āditya himself, and Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas). ||34||
Likewise, one should also recite "svāhā to Prāṇa" at the end of the mantra, and say: "This is for the god Āditya, not for me. (35)
Likewise, for the Apāna mantra, its form is white like cow's milk;
Śraddhā is the Ṛṣi, and Soma is indeed remembered as the deity here. (36)
One should likewise recite "To the Uṣṇik metre, svāhā! and "To Apāna, svāhā!
Here, the modification (ūha) is proclaimed as: "This is for Soma, not mine. ||37||
The fire-god Hutāśana is declared to be the seed-syllable of the Vyāna-mantra; Agni is said to be the seer (ṛṣi), Agni the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as the meter (chaṃdas). ||38||
"Also, 'To Vyāna, Svāhā! To Agni, this [is mine], not mine!
Likewise, the mantra for Udāna has the color of a *śakragopa* insect. (39)
The seer is declared to be Agni, and Vāyu is remembered as the deity;
the Bṛhatī is declared to be the metre, and it is for Udāna, as before. (40)
"Vāyave idaṃ na mama"—thus should the twice-born recite;
the mantra of the Samāna-vāyu has the color of lightning and is multiformed (virūpaka). ||41||
The seer is declared to be Agni; Parjanya is considered the deity.
Paṅkti is declared to be the metre, and for the Samāmnāya it is as before. 42.
Having said, "This [is] for Parjanya," one should cast the sixth oblation;
Vaiśvānara, the great fire, is proclaimed as the seer (ṛṣi). ||43||
The Gāyatrī is declared to be the metre, and the deity is the Self (Ātman).
The mantra, ending with "svāhā," is said to be that which one should utter for the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
"This is not mine"—when this realization has arisen, it becomes the Prāṇāgnihotra sacrifice.
Having understood this and performed the rite accordingly, one is fit for becoming Brahman.
Indeed, this Prāṇāgnihotra-vidyā has been described to you in brief.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 21 ||
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Having uttered "Amṛtāpidhānam," the best of practitioners—
The wise man should give food from the vessel to those entitled to receive the remnants of the meal.
"Whoever has been born in my family, including male and female servants who desire food—may they all attain satisfaction on this earth through what has been given by me. (2)
May the water given by me reach those who dwell for millions of aeons in the Raurava hell, that abode of demerit, and may it stand as an inexhaustible offering for those who seek it. (3)
Having untied the knot of the purifier (pavitra), one should cast it upon the ground within the mandala;
he who casts it instead into the vessel is a brahmin who defiles the row of diners.
A twice-born man who has been touched by a dog or a Śūdra while he is impure from eating remains is purified by fasting for one night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter twenty-three:
"If one is touched by something that has not been rendered impure by food remnants, bathing alone is prescribed."
By offering a single oblation, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
It is taught that for five times ten million [beings], the fruit thereof is infinite;
and he who indeed gives food at the Prāṇāgnihotra on a bamboo staff [attains this].
Whatever merit belongs to the giver and whatever fruit belongs to the enjoyer, both of them obtain that very same thing; thus, both go to heaven.
If a Brahmin eats according to the prescribed rule with his hand holding a strainer (pavitra),
for every morsel he consumes, the fruit thereof shall be equal to that of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Constant recitation, libation, fire-offering, and feeding of Brahmins at the three times of worship are called *puraścaraṇa*.
Sleeping on the ground, being righteous in soul, having conquered anger, and having subdued the senses— [these are its requirements]. (10)
Eating light, desirable, and wholesome food, he should be humble and tranquil in mind. || 11 ||
He should always bathe at the three periods of the day and always speak auspicious words;
[he must avoid] speaking with women, Śūdras, outcasts, those who have fallen from their caste, atheists, or those who have eaten the remnants of another's meal.
O best of sages, one should not speak the language of the Cāṇḍālas,
nor should one speak after having bowed down during recitations, fire-offerings, worship, and other such rites.
One should always, in all circumstances, avoid sexual intercourse, as well as talk about it or socializing with those devoted to it, by means of action, mind, and speech. (14)
The renunciation of sexual intercourse in all circumstances is declared to be celibacy (brahmacarya); indeed, this is cited as the celibacy of both the king and the householder. ||15||

Sexual union with one's wife according to the prescribed rule—after she has bathed following her menses, when she is consecrated and of the same caste, having carefully observed her period—[is the duty]. (16)
Traveling at night, however, should be undertaken; it does not destroy one's celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Yet, without having cleared the three debts and without having procreated sons, [one should not depart]. (17)
Likewise, one who desires liberation but remains devoted to sacrifices sinks downward;
that which is the birth of the "goat's neck" (ajāgala) is what is enjoined by the Vedas. 18.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, the purification of the three debts must be performed;
for you are thus indebted to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors. (19)
One should liberate the sages through celibacy, the ancestors with water and sesame seeds, and the gods with sacrifice; one should practice the dharma appropriate to one's own stage of life.

Subsisting on milk, or eating fruits, or eating vegetables, or consuming sacrificial ghee, or subsisting on alms, the wise man who performs the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances should recite [the mantra]. 21.
Salt, alkaline substances, and sour things; garlic, eating from bell-metal vessels, betel-leaf, eating twice a day, wearing foul-smelling clothes, and being intoxicated; 22.
One should avoid reciting [mantras] at night if it contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti; one should not spend time in vain through gambling, women, sleep, or idle talk. (23)
One should pass the time through the worship of deities, hymns of praise, and the study of the Āgamas, as well as by maintaining celibacy and practicing silence. (24)
Daily bathing at the three periods of the day, avoidance of the work of Śūdras, constant worship, regular giving, and the practice of bliss, praise, and recitation. (25)
Worship according to specific signs, as well as faith in the Guru and the Deity—these twelve are the duties of one devoted to japa, which bestow excellent accomplishment. (26)

Having performed the morning worship of the Sun, one should recite [the mantra] while facing him; or, having worshipped an image of a deity or the like, or the fire, one should face that [object]. (27)
Dedicated to bathing, worship, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and libations,
he is free from desire for the deity and offers all his actions as an oblation.
One who performs the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) should observe these and other such rules;
therefore, the twice-born man, with a serene mind, should be devoted to recitation (japa) and fire-oblations (homa). 29.
One should be devoted to austerity and study and be compassionate toward all living beings;
through austerity one attains heaven, and through austerity one finds the Great.
For one endowed with austerity and self-restraint, rites succeed:
incantations for causing enmity, subjugation, killing, and the destruction of disease. (31)
Whichever rishi praised whichever deity for whatever purpose,
that person's desire was fulfilled for each of them in exactly that manner.
I shall describe those rites and the procedures for performing them; first, I shall explain the *puraścaraṇa*, which brings about the accomplishment of all rituals.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter twenty-three:
A twice-born man who neglects the study of the Vedas and other such duties should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved off, he is then pure. ||34||
He should remain standing during the day, but at night he should sit while remaining pure and restrained in speech;
speaking the truth, he should recite purificatory texts as well as the vyāhṛtis.
Having recited those [mantras] beginning with Oṃkāra, as well as the Sāvitrī verse beginning with "tat," and the purifying hymn beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" which destroys sins; ||36||
The *pūrṇā* verses, the *svastimatī* verses, and likewise the *pāvamānī* verses—these should be employed at the beginning and at the end of all ritual acts. (37)
One may recite either a thousand, a hundred, or ten times; or else, one may recite the syllable *oṃ*, the three *vyāhṛtis*, and the *Sāvitrī* ten thousand times. (38)
Having gratified the teachers, the sages, the Vedas, and the deities with water, he should not converse with an ignoble person, nor even with a Śūdra or those who are censured. (39)
Nor with a woman in her menses, nor with a bride, nor with outcasts, nor with men of the lowest castes;
nor with those who hate the gods or Brahmins, nor with those who revile their teachers or gurus. (40)
One who is hated by his mother or father should not harbor resentment toward anyone;
this rule for all hardships has been declared in due order. (41)
The procedure for the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra, as well as for the Sāntapana,
the Parāka Kṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa, [is now described].
One is liberated from all five mortal sins and all misdeeds;
by the Taptakṛcchra penance, one burns away all sins in an instant. ||43||
Purified by three cāndrāyaṇa penances, one attains the world of Brahmā;
by eight, one shall then directly behold the deities who grant boons.
Having mastered the Vedas with ten [repetitions], one enjoys all desires;
for three days one should eat in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days one should eat what is obtained unasked.
A twice-born man should not eat for three days thereafter and should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
[the ingredients of which are] cow's urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with Kuśa grass.
A fast for one night is known as the *sāṃtapana* *kṛcchra*.
One should eat only a single morsel for three days, as previously described. (47)
A twice-born man should observe a fast for three days; this is the Atikṛcchra penance he should perform.
Likewise, that which is joined with three such periods is known as the Mahāsāṃtapana.
A Brahmin performing the Taptakṛcchra penance, being composed and having bathed once, should drink hot water, milk, ghee, and air, each for three days respectively.
One who drinks only water while remaining self-controlled and vigilant for twelve days is said to have performed the Prājāpatya rite according to the traditional rules. (50)
This penance called Parāka is the dispeller of all sins.
One should consume one morsel of food on the dark lunar days and increase it during the bright fortnight.
One should not eat on the new moon day; such is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Having performed ablutions at the three periods of the day, this is remembered as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
A Brahmin who has performed his daily rites should eat four morsels in the morning and four when the sun has set;
this is known as the Śiśu-Cāndrāyaṇa.
When the sun is at midday, one who has restrained the self should eat eight morsels of sacrificial food;
this is the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa vow. (54)
Indeed, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Vasus move about in this manner;
all the gods, along with the Maruts and Bhū, are well. (55)
Each one, when performed according to the rules, purifies [the body] in seven nights:
the skin, blood, flesh, bones, fat, marrow, and likewise the lymph.
Each one [of these] becomes purified in seven nights; of this there is no doubt. With his self thus purified by these, he should perform his duties constantly. (57)
Thus, for one who is pure, actions certainly succeed; of this there is no doubt.
A person of pure soul, truthful in speech and having conquered the senses, should perform action. (58)
Thereafter, he attains all his desired objects without a doubt;
he should fast for three nights, abstaining from all ritual activities.
Or one may perform it for three nights; thereafter, one should commence the ritual action.
Thus has the procedure been described, which bestows the fruit of *puraścaryā*.
O divine sage, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) of the Gāyatrī, which bestows all desires and destroys great sins, has been described to you. (61)
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the eleventh book, chapter twenty-four: First, the practitioner of mantra should perform that which effects the purification of the body.
Then one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā); thus, one shall become a partaker of all fruits. ||62||
Thus has this secret procedure for the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) been told to you;
it must not be spoken to another, since it is remembered as the very essence of the Vedas.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 23 ||
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Śrī Nārada said:
O highly fortunate Nārāyaṇa, [I shall describe] the Gāyatrī in brief.
O treasury of compassion, please explain the ritual applications for pacification and the other rites.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Brahmā, let this be yours;
it must not be told to anyone who is wicked or a slanderer.
This which you have asked is most secret; now, for the sake of pacification, a twice-born man should offer oblations with the prescribed sacrificial fuels.
With *śamī* wood fuel, spirits, diseases, planetary influences, and the like are pacified.
For the pacification of elemental diseases and other afflictions,
a twice-born man should offer oblations with the wood of a milk-tree during the Ārdrā asterism; or he may offer oblations with its chips,
or satisfy the Sun with water using both hands, whereby he shall attain peace.
Having recited [the mantra] in water reaching up to the knees, one shall remove all defects. ||5||
By reciting [the mantra] while submerged up to the neck in water, one is released from life-threatening danger;
for all rites of pacification (śāntika), recitation while immersed in water is prescribed.
In a vessel made of gold, or even silver, or one made of copper, or even one made from the wood of a milk-exuding tree, or even one made of flawless clay; || 7 ||
Having offered a thousand oblations with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into a well-kindled fire,
one should gradually complete the remainder of the rite using wood from milk-exuding trees.
One should sprinkle that place while recollecting the mantra of the kuśa grass.

Having recited [the mantra] a thousand times while touching the vessel containing the offerings at each oblation, and then scattering the *bali* with that [mixture], one should meditate upon the Supreme Deity therein;
thus, the sin arising from malevolent sorcery (*abhicāra*) is destroyed. || 10 ||
If gods, spirits, piśācas, and others bring [a person] under their control in this manner,
the entire household, village, city, and kingdom are liberated from them.
By burying [the image], one is liberated from those [sins]; by writing it down, one is liberated even from the middle [degree].
Having drawn a trident in a mandala, or according to the previously mentioned sequence.
Having consecrated it with a thousand recitations, one should bury it for the sake of all-pervading peace;
[using] either a golden, silver, or even copper jar.
Having placed a new, divine earthen vessel— free from cracks and wound with thread—
upon a sacrificial mound or a sandy bank, the knower of mantras should fill it with water.
Having brought sacred waters from the four directions by means of the best of the twice-born, one should place cardamom, sandalwood, camphor, jasmine, trumpet-flower, and jasmine;
likewise, bilva leaves, ākrāntā, the goddess [image], rice, barley, sesame seeds,
mustard seeds, and the sprouts of milk-exuding trees.
Having thus encompassed all [the rites], the wise and composed Brahmin, having bathed and equipped himself with a bundle of kuśa grass, should recite the mantra one thousand times.
In the various directions, Brahmins learned in the three Vedas should recite mantras dedicated to the Sun;
one should sprinkle him with water, make him drink it, and consecrate him with that same water.
He shall be liberated from elemental spirits, diseases, and malevolent spells, and become happy;
by means of this consecration, even a man who has entered the jaws of death shall be released.
A wise king who desires to live long must certainly cause this to be performed;
O Sage, at the consecration, a hundred cows should be given to the officiating priests.
Or, according to what is available for the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or according to one's capacity,
the twice-born man should touch an Aśvattha tree on a Saturday and recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
A twice-born man is liberated from elemental spirits, diseases, malevolent spells, and great fear if he offers oblations of *guḍūcī* cut at the joints, mixed with milk. 22.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter twenty-four.
Thus, the oblation for the Conqueror of Death destroys all diseases;
one should offer the leaves of the mango tree with milk for the pacification of fever.
Having offered oblations of vacā mixed with milk, one shall destroy consumption;
by the offering of the threefold honey, pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣmā) is destroyed. 24.
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) as food to the Sun-god preceded by a fire-oblation (homa), one should feed it to a person afflicted by consumption (rājayakṣman); thus he shall obtain peace.
The creeper: A twice-born man should offer oblations of Soma, having cut it at the joints, when the moon is conjoined with the sun; this is declared for the sake of quelling consumption. (26)
By offering oblations of the flowers of the Śaṅkhavṛkṣa tree, one shall destroy leprosy (kuṣṭha);
the destruction of epilepsy (apasmāra) occurs through the grain of the Apāmārga plant.
Through the offering of fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees, even insanity is destroyed;
through the offering of fuel-sticks from udumbara trees, excessive urination comes to an end.
One should pacify *prameha* by wearing [the mantra] with honey or sugarcane juice;
by offering oblations of the three types of honey, one brings *masūrikā* to peace.
Having offered oblations with the ghee of a tawny cow, one should bring about the pacification of smallpox;
by means of Udumbara, Vaṭa, and Aśvattha wood, one may remove diseases of cows, elephants, and horses.
If an anthill containing ants and honey is produced within one's house,
a twice-born man should offer oblations by the hundreds with sacrificial wood from the Śamī tree, along with food and clarified butter.
That [disturbance] arising from it attains pacification; one should offer oblations there with the remaining [mantras].
In the case of portents such as clouds, thunder, or earthquakes, [one should worship] Vanavetasa.
If one performs the oblation in this manner for seven days, the kingdom and the realm shall become happy.
In whichever direction one strikes with a clod of earth over which the mantra has been recited a hundred times, [in that direction the enemy shall be struck down]. || 33 ||
Then his fear of fire, wind, and other such things shall perish;
by reciting this with the mind alone, one who is bound shall be released from bondage.

By touching those afflicted by spirits, diseases, poisons, and the like, and reciting [the mantra], one may liberate them; by drinking water consecrated with the mantra, one shall be liberated from fear of the earth and other such dangers.
Having consecrated it a hundred times, one should apply the ashes for the pacification of spirits and other evils;
one should wear the ashes on the head, having consecrated them with the Ṛgvedic verse beginning with "tat".
Freed from all diseases, may he live happily for a hundred years.
If one is unable [to perform this], one should have a rite of peace performed by a Brahmin after giving him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 37.
Then, by offering flowers, a twice-born man may take away nourishment, fortune, and prosperity;
one desiring fortune should offer a lotus, and being red [in disposition], he shall obtain prosperity.
By offering auspicious, fresh *jātī* flowers, one attains prosperity;
by an oblation of *śāli* rice grains, one attains abundant prosperity. (39)
By offering oblations with the fuel-sticks of the bilva tree, one shall obtain prosperity;
likewise by offering oblations with the chips, leaves, flowers, or even the fruits of the bilva.
One attains supreme prosperity even by using pieces of the root,
as well as by fuel-sticks of the bilva tree, with milk-rice and clarified butter.
By offering oblations a hundred times each for seven days, one shall obtain prosperity;
by offering parched grain mixed with the three sweets in a fire sacrifice, one shall obtain a daughter.
By this method, a maiden obtains her desired husband;
by offering a hundred red lotuses for seven days, she shall obtain gold.
By offering water into the solar disc, she shall obtain gold situated within the water.
Having offered food, one shall obtain food; one shall become a lord of rice and grain.
By offering the powder of dried cow-dung from a calf into the fire, one obtains cattle;
and through oblations of priyaṅgu-gruel mixed with clarified butter, one shall have offspring.
Having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as food to the Sun-god preceded by a fire-oblation (*homa*), one should feed the woman who has bathed after her menses; thus she shall obtain a supreme son.
Having offered a hundred oblations of rice grains that are sprouting, moist, and red, along with the three sweets, one obtains gold and long life.
Having offered a golden bud, one shall obtain a lifespan of a hundred years;
this may be done with dūrvā grass, or with milk, honey, or even clarified butter.
By offering one hundred oblations each for seven days with *śamī* wood, food, milk, or clarified butter, one wards off untimely death.
By offering oblations of *nyagrodha* wood for seven hundred days, one wards off untimely death; thereafter, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as an oblation.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter twenty-four:
Reciting [the name] one hundred times each for seven days wards off the fear of untimely death.
Subsisting on milk alone, one should perform recitation; within seven days of death, one shall become victorious.
By fasting and reciting [the mantra] while restraining one's speech for three nights, one is liberated from Yama;
by merely immersing oneself in water and reciting it, one is instantly released from death.
By resorting to duality and reciting [the mantra] for a month, one shall obtain a kingdom;
by offering oblations of bilva fruits—along with their roots, fruits, and sprouts—one shall likewise obtain a kingdom. (53)
Having offered a hundred lotuses for a month, one obtains a kingdom free from thorns;
having offered rice-gruel mixed with śāli rice, one obtains a village.
Having offered oblations of *aśvattha* fuel-sticks, one shall obtain victory at the beginning of battle;
having offered oblations of *arka* fuel-sticks, one shall be victorious everywhere. (55)
By offering milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with the leaves or flowers of the cane (vetasa) tree for a hundred oblations over seven days, one shall obtain rain.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel for seven days, one shall obtain the vision [of the deity];
by offering ashes soaked in water into the fire, one may ward off a great rainstorm.
With fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood, one attains spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*);
having offered *palāśa* flowers, one shall obtain everything desired. (58)
By offering milk as an oblation, one attains my abode; by offering clarified butter, one attains intelligence.
Having consecrated it with mantras, one should drink the essence of Brahman and thereby attain wisdom.
From a flower-homa, a cloth of that same kind [as the flower] shall be obtained;
by offering salt mixed with honey, one shall bring whatever is desired under control.
Having offered oblations with flowers soaked in honey, one brings Lakṣmī under one's control;
standing in water, one should daily sprinkle oneself with a handful [of these offerings].

A Brahmin who performs [this rite] for another shall obtain intelligence, health, long life, and supreme well-being; and that other person for whom he acts shall likewise attain nourishment and prosperity. 62.
Furthermore, one who desires long life should recite the *cāruvidhi* mantra a thousand times every day for a month in a pure place; he shall obtain supreme longevity. (63)
A twice-born man desiring long life and health should recite it for two months; he shall obtain longevity and health. To attain prosperity, he should recite the three *sāmans*.
Through four [repetitions], one gains longevity, prosperity, sons, wives, and so forth; through recitation (japa), one gains fame.
Through five [repetitions], one gains sons, wives, longevity, health, prosperity, and knowledge.
In this very manner, one should proceed toward the higher desires by means of the higher months;
standing with arms raised and without support, one should recite the mantra on one foot.
By reciting it three hundred times for one month, one shall obtain all desires;
likewise, by reciting it one thousand and one hundred times, one shall obtain everything.
Having restrained both the prāṇa and apāna breaths, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred times for a month;
whatever one desires, that one obtains, and one may even attain the Thousandfold.
Standing on one foot with arms raised, the self-controlled practitioner should restrain his breath and recite [the mantra];
Kauśika says that he obtains a hundred [lives] within a month, if he so desires. (69)
Having thus recited it three hundred times, one shall obtain everything;
having immersed oneself in water, one should recite it a hundred times and obtain what is desired.
Having thus recited three hundred [times], one attains everything;
one should recite a thousand times standing on one leg, with arms raised upward, motionless and without support.
By eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) at night for a year, one attains the state of a ṛṣi;
likewise, by chanting this for a year, a cow becomes one that yields milk at will.
By reciting thus for three years, one shall obtain vision of the three times;
if one recites for four years, the Blessed Lord Śiva will appear.
In this manner, within five years, one shall possess the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest;
likewise, by chanting for six years, one shall attain the power of assuming any form at will (*kāmarūpitva*).
In this way, one may attain immortality in seven years;
lordship over men in nine, and the status of a god in ten.
Through eleven years, one attains the status of Prajāpati; likewise, through twelve years, one may attain the office of Brahman by means of speed.
By this very [practice], worlds have been conquered through austerity by Nārada and others;
some [subsisted] on vegetables, others on roots, others on fruits, and others on milk.
Some sages subsist on clarified butter, others on Soma, and still others on sacrificial porridge; some eat only once every fortnight, while others eat only once a day.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the eleventh book, chapter twenty-four.
Others, eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), perform the highest austerity;
furthermore, for the purification of secret sins, a twice-born man should recite the [Gāyatrī] three thousand times.
The best of the twice-born who has stolen gold shall become pure after one month;
one who has drunk liquor shall attain purification by reciting [the mantra] three thousand times for a month.
One who has violated the teacher’s bed shall become pure by reciting [the mantra] three thousand times for one month;
having built a hut and dwelling in the forest, one should recite it three thousand times for one month.
"A killer of a Brahmin is released from sin," so it was spoken by Kauśika.
Having immersed oneself in water for twelve days, one should mutter [the mantra] a thousand times every day. (82)

All twice-born men who have committed great sins shall be liberated from their transgression by reciting [the mantra] three thousand times for a month, while restraining the breath and remaining silent.
Even one joined with a great sin is liberated from great fear;
even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified by a thousand breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). 84.
Thereafter, being composed, one should practice the sixfold [breath control] while harmonizing the prāṇa and apāna;
this is prāṇāyāma, which destroys all sins. (85)
A king who practices this a thousand times for a month shall attain purity;
indeed, a twice-born man guilty of killing a cow should recite it three thousand times for twelve days.
For approaching those who should not be approached, theft, killing, and eating forbidden food,
the Gāyatrī, when recited ten thousand times as a repeated practice, shall purify the twice-born.
Having performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one is liberated from all sins;
this is for the sake of purification when there is a mixture of all kinds of evils. ||88||
One who dwells in the forest and constantly recites this verse three thousand times for a month shall have performed a recitation equal to a fast. (89)
When practiced twenty-four thousand times, it is designated as a *kṛcchra*;
when practiced sixty-four thousand times, however, it is equal to a *cāndrāyaṇa*.
Having restrained the breath at both twilights, one should constantly practice this hundred times;
thus one attains the supreme *Ṛc* beginning with "Tat," which brings about the destruction of all sins.

Having immersed oneself in the waters, one should daily recite the verse beginning with "tat" a hundred times while meditating on the Goddess in the form of the Sun; thus, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus have these conceptions of peace, purification, and so forth been correctly explained to you;
they are most secret and extremely esoteric, and must always be kept hidden by you. (93)
Thus has been briefly declared this compendium of right conduct;
by practicing it according to the prescribed rule, Māyā-Durgā becomes pleased. (14)
A person should perform occasional rites, daily rites, and rites for specific desires according to the prescribed rules;
such a person shall obtain the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 95.
"Good conduct is the primary dharma; the Lord is the master of dharma.
Thus it is stated in all the scriptures that the fruit of virtuous conduct is great. (96)
One who possesses good conduct is always pure; one who possesses good conduct is always happy;
one who possesses good conduct is always blessed—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Nārada. (97)
Even if a mortal should hear this work, which generates the grace of the Goddess and prescribes the rules of virtuous conduct, he shall partake in great prosperity and happiness. (98)
Through right conduct, one attains happiness both in this world and the next;
that alone has been declared by me to you—what else do you wish to hear? 99.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," in the eleventh book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
This eleventh book of the Devībhāgavata is declared to consist of one thousand two hundred and forty-three auspicious verses composed by Vyāsa. || 1 ||
This eleventh book is completed. === PAGE 787 === Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
The Śrīmad Devī Bhāgavata,
Twelfth Skandha; now the first chapter.
Nārada said:
O Lord, you have indeed described the rules for right conduct;
its incomparable majesty, which destroys all sins, has also been told. (1)
I have heard from the lotus of your mouth the nectar of divine stories,
as well as those vows you have described, beginning with the Cāndrāyaṇa.
We know those [deeds] to be difficult to accomplish and impossible for an agent to achieve;
therefore, let us now perform that which is easy for embodied beings to accomplish. (3)
O Lord, O Sovereign of the Gods, please graciously tell me that action which generates the grace of the Goddess and grants success in auspicious undertakings. (4)
In the procedure for the rules of right conduct, regarding that which is declared as the rule for the Gāyatrī, what among it would be the most primary, and what would bestow greater merit? (5)
O Sage, regarding those letters belonging to the Gāyatrī whose number as three has been stated by you— whom are they said to have as their seers (ṛṣis), and what are their meters (chandās)?
"O Lord, tell me everything: which deities are said to preside over them?
A great curiosity revolves within my mind. (7)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: Whether he performs other rites or not, and likewise whether he performs ritual observances or not,
a twice-born man who is devoted solely to the Gāyatrī becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
By offering arghya during the twilights and performing the recitation of the Gāyatrī three thousand times, one shall become worthy of worship by the gods in the highest state.
Whether he performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) or not, let him practice the Gāyatrī alone, meditating with a sincere disposition upon her whose form is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda).
By the mere perfection of a single syllable [of this mantra], the best of Brahmins rivals even Hari, Śakra, Brahmā, Sūrya, Candra, and Hutāśana. (10–11)
Now, therefore, let the Brahman-hood, the meters, the deities, and likewise the principles (tattvas) along with their ṛṣis and so forth be heard in their proper order:
Vāmadeva, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Śukra, Kaṇva, and Parāśara.
The immensely radiant Viśvāmitra, Kapila, and the great Śaunaka. 13.
Yājñavalkya, Bharadvāja, Jamadagni—the treasury of asceticism—Gautama, Mudgala, Vedavyāsa, and Lomaśa; || 14 ||
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the twelfth book, chapter two.
Agastya, Kauśika, Vatsa, Pulastya, Māṇḍuka, Durvāsas—the best among ascetics—Nārada, and Kaśyapa; ||15||
Thus, O sage, these sages of the social orders have been declared in sequence:
Gāyatrī, Uṣṇik, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti. (16)
The Triṣṭubh, the Jagatī, and likewise the Atijagatī are considered [metres]; as well as the Śakvarī, the Atiśakvarī, the Dhṛti, and the Atidhṛti. || 17 ||
Virāj, Prastārapaṅkti, Kṛti, Prakṛti, Ākṛti, Vikṛti, Saṃkṛti, and likewise Akṣarapaṅkti. || 18 ||
"Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ"—thus the meter known as Jyotiṣmatī is remembered;
these, O great sage, are the meters that have been proclaimed. (19)
O wise one, listen now to the deities of those very [sections] in their proper sequence:
the first is declared to be Āgneya, and the second is Prājāpatya. (20)
The third is likewise Somya, and Īśāna is the fourth;
the fifth is declared to be Sāvitra, and the sixth has Āditya as its deity.
The seventh is dedicated to Bṛhaspati, the eighth to Mitra and Varuṇa;
the ninth has Bhaga as its deity, and the tenth belongs to Aryaman and Īśvara.
The eleventh is remembered as Gaṇeśa, and the twelfth as Tvāṣṭra;
the thirteenth is declared to be Pauṣṇa, and the fourteenth Aindrāgna.
The fifteenth is dedicated to Vāyu, the sixteenth to Vāmadeva,
and the seventeenth, consisting of seventeen syllables, is said to have Mitrāvaruṇa as its deity. The eighteenth is dedicated to the Viśvedevas, and the nineteenth belongs to the Mothers (Mātṛkā).
The twentieth is the Vaiṣṇava, which is declared to have Vāsudeva as its presiding deity. ||25||
The twenty-first is numbered [as such], the twenty-second has Rudra as its deity;
the twenty-third is Kavi, and the one numbering the [twenty-five] principles belongs to the Aśvins.
The compendium of the twenty-four letters and their deities has been declared as supremely excellent, the sole purifier of great sins.
By merely hearing it, one obtains the full fruit of recitation along with its ancillaries.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Investigation of Gāyatrī," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O great sage, hear now what the powers of the social classes (varṇas) are.
Vāmadevī is beloved, truthful, all-auspicious, and playful. || 1 ||
Prabhāvatī, Jayā, Śāntā, Kāntā, Durgā, Sarasvatī, Vidrumā, Viśāleśā, Vyāpinī, and likewise Vimalā. (2)

She is remembered as the dispeller of darkness, the subtle one, the source of the universe, the victorious, the self-controlled, the one whose abode is the lotus, the supreme, the splendor, the auspicious one, and the three-stepped. || 3 ||
The powers of the twenty-four phonemes have been proclaimed; hereafter, I shall describe the phoneme-phonemes exactly as they are. (4)
The *capaka* is like the color of an *atasī* flower, as is the coral;
the crystal-like [bead] likewise has a radiance equal to that of a lotus flower. ||5||
Resembling the rising sun, like a conch shell, a jasmine flower, or the moon; possessing the luster of coral and lotus petals, and a radiance equal to a ruby.
Resembling a sapphire, with the luster of a pearl or saffron,
having the hue of collyrium, red, like lapis lazuli, and resembling honey.
It is yellow like turmeric, with the luster of jasmine or milk, possessing a radiance equal to that of a sun-gem;
it resembles the tail-feathers of a parrot and likewise resembles a hundred-petaled lotus.
Resembling the ketakī flower, possessing the luster of the mallikā blossom, and the karavīra—these are proclaimed in their respective order. ||9||
The elements have been declared as the purifiers of great sins for all classes:
earth, water, fire, air, and space. (10)
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter three:
Smell, taste, form, sound, and likewise touch—
The generative organ, the anus, the feet, the hands, and speech, in due order. || 11 ||
The vital breath (prāṇa), the tongue, the eye, the skin, and the ear thereafter;
then the out-breath (apāna), the diffused breath (vyāna), and the equalizing breath (samāna) thereafter. (12)
These essential principles of the phonemes have thus been proclaimed in sequence;
hereafter, I shall explain the mudrās of the phonemes in their proper order.
The *sumukha* (single-faced), the *saṃpuṭa* (joined), the *vitata* (stretched), and likewise the *vistṛta* (expanded);
as well as the two-faced, three-faced, four-faced, and five-faced [mudrās]. || 14 ||
The six-faced, the downward-facing, the pervasive, the cupped-hands gesture, the cart, the noose of Yama, the entwined, and the facing-both-ways. (15)
Vilaṃba, Muṣṭika, Matsya, Kūrma, Varāhaka, Siṃhākrānta, Mahākrānta, Mudgara, and likewise Pallava. || 16 ||
The trident-yoni, the surabhi, the rosary, the liṅga, and the lotus are proclaimed as the great mudrās, which are the forms of the fourth state. || 17 ||
Thus, O Great Sage, these mudrās of the letters have been proclaimed to you;
they cause the destruction of great sins and bestow fame and splendor, O Sage. (18)
Thus ends the second chapter in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter.
Nārada said:
"O Lord, O Master of the entire universe, O Sovereign, there is a doubt in my mind."
O knower of the sixty-four arts, O you who have transcended yoga through the destruction of sin! ||1||
By what merit may one be liberated, and how does one become the very form of Brahman? And how specifically does the body become the form of the deity and the form of the mantra? (2)

O Lord, I wish to hear about that ritual action (karma), as well as the ritual renunciation (nyāsa) according to the prescribed rules, along with the seers (ṛṣi), the meters (chandas), the presiding deities (adhidaiva), and the meditations (dhyāna) in accordance with the injunctions.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: There is a certain supreme secret, namely the Gāyatrī-kavaca;
by reciting and wearing it, a mortal is liberated from all sins.
One attains all desires and is born with the form of a goddess;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the [deities] of this Gāyatrī-kavaca. ||5||
O Nārada, the sages, the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, and the meters are said to be the deities whose form is Brahman; Gāyatrī is the supreme digit.
The seed-syllable of that is "bhargaḥ," which has been declared by the wise to be the Śakti;
and the "kīlaka" is said to be the application of the intellect for the sake of liberation.
The heart is said to consist of four [syllables], the head is remembered as having three syllables;
the crest (śikhā) should have four, and the armor (kavaca) is remembered as having three.
It is indicated by four [fingers] and with those four it becomes the weapon-mudrā.
Now I shall describe the meditation which bestows the desired objects upon the practitioner.

I bow to Gāyatrī, whose face possesses the luster of pearls, coral, gold, sapphire, and white [crystal], who is adorned with a jeweled crown set with the moon, whose nature consists of the syllables that express the meaning of reality, and who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a goad, a whip, a radiant skull, and a cord.
I worship her who bears in her hands a conch, a discus, and a pair of lotuses. 10.
May Gāyatrī protect me from the east; may Sāvitrī protect me from the south; may Brahma-sandhyā protect me from the west, and Sarasvatī from the north. (11)
Pārvatī shall protect the eastern direction, and Pāvakī, who reclines upon the waters, shall protect [the south];
Yātudhānī, who strikes fear into the Yātudhānas, shall protect the southern direction. (12)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter four:
Pāvamānī, the playful consort of Pavamāna, shall protect the northern direction.
May Rudrāṇī, who possesses the form of Rudra, protect the Raudrī direction for me.
May Brahmāṇī protect me above, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī from below;
thus may Bhuvaneśvarī protect all my limbs and the ten directions.
May that *tat-pada* protect my feet; may the *padam* of Savitṛ protect my shanks; may the *vareṇya* protect my waist, and likewise may *bhargaḥ* protect my navel. (15)
"May we meditate upon that heart of the God"—thus [he places it] on the two cheeks; "and may he grant the station of wisdom to my eyes," and "may he grant the station to my forehead. (16)
May *naḥ* protect my foot, may *me* impel my head;
may *tat* protect my crown, and may the syllable *sa-* protect my forehead. (17)
The syllable *bi* is in the two eyes, the syllable *tu* is on the two cheeks, the syllable *va* is in the nostrils, and likewise the syllable *re* is in the mouth. (18)
The syllable *ṇa* is the upper lip, while *ya* is the lower lip;
the letter *bha* is in the middle of the mouth, and likewise *ga* is on the chin. (19)
The syllable *de* is at the region of the throat, while *va* is at the region of the shoulders;
*sy* is the right hand, and *dhī* is the left hand.
The syllable *ma* shall protect the heart, and likewise the syllable *dhi* the belly; the syllable *dhi* is at the region of the navel, while the syllable *yo* is at the hips.
May the syllable *yo* protect the secret place; may the syllable *naḥ* protect our two thighs;
may the syllable *pra* protect the knees; and may the syllable *co* protect the region of the shanks.
May the letter *da* protect the region of my ankles, the letter *ya* my pair of feet, and the consonant *ta* always protect all my limbs. (23)
But this divine armor destroys hundreds of afflictions, bestows the knowledge of the sixty-four arts, and brings about liberation. (24)
One is liberated from all sins and attains the supreme Brahman;
by either reciting or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Armor of the Gāyatrī Mantra," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Sovereign of the past and future worlds!
And the divine armor has been heard, which is the very embodiment of the Gāyatrī mantra. || 1 ||
Now I wish to hear the supreme Gāyatrī-hṛdaya, by the retention of which all the merit that comes from the recitation of the Gāyatrī is obtained. (2)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Nārada, the Heart of the Goddess has been clearly proclaimed in the Atharvaṇa;
that very same [Heart], which is the most secret of secrets, I shall now proclaim.
Having meditated upon the Great Goddess Gāyatrī, the Mother of the Vedas, who possesses the form of Virāj, the practitioner should then meditate upon these deities within her limbs. Furthermore,
due to the identity between the microcosmic body (piṇḍa) and the macrocosmic universe (brahmāṇḍa),
the practitioner should contemplate his own body as being of the nature of the Goddess, in order to become one with Her.
"An non-god should not worship a god"—so the knowers of the Veda understand.
Therefore, for the sake of non-duality, one should contemplate these deities within one's own body. (6)
Now I shall fully declare that [state]; one should become absorbed in that.
Gāyatrī is the heart of this [mantra], and I alone am remembered as its seer (ṛṣi). (7)
The Gāyatrī meter is prescribed, and the deity is the Supreme Goddess;
one should perform the six limbs in sequence according to the manner previously described.
Seated in a secluded place, one should meditate with a one-pointed mind. ||8||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the twelfth book, chapter five.

Now follows the assignment of meanings (arthanyāsa). The deity of the sky is at the crown of the head; the Aśvins are in the rows of teeth; both twilights are in the two lips; and Agni is in the mouth.
Sarasvatī is in the tongue; Bṛhaspati is in the neck; the eight Vasus are in the two breasts; the Maruts are in the two arms; and Parjanya is in the heart.
