The sky is his belly; the intermediate space is his navel; Indra and Agni are his hips; Prajāpati, the mass of consciousness, is his buttocks; Kailāsa and Alaya are his thighs; the Viśvedevas are his knees; Kauśika is in his shanks; the secret path (guhyamayana) is his private parts; the ancestors are his thighs; the earth is his feet; the trees are in his fingers; the sages are his body hairs; and the muhūrtas are his nails.

The planets are in the bones; blood and flesh are the seasons. The years are indeed the twinkling of an eye; day and night are the sun and the moon. I take refuge in the preeminent, divine Gāyatrī, the thousand-eyed, for protection.

Oṃ, obeisance to the most excellent Savitṛ. Oṃ, obeisance to that primordial victory. Obeisance to the Āditya of the morning. Obeisance to the foundation of the Āditya of the morning. Studying this in the morning, one destroys the sin committed during the night; studying it in the evening, one destroys the sin committed during the day. Studying it both in the evening and in the morning, one becomes free from sin. One becomes as if bathed in all sacred fords (tīrthas).

One becomes known by all the gods. One becomes purified from speaking what should not be spoken. One becomes purified from eating what should not be eaten. One becomes purified from consuming what should not be consumed. One becomes purified from performing what cannot be accomplished. One becomes purified from hundreds of thousands of improper gifts. One becomes purified from all forms of receiving gifts. One becomes purified from defiling the company at a meal. One becomes purified from speaking untruth.
He becomes so. Furthermore, one who is not a student of sacred knowledge becomes a student of sacred knowledge. By studying this heart-mantra, it is as if a thousand sacrifices have been performed.

The fruits of reciting the Gāyatrī one hundred and sixty thousand times shall accrue. One should properly instruct eight Brāhmaṇas; for him, success (siddhi) comes to pass. That Brāhmaṇa who studies this daily, being pure in the morning, is liberated from all sins. He is glorified in the world of Brahmā. Thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Heart of Gāyatrī," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Nārada said:
O compassionate one toward devotees, O omniscient one, [reveal] the heart which destroys all sins.
Since the [merit] of the Gāyatrī has been told, therefore recite the hymn of the Gāyatrī. || 1 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
O primordial power, mother of the universe, bestower of grace upon devotees, all-pervading and infinite Śrī Sandhyā, salutations be unto you from me. 2.
You alone are the twilight, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī;
you are Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Raudrī, as well as red, white, and black.
In the morning she is a young girl, and at midday she becomes established in youth;
in the evening she is the Goddess Brahmā—thus she is always meditated upon by the sages.
Seated upon a swan, mounted on Garuḍa, and likewise borne by a bull—she who is seen on earth by ascetics as the one who studies the Ṛgveda. (5)
Reciting the Yajurveda, she shines in the intermediate space; likewise, as a singer of Sāmans, she wanders everywhere upon the earth.
For you have indeed gone to the world of Rudra, and you dwell in the world of Viṣṇu;
you alone are she who bestows grace upon mortals in the world of Brahmā.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the twelfth book, chapter six: Māyā, who generates joy for the Seven Sages and bestows many boons.
Indeed, she was born from the tears and sweat produced by the hands and eyes of Śiva and Śivā.
Durgā, the mother of bliss, is recited in ten forms:
Vareṇyā, Varadā, Variṣṭhā, and Varavarṇinī; || 9 ||
Gariṣṭhā, Varāhā, and Varārohā as the seventh;
likewise Nīlagaṅgā and Sandhyā—these always bestow both enjoyment and liberation.
The goddess Bhāgīrathī flows through the world of mortals, and Bhogavatī through Pātāla; she is the river that carries the three worlds and dwells in these three abodes.
In the world of Bhūḥ, you alone are the Earth, the sustainer of the worlds;
in the world of Bhuvaḥ, you are the power of the wind; and in the world of Svar, you are the treasury of splendors.
In Maharloka she is Mahāsiddhi; in Janaloka she is also Janā;
in Tapoloka she is Tapasvinī; and in Satyaloka she is Satyavāk.
Kamalā resides in the world of Viṣṇu, Gāyatrī bestows the world of Brahmā,
and Gaurī, dwelling in the world of Rudra, abides as half the body of Hara.

For you are indeed proclaimed to be the primordial nature (prakṛti) of both the individual soul (aṇu) and the Great Soul (mahat); you are indeed the essence of the state of equilibrium, possessing the form of the variegated Brahman.
Therefore, you are indeed praised as the supreme, transcendent Śakti;
you are the triadic power consisting of the power of will (icchā-śakti), the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti).
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, the Vipāśā and the Sarasvatī, the Sarayū, the Devikā, the Sindhu, the Narmadā, and likewise the Irāvatī. || 17 ||
The Godāvarī, the Śatadru, the Kāverī which flows to the world of the gods, the Kauśikī, the Candrabhāgā, the Vitastā, and the Sarasvatī. || 18 ||
The Gaṇḍakī, the Tāpinī, the Toyā, the Gomatī, and the Vetravatī;
and likewise the Iḍā, the Piṅgalā, and the Suṣumnā as the third.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and likewise Apūṣā;
Alambusā, Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, and Prāṇavāhinī. (20)
And you, O Wise One, are sung of by the ancients as the channel (nāḍī) residing within the body;
as the vital power (prāṇa-śakti) situated in the heart-lotus, and as the mistress of dreams (svapna-nāyikā) residing in the throat. 21.
You are always situated in the palate as the support; you are the Bindu-svā and the garlanded with Bindus.
At the root is the power Kuṇḍalinī, and Vyāpinī resides at the base of the hair.
For you, seated in the center of the crest-lock, are indeed Manonmanī before Śiva;
what more need be said? Whatever exists within the three worlds [is you]. 23.
"O Great Goddess, all that [is for] prosperity; O Twilight, salutations to you!
Thus has this hymn, which bestows great merit, been proclaimed for the twilight. (24)
It pacifies great sins and bestows great accomplishments;
whoever, being composed, recites this hymn at the time of the twilights, [attains these benefits]. (25)
One without a son shall obtain a city; one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth;
and he shall attain the fruit of visiting all sacred fords, performing austerities, giving gifts, sacrificing, and practicing yoga. ||26||
Having enjoyed pleasures for a long time, he shall attain liberation;
and whoever recites this hymn composed by ascetics at the time of bathing, [he too shall attain the same].
Whoever immerses himself in this yantra obtains the fruit arising from bathing at the twilight hours;
of this there is no doubt, O Nārada—this is the truth, the absolute truth. Even he who merely hears of it with devotion is liberated from sin.
Words like nectar were spoken, uttered by Nārada. ||29||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Hymn to Gāyatrī," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, expert in all the śāstras!
The secret of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas has been heard from your own mouth.
O God, by what means does the knowledge that removes all sins proceed? What is the realization of Brahman, and what indeed is the means to liberation? ||2||
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter six: By what means is the goal of the Brāhmaṇas attained, and by what is death destroyed?
O lotus-eyed one, by what means is the fruit of this world and the next attained? (3)
"You ought to explain everything in its entirety, from the very beginning.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one! You have asked rightly, O sinless one. (4)
Listen, I shall diligently recite the eight thousand auspicious and divine names of Gāyatrī, which destroy all sins. (5)
I shall tell you that which was previously proclaimed by the Blessed One at the beginning of creation:
Brahmā is celebrated as the seer (ṛṣi) of the one thousand and eight [verses].
The meter is known to be the goddess Anuṣṭubh, and Gāyatrī is remembered as the deity;
the consonants are its seeds (bījas), and the vowels are said to be its powers (śaktis). || 7 ||
The placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) are now described by means of the letters of the *mātṛkā*.
Next, I shall indeed proclaim the meditation (*dhyāna*) for the benefit of practitioners. (8)

I worship this maiden Gāyatrī, who is joined with red, white, golden, blue, and white [rays], radiant with three eyes, red in hue, wearing a fresh red garland, adorned with clusters of jewels, seated upon a lotus, holding a water-pot and a lotus in her palms, possessing lotus-like eyes, bearing a rosary, and mounted upon a swan. (9)
She is characterized by the unmanifest, yet she is manifest; she is both the Mother and Maheshvari.
Residing in the midst of the ocean of nectar, she is both unconquered and invincible.
Though she is the support of qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and resides within the solar orb,
she is ageless, unaging, free from sin, and holds a superior rosary in her lower hand.
Though she begins with the letter 'A' and ends with the letter 'Kṣa', she is the destroyer of the six internal enemies;
though she resembles collyrium, she dwells beyond all collyrium.
Aditi is the Ajapa-vidyā, whose eyes resemble lotuses;
she is the knowledge situated both within and without, the destroyer of ignorance, and the innermost self. 13.

She is the Unborn (Ajā) with the face of a goat (Ajamukhā), yet she is clothed in garments resembling lotuses; she is the knower of bestowing the meaning of the half-measure (ardhamātrā), yet she is the destroyer of the circle of enemies.
She is the slayer of demons (Asuraghnī), yet she is the New Moon (Amāvāsyā); she is the destroyer of misfortune (Alakṣmīghnī), yet she is unasked by the lowest-born (Antyajācitā).
She is the primordial Fortune (Ādilakṣmī), the primordial Power (Ādiśakti), the Embodiment (Ākṛti), and she whose face is vast (Āyatānanā).
She follows the path of the sun and is frequented by the sun;
she follows the conduct of the preceptor’s circle and dwells in the primordial form.
She is of the nature of fire, she holds a chowrie, she is the primordial one, she is free from fear, and she is seated upon her throne;
she is the support residing in the foundation, and she dwells within the limits of space.
Joined with the first letter, she has the form of the inner space;
she resides within the solar orb and destroys internal suffering and death.
Indirā, Ceṣṭadā, Ceṣṭā, Indīvaranibhekṣaṇā, Irāvatī, Indrapadā, Candrāṇī, and Indurūpiṇī. || 19 ||
Equipped with a sugarcane bow and drawing an arrow,
Ceḍā is the color of sapphire and has a tawny form.
Indrākṣī, the Goddess Īśvarī, who is here devoid of the three [qualities], Umā, Upā, she who resembles the stars, and she whose face is like the fruit of the urvāruka gourd. 21.
Uḍuprabhā, Coḍumatī, Haḍucūḍā, and Haḍucūḍamadhyagā;
Ūrdhvā, Ūrdhvakeśī, and Ūrdhvādhogatibhedinī. 22.
She who holds her arms aloft for her beloved, who bestows the knots of speech adorned with garlands of waves, who is the nourishing truth, and who is saluted by sages and gods. (23)
She is the Rigveda, the remover of debt, and the one who holds the circle of seers within her waters;
she is the bestower of prosperity, established on the straight path, the embodiment of upright dharma, and the giver of rectitude. 24.

She whose abode is the Ṛgveda, she who is straightforward, she who causes the lost Dharma to proceed; she who is born from the foremost of spiders, and she who sports among spiders and the like. || 25 ||
Consisting of a single syllable and a single mora, she is established as one and alone;
mounted upon Airāvata, she belongs to Indra and bestows both worldly and otherworldly fruits.
She is indeed the syllable *oṃ*, the medicinal herbs, the warp and the woof, and she who dwells within the woven cloth;
she is the submarine fire (*aurva*), endowed with medicinal plants, and the bestower of the fruits of the domestic fire (*aupāsana*).
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter six: The Goddess, situated within the cosmic egg, assumes a form corresponding to the letter 'A'.
Kātyāyanī, Kālarātri, Kāmākṣī, and Kāmasundarī. 28.
Kamalā, Kāminī, Kāntā, Kāmadā, Kālakaṇṭhinī;
she who bears breasts like the frontal globes of an elephant, and she who dwells in Karavīra-suvā. || 29 ||
She is auspicious, adorned with earrings, and dwells in Kurukṣetra;
she has the form of a kuruviṃda gem, possesses earrings, and resides in the white water-lily.
She whose tongue is Time, whose mouth is formidable, who is Kālikā, whose form is Time;
she who possesses lovely qualities, who is Splendor, the bearer of all arts, and the night-blooming lily.
Kauśikī is lotus-shaped, she who subdues the radiance of those who follow the path of desire;
Kaumārī has compassionate side-glances, she who reaches to the ends of the quarters, and she who is dear to the elephant.
She who is praised by Keśava, she who loves the kadamba flower, the daughter of Kalinda, the dark-hued one, the girdle of the earth, and she who is extolled by the pitcher-born Agastya. 33.
The mother of desire, possessed of ritual power, assuming forms at will, the compassionate one, the maiden, dwelling in the sacrificial pit, the Kirāti, whose vehicle is the parrot. ||34||
Kaikeyī, whose speech is like the warbling of the cuckoo, who is fond of the ketakī flower, who carries a water-pot, who is dark-hued, and who effects the uprooting of karma. || 35 ||
With the gait of a swan, her armpits adorned with auspicious festive marks, bearing a musk tilaka, lovely, with the stride of a lordly elephant, she was like the voice of the cuckoo. (36)
She who is smeared with camphor, she who is black, she who is tawny, she who dwells in caves;
she who is immutable, she who is the lord of the wicked, she who is beautiful, she who resides within the womb of all the worlds;
she who holds a sword and a shield in her hands, she who is short, she who moves through the sky, and she whose vehicle is a bird.
She is renowned as the bearer of the khaṭvāṅga staff, seated upon the king of birds. 38.

The destroyer of the threshing floor, the one who has shattered old age, the bestower of the Khaṇḍa narrative, she who bears the crescent moon as her tilaka, the Gaṅgā, worshipped by Gaṇeśa and Guha. (39)
She is Gāyatrī, Gomatī, Gītā, Gāndhārī, and she who is fond of singing;
she is Gotamī, Gāminī, and Gādhā, served by Gandharvas and Apsaras. ||40||
She is trodden upon by the feet of Govinda; she is manifested through the three qualities (guṇas); she is the Gandharvī, the Gahvarī, the Gotrā, the Girīśā, the Gahanā, and the Gamī. 41.
Dwelling in the cave, possessed of virtues, and the destroyer of great sins;
she is weighty, virtuous, secret, to be protected, and the bestower of qualities.
Girijā, Guhyamātaṅgī, the beloved of him whose banner bears Garuḍa;
she who removes pride, Godā, she who dwells in Gokula, and Gadādhara.
Residing in Gokarṇa, she dwells within the circle of the household;
she is the giver of Dharma and the giver of wealth, the bell that intoxicates the fierce Dānavas.
She consists of the mantra *ghṛṇi*, she is the bestower of wealth and prosperity, she is fond of the sound of the bell, she is the sense of smell, and she brings satisfaction to the sun. ||45||
She is the dense circle of enemies, the whirling one, Ghṛtācī, and she of dense velocity;
she consists of the element of knowledge, she is the anointing, the anointed one, and the sweetly smiling one.
She is agile, fierce, and wonderful, adorned with variegated garlands;
she has four arms and beautiful teeth, bestowing skill and righteous conduct.
Cūlikā, Citravastrāntā, Candramas, Karṇakuṇḍalā, Candrahāsā, Cārudātrī, Cakorī, and Candrahāsinī. || 48 ||
Candrikā, Candradhātrī, Caurī, Caurā, Caṇḍikā, Cañcadvāgvādinī, Candracūḍā, and Coravināśinī. || 49 ||
Her limbs were smeared with beautiful sandalwood paste, she was fanned by waving whisks, she possessed a lovely waist and a graceful gait; Candrikā was like the very embodiment of the moon.
She who loves beautiful oblations, whose conduct is lovely, who holds a discus in her arm;
she who dwells in the center of the lunar orb and for whom the lunar orb is a mirror.
She whose breasts are like ruddy geese, whose movements are variegated, who is beautiful and playful;
she whose nature is consciousness, who is like the moon, who is Chandravatī, and who is fond of sandalwood.
She is the impeller, possessed of ancient wisdom; she is the cātaka bird and the lovely cause.
She is considered the parasol, the bearer of the parasol, the shade, and her retinue is her own will.
The goddess Chāyā is bound by the gaps, pervading through the concealed senses;
she is established in the Anuṣṭubh meter and dispels the afflictions arising from defects. ||54||
Chedā, Chatreśvarī, Chitrā, Churikā, and she who delights in cutting;
the Mother, who is birthless, the knower of all beings (Jātavedā), and she who consists of the universe. ||55||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter six:
Jāhnavī, Jaṭilā, Jetrī, she who is devoid of old age and death.
Jambūdvīpavatī, Jvālā, Jayantī, and Jalaśālinī. ||56||
She who has conquered her senses, conquered anger, and conquered her enemies; she who is beloved by the world;
whose tongue is like gold; the daughter of Janaka; and the very earth itself, yet subject to decay.
The mother, the daughter of Jahnu, the one who desires the welfare of the three worlds, Jvālāmukhī, the practitioner of *japa*, the destroyer of fever, she who has conquered the universe. 58.
She consists of the conquest of all, she is a blazing flame, the ever-awake goddess of fever;
she is the radiant one, the giver of water, the eldest, and she causes the quarters of the sky to burst with the twang of her bowstring. 59.
Jaṃbhinī, Jṛmbhaṇā, Jṛmbhā, she whose earrings are blazing rubies, Jhijhikā, she whose sound is the jingling of ornaments, and she who possesses the speed of a violent tempest.
Skilled in playing the jhallarī cymbals, she is known as Narūpā, possessing three arms;
equipped with a ṭaṅka-weapon and arrows, she is Ṭaṅkinī, the piercer with the ṭaṅka.
She is the one who produces the sound of the ṭaṅka weapon, whose great chest is worthy of being struck by the ṭaṅka,
the Goddess who causes the sound of the ṭaṅka, and who resounds with the syllables "ṭhaṭha."
She is the Ḍāmarī, the Ḍākinī, the child-like Ḍiṃbhā, who has conquered the sole Ḍuṇḍamāra;
she stands on the path of the Ḍāmarī-tantra and resounds with the sound "ḍama-ḍuma."

She dwells in foam, is devoted to the play of the laughing child, is the mother of the elephant-headed Lord of Obstacles (Ḍhuṇḍhi), holds a drum (ḍhakkā) in her hand, and is the multitude of the ḍhili-sounds. 64.
The river Narmadā is eternal knowledge, incomparable, and devoid of qualities;
Tulasī is the three-stranded lute, consisting of the three qualities, possessing three steps, and is a youthful tree.
She is stepped upon by the three strides of Viṣṇu, yet she moves toward the fourth step;
she resembles the rising sun, yet she is dark and afflicted by the cold.
She is endowed with knowledge of the three times, possesses the three folds [of skin], and has three eyes;
she is the triple-power, Tripurā, the Exalted One, and likewise the Horse-faced One.
She is the devourer of the devourer of whales, the fierce one, the three-streamed river, the leader of the tamasic,
the knower of the secrets of ritual and mantra, the slender-waisted, and the triple-heavened.
She who is the three junctions of the day, she who has three breasts, she who is contentment, she who stands firm, she who shines with rhythmic beats,
she who wears earrings, she who has the luster of frost, and she who dwells on the snowy mountain.
She is entwined with a web of threads, fond of strings of bright pearls,
devoted to oblations of sesame seeds, the essence of sacred fords, and possessing the form of a *tamāla* flower.
She is joined with the three stars, slender of form, and surrounded by the trident.
She has a flat belly, is adorned with sesame seeds, and is fond of wearing earrings.
Trijatā, Tittirī, and Tṛṣṇā, possessing youthful forms of three kinds,
resemble molten gold and are adorned with ornaments of molten gold.
She who has three eyes, who possesses the three goals of life, who bestows knowledge of the three periods of time;
she who is the act of libation, who grants satisfaction, who is herself satisfied, who is characterized by *tamas*, and who is praised by Tumburu. (73)

Seated upon Tārkṣya, she is the creeper of the triple-folded form with three bends; she utters the sound "Thāt," she is the one whose voice is "Thāra," she is the one who goes, the milker, and the one who is compassionate toward the distressed. 74.
She is the destroyer of people, the invincible Durgā, the slayer of the demon Durgāsura;
she is the divine law, the day and night, Draupadī, and the sound of the kettledrum.
Devayānī, difficult to dwell with, the divider of poverty by day, beloved of Dāmodara, radiant, clothed in the directions, and the deluder of the quarters. 76.
Dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, she is the wielder of the staff (Daṇḍinī), worshipped by the gods,
revered by the deities, an enemy of those who dwell in heaven, and possesses the form of a Dānava.
She is praised by the poor and the helpless; she is initiation (dīkṣā) and the very embodiment of the deities and others;
she is the nurse, the wielder of the bow, the cow, the sustainer, and the practitioner of righteousness.
She is the sustainer of the earth, the support of the world, the giver of wealth, and the milker of grain;
she is virtuous by nature, the presiding deity of riches, and highly skilled in the science of archery.
She is steadfastness, she whose feet are firm, the beloved of the King of Dharma, and the eternal;
she is Dhūmāvatī, she whose hair is smoke-colored, and the illuminator of the scriptures of Dharma.
She is the river, the beloved of Nanda, sleep, praised by men, and whose nature is joy;
she is the Narmadā, the lotus-like one, the blue one, and she who has her refuge in the Blue-throated Lord.
She is the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, eternal, stainless, devoid of qualities, a treasure-house,
supportless, incomparable, perpetually pure, and untainted.

She who transcends sound, the drop, and the digit; whose nature consists of sound, the drop, and the digit; the lioness among men; the supporter of the mountain; adorned by kings and serpents. || 83 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter six.
She quiets the afflictions of hell, she is born from the feet of Nārāyaṇa;
she is irreproachable, formless, and acts for the pleasure of Nārada. (84)
She is known as the manifold light, pure in essence by her own nature;
she is the policy that wears the nine threads and brings about the absence of all affliction. 85.
Born from joy, enriched with the nine gems, dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest, fond of fresh butter, a woman whose voice resounds like a dark rain cloud. 86.
She who blinks, she whose form is like a river, she with the blue throat, the sovereign of the night,
she who is the destroyer of Śumbha through the recitation of her names, and she who dwells in the world of the Nagas.
Resembling freshly minted gold, the presiding deity of the world of the Nāgas, she captivates the hearts of men with her shanks adorned by anklets. (88)
Immersed [in thought], with blood-red eyes and a voice like the roar of a thunderclap,
she dwelt in the Nandana garden as a silent attendant.
Pārvatī is supremely generous, identical with the Supreme Brahman, and transcendent;
she is liberated from the five sheaths and is the destroyer of the five great sins.
She who knows the arrangement of the minds of others, the fivefold one, possessing five forms;
she is the full moon, supreme joy, and the illuminator of the splendor of the beyond. || 91 ||
Ancient, belonging to the city, meritorious, with eyes like lotuses, submerged in the depths of Pātāla, she is gracious and the increaser of joy. 92.
She is the purifier, accompanied by her feet, the graceful one, and the consumer of air;
she is Prajāpati, the weary one, and she whose breasts are the mountain ranges. 93.
She who loves the lotus, who resides in the lotus, whose eyes are like lotuses, who is born from the lotus;
she who has lotus-petals [as her garments], whose feet are like lotuses, who is the mistress of the lotus-pond, and who speaks with affection. ||94||
She is liberated from the bonds of the individual soul (paśupāśa), the lady of the city, the dweller in the city;
she is abundant, the Supreme Person, the knower of the joints of existence, and one who is fond of the flowers of the Pārijāta tree. || 95 ||
Devoted to her husband, with pure limbs, intent on flowers and smiles,
possessing offspring, daughters, and grandsons, she is rich in sons and abundant in milk. Honored by her sons,
holding the noose of authority, she is a lineage that bestows the world of the ancestors.
Ancient, virtuous in character, and the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before her. || 97 ||
She is the mother of Pradyumna, she is nourishing, she is the consort of the Grandfather (Brahmā),
she dwells in the city of Puṇḍarīka, and her face is like a white lotus.
She has broad shanks, broad arms, broad feet, and a broad belly;
she possesses the splendor of coral, has tawny eyes, wears yellow garments, and is exceedingly fickle.
She is the progenitor, the giver of nourishment, the meritorious one, the foundation, the syllable Om, and the goal;
she possesses five colors, the fivefold speech, and resides within the cage of the five elements.
She is the supreme light, supreme love, and the supreme goal; she is the ultimate limit, the sovereign of the highest, the purifier, and the ascetic who burns with purity. || 101 ||
Puṇyabhadrā, Paricchedyā, Puṣpahāsā, Pṛthūdarī, Pītāṅgī, Pītavasanā, Pītaśayyā, and Piśācinī. || 102 ||
She who loves yellow, the destroyer of Piśācas, she whose eyes are like the Pāṭala flower, she whose actions are clever,
she whose conduct is fond of the five kinds of food, and the one who takes away the life of Pūtanā.
Standing in the midst of a forest of *punnāga* trees, she has descended upon a holy bathing place;
she is the supreme power (*parā śakti*) in her five-limbed form, bestowing the highest bliss. (104)
She who dwells in the Puṣpaka arrow, who nourishes all the worlds, who is fond of drinking, who has five tufts of hair, and who reclines upon a serpent. 105.
The earth is five-fold in measure, the broad-yielding sustainer of travelers;
she is the mother of the Purāṇas and Nyāya, and is fragrant with the scent of Pāṭalī flowers. || 106 ||
She is the bestower of merit and progeny, whose sole range of vision is the supreme path;
she possesses the beauty of coral, her hopes are fulfilled, she is the sacred syllable *praṇava*, and her belly is like a tender sprout.
She is the fruitful one, the giver of fruits, she is the hollow reed, she is the hissing sound, and her form is that of a leaf.
She who reclines upon the coils of the lord of serpents as her bed, adorned by the circle of serpent-hoods.
The young woman is highly esteemed; her garments resemble the heat of the sun;
she is dear to Balabhadra; she is venerable; she is the mare (Vaḍavā); and she is praised by the wise.
Baṃdīdevī, Bilavatī, Vaḍiśanī, Balipriyā;
Bāṃdhava, Bodhitā, Buddhi, and Bandhūkakusumapriyā. (110)
She who possesses the radiance of the rising sun, the goddess Brāhmī, the deity of the Brahmins, praised by Bṛhaspati, Vṛndā, who wanders through Vṛndāvana. 111.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the twelfth book, chapter six:
Balākinī, Bilāhārā, Bilāvāsā, and Bahūdakā.
She has many eyes, many feet, and many earrings. || 112 ||
She whose form is the seed-syllable, she who possesses manifold forms;
she who transcends the bindu, nāda, and kalā, yet has the nature of bindu and nāda. || 113 ||
Possessing many arms, she dwells in the hermitage of Badarī;
she is the object of worship for the gods, broad-shouldered, vast, and the one who strikes down the arrows of the enemy.
The woman, possessing great prowess, had bound her fingers with leather guards;
she sat in the lotus posture (padmāsana) upon a surface of bilva leaves. || 115 ||
She is the presiding lady over the multitude, she who abides in abundance, she whose intellect is like a mirror,
she who possesses a bow as youthful as a child, and she whose speed is like that of the submarine fire.

She whose natural abode is the Bodhi tree, she who threads the Brahma-bracelet, she who is to be meditated upon, she who possesses a terrifying form, she who brings about existence, and she who removes fear. || 117 ||
Residing both outside and within the cosmic egg, she dwells in the heart of Bhārata;
she is Bhairavī of terrifying form, the bestower of prosperity, garlanded with auspiciousness.

Bhadrakālī, Bhujaṅgākṣī, Bhāratī, Bhāminī, she who is devoted to enjoyment, the bestower of prosperity, she of vast valor, the abode of spirits, the creeper-like tongue of Bhṛgu, the daughter of Bhṛgu, and she who is honored by the gods on earth. 119.
Bhāgīrathī, Bhogavatī, Bhavanasthā, Bhiṣagvarā, Bhāminī, Bhoginī, Bhāṣā, Bhavānī, and Bhūridakṣiṇā. 120.

She whose essence is splendor, who is formidable, who liberates from the bonds of worldly existence, who is to be worshipped, who is the sustainer of all beings, who is delighted, and who is the sovereign of the universe. || 122 ||
Bhujaṅgavalayā, Bhīmā, Bheruṇḍā, Bhāgadheyinī;
Mātā, Māyā, Madhumatī, Madhujihvā, Madhupriyā;
Mahādevī, Mahābhāgā, Mālinī, Mīnalocanā.
She is beyond illusion, full of sweetness, the month of Madhu, and flowing with honey. || 123 ||
She is born of Manu, produced from honey, and a resident of the city of Mithilā;
she is the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the piercer, and the one garlanded with clouds.
Maithilī, the smooth and beloved one! Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, Mahākalyā, Maheśvarī! || 125 ||

Mandodarī, Mahāmāyā, Māhendrī, daughter of Mount Meru, she who is worshipped with Mandāra flowers, she whose anklets and girdle are most charming, the bestower of liberation, and the sweet-spoken one. || 126 ||
Malayānvitā, Mevā, Marakatasyānā, Māgadhī, and Menakātmajā. 127.
Madhuradrāviṇī, Mudrā, Malayā,
Mahāmārī, Mahāvīrā, Mahāśyāmā, Manustutā,
Mātṛkā, Mihirābhāsā, and Mukundapadavikramā. || 128 ||
The bewildered one residing in the mūlādhāra, dwelling in the maṇipūraka, the deer-eyed one mounted upon a buffalo, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura. || 129 ||
She is the yogic posture, attainable through yoga, and the yoga that rests upon youth;
she is the youthful maiden, situated in the midst of battle, the Yamunā river, and the upholder of the cosmic age.
She was a Yakṣiṇī engaged in yoga, born from the lineage of the Yakṣa kings; she was skilled in the rites of processions and vehicles, and she was born into the Yadu dynasty.
Beginning with the letter *ya* and ending with the letter *ha*, she is the Yājuṣī, whose form is the sacrifice;
she is the night, devoted to yoga, and the terrifier of the Yātudhānas. 4132.
Rukmiṇī, the delightful Rāmā, Revatī, Reṇukā, and Rati;
Raudrī, whose form is dear to Rudra, the mother of Rāma, and she who is fond of Rati. || 133 ||
Rohiṇī, the bestower of sovereignty, Revā, Ramā, the lotus-eyed one, Rākeśī, endowed with beauty, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne. || 134 ||
Wearing red garlands and garments, anointed with red perfumes and unguents,
she is as majestic as a royal swan, as beautiful as a plantain tree, and fond of red lotuses.
She who has illumined the entire surface of the earth,
who is clothed in a tiger skin, who is a chariot-warrior, and who wears a garland of jewels.
She is the support of the delightful age, the daughter of Ravana, and the one who gladdens Rama;
she is trodden upon by the feet of Ramachandra and is the destroyer of the cries of distress.
The mistress of disease, the pacifier of disease, adorned with golden ornaments;
the presiding deity of modesty, the restless one, the graceful one, the bearer of the *liṅga*. 38.
Clad in garments of jewels, Lakṣmī stands upon her chariot; she is the fickle one, the destroyer of poison, the observer of the world, and renowned throughout the universe.
She is Modesty, the goddess Laṃbodari, the beautiful woman, and the sustainer of the world. 139.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter six.
The bestower of boons, the praised one, the knowledge (vidyā) of Viṣṇu, of pure form;
Vārāhī, free from passion, the showerer, she who sports with excellent Lakṣmī. 140.
Vinatā, who dwells in the midst of the sky; she who is seated upon the lotus-throne;
Vāruṇī, born from the flute; Vītihotrā, the multiformed one. 141.
Abiding in the midst of the circle of wind, she is the form of Viṣṇu, beloved of Brahmā;
she is the consort of Viṣṇu, the mother of Viṣṇu, the large-eyed one, and the earth. 142.
She is beloved by Vāmadeva, the shore, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the milker of wealth;
her limbs are encompassed by the syllables of the Vedas, and she bestows the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
She is the mother of Vāma, the consort of Vāsava, the supreme dweller in Vaikuṇṭha;
she is the beloved of Vyāsa, the wearer of armor, and she is served by Vālmīki.
Śākaṃbharī, Śivā, Śāntā, Śāradā, the refuge for those who seek shelter; she of the slender waist, of auspicious conduct, and the destroyer of the demon Śumbha. || 145 ||
She is the possessor of splendor, the embodiment of auspiciousness, and she who forms half the body of Śaṅkara;
she is crimson, pure in intention, radiant white, and the one who effects the union with the head. 146.
Śarāvatī, Śarānandā, Śarajjyotsnā, Śubhānanā, Śarabhā, Śūlinī, Śuddhā, Śavarī, and Śukavāhnā. || 147 ||
The illustrious Śrīdharānandā, who bestows the bliss of hearing;
Śarvāṇī, the night-like one worthy of worship; Pabhāṣā, who is fond of the six seasons. (148)
The Goddess, who dwells in the sixfold foundation, acts for the benefit of the lame and the unfortunate;
she possesses the excellent wisdom of the form of the six limbs and is saluted by gods and asuras alike. 149.
Sarasvatī is the eternal support, the bringer of all auspiciousness;
she is fond of the chanting of the Sāman, subtle, the mother Sāvitrī, and born from the Sāman. 150.
She dwells in all abodes, is eternally blissful, possesses beautiful breasts, and has the ocean as her garment;
she is the perfection (Siddhi) who delights in all sovereignty, and whose prowess is her virtuous kinsmen. || 151 ||
Residing within the orb of the seven sages and dwelling in the lunar sphere, she is omniscient, possesses intense compassion, and is free from those who are her equals or superiors. (152)
She is most exalted, free from false consciousness, possessed of true virtues, and the bestower of all desired things;
she is the honey-maker, the daughter of the Sun, the one with beautiful hair, and the embodiment of the Sāman chants. (153)
She is golden-hued, tawny, the embodiment of the syllable Hrīṃ, and she whose vehicle is the swan;
her limbs are draped in silken garments, she is the daughter of the Ocean of Milk, and she is Forgiveness personified. 154.
"Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Pārvatī, Sarasvatī, Vedagarbhā, Varārohā, Śrīgāyatrī, and Parāmbikā—
O Nārada, this is the thousand names of Gāyatrī,
which bestows merit, destroys all sins, and grants great prosperity. (155–156)
Indeed, these names of Gāyatrī are productive of satisfaction;
they should especially be recited on the eighth lunar day along with the twice-born.

Having performed the recitation (japa), and especially having performed the fire-oblation (homa), worship (pūjā), and meditation (dhyāna), [the mantra] should not be given to just anyone, especially in the case of the Gāyatrī. 158.
This should indeed be spoken to one who is pure, a good disciple, and a worshiper of the gods;
it must not be shown to fallen practitioners or even to kinsmen. || 159 ||
In whose house a scripture is written, there is no fear from anyone;
even though she is fickle, the Goddess of Fortune remains there, having become steadfast. 160.
This is a great secret, more hidden than the most hidden;
it bestows merit upon men and provides a treasure for the poor. (161)
It bestows liberation upon those seeking release and grants all desires to those possessed by longing; the sick are indeed freed from disease, and the bound are released from bondage. 962.
Men who have committed the murder of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the theft of gold, or even sexual intercourse with the teacher's wife, are released from that sin by bathing once. (163)
One is liberated simply by reciting [this] from the sin of accepting improper gifts, especially from eating what should not be eaten, and from heretics, falsehoods, and the like. 164.
O Lotus-born One, this stainless secret has been spoken by me; it bestows union with Brahman upon men. It is the truth, the absolute truth; there is no doubt about it. (165)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Thousand-Name Hymn of Gāyatrī," in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter seven.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Nārada said: I have heard the hymn known as the Thousand Names of the auspicious Gāyatrī, which bestows fruit, brings about great exaltation, and grants supreme good fortune. (1)
Now I wish to hear the supreme characteristics of initiation (dīkṣā), without which there can be no eligibility for the mantra of the Goddess. (2)
O Lord, tell me in detail everything according to the general rule for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and likewise for women.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Listen; I shall explain the initiation for disciples of purified soul, by which they obtain the qualification for the worship of the deity, the fire, the guru, and so forth. (4)
That which bestows divine knowledge and brings about the destruction of sins is indeed declared as *dīkṣā* by those expert in the Vedas and Tantras. (5)
That [initiation] must certainly be performed, since it is considered to yield great fruit;
for in this case, both the teacher and the disciple must be exceedingly pure.
The Guru, having duly performed all his morning duties,
and having performed everything such as the ritual bath and the twilight prayers according to the prescribed rules— (7)
Carrying his water-pot and observing silence, he should go from the riverbank to his home;
having reached the sacrificial pavilion, he should enter there and take his place upon the excellent seat.
Having sipped water and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should consecrate water mixed with fragrance and flowers by reciting the Astra-mantra seven times.
With that water, while reciting the Astra-mantra, the wise one should sprinkle the entire doorway; thereafter, he should perform the worship.
Above the Udumbara tree, one should worship the deity Gaṇanātha, as well as Śrī and Sarasvatī, with perfumes and flowers while reciting their respective name-mantras.
One should worship Gaṅgā and Vināyaka on the right jamb of the door,
and Kṣetrapāla and Sūryajā on the left jamb of the door.
One should worship the deity of the weapon at the threshold with the weapon-mantra,
while contemplating everywhere that all that is visible is composed of the Goddess.
One should then dispel divine obstacles by the recitation of the weapon-mantra.
One should strike down the obstacles moving in the intermediate space with blows from the feet, and those on the ground with kicks.
Touching the left branch, he should subsequently enter with his right foot;
having entered, he should place the water-pot and perform the general *arghya* offering.

And with that same water for the guest-offering (arghya), one should worship Vāstunātha, who is of lotus-origination, in the south-western direction with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings. || 16 ||
Then the Guru should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and, with that along with the sacred water (āryodaka),
sprinkle the pavilion as far as the arches and pillars.
One should indeed contemplate with the mind that all this is composed of the Goddess;
while reciting the root mantra with devotion, the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) should be performed with the Śara-mantra.
Having recited the Śara-mantra, one should strike the edge of the pavilion;
then, having likewise recited the mantra, one should perform the sprinkling.
One should fumigate the teeth-stick with incenses and then scatter the *vikirā* (scattering offerings) over it;
furthermore, one should sweep them away with a broom made of *kuśa* grass.
O Sage, having formed that heap in the northeastern direction, one should establish it;
then, having performed the Puṇyāhavācana rite, one should satisfy the poor and the helpless.
Afterwards, having prostrated before his own guru, he should sit upon a soft seat facing east and, according to the prescribed rule, meditate upon the deity of the mantra.

O Sage, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites by the very path previously described, one should indeed perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the seer (ṛṣi) and so forth for the deity's mantra.
One should place the Sage upon the head, the Metre upon the mouth,
the Deity in the lotus of the heart, and the Seed-syllable on the feet.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter seven.
Having placed the *śakti* [mantra], and then, following the sound of three claps (*tāla*),
the person should subsequently perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with three snaps of the fingers (*choṭikā*).
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) while recollecting the root mantra, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā upon the body; the method for that is now being told.
Having uttered "Oṃ Aṃ Namaḥ," the knower of mantras should place it upon his head;
O Sage, he should likewise place [the syllables] in all the other locations.
The best of beings performed the root mantra and the six-limbed ritual on the six limbs,
sequentially upon the fingers beginning with the thumb, and upon the heart and other centers.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with mantras joined by *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vapaṭ*, and *vaṣaṭ-phaṭ*, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), and consisting of five parts. ||29||

Thereafter, one should apply the placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*) and so forth of the root mantra in the specific locations prescribed in the respective ritual manuals; this is remembered as the procedure for placement (*nyāsavidhi*). 30.
Then, one should contemplate a beautiful seat within this body of one’s own;
one should place Dharma on the right shoulder and Jñāna on the left shoulder.
O Sage, one should place detachment on the left thigh and sovereignty on the right thigh; then one should meditate upon unrighteousness in the region of the face.
Furthermore, on the left side at the region of the navel, one should likewise place the right vessel,
as well as the negations (nañ) and so forth, and the knowledges (jñāna) and so forth, exactly as previously described.
O best of sages, dharma and the other [puruṣārthas] are said to be the feet of the throne;
whereas adharma and the others are recorded as the limbs by the preeminent sages. (34)
In the center, upon a soft seat in a clean place, one should place Ananta in the heart-center;
therein is the stainless lotus of the phenomenal world (prapañca), within which are the sun, moon, and fire.
I shall now briefly describe how the practitioner of mantras should perform the placement (nyāsa) accompanied by the constituent parts (kalās).
It is taught that the Sun has twelve kalās and the Moon has sixteen.
The ten digits (kalās) of Fire have been declared; one should meditate upon them as being endowed with those [digits]. One should then place Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas above them. (37)
The wise one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Self, the Inner Self, the Supreme Self, and the Self of Knowledge; such is the conceptualization of the pedestal (pīṭha). ||38||
Having worshipped the seat with the mantra "Obeisance to the seat of [Name]," the practitioner should then meditate upon the Supreme Mother within it.
Following the procedure prescribed in the Kalpa, the mantra-practitioner should worship the deity of the mantra to be given with mental offerings according to the rules. (40)
The wise one should display the mudrās prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa) which bring delight;
for by performing them, joy is produced for the Goddess. 41.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, on the front of his own left side, he should properly draw a circular maṇḍala upon a hexagon, joined with a square in its center. 42.
Having drawn a triangle in the center, one should display the conch mudrā;
and one should worship the six limbs within the six corners with flowers and other offerings.
O best of sages, one should perform the worship of the six limbs in the corners starting from the southeast;
then, O excellent sage, taking up the supporting vessel for the conch—
Having consecrated it with the Astra-mantra, one should place it there in the mandala;
then, having addressed the circle of mantras, one should address it as being of the nature of the ten kalās.
"Obeisance to the goddess so-and-so for the purpose of placing the arghya vessel"—this mantra is also declared by the wise for the placement of the base of the conch. (46)
On the base (ādhāra), beginning from the east and proceeding in a clockwise direction, one should worship the ten fire-potencies (vahnikalā) situated within the fire-mandala. || 47 ||
Then, having sprinkled the excellent conch with the root mantra, one should place it upon its base while recollecting the root mantra. (48)

Having addressed [the vessel] at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths] as "to the one whose nature is the digit (kalā), who is without the solar orb," he should then utter: "Obeisance to the arghya-vessel of such-and-such a goddess. (49)
Having sprinkled water upon the conch with the word "pada," one should utter "namaḥ.
With that [mantra], one should sprinkle the conch and worship it twelve times therein. ||50||

Having sprinkled [the materials] with the reverse-order Mātṛkā and the root mantra in reverse order, one should praise the twelve digits (kalās) of the Sun beginning with Taviṇī in their proper sequence. 51.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter seven. [Page 801] 804.
One should fill the conch with water and place there a digit of the moon, saying: "Oṃ, to the lunar orb, to the essence of the sixteen digits. (52)
The mantra ending with the heart-mantra, "To such-and-such deceased," is prescribed;
one should worship the water with that mantra using the *sṛṇi* mudrā.
Having invoked the sacred fords (tīrthas) right there, one should mutter the mantra eight times;
having assigned the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅgas) to the water, one should worship the waters with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
One should recite the root mantra eight times and cover [the vessel] with the fish-mudrā;
then, one should place the *prokṣaṇī* (sprinkling vessel) upon the conch in the southern direction.
Having sprinkled a little water from the conch, he should sprinkle everything all around;
then, he should contemplate the objects of worship and his own self as being completely purified.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Then, having drawn a Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala upon an altar in front of himself,
he should fill the center of the pericarp with rice grains.
Having spread darbha grass right there, one should place the seat (kūrca) endowed with its proper characteristics;
beginning with the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), one should worship that throne-mantra (pīṭhamaṃtra).
Having taken a flawless pitcher whose interior has been washed with water consecrated by mantras,
one should wrap it with a triple-stranded thread that is reddish in color.

The preceptor should place [the vessel], which has nine gems within it, is provided with a tuft of grass, and is worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, upon that pedestal while reciting the Tārā mantra.
O Sage, one should contemplate the oneness of the pitcher and the pedestal, and then fill it with water from sacred sites while reciting the Mātṛkā in reverse order.
Having recited the root mantra, one should fill [the vessel] with the mental conception of the deity,
using tender, fresh sprouts of the Aśvattha, Panasa, and Āmra trees.
One should cover the mouth of the jar with a cup containing fruit and unbroken rice;
the wise man should then establish it and wrap it with a pair of cloths.
One should perform the rite of establishing the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) with the mantra for establishing the vital breaths;
one should delight the supreme deity with the mudrās of invocation and the rest.

One should meditate upon that Supreme Goddess according to the method described in the Kalpa; then, one should utter words of welcome and inquiries after her well-being in the presence of the Goddess.
Then one should offer water for the feet (pādya), and after that, water for sipping (ācamanīyaka);
one should also present the honey-mixture (madhuparka) along with fragrant unguents, and offer a divine bath.
Then one should give two garments, bright red, made of fine linen and perfectly pure;
thereafter, one should arrange [the offerings] strewn with various collections of gems.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the limbs of the Goddess according to the prescribed method using the letters of the Mātṛkā as encapsulated by Manu, one should worship her with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
O Sage, the incense consists of black agallochum mixed with camphor,
as well as saffron and sandalwood combined with musk.
One should offer flowers such as the *kunda* and others to the Supreme Goddess; likewise, incense consisting of agallochum (*aguru*), turushka, ushira, sandalwood, and sugar. (70)
It is traditionally taught that honey mixed [with other ingredients] is always dear to the Goddess in the form of incense.
Then, having offered many lamps, the wise man should present the food offering (naivedya).
One should pour water from the *jala-dadhma* vessel into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel for each respective substance, and not otherwise;
thereafter, one should perform the limb-worship (*aṅgapūjā*) and the rites prescribed in the ritual manual (*kalpa*).
Then, having worshipped the Goddess together with her attendants, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the south, one should invoke the Fire there.
Having invoked the deity residing in the image there and worshipped it in due order,
one should then perform the oblation with the *tāra* (om), the *vyāhṛtis*, and indeed with the root mantra.
O Sage, one should then perform twenty-five oblations with milk-rice mixed with ghee, using the *vyāhṛtis*, and should offer further oblations once more.

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should join the Goddess to the pedestal; then, having dismissed the fire, one who is purified by the oblation should scatter and smear [the site]. (76)
Then, having offered the five services (pañcopacāra) consisting of perfumes, flowers, and so forth, along with betel, an umbrella, and chowries, to the attendants of the deity.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter seven.
Then one should offer the oblation to the Goddess and recite the mantra one thousand times;
having offered the recitation, one should scatter the remains of the portion in the direction where the deity is stationed.
One should place a water-pot (karkarī) upon it, invoke Durgā therein, and worship her while reciting "Protect! Protect! and sprinkling water from the mouth of its spout.
Chanting the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should sprinkle the site while circumambulating it clockwise;
one should place a karkarī jar in its proper place and worship the deity of the weapon.
The teacher, restrained in speech, should eat together with the disciple behind him;
on that night, he should diligently sleep upon that same altar.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: O Sage, I shall now describe in brief, according to the rules and the prescribed injunctions, the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the altar (sthaṇḍila).
Having recited the root mantra, one should gaze [at the object] with the weapon mantra;
one should sprinkle it and perform the striking with that very armor mantra.
Sprinkling is thus prescribed; thereafter, one should draw three lines each, extending all around, with their tips pointing eastward and northward.
Having sprinkled the pedestal with the Praṇava, one should worship the pedestal of the Goddess,
beginning from Ādhāraśakti and ending with the mantra of the pedestal.
Having invoked Śiva and the two supreme causes upon that pedestal, he,
being composed in mind, should worship them with offerings such as perfumes and other services.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, having bathed after her menses, closely united with Śaṅkara;
one should contemplate their amorous play for a short time while they are overcome by passion.
Then, having taken up the fire with a vessel, one should place it in front,
having set aside the portion for the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) by means of the previously mentioned rites of inspection (vīkṣaṇa) and so forth.
Having consecrated [the fire] and uttered the seed-syllable *raṃ*,
one should thereafter join consciousness (*caitanya*) into it and consecrate it with the *praṇava* (OM).
Then the Guru should display the Dhenu-mudrā seven times;
having placed [the disciple] under protection in the refuge, he should cover him with the armor-mantra.
Having circumambulated the water three times from left to right, that best of beings,
with his knees touching the ground, recited the Tāra-mantra over the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
With the thought that it is the seed of Śiva, one should cast the fire into the womb of the Goddess;
then one should offer water for sipping to the God and to the Goddess, the Mother of the World. 92.
"Cit piṅgala hana daha paca yugmam tataḥ paraṃ sarvajña ājñāpaya svāhā"—this is the mantra for kindling the fire. (93)
I bow to Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations; he who is golden-hued, stainless, kindled, and whose faces are turned in every direction. 14.
With this mantra, they should praise that fire with supreme devotion;
then the best of preceptors should invoke the six-limbed mantra of the fire.
Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa, Dhūmavyāpī, Saptāha, and Dhanurdhara are remembered in this order. (96)
One should place the six limbs, joined with their respective seed-syllables, in the previously mentioned locations;
one should meditate upon Fire, golden-hued, three-eyed, and seated upon a lotus.
Then, the knower of mantras should sprinkle the supreme auspicious vessel, which bears the svastika of the desired power,
over the rim of the sacrificial pit.
One should spread *darbha* grass around [the altar] from the west, and then place the boundary-sticks (*paridhi*).
[The mandala] consists of a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and an outer enclosure (*bhūpura*). 99.
One should visualize the yantra of Fire, or alternatively, draw it first;
then, O Sage, one should worship Fire in its center with this mantra:
"O Vaiśvānara! O Jātavedas! O Jātavedas, come hither! (vaiśvānara tato jātavedaḥ jātavedaḥ paścād ihāvaha).
Having uttered the word "Lohitākṣa," accomplish all rites.
The mantra ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā) is used; with that, one should worship Vahni in the center and in all six corners—namely Hiraṇyā and Gaganā as well.
One should worship those seven tongues— Red, Black, Radiant, Multiform, and Excessive— as well as the worship of the limbs upon the filaments.
On the petals, one should worship the two forms who hold the Śakti and the Svastika.
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and Havyavāhana; || 104 ||
Another is known as Aśvodaraja, while another is called Vaiśvānara;
there is also Komāratejas, and Viśvamukha is remembered as Devamukha. 105.

The forms of Fire, beginning with the word *tārāgnaye* and ending with *namaḥ*, are to be placed; likewise, the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in the four directions, accompanied by their weapons such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*). || 106 ||
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:

Then, having performed the purification of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles as well as the purification of the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should perform the *homa* offering; thereafter, taking the ghee with the thread, one should indeed proceed. (107)
From the portion taken from the south,
one should offer into the right eye of the fire with "Svāhā to Agni," and likewise from the other side, the left.
O best of men, having taken that which was brought from the center with the mantra "Svāhā to Soma," he should then offer it into the central eye with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni and Soma. || 109 ||
Then, taking ghee from the southern portion and placing it in the mouth, one should subsequently offer it with the mantra: "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. (110)
Then the practitioner should offer oblations with the seven vyāhṛtis;
thereafter, he should offer oblations into the fire with the fire-mantra three times.
Then, O Sage, for the sake of performing the purificatory rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna), one should offer eight oblations at a time with the syllable Om alone.

The rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana), followed by the birth-rite (jātakarma), the naming ceremony (nāmakarma), and likewise the first outing (niṣkramaṇa). || 113 ||
The first feeding of solid food, as well as the tonsure ceremony, the binding of the sacred thread, and likewise the Mahānāmnī vow, followed by the Upaniṣad vow. (114)
The purificatory rites (saṃskāras) enjoined by the Vedas are declared to be those beginning with the Godāna and ending with marriage;
thereafter, having worshipped Śiva and Pārvatī, one should dismiss them.
The practitioner should offer five fuel-sticks (samidh) directed toward the fire,
and thereafter, he should offer one oblation for each of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas).
O Sage, having taken ghee into the *sruk* ladle four times with the *sruva* spoon, and having covered it with that very same spoon while remaining seated on one's own seat; 117.
Then, one should offer oblations into the fire with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
one should offer ten oblations with the Mahāgaṇeśa mantra as prescribed.
Having worshipped the pedestal in the fire and meditated upon the deity of the mantra within the mouth of that fire twenty-five times; 119.
One should offer oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of unifying the [deity's] faces,
while contemplating the identity of the fire and the deity together with oneself.
Then the supreme practitioner should meditate upon [the deity] as unified;
he should offer oblations separately for each of the six limbs of the deities.
O best of sages, one should offer exactly eleven oblations;
by this, O sage, the union of the channels between the fire and the deity is accomplished.
O Sage, one should likewise offer oblations with clarified butter, following the same sequence for each of the repetitions according to the single-step method.
Then, one should perform oblations with the substances prescribed in the ritual manual, or alternatively with sesame seeds,
reciting the root mantra of the deity one thousand times, O Gajantaka.
O Sage, having thus taken the goddess, he meditated upon her as being satisfied;
likewise, he [meditated upon] the goddess Āvṛti and the deities beginning with Vahni.
Then, [he should initiate] the disciple who has bathed well, performed the twilight rites and other duties,
is provided with two garments, and is endowed with golden ornaments.

The disciple should bring the water-pot near the sacrificial pit for the purification of his hands; then, having offered salutations to the gurus and the members of the assembly, he should proceed. (127)
Having paid homage to the family deity, he should enter the seat;
then the Guru should look upon that disciple with a compassionate gaze. 128.
One should contemplate that consciousness as being united within one's own body;
thereafter follows the purification of the paths (adhvan) residing within the body of the disciple.
The wise one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) by means of divine vision, so that the self may become purified and fit for the grace of the gods and other beings. (130)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter seven.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: He should meditate upon the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) of the disciple’s body in their proper sequence:
first, the collection of the path of Kalās in the two feet; then, the path of Tattvas. 131.

The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is in the navel, the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan) likewise in the heart; the path of the words (padādhvan) is in the forehead, and the path of the mantras (mantrādhvan) in the head. || 132 ||
Touching the disciple with the *kūrca* grass while using sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter (*ājya*), he should recite the mantra: "I purify this path; svāhā! (133).
One should indeed offer oblations for each path in turn, beginning with the path rich in stars (tārāḍhya).
Then, one should contemplate those six paths as dissolved into Brahman.
Therefore, the Guru should indeed generate it again by means of the six measures;
he should then join that consciousness, which resides within himself, once more with the disciple.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should lead the deity into the water-pot (*kalaśa*).
Having again offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and likewise the limb-oblations (*aṅgāhuti*) to the fire; 136.
Having offered [the oblations] one by one, the Guru should dissolve the fire into himself;
then the Guru should bind the eyes of the disciple with a cloth.
With the Netra-mantra, he should lead that disciple around the mandala;
he should then cause the disciple to offer a handful of flowers to the principal goddess from his own hands.
Having removed the blindfold, he should instruct [the disciple] on a seat of kuśa grass;

he should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) in the body of the disciple according to the prescribed method. Then, having performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) of the mantras as they have been taught, [he should place them] upon the body of the disciple.
One should cause the disciple to enter the mandala, while those [deities] residing in other jars [are likewise invoked]. || 140 ||
Having placed the sprouts upon the head of the disciple, he should recite the Mātṛkā;
then he should bathe the disciple with the waters contained in the jar, which are of the nature of the deities.
And he should promptly perform the sprinkling of water from the *vardhanī* vessel for the sake of protection;
then the disciple, having risen and put on two garments, [should proceed]. (142)
Having smeared himself with ashes, he should lie down in the presence of the Guru.
Then, the Guru [visualizes] Śivā emerging from his own heart. 143.
The treasury of compassion should contemplate [the mantra] as having entered the heart of the disciple;
he should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, while indeed contemplating the identity of those two.
Then, placing his own hand upon the head of the disciple, the Guru should impart the great mantra of the Great Goddess into the disciple's right ear for the third time. (145)
O Sage, the disciple should also recite the mantra one hundred and eight times,
and prostrate himself on the ground like a staff before that preceptor who is the very embodiment of the deity.
One should offer all one's possessions to him for as long as one lives, with a mind focused on no other;
having given the sacrificial fee to the officiating priests, one should also feed the Brahmins.

One should [feed] married women, virgins, and young brahmin students (baṭuka) in every way, as well as the wretched, the helpless, and the poor, while remaining free from stinginess regarding wealth. 148.
Realizing that one's own purpose has been accomplished, one should constantly propitiate the Manu.
Thus has the unsurpassed ritual procedure for initiation been fully explained to you. 149.
Having reflected upon this in its entirety, take refuge in the lotus feet of the Goddess;
for no other supreme dharma exists here for a Brahmin. 150.

The Vaidika [teacher] should instruct the Manu according to the procedure prescribed in his own Gṛhya-sūtra, whereas the Tāntrika should do so according to the Tantric method; this is the eternal rule. 151.
Those various [beings] shall perform those specific applications as they have been described, and not otherwise.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said: "O Nārada, everything that was asked by you has thus been related by me."
Henceforth, worship eternally the lotus feet of Parāmbā;
by constantly propitiating them, I have attained supreme bliss. 153.
In the glorious *Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, in the twelfth book, chapter eight. Vyāsa said:
Having thus spoken all this unsurpassed teaching to Nārada, O King,
he closed his eyes in meditative absorption and meditated upon the lotus feet of the Goddess.
The blessed Nārāyaṇa, the crest-jewel of the best of sages,
and Nārada as well, having then bowed to their supreme teacher Nārāyaṇa, [departed].
Eager for a vision of the Goddess, he departed immediately to perform austerities. || 155 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Janamejaya said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, best among those who have mastered all the scriptures!
For all the twice-born, however, the practice of worship according to one's capacity is declared in the Śruti.
O All-pervading Lord, why did the twice-born, abandoning that [Sandhyā] which is obligatory at the three junctions of time and at other times as well, instead worship other deities?
Some are seen as Vaiṣṇavas, others likewise as Gāṇapatyas; some follow the path of the Kāpālikas, while others wear garments of bark.
Likewise, the Digambaras, the Buddhists, the Cārvākas,
and others such as these are seen in great numbers in the world, devoid of faith in the Vedas.
O Brahmā, you ought to tell me what the cause is here;
for these people are intelligent, learned, and experts in various systems of logic.
Indeed, they do exist even within the Vedas, though they are devoid of faith;
for no one here desires to abandon their own welfare through their own intelligence.
What is the reason for this? Therefore, speak, O best among the knowers of the Vedas!
Previously, the greatness of Maṇidvīpa was described by you. (7)
O sinless one, tell me, who am a faithful devotee, what that supreme and most exalted abode of the Goddess is like. || 8 ||
"When the gurus are pleased, they indeed speak even that which is secret.
Sūta said:
Having heard these words of the king, the venerable Vādarāyaṇa [spoke].
Then, O lords of sages, he narrated everything in due order, hearing which the faith of the twice-born in the Vedas increases. (10)
Vyāsa said:
You have asked well, O King, at the proper time and in a manner suited to that occasion. You are wise regarding the Vedas, and you appear to be truly endowed with faith.
Formerly, the Daityas, arrogant with pride, waged war against the gods;
they fought with the gods for a hundred years, O great king, a battle that caused immense wonder. (12)
O King, their battle was indeed one that brought about the destruction of the world, featuring various weapons and missiles and diversified by many kinds of illusions. (13)
Through the entry of the grace of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), the gods conquered the Daityas in battle;
abandoning the earth and heaven, they went to the abode of Pātāla.
Then, filled with great joy and overcome by delusion, the gods, full of pride, began to describe their own prowess to one another on all sides. || 15 ||
"How could victory not be ours, since our majesty is such? O Daityas, where is the Supreme Being? We are commoners, devoid of prowess. (16)
In the Śrī Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, Twelfth Skandha, Chapter 8:
"We are all illustrious ones who bring about creation, maintenance, and destruction."
What need is there to speak of commoners and even of the Daityas in our presence? || 17 ||
Not knowing the power of the Supreme Śakti, they fell into delusion;
at that very moment, the Mother of the Universe acted to bestow grace upon them.
O King, he appeared in the form of a Yakṣa, filled with compassion, resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons. (19)
Having seen that most beautiful light, never before seen, which was devoid of hands, feet, and other limbs, and possessed a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning; ||20||
Then, filled with wonder, they said: "What is this? What is this?
"Is it the deed of the Daityas, or some great illusion?"
Or was she created by someone as a source of wonder for the gods?
Then they all gathered together and held an excellent deliberation.
Having gone near the yakṣa, one should also ask, "Who are you?
Then, having ascertained his strength or weakness, the counter-measure should be undertaken. 23.
Then Indra, the lord of the gods, having summoned Agni, said:
"Go indeed to us, for you are our supreme mouth."
Then, having gone there, find out what this yakṣa is;
thus [spoke] the thousand-eyed one, his words filled with his own prowess. (25)
That fire, having emerged with speed, went into the presence of the Yakṣa;
then the Yakṣa spoke to that consumer of oblations, "Who are you?"
"Tell me truly before me what kind of valor you possess.
He replied, "I am Agni; likewise, I am Jātavedas."
"The power to burn everything resides within me regarding the entire universe.
Then the Yakṣa placed a blade of grass before that supreme splendor. (28)
If you indeed possess the power to burn this universe,
then the consumer of oblations (Agni) exerted his effort with all his might.
He was unable to burn even a blade of grass; filled with shame, he went before the gods.
When questioned by the gods regarding the matter, the consumer of oblations (Agni) told them everything:
"O gods, our pride in being the lords of all and so forth is indeed in vain."
Then the slayer of Vṛtra, having summoned Vāyu, spoke this: ||31||
The entire universe is woven upon you, and it moves by means of your activities;
you are the form of the vital breath of all beings and the sustainer of all powers.
Go yourself and find out what this yakṣa is;
there is no one else capable of knowing that supreme splendor which is the yakṣa.
Having heard the words of the Thousand-eyed One, which were woven with the weight of his virtues, he went quickly with pride to where the Yakṣa was resplendent. (34)
Having seen the yakṣa, he then spoke to Vāyu in gentle words:
"Who are you? What power do you possess? Tell me everything before me."
Then, having heard the words of the yakṣa, Marut spoke with pride:
"I am Mātariśvan," and he said, "I am Vāyu. (36)
Indeed, my power lies in the moving and grasping of everything; through my activity, the entire world comes to possess all its functions. (37)
Having heard these words of Vāyu, the Supreme Light replied:
"This [world] is but a blade of grass before you; move it as you wish. (38)
"Otherwise, abandon this bull and go bashfully to Vāsava.
Hearing these words of the Yakṣa, Vāyu, endowed with all powers, [departed]. (39)
He made an effort, yet he did not move from his own place;
ashamed, that Vāyu abandoned his pride and went to the side of the God.
He related the entire account, the cause for the quenching of his pride:
"We, who were possessed by false pride and arrogance, were not capable of knowing this. (41)
A supernatural, extremely terrible, and blazing spirit appeared;
then all the hosts of gods addressed the thousand-eyed Indra.
"O Devarāśi, since you know the yakṣa in its true nature, therefore Indra, out of great pride, rushed toward that yakṣa. (43)
Then that supreme splendor in the form of a yakṣa, higher than the highest, fled;
thereafter, that yakṣa vanished from the presence of Vāsava.
Thus,
even Vāsava, the king of the gods, became filled with shame. *Śrīmad-Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa*, Twelfth Skandha, Chapter 8.
Due to the absence of conversation with the yakṣa, he experienced lightness in his mind.
Henceforth, I must not go to the assembly of the gods;
for what could I say there to the deities that would not be a source of my own humiliation? (46)
Therefore, the abandonment of the body is better, for pride is indeed the wealth of the great;
when pride is lost, life is no different from death—of this there is no doubt.
Having thus resolved, the Lord of the Gods abandoned his horse right there and sought refuge in Him whose life-story is such as this. (48)
At that very moment, a voice from the sky arose in the firmament:
"O Thousand-eyed One, chant the seed-syllable of Māyā; by that, become happy. (49)
Then, subsisting on no food for a hundred thousand years with eyes closed in meditation, he recited the supreme seed-mantra of Māyā, which is higher than the highest.
Suddenly, on the ninth day of the month of Caitra, while the sun was at the meridian,
that very same light manifested once again in that very same place.
In the center of the circle of light is the Youthful Maiden, in the bloom of fresh youth, possessing the luster of a shining hibiscus flower and the brilliance of ten million rising suns.
She wears the cool-rayed moon as her crown, and her voice is revealed from within her garment;
with four excellent hands, she displays the gestures of granting boons, the noose, the goad, and fearlessness.
She possessed beautiful limbs and delicate, creeper-like members; she was auspicious Śivā, the Mother who is a wish-fulfilling tree for her devotees, adorned with various ornaments.
She has three eyes, is adorned with a garland of jasmine flowers and a mass of matted hair,
and is praised from the four directions by the four Vedas personified as wise sages.
Her teeth, like rows of rubies, adorned her face on all sides; with a serene and smiling countenance, she was as beautiful as ten million gods of love. (56)
[He saw] the goddess Umā, known as Haimavatī, the auspicious Śivā, standing before him, clothed in red garments and adorned with red sandalwood paste. (57)
There, Vāsava beheld her, the embodiment of unfeigned compassion and the cause of all causes, his inner heart faltering with love. (58)
Then, with eyes filled with tears of love and his body covered in horripilation,
he prostrated like a staff at the feet of the Lord of the Universe.
With his neck bowed in devotion, he praised [him] with various hymns;
being exceedingly pleased, he said, "What is this? Is it a Yakṣa? (60)
"And tell me everything, O most beautiful one, why did it manifest?
Having heard these words of his, she who was an ocean of compassion replied:
This form of mine is Brahman, the cause of all causes;
it is presided over by me, the witness of all, free from all affliction.
That goal which all the Vedas proclaim, which all the sacrificial rites declare, and desiring which they lead a life of celibate studentship—that goal I tell you in brief. (63)
"Oṃ' is the single-syllabled Brahman, and they say that very same thing is 'Hoṃ'.
O best of gods, these two seed-syllables are my primary mantras. (64)
Since I create the entire universe possessing two parts, one of those parts is proclaimed to be named Saccidānanda. (65)
That which is known as *māyā-prakṛti* is declared to be the second part;
and that *māyā* is the supreme power (*parā śakti*), while I, the Sovereign, am the possessor of that power (*śaktimatī*). (66)
O best of gods, this Māyā of mine has come to me as a state of identity, just as moonlight belongs to the moon. (67)
At the time of dissolution, she remains non-different from me alone;
indeed, by the power of the ripening of the karma of living beings, [she manifests] once again.
Thus, that form which is unmanifest attains the state of manifestation;
however, that internal-facing state is designated as Māyā. (69)
But that illusion which is outward-turned is designated by the word "tamas";
from that tamas which is outward-turned, the emergence of sattva arises. (70)
The Eighth Chapter of the Twelfth Book in the Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa.
O best of the gods, at the beginning of creation, the quality of rajas then arises;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are said to consist of the three qualities. (71)
Brahmā has an excess of the quality of rajas; Viṣṇu possesses an excess of sattva;
Rudra, who assumes the form of the cause of all, possesses an excess of tamas.
The gross body is Brahmā; the subtle body (liṅgadeha) is remembered as Hari; Rudra is the causal body; but I alone am indeed the fourth state (turiya).
That state of equilibrium which has been described as having the form of the inner ruler of all—
beyond that is the Supreme Brahman, my own form, devoid of all material form.
My own form is said to be twofold: devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) and endowed with attributes (saguṇa).
That which is devoid of attributes is free from māyā; that which is endowed with attributes is joined with māyā. (75)
Having created the entire world and having entered into its midst,
I incessantly impel the individual soul according to its karma and according to its sacred learning.
Indeed, I alone impel Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—who are of the nature of the cause—toward creation, maintenance, and dissolution. (77)
The wind blows out of fear of me, and the sun moves;
likewise do Indra, Agni, and Death. Therefore, I am remembered as the most excellent of all. (78)
"By my grace, victory has always been obtained by you;
yet I make you dance like wooden puppets. (79)
Sometimes there is victory for the gods and sometimes for the Daityas;
independent and by my own will, I perform everything in accordance with the law of karma.
Having forgotten me, who am the soul of all, out of your own pride, you—whose minds are shrouded by egoism—have fallen into endless delusion. 81.
Then, in order to bestow grace, my unsurpassed splendor suddenly issued forth from your body as a Yakṣa. (82)
Henceforth, having abandoned all states of being and the pride born of the body, take refuge in me alone, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss. 83.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Great Goddess, the Sovereign Mūlaprakṛti,
being praised by the gods with devotion, immediately vanished from sight.
Then, having abandoned all pride, they all properly worshipped the supreme-most lotus feet of the Blessed Lady. 85.
At all times, during the three junctions of the day, they were all devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī;
they constantly served the Goddess with their shares of the sacrificial offerings and other rites.
