Thus, in the Satya Yuga, all were intent on the recitation of the Gāyatrī,
and their minds were also thoroughly proficient in the recitation of the Tāra and Hṛllekhā mantras.
Nowhere in the Veda is the constant worship of Viṣṇu enjoined;
likewise, there is no constant initiation for Viṣṇu, nor indeed for Śiva.
The meditation on the Gāyatrī is eternal and proclaimed by all the Vedas;
without it, there is a downfall for the Brāhmaṇa in every respect. (89)
To that extent alone is the twice-born one fulfilled; indeed, he has no further dependence on anything else.
A twice-born man who is proficient in the Gāyatrī alone shall attain liberation.
"Whether one should perform other [rites] or not," so Manu himself has declared;
but having abandoned that [view], those devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu follow the Gāyatrī. (91)
A Brahmin devoted to the worship of Śiva goes to hell in every way;
therefore, O King, in the first age, those intent on the recitation of the Gāyatrī [attain their goal].
All those best of the twice-born were devoted to the lotus feet of the Goddess. || 92 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 8 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter nine.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Vyāsa said: Once, O Lord, after fifteen years had passed,
Śatakratu did not send rain due to the power of the karma of living beings.
Due to a lack of rain, there occurred an extreme famine that caused total destruction;
indeed, it was impossible to count the number of corpses in every single house.
Some, afflicted by hunger, devour horses or wild boars;
and other people eat the corpses of men.
The infant, the mother of the infant, the woman, and even the man—all set out to devour them; the men were tormented by agitation. (4)
Many Brahmins there held an excellent deliberation: "Gautama, whose wealth is asceticism, is here; he will remove our distress. (5)
"All of us must go together now to Gautama’s hermitage;
it is heard that there is plenty of food at Gautama’s hermitage, where many living beings have gone.
Having reflected thus, the Brahmins, who were householders maintaining the sacred fire-rituals, [prepared to depart].
Accompanied by cattle, cows, and horses, they went to the hermitage of Gautama; some came from the eastern region and others from the southern region.
Those from the west and those from the north arrived from various directions;
seeing that assembly of the distressed, Gautama approached them.
He honored the Brahmins with offerings such as seats and other services; then he inquired after their welfare and the reason for their arrival.
Smiling, they all related their respective accounts.
Seeing those brahmins distressed, the sage granted them fearlessness.
"This is your dwelling; I am your servant in every respect.
What anxiety can there be for me, a servant, when you are present? 12.
I am blessed at this moment, O you all whose wealth is asceticism; by the mere sight of you, even my evil deeds turn into meritorious acts.
May they all dust their feet upon my home;
who else but I could be so fortunate through your grace? (14)
"All must remain here in comfort, devoted to the twilight prayers and the recitation of mantras.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus consoled them all, the sage Gautama, the king of sages, then—
With his neck constantly bent in devotion, Gāyatrī offered this prayer:
"Obeisance, O Goddess Mahāvidyā, who are beyond the Vedas and higher than the highest! (16)

O Mother, who consists of the great mantras beginning with the *vyāhṛtis*, who are embodied in the *praṇava*, whose nature is the state of equilibrium, salutations to you who are the form of the syllable *hrīṃ*. 17.
I bow to you, O Goddess, who are the embodiment of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, the granter of all aims,
the wish-fulfilling creeper for devotees, and the witness of the three states of existence.
She whose nature is beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda),
who is to be known through all the Vedāntas, and who dwells within the solar orb.
In the morning I always bow to her as a red-colored girl; at midday, to the supreme young woman; and in the evening, to the dark-complexioned old woman. 20.
"O Goddess, who draws forth all beings, O Supreme Sovereign, forgive me!
Thus praised, the Mother of the World granted her direct vision.
She gave him a full vessel by which all nourishment could be obtained;
that Mother said to the sage, "Whatever desire you wish for in the evening," (22)
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter nine.
"A vessel that fulfills his religious merit shall be given by me.
Having spoken thus, the goddess Gāyatrī, the supreme power, vanished.
From that place, O King, heaps of food resembling mountains emerged,
containing various foods of six flavors as well as diverse kinds of grasses.
There were divine ornaments and silken garments,
as well as the commencement of sacrifices and various kinds of sacrificial vessels.
O King, whatever was desired by that high-souled sage,
all of that emerged from that full vessel of Gāyatrī.
Then, having summoned all the sages, the sage Aṅgautama joyfully gave them wealth, ornaments, and garments.
Cows, buffaloes, and other animals emerged from the full vessel;
he gave away the sacrificial implements that had been brought forth, such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
All of them, having gathered together at the word of the sage, performed sacrifices;
that very place became preeminent, resembling heaven itself. (29)
Whatever beautiful object is seen within the three worlds, all of that is produced there from the vessel bestowed by Gāyatrī. (30)
The wives, resembling celestial nymphs, shone with ornaments and other finery;
the sages, like unto gods, were adorned with garments, sandalwood paste, and jewelry. (31)
A perpetual festival proceeded within the circle of the sage’s hermitage;
there was no fear whatsoever of disease or the like, nor was there any fear of misery anywhere. 32.
That hermitage of the sage became a hundred yojanas in extent on all sides;
and whatever other living beings there were, they too gathered there. (33)
Then, having granted them all freedom from fear,
that self-possessed one nourished them with various kinds of great sacrifices performed according to the prescribed rites, O gods.
They attained supreme satisfaction and sang the praises of the sage;
then the highly illustrious slayer of Vṛtra again recited a verse in the assembly.

"Aha! This wish-fulfilling tree of ours has indeed been established, for it fulfills our desires; otherwise, where could we find such an unexpected offering of oblation or sacrificial fat, when even the hope for life itself is so difficult to sustain? (36)
In this manner, for twelve years,
he nurtured those bulls among sages like his own sons, being entirely free from the pride of the sagehood of Aṅga.
The best of sages established the supreme abode of Gāyatrī, where the Mother of the Universe is worshipped by all the foremost sages. (38)
Even today, that goddess is seen there in the form of a young girl, due to her supreme devotion and the performance of *puraścaraṇa* rites three times a day. (39)
At midday she appears as a young woman, but at evening she is seen as an old woman.
Once, the best of sages, Nārada, arrived there.
Jingling his ornaments and singing of the supreme qualities of Gāyatrī, he sat down in the midst of the assembly of sages whose souls were purified. 41.
Honored exceedingly by Gotama and others, he whose mind was perfectly tranquil recounted various stories concerning the glory of Gautama.
O Brahman-sage, in the assembly of the gods, the King of the Gods sang of your many kinds of pure and supreme fame, born from your nurturing of the sages. 43.
Having heard the words of the Lord of Śacī, I have come to see you;
you are blessed, O best of sages, by the grace of the Mother of the World. 44.
Having spoken thus to that sage, he went to the abode of Gāyatrī;
with eyes blossoming with love, he beheld that Mother of the World.
Having praised the Goddess according to the prescribed rites, he returned once more to heaven.
Then, those Brahmins who were staying there, supported by the sage, [remained].
Having heard of the sage’s excellence, they became distressed with envy, thinking, "We must certainly act in every way so that his fame shall not increase. (47)
"It shall happen later when the time has arrived"—this was decided by everyone.
Then, after some time had passed, rain fell upon the surface of the earth.
O best of kings, there was abundance of food in all lands;
hearing news of this plenty, all the brāhmaṇas gathered together. 49.
"Alas, alas! O King! they cried, as they saw Gautama cursed and making an effort [to depart].
Blessed are their parents, from whom such an origin as this has come.
O King, who indeed is able to describe the greatness of Time?
O monarch, a single cow was created by his illusory power as an old woman on the verge of death.
And at that time, as it was the hour for the sage's fire-oblation, she entered his hut;
being driven away by his shouts of "Hūṃ," she gave up her life at that very moment.
"By this wicked one, cows have been slaughtered"— thinking thus, O King, those twice-born ones completed the fire sacrifice, and the king of sages was filled with the utmost wonder.
With eyes closed in meditative concentration, he reflected upon the cause;
and having realized at that very moment that all this had been done by the twice-born, he [proceeded].
He harbored a supreme wrath like that of Rudra at the time of universal dissolution,
and with eyes bloodshot with anger, he cursed all the sages.
Those of you who are not always intent upon the Mother of the Vedas, upon Gāyatrī, upon meditation on her, and upon the recitation of her mantra, are the lowest of Brahmins. (56)
"You are always averse to the Vedas, to the sacrifices prescribed in the Vedas, and likewise to the occupations related to them; you are the lowest of Brahmins. (57)
O lowest of Brahmins, you have always been averse to Śiva, to his mantra, and likewise to the scripture of Śiva. (58)
You who are always averse to meditation upon and the stories of the Primordial Nature, the Illustrious Goddess, are the lowest of Brahmins. (59)
O lowest of Brahmins, you have always been averse to the mantra of the Goddess, to the station of the Goddess, and to the performance of her rites. (60)
O lowest of Brahmins, you are always averse to the desire to witness the festival of the Goddess and to the chanting of the names of the Goddesses. (61)
O lowest of Brahmins, you have always been averse to the presence of a devotee of the Goddess, as well as to the worship of a devotee of the Goddess. (62)
O you who dwell in the hermitages of Brahmins, you have always been averse to the desire of a devotee of Śiva to witness his festival and to his worship. (63)
O lowest of Brahmins, you who are always averse to Rudrākṣa beads, Bilva leaves, and pure sacred ash, shall forever remain so.
"You are always averse to the path of Vedic and Smṛti injunctions, as well as to the way of knowledge; you are all the lowest of Brāhmaṇas. (65)
You who are always averse to being intent upon non-dual knowledge and to the means of practice such as tranquility and self-control are the lowest of Brahmins. (66)
Even regarding the performance of obligatory rites and the means for the Agnihotra and other sacrifices, you are never inclined toward them;
you are the lowest of Brahmins. (67)
You are always averse to the study of the Vedas, as well as to their recitation; you are the lowest of Brahmins. (68)
Indeed, in matters such as the gift of cows and other charities, as well as in the ancestral śrāddha rites, you have always been averse to these; you are the lowest of Brahmins. (69)
"Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and likewise expiatory rites (prāyaścitta)—you base Brahmins are always averse to these. (70)
Those who, among the various gods, are endowed with faith and devotion toward Śrī Devī, yet are marked with the conch, discus, and other such signs, are the lowest of Brahmins. (71)
"O lowest of Brahmins, you shall become addicted to the Kāpālikas, always devoted to Buddhist scriptures, and intent upon the practices of heretics."
Likewise, those who sell their father, mother, son, brother, or daughter, as well as those who sell their wife—be it known that these are the lowest of Brahmins. (73)
Likewise, those who sell the Vedas, those who sell sacred fords, and those who sell dharma—such are the lowest of Brahmins. (74)
"O lowest of Brahmins, may you become possessed of faith in the Pāñcarātra, in the science of erotics (kāmaśāstra), in the Kāpālika doctrine, and in Buddhism! (75)
May you all become the lowest of Brahmins—those who approach their mothers' daughters, those who approach their sisters, and those who are lustful for the wives of others. (76)
Those born of your lineage— both women and men alike—
shall be consumed by the curse I have given and shall become just like you.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter nine.
What is the use of my speaking at length? Gāyatrī, the sovereign primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), shall indeed become supreme among you; for who, truly, is a father?
"May your residence always be in pits such as blind wells.
Vyāsa said:
Having uttered such a verbal punishment (vāgdaṇḍa), he then performed the ritual rinsing with water.
Extremely eager, he went for the purpose of seeing Gāyatrī;
he bowed down to the Great Goddess, and she too, the goddess who is higher than the highest, [bowed to him]. (80)
Seeing the composition of the Brāhmaṇas, he indeed felt wonder in his heart;
even today, her face is seen to be filled with that same wonder. (81)
With her lotus-like face smiling, she said to that best of sages:
"Milk offered to a serpent only results in poison. (82)
"O illustrious one, bring peace; such is the course of karma.
Having thus prostrated before the Goddess, he then departed for his own hermitage. 83.
Then, consumed by the curse, the brahmins forgot the masses of Vedic knowledge;
Gāyatrī was forgotten by them all, and that was like a marvel.
Then, having all gathered together and being purified by remorse,
they prostrated themselves on the ground like a staff before that best of sages.
But they did not utter a single word; standing with their faces cast down in shame, they said again and again, "Be gracious! Be gracious! Be gracious! (86)
They made their request, surrounding the lord of sages on all sides;
the sage, his heart filled with compassion, spoke to them.
"Until the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, your stay shall be in the Kumbhīpāka hell;
know this in every way that my word shall not be false. (88)
Thereafter, in the Kali age, you two shall indeed take birth on earth;
all this that I have spoken shall certainly come to pass, and not otherwise.
If there should be any fault on your part for the sake of liberating the fish-king, then everyone should always serve the lotus-feet of the Gāyatrī. 90.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus dismissed them all, Gautama, the best of sages,
considering that [his karma] had begun to bear fruit, attained peace within his mind.
For this reason, O King, when the wise Kṛṣṇa had departed and the Kali age had set in,
those Brāhmaṇas who had previously been consumed by curses emerged from the Kumbhīpāka hell and were born upon the earth. (92)
Those who are devoid of the three twilight prayers and are lacking in devotion to the Gāyatrī; || 93 ||
Devoid of devotion to the Vedas and following the doctrines of heretics, they are bereft of the performance of virtuous rites such as the Agnihotra, as well as the utterances of Svadhā and Svāhā.
Some never understand the unmanifest root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) at all; others, marked with heated seals, are devoted to licentious conduct.
The Kāpālikas, the Kaulikas, the Buddhists, the Jains, and others— even those who are scholars— all of them are promoters of wicked conduct.
Those who are lustful for the wives of others and devoted to wicked conduct shall all,
by their own actions, go again to the Kumbhīpāka hell.
Therefore, O King, the Supreme Goddess should be served with one's whole being;
neither the worship of Viṣṇu nor the worship of Śiva is as constant [as hers]. 98.
And the constant worship of Śakti, without which one falls downward—O sinless one, all that was asked by you has been explained in brief. 99.
Henceforth, listen to the beautiful description of Maṇidvīpa, which is the supreme abode of the primordial Bhuvaneśī, the forest-fire to the world of existence. 100.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, a compendium of eighteen thousand verses. || 9 ||
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, the twelfth book, chapter ten.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Above the realm of Brahmā lies that world which has been heard of;
it is Maṇidvīpa itself, where the Goddess shines resplendent.
Because he is superior to everything, he is therefore remembered as "Sarva" (All). In ancient times, this world was fashioned by Parāmbā herself through her mental will.
By nature, which is its fundamental basis, this entire world exists for the sake of its own dwelling;
it is superior to Kailāsa and even more excellent than Vaikuṇṭha. (3)
All the worlds are considered superior even to Goloka;
indeed, nothing as beautiful as this exists anywhere within the three worlds. (4)
O best of beings, that very one has become the parasol for the three worlds, destroying the torment of worldly existence;
he alone has become the shade for all the universes.
Extending for many yojanas and equally deep,
the ocean of nectar indeed surrounds the Maṇidvīpa on all sides.
It was crowded with hundreds of waves tossed up by the friction of the Maruts,
strewn with sands bright as jewels, and filled with fish and conch shells.
It was cooled by droplets from the waves produced by the friction of twenty [ships],
and it was filled with the coming and going of various boats equipped with diverse banners.
Then, from that [place], there appeared in the sky a great, radiant city constructed of refined gold, surrounded on all sides by trees with jewels for fruit upon its banks. ||1||
A great rampart seven yojanas in width stands there;
[its defenders] are skilled in various weapons and missiles and are experts in diverse modes of combat.
Guardians dwell here on all sides, rejoicing;
it is provided with four gates and attended by hundreds of gatekeepers.
O King, surrounded by various groups of goddesses filled with devotion, those gods who come for the sake of beholding the Lord of the Universe [arrive]. (12)
Their hosts dwell here, and their mounts are indeed present there; the place is filled with the sound of bells from the clashing of hundreds of celestial chariots (vimānas).
The quarters of the sky are deafened by the neighing of horses and the trampling of hooves, while the attendants, striking with canes in their hands, raise shouts of "kilakila."
O protector of the earth, the attendants of the hosts of gods shine there;
yet, O King, amidst that clamor, not a single sound was heard from anyone anywhere.
For someone else, it is heard that in the midst of the extremely crowded and diverse path,
at every step there are lakes filled with sweet water.
O King, there were various groves resplendent with jewel-bearing trees;
beyond that was a mandala fashioned from the great sāra-element.
There is another great *śāla* tree whose summit touches the sky;
by its splendor, this latter tree is a hundred times superior to the former *śāla*. (18)
It was provided with gate-towers and gates and endowed with many trees;
whatever species of trees exist, all of them were present there.
They were constantly covered with flowers, always endowed with fruit, possessed of fresh sprouts, and filled with mutual fragrance. ||20||
There were jackfruit trees, *vakula* trees, *lodhra* trees, *kaṇikāra* trees, and *śiṃśapā* trees;
as well as *devadāru*, *kāñcanāra*, mango trees, and *sumeru* trees. (21)
Likucas, hiṅgulās, elās, lavaṅgas, kaṭphalas, as well as pāṭalas, mucukundas, phalinīs, and jaghanephalas; ||22||
Tāla trees, astamālas, sāl trees, kaṅkolakas, nāgabhadrakas, punnāgas, pīlavas, sātvakas, and indeed camphor-bearing trees; || 23 ||
Aśvakarṇa, Hastikarṇa, Tālaparṇa, and pomegranates; Gaṇikā, Bandhujīva, citron, and Kuraṇḍaka. ||24||

Each goddess shines resplendent with her own attendant goddesses, accompanied by their respective ornaments and vehicles, possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns. 107.
Indeed, there dwell seventy million great mantra-deities;

Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
That very abode of the Goddess shines resplendent in the central region.
In those [four directions], there were four pavilions, each provided with a thousand pillars. || 1 ||
One is the Śṛṅgāra-maṇḍapa, and the other is the Mukti-maṇḍapa;
the third is proclaimed as being named the Jñāna-maṇḍapa. || 2 ||
And the fourth is proclaimed to be the solitary pavilion;
it is provided with various canopies and perfumed with various incenses. || 3 ||
The auspicious pavilions shine with a splendor equal to ten million suns;
surrounding those pavilions, it is said, are groves of saffron trees.
In the glorious Śrīmad Devībhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter twelve: Where groves of Mallikā and Kunda flowers stand in great abundance.
O King, those streams were filled with countless quantities of musk.
Similarly, it was constructed with jeweled staircases,
filled with the essence of nectar, and resounded with intoxicated bees.
The great forest of Mahāpadma;
and the fragrance of the merchants perfumes the jewel-island.
Filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, its quarters perfumed with fragrances,
the goddesses sing in various melodies within the pavilion of love; the best of gods are the members of the assembly, and in their midst is the illustrious Mother of the Universe.
The auspicious goddess liberates [beings] incessantly;
O King, she imparts the instruction of knowledge in the third pavilion.
And in the fourth pavilion, O King, the Mother of the World, together with her attendants, constantly contemplates the protection of the universe. Within the Pavilion of Liberation, however,
in the House of the Wish-fulfilling Gem, she exists as the supreme essence of the Śakti-tattva.
The couch, provided with ten steps, also shines resplendently. || 11 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
these are declared to be the five hooves, while Sadāśiva is the blade.
Above him shines the Great Goddess Bhuvaneśī,
that Goddess who, for the sake of her own divine play, became manifest in two forms.
At the beginning of creation, he himself was this Maheśvara, possessing half of her body; he who destroys the pride of Kandarpa, more beautiful than ten million Kandarapas,
five-faced, three-eyed, and adorned with jewel ornaments.
And he protected the man who was terrified of Hari with his own arms. || 15 ||
That great Lord of all, sixteen years of age, possesses the brilliance of ten million suns and the coolness of ten million moons.
Resembling pure crystal, three-eyed and of cooling luster, the Goddess Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī is seated upon his left lap. 17.
She is resplendent with a girdle-string studded with clusters of nine gems,
and adorned with armlets of vaidūrya set in refined gold.
The splendor of the radiance of her forehead surpassed that of the half-moon. ||19||
Her lotus-face was adorned with earrings in the form of golden śrī-cakras. ||20||
She was resplendent with lips that eclipsed the luster of a bimba fruit,
and her face was illuminated by a tilaka mark of shimmering saffron and musk.
With large, shimmering sun and moon ornaments on her divine crest-jewel,
she was radiant with a rising, level, and pure nose-ornament.
Adorned with clusters of clear pearls suspended from her funeral pyre,
her breasts were embellished with sandalwood paste, camphor, and saffron.
Her limbs were adorned with various and manifold ornaments, and her neck was like a conch shell;
she was resplendent with a row of teeth resembling the seeds of the pomegranate fruit,
and her lotus-face was filled with petals [of lips] darkened by swarms of intoxicated bees.
Her head was adorned with a crown fashioned from priceless jewels,
and her navel was beautified by a whirlpool-like fold resembling the Ganges.
Her face resembles the autumn moon, freed from both blemish and waning.
Her fingers were adorned with rings set with fragments of rubies,
and she was beautiful with three eyes shaped like the petals of a white lotus.
Her radiant luster is like that of a great ruby of pure passion fashioned from the imagined; she is adorned with jeweled bracelets joined by strings of tiny gem-bells;
a succession of necklaces shines upon her, consisting of strings of gems and pearls;
and her hands gleam with a spreading web of light emanating from jeweled fingers. 28.
Mallikā was adorned with jasmine flowers whose scent filled her hair and who were encircled by rows of pearls. ||29||
The bodice, woven with the boundless radiance of various jewels, shone brilliantly. ||30||
Śivā is languid from the weight of her well-rounded, firm, and lofty breasts; she possesses four arms resplendent with the gestures of granting boons, the noose, the goad, and the protection;
she is richly adorned in every erotic ornament, a delicate creeper of limbs, the very essence of the stream of beauty, and composed of unfeigned compassion. (31)
She possesses a supreme splendor that bears the luster of ten million times ten million suns and moons.
The sweetness of her own conversation utterly outshone that of Sarasvatī.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter twelve:
She was surrounded on all sides by various female companions, handmaidens, celestial nymphs, and all the deities. (33)

And among all the halls, the pinnacle of all splendors is declared to be the House of the Cintāmaṇi, wherein dwells the Goddess Mahāmāyī.
Whosoever the lay disciples (upāsakas) who exist throughout every universe—among the gods, in the worlds of the nāgas, among humans, and others. ||44||
O protector of the earth, all those who, devoted to the worship of the Goddess, cast off their lives here in this field of the Goddess belonging to Śrīdevī, go to that very place.
They all go to that very place where the goddess’s great festival is held,
where there are streams of ghee, streams of milk, streams of curd, and flows of honey.
All the rivers flow there, as do other supreme streams carrying nectar;
some carry grape juice, while others carry the juice of the jambu fruit.
There were thousands of rivers flowing with mango juice and sugarcane juice,
as well as trees that yielded the fruits of one's desires, along with ponds and wells.
It yields fruits and drinks according to one's desire; indeed, there is nothing lacking whatsoever.
Neither disease nor graying hair, nor even old age, ever occurs there. (49)
There was no anxiety nor any envy, nor likewise desire, anger, and so forth;
all were young men accompanied by their wives, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns.
There, some worship the goddess Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī constantly; some have attained the state of being in her world (sālokya), and some have reached the state of proximity (sāmīpya). 51.
Some have attained similarity of form, while others have attained equality;
such are the various deities residing within each respective cosmic egg.
Those collective powers abide there, serving the Sovereign of the Universe;
seven crores of great mantras worship Her in embodied form.
And all the Great Vidyās [worship] Śivā, whose nature is the state of equilibrium, who is the form of the causal Brahman, and whose body is variegated by Māyā. ||54||
Thus, O King, has the most magnificent Maṇidvīpa been described by me;
there neither the sun nor the moon shines, nor do millions of lightning flashes or even fire.
They are equal to not even a ten-millionth part of a ten-millionth part of its radiance;
in some places it resembles coral, and in others it has the luster of emerald.
In some places its splendor was like the light of lightning, and in others it was like the midday sun;
in some places it was pervaded by the intense radiance of a great torrent of ten million flashes of lightning.
In some places, its splendor was like that of distant sapphire and ruby; in others, the horizons blazed with the intense radiance of great diamonds and precious gems. 58.
In its radiance it was like a forest fire, resembling molten gold;
in some places it emitted moonstones, and in others it emitted sunstones.
It was endowed with jeweled peaks, possessed jeweled walls and gate-towers,
and was completely adorned with trees that had jeweled leaves and jeweled fruits.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter thirteen: [The place] resounded with the cries of flocks of dancing peacocks and was radiant with the cooing of pigeons.
It was beautified by the warbling songs of cuckoos and the speech of parrots. || 61 ||
It was surrounded by lakes extending for a distance of one hundred thousand *lakṣas*, exceedingly delightful and beautiful with waters,
and adorned in their central regions by blooming jewel-lotuses.

and the horizons on every side were set ablaze by the luster of jewels.
O King, it was filled with great fragrant breezes from the groves of trees,
perfumed by incense, and illuminated by rows of jewel-lamps.
With the flickering luster of its interior, which is more transparent than a honeycomb,
this [mirror], joined with the surface of a mirror, causes confusion regarding the directions.
Of complete sovereignty, of all aesthetic charm, of omniscience, and of all splendor; (67)
O King, here is the culmination of all valor, of every supreme quality, and of all compassion. (68)
Indeed, all those joys that exist throughout the realms from King Ānanda up to the Brahma-world are contained within this very [joy]. || 69 ||
Thus, O King, has this most magnificent Maṇidvīpa been described to you—the supreme abode of the Great Goddess, the most excellent of all worlds. (70)
By remembering this, all sin is instantly destroyed;
and by remembering it at the moment of the departure of the vital breaths, one goes to that very place.
If one should recite these five chapters daily with a concentrated mind,
there shall indeed be no affliction from ghosts, spirits, demons, and the like.
In the construction of a new house and likewise in the Vāstu ritual, this should be recited with effort; by that, auspiciousness arises.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 12 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Vyāsa said:
Thus has been told to you, O sinless king, everything that was asked by you.
That which was spoken by Nārāyaṇa to the high-souled Nārada.
Having heard this most wonderful Purāṇa of the Great Goddess, a mortal becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose; indeed, he is the most beloved of the Goddess.
O King, perform the Ambā sacrifice for the sake of rescuing your father,
since you, O Indra among kings, have become despondent upon learning of your father’s miserable state.
Receive from me, O Great Goddess, this mantra, the most excellent of all,
which, when practiced according to the prescribed rules and ritual, bestows the fulfillment of one's birth.
Sūta said:
Having heard that, the tiger among kings requested the lord of sages for that very great mantra known as the Devī-Pranava.
The best of kings undertook the initiation according to the prescribed ritual;
then, at the commencement of the nine-night festival, he summoned Dhaumya and the others.
Free from any stinginess regarding wealth, he quickly performed the Ambā-yajña;
he had this supreme Purāṇa recited by Brāhmaṇas.
In the presence of the Śrīdevī, for the pleasure of Ambikā, he fed an innumerable number of Brahmins and married women with the supreme Devībhāgavata.
The lord of the earth satisfied all of them— the maidens, the young students, and likewise the poor and the helpless— by bestowing wealth upon them.
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter thirteen:
While he remained established at the sacrificial site after having completed the sacrifice, for as long as he stayed there—
At that very moment, Nārada descended from the sky.
Sounding his great lute, resembling a blazing crest of fire,
he rose up in haste upon seeing that sage Nārada.
The lord of the earth honored him with offerings such as a seat and,
having inquired after his welfare, asked the reason for his arrival.
The king said:
"O virtuous one, tell me from where you have come; what may I do for you? By the reason of your arrival, I am truly well-protected and my purpose is fulfilled. (13)
Having heard these words of the king, the best of sages replied:
"O best of kings, today I beheld this very horse in the world of the gods."
Having reached your presence in great astonishment to report that matter,
your father has fallen into a miserable state due to the reversal of his own karma.
Indeed, having now assumed this very divine form and body,
the God of gods has been properly praised on all sides by the Apsarases.
He attained [liberation] through the fruit arising from hearing this Devībhāgavata. || 17 ||
Having ascended an excellent celestial chariot to the Island of Jewels by the fruit of the Ambā sacrifice, your father has gone to a happy state;
you are blessed, you have fulfilled your purpose, and your life is fruitful.
O ornament of your lineage!
Today your vast fame has spread throughout the world of the gods. (19)
"O Father, you have been rescued from hell by him," Sūta said,
having heard what was spoken by Nārada, his heart faltering with love.
He fell at the lotus feet of Vyāsa, whose deeds are miraculous.
O God, O Great Sage, by your grace I have achieved my purpose;
what else could I do for you in return, other than offer salutations? (21)
"O Sage, by you!
Having heard these words of the king and having greeted him with blessings, [he spoke]. || 22 ||
"I am always to be favored," [he thought];
thus spoke the venerable Vādarāyaṇa in gentle words:
"O King, renouncing everything, take refuge in the lotus feet of the Goddess. (23)
Always recite the Devībhāgavata with a concentrated mind; always perform the Ambāmakhya sacrifice with devotion, remaining ever vigilant. (24)
By that [means], you shall be liberated from the bonds of existence without effort;
there are other ancient [scriptures] as well, such as those headed by Hari and Rudra. (25)
This [Purāṇa] does not deserve even a sixteenth part of this Devībhāgavata;
it is the essence of all the Purāṇas and the Vedas in every respect. (26)
O best of kings, how could any other work be considered a Purāṇa that does not expound this very same primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti)? [27]
O Janamejaya, he who possesses merit equal to the study of the Vedas should recite this very work with diligence; such is the instruction of the best of the wise. (28)
Having spoken thus to the king, the sovereign of sages departed from there;
and the stainless sages, headed by Dhaumya, likewise returned to their respective abodes. (29)
They offered the highest praise for the Devībhāgavata alone;
thereafter, the king, with a satisfied mind, ruled the earth.
And likewise, one who constantly hears the Devībhāgavata five times [daily]. ||30||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the twelfth book of the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa. || 13 ||
In the glorious Devībhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the twelfth book, chapter fourteen. Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Sūta said:
That which consists of half a verse and emerged from the lotus-like mouth of the Goddess, known as the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, reveals the established conclusions of the Vedas. ||1||
That which was taught to Viṣṇu, who dwells on the island of Śveta-dvīpa,
was formerly composed by Brahmā in an extent of one hundred crores [of verses].
Having gathered its essence together for the sake of Śuka, Vyāsa composed it in eighteen thousand verses, consisting of twelve books (skandhas). ||3||
The Purāṇa named Devībhāgavata was composed in ancient times;
even today, it remains indeed very extensive in the world of the gods. ||4||
There is no merit equal to this, which is purifying and destructive of sin;
at every step, a human being obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice. ||5||
Having honored a reciter of the Purāṇas with garments, ornaments, and other gifts,
and having heard this from his mouth with the thought that he is Vyāsa himself, one should remain fasting.
O Sage, having had it written either by his own hand or by a scribe on the full moon day of the month of Proṣṭhapada, accompanied by a golden lion; ||7||
Then he should give a sacrificial fee to the reciter of the Purāṇa: a milk-yielding Kapila cow, adorned with ornaments, accompanied by her calf, and wearing a golden garland.
At the conclusion, he should also feed as many Brāhmaṇas as there are chapters in the recitation.
Likewise, there were as many married women and young maidens together with the *baṭuka* youths. ||9||
One should worship them with the thought that they are goddesses, offering garments, ornaments, and so forth, as well as milk-rice, incense, garlands, flowers, and other such items. ||10||
By this gift of a Purāṇa, one obtains the fruit of gifting land;
having become happy in this world, he shall attain and go to the city of the Goddess. ||11||
For one who constantly listens with devotion to the supreme Devībhāgavata,
there is indeed nothing whatsoever that is difficult to attain, anywhere or at any time.
A sonless man obtains sons, and one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth.
A seeker of knowledge shall obtain learning, adorning the earth with his fame.
Whether a woman is barren, or one who bears only a single child, or one whose children have died,
she shall undoubtedly be freed from those defects by hearing this.
In whichever house this book remains worshipped, Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī shall never abandon that home. (15)
There, the Vetālas, Ḍākinīs, Rākṣasas, and others do not look on;
having touched a man afflicted by fever, one should recite this with a concentrated mind.
From the mandala, fever accompanied by burning sensations meets its destruction;
by reciting this a hundred times, the disease of consumption (kṣaya) is eradicated.
Whoever, having performed the twilight devotions with a concentrated mind, recites even a single chapter at each junction of the day, that person shall become possessed of knowledge. (18)
One should indeed observe omens regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;

If one recites this daily with great devotion during the autumnal Navarātra, Ambikā, being well-pleased, grants him a fruit exceeding his desires. 20.

O Sage, for the constant propitiation of one's own Vedic Gāyatrī, this should be recited with effort during the four periods of nine nights.
There is no contradiction here for anyone regarding what should be recited by this [method];

Therefore, the twice-born should always recite it for the sake of pleasing that very power.
Neither a woman nor a Śūdra, being deluded, should ever read this. ||24||

What is the use of much speaking? I shall state the essence according to the truth. (25)
